Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Dīghanikāye

In the Dīgha Nikāya

Mahāvaggaṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Great Chapter

1. Mahāpadānasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Mahāpadāna Sutta

Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttakathā

The Discourse Connected with Previous Dwellings

1. Evaṃ [P 2.0407][V 2.0001][M 2.0001] me sutaṃ…pe… karerikuṭikāyanti mahāpadānasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – karerikuṭikāyanti karerīti varuṇarukkhassa nāmaṃ, karerimaṇḍapo tassā kuṭikāya dvāre ṭhito, tasmā “karerikuṭikā”ti vuccati, yathā kosambarukkhassa dvāre ṭhitattā “kosambakuṭikā”ti. Antojetavane kira karerikuṭi kosambakuṭi gandhakuṭi salaḷāgāranti cattāri mahāgehāni, ekekaṃ satasahassapariccāgena nipphannaṃ. Tesu salaḷāgāraṃ raññā pasenadinā kāritaṃ, sesāni anāthapiṇḍikena kāritāni. Iti bhagavā anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā thambhānaṃ upari kāritāya devavimānakappāya karerikuṭikāyaṃ viharati[V 2.0002]. Pacchābhattanti ekāsanikakhalupacchābhattikānaṃ pātova bhuttānaṃ antomajjhanhikepi pacchābhattameva. Idha pana pakatibhattassa pacchato “pacchābhatta”nti adhippetaṃ. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānanti piṇḍapātato paṭikkantānaṃ, bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhapetvā uṭṭhitānanti attho.

1. Thus have I heard... and so on... 'at the Kareri Hut'—this is the Mahāpadāna Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of terms not previously encountered. Regarding 'at the Kareri Hut': 'Kareri' is the name for the Varuṇa tree. A Kareri pavilion stood at the door of that hut; therefore, it is called the 'Kareri Hut,' just as the 'Kosamba Hut' is so called because a Kosamba tree stood at its door. It is said that within the Jeta Grove there were four great buildings: the Kareri Hut, the Kosamba Hut, the Fragrant Hut, and the Salaḷa House, each completed at the cost of one hundred thousand. Among them, the Salaḷa House was caused to be built by King Pasenadi, and the rest were caused to be built by Anāthapiṇḍika. Thus the Blessed One was dwelling in the Kareri Hut—which was like a celestial mansion, caused to be built upon pillars by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. Regarding 'after the meal': for those who practice eating in one sitting and those who refuse food after the proper time, even midday is 'after the meal' if they have already eaten in the early morning. Here, however, 'after the meal' is intended to mean the time after the regular meal. Regarding 'having returned from the alms round': the meaning is 'of those who have returned from collecting alms-food,' that is, 'of those who have risen after completing the business of the meal.'

Karerimaṇḍalamāḷeti tasseva karerimaṇḍapassa avidūre katāya nisīdanasālāya. So kira karerimaṇḍapo gandhakuṭikāya ca sālāya ca [M 2.0002] antare hoti, tasmā gandhakuṭīpi karerikuṭikāpi sālāpi – “karerimaṇḍalamāḷo”ti vuccati. Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttāti “ekampi jātiṃ, dvepi jātiyo”ti evaṃ vibhattena pubbenivutthakkhandhasantānasaṅkhātena pubbenivāsena saddhiṃ yojetvā pavattitā. Dhammīti dhammasaṃyuttā.

Regarding 'at the Kareri Pavilion Terrace': this refers to the sitting hall built not far from that same Kareri pavilion. It is said that the Kareri pavilion was between the Fragrant Hut and the hall; therefore, the Fragrant Hut, the Kareri Hut, and the hall are all called the 'Kareri Pavilion Terrace.' Regarding 'connected with previous dwellings': it is a talk that proceeded by being connected with previous dwellings—designated as the continuity of aggregates previously lived through and analyzed as 'one birth, two births,' and so on. Regarding 'a talk on the Teaching': it is a talk connected with the Dhamma.

Udapādīti aho acchariyaṃ dasabalassa pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ[P 2.0408], pubbenivāsaṃ nāma ke anussaranti, ke nānussarantīti. Titthiyā anussaranti, sāvakā ca paccekabuddhā ca buddhā ca anussaranti. Kataratitthiyā anussaranti? Ye aggappattakammavādino, tepi cattālīsaṃyeva kappe anussaranti, na tato paraṃ. Sāvakā kappasatasahassaṃ anussaranti. Dve aggasāvakā asaṅkhyeyyañceva kappasatasahassañca. Paccekabuddhā dve asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca. Buddhānaṃ pana ettakanti paricchedo natthi, yāvatakaṃ ākaṅkhanti, tāvatakaṃ anussaranti.

Regarding 'arose': Oh, how wonderful is the knowledge of previous dwellings of the One with Ten Powers! Who, indeed, recollects previous dwellings, and who does not? The sectarians recollect, and so do the disciples, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddhas. Which sectarians recollect? Those who are proponents of kamma who have reached the highest attainment. Even they recollect only forty eons, not beyond that. Disciples recollect one hundred thousand eons. The two chief disciples recollect one incalculable and one hundred thousand eons. Paccekabuddhas recollect two incalculables and one hundred thousand eons. For the Buddhas, however, there is no such limit as 'only this much'; they recollect as far as they wish.

Titthiyā khandhapaṭipāṭiyā anussaranti, paṭipāṭiṃ muñcitvā na sakkonti. Paṭipāṭiyā anussarantāpi asaññabhavaṃ patvā khandhappavattiṃ na passanti, jāle patitā kuṇṭhā viya, kūpe patitā paṅguḷā viya ca honti. Te tattha ṭhatvā “ettakameva, ito paraṃ natthī”ti diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhanti. Iti titthiyānaṃ pubbenivāsānussaraṇaṃ andhānaṃ yaṭṭhikoṭigamanaṃ viya hoti. Yathā hi andhā yaṭṭhikoṭiggāhake satiyeva gacchanti, asati tattheva nisīdanti, evameva titthiyā khandhapaṭipāṭiyāva anussarituṃ sakkonti, paṭipāṭiṃ vissajjetvā na sakkonti.

The sectarians recollect by way of the sequence of aggregates; they are unable to recollect having set aside the sequence. Even while recollecting by way of the sequence, on reaching the sphere of non-perception, they do not see the process of the aggregates, and they become like the crippled fallen into a net or the lame fallen into a well. Standing there, they grasp the view: 'There is only this much; there is nothing beyond this.' Thus, the sectarians' recollection of previous dwellings is like the blind going by means of the tip of a stick. For just as the blind can go only when there is someone holding the tip of the stick, and sit right there when there is not, so too the sectarians are able to recollect only by way of the sequence of aggregates; they are unable to do so having abandoned the sequence.

Sāvakāpi khandhapaṭipāṭiyāva anussaranti, asaññabhavaṃ patvā khandhappavattiṃ na passanti. Evaṃ santepi te vaṭṭe saṃsaraṇakasattānaṃ khandhānaṃ abhāvakālo nāma natthi. Asaññabhave pana pañcakappasatāni pavattantīti tattakaṃ kālaṃ atikkamitvā buddhehi dinnanaye ṭhatvā parato anussaranti; seyyathāpi āyasmā sobhito. Dve aggasāvakā pana paccekabuddhā ca [V 2.0003] cutipaṭisandhiṃ oloketvā anussaranti. Buddhānaṃ cutipaṭisandhikiccaṃ natthi, yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ passitukāmā honti, taṃ tadeva passanti.

Disciples, too, recollect only by way of the sequence of aggregates; on reaching the sphere of non-perception, they do not see the process of the aggregates. Even so, for beings wandering in the round of rebirth, there is no period of time when the aggregates are absent. In the sphere of non-perception, however, five hundred eons pass. Having transcended that period of time, standing in the method given by the Buddhas, they recollect beyond that, as did the Venerable Sobhita. The two chief disciples and the Paccekabuddhas, however, recollect by observing death and rebirth-linking. For the Buddhas, there is no need to observe death and rebirth-linking; whatever place they wish to see, that very place they see.

Titthiyā [M 2.0003] ca pubbenivāsaṃ anussaramānā attanā diṭṭhakatasutameva anussaranti. Tathā sāvakā ca paccekabuddhā [P 2.0409] ca. Buddhā pana attanā vā parehi vā diṭṭhakatasutaṃ sabbameva anussaranti.

And the sectarians, when recollecting previous dwellings, recollect only what has been seen, done, or heard by themselves. Likewise for the disciples and the Paccekabuddhas. The Buddhas, however, recollect everything that has been seen, done, or heard, whether by themselves or by others.

Titthiyānaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ khajjopanakaobhāsasadisaṃ, sāvakānaṃ padīpobhāsasadisaṃ, aggasāvakānaṃ osadhitārakobhāsasadisaṃ, paccekabuddhānaṃ candobhāsasadisaṃ, buddhānaṃ saradasūriyamaṇḍalobhāsasadisaṃ. Tassa ettakāni jātisatāni jātisahassāni jātisatasahassānīti vā ettakāni kappasatāni kappasahassāni kappasatasahassānīti vā natthi, yaṃ kiñci anussarantassa neva khalitaṃ, na paṭighātaṃ hoti, āvajjanapaṭibaddhameva ākaṅkhamanasikāracittuppādapaṭibaddhameva hoti. Dubbalapattapuṭe vegakkhittanārāco viya, sinerukūṭe vissaṭṭhaindavajiraṃ viya ca asajjamānameva gacchati. “Aho mahantaṃ bhagavato pubbenivāsañāṇa”nti evaṃ bhagavantaṃyeva ārabbha kathā uppannā, jātā pavattāti attho. Taṃ sabbampi saṅkhepato dassetuṃ “itipi pubbenivāso, itipi pubvenivāso”ti ettakameva pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha itipīti evampi.

The knowledge of previous dwellings of the sectarians is like the light of a firefly; that of the disciples is like the light of a lamp; that of the chief disciples is like the light of the morning star; that of the Paccekabuddhas is like the light of the moon; and that of the Buddhas is like the light of the autumn sun’s orb. For him, there is no limit of 'only so many hundreds of births, thousands of births, or hundreds of thousands of births,' or 'only so many hundreds of eons, thousands of eons, or hundreds of thousands of eons,' and in recollecting anything whatsoever, there is neither faltering nor obstruction. His recollection is bound only by advertence and by the arising of a thought connected with aspiration and attention. Like an arrow shot with speed through a weak leaf-wrap, or like Indra's thunderbolt hurled upon the peak of Mount Sineru, it proceeds without impediment. 'Ah, how vast is the Blessed One’s knowledge of past lives!'—thus a discussion concerning the Blessed One arose and proceeded. To show all this in brief, only this much is stated in the Pāli: 'Thus indeed it was about past lives; thus indeed it was about past lives.' Herein, 'Thus indeed' means 'in this manner also'.

2-3. Assosi kho…pe… atha bhagavā anuppattoti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva. Ayameva hi viseso – tattha sabbaññutaññāṇena assosi, idha dibbasotena. Tattha ca vaṇṇāvaṇṇakathā vippakatā, idha pubbenivāsakathā. Tasmā bhagavā – “ime bhikkhū mama pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ ārabbha guṇaṃ thomenti, pubbenivāsañāṇassa pana me nipphattiṃ na jānanti; handa nesaṃ tassa nipphattiṃ kathetvā dassāmī”ti āgantvā pakatiyāpi buddhānaṃ nisīditvā dhammadesanatthameva ṭhapite taṅkhaṇe bhikkhūhi papphoṭetvā dinne varabuddhāsane nisīditvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave”ti pucchāya ca “idha[P 2.0410], bhante”tiādipaṭivacanassa ca pariyosāne tesaṃ pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ kathetukāmo iccheyyātha notiādimāha. Tattha iccheyyātha noti iccheyyātha nu. Atha naṃ pahaṭṭhamānasā bhikkhū yācamānā etassa bhagavātiādimāhaṃsu. Tattha etassāti etassa dhammikathākaraṇassa.

2-3. 'The Blessed One heard…pe… then the Blessed One arrived.' Here, what should be said has already been stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. This is the only difference: there, he heard with the knowledge of omniscience, whereas here, with the divine ear. There, the discussion of praise and blame was left incomplete, whereas here, it is the discussion of past lives. Therefore, the Blessed One thought, 'These monks are praising my knowledge of past lives, but they do not know the accomplishment of this knowledge of mine. Well then, let me explain and show them its accomplishment.' Having arrived, he sat down on the excellent Buddha-seat, which was established for the very purpose of Buddhas sitting and teaching the Dhamma, and which at that moment had been dusted and offered by the monks. At the end of his question, 'What is the topic of your discussion, monks?' and their reply, 'Here, Lord…,' desiring to give them a Dhamma talk connected with past lives, he said, beginning with, 'Would you wish?' Here, 'iccheyyātha no' means 'iccheyyātha nu' (Would you wish?). Then, the monks, delighted in mind and making their request, said, beginning with, 'Of this, Blessed One…' Here, 'of this' means of this giving of a Dhamma talk.

4. Atha [M 2.0004] bhagavā tesaṃ yācanaṃ gahetvā kathetukāmo “tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇāthā”ti te [V 2.0004] sotāvadhāraṇasādhukamanasikāresu niyojetvā aññesaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇaṃ pakāsetukāmo ito so, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha yaṃ vipassīti yasmiṃ kappe vipassī. Ayañhi ‘ya’nti saddo “yaṃ me, bhante, devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sammukhā sutaṃ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ, ārocemi taṃ, bhagavato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.203) paccattavacane dissati. “Yaṃ taṃ apucchimha akittayī no, aññaṃ taṃ pucchāma tadiṅgha brūhī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 881) upayogavacane. “Aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 1.277) karaṇavacane. Idha pana bhummattheti daṭṭhabbo. Tena vuttaṃ – “yasmiṃ kappe”ti. Udapādīti dasasahassilokadhātuṃ unnādento uppajji.

4. Then the Blessed One, having accepted their request and wishing to speak, said, 'Well then, monks, listen.' Having directed them to attentive listening and careful attention, and wishing to reveal the recollection of the severed continuum which is exclusive to Buddhas, he began with, 'From this, monks…' Here, 'yaṃ Vipassī' means 'in which aeon Vipassī (appeared)'. For this word 'yaṃ' is seen in the nominative sense, as in passages like, 'That which I, venerable sir, heard face to face from the Tāvatiṃsa devas and received directly, I declare that to the Blessed One'; in the accusative sense, as in, 'What we asked, you did not explain; now we ask another, so please speak'; and in the instrumental sense, as in, 'It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen that in one world-system...' Here, however, it should be understood in the locative sense. Hence it is said, 'in which aeon.' 'Udapādī' (arose) means he arose, making the ten-thousandfold world-system resound.

Bhaddakappeti pañcabuddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitattā sundarakappe sārakappeti bhagavā imaṃ kappaṃ thomento evamāha. Yato paṭṭhāya kira amhākaṃ bhagavatā abhinīhāro kato, etasmiṃ antare ekakappepi pañca buddhā nibbattā nāma natthi. Amhākaṃ bhagavato abhinīhārassa purato pana taṇhaṅkaro, medhaṅkaro, saraṇaṅkaro, dīpaṅkaroti cattāro buddhā ekasmiṃ kappe nibbattiṃsu. Tesaṃ orabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ buddhasuññameva ahosi.

The Blessed One, praising this aeon, called it a 'fortunate aeon' because it is adorned with the appearance of five Buddhas, and also a 'beautiful aeon' and a 'meaningful aeon.' It is said that from the time our Blessed One made his resolution, there has not been even a single aeon in which five Buddhas have arisen. However, before our Blessed One’s resolution, four Buddhas—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—arose in a single aeon. In the time before them, there was one incalculable period devoid of Buddhas.

Asaṅkhyeyyakappapariyosāne pana koṇḍañño nāma buddho ekova ekasmiṃ kappe uppanno. Tatopi asaṅkhyeyyaṃ buddhasuññameva ahosi. Asaṅkhyeyyakappapariyosāne maṅgalo, sumano, revato, sobhitoti cattāro buddhā ekasmiṃ kappe uppannā[P 2.0411]. Tatopi asaṅkhyeyyaṃ buddhasuññameva ahosi. Asaṅkhyeyyakappapariyosāne pana ito kappasatasahassādhikassa asaṅkhyeyyassa upari anomadassī, padumo, nāradoti tayo buddhā ekasmiṃ kappe uppannā. Tatopi asaṅkhyeyyaṃ buddhasuññameva ahosi. Asaṅkhyeyyakappapariyosāne pana ito kappasatasahassānaṃ upari padumuttaro bhagavā ekova ekasmiṃ kappe uppanno. Tassa orabhāge ito tiṃsakappasahassānaṃ upari sumedho, sujātoti dve buddhā ekasmiṃ kappe uppannā. Tato orabhāge ito aṭṭhārasannaṃ kappasahassānaṃ upari piyadassī, atthadassī, dhammadassīti tayo buddhā [M 2.0005] ekasmiṃ kappe uppannā. Atha ito catunavutikappe siddhattho nāma buddho ekova ekasmiṃ kappe uppanno. Ito dve navutikappe tisso, phussoti dve buddhā ekasmiṃ kappe uppannā. Ito ekanavutikappe vipassī bhagavā uppanno. Ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhī, vessabhūti dve buddhā uppannā. Imasmiṃ bhaddakappe kakusandho, koṇāgamano, kassapo, gotamo amhākaṃ sammāsambuddhoti cattāro buddhā uppannā, metteyyo uppajjissati. Evamayaṃ kappo pañcabuddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitattā sundarakappo sārakappoti bhagavā imaṃ kappaṃ thomento evamāha.

At the end of an incalculable aeon, a Buddha named Koṇḍañña alone appeared in a single aeon. After that, there was an incalculable period without Buddhas. At the end of another incalculable aeon, four Buddhas—Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita—appeared in one aeon. Again, after that, there was an incalculable period without Buddhas. At the end of yet another incalculable aeon, more than an incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons ago, three Buddhas—Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada—appeared in a single aeon. After that too, there was an incalculable period without Buddhas. At the end of another incalculable aeon, more than one hundred thousand aeons ago, the Blessed One Padumuttara appeared alone in one aeon. After him, more than thirty thousand aeons ago, two Buddhas—Sumedha and Sujāta—appeared in a single aeon. After that, more than eighteen thousand aeons ago, three Buddhas—Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī—appeared in one aeon. Then, ninety-four aeons ago, a Buddha named Siddhattha appeared alone in one aeon. Ninety-two aeons ago, two Buddhas—Tissa and Phussa—appeared in a single aeon. Ninety-one aeons ago, the Blessed One Vipassī appeared. Thirty-one aeons ago, two Buddhas—Sikhī and Vessabhūti—appeared. In this fortunate aeon, four Buddhas have appeared: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and Gotama, our perfectly enlightened Buddha. Metteyya will appear. Thus, because this aeon is adorned with the appearance of five Buddhas, the Blessed One praised this aeon as a beautiful and meaningful aeon, saying so.

Kiṃ [V 2.0005] panetaṃ buddhānaṃyeva pākaṭaṃ hoti – “imasmiṃ kappe ettakā buddhā uppannā vā uppajjissantīti vā”ti, udāhu aññesampi pākaṭaṃ hotīti? Aññesampi pākaṭaṃ hoti. Kesaṃ? Suddhāvāsabrahmānaṃ. Kappasaṇṭhānakālasmiñhi ekamasaṅkhyeyyaṃ ekaṅgaṇaṃ hutvā ṭhite lokasannivāse lokassa saṇṭhānatthāya devo vassituṃ ārabhati. Āditova antaraṭṭhake himapāto viya hoti. Tato tilamattā kaṇamattā taṇḍulamattā mugga-māsa-badara-āmalaka-eḷāluka-kumbhaṇḍa-alābumattā udakadhārā hutvā anukkamena usabhadveusabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutadvegāvutaaḍḍhayojanayojanadviyojana…pe… yojanasatayojanasahassayojanasatasahassamattā [P 2.0412] hutvā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷabbhantare yāva avinaṭṭhabrahmalokā pūretvā tiṭṭhanti. Atha taṃ udakaṃ anupubbena bhassati, bhassante udake pakatidevalokaṭṭhānesu devalokā saṇṭhahanti, tesaṃ saṇṭhahanavidhānaṃ visuddhimagge pubbenivāsakathāyaṃ vuttameva.

But is this evident only to the Buddhas—"In this aeon, so many Buddhas have arisen or will arise"—or is it evident to others as well? It is evident to others as well. To whom? To the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās. For when, at the time of the aeon's formation, the world-system remains, having been a single expanse for one incalculable period, a deva begins to rain in order to establish the world. From the very beginning, it is like a fall of snow during the interim eight days. Then drops the size of sesame seeds, broken rice grains, rice grains, mung beans, black grams, jujubes, emblic myrobalans, cucumbers, ash gourds, and bottle gourds fall, gradually increasing in size up to the measure of a usabha, two usabhas, half a gāvuta, a gāvuta, two gāvutas, half a yojana, a yojana, two yojanas… up to a hundred yojanas, a thousand yojanas, a hundred thousand yojanas, filling the space within a hundred thousand koṭis of world-spheres as far as the imperishable Brahma-worlds. Then that water gradually recedes. As the water recedes, the deva-worlds re-establish themselves in their proper places. The manner of their re-establishment is as described in the Visuddhimagga's account of the recollection of past lives.

Manussalokasaṇṭhahanaṭṭhānaṃ pana patte udake dhamakaraṇamukhe pihite viya vātavasena taṃ udakaṃ santiṭṭhati, udakapiṭṭhe uppalinipaṇṇaṃ viya pathavī saṇṭhahati. Mahābodhipallaṅko vinassamāne loke pacchā vinassati, saṇṭhahamāne paṭhamaṃ saṇṭhahati. Tattha pubbanimittaṃ hutvā eko paduminigaccho uppajjati, tassa sace tasmiṃ kappe buddho nibbattissati, pupphaṃ uppajjati. No ce, nuppajjati. Uppajjamānañca sace eko buddho nibbattissati, ekaṃ uppajjati. Sace dve, tayo, cattāro, pañca buddhā nibbattissanti, pañca uppajjanti. Tāni ca kho ekasmiṃyeva nāḷe kaṇṇikābaddhāni hutvā. Suddhāvāsabrahmāno “āyāma[M 2.0006], mayaṃ mārisā, pubbanimittaṃ passissāmā”ti mahābodhipallaṅkaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti, buddhānaṃ anibbattanakappe pupphaṃ na hoti. Te pana apupphitagacchaṃ disvā – “andhakāro vata bho loko bhavissati, matā matā sattā apāye pūressanti, cha devalokā nava brahmalokā suññā bhavissantī”ti anattamanā honti. Pupphitakāle pana pupphaṃ disvā – “sabbaññubodhisattesu mātukucchiṃ okkamantesu nikkhamantesu sambujjhantesu dhammacakkaṃ pavattentesu yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karontesu devorohanaṃ karontesu āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajjantesu parinibbāyantesu dasasahassacakkavāḷakampanādīni pāṭihāriyāni dakkhissāmā”ti ca “cattāro apāyā parihāyissanti, cha devalokā nava brahmalokā paripūressantī”ti ca attamanā udānaṃ udānentā attano attano brahmalokaṃ gacchanti. Imasmiṃ bhaddakappe pañca padumāni uppajjiṃsu. Tesaṃ nimittānaṃ ānubhāvena cattāro buddhā uppannā, pañcamo uppajjissati. Suddhāvāsabrahmānopi [P 2.0413] tāni padumāni disvā imamatthaṃ jāniṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “aññesampi pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti.

But when the water reaches the place where the human world is to be established, that water settles due to the wind as if the mouth of a water-strainer were closed; and on the surface of that water, the earth establishes itself like a lotus leaf. The Great Bodhi Seat is the last to perish when the world is being destroyed and the first to be established when it is being established. There, as a preliminary sign, a single lotus bush arises. If a Buddha is to appear in that aeon, a flower arises from it. If not, it does not arise. And when it arises, if one Buddha is to appear, one [flower] arises. If two, two arise; if three, three arise; if four, four arise; if five Buddhas are to appear, five arise. And these are bound to a single stalk at the pericarp. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmās [think], "Come, friends, let us see the preliminary sign," and they approach the place of the Great Bodhi Seat. In an aeon when Buddhas do not appear, there is no flower. But seeing the flowerless bush, they are disheartened [thinking]: "Alas, the world will be in darkness! Beings, dying again and again, will fill the lower realms. The six deva-worlds and nine Brahma-worlds will be empty!" But at the time of flowering, seeing the flower, they rejoice and exclaim: "When the Omniscient Bodhisattas enter their mother's womb, emerge, attain full enlightenment, turn the Wheel of Dhamma, perform the Twin Miracle, descend from the deva-world, relinquish their life-force, and attain final Nibbāna, we will witness the quaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system and other miracles! The four lower realms will diminish, and the six deva-worlds and nine Brahma-worlds will be filled!" Delighted, uttering an inspired utterance, they return to their respective Brahma-worlds. In this auspicious aeon, five lotuses appeared. Due to the power of those signs, four Buddhas have arisen, and the fifth will arise. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmās too, seeing those lotuses, understood this matter. Therefore, it is said, "It is evident even to others."

Āyuparicchedavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Delimitation of the Lifespan

5-7. Iti [V 2.0006] bhagavā – “ito so, bhikkhave”tiādinā nayena kappaparicchedavasena pubbenivāsaṃ dassetvā idāni tesaṃ buddhānaṃ jātiparicchedādivasena dassetuṃ vipassī, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha āyuparicchede parittaṃ lahukanti ubhayametaṃ appakasseva vevacanaṃ. Yañhi appakaṃ, taṃ parittañceva lahukañca hoti.

5-7. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the past abodes by way of delimitation of aeons, beginning with "From here, monks," now, in order to show them by way of delimitation of births and so on, said, "Vipassī, monks," and so on. There, in delimiting the life-span, "limited" and "light" are both synonymous with "little." For what is little is both limited and light.

Appaṃ vā bhiyyoti vassasatato vā upari appaṃ, aññaṃ vassasataṃ apatvā vīsaṃ vā tiṃsaṃ vā cattālīsaṃ vā paṇṇāsaṃ vā saṭṭhi vā vassāni jīvati. Evaṃ dīghāyuko pana atidullabho, asuko kira evaṃ ciraṃ jīvatīti tattha tattha gantvā daṭṭhabbo hoti. Tattha visākhā upāsikā vīsavassasataṃ jīvati, tathā pokkharasāti brāhmaṇo, brahmāyu brāhmaṇo, selo brāhmaṇo, bāvariyabrāhmaṇo, ānandatthero, mahākassapattheroti. Anuruddhatthero pana vassasatañceva paṇṇāsañca vassāni, bākulatthero vassasatañceva saṭṭhi ca vassāni. Ayaṃ sabbadīghāyuko. Sopi dve vassasatāni na jīvati.

The phrase "a little more" means a little over one hundred years; that is, without reaching a further hundred years, one lives for an additional twenty, or thirty, or forty, or fifty, or sixty years. However, such a long-lived person is extremely rare; it is said, 'Such a one lives for so long!' and one has to go here and there to see them. In this regard, the laywoman Visākhā lived for one hundred and twenty years, as did the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, the Brahmin Brahmāyu, the Brahmin Sela, the Brahmin Bāvari, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Mahākassapa. The Elder Anuruddha, however, lived for one hundred and fifty years, and the Elder Bākula for one hundred and sixty years. He had the longest lifespan of all. Yet even he did not live for two hundred years.

Vipassīādayo [M 2.0007] pana sabbepi bodhisattā mettāpubbabhāgena somanassasahagatañāṇasampayuttaasaṅkhārikacittena mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Tena cittena gahitāya paṭisandhiyā asaṅkhyeyyaṃ āyu, iti sabbe buddhā asaṅkhyeyyāyukā. Te kasmā asaṅkhyeyyaṃ na aṭṭhaṃsu? Utubhojanavipattiyā. Utubhojanavasena hi āyu hāyatipi vaḍḍhatipi.

But all the Bodhisattas, beginning with Vipassī, took rebirth in their mother’s womb with an unprompted consciousness associated with joy and knowledge, having loving-kindness as the preliminary part. Due to the rebirth-consciousness taken with that consciousness, their lifespan was incalculable—thus all Buddhas have an incalculable lifespan. Why did they not live for an incalculable time? Due to the failure of climate and food. For lifespan decreases or increases based on climate and food.

Tattha yadā rājāno adhammikā honti, tadā uparājāno, senāpati, seṭṭhi, sakalanagaraṃ, sakalaraṭṭhaṃ adhammikameva hoti; atha tesaṃ ārakkhadevatā, tāsaṃ devatānaṃ mittā bhūmaṭṭhadevatā, tāsaṃ devatānaṃ mittā ākāsaṭṭhakadevatā, ākāsaṭṭhakadevatānaṃ mittā uṇhavalāhakā devatā, tāsaṃ mittā abbhavalāhakā devatā, tāsaṃ mittā sītavalāhakā devatā, tāsaṃ mittā vassavalāhakā devatā, tāsaṃ mittā cātumahārājikā [P 2.0414] devatā, tāsaṃ mittā tāvatiṃsā devatā, tāsaṃ mittā yāmā devatāti evamādi. Evaṃ yāva bhavaggā ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake sabbā devabrahmaparisāpi adhammikāva honti. Tāsaṃ adhammikatāya visamaṃ candimasūriyā pariharanti, vāto yathāmaggena na vāyati, ayathāmaggena vāyanto ākāsaṭṭhakavimānāni khobheti, vimānesu khobhitesu devatānaṃ kīḷanatthāya cittāni na namanti, devatānaṃ kīḷanatthāya cittesu anamantesu [V 2.0007] sītuṇhabhedo utu yathākālena na sampajjati, tasmiṃ asampajjante na sammā devo vassati, kadāci vassati, kadāci na vassati; katthaci vassati, katthaci na vassati, vassantopi vappakāle aṅkurakāle nāḷakāle pupphakāle khīraggahaṇādikālesu yathā yathā sassānaṃ upakāro na hoti, tathā tathā vassati ca vigacchati ca, tena sassāni visamapākāni honti, vigatagandhavaṇṇarasādisampannāni. Ekabhājane pakkhittataṇḍulesupi ekasmiṃ padese bhattaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ hoti, ekasmiṃ atikilinnaṃ, ekasmiṃ samapākaṃ. Taṃ paribhuttaṃ kucchiyampi tīhākārehi paccati. Tena sattā bahvābādhā ceva honti, appāyukā ca. Evaṃ tāva utubhojanavasena āyu hāyati.

Herein, when kings are unrighteous, then the viceroys, generals, treasurers, the entire city, and the entire kingdom become unrighteous as well. Then their guardian deities become unrighteous; and the friends of those deities, the earth-dwelling deities; and the friends of those deities, the sky-dwelling deities; and the friends of the sky-dwelling deities, the hot-cloud deities; and their friends, the mist-cloud deities; and their friends, the cold-cloud deities; and their friends, the rain-cloud deities; and their friends, the deities under the Four Great Kings; and their friends, the Tāvatiṃsa deities; and their friends, the Yāma deities—and so on. Thus, up to the peak of existence, excepting the noble disciples, all assemblies of devas and brahmās also become unrighteous. Due to their unrighteousness, the sun and moon move erratically. The wind does not blow along its proper course; blowing improperly, it shakes the celestial mansions. When the mansions are shaken, the minds of the deities do not incline towards amusement. When their minds do not incline towards amusement, the season, with its division of cold and heat, does not occur at the proper time. When it does not occur properly, the rain does not fall correctly: sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not; in some places it rains, in others it does not. Even when it does rain, it rains and ceases in such a way that it is of no benefit to the crops during the time of sowing, sprouting, stalk-growth, flowering, or the milky stage and so on. Consequently, the crops ripen unevenly and are devoid of fragrance, color, taste, and other good qualities. Even with rice grains placed in a single pot, in one part the cooked rice is underdone, in another it is mushy, and in another it is properly cooked. When eaten, that food is digested in the stomach in three ways. As a result, beings suffer from many illnesses and have short lifespans. Thus, on account of the seasons and food, the lifespan diminishes.

Yadā [M 2.0008] pana rājāno dhammikā honti, tadā uparājānopi dhammikā hontīti purimanayeneva yāva brahmalokā sabbepi dhammikā honti. Tesaṃ dhammikattā samaṃ candimasūriyā pariharanti, yathāmaggena vāto vāyati, yathāmaggena vāyanto ākāsaṭṭhakavimānāni na khobheti, tesaṃ akhobhā devatānaṃ kīḷanatthāya cittāni namanti. Evaṃ kālena utu sampajjati, devo sammā vassati, vappakālato paṭṭhāya sassānaṃ upakāraṃ karonto kāle vassati, kāle vigacchati, tena sassāni samapākāni sugandhāni suvaṇṇāni surasāni ojavantāni honti, tehi sampāditaṃ bhojanaṃ paribhuttampi sammā paripākaṃ gacchati[P 2.0415], tena sattā arogā dīghāyukā honti. Evaṃ utubhojanavasena āyu vaḍḍhati.

When, however, kings are righteous, then their viceroys are also righteous; in the same way as before, all beings up to the brahmā world become righteous. Due to their righteousness, the sun and moon move evenly. The wind blows along its proper course, and blowing along its proper course, it does not shake the celestial mansions. Because these are unshaken, the minds of the deities incline toward amusement. Thus, the season occurs at the proper time, and the rain falls correctly. From the time of sowing onwards, raining at the proper time and ceasing at the proper time, it benefits the crops. Consequently, the crops ripen evenly and are fragrant, of good color, delicious, and full of nutriment. The food prepared from these, when consumed, is properly digested. As a result, beings are free from illness and are long-lived. In this way, on account of the seasons and food, the lifespan increases.

Tattha vipassī bhagavā asītivassasahassāyukakāle nibbatto, sikhī sattativassasahassāyukakāleti idaṃ anupubbena parihīnasadisaṃ kataṃ, na pana evaṃ parihīnaṃ, vaḍḍhitvā vaḍḍhitvā parihīnanti veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Imasmiṃ tāva kappe kakusandho bhagavā cattālīsavassasahassāyukakāle nibbatto, āyuppamāṇaṃ pañca koṭṭhāse katvā cattāri ṭhatvā pañcame vijjamāneyeva parinibbuto. Taṃ āyu parihāyamānaṃ dasavassakālaṃ patvā puna vaḍḍhamānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ hutvā tato parihāyamānaṃ tiṃsavassasahassakāle ṭhitaṃ; tadā koṇāgamano bhagavā nibbatto. Tasmimpi tatheva parinibbute taṃ āyu dasavassakālaṃ patvā puna vaḍḍhamānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ hutvā parihāyitvā vīsativassasahassakāle ṭhitaṃ; tadā kassapo bhagavā nibbatto. Tasmimpi tatheva parinibbute taṃ āyu dasavassakālaṃ patvā puna vaḍḍhamānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ hutvā parihāyitvā vassasatakālaṃ pattaṃ, atha amhākaṃ sammāsambuddho nibbatto. Evaṃ anupubbena parihāyitvā parihāyitvā vaḍḍhitvā vaḍḍhitvā parihīnanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha yaṃ yaṃ āyuparimāṇesu [V 2.0008] manussesu buddhā nibbattanti, tesampi taṃ tadeva āyuparimāṇaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Among them, the Blessed One Vipassī arose when the lifespan was eighty thousand years, and Sikhī when it was seventy thousand years. This is presented as being similar to a gradual decline, but it did not, however, decline in this way; it should be understood that it declined after having increased and increased. How so? In this very eon, to begin with, the Blessed One Kakusandha arose when the lifespan was forty thousand years. Having divided that lifespan into five portions, he lived for four and attained parinibbāna while the fifth portion was still present. That lifespan, declining, reached a period of ten years, and then, increasing again, became incalculable. Thereafter, declining, it stood at a period of thirty thousand years; at that time, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana arose. When he too had attained parinibbāna in the same way, that lifespan reached a period of ten years, and then, increasing again, became incalculable, and declining, stood at a period of twenty thousand years; at that time, the Blessed One Kassapa arose. When he too had attained parinibbāna in the same way, that lifespan reached a period of ten years, and then, increasing again, became incalculable, and declining, reached a period of one hundred years; then our Perfectly Enlightened One arose. Thus, it should be understood that it declined sequentially after having declined and declined, and then increased and increased. Herein, it should be understood that whatever the measure of the human lifespan is when Buddhas arise, that very same measure of lifespan is theirs as well.

Āyuparicchedavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section on lifespan is concluded.

Bodhiparicchedavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on the Bodhi Tree

8. Bodhiparicchede [M 2.0009] pana pāṭaliyā mūleti pāṭalirukkhassa heṭṭhā. Tassā pana pāṭaliyā khandho taṃ divasaṃ paṇṇāsaratano hutvā abbhuggato, sākhā paṇṇāsaratanāti ubbedhena ratanasataṃ ahosi. Taṃ divasañca sā pāṭali kaṇṇikābaddhehi viya pupphehi mūlato paṭṭhāya ekasañchannā ahosi, dibbagandhaṃ vāyati. Na kevalañca tadā ayameva pupphitā, dasasahassacakkavāḷe sabbapāṭaliyo pupphitā. Na kevalañca pāṭaliyo, dasasahassacakkavāḷe sabbarukkhānaṃ khandhesu khandhapadumāni, sākhāsu sākhāpadumāni, latāsu latāpadumāni, ākāse ākāsapadumāni pupphitāni, pathavitalaṃ [P 2.0416] bhinditvāpi mahāpadumāni uṭṭhitāni. Mahāsamuddopi pañcavaṇṇehi padumehi nīluppalarattuppalehi ca sañchanno ahosi. Sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷaṃ dhajamālākulaṃ tattha tattha nibaddhapupphadāmavissaṭṭhamālāguḷavippakiṇṇaṃ nānāvaṇṇakusumasamujjalaṃ nandanavanacittalatāvanamissakavanaphārusakavanasadisaṃ ahosi. Puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ussitaddhajā pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiṃ abhihananti. Pacchimadakkhiṇauttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ussitaddhajā dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiṃ abhihananti. Evaṃ aññamaññasirīsampattāni cakkavāḷāni ahesuṃ. Abhisambuddhoti sakalaṃ buddhaguṇavibhavasiriṃ paṭivijjhamāno cattāri saccāni abhisambuddho.

8. Now, in the section on the Bodhi tree, 'at the foot of the Pāṭali' means beneath the Pāṭali tree. On that day, the trunk of that Pāṭali tree rose up to a height of fifty cubits, and its branches were fifty cubits; thus, its total height was one hundred cubits. And on that day, that Pāṭali tree was completely covered from its base with flowers as if bound in clusters, and a divine fragrance wafted from it. Not only was this particular tree in bloom at that time, but all the Pāṭali trees in the ten-thousandfold world-system were in bloom. And not only the Pāṭali trees, but in the ten-thousandfold world-system, lotuses bloomed on the trunks of all trees, lotuses on their branches, lotuses on their vines, and lotuses in the sky; and breaking through the surface of the earth, great lotuses also arose. The great ocean, too, was covered with lotuses of five colors, and with blue and red water lilies. The entire ten-thousandfold world-system was filled with banners and garlands, resplendent with bound floral wreaths, scattered garlands, and strewn flowers of various colors, resembling the Nandana, Cittalată, Missaka, and Phārusaka groves. Banners raised at the rim of the eastern world-system struck the rim of the western world-system, and those at the western rim struck the eastern. Those at the northern rim struck the southern, and those at the southern rim struck the northern. Thus the world-systems attained a state of mutual splendor. 'He was fully enlightened' means that by penetrating the entire glorious majesty of a Buddha's qualities, he became fully enlightened to the Four Truths.

“Sikhī, bhikkhave, bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho puṇḍarīkassa mūle abhisambuddho”tiādīsupi imināva nayena padavaṇṇanā veditabbā. Ettha pana puṇḍarīkoti setambarukkho. Tassāpi tadeva parimāṇaṃ. Taṃ divasañca sopi dibbagandhehi pupphehi susañchanno ahosi. Na kevalañca pupphehi, phalehipi sañchanno ahosi. Tassa ekato taruṇāni phalāni, ekato majjhimāni phalāni, ekato nātipakkāni phalāni, ekato supakkāni pakkhittadibbojāni viya surasāni olambanti. Yathā so, evaṃ sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷesu [V 2.0009] pupphūpagarukkhā pupphehi, phalūpagarukkhā phalehi paṭimaṇḍitā ahesuṃ.

In such passages as, 'Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was fully enlightened at the foot of the Puṇḍarīka tree,' and so on, the explanation of the words should be understood in this same way. Here, however, 'Puṇḍarīka' means a white mango tree. Its dimensions were also the same. And on that day, it too was beautifully covered with divinely fragrant flowers. It was covered not only with flowers, but also with fruits. On one side of it hung young fruits; on another, medium-sized fruits; on another, nearly ripe fruits; and on another, fully ripe fruits, as delicious as if infused with divine nectar. Just as with that tree, so too throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world-system, the flowering trees were adorned with flowers and the fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits.

Sāloti sālarukkho. Tassāpi tadeva parimāṇaṃ, tatheva pupphasirīvibhavo veditabbo. Sirīsarukkhepi eseva nayo. Udumbararukkhe pupphāni [M 2.0010] nāhesuṃ, phalavibhūti panettha ambe vuttanayāva, tathā nigrodhe, tathā assatthe. Iti sabbabuddhānaṃ ekova pallaṅko, rukkhā pana aññepi honti. Tesu yassa yassa rukkhassa mūle catumaggañāṇasaṅkhātabodhiṃ buddhā paṭivijjhanti, so so bodhīti vuccati. Ayaṃ bodhiparicchedo nāma.

'Sāla' means the sāla tree. Its dimensions were also the same, and the glorious splendor of its flowers should be understood in the same way. This same principle applies to the Sirīsa tree. On the Udumbara tree there were no flowers, but the majesty of its fruit was as described for the mango tree; likewise for the Banyan tree, and likewise for the Assattha tree. Thus, for all Buddhas the seat of awakening is one and the same, but the trees may be different. Among these, at the foot of whichever tree the Buddhas penetrate the enlightenment known as the knowledge of the four paths, that very tree is called the 'Bodhi'. This is the section on the Bodhi tree.

Sāvakayugaparicchedavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Pairs of Disciples

9. Sāvakayugaparicchede pana khaṇḍatissanti khaṇḍo ca tisso ca. Tesu khaṇḍo ekapitiko kaniṭṭhabhātā, tisso purohitaputto[P 2.0417]. Khaṇḍo paññāpāramiyā matthakaṃ patto, tisso samādhipāramiyā matthakaṃ patto. Agganti ṭhapetvā vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ avasesehi saddhiṃ asadisaguṇatāya uttamaṃ. Bhaddayuganti aggattāyeva bhaddayugaṃ. Abhibhūsambhavanti abhibhū ca sambhavo ca. Tesu abhibhū paññāpāramiyā matthakaṃ patto. Sikhinā bhagavatā saddhiṃ aruṇavatito brahmalokaṃ gantvā brahmaparisāya vividhāni pāṭihāriyāni dassento dhammaṃ desetvā dasasahassilokadhātuṃ andhakārena pharitvā – “kiṃ ida”nti sañjātasaṃvegānaṃ obhāsaṃ pharitvā – “sabbe me rūpañca passantu, saddañca suṇantū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā – “ārambhathā”ti gāthādvayaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.185) bhaṇanto saddaṃ sāvesi. Sambhavo samādhipāramiyā matthakaṃ patto ahosi.

9. Now, in the section on the pairs of disciples, 'Khaṇḍa and Tissa' refers to Khaṇḍa and Tissa. Of these two, Khaṇḍa was the younger brother of the Buddha by the same father, while Tissa was the son of the royal chaplain. Khaṇḍa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom; Tissa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration. 'Foremost' means they were supreme due to their incomparable qualities in comparison with the remaining disciples of the Blessed One Vipassī. 'Auspicious Pair' is so called simply because of their pre-eminence. 'Abhibhū and Sambhava' refers to Abhibhū and Sambhava. Of these two, Abhibhū reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom. He, together with the Blessed One Sikhī, went from Aruṇavatī to the Brahmā world. There, displaying various miracles before the assembly of Brahmās, he taught the Dhamma. He then pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system with darkness. For those who became spiritually stirred, wondering, 'What is this?', he spread light and made the resolution: 'May all see my form and hear my voice.' Then, reciting the two verses beginning 'Strive on...', he made his voice heard. Sambhava had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration.

Soṇuttaranti soṇo ca uttaro ca. Tesupi soṇo paññāpāramiṃ patto, uttaro samādhipāramiṃ patto ahosi. Vidhurasañjīvanti vidhuro ca sañjīvo ca. Tesu vidhuro paññāpāramiṃ patto ahosi, sañjīvo samādhipāramiṃ patto. Samāpajjanabahulo rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānakuṭileṇamaṇḍapādīsu samāpattibalena jhāyanto ekadivasaṃ araññe nirodhaṃ samāpajji, atha naṃ vanakammikādayo “mato”ti sallakkhetvā jhāpesuṃ. So yathāparicchedena samāpattito uṭṭhāya cīvarāni papphoṭetvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Tadupādāyeva ca naṃ “sañjīvo”ti sañjāniṃsu. Bhiyyosuttaranti bhiyyoso ca uttaro ca. Tesu bhiyyoso paññāya uttaro, uttaro samādhinā aggo ahosi. Tissabhāradvājanti tisso ca bhāradvājo ca[V 2.0010]. Tesu tisso paññāpāramiṃ patto, bhāradvājo samādhipāramiṃ patto ahosi[M 2.0011]. Sāriputtamoggallānanti sāriputto ca moggallāno ca. Tesu sāriputto paññāvisaye, moggallāno samādhivisaye aggo ahosi. Ayaṃ sāvakayugaparicchedo nāma.

'Soṇa and Uttara' refers to Soṇa and Uttara. Of these two, Soṇa attained the perfection of wisdom, while Uttara attained the perfection of concentration. 'Vidhura and Sañjīva' refers to Vidhura and Sañjīva. Of these two, Vidhura attained the perfection of wisdom, while Sañjīva attained the perfection of concentration. The latter, being one who frequently entered meditative attainments, would absorb himself in jhāna by the power of his attainment in places such as night-quarters, day-quarters, huts, caves, and pavilions. One day, in the forest, he entered the attainment of cessation. Then, forest workers and others, thinking he was dead, cremated him. But he, rising from his attainment at the pre-determined time, shook out his robes and entered the village for alms. On account of this, they came to know him as 'Sañjīva' (He Who Lives Again). 'Bhiyyosa and Uttara' refers to Bhiyyosa and Uttara. Of these two, Bhiyyosa was supreme in wisdom, and Uttara was foremost in concentration. 'Tissa and Bhāradvāja' refers to Tissa and Bhāradvāja. Of these two, Tissa attained the perfection of wisdom, and Bhāradvāja attained the perfection of concentration. 'Sāriputta and Moggallāna' refers to Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Of these two, Sāriputta was foremost in the domain of wisdom, and Moggallāna was foremost in the domain of concentration. This is the section on the pairs of disciples.

Sāvakasannipātaparicchedavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Assembly of Disciples

10. Sāvakasannipātaparicchede [P 2.0418] vipassissa bhagavato paṭhamasannipāto caturaṅgiko ahosi, sabbe ehibhikkhū, sabbe iddhiyā nibbattapattacīvarā, sabbe anāmantitāva āgatā, iti te ca kho pannarase uposathadivase. Atha satthā bījaniṃ gahetvā nisinno uposathaṃ osāresi. Dutiyatatiyesupi eseva nayo. Tathā sesabuddhānaṃ sabbasannipātesu. Yasmā pana amhākaṃ bhagavato paṭhamabodhiyāva sannipāto ahosi, idañca suttaṃ aparabhāge vuttaṃ, tasmā “mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi eko sāvakānaṃ sannipāto”ti aniṭṭhapetvā “ahosī”ti vuttaṃ.

10. In the section on the assembly of disciples, the first assembly of the Blessed One Vipassī was characterized by four factors: all were 'Come, bhikkhu' monks; all had robes and bowls created by psychic power; all had come uninvited; and it was the fifteenth day, the Uposatha day. Then the Teacher, taking a fan, sat down and recited the Pātimokkha. This same method applied to the second and third assemblies. Likewise for all assemblies of the remaining Buddhas. But since the assembly for our Blessed One occurred right at the time of his first enlightenment, and this sutta was spoken later, therefore, without completing the statement as, 'Bhikkhus, for me now there is one assembly of disciples,' it was said as, 'there was.'

Tattha aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatānīti purāṇajaṭilānaṃ sahassaṃ, dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ parivārāni aḍḍhateyyasatānīti aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatāni. Tattha dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya vatthuṃ kathetvā pabbajjā dīpetabbā. Pabbajitānaṃ pana tesaṃ mahāmoggallāno sattame divase arahattaṃ patto. Dhammasenāpati pannarasame divase gijjhakūṭapabbatamajjhe sūkarakhataleṇapabbhāre bhāgineyyassa dīghanakhaparibbājakassa sajjite dhammayāge vedanāpariggahasuttante (ma. ni. 2.201) desiyamāne desanaṃ anubujjhamānaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesetvā sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ patto. Bhagavā therassa arahattappattiṃ ñatvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā veḷuvaneyeva paccuṭṭhāsi. Thero – “kuhiṃ nu kho bhagavā gato”ti āvajjanto veḷuvane patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā sayampi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā veḷuvaneyeva paccuṭṭhāsi. Atha bhagavā pātimokkhaṃ osāresi. Taṃ sannipātaṃ sandhāya bhagavā – “aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatānī”ti āha. Ayaṃ sāvakasannipātaparicchedo nāma.

Herein, 'twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus' means the thousand former matted-hair ascetics and the two hundred and fifty followers of the two chief disciples, thus twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus. In this context, beginning from the aspiration of the two chief disciples, the story should be told to explain their going forth. Now, of those who had gone forth, Mahāmoggallāna attained arahantship on the seventh day. The General of the Dhamma, on the fifteenth day, while the discourse on the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being delivered in the middle of Gijjhakūṭa Mountain near the Boar's Cave slope, at the Dhamma-offering prepared for his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, sent forth his knowledge to comprehend the teaching and attained the disciple-perfection-knowledge. The Blessed One, knowing the elder’s attainment of arahantship, rose into the air and alighted in the Bamboo Grove. The elder, reflecting, 'Where can the Blessed One have gone?' and knowing that he was established in the Bamboo Grove, also rose into the air himself and alighted there in the Bamboo Grove. Then the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha. With reference to this assembly, the Blessed One said, 'Twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus.' This is called the Section on the Assembly of Disciples.

Upaṭṭhākaparicchedavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Attendants

11. Upaṭṭhākaparicchede [M 2.0012] pana ānandoti nibaddhupaṭṭhākabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Bhagavato hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ anibaddhā upaṭṭhākā ahesuṃ. Ekadā nāgasamālo pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vicari, ekadā nāgito, ekadā upavāno, ekadā sunakkhatto, ekadā cundo samaṇuddeso, ekadā sāgato[V 2.0011], ekadā meghiyo. Tattha [P 2.0419] ekadā bhagavā nāgasamālattherena saddhiṃ addhānamaggapaṭipanno dvedhāpathaṃ patto. Thero maggā okkamma – “bhagavā, ahaṃ iminā maggena gacchāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ bhagavā – “ehi bhikkhu, iminā maggena gacchāmā”ti āha. So – “handa, bhagavā, tumhākaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gaṇhatha, ahaṃ iminā maggena gacchāmī”ti vatvā pattacīvaraṃ chamāyaṃ ṭhapetuṃ āraddho. Atha naṃ bhagavā – “āhara, bhikkhū”ti vatvā pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā gato. Tassapi bhikkhuno itarena maggena gacchato corā pattacīvarañceva hariṃsu, sīsañca bhindiṃsu. So – “bhagavā idāni me paṭisaraṇaṃ, na añño”ti cintetvā lohitena gaḷitena bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. “Kimidaṃ bhikkhū”ti ca vutte taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ bhagavā – “mā cintayi, bhikkhu, etaṃyeva te kāraṇaṃ sallakkhetvā nivārayimhā”ti vatvā naṃ samassāsesi.

11. In the Section on Attendants, however, the name 'Ānanda' is mentioned with reference to his status as the permanent attendant. Indeed, in the period of the first enlightenment, the Blessed One had non-permanent attendants. At one time, Nāgasamāla took the bowl and robe and went about; at another time, Nāgita; at another time, Upavāna; at another time, Sunakkhatta; at another time, Cunda the novice; at another time, Sāgata; at another time, Meghiya. Among them, on one occasion the Blessed One was travelling along a road with the Elder Nāgasamāla when they came to a fork. The elder stepped off the path and said, 'Blessed One, I will go by this path.' Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Come, bhikkhu, let us go by this path.' He replied, 'Here, Blessed One, take your bowl and robe; I will go by this path,' and began to place the bowl and robe on the ground. Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Bring them, bhikkhu,' took the bowl and robe, and departed. As that bhikkhu was going by the other path, robbers stole his bowl and robe and also broke his head. He thought, 'The Blessed One is now my refuge, no other,' and with blood flowing, he went to the Blessed One. When asked, 'What is this, bhikkhu?' he related what had happened. Then the Blessed One consoled him, saying, 'Do not worry, bhikkhu. It was because we foresaw this very reason that we tried to prevent you.'

Ekadā pana bhagavā meghiyattherena saddhiṃ pācīnavaṃsamigadāye jantugāmaṃ agamāsi. Tatrāpi meghiyo jantugāme piṇḍāya caritvā nadītīre pāsādikaṃ ambavanaṃ disvā – “bhagavā, tumhākaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gaṇhatha, ahaṃ tasmiṃ ambavane samaṇadhammaṃ karomī”ti vatvā bhagavatā tikkhattuṃ nivāriyamānopi gantvā akusalavitakkehi upadduto anvāsatto (a. ni. 9.3; udāna paricchedo 31 daṭṭhabbo). Paccāgantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Tampi bhagavā – “idameva te kāraṇaṃ sallakkhetvā nivārayimhā”ti vatvā anupubbena sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Tattha gandhakuṭipariveṇe paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinno bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhave, idānimhi mahallako, ‘ekacce bhikkhū iminā maggena gacchāmā’ti vutte aññena gacchanti, ekacce mayhaṃ pattacīvaraṃ nikkhipanti, mayhaṃ nibaddhupaṭṭhākaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ jānāthā”ti. Bhikkhūnaṃ dhammasaṃvego udapādi. Athāyasmā sāriputto uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā – “ahaṃ[M 2.0013], bhante, tumheyeva patthayamāno satasahassakappādhikaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ pāramiyo pūrayiṃ, nanu mādiso mahāpañño upaṭṭhāko nāma vaṭṭati, ahaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti āha. Taṃ bhagavā – “alaṃ sāriputta, yassaṃ [P 2.0420] disāyaṃ tvaṃ viharasi, asuññāyeva me sā disā, tava ovādo buddhānaṃ ovādasadiso, na me tayā upaṭṭhākakiccaṃ atthī”ti paṭikkhipi. Etenevupāyena mahāmoggallānaṃ ādiṃ katvā asītimahāsāvakā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Te sabbepi bhagavā paṭikkhipi.

On another occasion, the Blessed One went with the Elder Meghiya to Jantugāma in the Pācīnavaṃsa Deer Park. There too, Meghiya, after going for alms in Jantugāma, saw a delightful mango grove on the riverbank and said, 'Blessed One, take your bowl and robe; I will perform the ascetic's practice in that mango grove.' Although he was prevented by the Blessed One three times, he went and was afflicted and obsessed by unwholesome thoughts. Returning, he reported what had happened. To him also the Blessed One said, 'It was because we foresaw this very reason that we tried to prevent you,' and then he proceeded in stages to Sāvatthī. There, seated on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat in the Perfumed Chamber's precinct, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus, I am now old. When it is said, "Let us go by this path," some bhikkhus go by another. Some put down my bowl and robe. You should find for me one bhikkhu to be a permanent attendant.' A sense of spiritual urgency arose in the bhikkhus. Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said: 'Venerable Sir, it was while aspiring for you alone that I fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable aeon and over one hundred thousand kappas. Surely it is fitting that one of great wisdom such as I be an attendant? I will attend upon you.' The Blessed One rejected him, saying: 'Enough, Sāriputta. In whatever direction you dwell, that direction is not empty for me. Your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas. I have no need for the service of an attendant from you.' In this same way, beginning with Mahāmoggallāna, the eighty great disciples arose. The Blessed One rejected them all.

Ānandatthero pana tuṇhīyeva nisīdi. Atha naṃ bhikkhū evamāhaṃsu – “āvuso, ānanda, bhikkhusaṅgho upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānaṃ yācati, tvampi yācāhī”ti. So āha – “yācitvā laddhupaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0012] nāma āvuso kīdisaṃ hoti, kiṃ maṃ satthā na passati, sace rocissati, ānando maṃ upaṭṭhātūti vakkhatī”ti. Atha bhagavā – “na, bhikkhave, ānando aññena ussāhetabbo, sayameva jānitvā maṃ upaṭṭhahissatī”ti āha. Tato bhikkhū – “uṭṭhehi, āvuso ānanda, uṭṭhehi āvuso ānanda, dasabalaṃ upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānaṃ yācāhī”ti āhaṃsu. Thero uṭṭhahitvā cattāro paṭikkhepe, catasso ca āyācanāti aṭṭha vare yāci.

The Venerable Ānanda, however, remained silent. Then the bhikkhus said to him: “Friend Ānanda, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is requesting the position of attendant. You too should request it.” He replied: “Friends, what sort of thing is an attendant’s position obtained by request? Does the Teacher not see me? If it is pleasing to him, he will say, ‘Let Ānanda attend upon me.’” Then the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, Ānanda is not to be urged by another; knowing for himself, he will attend upon me.” Then the bhikkhus said: “Rise, friend Ānanda, rise, friend Ānanda! Request the position of attendant from the Ten-Powered One.” The Elder arose and requested eight boons: four refusals and four requests.

Cattāro paṭikkhepā nāma – “sace me, bhante, bhagavā attanā laddhaṃ paṇītaṃ cīvaraṃ na dassati, piṇḍapātaṃ na dassati, ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasituṃ na dassati, nimantanaṃ gahetvā na gamissati, evāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti vatvā – “kiṃ panettha, ānanda, ādīnavaṃ passasī”ti vutte – “sacāhaṃ, bhante, imāni vatthūni labhissāmi, bhavissanti vattāro – ‘ānando dasabalena laddhaṃ paṇītaṃ cīvaraṃ paribhuñjati, piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjati, ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasati, ekato nimantanaṃ gacchati, etaṃ lābhaṃ labhanto tathāgataṃ upaṭṭhāti, ko evaṃ upaṭṭhahato bhāro’ti” ime cattāro paṭikkhepe yāci.

The four refusals are as follows: “Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One does not give me a fine robe that he himself has received, does not give me almsfood, does not allow me to dwell in the same perfumed chamber, and does not go to an invitation taking me with him, then I will attend upon the Blessed One.” When asked, “Ānanda, what disadvantage do you see in this?” he replied: “Venerable Sir, if I were to receive these things, there would be those who would say: ‘Ānanda uses the fine robe received by the Ten-Powered One, he uses the almsfood, he dwells in the same perfumed chamber, and he goes together with him to an invitation. It is because he is receiving this gain that he attends upon the Tathāgata. What burden is there for one who attends in this way?’ He requested these four refusals.

Catasso āyācanā nāma – “sace, bhante, bhagavā mayā gahitanimantanaṃ gamissati, sacāhaṃ tiroraṭṭhā tirojanapadā bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgataṃ parisaṃ āgatakkhaṇe eva bhagavantaṃ dassetuṃ lacchāmi, yadā me kaṅkhā uppajjati, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ lacchāmi, yaṃ bhagavā mayhaṃ parammukhā dhammaṃ deseti, taṃ āgantvā mayhaṃ kathessati, evāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ [M 2.0014] upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti vatvā – “kaṃ panettha, ānanda, ānisaṃsaṃ passasī”ti [P 2.0421] vutte – “idha, bhante, saddhā kulaputtā bhagavato okāsaṃ alabhantā maṃ evaṃ vadanti – ‘sve, bhante ānanda, bhagavatā saddhiṃ amhākaṃ ghare bhikkhaṃ gaṇheyyāthā’ti, sace bhante bhagavā tattha na gamissati, icchitakkhaṇeyeva parisaṃ dassetuṃ, kaṅkhañca vinodetuṃ okāsaṃ na lacchāmi, bhavissanti vattāro – ‘kiṃ ānando dasabalaṃ upaṭṭhāti, ettakampissa anuggahaṃ bhagavā na karotī’ti. Bhagavato ca parammukhā maṃ pucchissanti – ‘ayaṃ, āvuso ānanda, gāthā, idaṃ suttaṃ, idaṃ jātakaṃ, kattha desita’nti. Sacāhaṃ taṃ na sampādayissāmi, bhavissanti vattāro – ‘ettakampi, āvuso, na jānāsi, kasmā tvaṃ chāyā viya bhagavantaṃ avijahanto dīgharattaṃ vicarasī’ti. Tenāhaṃ parammukhā desitassapi dhammassa puna kathanaṃ icchāmī”ti imā catasso āyācanā yāci. Bhagavāpissa adāsi.

The four requests are as follows: “Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will go to an invitation that I have accepted; if I may be permitted to present to the Blessed One, at the very moment of their arrival, the assembly of people who have come from other regions and other districts to see him; if, whenever a doubt arises in me, I may be permitted to approach the Blessed One at that very moment; and if the Blessed One will repeat to me the Dhamma he has taught in my absence—then I will attend upon the Blessed One.” When asked, “Ānanda, what benefit do you see in this?” he replied: “Venerable Sir, in this matter, faithful clansmen, unable to get an opportunity with the Blessed One, say to me: ‘Venerable Ānanda, tomorrow, may you, together with the Blessed One, accept almsfood in our house.’ Now, if the Blessed One does not go there; or if I do not get the opportunity to present the assembly at the desired moment, or to dispel my doubt, there will be those who say: ‘Why does Ānanda attend upon the Ten-Powered One? The Blessed One does not grant him even this much of a favor.’ Furthermore, in the Blessed One’s absence, they will question me: ‘Friend Ānanda, where was this verse taught? Where was this sutta taught? Where was this jātaka taught?’ If I cannot answer them, there will be those who say: ‘Friend, you do not even know this much. Why do you follow the Blessed One for so long, never leaving him, like a shadow?’ It is for this reason that I desire the retelling of the Dhamma taught in my absence.” He made these four requests. The Blessed One granted them to him.

Evaṃ ime aṭṭha vare gahetvā nibaddhupaṭṭhāko ahosi. Tasseva ṭhānantarassatthāya kappasatasahassaṃ [V 2.0013] pūritānaṃ pāramīnaṃ phalaṃ pāpuṇīti imassa nibaddhupaṭṭhākabhāvaṃ sandhāya – “mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etarahi ānando bhikkhu upaṭṭhāko aggupaṭṭhāko”ti āha. Ayaṃ upaṭṭhākaparicchedo nāma.

Thus, having received these eight boons, he became the constant attendant. For the sake of that very position, he attained the fruit of the perfections he had fulfilled over a hundred thousand aeons. It was with reference to his state as constant attendant that the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, the bhikkhu Ānanda is now my attendant, my chief attendant.” This is called the Section on the Attendant.

12. Pitiparicchedo uttānatthoyeva.

12. The Section on the Father is self-evident in meaning.

Vihāraṃ pāvisīti kasmā vihāraṃ pāvisi? Bhagavā kira ettakaṃ kathetvā cintesi – “na tāva mayā sattannaṃ buddhānaṃ vaṃso nirantaraṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā kathito, ajja mayi pana vihāraṃ paviṭṭhe ime bhikkhū bhiyyoso mattāya pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ ārabbha vaṇṇaṃ kathayissanti. Athāhaṃ āgantvā nirantaraṃ buddhavaṃsaṃ kathetvā matthakaṃ pāpetvā dassāmī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ kathāvārassa okāsaṃ datvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi.

Why did he enter the dwelling? It is said that the Blessed One, having spoken thus much, thought: “The lineage of the seven Buddhas has not yet been narrated by me continuously to its conclusion. But today, when I have entered the dwelling, these bhikkhus will, to an even greater degree, speak in praise concerning the knowledge of past lives. Then I shall return and, having narrated the lineage of the Buddhas continuously and brought it to its conclusion, I will present it.” Having given the bhikkhus an opportunity for discussion, he rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.

Yañcetaṃ bhagavā tantiṃ kathesi, tattha kappaparicchedo, jātiparicchedo, gottaparicchedo, āyuparicchedo, bodhiparicchedo, sāvakayugaparicchedo, sāvakasannipātaparicchedo, upaṭṭhākaparicchedo, pitiparicchedoti navime vārā āgatā, sambahulavāro anāgato, ānetvā pana dīpetabbo.

And in this textual tradition that the Blessed One taught, these nine sections are included: the Section on the Aeon, the Section on Birth, the Section on the Clan, the Section on the Lifespan, the Section on the Enlightenment Tree, the Section on the Pair of Disciples, the Section on the Assembly of Disciples, the Section on the Attendant, and the Section on the Father. The section on numerous matters has not yet been included, but it should be brought in and explained.

Sambahulavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Numerous Matters.

Sabbabodhisattānañhi [P 2.0422][M 2.0015] ekasmiṃ kulavaṃsānurūpe putte jāte nikkhamitvā pabbajitabbanti ayameva vaṃso, ayaṃ paveṇī. Kasmā? Sabbaññubodhisattānañhi mātukucchiṃ okkamanato paṭṭhāya pubbe vuttappakārāni anekāni pāṭihāriyāni honti, tatra nesaṃ yadi neva jātanagaraṃ, na pitā, na mātā, na bhariyā, na putto paññāyeyya, “imassa neva jātanagaraṃ, na pitā, na bhariyā, na putto paññāyati, devo vā sakko vā māro vā brahmā vā esa maññe, devānañca īdisaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ anacchariya”nti maññamāno jano neva sotabbaṃ, na saddhātabbaṃ maññeyya. Tato abhisamayo na bhaveyya, abhisamaye asati niratthakova buddhuppādo, aniyyānikaṃ sāsanaṃ hoti. Tasmā sabbabodhisattānaṃ – “ekasmiṃ kulavaṃsānurūpe putte jāte nikkhamitvā pabbajitabba”nti ayameva vaṃso ayaṃ paveṇī. Tasmā puttādīnaṃ vasena sambahulavāro ānetvā dīpetabbo.

Indeed, for all Bodhisattas, 'When a son is born to them in a suitable family lineage, they are to go forth, having renounced'—this is precisely the lineage, this is the tradition. Why? Because from the time all Omniscient Bodhisattas enter their mother’s womb, many marvels of the kind previously described occur. If at that time neither a birth city nor a father nor a mother nor a wife nor a son were evident for them, people would think, 'This one has no birth city, no father, no mother, no wife, no son. I think he is a god, Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, and such a marvel is not surprising for gods.' Thinking thus, people would consider it not worth listening to or believing, and realization would not occur. Without realization, the arising of a Buddha would be utterly pointless, and the teaching would not lead to liberation. Therefore, for all Bodhisattas, 'When a son is born to them in a suitable family lineage, they are to go forth, having renounced'—this is precisely the lineage, this is the tradition. Therefore, the numerous topics regarding sons and others should be brought in and elucidated.

Sambahulaparicchedavaṇṇanā

Explanation of Numerous Sections

Tattha [V 2.0014] –

Therein:

Samavattakkhandho atulo, suppabuddho ca uttaro;

Satthavāho vijitaseno, rāhulo bhavati sattamoti.

Samavattakkhandho, Atulo, Suppabuddho and Uttaro; Satthavāho, Vijitaseno; and Rāhulo is the seventh.

Ete tāva sattannampi bodhisattānaṃ anukkameneva satta puttā veditabbā.

These, in the first place, should be known as the seven sons of the seven Bodhisattas, in due order.

Tattha rāhulabhadde tāva jāte paṇṇaṃ āharitvā mahāpurisassa hatthe ṭhapayiṃsu. Athassa tāvadeva sakalasarīraṃ khobhetvā puttasineho aṭṭhāsi. So cintesi – “ekasmiṃ tāva jāte evarūpo puttasineho, parosahassaṃ kira me puttā bhavissanti, tesu ekekasmiṃ jāte idaṃ sinehabandhanaṃ evaṃ vaḍḍhantaṃ dubbhejjaṃ bhavissati, rāhu jāto, bandhanaṃ jāta”nti āha. Taṃ divasameva ca rajjaṃ pahāya nikkhanto. Esa nayo sabbesaṃ puttuppattiyanti. Ayaṃ puttaparicchedo.

Therein, when Rāhula the Fortunate was born, they brought a leaf and placed it in the Great Being’s hand. Then, at that very moment, affection for his son arose, agitating his entire body. He thought: 'With just this one son born, such affection arises. It is said I will have more than a thousand sons. With each one born, this bond of affection, growing in this way, will become difficult to break.' He then said: 'A Rāhu is born, a fetter is born.' And on that very day, having relinquished the kingdom, he went forth. This is the way for all regarding the birth of a son. This is the section on sons.

Sutanā [M 2.0016] sabbakāmā ca, sucittā atha rocinī;

Rucaggatī sunandā ca, bimbā bhavati sattamāti.

Sutanā and Sabbakāmā, Sucittā and then Rocinī; Rucaggatī and Sunandā, and Bimbā is the seventh.

Etā tesaṃ sattannampi puttānaṃ mātaro ahesuṃ. Bimbādevī pana rāhulakumāre jāte rāhulamātāti paññāyittha. Ayaṃ bhariyaparicchedo.

These were the mothers of those seven sons. Furthermore, when Prince Rāhula was born, Queen Bimbā became known as Rāhulamātā (Rāhula's mother). This is the section on wives.

Vipassī [P 2.0423] kakusandhoti ime pana dve bodhisattā payuttaājaññarathamāruyha mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamiṃsu. Sikhī koṇāgamanoti ime dve hatthikkhandhavaragatā hutvā nikkhamiṃsu. Vessabhū suvaṇṇasivikāya nisīditvā nikkhami. Kassapo uparipāsāde mahātale nisinnova ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānā uṭṭhāya taṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā – “pāsādo uggantvā bodhimaṇḍe otaratū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Pāsādo ākāsena gantvā bodhimaṇḍe otari. Mahāpurisopi tato otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā – “pāsādo yathāṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhātū”ti cintesi. So yathāṭhāne patiṭṭhāsi. Mahāpurisopi satta divasāni padhānamanuyuñjitvā bodhipallaṅke [V 2.0015] nisīditvā sabbaññutaṃ paṭivijjhi. Amhākaṃ pana bodhisatto kaṇṭakaṃ assavaramāruyha nikkhantoti. Ayaṃ yānaparicchedo.

Furthermore, the two Bodhisattas Vipassī and Kakusandha, having mounted a chariot yoked with thoroughbreds, went forth on the Great Renunciation. The two, Sikhī and Koṇāgamana, went forth having mounted upon the back of a choice elephant. Vessabhū went forth seated in a golden palanquin. Kassapa, while seated on the great terrace of the upper palace, having produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, rising from that jhāna and making it his foundation, resolved: 'May the palace rise up and descend at the Bodhimaṇḍa!' The palace, going through the sky, descended at the Bodhimaṇḍa. The Great Being, having descended from it and stood on the ground, thought: 'May the palace be established in its original place!' It was established in its original place. The Great Being, having engaged in the striving for seven days, sat on the Bodhi-seat and penetrated to omniscience. Our Bodhisatta, however, went forth having mounted the excellent horse Kaṇṭaka. This is the section on vehicles.

Vipassissa pana bhagavato yojanappamāṇe padese vihāro patiṭṭhāsi, sikhissa tigāvute, vessabhussa aḍḍhayojane, kakusandhassa gāvute, koṇāgamanassa aḍḍhagāvute, kassapassa vīsatiusabhe. Amhākaṃ bhagavato pakatimānena soḷasakarīse, rājamānena aṭṭhakarīse padese vihāro patiṭṭhitoti. Ayaṃ vihāraparicchedo.

Furthermore, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the monastery was established in an area of one yojana; for Sikhī, three gāvutas; for Vessabhū, half a yojana; for Kakusandha, one gāvuta; for Koṇāgamana, half a gāvuta; and for Kassapa, twenty usabhas. For our Blessed One, the monastery was established in an area of sixteen karīsas by the standard measure, and eight karīsas by the royal measure. This is the section on monasteries.

Vipassissa pana bhagavato ekaratanāyāmā vidatthivitthārā aṭṭhaṅgulubbedhā suvaṇṇiṭṭhakā kāretvā cūḷaṃsena chādetvā vihāraṭṭhānaṃ kiṇiṃsu. Sikhissa suvaṇṇayaṭṭhiphālehi chādetvā kiṇiṃsu. Vessabhussa suvaṇṇahatthipādāni kāretvā tesaṃ cūḷaṃsena chādetvā kiṇiṃsu. Kakusandhassa vuttanayeneva suvaṇṇiṭṭhakāhi chādetvā kiṇiṃsu. Koṇāgamanassa vuttanayeneva suvaṇṇakacchapehi chādetvā kiṇiṃsu. Kassapassa [M 2.0017] suvaṇṇakaṭṭīhiyeva chādetvā kiṇiṃsu. Amhākaṃ bhagavato salakkhaṇānaṃ kahāpaṇānaṃ cūḷaṃsena chādetvā kiṇiṃsu. Ayaṃ vihārabhūmiggahaṇadhanaparicchedo.

Furthermore, for the Blessed One Vipassī, they purchased the monastery site by having golden bricks made—one cubit long, one span wide, and eight finger-widths thick—and covering the ground by setting them on edge. For Sikhī, they purchased it by covering it with golden bars. For Vessabhū, they purchased it by having golden elephant-foot ingots made and covering the ground by setting them on edge. For Kakusandha, they purchased it by covering it with golden bricks in the manner already described. For Koṇāgamana, they purchased it by covering it with golden tortoises in the manner already described. For Kassapa, they purchased it by covering it with golden ingots. For our Blessed One, they purchased it by covering it with marked kahāpaṇas set on edge. This is the section on the wealth for acquiring the monastery land.

Tattha [P 2.0424] vipassissa bhagavato tathā bhūmiṃ kiṇitvā vihāraṃ katvā dinnupaṭṭhāko punabbasumitto nāma ahosi, sikhissa sirivaḍḍhano nāma, vessabhussa sotthiyo nāma, kakusandhassa accuto nāma, koṇāgamanassa uggo nāma, kassapassa sumano nāma, amhākaṃ bhagavato sudatto nāma. Sabbe cete gahapatimahāsālā seṭṭhino ahesunti. Ayaṃ upaṭṭhākaparicchedo nāma.

Therein, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the attendant-donor who bought the land and had the monastery built was named Punabbasumitta; for Sikhī, Sirivaḍḍhana; for Vessabhū, Sotthiya; for Kakusandha, Accuta; for Koṇāgamana, Ugga; for Kassapa, Sumana; and for our Blessed One, Sudatta. All of these were great and wealthy householders and bankers. This is called the section on attendant-donors.

Aparāni cattāri avijahitaṭṭhānāni nāma honti. Sabbabuddhānañhi bodhipallaṅko avijahito, ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne hoti. Dhammacakkappavattanaṃ isipatane migadāye avijahitameva hoti. Devorohanakāle saṅkassanagaradvāre paṭhamapadagaṇṭhikā avijahitāva hoti. Jetavane gandhakuṭiyā cattāri mañcapādaṭṭhānāni avijahitāneva honti. Vihāro pana khuddakopi mahantopi hoti, vihāropi na vijahitoyeva, nagaraṃ pana vijahati. Yadā nagaraṃ pācīnato hoti, tadā vihāro pacchimato; yadā nagaraṃ dakkhiṇato, tadā vihāro uttarato. Yadā nagaraṃ pacchimato, tadā vihāro pācīnato; yadā nagaraṃ uttarato, tadā vihāro dakkhiṇato. Idāni pana nagaraṃ uttarato, vihāro dakkhiṇato.

There are four other places that are called unabandoned. For all Buddhas, the Bodhi-seat is unabandoned; it is in one and the same place. The turning of the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana in the Deer Park is indeed unabandoned. At the time of the descent from the deva world, the first footprint at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa is indeed unabandoned. In the Fragrant Chamber at Jetavana, the four places for the legs of the couch are indeed unabandoned. The monastery, however, may be small or large; the monastery itself is not abandoned, but the city is. When the city is to the east, the monastery is to the west; when the city is to the south, the monastery is to the north. When the city is to the west, the monastery is to the east; when the city is to the north, the monastery is to the south. Now, however, the city is to the north, and the monastery is to the south.

Sabbabuddhānañca [V 2.0016] āyuvemattaṃ, pamāṇavemattaṃ, kulavemattaṃ, padhānavemattaṃ, rasmivemattanti pañca vemattāni honti. Āyuvemattaṃ nāma keci dīghāyukā honti, keci appāyukā. Tathā hi dīpaṅkarassa vassasatasahassaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi, amhākaṃ bhagavato vassasataṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ.

For all Buddhas, there are five variations: variation in lifespan, variation in stature, variation in family, variation in striving, and variation in radiance. Regarding the variation in lifespan: some are long-lived, while others are short-lived. For instance, the lifespan of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was one hundred thousand years, whereas the lifespan of our Blessed One was one hundred years.

Pamāṇavemattaṃ nāma keci dīghā honti keci rassā. Tathā hi dīpaṅkaro asītihattho ahosi, sumano navutihattho, amhākaṃ bhagavā aṭṭhārasahattho.

Regarding the variation in stature: some are tall, while others are short. For instance, Dīpaṅkara was eighty cubits tall, Sumana was ninety cubits, and our Blessed One was eighteen cubits.

Kulavemattaṃ [M 2.0018] nāma keci khattiyakule nibbattanti, keci brāhmaṇakule. Padhānavemattaṃ nāma kesañci padhānaṃ ittarakālameva hoti, yathā kassapassa bhagavato. Kesañci addhaniyaṃ, yathā amhākaṃ bhagavato.

Regarding the variation in family: some are born in a khattiya family, others in a brahmin family. Regarding the variation in striving: for some, the striving lasts only a short time, as for the Blessed One Kassapa; for others, it is for a long period, as for our Blessed One.

Rasmivemattaṃ nāma maṅgalassa bhagavato sarīrarasmi dasasahassilokadhātuppamāṇā ahosi. Amhākaṃ bhagavato samantā byāmamattā[P 2.0425]. Tatra rasmivemattaṃ ajjhāsayappaṭibaddhaṃ, yo yattakaṃ icchati, tassa tattakaṃ sarīrappabhā pharati. Maṅgalassa pana niccampi dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharatūti ajjhāsayo ahosi. Paṭividdhaguṇesu pana kassaci vemattaṃ nāma natthi.

Regarding the variation in radiance: the bodily radiance of the Blessed One Maṅgala had the measure of ten thousand world-systems, whereas that of our Blessed One was a fathom in extent all around. Therein, the variation in radiance is connected to aspiration; to whatever extent one wishes, to that extent the bodily radiance pervades. The Blessed One Maṅgala's aspiration, however, was that it should always pervade ten thousand world-systems. But with regard to the qualities of penetration, there is no variation whatsoever for anyone.

Aparaṃ amhākaṃyeva bhagavato sahajātaparicchedañca nakkhattaparicchedañca dīpesuṃ. Sabbaññubodhisattena kira saddhiṃ rāhulamātā, ānandatthero, channo, kaṇṭako, nidhikumbho, mahābodhi, kāḷudāyīti imāni satta sahajātāni. Mahāpuriso ca uttarāsāḷhanakkhatteneva mātukucchiṃ okkami, mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhami, dhammacakkaṃ pavattesi, yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi. Visākhānakkhattena jāto ca abhisambuddho ca parinibbuto ca. Māghanakkhattenassa sāvakasannipāto ca ahosi, āyusaṅkhārossajjanañca, assayujanakkhattena devorohananti ettakaṃ āharitvā dīpetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ sambahulaparicchedo nāma.

Furthermore, they explained the section on the co-borns and the section on the constellations of our own Blessed One. It is said that these seven were co-born with the Omniscient Bodhisatta: Rāhula’s mother, the Elder Ānanda, Channa, Kaṇṭaka, the treasure jar, the great Bodhi tree, and Kāḷudāyī. The Great Being entered his mother’s womb under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation; under the same constellation he went forth in the Great Renunciation, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and performed the Twin Miracle. Under the Visākhā constellation, he was born, became fully enlightened, and passed into final nibbāna. Under the Māgha constellation, the assembly of disciples and the relinquishing of the life-force took place. Under the Assayuja constellation, the descent from the deva world occurred. This much should be presented and explained. This is called the Miscellaneous Section.

13. Idāni atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnantiādīsu te bhikkhū – “āvuso, pubbenivāsassa nāma ayaṃ gati, yadidaṃ cutito paṭṭhāya paṭisandhiārohanaṃ. Yaṃ pana idaṃ paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya pacchāmukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesetvā cuti gantabbaṃ, idaṃ atigarukaṃ. Ākāse padaṃ dassento viya bhagavā kathesī”ti ativimhayajātā hutvā – “acchariyaṃ, āvuso,”tiādīni vatvā puna aparampi kāraṇaṃ dassento – “yatra hi nāma tathāgato”tiādimāhaṃsu[V 2.0017]. Tattha yatra hi nāmāti acchariyatthe nipāto, yo nāma tathāgatoti attho. Chinnapapañceti ettha papañcā nāma taṇhā māno diṭṭhīti ime tayo kilesā. Chinnavaṭumeti ettha vaṭumanti kusalākusalakammavaṭṭaṃ vuccati. Pariyādinnavaṭṭeti tasseva vevacanaṃ, pariyādinnasabbakammavaṭṭeti attho. Sabbadukkhavītivatteti sabbaṃ vipākavaṭṭasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhaṃ vītivatte[M 2.0019]. Anussarissatīti idaṃ yatrāti nipātavasena anāgatavacanaṃ, attho panettha atītavasena veditabbo. Bhagavā hi te buddhe anussari, na idāni anussarissati. Evaṃsīlāti [P 2.0426] maggasīlena phalasīlena lokiyalokuttarasīlena evaṃsīlā. Evaṃdhammāti ettha samādhipakkhā dhammā adhippetā, maggasamādhinā phalasamādhinā lokiyalokuttarasamādhinā, evaṃsamādhayoti attho. Evaṃpaññāti maggapaññādivaseneva evaṃpaññā. Evaṃvihārīti ettha pana heṭṭhā samādhipakkhānaṃ dhammānaṃ gahitattā vihāro gahitova puna kasmā gahitameva gaṇhātīti ce; na idaṃ gahitameva, idañhi nirodhasamāpattidīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ nirodhasamāpattivihārī te bhagavanto ahesunti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

13. Now, regarding the passage beginning 'Then those monks...', those monks thought: 'Friends, this is the way of recollecting past lives, namely, ascending to rebirth starting from the preceding death. But this—sending knowledge backwards from rebirth to find the preceding death—is extremely difficult. The Blessed One spoke as if showing a footprint in the sky!' Becoming utterly amazed, they said, 'Wonderful, friends!' and so on. Then, pointing out yet another reason, they said, 'Indeed, where the Tathāgata...' and so on. Therein, the phrase 'indeed, where' (yatra hi nāma) is a particle in the sense of wonder; the meaning is 'such a Tathāgata'. In the phrase 'with proliferation cut off' (chinnapapañca), 'proliferation' refers to these three defilements: craving, conceit, and wrong view. In the phrase 'with the round cut off' (chinnavaṭuma), 'the round' (vaṭuma) refers to the round of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. The word pariyādinnavaṭṭa ('with the round exhausted') is a synonym for that very same thing; the meaning is 'one for whom the entire round of kamma is exhausted'. 'Having transcended all suffering' (sabbadukkhavītivatta) means: they have transcended all suffering, which is designated as the round of results. The word 'will recollect' (anussarissati) is a future tense verb due to the particle yatra, but the meaning here should be understood in the past tense. For the Blessed One did recollect those Buddhas; it is not that he will recollect them only now. 'Of such virtue' (evaṃsīlā) means they were of such virtue through the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, and mundane and supramundane virtue. In 'of such qualities' (evaṃdhammā), the qualities associated with concentration are intended; the meaning is 'of such concentration' through the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and mundane and supramundane concentration. 'Of such wisdom' (evaṃpaññā) means they were of such wisdom by way of the wisdom of the path and so on. As for 'dwelling thus' (evaṃvihārī): if it is asked, 'Since the qualities associated with concentration were already included below, dwelling is already included, so why include again what is already included?', the answer is: this is not what was already included, for this was stated to explain the attainment of cessation. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: 'Those Blessed Ones were dwellers in such an attainment of cessation.'

Evaṃvimuttāti ettha vikkhambhanavimutti, tadaṅgavimutti, samucchedavimutti, paṭippassaddhivimutti, nissaraṇavimuttīti pañcavidhā vimutti. Tattha aṭṭha samāpattiyo sayaṃ vikkhambhitehi nīvaraṇādīhi vimuttattā vikkhambhanavimuttīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Aniccānupassanādikā sattānupassanā sayaṃ tassa tassa paccanīkaṅgavasena pariccattāhi niccasaññādīhi vimuttattā tadaṅgavimuttīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Cattāro ariyamaggā sayaṃ samucchinnehi kilesehi vimuttattā samucchedavimuttīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Cattāri sāmaññaphalāni maggānubhāvena kilesānaṃ paṭippassaddhante uppannattā paṭippassaddhivimuttīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Nibbānaṃ sabbakilesehi nissaṭattā apagatattā dūre ṭhitattā nissaraṇavimuttīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Iti imāsaṃ pañcannaṃ vimuttīnaṃ vasena – “evaṃ vimuttā”ti ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

"Thus liberated"—herein, liberation is fivefold: liberation by suppression, liberation by substitution, liberation by eradication, liberation by tranquillization, and liberation by escape.
