Therein, the eight attainments are reckoned as liberation by suppression because they are liberated from the hindrances and so forth that have been suppressed. The seven contemplations, such as the contemplation of impermanence, are reckoned as liberation by substitution because they are liberated from the perceptions of permanence and so forth that have been abandoned by means of their respective opposing factors. The four noble paths are reckoned as liberation by eradication because they are liberated from the defilements that have been eradicated. The four fruits of the contemplative life are reckoned as liberation by tranquillization because they arise upon the calming of the defilements through the power of the paths. Nibbāna is reckoned as liberation by escape because it has escaped from all defilements, has departed, and stands afar. Thus, in the phrase "thus liberated," the meaning should be understood according to these five kinds of liberation.

14. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti ekībhāvā vuṭṭhito.

14. "Having emerged from seclusion" means having emerged from solitude.

16. “Ito so, bhikkhave”ti ko anusandhi? Idañhi suttaṃ – “tathāgatassevesā, bhikkhave, dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā”ti ca “devatāpi tathāgatassa etamatthaṃ ārocesu”nti ca imehi dvīhi padehi ābaddhaṃ. Tattha devatārocanapadaṃ suttantapariyosāne devacārikakolāhalaṃ dassento vicāressati[P 2.0427]. Dhammadhātupadānusandhivasena pana ayaṃ desanā [M 2.0020] āraddhā. Tattha khattiyo jātiyātiādīni ekādasapadāni nidānakaṇḍe vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

16. Regarding "From here, monks," what is the connection? This discourse is connected to these two phrases: "Indeed, monks, this Dhamma-element is well-penetrated by the Tathāgata," and "deities also informed the Tathāgata of this matter." Therein, the phrase about the deities' announcement will be examined at the end of the sutta when showing the commotion of the deities' visit. This teaching, however, is begun in connection with the phrase about the Dhamma-element. Therein, the eleven phrases beginning with "a khattiya by birth" should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the background.

Bodhisattadhammatāvaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Nature of a Bodhisatta

17. Atha [V 2.0018] kho, bhikkhave, vipassī bodhisattotiādīsu pana vipassīti tassa nāmaṃ, tañca kho vividhe atthe passanakusalatāya laddhaṃ. Bodhisattoti paṇḍitasatto bujjhanakasatto. Bodhisaṅkhātesu vā catūsu maggesu satto āsatto laggamānasoti bodhisatto. Sato sampajānoti ettha satoti satiyeva. Sampajānoti ñāṇaṃ. Satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā mātukucchiṃ okkamīti attho. Okkamīti iminā cassa okkantabhāvo pāḷiyaṃ dassito, na okkamanakkamo. So pana yasmā aṭṭhakathaṃ ārūḷho, tasmā evaṃ veditabbo –

17. Now, in the phrases beginning "Then, bhikkhus, Vipassī the Bodhisatta," "Vipassī" is his name, and it was obtained due to his skill in seeing various meanings. "Bodhisatta" means a wise being, a being who will awaken. Or, a being who is attached, devoted, and clinging to the four paths known as "bodhi" is a Bodhisatta. Herein, in "mindful and clearly comprehending," "mindful" refers to mindfulness itself. "Clearly comprehending" refers to knowledge. The meaning is that having made mindfulness well-established and having discerned with knowledge, he descended into his mother’s womb. By this word "descended," the fact of his descent is shown in the Pāli, but not the process of his descent. But since that process is set forth in the commentary, it should be understood thus:

Sabbabodhisattā hi samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā, pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajitvā, ñātatthacariyalokatthacariyabuddhacariyānaṃ koṭiṃ patvā, vessantarasadise tatiye attabhāve ṭhatvā, satta mahādānāni datvā, sattakkhattuṃ pathaviṃ kampetvā, kālaṅkatvā, dutiyacittavāre tusitabhavane nibbattanti. Vipassī bodhisattopi tatheva katvā tusitapure nibbattitvā saṭṭhisatasahassādhikā sattapaññāsa vassakoṭiyo tattha aṭṭhāsi. Aññadā pana dīghāyukadevaloke nibbattā bodhisattā na yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Kasmā? Tattha pāramīnaṃ duppūraṇīyattā. Te adhimuttikālakiriyaṃ katvā manussapatheyeva nibbattanti. Pāramīnaṃ pūrento pana yathā idāni ekena attabhāvena sabbaññutaṃ upanetuṃ sakkonti, evaṃ sabbaso pūritattā tadā vipassī bodhisatto tattha yāvatāyukaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

Indeed, all Bodhisattas, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having made the five great relinquishments, having reached the culmination of conduct for the benefit of relatives, for the benefit of the world, and for enlightenment, abiding in the third-to-last existence, which is like that of Vessantara, having given the seven great gifts, having caused the earth to quake seven times, and having passed away, are reborn in the Tusita heaven in the second thought-moment. The Bodhisatta Vipassī, having done likewise, was reborn in the city of Tusita and remained there for fifty-seven koṭis and six million years. However, at other times, Bodhisattas who are reborn in long-lived deva realms do not remain for their full lifespan. Why? Because there the perfections are difficult to fulfill. They effect a death by resolution and are reborn only in the human sphere. But because his perfections were so completely fulfilled that he was able to attain omniscience with only one intervening existence, the Bodhisatta Vipassī at that time remained there for his full lifespan.

Devatānaṃ pana – “manussānaṃ gaṇanāvasena idāni sattahi divasehi cuti bhavissatī”ti pañca pubbanimittāni uppajjanti – mālā milāyanti, vatthāni kilissanti, kacchehi sedā muccanti, kāye dubbaṇṇiyaṃ okkamati, devo devāsane na saṇṭhāti. Tattha [P 2.0428] mālāti paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase piḷandhanamālā[M 2.0021], tā kira saṭṭhisatasahassādhikā sattapaṇṇāsa vassakoṭiyo amilāyitvā tadā milāyanti. Vatthesupi eseva nayo. Ettakaṃ pana kālaṃ devānaṃ neva sītaṃ na uṇhaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ kāle sarīrā bindubinduvasena sedā muccanti. Ettakañca kālaṃ tesaṃ sarīre khaṇḍiccapāliccādivasena vivaṇṇatā na paññāyati, devadhītā soḷasavassuddesikā viya khāyanti, devaputtā vīsativassuddesikā viya khāyanti, maraṇakāle pana tesaṃ kilantarūpo attabhāvo hoti. Ettakañca tesaṃ kālaṃ devaloke ukkaṇṭhitā nāma natthi, maraṇakāle pana nissasanti vijambhanti, sake āsane nābhiramanti.

Now, for the devas, five portents appear, indicating, 'According to human reckoning, passing away will occur in seven days': their garlands wither, their garments become soiled, sweat is discharged from their armpits, discolouration comes upon their bodies, and the deva is unsteady in his divine seat. Therein, 'garlands' means the garlands worn on the day of rebirth-linking. It is said that those garlands, which had not withered for fifty-seven koṭis and six million years, then wither. The same principle applies to their garments. For all that time, the devas experience neither cold nor heat, but at that time, sweat is discharged from their bodies drop by drop. And for all that time, no sign of altered appearance, such as broken teeth or grey hair, is seen on their bodies; the devatās appear as if sixteen years of age, and the devaputtas appear as if twenty years of age. But at the time of death, their physical form becomes weary. And for all that time, there is nothing called discontent for them in the deva world, but at the time of death, they sigh and yawn, and do not delight in their own seats.

Imāni [V 2.0019] pana pubbanimittāni yathā loke mahāpuññānaṃ rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃyeva ukkāpātabhūmicālacandaggāhādīni nimittāni paññāyanti, na sabbesaṃ; evaṃ mahesakkhadevatānaṃyeva paññāyanti, na sabbesaṃ. Yathā ca manussesu pubbanimittāni nakkhattapāṭhakādayova jānanti, na sabbe; evaṃ tānipi na sabbadevatā jānanti, paṇḍitā eva pana jānanti. Tattha ye mandena kusalakammena nibbattā devaputtā, te tesu uppannesu – “idāni ko jānāti, ‘kuhiṃ nibbattessāmā’ti” bhāyanti. Ye mahāpuññā, te “amhehi dinnaṃ dānaṃ, rakkhitaṃ sīlaṃ, bhāvitaṃ bhāvanaṃ āgamma upari devalokesu sampattiṃ anubhavissāmā”ti na bhāyanti. Vipassī bodhisattopi tāni pubbanimittāni disvā “idāni anantare attabhāve buddho bhavissāmī”ti na bhāyati. Athassa tesu nimittesu pātubhūtesu dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā sannipatitvā – “mārisa, tumhehi dasa pāramiyo pūrentehi na sakkasampattiṃ, na mārasampattiṃ, na brahmasampattiṃ, na cakkavattisampattiṃ patthentehi pūritā, lokanittharaṇatthāya pana buddhattaṃ patthayamānehi pūritā. So vo, idāni kālo, mārisa, buddhattāya, samayo, mārisa, buddhattāyā”ti yācanti.

Moreover, just as in the world signs such as falling meteors, earthquakes, and lunar eclipses appear only to those of great merit—kings, royal ministers, and the like—and not to everyone; so too, these prior signs appear only to deities of great power, and not to all of them. And just as among humans, only astrologers and the like know of the prior signs, not everyone; so too, not all deities know of them—only the wise ones do. Among them, those devaputtas born from meager wholesome deeds become fearful when these signs arise, thinking, “Who knows now where we shall be reborn?” But those of great merit do not fear, thinking, “On account of the generosity we gave, the virtue we upheld, and the meditation we cultivated, we shall experience prosperity in the higher celestial realms.” The Bodhisatta Vipassī, too, upon seeing these prior signs, did not fear, thinking, “Now, in the very next existence, I shall become a Buddha.” Then, when these signs had appeared to him, the deities of the ten thousand world-systems assembled and entreated him: “Venerable Sir, when you fulfilled the ten perfections, you did so not aspiring to the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, nor to the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch; rather, you fulfilled them aspiring to Buddhahood for the sake of the world’s liberation. This, Venerable Sir, is now your time for Buddhahood; this, Venerable Sir, is the occasion for Buddhahood.”

Atha mahāsatto tāsaṃ devatānaṃ paṭiññaṃ adatvāva kāladīpadesakulajanettiāyuparicchedavasena pañcamahāvilokanaṃ nāma vilokesi. Tattha “kālo nu kho, na kālo”ti paṭhamaṃ kālaṃ vilokesi. Tattha [P 2.0429] vassasatasahassato uddhaṃ vaḍḍhitaāyukālo kālo nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Tadā hi sattānaṃ jātijarāmaraṇāni na [M 2.0022] paññāyanti, buddhānañca dhammadesanā nāma tilakkhaṇamuttā natthi. Te tesaṃ – “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti kathentānaṃ – “kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathentī”ti neva sotuṃ, na saddahituṃ maññanti, tato abhisamayo na hoti, tasmiṃ asati aniyyānikaṃ sāsanaṃ hoti. Tasmā so akālo. Vassasatato ūnaāyukālopi kālo na hoti. Kasmā? Tadā hi sattā ussannakilesā honti, ussannakilesānañca dinno ovādo ovādaṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, udake daṇḍarāji viya khippaṃ vigacchati. Tasmā sopi akālova. Vassasatasahassato paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, vassasatato paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ āyukālo kālo nāma, tadā ca asītivassasahassāyukā manussā. Atha mahāsatto – “nibbattitabbakālo”ti kālaṃ passi.

Then the Great Being, without yet giving his assent to those deities, made what is known as the five great surveyings, with respect to time, continent, region, lineage, and the mother’s lifespan. Therein, he first surveyed the time: “Is it now the time, or is it not the time?” In this regard, a time when the lifespan is increasing beyond one hundred thousand years is not called the proper time. Why is that? Because at such a time, birth, aging, and death are not apparent to beings, and the Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas is never apart from the three characteristics. When they are told, “Impermanent, suffering, non-self,” they think, “What is this they are saying?” and do not deem it worth listening to or believing. Consequently, there is no realization, and in its absence, the teaching does not lead to liberation. Therefore, that is an improper time. A time when the lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not the proper time. Why is that? Because at such a time, beings have rampant defilements, and advice given to those with rampant defilements does not take hold; it quickly vanishes, like a line drawn with a stick on water. Therefore, that too is an improper time. The period from one hundred thousand years downwards and from one hundred years upwards is called the proper time. At that time, the human lifespan was eighty thousand years. Then the Great Being saw: “It is the proper time to be born.”

Tato dīpaṃ vilokento saparivāre cattāro dīpe oloketvā – “tīsu dīpesu buddhā na nibbattanti, jambudīpeyeva nibbattantī”ti dīpaṃ passi.

Thereafter, surveying for the continent, he looked upon the four continents with their surrounding islands and saw: ‘Buddhas are not born in the other three continents; they are born only in Jambudīpa.’ Thus he determined the continent.

Tato [V 2.0020] – “jambudīpo nāma mahā, dasayojanasahassaparimāṇo, katarasmiṃ nu kho padese buddhā nibbattantī”ti desaṃ vilokento majjhimadesaṃ passi. Majjhimadeso nāma – “puratthimāya disāya gajaṅgalaṃ nāma nigamo”tiādinā (mahāva. 259) nayena vinaye vuttova. So āyāmato tīṇi yojanasatāni, vitthārato aḍḍhateyyāni, parikkhepato navayojanasatānīti. Etasmiñhi padese buddhā paccekabuddhā aggasāvakā asīti mahāsāvakā cakkavattirājāno aññe ca mahesakkhā khattiyabrāhmaṇagahapatimahāsālā uppajjanti. Idañcettha bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ, tattha mayā nibbattitabbanti niṭṭhaṃ agamāsi.

Then, surveying for the region, he considered: ‘Jambudīpa is vast, ten thousand yojanas in extent. In which region are Buddhas born?’ And he saw the Middle Country. The Middle Country is that which is described in the Vinaya by the passage beginning, ‘In the eastern direction, there is a market town named Gajaṅgala.’ It is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred in circumference. Indeed, it is in this region that Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, the eighty great disciples, wheel-turning monarchs, and other powerful beings—greatly influential khattiyas, brahmins, and householders—are born. ‘And herein is the city named Bandhumatī. It is there I must be born.’ Thus he made his decision.

Tato kulaṃ vilokento – “buddhā nāma lokasammate kule nibbattanti. Idāni ca khattiyakulaṃ lokasammataṃ, tattha nibbattissāmi, bandhumā nāma me rājā pitā bhavissatī”ti kulaṃ passi.

Thereafter, surveying for the lineage, he saw: ‘Buddhas are born into a lineage that is esteemed by the world. At present, the khattiya lineage is esteemed by the world. I shall be born into that. King Bandhumā will be my father.’ Thus he determined the lineage.

Tato [P 2.0430] mātaraṃ vilokento – “buddhamātā nāma lolā surādhuttā na hoti, kappasatasahassaṃ pūritapāramī, jātito paṭṭhāya akhaṇḍapañcasīlā hoti, ayañca bandhumatī nāma devī īdisā, ayaṃ me mātā bhavissati[M 2.0023], “kittakaṃ panassā āyū”ti āvajjanto “dasannaṃ māsānaṃ upari satta divasānī”ti passi.

Thereafter, surveying for the mother, he saw: ‘A Buddha’s mother is never fickle or given to intoxicants. She is one who has fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and has kept the five precepts unbroken from birth. This Queen Bandhumatī is just so. She shall be my mother.’ Then, reflecting, ‘But what is the extent of her lifespan?’ he saw: ‘Ten months and seven days from now.’

Iti imaṃ pañcamahāvilokanaṃ viloketvā “kālo, me mārisā, buddhabhāvāyā”ti devatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karonto paṭiññaṃ datvā – “gacchatha, tumhe”ti tā devatā uyyojetvā tusitadevatāhi parivuto tusitapure nandanavanaṃ pāvisi. Sabbadevalokesu hi nandanavanaṃ atthiyeva. Tatra naṃ devatā ito cuto sugatiṃ gacchāti pubbekatakusalakammokāsaṃ sārayamānā vicaranti. So evaṃ devatāhi kusalaṃ sārayamānāhi parivuto tattha vicarantoyeva cavi.

Thus, having made these five great surveyings, showing favor to the deities, he gave his assent, saying, “Venerable Sirs, it is time for my Buddhahood.” Then, dismissing those deities with the words, “You may go,” he entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita realm, surrounded by the Tusita deities. For in all celestial worlds there is a Nandana Grove. There, the deities wander about, reminding him of the opportunity created by his previously performed wholesome kamma, saying, “Having passed away from here, go to a good destination!” And so, surrounded by deities who were thus reminding him of his merit, he passed away while wandering there.

Evaṃ cuto ca ‘cavāmī’ti jānāti, cuticittaṃ na jānāti. Paṭisandhiṃ gahetvāpi jānāti, paṭisandhicittameva na jānāti. “Imasmiṃ me ṭhāne paṭisandhiṃ gahitā”ti evaṃ pana jānāti. Keci pana therā – “āvajjanapariyāyo nāma laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, dutiyatatiyacittavāre eva jānissatī”ti vadanti. Tipiṭakamahāsīvatthero pana āha – “mahāsattānaṃ paṭisandhi na aññesaṃ paṭisandhisadisā, koṭippattaṃ pana tesaṃ satisampajaññaṃ. Yasmā pana teneva cittena taṃ cittaṃ ñātuṃ na sakkā, tasmā cuticittaṃ na jānāti. Cutikkhaṇepi ‘cavāmī’ti jānāti. Paṭisandhicittaṃ na jānāti. ‘Asukasmiṃ me ṭhāne paṭisandhi gahitā’ti jānāti, tasmiṃ [V 2.0021] kāle dasasahassilokadhātu kampatī”ti. Evaṃ sato sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamanto pana ekūnavīsatiyā paṭisandhicittesu mettāpubbabhāgassa somanassasahagatañāṇasampayuttaasaṅkhārikakusalacittassa sadisamahāvipākacittena paṭisandhi gaṇhi. Mahāsīvatthero pana upekkhāsahagatenāti āha. Yathā [P 2.0431] ca amhākaṃ bhagavā, evaṃ sopi āsāḷhīpuṇṇamāyaṃ uttarāsāḷhanakkhatteneva paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi.

Thus, when passing away, he knows, “I am passing away,” but he does not know the death-consciousness. Even after taking rebirth-linking he knows, but he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness itself. However, he knows thus: “Rebirth-linking has been taken by me in this place.” But some elders say: “It is fitting that the turn for adverting be obtained; he will know only in the second or third consciousness-moment.” The Elder Mahāsīva, knower of the Tipiṭaka, however, said: “The rebirth-linking of great beings is not like the rebirth-linking of others; their mindfulness and clear comprehension, however, have reached the utmost. Yet, because that consciousness cannot be known by that very same consciousness, he does not know the death-consciousness. Even at the moment of death, he knows, ‘I am passing away.’ He does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness. He knows, ‘Rebirth-linking has been taken by me in such-and-such a place.’ At that time, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembles.” Thus, being mindful and clearly comprehending while descending into his mother’s womb, from among the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness, he took rebirth-linking with a great resultant consciousness similar to a wholesome, unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and preceded by loving-kindness. The Elder Mahāsīva, however, said it was with one accompanied by equanimity. And just as our Blessed One, so too did he take rebirth-linking on the Āsāḷhī full moon day, precisely under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation.

Tadā kira pure puṇṇamāya sattamadivasato paṭṭhāya vigatasurāpānaṃ mālāgandhādivibhūtisampannaṃ nakkhattakīḷaṃ anubhavamānā bodhisattamātā sattame divase pāto uṭṭhāya gandhodakena nahāyitvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitā varabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sirisayane nipannā niddaṃ okkamamānā idaṃ supinaṃ addasa – “cattāro kira [M 2.0024] naṃ mahārājāno sayaneneva saddhiṃ ukkhipitvā anotattadahaṃ netvā nahāpetvā dibbavatthaṃ nivāsetvā dibbagandhehi vilimpetvā dibbapupphāni piḷandhitvā, tato avidūre rajatapabbato, tassa anto kanakavimānaṃ atthi, tasmiṃ pācīnato sīsaṃ katvā nipajjāpesuṃ. Atha bodhisatto setavaravāraṇo hutvā tato avidūre eko suvaṇṇapabbato, tattha caritvā tato oruyha rajatapabbataṃ abhiruhitvā kanakavimānaṃ pavisitvā mātaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇapassaṃ phāletvā kucchiṃ paviṭṭhasadiso ahosi”.

At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta’s mother, beginning from the seventh day before the full moon, abstaining from intoxicants and endowed with the splendor of garlands, perfumes, and other adornments, was enjoying the star festival. On the seventh day, rising early, she bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all ornaments, partook of excellent food, undertook the Uposatha precepts, entered her splendid chamber, and lay down on her magnificent couch. As she was falling asleep, she saw this dream: “It is said, four great kings lifted her up together with her very couch, took her to Lake Anotatta, bathed her, clothed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine perfumes, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from there is a silver mountain, and within it a golden mansion. There, they laid her down with her head to the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a splendid white elephant, was on a golden mountain not far from there. After wandering there, he descended, ascended the silver mountain, entered the golden mansion, circumambulated his mother, and, splitting open her right side, he appeared to enter her womb.”

Atha pabuddhā devī taṃ supinaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā vibhātāya rattiyā catusaṭṭhimatte brāhmaṇapāmokkhe pakkosāpetvā haritūpalittāya lājādīhi katamaṅgalasakkārāya bhūmiyā mahārahāni āsanāni paññapetvā tattha nisinnānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ sappimadhusakkarābhisaṅkhatassa varapāyāsassa suvaṇṇarajatapātiyo pūretvā suvaṇṇarajatapātīheva paṭikujjitvā adāsi, aññehi ca ahatavatthakapilagāvīdānādīhi nesaṃ santappesi. Atha nesaṃ sabbakāmasantappitānaṃ taṃ supinaṃ ārocetvā – “kiṃ bhavissatī”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇā āhaṃsu – “mā cintayi, mahārāja, deviyā te kucchimhi gabbho patiṭṭhito, so ca kho purisagabbho na itthigabbho, putto te bhavissati. So sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasissati, rājā bhavissati cakkavattī. Sace agārā nikkhamma pabbajissati, buddho bhavissati loke vivaṭṭacchado”ti. Ayaṃ tāva – “mātukucchiṃ okkamī”ti ettha vaṇṇanākkamo.

Then the queen, upon awakening, related that dream to the king. When the night grew light, the king had sixty-four prominent brahmins summoned. On ground that was smeared with fresh cow-dung and auspiciously honored with roasted grain and other offerings, he had magnificent seats prepared. For the brahmins seated there, he filled golden and silver bowls with excellent milk-rice prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, and covering them with other golden and silver bowls, he presented them. He also satisfied them with other gifts, such as new cloth and tawny cows. Then, when they had been satisfied with all desirable things, he related the dream to them and asked, “What will be the result?” The brahmins replied: “Do not be anxious, great king. A conception has been established in the queen’s womb. And it is a male conception, not a female one; you will have a son. If he lives the household life, he will become a wheel-turning monarch. If he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he will become a Buddha in the world, one who has rolled back the covering.” This, for now, is the order of exposition here regarding “He descended into his mother’s womb.”

Ayamettha [P 2.0432] dhammatāti ayaṃ ettha mātukucchiokkamane dhammatā, ayaṃ sabhāvo, ayaṃ niyāmoti [V 2.0022] vuttaṃ hoti. Niyāmo ca nāmesa kammaniyāmo, utuniyāmo, bījaniyāmo, cittaniyāmo, dhammaniyāmoti pañcavidho (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 498).

“This here is the natural principle” means: this is the natural principle in the descent into the mother’s womb; this is the inherent nature; this is the fixed order. And this fixed order is fivefold: the order of kamma, the order of seasons, the order of seeds, the order of mind, and the order of phenomena.

Tattha kusalassa iṭṭhavipākadānaṃ, akusalassa aniṭṭhavipākadānanti ayaṃ kammaniyāmo. Tassa dīpanatthaṃ – “na antalikkhe”ti (khu. pā. 127) gāthāya vatthūni vattabbāni. Apica ekā kira itthī sāmikena saddhiṃ bhaṇḍitvā ubbandhitvā maritukāmā [M 2.0025] rajjupāse gīvaṃ pavesesi. Aññataro puriso vāsiṃ nisento taṃ itthikammaṃ disvā rajjuṃ chinditukāmo – “mā bhāyi, mā bhāyī”ti taṃ samassāsento upadhāvi. Rajju āsīviso hutvā aṭṭhāsi. So bhīto palāyi. Itarā tattheva mari. Evamādīni cettha vatthūni dassetabbāni.

Among these, the order of kamma is this: the giving of desirable results by wholesome kamma, and the giving of undesirable results by unwholesome kamma. To illustrate this, the stories connected with the verse beginning “Not in the sky…” should be told. Furthermore, it is said that a certain woman, having quarreled with her husband, wished to die by hanging herself and placed a noose around her neck. Another man, while sharpening an adze, saw what the woman was doing and, wishing to cut the rope, ran towards her, comforting her, saying, “Do not fear, do not fear!” The rope became a venomous snake and remained so. Frightened, he fled. The other, the woman, died right there. Stories such as these should be presented here.

Tesu tesu janapadesu tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle ekappahāreneva rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalagahaṇādīni, vātassa vāyanaṃ avāyanaṃ, ātapassa tikkhatā mandatā, devassa vassanaṃ avassanaṃ, padumānaṃ divā vikasanaṃ rattiṃ milāyananti evamādi utuniyāmo.

The order of seasons is as follows: in various regions at various times, the bearing of flowers and fruit by trees all at once; the blowing or not blowing of the wind; the intensity or mildness of the sun’s heat; the falling or not falling of rain; the blooming of lotuses by day and their fading by night, and so forth.

Yaṃ panetaṃ sālibījato sāliphalameva, madhurato madhurasaṃyeva, tittato tittarasaṃyeva phalaṃ hoti, ayaṃ bījaniyāmo.

Furthermore, that from a rice seed only rice fruit is produced; from a sweet seed, a sweet-tasting fruit; and from a bitter seed, a bitter-tasting fruit—this is the order of seeds.

Purimā purimā cittacetasikā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ upanissayapaccayena paccayoti evaṃ yadetaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ anantarā sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ nibbattanaṃ, ayaṃ cittaniyāmo.

The order of mind is this: preceding mental states and mental factors are a condition for subsequent mental states and mental factors by way of decisive support condition. Thus, that which is the arising of receiving consciousness and so on immediately after eye-consciousness and so on—this is the order of mind.

Yā panesā bodhisattānaṃ mātukucchiokkamanādīsu dasasahassilokadhātukampanādīnaṃ pavatti, ayaṃ dhammaniyāmo nāma. Tesu idha dhammaniyāmo adhippeto. Tasmā tamevatthaṃ dassento dhammatā esā bhikkhavetiādimāha.

Now, this occurrence—the trembling of the ten-thousand-world-system and so on at the Bodhisattas' descent into their mothers' wombs and so on—is what is called the fixed order of the Dhamma. Among the fixed orders, it is the fixed order of the Dhamma that is intended here. Therefore, to show that very meaning, he said, 'This, monks, is the natural state,' and so on.

18. Tattha kucchiṃ okkamatīti ettha kucchiṃ okkanto hotīti ayamevattho[P 2.0433]. Okkante hi tasmiṃ evaṃ hoti, na okkamamāne. Appamāṇoti vuḍḍhippamāṇo, vipuloti attho. Uḷāroti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Uḷārāni uḷārāni khādanīyāni khādantītiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.399) hi madhuraṃ uḷāranti vuttaṃ. Uḷārāya khalu bhavaṃ vacchāyano samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pasaṃsāya pasaṃsatītiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.288) seṭṭhaṃ uḷāranti vuttaṃ. Idha pana vipulaṃ [V 2.0023] adhippetaṃ. Devānaṃ devānubhāvanti ettha devānaṃ ayamānubhāvo nivatthavatthassa pabhā dvādasayojanāni pharati, tathā sarīrassa, tathā alaṅkārassa, tathā vimānassa, taṃ atikkamitvāti attho.

18. Here, in the phrase 'enters the womb,' the meaning is precisely this: 'he has entered the womb.' For this occurs when he has entered, not while he is in the process of entering. 'Immeasurable' means having a measure of growth; the meaning is 'vast.' 'Sublime' is a synonym for that very word. For in passages such as, 'eating sublime, sublime delicacies,' 'sublime' is said to mean sweet. In passages such as, 'Surely, the venerable Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with sublime praise,' 'sublime' is said to mean excellent. Here, however, 'vast' is what is intended. In the phrase 'with the splendor of the devas,' the meaning is 'surpassing it'—that is, this is the splendor of the devas: the radiance of a worn garment spreads for twelve yojanas, likewise that of the body, likewise that of the ornaments, and likewise that of the celestial mansion.

Lokantarikāti [M 2.0026] tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ antarā ekeko lokantariko hoti, tiṇṇaṃ sakaṭacakkānaṃ vā tiṇṇaṃ pattānaṃ vā aññamaññaṃ āhacca ṭhapitānaṃ majjhe okāso viya. So pana lokantarikanirayo parimāṇato aṭṭhayojanasahasso hoti. Aghāti niccavivaṭā. Asaṃvutāti heṭṭhāpi appatiṭṭhā. Andhakārāti tamabhūtā. Andhakāratimisāti cakkhuviññāṇuppattinivāraṇato andhabhāvakaraṇatimisena samannāgatā. Tattha kira cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na jāyati. Evaṃmahiddhikāti candimasūriyā kira ekappahāreneva tīsu dīpesu paññāyanti, evaṃ mahiddhikā. Ekekāya disāya nava nava yojanasatasahassāni andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokaṃ dassenti, evaṃmahānubhāvā. Ābhāya nānubhontīti attano pabhāya nappahonti. Te kira cakkavāḷapabbatassa vemajjhena vicaranti, cakkavāḷapabbatañca atikkamma lokantarikanirayā. Tasmā te tattha ābhāya nappahonti.

The inter-world hell is the space between every three world-systems, where one such hell is found, like the space in the middle of three cart-wheels or three bowls placed touching one another. That inter-world hell is eight thousand yojanas in extent. 'Woeful' means always open. 'Unenclosed' means without a foundation below. 'Dark' means it is sheer blackness. 'Shrouded in darkness' means it is possessed of a blinding darkness that prevents the arising of eye-consciousness. It is said that eye-consciousness does not arise there. 'So mighty' refers to the moon and sun, which, it is said, appear in three continents at once—so mighty are they. 'So powerful' means they dispel the darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction and provide light. 'They do not illumine with their radiance' means they are not able with their own light. For it is said they travel along the middle of the world-encircling mountain, and the inter-world hells are beyond the world-encircling mountain. Therefore, they are not able to illumine that place with their radiance.

Yepi tattha sattāti yepi tasmiṃ lokantarikamahāniraye sattā uppannā. Kiṃ pana kammaṃ katvā tattha uppajjantīti. Bhāriyaṃ dāruṇaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānañca upari aparādhaṃ, aññañca divase divase pāṇavadhādisāhasikakammaṃ katvā uppajjanti, tambapaṇṇidīpe abhayacoranāgacorādayo viya. Tesaṃ attabhāvo tigāvutiko hoti, vaggulīnaṃ viya dīghanakhā honti. Te rukkhe vagguliyo viya nakhehi cakkavāḷapabbate lagganti. Yadā [P 2.0434] saṃsappantā aññamaññassa hatthapāsaṃ gatā honti, atha “bhakkho no laddho”ti maññamānā tattha vāvaṭā viparivattitvā lokasandhārakaudake patanti, vāte paharantepi madhukaphalāni viya chijjitvā udake patanti, patitamattāva accantakhāre udake piṭṭhapiṇḍi viya vilīyanti.

'And those beings who are there' means those beings who have arisen in that great inter-world hell. But what kamma did they do to arise there? They arise there for having committed grave and cruel offenses against their parents and against righteous ascetics and brahmins, and for having done other violent deeds day after day, such as killing living beings—like Abhaya the robber, Nāga the robber, and others on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Their bodies are three gāvutas in size, and they have long nails like bats. They cling to the world-encircling mountain with their nails, just as bats cling to a tree. When, crawling about, they come within each other's reach, they think, 'We have found food!' Exerting themselves there, they turn over and fall into the world-sustaining water. Even when the wind blows, they are cut off like madhuka fruits and fall into the water. As soon as they have fallen, they dissolve in the extremely cold water like a lump of flour.

Aññepi kira bho santi sattāti bho yathā mayaṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhavāma, evaṃ aññe kira sattāpi imaṃ dukkhamanubhavanatthāya idhūpapannāti taṃ divasaṃ passanti. Ayaṃ pana obhāso ekayāgupānamattampi na tiṭṭhati, accharāsaṅghāṭamattameva vijjobhāso viya niccharitvā – “kiṃ ida”nti bhaṇantānaṃyeva antaradhāyati. Saṅkampatīti samantato kampati. Itaradvayaṃ purimapadasseva vevacanaṃ. Puna appamāṇo cātiādi nigamanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Friends, it seems there are other beings!' means: on that day they see, thinking, 'Friends, just as we are experiencing great suffering, so it seems other beings have also arisen here to experience this suffering.' This radiance, however, does not last even for the time it takes to drink a measure of gruel; it lasts only for the duration of a finger-snap. Having flashed forth like lightning, it vanishes even as they are saying, 'What is this?' 'It trembled' means it shook all around. The other two terms are synonyms of the first. Again, the passage beginning 'immeasurable' was stated for the purpose of conclusion.

19. Cattāro [V 2.0024][M 2.0027] naṃ devaputtā cātuddisaṃ rakkhāya upagacchantīti ettha cattāroti catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Dasasahassacakkavāḷesu pana cattāro cattāro katvā cattālīsasahassāni honti. Tattha imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe mahārājāno khaggahatthā bodhisattassa ārakkhatthāya upagantvā sirigabbhaṃ paviṭṭhā, itare gabbhadvārato paṭṭhāya avaruddhake paṃsupisācakādiyakkhagaṇe paṭikkamāpetvā yāva cakkavāḷā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu.

19. In the phrase, 'Four devaputtas approached from the four directions to provide protection,' the word 'four' is stated with reference to the Four Great Kings. In the ten-thousand world-systems, however, taking four in each, there are forty thousand. Among them, the Great Kings in this world-system, with swords in hand, approached to protect the Bodhisatta and entered the glorious chamber. The others, starting from the door of the chamber, drove back the obstructive hordes of yakṣas, such as dust-pīsacas, and took up guard as far as the edge of the world-system.

Kimatthāya panāyaṃ rakkhā? Nanu paṭisandhikkhaṇe kalalakālato paṭṭhāya sacepi koṭisatasahassamārā koṭisatasahassasineruṃ ukkhipitvā bodhisattassa vā bodhisattamātuyā vā antarāyakaraṇatthaṃ āgaccheyyuṃ, sabbe antarāva antaradhāyeyyuṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā ruhiruppādavatthusmiṃ – “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ parupakkamena tathāgataṃ jīvitā voropeyya. Anupakkamena, bhikkhave, tathāgatā parinibbāyanti. Gacchatha, tumhe bhikkhave, yathāvihāraṃ, arakkhiyā, bhikkhave tathāgatā”ti (cūḷava. 341). Evameva, tena parupakkamena na tesaṃ jīvitantarāyo [P 2.0435] atthi, santi kho pana amanussā virūpā duddasikā bheravarūpā migapakkhino, yesaṃ rūpaṃ vā disvā saddaṃ vā sutvā bodhisattamātu bhayaṃ vā santāso vā uppajjeyya, tesaṃ nivāraṇatthāya rakkhaṃ aggahesuṃ. Apica bodhisattassa puññatejena sañjātagāravā attano gāravacoditāpi te evamakaṃsu.

But for what purpose is this protection? Indeed, from the moment of conception, from the kalala stage, even if a trillion Māras were to come, lifting a trillion Mount Merus with the intention of causing harm to the Bodhisatta or the Bodhisatta’s mother, they would all vanish midway. This, too, has been said by the Blessed One in the Ruhiruppādavatthu: 'Monks, this is impossible, there is no possibility, that one could take the Tathāgata’s life by violent means. Monks, without violent means, Tathāgatas attain final Nibbāna. Go, monks, dwell as you please. Monks, Tathāgatas do not need protection.' Likewise, through such violent means, there is no danger to their lives. However, there are non-human beings, beasts, and birds that are deformed, ugly, and terrifying in form. Upon seeing their forms or hearing their sounds, fear or terror might arise in the Bodhisatta’s mother. It was to ward them off that they provided protection. Moreover, reverence having arisen in them due to the Bodhisatta’s power of merit, they also acted thus, prompted by their own reverence.

Kiṃ pana te antogabbhaṃ pavisitvā ṭhitā cattāro mahārājāno bodhisattassa mātuyā attānaṃ dassenti, na dassentīti? Nahānamaṇḍanabhojanādisarīrakiccakāle na dassenti, sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā varasayane nipannakāle pana dassenti. Tattha kiñcāpi amanussadassanaṃ nāma manussānaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ hoti, bodhisattassa mātā pana attano ceva puttassa ca puññānubhāvena te disvā na bhāyati, pakatiantepurapālakesu viya assā etesu cittaṃ uppajjati.

But do those four great kings, having entered and stationed themselves in the inner chamber, show themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother, or do they not? They do not show themselves at the time of bathing, adorning, eating, and other bodily activities; but when she enters the splendid chamber and lies down on the excellent bed, they do show themselves. And although the sight of non-humans is indeed frightening to humans, the Bodhisatta’s mother, through the powerful merit of both herself and her son, is not afraid upon seeing them; her mind arises towards them just as it would towards the regular palace guards.

20. Pakatiyā sīlavatīti sabhāveneva sīlasampannā. Anuppanne kira buddhe manussā tāpasaparibbājakānaṃ santike vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā sīlaṃ gaṇhanti. Bodhisattamātāpi kāladevilassa isino santike [M 2.0028] sīlaṃ gaṇhāti. Bodhisatte pana kucchigate aññassa pādamūle nisīdituṃ nāma na sakkā, samānāsane nisīditvā gahitasīlampi āvajjanakaraṇamattaṃ hoti. Tasmā sayameva sīlaṃ aggahesīti vuttaṃ hoti.

20. ‘Naturally virtuous’ means she was endowed with virtue by her very nature. It is said that when a Buddha has not arisen, people approach ascetics and wanderers, pay homage, sit squatting, and undertake the precepts. The Bodhisatta’s mother also used to undertake the precepts from the sage Kāladevila. However, once the Bodhisatta was in her womb, it was not possible for her to sit at another’s feet; even undertaking the precepts while sitting on an equal seat would amount to an act of disrespect. Therefore, it is said that she undertook the precepts by herself.

21. Purisesūti [V 2.0025] bodhisattassa pitaraṃ ādiṃ katvā kesuci manussesu purisādhippāyacittaṃ nuppajjati. Bodhisattamāturūpaṃ pana kusalā sippikā potthakammādīsupi kātuṃ na sakkonti. Taṃ disvā purisassa rāgo nuppajjatīti na sakkā vattuṃ, sace pana taṃ rattacitto upasaṅkamitukāmo hoti, pādā na vahanti, dibbasaṅkhalikā viya bajjhanti. Tasmā “anatikkamanīyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

21. ‘Among men’ means that no lustful thought towards any man, beginning with the Bodhisatta’s father, arose in her. Furthermore, skilled artisans were unable to depict the form of the Bodhisatta’s mother, even in paintings and the like. It cannot be said that lust would not arise in a man upon seeing her; but if a man with a lustful mind wished to approach her, his feet would not carry him; they would become bound as if by divine fetters. Therefore, it was said, ‘She is not to be transgressed,’ and so on.

22. Pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānanti pubbe kāmaguṇūpasañhitanti iminā purisādhippāyavasena vatthupaṭikkhepo kato, idha ārammaṇappaṭilābho dassito. Tadā kira deviyā evarūpo putto kucchiṃ upapannoti sutvā samantato rājāno [P 2.0436] mahagghaābharaṇatūriyādivasena pañcadvārārammaṇavatthubhūtaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesenti. Bodhisattassa ca bodhisattamātu ca katakammassa ussannattā lābhasakkārassa pamāṇaparicchedo natthi.

22. Regarding ‘the five strands of sensual pleasure’: previously, with the words ‘associated with sensual pleasures,’ the rejection of the object of lust was made with reference to her intention towards men. Here, the acquisition of sense-objects is shown. It is said that at that time, upon hearing, ‘Such a son has entered the queen’s womb,’ kings from all around sent gifts—consisting of valuable ornaments, musical instruments, and so on—that became objects for the five sense-doors. And due to the abundance of the past kamma of both the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta’s mother, there was no measure or limit to their gain and honour.

23. Akilantakāyāti yathā aññā itthiyo gabbhabhārena kilamanti hatthapādā uddhumātatādīni pāpuṇanti, evaṃ tassā koci kilamatho nāhosi. Tirokucchigatanti antokucchigataṃ. Passatīti kalalādikālaṃ atikkamitvā sañjātaaṅgapaccaṅgaahīnindriyabhāvaṃ upagataṃyeva passati. Kimatthaṃ passati? Sukhavāsatthaṃyeva. Yatheva hi mātā puttena saddhiṃ nipannā vā nisinnā vā – “hatthaṃ vāssa pādaṃ vā olambantaṃ ukkhipitvā saṇṭhapessāmī”ti sukhavāsatthaṃ puttaṃ oloketi, evaṃ bodhisattamātāpi yaṃ taṃ mātu uṭṭhānagamanaparivattananisajjādīsu uṇhasītaloṇikatittakakaṭukāhāraajjhoharaṇakālesu ca gabbhassa dukkhaṃ uppajjati, “atthi nu kho me taṃ puttassā”ti sukhavāsatthaṃ olokayamānā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinnaṃ bodhisattaṃ passati. Yathā hi aññe antokucchigatā pakkāsayaṃ avattharitvā āmāsayaṃ ukkhipitvā udarapaṭalaṃ piṭṭhito katvā piṭṭhikaṇḍakaṃ nissāya ukkuṭikaṃ dvīsu muṭṭhīsu hanukaṃ ṭhapetvā deve [M 2.0029] vassante rukkhasusire makkaṭā viya nisīdanti, na evaṃ bodhisatto, bodhisatto pana piṭṭhikaṇḍakaṃ piṭṭhito katvā dhammāsane dhammakathiko viya pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā puratthābhimukho nisīdati. Pubbekatakammaṃ panassā vatthuṃ sodheti, suddhe vatthumhi sukhumacchavilakkhaṇaṃ nibbattati. Atha naṃ kucchitaco paṭicchādetuṃ na sakkoti, olokentiyā bahiṭhito viya paññāyati. Tamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvento bhagavā seyyathāpītiādimāha. Bodhisatto pana antokucchigato mātaraṃ na passati. Na hi antokucchiyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjati.

23. ‘With an unwearied body’ means that unlike other women who become weary from the burden of pregnancy, their hands and feet swelling and so on, she experienced no such fatigue. ‘Visible through the womb’ means inside the womb. ‘She sees’ means she sees him only after he has passed the embryonic stage and has attained fully formed major and minor limbs and complete faculties. For what reason does she see him? For her own comfort. Just as a mother, lying or sitting with her child, looks at the child for his comfort, thinking, “I will lift and properly place his hand or foot if it is dangling,” so too the Bodhisatta’s mother, looking for his comfort—wondering, “Does any suffering arise for my son?” when suffering might arise for the fetus during her own standing, walking, turning, sitting, or eating of hot, cold, salty, bitter, or pungent food—sees the Bodhisatta seated with his legs crossed. For whereas other beings inside the womb—pressing down on the digestive stomach, pushing up the undigested food, with the abdominal lining to their back, leaning against the spine—sit squatting like little monkeys in a tree hollow when it rains, with their chin resting on their two fists, the Bodhisatta is not like that. Rather, the Bodhisatta, with his back to the mother’s spine, sits facing forward with his legs crossed, like a Dhamma teacher on the Dhamma seat. Furthermore, her past kamma purifies the womb; in a purified womb, a body with the characteristic of very fine skin is produced. Then the skin of the womb cannot conceal him; to her looking, he appears as if he were outside. To illustrate this point with a simile, the Blessed One said, ‘Just as if…’ and so on. The Bodhisatta, however, being inside the womb, does not see his mother, for eye-consciousness does not arise inside the womb.

24. Kālaṅkarotīti [V 2.0026] na vijātabhāvapaccayā, āyuparikkhayeneva. Bodhisattena vasitaṭṭhānañhi cetiyakuṭisadisaṃ hoti, aññesaṃ aparibhogārahaṃ, na ca sakkā bodhisattamātaraṃ [P 2.0437] apanetvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapetunti tattakaṃyeva bodhisattamātu āyuppamāṇaṃ hoti, tasmā tadā kālaṅkaroti. Katarasmiṃ pana vaye kālaṃ karotīti? Majjhimavaye. Paṭhamavayasmiñhi sattānaṃ attabhāve chandarāgo balavā hoti, tena tadā sañjātagabbhā itthī gabbhaṃ anurakkhituṃ na sakkoti, gabbho bahvābādho hoti. Majjhimavayassa pana dve koṭṭhāse atikkamma tatiye koṭṭhāse vatthu visadaṃ hoti, visade vatthumhi nibbattadārakā arogā honti, tasmā bodhisattamātāpi paṭhamavaye sampattiṃ anubhavitvā majjhimavayassa tatiye koṭṭhāse vijāyitvā kālaṃ karotīti ayamettha dhammatā.

24. ‘She passes away’: This is not on account of childbirth, but solely due to the exhaustion of her lifespan. For the place where the Bodhisatta has dwelt is like the chamber of a cetiya, unfit for use by any other. And it is not possible to remove the Bodhisatta’s mother and install another in the position of chief queen. Thus, the lifespan of the Bodhisatta’s mother is just that long; therefore, she passes away at that time. But at what age does she pass away? In middle age. For in the first stage of life, beings have strong sensual desire and passion in their existence; because of that, a woman who conceives then cannot protect the fetus, and the fetus is subject to many illnesses. But in middle age, after two parts have passed, in the third part the womb is pure. Children conceived in a pure womb are free from illness. Therefore, the Bodhisatta’s mother, having enjoyed prosperity in the first stage of life, gives birth in the third part of middle age and passes away. This, herein, is the fixed nature of things.

25. Nava vā dasa vāti ettha vā saddassa vikappanavasena satta vā aṭṭha vā ekādasa vā dvādasa vāti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo. Tattha sattamāsajāto jīvati, sītuṇhakkhamo pana na hoti. Aṭṭhamāsajāto na jīvati, avasesā jīvanti.

25. Regarding ‘nine or ten months’: here, by way of the word ‘or’ indicating alternatives, the inclusion of ‘seven or eight, or eleven or twelve,’ and so on, should be understood. Among these, one born at seven months lives, but is not able to endure cold and heat. One born at eight months does not live. The rest live.

27. Devā paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhantīti khīṇāsavā suddhāvāsabrahmāno paṭiggaṇhanti. Kathaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti? “Sūtivesaṃ gaṇhitvā”ti eke. Taṃ pana paṭikkhipitvā idaṃ vuttaṃ – ‘tadā bodhisattamātā suvaṇṇakhacitaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsetvā macchakkhisadisaṃ dukūlapaṭaṃ yāva pādantā pārupitvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassā sallahukagabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi, dhamakaraṇato udakanikkhamanasadisaṃ. Atha te pakatibrahmaveseneva upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamaṃ suvaṇṇajālena [M 2.0030] paṭiggahesuṃ. Tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno ajinappaveṇiyā paṭiggahesuṃ. Tato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena paṭiggahesuṃ’. Tena vuttaṃ – “devā paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti, pacchā manussā”ti.

27. The gods receive him first—that is, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās, those with taints destroyed, receive him. How do they receive him? Some say, 'Having taken the guise of birth attendants.' But rejecting that, this is said: 'Then the Bodhisatta's mother, having put on a gold-embroidered garment and draped herself down to her feet in a fine cloth like a fish's eye, stood there. Then for her, the emergence from the womb was light, like water flowing from a water filter. Then those Brahmās, approaching in their natural Brahma appearance, first received him with a golden net. From their hands, the Four Great Kings received him with a garment of fine antelope hide. From them, humans received him with a cushion of fine cloth.' Therefore it is said: 'The gods receive him first, afterwards the humans.'

28. Cattāro naṃ devaputtāti cattāro mahārājāno. Paṭiggahetvāti ajinappaveṇiyā paṭiggahetvā. Mahesakkhoti mahātejo mahāyaso lakkhaṇasampanno.

28. The four devaputtas—these are the Four Great Kings. Having received him—means having received him with a garment of fine antelope hide. Of great majesty—means possessing great power, great renown, and endowed with the characteristic marks.

29. Visadova nikkhamatīti yathā aññe sattā yonimagge laggantā bhaggavibhaggā nikkhamanti, na evaṃ nikkhamati, alaggo [P 2.0438] hutvā nikkhamatīti attho udenāti udakena. Kenaci asucināti yathā aññe sattā kammajavātehi uddhaṃpādā adhosirā yonimagge pakkhittā sataporisaṃ narakapapātaṃ patantā viya, tāḷacchiddena nikkaḍḍhiyamānā hatthī viya mahādukkhaṃ anubhavantā nānāasucimakkhitāva nikkhamanti, na evaṃ bodhisatto. Bodhisattañhi kammajavātā [V 2.0027] uddhapādaṃ adhosiraṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti. So dhammāsanato otaranto dhammakathiko viya, nisseṇito otaranto puriso viya ca dve hatthe ca dve pāde ca pasāretvā ṭhitakova mātukucchisambhavena kenaci asucinā amakkhitova nikkhamati.

29. 'He emerges pure': Just as other beings emerge from the birth canal stuck, broken, and shattered, he does not emerge thus; the meaning is that he emerges unstuck. 'By water' means by water. 'By any impurity': Just as other beings, cast into the birth canal by the winds born of kamma with feet up and head down, as if falling into a hell-chasm a hundred persons deep, or like an elephant being dragged through a narrow aperture with a hook, experience great suffering and emerge smeared with various impurities, it is not so for the Bodhisatta. For the winds born of kamma are unable to make the Bodhisatta have his feet up and head down. He, like a Dhamma-preacher descending from the Dhamma-seat or like a man descending a ladder, emerges standing with both hands and both feet outstretched, unsullied by any impurity arising from his mother's womb.

Udakassa dhārāti udakavaṭṭiyo. Tāsu sītā suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patati uṇhā rajatakaṭāhe. Idañca pathavitale kenaci asucinā asammissaṃ tesaṃ pānīyaparibhojanīyaudakañceva aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ kīḷāudakañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, aññassa pana suvaṇṇarajataghaṭehi āhariyamānaudakassa ceva haṃsavattakādipokkharaṇīgatassa ca udakassa paricchedo natthi.

Streams of water—these are globes of water. Of these, the cold one falls into a golden basin, and the hot one into a silver basin. And this is said to show that their water for drinking and use, as well as the water for play not shared with others, was unmixed with any impurity on the surface of the earth. For other water, however, such as that brought in golden and silver pots or that from ponds like Haṃsavattaka and so forth, there is no limit.

31. Sampatijātoti muhuttajāto. Pāḷiyaṃ pana mātukucchito nikkhantamatto viya dassito, na evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nikkhantamattañhi naṃ paṭhamaṃ brahmāno suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno ajinappaveṇiyā, tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena. Manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhito. Setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāneti dibbasetacchatte anudhāriyamānamhi. Ettha ca chattassa parivārāni khaggādīni [M 2.0031] pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍānipi āgatāneva. Pāḷiyaṃ pana rājagamane rājā viya chattameva vuttaṃ. Tesu chattameva paññāyati, na chattaggāhako. Tathā khaggatālavaṇṭamorahatthakavāḷabījanīuṇhīsamattāyeva paññāyanti, na tesaṃ gāhakā. Sabbāni kira tāni adissamānarūpā devatā gaṇhiṃsu. Vuttañcetaṃ –

31. ‘Just born’ means born just a moment before. In the Pāli, however, he is shown as if he had just emerged from his mother’s womb, but it should not be understood thus. For, having just emerged, the Brahmās first received him with a golden net; from their hands, the Four Great Kings received him with a garment of fine antelope hide; and from their hands, humans received him with a cushion of fine cloth. Released from the hands of humans, he stood firm on the ground. ‘While a white parasol was being held aloft’ means while a divine white parasol was being held aloft. And here, the parasol’s accompaniments—the five items of royal insignia, such as the sword—also arrived. In the Pāli, however, just as the king is mentioned in a royal procession, only the parasol is mentioned. Among these, only the parasol is perceived, not the parasol-bearer. Likewise, only the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan, the chowrie whisk, and the diadem are perceived, not their bearers. It is said that all these were held by deities in invisible form. And this was said:

“Anekasākhañca [P 2.0439] sahassamaṇḍalaṃ,

Chattaṃ marū dhārayumantalikkhe;

Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vipatanti cāmarā,

Na dissare cāmarachattagāhakā”ti. (su. ni. 693);

“With its many ribs and a thousand circles, a parasol the Maruts held in the sky; golden-handled chowries were waved, but the bearers of the chowries and parasol were not seen.”

Sabbā ca disāti idaṃ sattapadavītihārūpari ṭhitassa viya sabbadisānuvilokanaṃ vuttaṃ, na kho panevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahāsatto hi manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā paṭhaviyaṃ patiṭṭhito puratthimaṃ disaṃ olokesi. Anekāni cakkavāḷasahassāni ekaṅgaṇāni ahesuṃ. Tattha devamanussā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamānā – “mahāpurisa, idha tumhehi sadisopi natthi, kuto uttaritaro”ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ catasso disā, catasso anudisā, heṭṭhā, uparīti dasa disā anuviloketvā attanā sadisaṃ adisvā – “ayaṃ uttarā disā”ti uttarābhimukho sattapadavītihārena agamāsīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Āsabhinti uttamaṃ. Aggoti guṇehi sabbapaṭhamo. Itarāni [V 2.0028] dve padāni etasseva vevacanāni. Ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavoti padadvayena imasmiṃ attabhāve pattabbaṃ arahattaṃ byākāsi.

‘And all directions’: This is stated as if it were a surveying of all directions by one standing after having taken the seven steps, but it should not be understood in this way. For the Great Being, released from the hands of humans, stood firm on the ground and looked toward the eastern direction. Many thousands of world-systems became as a single open space. There, gods and humans, honoring him with perfumes, garlands, and so on, said: ‘O Great Being, here there is no one equal to you, whence one superior?’ In this way, having surveyed the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—the ten directions—and not seeing anyone equal to himself, thinking, ‘This is the supreme direction,’ he faced north and went forward with a seven-step stride. Thus is the meaning here to be understood. ‘A noble utterance’ means a supreme one. ‘Chief’ means foremost of all in virtues. The other two words are synonyms of this one. With the two phrases, ‘This is my last birth, now there is no more re-becoming,’ he declared the Arahantship to be attained in this very existence.

Ettha ca samehi pādehi pathaviyā patiṭṭhānaṃ caturiddhipādapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, uttarābhimukhabhāvo mahājanaṃ ajjhottharitvā abhibhavitvā gamanassa pubbanimittaṃ, sattapadagamanaṃ sattabojjhaṅgaratanapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, dibbasetacchattadhāraṇaṃ vimuttivarachattapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, pañcarājakakudhabhaṇḍānaṃ paṭilābho pañcahi vimuttīhi vimuccanassa pubbanimittaṃ, sabbadisānuvilokanaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, āsabhivācābhāsanaṃ appaṭivattiyadhammacakkappavattanassa pubbanimittaṃ, “ayamantimā jātī”ti sīhanādo anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānassa pubbanimittanti veditabbaṃ[M 2.0032]. Ime [P 2.0440] vārā pāḷiyaṃ āgatā, sambahulavāro pana nāgato, āharitvā dīpetabbo.

And here, standing on the earth with level feet is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the four bases of spiritual power. Facing northward, overwhelming and surpassing the great multitude, is the preliminary sign for his journey. Taking seven steps is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the seven enlightenment-factor jewels. The holding of the divine white parasol is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the supreme parasol of liberation. The acquisition of the five royal regalia is the preliminary sign for liberation by the five liberations. Looking around in all directions is the preliminary sign for the attainment of unobstructed knowledge. Uttering the bull-like speech is the preliminary sign for setting in motion the irreversible Wheel of Dhamma. The lion’s roar, “This is my last birth,” is to be known as the preliminary sign for the final passing away into the Nibbāna element without residue. These passages have come in the Pāli, but the section on many things has not come; it should be brought forth and explained.

Mahāpurisassa hi jātadivase dasasahassilokadhātu kampi. Dasasahassilokadhātumhi devatā ekacakkavāḷe sannipatiṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ devā paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, pacchā manussā. Tantibaddhā vīṇā cammabaddhā bheriyo ca kenaci avāditā sayameva vajjiṃsu. Manussānaṃ andubandhanādīni khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ chijjiṃsu. Sabbarogā vūpasamiṃsu, ambilena dhotatambamalaṃ viya vigacchiṃsu. Jaccandhā rūpāni passiṃsu. Jaccabadhirā saddaṃ suṇiṃsu. Pīṭhasappī javasampannā ahesuṃ. Jātijaḷānampi eḷamūgānaṃ sati patiṭṭhāsi. Videsapakkhandā nāvā supaṭṭanaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Ākāsaṭṭhakabhūmaṭṭhakaratanāni sakatejobhāsitāni ahesuṃ. Verino mettacittaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Avīcimhi aggi nibbāyi. Lokantaresu āloko udapādi. Nadīsu jalaṃ nappavattati. Mahāsamudde madhurasaṃ udakaṃ ahosi. Vāto na vāyi. Ākāsapabbatarukkhagatā sakuṇā bhassitvā pathavigatā ahesuṃ. Cando ativiroci. Sūriyo na uṇho, na sītalo, nimmalo utusampanno ahosi. Devatā attano attano vimānadvāre ṭhatvā apphoṭanaseḷanacelukkhepādīhi mahākīḷakaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Cātuddīpikamahāmegho vassi. Mahājanaṃ neva khudā na pipāsā pīḷesi. Dvārakavāṭāni sayameva vivariṃsu. Pupphūpagaphalūpagā rukkhā pupphaphalāni gaṇhiṃsu. Dasasahassilokadhātu ekaddhajamālā ahosi.

Indeed, on the day the Great Being was born, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. The deities in the ten-thousandfold world system gathered in one world-sphere. First, the deities received him, and afterward, humans. Lutes bound with strings and drums bound with hide played by themselves without anyone playing them. The fetters and bonds of humans broke into pieces. All diseases were pacified, vanishing like copper tarnish washed away with acid. The blind from birth saw forms. The deaf from birth heard sounds. The crippled became swift-footed. For even the congenitally dull-witted and mute, mindfulness was established. Ships scattered to foreign lands reached safe harbors. Jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shone with their own brilliance. Enemies developed a mind of loving-kindness. The fire in the Avīci hell was extinguished. Light arose in the inter-cosmic spaces. The water in the rivers did not flow. The water in the great ocean became sweet. The wind did not blow. Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees, having dropped down, came to be on the ground. The moon shone exceedingly brightly. The sun was neither hot nor cold, but clear and seasonably perfect. Deities stood at the gates of their own celestial mansions and engaged in great sport with hand-clapping, shouts of joy, and the tossing of garments. A great cloud rained over the four continents. The great populace was afflicted by neither hunger nor thirst. Door panels opened by themselves. Flower-bearing and fruit-bearing trees produced their flowers and fruits. The ten-thousandfold world system became a single garland of banners.

Tatrāpi dasasahassilokadhātukampo sabbaññutaññāṇapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Devatānaṃ ekacakkavāḷe sannipāto dhammacakkappavattanakāle ekappahāreneva sannipatitvā dhammaṃ paṭiggaṇhanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ devatānaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa [V 2.0029] pubbanimittaṃ. Pacchā manussānaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ [P 2.0441] catunnaṃ arūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Tantibaddhavīṇānaṃ sayaṃ vajjanaṃ anupubbavihārapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Cammabaddhabherīnaṃ vajjanaṃ mahatiyā dhammabheriyā anussāvanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Andubandhanādīnaṃ chedo asmimānasamucchedassa pubbanimittaṃ. Mahājanassa rogavigamo catusaccapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Jaccandhānaṃ rūpadassanaṃ dibbacakkhupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ[M 2.0033]. Badhirānaṃ saddassavanaṃ dibbasotadhātupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Pīṭhasappīnaṃ javasampadā caturiddhipādapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Jaḷānaṃ satipatiṭṭhānaṃ catusatipaṭṭhānapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Videsapakkhandanāvānaṃ supaṭṭanasampāpuṇanaṃ catupaṭisambhidādhigamassa pubbanimittaṃ. Ratanānaṃ sakatejobhāsitattaṃ yaṃ lokassa dhammobhāsaṃ dassessati, tassa pubbanimittaṃ.

Therein also, the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system is the preliminary sign for the attainment of omniscient knowledge. The gathering of deities in one world-sphere is the preliminary sign for their gathering together at the time of the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma and receiving the Dhamma all at once. The initial reception by the deities is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the four form-sphere jhānas. The subsequent reception by humans is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the four formless-sphere jhānas. The spontaneous playing of string-bound lutes is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the successive abidings. The sounding of hide-bound drums is the preliminary sign for the proclamation of the great drum of the Dhamma. The breaking of fetters and bonds is the preliminary sign for the complete cutting off of the conceit ‘I am.’ The departure of disease from the great populace is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the Four Truths. The seeing of forms by the blind from birth is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the divine eye. The hearing of sound by the deaf is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the divine ear element. The swiftness of the crippled is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the four bases of spiritual power. The establishment of mindfulness in the dull-witted is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness. The reaching of a good port by ships scattered to foreign lands is the preliminary sign for the mastery of the four analytical knowledges. The state of jewels shining with their own brilliance is the preliminary sign of the light of the Dhamma that he will show to the world.

Verīnaṃ mettacittapaṭilābho catubrahmavihārapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Avīcimhi agginibbāyanaṃ ekādasaagginibbāyanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Lokantarikāloko avijjandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ñāṇālokadassanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Mahāsamuddassa madhuratā nibbānarasena ekarasabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Vātassa avāyanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatabhindanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Sakuṇānaṃ pathavigamanaṃ mahājanassa ovādaṃ sutvā pāṇehi saraṇagamanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Candassa ativirocanaṃ bahujanakantatāya pubbanimittaṃ. Sūriyassa uṇhasītavivajjanautusukhatā kāyikacetasikasukhappattiyā pubbanimittaṃ. Devatānaṃ vimānadvāresu ṭhatvā apphoṭanādīhi kīḷanaṃ buddhabhāvaṃ patvā udānaṃ udānassa pubbanimittaṃ. Cātuddīpikamahāmeghavassanaṃ mahato dhammameghavassanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Khudāpīḷanassa abhāvo kāyagatāsatiamatapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Pipāsāpīḷanassa abhāvo vimuttisukhena [P 2.0442] sukhitabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Dvārakavāṭānaṃ sayameva vivaraṇaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikamaggadvāravivaraṇassa pubbanimittaṃ. Rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalaggahaṇaṃ vimuttipupphehi pupphitassa ca sāmaññaphalabhārabharitabhāvassa ca pubbanimittaṃ. Dasasahassilokadhātuyā ekaddhajamālitā ariyaddhajamālamālitāya pubbanimittanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ sambahulavāro nāma.

The attainment of a mind of loving-kindness towards enemies is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the four divine abidings. The quenching of the fire in Avīci is the preliminary sign for the quenching of the eleven fires. The light in the inter-world space, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, is the preliminary sign for the vision of the light of wisdom. The sweetness of the great ocean is the preliminary sign for the state of having a single taste through the taste of Nibbāna. The non-blowing of the wind is the preliminary sign for the shattering of the sixty-two kinds of wrong views. The coming of birds to the ground is the preliminary sign for the great populace, having heard his instruction, going for refuge with their very lives. The surpassing radiance of the moon is the preliminary sign for being beloved by many people. The sun's pleasantness of season, being devoid of heat and cold, is the preliminary sign for the attainment of physical and mental happiness. The playing of deities, standing at the doors of their mansions and clapping their hands and so on, is the preliminary sign for uttering an inspired utterance upon attaining Buddhood. The raining of a great cloud over the four continents is the preliminary sign for the raining of the great Dhamma-cloud. The absence of the affliction of hunger is the preliminary sign for the attainment of the deathless through mindfulness directed to the body. The absence of the affliction of thirst is the preliminary sign for the state of being blissful with the bliss of liberation. The spontaneous opening of door-panels is the preliminary sign for the opening of the door of the Noble Eightfold Path. The trees' bearing of flowers and fruits is the preliminary sign for being flowered with the flowers of liberation and for the state of being laden with the burden of the fruits of recluseship. The state of the ten-thousandfold world-system being garlanded with a single banner is to be understood as the preliminary sign for being garlanded with the garland of the noble banner. This is called the Section on Various Matters.

Ettha pañhaṃ pucchanti – “yadā mahāpuriso pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā uttarābhimukho padasā gantvā āsabhiṃ vācaṃ abhāsi, tadā kiṃ pathaviyā gato, udāhu ākāsena; dissamāno gato, udāhu adissamāno; acelako gato, udāhu alaṅkatapaṭiyatto; daharo hutvā gato[M 2.0034], udāhu mahallako; pacchāpi kiṃ tādisova ahosi, udāhu puna bāladārako”ti? Ayaṃ pana pañho heṭṭhālohapāsāde samuṭṭhito tipiṭakacūḷābhayattherena vissajjitova. Thero kira ettha niyatipubbekatakammaissaranimmānavādavasena [V 2.0030] taṃ taṃ bahuṃ vatvā avasāne evaṃ byākari – “mahāpuriso pathaviyā gato, mahājanassa pana ākāsena gacchanto viya ahosi. Dissamāno gato, mahājanassa pana adissamāno viya ahosi. Acelako gato, mahājanassa pana alaṅkatapaṭiyatto viya upaṭṭhāsi. Daharova gato, mahājanassa pana soḷasavassuddesiko viya ahosi. Pacchā pana bāladārakova ahosi, na tādiso”ti. Parisā cassa – “buddhena viya hutvā bho therena pañho kathito”ti attamanā ahosi. Lokantarikavāro vuttanayo eva.

Here, a question is asked: 'When the Great Being, having stood on the ground, walked facing north on foot and uttered a noble speech, did he go on the ground or in the sky? Did he go while visible or invisible? Did he go naked or adorned and prepared? Did he go as a youth or as an old man? And afterward, was he still the same or again a child?' This question, however, arose at the lower Brazen Palace and was answered by the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. The Elder, it is said, spoke much here concerning the doctrines of fatalism, past actions, and divine creation, and at the end declared thus: 'The Great Being went on the ground, but to the multitude, it seemed as though he went in the sky. He went while visible, but to the multitude, it seemed as though he was invisible. He went naked, but to the multitude, he appeared as though he were adorned and prepared. He went as a youth, but to the multitude, it seemed as though he was about sixteen years old. Afterward, however, he was indeed a child, not such a one.' And his assembly was delighted, saying, 'Sirs, the Elder has answered the question as if he were the Buddha.' The section on the inter-world space is just as has been stated.

Imā ca pana ādito paṭṭhāya kathitā sabbadhammatā sabbabodhisattānaṃ hontīti veditabbā.

And it should be understood that all these fixed principles, described from the beginning, belong to all Bodhisattas.

Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man.

33. Addasa khoti dukūlacumbaṭake nipajjāpetvā ānītaṃ addasa. Mahāpurisassāti jātigottakulapadesādivasena mahantassa purisassa. Dve gatiyoti dve niṭṭhā, dve nipphattiyo. Ayañhi gatisaddo – “pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo”ti (ma. ni. 1.153) ettha nirayādibhedāya sattehi gantabbagatiyā [P 2.0443] vattati. “Imesaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ kalyāṇadhammānaṃ neva jānāmi āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.508) ettha ajjhāsaye. “Nibbānaṃ arahato gatī”ti (pari. 339) ettha paṭissaraṇe. “Api ca tyāhaṃ brahme gatiñca pajānāmi, jutiñca pajānāmi evaṃmahiddhiko bako brahmā”ti (ma. ni. 1.503) ettha nipphattiyaṃ vattati. Svāyamidhāpi nipphattiyaṃ vattatīti veditabbo. Anaññāti aññā gati nipphatti nāma natthi.

33. As to Addasa kho ('He saw indeed'): it means he saw him brought and laid down on a roll of fine cloth. As to Mahāpurisassa ('of a great man'): it means of a man who is great by way of birth, clan, family, region, and so forth. As to Dve gatiyo ('two destinies'): it means two conclusions, two fulfillments. For this word gati ('destiny')—as in 'Sāriputta, there are these five destinies'—is used in the sense of a destination to be gone to by beings, distinguished as hell and so forth. As in 'Of these monks who are virtuous and of good character, I know not their coming or their going'—it is used in the sense of inclination. As in 'Nibbāna is the refuge of the Arahant'—it is used in the sense of refuge. And as in 'But, Brahmā, I understand your fulfillment and your splendor, so mighty is Baka Brahmā'—it is used in the sense of fulfillment. Here too, it should be understood that this word is used in the sense of fulfillment. As to Anaññā ('no other'): it means there is no other destiny or fulfillment.

Dhammikoti dasakusaladhammasamannāgato agatigamanavirahito. Dhammarājāti idaṃ purimapadasseva vevacanaṃ. Dhammena vā laddharajjattā dhammarājā. Cāturantoti [M 2.0035] puratthimasamuddādīnaṃ catunnaṃ samuddānaṃ vasena caturantāya pathaviyā issaro. Vijitāvīti vijitasaṅgāmo. Janapado asmiṃ thāvariyaṃ thirabhāvaṃ pattoti janapadatthāvariyappatto. Caṇḍassa hi rañño balidaṇḍādīhi lokaṃ pīḷayato manussā majjhimajanapadaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbatasamuddatīrādīni nissāya paccante vāsaṃ kappenti. Atimudukassa rañño corehi sāhasikadhanavilopapīḷitā manussā paccantaṃ pahāya janapadamajjhe vāsaṃ kappenti, iti evarūpe rājini janapado thirabhāvaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Imasmiṃ pana [V 2.0031] kumāre rajjaṃ kārayamāne etassa janapado pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapetvā ayopaṭṭena parikkhitto viya thiro bhavissatīti dassento – “janapadatthāvariyappatto”ti āhaṃsu.

As to Dhammiko ('righteous'): it means one endowed with the ten wholesome principles and free from following wrong courses. As to Dhammarājā ('righteous king'): this is a synonym for the preceding word. Or, he is a righteous king because he has obtained the kingdom righteously. As to Cāturanto ('ruler of the four quarters'): it means he is the master of the earth which has the four oceans, beginning with the eastern ocean, as its boundaries. As to Vijitāvī ('victorious'): it means one who has been victorious in battle. Janapadatthāvariyappatto ('one whose country has attained stability') means: the country (janapado) has attained (patto) stability (thāvariyaṃ), a firm state (thirabhāvaṃ), under him (asmiṃ). For when a cruel king oppresses the populace with taxes, punishments, and so on, the people abandon the central country and, relying on mountains, seashores, and the like, they make their dwelling in the border regions. In the case of an overly lenient king, the people, afflicted by the violent plundering of wealth by robbers, abandon the border regions and make their dwelling in the middle of the country. Thus, under such a king, the country does not attain stability. But when this prince is exercising kingship, his country will be as firm as if placed on a stone slab and encircled by an iron plate. To show this, they said, janapadatthāvariyappatto.

Sattaratanasamannāgatoti ettha ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Apica –

Here, in the phrase Sattaratanasamannāgato ('possessed of the seven treasures'), a 'treasure' (ratana) is so called in the sense that it generates delight (rati). Moreover:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccati”.

That which is esteemed, of great value, incomparable, rare to see, and enjoyed by superior beings—for these reasons it is called a 'treasure'.

Cakkaratanassa ca nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya aññaṃ devaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na hoti, sabbe gandhapupphādīhi tasseva pūjañca abhivādanādīni ca karontīti cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Cakkaratanassa ca ettakaṃ nāma dhanaṃ agghatīti [P 2.0444] aggho natthi, iti mahagghaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Cakkaratanañca aññehi loke vijjamānaratanehi asadisanti atulaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Yasmā ca pana yasmiṃ kappe buddhā uppajjanti, tasmiṃyeva cakkavattino uppajjanti, buddhā ca kadāci karahaci uppajjanti, tasmā dullabhadassanaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Tadetaṃ jātirūpakulaissariyādīhi anomassa uḷārasattasseva uppajjati, na aññassāti anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Yathā cakkaratanaṃ, evaṃ sesānipīti. Imehi sattahi ratanehi parivārabhāvena ceva sabbabhogūpakaraṇabhāvena ca samannāgatoti sattaratanasamannāgato.

And from the moment the Wheel-Treasure arises, there is no other divine place of worship; all people offer it perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and perform acts of reverence—thus, it is a treasure by virtue of being esteemed. And the Wheel-Treasure has no price such that it could be valued by a certain amount of wealth; thus, it is a treasure also by virtue of being of great value. And the Wheel-Treasure is unlike other treasures existing in the world; thus, it is a treasure also by virtue of being incomparable. And since Wheel-Turning Monarchs arise only in an aeon in which Buddhas arise, and Buddhas arise only rarely and occasionally, it is therefore a treasure also by virtue of being rarely seen. This treasure arises only for a peerless and noble being on account of birth, beauty, lineage, sovereignty, and so forth, and not for any other; thus, it is a treasure also by virtue of being used by a peerless being. Just as the Wheel-Treasure is, so too are the remaining treasures. Thus, he is 'possessed of the seven treasures' because he is endowed with these seven treasures, both as his retinue and as all his instruments of enjoyment.

Idāni tesaṃ sarūpato dassanatthaṃ tassimānītiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cakkaratanantiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepādhippāyo – dvesahassadīpaparivārānaṃ catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ sirivibhavaṃ gahetvā dātuṃ samatthaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati. Tathā purebhattameva sāgarapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anusaṃyāyanasamatthaṃ vehāsaṅgamaṃ hatthiratanaṃ, tādisameva assaratanaṃ, caturaṅgasamannāgate andhakāre [M 2.0036] yojanappamāṇaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokadassanasamatthaṃ maṇiratanaṃ, chabbidhadosavivajjitaṃ manāpacāri itthiratanaṃ, yojanappamāṇe antopathavigataṃ nidhiṃ dassanasamatthaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ, aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā sakalarajjamanusāsanasamatthaṃ jeṭṭhaputtasaṅkhātaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavati.

Now, in order to show them according to their individual nature, the passage beginning 'tassimāni' was spoken. Therein, regarding 'the wheel-treasure' and so forth, this is the meaning in brief: The wheel-treasure appears, capable of taking and bestowing the splendor and prosperity of the four great continents with their retinue of two thousand islands. Similarly, the elephant-treasure appears, capable of traveling through the air and traversing the earth as far as the ocean even before the morning meal. Likewise, the horse-treasure is of the same kind. The gem-treasure appears, capable of dispelling darkness for the extent of a yojana and providing light for sight, even in a darkness endowed with four factors. The woman-treasure appears, delightful in conduct and free from the six kinds of faults. The householder-treasure appears, capable of seeing a treasure hidden within the earth at a depth of a yojana. The leader-treasure appears, known as the eldest son, born in the womb of the chief queen and capable of governing the entire kingdom.

Parosahassanti atirekasahassaṃ. Sūrāti abhīrukā. Vīraṅgarūpāti vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ vīraṅgaṃ, vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ, vīraṅgaṃ rūpametesanti vīraṅgarūpā, vīriyajātikā vīriyasabhāvā vīriyamayā akilāsuno ahesuṃ. Divasampi yujjhantā na kilamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāgarapariyantanti cakkavāḷapabbataṃ sīmaṃ katvā ṭhitasamuddapariyantaṃ. Adaṇḍenāti ye katāparādhe satte satampi sahassampi [V 2.0032] gaṇhanti, te dhanadaṇḍena rajjaṃ kārenti. Ye chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsanti, te satthadaṇḍena. Ayaṃ pana duvidhampi daṇḍaṃ pahāya adaṇḍena ajjhāvasati. Asatthenāti [P 2.0445] ye ekatodhārādinā satthena paraṃ vihesanti, te satthena rajjaṃ kārenti nāma. Ayaṃ pana satthena khuddamakkhikāyapi pivanamattaṃ lohitaṃ kassaci anuppādetvā dhammeneva – “ehi kho mahārājā”ti evaṃ paṭirājūhi sampaṭicchitāgamano vuttappakāraṃ pathaviṃ abhivijinitvā ajjhāvasati, abhibhavitvā sāmī hutvā vasatīti attho.

'More than a thousand' means exceeding a thousand. 'Valiant' means fearless. 'Of heroic form' means the limb of heroes is 'vīraṅga'; this is a name for vigor. They are 'of heroic form' because vigor is their nature; they were of vigorous birth, of a vigorous nature, made of vigor, and untiring. It is said that they do not tire even when fighting for a whole day. 'Up to the ocean's edge' means up to the ocean that stands with the Cakkavāḷa mountain as its boundary. 'Without punishment' means that some rulers, who seize offenders for a hundred or a thousand, rule by means of financial penalties. Those who instruct with cutting and piercing rule by means of punishment by weapons. This one, however, having abandoned both kinds of punishment, dwells without punishment. 'Without a weapon' means that some rulers oppress others with a weapon, such as a single-edged blade; they are said to rule by means of a weapon. This one, however, without causing anyone to shed even a drop of blood the size of a gnat's drink by means of a weapon, rules righteously. 'Come, great king'—thus, with his arrival welcomed by rival kings, he conquers the aforementioned earth and dwells there, having subdued it and become its master. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ ekaṃ nipphattiṃ kathetvā dutiyaṃ kathetuṃ sace kho panātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhikilesataṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ chadanaṃ āvaraṇaṃ vivaṭaṃ viddhaṃsitaṃ vivaṭakaṃ etenāti vivaṭacchado. “Vivaṭṭacchadā”tipi pāṭho, ayameva attho.

Having thus explained the first fulfillment, the passage beginning 'But if...' was spoken in order to explain the second. Therein, 'with covering removed' (vivaṭacchado) means that the covering and obstruction—that is, the defilements and craving known as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wrong views—has been opened and destroyed by him. There is also the reading 'vivaṭṭacchadā', and the meaning is the same.

35. Evaṃ dutiyaṃ nipphattiṃ kathetvā tāsaṃ nimittabhūtāni lakkhaṇāni dassetuṃ ayañhi, deva, kumārotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha suppatiṭṭhitapādoti yathā aññesaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pādaṃ ṭhapentānaṃ aggapādatalaṃ vā paṇhi vā passaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ phusati, vemajjhe vā pana chiddaṃ hoti, ukkhipantānaṃ aggatalādīsu ekakoṭṭhāsova paṭhamaṃ uṭṭhahati, na evamassa. Assa pana suvaṇṇapādukatalamiva ekappahāreneva sakalaṃ pādatalaṃ bhūmiṃ phusati, ekappahāreneva bhūmito uṭṭhahati. Tasmā ayaṃ suppatiṭṭhitapādo.

35. Having thus explained the second fulfillment, the passage beginning 'Indeed, sire, this prince...' was spoken in order to show the marks that are their signs. Therein, 'with well-placed feet' means that it is not like with others, who, when placing a foot on the ground, touch first with the front of the sole, or the heel, or the side, or there is a gap in the middle, and who, when lifting it, raise only one part, such as the front of the sole, first. With him, it is not so. Rather, his entire sole touches the ground all at once, like the sole of a golden slipper, and lifts from the ground all at once. Therefore, he is one 'with well-placed feet'.

Cakkānīti [M 2.0037] dvīsu pādatalesu dve cakkāni, tesaṃ arā ca nemi ca nābhi ca pāḷiyaṃ vuttāva. Sabbākāraparipūrānīti iminā pana ayaṃ viseso veditabbo, tesaṃ kira cakkānaṃ pādatalassa majjhe nābhi dissati, nābhiparicchinnā vaṭṭalekhā dissati, nābhimukhaparikkhepapaṭṭo dissati, panāḷimukhaṃ dissati, arā dissanti, aresu vaṭṭilekhā dissanti, nemimaṇikā dissanti. Idaṃ tāva pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva. Sambahulavāro pana anāgato, so evaṃ daṭṭhabbo – satti, sirivaccho, nandi, sovattiko, vaṭaṃsako, vaḍḍhamānakaṃ, macchayugaḷaṃ, bhaddapīṭhaṃ, aṅkusako, pāsādo, toraṇaṃ, setacchattaṃ, khaggo, tālavaṇṭaṃ, morahatthako, vāḷabījanī, uṇhīsaṃ, maṇi, patto, sumanadāmaṃ, nīluppalaṃ, rattuppalaṃ, setuppalaṃ, padumaṃ, puṇḍarīkaṃ, puṇṇaghaṭo[P 2.0446], puṇṇapāti, samuddo, cakkavāḷo, himavā, sineru, candimasūriyā, nakkhattāni, cattāro mahādīpā, dviparittadīpasahassāni, antamaso cakkavattirañño parisaṃ upādāya sabbo cakkalakkhaṇasseva parivāro.

'Wheels' means there are two wheels on the two soles of his feet; their spokes, rims, and hubs are as stated in the Pāḷi. By 'complete in all aspects', however, this distinction should be understood: it is said that in the middle of the sole of the foot of those wheels, a hub is seen; a circular line defined by the hub is seen; a band surrounding the mouth of the hub is seen; the mouth of the channel is seen; spokes are seen; circular lines on the spokes are seen; and jewel-beads on the rim are seen. This much is indeed found in the Pāḷi.
