The section with numerous details, however, is not found in the canon; it should be understood thus: a spear, a śrīvatsa, a nandyāvarta, a svastika, a diadem, a 'growing' vessel, a pair of fish, an auspicious seat, a goad, a palace, a gateway, a white parasol, a sword, a palm-leaf fan, a peacock-feather fan, a yak-tail whisk, a turban, a jewel, a bowl, a jasmine garland, a blue water lily, a red water lily, a white water lily, a paduma lotus, a puṇḍarīka lotus, a full pitcher, a full vessel, the ocean, the world-sphere, the Himālaya, Mount Sineru, the moon and sun, the constellations, the four great continents, the two thousand minor islands, and even, down to the last, the retinue of a wheel-turning monarch—all this is the retinue of the wheel-mark itself.

Āyatapaṇhīti [V 2.0033] dīghapaṇhi, paripuṇṇapaṇhīti attho. Yathā hi aññesaṃ aggapādo dīgho hoti, paṇhimatthake jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti, paṇhiṃ tacchetvā ṭhapitā viya hoti, na evaṃ mahāpurisassa. Mahāpurisassa pana catūsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāsā aggapādo hoti, tatiye koṭṭhāse jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti, catutthakoṭṭhāse āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitā viya rattakambalageṇḍukasadisā paṇhi hoti.

“Long-heeled” (Āyatapaṇhi) means having long heels; that is, having fully developed heels. For whereas with others the forepart of the foot is long, the shin rests upon the top of the heel, and the heel appears as if it were trimmed and set in place, it is not so for the Great Man. For the Great Man, however, of four parts of the foot, two parts constitute the forefoot, in the third part the shin is established, and in the fourth part is the heel, which is like a ball of red wool, as if rounded with an awl and set in place.

Dīghaṅgulīti yathā aññesaṃ kāci aṅguliyo dīghā honti, kāci rassā, na evaṃ mahāpurisassa. Mahāpurisassa pana makkaṭasseva dīghā hatthapādaṅguliyo mūle thūlā, anupubbena gantvā agge tanukā, niyyāsatelena madditvā vaṭṭitaharitālavaṭṭisadisā honti. Tena vuttaṃ – “dīghaṅgulī”ti.

“Long-fingered” (Dīghaṅgulī): Whereas with others some fingers and toes are long and some are short, it is not so for the Great Man. For the Great Man, however, his fingers and toes are long like a monkey’s, thick at the base and gradually tapering to slender tips, resembling rounded sticks of orpiment that have been kneaded with resinous oil. Therefore, it is said: “long-fingered.”

Mudutalunahatthapādoti sappimaṇḍe osāretvā ṭhapitaṃ satavāravihatakappāsapaṭalaṃ viya mudu. Yathā ca idāni jātamattassa, evaṃ vuḍḍhakālepi mudutalunāyeva bhavissanti, mudutalunā hatthapādā etassāti mudutalunahatthapādo.

“Soft and tender hands and feet” (Mudutalunahatthapādo) means they are as soft as a layer of cotton that has been beaten a hundred times, immersed in the finest ghee, and set aside. And just as they are now at the time of his birth, so too in old age will they remain soft and tender. Because his hands and feet are soft and tender, he is called “one with soft and tender hands and feet.”

Jālahatthapādoti na cammena paṭibaddhaaṅgulantaro. Ediso hi phaṇahatthako purisadosena upahato pabbajjaṃ na paṭilabhati. Mahāpurisassa pana [M 2.0038] catasso hatthaṅguliyo pañcapi pādaṅguliyo ekappamāṇā honti, tāsaṃ ekappamāṇatāya yavalakkhaṇaṃ aññamaññaṃ paṭivijjhitvā tiṭṭhati. Athassa hatthapādā kusalena vaḍḍhakinā yojitajālavātapānasadisā honti. Tena vuttaṃ – “jālahatthapādo”ti.

“Net-like hands and feet” (Jālahatthapādo) does not mean that the spaces between his fingers are bound by skin. Indeed, a person with such webbed hands, being afflicted by a human defect, cannot receive ordination. For the Great Man, however, his four fingers and five toes are of equal length. Because of their equal length, the barleycorn marks on them stand touching one another. Thus his hands and feet are like a lattice window skillfully fashioned by a carpenter. Therefore, it is said: “net-like hands and feet.”

Uddhaṃ patiṭṭhitagopphakattā ussaṅkhā pādā assāti ussaṅkhapādo. Aññesañhi piṭṭhipāde gopphakā honti, tena tesaṃ pādā āṇibaddhā viya baddhā honti, na yathāsukhaṃ parivaṭṭanti, gacchantānaṃ pādatalānipi na dissanti. Mahāpurisassa pana āruhitvā upari gopphakā patiṭṭhahanti, tenassa nābhito paṭṭhāya uparimakāyo nāvāya ṭhapitasuvaṇṇapaṭimā viya niccalo hoti, adhokāyova iñjati, sukhena pādā [P 2.0447] parivaṭṭanti, puratopi pacchatopi ubhayapassesupi ṭhatvā passantānaṃ pādatalāni paññāyanti, na hatthīnaṃ viya pacchatoyeva.

“Feet with high insteps” (Ussaṅkhapādo) means he has feet with high insteps because his ankles are set high. For with others, the ankles are on the instep, and because of this their feet are bound as if fastened with pins and cannot turn with ease, nor are the soles of their feet visible when they walk. For the Great Man, however, the ankles are set high up; because of this, his upper body from the navel upwards is as motionless as a golden statue placed on a boat, and only his lower body moves. His feet turn with ease, and for those who stand and look from the front, from behind, or from either side, the soles of his feet are visible, not as with elephants, whose soles are visible only from behind.

Eṇijaṅghoti eṇimigasadisajaṅgho maṃsussadena paripuṇṇajaṅgho, na ekato baddhapiṇḍikamaṃso[V 2.0034], samantato samasaṇṭhitena maṃsena parikkhittāhi suvaṭṭitāhi sāligabbhayavagabbhasadisāhi jaṅghāhi samannāgatoti attho.

“Antelope-like calves” (Eṇijaṅgho) means he has calves like those of an eṇi antelope, full due to an abundance of flesh; the muscle is not bound into a lump on one side, but he is endowed with well-rounded calves, encircled on all sides by evenly arranged flesh, resembling the sheaths of rice and barley plants. This is the meaning.

Anonamantoti anamanto, etenassa akhujjaavāmanabhāvo dīpito. Avasesajanā hi khujjā vā honti vāmanā vā. Khujjānaṃ uparimakāyo aparipuṇṇo hoti, vāmanānaṃ heṭṭhimakāyo. Te aparipuṇṇakāyattā na sakkonti anonamantā jaṇṇukāni parimajjituṃ. Mahāpuriso pana paripuṇṇaubhayakāyattā sakkoti.

“Not bending down” (Anonamanto) means not stooping; by this, his state of being neither hunchbacked nor dwarfish is shown. For other people are either hunchbacked or dwarfish. The upper body of hunchbacks is incomplete, and the lower body of dwarfs is incomplete. Because their bodies are incomplete, they are not able to stroke their knees without bending down. The Great Man, however, is able to do so because both parts of his body are complete.

Kosohitavatthaguyhoti usabhavāraṇādīnaṃ viya suvaṇṇapadumakaṇṇikasadisehi kosehi ohitaṃ paṭicchannaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ assāti kosohitavatthaguyho. Vatthaguyhanti vatthena guhitabbaṃ aṅgajātaṃ vuccati.

“Male organ concealed in a sheath” (Kosohitavatthaguyho) means he is one whose male organ is placed within and concealed by a sheath, like that of a bull, an elephant, and so on, the sheath resembling the pericarp of a golden lotus. “The part to be concealed by cloth” (Vatthaguyha) is the name for the generative organ, which ought to be concealed by a cloth.

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti jātihiṅgulakena majjitvā dīpidāṭhāya ghaṃsitvā gerukaparikammaṃ katvā ṭhapitaghanasuvaṇṇarūpasadisoti attho. Etenassa ghanasiniddhasaṇhasarīrataṃ dassetvā chavivaṇṇadassanatthaṃ kañcanasannibhattacoti vuttaṃ. Purimassa vā vevacanametaṃ.

“Golden-hued” (Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo) means his complexion is like a solid golden image that has been smeared with natural cinnabar, rubbed with a leopard’s tooth, and prepared with red ochre. This shows that his body is solid, smooth, and tender. To show the color of his skin, the phrase “skin like gold” (kañcanasannibhattaco) is used. Or, this is a synonym for the former term.

Rajojallanti [M 2.0039] rajo vā malaṃ vā. Na upalimpatīti na laggati padumapalāsato udakabindu viya vivaṭṭati. Hatthadhovanādīni pana utuggahaṇatthāya ceva dāyakānaṃ puññaphalatthāya ca buddhā karonti, vattasīsenāpi ca karontiyeva. Senāsanaṃ pavisantena hi bhikkhunā pāde dhovitvā pavisitabbanti vuttametaṃ.

“Dust and dirt” (Rajojalla) means fine dust or coarse dirt. “Is not smeared on him” (na upalimpati) means it does not stick; it rolls off like a drop of water from a lotus leaf. However, the Buddhas perform acts such as washing their hands both for the sake of refreshment and for the sake of the fruit of merit for donors, and they also do so as a matter of observance. For it has been said: “A monk, when entering a lodging, should wash his feet before entering.”

Uddhaggalomoti āvaṭṭapariyosāne uddhaggāni hutvā mukhasobhaṃ ullokayamānāni viya ṭhitāni lomāni assāti uddhaggalomo.

'One with upward-pointing body hairs' (Uddhaggalomo) means he has body hairs that stand upright with curled tips, appearing as if they are gazing upon the beauty of his face.

Brahmujugattoti brahmā viya ujugatto, ujumeva uggatadīghasarīro bhavissati. Yebhuyyena hi sattā khandhe kaṭiyaṃ [P 2.0448] jāṇūsūti tīsu ṭhānesu namanti, te kaṭiyaṃ namantā pacchato namanti, itaresu dvīsu ṭhānesu purato. Dīghasarīrā pana eke passavaṅkā honti, eke mukhaṃ unnametvā nakkhattāni gaṇayantā viya caranti, eke appamaṃsalohitā sūlasadisā honti, eke purato pabbhārā honti, pavedhamānā gacchanti. Ayaṃ pana ujumeva uggantvā dīghappamāṇo devanagare ussitasuvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya bhavissatīti dīpenti. Yathā cetaṃ, evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ jātamattassa [V 2.0035] sabbaso aparipuṇṇaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ āyatiṃ tathābhāvitaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“Body as straight as Brahmā’s” (Brahmujugatto) means his body is straight like that of a Brahmā; he will have a tall body that has grown perfectly erect. For most beings bend at three points—the shoulders, the waist, and the knees. When they bend at the waist, they bend backward; at the other two points, they bend forward. Some tall beings, however, are crooked at the side; some walk with their faces upturned as if counting the stars; some have little flesh and blood and are like stakes; some are stooped forward and walk trembling. But this one, rising up perfectly straight, will be of great height, like a golden archway erected in a city of the gods—thus they indicate. And just as this is so, it should be understood that whatever mark of a Great Man is not entirely complete at the time of birth is spoken of with reference to its becoming so in the future.

Sattussadoti dve hatthapiṭṭhiyo dve pādapiṭṭhiyo dve aṃsakūṭāni khandhoti imesu sattasu ṭhānesu paripuṇṇo maṃsussado assāti sattussado. Aññesaṃ pana hatthapādapiṭṭhādīsu sirājālaṃ paññāyati, aṃsakūṭakkhandhesu aṭṭhikoṭiyo. Te manussā petā viya khāyanti, na tathā mahāpuriso, mahāpuriso pana sattasu ṭhānesu paripuṇṇamaṃsussadattā nigūḷhasirājālehi hatthapiṭṭhādīhi vaṭṭetvā suṭṭhapitasuvaṇṇāḷiṅgasadisena khandhena silārūpakaṃ viya khāyati, cittakammarūpakaṃ viya ca khāyati.

“Seven-raised” (Sattussado) means he has a fullness of raised flesh in these seven places: the backs of both hands, the backs of both feet, both shoulder-points, and the nape of the neck. For others, however, networks of veins are visible on the backs of their hands and feet, and so on, and the points of their bones are visible at their shoulder-points and napes. Such people appear like human specters, but not so the Great Being. The Great Being, on account of the fullness of his flesh in these seven places, with the backs of his hands and so forth being rounded and having concealed networks of veins, and with a nape like a well-placed golden drum, appears like a stone statue or a painted figure.

Sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya kāyo assāti sīhapubbaddhakāyo. Sīhassa hi puratthimakāyova paripuṇṇo hoti, pacchimakāyo aparipuṇṇo. Mahāpurisassa pana sīhassa pubbaddhakāyo viya sabbo kāyo paripuṇṇo. Sopi sīhasseva tattha tattha vinatunnatādivasena dussaṇṭhitavisaṇṭhito [M 2.0040] na hoti, dīghayuttaṭṭhāne pana dīgho, rassathūlakisaputhulaanuvaṭṭitayuttaṭṭhānesu tathāvidhova hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

“Having the forepart of a lion” (Sīhapubbaddhakāyo) means his body is like the forepart of a lion. For a lion, only its forepart is full, while its hind part is not full. But for the Great Being, his entire body is full, like the forepart of a lion. Furthermore, his body is not ill-formed and misshapen—as a lion's is, with its various sunken and raised parts—but rather, where length is suitable, it is long; and in places where shortness, thickness, thinness, breadth, or successive roundness are suitable, it is just so. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Manāpiyeva kho, bhikkhave, kammavipāke paccupaṭṭhite yehi aṅgehi dīghehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni dīghāni saṇṭhanti. Yehi aṅgehi rassehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni rassāni saṇṭhanti. Yehi aṅgehi thūlehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni thūlāni saṇṭhanti. Yehi aṅgehi kisehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni kisāni saṇṭhanti. Yehi aṅgehi puthulehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni [P 2.0449] puthulāni saṇṭhanti. Yehi aṅgehi vaṭṭehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni vaṭṭāni saṇṭhantī”ti.

“Indeed, Bhikkhus, when the agreeable result of kamma manifests, those limbs that are beautiful when long are established as long; those limbs that are beautiful when short are established as short; those limbs that are beautiful when thick are established as thick; those limbs that are beautiful when thin are established as thin; those limbs that are beautiful when broad are established as broad; and those limbs that are beautiful when round are established as round.”

Iti nānācittena puññacittena cittito dasahi pāramīhi sajjito mahāpurisassa attabhāvo, loke sabbasippino vā sabbaiddhimanto vā patirūpakampi kātuṃ na sakkonti.

Thus, the personal existence of the Great Being—adorned by various meritorious thoughts and prepared by the ten perfections—is such that all the artisans or all those with psychic power in the world are unable to create even a likeness of it.

Citantaraṃsoti antaraṃsaṃ vuccati dvinnaṃ koṭṭānaṃ antaraṃ, taṃ citaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ antaraṃsaṃ assāti citantaraṃso. Aññesañhi taṃ ṭhānaṃ ninnaṃ hoti, dve piṭṭhikoṭṭā pāṭiyekkā paññāyanti. Mahāpurisassa pana kaṭito paṭṭhāya maṃsapaṭalaṃ yāva khandhā uggamma samussitasuvaṇṇaphalakaṃ viya piṭṭhiṃ chādetvā patiṭṭhitaṃ.

“With the space between his shoulders filled” (citantaraṃso) means that the space between the two shoulder blades is called the antaraṃsa; and because that antaraṃsa is filled and full, he is called citantaraṃso. For others, that place is sunken, and the two shoulder blades appear separately. For the Great Being, however, a layer of flesh, rising from his waist up to his shoulders, is established covering his back like a well-raised golden plank.

Nigrodhaparimaṇḍaloti [V 2.0036] nigrodho viya parimaṇḍalo. Yathā paññāsahatthatāya vā satahatthatāya vā samakkhandhasākho nigrodho dīghatopi vitthāratopi ekappamāṇova hoti, evaṃ kāyatopi byāmatopi ekappamāṇo. Yathā aññesaṃ kāyo dīgho vā hoti byāmo vā, na evaṃ visamappamāṇoti attho. Teneva yāvatakvassa kāyotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yāvatako assāti yāvatakvassa.

“Having the proportions of a banyan tree” (Nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo) means he is perfectly proportioned like a banyan tree. Just as a banyan tree with a balanced trunk and branches of fifty or a hundred cubits is of a single measure in both height and breadth, so too is he of a single measure in his height and his arm-span. It is not that his proportions are unequal, as with others for whom either the body is long or the arm-span is long; this is the meaning. For that very reason, the phrase beginning “As is his body...” was spoken. Therein, the words yāvatako assa become yāvatakvassa.

Samavaṭṭakkhandhoti samavaṭṭitakkhandho. Yathā eke koñcā viya ca bakā viya ca varāhā viya ca dīghagalā vaṅkagalā puthulagalā ca honti[M 2.0041], kathanakāle sirājālaṃ paññāyati, mando saro nikkhamati, na evaṃ mahāpurisassa. Mahāpurisassa pana suvaṭṭitasuvaṇṇāḷiṅgasadiso khandho hoti, kathanakāle sirājālaṃ na paññāyati, meghassa viya gajjito saro mahā hoti.

“Having an evenly rounded neck” (Samavaṭṭakkhandho) means having a well-rounded neck. Unlike some who, like curlews, herons, or wild boars, have long necks, crooked necks, or broad necks, and for whom a network of veins appears and a weak sound emerges when they speak—it is not so for the Great Being. Rather, the Great Being's neck is like a well-rounded golden drum; when he speaks, no network of veins is visible, and his voice is as mighty as the thunder of a cloud.

Rasaggasaggīti ettha rasaṃ gasanti harantīti rasaggasā. Rasaharaṇīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tā aggā assāti rasaggasaggī. Mahāpurisassa kira sattarasaharaṇīsahassāni uddhaggāni hutvā gīvāyameva paṭimukkāni. Tilaphalamattopi āhāro jivhagge ṭhapito sabbakāyaṃ anupharati. Teneva mahāpadhānaṃ padahantassa ekataṇḍulādīhipi kaḷāyayūsapasatamattenāpi kāyassa yāpanaṃ ahosi. Aññesaṃ pana tathā abhāvā na sakalaṃ kāyaṃ ojā pharati. Tena te bahvābādhā honti.

Regarding “possessing the supreme taste” (rasaggasaggī): herein, rasaggasā means 'they convey taste' (rasaṃ gasanti). This is a term for the taste-conveying nerves. Because those nerves are supreme (aggā) in him, he is called rasaggasaggī. It is said that the Great Being has seven thousand taste-conveying nerves that, with their tips pointing upwards, are connected within his neck. Even a morsel of food the size of a sesame seed, when placed on the tip of his tongue, pervades his entire body. For this reason, while he was undertaking the Great Striving, the sustenance of his body was possible even with single grains of rice and so on, or with just a handful of bean soup. For others, however, because this is not the case, the nutritive essence does not pervade the entire body. Therefore, they suffer from many illnesses.

Sīhasseva [P 2.0450] hanu assāti sīhahanu. Tattha sīhassa heṭṭhimahanumeva paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, na uparimaṃ. Mahāpurisassa pana sīhassa heṭṭhimaṃ viya dvepi paripuṇṇāni dvādasiyā pakkhassa candasadisāni honti. Atha nemittakā hanukapariyantaṃ olokentāva imesu hanukesu heṭṭhime vīsati uparime vīsatīti cattālīsadantā samā aviraḷā patiṭṭhahissantīti sallakkhetvā ayañhi deva, kumāro cattālīsadanto hotītiādimāhaṃsu. Tatrāyamattho, aññesañhi paripuṇṇadantānampi dvattiṃsa dantā honti. Imassa pana cattālīsaṃ bhavissanti. Aññesañca keci dantā uccā, keci nīcāti visamā honti, imassa pana ayapaṭṭakena chinnasaṅkhapaṭalaṃ viya samā bhavissanti. Aññesaṃ kumbhilānaṃ viya dantā viraḷā honti, macchamaṃsāni khādantānaṃ dantantaraṃ pūrenti. Imassa pana kanakaphalakāyaṃ samussitavajirapanti viya aviraḷā tūlikāya dassitaparicchedā viya dantā bhavissanti. Aññesañca pūtidantā uṭṭhahanti. Tena kāci dāṭhā kāḷāpi vivaṇṇāpi honti. Ayaṃ pana suṭṭhu sukkadāṭho osadhitārakampi atikkamma virocamānāya pabhāya samannāgatadāṭho bhavissati.

“Having jaws like a lion” (sīhahanu) means his jaw is like a lion's. In a lion, only the lower jaw is full, not the upper. But for the Great Being, both jaws are full, like the moon on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight. Then the soothsayers, observing the extent of his jawbones, discerned, 'In these jaws, twenty teeth below and twenty above—forty teeth in total—will be established, even and without gaps,' and thus they declared, 'Indeed, Your Majesty, the prince will have forty teeth,' and so on. The meaning here is this: for others, even those with a full set of teeth have only thirty-two. But this one will have forty. And for others, some teeth are high and some low, and thus they are uneven; but his will be even, like a slice of conch shell cut with an iron saw. For others, their teeth are gapped like a crocodile's, and when they eat fish and meat, the spaces between their teeth are filled. But his teeth will be without gaps, like a row of diamonds set on a golden plank, their divisions as clear as if drawn with a fine brush. Furthermore, others have decaying teeth, and because of this, some of their canines are dark or discolored. But this prince will have perfectly white canines, possessing canines endowed with a radiance that surpasses even the morning star.

Pahūtajivhoti [V 2.0037] puthulajivho. Aññesaṃ jivhā thūlāpi honti kisāpi rassāpi thaddhāpi visamāpi, mahāpurisassa pana jivhā mudu dīghā puthulā vaṇṇasampannā hoti. So hi etaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ pariyesituṃ āgatānaṃ kaṅkhāvinodanatthaṃ mudukattā taṃ jivhaṃ kathinasūciṃ viya vaṭṭetvā ubho nāsikasotāni parāmasati, dīghattā ubho kaṇṇasotāni parāmasati[M 2.0042], puthulattā kesantapariyosānaṃ kevalampi nalāṭaṃ paṭicchādeti. Evamassa mududīghaputhulabhāvaṃ pakāsento tesaṃ kaṅkhaṃ vinodeti. Evaṃ tilakkhaṇasampannaṃ jivhaṃ sandhāya “pahūtajivho”ti vuttaṃ.

He has a broad tongue (pahūtajivho); that is, a wide tongue. The tongues of others may be thick, or thin, or short, or stiff, or uneven, but the Great Man’s tongue is soft, long, broad, and endowed with fine color. To dispel the doubts of those who come seeking this mark, because of its softness, he rolls his tongue like a firm needle and touches both nostrils; because of its length, he touches both orifices of the ears; and because of its breadth, it covers his entire forehead up to the hairline. In this way, by revealing the softness, length, and breadth of his tongue, he removes their uncertainty. Thus, with reference to the tongue endowed with these three characteristics, it is said, 'He has a broad tongue.'

Brahmassaroti aññe chinnassarāpi bhinnassarāpi kākassarāpi honti, ayaṃ pana mahābrahmuno sarasadisena sarena samannāgato bhavissati, mahābrahmuno hi pittasemhehi apalibuddhattā saro visado hoti. Mahāpurisenāpi katakammaṃ tassa vatthuṃ sodheti. Vatthuno suddhattā nābhito [P 2.0451] paṭṭhāya samuṭṭhahanto saro visado aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatova samuṭṭhāti. Karavīko viya bhaṇatīti karavīkabhāṇī, mattakaravīkarutamañjughosoti attho.

He has a voice like Brahmā's (brahmassaro). Others may have interrupted voices, broken voices, or voices like a crow, but this one will possess a voice resembling that of the Great Brahmā. For the Great Brahmā's voice is clear because it is unimpaired by bile and phlegm. The kamma done by the Great Man also purifies its physical basis. Due to the purity of that basis, the voice, arising from the navel, is clear and arises endowed with eight factors. He speaks like the karavīka bird, thus he is 'one who speaks like a karavīka'; the meaning is that his voice is as sweet and melodious as the cry of an intoxicated karavīka.

Abhinīlanettoti na sakalanīlanetto, nīlayuttaṭṭhāne panassa umāpupphasadisena ativisuddhena nīlavaṇṇena samannāgatāni nettāni honti, pītayuttaṭṭhāne kaṇikārapupphasadisena pītavaṇṇena, lohitayuttaṭṭhāne bandhujīvakapupphasadisena lohitavaṇṇena, setayuttaṭṭhāne osadhitārakasadisena setavaṇṇena, kāḷayuttaṭṭhāne addāriṭṭhakasadisena kāḷavaṇṇena samannāgatāni. Suvaṇṇavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇisīhapañjarasadisāni khāyanti.

He has deep blue eyes (abhinīlanetto)—not entirely blue, but in the places where blue is appropriate, his eyes are endowed with an exceedingly pure blue color like the flax flower; in the places where yellow is appropriate, with a yellow color like the kaṇikāra flower; in the places where red is appropriate, with a red color like the bandhujīvaka flower; in the places where white is appropriate, with a white color like the morning star; and in the places where black is appropriate, with a black color like the soapberry seed. They appear like an opened, jeweled lion-window in a golden mansion.

Gopakhumoti ettha pakhumanti sakalacakkhubhaṇḍaṃ adhippetaṃ, taṃ kāḷavacchakassa bahaladhātukaṃ hoti, rattavacchakassa vippasannaṃ, taṃmuhuttajātataruṇarattavacchakasadisacakkhubhaṇḍoti attho. Aññesañhi cakkhubhaṇḍā aparipuṇṇā honti, hatthimūsikādīnaṃ akkhisadisehi viniggatehipi gambhīrehipi akkhīhi samannāgatā honti. Mahāpurisassa pana dhovitvā majjitvā ṭhapitamaṇiguḷikā viya mudusiniddhanīlasukhumapakhumācitāni akkhīni.

He has eyelashes like a cow's (gopakhumo). Here, 'pakhuma' refers to the entire eye apparatus. In a black calf, this is thick with substance, while in a red calf, it is very clear. The meaning is that his eye apparatus resembles that of a tender, red calf just born. For the eye apparatuses of others are incomplete; they are endowed with protruding or deep-set eyes, like those of elephants, mice, and so on. But the Great Man’s eyes are adorned with soft, smooth, dark, and fine eyelashes, like a polished jewel-bead that has been washed and set.

Uṇṇāti uṇṇalomaṃ. Bhamukantareti dvinnaṃ bhamukānaṃ vemajjhe nāsikamatthakeyeva jātā, uggantvā pana nalāṭavemajjhe jātā. Odātāti parisuddhā, osadhitārakasamānavaṇṇā. Mudūti sappimaṇḍe osāretvā ṭhapitasatavāravihatakappāsapaṭalasadisā. Tūlasannibhāti simbalitūlalatātūlasamānā, ayamassa odātatāya upamā. Sā panesā koṭiyaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhiyamānā upaḍḍhabāhuppamāṇā hoti, vissaṭṭhā [M 2.0043] dakkhiṇāvaṭṭavasena āvaṭṭitvā uddhaggā hutvā [V 2.0038] santiṭṭhati. Suvaṇṇaphalakamajjhe ṭhapitarajatapubbuḷakaṃ viya, suvaṇṇaghaṭato nikkhamamānā khīradhārā viya, aruṇappabhārañjite gaganappadese osadhitārakā viya ca atimanoharāya siriyā virocati.

He has an uṇṇā (uṇṇā), that is, the uṇṇa-hair. It grows right at the midpoint between the two eyebrows, on the top of the nose, but rising up, it is situated in the center of the forehead. It is pure white (odātā), with a color like the morning star. It is soft (mudū), like a layer of cotton that has been teased a hundred times, dipped in the finest butter, and set down. It resembles cotton (tūlasannibhā), like silk-cotton or creeper-cotton—this is a simile for its whiteness. When grasped at the tip and pulled, it is half an arm-span in length. When released, it coils in a clockwise direction and stays fixed with its tip pointing upwards. It shines with a most captivating splendor, like a silver bubble placed in the middle of a golden plank, like a stream of milk flowing from a golden pot, or like the morning star in a region of the sky tinged with the light of dawn.

Uṇhīsasīsoti [P 2.0452] idaṃ paripuṇṇanalāṭatañca paripuṇṇasīsataṃ cāti dve atthavase paṭicca vuttaṃ. Mahāpurisassa hi dakkhiṇakaṇṇacūḷikato paṭṭhāya maṃsapaṭalaṃ uṭṭhahitvā sakalanalāṭaṃ chādayamānaṃ pūrayamānaṃ gantvā vāmakaṇṇacūḷikāyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ, taṃ rañño bandhauṇhīsapaṭṭo viya virocati. Mahāpurisassa kira imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ disvā rājūnaṃ uṇhīsapaṭṭaṃ akaṃsu. Ayaṃ tāva eko attho. Aññe pana janā aparipuṇṇasīsā honti, keci kapisīsā, keci phalasīsā, keci aṭṭhisīsā, keci hatthisīsā, keci tumbasīsā, keci pabbhārasīsā. Mahāpurisassa pana āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitaṃ viya suparipuṇṇaṃ udakapubbuḷasadisaṃ sīsaṃ hoti. Tattha purimanaye uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso viyāti uṇhīsasīso. Dutiyanaye uṇhīsaṃ viya sabbattha parimaṇḍalasīsoti uṇhīsasīso.

The characteristic 'having a head like a turban' (uṇhīsasīso) is stated with reference to two meanings: the fullness of the forehead and the completeness of the head. For the Great Man, a layer of flesh rises from the tip of the right ear, covers and fills the entire forehead, and settles at the tip of the left ear; it shines like a king’s bound turban-cloth. It is said that upon seeing this characteristic of the Great Man, kings began to make turban-cloths. This is the first meaning. As for the second, other people have incomplete heads: some have heads like a monkey, some like a fruit, some like a bone, some like an elephant, some like a gourd, and some have sloping heads. But the Great Man’s head is perfectly complete, like a water bubble, as if shaped by a lathe. In this context, according to the first interpretation, he is 'turban-headed' because his head is like one wrapped with a turban. According to the second interpretation, he is 'turban-headed' because his head is perfectly round all over, like a turban.

Vipassīsamaññāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Designation 'Vipassī'

37. Sabbakāmehīti idaṃ lakkhaṇāni pariggaṇhāpetvā pacchā kataṃ viya vuttaṃ, na panevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṭhamañhi te nemittake santappetvā pacchā lakkhaṇapariggaṇhanaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Tassa vitthāro gabbhokkantiyaṃ vuttoyeva. Pāyentīti thaññaṃ pāyenti. Tassa kira niddosena madhurena khīrena samannāgatā saṭṭhi dhātiyo upaṭṭhāpesi, tathā sesāpi tesu tesu kammesu kusalā saṭṭhisaṭṭhiyeva. Tāsaṃ pesanakārake saṭṭhi purise, tassa tassa katākatabhāvaṃ sallakkhaṇe saṭṭhi amacce upaṭṭhāpesi. Evaṃ cattāri saṭṭhiyo itthīnaṃ, dve saṭṭhiyo purisānanti cha saṭṭhiyo upaṭṭhakānaṃyeva ahesuṃ. Setacchattanti dibbasetacchattaṃ. Kuladattiyaṃ pana sirigabbheyeva tiṭṭhati. Mā naṃ sītaṃ vātiādīsu mā abhibhavīti attho veditabbo. Svāssudanti so assudaṃ. Aṅkeneva aṅkanti aññassa bāhunāva aññassa bāhuṃ. Aññassa ca aṃsakūṭeneva [M 2.0044] aññassa aṃsakūṭaṃ. Parihariyatīti nīyati, sampāpiyatīti attho.

37. The phrase 'with all desires' (sabbakāmehi) was stated as if it were done after the marks had been ascertained, but it should not be understood thus. For it should be understood that first the soothsayers were satisfied, and only afterwards was the ascertainment of the marks performed. The details of this are indeed stated in the section on the descent into the womb. 'They fed' means they gave milk to drink. It is said that sixty wet nurses, endowed with faultless, sweet milk, were appointed for him; similarly, for the other tasks, sixty women skilled in each were appointed. Sixty men were appointed to act as their messengers, and sixty ministers to observe what was done and not done in each case. Thus, there were four groups of sixty women and two groups of sixty men, making six groups of sixty attendants in total. 'The white parasol' means the divine white parasol. The one given by the family, however, remains in the royal chamber. In the phrase 'Lest cold...' and so on, the meaning should be understood as 'lest it overpower him.' The word `svāssudaṃ` is to be analyzed as `so assu daṃ`. 'From lap to lap' means from one person's arm to another's arm. And 'from shoulder-tip to shoulder-tip' means from one person's shoulder-tip to another's. 'Was carried around' means was led, was conveyed; that is the meaning.

38. Mañjussaroti akharassaro. Vaggussaroti chekanipuṇassaro. Madhurassaroti sātassaro. Pemaniyassaroti pemajanakassaro. Tatridaṃ [P 2.0453] karavīkānaṃ madhurassaratāya – karavīkasakuṇe kira madhurarasaṃ ambapakkaṃ mukhatuṇḍakena paharitvā paggharitarasaṃ pivitvā pakkhena [V 2.0039] tālaṃ datvā vikūjamāne catuppadā mattā viya laḷituṃ ārabhanti. Gocarapasutāpi catuppadā mukhagatāni tiṇāni chaḍḍetvā taṃ saddaṃ suṇanti. Vāḷamigā khuddakamige anubandhamānā ukkhittaṃ pādaṃ anikkhipitvāva tiṭṭhanti. Anubaddhamigā ca maraṇabhayaṃ jahitvā tiṭṭhanti. Ākāse pakkhandā pakkhinopi pakkhe pasāretvā taṃ saddaṃ suṇamānāva tiṭṭhanti. Udake macchāpi kaṇṇapaṭalaṃ papphoṭetvā taṃ saddaṃ suṇamānāva tiṭṭhanti. Evaṃ madhurassarā karavīkā.

38. 'A lovely voice' (mañjussara) means a voice that is not harsh. 'An articulate voice' (vaggussara) means a skillful and refined voice. 'A sweet voice' (madhurassara) means a delightful voice. 'An endearing voice' (pemaniyassara) means a voice that generates love. In this regard, this is the account of the sweetness of the karavīka birds' voice: It is said that when a karavīka bird, having pierced a sweet, ripe mango with its beak, drinks the dripping juice and, beating time with its wings, begins to sing, four-footed animals begin to sport about as if intoxicated. Even four-footed animals intent on grazing drop the grass from their mouths and listen to that sound. Predatory animals chasing small prey stop with a foot raised, not putting it down. And the pursued animals, abandoning their fear of death, also stand still. Birds flying in the sky, spreading their wings, also stop to listen to that sound. Even fish in the water, flapping their gill-covers, remain still, listening to that sound. So sweet-voiced are the karavīka birds.

Asandhimittāpi dhammāsokassa devī – “atthi nu kho, bhante, buddhassarena sadiso kassaci saro”ti saṅghaṃ pucchi. Atthi karavīkasakuṇassāti. Kuhiṃ, bhante, te sakuṇāti? Himavanteti. Sā rājānaṃ āha – “deva, ahaṃ karavīkasakuṇaṃ passitukāmāmhī”ti. Rājā – “imasmiṃ pañjare nisīditvā karavīko āgacchatū”ti suvaṇṇapañjaraṃ vissajjesi. Pañjaro gantvā ekassa karavīkassa purato aṭṭhāsi. So – “rājāṇāya āgato pañjaro, na sakkā na gantu”nti tattha nisīdi. Pañjaro āgantvā rañño purato aṭṭhāsi. Na karavīkasaddaṃ kārāpetuṃ sakkonti. Atha rājā – “kathaṃ, bhaṇe, ime saddaṃ na karontī”ti āha. Ñātake adisvā devāti. Atha naṃ rājā ādāsehi parikkhipāpesi. So attano chāyaṃ disvā – “ñātakā me āgatā”ti maññamāno pakkhena tālaṃ datvā madhurassarena maṇivaṃsaṃ dhamamāno viya viravi. Sakalanagare manussā mattā viya laḷiṃsu. Asandhimittā cintesi – “imassa tāva tiracchānagatassa evaṃ madhuro saddo, kīdiso nu kho sabbaññutaññāṇasiripattassa bhagavato saddo ahosī”ti pītiṃ uppādetvā taṃ pītiṃ avijahitvā sattahi jaṅghasatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ madhuro kira [M 2.0045] karavīkasaddoti. Tato pana satabhāgena sahassabhāgena ca madhurataro vipassissa kumārassa saddo ahosīti veditabbo.

Asandhimittā, the queen of King Dhammāsoka, asked the Saṅgha: 'Venerable sirs, is there anyone's voice that is similar to the Buddha's voice?' 'There is: that of the karavīka bird.' 'Where, venerable sirs, are those birds?' 'In the Himalayas.' She then said to the king: 'Your Majesty, I wish to see a karavīka bird.' The king, saying, 'Let a karavīka come and sit in this cage,' dispatched a golden cage. The cage went and stood before a karavīka bird. The bird, thinking, 'This cage has come by the king's command; it is not possible not to go,' sat in it. The cage returned and stood before the king. They were unable to make the karavīka sing. Then the king asked: 'Sirs, why do these birds not make a sound?' 'Because they do not see their kin, Your Majesty.' Then the king had it surrounded with mirrors. Seeing its own reflection and thinking, 'My kin have come,' it beat time with its wings and sang with a sweet voice, as if one were playing a jeweled flute. All the people in the city sported about as if intoxicated. Asandhimittā reflected: 'If the voice of this creature, a mere animal, is so sweet, how sweet must have been the voice of the Blessed One, who attained the splendor of omniscient knowledge!' Generating rapture, and not abandoning that rapture, she, together with seven hundred female attendants, became established in the fruit of stream-entry. So sweet, it is said, is the voice of the karavīka. However, it should be understood that the voice of Prince Vipassī was a hundred times, a thousand times sweeter than that.

39. Kammavipākajanti na bhāvanāmayaṃ, kammavipākavasena pana devatānaṃ cakkhusadisameva maṃsacakkhu ahosi[P 2.0454], yena nimittaṃ katvā tilavāhe pakkhittaṃ ekatilampi ayaṃ soti uddharitvā dātuṃ sakkoti.

39. 'Born of the result of kamma' means it was not produced by meditative development. Rather, by the power of the result of kamma, his fleshly eye became just like the eye of the devas, with which, having made a mental note, he was able to pick out even a single sesame seed that had been put into a cart of sesame seeds and give it, saying, 'This is it.'

40. Vipassīti ettha ayaṃ vacanattho, antarantarā nimīlajanitandhakāravirahena visuddhaṃ passati, vivaṭehi ca akkhīhi passatīti vipassī; dutiyavāre viceyya viceyya passatīti vipassī; vicinitvā vicinitvā passatīti attho.

40. Regarding the name 'Vipassī,' this is the explanation of the word: because he sees with special clarity, being free from the darkness caused by intermittent blinking, and because he sees with open eyes, he is called 'Vipassī.' In a second explanation, because he sees after repeatedly investigating, he is called 'Vipassī'; the meaning is that he sees after thoroughly examining.

Atthe panāyatīti atthe jānāti passati, nayati vā pavattetīti attho. Ekadivasaṃ kira [V 2.0040] vinicchayaṭṭhāne nisīditvā atthe anusāsantassa rañño alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mahāpurisaṃ ānetvā hatthe ṭhapayiṃsu. Tassa taṃ aṅkekatvā upalāḷayamānasseva amaccā sāmikaṃ assāmikaṃ akaṃsu. Bodhisatto anattamanasaddaṃ nicchāresi. Rājā – “kimetaṃ, upadhārethā”ti āha. Upadhāriyamānā aññaṃ adisvā – “aḍḍassa dubbinicchitattā evaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti puna sāmikaṃyeva sāmikaṃ katvā “ñatvā nu kho kumāro evaṃ karotī”ti vīmaṃsantā puna sāmikaṃ assāmikaṃ akaṃsu. Punapi bodhisatto tatheva saddaṃ nicchāresi. Atha rājā – “jānāti mahāpuriso”ti tato paṭṭhāya appamatto ahosi. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “viceyya viceyya kumāro atthe panāyatī”ti.

'He discerns the matter' (atthe panāyati) means he knows and sees the matter, or he guides and brings it about; that is the meaning. It is said that one day, while the king was seated in the hall of justice instructing on legal matters, they brought the Great Being, adorned and prepared, and placed him in the king's hands. While the king was holding him on his lap and fondling him, the ministers made the rightful owner a non-owner. The Bodhisatta uttered a sound of displeasure. The king said, 'What is this? Investigate it.' While investigating, seeing no other cause, they thought, 'This must have happened because the case was poorly judged.' They then made the rightful owner the owner again. Wondering, 'Does the prince know this and act thus?', they again made the owner a non-owner. Once more, the Bodhisatta uttered the same sound. Then the king, realizing, 'The Great Being knows,' became heedful from that day forward. It was with reference to this that it was said: 'Investigating again and again, the prince discerns the matter.'

42. Vassikantiādīsu yattha sukhaṃ hoti vassakāle vasituṃ, ayaṃ vassiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho vassāvāso vassaṃ, vassaṃ arahatīti vassiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo.

42. Regarding 'vassika' and other such terms: wherever it is pleasant to dwell during the rainy season, that dwelling is called 'vassika' (suitable for the rainy season). This same principle applies to the other terms as well. Herein, this is the verbal explanation: 'vassāvāso' is a residence for the rainy season (vassaṃ); because it is suitable for the rainy season (vassaṃ arahati), it is called 'vassiko'. This same principle applies to the other terms as well.

Tattha vassiko pāsādo nātiucco hoti, nātinīco, dvāravātapānānipissa nātibahūni nātitanūni, bhūmattharaṇapaccattharaṇakhajjabhojjānipettha missakāneva vaṭṭanti. Hemantike thambhāpi bhittiyopi nīcā honti, dvāravātapānāni tanukāni sukhumacchiddāni, uṇhappavesanatthāya bhittiniyūhāni nīhariyanti. Bhūmattharaṇapaccattharaṇanivāsanapārupanāni panettha uṇhaviriyāni [M 2.0046] kambalādīni vaṭṭanti. Khajjabhojjaṃ siniddhaṃ kaṭukasannissitaṃ nirudakasannissitañca. Gimhike thambhāpi bhittiyopi uccā honti, dvāravātapānāni panettha bahūni vipulajātāni honti, bhūmattharaṇādīni dukūlamayāni vaṭṭanti. Khajjabhojjāni madhurasasannissitabharitāni. Vātapānasamīpesu cettha [P 2.0455] nava cāṭiyo ṭhapetvā udakassa pūretvā nīluppalādīhi sañchādenti. Tesu tesu padesesu udakayantāni karonti, yehi deve vassante viya udakadhārā nikkhamanti.

Therein, the palace for the rainy season is neither too high nor too low. Its doors and windows are neither too many nor too few. Here, the floor coverings, spreads, and foods both hard and soft are of a moderate nature. In the winter residence, the pillars and walls are low; the doors and windows are small and have fine apertures; and projecting windows are extended from the walls to let in the heat. Here, the floor coverings, spreads, undergarments, and outer robes, such as woolen blankets and the like, are suitable for providing warmth. The food, both hard and soft, is rich, spicy, and prepared with little water. In the summer residence, the pillars and walls are high. Here, the doors and windows are numerous and wide. The floor coverings and so forth are made of fine linen. The foods, both hard and soft, are full of sweet tastes. And here, near the windows, they place new pots, fill them with water, and cover them with blue lotuses and the like. In various places, they construct water-machines from which streams of water flow forth as if it were raining from the sky.

Nippurisehīti purisavirahitehi. Na kevalañcettha tūriyāneva nippurisāni, sabbaṭṭhānānipi nippurisāneva, dovārikāpi itthiyova, nahāpanādiparikammakarāpi itthiyova. Rājā kira – “tathārūpaṃ issariyasukhasampattiṃ anubhavamānassa purisaṃ disvā purisāsaṅkā uppajjati, sā me puttassa mā ahosī”ti sabbakiccesu itthiyova ṭhapesīti.

'Without men' means devoid of men. And here, not only were the musical instruments without men, but all places were without men. The doorkeepers were only women, and those who performed services such as bathing were also only women. It is said that the king thought, 'While my son is experiencing such sovereign pleasure and felicity, upon seeing a man, a suspicion concerning men might arise in him. May that not happen to my son!' Thus, he appointed only women for all duties.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Recitation Section is concluded.

Jiṇṇapurisavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Aged Man.

43. Dutiyabhāṇavāre [V 2.0041] gopānasivaṅkanti gopānasī viya vaṅkaṃ. Bhogganti khandhe, kaṭiyaṃ, jāṇūsūti tīsu ṭhānesu bhoggavaṅkaṃ. Daṇḍaparāyananti daṇḍagatikaṃ daṇḍapaṭisaraṇaṃ. Āturanti jarāturaṃ. Gatayobbananti atikkantayobbanaṃ pacchimavaye ṭhitaṃ. Disvāti aḍḍhayojanappamāṇena balakāyena parivuto susaṃvihitārakkhopi gacchanto yadā ratho purato hoti, pacchā balakāyo, tādise okāse suddhāvāsakhīṇāsavabrahmehi attano ānubhāvena rathassa puratova dassitaṃ, taṃ purisaṃ passitvā. Suddhāvāsā kira – “mahāpuriso paṅke gajo viya pañcasu kāmaguṇesu laggo, satimassa uppādessāmā”ti taṃ dassesuṃ. Evaṃ dassitañca taṃ bodhisatto ceva passati sārathi ca. Brahmāno hi bodhisattassa appamādatthaṃ sārathissa ca kathāsallāpatthaṃ taṃ dassesuṃ. Kiṃ panesoti “eso jiṇṇoti kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti, nāhaṃ, bho ito pubbe evarūpaṃ addasa”nti pucchi.

43. In the Second Recitation Section, 'bent like a roof rafter' means bent like a roof rafter. 'Stooped' means stooped and bent in three places: at the shoulders, the waist, and the knees. 'Reliant on a staff' means one whose movement depends on a staff, one who is supported by a staff. 'Ailing' means ailing with old age. 'Whose youth is gone' means one who has passed beyond youth and is in the final stage of life. 'Having seen': Though he was traveling surrounded by an army half a yojana in size and with well-arranged protection, when the chariot was in front and the army behind, in such a space, he saw that man who was manifested right in front of the chariot through the power of the Arahant Brahmās of the Pure Abodes. It is said that the Brahmās of the Pure Abodes thought, 'The Great Being is stuck in the five strands of sensual pleasure like a great elephant in the mud. We shall arouse mindfulness in him.' And so they manifested that man. And being thus manifested, both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw him. Indeed, the Brahmās manifested him for the sake of the Bodhisatta's heedfulness and so that the charioteer would have a topic of conversation. Regarding the phrase, 'What, then, is this aged man?': this means he asked, 'Friend, I have never before seen such a being. What is this thing called an aged man?'

Tena [M 2.0047] hīti yadi mayhampi evarūpehi kesehi evarūpena ca kāyena bhavitabbaṃ, tena hi samma sārathi. Alaṃ dānajja uyyānabhūmiyāti – “ajja uyyānabhūmiṃ passissāmā”ti gacchāma, alaṃ tāya uyyānabhūmiyāti saṃviggahadayo saṃvegānurūpamāha. Antepuraṃ gatoti itthijanaṃ vissajjetvā sirigabbhe ekakova nisinno. Yatra hi nāmāti yāya jātiyā sati jarā paññāyati, sā jāti dhiratthu [P 2.0456] dhikkatā atthu, jigucchāmetaṃ jātinti, jātiyā mūlaṃ khaṇanto nisīdi, paṭhamena sallena hadaye viddho viya.

Regarding 'Then indeed': 'If I too am destined to have such hair and such a body, then indeed, good charioteer...' Regarding 'Enough now for today with the pleasure garden!': He spoke in accordance with his sense of spiritual urgency, with a heart stirred, saying, 'We are going today to see the pleasure garden, but enough with that pleasure garden!' Having gone to the inner palace, he dismissed the women and sat all alone in the glorious inner chamber. Regarding 'Woe unto it!': 'Woe unto that birth, because of which old age is manifest! Let it be condemned! I am disgusted by this birth!' Thus, digging at the root of birth, he sat as if pierced in the heart by the first arrow.

45. Sārathiṃ āmantāpetvāti rājā kira nemittakehi kathitakālato paṭṭhāya ohitasoto vicarati, so “kumāro uyyānaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge nivatto”ti sutvā sārathiṃ āmantāpesi. Mā heva khotiādīsu rajjaṃ kāretu, mā pabbajatu, brāhmaṇānaṃ vacanaṃ mā saccaṃ hotūti evaṃ cintesīti attho.

45. 'Having had the charioteer summoned': It is said that from the time the fortune-tellers had spoken, the king went about with attentive ears. So, having heard, 'The prince, while going to the park, turned back midway,' he had the charioteer summoned. Regarding 'May it not be so' and other such phrases, the meaning is that he thought thus: 'Let him exercise kingship, may he not go forth into homelessness! May the words of the brahmins not come true!'

Byādhipurisavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Sick Man.

47. Addasa khoti pubbe vuttanayeneva suddhāvāsehi dassitaṃ addasa. Ābādhikanti iriyāpathabhañjanakena visabhāgabādhena ābādhikaṃ. Dukkhitanti rogadukkhena dukkhitaṃ. Bāḷhagilānanti adhimattagilānaṃ. Palipannanti nimuggaṃ. Jarā paññāyissati byādhi paññāyissatīti [V 2.0042] idhāpi yāya jātiyā sati idaṃ dvayaṃ paññāyati, dhikkatā sā jāti, ajātaṃ khemanti jātiyā mūlaṃ khaṇanto nisīdi, dutiyena sallena viddho viya.

47. 'He saw indeed': He saw him who was manifested by the deities of the Pure Abodes in the same way as stated before. 'Diseased' means afflicted with a contrary ailment that destroys the bodily postures. 'Suffering' means afflicted with the suffering of sickness. 'Gravely ill' means ill in the highest degree. 'Wallowing' means sunk down. Here too, regarding 'Old age will be known, sickness will be known': 'Woe unto that birth, because of which this pair is manifest! The unborn is security!' Thus, digging at the root of birth, he sat as if pierced by the second arrow.

Kālaṅkatapurisavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Deceased Man.

50. Vilātanti sivikaṃ. Petanti ito paṭigataṃ. Kālaṅkatanti katakālaṃ, yattakaṃ tena kālaṃ jīvitabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ katvā niṭṭhapetvā matanti attho. Imampissa purimanayeneva brahmāno dassesuṃ. Yatra hi nāmāti idhāpi yāya jātiyā sati idaṃ tayaṃ paññāyati, dhikkatā sā jāti, ajātaṃ khemanti jātiyā mūlaṃ khaṇanto nisīdi, tatiyena sallena viddho viya.

50. 'A bier' means a palanquin. 'Departed' means gone from this world. 'One who has made his time' means one whose time is done; the meaning is that, having done and completed all the time that he was to live, he is dead. This too the Brahmā deities manifested to him in the same way as before. Here too, regarding 'Woe unto it!': 'Woe unto that birth, because of which this triad is manifest! The unborn is security!' Thus, digging at the root of birth, he sat as if pierced by the third arrow.

Pabbajitavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Renunciant.

52. Bhaṇḍunti [M 2.0048] muṇḍaṃ. Imampissa purimanayeneva brahmāno dassesuṃ. Sādhu dhammacariyātiādīsu ayaṃ deva dhammacaraṇabhāvo sādhūti cintetvā pabbajitoti evaṃ ekamekassa padassa yojanā veditabbā. Sabbāni cetāni dasakusalakammapathavevacanāneva. Avasāne pana avihiṃsāti karuṇāya pubbabhāgo. Anukampāti mettāya pubbabhāgo. Tenahīti uyyojanatthe nipāto. Pabbajitaṃ hissa disvā cittaṃ pabbajjāya ninnaṃ jātaṃ. Atha tena saddhiṃ kathetukāmo hutvā sārathiṃ uyyojento tena hītiādimāha.

52. ‘Shaven’ (bhaṇḍu) means a shaven head. This one too, the Brahmā deities showed him as before. In phrases like ‘Good is the practice of the Dhamma,’ it should be understood that the connection of each word is thus: ‘Thinking, “This state of practicing the Dhamma is good,” he went forth.’ All these are indeed synonyms for the ten wholesome courses of action. At the end, ‘non-violence’ (avihiṃsā) is the precursor of compassion (karuṇā). ‘Sympathy’ (anukampā) is the precursor of loving-kindness (mettā). ‘Then indeed’ (tenahi) is a particle in the sense of urging on. For upon seeing the renunciant, his mind became inclined to renunciation. Then, wishing to speak with him, he urged on the charioteer, saying, ‘Then indeed,’ and so on.

Bodhisattapabbajjāvaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Bodhisatta’s Renunciation

54. Atha [P 2.0457] kho, bhikkhaveti – “pabbajitassa sādhu dhammacariyā”tiādīni ca aññañca bahuṃ mahājanakāyena rakkhiyamānassa puttadārasambādhe ghare vasato ādīnavapaṭisaṃyuttañceva migabhūtena cetasā yathāsukhaṃ vane vasato pabbajitassa vivekānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttañca dhammiṃ kathaṃ sutvā pabbajitukāmo hutvā – atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassī kumāro sārathiṃ āmantesi.

54. ‘Then, bhikkhus’—having heard a Dhamma talk connected with the drawbacks for one living in a home crowded with wife and children while being guarded by a great multitude, and also connected with the benefits of seclusion for a renunciant living at ease in the forest with a mind like a deer's, along with other teachings such as, ‘Good is the practice of the Dhamma for a renunciant,’ he became desirous of going forth. Then, bhikkhus, Prince Vipassī addressed the charioteer.

Imāni cattāri disvā pabbajitaṃ nāma sabbabodhisattānaṃ vaṃsova tantiyeva paveṇīyeva. Aññepi ca bodhisattā yathā ayaṃ vipassī kumāro, evaṃ cirassaṃ cirassaṃ passanti. Amhākaṃ pana bodhisatto cattāripi ekadivasaṃyeva disvā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā anomānadītīre [V 2.0043] pabbajito. Teneva rājagahaṃ patvā tattha raññā bimbisārena – “kimatthaṃ, paṇḍita, pabbajitosīti” puṭṭho āha –

Seeing these four sights, what is called ‘the going forth’ is indeed the lineage, the tradition, the custom of all Bodhisattas. Other Bodhisattas too, like this Prince Vipassī, see them only after a very long time. Our Bodhisatta, however, having seen all four in a single day, made the Great Renunciation and went forth on the banks of the Anomā River. For that reason, having arrived at Rājagaha, when asked by King Bimbisāra, ‘For what reason, wise one, have you gone forth?’ he replied:

“Jiṇṇañca disvā dukhitañca byādhitaṃ,

Matañca disvā gatamāyusaṅkhayaṃ;

Kāsāyavatthaṃ pabbajitañca disvā,

Tasmā ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rājā”ti.

‘Seeing the aged, the suffering, and the sick,

And seeing the dead whose life-span was spent;

Seeing one gone forth in ochre-colored robes,

Therefore, O king, I have gone forth.’

Mahājanakāyaanupabbajjāvaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Great Multitude Following into Homelessness

55. Sutvāna tesanti tesaṃ caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ sutvā etadahosi. Orakoti ūnako lāmako. Anupabbajiṃsūti anupabbajitāni[M 2.0049]. Kasmā panettha yathā parato khaṇḍatissānaṃ anupabbajjāya – “bandhumatiyā rājadhāniyā nikkhamitvā”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ na vuttanti? Nikkhamitvā sutattā. Ete kira sabbepi vipassissa kumārassa upaṭṭhākaparisāva, te pātova upaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā kumāraṃ adisvā pātarāsatthāya gantvā bhuttapātarāsā āgamma “kuhiṃ kumāro”ti pucchitvā “uyyānabhūmiṃ gato”ti sutvā “tattheva naṃ dakkhissāmā”ti nikkhamantā nivattamānaṃ sārathiṃ disvā – “kumāro pabbajito”ti cassa vacanaṃ sutvā sutaṭṭhāneyeva sabbābharaṇāni omuñcitvā antarāpaṇato kāsāvapītāni vatthāni āharāpetvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā pabbajiṃsu. Iti nagarato nikkhamitvā bahinagare sutattā ettha – “bandhumatiyā rājadhāniyā nikkhamitvā”ti na vuttaṃ.

55. ‘Having heard them’ (sutvāna tesaṃ) means that upon hearing this, it occurred to those eighty-four thousand beings. ‘Inferior’ (orako) means lesser, base. ‘They went forth after him’ (anupabbajiṃsu) means they followed him into homelessness. Why is it not stated here, as it is stated later regarding the going forth of Khaṇḍatissa’s followers, ‘having left the royal city of Bandhumatī’? Because they heard after having left. It is said that all these were indeed the attendant retinue of Prince Vipassī. In the morning, they came to attend upon him, but not seeing the prince, they went for their morning meal. After eating, they returned and asked, ‘Where is the prince?’ Hearing he had gone to the pleasure grove, they thought, ‘We will see him there.’ As they were setting out, they saw the charioteer returning and heard his words: ‘The prince has gone forth.’ Right there, at the place where they heard, they removed all their ornaments, had ochre robes brought from a shop in the market, shaved off their hair and beards, and went forth. Thus, because they had left the city and heard the news outside the city, it is not stated here, ‘having left the royal city of Bandhumatī.’

Cārikaṃ [P 2.0458] caratīti gatagataṭṭhāne mahāmaṇḍapaṃ katvā dānaṃ sajjetvā āgamma svātanāya nimantito janassa āyācitabhikkhameva paṭiggaṇhanto cattāro māse cārikaṃ cari.

‘He wandered on tour’ (cārikaṃ carati) means: In every place he went, after people had built a great pavilion, prepared alms, and come to invite him for the next day, he would accept only the alms thus requested by the people, and in this way he wandered on tour for four months.

Ākiṇṇoti iminā gaṇena parivuto. Ayaṃ pana vitakko bodhisattassa kadā uppannoti? Sve visākhapuṇṇamā bhavissatīti cātuddasīdivase. Tadā kira so – “yatheva maṃ ime pubbe gihibhūtaṃ parivāretvā caranti, idānipi tatheva, kiṃ iminā gaṇenā”ti gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya ukkaṇṭhitvā “ajjeva gacchāmī”ti cintetvā puna “ajja avelā, sace idāni gamissāmi, sabbeva ime jānissanti, sveva gamissāmī”ti cintesi. Taṃ divasañca uruvelagāmasadise gāme gāmavāsino svātanāya nimantayiṃsu. Te caturāsītisahassānampi tesaṃ [V 2.0044] pabbajitānaṃ mahāpurisassa ca pāyāsameva paṭiyādayiṃsu. Atha mahāpuriso punadivase tasmiṃyeva gāme tehi pabbajitehi saddhiṃ bhattakiccaṃ katvā vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Tattha te pabbajitā mahāpurisassa vattaṃ dassetvā attano attano rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni paviṭṭhā. Bodhisattopi paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nisinno.

‘Crowded’ (ākiṇṇa) means surrounded by this group. But when did this thought arise in the Bodhisatta? On the fourteenth day, when it was realized that ‘Tomorrow will be the full moon of Visākha.’ Then, it is said, he thought: ‘Just as these people surrounded me when I was a householder, so they do now. What is the use of this group?’ Discontented with the company of the group, he thought, ‘I will go today.’ Then he reconsidered: ‘Today is not the right time. If I go now, all of them will know. I will go tomorrow.’ On that day, the villagers of a village similar to Uruvelā invited them for the next day’s meal. They prepared milk-rice for those eighty-four thousand renunciants and for the Great Being. Then, on the next day, the Great Being, after taking his meal with those renunciants in that very village, went back to his dwelling place. There, those renunciants, having completed their duties to the Great Being, entered their respective day and night quarters. The Bodhisatta also entered his leaf hut and sat down.

“Ṭhite majjhanhike kāle, sannisīvesu pakkhisu;

Saṇateva brahāraññaṃ, taṃ bhayaṃ paṭibhāti ma”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.15);

‘When it is midday,

And the birds have settled down,

The great forest seems to resound—

That fear appears to me.’

Evarūpe [M 2.0050] avivekārāmānaṃ bhayakāle sabbasattānaṃ sadarathakāleyeva – “ayaṃ kālo”ti nikkhamitvā paṇṇasālāya dvāraṃ pidahitvā bodhimaṇḍābhimukho pāyāsi. Aññadāpi ca tasmiṃ ṭhāne vicaranto bodhimaṇḍaṃ passati, nisīdituṃ panassa cittaṃ na namitapubbaṃ. Taṃ divasaṃ panassa ñāṇaṃ paripākagataṃ, tasmā alaṅkataṃ bodhimaṇḍaṃ disvā ārohanatthāya cittaṃ uppannaṃ. So dakkhiṇadisābhāgena upagamma padakkhiṇaṃ katvā puratthimadisābhāge cuddasahatthaṃ pallaṅkaṃ paññapetvā caturaṅgavīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā – “yāva buddho na homi, na tāva ito vuṭṭhahāmī”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā nisīdi. Idamassa vūpakāsaṃ sandhāya – “ekova gaṇamhā vūpakaṭṭho vihāsī”ti vuttaṃ.

At such a time—a time of fear for those who do not delight in seclusion, a time of agitation for all beings—thinking, ‘This is the time,’ he went out, closed the door of the leaf-hut, and set out facing the Bodhi-maṇḍa. Although on other occasions while wandering in that place he would see the Bodhi-maṇḍa, his mind had never before inclined to sit there. On that day, however, his wisdom had reached maturity; therefore, upon seeing the adorned Bodhi-maṇḍa, the thought to ascend it arose. Approaching from the southern side, he circumambulated it to the right, and on the eastern side he prepared a seat fourteen hands in length. Having resolved on the fourfold effort, he made the vow, ‘I will not rise from this seat until I am a Buddha,’ and sat down. It was in reference to this seclusion of his that it was said: ‘Alone, withdrawn from the group, he dwelt.’

Aññeneva [P 2.0459] tānīti te kira sāyaṃ bodhisattassa upaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā paṇṇasālaṃ parivāretvā nisinnā “ativikālo jāto, upadhārethā”ti vatvā paṇṇasālaṃ vivaritvā taṃ apassantāpi “kuhiṃ gato”ti nānubandhiṃsu, “gaṇavāse nibbinno eko viharitukāmo maññe mahāpuriso, buddhabhūtaṃyeva naṃ passissāmā”ti vatvā antojambudīpābhimukhā cārikaṃ pakkantā.

It is said that in the evening, they came to attend on the Bodhisatta. Having surrounded the leaf-hut and sat down, they said, 'It has become very late; let us ascertain.' Then, opening the leaf-hut and not seeing him, they did not follow, though wondering, 'Where has he gone?' They thought, 'The Great Being, weary of living in a community, desires to dwell alone, we suppose. We shall see him only when he has become a Buddha.' Having said this, facing towards the interior of Jambudīpa, they departed on their journey.

Bodhisattaabhivesavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Bodhisatta's Resolve

57. Vāsūpagatassāti bodhimaṇḍe ekarattivāsaṃ upagatassa. Rahogatassāti rahasi gatassa. Paṭisallīnassāti ekībhāvavasena nilīnassa. Kicchanti dukkhaṃ. Cavati ca upapajjati cāti idaṃ dvayaṃ pana aparāparaṃ cutipaṭisandhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Jarāmaraṇassāti ettha yasmā pabbajanto jiṇṇabyādhimatteyeva disvā pabbajito, tasmāssa jarāmaraṇameva upaṭṭhāti. Tenevāha [V 2.0045] – “jarāmaraṇassā”ti. Iti jarāmaraṇaṃ mūlaṃ katvā abhiniviṭṭhassa bhavaggato otarantassa viya – atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassissa bodhisattassa etadahosi.

57. 'Of one who has taken up residence' (vāsūpagatassa) means: of one who has undertaken a one-night residence at the Bodhi-seat. 'Of one who has gone to a solitary place' (rahogatassa) means: of one who has gone into seclusion. 'Of one who is in seclusion' (paṭisallīnassa) means: of one who is secluded by way of being alone. 'Distress' (kicchaṃ) means suffering. The pair 'passes away and is reborn' refers to the successive cycle of death and rebirth-linking. Regarding 'of old age and death' (jarāmaraṇassa): here, because when he went forth, he did so having seen only an old person, a sick person, and a dead person, therefore only old age and death were present to his mind. For that reason, it is said, 'of old age and death.' Thus, for him who was firmly intent, having made old age and death the foundation, as if descending from the summit of existence—then, monks, this thought arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī:

Yonisomanasikārāti upāyamanasikārā pathamanasikārā. Aniccādīni hi aniccāditova manasikaroto yonisomanasikāro nāma hoti. Ayañca – “kismiṃ nu kho satijātiādīni honti, kismiṃ asati na hontī”ti udayabbayānupassanāvasena pavattattā tesaṃ aññataro[M 2.0051]. Tasmāssa ito yonisomanasikārā iminā upāyamanasikārena ahu paññāya abhisamayo, bodhisattassa paññāya yasmiṃ sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, tena jarāmaraṇakāraṇena saddhiṃ samāgamo ahosi. Kiṃ pana tanti? Jāti. Tenāha – “jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī”ti. Yā cāyaṃ jarāmaraṇassa kāraṇapariggāhikā paññā, tāya saddhiṃ bodhisattassa samāgamo ahosīti ayamettha attho. Etenupāyena sabbapadāni veditabbāni.

'Wise attention' (yonisomanasikāra) means attention through the right means, attention to the path. For when one attends to impermanence and so on as impermanence, it is called wise attention. And this attention—which proceeds by way of contemplating arising and passing away, asking, 'When what exists, do birth and so on occur? When what does not exist, do they not occur?'—is one of those types. Therefore, from this wise attention, from this attention through the right means, there arose for him a realization through wisdom; there was a meeting for the Bodhisatta, through wisdom, with that cause in the presence of which aging and death occur. But what is that? Birth. Therefore, he said, 'When there is birth, aging and death occur.' The meaning here is this: there was a meeting of the Bodhisatta with that wisdom which grasps the cause of aging and death. By this method, all the terms should be understood.

Nāmarūpe kho sati viññāṇanti ettha pana saṅkhāresu sati viññāṇanti ca, avijjāya sati saṅkhārāti ca vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, tadubhayampi na gahitaṃ. Kasmā? Avijjāsaṅkhārā hi atīto bhavo tehi saddhiṃ ayaṃ vipassanā na ghaṭiyati. Mahāpuriso hi paccuppannavasena abhiniviṭṭhoti. Nanu ca avijjāsaṅkhārehi adiṭṭhehi na sakkā buddhena bhavitunti. Saccaṃ na sakkā, iminā pana te bhavaupādānataṇhāvaseneva diṭṭhāti. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne [P 2.0460] vitthārato paṭiccasamuppādakathā kathetabbā. Sā panesā visuddhimagge kathitāva.

Regarding the statement, 'When there is name-and-form, there is consciousness': here, it should have been said, 'When there are formations, there is consciousness,' and 'When there is ignorance, there are formations,' but both of these were not taken up. Why? Because ignorance and formations are a past existence, and this insight meditation does not connect with them. For the Great Being was intent on the present existence. 'Is it not so that one cannot become a Buddha without having seen ignorance and formations?' Truly, one cannot. However, by this Bodhisatta, they were seen by way of existence, clinging, and craving. At this point, the discourse on dependent origination should be explained in detail, but that has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga.

58. Paccudāvattatīti paṭinivattati. Katamaṃ panettha viññāṇaṃ paccudāvattatīti? Paṭisandhiviññāṇampi vipassanāñāṇampi. Tattha paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ paccayato paṭinivattati, vipassanāñāṇaṃ ārammaṇato. Ubhayampi nāmarūpaṃ nātikkamati, nāmarūpato paraṃ na gacchati. Ettāvatā jāyetha vātiādīsu viññāṇe nāmarūpassa paccaye honte, nāmarūpe ca viññāṇassa paccaye honte, dvīsupi aññamaññapaccayesu hontesu ettakena jāyetha vā…pe… upapajjetha vā, ito hi paraṃ kiṃ aññaṃ jāyeyya vā…pe… upapajjeyya vā. Nanu etadeva jāyati ca…pe… upapajjati cāti? Evaṃ saddhiṃ aparāparacutipaṭisandhīhi pañca padāni dassetvā puna taṃ ettāvatāti vuttamatthaṃ niyyātento – “yadidaṃ nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti vatvā tato paraṃ anulomapaccayākāravasena viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpamūlaṃ [V 2.0046] āyatimpi jātijarāmaraṇaṃ dassetuṃ nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanantiādimāha. Tattha kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotīti sakalassa jātijarāmaraṇasokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsādibhedassa dukkharāsissa nibbatti hoti. Iti mahāpuriso sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa nibbattiṃ addasa.

58. 'It turns back' (paccudāvattati) means it reverts. Which consciousness turns back here? Both rebirth-linking consciousness and insight knowledge. Of these, rebirth-linking consciousness turns back from its cause, while insight knowledge turns back from its object. Neither transcends name-and-form; neither goes beyond name-and-form. In phrases such as 'To this extent one might be born,' when consciousness is a condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form is a condition for consciousness—when both exist as mutual conditions—to that extent one might be born... or reappear. For what else beyond this could be born... or reappear? Is it not just this that is born... and reappears? Thus, having shown the five terms together with successive deaths and rebirths, and then concluding the meaning stated as 'to this extent,' he said: 'That is to say, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form.' After that, to show future birth, aging, and death rooted in name-and-form with consciousness as condition, by way of the forward order of conditions, he said, 'With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases,' and so on. Therein, 'the arising of this whole mass of suffering occurs' means the production of the entire mass of suffering, differentiated as birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, the Great Being saw the arising of the entire round of suffering.

59. Samudayo [M 2.0052] samudayoti khoti nibbatti nibbattīti kho. Pubbe ananussutesūti na anussutesu assutapubbesu. Cakkhuṃ udapādītiādīsu udayadassanapaññāvesā. Dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu, ñātakaraṇaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, pajānanaṭṭhena paññā, nibbijjhitvā paṭivijjhitvā uppannaṭṭhena vijjā, obhāsaṭṭhena ca ālokoti vuttā. Yathāha – “cakkhuṃ udapādīti dassanaṭṭhena. Ñāṇaṃ udapādīti ñātaṭṭhena. Paññā udapādīti pajānanaṭṭhena. Vijjā udapādīti paṭivedhaṭṭhena. Āloko udapādīti obhāsaṭṭhena. Cakkhudhammo dassanaṭṭho attho. Ñāṇadhammo ñātaṭṭho attho. Paññādhammo pajānanaṭṭho attho. Vijjādhammo paṭivedhaṭṭho attho. Āloko dhammo obhāsaṭṭho attho”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.39). Ettakehi padehi kiṃ [P 2.0461] kathitanti? Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotīti paccayasañjānanamattaṃ kathitaṃ. Athavā vīthipaṭipannā taruṇavipassanā kathitāti.

59. 'Arising, arising' (samudayo, samudayo) means origination, origination. 'In things not previously heard' (pubbe ananussutesu) means in things not learned, not heard before. In phrases such as 'the eye arose,' this refers to the wisdom that sees arising. It is called 'eye' (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing; 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of the function of knowing; 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of understanding; 'true knowledge' (vijjā) in the sense of having arisen after breaking through and penetrating; and 'light' (āloko) in the sense of illumination. As it is said: '“The eye arose” in the sense of seeing. “Knowledge arose” in the sense of knowing. “Wisdom arose” in the sense of understanding. “True knowledge arose” in the sense of penetration. “Light arose” in the sense of illumination' (Paṭis I 1). What is taught by these terms? Merely the recognition of conditions—'When this exists, that comes to be'—is taught. Or, fledgling insight that has entered upon the path is taught.

61. Adhigato kho myāyanti adhigato kho me ayaṃ. Maggoti vipassanāmaggo. Bodhāyāti catusaccabujjhanatthāya, nibbānabujjhanatthāya eva vā. Api ca bujjhatīti bodhi, ariyamaggassetaṃ nāmaṃ, tadatthāyātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Vipassanāmaggamūlako hi ariyamaggoti. Idāni taṃ maggaṃ niyyātento – “yadidaṃ nāmarūpanirodhātiādimāha. Ettha ca viññāṇanirodhotiādīhi paccattapadehi nibbānameva kathitaṃ. Iti mahāpuriso sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa anibbattinirodhaṃ addasa.

61. Indeed, this path has been attained by me. The path means the path of insight. For awakening means for the purpose of understanding the Four Noble Truths, or indeed for the realization of Nibbāna. Furthermore, awakening is so called because one awakens; this is a name for the Noble Path, and it is also said to be for that purpose. For the Noble Path has its root in the path of insight. Now, presenting that path, he said, 'That is, this cessation of name-and-form,' and so on. And here, with terms such as 'with the cessation of consciousness,' Nibbāna itself is described. Thus, the Great Being saw the non-re-arising cessation of all the suffering of the round.

62. Nirodho nirodhoti khoti anibbatti anibbattiti kho. Cakkhuntiādīni vuttatthāneva. Idha pana sabbeheva etehi padehi – “imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hotī”ti nirodhasañjānanamattameva kathitaṃ, athavā vuṭṭhānagāminī balavavipassanā kathitāti.

62. 'Cessation, cessation,' indeed, means 'non-re-arising, non-re-arising,' indeed. The terms 'eye' and so on have the same meaning as already stated. Here, however, with all these terms—'When this is not, this does not come to be'—only the mere recognition of cessation is stated, or else powerful insight leading to emergence is stated.

63. Aparena samayenāti evaṃ paccayañca paccayanirodhañca viditvā tato aparabhāge. Upādānakkhandhesūti upādānassa paccayabhūtesu khandhesu. Udayabbayānupassīti tameva paṭhamaṃ diṭṭhaṃ udayañca vayañca anupassamāno. Vihāsīti sikhāpattaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanaṃ vahanto vihari. Idaṃ kasmā vuttaṃ? Sabbeyeva hi pūritapāramino bodhisattā pacchimabhave puttassa jātadivase [V 2.0047][M 2.0053] mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā pabbajitvā padhānamanuyuñjitvā bodhipallaṅkamāruyha mārabalaṃ vidhamitvā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussaranti, dutiyayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhenti, tatiyayāme paccayākāraṃ sammasitvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānato uṭṭhāya pañcasu khandhesu abhinivisitvā udayabbayavasena samapaññāsa lakkhaṇāni disvā yāva gotrabhuñāṇā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā ariyamaggena sakale buddhaguṇe paṭivijjhanti. Ayampi mahāpuriso pūritapāramī. So yathāvuttaṃ sabbaṃ anukkamaṃ katvā pacchimayāme ānāpānacatutthajjhānato uṭṭhāya pañcasu khandhesu abhinivisitvā vuttappakāraṃ udayabbayavipassanaṃ ārabhi. Taṃ dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ.

63. 'At another time' means: thus having understood both the condition and the cessation of the condition, in the period thereafter. 'In the aggregates of clinging' means: in the aggregates that are the condition for clinging. 'Observing arising and passing away' means: repeatedly observing that very arising and passing away seen at first. 'He dwelt' means: he dwelt maintaining the insight leading to emergence that had reached its peak. Why was this said? Because all Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections, in their final existence, on the day their son is born, go forth in the great renunciation, and having gone forth and applied themselves to the striving, they ascend the seat of awakening, dispel Māra’s forces, and in the first watch of the night recollect their past lives; in the second watch, they purify the divine eye; and in the third watch, having reflected on the causal pattern, they rise from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, attend to the five aggregates, and seeing the fifty characteristics by way of arising and passing away, they develop insight up to the change-of-lineage knowledge and with the noble path penetrate all the qualities of a Buddha. This Great Being, too, had fulfilled the perfections. Having followed the entire sequence as described, in the last watch of the night, rising from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, he attended to the five aggregates and began the insight into arising and passing away of the kind described. To show that, this was said.

Tattha [P 2.0462] iti rūpanti idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, ito uddhaṃ rūpaṃ natthīti ruppanasabhāvañceva bhūtupādāyabhedañca ādiṃ katvā lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānavasena anavasesarūpapariggaho vutto. Iti rūpassa samudayoti iminā evaṃ pariggahitassa rūpassa samudayadassanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha itīti evaṃ samudayo hotīti attho. Tassa vitthāro – “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo, taṇhāsamudayā rūpasamudayo, kammasamudayā rūpasamudayo, āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayoti, nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passatī”ti evaṃ veditabbo. Atthaṅgamepi “avijjānirodhā rūpanirodho…pe… vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa nirodhaṃ passatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) ayamassa vitthāro.

Herein, by 'Thus is form' is meant: 'This is form, this much is form, beyond this there is no form.' In this way, beginning with the nature of being afflicted and the distinction between primary and derived matter, the exhaustive comprehension of form by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause is stated. By 'Thus is the arising of form,' the seeing of the arising of form so comprehended is stated. Therein, 'thus' means 'in this way arising occurs.' Its detailed explanation is to be understood thus: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is an arising of form; with the arising of craving, there is an arising of form; with the arising of kamma, there is an arising of form; with the arising of nutriment, there is an arising of form.' In this way, by seeing the characteristic of generation, one sees the arising of the form aggregate. In the case of passing away also: 'With the cessation of ignorance, there is cessation of form…' and so on. By seeing the characteristic of alteration, one sees the cessation of the form aggregate. This is its detailed explanation.

Iti vedanātiādīsupi ayaṃ vedanā, ettakā vedanā, ito uddhaṃ vedanā natthi. Ayaṃ saññā, ime saṅkhārā, idaṃ viññāṇaṃ, ettakaṃ viññāṇaṃ, ito uddhaṃ viññāṇaṃ natthīti vedayitasañjānanaabhisaṅkharaṇavijānanasabhāvañceva sukhādirūpasaññādi phassādi cakkhuviññāṇādi bhedañca ādiṃ katvā lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānavasena anavasesavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇapariggaho vutto. Iti vedanāya samudayotiādīhi pana evaṃ pariggahitānaṃ vedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇānaṃ samudayadassanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāpi itīti evaṃ samudayo hotīti attho. Tesampi vitthāro – “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) rūpe vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tīsu khandhesu “āhārasamudayā”ti avatvā “phassasamudayā”ti vattabbaṃ. Viññāṇakkhandhe “nāmarūpasamudayā”ti [M 2.0054] atthaṅgamapadampi tesaṃyeva vasena yojetabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana udayabbayavinicchayo sabbākāraparipūro visuddhimagge vutto. Tassa pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassino viharatoti tassa vipassissa bodhisattassa imesu rūpādīsu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu samapaññāsalakkhaṇavasena udayabbayānupassino viharato yathānukkamena vaḍḍhite vipassanāñāṇe anuppādanirodhena nirujjhamānehi [V 2.0048] āsavasaṅkhātehi kilesehi anupādāya aggahetvāva cittaṃ vimuccati, tadetaṃ [P 2.0463] maggakkhaṇe vimuccati nāma, phalakkhaṇe vimuttaṃ nāma; maggakkhaṇe vā vimuttañceva vimuccati ca, phalakkhaṇe vimuttameva.

In the case of 'Thus is feeling,' and so on, it is also the same: 'This is feeling, this much is feeling, beyond this there is no feeling. This is perception... These are formations... This is consciousness, this much is consciousness, beyond this there is no consciousness.' In this way, beginning with the natures of experiencing, perceiving, forming, and cognizing, and with the distinctions of pleasant feeling etc., perception of form etc., contact etc., and eye-consciousness etc., the exhaustive comprehension of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause is stated. Furthermore, by 'Thus is the arising of feeling,' and so on, the seeing of the arising of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, so comprehended, is stated. Therein also, 'thus' means 'in this way arising occurs.' Their detailed explanation should be understood in the same way as stated for form: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling.' This, however, is the difference: for the three mental aggregates, instead of saying 'from the arising of nutriment,' it should be said 'from the arising of contact.' For the consciousness aggregate, it should be said 'from the arising of name-and-form.' The term for passing away should also be applied in relation to these respective causes. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, the determination of arising and passing away, complete in all aspects, is stated by me in the Visuddhimagga. 'For him who dwells observing the arising and passing away in the five aggregates of clinging' means: for that Bodhisatta Vipassī, while he was dwelling observing the arising and passing away in these five aggregates of clinging—form and so on—by way of the fifty characteristics, as his insight knowledge developed in sequence, his mind was liberated from the defilements known as taints as they ceased with a non-re-arising cessation, by not clinging, by not grasping. That mind, at the moment of the path, is called 'is being liberated'; at the moment of fruition, it is called 'has been liberated.' Or, at the moment of the path, it is both 'has been liberated' and 'is being liberated'; at the moment of fruition, it is simply 'has been liberated'.

Ettāvatā ca mahāpuriso sabbabandhanā vippamutto sūriyarasmisamphuṭṭhamiva padumaṃ suvikasitacittasantāno cattāri maggañāṇāni, cattāri phalañāṇāni, catasso paṭisambhidā, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ, cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni, sakale ca buddhaguṇe hatthagate katvā paripuṇṇasaṅkappo bodhipallaṅke nisinnova –

And thus the Great Being, completely freed from all bonds, with a mental continuum as fully blossomed as a lotus touched by the sun's rays, having brought into his grasp the four path-knowledges, the four fruit-knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, the knowledge that discerns the four kinds of birth, the knowledge that discerns the five destinies, the six unshared knowledges, and all the qualities of a Buddha, with his aspiration fulfilled, was seated upon the seat of enlightenment—

“Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ;

Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

“Through countless births in saṃsāra have I wandered, not finding, seeking the house-builder. Painful is birth again and again.

Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhataṃ;

Visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā”ti. (dha. pa. 153, 154);

O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build a house again. All your rafters are broken; the ridgepole is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of cravings.”

“Ayoghanahatasseva, jalato jātavedaso;

Anupubbūpasantassa, yathā na ñāyate gati.

“Just as of a blazing fire on iron struck by a hammer, when gradually it is extinguished, the destination is not known;

Evaṃ sammāvimuttānaṃ, kāmabandhoghatārinaṃ;

Paññāpetuṃ gati natthi, pattānaṃ acalaṃ sukha”nti. (udā. 80);

So it is for those rightly liberated, who have crossed the flood of the bond of sensuality, who have attained unshakable happiness: there is no means to designate their destination.”

Evaṃ manasi karonto sarade sūriyo viya, puṇṇacando viya ca virocitthāti.

Reflecting thus in his mind, he was resplendent, like the sun in autumn and like the full moon.

Dutiyabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the commentary on the second recitation portion.

Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse of Brahmā's Request

64. Tatiyabhāṇavāre [V 2.0049][M 2.0055] yaṃnūnāhaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyanti yadi panāhaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ. Ayaṃ pana vitakko kadā uppannoti? Buddhabhūtassa aṭṭhame sattāhe. So kira buddho hutvā sattāhaṃ bodhipallaṅke nisīdi, sattāhaṃ bodhipallaṅkaṃ olokento aṭṭhāsi, sattāhaṃ ratanacaṅkame caṅkami, sattāhaṃ ratanagabbhe dhammaṃ vicinanto nisīdi, sattāhaṃ ajapālanigrodhe nisīdi, sattāhaṃ mucalinde nisīdi, sattāhaṃ rājāyatane nisīdi. Tato uṭṭhāya aṭṭhame sattāhe puna āgantvā ajapālanigrodhe nisinnamattasseva [P 2.0464] sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo ayañceva ito anantaro ca vitakko uppannoti.

64. In the third recitation portion, regarding the phrase, 'What if I were to teach the Dhamma?', this means, 'If I were to teach the Dhamma.' As to this thought, when did it arise? It arose in the eighth week after he had become a Buddha. For, it is said, having become a Buddha, he sat for one week at the seat of enlightenment; for one week he stood gazing at the seat of enlightenment; for one week he walked on the jeweled promenade; for one week he sat in the jeweled chamber contemplating the Dhamma; for one week he sat at the Goatherd's Banyan tree; for one week he sat at the Mucalinda tree; for one week he sat at the Rājāyatana tree. Then, having arisen from there, in the eighth week, upon returning and just as he was seated at the Goatherd's Banyan tree, this very thought, which is practiced and well-practiced by all Buddhas, and the one immediately following it, arose.

Tattha adhigatoti paṭividdho. Dhammoti catusaccadhammo. Gambhīroti uttānabhāvapaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ. Duddasoti gambhīrattāva duddaso dukkhena daṭṭhabbo, na sakkā sukhena daṭṭhuṃ. Duddasattāva duranubodho dukkhena avabujjhitabbo, na sakkā sukhena avabujjhituṃ. Santoti nibbuto. Paṇītoti atappako. Idaṃ dvayaṃ lokuttarameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atakkāvacaroti takkena avacaritabbo ogāhitabbo na hoti, ñāṇeneva avacaritabbo. Nipuṇoti saṇho. Paṇḍitavedanīyoti sammāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipannehi paṇḍitehi veditabbo. Ālayarāmāti sattā pañcasu kāmaguṇesu allīyanti, tasmā te ālayāti vuccanti. Aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni ālayanti, tasmā ālayāti vuccanti. Tehi ālayehi ramantīti ālayarāmā. Ālayesu ratāti ālayaratā. Ālayesu suṭṭhu muditāti ālayasammuditā.
