Yatheva hi susajjitaṃ pupphaphalabharitarukkhādisampannaṃ uyyānaṃ paviṭṭho rājā tāya tāya sampattiyā ramati, pamudito āmodito hoti, na ukkaṇṭhati, sāyaṃ nikkhamituṃ na icchati, evamimehipi kāmālayataṇhālayehi sattā ramanti, saṃsāravaṭṭe pamuditā anukkaṇṭhitā vasanti. Tena nesaṃ bhagavā duvidhampi ālayaṃ uyyānabhūmiṃ viya dassento – “ālayarāmā”tiādimāha.

Therein, realized means penetrated. Dhamma means the four-truth Dhamma. Profound: this is a term that negates a state of being obvious. Hard to see: because it is profound, it is hard to see; it is to be seen with difficulty, it cannot be seen with ease. Hard to understand: because it is hard to see, it is hard to understand; it is to be understood with difficulty, it cannot be understood with ease. Peaceful means extinguished. Sublime means excellent. These two are spoken of with reference only to the supramundane. Beyond the scope of logic means it is not to be traversed or penetrated by logic; it is to be traversed only by knowledge. Subtle means fine. To be experienced by the wise means to be known by the wise who have undertaken the right practice. Delighting in attachments: beings cling to the five strands of sensual pleasure, therefore these are called attachments (`ālaya`). Or, the one hundred and eight elaborations of craving are what they cling to, therefore these are called attachments. Because they delight in these attachments, they are delighting in attachments. Because they are fond of attachments, they are fond of attachments. Because they greatly rejoice in attachments, they are greatly rejoicing in attachments. For just as a king, having entered a well-adorned park complete with trees laden with flowers and fruit, delights in its various splendors, is joyful and happy, does not become weary, and does not wish to leave even in the evening, so too do these beings delight in these attachments to sensual pleasures and attachments to craving; they dwell in the round of saṃsāra, joyful and not weary. Therefore the Blessed One, showing both kinds of attachment to be like the grounds of a park, said, 'delighting in attachments,' and so on.

Yadidanti nipāto, tassa ṭhānaṃ sandhāya – “yaṃ ida”nti, paṭiccasamuppādaṃ sandhāya – “yo aya”nti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādoti imesaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā, idappaccayatā ca sā paṭiccasamuppādo cāti idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo. Saṅkhārādipaccayānaṃ [M 2.0056] avijjādīnaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbaṃ nibbānameva. Yasmā hi taṃ āgamma sabbasaṅkhāravipphanditāni sammanti [V 2.0050] vūpasammanti tasmā – “sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti vuccati. Yasmā ca taṃ āgamma sabbe upadhayo paṭinissaṭṭhā honti, sabbā taṇhā khīyanti[P 2.0465], sabbe kilesarāgā virajjanti, sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, tasmā “sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho”ti vuccati. Sā panesā taṇhā bhavena bhavaṃ, phalena vā saddhiṃ kammaṃ vinati saṃsibbatīti katvā vānanti vuccati. Tato vānato nikkhantanti nibbānaṃ. So mamassa kilamathoti yā ajānantānaṃ desanā nāma, so mama kilamatho assa, sā mama vihesā assāti attho. Kāyakilamatho ceva kāyavihesā ca assāti vuttaṃ hoti, citte pana ubhayampetaṃ buddhānaṃ natthi.

Yadidaṃ is a particle. With reference to its position, the meaning should be seen as yaṃ idaṃ ('this which is'); with reference to dependent origination, as yo ayaṃ ('this which is'). Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo (specific conditionality as dependent origination): the conditions of these things are 'specific conditions' (`idappaccayā`); 'specific conditions' themselves are 'specific conditionality' (`idappaccayatā`); and that which is specific conditionality and is dependent origination is thus idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo. This is a designation for the conditions beginning with ignorance which are the conditions for formations and so on. The stilling of all formations, and so on, all refer to Nibbāna itself. For, since on account of it all agitations of formations are stilled and quieted, it is called 'the stilling of all formations.' And since on account of it all substrates are relinquished, all cravings are destroyed, all passions of defilement fade away, and all suffering ceases, it is therefore called 'the relinquishing of all substrates, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation.' Furthermore, that craving is called vāna because it weaves or stitches one existence to another, or karma with its result. Nibbāna means 'gone forth from that vāna (weaving).' That would be a weariness for me: the meaning is that this teaching to those who do not know would be a weariness for me, would be a vexation for me. This means it would be a bodily weariness and a bodily vexation. But in the minds of Buddhas, neither of these two exists.

65. Apissūti anubrūhanatthe nipāto. So – “na kevalaṃ etadahosi, imāpi gāthā paṭibhaṃsū”ti dīpeti. Vipassintiādīsu vipassissa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassāti attho. Anacchariyāti anuacchariyā. Paṭibhaṃsūti paṭibhānasaṅkhātassa ñāṇassa gocarā ahesuṃ, parivitakkayitabbataṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

65. The particle apissu is used in the sense of amplification. It indicates: 'Not only did this thought occur, but these verses also appeared to him.' In phrases such as of Vipassī, the meaning is 'of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Vipassī.' Anacchariyā means repeatedly marvelous. Paṭibhaṃsū means they became the object of the knowledge known as inspiration (`paṭibhāna`); they attained a state fit to be repeatedly reflected upon.

Kicchenāti dukkhena, na dukkhāya paṭipadāya. Buddhānañhi cattāropi maggā sukhapaṭipadāva honti. Pāramīpūraṇakāle pana sarāgasadosasamohasseva sato āgatāgatānaṃ yācakānaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ sīsaṃ chinditvā galalohitaṃ nīharitvā suañjitāni akkhīni uppāṭetvā kulavaṃsapadīpakaṃ puttaṃ manāpacāriniṃ bhariyanti evamādīni dentassa aññāni ca khantivādisadisesu attabhāvesu chejjabhejjādīni pāpuṇantassa āgamanīyapaṭipadaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Halanti ettha hakāro nipātamatto, alanti attho. Pakāsitunti desetuṃ; evaṃ kicchena adhigatassa dhammassa alaṃ desetuṃ; ko attho desitenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rāgadosaparetehīti rāgadosaphuṭṭhehi rāgadosānugatehi vā.

"Kicchena" means with difficulty, that is, with suffering; not by a difficult practice. For the Buddhas, all four paths are indeed paths of ease. However, this was said with reference to the practice that leads to the path, which one undertakes during the time of fulfilling the perfections while still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion: of one who gives to beggars who come again and again an adorned and prepared head, having cut it off; who extracts the blood from his throat; who plucks out his well-anointed eyes; who gives away his son, the lamp of his lineage, and his beloved wife, and so forth; and of one who, in other existences such as that of the Khantivādi ascetic, undergoes cutting, breaking, and the like. Herein, in the word ‘halaṃ,’ the ‘ha’ is merely a particle; the meaning is ‘alaṃ,’ that is, ‘of no use.’ ‘Pakāsituṃ’ means ‘to teach’; thus, it is of no use to teach the Dhamma attained with difficulty. What is the benefit of teaching it? This is what is said. ‘Overcome by lust and hatred’ means touched by lust and hatred, or followed by lust and hatred.

Paṭisotagāminti niccādīnaṃ paṭisotaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāsubhanti evaṃ gataṃ catusaccadhammaṃ. Rāgarattāti kāmarāgena bhavarāgena diṭṭhirāgena ca rattā. Na dakkhantīti aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā asubhanti iminā sabhāvena na passissanti[M 2.0057], te apassante ko sakkhissati evaṃ gāhāpetuṃ? Tamokhandhena āvuṭāti [P 2.0466] avijjārāsinā ajjhotthaṭā.

Going against the stream: this means the Four Noble Truths, which go against the stream of permanence, pleasure, self, and beauty, being themselves impermanent, suffering, not-self, and foul. Infatuated with lust: they are infatuated with sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust associated with wrong views. They will not see: they will not see it as having this nature of being impermanent, suffering, not-self, and foul. Who will be able to make them, who do not see, grasp it thus? Shrouded by the mass of darkness: they are overwhelmed by the heap of ignorance.

Appossukkatāyāti nirussukkabhāvena, adesetukāmatāyāti attho. Kasmā panassa evaṃ cittaṃ nami? Nanu esa – “mutto mocessāmī, tiṇṇo tāressāmi”,

To disinclination: this means to a state of being without zeal; the meaning is a state of not wishing to teach. But why did his mind incline thus? Is it not so that he thought: “Being freed, I will free others; having crossed over, I will help others cross over”?

“Kiṃ [V 2.0051] me aññātavesena, dhammaṃ sacchikatenidha;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, santāressaṃ sadevaka”nti.

“What use is it for me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown guise? Having attained omniscience, I shall lead the world with its gods to deliverance.”

Patthanaṃ katvā pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ pattoti. Saccametaṃ, paccavekkhaṇānubhāvena panassa evaṃ cittaṃ nami. Tassa hi sabbaññutaṃ patvā sattānaṃ kilesagahanataṃ dhammassa ca gambhīrataṃ paccavekkhantassa sattānaṃ kilesagahanatā ca dhammagambhīratā ca sabbākārena pākaṭā jātā. Athassa – “ime sattā kañjikapuṇṇalābu viya takkabharitacāṭi viya vasātelapītapilotikā viya añjanamakkhitahatthā viya kilesabharitā atisaṃkiliṭṭhā rāgarattā dosaduṭṭhā mohamūḷhā, te kiṃ nāma paṭivijjhissantī”ti cintayato kilesagahanapaccavekkhaṇānubhāvenāpi evaṃ cittaṃ nami.

(It is objected:) Did he not attain omniscience after making the aspiration and fulfilling the perfections? This is true. However, his mind inclined thus through the power of reflection. For when he, having attained omniscience, reflected on the thicket of beings' defilements and the profundity of the Dhamma, the thicket of beings' defilements and the profundity of the Dhamma became fully apparent in every way. Then, as he considered—“These beings are filled with defilements, like a gourd filled with sour gruel, like a pot filled with buttermilk, like a rag soaked in fat and oil, like hands smeared with sooty unguent; they are excessively defiled, infatuated with lust, corrupted by hatred, and deluded by ignorance. What, then, will they penetrate?”—his mind inclined thus also through the power of reflecting on the thicket of defilements.

“Ayañca dhammo pathavīsandhārakaudakakkhandho viya gambhīro, pabbatena paṭicchādetvā ṭhapito sāsapo viya duddaso, satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādanaṃ viya duranubodho, nanu mayā hi imaṃ dhammaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ vāyamantena adinnaṃ dānaṃ nāma natthi, arakkhitaṃ sīlaṃ nāma natthi, aparipūritā kāci pāramī nāma natthi. Tassa me nirussāhaṃ viya mārabalaṃ vidhamantassāpi pathavī na kampittha, paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantassāpi na kampittha, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhentassāpi na kampittha, pacchimayāme pana paṭiccasamuppādaṃ paṭivijjhantasseva me dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha. Iti mādisenāpi tikkhañāṇena kicchenevāyaṃ dhammo paṭividdho taṃ lokiyamahājanā kathaṃ paṭivijjhissantī”ti dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇānubhāvenāpi evaṃ cittaṃ namīti veditabbaṃ.

“And this Dhamma is as deep as the mass of water that supports the earth, as hard to see as a mustard seed placed and covered by a mountain, as difficult to penetrate as touching tip to tip of a hair split a hundredfold. Indeed, for me, while striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift left ungiven, no virtue left unguarded, no perfection left unfulfilled. Even when I was scattering the army of Māra as if without effort, the earth did not tremble. Nor did it tremble when I recollected past lives in the first watch of the night, nor when I purified the divine eye in the middle watch. But in the last watch, only when I was penetrating dependent origination did the ten-thousandfold world system tremble. Thus, this Dhamma was penetrated only with difficulty even by one like me with sharp wisdom—how then will the great mass of worldly people penetrate it?” It should be understood that his mind inclined thus also through the power of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma.

Apica [M 2.0058] brahmunā yācite desetukāmatāyapissa evaṃ cittaṃ [P 2.0467] nami. Jānāti hi bhagavā – “mama appossukkatāya citte namamāne maṃ mahābrahmā dhammadesanaṃ yācissati, ime ca sattā brahmagarukā, te ‘satthā kira dhammaṃ na desetukāmo ahosi, atha naṃ mahābrahmā yācitvā desāpesi, santo vata bho dhammo, paṇīto vata bho dhammo’ti maññamānā sussūsissantī”ti. Imampissa kāraṇaṃ paṭicca appossukkatāya cittaṃ nami, no dhammadesanāyāti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, his mind also inclined thus due to his desire to teach only when requested by Brahmā. For the Blessed One knows: “When my mind inclines to disinclination, the Great Brahmā will request me to teach the Dhamma. And these beings are respectful of Brahmā. Thinking, ‘It seems the Teacher was unwilling to teach the Dhamma, but then the Great Brahmā, having requested him, caused him to teach. Oh, how peaceful is the Dhamma! Oh, how excellent is the Dhamma!’ they will want to listen carefully.” It should be understood that, on account of this reason also, his mind inclined to disinclination, not away from teaching the Dhamma.

66. Aññatarassāti ettha kiñcāpi “aññataro”ti vuttaṃ, atha kho imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe jeṭṭhakamahābrahmā esoti veditabbo. Nassati vata bho lokoti so kira imaṃ saddaṃ tathā nicchāresi, yathā dasasahassilokadhātubrahmāno sutvā sabbe sannipatiṃsu. Yatra hi nāmāti [V 2.0052] yasmiṃ nāma loke. Purato pāturahosīti tehi dasahi brahmasahassehi saddhiṃ pāturahosi. Apparajakkhajātikāti paññāmaye akkhimhi appaṃ parittaṃ rāgadosamoharajaṃ etesaṃ, evaṃ sabhāvāti apparajakkhajātikā. Assavanatāti assavanatāya. Bhavissantīti purimabuddhesu dasapuññakiriyavatthuvasena katādhikārā paripākagatā padumāni viya sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ, dhammadesanaṃyeva ākaṅkhamānā catuppadikagāthāvasāne ariyabhūmiṃ okkamanārahā na eko, na dve, anekasatasahassā dhammassa aññātāro bhavissantīti dasseti.

66. Of a certain one: here, though it is said “a certain one,” it should be understood that this is the chief Great Brahmā in this world-system. “Alas, the world is perishing!”: it is said that he uttered this sound in such a way that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system, having heard it, all gathered. Where indeed: in whatever world. Appeared before him: he appeared before him, together with those ten thousand Brahmās. Of a nature with little dust in the eyes: for them, in the wisdom-eye, there is little, a small amount of, the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion; being of such a nature, they are “of a nature with little dust in the eyes.” From not hearing: due to not hearing. There will be: this shows that those who, through the ten bases of meritorious deeds in the presence of past Buddhas, have made their aspiration and have reached maturity, like lotuses longing for the touch of the sun’s rays, they long only for the teaching of the Dhamma; at the end of a four-line verse, there will be knowers of the Dhamma worthy of entering the noble stage—not one, not two, but many hundreds of thousands.

69. Ajjhesananti evaṃ tikkhattuṃ yācanaṃ. Buddhacakkhunāti indriyaparopariyattañāṇena ca āsayānusayañāṇena ca. Imesañhi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti nāmaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇassa “samantacakkhū”ti, tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānaṃ “dhammacakkhū”ti. Apparajakkhetiādīsu yesaṃ vuttanayeneva paññācakkhumhi rāgādirajaṃ appaṃ, te apparajakkhā. Yesaṃ taṃ mahantaṃ, te mahārajakkhā. Yesaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni tikkhāni, te tikkhindriyā. Yesaṃ tāni mudūni, te mudindriyā. Yesaṃ teyeva saddhādayo ākārā sundarā, te svākārā. Ye kathitakāraṇaṃ sallakkhenti, sukhena sakkā honti viññāpetuṃ, te suviññāpayā. Ye paralokañceva vajjañca bhayato passanti, te paralokavajjabhayadassāvino nāma.

69. “Requesting”—thus is the request. “With the Buddha’s eye”—with the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties and the knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies. For of these two knowledges, the name is “the Buddha’s eye”; of the omniscient knowledge, it is “the all-seeing eye”; and of the three path-knowledges, it is “the Dhamma eye.” In “of little dust,” etc., those for whom the dust of greed and so on in the wisdom-eye is little, as stated, are “of little dust.” Those for whom it is great are “of great dust.” Those whose faculties of faith and so on are sharp are “of sharp faculties.” Those for whom they are dull are “of dull faculties.” Those whose very qualities of faith and so on are beautiful are “of beautiful qualities.” Those who discern the stated reason and can be easily made to understand are “easily instructed.” Those who see the next world and faults as fearful are called “seers of danger in the next world and in faults.”

Ayaṃ [M 2.0059][P 2.0468] panettha pāḷi – “saddho puggalo apparajakkho, assaddho puggalo mahārajakkho.… Āraddhavīriyo…pe… kusīto… upaṭṭhitassati… muṭṭhassati… samāhito… asamāhito… paññavā… duppañño puggalo mahārajakkho. Tathā saddho puggalo tikkhindriyo…pe… paññavā puggalo paralokavajjabhayadassāvī, duppañño puggalo na paralokavajjabhayadassāvī. Lokoti khandhaloko, dhātuloko, āyatanaloko, sampattibhavaloko, vipattibhavaloko, sampattisambhavaloko, vipattisambhavaloko. Eko loko – sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Dve lokā – nāmañca rūpañca. Tayo lokā – tisso vedanā. Cattāro lokā – cattāro āhārā. Pañca lokā – pañcupādānakkhandhā. Cha lokā – cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni. Satta lokā – satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Aṭṭha lokā – aṭṭha lokadhammā. Nava lokā – nava sattāvāsā. Dasa lokā – dasāyatanāni. Dvādasa lokā – dvādasāyatanāni. Aṭṭhārasa lokā – aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo. Vajjanti sabbe kilesā vajjaṃ, sabbe duccaritā vajjaṃ, sabbe abhisaṅkhārā vajjaṃ, sabbe bhavagāmikammā vajjaṃ. Iti imasmiñca loke imasmiñca vajje tibbā bhayasaññā paccupaṭṭhitā hoti, seyyathāpi ukkhittāsike vadhake[V 2.0053]. Imehi paññāsāya ākārehi imāni pañcindriyāni jānāti passati aññāti paṭivijjhati, idaṃ tathāgatassa indriyaparopariyatte ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.112).

Herein, this is the Pāli text: “A faithful person is one of little dust; an unfaithful person is one of great dust.… One with aroused energy… a lazy one… one with established mindfulness… one with muddled mindfulness… one who is composed… one who is uncomposed… one with wisdom… a person without wisdom is one of great dust. Likewise, a faithful person is one of keen faculties… a wise person is a seer of danger in the next world and in faults; a person without wisdom is not a seer of danger in the next world and in faults. ‘World’ means the world of aggregates, the world of elements, the world of sense bases, the world of fortunate existences, the world of unfortunate existences, the world of fortunate arising, the world of unfortunate arising. One world: all beings are sustained by nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds: the three feelings. Four worlds: the four nutriments. Five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging. Six worlds: the six internal sense bases. Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: the ten sense bases. Twelve worlds: the twelve sense bases. Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements. ‘Fault’ means all defilements are a fault, all misconduct is a fault, all volitional formations are a fault, all actions leading to becoming are a fault. Thus, in this world and in this fault, a keen perception of danger is present, like that toward an executioner with an upraised sword. With these fifty modes, one knows these five faculties. This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties.”

Uppaliniyanti uppalavane. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Antonimuggaposīnīti yāni aññānipi padumāni antonimuggāneva posayanti. Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitānīti udakaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitāni. Tattha yāni accuggamma ṭhitāni, tāni sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ āgamayamānāni ṭhitāni ajja pupphanakāni. Yāni samodakaṃ ṭhitāni, tāni sve pupphanakāni. Yāni udakānuggatāni antoudakaposīni, tāni tatiyadivase pupphanakāni. Udakā pana anuggatāni aññānipi sarojauppalādīni nāma [P 2.0469] atthi, yāni neva pupphissanti, macchakacchapabhakkhāneva bhavissanti, tāni pāḷiṃ nārūḷhāni. Āharitvā pana dīpetabbānīti dīpitāni. Yatheva hi tāni catubbidhāni pupphāni, evameva ugghaṭitaññū, vipañcitaññū, neyyo, padaparamoti cattāro puggalā. Tattha yassa [M 2.0060] puggalassa saha udāhaṭavelāya dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ugghaṭitaññū. Yassa puggalassa saṅkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo vipañcitaññū. Yassa puggalassa uddesato paripucchato yonisomanasikaroto kalyāṇamitte sevato bhajato payirupāsato anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo neyyo. Yassa puggalassa bahumpi suṇato bahumpi bhaṇato bahumpi gaṇhato bahumpi dhārayato bahumpi vācayato na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamo (pu. pa. 148, 149, 150, 151).

“In a pond of blue lotuses” means in a blue lotus grove. In the other cases, it is the same method. “Nourished while submerged” refers to other lotuses that are nourished while remaining submerged. “Standing having risen above the water” means standing having surpassed the water. Therein, those that stand having risen above the water, awaiting the touch of the sun’s rays, are those that will bloom today. Those that stand level with the water are those that will bloom tomorrow. Those that have not emerged from the water and are nourished within it are those that will bloom on the third day. However, there are other lotuses and water lilies that have not emerged from the water, which will not bloom at all but will become food for fish and turtles; these are not included in the Pāli text. But they were explained because they should be brought forth and shown. For just as there are these four kinds of flowers, so too are there four kinds of individuals: the one who understands quickly, the one who understands through explanation, the one who can be led, and the one who is limited to words. Among these, the individual for whom the attainment of Dhamma occurs at the very moment of utterance is called ‘one who understands quickly.’ The individual for whom the attainment of Dhamma occurs when the meaning of a brief statement is analyzed in detail is called ‘one who understands through explanation.’ The individual for whom the attainment of Dhamma occurs gradually through instruction, questioning, wise consideration, and by serving, attending to, and associating with virtuous friends is called ‘one who can be led.’ The individual for whom, despite much listening, speaking, learning, retaining, and reciting, the attainment of Dhamma does not occur in that life is called ‘one who is limited to words.’

Tattha bhagavā uppalavanādisadisaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ olokento – “ajja pupphanakāni viya ugghaṭitaññū, sve pupphanakāni viya vipañcitaññū, tatiyadivase pupphanakāni viya neyyo, macchakacchapabhakkhāni viya padaparamo”ti addasa. Passanto ca – “ettakā apparajakkhā, ettakā mahārajakkhā. Tatrāpi ettakā ugghaṭitaññū”ti evaṃ sabbākārato addasa. Tattha tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve bhagavato dhammadesanā atthaṃ sādheti, padaparamānaṃ anāgate vāsanatthāya hoti.

There, the Blessed One, surveying the ten-thousandfold world-system, which was like a lotus grove, saw: 'Like the flowers that will bloom today are those of quick understanding; like the flowers that will bloom tomorrow are those who understand through explanation; like the flowers that will bloom on the third day are those who can be led; and like those that become food for fish and turtles are those who are limited to words.' And while seeing, he saw in all aspects thus: 'This many are of little dust, this many are of great dust. And among them, this many are of quick understanding.' For the three types of individuals, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma accomplishes its purpose in this very existence; for those who are limited to words, it serves as a basis for future habituation.

Atha bhagavā imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ atthāvahaṃ dhammadesanaṃ viditvā desetukamyataṃ uppādetvā puna te sabbesupi tīsu bhavesu sabbe satte bhabbābhabbavasena dve koṭṭhāse akāsi. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ – “ye te sattā kammāvaraṇena samannāgatā, vipākāvaraṇena samannāgatā, kilesāvaraṇena [V 2.0054] samannāgatā, assaddhā acchandikā duppaññā abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ, ime te sattā abhabbā. Katame sattā bhabbā? Ye te sattā na kammāvaraṇena…pe…ime te sattā bhabbā”ti (vibha. 827; paṭi. ma. 1.114).

Then the Blessed One, knowing the Dhamma teaching that would bring benefit to these four individuals, gave rise to the desire to teach. Again, in all three realms of existence, he divided all beings into two categories: the capable and the incapable. In reference to them, it was said: “Those beings who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma, possessed of the obstruction of results, possessed of the obstruction of defilements, who are faithless, without desire, of little wisdom, and incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states—these beings are incapable. Which beings are capable? Those beings who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma… and so on… these beings are capable” (Vibhanga 827; Patisambhidāmagga 1.114).

Tattha sabbepi abhabbapuggale [P 2.0470] pahāya bhabbapuggaleyeva ñāṇena pariggahetvā – “ettakā rāgacaritā, ettakā dosamohavitakkasaddhābuddhicaritā”ti cha koṭṭhāse akāsi. Evaṃ katvā – “dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti cintesi[M 2.0061]. Brahmā taṃ ñatvā somanassajāto bhagavantaṃ gāthāhi ajjhabhāsi. Idaṃ sandhāya – “atha kho so, bhikkhave, mahābrahmā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Therein, having set aside all incapable individuals and having encompassed only the capable individuals with his knowledge, he divided them into six categories: “So many are of a lustful temperament, so many are of a hateful, deluded, speculative, faithful, and intelligent temperament.” Having done so, he thought, “I will teach the Dhamma.” Knowing this, Brahmā, filled with joy, addressed the Blessed One with verses. In reference to this, it was said: “Then, monks, that Great Brahmā…”

70. Tattha ajjhabhāsīti adhiabhāsi, adhikicca ārabbha abhāsīti attho.

70. Therein, ajjhabhāsi means adhi-abhāsi (he addressed); that is, he spoke concerning, he spoke with reference to—this is the meaning.

Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhitoti selamaye ekagghane pabbatamuddhani yathāṭhitova, na hi tattha ṭhitassa dassanatthaṃ gīvukkhipanapasāraṇādikiccaṃ atthi. Tathūpamanti tappaṭibhāgaṃ selapabbatūpamaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho, yathā selapabbatamuddhani yathāṭhitova cakkhumā puriso samantato janataṃ passeyya, tathā tvampi sumedha, sundarapaññasabbaññutaññāṇena samantacakkhu bhagavā dhammamayaṃ paññāmayaṃ pāsādamāruyha sayaṃ apetasoko sokāvatiṇṇaṃ jātijarābhibhūtaṃ janataṃ apekkhassu, upadhāraya upaparikkha.

Regarding the phrase Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito (As one standing on a mountain peak of rock): this means just as one standing on a solid mountain peak made of rock. For one standing there, there is no need to raise or stretch the neck in order to see. Tathūpamaṃ (similar to that) means comparable to that, having the simile of a rocky mountain. This is the brief meaning here: Just as a man with good sight, standing on a mountain peak of rock, might see the people all around, so too, O wise one, O all-seeing Blessed One, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and wisdom with your beautiful wisdom and omniscient knowledge, being yourself free from sorrow, look upon the people sunk in sorrow, overcome by birth and aging. Observe, consider, and examine them.

Ayamettha adhippāyo – yathā hi pabbatapāde samantā mahantaṃ khettaṃ katvā tattha kedārapāḷīsu kuṭikāyo katvā rattiṃ aggiṃ jāleyyuṃ. Caturaṅgasamannāgatañca andhakāraṃ assa. Athassa pabbatassa matthake ṭhatvā cakkhumato purisassa bhūmiṃ olokayato neva khettaṃ, na kedārapāḷiyo, na kuṭiyo, na tattha sayitamanussā paññāyeyyuṃ, kuṭikāsu pana aggijālamattameva paññāyeyya. Evaṃ dhammapāsādamāruyha sattanikāyaṃ olokayato tathāgatassa ye te akatakalyāṇā sattā, te ekavihāre dakkhiṇajāṇupasse nisinnāpi buddhacakkhussa āpāthaṃ nāgacchanti, rattiṃ khittasarā viya honti. Ye pana katakalyāṇā veneyyapuggalā, te tassa dūre ṭhitāpi āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, so aggi viya himavantapabbato viya ca. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

This is the intended meaning here: Suppose that at the foot of a mountain, a large field was prepared all around, and on the dykes of that field, huts were built and fires lit in them at night. And suppose there was a darkness endowed with its four factors. Then, if a man with good sight were to stand on the summit of that mountain and look down at the ground, neither the field, nor the dykes, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping therein would be visible; only the flames of the fires in the huts would be seen. Similarly, when the Tathāgata, having ascended the palace of the Dhamma, surveys the host of beings, those beings who have not done meritorious deeds do not come into the range of the Buddha’s eye, even if they are seated near his right knee in the same monastery; they are like arrows shot in the night. But those trainable individuals who have done meritorious deeds come into his range even when they are far away, like that fire or like the Himavant mountain. And this has been said:

“Dūre santo pakāsenti, himavantova pabbato;

Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṃ khittā yathā sarā”ti. (dha. pa. 304);

“The good are visible from afar, like the Himavant mountain; the wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.”

Uṭṭhehīti [P 2.0471][V 2.0055] bhagavato dhammadesanatthaṃ cārikacaraṇaṃ yācanto bhaṇati. Vīrātiādīsu bhagavā vīriyavantatāya vīro, devaputtamaccukilesamārānaṃ vijitattā [M 2.0062] vijitasaṅgāmo, jātikantarādinittharaṇatthāya veneyyasatthavāhanasamatthatāya satthavāho, kāmacchandaiṇassa abhāvato aṇaṇoti veditabbo.

He says Uṭṭhehi (Arise!), requesting the Blessed One to wander forth for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. In phrases such as vīra (hero), the Blessed One is a hero on account of his energy; he is vijitasaṅgāma (a victor in battle) because he has conquered the devaputta-māra, the death-māra, and the defilement-māra; he is a satthavāha (caravan leader) because of his ability to lead the caravan of trainable beings across the wilderness of birth and so on; and he is to be understood as aṇaṇa (debt-free) because of the absence of the debt of sensual desire.

71. Apārutāti vivaṭā. Amatassa dvārāti ariyamaggo. So hi amatasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa dvāraṃ. So mayā vivaritvā ṭhapitoti dasseti. Pamuñcantu saddhanti sabbe attano saddhaṃ pamuñcantu vissajjentu. Pacchimapadadvaye ayamattho, ahañhi attano paguṇaṃ suppavattitampi imaṃ paṇītaṃ uttamaṃ dhammaṃ kāyavācākilamathasaññī hutvā na bhāsiṃ, idāni pana sabbe janā saddhābhājanaṃ upanentu, pūressāmi tesaṃ saṅkappanti.

71. Apāruta means opened (vivaṭa). Amatassa dvāra (the door to the Deathless) means the Noble Path. For that is the door to Nibbāna, which is known as the Deathless. He shows: 'That has been opened and established by me.' Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ (Let them release faith) means let all release, let them send forth their faith. This is the meaning of the last two lines: 'For I, perceiving it as wearisome to body and speech, did not teach this excellent, supreme Dhamma, though it was well-mastered and readily available to me. But now, let all people bring forth the vessel of faith; I will fulfill their aspiration.'

Aggasāvakayugavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Pair of Chief Disciples

73. Bodhirukkhamūleti bodhirukkhassa avidūre ajapālanigrodhe antarahitoti attho. Kheme migadāyeti isipatanaṃ tena samayena khemaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ hoti, migānaṃ pana abhayavāsatthāya dinnattā migadāyoti vuccati. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “kheme migadāye”ti. Yathā ca vipassī bhagavā, evaṃ aññepi buddhā paṭhamaṃ dhammadesanatthāya gacchantā ākāsena gantvā tattheva otaranti. Amhākaṃ pana bhagavā upakassa ājīvakassa upanissayaṃ disvā – “upako imaṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno, so maṃ disvā sallapitvā gamissati. Atha puna nibbindanto āgamma arahattaṃ sacchikarissatī”ti ñatvā aṭṭhārasayojanamaggaṃ padasāva agamāsi. Dāyapālaṃ āmantesīti disvāva punappunaṃ oloketvā – “ayyo no, bhante, āgato”ti vatvā upagataṃ āmantesi.

73. Regarding Bodhirukkhamūle (at the foot of the Bodhi tree): the meaning is that he was at the Ajapāla banyan tree, not far from the Bodhi tree. Regarding Kheme migadāye (in the Khemā deer park): At that time, Isipatana was a park named Khemā; but because it was given for the deer to live in safety, it is called the Migadāya (Deer Sanctuary). In reference to that, it was said: kheme migadāye. And just as the Blessed One Vipassī, so also other Buddhas, when going to deliver their first Dhamma discourse, travel through the air and descend in that very place. Our Blessed One, however, seeing the strong supporting condition of the ascetic Upaka, and knowing, 'Upaka has set out on this long journey. He will see me, converse with me, and then go on his way. Then later, becoming dispassionate, he will return and realize arahantship,' he traveled the eighteen-yojana path on foot. Regarding Dāyapālaṃ āmantesi (He addressed the park keeper): The keeper, upon seeing him and looking again and again, approached and said, 'Venerable sir, has our master come?' The Buddha then addressed him.

75-6. Anupubbiṃ kathanti dānakathaṃ, dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ, sīlānantaraṃ saggaṃ, saggānantaraṃ magganti evaṃ anupaṭipāṭikathaṃ kathesi. Tattha dānakathanti idaṃ dānaṃ nāma sukhānaṃ nidānaṃ, sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ, bhogānaṃ patiṭṭhā, visamagatassa tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ, idhalokaparalokesu dānasadiso avassayo [P 2.0472] patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi. Idañhi avassayaṭṭhena ratanamayasīhāsanasadisaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena mahāpathavīsadisaṃ, ārammaṇaṭṭhena [M 2.0063] ālambanarajjusadisaṃ. Idañhi dukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhena nāvā, samassāsanaṭṭhena saṅgāmasūro, bhayaparittāṇaṭṭhena susaṅkhatanagaraṃ, maccheramalādīhi anupalittaṭṭhena padumaṃ, tesaṃ nidahanaṭṭhena aggi, durāsadaṭṭhena [V 2.0056] āsīviso, asantāsanaṭṭhena sīho, balavantaṭṭhena hatthī, abhimaṅgalasammataṭṭhena setausabho, khemantabhūmisampāpanaṭṭhena valāhakaassarājā. Dānañhi loke sakkasampattiṃ mārasampattiṃ brahmasampattiṃ cakkavattisampattiṃ sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ abhisambodhiñāṇaṃ detīti evamādidānaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ.

75-6. He gave a gradual discourse: a discourse on giving, then after giving, on virtue, after virtue, on heaven, and after heaven, on the path—thus he spoke a discourse in sequential order. Herein, the discourse on giving is as follows: This giving is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, the foundation of wealth, a protection, shelter, destination, and final resort for one in adversity. In this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, handhold, protection, shelter, destination, or final resort comparable to giving. For, as a support, it is like a jeweled lion-throne; as a foundation, like the great earth; as a handhold, like a supporting rope. It is a boat for crossing over suffering, a hero in battle for giving solace, a well-fortified city for protection from fear, a lotus for being unstained by the defilements of stinginess and so forth. It is a fire for burning them, a venomous snake for being difficult to approach, a lion for not causing fear, an elephant for its strength, a white bull for being deemed highly auspicious, and a cloud-horse king for reaching the land of safety. For in this world, giving grants the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā, the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch, the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection, the knowledge of a paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of supreme enlightenment. Such was the discourse connected with the virtues of giving.

Yasmā pana dānaṃ dadanto sīlaṃ samādātuṃ sakkoti, tasmā tadanantaraṃ sīlakathaṃ kathesi. Sīlakathanti sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ avassayo patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ. Idhalokaparalokasampattīnañhi sīlasadiso avassayo patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi, sīlasadiso alaṅkāro natthi, sīlapupphasadisaṃ pupphaṃ natthi, sīlagandhasadiso gandho natthi, sīlālaṅkārena hi alaṅkataṃ sīlakusumapiḷandhanaṃ sīlagandhānulittaṃ sadevakopi loko olokento tittiṃ na gacchatīti evamādisīlaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ.

Since one who gives is able to undertake virtue, therefore, immediately after, he spoke the discourse on virtue. The discourse on virtue: This which is called virtue is a support, a foundation, a handhold, a protection, a shelter, a destination, and a final resort. For the prosperity of this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, handhold, protection, shelter, destination, or final resort equal to virtue. There is no adornment equal to virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue. For even the world with its devas, gazing upon one adorned with the adornment of virtue, wearing the garland of virtue-flowers, and anointed with the fragrance of virtue, does not reach satisfaction—such was the discourse connected with the qualities of virtue.

Idaṃ pana sīlaṃ nissāya ayaṃ saggo labbhatīti dassetuṃ sīlānantaraṃ saggakathaṃ kathesi. Saggakathanti ayaṃ saggo nāma iṭṭho kanto manāpo, niccamettha kīḷā, niccaṃ sampattiyo labbhanti, cātumahārājikā devā navutivassasatasahassāni dibbasukhaṃ dibbasampattiṃ paṭilabhanti, tāvatiṃsā tisso ca vassakoṭiyo saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassānīti evamādisaggaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ. Saggasampattiṃ kathayantānañhi buddhānaṃ mukhaṃ nappahoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “anekapariyāyena kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, saggakathaṃ katheyya”ntiādi.

Now, to show that this heaven is attained by relying on this virtue, he spoke the discourse on heaven immediately after the discourse on virtue. The discourse on heaven: This heaven is wished for, lovely, and pleasing; there, one enjoys constant sport and obtains constant prosperity. The devas of the Four Great Kings obtain divine happiness and divine prosperity for nine million years; the devas of Tāvatiṃsa, for thirty-six million years—such is the discourse connected with the qualities of heaven. Indeed, the mouths of the Buddhas are not sufficient to describe the prosperity of heaven. And this was also said: 'Monks, in many ways I could speak the discourse on heaven,' and so on.

Evaṃ saggakathāya palobhetvā puna hatthiṃ alaṅkaritvā tassa soṇḍaṃ chindanto viya – “ayampi saggo anicco addhuvo, na ettha chandarāgo [P 2.0473] kātabbo”ti dassanatthaṃ – “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.235; 2.42) nayena kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ [M 2.0064] okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ kathesi. Tattha ādīnavoti doso. Okāroti avakāro lāmakabhāvo. Saṃkilesoti tehi sattānaṃ saṃsāre saṃkilissanaṃ. Yathāha – “kilissanti vata bho sattā”ti (ma. ni. 2.351). Evaṃ kāmādīnavena tejjatvā nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesi, pabbajjāya guṇaṃ pakāsesīti attho. Sesaṃ ambaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayañceva uttānatthañca.

Having thus enticed them with the discourse on heaven, he then, as if adorning an elephant and cutting off its trunk, showed that 'This heaven too is impermanent, not lasting; one should not develop desire or lust for it.' To demonstrate this, he expounded on the danger, inferiority, and defilement of sensual pleasures in the manner of: 'Sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is greater' (MN 1.235; 2.42). Herein, 'danger' (ādīnava) means fault. 'Inferiority' (okāra) means baseness. 'Defilement' (saṃkilesa) refers to beings becoming defiled in saṃsāra by them. As it is said: 'Truly, beings are defiled' (MN 2.351). Having thus intimidated them with the danger of sensual pleasures, he revealed the benefits of renunciation and proclaimed the virtues of going forth—this is the meaning. The rest follows the method explained in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta commentary and is straightforward in meaning.

77. Alatthunti kathaṃ alatthuṃ? Ehibhikkhubhāvena. Bhagavā kira tesaṃ iddhimayapattacīvarassūpanissayaṃ olokento anekāsu jātīsu cīvaradānādīni disvā etha bhikkhavotiādimāha[V 2.0057]. Te tāvadeva bhaṇḍū kāsāyavasanā aṭṭhahi bhikkhuparikkhārehi sarīrapaṭimukkeheva vassasatikattherā viya bhagavantaṃ namassamānāva nisīdiṃsu.

77. How did they attain it? By the state of being an 'ehi bhikkhu.' It is said that the Blessed One, looking into their supporting condition for robes and a bowl created by psychic power, saw that in many existences they had given robes and other items, and said, 'Come, monks.' At that very moment, with their heads shaven and wearing ochre robes, with the eight monastic requisites just placed upon their bodies, they sat down paying homage to the Blessed One, appearing just like elders of a hundred years' standing.

Sandassesītiādīsu idhalokatthaṃ sandassesi, paralokatthaṃ sandassesi. Idhalokatthaṃ dassento aniccanti dassesi, dukkhanti dassesi, anattāti dassesi, khandhe dassesi, dhātuyo dassesi, āyatanāni dassesi, paṭiccasamuppādaṃ dassesi, rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ dassento pañca lakkhaṇāni dassesi, tathā vedanākkhandhādīnaṃ, tathā vayaṃ dassentopi udayabbayavasena paññāsalakkhaṇāni dassesi, paralokatthaṃ dassento nirayaṃ dassesi, tiracchānayoniṃ, pettivisayaṃ, asurakāyaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ kusalānaṃ vipākaṃ, channaṃ devalokānaṃ, navannaṃ brahmalokānaṃ sampattiṃ dassesi.

In the passage beginning 'He demonstrated,' etc.: he demonstrated the subject of this world and the subject of the next world. Demonstrating the subject of this world, he demonstrated impermanence, suffering, and not-self; he demonstrated the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination. Showing the arising of the form aggregate, he demonstrated five characteristics, and likewise for the aggregates of feeling and so on. Likewise, also showing their passing away, by way of arising and passing away he demonstrated fifty characteristics. Demonstrating the subject of the next world, he demonstrated hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, the host of asuras, the result of the three kinds of wholesome kamma, the prosperity of the six deva worlds, and the prosperity of the nine Brahmā worlds.

Samādapesīti catupārisuddhisīlaterasadhutaṅgadasakathāvatthuādike kalyāṇadhamme gaṇhāpesi.

'He caused them to undertake' means he had them take up wholesome qualities such as the fourfold purity of conduct, the thirteen ascetic practices, and the ten topics of discourse.

Samuttejesīti suṭṭhu uttejesi, abbhussāhesi. Idhalokatthañceva paralokatthañca tāsetvā tāsetvā adhigataṃ viya katvā kathesi. Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇapañcavīsatimahābhayappabhedañhi idhalokatthaṃ buddhe bhagavati tāsetvā tāsetvā kathayante pacchābāhaṃ, gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cātumahāpathe pahārasatena tāḷetvā dakkhiṇadvārena [P 2.0474] niyyamāno viya āghātanabhaṇḍikāya ṭhapitasīso viya sūle uttāsito viya mattahatthinā maddiyamāno viya ca saṃviggo hoti. Paralokatthañca [M 2.0065] kathayante nirayādīsu nibbatto viya devalokasampattiṃ anubhavamāno viya ca hoti.

“He inspired them”—he thoroughly roused and urged them on; he encouraged them. By repeatedly frightening them about both this world and the next, he spoke as if they had already attained it. For when the Buddha, the Blessed One, speaks, frightening them again and again about the thirty-two modes of punishment and the twenty-five varieties of great fears concerning this world, one becomes agitated as if being led away with hands bound tightly behind the back, struck a hundred times at the crossroads, led out through the southern gate, with one's head placed on the executioner's block, as if impaled on a stake, or as if being crushed by a maddened elephant. And when he speaks concerning the next world, one feels as if reborn in hell and so on, or as if experiencing the bliss of the celestial worlds.

Sampahaṃsesīti paṭiladdhaguṇena codesi, mahānisaṃsaṃ katvā kathesīti attho.

“He gladdened them”—he exhorted them by means of the virtue they had attained, meaning that he spoke of the great benefits.

Saṅkhārānaṃ ādīnavanti heṭṭhā paṭhamamaggādhigamatthaṃ kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ kathesi, idha pana uparimaggādhigamatthaṃ – “aniccā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā addhuvā anassāsikā, yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṃ alaṃ virajjituṃ alaṃ vimuccitu”ntiādinā (a. ni. 7.66; saṃ. ni. 2.134) nayena saṅkhārānaṃ ādīnavañca lāmakabhāvañca tappaccayañca kilamathaṃ pakāsesi. Yathā ca tattha nekkhamme, evamidha – “santamidaṃ, bhikkhave, nibbānaṃ nāma paṇītaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇa”ntiādinā nayena nibbāne ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesi.

As to “the danger of formations”: previously, for the attainment of the first path, he taught the danger of sensual pleasures. But here, for the attainment of the higher paths, by the method beginning, “Monks, formations are impermanent, unstable, unreliable; truly, monks, it is quite enough to become disenchanted with all formations, enough to become dispassionate, enough to be liberated,” he revealed the danger of formations, their wretchedness, and the weariness conditioned by them. And just as there he revealed the benefit in renunciation, so here, by the method beginning, “Monks, this is peaceful, this is sublime: Nibbāna, namely, the secure protection, the refuge,” he revealed the benefit in Nibbāna.

Mahājanakāyapabbajjāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Going Forth of the Great Multitude

78. Mahājanakāyoti [V 2.0058] tesaṃyeva dvinnaṃ kumārānaṃ upaṭṭhākajanakāyoti.

78. “The great multitude” means the multitude of attendants of those same two princes.

80. Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāma, dhammañcāti saṅghassa aparipuṇṇattā dvevācikameva saraṇamagamaṃsu.

80. “We go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma”—because the Saṅgha was not yet complete, they took refuge with only a twofold declaration.

81. Alatthunti pubbe vuttanayeneva ehibhikkhubhāveneva alatthuṃ. Ito anantare pabbajitavārepi eseva nayo.

81. “They attained”: in the manner previously stated, they attained it through the “Come, monk” state itself. This same method applies also in the case of the ordinations immediately following.

Cārikāanujānanavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Permission to Wander

85. Parivitakko udapādīti kadā udapādi? Sambodhito satta saṃvaccharāni satta māse satta divase atikkamitvā udapādi. Bhagavā kira pitusaṅgahaṃ karonto vihāsi. Rājāpi cintesi – “mayhaṃ jeṭṭhaputto nikkhamitvā buddho jāto, dutiyaputto me nikkhamitvā aggasāvako jāto, purohitaputto dutiyaaggasāvako, ime ca avasesā bhikkhū gihikālepi mayhaṃ puttameva parivāretvā vicariṃsu. Ime sabbe idānipi [M 2.0066] mayhaṃyeva bhāro, ahameva ca ne catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahissāmi, aññesaṃ okāsaṃ na dassāmī”ti vihāradvārakoṭṭhakato paṭṭhāya yāva rājagehadvārā ubhayato khadirapākāraṃ kārāpetvā kilañjehi chādāpetvā vatthehi paṭicchādāpetvā upari ca chādāpetvā suvaṇṇatārakavicittaṃ samolambitatālakkhandhamattaṃ vividhapupphadāmavitānaṃ kārāpetvā heṭṭhā bhūmiyaṃ cittattharaṇehi [P 2.0475] santharāpetvā anto ubhosu passesu mālāvacchake puṇṇaghaṭe, sakalamaggavāsatthāya ca gandhantare pupphāni pupphantare gandhe ca ṭhapāpetvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocāpesi.

85. “A thought arose”—when did it arise? It arose after seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since his enlightenment. The Blessed One, it is said, was staying, showing favour to his father. The king also thought: “My eldest son went forth and became a Buddha; my second son went forth and became the chief disciple; the royal chaplain's son became the second chief disciple. And these remaining monks, even in their time as householders, wandered in the company of my son. Now, all of them are my responsibility. I alone will attend to them with the four requisites; I will not give the opportunity to others.” Thus, starting from the monastery gatehouse and extending to the palace door, he had an acacia-wood fence erected on both sides, had it covered with mats, overlaid with cloth, and also roofed over. He had a canopy of diverse flower garlands made, variegated with golden stars, from which hung down tassels the measure of a palm trunk. Below, on the ground, he had variegated coverings spread. Inside, along both sides, he had small flowering plants and full water-pots placed, and for the purpose of perfuming the entire path, he had flowers placed among perfumes and perfumes among flowers. Then he had the time announced to the Blessed One.

Bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto antosāṇiyāva rājagehaṃgantvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā vihāraṃ paccāgacchati. Añño koci daṭṭhumpi na labhati, kuto pana bhikkhaṃ vā dātuṃ, pūjaṃ vā kātuṃ, dhammaṃ vā sotuṃ. Nāgarā cintesuṃ – “ajja satthu loke uppannassa sattamāsādhikāni sattasaṃvaccharāni, mayañca daṭṭhumpi na labhāma, pageva bhikkhaṃ vā dātuṃ, pūjaṃ vā kātuṃ, dhammaṃ vā sotuṃ. Rājā – ‘mayhameva buddho, mayhameva dhammo, mayhameva saṅgho’ti mamāyitvā sayameva upaṭṭhahi. Satthā ca uppajjamāno sadevakassa lokassa atthāya hitāya uppanno. Na hi raññoyeva [V 2.0059] nirayo uṇho assa, aññesaṃ nīluppalavanasadiso. Tasmā rājānaṃ vadāma. Sace no satthāraṃ deti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce deti, raññā saddhiṃ yujjhitvāpi saṅghaṃ gahetvā dānādīni puññāni karoma. Na sakkā kho pana suddhanāgareheva evaṃ kātuṃ, ekaṃ jeṭṭhapurisampi gaṇhāmā”ti.

The Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, would go to the royal palace only within that enclosure, and having completed his meal, would return to the monastery. No one else could even see him, much less give alms, offer worship, or listen to the Dhamma. The citizens thought: “It has now been seven years and seven months since the Teacher appeared in the world, yet we cannot even see him, let alone give alms, offer worship, or listen to the Dhamma. The king, thinking, ‘The Buddha is mine, the Dhamma is mine, the Saṅgha is mine,’ has appropriated them and attends to them himself. But the Teacher arose for the welfare and benefit of the world with its gods. Surely, hell is not hot for the king alone, while for others it is like a forest of blue water lilies. Therefore, let us speak to the king. If he gives us the Teacher, that is good. If he does not, then we will fight with the king, invite the Saṅgha, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms. But this cannot be done by ordinary citizens alone; let us get a leading man on our side.”

Te senāpatiṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassetamatthaṃ ārocetvā – “sāmi, kiṃ amhākaṃ pakkho hosi, udāhu rañño”ti āhaṃsu. So – “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pakkho homi, api ca kho pana paṭhamadivaso mayhaṃ dātabbo”ti. Te sampaṭicchiṃsu. So rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “nāgarā, deva, tumhākaṃ kupitā”ti āha. Kimatthaṃ tātāti? Satthāraṃ kira tumheyeva upaṭṭhahatha, amhe na labhāmāti. Sace idānipi labhanti, na kuppanti, alabhantā tumhehi saddhiṃ yujjhitukāmā devāti. Yujjhāmi, tāta, nāhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ demīti. Deva tumhākaṃ dāsā tumhehi saddhiṃ yujjhāmāti vadanti, tumhe kaṃ gaṇhitvā yujjhissathāti? Nanu tvaṃ senāpatīti? Nāgarehi vinā na [M 2.0067] samattho ahaṃ devāti. Tato rājā – “balavanto nāgarā, senāpatipi tesaññeva pakkho”ti ñatvā “aññānipi sattamāsādhikāni sattasaṃvaccharāni mayhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ dadantū”ti āha. Nāgarā [P 2.0476] na sampaṭicchiṃsu. Rājā – “cha vassāni, pañca, cattāri, tīṇi, dve, ekavassa”nti hāpesi. Evaṃ hāpentepi na sampaṭicchiṃsu. Aññe satta divase yāci. Nāgarā – “atikakkhaḷaṃ dāni raññā saddhiṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti anujāniṃsu.

They approached the commander, explained the matter, and asked, "Sir, will you be on our side, or on the king's?" He replied, "I am on your side, but the first day must be given to me." They agreed. The commander then went to the king and said, "Sire, the citizens are angry with you." "For what reason, dear?" "Because, they say, you alone attend to the Teacher, while we do not get the chance. If they get the chance even now, they will not be angry; but if they do not, they wish to fight with you, sire." "I will fight, dear, but I will not give the community of monks." "Sire, they say, 'We are your slaves; we will fight with you.' With whom will you fight?" "Are you not the commander?" "Without the citizens, I am not able, sire." Then the king, realizing, 'The citizens are strong, and even the commander is on their side,' said, 'Let them give me the community of monks for another seven years and seven months.' The citizens did not agree. The king reduced it to six years, five, four, three, two, and one year, but even as he reduced it, they did not agree. He then asked for another seven days. The citizens, thinking, "Now it is not proper to act so harshly towards the king," consented.

Rājā sattamāsādhikānaṃ sattannaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ sajjitaṃ dānamukhaṃ sattannameva divasānaṃ vissajjetvā cha divase kesañci apassantānaṃyeva dānaṃ datvā sattame divase nāgare pakkosāpetvā – “sakkhissatha, tāta, evarūpaṃ dānaṃ dātu”nti āha. Tepi – “nanu amheyeva nissāya taṃ devassa uppanna”nti vatvā – “sakkhissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā piṭṭhihatthena assūni puñchamāno bhagavantaṃ vanditvā – “bhante, ahaṃ aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassaṃ aññassa vāraṃ akatvā yāvajīvaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahissāmīti cintesiṃ. Nāgarā na dāni me anuññātā, nāgarā hi ‘mayaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ na labhāmā’ti kuppanti. Bhagavā sve paṭṭhāya tesaṃ anuggahaṃ karothā”ti āha.

The king, taking the provisions for the offering that had been prepared for seven years and seven months, distributed them over just seven days. For six days, he gave alms while being unseen by anyone, and on the seventh day, he had the citizens summoned and said, "Dears, will you be able to give such an offering?" They replied, "Was it not on account of us that this arose for you, sire? We will be able." The king, wiping his tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I had resolved, 'I will support one hundred sixty-eight thousand monks for as long as they live with the four requisites, without giving a turn to anyone else.' But now the citizens have not permitted me, for the citizens are angry, thinking, 'We do not get to give alms.' May the Blessed One, starting from tomorrow, show them favor."

Atha dutiyadivase senāpati mahādānaṃ sajjetvā – “ajja yathā añño koci ekabhikkhampi na deti, evaṃ rakkhathā”ti samantā purise ṭhapesi. Taṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhibhariyā rodamānā dhītaraṃ āha – “sace, amma, tava pitā jīveyya, ajjāhaṃ paṭhamaṃ dasabalaṃ bhojeyya”nti[V 2.0060]. Sā taṃ āha – “amma, mā cintayi, ahaṃ tathā karissāmi yathā buddhappamukho bhikkhusaṅgho paṭhamaṃ amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ paribhuñjissatī”ti. Tato satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇapātiyā nirudakapāyāsassa pūretvā sappimadhusakkarādīhi abhisaṅkharitvā aññāya pātiyā paṭikujjitvā taṃ sumanamālāguḷehi parikkhipitvā mālāguḷasadisaṃ katvā bhagavato gāmaṃ pavisanavelāya sayameva ukkhipitvā dāsigaṇaparivutā nagarā nikkhami. Antarāmagge senāpatiupaṭṭhākā – “amma, mā ito agamā”ti vadanti. Mahāpuññā nāma manāpakathā honti, na ca tesaṃ punappunaṃ bhaṇantānaṃ kathā paṭikkhipituṃ sakkā hoti. Sā – “cūḷapitā mahāpitā mātulā kissa tumhe gantuṃ na dethā”ti āha. Senāpatinā [P 2.0477] – “aññassa kassaci khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ dātuṃ mā dethā”ti ṭhapitamha ammāti. Kiṃ pana me hatthe khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ passathāti? Mālāguḷaṃ passāmāti[M 2.0068]. Kiṃ tumhākaṃ senāpati mālāguḷapūjampi kātuṃ na detīti? Deti, ammāti. Tena hi, apetha, apethāti bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā mālāguḷaṃ gaṇhāpetha bhagavāti āha. Bhagavā ekaṃ senāpatissupaṭṭhākaṃ oloketvā mālāguḷaṃ gaṇhāpesi. Sā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā – “bhagavā, bhavābhave nibbattiyaṃ me sati paritassanajīvitaṃ nāma mā hotu, ayaṃ sumanamālā viya nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne piyāva homi, nāmena ca sumanā yevā”ti patthanaṃ katvā satthārā – “sukhinī hohī”ti vuttā vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

Then on the second day, the commander prepared a great alms-giving and stationed men all around, saying, "Today, guard in such a way that no one else gives anything even to a single monk." That day, the merchant’s wife, weeping, said to her daughter, "Dear, if your father were alive, today I would have been the first to feed the Ten-Powered One." Her daughter replied, "Mother, do not worry. I will act in such a way that the community of monks headed by the Buddha will first consume our alms-food." Then, filling a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with milk-rice made without water and preparing it with ghee, honey, and sugar, she covered it by inverting another bowl over it, surrounded it with garlands of jasmine flowers, and made it resemble a flower garland. At the time the Blessed One was entering the village, she lifted it herself and, surrounded by a retinue of female servants, went out from the city. Along the way, the commander’s attendants said, "Lady, do not go from here." For those of great merit are said to have pleasing speech, and it is not possible to reject their words when they speak repeatedly. She said, "Uncles, why do you not let me go?" They replied, "Lady, we have been stationed by the commander with the order, 'Do not let anyone else give hard or soft food.'" "But do you see any hard or soft food in my hands?" "We see a flower garland." "Does your commander not allow even the offering of a flower garland?" "He allows it, lady." "In that case, step aside, step aside!" she said. Approaching the Blessed One, she said, "Blessed One, please have this flower garland accepted." The Blessed One, glancing at one of the commander’s attendants, had the flower garland accepted. She paid homage to the Blessed One and made an aspiration: "Blessed One, in my rebirths in existence after existence, may I not have a life of fear and trembling. Like this jasmine flower, may I be beloved in every place I am reborn, and may my name be Sumanā." The Teacher said to her, "Be happy." Having paid homage and circumambulated him respectfully, she departed.

Bhagavā senāpatissa gehaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīdi. Senāpati yāguṃ gahetvā upagañchi, satthā pattaṃ pidahi. Nisinno, bhante, bhikkhusaṅghoti. Atthi no eko antarā piṇḍapāto laddhoti. So mālaṃ apanetvā piṇḍapātaṃ addasa. Cūḷupaṭṭhāko āha – “sāmi, mālāti maṃ vatvā mātugāmo vañcesī”ti. Pāyāso bhagavantaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pahoti. Senāpatipi attano deyyadhammaṃ adāsi. Satthā bhattakiccaṃ katvā maṅgalaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. Senāpati – “kā nāma sā piṇḍapātamadāsī”ti pucchi. Seṭṭhidhītā, sāmīti. Sappaññā sā itthī, evarūpāya ghare vasantiyā purisassa saggasampatti nāma na dullabhāti taṃ ānetvā jeṭṭhikaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

The Blessed One went to the commander’s house and sat down on the prepared seat. The commander, taking rice gruel, approached; the Teacher covered his bowl. "Venerable sir, the community of monks is seated." "There is an alms-meal that we received in between," he said. The commander removed the garland and saw the alms-food. The junior attendant said, “Master, a woman deceived me, saying ‘it is a garland.’” The milk-rice was sufficient for all the monks, beginning with the Blessed One. The commander also gave his own offering. The Teacher, having finished his meal duties, spoke a blessing and departed. The commander asked, “Who was she that gave the alms-food?” “The merchant’s daughter, master.” Thinking, “That woman is wise; for a man living in a house with such a woman, the attainment of heavenly bliss is not difficult to obtain,” he had her brought and established her in the position of chief wife.

Punadivase nāgarā dānamadaṃsu, punadivase rājāti ekantarikāya dānaṃ dātuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Rājāpi carapurise ṭhapetvā nāgarehi dinnadānato atirekataraṃ deti, nāgarāpi tatheva katvā raññā dinnadānato atirekataraṃ. Rājagehe nāṭakitthiyo daharasāmaṇere vadanti – “gaṇhatha, tātā, na gahapatikānaṃ gattavatthādīsu puñchitvā bāḷadārakānaṃ kheḷasiṅghāṇikādidhovanahatthehi kataṃ[V 2.0061], suciṃ paṇītaṃ kata”nti. Punadivase nāgarāpi dadamānā vadanti – “gaṇhatha, tātā, na nagaragāmanigamādīsu saṅkaḍḍhitataṇḍulakhīradadhisappiādīhi, na aññesaṃ jaṅghasīsapiṭṭhiādīni [P 2.0478] bhañjitvā āharāpitehi kataṃ, jātisappikhīrādīhiyeva kata”nti. Evaṃ sattasu saṃvaccharesu sattasu māsesu sattasu divasesu ca atikkantesu atha bhagavato ayaṃ vitakko udapādi. Tena vuttaṃ – “sambodhito satta saṃvaccharāni satta māsāni satta divasāni atikkamitvā udapādī”ti.

On the following day, the citizens gave alms; on the day after that, the king gave alms. Thus they began to give alms on alternate days. The king, having stationed spies, gave an offering even more lavish than that given by the citizens; the citizens, too, doing likewise, gave an offering even more lavish than that given by the king. In the royal palace, the dancing women would say to the young novices: “Take this, dear sirs. It was not prepared after wiping hands on the bodies and clothes of householders, nor with hands that have washed away the spittle and snot of young children; it is pure and excellently prepared.” On the following day, the citizens, while giving alms, would also say: “Take this, dear sirs. It was not prepared with rice, milk, curd, ghee, and so on, scraped together from cities, villages, and towns, nor was it prepared with provisions brought after breaking the shins, heads, and backs of others; it was prepared only with genuine ghee, milk, and so on.” In this way, after seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed, a certain thought arose in the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: “It arose after seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since his full enlightenment.”

87. Aññataro [M 2.0069] mahābrahmāti dhammadesanaṃ āyācitabrahmāva.

87. A certain Great Brahmā: This is the very Brahmā who requested the teaching of the Dhamma.

89. Caturāsīti āvāsasahassānīti caturāsīti vihārasahassāni. Te sabbepi dvādasasahassabhikkhugaṇhanakā mahāvihārā abhayagiricetiyapabbatacittalapabbatamahāvihārasadisāva ahesuṃ.

89. Eighty-four thousand residences means eighty-four thousand monasteries. All of them were great monasteries capable of accommodating twelve thousand bhikkhus, just like the Mahāvihāra, Abhayagiri, Cetiyapabbata, and Cittalapabbata monasteries.

90. Khantī paramaṃ tapoti adhivāsanakhanti nāma paramaṃ tapo. Titikkhāti khantiyā eva vevacanaṃ. Titikkhā saṅkhātā adhivāsanakhanti uttamaṃ tapoti attho. Nibbānaṃ paramanti sabbākārena pana nibbānaṃ paramanti vadanti buddhā. Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātīti yo adhivāsanakhantivirahitattā paraṃ upaghāteti bādheti hiṃsati, so pabbajito nāma na hoti. Catutthapādo pana tasseva vevacanaṃ. “Na hi pabbajito”ti etassa hi na samaṇo hotīti vevacanaṃ. Parūpaghātīti etassa paraṃ viheṭhayantoti vevacanaṃ. Atha vā parūpaghātīti sīlūpaghātī. Sīlañhi uttamaṭṭhena paranti vuccati. Yo ca samaṇo paraṃ yaṃ kañci sattaṃ viheṭhayanto parūpaghātī hoti, attano sīlaṃ vināsako, so pabbajito nāma na hotīti attho. Athavā yo adhivāsanakhantiyā abhāvato parūpaghātī hoti, paraṃ antamaso ḍaṃsamakasampi sañcicca jīvitā voropeti, so na hi pabbajito. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Malassa apabbājitattā. “Pabbājayamattano malaṃ, tasmā pabbajitoti vuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 388) idañhi pabbajitalakkhaṇaṃ. Yopi na heva kho upaghāteti, na māreti, api ca daṇḍādīhi viheṭheti, so paraṃ viheṭhayanto samaṇo na hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Vihesāya asamitattā. “Samitattā hi pāpānaṃ[P 2.0479], samaṇoti pavuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 265) idañhi samaṇalakkhaṇaṃ.

90. Patience is the highest austerity: this means that forbearance is the highest austerity. 'Endurance' is a synonym for patience. The meaning is that endurance, known as forbearance, is the supreme austerity. Nibbāna is the highest: the Buddhas declare that in every way, Nibbāna is the highest. A renunciate is not one who harms others: one who, due to a lack of forbearance, harms, troubles, or injures another is not called a renunciate. The fourth line, moreover, is a synonym for the third. For 'is not a renunciate' is a synonym for 'is not an ascetic.' 'One who harms others' is a synonym for 'one who torments others.' Alternatively, 'one who harms others' means one who destroys virtue. For virtue, in the ultimate sense, is called 'supreme' (para). And whichever ascetic, by tormenting any other being, becomes a harmer of others and a destroyer of his own virtue, is not called a renunciate—this is the meaning. Alternatively, one who, from a lack of forbearance, becomes a harmer of others, who intentionally deprives even a fly or a mosquito of life, is not a renunciate. For what reason? Because his defilements have not been expelled. For 'He expels his own defilements, therefore he is called a "renunciate"' (Dhp 388)—this is the characteristic of a renunciate. And one who does not actually harm or kill, but torments another with a stick or the like—he, by tormenting another, is not an ascetic. For what reason? Because harm has not been pacified by him. For 'Because evils have been pacified, one is called an "ascetic"' (Dhp 265)—this is the characteristic of an ascetic.

Dutiyagāthāya sabbapāpassāti sabbākusalassa. Akaraṇanti anuppādanaṃ. Kusalassāti catubhūmikakusalassa. Upasampadāti paṭilābho. Sacittapariyodapananti attano cittajotanaṃ, taṃ pana [V 2.0062] arahattena hoti. Iti sīlasaṃvarena sabbapāpaṃ pahāya samathavipassanāhi kusalaṃ sampādetvā arahattaphalena cittaṃ pariyodāpetabbanti etaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādo anusiṭṭhī ti.

In the second verse, sabbapāpassa (of all evil) means of all that is unwholesome. Akaraṇaṃ (the non-doing) means the non-arising. Kusalassa (of the wholesome) refers to the wholesome of the four planes. Upasampadā (the undertaking) means the attainment. Sacittapariyodapanaṃ (the purification of one’s own mind) means the illuminating of one’s own mind, and that occurs through Arahantship. Thus: having abandoned all evil by restraint in virtue, having accomplished the wholesome through serenity and insight, one should purify the mind through the fruit of Arahantship—this is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas.

Tatiyagāthāya [M 2.0070] anūpavādoti vācāya kassaci anupavadanaṃ. Anūpaghātoti kāyena upaghātassa akaraṇaṃ. Pātimokkheti yaṃ taṃ paatimokkhaṃ, atipamokkhaṃ, uttamasīlaṃ, pāti vā agativisesehi mokkheti duggatibhayehi, yo vā naṃ pāti, taṃ mokkhetīti “pātimokkha”nti vuccati. Tasmiṃ pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro. Mattaññutāti paṭiggahaṇaparibhogavasena pamāṇaññutā. Pantañca sayanāsananti sayanāsanañca saṅghaṭṭanavirahitanti attho. Tattha dvīhiyeva paccayehi catupaccayasantoso dīpito hotīti veditabbo. Etaṃ buddhāna sāsananti etaṃ parassa anupavadanaṃ anupaghātanaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaro paṭiggahaṇaparibhogesu mattaññutā aṭṭhasamāpattivasibhāvāya vivittasenāsanasevanañca buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādo anusiṭṭhīti. Imā pana sabbabuddhānaṃ pātimokkhuddesagāthā hontīti veditabbā.

In the third verse, anūpavādo (non-reproach) means not reproaching anyone by way of speech. Anūpaghāto (non-harming) means the non-doing of harm by way of body. Pātimokkha: this refers to that which is the foremost, the most excellent, the supreme virtue. Or, it protects (pāti) from particular wrong courses and liberates (mokkheti) from the fears of bad destinations. Or, he who protects (pāti) it, it liberates (mokkheti) him—thus it is called ‘Pātimokkha.’ And in that Pātimokkha, there is restraint (saṃvaro). Mattaññutā (knowing the measure) means knowing the proper measure with regard to receiving and using. And pantañca sayanāsanaṃ (a secluded bed and seat) means a lodging that is free from commotion—this is the meaning. It should be understood that herein, contentment with the four requisites is shown by means of just two requisites. This—not reproaching another, not harming another, restraint in the Pātimokkha, knowing the measure in receiving and using, and frequenting secluded lodgings for the sake of mastery over the eight attainments—is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas. These, however, should be known as the verses for the recitation of the Pātimokkha of all the Buddhas.

Devatārocanavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Devas' Announcement

91. Ettāvatā ca iminā vipassissa bhagavato apadānānusārena vitthārakathanena – “tathāgatassevesā, bhikkhave, dhammadhātu suppaṭividdhā”ti evaṃ vuttāya dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā idāni – “devatāpi tathāgatassa etamatthaṃ ārocesu”nti vuttaṃ devatārocanaṃ pakāsetuṃ ekamidāhantiādimāha.

91. Thus far, by means of this detailed exposition in accordance with the life story of the Blessed One Vipassī, having revealed the well-penetrated nature of the Dhamma-principle, concerning which it was said, "Monks, this Dhamma-principle has been well-penetrated by the Tathāgata," he now began with "ekamidāhaṃ" to reveal the declaration of the devas, concerning which it was said, "The devas also informed the Tathāgata of this matter."

Tattha subhagavaneti evaṃnāmake vane. Sālarājamūleti vanappatijeṭṭhakassa mūle. Kāmacchandaṃ virājetvāti anāgāmimaggena mūlasamugghātavasena virājetvā. Yathā ca vipassissa, evaṃ sesabuddhānampi sāsane vutthabrahmacariyā devatā ārocayiṃsu, pāḷi pana vipassissa [P 2.0480] ceva amhākañca bhagavato vasena āgatā.

Therein, subhagavane means: in a forest so named. Sālarājamūle means: at the foot of the lord of the forest. Kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā means: having become dispassionate towards sensual desire, having eradicated it by way of uprooting through the path of the non-returner. And just as devas who had lived the holy life in the dispensation of Vipassī made this announcement, so too did devas in the dispensations of the other Buddhas. The Pāli text, however, has come down with reference to both the Blessed One Vipassī and our own Blessed One.

Tattha attano sampattiyā na hāyanti, na vihāyantīti avihā. Na kañci sattaṃ tapantīti atappā. Sundaradassanā abhirūpā pāsādikāti sudassā. Suṭṭhu passanti, sundarametesaṃ vā dassananti sudassī. Sabbeheva ca saguṇehi bhavasampattiyā ca jeṭṭhā, natthettha kaniṭṭhāti akaniṭṭhā.

Herein, because they do not fall away from or diminish in their own attainment, they are the Avihā. Because they do not torment any being, they are the Atappā. Because they are of beautiful appearance, exceedingly fair, and inspiring, they are the Sudassā. Because they see well, or because their sight is beautiful, they are the Sudassī. They are foremost in all their own qualities and in the attainments of existence, and there are no juniors among them, thus they are the Akaniṭṭhā.

Idha [V 2.0063][M 2.0071] ṭhatvā bhāṇavārā samodhānetabbā. Imasmiñhi sutte vipassissa bhagavato apadānavasena tayo bhāṇavārā vuttā. Yathā ca vipassissa, evaṃ sikhīādīnampi apadānavasena vuttāva. Pāḷi pana saṅkhittā. Iti sattannaṃ buddhānaṃ vasena amhākaṃ bhagavatā ekavīsati bhāṇavārā kathitā. Tathā avihehi. Tathā atappehi. Tathā sudassehi. Tathā sudassīhi. Tathā akaniṭṭhehīti sabbampi chabbīsatibhāṇavārasataṃ hoti. Tepiṭake buddhavacane aññaṃ suttaṃ chabbīsatibhāṇavārasataparimāṇaṃ nāma natthi, suttantarājā nāma ayaṃ suttantoti veditabbo. Ito paraṃ anusandhidvayampi niyyātento iti kho bhikkhavetiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānamevāti.

Here, pausing, the recitation sections should be reckoned. For in this discourse, three recitation sections are spoken concerning the Blessed One Vipassī by way of his life story. And just as for Vipassī, so too for Sikhī and the others, they are spoken by way of their life stories. The Pāli text, however, is abbreviated. Thus, with reference to the seven Buddhas, twenty-one recitation sections were spoken by our Blessed One. Likewise by the Avihā devas. Likewise by the Atappā devas. Likewise by the Sudassā devas. Likewise by the Sudassī devas. Likewise by the Akaniṭṭhā devas. Thus, in total, it amounts to one hundred and twenty-six recitation sections. In the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, there is no other discourse named that has the measure of one hundred and twenty-six recitation sections; this discourse should be understood as the king of discourses. Hereafter, concluding the two connections, he spoke the words beginning, 'Thus, O monks...' All of that is self-evident.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya,

Mahāpadānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Great Discourse on the Lineage is concluded.

2. Mahānidānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Great Discourse on Causation

Nidānavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Nidāna

95. Evaṃ [V 2.0064][P 2.0481][M 2.0072] me sutaṃ…pe… kurūsūti mahānidānasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā. Kurūsu viharatīti kurū nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīsaddena “kurū”ti vuccati. Tasmiṃ kurūsu janapade. Aṭṭhakathācariyā panāhu – mandhātukāle tīsu dīpesu manussā “jambudīpo nāma buddhapaccekabuddhamahāsāvakacakkavattippabhutīnaṃ uttamamanussānaṃ uppattibhūmi uttamadīpo atiramaṇīyo”ti sutvā raññā mandhātucakkavattinā cakkaratanaṃ purakkhatvā cattāro dīpe anusaṃyāyantena saddhiṃ āgamaṃsu. Tato rājā pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pucchi – “atthi nu kho manussalokato ramaṇīyataraṃ ṭhāna”nti. Kasmā deva evaṃ bhaṇasi? Kiṃ na passasi candimasūriyānaṃ ānubhāvaṃ, nanu etesaṃ ṭhānaṃ ito ramaṇīyataranti? Rājā cakkaratanaṃ purakkhatvā tattha agamāsi. Cattāro mahārājāno – “mandhātumahārājā āgato”ti sutvāva “mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo rājā, na sakkā yuddhena paṭibāhitu”nti sakaṃ rajjaṃ niyyātesuṃ. So taṃ gahetvā puna pucchi – “atthi nu kho ito ramaṇīyataraṃ ṭhāna”nti?

95. The Mahānidāna Sutta begins with the words, 'Thus have I heard... in the Kuru country.' Herein is the explanation of obscure terms. Regarding the phrase 'dwelling in the Kuru country': the Kuru are princes native to that country. Their residence, even a single country, is called 'Kuru' by a conventional term. In that Kuru country. The ancient commentators, however, have said: In the time of Mandhātā, people on three continents, having heard, 'Jambudīpa is the birthplace of supreme beings such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, great disciples, and wheel-turning monarchs; it is the supreme and most delightful continent,' came along with the wheel-turning monarch, King Mandhātā, as he journeyed through the four continents, preceded by his wheel-treasure. Then the king asked his guide-treasure, 'Is there, indeed, any place more delightful than the human world?' 'Why, Your Majesty, do you say so? Do you not see the majesty of the moon and sun? Is not their abode more delightful than this?' The king, preceded by his wheel-treasure, went there. The Four Great Kings, as soon as they heard, 'King Mandhātā has arrived,' thinking, 'The king is of great psychic power and majesty; he cannot be repelled by battle,' they handed over their own kingdom. Having received it, he asked again, 'Is there, indeed, any place more delightful than this?'

Athassa tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ kathayiṃsu. “Tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ, deva, ito ramaṇīyataraṃ. Tattha sakkassa devarañño ime cattāro mahārājāno paricārakā dovārikabhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhanti, sakko devarājā mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo, tassimāni upabhogaṭṭhānāni – yojanasahassubbedho vejayanto pāsādo, pañcayojanasatubbedhā sudhammā devasabhā, diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko vejayantaratho tathā erāvaṇo hatthī[P 2.0482], dibbarukkhasahassappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nandanavanaṃ, cittalatāvanaṃ, phārusakavanaṃ, missakavanaṃ, yojanasatubbedho pāricchattako koviḷāro, tassa heṭṭhā saṭṭhiyojanāyāmā paññāsayojanavitthatā [V 2.0065] pañcadasayojanubbedhā jayakusumapupphavaṇṇā paṇḍukambalasilā, yassā mudutāya sakkassa nisīdato upaḍḍhakāyo anupavisatī”ti.

Then they told him of the Tāvatiṃsa realm. 'The Tāvatiṃsa realm, Your Majesty, is more delightful than this. There, these Four Great Kings stand as attendants in the position of gatekeepers for Sakka, the king of the devas. Sakka, the king of the devas, is of great psychic power and majesty. These are his articles of enjoyment: the Vejayanta palace, a thousand yojanas in height; the Sudhammā assembly hall of the devas, five hundred yojanas in height; the Vejayanta chariot, one hundred and fifty yojanas in size, and likewise the elephant Erāvaṇa; the Nandana grove, adorned with a thousand celestial trees; the Cittalatā grove; the Phārusaka grove; the Missaka grove; the Pāricchattaka coral tree, one hundred yojanas in height; beneath it, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, sixty yojanas in length, fifty yojanas in width, and fifteen yojanas in height, the color of jasmine flowers, which is so soft that when Sakka sits upon it, half of his body sinks in.'

Taṃ [M 2.0073] sutvā rājā tattha gantukāmo cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkiri. Taṃ ākāse patiṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Atha dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ vemajjhato cakkaratanaṃ otaritvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ pariṇāyakaratanapamukhāya caturaṅginiyā senāya. Rājā ekakova tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ agamāsi. Sakko – “mandhātā āgato”ti sutvāva tassa paccuggamanaṃ katvā – “svāgataṃ, te mahārāja, sakaṃ te mahārāja, anusāsa mahārājā”ti vatvā saddhiṃ nāṭakehi rajjaṃ dve bhāge katvā ekaṃ bhāgamadāsi. Rañño tāvatiṃsabhavane patiṭṭhitamattasseva manussabhāvo vigacchi, devabhāvo pāturahosi. Tassa kira sakkena saddhiṃ paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ nisinnassa akkhinimisamattena nānattaṃ paññāyati. Taṃ asallakkhentā devā sakkassa ca tassa ca nānatte muyhanti. So tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamāno yāva chattiṃsa sakkā uppajjitvā cutā, tāva rajjaṃ kāretvā atittova kāmehi tato cavitvā attano uyyāne patiṭṭhito vātātapena phuṭṭhagatto kālamakāsi.

Hearing that, the king, wishing to go there, projected the wheel-treasure upwards. It established itself in the sky together with his fourfold army. Then, descending from between the two deva worlds, the wheel-treasure established itself on the earth together with the fourfold army, headed by the guide-treasure. The king went alone to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Sakka, as soon as he heard, 'Mandhātā has arrived,' went out to meet him and, after saying, 'Welcome, great king! It is yours, great king! Rule, great king!', he divided the kingdom into two parts along with the celestial dancers and gave one part to him. As soon as the king was established in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, his human state vanished and a deva state appeared. It is said that when he was seated with Sakka on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, the difference between them was discernible only by the blinking of their eyes. The devas, not noticing this, were perplexed by the difference between Sakka and him. While enjoying divine fortune there, he reigned for as long as it took for thirty-six Sakkas to arise and pass away. Still insatiate in his sensual desires, he fell from there and was established in his own park where, his body afflicted by wind and sun, he passed away.

Cakkaratane pana puna pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhite pariṇāyakaratanaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe mandhātu upāhanaṃ likhāpetvā idaṃ mandhātu rajjanti rajjamanusāsi. Tepi tīhi dīpehi āgatamanussā puna gantuṃ asakkontā pariṇāyakaratanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “deva, mayaṃ rañño ānubhāvena āgatā, idāni gantuṃ na sakkoma, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ no dehī”ti yāciṃsu. So tesaṃ ekamekaṃ janapadamadāsi. Tattha pubbavidehato āgatamanussehi āvasitapadeso tāyeva purimasaññāya – “videharaṭṭha”nti nāmaṃ labhi, aparagoyānato āgatamanussehi āvasitapadeso “aparantajanapado”ti nāmaṃ labhi, uttarakuruto āgatamanussehi āvasitapadeso “kururaṭṭha”nti nāmaṃ [P 2.0483] labhi, bahuke pana gāmanigamādayo upādāya bahuvacanena vohariyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “kurūsu viharatī”ti.

When, however, the wheel-treasure was again established on the earth, the guide-jewel had Mandhātā's sandal inscribed on golden plates and governed the kingdom, declaring, 'This is Mandhātā's realm.' Those people who had come from the three continents, being unable to return, approached the guide-jewel and requested, 'Lord, we came through the king's power, but now we are unable to return. Give us a dwelling place!' He gave each of them a separate territory. The area inhabited by the people who had come from Pubbavideha received the name 'Videha country' by that same former designation. The area inhabited by the people who had come from Aparagoyāna received the name 'Aparanta territory.' The area inhabited by the people who had come from Uttarakuru received the name 'Kuru country.' But on account of its many villages, market towns, and so forth, it is referred to in the plural. Therefore, it is said, 'He dwells among the Kurus.'

Kammāsadhammaṃ nāma kurūnaṃ nigamoti kammāsadhammanti ettha keci dha-kārassa da-kārena atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti. Kammāso ettha damitoti kammāsadammo. Kammāsoti kammāsapādo porisādo vuccati.
