Tassa kira pāde khāṇukena viddhaṭṭhāne vaṇo ruhanto cittadārusadiso hutvā ruhi. Tasmā kammāsapādoti paññāyittha. So ca tasmiṃ okāse damito porisādabhāvato [M 2.0074] paṭisedhito[V 2.0066]. Kena? Mahāsattena. Katarasmiṃ jātaketi? Mahāsutasomajātaketi eke. Ime pana therā jayaddisajātaketi vadanti. Tadā hi mahāsattena kammāsapādo damito. Yathāha –

Regarding 'Kammāsadhamma, a market town of the Kurus': Here, concerning the word 'Kammāsadhamma', some explain the meaning by using the letter 'da' for the letter 'dha'. 'Kammāsa was tamed here' (Kammāso ettha damito), thus it is 'Kammāsadamma'. 'Kammāsa' refers to the man-eater Kammāsapāda. And he was tamed in that place, restrained from his state of being a man-eater. By whom? By the Great Being. In which Jātaka? Some say it was in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka. These elders, however, say it was in the Jayaddisa Jātaka. For at that time, Kammāsapāda was tamed by the Great Being. As it is said:

“Putto yadā homi jayaddisassa;

Pañcālaraṭṭhadhipatissa atrajo.

Cajitvāna pāṇaṃ pitaraṃ pamocayiṃ;

Kammāsapādampi cahaṃ pasādayi”nti.

“When I was the son of Jayaddisa, the ruler of the Pañcāla country, his true-born son, having given up my life, I liberated my father; and I also brought contentment to Kammāsapāda.”

Keci pana dha-kāreneva atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti. Kurūraṭṭhavāsīnaṃ kira kuruvattadhammo, tasmiṃ kammāso jāto, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ kammāso ettha dhammo jātoti kammāsadhammanti vuccati. Tattha niviṭṭhanigamassāpi etadeva nāmaṃ. Bhummavacanena kasmā na vuttanti. Avasanokāsato. Bhagavato kira tasmiṃ nigame vasanokāso koci vihāro nāma nāhosi. Nigamato pana apakkamma aññatarasmiṃ udakasampanne ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge mahāvanasaṇḍo ahosi tattha bhagavā vihāsi, taṃ nigamaṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā. Tasmā evamettha attho veditabbo – “kurūsu viharati kammāsadhammaṃ nāma kurūnaṃ nigamo, taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā”ti.

Some, however, explain the meaning with the letter 'dha' itself. It is said that for the inhabitants of the Kuru country, their practice of the Kuru observance became variegated in that place. Therefore, that place is called Kammāsadhamma, meaning, 'Here the practice (dhamma) became variegated (kammāsa).' The market town established there also has this very name. Why was it not stated in the locative case? Because it was not a dwelling place. It is said that in that market town, the Blessed One had no dwelling place called a monastery. Rather, having departed from the market town, there was a great forest grove in a certain delightful region endowed with water. The Blessed One dwelt there, having made that market town his alms-resort village. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'He dwells among the Kurus, having made Kammāsadhamma, a market town of the Kurus, his alms-resort village.'

Āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ, gāravavacanametaṃ. Ānandoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso – “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Tasmā yathā nisinno ekamantaṃ nisinno hoti, tathā nisīdīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ nisīdīti [P 2.0484] upāvisi. Paṇḍitā hi garuṭṭhāniyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ nisīdanti. Ayañca tesaṃ aññataro, tasmā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

'Venerable' is a term of affection; it is a term of respect. 'Ānanda' is the name of that elder. 'Ekamantaṃ' (to one side) is an adverbial expression in the neuter gender, as in 'unevenly the moon and sun revolve' and so on. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: he sat in such a way that he was seated to one side. Alternatively, this is an accusative expression used in the sense of the locative; 'he sat down' means he took a seat. For the wise, when approaching one worthy of respect, they sit to one side out of skill in seating etiquette. And this was one of them, so he sat to one side.

Kathaṃ nisinno kho pana ekamantaṃ nisinno hotīti? Cha nisajjadose vajjetvā. Seyyathidaṃ – atidūraṃ, accāsannaṃ, uparivātaṃ, unnatappadesaṃ, atisammukhaṃ, atipacchāti. Atidūre nisinno hi sace kathetukāmo hoti, uccāsaddena kathetabbaṃ hoti. Accāsanne nisinno saṅghaṭṭanaṃ karoti. Uparivāte nisinno sarīragandhena bādhati. Unnatappadese nisinno [M 2.0075] agāravaṃ pakāseti. Atisammukhā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Atipacchā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, gīvaṃ parivattetvā daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā ayampi tikkhattuṃ bhagavantaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā sakkaccaṃ vanditvā ete cha nisajjadose vajjetvā [V 2.0067] dakkhiṇajāṇumaṇḍalassa abhimukhaṭṭhāne chabbaṇṇānaṃ buddharasmīnaṃ anto pavisitvā pasannalākhārasaṃ vigāhanto viya suvaṇṇapaṭaṃ pārupanto viya rattuppalamālāvitānamajjhaṃ pavisanto viya ca dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko āyasmā ānando nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”ti.

How, then, is one who is seated seated to one side? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. Namely: being too far, too close, upwind, on higher ground, too directly in front, and too far behind. For if one sits too far and wishes to speak, one must speak loudly. If one sits too close, one causes physical contact. If one sits upwind, one afflicts with body odor. If one sits on higher ground, one shows disrespect. If one sits too directly in front and wishes to look, one must look by meeting eye to eye. If one sits too far behind and wishes to look, one must turn the neck. Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda—the Treasurer of the Dhamma—after circumambulating the Blessed One three times and respectfully paying homage, avoided these six faults of sitting and sat down in a place facing the right knee, as if entering into the six-colored rays of the Buddha, like plunging into clear lac juice, like wrapping himself in a golden cloth, and like entering beneath a canopy of red lotuses. Thus it is said: 'He sat down to one side.'

Kāya pana velāya, kena kāraṇena ayamāyasmā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamantoti? Sāyanhavelāyaṃ paccayākārapañhapucchanakāraṇena. Taṃ divasaṃ kirāyamāyasmā kulasaṅgahatthāya gharadvāre gharadvāre sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ nikkhipanto viya kammāsadhammagāmaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto satthu vattaṃ dassetvā satthari gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe satthāraṃ vanditvā attano divāṭṭhānaṃ gantvā antevāsikesu vattaṃ dassetvā paṭikkantesu divāṭṭhānaṃ paṭisammajjitvā cammakkhaṇḍaṃ paññapetvā udakatumbato udakaṃ gahetvā udakena hatthapāde sītale katvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno sotāpattiphalasamāpattiṃ samāpajji. Atha paricchinnakālavasena samāpattito uṭṭhāya paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ otāresi. So – “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādito paṭṭhāya antaṃ, antato paṭṭhāya ādiṃ, ubhayantato paṭṭhāya majjhaṃ, majjhato paṭṭhāya ubho ante pāpento tikkhattuṃ dvādasapadaṃ paccayākāraṃ sammasi. Tassevaṃ sammasantassa paccayākāro vibhūto [P 2.0485] hutvā uttānakuttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi.

At what time, and for what reason, did this venerable one approach the Blessed One? In the evening, for the purpose of asking a question about dependent origination. That very day, it is said, this venerable one, as if placing a bundle of goods worth a thousand at each house door for the sake of winning support from families, wandered for alms in the village of Kammāsadhamma. Having returned from his alms round, having performed his duties towards the Teacher, and having paid homage to the Teacher when the Teacher had entered the fragrant hut, he went to his own day quarters. There, having performed his duties towards his pupils, and after they had departed, he swept his day quarters, spread out his leather mat, took water from the water pot, cooled his hands and feet with water, sat down cross-legged, and attained the fruition-attainment of stream-entry. Then, emerging from that attainment at the end of the allotted time, he directed his knowledge to dependent origination. Starting from 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise,' he examined the twelve-linked dependent origination three times: from the beginning to the end, from the end to the beginning, from both ends to the middle, and from the middle to both ends. As he thus examined, dependent origination became clear and manifest to him, appearing as if utterly plain.

Tato cintesi – “ayaṃ paccayākāro sabbabuddhehi – ‘gambhīro ceva gambhīrāvabhāso cā’ti kathito, mayhaṃ kho pana padesañāṇe ṭhitassa sāvakassa sato uttāno vibhūto pākaṭo hutvā upaṭṭhāti, mayhaṃyeva nu kho esa uttānako hutvā upaṭṭhāti, udāhu aññesampī”ti? Athassa etadahosi – “handāhaṃ imaṃ pañhaṃ gahetvā bhagavantaṃ pucchāmi, addhā me bhagavā imaṃ atthuppattiṃ katvā sālindaṃ sineruṃ ukkhipanto viya ekaṃ suttantakathaṃ kathetvā dassessati. Buddhānañhi vinayapaññattiṃ, bhummantaraṃ, paccayākāraṃ, samayantaranti imāni cattāri ṭhānāni patvā gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, ñāṇaṃ anupavisati, buddhañāṇassa mahantabhāvo [M 2.0076] paññāyati, desanā gambhīrā hoti tilakkhaṇabbhāhatā suññatapaṭisaṃyuttā”ti.

Then he thought: 'This dependent origination has been described by all Buddhas as "profound and with a profound appearance." Yet for me, a disciple established in partial knowledge, it appears plain, distinct, and evident. Does it appear so plainly only to me, or to others as well?' Then it occurred to him: 'Let me take this question and ask the Blessed One. Surely the Blessed One, taking this matter as the occasion, will deliver a discourse, as if lifting up Mount Sineru with its surrounding peaks. For when the Buddhas reach these four topics—the Vinaya rules, the divisions between realms, dependent origination, and other philosophical systems—their roar becomes mighty, knowledge penetrates, the greatness of the Buddha’s knowledge becomes evident, and the teaching becomes profound, stamped with the three characteristics, and connected with emptiness.'

So kiñcāpi pakatiyāva ekadivase satavārampi sahassavārampi bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamanto na ahetuakāraṇena upasaṅkamati, taṃ divasaṃ pana imaṃ pañhaṃ gahetvā – “imaṃ buddhagandhahatthiṃ āpajja ñāṇakoñcanādaṃ sossāmi, buddhasīhaṃ āpajja ñāṇasīhanādaṃ sossāmi, buddhasindhavaṃ āpajja ñāṇapadavikkamaṃ passissāmī”ti cintetvā divāṭṭhānā uṭṭhāya cammakkhaṇḍaṃ papphoṭetvā [V 2.0068] ādāya sāyanhasamaye bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami. Tena vuttaṃ – “sāyanhavelāyaṃ paccayākārapañhapucchanakāraṇena upasaṅkamanto”ti.

Although by nature he would approach the Blessed One a hundred or even a thousand times a day, he would not approach without cause or reason. On that day, however, taking up this question, he thought: 'Having approached this Buddha, this fragrant elephant, I will hear the trumpeting of knowledge. Having approached this Buddha, this lion, I will hear the lion's roar of knowledge. Having approached this Buddha, this thoroughbred, I will witness the stride of knowledge.' Having thought thus, rising from his day quarters, he shook out the leather mat, took it up, and approached the Blessed One in the evening. Hence it was said: 'He approached in the evening for the purpose of asking a question about dependent origination.'

Yāva gambhīroti ettha yāvasaddo pamāṇātikkame, atikkamma pamāṇaṃ gambhīro, atigambhīroti attho. Gambhīrāvabhāsoti gambhīrova hutvā avabhāsati, dissatīti attho. Ekañhi uttānameva gambhīrāvabhāsaṃ hoti pūtipaṇṇādivasena kāḷavaṇṇapurāṇaudakaṃ viya. Tañhi jāṇuppamāṇampi sataporisaṃ viya dissati. Ekaṃ gambhīraṃ [P 2.0486] uttānāvabhāsaṃ hoti maṇigaṅgāya vippasannaudakaṃ viya. Tañhi sataporisampi jāṇuppamāṇaṃ viya khāyati. Ekaṃ uttānaṃ uttānāvabhāsaṃ hoti cāṭiādīsu udakaṃ viya. Ekaṃ gambhīraṃ gambhīrāvabhāsaṃ hoti sinerupādakamahāsamudde udakaṃ viya. Evaṃ udakameva cattāri nāmāni labhati. Paṭiccasamuppāde panetaṃ natthi. Ayañhi gambhīro ceva gambhīrāvabhāso cāti ekameva nāmaṃ labhati. Evarūpo samānopi atha ca pana me uttānakuttānako viya khāyati, yadidaṃ acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ bhanteti. Evaṃ attano vimhayaṃ pakāsento pañhaṃ pucchitvā tuṇhībhūto nisīdi.

Here, in the phrase 'yāva gambhīro,' the word 'yāva' signifies exceeding a measure; the meaning is 'deep beyond measure,' 'exceedingly deep.' 'Gambhīrāvabhāso' means that being deep, it also appears, or is seen, as deep. For some water, though shallow, appears deep, like dark, old water discolored by putrid leaves and so on. Though only knee-deep, it may seem a hundred fathoms deep. Some water, though deep, appears shallow, like the very clear water of the Maṇigaṅgā river. Though a hundred fathoms deep, it may seem only knee-deep. Some water is shallow and appears shallow, like water in a pot. Some water is deep and appears deep, like the water in the great ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru. Thus, water alone acquires four designations. But this is not so with dependent origination. For it is both deep and appears deep—it bears only this one designation. 'Though it is of such a nature, yet to me it appears utterly plain. This is wonderful, venerable sir, this is marvelous, venerable sir!' Thus, expressing his astonishment, he asked the question and then sat down in silence.

Bhagavā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā – “ānando bhavaggaggahaṇāya hatthaṃ pasārento viya, sineruṃ chinditvā miñjaṃ nīharituṃ vāyamamāno viya, vinā nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmo viya, pathaviṃ parivattetvā pathavojaṃ gahetuṃ vāyamamāno viya buddhavisayapañhaṃ attano uttānaṃ vadati. Handassa gambhīrabhāvaṃ ācikkhissāmī”ti cintetvā mā hevantiādimāha.

Having heard his words, the Blessed One thought: "Ānanda speaks of a question that is the domain of a Buddha as if it were plain to him—like one stretching out his hand to grasp the summit of existence, like one trying to extract the pith by splitting Mount Sineru, like one wishing to cross the great ocean without a boat, like one striving to take the earth's essence by turning it over. Well then, I shall explain its profound nature to him." Reflecting thus, he said, "Do not say so, Ānanda," and so forth.

Tattha mā hevanti ha-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Evaṃ mā bhaṇīti attho. Mā hevanti ca idaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ ussādentopi bhaṇati apasādentopi.

Therein, in 'mā hevaṃ,' the 'ha' is a mere particle, an expletive. The meaning is, 'Do not speak thus.' The Blessed One utters this expression, 'mā hevaṃ,' to the Venerable Ānanda both to commend him and to disparage him.

Ussādanāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Commendation

Tattha [M 2.0077] ussādento – ānanda, tvaṃ mahāpañño visadañāṇo, tena te gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako viya khāyati. Aññesaṃ panesa uttānakoti na sallakkhetabbo, gambhīroyeva ca gambhīrāvabhāso ca. Tattha catasso upamā vadanti. Chamāse subhojanarasapuṭṭhassa kira katayogassa mahāmallassa samajjasamaye katamallapāsāṇaparicayassa yuddhabhūmiṃ gacchantassa antarā mallapāsāṇaṃ dassesuṃ, so – kiṃ etanti āha. Mallapāsāṇoti. Āharatha nanti. Ukkhipituṃ [V 2.0069] na sakkomāti vutte sayaṃ gantvā kuhiṃ imassa bhāriyaṭṭhānanti vatvā dvīhi hatthehi dve pāsāṇe ukkhipitvā kīḷāguḷe viya khipitvā agamāsi. Tattha mallassa mallapāsāṇo lahukopi na aññesaṃ lahukoti vattabbo. Chamāse subhojanarasapuṭṭho mallo viya hi kappasatasahassaṃ abhinīhārasampanno āyasmā ānando, yathā mallassa mahābalatāya mallapāsāṇo lahuko, evaṃ therassa mahāpaññatāya [P 2.0487] paṭiccasamuppādo uttāno, so aññesaṃ uttānoti na vattabbo.

Here, by way of encouragement: 'Ānanda, you are of great wisdom and clear understanding; therefore, even the profound dependent origination appears shallow to you. But for others, it should not be regarded as shallow; it is indeed deep and has the appearance of being deep.' In this regard, they cite four similes. It is said that a great, well-trained wrestler, who had been well-nourished with fine food for six months and was familiar with the wrestler's stone, was going to the wrestling ground during a festival. On the way, they showed him a wrestler's stone. He asked, 'What is this?' 'A wrestler's stone,' they replied. 'Bring it here,' he said. When they said, 'We cannot lift it,' he went himself, and saying, 'Where is the heavy part of this?' he lifted two stones with his two hands, tossed them like play-balls, and went on his way. In this case, although the wrestler's stone is light for the wrestler, it should not be called light for others. For just as the wrestler was well-nourished with fine food for six months, so the Venerable Ānanda was endowed with the aspiration for a hundred thousand eons. Just as the wrestler's stone was light for the wrestler due to his great strength, so dependent origination is shallow for the Elder due to his great wisdom. But it should not be called shallow for others.

Mahāsamudde ca timināma maccho dviyojanasatiko timiṅgalo tiyojanasatiko, timipiṅgalo catuyojanasatiko timirapiṅgalo pañcayojanasatiko, ānando timinando ajjhāroho mahātimīti ime cattāro yojanasahassikā. Tattha timirapiṅgaleneva dīpenti. Tassa kira dakkhiṇakaṇṇaṃ cālentassa pañcayojanasate padese udakaṃ calati. Tathā vāmakaṇṇaṃ. Tathā naṅguṭṭhaṃ, tathā sīsaṃ. Dve pana kaṇṇe cāletvā naṅguṭṭhena udakaṃ paharitvā sīsaṃ aparāparaṃ katvā kīḷituṃ āraddhassa sattaṭṭhayojanasate padese bhājane pakkhipitvā uddhane āropitaṃ viya udakaṃ pakkuthati, tiyojanasatamatte padese udakaṃ piṭṭhiṃ chādetuṃ na sakkoti. So evaṃ vadeyya – “ayaṃ mahāsamuddo gambhīro gambhīroti vadanti kutassa gambhīratā, mayaṃ piṭṭhipaṭicchādanamattampi udakaṃ na labhāmā”ti. Tattha kāyupapannassa timirapiṅgalassa mahāsamuddo uttānoti, aññesaṃ khuddakamacchānaṃ uttānoti na vattabbo, evameva ñāṇupapannassa therassa paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti, aññesampi uttānoti na vattabbo.

Furthermore, in the great ocean, there is a fish named Timi, two hundred yojanas in size; the Timiṅgala is three hundred yojanas; the Timipiṅgala is four hundred yojanas; the Timirapiṅgala is five hundred yojanas. The Ānanda, Timinanda, Ajjhāroha, and Mahātimi—these four are each a thousand yojanas in size. In this context, they illustrate with the Timirapiṅgala. It is said that when it moves its right ear, the water stirs across a region of five hundred yojanas. The same with its left ear. The same with its tail, and the same with its head. But when it begins to play by moving both ears, striking the water with its tail, and moving its head back and forth, the water across a region of seven or eight hundred yojanas boils as if placed in a pot over a fire. In water a mere three hundred yojanas deep, it cannot cover its back. It might say: 'They call this great ocean deep, deep—but where is its depth? We cannot even find enough water to cover our backs.' In this case, for the Timirapiṅgala, endowed with such a body, the great ocean is shallow, but it should not be called shallow for other small fish. In the same way, for the Elder endowed with wisdom, dependent origination is shallow, but it should not be called shallow for others.

Supaṇṇarājā [M 2.0078] ca diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko, tassa dakkhiṇapakkho paññāsayojaniko hoti tathā vāmapakkho, piñchavaṭṭi saṭṭhiyojanikā, gīvā tiṃsayojanikā, mukhaṃ navayojanaṃ, pādā dvādasayojanikā. Tasmiṃ supaṇṇavātaṃ dassetuṃ āraddhe sattaṭṭhayojanasataṃ ṭhānaṃ nappahoti. So evaṃ vadeyya – “ayaṃ ākāso ananto anantoti vadanti, kutassa anantatā, mayaṃ pakkhavātappasāraṇokāsampi na labhāmā”ti. Tattha kāyupapannassa supaṇṇarañño ākāso parittoti, aññesaṃ khuddakapakkhīnaṃ parittoti na vattabbo, evameva ñāṇupapannassa therassa paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti, aññesampi uttānoti na vattabbo.

And the Supaṇṇa king is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. His right wing is fifty yojanas, and so is his left wing. His tail-fan is sixty yojanas, his neck thirty yojanas, his mouth nine yojanas, and his feet twelve yojanas. When he begins to generate the Supaṇṇa wind, a space of seven or eight hundred yojanas is not enough. He might say: 'They call this sky endless, endless—but where is its endlessness? We cannot even find space to spread the wind of our wings.' In this case, for the Supaṇṇa king, endowed with such a body, the sky is limited, but it should not be called limited for other small birds. In the same way, for the Elder endowed with wisdom, dependent origination is shallow, but it should not be called shallow for others.

Rāhu asurindo pana pādantato yāva kesantā yojanānaṃ cattāri sahassāni aṭṭha ca satāni hoti. Tassa dvinnaṃ bāhānaṃ antaraṃ dvādasayojanasatikaṃ. Bahalattena chayojanasatikaṃ[P 2.0488]. Hatthapādatalāni [V 2.0070] tiyojanasatikāni, tathā mukhaṃ. Ekekaṃ aṅgulipabbaṃ paññāsayojanaṃ, tathā bhamukantaraṃ. Nalāṭaṃ tiyojanasatikaṃ. Sīsaṃ navayojanasatikaṃ. Tassa mahāsamuddaṃ otiṇṇassa gambhīraṃ udakaṃ jāṇuppamāṇaṃ hoti. So evaṃ vadeyya – “ayaṃ mahāsamuddo gambhīro gambhīroti vadanti, kutassa gambhīratā, mayaṃ jāṇuppaṭicchādanamattampi udakaṃ na labhāmā”ti. Tattha kāyupapannassa rāhuno mahāsamuddo uttānoti, aññesaṃ uttānoti na vattabbo, evameva ñāṇupapannassa therassa paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti, aññesampi uttānoti na vattabbo. Etamatthaṃ sandhāya bhagavā – “mā hevaṃ, ānanda, avaca; mā hevaṃ, ānanda avacā”ti āha.

Rāhu, the lord of the Asuras, measures four thousand eight hundred yojanas from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair. The span between his two arms is twelve hundred yojanas. His thickness is six hundred yojanas. The palms of his hands and soles of his feet are three hundred yojanas each, as is his mouth. Each finger joint is fifty yojanas, and so is the space between his eyebrows. His forehead is three hundred yojanas, and his head nine hundred yojanas. When he enters the great ocean, the deep water only reaches his knees. He might say: 'They call this great ocean deep, deep—but where is its depth? We cannot even find enough water to cover our knees.' In this case, for Rāhu, endowed with such a body, the great ocean is shallow, but it should not be called shallow for others. In the same way, for the Elder endowed with wisdom, dependent origination is shallow, but it should not be called shallow for others. It was with reference to this meaning that the Blessed One said: 'Do not say so, Ānanda; do not say so, Ānanda.'

Therassa hi catūhi kāraṇehi gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānoti upaṭṭhāti. Katamehi catūhi? Pubbūpanissayasampattiyā, titthavāsena, sotāpannatāya, bahussutabhāvenāti.

Indeed, for the Elder, even the profound dependent origination appears shallow for four reasons. What four? Due to the perfection of supporting conditions from the past, due to residing at the ford of the Teacher, due to being a stream-enterer, and due to being greatly learned.

Pubbūpanissayasampattikathā

The Story of the Perfection of Supporting Conditions from the Past

Ito kira satasahassime kappe padumuttaro nāma satthā loke uppajji. Tassa haṃsavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, ānando nāma rājā pitā[M 2.0079], sumedhā nāma devī mātā, bodhisatto uttarakumāro nāma ahosi. So puttassa jātadivase mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamma pabbajitvā padhānamanuyuñjanto anukkamena sabbaññutaṃ patvā – “anekajātisaṃsāra”nti udānaṃ udānetvā sattāhaṃ bodhipallaṅke vītināmetvā pathaviyaṃ ṭhapessāmīti pādaṃ abhinīhari. Atha pathaviṃ bhinditvā mahantaṃ padumaṃ uṭṭhāsi. Tassa dhurapattāni navutihatthāni, kesaraṃ tiṃsahatthaṃ, kaṇṇikā dvādasahatthā, navaghaṭappamāṇo reṇu ahosi.

It is said that one hundred thousand eons from this present one, in that eon, a Teacher named Padumuttara arose in the world. His city was named Haṃsavatī, his father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was the prince named Uttara. On the day of his son's birth, he undertook the great renunciation, went forth, and engaging in diligent striving, he gradually attained omniscience. Having uttered the inspired utterance, 'Through countless births in saṃsāra...', he spent seven days on the throne of enlightenment. Then, thinking, 'I will place my foot on the earth,' he extended his foot. At that moment, the earth split open, and a great lotus arose. Its principal petals were ninety cubits, its filaments thirty cubits, its pericarp twelve cubits, and its pollen was the measure of nine pots.

Satthā pana ubbedhato aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedho ahosi. Tassa ubhinnaṃ bāhānamantaraṃ aṭṭhārasahatthaṃ, nalāṭaṃ pañcahatthaṃ, hatthapādā ekādasahatthā. Tassa ekādasahatthena pādena dvādasahatthāya kaṇṇikāya akkantamattāya navaghaṭappamāṇo reṇu uṭṭhāya aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthaṃ padesaṃ uggantvā okiṇṇamanosilācuṇṇaṃ viya paccokiṇṇo. Tadupādāya bhagavā padumuttarotveva paññāyittha. Tassa devilo [P 2.0489] ca sujāto ca dve aggasāvakā ahesuṃ. Amitā ca asamā ca dve aggasāvikā. Sumano nāma upaṭṭhāko. Padumuttaro bhagavā pitusaṅgahaṃ kurumāno bhikkhusatasahassaparivāro haṃsavatiyā rājadhāniyā vasati.

The Teacher, furthermore, was fifty-eight cubits in height. The distance between his two arms was eighteen cubits, his forehead five cubits, and his hands and feet eleven cubits. When he placed his eleven-cubit foot on the twelve-cubit pericarp, pollen amounting to nine jars rose up and, ascending over an area of fifty-eight cubits, settled down like scattered vermilion powder. On account of that, the Blessed One was known as Padumuttara. His two foremost disciples were Devila and Sujāta. His two foremost female disciples were Amitā and Asamā. His attendant was named Sumana. The Blessed One Padumuttara, showing favor to his father, dwelt in the royal city of Haṃsavatī, surrounded by one hundred thousand bhikkhus.

Kaniṭṭhabhātā [V 2.0071] panassa sumanakumāro nāma. Tassa rājā haṃsavatito vīsatiyojanasate ṭhāne bhogagāmaṃ adāsi. So kadāci āgantvā pitarañca satthārañca passati. Athekadivasaṃ paccanto kupito. Sumano rañño pesesi – “paccanto kupito”ti. Rājā “mayā tvaṃ tattha kasmā ṭhapito”ti paṭipesesi. So nikkhamma core vūpasametvā – “upasanto, deva, janapado”ti rañño pesesi. Rājā tuṭṭho – “sīghaṃ mama putto āgacchatū”ti āha. Tassa sahassamattā amaccā honti. So tehi saddhiṃ antarāmagge mantesi – “mayhaṃ pitā tuṭṭho, sace me varaṃ deti, kiṃ gaṇhāmī”ti. Atha naṃ ekacce “hatthiṃ gaṇhatha, assaṃ gaṇhatha, rathaṃ gaṇhatha, janapadaṃ gaṇhatha, sattaratanāni gaṇhathā”ti āhaṃsu. Apare – “tumhe pathavissarassa puttā, tumhākaṃ dhanaṃ na dullabhaṃ, laddhampi cetaṃ sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyaṃ, puññameva ekaṃ ādāya gamanīyaṃ; tasmā te deve varaṃ dadamāne temāsaṃ padumuttaraṃ bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ varaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. So – “tumhe mayhaṃ kalyāṇamittā, na mametaṃ cittaṃ atthi, tumhehi pana uppāditaṃ, evaṃ karissāmī”ti gantvā pitaraṃ vanditvā [M 2.0080] pitarāpi āliṅgetvā tassa matthake cumbitvā – “varaṃ te putta, demī”ti vutte “sādhu mahārāja, icchāmahaṃ mahārāja bhagavantaṃ temāsaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahanto jīvitaṃ avañjhaṃ kātuṃ, imameva varaṃ dehī”ti āha. “Na sakkā tāta, aññaṃ varehī”ti vutte “deva, khattiyānaṃ nāma dve kathā natthi, etameva dehi, na me aññenattho”ti. Tāta buddhānaṃ nāma cittaṃ dujjānaṃ, sace bhagavā na icchissati, mayā dinnepi kiṃ bhavissatīti? So – “sādhu, deva, ahaṃ bhagavato cittaṃ jānissāmī”ti vihāraṃ gato.

Furthermore, his youngest brother was named Prince Sumana. The king gave him a revenue village at a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas from Haṃsavatī. Occasionally, he would come to see his father and the Teacher. Then one day, the border region became agitated. Sumana sent a message to the king: “The border is in turmoil.” The king replied, “Why then have I placed you there?” He then went out, pacified the robbers, and sent word to the king: “The country is now peaceful, sire.” Pleased, the king said, “Let my son come to me quickly.” Sumana had about a thousand ministers. Along the way, he consulted with them: “My father is pleased. If he grants me a boon, what should I ask for?” Some advised, “Ask for an elephant, a horse, a chariot, a country, or the seven treasures.” Others said, “You are the son of a world monarch. Wealth is not hard for you to obtain. Even if you gain all this, you must leave it behind. Only merit can be taken with you. Therefore, when the king offers you a boon, ask for the opportunity to attend upon the Blessed One Padumuttara for three months.” Sumana replied, “You are my good friends. This thought did not occur to me, but you have suggested it. I will do so.” He went to his father, paid homage, and was embraced by him. His father kissed his forehead and said, “I will give you a boon, my son.” When this was said, Sumana replied, “Great king, I wish to attend upon the Blessed One for three months with the four requisites, making my life not in vain. Grant me this very boon.” The king replied, “My dear, this is not possible. Ask for something else.” Sumana said, “Sire, for a khattiya, there are not two words. Grant me this; I have no need of anything else.” The king said, “Dear son, the minds of Buddhas are hard to know. If the Blessed One does not consent, what use will my granting it be?” Sumana said, “Very well, sire. I will ascertain the Blessed One’s mind.” And he went to the monastery.

Tena ca samayena bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhapetvā bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭho hoti. So maṇḍalamāḷe sannisinnānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Te taṃ āhaṃsu – “rājaputta, kasmā āgatosī”ti? Bhagavantaṃ dassanāya, dassetha me bhagavantanti. Na [P 2.0490] mayaṃ, rājaputta, icchiticchitakkhaṇe satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhāmāti. Ko pana, bhante, labhatīti? Sumanatthero nāma rājaputtāti. “So kuhiṃ, bhante, thero”ti. Therassa nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā gantvā vanditvā – “icchāmahaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ passituṃ, dassetha me”ti āha. Thero – “ehi rājaputtā”ti taṃ gahetvā taṃ gandhakuṭipariveṇe ṭhapetvā gandhakuṭiṃ abhiruhi. Atha naṃ bhagavā – “sumana, kasmā āgatosī”ti āha. Rājaputto, bhante, bhagavantaṃ dassanāya āgatoti. Tena hi bhikkhu āsanaṃ paññāpehīti. Thero āsanaṃ paññāpesi, nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Rājaputto bhagavantaṃ vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ akāsi. Kadā āgatosi rājaputtāti? Bhante, tumhesu gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhesu. Bhikkhū pana – “na mayaṃ icchiticchitakkhaṇe bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhāmā”ti maṃ [V 2.0072] therassa santikaṃ pāhesuṃ. Thero pana ekavacaneneva dassesi. Thero, bhante, tumhākaṃ sāsane vallabho maññeti. Āma rājakumāra, vallabho esa bhikkhu mayhaṃ sāsaneti. Bhante, buddhānaṃ sāsane kiṃ katvā vallabho hotīti? Dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā kumārāti. Bhagavā, ahaṃ thero viya buddhasāsane vallabho hotukāmo, temāsaṃ me vassāvāsaṃ adhivāsethāti. Bhagavā – “atthi nu kho tattha gatena attho”ti oloketvā atthīti disvā “suññāgāre, kho rājakumāra tathāgatā abhiramantī”ti [M 2.0081] āha. Kumāro “aññātaṃ bhagavā, aññātaṃ sugatā”ti vatvā “ahaṃ, bhante, purimataraṃ gantvā vihāraṃ kāremi, mayā pesite bhikkhusatasahassena saddhiṃ āgacchathā”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā pitusantikaṃ gantvā “dinnā me, deva, bhagavatā paṭiññā, mayā pahite bhagavantaṃ peseyyāthā”ti pitaraṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā yojane yojane vihāraṃ kāretvā vīsayojanasataṃ addhānaṃ gantvā attano nagare vihāraṭṭhānaṃ vicinanto sobhanaṃ nāma kuṭumbikassa uyyānaṃ disvā satasahassena kiṇitvā satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā vihāraṃ kāresi. Tattha bhagavato gandhakuṭiṃ sesabhikkhūnañca rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānatthāya kuṭileṇamaṇḍape kārāpetvā [P 2.0491] pākāraparikkhepe katvā dvārakoṭṭhakañca niṭṭhapetvā pitusantikaṃ pesesi – “niṭṭhitaṃ mayhaṃ kiccaṃ, satthāraṃ pahiṇathā”ti.

At that time, having finished his meal, the Blessed One had entered his fragrant hut. The prince then approached the monks who were sitting in the assembly hall. They asked him, "Prince, why have you come?" "To see the Blessed One—please show me the Blessed One." "We, prince, cannot see the Teacher at will whenever we wish." "Who then, sir, can?" "The elder named Sumana, prince." "Where, sir, is the elder?" After asking where the elder was seated, he went, paid homage, and said, "I wish to see the Blessed One—please show him to me." The elder said, "Come, prince," and taking him, placed him in the fragrant hut’s enclosure, then ascended to the fragrant hut. Then the Blessed One asked, "Sumana, why have you come?" "Venerable sir, the prince has come to see the Blessed One." "Then, monk, prepare a seat." The elder prepared a seat, and the Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The prince paid homage to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings. "When did you arrive, prince?" "Sir, when you had entered the fragrant hut. The monks, however, sent me to the elder, saying, 'We cannot see the Blessed One at will whenever we wish.' But the elder showed him to me with just one word. Sir, the elder seems to be favored in your dispensation." "Yes, prince, this monk is favored in my dispensation." "Sir, what must one do to become favored in the dispensation of the Buddhas?" "By giving gifts, undertaking virtuous conduct, and observing the uposatha, prince." "Blessed One, I wish to become favored in the Buddha’s dispensation like the elder. Please accept from me the invitation for the three-month rains-residence." The Blessed One, considering whether there was any benefit in going there, saw that there was and said, "Tathāgatas delight in secluded dwellings, prince." The prince said, "It is understood, Blessed One; it is understood, Sugata," and then declared, "Sir, I will go ahead and have a monastery built. When I send a message, please come with a hundred thousand monks." Having received this promise, he went to his father, paid homage, and said, "Sire, the Blessed One has given me his promise. When I send word, please send the Blessed One." Then he departed and had a monastery built every yojana, traveling a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas until he reached his own city. Searching for a suitable monastery site, he saw a park belonging to a householder named Sobhana. He bought it for a hundred thousand, spent another hundred thousand, and had a monastery built there. He had a fragrant hut constructed for the Blessed One, and for the other monks, he had cells, caves, and pavilions built for their residence by day and night. Having had walls, enclosures, and a gatehouse completed, he sent a message to his father: "My task is complete—please send the Teacher."

Rājā bhagavantaṃ bhojetvā – “bhagavā, sumanassa kiccaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ, tumhākaṃ gamanaṃ paccāsīsatī”ti āha. Bhagavā satasahassabhikkhuparivāro yojane yojane vihāresu vasamāno agamāsi. Kumāro “satthā āgato”ti sutvā yojanaṃ paccuggantvā mālādīhi pūjayamāno vihāraṃ pavesetvā –

The king, having offered food to the Blessed One, said, "Venerable sir, Sumana’s task is finished; he awaits your coming." The Blessed One, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand monks, dwelling in monasteries at every yojana along the way, departed. The prince, hearing that "the Teacher has arrived," went a yojana to meet him, honoring him with garlands and other offerings, and led him into the monastery, saying:

“Satasahassena me kītaṃ, satasahassena māpitaṃ;

Sobhanaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ, paṭiggaṇha mahāmunī”ti.

"With a hundred thousand I purchased it, with a hundred thousand I had it built; the park named Sobhana, O Great Sage, please accept it."

Vihāraṃ niyyātesi. So vassūpanāyikadivase dānaṃ datvā attano puttadāre ca amacce ca pakkosāpetvā āha – “ayaṃ satthā amhākaṃ santikaṃ dūrato āgato, buddhā ca nāma dhammagaruno na āmisagarukā. Tasmā ahaṃ temāsaṃ dve sāṭake nivāsetvā dasa sīlāni samādiyitvā idheva vasissāmi, tumhe khīṇāsavasatasahassassa imināva nīhārena temāsaṃ dānaṃ dadeyyāthā”ti.

He offered the monastery. On the day for entering the rains-residence, after giving alms, he summoned his wife, children, and ministers and said: "This Teacher has come to us from afar, and Buddhas are reverent toward the Dhamma, not toward material things. Therefore, I will stay here for three months, wearing two cloths and undertaking the ten precepts. You should give alms to the hundred thousand arahants in this same manner for three months."

So sumanattherassa vasanaṭṭhānasabhāgeyeva ṭhāne vasanto yaṃ thero bhagavato vattaṃ karoti, taṃ [V 2.0073] sabbaṃ disvā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne ekantavallabho esa thero, etasseva me ṭhānantaraṃ patthetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā upakaṭṭhāya pavāraṇāya gāmaṃ pavisitvā sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā sattame divase bhikkhusatasahassassa pādamūle ticīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ [M 2.0082] vanditvā – “bhante, yadetaṃ mayā magge yojanantarikaṃ yojanantarikaṃ vihāraṃ kārāpanato paṭṭhāya puññaṃ kataṃ, taṃ neva sakkasampattiṃ, na mārasampattiṃ, na brahmasampattiṃ patthayantena, buddhassa pana upaṭṭhākabhāvaṃ patthayantena kataṃ. Tasmā ahampi, bhagavā, anāgate sumanatthero viya buddhassa upaṭṭhāko bhaveyya”nti pañcapatiṭṭhitena nipatitvā vandi.

Staying in a place similar to the Elder Sumana's dwelling, he observed all the duties the elder performed for the Blessed One and thought: "This elder is exceedingly favored in this place; it is fitting for me to aspire to a position like his." As the Pavāraṇā approached, he entered the village, gave a great alms-giving for seven days, and on the seventh day placed sets of the triple robe at the feet of one hundred thousand monks. Paying homage to the Blessed One, he said: "Venerable sir, whatever merit I have made, beginning with having monasteries built at intervals of a yojana along the road, I have not done so aspiring for Sakka’s prosperity, Māra’s prosperity, or Brahmā’s prosperity, but only aspiring to the state of being an attendant of a Buddha. Therefore, may I too, Blessed One, in the future, become an attendant of a Buddha like the Elder Sumana." He prostrated with the five points touching the ground and paid homage.

Bhagavā – “mahantaṃ kulaputtassa cittaṃ, samijjhissati nu kho no”ti olokento – “anāgate ito satasahassime kappe gotamo nāma [P 2.0492] buddho uppajjissati, tasseva upaṭṭhāko bhavissatī”ti ñatvā –

The Blessed One, contemplating, "Great is the aspiration of this noble son; will it succeed or not?" saw with his knowledge: "In the future, in the one hundred thousandth aeon from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; he will be his attendant."

“Icchitaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, sabbameva samijjhatu;

Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā, cando pannaraso yathā”ti.

"May all that you have wished and longed for be fulfilled; may all your aspirations be accomplished, like the moon on the fifteenth day."

Āha. Kumāro taṃ sutvā – “buddhā nāma advejjhakathā hontī”ti dutiyadivaseyeva tassa bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito gacchanto viya ahosi. So tasmiṃ buddhuppāde vassasatasahassaṃ dānaṃ datvā sagge nibbattitvā kassapabuddhakālepi piṇḍāya carato therassa pattaggahaṇatthaṃ uttarisāṭakaṃ datvā pūjamakāsi. Puna sagge nibbattitvā tato cuto bārāṇasirājā hutvā aṭṭhannaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ paṇṇasālāyo kāretvā maṇiādhārake upaṭṭhapetvā catūhi paccayehi dasavassasahassāni upaṭṭhānaṃ akāsi. Etāni pākaṭaṭṭhānāni.

Hearing this, the prince thought, 'Indeed, Buddhas do not speak in two ways,' and on the very next day, taking the Blessed One's bowl and robe, he was as if following closely behind him. During that Buddha-era, having given alms for a hundred thousand years, he was reborn in heaven. And during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he made an offering by giving his upper robe to an elder who was wandering for alms, for the purpose of taking his bowl. Again reborn in heaven and having passed away from there, he became the king of Bārāṇasī. He had leaf-huts built for eight Paccekabuddhas, set up jeweled bowl-stands, and attended to them with the four requisites for ten thousand years. These are the well-known instances.

Kappasatasahassaṃ pana dānaṃ dadamānova amhākaṃ bodhisattena saddhiṃ tusitapure nibbattitvā tato cuto amitodanasakkassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā anupubbena katābhinikkhamano sammāsambodhiṃ patvā paṭhamagamanena kapilavatthuṃ āgantvā tato nikkhamante bhagavati bhagavato parivāratthaṃ rājakumāresu pabbajitesu bhaddiyādīhi saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā nacirasseva āyasmato puṇṇassa mantāṇiputtassa santike dhammakathaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi (saṃ. ni. 3.83). Evamesa āyasmā pubbūpanissayasampanno tassimāya pubbūpanissayasampattiyā gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi.

However, for a hundred thousand aeons, while continuously giving alms, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta. Having passed away from there, he took rebirth in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan. Later, when the Blessed One—who had in due course made the great renunciation, attained perfect self-enlightenment, and come to Kapilavatthu on his first visit—was departing from there, and when the royal princes were going forth to form the Blessed One's retinue, he went forth together with Bhaddiya and the others. Having been ordained in the presence of the Blessed One, not long after, upon hearing a Dhamma discourse from the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus this venerable one, being endowed with supporting conditions from the past, due to this endowment with supporting conditions from the past, even the profound dependent origination appeared to him as if it were plain.

Titthavāsādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on Titthavāsa and so forth

Titthavāsoti [V 2.0074][M 2.0083] punappunaṃ garūnaṃ santike uggahaṇasavanaparipucchanadhāraṇāni vuccanti. So therassa ativiya parisuddho, tenāpissāyaṃ gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi.

'Titthavāsa' refers to the repeated learning, hearing, questioning, and memorizing in the presence of teachers. This was exceedingly pure for the elder; for that reason also, this profound dependent origination appeared to him as if it were plain.

Sotāpannānañca nāma paccayākāro uttānakova hutvā upaṭṭhāti, ayañca āyasmā sotāpanno. Bahussutānañca catuhatthe ovarake padīpe jalamāne mañcapīṭhaṃ viya nāmarūpaparicchedo [P 2.0493] pākaṭo hoti, ayañca āyasmā bahussutānaṃ aggo hoti, bāhusaccānubhāvenapissa gambhīropi paccayākāro uttānako viya upaṭṭhāsi.

Furthermore, for stream-enterers, the structure of conditionality appears as if plain, and this venerable one is a stream-enterer. And for the very learned, the discernment of name-and-form is as manifest as a bed and a chair when a lamp is burning in a four-cubit chamber; and this venerable one is the foremost among the very learned. Through the power of his great learning, too, even the profound structure of conditionality appeared to him as if it were plain.

Paṭiccasamuppādagambhīratā

The Profundity of Dependent Origination

Tattha atthagambhīratāya, dhammagambhīratāya, desanāgambhīratāya, paṭivedhagambhīratāyāti catūhi ākārehi paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīro nāma.

Therein, dependent origination is called profound in four aspects: profundity of meaning, profundity of the principle, profundity of the teaching, and profundity of penetration.

Tattha jarāmaraṇassa jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho gambhīro…pe… saṅkhārānaṃ avijjāpaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho gambhīroti ayaṃ atthagambhīratā.

Therein, the meaning of aging-and-death being well-arisen and having come together conditioned by birth is profound... and so on... the meaning of volitional formations being well-arisen and having come together conditioned by ignorance is profound. This is the profundity of meaning.

Avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho gambhīro…pe… jātiyā jarāmaraṇassa paccayaṭṭho gambhīroti ayaṃ dhammagambhīratā.

The meaning of ignorance being a condition for volitional formations is profound... and so on... the meaning of birth being a condition for aging-and-death is profound. This is the profundity of the principle.

Katthaci sutte paṭiccasamuppādo anulomato desiyati, katthaci paṭilomato, katthaci anulomapaṭilomato, katthaci majjhato paṭṭhāya anulomato vā paṭilomato vā anulomapaṭilomato vā, katthaci tisandhi catusaṅkhepo, katthaci dvisandhi tisaṅkhepo, katthaci ekasandhi dvisaṅkhepoti ayaṃ desanāgambhīratā.

In some suttas, dependent origination is taught in forward order; in some, in reverse order; in some, in both forward and reverse order; in some, starting from the middle, in forward, reverse, or both forward and reverse order; in some, with three connections and four groups; in some, with two connections and three groups; in some, with one connection and two groups. This is the profundity of the teaching.

Avijjāya pana aññāṇaadassanasaccāpaṭivedhaṭṭho gambhīro, saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇāyūhanasarāgavirāgaṭṭho, viññāṇassa suññataabyāpāraasaṅkantipaṭisandhipātubhāvaṭṭho, nāmarūpassa ekuppādavinibbhogāvinibbhoganamanaruppanaṭṭho, saḷāyatanassa adhipatilokadvārakkhettavisayibhāvaṭṭho[V 2.0075], phassassa [M 2.0084] phusanasaṅghaṭṭanasaṅgatisannipātaṭṭho, vedanāya ārammaṇarasānubhavanasukhadukkhamajjhattabhāvanijjīvavedayitaṭṭho, taṇhāya abhinanditaajjhosānasaritālatātaṇhānadītaṇhāsamuddaduppūraṇaṭṭho, upādānassa ādānaggahaṇābhinivesaparāmāsaduratikkamaṭṭho, bhavassa āyūhanābhisaṅkharaṇayonigatiṭhitinivāsesu khipanaṭṭho, jātiyā jātisañjātiokkantinibbattipātubhāvaṭṭho, jarāmaraṇassa khayavayabhedavipariṇāmaṭṭho gambhīroti. Evaṃ yo avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvo, yena paṭivedhena avijjādayo sarasalakkhaṇato paṭividdhā honti; so gambhīroti ayaṃ paṭivedhagambhīratāti veditabbā. Sā sabbāpi therassa uttānakā viya upaṭṭhāsi. Tena bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ ussādento – “mā heva”ntiādimāha. Ayañcettha [P 2.0494] adhippāyo – ānanda, tvaṃ mahāpañño visadañāṇo, tena te gambhīropi paṭiccasamuppādo uttānako viya khāyati, tasmā – “mayhameva nu kho esa uttānako hutvā upaṭṭhāti, udāhu aññesampī”ti mā evaṃ avacāti.

Furthermore, the meaning of ignorance as not-knowing, not-seeing, and non-penetration of the truths is profound. The meaning of volitional formations as constructing, accumulating, being with passion, and being without passion is profound. The meaning of consciousness as emptiness, non-activity, non-transference, and manifestation at rebirth-linking is profound. The meaning of name-and-form as co-arising, being separable, being inseparable, inclining, and being afflicted is profound. The meaning of the six sense bases as dominance, world, door, field, and having an object is profound. The meaning of contact as touching, impact, coming together, and convergence is profound. The meaning of feeling as experiencing the flavor of an object, as pleasure, pain, or neutrality, and as being felt without a living soul is profound. The meaning of craving as delighting, clinging, flowing, being a creeper, a river of craving, an ocean of craving, and being difficult to fill is profound. The meaning of clinging as taking up, grasping, adherence, misapprehension, and being difficult to transcend is profound. The meaning of becoming as accumulating, constructing, and casting into wombs, destinations, stations, and abodes is profound. The meaning of birth as being born, coming to be, descending, being produced, and manifesting is profound. The meaning of aging-and-death as decay, perishing, breaking up, and changing is profound. Thus, that intrinsic nature of ignorance and so on, which is penetrated by means of insight according to its individual characteristics, is profound. This should be understood as the profundity of penetration. All this appeared to the Elder as if it were plain. Therefore, the Blessed One, encouraging Venerable Ānanda, said, 'Do not say so,' and so on. And this is the intended meaning here: 'Ānanda, you are of great wisdom and clear knowledge; therefore, even the profound dependent origination appears to you as if it were plain. Therefore, do not say, "Does this appear plain only to me, or to others as well?"'

Apasādanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Admonition

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “apasādento”ti, tattha ayaṃ adhippāyo – ānanda, “atha ca pana me uttānakuttānako viya khāyatī”ti mā hevaṃ avaca. Yadi hi te esa uttānakuttānako viya khāyati, kasmā tvaṃ attano dhammatāya sotāpanno nāhosi, mayā dinnanayeva ṭhatvā sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭivijjhasi. Ānanda, idaṃ nibbānameva gambhīraṃ, paccayākāro pana tava uttānako jāto, atha kasmā oḷārikaṃ kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ, oḷārikaṃ kāmarāgānusayaṃ paṭighānusayanti ime cattāro kilese samugghāṭetvā sakadāgāmiphalaṃ na sacchikarosi? Teyeva aṇusahagate cattāro kilese samugghāṭetvā anāgāmiphalaṃ na sacchikarosi? Rūparāgādīni pañca saṃyojanāni, bhavarāgānusayaṃ, mānānusayaṃ, avijjānusayanti ime aṭṭha kilese samugghāṭetvā arahattaṃ na sacchikarosi?

As for what was said, 'admonishing,' here is the intended meaning: Ānanda, do not speak thus: 'And yet, it appears to me as if it were exceedingly shallow.' For if this appears to you as if it were exceedingly shallow, why did you not become a stream-enterer by your own nature, but instead penetrate the path of stream-entry only by standing in the method given by me? Ānanda, is it that only this Nibbāna is profound, and that dependent origination has become shallow for you? If so, why do you not realize the fruit of once-returning by uprooting these four defilements: the gross fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of aversion, the gross latent tendency of sensual desire, and the latent tendency of aversion? Why do you not realize the fruit of non-returning by uprooting those same four defilements that are accompanied by subtlety? Why do you not realize Arahantship by uprooting these eight defilements: the five fetters beginning with lust for form, the latent tendency of becoming, the latent tendency of conceit, and the latent tendency of ignorance?

Kasmā [M 2.0085] ca satasahassakappādhikaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ pūritapāramino sāriputtamoggallānā viya sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ nappaṭivijjhasi? Satasahassakappādhikāni dve asaṅkhyeyyāni pūritapāramino paccekabuddhā viya ca paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nappaṭivijjhasi? Yadi vā te sabbathāva esa uttānako hutvā upaṭṭhāti, atha kasmā satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri aṭṭha soḷasa vā asaṅkhyeyyāni pūritapāramino buddhā viya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ na sacchikarosi? Kiṃ anatthikosi etehi visesādhigamehi, passa yāvañca te aparaddhaṃ, tvaṃ nāma sāvako padesañāṇe [V 2.0076] ṭhito atigambhīraṃ paccayākāraṃ – “uttānako me upaṭṭhātī”ti vadasi, tassa te idaṃ vacanaṃ buddhānaṃ kathāya paccanīkaṃ hoti, na tādisena nāma bhikkhunā buddhānaṃ kathāya paccanīkaṃ kathetabbanti yuttametaṃ.

And why do you not penetrate the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple, like Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable aeon and over one hundred thousand kappas? And why do you not penetrate the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, like the Paccekabuddhas who fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable aeons and over one hundred thousand kappas? Or if this dependent origination appears to you as entirely shallow, then why do you not realize the knowledge of omniscience, like the Buddhas who fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable aeons and over one hundred thousand kappas? Are you uninterested in these special attainments? See how great your error is! You, a disciple standing in partial knowledge, say of the exceedingly profound causal structure, 'It appears shallow to me.' This statement of yours is contrary to the speech of the Buddhas. It is not fitting that a bhikkhu such as you should speak in contradiction to the speech of the Buddhas.

Nanu mayhaṃ, ānanda, idaṃ paccayākāraṃ paṭivijjhituṃ vāyamantasseva satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni atikkantāni? Paccayākāraṃ paṭivijjhanatthāya ca pana me adinnaṃ dānaṃ nāma natthi, apūritapāramī nāma natthi. Paccayākāraṃ [P 2.0495] paṭivijjhassāmīti pana me nirussāhaṃ viya mārabalaṃ vidhamantassa ayaṃ mahāpathavī dvaṅgulamattampi na kampi tathā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ sampādentassa. Pacchimayāme pana me balavapaccūsasamaye – “avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ navahi ākārehi paccayo hotī”ti diṭṭhamatteva dasasahassilokadhātu ayadaṇḍakena ākoṭitakaṃsatālaṃ viya viravasataṃ viravasahassaṃ muñcamānā vātāhate paduminipaṇṇe udakabindu viya kampittha. Evaṃ gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo, gambhīrāvabhāso ca. Etassa ānanda, dhammassa ananubodhā…pe… nātivattatīti.

Is it not so, Ānanda, that for me, while striving to penetrate this causal structure, four incalculable aeons and over one hundred thousand kappas have passed? Furthermore, for the sake of penetrating the causal structure, there is no gift that was not given by me, no perfection that was not fulfilled by me. And while I was dispelling the forces of Māra as if without effort, thinking, 'I will penetrate the causal structure,' this great earth did not tremble even two finger-breadths, just as it did not when I was attaining knowledge of past lives in the first watch and the divine eye in the middle watch. But in the last watch, at the time of the powerful dawn, just upon seeing that 'ignorance is a condition for formations in nine aspects,' the ten-thousandfold world-system, emitting a hundred, a thousand sounds like a bronze cymbal struck with an iron rod, trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind. So profound, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and profound is its appearance. Ānanda, from not awakening to this principle… one does not transcend.

Etassa dhammassāti etassa paccayadhammassa. Ananubodhāti ñātapariññāvasena ananubujjhanā. Appaṭivedhāti tīraṇappahānapariññāvasena appaṭivijjhanā. Tantākulakajātāti tantaṃ viya ākulakajātā. Yathā nāma dunnikkhittaṃ mūsikacchinnaṃ pesakārānaṃ tantaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ ākulaṃ hoti, idaṃ aggaṃ idaṃ mūlanti aggena vā aggaṃ mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaraṃ hoti; evameva sattā imasmiṃ paccayākāre khalitā ākulā byākulā honti, na sakkonti taṃpaccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ. Tattha tantaṃ paccattapurisakāre ṭhatvā sakkāpi bhaveyya ujuṃ kātuṃ, ṭhapetvā pana [M 2.0086] dve bodhisatte aññe sattā attano dhammatāya paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ samatthā nāma natthi. Yathā pana ākulaṃ tantaṃ kañjiyaṃ datvā kocchena pahataṃ tattha tattha guḷakajātaṃ hoti gaṇṭhibaddhaṃ, evamime sattā paccayesu pakkhalitvā paccaye ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontā dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatavasena ākulakajātā honti, gaṇṭhibaddhā. Ye hi keci diṭṭhigatanissitā, sabbe paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontāyeva.

'Of this principle' means of this principle of conditionality. 'From not awakening to' means from not understanding by way of comprehension as knowing. 'From not penetrating' means from not piercing through by way of comprehension by judgment and comprehension by abandoning. 'Become like a tangled skein of thread' means become tangled like a thread. For just as a weaver's thread, badly laid down and gnawed by mice, becomes tangled in places, and it is difficult to align end with end or beginning with beginning; even so, beings, having faltered regarding this causal structure, become confused, bewildered, and entangled; they are unable to straighten out that causal structure. In that case, it might be possible to straighten the thread by relying on individual human effort, but apart from the two Bodhisattas, no other beings are capable of straightening out the causal structure by their own nature. Furthermore, just as a tangled thread, after applying rice-gruel and combing it with a brush, becomes lumpy and knotted in places, even so these beings, having faltered regarding conditions and being unable to straighten out the conditions, become tangled and knotted by way of the sixty-two kinds of wrong views. For whoever relies on wrong views are all incapable of straightening out the causal structure.

Kulāgaṇṭhikajātāti kulāgaṇṭhikaṃ vuccati pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ. Kulā nāma sakuṇikā, tassā kulāvakotipi eke. Yathā hi tadubhayampi ākulaṃ aggena vā aggaṃ mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaranti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

Regarding 'become like a knotted ball of thread': the weaver's starched thread is called a 'knotted ball.' Some say `kulā` is a small bird, and thus it means like its nest (`kulāvaka`). For just as both of these are tangled, so that it is difficult to align end with end or beginning with beginning, this should be connected in the same way as before.

Muñjapabbajabhūtāti [P 2.0496][V 2.0077] muñjatiṇaṃ viya pabbajatiṇaṃ viya ca bhūtā. Yathā tāni tiṇāni koṭṭetvā katarajju jiṇṇakāle katthaci patitaṃ gahetvā tesaṃ tiṇānaṃ idaṃ aggaṃ, idaṃ mūlanti aggena vā aggaṃ mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ dukkaranti. Tampi paccattapurisakāre ṭhatvā sakkā bhaveyya ujuṃ kātuṃ, ṭhapetvā pana dve bodhisatte aññe sattā attano dhammatāya paccayākāraṃ ujuṃ kātuṃ samatthā nāma natthi. Evamayaṃ pajā paccayākāre ujuṃ kātuṃ asakkontī diṭṭhigatavasena gaṇṭhikajātā hutvā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattati.

Regarding 'become like muñja and babbaja grass': it means having become like muñja grass and babbaja grass. Just as when those grasses are pounded and a rope is made, and when that rope, in its old age, has fallen somewhere, one picks it up and it is difficult to align the tips of those grasses with the tips, or the roots with the roots. Even that might be straightened by relying on individual human effort. However, apart from the two Bodhisattas, no other beings are capable of straightening out the causal structure by their own nature. Thus this generation, unable to straighten out the causal structure, becomes knotted by way of wrong views and does not transcend the plane of misery, the bad destination, the state of ruin, and saṃsāra.

Tattha apāyoti nirayatiracchānayonipettivisayaasurakāyā. Sabbepi hi te vaḍḍhisaṅkhātassa ayassa abhāvato – “apāyo”ti vuccanti. Tathā dukkhassa gatibhāvato duggati. Sukhasamussayato vinipatitattā vinipāto. Itaro pana –

Herein, ‘apāya’ refers to the hells, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, and the realm of asuras. Indeed, all these are called ‘apāya’ because of the absence of welfare (aya), which is known as ‘increase’ (vaḍḍhi). Likewise, because it is a destination (gati) of suffering, it is called ‘duggati.’ Because of having fallen away from the collection of happiness, it is called ‘vinipāta.’ As for the other—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti.

“The unbroken continuity of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, occurring without interruption, is called saṃsāra.”

Taṃ sabbampi nātivattati nātikkamati. Atha kho cutito paṭisandhiṃ, paṭisandhito cutinti evaṃ punappunaṃ cutipaṭisandhiyo gaṇhantā tīsu bhavesu catūsu yonīsu pañcasu gatīsu sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu navasu sattāvāsesu mahāsamudde vātukkhittanāvā viya yantesu yuttagoṇo viya ca paribbhamatiyeva[M 2.0087]. Iti sabbaṃ petaṃ bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ apasādento āhāti veditabbaṃ.

One does not overcome or transgress all that. Instead, from death to rebirth, and from rebirth to death, thus repeatedly taking up death and rebirth, one wanders among the three planes of existence, the four modes of generation, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a boat tossed by the wind on the great ocean or like an ox yoked to a machine. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke all this, admonishing the Venerable Ānanda.

Paṭiccasamuppādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Dependent Origination

96. Idāni yasmā idaṃ suttaṃ – “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo”ti ca “tantākulakajātā”ti ca dvīhiyeva padehi ābaddhaṃ, tasmā – “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo”ti iminā tāva anusandhinā paccayākārassa gambhīrabhāvadassanatthaṃ desanaṃ ārabhanto atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇantiādimāha. Tatrāyamattho – imassa jarāmaraṇassa paccayo idappaccayo, tasmā idappaccayā atthi jarāmaraṇaṃ, atthi nu kho jarāmaraṇassa paccayo, yamhā paccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ bhaveyyāti [P 2.0497] evaṃ puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, paṇḍitena puggalena yathā – “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti vutte ṭhapanīyattā pañhassa tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ hoti, “abyākatametaṃ [V 2.0078] tathāgatenā”ti vā vattabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ appaṭipajjitvā, yathā – “cakkhu sassataṃ asassata”nti vutte asassatanti ekaṃseneva vattabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ ekaṃseneva atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. Puna kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ, ko nāma so paccayo, yato jarāmaraṇaṃ hotīti vutte jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iccassa vacanīyaṃ, evaṃ vattabbaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. Esa nayo sabbapadesu.

96. Now, since this discourse is bound by just two phrases— “Ānanda, this dependent origination is profound” and “like a tangled skein”—therefore, beginning the teaching with the connection, “Ānanda, this dependent origination is profound,” in order to show the profundity of the causal pattern, he said, “Does aging-and-death exist with this as condition?” and so on. Herein, this is the meaning: The condition for this aging-and-death is this condition; therefore, with this as condition, aging-and-death exists. “Is there, then, a condition for aging-and-death, from which condition aging-and-death might arise?” When asked thus, Ānanda, a wise person should not respond as one would to a question that should be set aside, such as when asked, “Is the life principle the same as the body?” where one should remain silent or say, “This has not been declared by the Tathāgata.” Not proceeding in that way, just as when asked, “Is the eye permanent or impermanent?” one should answer decisively, “It is impermanent,” so too here one should state decisively, “It exists.” Further, when asked, “With what as condition is there aging-and-death? What is that condition from which aging-and-death arises?” one should answer, “With birth as condition, there is aging-and-death.” This is what should be said; this is the meaning. This method applies to all clauses.

Nāmarūpapaccayā phassoti idaṃ pana yasmā saḷāyatanapaccayāti vutte cakkhusamphassādīnaṃ channaṃ vipākasamphassānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ hoti, idha ca “saḷāyatanapaccayā”ti iminā padena gahitampi agahitampi paccayuppannavisesaṃ phassassa ca saḷāyatanato atirittaṃ aññampi visesapaccayaṃ dassetukāmo, tasmā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iminā pana vārena bhagavatā kiṃ kathitanti? Paccayānaṃ nidānaṃ kathitaṃ. Idañhi suttaṃ paccaye nijjaṭe niggumbe katvā kathitattā mahānidānanti vuccati.

As for the statement, “With name-and-form as condition, there is contact,” it should be understood that this was stated because when it is said, “With the six sense bases as condition,” only the six kinds of resultant contacts—such as eye-contact—are included. But here, he wished to show the specific conditioned phenomenon—both that which is included by the phrase “with the six sense bases as condition” and that which is not—and also another specific condition for contact that is additional to the six sense bases. But what was taught by the Blessed One by means of this section? The source of conditions was taught. Indeed, because this discourse was taught having made the conditions free of tangles and thickets, it is called the “Great Discourse on the Source.”

98. Idāni tesaṃ tesaṃ paccayānaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti kho panetaṃ vuttantiādimāha. Tattha pariyāyenāti kāraṇena. Sabbenasabbaṃ sabbathāsabbanti nipātadvayametaṃ. Tassattho – “sabbākārena sabbā sabbena sabhāvena [M 2.0088] sabbā jāti nāma yadi na bhaveyyā”ti. Bhavādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Kassacīti aniyamavacanametaṃ, devādīsu yassa kassaci. Kimhicīti idampi aniyamavacanameva, kāmabhavādīsu navasu bhavesu yattha katthaci. Seyyathidanti aniyamitanikkhittaatthavibhajanatthe nipāto, tassattho – “yaṃ vuttaṃ ‘kassaci kimhicī’ti, tassa te atthaṃ vibhajissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ vibhajanto – “devānaṃ vā devattāyā”tiādimāha. Tattha devānaṃ vā devattāyāti yā ayaṃ devānaṃ devabhāvāya khandhajāti, yāya khandhajātiyā devā “devā”ti vuccanti. Sace [P 2.0498] hi jāti sabbena sabbaṃ nābhavissāti iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Ettha ca devāti upapattidevā. Gandhabbāti mūlakhandhādīsu adhivatthadevatāva. Yakkhāti amanussā. Bhūtāti ye keci nibbattasattā. Pakkhinoti ye keci aṭṭhipakkhā vā cammapakkhā vā lomapakkhā vā. Sarīsapāti ye keci bhūmiyaṃ sarantā gacchanti. Tesaṃ tesanti tesaṃ tesaṃ devagandhabbādīnaṃ. Tadatthāyāti devagandhabbādibhāvāya. Jātinirodhāti jātivigamā, jātiabhāvāti attho.

98. Now, to show the true, undeviating, and unalterable nature of those various conditions as conditions, he begins by saying: “That it was said: ‘With birth as condition, there is aging-and-death,’” and so on. Here, by ‘pariyāyena’ is meant ‘by reason’ (kāraṇena). ‘Sabbenasabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ’ are two particles. Their meaning is: “If birth did not exist at all, in any way, in its entire nature.” The meaning should be understood in the same way for terms beginning with “becoming” and so forth. ‘Kassaci’ (of anyone) is an indefinite term, referring to anyone among gods and others. ‘Kimhici’ (in anything) is also an indefinite term, referring to anywhere among the nine realms of becoming, such as the desire realm. ‘Seyyathidaṃ’ (that is) is a particle used for analyzing a meaning that has been stated indefinitely. Its meaning is: “I will analyze for you the meaning of what was said as ‘of anyone, in anything.’” Then, analyzing it, he says: “For gods, in their divine state…” and so on. Here, “for gods, in their divine state” refers to that birth of aggregates for the divine state of gods, by which birth of aggregates gods are called “gods.” The meaning should be understood in this way for all clauses: “If birth did not exist at all, in any way…” Here, “gods” refers to gods by rebirth. “Gandhabbas” refers to deities dwelling in the roots of trees, their trunks, and so forth. “Yakkhas” are non-humans. “Beings” (bhūtā) refers to any creatures that have come into being. “Birds” (pakkhino) refers to any with wings of bone, wings of skin, or wings of feathers. “Creeping things” (sarīsapā) refers to any that move by crawling on the ground. “Of those various” refers to those various gods, gandhabbas, and so forth. “For that state” means for the state of being a god, gandhabba, and so forth. “With the cessation of birth” means with the passing away of birth, with the absence of birth; this is the meaning.

Hetūtiādīni sabbānipi kāraṇavevacanāni eva. Kāraṇañhi yasmā attano phalatthāya hinoti [V 2.0079] pavattati, tasmā “hetū”ti vuccati. Yasmā taṃ phalaṃ nideti – “handa, naṃ gaṇhathā”ti appeti viya tasmā nidānaṃ. Yasmā phalaṃ tato samudeti uppajjati, tañca paṭicca eti pavattati, tasmā samudayoti ca paccayoti ca vuccati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Api ca yadidaṃ jātīti ettha yadidanti nipāto. Tassa sabbapadesu liṅgānurūpato attho veditabbo. Idha pana – “yā esā jātī”ti ayamassa attho. Jarāmaraṇassa hi jāti upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti.

‘Hetu’ and so forth—all these are indeed synonyms for ‘kāraṇa’ (cause). For a cause (kāraṇa), because it proceeds (hinoti) for the sake of its own fruit, is called ‘hetu’ (root cause). Because it assigns (nideti) that fruit—as if presenting it, saying, “Here, take it!”—it is called ‘nidāna’ (source). Because the fruit arises (samudeti) from it, and depending on it (paṭicca), it proceeds (eti), it is called ‘samudaya’ (origin) and ‘paccaya’ (condition). This method applies everywhere. Moreover, in the phrase ‘yadidaṃ jāti’ (that is, birth), ‘yadidaṃ’ is a particle. Its meaning should be understood in all clauses according to the gender. Here, however, its meaning is: “that which is birth.” For birth is a condition for aging-and-death by way of decisive support.

99. Bhavapade – “kimhicī”ti iminā okāsapariggaho kato. Tattha heṭṭhā avīcipariyantaṃ katvā upari paranimmitavasavattideve antokaritvā kāmabhavo veditabbo. Ayaṃ nayo upapattibhave. Idha pana kammabhave yujjati. So hi jātiyā upanissayakoṭiyāva paccayo hoti. Upādānapadādīsupi – “kimhicī”ti iminā okāsapariggahova katoti veditabbo.

99. In the term on becoming, the delimitation of the sphere is made by 'in anything' (kimhici). Herein, sense-sphere existence should be understood by taking Avīci as the lower limit and including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas as the upper limit. This method applies in the case of rebirth-existence. But here, it is applicable to kamma-existence. For that is a condition for birth only by way of the category of decisive support. Also, in the terms beginning with 'clinging', it should be understood that the delimitation of the sphere is indeed made by 'in anything'.

100. Upādānapaccayā [M 2.0089] bhavoti ettha kāmupādānaṃ tiṇṇampi kammabhavānaṃ tiṇṇañca upapattibhavānaṃ paccayo, tathā sesānipīti upādānapaccayā catuvīsatibhavā veditabbā. Nippariyāyenettha dvādasa kammabhavā labbhanti. Tesaṃ upādānāni sahajātakoṭiyāpi upanissayakoṭiyāpi paccayo.

100. In the text, 'With clinging as condition, becoming [arises],' sensual clinging is a condition for the three kamma-existences and the three rebirth-existences. Likewise for the remaining clingings. Thus, conditioned by clinging, twenty-four kinds of existence are to be understood. Here, in the primary sense, twelve kamma-existences are obtained. For these, the clingings are a condition by way of the category of co-nascence and by way of the category of decisive support.

101. Rūpataṇhāti rūpārammaṇe taṇhā. Esa nayo saddataṇhādīsu. Sā panesā taṇhā upādānassa sahajātakoṭiyāpi upanissayakoṭiyāpi paccayo hoti.

101. 'Craving for forms' is craving for a form-object. This is the method for craving for sounds and so forth. This craving, however, is a condition for clinging by way of the category of co-nascence and by way of the category of decisive support.

102. Esa paccayo taṇhāya, yadidaṃ [P 2.0499] vedanāti ettha vipākavedanā taṇhāya upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti, aññā aññathāpīti.

102. In the text, 'This is a condition for craving, namely, feeling,' resultant feeling is a condition for craving by way of the category of decisive support; other feelings are conditions in other ways as well.

103. Ettāvatā pana bhagavā vaṭṭamūlabhūtaṃ purimataṇhaṃ dassetvā idāni desanaṃ, piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā kesesu vā gahetvā viravantaṃ viravantaṃ maggato okkamento viya navahi padehi samudācārataṇhaṃ dassento – “iti kho panetaṃ, ānanda, vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā”tiādimāha. Tattha taṇhāti dve taṇhā esanataṇhā ca, esitataṇhā ca. Yāya taṇhāya ajapathasaṅkupathādīni paṭipajjitvā bhoge esati gavesati, ayaṃ esanataṇhā nāma. Yā tesu esitesu gavesitesu paṭiladdhesu taṇhā, ayaṃ esitataṇhā nāma. Tadubhayampi samudācārataṇhāya eva adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā [V 2.0080] duvidhāpesā vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā nāma. Pariyesanā nāma rūpādiārammaṇapariyesanā, sā hi taṇhāya sati hoti. Lābhoti rūpādiārammaṇapaṭilābho, so hi pariyesanāya sati hoti. Vinicchayo pana ñāṇataṇhādiṭṭhivitakkavasena catubbidho. Tattha – “sukhavinicchayaṃ jaññā, sukhavinicchayaṃ ñatvā ajjhattaṃ sukhamanuyuñjeyyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.323) ayaṃ ñāṇavinicchayo. “Vinicchayoti dve vinicchayā – taṇhāvinicchayo ca diṭṭhivinicchayo cā”ti (mahāni. 102). Evaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni taṇhāvinicchayo. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhivinicchayo. “Chando kho, devānaminda, vitakkanidāno”ti (dī. ni. 2.358) imasmiṃ pana sutte idha vinicchayoti vutto vitakkoyeva āgato. Lābhaṃ labhitvā hi iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ sundarāsundarañca vitakkeneva vinicchināti [M 2.0090] – “ettakaṃ me rūpārammaṇatthāya bhavissati, ettakaṃ saddādiārammaṇatthāya, ettakaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissati, ettakaṃ parassa, ettakaṃ paribhuñjissāmi, ettakaṃ nidahissāmī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ – “lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo”ti.

103. Thus far, the Blessed One, having shown the prior craving which is the root of the cycle of rebirth, now, as if striking one on the back or seizing one by the hair and forcing one who is wailing and wailing off the path, demonstrates craving in its active phase with nine terms, saying: 'Thus, Ānanda, with feeling as condition, there is craving,' and so on. Therein, 'craving' refers to two types: craving in seeking and craving for what has been sought. The craving by which one, having taken to goat-paths, stake-paths, and the like, seeks and searches for possessions, is called 'craving in seeking.' The craving that arises for those possessions once they have been sought, searched for, and obtained, is called 'craving for what has been sought.' Both are designations for craving in its active phase. Therefore, this two-fold craving is what is called 'craving conditioned by feeling.' 'Searching' means the searching for objects such as forms; for that occurs when there is craving. 'Gain' is the acquisition of objects such as forms; for that occurs when there is searching. 'Discernment,' however, is fourfold, by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought. Therein, 'One should know the discernment of pleasure; having known the discernment of pleasure, one should pursue internal pleasure'—this is discernment by knowledge. 'Discernment is of two kinds: discernment by craving and discernment by views.' Thus, the one hundred and eight courses of craving that are mentioned are 'discernment by craving.' The sixty-two views are 'discernment by views.' But in the Sutta that says, 'Desire, O king of the devas, is rooted in thought,' it is thought itself that is meant here by 'discernment.' For having obtained a gain, one discerns what is desirable and undesirable, beautiful and ugly, only through thought, thus: 'This much will be for my purpose of form-objects, this much for the purpose of sound-objects and so on; this much will be for me, this much for another; this much I will enjoy, this much I will store away.' Therefore it was said: 'Conditioned by gain, there is discernment.'

Chandarāgoti evaṃ akusalavitakkena vitakkitavatthusmiṃ dubbalarāgo ca balavarāgo ca uppajjati, idañhi idha taṇhā. Chandoti dubbalarāgassādhivacanaṃ. Ajjhosānanti ahaṃ mamanti balavasanniṭṭhānaṃ. Pariggahoti taṇhādiṭṭhavasena pariggahaṇakaraṇaṃ. Macchariyanti parehi sādhāraṇabhāvassa asahanatā. Tenevassa porāṇā evaṃ [P 2.0500] vacanatthaṃ vadanti – “idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayhameva hotu, mā aññesaṃ acchariyaṃ hotūti pavattattā macchariyanti vuccatī”ti. Ārakkhoti dvārapidahanamañjūsagopanādivasena suṭṭhu rakkhaṇaṃ. Adhikarotīti adhikaraṇaṃ, kāraṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ārakkhādhikaraṇanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, ārakkhahetūti attho. Daṇḍādānādīsu paranisedhanatthaṃ daṇḍassa ādānaṃ daṇḍādānaṃ. Ekato dhārādino satthassa ādānaṃ satthādānaṃ. Kalahoti kāyakalahopi vācākalahopi. Purimo purimo virodho viggaho. Pacchimo pacchimo vivādo. Tuvaṃtuvanti agāravavacanaṃ tuvaṃtuvaṃ.

'Desire-lust' (chandarāga): thus, in regard to an object conceived with unwholesome thought, both weak lust and strong lust arise; for this here is craving. 'Desire' (chanda) is a designation for weak lust. 'Tenacity' (ajjhosāna) is the strong conviction, 'I,' 'mine.' 'Appropriation' (pariggaha) is the act of taking possession by means of craving and views. 'Stinginess' (macchariya) is the inability to bear something being shared with others. For this reason, the ancients state its etymology thus: 'Because it occurs with the thought, "Let this marvel be for me alone, let it not be a marvel for others," it is called stinginess.' 'Guarding' (ārakkha) is protecting well by means of barring doors, securing chests, and so on. Because it is a basis for results (adhikaroti), it is called a 'ground' (adhikaraṇa); this is a name for a cause. The term 'on account of guarding' (ārakkhādhikaraṇa) is a neuter abstract noun; the meaning is 'due to the cause of guarding.' In the terms beginning with 'taking up the rod' (daṇḍādāna), the taking up of a rod to obstruct another is 'taking up the rod.' The taking up of a weapon, such as a single-edged blade, is 'taking up the weapon.' 'Conflict' (kalaha) is both bodily conflict and verbal conflict. An earlier stage of opposition is a 'quarrel' (viggaha). A later stage is a 'dispute' (vivāda). 'You-you' (tuvaṃtuvaṃ) is a disrespectful expression.

112. Idāni paṭilomanayenāpi taṃsamudācārataṇhaṃ dassetuṃ puna – “ārakkhādhikaraṇa”nti ārabhanto desanaṃ nivattesi. Tattha kāmataṇhāti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasena uppannā rūpāditaṇhā. Bhavataṇhāti sassatadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo. Vibhavataṇhāti ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo. Ime dve dhammāti vaṭṭamūlataṇhā ca samudācārataṇhā cāti ime dve dhammā. Dvayenāti taṇhālakkhaṇavasena ekabhāvaṃ gatāpi vaṭṭamūlasamudācāravasena dvīhi koṭṭhāsehi vedanāya ekasamosaraṇā bhavanti, vedanāpaccayena ekapaccayāti attho. Tividhañhi samosaraṇaṃ osaraṇasamosaraṇaṃ, sahajātasamosaraṇaṃ, paccayasamosaraṇañca. Tattha – “atha [V 2.0081] kho sabbāni tāni kāmasamosaraṇāni bhavantī”ti idaṃ osaraṇasamosaraṇaṃ nāma. “Chandamūlakā, āvuso, ete dhammā phassasamudayā vedanāsamosaraṇā”ti (a. ni. 8.83) idaṃ sahajātasamosaraṇaṃ nāma. “Dvayena vedanāya ekasamosaraṇā”ti idaṃ pana paccayasamosaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.

112. Now, to show that conduct-craving also by the reverse method, beginning with 'ārakkhādhikaraṇa,' he turned back the discourse. Herein, 'sensual craving' is craving for forms, etc., arisen through lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Craving for existence' is lust accompanied by the eternalism-view. 'Craving for non-existence' is lust accompanied by the annihilation-view. These two phenomena are root-craving and conduct-craving. 'By way of duality'—though they become one in nature by the characteristic of craving, they become a single convergence into feeling through two divisions, by way of root-craving and conduct-craving; the meaning is that they have a single condition because of feeling as condition. For there are three kinds of convergence: convergence by approach, convergence by co-arising, and convergence by condition. Herein, 'Then all those converge upon sensual pleasures'—this is called 'convergence by approach'. 'These phenomena, friend, are rooted in desire, arisen from contact, converging upon feeling'—this is called 'convergence by co-arising'. 'Converging into feeling by way of duality'—this should be understood as 'convergence by condition'.

113. Cakkhusamphassoti [M 2.0091] ādayo sabbe vipākaphassāyeva. Tesu ṭhapetvā cattāro lokuttaravipākaphasse avasesā dvattiṃsa phassā honti. Yadidaṃ phassoti ettha pana phasso bahudhā vedanāya paccayo hoti.

113. 'Eye-contact' and so on are all resultant contacts. Excluding the four supramundane resultant contacts, the remaining thirty-two contacts are meant. But here, in the phrase 'this contact', contact is a condition for feeling in many ways.

114. Yehi, ānanda, ākārehītiādīsu ākārā vuccanti vedanādīnaṃ aññamaññaṃ asadisasabhāvā. Teyeva sādhukaṃ dassiyamānā taṃ taṃ līnamatthaṃ gamentīti liṅgāni. Tassa tassa sañjānanahetuto nimittāni. Tathā tathā uddisitabbato uddesā[P 2.0501]. Tasmā ayamettha attho – “ānanda, yehi ākārehi…pe… yehi uddesehi nāmakāyassa nāmasamūhassa paññatti hoti, yā esā ca vedanāya vedayitākāre vedayitaliṅge vedayitanimitte vedanāti uddese sati, saññāya sañjānanākāre sañjānanaliṅge sañjānananimitte saññāti uddese sati, saṅkhārānaṃ cetanākāre cetanāliṅge cetanānimitte cetanāti uddese sati, viññāṇassa vijānanākāre vijānanaliṅge vijānananimitte viññāṇanti uddese sati – ‘ayaṃ nāmakāyo’ti nāmakāyassa paññatti hoti. Tesu nāmakāyappaññattihetūsu vedanādīsu ākārādīsu asati api nu kho rūpakāye adhivacanasamphasso paññāyetha? Yvāyaṃ cattāro khandhe vatthuṃ katvā manodvāre adhivacanasamphassavevacano manosamphasso uppajjati, api nu kho so rūpakāye paññāyetha, pañca pasāde vatthuṃ katvā katvā uppajjeyyā”ti. Atha āyasmā ānando ambarukkhe asati jamburukkhato ambapakkassa uppattiṃ viya rūpakāyato tassa uppattiṃ asampaṭicchanto no hetaṃ bhanteti āha.

114. In 'Ānanda, by what modes...', modes are said to be the dissimilar individual natures of feeling, etc., in relation to one another. These very modes, when carefully shown, lead to the understanding of the respective hidden meaning; thus they are called signs. They are called marks because they are the cause for recognizing each particular thing. They are called designations because they are to be pointed out in such and such a way. Therefore, the meaning here is: 'Ānanda, by whatever modes... or by whatever designations the designation of the mental body, the aggregate of mental phenomena, occurs; that is, when for feeling there is the mode of feeling, the sign of feeling, the mark of feeling, and the designation 'feeling'; when for perception there is the mode of perceiving, the sign of perceiving, the mark of perceiving, and the designation 'perception'; when for volitional formations there is the mode of volition, the sign of volition, the mark of volition, and the designation 'volition'; when for consciousness there is the mode of cognizing, the sign of cognizing, the mark of cognizing, and the designation 'consciousness'—then the designation 'this is the mental body' occurs. If these causes for the designation of the mental body—namely feeling, etc., along with their modes, signs, and marks—were absent, could verbal contact be discerned in the physical body? That is, could the mental contact called verbal contact, which arises in the mind-door having made the four aggregates its basis, be discerned in the physical body? Could it arise having made the five sense faculties its basis?'
