Then, the Venerable Ānanda, not accepting its arising from the physical body, like the arising of a mango fruit from a rose-apple tree when there is no mango tree, said, 'No, venerable sir.'

Dutiyapañhe ruppanākāraruppanaliṅgaruppananimittavasena rūpanti uddesavasena ca ākārādīnaṃ attho veditabbo. Paṭighasamphassoti sappaṭighaṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ vatthuṃ katvā uppajjanakasamphasso. Idhāpi thero jamburukkhe asati ambarukkhato jambupakkassa uppattiṃ viya nāmakāyato tassa uppattiṃ asampaṭicchanto “no hetaṃ bhante”ti āha.

In the second question, the meaning of 'mode', 'sign', and 'mark' should be understood in relation to the designation 'form' (rūpa), by way of the mode of being afflicted, the sign of being afflicted, and the mark of being afflicted. 'Resistance-contact' refers to contact that arises having made the resistant form-aggregate its basis. Here too, the elder, not accepting its arising from the mental body—like the arising of a rose-apple fruit from a mango tree when there is no rose-apple tree—replied, 'No, venerable sir.'

Tatiyapañho [V 2.0082][M 2.0092] ubhayavaseneva vutto. Tatra thero ākāse ambajambupakkānaṃ uppattiṃ viya nāmarūpābhāve dvinnampi phassānaṃ uppattiṃ asampaṭicchanto “no hetaṃ bhante”ti āha.

The third question was stated in terms of both. There, the elder, not accepting that both contacts could arise in the absence of name-and-form—just as mango and rose-apple fruits do not arise in space—replied, 'No, venerable sir.'

Evaṃ dvinnaṃ phassānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ paccayaṃ dassetvā idāni dvinnampi tesaṃ avisesato nāmarūpapaccayataṃ dassetuṃ – “yehi ānanda ākārehī”ti catutthaṃ pañhaṃ ārabhi. Yadidaṃ nāmarūpanti yaṃ idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, yaṃ idaṃ chasupi dvāresu nāmarūpaṃ, eseva hetu eseva paccayoti attho. Cakkhudvārādīsu hi cakkhādīni ceva rūpārammaṇādīni ca rūpaṃ, sampayuttakā khandhā nāmanti evaṃ pañcavidhopi so phasso nāmarūpapaccayāva [P 2.0502] phasso. Manodvārepi hadayavatthuñceva yañca rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti, idaṃ rūpaṃ. Sampayuttadhammā ceva yañca arūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti, idaṃ arūpaṃ nāma. Evaṃ manosamphassopi nāmarūpapaccayā phassoti veditabbo. Nāmarūpaṃ panassa bahudhā paccayo hoti.

Having thus shown the separate conditions for these two types of contact, now, to demonstrate their conditioning by name-and-form without distinction, the fourth question begins with: 'Ānanda, by whatever modes...' Here, 'this name-and-form' means that name-and-form which is present in the six sense doors. This itself is the cause, this itself is the condition—this is the meaning. For in the eye-door etc., the eye etc., as well as visible objects etc., are materiality, while the associated aggregates are mentality; thus, that fivefold contact is contact conditioned only by name-and-form. In the mind-door as well, the heart-base and whatever material object is the object, this is materiality. The associated phenomena and whatever immaterial thing is the object, this is immateriality, or mentality. Thus, mind-contact too should be understood as contact conditioned by name-and-form. Moreover, name-and-form is a condition for it in many ways.

115. Na okkamissathāti pavisitvā pavattamānaṃ viya paṭisandhivasena na vattissatha. Samuccissathāti paṭisandhiviññāṇe asati api nu kho suddhaṃ avasesaṃ nāmarūpaṃ antomātukucchismiṃ kalalādibhāvena samuccitaṃ missakabhūtaṃ hutvā vattissatha. Okkamitvā vokkamissathāti paṭisandhivasena okkamitvā cutivasena vokkamissatha, nirujjhissathāti attho. So panassa nirodho na tasseva cittassa nirodhena, na tato dutiyatatiyānaṃ nirodhena hoti. Paṭisandhicittena hi saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitāni samatiṃsa kammajarūpāni nibbattanti. Tesu pana ṭhitesuyeva soḷasa bhavaṅgacittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. Etasmiṃ antare gahitapaṭisandhikassa dārakassa vā mātuyā vā panassa antarāyo natthi. Ayañhi anokāso nāma. Sace pana paṭisandhicittena saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitarūpāni sattarasamassa bhavaṅgassa paccayaṃ dātuṃ sakkonti, pavatti pavattati, paveṇī ghaṭiyati. Sace pana na sakkonti, pavatti nappavattati, paveṇī na ghaṭiyati, vokkamati nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāya “okkamitvā vokkamissathā”ti vuttaṃ.

115. "Will you not descend?" means: will you not come to be by way of rebirth-linking, as if entering and continuing? "Will it be formed?" means: in the absence of rebirth-linking consciousness, will the mere remaining name-and-form come to be, gathered together and mixed within the mother's womb in the state of an embryo and so forth? "Having descended, will you depart?" means: having descended by way of rebirth-linking, will you depart by way of death; the meaning is, will you cease. But its cessation does not occur by the cessation of that very consciousness, nor by the cessation of the second or third consciousnesses after that. For, together with the rebirth-linking consciousness, thirty kamma-born material phenomena arise. While these persist, sixteen life-continuum consciousnesses arise and cease. During this interval, there is no danger for the child who has taken rebirth-linking, nor for its mother. This is indeed called a "non-opportunity" for death. But if the material phenomena that arose together with the rebirth-linking consciousness are able to provide a condition for the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness, the process continues, the lineage connects. But if they are not able, the process does not continue, the lineage does not connect; this is called "departure." It is with reference to this that it was said, "Having descended, will you depart?"

Itthattāyāti itthabhāvāya, evaṃ paripuṇṇapañcakkhandhabhāvāyāti attho. Daharasseva satoti mandassa bālasseva santassa. Vocchijjissathāti upacchijjissatha [M 2.0093] vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullanti viññāṇe upacchinne suddhaṃ nāmarūpameva uṭṭhahitvā paṭhamavayavasena vuḍḍhiṃ, majjhimavayavasena virūḷhiṃ, pacchimavayavasena vepullaṃ api nu kho āpajjissathāti. Dasavassavīsativassavassasatavassasahassasampāpanena [V 2.0083] vā api nu kho vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissathāti attho.

"For this state" means for the state of being thus; that is, for the state of the five aggregates being thus complete. "While being a mere child" means while being a dull infant. "Will you be cut off?" means: will you be terminated? When consciousness is cut off, will mere name-and-form by itself arise and attain growth by way of the first stage of life, development by way of the middle stage of life, and abundance by way of the last stage of life? Or, by reaching ten, twenty, a hundred, or a thousand years, will you attain growth, development, and abundance? This is the meaning.

Tasmātihānandāti yasmā mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇepi [P 2.0503] kucchivāsepi kucchito nikkhamanepi, pavattiyaṃ dasavassādikālepi viññāṇamevassa paccayo, tasmā eseva hetu esa paccayo nāmarūpassa, yadidaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Yathā hi rājā attano parisaṃ niggaṇhanto evaṃ vadeyya – “tvaṃ uparājā, tvaṃ senāpatīti kena kato nanu mayā kato, sace hi mayi akaronte tvaṃ attano dhammatāya uparājā vā senāpati vā bhaveyyāsi, jāneyyāma vo bala”nti; evameva viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpassa paccayo hoti. Atthato evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ vadati viya “tvaṃ nāmaṃ, tvaṃ rūpaṃ, tvaṃ nāmarūpaṃ nāmāti kena kataṃ, nanu mayā kataṃ, sace hi mayi purecārike hutvā mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ agaṇhante tvaṃ nāmaṃ vā rūpaṃ vā nāmarūpaṃ vā bhaveyyāsi, jāneyyāma vo bala”nti. Taṃ panetaṃ viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpassa bahudhā paccayo hoti.

"Therefore, Ānanda" means: because consciousness is its condition at the time of taking rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, while dwelling in the womb, while exiting from the womb, and during the process of existence at the time of ten years and so forth, therefore this is the cause, this is the condition for name-and-form, that is, this consciousness. Just as a king, while rebuking his retinue, might say: "You, the viceroy, and you, the general—by whom were you made? Was it not by me that you were made? Indeed, if I had not made you, and you could become a viceroy or a general by your own nature, we would know your strength!" In the same way, consciousness is a condition for name-and-form. In meaning, it is as if consciousness says to name-and-form: "You, name; you, form; you, called name-and-form—by whom were you made? Was it not by me that you were made? Indeed, if I, having been the forerunner, had not taken rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, and you could become name, or form, or name-and-form, we would know your strength!" Now, this consciousness is a condition for name-and-form in many ways.

116. Dukkhasamudayasambhavoti dukkharāsisambhavo. Yadidaṃ nāmarūpanti yaṃ idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, eseva hetu esa paccayo. Yathā hi rājapurisā rājānaṃ niggaṇhanto evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “tvaṃ rājāti kena kato, nanu mayā kato, sace hi mayi uparājaṭṭhāne, mayi senāpatiṭṭhāne atiṭṭhante tvaṃ ekakova rājā bhaveyyāsi, passeyyāma te rājabhāva”nti; evameva nāmarūpampi atthato evaṃ viññāṇaṃ vadati viya “tvaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇanti kena kataṃ, nanu amhehi kataṃ, sace hi tvaṃ tayo khandhe hadayavatthuñca anissāya paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ nāma bhaveyyāsi, passeyyāma te paṭisandhiviññāṇabhāva”nti. Tañca panetaṃ nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇassa bahudhā paccayo hoti.

116. "The arising of the origin of suffering" means the arising of the mass of suffering. "That is, name-and-form" means: this name-and-form, this very thing is the cause, this is the condition. Just as the king's men, while rebuking the king, might say: "You, the king—by whom were you made? Was it not by us that you were made? Indeed, if we were not established in the positions of viceroy and general, could you be king all by yourself? We would see your state of being king!" In the same way, name-and-form also, in meaning, says to consciousness as it were: "You, rebirth-linking consciousness—by whom were you made? Was it not by us that you were made? Indeed, if you, without depending on the three aggregates and the heart-base, could be what is called rebirth-linking consciousness, we would see your state of being rebirth-linking consciousness!" And this name-and-form is a condition for consciousness in many ways.

Ettāvatā khoti viññāṇe nāmarūpassa paccaye honte, nāmarūpe viññāṇassa paccaye honte, dvīsu aññamaññapaccayavasena pavattesu ettakena [M 2.0094] jāyetha vā…pe… upapajjetha vā, jātiādayo paññāyeyyuṃ aparāparaṃ vā cutipaṭisandhiyoti.

"To this extent" means: when consciousness is a condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form is a condition for consciousness, with the two proceeding by way of mutual conditionality—by this much one might be born, or grow old, or die, or pass away, or reappear. Birth and so forth would be discerned, or successively, death and rebirth-linking.

Adhivacanapathoti “sirivaḍḍhako dhanavaḍḍhako”tiādikassa atthaṃ adisvā vacanamattameva adhikicca pavattassa vohārassa patho. Niruttipathoti saratīti sato, sampajānātīti sampajānotiādikassa [P 2.0504] kāraṇāpadesavasena pavattassa vohārassa patho. Paññattipathoti – “paṇḍito [V 2.0084] byatto medhāvī nipuṇo kataparappavādo”tiādikassa nānappakārato ñāpanavasena pavattassa vohārassa patho. Iti tīhi padehi adhivacanādīnaṃ vatthubhūtā khandhāva kathitā. Paññāvacaranti paññāya avacaritabbaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Vaṭṭaṃ vattatīti saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ vattati. Itthattanti itthaṃbhāvo, khandhapañcakassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Paññāpanāyāti nāmapaññattatthāya. “Vedanā saññā”tiādinā nāmapaññattatthāya, khandhapañcakampi ettāvatā paññāyatīti attho. Yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇenāti yaṃ idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇena aññamaññapaccayatāya pavattati, ettāvatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañhettha niyyātitavacanaṃ.

"The path of designation" is the path of conventional speech that proceeds by relying only on the term itself, without regard for the meaning, such as in "Sirivaḍḍhaka" or "Dhanavaḍḍhaka." "The path of language" is the path of conventional speech that proceeds by way of indicating a reason, such as in "one remembers (sarati), thus one is mindful (sato)," or "one clearly comprehends (sampajānāti), thus one is clearly comprehending (sampajāno)." "The path of concept" is the path of conventional speech that proceeds by way of making known in various ways, such as in "wise," "learned," "intelligent," "skillful," "one who has mastered the doctrines of others." Thus, by these three terms, the aggregates themselves, which are the basis for designation and so on, are spoken of. "The domain of wisdom" is that which is to be penetrated and known by wisdom. "The round turns" means the round of saṃsāra turns. "This state" means the state of being thus; this is a name for the five aggregates. "For designation" means for the purpose of name-concept. By terms such as "feeling" and "perception," it is for the purpose of name-concept; the meaning is that the five aggregates are also discerned to this extent. "That is, name-and-form together with consciousness" means: that name-and-form which proceeds together with consciousness by way of mutual conditionality—to this extent is what is said. And this here is the concluding statement.

Attapaññattivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Designation of Self.

117. Iti bhagavā – “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo, gambhīrāvabhāso cā”ti padassa anusandhiṃ dassetvā idāni “tantākulakajātā”ti padassa anusandhiṃ dassento “kittāvatā cā”tiādikaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha rūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānantiādīsu yo avaḍḍhitaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ attāti gaṇhāti, so rūpiṃ parittaṃ paññapeti. Yo pana nānākasiṇalābhī hoti, so taṃ kadāci nīlo, kadāci pītakoti paññapeti. Yo vaḍḍhitaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ attāti gaṇhāti, so rūpiṃ anantaṃ paññapeti. Yo vā pana avaḍḍhitaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ ugghāṭetvā nimittaphuṭṭhokāsaṃ vā tattha pavatte cattāro khandhe vā tesu viññāṇamattameva vā attāti gaṇhāti, so arūpiṃ parittaṃ paññapeti. Yo vaḍḍhitaṃ nimittaṃ ugghāṭetvā nimittaphuṭṭhokāsaṃ vā tattha pavatte cattāro khandhe vā tesu viññāṇamattameva vā attāti gaṇhāti, so arūpiṃ anantaṃ paññapeti.

117. Thus the Blessed One—having shown the connection of the phrase, 'This dependent origination, Ānanda, is deep and appears deep,' and now showing the connection of the phrase, 'entangled like a ball of thread,' began the discourse with 'To what extent,' and so on. Herein, Ānanda, in the statements beginning with 'a limited material self,' and so on, one who grasps an undeveloped kasiṇa-sign as the self designates a limited material self. But one who has attained various kasiṇas designates it sometimes as blue, sometimes as yellow. One who grasps a developed kasiṇa-sign as the self designates an infinite material self. Or one who, having discarded the undeveloped kasiṇa-sign, grasps either the space touched by the sign, or the four aggregates occurring there, or merely the consciousness among them as the self, designates a limited immaterial self. One who, having discarded the developed sign, grasps either the space touched by the sign, or the four aggregates occurring there, or merely the consciousness among them as the self, designates an infinite immaterial self.

118. Tatrānandāti [M 2.0095] ettha tatrāti tesu catūsu diṭṭhigatikesu. Etarahi vāti idāneva, na ito paraṃ. Ucchedavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatthabhāviṃ vāti tattha vā paraloke bhāviṃ. Sassatavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Atathaṃ vā pana santanti atathasabhāvaṃ samānaṃ. Tathattāyāti tathabhāvāya. Upakappessāmīti sampādessāmi. Iminā vivādaṃ dasseti. Ucchedavādī hi “sassatavādino attānaṃ atathaṃ anucchedasabhāvampi samānaṃ tathatthāya [P 2.0505] ucchedasabhāvāya upakappessāmi, sassatavādañca jānāpetvā ucchedavādameva naṃ gāhessāmī”ti cinteti. Sassatavādīpi “ucchedavādino attānaṃ atathaṃ asassatasabhāvampi samānaṃ tathatthāya sassatabhāvāya upakappessāmi, ucchedavādañca jānāpetvā sassatavādameva naṃ gāhessāmī”ti cinteti.

118. Herein, 'Ānanda'—here, 'herein' refers to those four with speculative views. 'Now' means in this very life, not hereafter. This is said with reference to annihilationism. 'Or existing there' means existing in that other world. This is said with reference to eternalism. 'But being unreal' means being of an unreal nature. 'For the sake of suchness' means for the sake of being so. 'I will bring about' means I will accomplish. By this, he shows the dispute. For the annihilationist thinks: 'Though the eternalist's self is unreal and not of an annihilating nature, I will bring it about for the sake of suchness, for the nature of annihilation; and having shown eternalism to be false, I will make him adopt annihilationism itself.' The eternalist also thinks: 'Though the annihilationist's self is unreal and not of an eternal nature, I will bring it about for the sake of suchness, for the nature of eternity; and having shown annihilationism to be false, I will make him adopt eternalism itself.'

Evaṃ [V 2.0085] santaṃ khoti evaṃ samānaṃ rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapentanti attho. Rūpinti rūpakasiṇalābhiṃ. Parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti paritto attāti ayaṃ diṭṭhi anuseti, sā pana na valli viya ca latā viya ca anuseti. Appahīnaṭṭhena anusetīti veditabbo. Iccālaṃ vacanāyāti taṃ puggalaṃ evarūpā diṭṭhi anusetīti vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

'Being thus' means being in such a state, designating a limited material self. 'Material' refers to one who has attained the material kasiṇa. 'The view of a limited self lies latent' means this view, 'the self is limited,' lies latent; and it lies latent like a short creeper and a long vine. It should be understood as 'lying latent' in the sense of not having been abandoned. 'Thus, it is fit to say' means it is proper to say that such a view lies latent in that person. This is the method in all cases.

Arūpinti ettha pana arūpakasiṇalābhiṃ, arūpakkhandhagocaraṃ vāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Ettāvatā lābhino cattāro, tesaṃ antevāsikā cattāro, takkikā cattāro, tesaṃ antevāsikā cattāroti attato soḷasa diṭṭhigatikā dassitā honti.

Here, regarding 'immaterial,' the meaning should be understood as one who has attained an immaterial kasiṇa, or one whose domain is the immaterial aggregates. To this extent, sixteen types of view-holders have been shown in substance: four who have attained meditative states, their four disciples, four reasoners, and their four disciples.

Naattapaññattivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Non-Designation of Self

119. Evaṃ ye attānaṃ paññapenti, te dassetvā idāni ye na paññapenti, te dassetuṃ – “kittāvatā ca ānandā”tiādimāha. Ke pana na paññapenti? Sabbe tāva ariyapuggalā na paññapenti. Ye ca bahussutā tipiṭakadharā dvipiṭakadharā ekapiṭakadharā, antamaso ekanikāyampi sādhukaṃ vinicchinitvā uggahitadhammakathikopi āraddhavipassakopi puggalo, te na paññapentiyeva. Etesañhi paṭibhāgakasiṇe paṭibhāgakasiṇamicceva ñāṇaṃ hoti. Arūpakkhandhesu ca arūpakkhandhā icceva.

119. Thus, having shown those who designate a self, now to show those who do not designate a self, he said, 'And to what extent, Ānanda…' But who are they that do not designate a self? Firstly, all noble individuals do not designate a self. And also those who are learned—bearers of the three Piṭakas, bearers of two Piṭakas, bearers of one Piṭaka, or even, at the very least, a person who, having thoroughly investigated one Nikāya, has mastered the teaching of the Dhamma, or a person who has undertaken insight meditation—they certainly do not designate a self. For them, regarding a counterpart sign, there is only the knowledge, 'It is a counterpart sign.' And regarding the formless aggregates, there is only the knowledge, 'They are formless aggregates.'

Attasamanupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Contemplating Self

121. Evaṃ [M 2.0096] ye na paññapenti, te dassetvā idāni ye te paññapenti, te yasmā diṭṭhivasena samanupassitvā paññapenti, sā ca nesaṃ samanupassanā vīsativatthukāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā appahīnattā hoti, tasmā taṃ vīsativatthukaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ dassetuṃ puna kittāvatā ca ānandātiādimāha.

121. Thus, having shown those who do not designate a self, now, as for those who do designate a self—since they designate after contemplating by way of views, and that contemplation of theirs occurs because the twenty-based identity view has not been abandoned—therefore, to show that twenty-based identity view, he spoke again, beginning with, 'And to what extent, Ānanda...'

Tattha vedanaṃ vā hīti iminā vedanākkhandhavatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi kathitā. Appaṭisaṃvedano me attāti iminā rūpakkhandhavatthukā. Attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attāti iminā saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhavatthukā[P 2.0506]. Idañhi khandhattayaṃ vedanāsampayuttattā vediyati. Etassa ca vedanādhammo avippayuttasabhāvo.

Therein, by the phrase 'or feeling,' the identity view based on the aggregate of feeling is stated. By 'my self is insentient,' the one based on the aggregate of form is stated. By 'my self feels, for my self has feeling as its nature,' the one based on the aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness is stated. For this triad of aggregates feels because it is associated with feeling. And for this triad, having feeling as its nature is an inseparable quality.

122. Idāni [V 2.0086] tattha dosaṃ dassento – “tatrānandā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatrāti tesu tīsu diṭṭhigatikesu. Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samayetiādi yo yo yaṃ yaṃ vedanaṃ attāti samanupassati, tassa tassa attano kadāci bhāvaṃ, kadāci abhāvanti evamādidosadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

122. Now, showing the fault therein, he said, beginning with 'Therein, Ānanda...' Therein, 'therein' refers to those three speculative views. The passage beginning 'Ānanda, at whatever time...' is said for the purpose of showing such faults as this: for whomever regards whatever feeling as self, for that very self there is sometimes existence and sometimes non-existence.

123. Aniccādīsu hutvā abhāvato aniccā. Tehi tehi kāraṇehi saṅgamma samāgamma katāti saṅkhatā. Taṃ taṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca sammā kāraṇeneva uppannāti paṭiccasamuppannā. Khayotiādi sabbaṃ bhaṅgassa vevacanaṃ. Yañhi bhijjati, taṃ khiyatipi vayatipi virajjhatipi nirujjhatipi, tasmā khayadhammātiādi vuttaṃ.

123. Regarding 'impermanent' and so on: they are impermanent because, having come to be, they cease to exist. They are conditioned because they are made by coming together and combining from various causes. They are dependently arisen because, depending on this or that condition, they have arisen rightly from a cause. 'Decay' and so on are all synonyms for dissolution. For that which breaks up also wastes away, perishes, fades away, and ceases. Therefore, 'subject to decay' and so on is said.

Byagā meti viagāti byagā, vigato niruddho me attāti attho. Kiṃ pana ekasseva tīsupi kālesu – “eso me attā”ti hotīti, kiṃ pana na bhavissati? Diṭṭhigatikassa hi thusarāsimhi nikkhittakhāṇukasseva niccalatā nāma natthi, vanamakkaṭo viya aññaṃ gaṇhāti, aññaṃ muñcati. Aniccasukhadukkhavokiṇṇanti visesena taṃ taṃ vedanaṃ attāti samanupassanto aniccañceva sukhañca dukkhañca attānaṃ samanupassati avisesena vedanaṃ attāti samanupassanto vokiṇṇaṃ uppādavayadhammaṃ [M 2.0097] attānaṃ samanupassati. Vedanā hi tividhā ceva uppādavayadhammā ca, tañcesa attāti samanupassati. Iccassa anicco ceva attā āpajjati, ekakkhaṇe ca bahūnaṃ vedanānaṃ uppādo. Taṃ kho panesa aniccaṃ attānaṃ anujānāti, na ekakkhaṇe bahūnaṃ vedanānaṃ uppatti atthi. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya – “tasmātihānanda, etenapetaṃ nakkhamati ‘vedanā me attā’ti samanupassitu”nti vuttaṃ.

The meaning of 'Byagā me' is 'it has vanished from me' (`vi agā`), that is, 'my self has departed, has ceased.' But could it be that for one and the same person, 'this is my self' holds true in all three periods of time? Why would it not be so? For one who holds wrong views has no stability, like a stake placed in a heap of chaff; like a forest monkey, he grasps one thing and lets go of another. Regarding 'mixed with impermanence, pleasure, and pain': one who specifically regards this or that feeling as self perceives the self as impermanent, pleasant, and painful. One who regards feeling without distinction as self perceives the self as mixed, subject to arising and passing away. For feeling is threefold and is subject to arising and passing away, and this he regards as self. Thus, for him, the self becomes impermanent, and it follows that many feelings arise in a single moment. But while this person accepts that self as impermanent, the arising of many feelings in a single moment is not possible. With reference to this meaning, it was said: 'Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason also it is not fitting to regard it thus: "Feeling is my self."'

124. Yattha panāvusoti yattha suddharūpakkhandhe sabbaso vedayitaṃ natthi. Api nu kho tatthāti api nu kho tasmiṃ vedanāvirahite tālavaṇṭe vā vātapāne vā asmīti evaṃ ahaṃkāro uppajjeyyāti attho. Tasmātihānandāti yasmā suddharūpakkhandho uṭṭhāya ahamasmīti na vadati, tasmā etenapi etaṃ nakkhamatīti attho. Api nu kho tattha ayamahamasmīti siyāti api nu kho tesu [P 2.0507] vedanādhammesu tīsu khandhesu ekadhammopi ayaṃ nāma ahamasmīti evaṃ vattabbo siyā. Atha vā vedanānirodhā saheva vedanāya niruddhesu tesu tīsu khandhesu api nu kho ayamahamasmīti vā ahamasmīti vā uppajjeyyāti attho. Athāyasmā ānando sasavisāṇassa tikhiṇabhāvaṃ viya taṃ asampaṭicchanto no hetaṃ bhanteti āha.

124. 'But where, friends,' means where in the pure aggregate of form there is absolutely no feeling whatsoever. 'Could there be there?' means: could the notion 'I am' arise in that which is devoid of feeling, such as in a palm-leaf fan or a window? 'Therefore, Ānanda,' means: because the pure aggregate of form does not stand up and declare 'I am,' therefore this too is not fitting. 'Could there be in that case the thought "I am this"?' means: could even one phenomenon among those three aggregates related to feeling be spoken of as 'I am this'? Or, with the cessation of feeling, when those three aggregates have ceased together with feeling, could the thought 'I am this' or 'I am' arise? Then the Venerable Ānanda, not accepting this, just as one would not accept the sharpness of a hare's horn, said: 'No, venerable sir, it is not so.'

Ettāvatā [V 2.0087] kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Vaṭṭakathā kathitā hoti. Bhagavā hi vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento katthaci avijjāsīsena kathesi, katthaci taṇhāsīsena, katthaci diṭṭhisīsena. Tattha “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi nappaññāyati avijjāya, ‘ito pubbe avijjā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti. Evañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati. Atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā avijjā”ti (a. ni. 10.61) evaṃ avijjāsīsena kathitā. “Purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi nappaññāyati bhavataṇhāya, ‘ito pubbe bhavataṇhā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti. Evañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati. Atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā bhavataṇhā”ti (a. ni. 10.62) evaṃ taṇhāsīsena kathitā. “Purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi nappaññāyati bhavadiṭṭhiyā, ‘ito pubbe bhavadiṭṭhi nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti, evañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati. Atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā bhavadiṭṭhī”ti evaṃ diṭṭhisīsena kathitā. Idhāpi diṭṭhisīseneva kathitā.

What has been said up to this point? The discourse on the round of existence has been spoken. The Blessed One, when teaching the discourse on the round, sometimes taught with ignorance as the head, sometimes with craving as the head, and sometimes with views as the head. Therein, it was taught with ignorance as the head thus: “Monks, a first point of ignorance is not discerned, of which it can be said: ‘Before this, there was no ignorance, and it came to be after.’ And this, monks, is what is said. And yet it is discerned that ignorance is dependently arisen.” It was taught with craving as the head thus: “Monks, a first point of craving for existence is not discerned, of which it can be said: ‘Before this, there was no craving for existence, and it came to be after.’ And this, monks, is what is said. And yet it is discerned that craving for existence is dependently arisen.” It was taught with views as the head thus: “Monks, a first point of the view of existence is not discerned, of which it can be said: ‘Before this, there was no view of existence, and it came to be after.’ And this, monks, is what is said. And yet it is discerned that the view of existence is dependently arisen.” Here too, it has been taught with views as the head.

Diṭṭhigatiko [M 2.0098] hi sukhādivedanaṃ attāti gahetvā ahaṅkāramamaṅkāraparāmāsavasena sabbabhavayonigati – viññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu tato tato cavitvā tattha tattha upapajjanto mahāsamudde vātukkhittanāvā viya satataṃ samitaṃ paribbhamati, vaṭṭato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃyeva na sakkoti.

For one who holds wrong views, taking pleasant feeling and so on as self, by way of the misapprehension of 'I-making' and 'mine-making,' wanders constantly and endlessly through all states of existence, births, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings—passing away from here and being reborn there, like a ship tossed by the wind on the great ocean. He is unable even to lift his head from the round of existence.

126. Iti bhagavā paccayākāramūḷhassa diṭṭhigatikassa ettakena kathāmaggena vaṭṭaṃ kathetvā idāni vivaṭṭaṃ kathento yato kho pana, ānanda, bhikkhūtiādimāha.

126. Thus the Blessed One, having taught the round of existence through this course of discussion to one who is deluded about the causal process and who holds wrong views, now, teaching about what is not the round, said, “But when, Ānanda, a monk…” and so on.

Tañca pana vivaṭṭakathaṃ bhagavā desanāsu kusalattā vissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhānaṃ navakammādivasena vikkhittapuggalaṃ anāmasitvā kārakassa satipaṭṭhānavihārino puggalassa vasena ārabhanto neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassatītiādimāha. Evarūpo hi bhikkhu – “yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ [P 2.0508] vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre vā santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Dukkhato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Anattato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasana”ntiādinā nayena vuttassa sammasanañāṇassa vasena sabbadhammesu pavattattā neva vedanaṃ attāti samanupassati, na aññaṃ, so evaṃ asamanupassanto na kiñci loke upādiyatīti khandhalokādibhede loke rūpādīsu dhammesu kiñci ekadhammampi attāti vā attaniyanti vā na upādiyati.

And this discourse on what is not the round, the Blessed One, being skilled in teaching, does not begin by addressing the distracted person who, occupied with new construction work and the like, has abandoned his meditation subject. Instead, he begins with reference to the practitioner, the person who dwells established in mindfulness, saying: 'He does not regard feeling as self,' and so on. For such a monk, because the knowledge of contemplation proceeds in regard to all phenomena according to the stated method—'Whatever form, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, he defines all form as impermanent: one contemplation. He defines it as suffering: one contemplation. He defines it as not-self: one contemplation'—he does not regard feeling as self, nor anything else. Not regarding it thus, he does not cling to anything in the world. That is, in the world with its divisions, such as the world of the aggregates, among phenomena such as form, he does not cling to any single phenomenon as 'self' or as 'belonging to self.'

Anupādiyaṃ [V 2.0088] na paritassatīti anupādiyanto taṇhādiṭṭhimānaparitassanāyāpi na paritassati. Aparitassanti aparitassamāno. Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatīti attanāva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyati. Evaṃ parinibbutassa panassa paccavekkhaṇāpavattidassanatthaṃ khīṇā jātītiādi vuttaṃ.

'Not clinging, he is not agitated' means: not clinging, he is not agitated even by the agitation born of craving, views, and conceit. 'Not agitated' means being unagitated. 'He attains final Nibbāna within himself' means: he attains Nibbāna by the final Nibbāna of the defilements within himself. For one thus attained to final Nibbāna, in order to show the arising of the reviewing knowledge, it was said, “Destroyed is birth,” and so on.

Iti sā diṭṭhīti yā tathāvimuttassa arahato diṭṭhi, sā evaṃ diṭṭhi. “Itissa diṭṭhī”tipi pāṭho. Yo tathāvimutto arahā, evamassa diṭṭhīti attho. Tadakallanti taṃ na yuttaṃ. Kasmā? Evañhi sati – “arahā na kiñci jānātī”ti vuttaṃ bhaveyya, evaṃ ñatvā vimuttañca arahantaṃ “na kiñci jānātī”ti vattuṃ [M 2.0099] na yuttaṃ. Teneva catunnampi nayānaṃ avasāne – “taṃ kissa hetū”tiādimāha.

To say, 'Thus, this is a wrong view,' means that whatever wrong view a thus-liberated Arahant has, that is such a wrong view. There is also the reading, 'This is his wrong view.' The meaning is: 'The Arahant, thus liberated, has such a wrong view.' That is not proper. Why? For if it were so, it would be said, 'The Arahant knows nothing.' And it is not proper to say of the Arahant, who is liberated through knowing thus, 'He knows nothing.' Therefore, at the conclusion of all four methods, it is said, 'For what reason?' and so on.

Tattha yāvatā ānanda adhivacananti yattako adhivacanasaṅkhāto vohāro atthi. Yāvatā adhivacanapathoti yattako adhivacanassa patho, khandhā āyatanāni dhātuyo vā atthi. Esa nayo sabbattha. Paññāvacaranti paññāya avacaritabbaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Tadabhiññāti taṃ abhijānitvā. Ettakena bhagavatā kiṃ dassitaṃ? Tantākulapadasseva anusandhi dassito.

Herein, Ānanda, 'as far as there is designation' means as far as there is conventional expression known as designation. 'As far as the path of designation extends' means as far as there is a path for designation, that is, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements. This is the method in all cases. 'The range of wisdom' means the five aggregates to be comprehended by wisdom. 'Having directly known that' means having directly known it. By this much, what has the Blessed One shown? The connection with the very phrase 'like a tangled skein' has been shown.

Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitivaṇṇanā

An Exposition of the Seven Stations of Consciousness

127. Idāni yo – “na paññapetī”ti vutto, so yasmā gacchanto gacchanto ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma hoti. Yo ca – “na samanupassatī”ti vutto, so yasmā gacchanto gacchanto paññāvimutto nāma hoti. Tasmā tesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nigamanañca nāmañca dassetuṃ satta kho imānanda viññāṇaṭṭhitiyotiādimāha.

127. Now, the one of whom it was said, 'he is not designated,' is so because, in his progress, he becomes one called 'liberated in both ways.' And the one of whom it was said, 'he does not see,' is so because, in his progress, he becomes one called 'liberated by wisdom.' Therefore, to show the conclusion and the names of these two bhikkhus mentioned previously, he said, 'Ānanda, there are these seven stations of consciousness,' and so on.

Tattha sattāti paṭisandhivasena vuttā, ārammaṇavasena saṅgītisutte (dī. ni. 3.311) vuttā catasso āgamissanti. Viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhati etthāti [P 2.0509] viññāṇaṭṭhiti, viññāṇapatiṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Dve ca āyatanānīti dve nivāsaṭṭhānāni. Nivāsaṭṭhānañhi idhāyatananti adhippetaṃ. Teneva vakkhati – “asaññasattāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanameva dutiya”nti. Kasmā panetaṃ sabbaṃ gahitanti? Vaṭṭapariyādānatthaṃ. Vaṭṭañhi na suddhaviññāṇaṭṭhitivasena suddhāyatanavasena vā pariyādānaṃ gacchati, bhavayonigatisattāvāsavasena pana gacchati, tasmā sabbametaṃ gahitaṃ.

Herein, 'seven' are spoken of in terms of rebirth-linking. In terms of objects, the four spoken of in the Saṅgīti Sutta will be mentioned. 'Consciousness stands herein,' thus it is a station of consciousness; this is a designation for a basis for consciousness. 'And the two spheres' means two dwelling places. For here 'sphere' is intended to mean 'dwelling place.' Therefore it will be said: 'The sphere of non-percipient beings, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the second.' But why is all this taken up? For the sake of the full comprehension of the round of existence. For the round is not fully comprehended merely by way of pure stations of consciousness or by way of pure spheres alone, but it is comprehended by way of existences, origins, destinations, and abodes of beings. Therefore, all this is taken up.

Idāni [V 2.0089] anukkamena tamatthaṃ vibhajanto katamā sattātiādimāha. Tattha seyyathāpīti nidassanatthe nipāto, yathā manussāti attho. Aparimāṇesu hi cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇānaṃ manussānaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena dvepi ekasadisā natthi. Yepi hi katthaci yamakabhātaro vaṇṇena vā saṇṭhānena vā ekasadisā honti, tesampi ālokitavilokitakathitahasitagamanaṭhānādīhi viseso hotiyeva. Tasmā [M 2.0100] nānattakāyāti vuttā. Paṭisandhisaññā pana nesaṃ tihetukāpi dvihetukāpi ahetukāpi honti, tasmā nānattasaññinoti vuttā. Ekacce ca devāti cha kāmāvacaradevā. Tesu hi kesañci kāyo nīlo hoti, kesañci pītakādivaṇṇo. Saññā pana nesaṃ dvihetukāpi tihetukāpi honti, ahetukā natthi. Ekacce ca vinipātikāti catuapāyavinimuttā uttaramātā yakkhinī, piyaṅkaramātā, phussamittā, dhammaguttāti evamādikā aññe ca vemānikā petā. Etesañhi pītaodātakāḷamaṅguracchavisāmavaṇṇādivasena ceva kisathūlarassadīghavasena ca kāyo nānā hoti, manussānaṃ viya dvihetukatihetukaahetukavasena saññāpi. Te pana devā viya na mahesakkhā, kapaṇamanussā viya appesakkhā, dullabhaghāsacchādanā dukkhapīḷitā viharanti. Ekacce kāḷapakkhe dukkhitā juṇhapakkhe sukhitā honti, tasmā sukhasamussayato vinipatitattā vinipātikāti vuttā. Ye panettha tihetukā tesaṃ dhammābhisamayopi hoti, piyaṅkaramātā hi yakkhinī paccūsasamaye anuruddhattherassa dhammaṃ sajjhāyato sutvā –

Now, analyzing that meaning in sequence, he began with, 'Which are the seven?' Herein, 'just as' is a particle in the sense of an example; the meaning is 'like humans.' For in countless world-systems, among countless humans, not even two are identical in appearance, shape, and so on. Even those who are similar in appearance or shape, such as twin brothers, still have their own distinction in looking ahead, looking aside, speaking, smiling, walking, standing, and so on. Therefore, they are called 'diverse in body.' But their rebirth-linking perception can be three-rooted, two-rooted, or rootless. Therefore, they are called 'diverse in perception.' 'And some devas' means the six kinds of sense-sphere devas. Among them, some have blue bodies, while others have bodies of yellow or other colors. Their perception can be two-rooted or three-rooted, but not rootless. 'And some beings in the state of loss' refers to those apart from the four states of woe, such as the yakkhiṇī Uttaramātā, Piyangkaramātā, Phussamittā, and Dhammaguttā, and other such petas dwelling in mansions. For their bodies are diverse in color—yellow, white, black, the color of catfish skin, dark, and so on—and in size—thin, stout, short, and tall. And like humans, their perception can be two-rooted, three-rooted, or rootless. But they are not powerful like devas; they are of little power like destitute humans, and they live afflicted by suffering, with food and clothing difficult to obtain. Some are afflicted in the dark fortnight and happy in the bright fortnight. Therefore, because they have fallen from an accumulation of happiness, they are called 'beings in the state of loss.' Among them, those who are three-rooted can also attain the penetration of the Dhamma. For the yakkhiṇī Piyangkaramātā, hearing the Venerable Anuruddha reciting the Dhamma at dawn,

“Mā [P 2.0510] saddamakari piyaṅkara, bhikkhu dhammapadāni bhāsati;

Api dhammapadaṃ vijāniya, paṭipajjema hitāya no siyā;

“Make no noise, Piyaṅkara, the bhikkhu is reciting verses of the Dhamma; should we come to understand a verse of the Dhamma, let us practice it; it would be for our welfare.

Pāṇesu ca saṃyamāmase, sampajānamusā na bhaṇāmase;

Sikkhema susīlyamattano, api muccema pisācayoniyā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 2.40);

Let us restrain ourselves regarding living beings, let us not knowingly speak a falsehood; let us train in our own good virtue, that we might be freed from this demonic womb.”

Evaṃ puttakaṃ saññāpetvā taṃ divasaṃ sotāpattiphalaṃ pattā. Uttaramātā pana bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvāva sotāpannā jātā.

Having instructed her son in this way, she attained the fruit of stream-entry that very day. As for Uttaramātā, she became a stream-enterer just by hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One.

Brahmakāyikāti brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitamahābrahmāno. Paṭhamābhinibbattāti te sabbepi paṭhamena jhānena abhinibbattā. Tesu brahmapārisajjā pana parittena abhinibbattā, tesaṃ kappassa tatiyo bhāgo āyuppamāṇaṃ. Brahmapurohitā majjhimena, tesaṃ upaḍḍhakappo āyuppamāṇaṃ, kāyo [V 2.0090] ca tesaṃ vipphārikataro hoti. Mahābrahmāno paṇītena, tesaṃ kappo āyuppamāṇaṃ, kāyo pana tesaṃ ativipphāriko hoti. Iti te kāyassa nānattā, paṭhamajjhānavasena saññāya ekattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññinoti veditabbā.

'Beings of the Brahmā group' means the Brahmās of the Assembly, the Ministers of Brahmā, and the Great Brahmās. 'First arisen' means they are all reborn through the first jhāna. Among them, the Brahmās of the Assembly are reborn through the minor development of jhāna; their lifespan is a third of an eon. The Ministers of Brahmā are reborn through the medium development; their lifespan is half an eon, and their bodies are more extensive. The Great Brahmās are reborn through the superior development; their lifespan is an eon, and their bodies are exceedingly extensive. Thus, because of the diversity of their bodies and the unity of their perception by way of the first jhāna, they are to be known as 'beings of diverse bodies and uniform perception'.

Yathā [M 2.0101] ca te, evaṃ catūsu apāyesu sattā. Nirayesu hi kesañci gāvutaṃ, kesañci aḍḍhayojanaṃ, kesañci yojanaṃ attabhāvo hoti, devadattassa pana yojanasatiko jāto. Tiracchānesupi keci khuddakā, keci mahantā. Pettivisayepi keci saṭṭhihatthā, keci sattatihatthā, keci asītihatthā honti, keci suvaṇṇā, keci dubbaṇṇā honti. Tathā kālakañjikā asurā. Api cettha dīghapiṭṭhikapetā nāma saṭṭhiyojanikāpi honti. Saññā pana sabbesampi akusalavipākaahetukāva honti. Iti āpāyikāpi nānattakāyā ekattasaññinotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti.

Just as those are, so too are beings in the four woeful states. Indeed, in the hells, the bodies of some are a gāvuta in size, some half a yojana, and some a yojana; Devadatta’s, however, was born a hundred yojanas in size. Among animals, too, some are small and some are large. In the realm of petas, some are sixty cubits, some seventy cubits, and some eighty cubits; some are of golden complexion, and some are of ugly complexion. Likewise are the Kālakañjika asuras. Moreover, herein, there are also petas named Dīghapiṭṭhika who are sixty yojanas in size. The perception of all of them, however, is solely a rootless unwholesome resultant. Thus, beings of the woeful states, though diverse in body, are indeed counted as having a single perception.

Ābhassarāti daṇḍaukkāya acci viya etesaṃ sarīrato ābhā chijjitvā chijjitvā patantī viya sarati vissaratīti ābhassarā. Tesu pañcakanayena dutiyatatiyajjhānadvayaṃ parittaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā parittābhā nāma honti, tesaṃ dve kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Majjhimaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā appamāṇābhā nāma honti, tesaṃ cattāro kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Paṇītaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā ābhassarā [P 2.0511] nāma honti, tesaṃ aṭṭha kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Idha pana ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena sabbepi te gahitā. Sabbesañhi tesaṃ kāyo ekavipphārova hoti, saññā pana avitakkavicāramattā vā avitakkaavicārā vāti nānā.

The Ābhassarā (Radiant) are so called because light flows and spreads from their bodies as if breaking off and falling, like a flame from a torch. Among them, by way of the fivefold method, those reborn there having developed the pair of the second and third jhānas to a limited degree are called the Parittābhā (Limited Radiance), with a lifespan of two great eons. Those who developed them to a middling degree are called the Appamāṇābhā (Immeasurable Radiance), with a lifespan of four great eons. Those who developed them to a superior degree are called the Ābhassarā (Radiant), with a lifespan of eight great eons. Here, however, all are included by way of the highest classification. For the body of all of them is of a single radiance, but their perception is diverse, being either with only sustained thought and without initial thought, or without initial and sustained thought.

Subhakiṇhāti subhena okiṇṇā vikiṇṇā, subhena sarīrappabhāvaṇṇena ekagghanāti attho. Etesañhi ābhassarānaṃ viya na chijjitvā chijjitvā pabhā gacchati. Pañcakanaye pana parittamajjhimapaṇītassa catutthajjhānassa vasena soḷasadvattiṃsacatusaṭṭhikappāyukā parittasubhaappamāṇasubhasubhakiṇhā nāma hutvā nibbattanti. Iti sabbepi te ekattakāyā ceva catutthajjhānasaññāya ekattasaññino cāti veditabbā. Vehapphalāpi catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitimeva bhajanti. Asaññasattā viññāṇābhāvā ettha saṅgahaṃ na gacchanti, sattāvāsesu gacchanti.

The Subhakiṇhā (Lustrous Beauty) are so called because they are entirely suffused and pervaded by beauty; the meaning is that their bodies have a uniform radiance and color of beauty. For their radiance does not go forth breaking off again and again, unlike that of the Ābhassarā. In the fivefold classification, based on the limited, middling, or superior attainment of the fourth jhāna, they are born as the Parittasubha (Limited Beauty), Appamāṇasubha (Immeasurable Beauty), or Subhakiṇhā (Lustrous Beauty), with lifespans of sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four great eons, respectively. Thus, all of them are to be understood as having uniform bodies and a single perception due to the perception of the fourth jhāna. The Vehapphalā (Great Fruit) also pertain to the fourth station of consciousness. The non-percipient beings, due to the absence of consciousness, are not included here, but are included among the abodes of beings.

Suddhāvāsā vivaṭṭapakkhe ṭhitā na sabbakālikā, kappasatasahassampi asaṅkhyeyyampi buddhasuññe loke nuppajjanti. Soḷasakappasahassabbhantare buddhesu uppannesuyeva uppajjanti, dhammacakkappavattassa bhagavato khandhavāraṭṭhānasadisā honti. Tasmā neva viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ na sattāvāsaṃ [V 2.0091] bhajanti. Mahāsīvatthero pana – “na kho pana so sāriputta sattāvāso sulabharūpo [M 2.0102] yo mayā anivutthapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.160) iminā suttena suddhāvāsāpi catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ catutthasattāvāsaṃyeva bhajantīti vadati, taṃ appaṭibāhiyattā suttassa anuññātaṃ.

The beings of the Pure Abodes, being on the side of the unfolding away from the cycle of existence, are not perpetual. For a hundred thousand great eons, or even an incalculable period, they do not arise in a world devoid of Buddhas. They arise only within a period of sixteen thousand great eons when Buddhas have appeared, and they are like the fortified camp of the Blessed One who sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. Therefore, they belong neither to the stations of consciousness nor to the abodes of beings. The Elder Mahāsīva, however, states that based on the sutta—'Sāriputta, there is no common abode of beings where I have not dwelt before during this long time, with the exception of the gods of the Pure Abodes'—the Pure Abodes do belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings. Since this is not contradicted by the sutta, it is permitted.

Sabbaso rūpasaññānantiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pana yatheva saññāya, evaṃ viññāṇassapi sukhumattā neva viññāṇaṃ nāviññāṇaṃ. Tasmā viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu avatvā āyatanesu vuttaṃ.

The meaning of 'by completely overcoming perceptions of form,' and so on, has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. As for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, however, just as its perception is subtle, so too is its consciousness; due to this subtlety, it is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness. Therefore, it is spoken of among the bases and not among the stations of consciousness.

128. Tatrāti tāsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu. Tañca pajānātīti tañca viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ pajānāti. Tassā ca samudayanti “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.49) nayena tassā samudayañca pajānāti. Tassā ca atthaṅgamanti – “avijjānirodhā [P 2.0512] rūpanirodho”tiādinā nayena tassā atthaṅgamañca pajānāti. Assādanti yaṃ rūpaṃ paṭicca…pe… yaṃ viññāṇaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ viññāṇassa assādoti, evaṃ tassā assādañca pajānāti. Ādīnavanti yaṃ rūpaṃ…pe… yaṃ viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, ayaṃ viññāṇassa ādīnavoti, evaṃ tassā ādīnavañca pajānāti. Nissaraṇanti yo rūpasmiṃ…pe… yo viññāṇe chandarāgavinayo, chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ viññāṇassa nissaraṇanti (saṃ. ni. 2.26) evaṃ tassā nissaraṇañca pajānāti. Kallaṃ nu tenāti yuttaṃ nu tena bhikkhunā taṃ viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena ahanti vā mamanti vā abhinanditunti. Etenupāyena sabbattha veditabbo. Yattha pana rūpaṃ natthi, tattha catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ vasena, yattha viññāṇaṃ natthi, tattha ekassa khandhassa vasena samudayo yojetabbo. Āhārasamudayā āhāranirodhāti idañcettha padaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

128. 'Therein' means: in those stations of consciousness. 'And he understands that' means: he understands that station of consciousness. 'And its origin' means: he understands its origin by the method beginning, 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form.' 'And its passing away' means: he understands its passing away by the method beginning, 'With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form.' 'Gratification' means: 'Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on form... in dependence on consciousness, this is the gratification of consciousness'; in this way, he understands its gratification. 'Danger' means: 'That form... that consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is the danger of consciousness'; in this way, he understands its danger. 'Escape' means: 'Whatever is the removal of desire and lust for form... for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust, this is the escape from consciousness'; in this way, he understands the escape from it. 'Is it fitting for him?' means: Is it proper for that monk to delight in that station of consciousness by way of craving, conceit, and views, as 'I' or 'mine'? This method should be understood in all cases. However, where there is no form, the origin should be connected by way of the four aggregates; where there is no consciousness, it should be connected by way of the one aggregate. And here the phrase 'with the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment' should not be connected.

Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhūti yadā kho ānanda, bhikkhu. Anupādā vimuttoti catūhi upādānehi aggahetvā vimutto. Paññāvimuttoti paññāya vimutto. Aṭṭha vimokkhe asacchikatvā paññābaleneva nāmakāyassa ca rūpakāyassa ca appavattiṃ katvā vimuttoti attho. So sukkhavipassako ca paṭhamajjhānādīsu aññatarasmiṃ ṭhatvā arahattaṃ patto [M 2.0103] cāti pañcavidho. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “katamo ca puggalo paññāvimutto? Idhekacco puggalo na heva kho aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo paññāvimutto”ti (pu. pa. 15).

'And when, Ānanda, a monk...' means at the time when, Ānanda, a monk. 'Freed by non-clinging' means freed without grasping with the four kinds of clinging. 'Freed by wisdom' means freed by wisdom, the meaning being that, without personally experiencing the eight liberations, he, by the power of wisdom alone, having brought about the non-occurrence of mentality and materiality, is freed. He is of five kinds: a dry-insight meditator, and one who, having established himself in any of the first jhāna and so on, attains arahantship. It is also stated: 'And what person is freed by wisdom? Here, a certain person does not dwell having personally experienced the eight liberations with the body, but his taints are destroyed by seeing with wisdom. This person is called one freed by wisdom' (Pu. Pa. 15).

Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Eight Liberations

129. Evaṃ [V 2.0092] ekassa bhikkhuno nigamanañca nāmañca dassetvā itarassa dassetuṃ aṭṭha kho imetiādimāha. Tattha vimokkhoti kenaṭṭhena vimokkho? Adhimuccanaṭṭhena. Ko panāyaṃ adhimuccanaṭṭho nāma? Paccanīkadhammehi ca suṭṭhu muccanaṭṭho, ārammaṇe ca abhirativasena suṭṭhu muccanaṭṭho, pituaṅke vissaṭṭhaṅgapaccaṅgassa dārakassa sayanaṃ viya aniggahitabhāvena nirāsaṅkatāya ārammaṇe pavattīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ panattho pacchime [P 2.0513] vimokkhe natthi, purimesu sabbesu atthi.

129. Having thus shown the conclusion and the name for one monk, in order to show it for the other, he began with 'eight, indeed...'. Herein, in what sense is it a liberation (vimokkha)? In the sense of release (adhimuccana). And what is this sense of release? It is the sense of being thoroughly freed from opposing qualities, and the sense of being thoroughly released through delight in the object. It is said to be the occurrence in the object in an un-oppressed state and without anxiety, like the lying down of a child whose limbs and minor limbs are relaxed on its father's lap. This meaning, however, is not present in the final liberation, but it is present in all the preceding ones.

Rūpī rūpāni passatīti ettha ajjhattaṃ kesādīsu nīlakasiṇādīsu nīlakasiṇādivasena uppāditaṃ rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ, tadassatthīti rūpī. Bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti bahiddhāpi nīlakasiṇādīni rūpāni jhānacakkhunā passati. Iminā ajjhattabahiddhāvatthukesu kasiṇesu uppāditajjhānassa puggalassa cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni dassitāni. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti ajjhattaṃ na rūpasaññī, attano kesādīsu anuppāditarūpāvacarajjhānoti attho. Iminā bahiddhā parikammaṃ katvā bahiddhāva uppāditajjhānassa puggalassa rūpāvacarajjhānāni dassitāni.

Regarding 'Having form, he sees forms': here, 'form' is the form-sphere jhāna produced by means of the blue kasiṇa, etc., in the hair, etc., internally; one who possesses that is 'having form.' 'He sees forms externally' means that he sees forms such as the blue kasiṇa, etc., externally with the jhāna-eye. By this, the four form-sphere jhānas are shown for a person who has produced jhāna in kasiṇas with internal and external bases. 'Internally without perception of form' means that internally he is without perception of form; the meaning is that he has not produced form-sphere jhāna in regard to his own hair and so on. By this, the form-sphere jhānas are shown for a person who, having done the preliminary work externally, has produced jhāna only externally.

Subhantveva adhimutto hotīti iminā suvisuddhesu nīlādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇesu jhānāni dassitāni. Tattha kiñcāpi antoappanāyaṃ subhanti ābhogo natthi, yo pana visuddhaṃ subhaṃ kasiṇamārammaṇaṃ karitvā viharati, so yasmā subhanti adhimutto hotīti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, tasmā evaṃ desanā katā. Paṭisambhidāmagge pana – “kathaṃ subhantveva adhimutto hotīti vimokkho? Idha bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati…pe… mettāya bhāvitattā sattā appaṭikūlā honti. Karuṇā, muditā, upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati…pe… upekkhāya bhāvitattā sattā appaṭikūlā [M 2.0104] honti. Evaṃ subhaṃ tveva adhimutto hotīti vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.212) vuttaṃ.

'He is resolved only upon the 'beautiful''—by this, the jhānas in the very pure color kasiṇas, such as blue, etc., are shown. Here, although there is no advertence towards 'beautiful' within absorption, one who dwells having made a pure, beautiful kasiṇa his object comes to be called one who is 'resolved upon the beautiful,' and therefore the teaching was given in this way. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, it is said: 'How is being resolved only upon the 'beautiful' a liberation? Here, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness... because loving-kindness has been developed, beings are not repulsive. With a mind accompanied by compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction... because equanimity has been developed, beings are not repulsive. Thus, 'being resolved only upon the beautiful' is a liberation' (Paṭi. Ma. 1.212).

Sabbaso rūpasaññānantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo vimokkhoti ayaṃ catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ sabbaso visuddhattā vimuttattā aṭṭhamo uttamo vimokkho nāma.

Regarding 'With the complete transcendence of perceptions of form,' etc., whatever needs to be said has already been said in the Visuddhimagga. 'This is the eighth liberation'—this is called the eighth, supreme liberation because of the complete purification from and liberation from the four aggregates.

130. Anulomanti [V 2.0093] ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā. Paṭilomanti pariyosānato paṭṭhāya yāva ādito. Anulomapaṭilomanti idaṃ atipaguṇattā samāpattīnaṃ aṭṭhatvāva ito cito ca sañcaraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Yatthicchakanti okāsaparidīpanaṃ, yattha yattha okāse icchati. Yadicchakanti samāpattidīpanaṃ, yaṃ yaṃ samāpattiṃ icchati. Yāvaticchakanti addhānaparicchedadīpanaṃ[P 2.0514], yāvatakaṃ addhānaṃ icchati. Samāpajjatīti taṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ pavisati. Vuṭṭhātīti tato uṭṭhāya tiṭṭhati.

130. 'Forward order' means from the beginning to the end. 'Reverse order' means from the end to the beginning. 'Forward and reverse order' is said by way of moving from this to that without stopping, due to great proficiency with the attainments. 'As he wishes in place' is an indication of location: in whatever location he wishes. 'As he wishes in attainment' is an indication of the attainment: whatever attainment he wishes. 'As he wishes in duration' is an indication of the extent of time: for whatever length of time he wishes. 'He attains' means he enters that particular attainment. 'He emerges' means he rises from that and stands.

Ubhatobhāgavimuttoti dvīhi bhāgehi vimutto, arūpasamāpattiyā rūpakāyato vimutto, maggena nāmakāyato vimuttoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'Liberated in both ways' means liberated in two parts: liberated from the material body by the formless attainments, and liberated from the mental body by the path. And this was said:

“Accī yathā vātavegena khittā, (upasivāti bhagavā)

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkhaṃ;

Evaṃ munī nāmakāyā vimutto,

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkha”nti. (su. ni. 1080);

'As a flame tossed by the force of the wind, (said the Blessed One to Upasiva), goes to its setting and cannot be reckoned; so too a sage, freed from the mental body, goes to his setting and cannot be reckoned.' (Sn. 1080)

So panesa ubhatobhāgavimutto ākāsānañcāyatanādīsu aññatarato uṭṭhāya arahattaṃ patto ca anāgāmī hutvā nirodhā uṭṭhāya arahattaṃ patto cāti pañcavidho. Keci pana – “yasmā rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānampi duvaṅgikaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ, arūpāvacarajjhānampi tādisameva. Tasmā rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānato uṭṭhāya arahattaṃ pattopi ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti.

Furthermore, this one liberated in both ways is fivefold: one who attains arahantship after emerging from one or another of the base of infinite space and so on, and one who, having been a non-returner, attains arahantship after emerging from cessation. Some, however, say: 'Since the fourth jhāna of the form-sphere is also two-factored and accompanied by equanimity, and the jhānas of the formless-sphere are just the same, therefore one who attains arahantship after emerging from the fourth jhāna of the form-sphere is also one liberated in both ways.'

Ayaṃ pana ubhatobhāgavimuttapañho heṭṭhā lohapāsāde samuṭṭhahitvā tipiṭakacūḷasumanattherassa vaṇṇanaṃ nissāya cirena vinicchayaṃ patto[M 2.0105]. Girivihāre kira therassa antevāsiko ekassa piṇḍapātikassa mukhato taṃ pañhaṃ sutvā āha – “āvuso, heṭṭhālohapāsāde amhākaṃ ācariyassa dhammaṃ vaṇṇayato na kenaci sutapubba”nti. Kiṃ pana, bhante, thero avacāti? Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ kiñcāpi duvaṅgikaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ kilese vikkhambheti, kilesānaṃ pana āsannapakkhe virūhanaṭṭhāne samudācarati. Ime hi kilesā nāma pañcavokārabhave nīlādīsu aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ upanissāya samudācaranti, rūpāvacarajjhānañca taṃ ārammaṇaṃ na samatikkamati. Tasmā sabbaso rūpaṃ nivattetvā arūpajjhānavasena kilese vikkhambhetvā arahattaṃ pattova ubhatobhāgavimuttoti, idaṃ āvuso thero avaca. Idañca pana vatvā idaṃ suttaṃ āhari – “katamo ca puggalo ubhatobhāgavimutto. Idhekacco puggalo aṭṭhavimokkhe [P 2.0515][V 2.0094] kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti (pu. pa. 24).

This question regarding one liberated in both ways arose below the Lohapāsāda and, after a long time, was resolved by relying on the explanation of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷasumana. It is said that in Girivihāra, a resident pupil of the Elder heard this question from the mouth of a certain alms-food-goer and said, 'Friend, when our teacher was expounding the Dhamma below the Lohapāsāda, this had never been heard by anyone.' 'But what, venerable sir, did the Elder say?' 'Although the fourth form-sphere jhāna, being two-factored and accompanied by equanimity, suppresses the defilements, it operates in a place where defilements grow, in close proximity. For these defilements arise in the five-constituent existence depending on some object or other among the blue, etc., and the form-sphere jhāna does not transcend that object. Therefore, only one who has attained arahantship by completely turning away from form and suppressing the defilements by means of the formless jhānas is called one liberated in both ways. This, friend, is what the Elder said.' And having said this, he cited this sutta: 'And what sort of person is liberated in both ways? Here, a certain person dwells having contacted the eight liberations with the body, and his taints are destroyed through seeing with wisdom. This person is called one liberated in both ways.' (Pug. Pa. 24)

Imāya ca ānanda ubhatobhāgavimuttiyāti ānanda ito ubhatobhāgavimuttito. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Regarding the phrase 'And, Ānanda, than this liberation in both ways' (Imāya ca ānanda ubhatobhāgavimuttiyā), this means: Ānanda, than this liberation in both ways. The rest is clear in every respect.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Mahānidānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Great Discourse on Causation is concluded.

3. Mahāparinibbānasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Great Discourse on the Final Emancipation

131. Evaṃ [P 2.0516][V 2.0095][M 2.0106] me sutanti mahāparinibbānasuttaṃ. Tatrāyamanupubbapadavaṇṇanā – gijjhakūṭeti gijjhā tassa kūṭesu vasiṃsu, gijjhasadisaṃ vā tassa kūṭaṃ atthīti gijjhakūṭo, tasmiṃ gijjhakūṭe. Abhiyātukāmoti abhibhavanatthāya yātukāmo. Vajjīti vajjirājāno. Evaṃmahiddhiketi evaṃ mahatiyā rājiddhiyā samannāgate, etena nesaṃ samaggabhāvaṃ kathesi. Evaṃmahānubhāveti evaṃ mahantena ānubhāvena samannāgate, etena nesaṃ hatthisippādīsu katasikkhataṃ kathesi, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “sikkhitā vatime licchavikumārakā, susikkhitā vatime licchavikumārakā, yatra hi nāma sukhumena tāḷacchiggalena asanaṃ atipātayissanti poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhita”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1115). Ucchecchāmīti ucchindissāmi. Vināsessāmīti nāsessāmi, adassanaṃ pāpessāmi. Anayabyasananti ettha na ayoti anayo, avaḍḍhiyā etaṃ nāmaṃ. Hitañca sukhañca viyassati vikkhipatīti byasanaṃ, ñātipārijuññādīnaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Āpādessāmīti pāpayissāmi.

131. Thus have I heard—this is the Great Discourse on the Final Emancipation. Herein, this is the sequential explanation of terms: 'Gijjhakūṭa' (Vulture Peak) is so called because vultures lived on its peaks (gijjhā tassa kūṭesu vasiṃsu), or because its peak resembled a vulture (gijjhasadisaṃ vā tassa kūṭaṃ atthi); on that Gijjhakūṭa. 'Desiring to attack' (Abhiyātukāmo) means desiring to go for the purpose of overpowering. 'The Vajjis' (Vajjī) refers to the Vajjian kings. 'Of such great might' (Evaṃmahiddhike) means endowed with such great royal might; by this, he spoke of their unity. 'Of such great power' (Evaṃmahānubhāve) means endowed with such great authority; by this, he spoke of their training in skills such as the art of the elephant, with reference to which it was said: 'Indeed, these Licchavi youths are well-trained, thoroughly trained, in that they can shoot an arrow through a narrow keyhole, shot after shot, without missing.' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1115) 'I will uproot' (Ucchecchāmi) means I will eradicate. 'I will destroy' (Vināsessāmi) means I will annihilate, I will cause to disappear. Regarding 'ruin and calamity' (Anayabyasanaṃ), here, 'not prosperity' (na ayo) is 'ruin' (anayo); this is a term for decline. That which scatters or casts away welfare and happiness (hitañca sukhañca viyassati vikkhipati) is 'calamity' (byasanaṃ); this is a term for the loss of relatives and so on. 'I will bring upon them' (Āpādessāmi) means I will cause them to reach.

Iti kira so ṭhānanisajjādīsu imaṃ yuddhakathameva katheti, gamanasajjā hothāti evaṃ balakāyaṃ āṇāpeti. Kasmā? Gaṅgāyaṃ kira ekaṃ paṭṭanagāmaṃ nissāya aḍḍhayojanaṃ ajātasattuno āṇā, aḍḍhayojanaṃ licchavīnaṃ. Ettha pana āṇāpavattiṭṭhānaṃ hotīti attho. Tatrāpi ca pabbatapādato mahagghabhaṇḍaṃ otarati. Taṃ sutvā – “ajja yāmi, sve yāmī”ti ajātasattuno saṃvidahantasseva licchavirājāno samaggā sammodamānā puretaraṃ gantvā sabbaṃ gaṇhanti. Ajātasattu pacchā āgantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā [P 2.0517] kujjhitvā gacchati. Te punasaṃvaccharepi tatheva karonti. Atha so balavāghātajāto tadā evamakāsi.

Thus, it is said, in various postures such as standing and sitting, he spoke only of this matter of war, and he would command the army, saying, 'Be prepared to march.' Why? It is said that near the Ganges, by a certain port village, half a yojana was under Ajātasattu's authority, and half a yojana was under the Licchavis'. Here, the meaning is that it was a place where their authority was exercised. And there, valuable goods would come down from the foothills. Hearing of this, while Ajātasattu was still making arrangements, thinking, 'I will go today, I will go tomorrow,' the Licchavi kings, united and rejoicing together, would go before him and take everything. Ajātasattu, arriving afterwards and learning of the matter, would become angry and depart. They did the same thing again the following year. Then, with a powerful animosity having arisen in him, he acted thus at that time.

Tato cintesi – “gaṇena saddhiṃ yuddhaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, ekopi moghappahāro nāma natthi, ekena kho pana paṇḍitena saddhiṃ mantetvā karonto nipparādho hoti, paṇḍito ca satthārā sadiso [V 2.0096] natthi, satthā ca avidūre dhuravihāre vasati, handāhaṃ pesetvā pucchāmi[M 2.0107]. Sace me gatena koci attho bhavissati, satthā tuṇhī bhavissati, anatthe pana sati kiṃ rañño tattha gamanenāti vakkhatī”ti. So vassakārabrāhmaṇaṃ pesesi. Brāhmaṇo gantvā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho rājā…pe… āpādessāmī”ti.

Then he thought: 'War with a confederacy is a heavy burden, and not a single blow can be in vain. But one who acts after consulting with a wise person is without fault, and there is no wise person like the Teacher. The Teacher, moreover, dwells nearby in the Dhura Monastery. Come, I shall send someone to inquire. If there is some benefit in my going, the Teacher will remain silent. But if there is a disadvantage, he will say, “What is the use of the king going there?”' So he sent the brahmin Vassakāra. The brahmin went and reported this matter to the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: 'Then the king... I will bring upon them...'

Rājaaparihāniyadhammavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Conditions of Non-Decline for a King

134. Bhagavantaṃ bījayamānoti thero vattasīse ṭhatvā bhagavantaṃ bījati, bhagavato pana sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā natthi. Bhagavā brāhmaṇassa vacanaṃ sutvā tena saddhiṃ amantetvā therena saddhiṃ mantetukāmo kinti te, ānanda, sutantiādimāha. Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātāti divasassa tikkhattuṃ sannipatantāpi antarantarā sannipatantāpi abhiṇhaṃ sannipātāva. Sannipātabahulāti hiyyopi sannipatimhā, purimadivasampi sannipatimhā, puna ajja kimatthaṃ sannipatitā homāti vosānaṃ anāpajjantā sannipātabahulā nāma honti. Yāvakīvañcāti yattakaṃ kālaṃ. Vuddhiyeva, ānanda, vajjīnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihānīti – abhiṇhaṃ asannipatantā hi disāvidisāsu āgataṃ sāsanaṃ na suṇanti, tato – “asukagāmasīmā vā nigamasīmā vā ākulā, asukaṭṭhāne corā vā pariyuṭṭhitā”ti na jānanti, corāpi “pamattā rājāno”ti ñatvā gāmanigamādīni paharantā janapadaṃ nāsenti. Evaṃ rājūnaṃ parihāni hoti. Abhiṇhaṃ sannipatantā pana taṃ taṃ pavattiṃ suṇanti, tato balaṃ pesetvā amittamaddanaṃ karonti, corāpi – “appamattā rājāno, na sakkā amhehi vaggabandhehi vicaritu”nti bhijjitvā palāyanti. Evaṃ rājūnaṃ vuddhi hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “vuddhiyeva, ānanda, vajjīnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā no parihānī”ti. Tattha pāṭikaṅkhāti icchitabbā, avassaṃ bhavissatīti evaṃ daṭṭhabbāti attho.

134. The Elder, standing in performance of his duty, was fanning the Blessed One; for the Blessed One, however, there was neither cold nor heat. Having heard the brahmin's words, the Blessed One did not discuss them with him, but wishing to confer with the Elder, he said, 'What have you heard, Ānanda?' and so on. 'Meeting frequently' means gathering three times a day, or gathering from time to time; both constitute 'meeting frequently.' 'Given to meetings' means they are those who do not become reluctant, thinking, 'We met yesterday, and we met the day before; for what purpose should we meet again today?' 'As long as' means for whatever period of time. 'Growth, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline'—for those who do not meet frequently fail to hear the news coming from various directions. Consequently, they do not know, 'The border of such and such a village or town is in disorder,' or 'Thieves have risen up in such and such a place.' The thieves, knowing that 'the kings are negligent,' attack villages and towns, destroying the countryside. Thus, the kings decline. But those who meet frequently hear about each event and dispatch forces to suppress their enemies. The thieves, realizing, 'The kings are vigilant—we cannot roam in gangs,' break up and flee. Thus, the kings prosper. Therefore, it is said, 'Growth, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.' Here, 'to be expected' means it should be desired and should be understood as 'it will certainly happen.'

Samaggātiādīsu sannipātabheriyā niggatāya – “ajja me kiccaṃ atthi, maṅgalaṃ atthī”ti vikkhepaṃ [P 2.0518] karontā na samaggā sannipatanti nāma. Bherisaddaṃ pana sutvāva bhuñjantāpi alaṅkariyamānāpi vatthāni nivāsentāpi aḍḍhabhuttā vā aḍḍhālaṅkatā vā vatthaṃ nivāsayamānā vā sannipatantā samaggā sannipatanti nāma. Sannipatitā pana cintetvā mantetvā kattabbaṃ katvā ekatova avuṭṭhahantā [M 2.0108] na samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma. Evaṃ vuṭṭhitesu hi ye paṭhamaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ evaṃ hoti – “amhehi bāhirakathāva sutā, idāni vinicchayakathā bhavissatī”ti. Ekato vuṭṭhahantā pana samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma. Apica – “asukaṭṭhānesu gāmasīmā [V 2.0097] vā nigamasīmā vā ākulā, corā pariyuṭṭhitā”ti sutvā – “ko gantvā imaṃ amittamaddanaṃ karissatī”ti vutte – “ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ, ahaṃ paṭhama”nti vatvā gacchantāpi samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma. Ekassa pana kammante osīdamāne sesā rājāno puttabhātaro pesetvā tassa kammantaṃ upatthambhayamānāpi, āgantukarājānaṃ – “asukassa gehaṃ gacchatu, asukassa gehaṃ gacchatū”ti avatvā sabbe ekato saṅgaṇhantāpi, ekassa maṅgale vā roge vā aññasmiṃ vā pana tādise sukhadukkhe uppanne sabbe tattha sahāyabhāvaṃ gacchantāpi samaggā vajjikaraṇīyāni karonti nāma.

Regarding 'united' and so on: when the drum signaling the assembly has sounded, those who make excuses, saying, 'I have work to do today,' or 'I have an auspicious event,' are not said to assemble in unity. However, those who, upon hearing the drum's sound, assemble even while eating, being adorned, or dressing—whether they are halfway through their meal, halfway through being adorned, or in the midst of dressing—are said to assemble in unity. Furthermore, once assembled, having deliberated, discussed, and done what was to be done, if they do not rise all at once, they are not said to disperse in unity. For when they disperse in this way, those who leave first think, 'We have only heard the preliminary discussions; now the decisive discussions will take place.' But those who rise together are said to disperse in unity. Moreover, upon hearing that 'In such-and-such places, village or town boundaries are in disorder, and thieves have risen up,' if it is asked, 'Who will go and subdue this enemy?' and they respond, 'I will go first, I will go first,' and set out, they are also said to act in unity. And if one ruler's work is faltering, and the other rulers send their sons and brothers to support that work; or if, instead of telling a visiting king, 'Go to this one's house,' or 'Go to that one's house,' they all receive him together; or if, when an auspicious event, an illness, or any similar joy or sorrow arises for one of them, they all go there to offer support—in doing so, they are said to perform the duties of the Vajjis in unity.

Apaññattantiādīsu pubbe akataṃ suṅkaṃ vā baliṃ vā daṇḍaṃ vā āharāpentā apaññattaṃ paññapenti nāma. Porāṇapaveṇiyā āgatameva pana anāharāpentā paññattaṃ samucchindanti nāma. Coroti gahetvā dassite avicinitvāva chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsentā porāṇaṃ vajjidhammaṃ samādāya na vattanti nāma. Tesaṃ apaññattaṃ paññapentānaṃ abhinavasuṅkādīhi pīḷitā manussā – “atiupaddutamha, ko imesaṃ vijite vasissatī”ti paccantaṃ pavisitvā corā vā corasahāyā vā hutvā janapadaṃ paharanti. Paññattaṃ samucchindantānaṃ paveṇīāgatāni suṅkādīni agaṇhantānaṃ koso parihāyati. Tato hatthiassabalakāyaorodhādayo yathānibaddhaṃ vaṭṭaṃ alabhamānā thāmena balena parihāyanti. Te neva yuddhakkhamā honti, na pāricariyakkhamā. Porāṇaṃ vajjidhammaṃ samādāya avattantānaṃ vijite manussā – “amhākaṃ puttaṃ pitaraṃ bhātaraṃ acoraṃyeva coroti [P 2.0519] katvā chindiṃsu bhindiṃsū”ti kujjhitvā paccantaṃ pavisitvā corā vā corasahāyā vā hutvā janapadaṃ paharanti, evaṃ rājūnaṃ parihāni hoti, paññattaṃ paññapentānaṃ pana “paveṇīāgatameva rājāno karontī”ti manussā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā kasivāṇijjādike kammante sampādenti. Paññattaṃ asamucchindantānaṃ paveṇīāgatāni suṅkādīni gaṇhantānaṃ [M 2.0109] koso vaḍḍhati, tato hatthiassabalakāyaorodhādayo yathānibaddhaṃ vaṭṭaṃ labhamānā thāmabalasampannā yuddhakkhamā ceva pāricariyakkhamā ca honti.

Regarding 'not previously established' and so on: those who impose taxes, tributes, or fines that were not made before are said to establish what was not established. However, by not collecting taxes that have come down by ancient tradition, they are said to uproot what has been established. Those who, when a person is presented after being arrested as a thief, impose punishments like mutilation or execution without investigation, are said not to act in accordance with the ancient Vajjian custom. When such rulers establish what was not established, the people, oppressed by new taxes and other such things, become distressed and think, 'We are greatly harassed; who can live in their domain?' They then enter the border regions and, becoming thieves or allies of thieves, attack the countryside. When rulers uproot what has been established and do not collect the taxes and other revenues that have come down by tradition, their treasury declines. Consequently, the elephant corps, cavalry, the army, and the royal household, not receiving their regular stipends, decline in physical strength and power. They become unfit for battle and unfit for service. In the domain of rulers who do not act in accordance with the ancient Vajjian custom, the people become angry, thinking, 'They have cut down and broken our son, father, or brother, who was not a thief, after declaring him a thief.' They then enter the border regions and, becoming thieves or allies of thieves, attack the countryside. In this way, the rulers decline. But when rulers uphold what has been established, the people, happy and delighted, think, 'The kings are only acting according to tradition,' and they successfully carry out their work in agriculture, trade, and other areas. When rulers do not uproot what has been established and collect the taxes and other revenues that have come down by tradition, their treasury grows. Consequently, the elephant corps, cavalry, the army, and the royal household, receiving their regular stipends, become endowed with physical strength and power, and are fit for battle and for service.

Porāṇaṃ vajjidhammanti ettha pubbe kira vajjirājāno “ayaṃ coro”ti ānetvā dassite “gaṇhatha naṃ cora”nti avatvā vinicchayamahāmattānaṃ denti. Te vinicchinitvā sace acoro hoti, vissajjenti. Sace coro, attanā kiñci avatvā vohārikānaṃ denti. Tepi acoro ce, vissajjenti. Coro ce, suttadharānaṃ denti. Tepi vinicchinitvā acoro ce, vissajjenti. Coro ce, aṭṭhakulikānaṃ denti. Tepi tatheva katvā senāpatissa, senāpati uparājassa, uparājā rañño, rājā vinicchinitvā acoro ce, vissajjeti. Sace [V 2.0098] pana coro hoti, paveṇīpotthakaṃ vācāpeti. Tattha – “yena idaṃ nāma kataṃ, tassa ayaṃ nāma daṇḍo”ti likhitaṃ. Rājā tassa kiriyaṃ tena samānetvā tadanucchavikaṃ daṇḍaṃ karoti. Iti etaṃ porāṇaṃ vajjidhammaṃ samādāya vattantānaṃ manussā na ujjhāyanti, “rājāno porāṇapaveṇiyā kammaṃ karonti, etesaṃ doso natthi, amhākaṃyeva doso”ti appamattā kammante karonti. Evaṃ rājūnaṃ vuddhi hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “vuddhiyeva, ānanda, vajjīnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihānī”ti.

Herein, regarding 'the ancient Vajjian law': it is said that in former times, when a person was brought and presented as 'a thief,' the Vajjian kings would not say, 'Seize this thief!' but would hand him over to the judicial ministers. If, after investigation, he was found to be no thief, they would release him. If he was a thief, without saying anything themselves, they would hand him over to the legal experts. If they too found him to be no thief, they would release him. If he was a thief, they would hand him over to the keepers of the legal texts. If they too, after investigation, found him to be no thief, they would release him. If he was a thief, they would hand him over to the council of eight. They too, having acted in the same way, would hand him to the commander-in-chief; the commander-in-chief to the viceroy; the viceroy to the king. The king, after investigation, if he was found to be no thief, would release him. If, however, he was a thief, the king would have the book of precedents recited. Therein it is written: 'For one who has done such-and-such a deed, this is the punishment.' The king, having compared the person's action with that, would inflict the appropriate punishment. Thus, for those who conducted themselves according to this ancient Vajjian law, the people did not complain, thinking, 'The kings act according to ancient precedent; there is no fault in them, the fault is ours alone.' Being diligent, they would carry on their work. In this way, the kings experienced growth. Therefore it was said: 'Growth, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.'

Sakkarontīti yaṃkiñci tesaṃ sakkāraṃ karontā sundarameva karonti. Garuṃ karontīti garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvāva karonti. Mānentīti manena piyāyanti. Pūjentīti nipaccakāraṃ dassenti. Sotabbaṃ maññantīti divasassa dve tayo vāre upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tesaṃ kathaṃ sotabbaṃ saddhātabbaṃ maññanti. Tattha ye evaṃ mahallakānaṃ rājūnaṃ sakkārādīni na karonti, ovādatthāya ca nesaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchanti, te tehi vissaṭṭhā anovadiyamānā kīḷāpasutā rajjato parihāyanti. Ye pana tathā paṭipajjanti, tesaṃ mahallakarājāno – “idaṃ kātabbaṃ, idaṃ na kātabba”nti [P 2.0520] porāṇaṃ paveṇiṃ ācikkhanti. Saṅgāmaṃ patvāpi – “evaṃ pavisitabbaṃ, evaṃ nikkhamitabba”nti upāyaṃ dassenti. Te tehi ovadiyamānā yathāovādaṃ paṭipajjantā sakkonti rājappaveṇiṃ sandhāretuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “vuddhiyeva, ānanda, vajjīnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihānī”ti.

'They honor' means that whatever honor they show them, they perform it well. 'They respect' means they act only after establishing a state of reverence. 'They esteem' means they hold them dear in their minds. 'They venerate' means they show humility. 'They deem them worthy of being heard' means that, going to attend upon them two or three times a day, they consider their speech should be heard and should be trusted. Herein, those younger Vajjis who do not show such honor and so forth to the elder kings, and do not go to attend upon them for instruction, are abandoned by them; being unadmonished and devoted to amusement, they decline from their sovereignty. But for those who conduct themselves thus, the elder kings explain the ancient precedent: 'This should be done; this should not be done.' Even when it comes to battle, they show the strategy: 'One should advance thus; one should withdraw thus.'
