Those who are thus admonished and conduct themselves according to that advice are able to uphold the royal tradition. Therefore it was said: 'Growth, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.'

Kulitthiyoti [M 2.0110] kulagharaṇiyo. Kulakumāriyoti anividdhā tāsaṃ dhītaro. Okkassa pasayhāti ettha “okkassā”ti vā “pasayhā”ti vā pasayhākārassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. “Ukkassā”tipi paṭhanti. Tattha okkassāti avakassitvā ākaḍḍhitvā. Pasayhāti abhibhavitvā ajjhottharitvāti ayaṃ vacanattho. Evañhi karontānaṃ vijite manussā – “amhākaṃ gehe puttamātaropi, kheḷasiṅghāṇikādīni mukhena apanetvā saṃvaḍḍhitadhītaropi ime rājāno balakkārena gahetvā attano ghare vāsentī”ti kupitā paccantaṃ pavisitvā corā vā corasahāyā vā hutvā janapadaṃ paharanti. Evaṃ akarontānaṃ pana vijite manussā appossukkā sakāni kammāni karontā rājakosaṃ vaḍḍhenti. Evamettha vuddhihāniyo veditabbā.

'Women of good family' means the matrons of the clan. 'Maidens of good family' means their virginal daughters. Regarding 'by dragging and by force': herein, 'by dragging' or 'by force' is a term for an act of violence. Some also read it as 'by seizing.' Herein, 'by dragging' means having pulled and dragged away. 'By force' means having overpowered and overwhelmed; this is the meaning of the words. For when rulers act in this way, the people in their domain become angry, thinking, 'These kings, by violence, seize and keep in their own homes even the mothers of our sons, and the daughters we have raised, wiping away their spittle and snot with our own mouths!' Enraged, they go to the borderlands and, becoming thieves or the companions of thieves, they strike at the country. But when rulers do not act in this way, the people in their domain, being free from anxiety, attend to their own work and increase the royal treasury. Thus should growth and decline be understood in this matter.

Vajjīnaṃ vajjicetiyānīti vajjirājūnaṃ vajjiraṭṭhe cittīkataṭṭhena cetiyānīti laddhanāmāni yakkhaṭṭhānāni. Abbhantarānīti antonagare ṭhitāni. Bāhirānīti bahinagare ṭhitāni[V 2.0099]. Dinnapubbanti pubbe dinnaṃ. Katapubbanti pubbe kataṃ. No parihāpessantīti aparihāpetvā yathāpavattameva karissanti dhammikaṃ baliṃ parihāpentānañhi devatā ārakkhaṃ susaṃvihitaṃ na karonti, anuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ janetuṃ asakkontāpi uppannaṃ kāsasīsarogādiṃ vaḍḍhenti, saṅgāme patte sahāyā na honti. Aparihāpentānaṃ pana ārakkhaṃ susaṃvihitaṃ karonti, anuppannaṃ sukhaṃ uppādetuṃ asakkontāpi uppannaṃ kāsasīsarogādiṃ hananti, saṅgāmasīse sahāyā hontīti evamettha vuddhihāniyo veditabbā.

By 'the Vajjian shrines of the Vajjis' are meant the yakkha-shrines in the Vajjian country which received the name 'shrines' (cetiyāni) because they were made objects of veneration by the Vajjian kings. 'Internal' means those situated inside the city. 'External' means those situated outside the city. 'Previously given' means given in the past. 'Previously made' means made in the past. 'They will not cause to be diminished' means that they will perform the righteous offerings as they have always been performed, without allowing them to be diminished. For indeed, for those who diminish the righteous offerings, the deities do not provide well-arranged protection; though unable to generate suffering that has not yet arisen, they increase existing ailments such as coughs and headaches, and they are not allies when battle is joined. But for those who do not diminish them, the deities provide well-arranged protection; though unable to produce happiness that has not yet arisen, they destroy existing ailments such as coughs and headaches, and they are allies at the forefront of battle. Thus should growth and decline be understood in this matter.

Dhammikā rakkhāvaraṇaguttīti ettha rakkhā eva yathā anicchitaṃ na gacchati, evaṃ āvaraṇato āvaraṇaṃ. Yathā icchitaṃ na vinassati, evaṃ gopāyanato gutti. Tattha balakāyena parivāretvā rakkhaṇaṃ pabbajitānaṃ dhammikā rakkhāvaraṇagutti [P 2.0521] nāma na hoti. Yathā pana vihārassa upavane rukkhe na chindanti, vājikā vajjhaṃ na karonti, pokkharaṇīsu macche na gaṇhanti, evaṃ karaṇaṃ dhammikā rakkhāvaraṇagutti nāma. Kinti anāgatā cāti iminā pana nesaṃ evaṃ paccupaṭṭhitacittasantānoti cittappavattiṃ pucchati.

Herein, regarding 'righteous protection, shielding, and guarding': 'protection' (rakkhā) is so called because it prevents, such that what is undesired does not approach. 'Shielding' (āvaraṇa) is so called because it obstructs. 'Guarding' (gutti) is so called because it secures, such that what is desired does not perish. In this context, protection by surrounding with a body of troops is not what is called 'righteous protection, shielding, and guarding' for the renunciants. Rather, acting in such a way that trees in the monastery's grove are not cut, that hunters do not kill game there, and that fish in the ponds are not taken—this is what is called 'righteous protection, shielding, and guarding.' As for the phrase, 'And that future ones might come': with this, he asks about the process of their thought, inquiring, 'Is their stream of consciousness thus established?'

Tattha [M 2.0111] ye anāgatānaṃ arahantānaṃ āgamanaṃ na icchanti, te assaddhā honti appasannā. Pabbajite ca sampatte paccuggamanaṃ na karonti, gantvā na passanti, paṭisanthāraṃ na karonti, pañhaṃ na pucchanti, dhammaṃ na suṇanti, dānaṃ na denti, anumodanaṃ na suṇanti, nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ na saṃvidahanti. Atha nesaṃ avaṇṇo abbhuggacchati – “asuko nāma rājā assaddho appasanno, pabbajite sampatte paccuggamanaṃ na karoti…pe… nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ na saṃvidahatī”ti. Taṃ sutvā pabbajitā tassa nagaradvārena na gacchanti, gacchantāpi nagaraṃ na pavisanti. Evaṃ anāgatānaṃ arahantānaṃ anāgamanameva hoti. Āgatānampi phāsuvihāre asati yepi ajānitvā āgatā, te – “vasissāmāti tāva cintetvā āgatamhā, imesaṃ pana rājūnaṃ iminā nīhārena ko vasissatī”ti nikkhamitvā gacchanti. Evaṃ anāgatesu anāgacchantesu, āgatesu dukkhaṃ viharantesu so deso pabbajitānaṃ anāvāso hoti. Tato devatārakkhā na hoti, devatārakkhāya asati amanussā okāsaṃ labhanti. Amanussā ussannā anuppannaṃ byādhiṃ uppādenti, sīlavantānaṃ dassanapañhāpucchanādivatthukassa puññassa anāgamo hoti. Vipariyāyena pana yathāvuttakaṇhapakkhaviparītassa sukkapakkhassa sambhavo hotīti evamettha vuddhihāniyo veditabbā.

Therein, those who do not desire the arrival of future arahants are faithless and lacking in confidence. When monastics arrive, they do not go out to meet them, do not go to see them, do not offer hospitality, do not ask questions, do not listen to the Dhamma, do not give alms, do not listen to the words of rejoicing, and do not arrange a place to stay. Then, their ill repute spreads: ‘Such and such a king is faithless and lacking in confidence; when monastics arrive, he does not go out to meet them… and does not arrange a place to stay.’ Hearing this, monastics do not go by way of his city gate, and even if they are going there, they do not enter the city. Thus, there is simply no arrival of future arahants. And for those who have already arrived, if there is no comfortable dwelling, even those who came without knowing this depart, thinking, ‘We came intending to stay, but who would stay with these kings, given this kind of treatment?’ Thus, with future monastics not arriving and those who have arrived dwelling in discomfort, that country becomes uninhabitable for monastics. Consequently, there is no protection from deities. When there is no protection from deities, non-human beings find an opportunity. When non-human beings become numerous, they cause unarisen diseases to arise, and there is no acquisition of merit that is based on seeing virtuous ones, asking questions, and so on. Conversely, however, there is the arising of the bright side, which is the opposite of the dark side as described. In this way, growth and decline are to be understood in this matter.

135. Ekamidāhanti idaṃ bhagavā pubbe vajjīnaṃ imassa vajjisattakassa desitabhāvappakāsanatthamāha[V 2.0100]. Tattha sārandade cetiyeti evaṃnāmake vihāre. Anuppanne kira buddhe tattha sārandadassa yakkhassa nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ cetiyaṃ ahosi. Athettha bhagavato vihāraṃ kārāpesuṃ, so sārandade cetiye katattā sārandadacetiyantveva saṅkhyaṃ gato.

135. The Blessed One said this—'At one time, I...'—to make it known that this set of seven Vajjian principles had been taught to the Vajjis previously. Therein, 'at the Sārandada Cetiya' means at the monastery so named. It is said that before the Buddha arose, there was a shrine in that place, the dwelling of the yakkha Sārandada. Then, they had a monastery built there for the Blessed One. Because it was built at the Sārandada shrine, it came to be known as the Sārandada Cetiya.

Akaraṇīyāti akātabbā, aggahetabbāti attho. Yadidanti [P 2.0522] nipātamattaṃ. Yuddhassāti karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, abhimukhayuddhena gahetuṃ na sakkāti attho. Aññatra upalāpanāyāti ṭhapetvā upalāpanaṃ. Upalāpanā nāma – “alaṃ vivādena, idāni samaggā homā”ti hatthiassarathahiraññasuvaṇṇādīni pesetvā saṅgahakaraṇaṃ. Evañhi saṅgahaṃ katvā kevalaṃ vissāsena sakkā gaṇhitunti attho. Aññatra mithubhedāyāti ṭhapetvā mithubhedaṃ. Iminā aññamaññabhedaṃ katvāpi sakkā ete gahetunti [M 2.0112] dasseti. Idaṃ brāhmaṇo bhagavato kathāya nayaṃ labhitvā āha.

'They cannot be overcome' means they should not be acted against, they should not be seized—this is the meaning. 'That is' (`yadidaṃ`) is merely a particle. 'By war' (`yuddhassa`) is the genitive case used in the instrumental sense; the meaning is that it is not possible to seize them by direct combat. 'Except by conciliation' means setting aside conciliation. Conciliation is the act of showing favor by sending gifts of elephants, horses, chariots, silver, gold, and so on, saying, 'Enough of conflict; let us now be united.' The meaning is that by showing favor in this way, it is possible to seize them simply through gaining their trust. 'Except by sowing internal discord' means setting aside sowing internal discord. By this, it is shown that it is also possible to seize them by creating division among them. The brahmin said this, having grasped the method from the Blessed One’s discourse.

Kiṃ pana bhagavā brāhmaṇassa imāya kathāya nayalābhaṃ na jānātīti? Āma, jānāti. Jānanto kasmā kathesīti? Anukampāya. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “mayā akathitepi katipāhena gantvā sabbe gaṇhissati, kathite pana samagge bhindanto tīhi saṃvaccharehi gaṇhissati, ettakampi jīvitameva varaṃ, ettakañhi jīvantā attano patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ puññaṃ karissantī”ti.

But does the Blessed One not know that the brahmin is gaining a method from this discourse? Yes, he knows. Knowing this, why did he speak? Out of compassion. For it is said that this occurred to him: 'Even if I do not speak, in a few days he will go and seize them all. But if I do speak, by sowing discord among the united, he will seize them in three years. Even this much life is better, for by living this long, they will make merit that will be a foundation for them.'

Abhinanditvāti cittena abhinanditvā. Anumoditvāti “yāva subhāsitañcidaṃ bhotā gotamenā”ti vācāya anumoditvā. Pakkāmīti rañño santikaṃ gato. Tato naṃ rājā – “kiṃ ācariya, bhagavā avacā”ti pucchi. So – “yathā bho samaṇassa gotamassa vacanaṃ na sakkā vajjī kenaci gahetuṃ, api ca upalāpanāya vā mithubhedena vā sakkā”ti āha. Tato naṃ rājā – “upalāpanāya amhākaṃ hatthiassādayo nassissanti, bhedeneva te gahessāmi, kiṃ karomā”ti pucchi. Tena hi, mahārāja, tumhe vajjiṃ ārabbha parisati kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetha. Tato ahaṃ – “kiṃ te mahārāja tehi, attano santakehi kasivāṇijjādīni katvā jīvantu ete rājāno”ti vatvā pakkamissāmi. Tato tumhe – “kinnu kho bho esa brāhmaṇo vajjiṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ kathaṃ paṭibāhatī”ti vadeyyātha, divasabhāge cāhaṃ tesaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesessāmi, tampi gāhāpetvā tumhepi mama dosaṃ āropetvā bandhanatālanādīni akatvāva kevalaṃ khuramuṇḍaṃ maṃ katvā nagarā nīharāpetha. Athāhaṃ – “mayā te nagare pākāro parikhā ca kāritā, ahaṃ kira dubbalaṭṭhānañca uttānagambhīraṭṭhānañca jānāmi, na cirasseva dāni [V 2.0101] ujuṃ karissāmī”ti [P 2.0523] vakkhāmi. Taṃ sutvā tumhe – “gacchatū”ti vadeyyāthāti. Rājā sabbaṃ akāsi.

'Having delighted' means having delighted in mind. 'Having rejoiced' means having rejoiced with the words, 'How well-spoken this is by the venerable Gotama!' 'He departed' means he went into the king's presence. Then the king asked him, 'Teacher, what did the Blessed One say?' He replied, 'Venerable one, according to the words of the ascetic Gotama, the Vajjis cannot be seized by anyone. However, they can be seized by conciliation or by sowing internal discord.' Then the king asked him, 'By conciliation, our elephants, horses, and so forth will be lost. I will seize them by sowing discord alone. What should we do?' 'In that case, great king, you should start a discussion in the assembly concerning the Vajjis. Then I will say, "Great king, what are they to you? Let these kings live by their own means, engaging in agriculture, trade, and so on," and then I will depart. Then you should say, "Sirs, why on earth does this brahmin obstruct the discussion that has arisen concerning the Vajjis?" And during the day, I will send them a tribute with a letter. Having had that tribute intercepted, you should then lay the blame on me, and without having me bound or beaten, simply have my head shaven with a razor and have me banished from the city. Then I will say, "I had the city walls and moats built for you. I know the strong and weak points, the shallow and deep places. Now, in no long time, I will make things straight!" Hearing that, you should say, "Let him go."' The king did everything.

Licchavī tassa nikkhamanaṃ sutvā – “saṭho brāhmaṇo, mā tassa gaṅgaṃ uttarituṃ adatthā”ti āhaṃsu. Tatra ekaccehi – “amhe ārabbha kathitattā kira so evaṃ kato”ti vutte “tena hi, bhaṇe, etū”ti bhaṇiṃsu. So gantvā licchavī disvā “kiṃ āgatatthā”ti pucchito taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi, licchavino – “appamattakena nāma evaṃ garuṃ daṇḍaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti [M 2.0113] vatvā – “kiṃ te tatra ṭhānantara”nti pucchiṃsu. “Vinicchayāmaccohamasmī”ti. Tadeva te ṭhānantaraṃ hotūti. So suṭṭhutaraṃ vinicchayaṃ karoti, rājakumārā tassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhanti.

Having heard of his banishment, the Licchavis said, "That brahmin is deceitful; do not allow him to cross the Ganges." When some there remarked, "It seems he was treated thus because of what was said concerning us," they said, "Well then, sirs, let him come." He went, and when the Licchavis saw him and asked, "Why have you come?", he explained the situation to them. The Licchavis, saying, "It is not right to impose such a heavy punishment for such a trifling matter," asked, "What was your position there?" "I was a minister of justice," he replied. They said, "Let that very position be yours here." He then judged cases exceedingly well, and the royal princes learned their arts from him.

So patiṭṭhitaguṇo hutvā ekadivasaṃ ekaṃ licchaviṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ gantvā – dārakā kasantīti pucchi. Āma, kasanti. Dve goṇe yojetvāti? Āma, dve goṇe yojetvāti. Ettakaṃ vatvā nivatto. Tato taṃ añño – “kiṃ ācariyo āhā”ti pucchitvā tena vuttaṃ asaddahanto “na me esa yathābhūtaṃ kathetī”ti tena saddhiṃ bhijji. Brāhmaṇo aññasmiṃ divase ekaṃ licchaviṃ ekamantaṃ netvā – “kena byañjanena bhuttosī”ti pucchitvā nivatto. Tampi añño pucchitvā asaddahanto tatheva bhijji. Brāhmaṇo aparampi divasaṃ ekaṃ licchaviṃ ekamantaṃ netvā – “atiduggatosi kirā”ti pucchi. Ko evamāhāti pucchito asuko nāma licchavīti. Aparampi ekamantaṃ netvā – “tvaṃ kira bhīrukajātiko”ti pucchi. Ko evamāhāti? Asuko nāma licchavīti. Evaṃ aññena akathitameva aññassa kathento tīhi saṃvaccharehi te rājāno aññamaññaṃ bhinditvā yathā dve ekamaggena na gacchanti, tathā katvā sannipātabheriṃ carāpesi. Licchavino – “issarā sannipatantu, sūrā sannipatantū”ti vatvā na sannipatiṃsu.

Having established his good reputation, one day he took a Licchavi aside and asked, "Do the boys plow?" "Yes, they plow." "Having yoked two oxen?" Having said just this much, he returned. Then another asked that Licchavi, "What did the teacher say?" Not believing what he was told, he thought, "This one is not telling me the truth," and broke with him. On another day, the brahmin took a Licchavi aside, asked, "With what curry did you eat?" and then returned. Another also asked that one, and not believing him, broke with him in the same way. On yet another day, the brahmin took a Licchavi aside and asked, "It is said you are very poor, is it not?" When asked, "Who says so?" he replied, "Such-and-such a Licchavi." Again, taking another aside, he asked, "It is said you are of a timid nature, is it not?" "Who says so?" "Such-and-such a Licchavi." Thus, by telling one what another had not said, within three years he caused those rulers to be divided against one another, so that two would not walk on the same road. Having done so, he had the assembly drum sounded. The Licchavis, saying, "Let the powerful assemble, let the valiant assemble," did not assemble.

Brāhmaṇo – “ayaṃ dāni kālo, sīghaṃ āgacchatū”ti rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi. Rājā sutvāva balabheriṃ carāpetvā nikkhami. Vesālikā sutvā – “rañño gaṅgaṃ uttarituṃ na dassāmā”ti bheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Tampi sutvā – “gacchantu sūrarājāno”tiādīni vatvā na [P 2.0524] sannipatiṃsu. “Nagarappavesanaṃ na dassāma, dvārāni pidahitvā ṭhassāmā”ti bheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Ekopi na sannipati. Yathāvivaṭeheva dvārehi pavisitvā sabbe anayabyasanaṃ pāpetvā gato.

The brahmin sent a message to the king, saying, "Now is the time, let him come quickly." The king, as soon as he heard, had the war drum beaten and set out. The Vesālians, hearing this, had their drum beaten, saying, "We will not allow the king to cross the Ganges." Hearing that too, they said, "Let the heroic kings go," and so forth, and did not assemble. They had their drum beaten, saying, "We will not allow entry into the city; we will close the gates and stand our ground." Not even one assembled. He entered through the very gates that were left open, brought them all to misfortune and ruin, and departed.

Bhikkhuaparihāniyadhammavaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Principles of Non-Decline for Monks

136. Atha [V 2.0102] kho bhagavā acirapakkantetiādimhi sannipātetvāti dūravihāresu iddhimante pesetvā santikavihāresu sayaṃ gantvā – “sannipatatha, āyasmanto; bhagavā vo sannipātaṃ icchatī”ti sannipātetvā. Aparihāniyeti [M 2.0114] aparihānikare, vuddhihetubhūteti attho. Dhamme desessāmīti candasahassaṃ sūriyasahassaṃ uṭṭhapento viya catukuṭṭake gehe anto teladīpasahassaṃ ujjālento viya pākaṭe katvā kathayissāmīti.

136. Now, in the passage beginning, "Then the Blessed One, not long after they had departed," the phrase "having assembled them" means: having sent those with psychic powers to distant monasteries and having gone himself to nearby monasteries, saying, “Assemble, venerable ones; the Blessed One wishes for your assembly,” thus he assembled them. The term “for non-decline” means “conducive to non-decline,” that is, being a cause for growth. The phrase “I will teach the principles” means: “I will speak, making them manifest, as if causing a thousand moons and a thousand suns to arise, or as if lighting a thousand oil lamps inside a four-cornered house.”

Tattha abhiṇhaṃ sannipātāti idaṃ vajjisattake vuttasadisameva. Idhāpi ca abhiṇhaṃ asannipatitā disāsu āgatasāsanaṃ na suṇanti. Tato – “asukavihārasīmā ākulā, uposathapavāraṇā ṭhitā, asukasmiṃ ṭhāne bhikkhū vejjakammadūtakammādīni karonti, viññattibahulā pupphadānādīhi jīvikaṃ kappentī”tiādīni na jānanti, pāpabhikkhūpi “pamatto bhikkhusaṅgho”ti ñatvā rāsibhūtā sāsanaṃ osakkāpenti. Abhiṇhaṃ sannipatitā pana taṃ taṃ pavattiṃ suṇanti, tato bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pesetvā sīmaṃ ujuṃ karonti, uposathapavāraṇādayo pavattāpenti, micchājīvānaṃ ussannaṭṭhāne ariyavaṃsake pesetvā ariyavaṃsaṃ kathāpenti, pāpabhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharehi niggahaṃ kārāpenti, pāpabhikkhūpi “appamatto bhikkhusaṅgho, na sakkā amhehi vaggabandhena vicaritu”nti bhijjitvā palāyanti. Evamettha hānivuddhiyo veditabbā.

Therein, the phrase “frequent assembly” is just like what was stated in the seven principles for the Vajjians. Here too, monks who do not assemble frequently do not hear the news that has come from the various directions. Consequently, they do not know of matters such as: ‘the boundary of such-and-such monastery is in disorder, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have been suspended, in such-and-such a place monks are practicing medicine, acting as messengers, and so on; being given to much requesting, they make their living by such means as giving flowers.’ Furthermore, corrupt monks, knowing that ‘the Saṅgha of monks is negligent,’ form groups and cause the Dispensation to decline. But those who assemble frequently hear of these various events. Consequently, they send a Saṅgha of monks to set the boundary straight and to have the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other such ceremonies proceed. In places where wrong livelihood is rampant, they send those who uphold the noble lineage to teach the noble lineage. They have the Vinaya-holders impose censure on the corrupt monks. The corrupt monks, realizing that ‘the Saṅgha of monks is vigilant; it is not possible for us to go about forming factions,’ break up and flee. In this way, decline and growth in this matter should be understood.

Samaggātiādīsu cetiyapaṭijagganatthaṃ vā bodhigehauposathāgāracchādanatthaṃ vā katikavattaṃ vā ṭhapetukāmatāya ovādaṃ vā dātukāmatāya – “saṅgho sannipatatū”ti bheriyā vā ghaṇṭiyā vā ākoṭitāya – “mayhaṃ cīvarakammaṃ atthi, mayhaṃ patto pacitabbo, mayhaṃ navakammaṃ atthī”ti vikkhepaṃ karontā na samaggā sannipatanti nāma. Sabbaṃ pana taṃ kammaṃ ṭhapetvā – “ahaṃ purimataraṃ, ahaṃ purimatara”nti ekappahāreneva sannipatantā samaggā sannipatanti nāma. Sannipatitā pana cintetvā mantetvā kattabbaṃ [P 2.0525] katvā ekato avuṭṭhahantā samaggā na vuṭṭhahanti nāma. Evaṃ vuṭṭhitesu hi ye paṭhamaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ evaṃ hoti – “amhehi bāhirakathāva sutā, idāni vinicchayakathā bhavissatī”ti. Ekappahāreneva vuṭṭhahantā pana samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma. Apica “asukaṭṭhāne vihārasīmā ākulā, uposathapavāraṇā ṭhitā, asukaṭṭhāne vejjakammādikārakā pāpabhikkhū ussannā”ti sutvā – “ko gantvā [M 2.0115] tesaṃ niggahaṃ karissatī”ti [V 2.0103] vutte – “ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ, ahaṃ paṭhama”nti vatvā gacchantāpi samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma.

In the context of “harmonious” and so forth: when the drum or bell is struck with the announcement, “Let the Sangha assemble,” for the purpose of maintaining a shrine, or roofing a Bodhi-tree house or an Uposatha hall, or for establishing a disciplinary code, or for giving advice—if they assemble while making excuses like, “I have robe-making to do,” “my bowl needs to be fired,” or “I have new work to attend to,” they are not said to assemble harmoniously. However, if they set aside all such tasks and assemble promptly, each thinking, “I will be first, I will be first,” then they are said to assemble harmoniously. Once assembled, if they deliberate, discuss, and complete what needs to be done, but do not rise together, they are not said to rise harmoniously. For when they rise in this manner, those who leave first think, “We have only heard the external discussion; now the decisive discussion will take place.” But if they rise at once, they are said to rise harmoniously. Furthermore, upon hearing that in a certain place the monastery boundary is in disarray, the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā is stalled, or that wicked monks engaged in medical practices and the like are rampant—if someone asks, “Who will go and restrain them?” and they say, “I will be first, I will be first,” and then go, they are also said to rise harmoniously.

Āgantukaṃ pana disvā – “imaṃ pariveṇaṃ yāhi, etaṃ pariveṇaṃ yāhi, ayaṃ ko”ti avatvā sabbe vattaṃ karontāpi, jiṇṇapattacīvarakaṃ disvā tassa bhikkhācāravattena pattacīvaraṃ pariyesamānāpi, gilānassa gilānabhesajjaṃ pariyesamānāpi, gilānameva anāthaṃ – “asukapariveṇaṃ yāhi, asukapariveṇaṃ yāhī”ti avatvā attano attano pariveṇe paṭijaggantāpi, eko oliyamānako gantho hoti, paññavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ saṅgaṇhitvā tena taṃ ganthaṃ ukkhipāpentāpi samaggā saṅghaṃ karaṇīyāni karonti nāma.

Furthermore, upon seeing a newcomer, without saying, “Go to this dwelling, go to that dwelling,” or “Who is this?” all perform their duties; upon seeing a monk with a worn-out bowl and robe, they seek a bowl and robe for him according to the alms-round duty; they seek medicine for the sick; and for a helpless sick person, without saying, “Go to such-and-such dwelling, go to such-and-such dwelling,” they care for him in their own dwellings; and if there is a neglected text, they support a wise monk and have him revive that text—by these actions, they are said to perform the duties of the Sangha in harmony.

Apaññattantiādīsu navaṃ adhammikaṃ katikavattaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ vā bandhantā apaññattaṃ paññapenti nāma, purāṇasanthatavatthusmiṃ sāvatthiyaṃ bhikkhū viya. Uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ sāsanaṃ dīpentā paññattaṃ samucchindanti nāma, vassasataparinibbute bhagavati vesālikā vajjiputtakā viya. Khuddānukhuddakā pana āpattiyo sañcicca vītikkamantā yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya na vattanti nāma, assajipunabbasukā viya. Navaṃ pana katikavattaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ vā abandhantā, dhammavinayato sāsanaṃ dīpentā, khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni asamūhanantā apaññattaṃ na paññapenti, paññattaṃ na samucchindanti, yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya vattanti nāma, āyasmā upaseno viya, āyasmā yaso kākaṇḍakaputto viya ca.

In the context of “not prescribed” and so forth: those who establish a new unrighteous agreement or training precept are said to “prescribe what is not prescribed,” like the monks at Sāvatthī in the case of the old felt-rug matter. Those who present the teaching as being contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya are said to “abolish what is prescribed,” like the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī a hundred years after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna. Those who intentionally transgress minor and trifling offenses and do not conduct themselves, having undertaken them, in the prescribed training rules are said to “not conduct themselves according to what is prescribed,” like Assaji and Punabbasuka. But those who do not establish new agreements or training precepts, who present the teaching in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya, who do not abolish minor and trifling training rules, who neither prescribe what is not prescribed nor abolish what is prescribed, and who conduct themselves, having undertaken them, in the prescribed training rules—they are said to conduct themselves in accordance with what is prescribed, like the Venerable Upasena and the Venerable Yasa, son of Kākaṇḍa.

“Suṇātu, me āvuso saṅgho, santamhākaṃ sikkhāpadāni gihigatāni, gihinopi jānanti, ‘idaṃ vo samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ kappati, idaṃ vo na kappatī’ti. Sace hi mayaṃ khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni [P 2.0526] samūhanissāma, bhavissanti vattāro – ‘dhūmakālikaṃ samaṇena gotamena sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, yāvimesaṃ satthā aṭṭhāsi, tāvime sikkhāpadesu sikkhiṃsu. Yato imesaṃ satthā parinibbuto, na dānime sikkhāpadesu sikkhantī’ti. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho apaññattaṃ [M 2.0116] na paññapeyya, paññattaṃ na samucchindeyya, yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya vatteyyā”ti (cuḷava. 442) –

“Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. There are training rules of ours that are known to householders; even householders know, ‘This is allowable for you ascetics, sons of the Sakyan; this is not allowable for you.’ If we were to abolish the minor and lesser training rules, there would be those who would say, ‘A training rule for a time of smoke was prescribed by the ascetic Gotama for his disciples. As long as their Teacher was present, they trained in the training rules. Since their Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, they no longer train in the training rules.’ If it seems fitting to the Sangha, the Sangha should not prescribe what has not been prescribed, nor abolish what has been prescribed, but should conduct itself in accordance with the training rules as they have been prescribed.”

Imaṃ tantiṃ ṭhapayanto āyasmā mahākassapo viya ca. Vuddhiyevāti sīlādīhi guṇehi vuḍḍhiyeva, no parihāni.

And like the Venerable Mahākassapa, who established this textual tradition. “Growth indeed” means growth in virtues such as morality and so forth, not decline.

Therāti [V 2.0104] thirabhāvappattā therakārakehi guṇehi samannāgatā. Bahū rattiyo jānantīti rattaññū. Ciraṃ pabbajitānaṃ etesanti cirapabbajitā. Saṅghassa pituṭṭhāne ṭhitāti saṅghapitaro. Pituṭṭhāne ṭhitattā saṅghaṃ parinenti pubbaṅgamā hutvā tīsu sikkhāsu pavattentīti saṅghapariṇāyakā.

“Elders” (therā) are those who have attained a state of firmness (thirabhāva), endowed with the qualities that make one an elder. They “know many nights” (bahū rattiyo jānanti), thus they are “of long standing” (rattaññū). They have been ordained for a long time (ciraṃ pabbajitā), thus they are “long-ordained” (cirapabbajitā). They stand in the position of a father to the Sangha (saṅghassa pituṭṭhāne ṭhitā), thus they are “fathers of the Sangha” (saṅghapitaro). Standing in the position of a father, they lead the Sangha (saṅghaṃ parinenti), and being leaders, they establish others in the three trainings, thus they are “leaders of the Sangha” (saṅghapariṇāyakā).

Ye tesaṃ sakkārādīni na karonti, ovādatthāya dve tayo vāre upaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchanti, tepi tesaṃ ovādaṃ na denti, paveṇīkathaṃ na kathenti, sārabhūtaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ na sikkhāpenti. Te tehi vissaṭṭhā sīlādīhi dhammakkhandhehi sattahi ca ariyadhanehīti evamādīhi guṇehi parihāyanti. Ye pana tesaṃ sakkārādīni karonti, upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti, tepi tesaṃ ovādaṃ denti. “Evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te ālokitabbaṃ, evaṃ te vilokitabbaṃ, evaṃ te samiñjitabbaṃ, evaṃ te pasāritabbaṃ, evaṃ te saṅghāṭipattacīvaraṃ dhāretabba”nti paveṇīkathaṃ kathenti, sārabhūtaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sikkhāpenti, terasahi dhutaṅgehi dasahi kathāvatthūhi anusāsanti. Te tesaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā sīlādīhi guṇehi vaḍḍhamānā sāmaññatthaṃ anupāpuṇanti. Evamettha hānivuddhiyo veditabbā.

Those who do not pay them honor and so forth, who do not attend upon them two or three times for instruction—to them the elders also do not give instruction, nor do they engage in traditional talk, nor do they teach the essential Dhamma discourses. Thus, abandoned by them, they decline in qualities such as the aggregates of Dhamma beginning with morality, the seven noble treasures, and so forth. But those who pay them honor and so forth, who attend upon them—to them the elders also give instruction. They engage in traditional talk, saying: “Thus should you go forward, thus should you go back; thus should you look ahead, thus should you look around; thus should you bend, thus should you stretch; thus should you wear your upper robe, bowl, and outer robe.” They teach the essential Dhamma discourses, and instruct them with the thirteen ascetic practices and the ten topics of discussion. Abiding by their instruction, growing in virtues such as morality, they attain the goal of the ascetic life. Thus, decline and growth should be understood in this context.

Punabbhavadānaṃ punabbhavo, punabbhavo sīlamassāti ponobbhavikā, punabbhavadāyikāti attho, tasmā ponobbhavikāya. Na vasaṃ gacchantīti ettha ye catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ kāraṇā upaṭṭhākānaṃ padānupadikā hutvā gāmato gāmaṃ vicaranti, te tassā taṇhāya vasaṃ gacchanti nāma, itare na gacchanti [P 2.0527] nāma. Tattha hānivuddhiyo pākaṭāyeva.

Giving rebirth is rebirth. Because its nature is rebirth, it is called 'leading to rebirth' (ponobbhavikā), meaning 'giver of rebirth'. Therefore, of that which leads to rebirth. Here, regarding 'they do not fall under its power': those who, for the sake of the four requisites, become followers of their supporters and wander from village to village, are said to fall under the power of that craving; the others are said not to. In this matter, the decline and growth are quite manifest.

Āraññakesūti pañcadhanusatikapacchimesu. Sāpekkhāti sataṇhā sālayā. Gāmantasenāsanesu hi jhānaṃ appetvāpi tato vuṭṭhitamattova itthipurisadārikādisaddaṃ suṇāti, yenassa adhigatavisesopi hāyatiyeva. Araññe pana niddāyitvā paṭibuddhamatto sīhabyagghamorādīnaṃ saddaṃ [M 2.0117] suṇāti, yena āraññakaṃ pītiṃ labhitvā tameva sammasanto aggaphale patiṭṭhāti. Iti bhagavā gāmantasenāsane jhānaṃ appetvā nisinnabhikkhuno araññe niddāyantameva pasaṃsati. Tasmā tameva atthavasaṃ paṭicca – “āraññakesu senāsanesu sāpekkhā bhavissantī”ti āha.

In forest dwellings: in those at a minimum of five hundred bow-lengths. 'With longing' (sāpekkhā) means with craving, with attachment. For in dwellings near a village, even having entered jhāna, just upon rising from it one hears the sounds of women, men, girls, and so on, by which even the special attainment one has gained diminishes. But in the forest, just upon awakening from sleep, one hears the sounds of lions, tigers, peacocks, and so on, by which, having obtained forest joy and by contemplating that very thing, one becomes established in the highest fruit. Thus, the Blessed One praises a monk sleeping in the forest more than a monk sitting having entered jhāna in a dwelling near a village. Therefore, with reference to this very benefit, he said: 'They will have longing for dwellings in the forest.'

Paccattaññeva satiṃ upaṭṭhapessantīti attanāva attano abbhantare satiṃ upaṭṭhapessanti. Pesalāti piyasīlā. Idhāpi sabrahmacārīnaṃ āgamanaṃ anicchantā nevāsikā assaddhā honti appasannā[V 2.0105]. Sampattabhikkhūnaṃ paccuggamanapattacīvarappaṭiggahaṇaāsanapaññāpanatālavaṇṭaggahaṇādīni na karonti, atha nesaṃ avaṇṇo uggacchati – “asukavihāravāsino bhikkhū assaddhā appasannā vihāraṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ na karontī”ti. Taṃ sutvā pabbajitā vihāradvārena gacchantāpi vihāraṃ na pavisanti. Evaṃ anāgatānaṃ anāgamanameva hoti. Āgatānaṃ pana phāsuvihāre asati yepi ajānitvā āgatā, te – “vasissāmāti tāva cintetvā āgatāmha, imesaṃ pana nevāsikānaṃ iminā nīhārena ko vasissatī”ti nikkhamitvā gacchanti. Evaṃ so vihāro aññesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anāvāsova hoti. Tato nevāsikā sīlavantānaṃ dassanaṃ alabhantā kaṅkhāvinodanaṃ vā ācārasikkhāpakaṃ vā madhuradhammassavanaṃ vā na labhanti, tesaṃ neva aggahitadhammaggahaṇaṃ, na gahitasajjhāyakaraṇaṃ hoti. Iti nesaṃ hāniyeva hoti, na vuddhi.

They will establish mindfulness within themselves: this means they themselves will establish mindfulness within their own interior. 'Pesalā' means those of amiable virtue. Here too, resident monks who do not wish for the arrival of their fellow practitioners become faithless and displeased. They do not perform duties such as going out to meet arriving monks, receiving their bowls and robes, preparing seats, or taking a palm-leaf fan. Then, a bad reputation arises for them: 'The monks residing in such-and-such a monastery are faithless and displeased; they do not perform the proper duties for those who enter the monastery.' Hearing this, monastics, even when passing by the monastery gate, do not enter. Thus, those who have not yet come do not come at all. As for those who have arrived, when there is no comfortable dwelling, even those who came without knowing the situation think, 'We came intending to stay, but with such conduct from these resident monks, who would stay?' and they depart. Thus, that monastery becomes uninhabitable for other monks. Then, the resident monks, not getting to see virtuous ones, do not obtain the dispelling of doubt, or instruction in conduct, or the hearing of the sweet Dhamma. For them, there is neither the grasping of the ungrasped Dhamma nor the recitation of what has been grasped. Thus, for them, there is only decline, not growth.

Ye pana sabrahmacārīnaṃ āgamanaṃ icchanti, te saddhā honti pasannā, āgatānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ paccuggamanādīni katvā senāsanaṃ paññapetvā denti, te gahetvā bhikkhācāraṃ pavisanti, kaṅkhaṃ vinodenti, madhuradhammassavanaṃ labhanti. Atha nesaṃ kittisaddo uggacchati – “asukavihārabhikkhū evaṃ saddhā pasannā vattasampannā saṅgāhakā”ti. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū dūratopi enti, tesaṃ nevāsikā vattaṃ karonti[P 2.0528], samīpaṃ āgantvā vuḍḍhataraṃ āgantukaṃ vanditvā nisīdanti, navakatarassa santike āsanaṃ gahetvā nisīdanti. Nisīditvā – “imasmiṃ vihāre vasissatha gamissathā”ti pucchanti. ‘Gamissāmī’ti vutte – “sappāyaṃ senāsanaṃ, sulabhā bhikkhā”tiādīni vatvā gantuṃ na denti. Vinayadharo ce hoti, tassa santike vinayaṃ sajjhāyanti. Suttantādidharo ce, tassa santike taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ sajjhāyanti. Āgantukānaṃ therānaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇanti. Āgantukā “ekaṃ [M 2.0118] dve divasāni vasissāmāti āgatāmha, imesaṃ pana sukhasaṃvāsatāya dasadvādasavassāni vasissāmā”ti vattāro honti. Evamettha hānivuddhiyo veditabbā.

But those who wish for the arrival of their fellow monastics are faithful and serene. For the arriving fellow monastics, they perform duties such as going out to meet them, and after preparing lodgings, they offer them. Taking the visitors with them, they enter the village for alms. They have their doubts dispelled and get to hear the sweet Dhamma. Then, a good reputation arises for them: 'The monks of such-and-such a monastery are so faithful, serene, accomplished in their duties, and hospitable.' Hearing this, monks come even from afar. The resident monks perform their duties for them. Approaching a more senior visitor, they pay respects and sit down. They take a seat near a more junior one and sit down. Having sat down, they ask, 'Will you stay in this monastery or will you go?' If one says, 'I will go,' they do not let them go, saying things like, 'The lodging is suitable, alms are easy to obtain.' If a visitor is an expert in the Vinaya, they recite the Vinaya in his presence. If he is an expert in the Suttas and so on, they recite that particular Dhamma in his presence. Abiding in the instruction of the visiting elders, they attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The visitors, who had come thinking, 'We will stay for one or two days,' become ones who say, 'Due to the pleasant company of these monks, we will stay for ten or twelve years.' In this way, decline and growth should be understood here.

137. Dutiyasattake kammaṃ ārāmo etesanti kammārāmāti. Kamme ratāti kammaratā. Kammārāmatamanuyuttāti yuttā payuttā anuyuttā. Tattha kammanti itikātabbakammaṃ vuccati. Seyyathidaṃ – cīvaravicāraṇaṃ, cīvarakaraṇaṃ, upatthambhanaṃ, sūcigharaṃ, pattatthavikaṃ, asaṃbaddhakaṃ, kāyabandhanaṃ, dhamakaraṇaṃ, ādhārakaṃ, pādakathalikaṃ, sammajjanīādīnaṃ karaṇanti. Ekacco hi etāni karonto sakaladivasaṃ etāneva karoti. Taṃ sandhāyesa paṭikkhepo. Yo pana etesaṃ karaṇavelāyameva etāni karoti, uddesavelāyaṃ uddesaṃ gaṇhāti, sajjhāyavelāyaṃ sajjhāyati, cetiyaṅgaṇavattavelāyaṃ [V 2.0106] cetiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ karoti, manasikāravelāyaṃ manasikāraṃ karoti, na so kammārāmo nāma.

137. In the second septet: 'kammārāma' means those for whom work (kamma) is their delight (ārāma). 'Kammarata' means those who delight (ratā) in work. 'Devoted to delighting in work' means yoked, thoroughly yoked, and repeatedly yoked. Here, 'work' refers to tasks that should be done. For example: managing robes, making robes, reinforcing robes, making a needle case, a bowl bag, a shoulder strap, a waistband, a water strainer, a bowl stand, a foot-scraper, making brooms, and so on. For a certain person, while doing these things, spends the entire day doing only them. This prohibition is stated with reference to him. But one who does these things only at the time for doing them, who takes up a text at the time for learning, recites at the time for recitation, performs the duties of the cetiya-courtyard at the time for those duties, and practices meditation at the time for meditation—such a person is not called a 'kammārāma'.

Na bhassārāmāti ettha yo itthivaṇṇapurisavaṇṇādivasena ālāpasallāpaṃ karontoyeva divasañca rattiñca vītināmeti, evarūpe bhasse pariyantakārī na hoti, ayaṃ bhassārāmo nāma. Yo pana rattindivaṃ dhammaṃ katheti, pañhaṃ vissajjeti, ayaṃ appabhassova bhasse pariyantakārīyeva. Kasmā? “Sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ – dhammī vā kathā, ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti (ma. ni. 1.273) vuttattā.

Here, regarding 'not delighting in talk': whoever passes the day and night making conversation and chatter about things such as the beauty of women and the beauty of men, and does not make an end to such talk, is called one who delights in talk (bhassārāma). But one who speaks on the Dhamma and answers questions day and night—this one is of little talk and is indeed one who makes an end to talk. Why? Because it has been said: 'When you have gathered, monks, there are two things to be done: either talk on the Dhamma or the noble silence' (MN 26).

Na niddārāmāti ettha yo gacchantopi nisinnopi nipannopi thinamiddhābhibhūto niddāyatiyeva, ayaṃ niddārāmo nāma. Yassa pana karajakāyagelaññena cittaṃ bhavaṅge otarati[P 2.0529], nāyaṃ niddārāmo. Tenevāha – “abhijānāmahaṃ aggivessana, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno niddaṃ okkamitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.387).

Herein, regarding 'not delighting in drowsiness': whoever, whether walking, sitting, or lying down, being overcome by sloth and torpor, only drowses, this one is called 'one who delights in drowsiness.' However, one whose mind sinks into the life-continuum due to the weariness of the perishable body, this one is not one who delights in drowsiness. For that very reason, He said: 'I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, having folded my outer robe in four, I fell asleep on my right side, mindful and fully aware.'

Na saṅgaṇikārāmāti ettha yo ekassa dutiyo dvinnaṃ tatiyo tiṇṇaṃ catutthoti evaṃ saṃsaṭṭhova viharati, ekako assādaṃ na labhati, ayaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmo. Yo pana catūsu iriyāpathesu ekako assādaṃ labhati, nāyaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmoti veditabbo.

Herein, regarding 'not delighting in company': whoever dwells only intermingled with others—being a second to one, a third to two, a fourth to three, and so on—and does not find enjoyment when alone, this one is one who delights in company. But whoever finds enjoyment when alone in the four postures, this one is to be understood as not one who delights in company.

Na [M 2.0119] pāpicchāti ettha asantasambhāvanāya icchāya samannāgatā dussīlā pāpicchā nāma.

Herein, regarding 'not having evil desires': immoral ones who are endowed with the desire to be esteemed for qualities they do not possess are called 'those with evil desires.'

Na pāpamittādīsu pāpā mittā etesanti pāpamittā. Catūsu iriyāpathesu saha ayanato pāpā sahāyā etesanti pāpasahāyā. Tanninnatappoṇatappabbhāratāya pāpesu sampavaṅkāti pāpasampavaṅkā.

Herein, regarding 'not having evil friends, etc.': 'Those with evil friends' (pāpamittā) are so called because they have evil friends. 'Those with evil companions' (pāpasahāyā) are so called because they have evil companions due to associating together in the four postures. 'Those bent towards evil' (pāpasampavaṅkā) are so called because they are bent towards evil, due to their inclination, bent, and leaning towards it.

Oramattakenāti avaramattakena appamattakena. Antarāti arahattaṃ apatvāva etthantare. Vosānanti pariniṭṭhitabhāvaṃ – “alamettāvatā”ti osakkanaṃ ṭhitakiccataṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yāva sīlapārisuddhimattena vā vipassanāmattena vā jhānamattena vā sotāpannabhāvamattena vā sakadāgāmibhāvamattena vā anāgāmibhāvamattena vā vosānaṃ na āpajjissanti, tāva vuddhiyeva bhikkhūnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihānī”ti.

`Oramattakena` means: by a lesser measure, by a small measure. `Antarā` means: in the interval, without having yet attained Arahantship. `Vosānaṃ` means: a state of completion, a withdrawal thinking, 'This much is enough,' a state where the task is halted. This is what is said: 'So long as the monks do not come to a conclusion with the mere purity of virtue, or with mere insight, or with mere jhāna, or with the mere state of a stream-enterer, or with the mere state of a once-returner, or with the mere state of a non-returner, for so long, growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline.'

138. Tatiyasattake [V 2.0107] saddhāti saddhāsampannā. Tattha āgamanīyasaddhā, adhigamasaddhā, pasādasaddhā, okappanasaddhāti catubbidhā saddhā. Tattha āgamanīyasaddhā sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ hoti. Adhigamasaddhā ariyapuggalānaṃ. Buddho dhammo saṅghoti vutte pana pasādo pasādasaddhā. Okappetvā pakappetvā pana saddahanaṃ okappanasaddhā. Sā duvidhāpi idhādhippetā. Tāya hi saddhāya samannāgato saddhāvimutto, vakkalittherasadiso hoti. Tassa hi cetiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ vā, bodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ vā katameva hoti. Upajjhāyavattaācariyavattādīni sabbavattāni pūreti. Hirimanāti pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya hiriyā yuttacittā. Ottappīti pāpato bhāyanalakkhaṇena ottappena samannāgatā.

138. In the third septet, `saddhā` means 'endowed with faith.' Herein, faith is of four kinds: faith of arrival, faith of attainment, faith of serene confidence, and faith of conviction. Among these, faith of arrival belongs to the Omniscient Bodhisattas. Faith of attainment belongs to noble individuals. When it is said, 'the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha,' the resulting serene confidence is faith of serene confidence. And the belief that comes from accepting and deciding is faith of conviction. Both of these latter two kinds are intended here. Indeed, one endowed with such faith is liberated by faith and is like the Elder Vakkali. For such a one, the duties at the stupa courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard are certainly fulfilled. He fulfills all duties, such as those towards his preceptor and teacher. `Hirimanā` means having a mind connected with moral shame, which has the characteristic of disgust for evil. `Ottappī` means endowed with moral dread, which has the characteristic of fear of evil.

Bahussutāti ettha pana pariyattibahussuto, paṭivedhabahussutoti [P 2.0530] dve bahussutā. Pariyattīti tīṇi piṭakāni. Paṭivedhoti saccappaṭivedho. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne pariyatti adhippetā. Sā yena bahu sutā, so bahussuto. So panesa nissayamuccanako, parisupaṭṭhāko, bhikkhunovādako, sabbatthakabahussutoti catubbidho hoti. Tattha tayo bahussutā samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya ovādavagge vuttanayena gahetabbā. Sabbatthakabahussutā pana ānandattherasadisā honti. Te idha adhippetā.

Regarding `bahussutā` (the learned): Herein, there are two kinds of learned ones: one learned in the scriptures (pariyatti) and one learned in penetration (paṭivedha). The scriptures are the three Piṭakas. Penetration is the penetration of the truths. In this context, however, the scriptures are intended. One by whom much has been heard is 'learned.' This learned one is of four kinds: one who is a cause for freedom from dependence, one who attends to the assembly, an exhorter of nuns, and one learned in all subjects. Among these, the first three kinds of learned ones should be understood according to the method stated in the Ovādavagga of the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā. But those learned in all subjects are like the Elder Ānanda. They are the ones intended here.

Āraddhavīriyāti [M 2.0120] yesaṃ kāyikañca cetasikañca vīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ hoti. Tattha ye kāyasaṅgaṇikaṃ vinodetvā catūsu iriyāpathesu aṭṭhaārabbhavatthuvasena ekakā honti, tesaṃ kāyikavīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ nāma hoti. Ye cittasaṅgāṇikaṃ vinodetvā aṭṭhasamāpattivasena ekakā honti, gamane uppannakilesassa ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na denti, ṭhāne uppannakilesassa nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya uppannakilesassa sayanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na denti, uppannuppannaṭṭhāneyeva kilese niggaṇhanti, tesaṃ cetasikavīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ nāma hoti.

`Āraddhavīriyā` means those whose bodily and mental energy is aroused. Herein, those who, having dispelled physical association with company, remain alone in the four postures by way of the eight grounds for arousing effort—their bodily energy is said to be aroused. Those who, having dispelled mental association with defilements, remain alone by way of the eight attainments; who do not allow a defilement that has arisen while walking to persist until standing, nor one that has arisen while standing to persist until sitting, nor one that has arisen while sitting to persist until lying down, but who suppress defilements right where they have arisen—their mental energy is said to be aroused.

Upaṭṭhitassatīti cirakatādīnaṃ saritā anussaritā mahāgatimbayaabhayattheradīghabhāṇaabhayattheratipiṭakacūḷābhayattherā viya. Mahāgatimbayaabhayatthero kira jātapañcamadivase maṅgalapāyāse tuṇḍaṃ pasārentaṃ vāyasaṃ disvā huṃ hunti saddamakāsi. Atha so therakāle – “kadā paṭṭhāya, bhante, sarathā”ti bhikkhūhi pucchito “jātapañcamadivase katasaddato paṭṭhāya āvuso”ti āha.

`Upaṭṭhitassatī` means one who remembers and recollects things done long ago and so forth, like the Elders Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya, Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, and Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. It is said that the Elder Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya, on the fifth day after his birth, saw a crow stretching its beak toward the auspicious milk-rice and made the sound 'huṃ, huṃ.' Then, when he was an elder, upon being asked by the monks, 'Venerable sir, from when do you remember?' he replied, 'Friends, from the sound I made on the fifth day after my birth.'

Dīghabhāṇakaabhayattherassa jātanavamadivase mātā cumbissāmīti onatā tassā moḷi muccittha[V 2.0108]. Tato tumbamattāni sumanapupphāni dārakassa ure patitvā dukkhaṃ janayiṃsu. So therakāle – “kadā paṭṭhāya, bhante, sarathā”ti pucchito – “jātanavamadivasato paṭṭhāyā”ti āha.

On the ninth day after the birth of the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, his mother bent down, intending to kiss him, and her topknot came loose. From it, a gourd's measure of jasmine flowers fell onto the child's chest, causing him pain. When he was an elder, upon being asked, 'Venerable sir, from when do you remember?' he replied, 'From the ninth day after my birth.'

Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero – “anurādhapure tīṇi dvārāni pidahāpetvā manussānaṃ ekena dvārena nikkhamanaṃ katvā – ‘tvaṃ kinnāmo, tvaṃ kinnāmo’ti pucchitvā sāyaṃ puna apucchitvāva tesaṃ nāmāni sampaṭicchāpetuṃ – “sakkā āvuso”ti āha. Evarūpe bhikkhū sandhāya – “upaṭṭhitassatī”ti vuttaṃ.

The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: 'Friends, it is possible in Anurādhapura, after having three gates closed and making the people exit through one gate, to ask each one, "What is your name? What is your name?" and then in the evening, without asking again, to correctly identify their names.' Referring to such monks, it was said, `upaṭṭhitassatī` (one with mindfulness established).

Paññavantoti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ udayabbayapariggāhikāya paññāya samannāgatā. Api ca dvīhipi etehi padehi vipassakānaṃ [P 2.0531] bhikkhūnaṃ vipassanāsambhārabhūtā sammāsati ceva vipassanāpaññā ca kathitā.

'Wise' means endowed with the wisdom that comprehends the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. Moreover, by these two terms, both right mindfulness and insight-wisdom, which are the requisites for insight of meditating monks, are described.

139. Catutthasattake satiyeva sambojjhaṅgo satisambojjhaṅgoti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Tattha upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇo satisambojjhaṅgo, pavicayalakkhaṇo dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo, paggahalakkhaṇo vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, pharaṇalakkhaṇo [M 2.0121] pītisambojjhaṅgo, upasamalakkhaṇo passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, avikkhepalakkhaṇo samādhisambojjhaṅgo, paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo. Bhāvessantīti satisambojjhaṅgaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpentā, chahi kāraṇehi dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpentā, navahi kāraṇehi vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpentā, dasahi kāraṇehi pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpentā, sattahi kāraṇehi passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpentā, dasahi kāraṇehi samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpentā, pañcahi kāraṇehi upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpentā vaḍḍhessantīti attho. Iminā vipassanāmaggaphalasampayutte lokiyalokuttaramissake sambojjhaṅge kathesi.

139. In the fourth septet, mindfulness itself is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. This method applies everywhere. Herein, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing; the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena has the characteristic of scrutinizing; the enlightenment factor of energy has the characteristic of exertion; the enlightenment factor of joy has the characteristic of suffusing; the enlightenment factor of tranquility has the characteristic of pacifying; the enlightenment factor of concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction; the enlightenment factor of equanimity has the characteristic of regarding with balance. 'They will develop' means they will increase, arousing the enlightenment factor of mindfulness through four causes, arousing the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena through six causes, arousing the enlightenment factor of energy through nine causes, arousing the enlightenment factor of joy through ten causes, arousing the enlightenment factor of tranquility through seven causes, arousing the enlightenment factor of concentration through five causes, and arousing the enlightenment factor of equanimity through five causes. By this, he described the enlightenment factors associated with insight, path, and fruition, mixed with the mundane and supramundane.

140. Pañcamasattake aniccasaññāti aniccānupassanāya saddhiṃ uppannasaññā. Anattasaññādīsupi eseva nayo. Imā satta lokiyavipassanāpi honti. “Etaṃ santaṃ, etaṃ paṇītaṃ, yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho virāgo nirodho”ti (a. ni. 9.36) āgatavasenettha dve lokuttarāpi hontīti veditabbā.

140. In the fifth septet, the perception of impermanence is the perception that arises together with the contemplation of impermanence. The same method applies to the perception of not-self and so on. These seven are also mundane insights. By the authority of the text that states, 'This is peaceful, this is excellent, namely the stilling of all formations, dispassion, cessation' (AN 9.36), it should be understood that two of these are also supramundane.

141. Chakke mettaṃ kāyakammanti mettacittena kattabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Vacīkammamanokammesupi eseva nayo. Imāni pana bhikkhūnaṃ vasena āgatāni gihīsupi labbhanti[V 2.0109]. Bhikkhūnañhi mettacittena ābhisamācārikadhammapūraṇaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya bodhivandanatthāya saṅghanimantanatthāya gamanaṃ, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā paccuggamanaṃ, pattappaṭiggahaṇaṃ, āsanapaññāpanaṃ, anugamananti evamādikaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma.

141. In the group of six, 'loving-kindness in bodily action' means bodily action that should be done with a mind of loving-kindness. The same method applies to verbal and mental actions. However, these, though presented in reference to monks, are also found among laypeople. For monks, the fulfillment of the code of proper conduct with a mind of loving-kindness is called loving-kindness in bodily action. For laypeople, going to pay homage at a shrine, to venerate the Bodhi tree, or to invite the Sangha; seeing a monk who has entered a village for alms and going out to greet him, receiving his bowl, offering a seat, or accompanying him—such actions are called loving-kindness in bodily action.

Bhikkhūnaṃ mettacittena ācārapaññattisikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ, kammaṭṭhānakathanaṃ, dhammadesanā, tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya gacchāma[P 2.0532], bodhivandanatthāya gacchāma, dhammassavanaṃ karissāma, dīpamālapupphapūjaṃ karissāma, tīṇi sucaritāni samādāya vattissāma, salākabhattādīni dassāma, vassavāsikaṃ dassāma, ajja saṅghassa cattāro paccaye dassāma, saṅghaṃ nimantetvā khādanīyādīni saṃvidahatha, āsanāni paññāpetha, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetha, saṅghaṃ paccuggantvā ānetha, paññattāsane [M 2.0122] nisīdāpetha, chandajātā ussāhajātā veyyāvaccaṃ karothātiādikathanakāle mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma.

For monks, prescribing rules of conduct and making known the training rules with a mind of loving-kindness, giving instructions on meditation subjects, teaching the Dhamma, and even the three baskets of the Buddha’s words—this is called loving-kindness in verbal action. For laypeople, at the time of speaking such as: 'Let us go to pay homage at the shrine'; 'Let us go to venerate the Bodhi tree'; 'We will listen to the Dhamma'; 'We will offer lamps, garlands, and flowers'; 'We will undertake and practice the three kinds of good conduct'; 'We will give ticket-food and other alms'; 'We will offer the rains-residence robe'; 'Today we will offer the four requisites to the Sangha'; 'Having invited the Sangha, prepare food and other offerings'; 'Prepare the seats'; 'Set out drinking water'; 'Go out to meet the Sangha and bring them here'; 'Have them sit on the prepared seats'; 'With willingness and enthusiasm, perform your duties'—this is called loving-kindness in verbal action.

Bhikkhūnaṃ pātova uṭṭhāya sarīrappaṭijagganaṃ, cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīni ca katvā vivittāsane nisīditvā imasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjāti cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ ‘ayyā sukhī hontu, averā abyāpajjā’ti cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma.

For monks, having risen early in the morning, attended to their bodily needs, and performed duties such as those pertaining to the shrine courtyard, then sitting in a secluded place and thinking, 'May the monks in this monastery be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction'—this is called loving-kindness as a mental action. For laypeople, thinking, 'May the venerables be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction'—this is called loving-kindness as a mental action.

Āvi ceva raho cāti sammukhā ca parammukhā ca. Tattha navakānaṃ cīvarakammādīsu sahāyabhāvagamanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Therānaṃ pana pādadhovanavandanabījanadānādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Ubhayehipi dunnikkhittānaṃ dārubhaṇḍādīnaṃ tesu avamaññaṃ akatvā attanā dunnikkhittānaṃ viya paṭisāmanaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma.

'Openly and privately' means both in one's presence and in one's absence. Herein, assisting junior monks with robe-making and other tasks in their presence is called loving-kindness in bodily action. For elders, all proper conduct such as washing their feet, paying respects, and offering a fan in their presence is called loving-kindness in bodily action. For both junior and senior monks, when their wooden items and other belongings are poorly placed, putting them away properly without contempt for those monks, as if they were one's own poorly placed items—this is called loving-kindness in bodily action in their absence.

Devatthero tissattheroti evaṃ paggayha vacanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Vihāre asantaṃ pana paṭipucchantassa kuhiṃ amhākaṃ devatthero, kuhiṃ amhākaṃ tissatthero, kadā nu kho āgamissatīti evaṃ mamāyanavacanaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma.

Speaking in an uplifting manner, such as 'Deva Thera' or 'Tissa Thera,' in their presence is called loving-kindness in verbal action. But when inquiring about someone not present in the monastery, speech that expresses endearment, such as, 'Where is our Deva Thera? Where is our Tissa Thera? When will he return?'—this is called loving-kindness in verbal action in their absence.

Mettāsinehasiniddhāni pana nayanāni ummīletvā pasannena mukhena olokanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ [V 2.0110] manokammaṃ nāma. Devatthero tissatthero arogo hotu, appābādhoti samannāharaṇaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma.

Opening one's eyes, which are gentle with loving-kindness and affection, and looking with a serene face in their presence—this is called loving-kindness as a mental action. Bringing to mind, 'May Deva Thera and Tissa Thera be free from illness and have few ailments,' in their absence—this is called loving-kindness as a mental action.

Lābhāti cīvarādayo laddhapaccayā. Dhammikāti kuhanādibhedaṃ micchājīvaṃ vajjetvā dhammena samena bhikkhācāravattena uppannā. Antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampīti pacchimakoṭiyā patte pariyāpannaṃ pattassa antogataṃ dvitikaṭacchubhikkhāmattampi[P 2.0533]. Appaṭivibhattabhogīti ettha dve paṭivibhattā nāma – āmisappaṭivibhattañca, puggalappaṭivibhattañca. Tattha – “ettakaṃ dassāmi, ettakaṃ na dassāmī”ti evaṃ cittena vibhajanaṃ āmisappaṭivibhattaṃ nāma. “Asukassa dassāmi, asukassa na dassāmī”ti evaṃ cittena vibhajanaṃ pana puggalappaṭivibhattaṃ nāma. Tadubhayampi akatvā yo appaṭivibhattaṃ bhuñjati, ayaṃ appaṭivibhattabhogī nāma.

“Gains” refers to requisites such as robes that have been obtained. “Righteous” means that they have arisen by avoiding wrong livelihood in its various forms, such as deception, and by means of the Dhamma, justly, and through the practice of the alms-round. “Even as little as what is contained in the bowl” means, at the lowest limit, what is contained within the bowl, even just two or three spoonfuls of alms-food. Regarding “one who enjoys without dividing,” there are two kinds of dividing: dividing by material items and dividing by person. Of these, dividing with the thought, “I will give this much, I will not give that much,” is called dividing by material items. But dividing with the thought, “I will give to this person, I will not give to that person,” is called dividing by person. One who does not do either of these and enjoys without dividing is called “one who enjoys without dividing.”

Sīlavantehi [M 2.0123] sabrahmacārīhi sādhāraṇabhogīti ettha sādhāraṇabhogino idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ, yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ labbhati, taṃ taṃ neva lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāmukhena gihīnaṃ deti, na attanā bhuñjati, paṭiggaṇhanto ca – “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotū”ti gahetvā ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ saṅghasantakaṃ viya passati.

“One who partakes in common with virtuous fellow monastics”—herein, this is the characteristic of one who partakes in common: whatever excellent thing is obtained, he neither gives it to householders with the aim of acquiring a greater gain by means of a lesser one, nor does he consume it himself. And when receiving it, he takes it thinking, “Let this be common to the Sangha,” and regards it as if it were the property of the Sangha, to be partaken of after striking the bell.

Imaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammaṃ ko pūreti, ko na pūretīti? Dussīlo tāva na pūreti. Na hi tassa santakaṃ sīlavantā gaṇhanti. Parisuddhasīlo pana vattaṃ akhaṇḍento pūreti. Tatridaṃ vattaṃ – yo hi odissakaṃ katvā mātu vā pitu vā ācariyupajjhāyādīnaṃ vā deti, so dātabbaṃ deti, sāraṇīyadhammo panassa na hoti, palibodhajagganaṃ nāma hoti. Sāraṇīyadhammo hi muttapalibodhasseva vaṭṭati. Tena pana odissakaṃ dentena gilānagilānupaṭṭhākaāgantukagamikānañceva navapabbajitassa ca saṅghāṭipattaggahaṇaṃ ajānantassa dātabbaṃ. Etesaṃ datvā avasesaṃ therāsanato paṭṭhāya thokaṃ adatvā yo yattakaṃ gaṇhāti, tassa tattakaṃ dātabbaṃ. Avasiṭṭhe asati puna piṇḍāya caritvā therāsanato paṭṭhāya yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ, taṃ datvā sesaṃ paribhuñjitabbaṃ. “Sīlavantehī”ti vacanato dussīlassa adātumpi vaṭṭati.

Now, who fulfills this principle of cordiality, and who does not? First, the immoral one does not fulfill it, for the virtuous do not accept what belongs to him. But the one with purified virtue, who does not break the practice, fulfills it. Herein is the practice: if one, having designated something for a specific recipient, gives it to one’s mother, father, preceptor, teacher, or others, one gives what should be given, but this is not the principle of cordiality for him—it is called the dispelling of an encumbrance. The principle of cordiality is proper only for one who is free from encumbrances. Therefore, when giving a designated portion, one should give to the sick, those who attend to the sick, visitors, those about to depart, and a newly ordained monk who does not yet know how to handle the outer robe and bowl. After giving to these, starting from the elder’s seat, one should give to whoever takes any amount that much, without being stingy. If nothing remains, one should go for alms again and, starting from the elder’s seat, give whatever is excellent and consume the rest. From the words “with the virtuous,” it is permissible not to give to the immoral.

Ayaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammo susikkhitāya parisāya supūro hoti, no asikkhitāya parisāya. Susikkhitāya hi parisāya yo aññato labhati, so na gaṇhāti. Aññato alabhantopi pamāṇayuttameva gaṇhāti, nātirekaṃ. Ayaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammo evaṃ punappunaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā laddhaṃ laddhaṃ dentassāpi dvādasahi vassehi pūrati, na tato oraṃ. Sace hi dvādasame [V 2.0111] vasse sāraṇīyadhammapūrako piṇḍapātapūraṃ pattaṃ āsanasālāyaṃ ṭhapetvā nahāyituṃ gacchati saṅghatthero ca kasseso pattoti, “sāraṇīyadhammapūrakassā”ti [P 2.0534] vutte “āharatha na”nti sabbaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ vicāretvā bhuñjitvā ca rittaṃ pattaṃ ṭhapeti, atha so bhikkhu rittaṃ pattaṃ disvā “mayhaṃ anavasesetvāva paribhuñjiṃsū”ti domanassaṃ uppādeti, sāraṇīyadhammo bhijjati, puna dvādasavassāni pūretabbo hoti. Titthiyaparivāsasadiso hesa, sakiṃ khaṇḍe jāte puna pūretabbova. Yo pana – “lābhā vata [M 2.0124] me, suladdhaṃ vata me, yassa me pattagataṃ anāpucchāva sabrahmacārī paribhuñjantī”ti somanassaṃ janeti, tassa puṇṇo nāma hoti.

This principle of cordiality is easy to fulfill in a well-trained community, but not in an untrained one. For in a well-trained community, one who obtains alms from another place does not take from the common store. Even one who obtains nothing from another place takes only a suitable amount, not an excessive one. This principle of cordiality, even for one who repeatedly goes for alms and gives away whatever is received, is fulfilled only after twelve years, not before. For if in the twelfth year, a monk who is fulfilling this principle of cordiality places his bowl, full of alms-food, in the assembly hall and goes to bathe, and the elder of the Sangha asks, “Whose bowl is this?” and upon being told, “It belongs to the one fulfilling the principle of cordiality,” he says, “Bring it,” and after examining all the alms-food and eating it, he leaves the bowl empty—if that monk then sees the empty bowl and gives rise to displeasure, thinking, “They have consumed it without leaving anything for me,” the principle of cordiality is broken, and it must be fulfilled for another twelve years. For this is similar to the probation of the sectarians—once broken, it must be fulfilled anew. But for one who generates joy, thinking, “Ah, what a gain for me! Ah, how well-gained for me, that my fellow monastics partake of what is in my bowl without even asking!”—for him, it is called fulfilled.

Evaṃ pūritasāraṇīyadhammassa pana neva issā, na macchariyaṃ hoti. So manussānaṃ piyo hoti, sulabhapaccayo ca, pattagatamassa diyyamānampi na khīyati, bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ labhati, bhaye vā chātake vā sampatte devatā ussukkaṃ āpajjanti.

For one who has thus fulfilled the principle of cordiality, there is neither envy nor stinginess. He is dear to people and easily obtains requisites. What is in his bowl, even when given away, is not exhausted; he obtains the best item in the place where goods are distributed. When danger or famine arises, deities become solicitous on his behalf.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – senagirivāsī tissatthero kira mahāgirigāmaṃ upanissāya viharati. Paññāsa mahātherā nāgadīpaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya gacchantā girigāme piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci aladdhā nikkhamiṃsu. Thero pana pavisanto te disvā pucchi – “laddhaṃ, bhante”ti? Vicarimha āvusoti. So tesaṃ aladdhabhāvaṃ ñatvā āha – “bhante yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva idheva hothā”ti. Mayaṃ, āvuso, paññāsa janā pattatemanamattampi na labhimhāti. Bhante, nevāsikā nāma paṭibalā honti, alabhantāpi bhikkhācāramaggasabhāgaṃ jānantīti. Therā āgamesuṃ. Thero gāmaṃ pāvisi. Dhurageheyeva mahāupāsikā khīrabhattaṃ sajjetvā theraṃ olokayamānā ṭhitā. Atha therassa dvāraṃ sampattasseva pattaṃ pūretvā adāsi, so taṃ ādāya therānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā gaṇhatha, bhanteti, saṅghattheraṃ āha. Thero – “amhehi ettakehi kiñci na laddhaṃ, ayaṃ sīghameva gahetvā āgato, kiṃ nu kho”ti sesānaṃ mukhaṃ olokesi. Thero olokanākāreneva ñatvā “bhante, dhammena samena laddhapiṇḍapāto, nikkukkuccā gaṇhathā”tiādito paṭṭhāya sabbesaṃ yāvadatthaṃ datvā attanāpi yāvadatthaṃ bhuñji.

Herein are these stories: It is said that the elder Tissa, a resident of Senagiri, was staying near Mahāgirigāma. Fifty great elders, on their way to Nāgadīpa to pay homage to the shrine, went for alms in the mountain village, but obtained nothing and departed. The elder, however, upon entering, saw them and asked, “Did you receive anything, venerable sirs?” “We wandered about, friend,” they replied. Knowing they had received nothing, he said, “Venerable sirs, wait here until I return.” “Friend, we are fifty persons and did not receive even enough to wet the bowl.” “Venerable sirs, resident monks are capable; even when not receiving alms, they know the proper alms-round route.” The elders waited. The elder entered the village. In the main house of the village, a great laywoman, having prepared milk-rice, stood watching for the elder. As soon as the elder arrived at her door, she filled his bowl and gave it to him. Taking it, he went to the elders and said to the Sangha-elder, “Take this, venerable sirs.” The elder thought, “We, so many, received nothing, yet this one has returned quickly with this. What can this be?” and looked at the faces of the others. The elder Tissa, understanding just by the way they looked, said, “Venerable sirs, this alms-food was obtained righteously and fairly. Take it without hesitation.” Starting from the first, he gave to all of them as much as they wanted, and he himself also ate to his satisfaction.

Atha naṃ bhattakiccāvasāne therā pucchiṃsu – “kadā, āvuso, lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhī”ti? Natthi me, bhante, lokuttaradhammoti. Jhānalābhīsi, āvusoti? Etampi [P 2.0535] me, bhante, natthīti. Nanu, āvuso, pāṭihāriyanti? Sāraṇīyadhammo me, bhante, pūrito, tassa me dhammassa pūritakālato paṭṭhāya sacepi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ hoti, pattagataṃ na khīyatīti. Te sutvā [V 2.0112] – “sādhu sādhu sappurisa, anucchavikamidaṃ tuyha”nti āhaṃsu. Idaṃ tāva – “pattagataṃ na khīyatī”ti ettha vatthu.

Then, at the conclusion of the meal duties, the elders asked him: “Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma?” “Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma.” “Friend, are you an attainer of jhāna?” “Venerable sirs, I do not have that either.” “Is it not a psychic power, friend?” “Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the qualities conducive to being remembered. From the time that Dhamma was fulfilled in me, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, what has come into my bowl is not exhausted.” Hearing this, they said: “Good, good, excellent man! This is fitting for you.” This, for now, is the story here concerning “what has come into the bowl is not exhausted.”

Ayameva pana thero cetiyapabbate giribhaṇḍamahāpūjāya dānaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne kiṃ varabhaṇḍanti pucchi. Dve sāṭakā, bhanteti. Ete mayhaṃ [M 2.0125] pāpuṇissantīti. Taṃ sutvā amacco rañño ārocesi – “eko daharo evaṃ vadatī”ti. Daharassa evaṃ cittaṃ, mahātherānaṃ pana sukhumasāṭakā vaṭṭantīti vatvā mahātherānaṃ dassāmīti ṭhapeti. Tassa bhikkhusaṅghe paṭipāṭiyā ṭhite dentassa matthake ṭhapitāpi te sāṭakā hatthaṃ nārohanti. Aññe ārohanti. Daharassa dānakāle pana hatthaṃ āruḷhā. So tassa hatthe pātetvā amaccassa mukhaṃ oloketvā daharaṃ nisīdāpetvā dānaṃ datvā saṅghaṃ vissajjetvā daharassa santike nisīditvā – “bhante, imaṃ dhammaṃ kadā paṭivijjhitthā”ti āha. So pariyāyenāpi asantaṃ avadanto – “natthi mayhaṃ mahārāja lokuttaradhammo”ti āha. Nanu, bhante, pubbe avacutthāti. Āma, mahārāja, sāraṇīyadhammapūrako ahaṃ, tassa me dhammassa pūritakālato paṭṭhāya bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ pāpuṇātīti. “Sādhu sādhu, bhante, anucchavikamidaṃ tuyha”nti vanditvā pakkāmi. Idaṃ – “bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti ettha vatthu.

Now, this same elder, during the great offering of goods on the mountain at Cetiyapabbata, went to the place of giving and asked: “What is the choice item in this place?” “Two cloths, venerable sir.” “These will come to me.” Hearing this, a minister informed the king: “A certain young monk speaks thus.” The king, thinking, “Such is the thought of a young one, but fine cloths are suitable for the great elders,” set them aside, intending, “I will give them to the great elders.” While he was giving as the community of monks stood in order, those cloths, even when placed on the heads of the elders, did not ascend to their hands. Other items did ascend. But at the time of giving to the young monk, they ascended to his hand. The king, having caused them to fall into the monk's hand and having looked at the minister’s face, dismissed the Sangha, sat down near the young monk, and said: “Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma?” He, not speaking of what was non-existent even indirectly, said: “Great king, I have no supramundane Dhamma.” “But, venerable sir, did you not speak so before?” “Yes, great king. I am one who has fulfilled the qualities conducive to being remembered. From the time that Dhamma was fulfilled in me, in a place of distributable items, the choice item comes to me.” “Good, good, venerable sir! This is fitting for you,” the king said, and having paid homage, he departed. This is the story here concerning “in a place of distributable items, the choice item comes to me.”

Brāhmaṇatissabhaye pana bhātaragāmavāsino nāgattheriyā anārocetvāva palāyiṃsu. Therī paccūsasamaye – “ativiya appanigghoso gāmo, upadhāretha tāvā”ti daharabhikkhuniyo āha. Tā gantvā sabbesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgamma theriyā ārocesuṃ. Sā sutvā “mā tumhe tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ cintayittha, attano uddesaparipucchāyonisomanasikāresuyeva yogaṃ karothā”ti vatvā bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ pārupitvā attadvādasamā gāmadvāre nigrodhamūle aṭṭhāsi. Rukkhe adhivatthādevatā dvādasannampi bhikkhunīnaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ datvā “ayye, mā aññattha gacchatha, niccaṃ [P 2.0536] idheva ethā”ti āha. Theriyā pana kaniṭṭhabhātā nāgatthero nāma atthi, so – “mahantaṃ bhayaṃ, na sakkā idha yāpetuṃ, paratīraṃ gamissāmī”ti attadvādasamova attano vasanaṭṭhānā nikkhanto theriṃ disvā gamissāmīti bhātaragāmaṃ āgato. Therī – “therā āgatā”ti sutvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā kiṃ ayyāti pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Sā – “ajja ekadivasaṃ vihāreyeva vasitvā sve gamissathā”ti āha. Therā vihāraṃ agamaṃsu.

Now, during the time of fear from Brāhmaṇa Tissa, the residents of Bhātaragāma fled without informing the elder nun Nāga. At dawn, the elder nun said to the young nuns: “The village is extremely quiet; first, go and investigate.” They went, and having learned that everyone had departed, they returned and informed the elder nun. Hearing this, she said: “Do not concern yourselves with their departure. Apply yourselves only to your own recitation, questioning, and wise attention.” Then, at the time for the alms-round, she dressed and, as the twelfth, stood at the village gate under a banyan tree. The deity dwelling in the tree gave almsfood to all twelve of the nuns and said: “Noble ladies, do not go elsewhere; always come right here.” Now, the elder nun had a younger brother, an elder named Nāga. He, thinking, “There is great danger; it is not possible to live here. I will go to the other shore,” departed from his own dwelling place as the twelfth and came to Bhātaragāma with the thought, “I will go after seeing the elder nun.” Hearing, “The elders have come,” she went to them and asked: “What is it, venerable sirs?” He explained the situation. She said: “Having stayed in the monastery for just one day today, you may go tomorrow.” The elders went to the monastery.

Therī [M 2.0126] punadivase rukkhamūle piṇḍāya caritvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti āha. Thero – “vaṭṭissati therī”ti vatvā tuṇhī aṭṭhāsi. Dhammiko tāta piṇḍapāto[V 2.0113], kukkuccaṃ akatvā paribhuñjathāti. “Vaṭṭissati therī”ti. Sā pattaṃ gahetvā ākāse khipi. Patto ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Thero – “sattatālamatte ṭhitampi bhikkhunibhattameva therī”ti vatvā – “bhayaṃ nāma sabbakālaṃ na hoti, bhaye vūpasante ariyavaṃsaṃ kathayamāno, ‘bho piṇḍapātika, bhikkhunibhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vītināmayitthā’ti cittena anuvadiyamāno santhambhetuṃ na sakkhissāmi, appamattā hotha theriyo”ti maggaṃ āruhi.

On the next day, the elder nun, having gone for alms at the foot of a tree, approached the elder and said, “Please partake of this almsfood.” The elder, saying, “Will it be proper, elder nun?” stood silent. “This almsfood is righteous, dear brother; partake of it without scruple.” “Will it be proper, elder nun?” She took the bowl and tossed it into the sky. The bowl stood still in the sky. The elder said, “Elder nun, even standing at the height of seven palm trees, it is still a nun’s almsfood,” and continued, “Fear does not last for all time. When the fear has subsided and I am speaking on the noble lineage, if I am reproached in someone's mind with the thought, ‘Ho, alms-goer, you passed your time having eaten a nun’s almsfood!’, I will not be able to remain firm. Be heedful, elder nuns,” and he set out on the road.

Rukkhadevatāpi – “sace thero theriyā hatthato piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjissati, na naṃ nivattessāmi. Sace na paribhuñjissati, nivattessāmī”ti cintayamānā ṭhatvā therassa gamanaṃ disvā rukkhā oruyha pattaṃ, bhante, dethāti pattaṃ gahetvā theraṃ rukkhamūlaṃyeva ānetvā āsanaṃ paññapetvā piṇḍapātaṃ datvā katabhattakiccaṃ paṭiññaṃ kāretvā dvādasa bhikkhuniyo dvādasa bhikkhū ca sattavassāni upaṭṭhahi. Idaṃ – “devatā ussukkaṃ āpajjantī”ti ettha vatthu. Tatra hi therī sāraṇīyadhammapūrikā ahosi.

The tree deity, for her part, stood thinking: “If the elder partakes of the almsfood from the elder nun’s hand, I will not turn him back. If he does not partake, I will turn him back.” Seeing the elder’s departure, she descended from the tree and, saying, “Venerable sir, give me the bowl,” she took the bowl. Having brought the elder right back to the foot of the tree, she prepared a seat, gave him the almsfood, and after he had finished his meal, she had him make a promise. She then attended to the twelve nuns and the twelve monks for seven years. This is the story here concerning “the deity makes an effort.” For in that case, the elder nun was a fulfiller of the qualities conducive to being remembered.

Akhaṇḍānītiādīsu yassa sattasu āpattikkhandhesu ādimhi vā ante vā sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti, tassa sīlaṃ pariyante chinnasāṭako viya khaṇḍaṃ nāma. Yassa pana vemajjhe bhinnaṃ, tassa majjhe chiddasāṭako viya chiddaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa pana paṭipāṭiyā dve tīṇi bhinnāni, tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ vā kucchiyaṃ vā uṭṭhitena visabhāgavaṇṇena kāḷarattādīnaṃ aññataravaṇṇā gāvī viya sabalaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa pana antarantarā visabhāgabinducitrā gāvī [P 2.0537] viya kammāsaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa pana sabbenasabbaṃ abhinnāni, tassa tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni nāma honti. Tāni panetāni taṇhādāsabyato mocetvā bhujissabhāvakaraṇato bhujissāni. Buddhādīhi viññūhi pasatthattā viññupasatthāni, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhattā – “idaṃ nāma tvaṃ āpannapubbo”ti kenaci parāmaṭṭhuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā ca aparāmaṭṭhāni, upacārasamādhiṃ vā appanāsamādhiṃ vā saṃvattayantīti samādhisaṃvattanikānīti vuccanti.

In the passage beginning with 'unbroken,' for one whose training rule among the seven groups of offenses is broken at the beginning or at the end, their virtue is called 'broken,' like a garment torn at the edge. For one whose training rule is broken in the middle, it is called 'pierced,' like a garment with a hole in the middle. For one whose two or three training rules are broken sequentially, their virtue is called 'spotted,' like a cow with patches of a dissimilar color, such as black or red, on its back or belly. For one whose training rules are broken here and there, their virtue is called 'speckled,' like a cow variegated with spots of dissimilar color. For one whose training rules are entirely unbroken, those virtues are called 'unbroken,' 'unpierced,' 'unspotted,' and 'unspeckled.' These virtues, by liberating from the state of slavery to craving and by bringing about a state of freedom, are called 'liberating.' Praised by the wise, such as the Buddha, they are called 'praised by the wise.'
