Ungrasped by craving and wrong view—and because it is not possible for anyone to reproach them, saying, 'You have previously committed this offense'—they are called 'ungrasped.' As they are conducive to access concentration or absorption concentration, they are called 'conducive to concentration.'

Sīlasāmaññagatā [M 2.0127] viharissantīti tesu tesu disābhāgesu viharantehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ samānabhāvūpagatasīlā viharissanti. Sotāpannādīnañhi sīlaṃ samuddantarepi devalokepi vasantānaṃ aññesaṃ sotāpannādīnaṃ sīlena samānameva hoti, natthi maggasīle nānattaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘They will dwell having attained to a commonality of virtue’ means that they will dwell with monks dwelling in various regions, their virtue having attained a state of sameness. For the virtue of stream-enterers and the like is the very same as the virtue of other stream-enterers and the like, even those dwelling in the middle of the ocean or in the deva world; there is no difference in the virtue of the path. This was said in reference to that.

Yāyaṃ [V 2.0114] diṭṭhīti maggasampayuttā sammādiṭṭhi. Ariyāti niddosā. Niyyātīti niyyānikā. Takkarassāti yo tathākārī hoti. Sabbadukkhakkhayāyāti sabbadukkhakkhayatthaṃ. Diṭṭhisāmaññagatāti samānadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ upagatā hutvā viharissanti. Vuddhiyevāti evaṃ viharantānaṃ vuddhiyeva bhikkhūnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihānīti.

‘This view’ means right view associated with the path. ‘Noble’ means stainless. Because it ‘leads out,’ it is ‘conducive to deliverance.’ ‘For one who does that’ means one who acts accordingly. ‘For the complete destruction of all suffering’ means for the purpose of the complete destruction of all suffering. ‘Having attained to a commonality of view’ means they will dwell having attained a state of same view. ‘Only growth’ means: for bhikkhus who dwell thus, growth is indeed to be expected, not decline.

142. Etadeva bahulanti āsannaparinibbānattā bhikkhu ovadanto punappunaṃ etaṃyeva dhammiṃ kathaṃ karoti. Iti sīlanti evaṃ sīlaṃ, ettakaṃ sīlaṃ. Ettha catupārisuddhisīlaṃ sīlaṃ cittekaggatā samādhi, vipassanāpaññā paññāti veditabbā. Sīlaparibhāvitoti ādīsu yasmiṃ sīle ṭhatvāva maggasamādhiṃ phalasamādhiṃ nibbattenti. Eso tena sīlena paribhāvito mahapphalo hoti, mahānisaṃso. Yamhi samādhimhi ṭhatvā maggapaññaṃ phalapaññaṃ nibbattenti, sā tena samādhinā paribhāvitā mahapphalā hoti, mahānisaṃsā. Yāya paññāya ṭhatvā maggacittaṃ phalacittaṃ nibbattenti, taṃ tāya paribhāvitaṃ sammadeva āsavehi vimuccati.

142. ‘This very thing frequently’ means that because his final Nibbāna was near, the Blessed One, while instructing the monks, repeatedly gave this very Dhamma talk. ‘Thus virtue’ means: virtue is of this kind, virtue is of this extent. Here, the fourfold purified virtue is to be understood as ‘virtue,’ unification of mind as ‘concentration,’ and insight-wisdom as ‘wisdom.’ In the passage beginning with ‘developed by virtue’: having established themselves in which virtue, they produce the concentration of the path and the concentration of the fruit. This concentration, developed by that virtue, becomes of great fruit and great benefit. Having established themselves in which concentration, they produce the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit. That wisdom, developed by that concentration, becomes of great fruit and great benefit. Having established themselves in which wisdom, they produce the path-mind and the fruit-mind. That mind, developed by that wisdom, is rightly liberated from the taints.

Yathābhirantanti buddhānaṃ anabhiratiparitassitaṃ nāma natthi, yathāruci yathāajjhāsayanti pana vuttaṃ hoti. Āyāmāti ehi yāma. “Ayāmā”tipi pāṭho, gacchāmāti [P 2.0538] attho. Ānandāti bhagavā santikāvacarattā theraṃ ālapati. Thero pana – “gaṇhathāvuso pattacīvarāni, bhagavā asukaṭṭhānaṃ gantukāmo”ti bhikkhūnaṃ āroceti.

‘As they pleased’ means that for Buddhas there is no such thing as discontent or agitation; rather, it is said to mean according to their wish and inclination. ‘Āyāma’ means ‘come, let us go.’ There is also the reading ‘Ayāma,’ the meaning of which is ‘let us go.’ ‘Ānanda’: the Blessed One addressed the elder because he was his constant attendant. The elder then informed the monks, saying: “Take your bowls and robes, friends, the Blessed One intends to go to such-and-such a place.”

144. Ambalaṭṭhikāgamanaṃ uttānameva. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputtotiādi (dī. ni. 3.141) sampasādanīye vitthāritaṃ.

144. The going to Ambalaṭṭhikā is straightforward. The part beginning “Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, etc.,” is explained in detail in the Sampasādanīya Sutta.

Dussīlaādīnavavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Dangers of Immorality.

148. Pāṭaligamane [M 2.0128] āvasathāgāranti āgantukānaṃ āvasathagehaṃ. Pāṭaligāme kira niccakālaṃ dvinnaṃ rājūnaṃ sahāyakā āgantvā kulāni gehato nīharitvā māsampi aḍḍhamāsampi vasanti. Te manussā niccupaddutā – “etesaṃ āgatakāle vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti nagaramajjhe mahatiṃ sālaṃ karitvā tassā ekasmiṃ padese bhaṇḍapaṭisāmanaṭṭhānaṃ, ekasmiṃ padese nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ akaṃsu. Te – “bhagavā āgato”ti sutvāva – “amhehi gantvāpi bhagavā ānetabbo siyā, so sayameva amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sampatto, ajja bhagavantaṃ āvasathe maṅgalaṃ vadāpessāmā”ti etadatthameva upasaṅkamantā. Tasmā evamāhaṃsu. Yena āvasathāgāranti te kira [V 2.0115] – “buddhā nāma araññajjhāsayā araññārāmā antogāme vasituṃ iccheyyuṃ vā no vā”ti bhagavato manaṃ ajānantā āvasathāgāraṃ appaṭijaggitvāva āgamaṃsu. Idāni bhagavato manaṃ ñatvā puretaraṃ gantvā paṭijaggissāmāti yenāvasathāgāraṃ, tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Sabbasantharinti yathā sabbaṃ santhataṃ hoti, evaṃ santhariṃ.

148. In the section on going to Pāṭaligāma, ‘guest house’ means a lodging house for visitors. It is said that in Pāṭaligāma, the allies of two kings would regularly come, displace families from their homes, and stay for a month or even half a month. The people, being constantly harassed, thought, “There will be a place for them to stay when they come,” and so they built a large hall in the middle of the city, with one area for storing goods and another for lodging. Hearing, “The Blessed One has come,” they thought, “We might have had to go and invite the Blessed One, but he has come to our lodging place on his own. Today we will have the Blessed One speak on what is auspicious in the guest house.” It was for this very purpose that they approached. Therefore, they spoke thus. As for the phrase, ‘to where the guest house was,’ it is said that they, not knowing the Blessed One’s mind—thinking, “Buddhas, by nature, have an inclination for the forest and delight in the forest; would they wish to stay inside a village or not?”—came without having prepared the guest house. Now, having understood the Blessed One’s mind, they went ahead to prepare it, and so they approached the guest house. ‘With everything spread’ means they spread coverings so that the entire place was covered.

149. Dussīloti asīlo nissīlo. Sīlavipannoti vipannasīlo bhinnasaṃvaro. Pamādādhikaraṇanti pamādakāraṇā.

149. ‘Immoral’ means one without virtue, devoid of virtue. ‘One whose virtue is corrupt’ means one of corrupt virtue, whose restraint is broken. ‘A ground for heedlessness’ means a cause of heedlessness.

Idañca suttaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ vasena āgataṃ pabbajitānampi pana labbhateva. Gahaṭṭho hi yena yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvitaṃ kappeti – yadi kasiyā, yadi vaṇijjāya, pāṇātipātādivasena pamatto taṃ taṃ yathākālaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkoti, athassa mūlampi vinassati. Māghātakāle pāṇātipātaṃ pana adinnādānādīni ca karonto daṇḍavasena mahatiṃ bhogajāniṃ nigacchati. Pabbajito dussīlo ca pamādakāraṇā sīlato buddhavacanato jhānato sattaariyadhanato ca jāniṃ nigacchati.

This discourse has come down in connection with householders, but it is also applicable to those who have gone forth. A householder who makes a living by any craft—whether by farming or by trade—if he is heedless through killing living beings and other such actions, he is not able to complete those tasks in due time, and thus even his capital is destroyed. Furthermore, by engaging in killing, stealing, and other wrongdoings at a time when killing is prohibited, he may incur a great loss of wealth through punishment. An immoral monk, due to heedlessness, incurs a loss of virtue, the Buddha’s teachings, jhāna, and the seven noble treasures.

Gahaṭṭhassa – “asuko nāma asukakule jāto dussīlo pāpadhammo [P 2.0539] pariccattaidhalokaparaloko salākabhattamattampi na detī”ti catuparisamajjhe pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati. Pabbajitassa vā – “asuko nāma nāsakkhi sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ, na buddhavacanaṃ uggahetuṃ, vejjakammādīhi [M 2.0129] jīvati, chahi agāravehi samannāgato”ti evaṃ abbhuggacchati.

For a householder: ‘This person, named so-and-so, born in such-and-such a family, is immoral, of wicked character, has abandoned this world and the next, and does not give even so much as a meal distributed by ticket’—thus a bad report spreads amidst the four assemblies. Or for a renunciant: ‘This person was not able to guard his morality, was not able to learn the Buddha's word, makes a living by medical practice and so on, and is endowed with the six kinds of disrespect’—thus it spreads.

Avisāradoti gahaṭṭho tāva – “avassaṃ bahūnaṃ sannipātaṭṭhāne keci mama kammaṃ jānissanti, atha maṃ niggaṇhissantī”ti vā, “rājakulassa vā dassantī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati, maṅkubhūto pattakkhandho adhomukho aṅgulikena bhūmiṃ kasanto nisīdati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti. Pabbajitopi – “bahū bhikkhū sannipatitā, avassaṃ koci mama kammaṃ jānissati, atha me uposathampi pavāraṇampi ṭhapetvā sāmaññato cāvetvā nikkaḍḍhissantī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti. Ekacco pana dussīlopi dappito viya vicarati, sopi ajjhāsayena maṅku hotiyeva.

Lacking confidence—a householder, for instance, thinking, ‘Surely, in a gathering of many, some will know of my deeds, and then they will censure me,’ or, ‘They will report me to the royal family,’ approaches fearfully. Disconcerted, with drooping shoulders, downcast, he sits scratching the ground with his finger, unable to speak with confidence. A renunciant, too, thinking, ‘Many monks have gathered; surely, someone will know of my deeds, and then, having suspended my Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, they will make me fall from the state of a monk and expel me,’ approaches fearfully, unable to speak with confidence. Some immoral persons, however, walk about as if proud, yet even they are inwardly disconcerted.

Sammūḷho kālaṅkarotīti tassa hi maraṇamañce nipannassa dussīlakamme samādāya pavattitaṭṭhānaṃ āpāthamāgacchati, so ummīletvā idhalokaṃ passati, nimīletvā paralokaṃ passati[V 2.0116], tassa cattāro apāyā upaṭṭhahanti, sattisatena sīse pahariyamāno viya hoti. So – “vāretha, vārethā”ti viravanto marati. Tena vuttaṃ – “sammūḷho kālaṃ karotī”ti. Pañcamapadaṃ uttānameva.

He dies in a state of bewilderment: for one lying on his deathbed, the immoral deeds he has undertaken and engaged in come into his presence. Opening his eyes, he sees this world; closing his eyes, he sees the next world. The four states of deprivation appear to him; it is as if he is being struck on the head with a hundred spears. Crying out, ‘Ward them off! Ward them off!’ he dies. Therefore it is said: ‘He dies in a state of bewilderment.’ The fifth point is self-evident.

150. Ānisaṃsakathā vuttavipariyāyena veditabbā.

150. The discourse on the benefits should be understood as the reverse of what has been said.

151. Bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāyāti aññāya pāḷimuttakāya dhammikathāya ceva āvasathānumodanāya ca ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya yojanappamāṇaṃ mahāmadhuṃ pīḷetvā madhupānaṃ pāyento viya bahudeva rattiṃ sandassetvā sampahaṃsetvā uyyojesi. Abhikkantāti atikkantā khīṇā khayavayaṃ upetā. Suññāgāranti pāṭiyekkaṃ suññāgāraṃ nāma natthi, tattheva pana ekapasse sāṇipākārena parikkhipitvā – “idha satthā vissamissatī”ti mañcakaṃ paññapesuṃ. Bhagavā – “catūhipi iriyāpathehi paribhuttaṃ etesaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti tattha sīhaseyyaṃ [P 2.0540] kappesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “suññāgāraṃ pāvisī”ti.

151. For much of the night with a righteous talk: that is, with a righteous talk apart from the Pāḷi canon and with a discourse of appreciation for the rest house, as if drawing down the celestial Ganges, or as if squeezing a great honeycomb of a yojana in size and giving a honey-drink to drink, for much of the night he instructed, inspired, and then dismissed them. The night had passed: it was over, spent, had come to an end. An empty dwelling: there was no separate dwelling called an empty dwelling, but in that very rest house, in one corner, they set up a couch, having enclosed it with a cloth curtain, thinking, ‘Here the Teacher will rest.’ The Blessed One, thinking, ‘Used by me in all four postures, it will be of great fruit for them,’ there adopted the lion’s posture. With reference to this it is said: ‘He entered an empty dwelling.’

Pāṭaliputtanagaramāpanavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Building of the City of Pāṭaliputta.

152. Sunidhavassakārāti [M 2.0130] sunidho ca vassakāro ca dve brāhmaṇā. Magadhamahāmattāti magadharañño mahāmattā mahāamaccā, magadharaṭṭhe vā mahāmattā mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgatāti magadhamahāmattā. Pāṭaligāme nagaranti pāṭaligāmaṃ nagaraṃ katvā māpenti. Vajjīnaṃ paṭibāhāyāti vajjirājakulānaṃ āyamukhapacchindanatthaṃ. Sahassevāti ekekavaggavasena sahassaṃ sahassaṃ hutvā. Vatthūnīti gharavatthūni. Cittāni namanti nivesanāni māpetunti raññañca rājamahāmattānañca nivesanāni māpetuṃ vatthuvijjāpāṭhakānaṃ cittāni namanti. Te kira attano sippānubhāvena heṭṭhā pathaviyaṃ tiṃsahatthamatte ṭhāne – “idha nāgaggāho, idha yakkhaggāho, idha bhūtaggāho, pāsāṇo vā khāṇuko vā atthī”ti passanti. Te tadā sippaṃ jappitvā devatāhi saddhiṃ mantayamānā viya māpenti. Athavā nesaṃ sarīre devatā adhimuccitvā tattha tattha nivesanāni māpetuṃ cittaṃ nāmenti. Tā catūsu koṇesu khāṇuke koṭṭetvā vatthumhi gahitamatte paṭivigacchanti. Saddhānaṃ kulānaṃ saddhā devatā tathā karonti, assaddhānaṃ kulānaṃ assaddhā devatāva. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Saddhānañhi evaṃ hoti – “idha manussā nivesanaṃ māpetvā paṭhamaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā maṅgalaṃ vaḍḍhāpessanti. Atha mayaṃ sīlavantānaṃ dassanaṃ, dhammakathaṃ, pañhāvissajjanaṃ[V 2.0117], anumodanañca sotuṃ labhissāma, manussā dānaṃ datvā amhākaṃ pattiṃ dassantī”ti.

152. Sunidha and Vassakāra: these are two brahmins, Sunidha and Vassakāra. Great ministers of Magadha: they are the great ministers, the chief counselors, of the king of Magadha; or, they are great officials in the Magadhan kingdom, meaning they are endowed with a great measure of authority. Building a city at Pāṭaligāma: they are making the village of Pāṭali into a city. For warding off the Vajjīs: for the purpose of cutting off the revenue stream of the Vajjī royal families. By the thousand: in groups of one thousand each. Sites: sites for houses. Their minds are inclined to build residences: the minds of the experts in site-lore are inclined to build residences for the king and the king’s great ministers. It is said that they, by the power of their craft, see down into the earth for a distance of thirty cubits, thinking: ‘Here is a nāga’s haunt, here a yakkha’s haunt, here a spirit’s haunt; here there is a rock or a stump.’ Then, reciting their craft, they build as if consulting with the deities. Or, deities possess their bodies and incline their minds to build residences in such and such a place. Having driven stakes into the four corners, as soon as the site is taken, those deities depart. For faithful families, faithful deities act thus; for faithless families, it is faithless deities who do so. For what reason? Because for the faithful deities, it occurs to them: ‘Here, people will build a residence and first have the Saṅgha of monks take a seat and perform a blessing ceremony. Then we will get to see the virtuous ones, and to hear the Dhamma talk, the answering of questions, and the discourse of appreciation. When people give a gift, they will share the merit with us.’

Tāvatiṃsehīti yathā hi ekasmiṃ kule ekaṃ paṇḍitamanussaṃ, ekasmiṃ vā vihāre ekaṃ bahussutabhikkhuṃ upādāya – “asukakule manussā paṇḍitā, asukavihāre bhikkhū bahussutā”ti saddo abbhuggacchati, evameva sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ vissakammañca devaputtaṃ upādāya – “tāvatiṃsā paṇḍitā”ti saddo abbhuggato. Tenāha – “tāvatiṃsehī”ti. Tāvatiṃsehi saddhiṃ mantetvāpi viya māpentīti attho.

With the Tāvatiṃsa gods: Just as, on account of a single wise person in a family, or a single learned monk in a monastery, a report spreads—‘The people in such-and-such a family are wise,’ or ‘The monks in such-and-such a monastery are learned’—in the very same way, on account of Sakka, king of the gods, and the god Vissakamma, the report has spread: ‘The Tāvatiṃsa gods are wise.’ Therefore, he said: ‘With the Tāvatiṃsa gods.’ The meaning is that they build as if having consulted with the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

Yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatananti yattakaṃ ariyakamanussānaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ [P 2.0541] nāma atthi. Yāvatā vaṇippathoti yattakaṃ vāṇijānaṃ ābhatabhaṇḍassa [M 2.0131] rāsivaseneva kayavikkayaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, vāṇijānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vā atthi. Idaṃ agganagaranti tesaṃ ariyāyatanavaṇippathānaṃ idaṃ agganagaraṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ pāmokkhaṃ bhavissatīti. Puṭabhedananti bhaṇḍapuṭabhedanaṭṭhānaṃ, bhaṇḍabhaṇḍikānaṃ mocanaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakalajambudīpe aladdhabhaṇḍampi hi idheva labhissanti, aññattha vikkayena agacchantampi ca idheva gamissati. Tasmā idheva puṭaṃ bhindissantīti attho. Catūsu hi dvāresu cattāri sabhāyaṃ ekanti evaṃ divase divase pañcasatasahassāni uṭṭhahissantīti dasseti.

Yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatananti: As far as the resort of noble people extends. Yāvatā vaṇippathoti: As far as there is a trade route, a place for buying and selling by way of heaps of merchandise brought by merchants, or a dwelling place for merchants. Idaṃ agganagaranti: This will be the foremost city, the chief and principal, among those noble resorts and trade routes. Puṭabhedananti: A place for opening bundles of goods; that is, a place for untying bundles of merchandise, it is said. Indeed, even goods not found anywhere else in all of Jambudīpa will be obtained right here, and even those not going elsewhere for sale will come here. Therefore, it means they will break open their bundles here. For at the four gates, four hundred thousand, and at the assembly hall, one hundred thousand—thus it is shown that five hundred thousand will accrue each and every day.

Aggito vātiādīsu cakārattho vā-saddo. Agginā ca udakena ca mithubhedena ca nassissatīti attho. Ekakoṭṭhāso agginā nassissati, nibbāpetuṃ na sakkhissanti. Ekaṃ gaṅgā gahetvā gamissati. Eko – “iminā akathitaṃ amussa, amunā akathitaṃ imassā”ti vadantānaṃ pisuṇavācānaṃ vasena bhinnānaṃ manussānaṃ aññamaññabhedeneva nassissatīti attho. Iti vatvā bhagavā paccūsakāle gaṅgāya tīraṃ gantvā katamukhadhovano bhikkhācāravelaṃ āgamayamāno nisīdi.

In phrases like 'aggito vā' (by fire or), the word 'vā' (or) has the meaning of 'ca' (and). It means it will perish by fire, and by water, and by internal discord. One portion will perish by fire—they will not be able to extinguish it. The Ganges will carry one portion away. Another portion will perish simply through the mutual discord of people divided by the slanderous speech of those saying, 'What was unsaid by this person to that person,' and 'what was unsaid by that person to this person.' Having said this, the Blessed One went to the bank of the Ganges at dawn, washed his face, and sat down while waiting for the time for the alms-round.

153. Sunidhavassakārāpi – “amhākaṃ rājā samaṇassa gotamassa upaṭṭhāko, so amhe pucchissati, ‘satthā kira pāṭaligāmaṃ agamāsi, tassa santikaṃ upasaṅkamittha, na upasaṅkamitthā’ti. Upasaṅkamimhāti ca vutte – ‘nimantayittha, na nimantayitthā’ti ca pucchissati. Na nimantayimhāti ca vutte amhākaṃ dosaṃ āropetvā niggaṇhissati. Idaṃ cāpi mayaṃ āgataṭṭhāne nagaraṃ māpema, samaṇassa kho pana gotamassa gatagataṭṭhāne kāḷakaṇṇisattā [V 2.0118] paṭikkamanti, taṃ mayaṃ nagaramaṅgalaṃ vadāpessāmā”ti cintetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā nimantayiṃsu. Tasmā – “atha kho sunidhavassakārā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

153. Sunidha and Vassakāra also thought: "Our king is a supporter of the ascetic Gotama. He will ask us, 'Did the Teacher go to Pāṭaligāma? Did you approach him, or did you not approach him?' If we say we approached him, he will ask, 'Did you invite him, or did you not invite him?' And if we say we did not invite him, he will find fault with us and punish us. Moreover, we are building a city at this place where we have arrived. Wherever the ascetic Gotama has gone, inauspicious beings depart. Therefore, we will have him pronounce a blessing for the city." Having considered this, they approached the Teacher and invited him. Hence, it is said: "Then Sunidha and Vassakāra..."

Pubbaṇhasamayanti pubbaṇhakāle. Nivāsetvāti gāmappavesananīhārena nivāsanaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ [P 2.0542] bandhitvā. Pattacīvaramādāyāti pattañca cīvarañca ādiyitvā kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ katvā.

‘In the morning’ means in the forenoon. ‘Having dressed’ means having put on the lower robe in a manner suitable for entering a village and having tied the belt. ‘Taking the bowl and robe’ means having taken both bowl and robe and attaching them to the body.

Sīlavantetthāti sīlavante ettha. Saññateti kāyavācāmanehi saññate.

‘Sīlavantettha’ means the virtuous here. ‘Saññate’ means restrained by body, speech, and mind.

Tāsaṃ [M 2.0132] dakkhiṇamādiyeti saṅghassa dinne cattāro paccaye tāsaṃ gharadevatānaṃ ādiseyya, pattiṃ dadeyya. Pūjitā pūjayantīti – “ime manussā amhākaṃ ñātakāpi na honti, evampi no pattiṃ dentī”ti ārakkhaṃ susaṃvihitaṃ karothāti suṭṭhu ārakkhaṃ karonti. Mānitā mānayantīti kālānukālaṃ balikammakaraṇena mānitā “ete manussā amhākaṃ ñātakāpi na honti, catumāsachamāsantare no balikammaṃ karontī”ti mānenti, mānentiyo uppannaṃ parissayaṃ haranti.

‘One should dedicate the offering to them’ means one should dedicate to the household deities the four requisites given to the Saṅgha, and give them a share of merit. ‘Being honored, they honor in return’—thinking, 'These humans are not even our relatives, yet they give us a share of merit,' they provide well-arranged protection. ‘Being respected, they respect in return’—being respected by the performance of timely offerings, they think, 'These humans are not even our relatives, yet every four or six months they perform offerings for us,' and thus they respect them in return, removing any arisen dangers.

Tato nanti tato naṃ paṇḍitajātikaṃ manussaṃ. Orasanti ure ṭhapetvā saṃvaḍḍhitaṃ, yathā mātā orasaṃ puttaṃ anukampati, uppannaparissayaharaṇatthameva tassa vāyamati, evaṃ anukampantīti attho. Bhadrāni passatīti sundarāni passati.

‘Tato naṃ’: refers to that wise person. ‘Orasaṃ’ means just as a mother has compassion for her own son, raised at her breast, and strives only to remove any danger that has arisen for him, so too do they have compassion for him. This is the meaning. ‘Sees auspicious things’ means sees beautiful things.

154. Uḷumpanti pāragamanatthāya āṇiyo koṭṭetvā kataṃ. Kullanti valliādīhi bandhitvā kataṃ.

154. ‘Uḷumpa’ means a raft made for the purpose of crossing over by hammering in pegs. ‘Kulla’ means a raft made by binding with vines and the like.

“Ye taranti aṇṇava”nti gāthāya aṇṇavanti sabbantimena paricchedena yojanamattaṃ gambhīrassa ca puthulassa ca udakaṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saranti idha nadī adhippetā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, ye gambhīravitthataṃ taṇhāsaraṃ taranti, te ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ setuṃ katvāna. Visajja pallalāni anāmasitvā udakabharitāni ninnaṭṭhānāni. Ayaṃ pana idaṃ appamattakaṃ taritukāmopi kullañhi jano pabandhati. Buddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca vināyeva kullena tiṇṇā medhāvino janāti.

In the verse, 'Those who cross the ocean…': ‘ocean’ (`aṇṇava`) is a designation for a body of water that is a yojana deep and wide, with its boundary at the very end. Here, ‘stream’ (`saraṃ`) is intended to mean a river. This is what is said: Those who cross the deep and wide river of craving do so having made the bridge called the Noble Path. Abandoning the marshes, and not touching the low-lying places filled with water, they cross. But this person, desiring to cross even this small amount of water, binds together a raft. The Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha, the wise people, have crossed over without a raft at all.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Recitation Section is concluded.

Ariyasaccakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble Truths

155. Koṭigāmoti [V 2.0119] mahāpanādassa pāsādakoṭiyaṃ katagāmo. Ariyasaccānanti ariyabhāvakarānaṃ saccānaṃ. Ananubodhāti abujjhanena ajānanena. Appaṭivedhāti appaṭivijjhanena. Sandhāvitanti bhavato bhavaṃ gamanavasena [P 2.0543] sandhāvitaṃ. Saṃsaritanti punappunaṃ gamanāgamanavasena saṃsaritaṃ. Mamañceva [M 2.0133] tumhākañcāti mayā ca tumhehi ca. Atha vā sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritanti sandhāvanaṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ mamañceva tumhākañca ahosīti emamettha attho veditabbo. Bhavanetti samūhatāti bhavato bhavaṃ nayanasamatthā taṇhārajju suṭṭhu hatā chinnā appavattikatā.

155. ‘Koṭigāma’: a village built at the pinnacle of Mahāpanāda's palace. ‘Ariyasaccānaṃ’: of the truths that make one noble. ‘Ananubodhā’: through not awakening, through not knowing. ‘Appaṭivedhā’: through not penetrating. ‘Sandhāvitaṃ’: wandered from existence to existence, in the sense of going. ‘Saṃsaritaṃ’: transmigrated by repeatedly going and coming. ‘Mamañceva tumhākañca’: by me and by you. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'the wandering and transmigration were both mine and yours.' ‘Bhavanetti samūhatā’: the guide to existence—the rope of craving, capable of leading from existence to existence—is well destroyed, cut off, and made incapable of future arising.

Anāvattidhammasambodhiparāyaṇavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Nature of Non-Returning and Being Destined for Supreme Enlightenment

156. Nātikāti ekaṃ taḷākaṃ nissāya dvinnaṃ cūḷapitumahāpituputtānaṃ dve gāmā. Nātiketi ekasmiṃ ñātigāmake. Giñjakāvasatheti iṭṭhakāmaye āvasathe.

156. ‘Nātikā’: two villages dependent on one reservoir, belonging to the sons of the younger and elder paternal uncles. ‘Nātike’: in a certain village of relatives. ‘Giñjakāvasathe’: in a brick dwelling.

157. Orambhāgiyānanti heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ, kāmabhaveyeva paṭisandhiggāhāpakānanti attho. Oranti laddhanāmehi vā tīhi maggehi pahātabbānītipi orambhāgiyāni. Tattha kāmacchando, byāpādoti imāni dve samāpattiyā vā avikkhambhitāni, maggena vā asamucchinnāni nibbattavasena uddhaṃ bhāgaṃ rūpabhavañca arūpabhavañca gantuṃ na denti. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīni tīṇi tattha nibbattampi ānetvā puna idheva nibbattāpentīti sabbānipi orambhāgiyāneva. Anāvattidhammāti paṭisandhivasena anāgamanasabhāvā.

157. Orambhāgiyāna: Pertaining to the lower part, meaning those that cause one to take rebirth in the sense-sphere existence. Alternatively, because they are to be abandoned by the three paths that have received the name 'lower' (ora), they are also called 'pertaining to the lower part.' Herein, sensual desire and ill will—these two, if not suppressed by an attainment or not eradicated by the path, do not, by way of their causing rebirth, allow one to go to the upper part, that is, the form realm and the formless realm. The three fetters beginning with identity view, having brought back even one who has been reborn there, cause them to be reborn right here again. Thus, all five are indeed 'pertaining to the lower part.' Anāvattidhammā: Having the nature of not returning by way of rebirth.

Rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttāti ettha kadāci karahaci uppattiyā ca, pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya cāti dvedhāpi tanubhāvo veditabbo. Sakadāgāmissa hi puthujjanānaṃ viya abhiṇhaṃ rāgādayo nuppajjanti, kadāci karahaci uppajjanti. Uppajjamānā ca puthujjanānaṃ viya bahalabahalā nuppajjanti, makkhikāpattaṃ viya tanukatanukā uppajjanti. Dīghabhāṇakatipiṭakamahāsīvatthero panāha – “yasmā sakadāgāmissa puttadhītaro honti, orodhā ca honti, tasmā bahalā kilesā. Idaṃ pana bhavatanukavasena kathita”nti. Taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ – “sotāpannassa sattabhave ṭhapetvā aṭṭhame bhave bhavatanukaṃ natthi. Sakadāgāmissa dve bhave ṭhapetvā pañcasu bhavesu bhavatanukaṃ natthi. Anāgāmissa rūpārūpabhave ṭhapetvā kāmabhave bhavatanukaṃ natthi. Khīṇāsavassa kismiñci bhave bhavatanukaṃ natthī”ti vuttattā paṭikkhittaṃ hoti.

Rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā: Herein, the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion should be understood in two ways: by their arising only occasionally and by the weakness of their obsession. For a once-returner, lust and other defilements do not arise frequently as they do for worldlings, but arise only occasionally. And when they do arise, they do not arise as thickly as for worldlings, but arise as very thin, like a fly’s wing. However, the great elder Mahāsīva, the Tipiṭaka-reciter and Dīgha-reciter, said: 'Because a once-returner has sons and daughters, and also has wives, their defilements are thick. This, however, was spoken of in terms of the attenuation of existence.' That view is refuted in this commentary, because it is stated: 'For a stream-enterer, setting aside seven existences, there is no attenuation of existence in an eighth existence. For a once-returner, setting aside two existences, there is no attenuation of existence in the subsequent five existences. For a non-returner, setting aside the form and formless realms, there is no attenuation of existence in the sense-sphere realm. For one whose taints are destroyed, there is no attenuation of existence in any existence whatsoever.' This is how that view is refuted.

Imaṃ [V 2.0120] lokanti imaṃ kāmāvacaralokaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ayañcettha [P 2.0544] adhippāyo, sace hi manussesu sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patto devesu nibbattitvā [M 2.0134] arahattaṃ sacchikaroti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. Asakkonto pana avassaṃ manussalokaṃ āgantvā sacchikaroti. Devesu sakadāgāmiphalaṃ pattopi sace manussesu nibbattitvā arahattaṃ sacchikaroti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. Asakkonto pana avassaṃ devalokaṃ gantvā sacchikarotīti.

Imaṃ lokaṃ: This is said with reference to this sense-sphere world. And the intention here is this: If one who has attained the fruit of once-returning among humans is reborn among the devas and realizes arahantship, that is good. But if unable to do so, they must inevitably come to the human world and realize it. And if one who has attained the fruit of once-returning among the devas is reborn among humans and realizes arahantship, that is good. But if unable to do so, they must inevitably go to the deva world and realize it.

Avinipātadhammoti ettha vinipatanaṃ vinipāto, nāssa vinipāto dhammoti avinipātadhammo. Catūsu apāyesu avinipātadhammo catūsu apāyesu avinipātasabhāvoti attho. Niyatoti dhammaniyāmena niyato. Sambodhiparāyaṇoti uparimaggattayasaṅkhātā sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ assa gati paṭisaraṇaṃ avassaṃ pattabbāti sambodhiparāyaṇo.

Avinipātadhammo: Herein, 'falling ruinously' (vinipatanaṃ) is a 'ruinous fall' (vinipāto). 'One whose nature is not to fall ruinously' (nāssa vinipāto dhammo) is an avinipātadhammo. This means one who is not of a nature to fall into the four woeful states; one who has the nature of not falling into the four woeful states. Niyato: Fixed by the fixed order of the Dhamma. Sambodhiparāyaṇo: For whom enlightenment—reckoned as the three higher paths—is the supreme goal, the destination, the refuge, which is inevitably to be attained; therefore, one who is destined for enlightenment.

Dhammādāsadhammapariyāyavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Mirror of the Dhamma

158. Vihesāti tesaṃ tesaṃ ñāṇagatiṃ ñāṇūpapattiṃ ñāṇābhisamparāyaṃ olokentassa kāyakilamathova esa, ānanda, tathāgatassāti dīpeti, cittavihesā pana buddhānaṃ natthi. Dhammādāsanti dhammamayaṃ ādāsaṃ. Yenāti yena dhammādāsena samannāgato. Khīṇāpāyaduggativinipātoti idaṃ nirayādīnaṃyeva vevacanavasena vuttaṃ. Nirayādayo hi vaḍḍhisaṅkhātato ayato apetattā apāyā. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati. Ye dukkaṭakārino, te ettha vivasā nipatantīti vinipātā.

158. Vihesā: This indicates: 'This, Ānanda, is only bodily fatigue for the Tathāgata who observes, for various beings, their course of knowledge, their arising with knowledge, and their future destiny with knowledge.' For the Buddhas, however, there is no mental fatigue. Dhammādāsa: A mirror made of the Dhamma. Khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto: This is stated as a synonym for hell and other such states. For hell and the like are called apāya because they are devoid of (apeta) gain (aya), which is known as growth. They are called duggati because they are a bad destination (gati) and resort for suffering. They are called vinipātā because those who do evil deeds fall (nipatanti) therein helplessly.

Aveccappasādenāti buddhaguṇānaṃ yathābhūtato ñātattā acalena accutena pasādena. Upari padadvayepi eseva nayo. Itipi so bhagavātiādīnaṃ pana vitthāro visuddhimagge vutto.

Aveccappasādena: With unshakable (acalena), immovable (accutena) confidence, which is due to knowing the qualities of the Buddha as they truly are. This same method applies to the two subsequent phrases as well. The detailed explanation of the passages beginning with 'Itipi so Bhagavā...' however, is given in the Visuddhimagga.

Ariyakantehīti ariyānaṃ kantehi piyehi manāpehi. Pañca sīlāni hi ariyasāvakānaṃ kantāni honti, bhavantarepi avijahitabbato. Tāni sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbopi panettha saṃvaro labbhatiyeva.

Ariyakantehi: By those [precepts] that are dear (kantehi), beloved (piyehi), and pleasing (manāpehi) to the noble ones. For the five precepts are dear to the noble disciples because they are not to be abandoned even in another existence. This was said with reference to them. Herein, all manner of restraint is indeed obtained.

Sotāpannohamasmīti idaṃ desanāsīsameva. Sakadāgāmiādayopi pana sakadāgāmīhamasmītiādinā nayena byākaronti yevāti. Sabbesampi hi sikkhāpadāvirodhena yuttaṭṭhāne byākaraṇaṃ anuññātameva hoti.

'I am a stream-enterer': this is merely the pinnacle of the teaching. For once-returners and others also declare themselves in the same way, saying, 'I am a once-returner,' and so on. Indeed, for all of them, such a declaration is permitted in a suitable situation, provided it does not violate a training rule.

Ambapālīgaṇikāvatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Ambapālī the Courtesan

161. Vesāliyaṃ [V 2.0121][M 2.0135] viharatīti ettha tena kho pana samayena vesālī iddhā ceva hoti phītācātiādinā khandhake vuttanayena [P 2.0545] vesāliyā sampannabhāvo veditabbo. Ambapālivaneti ambapāliyā gaṇikāya uyyānabhūte ambavane. Sato bhikkhaveti bhagavā ambapālidassane satipaccupaṭṭhānatthaṃ visesato idha satipaṭṭhānadesanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha saratīti sato. Sampajānātīti sampajāno. Satiyā ca sampajaññena ca samannāgato hutvā vihareyyāti attho. Kāye kāyānupassītiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhāne vakkhāma.

161. Vesāliyaṃ viharati: Herein, the prosperity of Vesālī should be understood according to the method stated in the Khandhaka, beginning with: 'Now at that time, Vesālī was prosperous and flourishing...' Ambapālivane: In the mango grove that was the park of the courtesan Ambapālī. Sato, bhikkhaveti: Here, on the occasion of seeing Ambapālī, the Blessed One began this discourse on the foundations of mindfulness specifically for the purpose of establishing mindfulness. Therein, 'one who is mindful' (sato) is so called because 'one remembers' (sarati). 'One who is clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) is so called because 'one clearly comprehends' (sampajānāti). The meaning is that one should dwell endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension. As for what is to be said regarding 'contemplating the body in the body' and so on, that we shall explain in the commentary to the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

Nīlāti idaṃ sabbasaṅgāhakaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇātiādi tasseva vibhāgadassanaṃ. Tattha na tesaṃ pakativaṇṇo nīlo, nīlavilepanavilittattā panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Nīlavatthāti paṭadukūlakoseyyādīnipi tesaṃ nīlāneva honti. Nīlālaṅkārāti nīlamaṇīhi nīlapupphehi alaṅkatā, rathāpi tesaṃ nīlamaṇikhacitā nīlavatthaparikkhittā nīladdhajā nīlavammikehi nīlābharaṇehi nīlaassehi yuttā, patodalaṭṭhiyopi nīlā yevāti. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Parivaṭṭesīti pahari. Kiṃ je ambapālīti jeti ālapanavacanaṃ, bhoti ambapāli, kiṃ kāraṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Kiñcā”tipi pāṭho, ayamevettha attho. Sāhāranti sajanapadaṃ. Aṅguliṃ phoṭesunti aṅguliṃ cālesuṃ. Ambakāyāti itthikāya.

The term 'Nīla' (blue/dark) is here all-encompassing. 'Blue in color,' and so on, shows its divisions. In this context, their natural color is not blue; rather, this is said because they were smeared with blue unguent. 'Blue garments' means that their cloths, fine cloths, and silks were all blue. 'Blue ornaments' means they were adorned with blue gems and blue flowers. Their chariots, too, were studded with blue gems, draped in blue cloth, had blue banners, were furnished with blue armor, adorned with blue ornaments, and yoked with blue horses; even their goad-sticks were blue. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances. 'Parivaṭṭesi' means he struck. In 'Kiṃ je ambapālī,' 'je' is a term of address, meaning, 'Venerable Ambapālī, for what reason?' There is also the reading 'Kiñcā,' which has the same meaning here. 'Sāhāraṃ' means with its countryside. 'Aṅguliṃ phoṭesuṃ' means they snapped their fingers. 'Ambakāya' refers to the woman.

Yesanti karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, yehi adiṭṭhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Olokethāti passatha. Avalokethāti punappunaṃ passatha. Upasaṃharathāti upanetha. Imaṃ licchaviparisaṃ tumhākaṃ cittena tāvatiṃsasadisaṃ upasaṃharatha upanetha allīyāpetha. Yatheva tāvatiṃsā abhirūpā pāsādikā nīlādinānāvaṇṇā, evamime licchavirājānopīti tāvatiṃsehi samake katvā passathāti attho.

The genitive 'yesaṃ' is used here in the sense of the instrumental ('karaṇa'), meaning 'by whom it has not been seen.' 'Oloketha' means 'look.' 'Avaloketha' means 'look again and again.' 'Upasaṃharatha' means 'bring near.' The meaning is: 'Bring this assembly of the Licchavis near to your minds, apply it to them, making them similar to the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods are beautiful, pleasing, and of various colors such as blue, so too should you see these Licchavi kings as being equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.'

Kasmā pana bhagavā anekasatehi suttehi cakkhādīnaṃ rūpādīsu nimittaggāhaṃ paṭisedhetvā idha mahantena ussāhena nimittaggāhe uyyojetīti? Hitakāmatāya. Tatra kira ekacce bhikkhū osannavīriyā, tesaṃ [M 2.0136] sampattiyā palobhento – “appamādena samaṇadhammaṃ karontānaṃ evarūpā issariyasampatti sulabhā”ti samaṇadhamme ussāhajananatthaṃ āha. Aniccalakkhaṇavibhāvanatthañcāpi [P 2.0546] evamāha. Nacirasseva hi sabbepime ajātasattussa vasena vināsaṃ pāpuṇissanti. Atha nesaṃ rajjasirisampattiṃ disvā ṭhitabhikkhū – “tathārūpāyapi nāma [V 2.0122] sirisampattiyā vināso paññāyissatī”ti aniccalakkhaṇaṃ bhāvetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇissantīti aniccalakkhaṇavibhāvanatthaṃ āha.

But why does the Blessed One, after having prohibited in hundreds of suttas the grasping of signs in forms and so on, here encourage the grasping of signs with great effort? Out of a desire for their welfare. For it seems that some monks there were lacking in energy. To entice them with this attainment—'Such sovereign splendor is easily gained by those who practice the ascetic's duties with diligence'—he spoke to arouse energy for the ascetic's duties. And he also spoke thus for the purpose of making manifest the characteristic of impermanence. For before long, all these Licchavis will come to destruction on account of Ajātasattu. Then, monks who are established, seeing their royal glory and prosperity, will think, 'The destruction of even such glorious prosperity will become apparent,' and by developing the characteristic of impermanence, they will attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thus, he spoke for the purpose of making manifest the characteristic of impermanence.

Adhivāsetūti ambapāliyā nimantitabhāvaṃ ñatvāpi kasmā nimantentīti? Asaddahanatāya ceva vattasīsena ca. Sā hi dhuttā itthī animantetvāpi nimantemīti vadeyyāti tesaṃ cittaṃ ahosi, dhammaṃ sutvā gamanakāle ca nimantetvā gamanaṃ nāma manussānaṃ vattameva.

Why did they invite the Blessed One, even though they knew that Ambapālī had already invited him? Because of their disbelief and because it was their custom. For this was their thought: 'She is a wanton woman; she might say, "I have invited him," even without having done so.' Furthermore, it is indeed the custom for people to extend an invitation at the time of departure after having heard the Dhamma.

Veḷuvagāmavassūpagamanavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of Entering the Rains-Residence at Veḷuvagāma

163. Veḷuvagāmakoti vesāliyā samīpe veḷuvagāmo. Yathāmittantiādīsu mittā mittāva. Sandiṭṭhāti tattha tattha saṅgamma diṭṭhamattā nātidaḷhamittā. Sambhattāti suṭṭhu bhattā sinehavanto daḷhamittā. Yesaṃ yesaṃ yattha yattha evarūpā bhikkhū atthi, te te tattha tattha vassaṃ upethāti attho. Kasmā evamāha? Tesaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya. Tesañhi veḷuvagāmake senāsanaṃ nappahoti, bhikkhāpi mandā. Samantā vesāliyā pana bahūni senāsanāni, bhikkhāpi sulabhā, tasmā evamāha. Atha kasmā – “yathāsukhaṃ gacchathā”ti na vissajjesi? Tesaṃ anukampāya. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ahaṃ dasamāsamattaṃ ṭhatvā parinibbāyissāmi, sace ime dūraṃ gacchissanti, mama parinibbānakāle daṭṭhuṃ na sakkhissanti. Atha nesaṃ – “satthā parinibbāyanto amhākaṃ satimattampi na adāsi, sace jāneyyāma, evaṃ na dūre vaseyyāmā”ti vippaṭisāro bhaveyya. Vesāliyā samantā pana vasantā māsassa aṭṭha vāre āgantvā dhammaṃ suṇissanti, sugatovādaṃ labhissantī”ti na vissajjesi.

163. Veḷuvagāma is a village near Vesālī. In the phrase 'yathāmittantiādīsu,' 'mittā' simply means friends. 'Sandiṭṭhā' refers to those who, having met here and there, are merely acquaintances, not very firm friends. 'Sambhattā' means those who are well-devoted, affectionate, and firm friends. The meaning is: for whichever monks, in whichever place, there are such friends, those monks should enter the rains-residence in that place. Why did he speak thus? For the sake of their comfortable dwelling. For in Veḷuvagāma, lodging was insufficient, and alms-food was scarce. Around Vesālī, however, there were many lodgings, and alms-food was easy to obtain; therefore, he spoke thus. Then why did he not dismiss them by saying, 'Go as you please'? Out of compassion for them. It is said that this was his thought: 'I will attain final Nibbāna after about ten months. If these monks go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my final Nibbāna. Then they might have remorse, thinking, "The Teacher, when attaining final Nibbāna, did not give us even a reminder. Had we known, we would not have stayed so far away." But if they dwell around Vesālī, they can come eight times a month to listen to the Dhamma and receive the Sugata’s teaching.' For this reason, he did not dismiss them.

164. Kharoti pharuso. Ābādhoti visabhāgarogo. Bāḷhāti balavatiyo. Māraṇantikāti maraṇantaṃ maraṇasantikaṃ pāpanasamatthā. Sato sampajāno adhivāsesīti satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā adhivāsesi. Avihaññamānoti vedanānuvattanavasena aparāparaṃ [M 2.0137] parivattanaṃ akaronto apīḷiyamāno adukkhiyamānova adhivāsesi[P 2.0547]. Anāmantetvāti ajānāpetvā. Anapaloketvāti na apaloketvā ovādānusāsaniṃ adatvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vīriyenāti pubbabhāgavīriyena ceva phalasamāpattivīriyena ca. Paṭipaṇāmetvāti vikkhambhetvā. Jīvitasaṅkhāranti ettha jīvitampi jīvitasaṅkhāro. Yena jīvitaṃ saṅkhariyati chijjamānaṃ ghaṭetvā ṭhapiyati, so phalasamāpattidhammopi jīvitasaṅkhāro. So idha adhippeto. Adhiṭṭhāyāti [V 2.0123] adhiṭṭhahitvā pavattetvā, jīvitaṭṭhapanasamatthaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjeyyanti ayamettha saṅkhepattho.

164. ‘Kharo’ means harsh. ‘Ābādho’ refers to a disease of elemental imbalance. ‘Bāḷhā’ means strong. ‘Māraṇantikā’ means capable of leading to death, close to death. ‘He endured, mindful and fully aware’ means that having established mindfulness well and having defined the experience with wisdom, he endured. ‘Without being troubled’ means he endured without tossing and turning in accordance with the arising of feelings, being neither oppressed nor afflicted by them. ‘Without having addressed’ means without having informed. ‘Without having taken leave’ means without having taken leave or given his final counsel and instruction. ‘By means of energy’ refers to both the preliminary energy and the energy of the attainment of fruition. ‘Having pushed it back’ means having suppressed it. Regarding ‘the life-formation’: here, life itself is a life-formation. Also, that principle of the attainment of fruition by which life, when it is being cut off, is repaired and maintained, is a life-formation. This latter meaning is intended here. ‘Having resolved’ means having made a resolution and sustained it, thinking, ‘May I enter the attainment of fruition that is capable of maintaining life.’ This is the meaning in brief.

Kiṃ pana bhagavā ito pubbe phalasamāpattiṃ na samāpajjatīti? Samāpajjati. Sā pana khaṇikasamāpatti. Khaṇikasamāpatti ca antosamāpattiyaṃyeva vedanaṃ vikkhambheti, samāpattito vuṭṭhitamattassa kaṭṭhapātena vā kaṭhalapātena vā chinnasevālo viya udakaṃ puna sarīraṃ vedanā ajjhottharati. Yā pana rūpasattakaṃ arūpasattakañca niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā mahāvipassanāvasena samāpannā samāpatti, sā suṭṭhu vikkhambheti. Yathā nāma purisena pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā hatthehi ca pādehi ca suṭṭhu apabyūḷho sevālo cirena udakaṃ ottharati; evameva tato vuṭṭhitassa cirena vedanā uppajjati. Iti bhagavā taṃ divasaṃ mahābodhipallaṅke abhinavavipassanaṃ paṭṭhapento viya rūpasattakaṃ arūpasattakaṃ niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā cuddasahākārehi sannetvā mahāvipassanāya vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā – “dasamāse mā uppajjitthā”ti samāpattiṃ samāpajji. Samāpattivikkhambhitā vedanā dasamāse na uppajji yeva.

But did the Blessed One not enter upon fruition attainment before this? He did. But that was momentary attainment. Momentary attainment suppresses feeling only within the attainment itself. For one who has just emerged from the attainment, feeling floods the body again, just as water covers a spot where algae has been parted by the fall of a stick or a potsherd. However, the attainment entered by way of great insight—after having made the septad of form and the septad of formlessness free of thickets and tangles—suppresses it well. Just as when a man, having entered a pond, thoroughly pushes aside the algae with his hands and feet, the water is covered again only after a long time; even so, for one who has emerged from that attainment, feeling arises only after a long time. Thus, on that day, as if establishing fresh insight upon the great seat of enlightenment, the Blessed One, having made the septad of form and the septad of formlessness free of thickets and tangles and having investigated them with fourteen modes, suppressed feeling by means of great insight and entered the attainment with the resolve, 'May it not arise for ten months.' The feeling, suppressed by the attainment, did not arise at all for ten months.

Gilānā vuṭṭhitoti gilāno hutvā puna vuṭṭhito. Madhurakajāto viyāti sañjātagarubhāvo sañjātathaddhabhāvo sūle uttāsitapuriso viya. Na pakkhāyantīti nappakāsanti, nānākārato na upaṭṭhahanti. Dhammāpi maṃ na paṭibhantīti satipaṭṭhānādidhammā mayhaṃ pākaṭā na hontīti dīpeti. Tantidhammā pana therassa supaguṇā. Na udāharatīti pacchimaṃ ovādaṃ na deti. Taṃ sandhāya vadati.

'Gilānā vuṭṭhito' means having been ill and then having recovered. 'As if become stiff' means having become heavy and rigid, like a man terrified by an impaling stake. 'Na pakkhāyanti' means they do not appear clearly, they do not present themselves in various ways. 'Even the teachings do not occur to me' shows: 'The teachings such as the foundations of mindfulness are not clear to me.' The textual teachings, however, were very familiar to the elder. 'He does not speak' means He does not give a final exhortation. He (Ānanda) speaks with reference to that.

165. Anantaraṃ [M 2.0138] abāhiranti dhammavasena vā puggalavasena vā ubhayaṃ akatvā. “Ettakaṃ dhammaṃ parassa na desessāmī”ti [P 2.0548] hi cintento dhammaṃ abbhantaraṃ karoti nāma. “Ettakaṃ parassa desessāmī”ti cintento dhammaṃ bāhiraṃ karoti nāma. “Imassa puggalassa desessāmī”ti cintento pana puggalaṃ abbhantaraṃ karoti nāma. “Imassa na desessāmī”ti cintento puggalaṃ bāhiraṃ karoti nāma. Evaṃ akatvā desitoti attho. Ācariyamuṭṭhīti yathā bāhirakānaṃ ācariyamuṭṭhi nāma hoti. Daharakāle kassaci akathetvā pacchimakāle maraṇamañce nipannā piyamanāpassa antevāsikassa kathenti, evaṃ tathāgatassa – “idaṃ mahallakakāle pacchimaṭṭhāne kathessāmī”ti muṭṭhiṃ katvā “pariharissāmī”ti ṭhapitaṃ kiñci natthīti dasseti.

165. 'Anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ' means not having made anything inner or outer, either with respect to the teaching or with respect to persons. For one who thinks, 'I will not teach this much of the teaching to another,' is said to make the teaching internal. One who thinks, 'I will teach this much to another,' is said to make the teaching external. Furthermore, one who thinks, 'I will teach this person,' is said to make the person internal. One who thinks, 'I will not teach this person,' is said to make the person external. The meaning is that He taught without doing so. 'Ācariyamuṭṭhi' (teacher's fist): just as among outsiders there is what is called a 'teacher's fist.' Having told nothing to anyone in their youth, when lying on their deathbed in their final time, they tell it to a dear and beloved disciple. It is shown that, similarly, there is nothing set aside by the Tathāgata, who, having made a 'fist' with the thought, 'I will teach this in my old age, at the final stage,' would think, 'I will carry it thus.'

Ahaṃ [V 2.0124] bhikkhusaṅghanti ahameva bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmīti vā mamuddesikoti ahaṃ uddisitabbaṭṭhena uddeso assāti mamuddesiko. Maṃyeva uddisitvā mama paccāsīsamāno bhikkhusaṅgho hotu, mama accayena vā mā ahesuṃ, yaṃ vā taṃ vā hotūti iti vā yassa assāti attho. Na evaṃ hotīti bodhipallaṅkeyeva issāmacchariyānaṃ vihatattā evaṃ na hoti. Sa kinti so kiṃ. Āsītikoti asītisaṃvacchariko. Idaṃ pacchimavayaanuppattabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Veṭhamissakenāti bāhabandhacakkabandhādinā paṭisaṅkharaṇena veṭhamissakena. Maññeti jiṇṇasakaṭaṃ viya veṭhamissakena maññe yāpeti. Arahattaphalaveṭhanena catuiriyāpathakappanaṃ tathāgatassa hotīti dasseti.

'Ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmi' means 'I alone will lead the Saṅgha of monks.' Or 'mamuddesiko': the Saṅgha is 'one that looks to me' because I am the one to be pointed to, in the sense of being the one to be designated. The meaning is for one who might think: 'May the Saṅgha of monks exist looking only to me, expecting from me; or after my passing, may they cease to be, or may they become whatever they will.' It is not so: because envy and stinginess were destroyed at the very seat of enlightenment, it is not so for him. 'Sa kiṃ' is 'so kiṃ' (what then?). 'Āsītiko' means eighty years of age. This is said to show the fact of having reached the final stage of life. 'Veṭhamissakena' means with a binding, with repairs such as straps for the shafts and rims. 'Maññe' means: 'like an old cart, I think it keeps going with the help of bindings.' He shows that for the Tathāgata, the maintenance of the four postures occurs by means of the binding that is the fruit of Arahantship.

Idāni tamatthaṃ pakāsento yasmiṃ, ānanda, samayetiādimāha. Tattha sabbanimittānanti rūpanimittādīnaṃ. Ekaccānaṃ vedanānanti lokiyānaṃ vedanānaṃ. Tasmātihānandāti yasmā iminā phalasamāpattivihārena phāsu hoti, tasmā tumhepi tadatthāya evaṃ viharathāti dasseti. Attadīpāti mahāsamuddagatadīpaṃ viya attānaṃ dīpaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ katvā viharatha. Attasaraṇāti attagatikāva hotha, mā aññagatikā. Dhammadīpadhammasaraṇapadesupi eseva nayo. Tamataggeti tamaagge. Majjhe takāro padasandhivasena vutto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ime aggatamāti tamataggā”ti. Evaṃ sabbaṃ tamayogaṃ chinditvā ativiya agge uttamabhāve ete[M 2.0139], ānanda[P 2.0549], mama bhikkhū bhavissanti. Tesaṃ atiagge bhavissanti, ye keci sikkhākāmā, sabbepi te catusatipaṭṭhānagocarāva bhikkhū agge bhavissantīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Now, to clarify that meaning, He said, 'At that time, Ānanda,' and so on. Therein, 'of all signs' means of the signs of form and so on. 'Of certain feelings' means of worldly feelings. 'Therefore, Ānanda': it is shown that because one is at ease through this abiding in the attainment of fruition, 'Therefore, you too should abide in this way for that purpose.' 'Be islands unto yourselves': having made the self an island, a support, like an island in the great ocean, you should abide. 'Be your own refuge': be ones who have the self as your resort, not another as your resort. This is the same method for the phrases 'the Dhamma as your island' and 'the Dhamma as your refuge.' As for 'tamatagge,' the division of the words is 'tama-agge.' The 't' in the middle is spoken for the sake of euphonic combination. This is what is said: 'These are the most excellent (aggatamā), therefore they are tamataggā.' Or, the meaning is: 'Thus, Ānanda, having cut off all application of the superlative suffix (tamayoga), these monks of mine will be exceedingly excellent (agge), in the supreme state. Among all those who are desirous of training, they will be the most excellent. All those monks who have the four foundations of mindfulness as their pasture will be the highest.' Thus He concludes the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Dutiyabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second recitation portion is finished.

Nimittobhāsakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on the Radiance of the Sign.

166. Vesāliṃ piṇḍāya pāvisīti kadā pāvisi? Ukkacelato nikkhamitvā vesāliṃ gatakāle. Bhagavā kira vuṭṭhavasso veḷuvagāmakā nikkhamitvā sāvatthiṃ gamissāmīti āgatamaggeneva paṭinivattanto anupubbena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanaṃ pāvisi. Dhammasenāpati bhagavato vattaṃ dassetvā divāṭṭhānaṃ gato. So tattha antevāsikesu vattaṃ dassetvā paṭikkantesu divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā cammakkhaṇḍaṃ paññapetvā pāde pakkhāletvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā phalasamāpattiṃ [V 2.0125] pāvisi. Athassa yathāparicchedena tato vuṭṭhitassa ayaṃ parivitakko udapādi – “buddhā nu kho paṭhamaṃ parinibbāyanti, agasāvakā nu kho”ti? Tato – “aggasāvakā paṭhama”nti ñatvā attano āyusaṅkhāraṃ olokesi. So – “sattāhameva me āyusaṅkhāro pavattatī”ti ñatvā – “kattha parinibbāyissāmī”ti cintesi. Tato – “rāhulo tāvatiṃsesu parinibbuto, aññāsikoṇḍaññatthero chaddantadahe, ahaṃ kattha parinibbāyissāmī”ti puna cintento mātaraṃ ārabbha satiṃ uppādesi – “mayhaṃ mātā sattannaṃ arahantānaṃ mātā hutvāpi buddhadhammasaṅghesu appasannā, atthi nu kho tassā upanissayo, natthi nu kho”ti āvajjetvā sotāpattimaggassa upanissayaṃ disvā – “kassa desanāya abhisamayo bhavissatī”ti olokento – “mameva dhammadesanāya bhavissati, na aññassa. Sace kho panāhaṃ appossukko bhaveyyaṃ, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘sāriputtatthero avasesajanānampi avassayo hoti. Tathā hissa samacittasuttadesanādivase (a. ni. 1.37) koṭisatasahassadevatā arahattaṃ pattā[M 2.0140]. Tayo magge paṭividdhadevatānaṃ gaṇanā natthi. Aññesu ca ṭhānesu anekā abhisamayā [P 2.0550] dissanti. Thereva cittaṃ pasādetvā sagge nibbattāneva asītikulasahassāni. So dāni sakamātumicchādassanamattampi harituṃ nāsakkhī’ti. Tasmā mātaraṃ micchādassanā mocetvā jātovarakeyeva parinibbāyissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā – “ajjeva bhagavantaṃ anujānāpetvā nikkhamissāmī”ti cundattheraṃ āmantesi. “Āvuso, cunda, amhākaṃ pañcasatāya bhikkhuparisāya saññaṃ dehi – ‘gaṇhathāvuso pattacīvarāni, dhammasenāpati nāḷakagāmaṃ gantukāmo’ti”. Thero tathā akāsi. Bhikkhū senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya therassa santikaṃ āgamaṃsu. Thero senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā divāṭṭhānadvāre ṭhatvā divāṭṭhānaṃ olokento – “idaṃ dāni pacchimadassanaṃ, puna āgamanaṃ natthī”ti pañcasatabhikkhuparivuto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā etadavoca –

166. Regarding the words, 'He entered Vesāli for alms,' when did he enter? When he had departed from Ukkacela and was on his way to Vesāli. It is said that the Blessed One, having completed the rains-residence, departed from Veḷuvagāmaka with the intention, 'I will go to Sāvatthī.' Returning by the same path he had come, he arrived in due course at Sāvatthī and entered Jetavana. The General of the Dhamma, having attended to his duties for the Blessed One, went to his daytime dwelling. There, having instructed his resident pupils in their duties and after they had departed, he swept the daytime dwelling, spread out a piece of leather, washed his feet, sat with his legs crossed, and entered the attainment of fruition. Then, having emerged from it after the determined period, this reflection arose in him: 'Do the Buddhas attain final Nibbāna first, or do the chief disciples?' Then, knowing, 'The chief disciples attain it first,' he examined his own life-formation. Realizing, 'My life-formation will continue for only seven days,' he considered, 'Where shall I attain final Nibbāna?' Then, reflecting further, 'Rāhula attained final Nibbāna in Tāvatiṃsa, the elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña at the Chaddanta Lake; where shall I attain final Nibbāna?' he brought his mother to mind and this thought arose: 'My mother, despite being the mother of seven arahants, is not confident in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Does she have the supporting condition for awakening, or not?' Having reflected thus, he saw that she had the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry. Considering, 'Through whose teaching will her realization occur?' he saw, 'It will occur through my own teaching, not another’s. But if I were to be unconcerned, there will be those who say of me: “The elder Sāriputta is a refuge even for other people. For instance, on the day he taught the Samacittasutta, a hundred thousand koṭis of devas attained arahantship. The number of devas who penetrated the three lower paths is countless. And in other places, many realizations are seen. Merely by gaining confidence in the elder, eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven. Yet now he was unable to remove even the wrong view of his own mother.” Therefore, I will free my mother from wrong view and attain final Nibbāna in the very chamber where I was born.' Having made this resolution, he thought, 'Today itself I will ask for the Blessed One’s permission and depart.' He then addressed the elder Cunda: 'Friend Cunda, give the signal to our company of five hundred bhikkhus: “Friends, take your bowls and robes; the General of the Dhamma wishes to go to the village of Nāḷaka.”' The elder did so. The bhikkhus, having put their lodgings in order, took their bowls and robes and came to the elder’s presence. The elder, having put his lodging in order and swept his daytime dwelling, stood at the doorway of the daytime dwelling and, looking at it, thought, 'This is now the final sight; there will be no return.' Surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said this:

“Chinno dāni bhavissāmi, lokanātha mahāmuni;

Gamanāgamanaṃ natthi, pacchimā vandanā ayaṃ.

“Now I shall be cut off, O Great Sage, Protector of the World; there is no more coming or going, this is my last homage.

Jīvitaṃ appakaṃ mayhaṃ, ito sattāhamaccaye;

Nikkhipeyyāmahaṃ dehaṃ, bhāravoropanaṃ yathā.

My life is short; in seven days hence, I shall lay down this body, like setting down a burden.

Anujānātu me bhante, bhagavā, anujānātu sugato;

Parinibbānakālo me, ossaṭṭho āyusaṅkhāro”ti.

Venerable sir, may the Blessed One grant me leave, may the Sugata grant me leave; the time for my Parinibbāna has come, my life-formation is relinquished.”

Buddhā [V 2.0126] pana yasmā “parinibbāhī”ti vutte maraṇasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ saṃvaṇṇenti nāma, “mā parinibbāhī”ti vutte vaṭṭassa guṇaṃ kathentīti micchādiṭṭhikā dosaṃ āropessanti, tasmā tadubhayampi na vadanti. Tena naṃ bhagavā āha – “kattha parinibbāyissasi sāriputtā”ti? “Atthi, bhante, magadhesu nāḷakagāme jātovarako, tatthāhaṃ parinibbāyissāmī”ti vutte “yassa dāni tvaṃ, sāriputta, kālaṃ maññasi, idāni pana te jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhabhātikānaṃ tādisassa bhikkhuno dassanaṃ dullabhaṃ bhavissatīti desehi tesaṃ dhamma”nti āha.

Now, because if it were said, 'You should attain Parinibbāna,' the Buddhas would be, as it were, praising death, and if it were said, 'You should not attain Parinibbāna,' they would be speaking of the virtue of the round of existence, those of wrong view would find fault. Therefore, they say neither of these two things. For that reason, the Blessed One said to him: 'Where will you attain final Nibbāna, Sāriputta?' 'Venerable sir, in the land of the Magadhans, in the village of Nāḷaka, there is the chamber where I was born. There I will attain final Nibbāna.' When this was said, the Blessed One replied: 'Sāriputta, you may do now what you deem the time for. However, for your elder and younger brothers, the sight of such a bhikkhu will henceforth be difficult to obtain. Therefore, teach them the Dhamma.'

Thero – “satthā mayhaṃ iddhivikubbanapubbaṅgamaṃ dhammadesanaṃ paccāsīsatī”ti ñatvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā tālappamāṇaṃ abbhuggantvā puna oruyha bhagavantaṃ vanditvā [P 2.0551] sattatālappamāṇe [M 2.0141] antalikkhe ṭhito iddhivikubbanaṃ dassetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Sakalanagaraṃ sannipati. Thero oruyha bhagavantaṃ vanditvā “gamanakālo me, bhante”ti āha. Bhagavā “dhammasenāpatiṃ paṭipādessāmī”ti dhammāsanā uṭṭhāya gandhakuṭiabhimukho gantvā maṇiphalake aṭṭhāsi. Thero tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā – “bhagavā ito kappasatasahassādhikassa asaṅkhyeyyassa upari anomadassisammāsambuddhassa pādamūle nipatitvā tumhākaṃ dassanaṃ patthesiṃ. Sā me patthanā samiddhā, diṭṭhā tumhe, taṃ paṭhamadassanaṃ, idaṃ pacchimadassanaṃ. Puna tumhākaṃ dassanaṃ natthī”ti – vatvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha yāva dassanavisayo, tāva abhimukhova paṭikkamitvā “ito paṭṭhāya cutipaṭisandhivasena kismiñci ṭhāne gamanāgamanaṃ nāma natthī”ti vanditvā pakkāmi. Udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahābhūmicālo ahosi. Bhagavā parivāretvā ṭhite bhikkhū āha – “anugacchatha, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātika”nti. Bhikkhū yāva dvārakoṭṭhakā agamaṃsu. Thero – “tiṭṭhatha, tumhe āvuso, appamattā hothā”ti nivattāpetvā attano parisāyeva saddhiṃ pakkāmi. Manussā – “pubbe ayyo paccāgamanacārikaṃ carati, idaṃ dāni gamanaṃ na puna paccāgamanāyā”ti paridevantā anubandhiṃsu. Tepi “appamattā hotha āvuso, evaṃbhāvino nāma saṅkhārā”ti nivattāpesi.

The elder, knowing, “The Teacher expects me to teach the Dhamma, preceded by a display of psychic power,” paid homage to the Blessed One, rose into the air to the height of a palm tree, descended again, paid homage to the Blessed One, stood in the sky at a height of seven palm trees, displayed psychic powers, and then taught the Dhamma. The entire city gathered. The elder descended, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, “Venerable sir, it is time for me to go.” The Blessed One, thinking, “I will see the General of the Dhamma off,” rose from the Dhamma seat and stood on the jeweled slab facing the Fragrant Chamber. The elder circumambulated three times, paid homage in four places, and said: “O Blessed One, more than an incalculable aeon and a hundred thousand aeons ago, at the feet of Anomadassi, the Perfectly Enlightened One, I fell down and aspired to see you. That aspiration of mine has been fulfilled—I have seen you. That was the first sight, this is the last. There will be no seeing you again.” Having spoken thus, he raised his joined hands, shining with the radiance of his fingernails, and stepped backward as far as the range of vision allowed. He then said, “From now on, there will be no coming or going by way of rebirth in any place,” paid homage, and departed. A great earthquake occurred, reaching to the water’s limit. The Blessed One said to the monks who stood surrounding him, “Monks, follow your elder brother.” The monks followed him as far as the gatehouse. The elder said, “Stay, friends, be heedful,” and turned them back, departing only with his own retinue. The people lamented, “Before, the venerable one would make return journeys, but now he goes, never to return,” and followed him. He turned them back too, saying, “Be heedful, friends, such is the nature of conditioned things.”

Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto antarāmagge sattāhaṃ manussānaṃ anuggahaṃ karonto sāyaṃ nāḷakagāmaṃ patvā gāmadvāre nigrodharukkhamūle aṭṭhāsi. Atha uparevato nāma therassa bhāgineyyo bahigāmaṃ gacchanto theraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Thero taṃ āha – “atthi gehe te ayyikā”ti? Āma, bhanteti. Gaccha amhākaṃ idhāgatabhāvaṃ ārocehi. “Kasmā āgato”ti ca vutte “ajja kira ekadivasaṃ antogāme bhavissati, jātovarakaṃ paṭijaggatha, pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ jānāthā”ti. So gantvā “ayyike, mayhaṃ mātulo [V 2.0127] āgato”ti āha. Idāni kuhinti? Gāmadvāreti. Ekakova, aññopi koci atthīti[P 2.0552]? Atthi pañcasatā bhikkhūti. Kiṃ kāraṇā āgatoti? So taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Brāhmaṇī – “kiṃ nu kho ettakānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggāpeti[M 2.0142], daharakāle pabbajitvā mahallakakāle gihī hotukāmo”ti cintentī jātovarakaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kāretvā daṇḍadīpikāyo jāletvā therassa pāhesi.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, after helping people along the way for seven days, arrived in the evening at the village of Nāḷaka and stood at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate. Then a nephew of the elder named Uparevata, while going out of the village, saw the elder, approached him, paid homage, and stood there. The elder said to him: “Is your grandmother at home?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Go and inform her of our arrival here.” And if asked, “Why has he come?” say, “It seems he will stay in the village for one day today. Prepare the birth chamber and ascertain a dwelling place for five hundred monks.” He went and said, “Grandmother, my uncle has come.” “Where is he now?” “At the village gate.” “Is he alone, or is there someone else?” “There are five hundred monks.” “What is the reason for his coming?” He told her the matter. The brahmin woman thought, “Why does he ask for a dwelling place to be prepared for so many? Having gone forth in youth, does he now wish to become a householder in old age?” But she had the birth chamber prepared and arranged a dwelling place for the five hundred monks. She lit torches and sent them to the elder.

Thero bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Abhiruhitvā ca jātovarakaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Nisajjeva – “tumhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchathā”ti bhikkhū uyyojesi. Tesu gatamattesuyeva therassa kharo ābādho uppajji, lohitapakkhandikā māraṇantikā vedanā vattanti, ekaṃ bhājanaṃ pavisati, ekaṃ nikkhamati. Brāhmaṇī – “mama puttassa pavatti mayhaṃ na ruccatī”ti attano vasanagabbhadvāraṃ nissāya aṭṭhāsi. Cattāro mahārājāno “dhammasenāpati kuhiṃ viharatī”ti olokentā “nāḷakagāme jātovarake parinibbānamañce nipanno, pacchimadassanaṃ gamissāmā”ti āgamma vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Thero – ke tumheti? Mahārājāno, bhanteti. Kasmā āgatatthāti? Gilānupaṭṭhākā bhavissāmāti. Hotu, atthi gilānupaṭṭhāko, gacchatha tumheti uyyojesi. Tesaṃ gatāvasāne teneva nayena sakko devānamindo, tasmiṃ gate suyāmādayo mahābrahmā ca āgamiṃsu. Tepi tatheva thero uyyojesi.

The elder ascended the mansion with the monks. Having ascended, he entered the lying-in chamber and sat down. As soon as he sat down, he dismissed the monks, saying, “Go to your dwelling place.” Just as they had left, a severe illness arose in the elder—bloody dysentery, bringing death near, with one vessel filling, and another emptying. The brahmin woman, thinking, “I do not approve of my son’s behavior,” stood leaning against the door of her own chamber. The Four Great Kings, looking to see, “Where is the General of the Dhamma staying?” perceived, “He is lying on the deathbed in the lying-in chamber at Nāḷaka village. Let us go for a final sight of him.” They approached, paid homage, and stood there. The elder asked, “Who are you?” “The Great Kings, venerable sir.” “Why have you come?” “To attend to you in your illness.” “Let it be, there is an attendant. You may go,” and he dismissed them. After they had left, in the same manner, Sakka, the king of the gods, came. When he had gone, Suyāma and the other devas, and the Great Brahmā, arrived. The elder dismissed them in the same way.

Brāhmaṇī devatānaṃ āgamanañca gamanañca disvā – “ke nu kho ete mama puttaṃ vanditvā gacchantī”ti therassa gabbhadvāraṃ gantvā – “tāta, cunda, kā pavattī”ti pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā – “mahāupāsikā, bhante āgatā”ti āha. Thero kasmā avelāya āgatatthāti pucchi. Sā tuyhaṃ tāta dassanatthāyāti vatvā “tāta ke paṭhamaṃ āgatā”ti pucchi. Cattāro mahārājāno, upāsiketi. Tāta, tvaṃ catūhi mahārājehi mahantataroti? Ārāmikasadisā ete upāsike, amhākaṃ satthu paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya khaggahatthā hutvā ārakkhaṃ akaṃsūti. Tesaṃ tāta, gatāvasāne ko āgatoti? Sakko devānamindoti. Devarājatopi tvaṃ tāta, mahantataroti? Bhaṇḍagāhakasāmaṇerasadiso [P 2.0553] esa upāsike, amhākaṃ satthu tāvatiṃsato otaraṇakāle pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā otiṇṇoti. Tassa tāta gatāvasāne jotamāno viya ko āgatoti? Upāsike tuyhaṃ bhagavā ca satthā ca mahābrahmā nāma esoti. Mayhaṃ bhagavato mahābrahmatopi tvaṃ tāta mahantataroti? Āma upāsike, ete nāma kira amhākaṃ satthu [M 2.0143] jātadivase cattāro mahābrahmāno mahāpurisaṃ suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsūti.

The brahmin woman, seeing the deities coming and going, thought, 'Who can these be who pay homage to my son and then depart?' She went to the elder’s chamber door and asked, 'Dear Cunda, what is happening?' He explained the matter and then said to the elder, 'Venerable sir, the great laywoman has arrived.' The elder asked, 'Why have you come at this untimely hour?' She replied, 'Dear son, I have come to see you,' and then asked, 'Dear son, who came first?' 'The Four Great Kings, laywoman.' 'Dear son, are you greater than the Four Great Kings?' 'They are like monastery attendants, laywoman. From the time of our Teacher’s conception, they stood guard with swords in hand.' 'Dear son, after they left, who came?' 'Sakka, the lord of the gods.' 'Dear son, are you greater even than the king of the gods?' 'He is like a novice who carries the requisites, laywoman. When our Teacher descended from Tāvatiṃsa, he was the one who descended carrying the bowl and robe.' 'Dear son, after he left, who was it that came, shining brightly?' 'Laywoman, this was the one named Mahābrahmā, who is your lord and teacher.' 'Dear son, are you greater even than my lord, Mahābrahmā?' 'Yes, laywoman. Indeed, it is said that on the day of our Teacher's birth, four such Mahābrahmās received the Great Being in a golden net.'

Atha [V 2.0128] brāhmaṇiyā – “puttassa tāva me ayaṃ ānubhāvo, kīdiso vata mayhaṃ puttassa bhagavato satthu ānubhāvo bhavissatī”ti cintayantiyā sahasā pañcavaṇṇā pīti uppajjitvā sakalasarīre phari. Thero – “uppannaṃ me mātu pītisomanassaṃ, ayaṃ dāni kālo dhammadesanāyā”ti cintetvā – “kiṃ cintesi mahāupāsike”ti āha. Sā – “puttassa tāva me ayaṃ guṇo, satthu panassa kīdiso guṇo bhavissatīti idaṃ, tāta, cintemī”ti āha. Mahāupāsike, mayhaṃ satthu jātakkhaṇe, mahābhinikkhamane, sambodhiyaṃ, dhammacakkappavattane ca dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha, sīlena samādhinā paññāya vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanena samo nāma natthi, itipi so bhagavāti vitthāretvā buddhaguṇappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammadesanaṃ kathesi.

Then, as the brahmin woman was thinking, 'If this is the spiritual power of my son, what must be the spiritual power of my son’s Teacher, the Blessed One!', joy of five kinds suddenly arose and pervaded her entire body. The elder, thinking, 'Joy and gladness have arisen in my mother; now is the time for a discourse on the Dhamma,' asked, 'Great laywoman, what are you thinking?' She replied, 'Dear son, I am thinking this: if this is the quality of my son, what must be the quality of his Teacher?' 'Great laywoman, at the moment of my Teacher’s birth, at his great renunciation, at his full enlightenment, and at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system quaked. In virtue, in concentration, in wisdom, in liberation, and in the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no one equal to him. For these reasons also, he is the Blessed One.' Thus elaborating, he gave a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the qualities of the Buddha.

Brāhmaṇī piyaputtassa dhammadesanāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya puttaṃ āha – “tāta, upatissa, kasmā evamakāsi, evarūpaṃ nāma amataṃ mayhaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ na adāsī”ti. Thero – “dinnaṃ dāni me mātu rūpasāriyā brāhmaṇiyā posāvanikamūlaṃ, ettakena vaṭṭissatī”ti cintetvā “gaccha mahāupāsike”ti brāhmaṇiṃ uyyojetvā “cunda kā velā”ti āha. Balavapaccūsakālo, bhanteti. Tena hi bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātehīti. Sannipatito, bhante, saṅghoti. Maṃ ukkhipitvā nisīdāpehi cundāti ukkhipitvā nisīdāpesi. Thero bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso catucattālīsaṃ vo vassāni mayā saddhiṃ vicarantānaṃ yaṃ me kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā na rocetha, khamatha taṃ āvusoti. Ettakaṃ, bhante, amhākaṃ chāyā viya tumhe amuñcitvā vicarantānaṃ aruccanakaṃ nāma natthi, tumhe pana amhākaṃ khamathāti. Atha [P 2.0554] thero aruṇasikhāya paññāyamānāya mahāpathaviṃ unnādayanto anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Bahū devamanussā therassa parinibbāne sakkāraṃ kariṃsu.

At the conclusion of her beloved son’s Dhamma discourse, the brahmin woman, having become established in the fruit of stream-entry, said to her son: 'Dear Upatissa, why have you done this? Why for so long did you not give me such deathlessness?' The elder, thinking, 'Now the payment for my upbringing has been given by me to my mother, the brahmin woman Rūpasārī; this much will suffice,' sent the brahmin woman away, saying, 'You may go, great laywoman.' Then he asked, 'Cunda, what is the time?' 'Venerable sir, it is the hour just before dawn.' 'In that case, assemble the community of monks.' 'Venerable sir, the community is assembled.' 'Cunda, lift me up and help me to sit.' He lifted him and helped him to sit. The elder addressed the monks: 'Friends, in the forty-four years you have wandered with me, if there was any action of mine, bodily or verbal, that did not please you, forgive me for it, friends.' 'Venerable sir, for us who have wandered with you for so long, never leaving you, like a shadow, there is nothing at all that was not pleasing. Rather, may you, venerable sir, forgive us.' Then, as the first light of dawn appeared, the elder, causing the great earth to resound, attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue. Many gods and humans paid homage at the elder's final passing.

Āyasmā [M 2.0144] cundo therassa pattacīvarañca dhātuparissāvanañca gahetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā ānandattheraṃ gahetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami. Bhagavā dhātuparissāvanaṃ gahetvā pañcahi gāthāsatehi therassa guṇaṃ kathetvā dhātucetiyaṃ kārāpetvā rājagahagamanatthāya ānandattherassa saññaṃ adāsi. Thero bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi. Bhagavā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto rājagahaṃ agamāsi. Tattha gatakāle mahāmoggallānatthero parinibbāyi. Bhagavā tassa dhātuyo gahetvā cetiyaṃ kārāpetvā rājagahato nikkhamitvā anupubbena gaṅgābhimukho gantvā ukkacelaṃ agamāsi. Tattha gaṅgātīre bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto nisīditvā tattha sāriputtamoggallānānaṃ parinibbānappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ suttaṃ desetvā ukkacelato nikkhamitvā vesāliṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ gate atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ [V 2.0129] nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya vesāliṃ piṇḍāya pāvisīti ayamettha anupubbī kathā.

The Venerable Cunda, taking the elder’s bowl and robe and the water-strainer containing the relics, went to Jetavana, and taking the Venerable Ānanda with him, he approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking the water-strainer with the relics, spoke of the elder’s qualities in five hundred verses, had a relic stupa built, and gave a sign to the Venerable Ānanda for the journey to Rājagaha. The elder informed the monks. The Blessed One, surrounded by the great community of monks, went to Rājagaha. Upon his arrival there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained final Nibbāna. The Blessed One, taking his relics, had a stupa built, and departing from Rājagaha, he journeyed in stages towards the Ganges and arrived at Ukkacelā. There, on the bank of the Ganges, surrounded by the community of monks, he sat down and delivered a discourse connected with the final Nibbāna of Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Then, departing from Ukkacelā, he went to Vesālī. Having gone there, the Blessed One dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms—this is the sequential narrative here.

Nisīdananti ettha cammakkhaṇḍaṃ adhippetaṃ. Udenacetiyanti udenayakkhassa cetiyaṭṭhāne katavihāro vuccati. Gotamakādīsupi eseva nayo. Bhāvitāti vaḍḍhitā. Bahulīkatāti punappunaṃ katā. Yānīkatāti yuttayānaṃ viya katā. Vatthukatāti patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena vatthu viya katā. Anuṭṭhitāti adhiṭṭhitā. Paricitāti samantato citā suvaḍḍhitā. Susamāraddhāti suṭṭhu samāraddhā.

Here, by 'a seat' is meant a piece of leather. By 'Udena Cetiya' is meant the monastery built at the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena. The same method applies to 'Gotamaka' and the others. 'Developed' (bhāvitā) means increased (vaḍḍhitā). 'Made much of' (bahulīkatā) means done again and again. 'Made into a vehicle' (yānīkatā) means made like a yoked vehicle. 'Made into a foundation' (vatthukatā) means made like a basis, in the sense of being a foundation. 'Established' (anuṭṭhitā) means resolved upon (adhiṭṭhitā). 'Familiarized' (paricitā) means accumulated all around and well-developed. 'Well undertaken' (susamāraddhā) means thoroughly undertaken.

Iti aniyamena kathetvā puna niyametvā dassento tathāgatassa khotiādimāha. Ettha ca kappanti āyukappaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle yaṃ manussānaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ hoti, taṃ paripuṇṇaṃ karonto tiṭṭheyya. Kappāvasesaṃ vāti – “appaṃ vā bhiyyo”ti (dī. ni. 2.7; a. ni. 6.74) vuttavassasatato atirekaṃ vā. Mahāsīvatthero panāha – “buddhānaṃ aṭṭhāne gajjitaṃ nāma natthi. Yatheva hi veḷuvagāmake uppannaṃ māraṇantikaṃ vedanaṃ dasa māse vikkhambheti, evaṃ punappunaṃ [P 2.0555] taṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā dasa dasa māse vikkhambhento imaṃ bhaddakappameva tiṭṭheyya, kasmā pana na ṭhitoti? Upādinnakasarīraṃ nāma khaṇḍiccādīhi abhibhuyyati, buddhā ca khaṇḍiccādibhāvaṃ apatvā pañcame āyukoṭṭhāse bahujanassa piyamanāpakāleyeva parinibbāyanti. Buddhānubuddhesu ca mahāsāvakesu parinibbutesu ekakeneva khāṇukena viya [M 2.0145] ṭhātabbaṃ hoti, daharasāmaṇeraparivāritena vā. Tato – ‘aho buddhānaṃ parisā’ti hīḷetabbataṃ āpajjeyya. Tasmā na ṭhito”ti. Evaṃ vuttepi so na ruccati, “āyukappo”ti idameva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ niyamitaṃ.

Having spoken thus without specification, then teaching with specification, he said, 'The Tathāgata...' and so on. Herein, 'kappa' means the life-span. At any given time, whatever the life-expectancy of humans may be, he could remain, fulfilling it completely. As for 'or for the remainder of the kappa,' it means exceeding the aforementioned hundred years by 'a little or even more.' However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: 'There is no such thing as an unfounded boast made by the Buddhas. For just as he suppressed the mortal pain that arose in Veḷuvagāma for ten months, so too, by repeatedly entering that attainment, he could suppress it for ten months at a time and remain for this entire auspicious aeon. Why then did he not remain? A body produced by clinging is overcome by such things as having broken teeth. And the Buddhas, without reaching a state of having broken teeth, attain parinibbāna in the fifth portion of their lifespan, while they are still dear and pleasing to the multitude. Moreover, when the great disciples who have understood following the Buddha have attained parinibbāna, he would have to remain alone like a tree stump, or surrounded only by young monks and novices. Then, the Buddha's assembly would become an object of contempt, with people thinking, 'Alas, what has become of the Buddha's assembly!' Therefore, he did not remain.'
