Even though this was stated, that view is not accepted. 'The life-span'—this alone is the determined meaning in the commentary.

167. Yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacittoti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ. Yathā mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto ajjhotthaṭacitto aññopi koci puthujjano paṭivijjhituṃ na sakkuṇeyya, evameva nāsakkhi paṭivijjhitunti attho. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Māro hi yassa sabbena sabbaṃ dvādasa vipallāsā appahīnā, tassa cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti. Therassa cattāro vipallāsā appahīnā, tenassa māro cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti. So pana cittapariyuṭṭhānaṃ karonto kiṃ karotīti? Bheravaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vā dasseti, saddārammaṇaṃ vā sāveti, tato sattā taṃ disvā vā sutvā vā satiṃ vissajjetvā vivaṭamukhā honti. Tesaṃ mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetvā hadayaṃ maddati. Tato visaññāva hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Therassa panesa mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetuṃ kiṃ sakkhissati[V 2.0130]? Bheravārammaṇaṃ pana dasseti. Taṃ disvā thero nimittobhāsaṃ na paṭivijjhi. Bhagavā jānantoyeva – “kimatthaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ āmantesī”ti? Parato “tiṭṭhatu, bhante, bhagavā”ti yācite “tuyhevetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ, tuyhevetaṃ aparaddha”nti dosāropanena sokatanukaraṇatthaṃ.

167. Regarding the phrase 'as one whose mind was assailed by Māra,' herein the word 'taṃ' is a mere particle. The meaning is that just as some ordinary person whose mind is assailed and overwhelmed by Māra would be unable to penetrate the meaning, in the same way, he was unable to penetrate it. For what reason? Māra assails the mind of one for whom the twelve perversions have not been entirely abandoned. For the Elder, four perversions were not abandoned; therefore, Māra assailed his mind. And what does Māra do when assailing the mind? He shows a terrifying visual object or makes one hear a terrifying sound. Then, having seen or heard it, beings let go of their mindfulness and stand with mouths agape. Inserting his hand through their mouths, he crushes their hearts. Then they stand as if unconscious. But how could he insert his hand into the Elder's mouth? He only showed a terrifying object. Seeing it, the Elder did not penetrate the sign and the hint. Although the Blessed One knew this, why did he invite him up to a third time? It was for the purpose of lessening Ānanda's sorrow later by placing the blame on him when he was requested, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain,' saying, 'This itself was your misdeed, this itself was your offense.'

Mārayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Māra's Request

168. Māro pāpimāti ettha māroti satte anatthe niyojento māretīti māro. Pāpimāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. So hi pāpadhammasamannāgatattā “pāpimā”ti vuccati. Kaṇho, antako, namuci, pamattabandhūtipi tasseva nāmāni. Bhāsitā kho panesāti ayañhi bhagavato sambodhipattiyā aṭṭhame sattāhe bodhimaṇḍeyeva āgantvā – “bhagavā yadatthaṃ tumhehi pāramiyo pūritā, so vo attho anuppatto, paṭividdhaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, kiṃ te lokavicāraṇenā”ti vatvā, yathā ajja[P 2.0556], evameva “parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā”ti yāci. Bhagavā cassa – “na [M 2.0146] tāvāha”ntiādīni vatvā paṭikkhipi. Taṃ sandhāya “bhāsitā kho panesā bhante”tiādimāha.

168. Regarding 'Māra, the Evil One': herein, he is called 'Māra' because he kills beings by engaging them in what is unbeneficial. 'Pāpimā' (the Evil One) is a synonym for him. Indeed, because he is endowed with evil qualities, he is called 'Pāpimā.' Kaṇha, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu are also his names. As for 'This was spoken...': in the eighth week after the Blessed One's attainment of enlightenment, Māra came to the very Bodhi-maṇḍa and said: 'Blessed One, the purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has been attained by you; all-knowing knowledge has been penetrated. What use is your involvement with the world?' Then, just as today, he requested, 'Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now attain parinibbāna.' But the Blessed One rejected him, saying, 'Not yet...' and so on. It was with reference to this that he said, 'This was spoken, venerable sir...'

Tattha viyattāti maggavasena viyattā. Tatheva vinītā tathā visāradā. Bahussutāti tepiṭakavasena bahu sutametesanti bahussutā. Tameva dhammaṃ dhārentīti dhammadharā. Athavā pariyattibahussutā ceva paṭivedhabahussutā ca. Pariyattipaṭivedhadhammānaṃyeva dhāraṇato dhammadharāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Dhammānudhammapaṭipannāti ariyadhammassa anudhammabhūtaṃ vipassanādhammaṃ paṭipannā. Sāmīcippaṭipannāti anucchavikapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā. Anudhammacārinoti anudhammacaraṇasīlā. Sakaṃ ācariyakanti attano ācariyavādaṃ. Ācikkhissantītiādīni sabbāni aññamaññassa vevacanāni. Sahadhammenāti sahetukena sakāraṇena vacanena. Sappāṭihāriyanti yāva na niyyānikaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desessanti.

Therein, 'viyattā' means accomplished by way of the path. Likewise, 'vinītā' means well-trained, and 'visāradā' means confident. 'Bahussutā' means they are learned, having heard much by way of the Tipiṭaka. They uphold that very Dhamma, hence they are 'dhammadharā' (upholders of the Dhamma). Alternatively, they are learned in both the scriptures (pariyatti) and the penetration (paṭivedha). Because they uphold the Dhamma of both the scriptures and the penetration, they are called 'dhammadharā'; thus the meaning should be understood here. 'Dhammānudhammapaṭipannā' means they are practicing the insight-Dhamma, which is in conformity with the noble Dhamma. 'Sāmīcippaṭipannā' means they are practicing the proper way. 'Anudhammacārino' means they are of a nature to act in accordance with the Dhamma. 'Sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ' means their own teacher's doctrine. 'Ācikkhissanti' and the other terms are all synonyms for one another. 'Sahadhammena' means with speech that has a basis and a reason. 'Sappāṭihāriyaṃ' means until they teach the Dhamma in a way that leads to emancipation.

Brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ. Iddhanti samiddhaṃ jhānassādavasena. Phītanti vuddhippattaṃ sabbaphāliphullaṃ viya abhiññāya sampattivasena. Vitthārikanti vitthataṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ disābhāge patiṭṭhitavasena. Bāhujaññanti bahujanehi ñātaṃ paṭividdhaṃ mahājanābhisamayavasena. Puthubhūtanti sabbākāravasena puthulabhāvappattaṃ. Kathaṃ? Yāva devamanussehi [V 2.0131] suppakāsitanti yattakā viññujātikā devā ceva manussā ca atthi sabbehi suṭṭhu pakāsitanti attho.

‘Brahmacariya’ (the holy life) is the entire holy life of the Dispensation, comprised of the threefold training. ‘Iddha’ means prosperous, flourishing by way of the savor of jhāna. ‘Phīta’ means thriving, having reached its full growth, like a tree in full fruit and flower, by way of the attainment of the higher knowledges. ‘Vitthārika’ means widespread, by way of being established in various regions. ‘Bāhujañña’ means widely known, known and penetrated by many people, by way of the realization of the great multitude. ‘Puthubhūta’ means having become extensive, having attained a state of breadth in all aspects. How so? ‘So that it is well-proclaimed by gods and humans’ means that it is well-proclaimed by all intelligent beings that exist, both gods and humans.

Appossukkoti nirālayo. Tvañhi pāpima, aṭṭhamasattāhato paṭṭhāya – “parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā parinibbātu, sugato”ti viravanto āhiṇḍittha. Ajja dāni paṭṭhāya vigatussāho hohi; mā mayhaṃ parinibbānatthaṃ vāyāmaṃ karohīti vadati.

‘Appossukko’ means unconcerned, without attachment. 'For you, O Evil One, from the eighth week onwards, have wandered about crying out, “Now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One attain parinibbāna! Let the Sugata attain parinibbāna!” From today onwards, be without enthusiasm; do not make an effort for my parinibbāna,' he says.

Āyusaṅkhāraossajjanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Relinquishing of the Life-Formation

169. Sato sampajāno āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajīti satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā āyusaṅkhāraṃ vissajji, pajahi. Tattha na bhagavā hatthena leḍḍuṃ viya āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossaji, temāsamattameva pana samāpattiṃ [M 2.0147] samāpajjitvā tato paraṃ na samāpajjissāmīti cittaṃ uppādesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “ossajī”ti. “Ussajjī”ti pi pāṭho. Mahābhūmicāloti [P 2.0557] mahanto pathavīkampo. Tadā kira dasasahassī lokadhātu kampittha. Bhiṃsanakoti bhayajanako. Devadundubhiyo ca phaliṃsūti devabheriyo phaliṃsu, devo sukkhagajjitaṃ gajji, akālavijjulatā nicchariṃsu, khaṇikavassaṃ vassīti vuttaṃ hoti.

169. Mindful and fully aware, he relinquished the life-formation. This means: having established mindfulness well and having discerned with wisdom, he released and abandoned the life-formation. In this context, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-formation as one might toss away a clod of earth with the hand; rather, having entered a meditative attainment for a period of only three months, he generated the thought, 'Henceforth, I shall not enter it again.' With reference to this was it said, 'he relinquished.' There is also the reading 'ussajji.' A great earthquake means a great trembling of the earth. At that time, it is said, the ten-thousandfold world-system shook. 'Terrifying' means fear-inducing. 'And the celestial drums resounded' means: the celestial kettle-drums resounded, the heavens uttered a dry thunder, untimely lightning flashed forth, and a momentary rain fell—this is what is meant.

Udānaṃ udānesīti kasmā udānesi? Koci nāma vadeyya – “bhagavā pacchato pacchato anubandhitvā – ‘parinibbāyatha, bhante, parinibbāyatha, bhante’ti upadduto bhayena āyusaṅkhāraṃ vissajjesī”ti. “Tassokāso mā hotu, bhītassa udānaṃ nāma natthī”ti etassa dīpanatthaṃ pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

He uttered an inspired utterance. Why did he utter it? Someone might say, “The Blessed One, being harassed and repeatedly pursued with the words, ‘Attain final Nibbāna, Lord; attain final Nibbāna, Lord,’ relinquished the life-formation out of fear.” To clarify this matter, he uttered an inspired utterance released by the force of joy, thinking, “Let there be no opportunity for such a claim; for one who is afraid, there is no such thing as an inspired utterance.”

Tattha sabbesaṃ soṇasiṅgālādīnampi paccakkhabhāvato tulitaṃ paricchinnanti tulaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Kāmāvacarakammaṃ. Na tulaṃ, na vā tulaṃ sadisamassa aññaṃ lokiyaṃ kammaṃ atthīti atulaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Mahaggatakammaṃ. Athavā kāmāvacararūpāvacaraṃ tulaṃ, arūpāvacaraṃ atulaṃ. Appavipākaṃ vā tulaṃ, bahuvipākaṃ atulaṃ. Sambhavanti sambhavassa hetubhūtaṃ, piṇḍakārakaṃ rāsikārakanti attho. Bhavasaṅkhāranti punabbhavasaṅkhāraṇakaṃ. Avassajīti vissajjesi. Munīti buddhamuni. Ajjhattaratoti niyakajjhattarato. Samāhitoti upacārappanāsamādhivasena samāhito. Abhindi kavacamivāti kavacaṃ viya abhindi. Attasambhavanti attani sañjātaṃ kilesaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “savipākaṭṭhena sambhavaṃ, bhavābhisaṅkhāraṇaṭṭhena bhavasaṅkhāranti ca laddhanāmaṃ tulātulasaṅkhātaṃ [V 2.0132] lokiyakammañca ossaji. Saṅgāmasīse mahāyodho kavacaṃ viya attasambhavaṃ kilesañca ajjhattarato samāhito hutvā abhindī”ti.

In this context, `tula` (measurable) means that which is weighed and measured, being directly perceptible to all, even to dogs and jackals. What is that? Kamma of the sense-sphere. `Atula` (immeasurable) means that which is not measurable, or for which there is no other worldly kamma that is its equal. What is that? Exalted kamma. Alternatively, kamma of the sense-sphere and the form-sphere is measurable, while that of the formless sphere is immeasurable. Or, kamma with little result is measurable, while that with great result is immeasurable. `Sambhava` (arising) means that which is the cause of existence, that which creates a mass, that which creates a heap—this is the meaning. `Bhavasaṅkhāra` (formation of existence) means that which conditions renewed existence. `Avassaji` means he relinquished. `Munī` means the Buddha-sage. `Ajjhattarato` means delighted in his own interior. `Samāhito` means composed by way of access and absorption concentration. `Abhindi kavacamiva` means he shattered it like armor. `Attasambhava` means the defilement arisen within oneself. This is what is said: 'He relinquished worldly kamma—which is named ‘arising’ because it has a result, and ‘formation of existence’ because it conditions existence, and which is designated as measurable and immeasurable. And, like a great warrior at the head of the battle, being inwardly delighted and composed, he shattered the defilement born within himself as one shatters armor.'

Atha vā tulanti tulento tīrento. Atulañca sambhavanti nibbānañceva sambhavañca. Bhavasaṅkhāranti bhavagāmikammaṃ. Avassaji munīti “pañcakkhandhā aniccā, pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ nirodho nibbānaṃ nicca”ntiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.38) nayena tulayanto buddhamuni bhave ādīnavaṃ, nibbāne ca ānisaṃsaṃ disvā taṃ khandhānaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ bhavasaṅkhārakammaṃ – “kammakkhayāya saṃvattatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.81) evaṃ vuttena kammakkhayakarena ariyamaggena [P 2.0558] avassaji. Kathaṃ? Ajjhattarato samāhito abhindi kavacamiva attani [M 2.0148] sambhavaṃ. So hi vipassanāvasena ajjhattarato samathavasena samāhitoti evaṃ pubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya samathavipassanābalena kavacamiva attabhāvaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ, attani sambhavattā “attasambhava”nti laddhanāmaṃ sabbakilesajālaṃ abhindi. Kilesābhāvena ca katakammaṃ appaṭisandhikattā avassaṭṭhaṃ nāma hotīti evaṃ kilesappahānena kammaṃ pajahi, pahīnakilesassa ca bhayaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā abhītova āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossaji, abhītabhāvañāpanatthañca udānaṃ udānesīti veditabbo.

Alternatively, `tula` means weighing, considering. And `atula` and `sambhava` mean Nibbāna and existence respectively. `Bhavasaṅkhāra` (formation of existence) means kamma that leads to existence. The sage relinquished. This means: weighing by the method that begins, 'The five aggregates are impermanent; the cessation of the five aggregates, Nibbāna, is permanent,' the Buddha-sage, having seen the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna, relinquished by means of the noble path—which destroys kamma and is said to 'conduce to the destruction of kamma'—that kamma which is the formation of existence and the root of the aggregates. How? 'Inwardly delighted and composed, he shattered what had arisen in himself as if it were armor.' For he was 'inwardly delighted' by way of insight, and 'composed' by way of serenity. Thus, beginning from the preliminary stage, with the power of serenity and insight, he shattered the entire net of defilements—which is named 'self-arisen' because it arises in oneself and which stood enveloping his personal existence like armor. And because, in the absence of defilements, kamma that has been done does not lead to a future rebirth, it is called 'relinquished.' Thus, by abandoning the defilements, he abandoned kamma. For one who has abandoned the defilements, there is no such thing as fear. Therefore, being fearless, he relinquished the life-formation; and it should be understood that he uttered the inspired utterance in order to make known his state of fearlessness.

Mahābhūmicālavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Great Earthquake

171. Yaṃ mahāvātāti yena samayena yasmiṃ vā samaye mahāvātā vāyanti, mahāvātā vāyantāpi ukkhepakavātā nāma uṭṭhahanti, te vāyantā saṭṭhisahassādhikanavayojanasatasahassabahalaṃ udakasandhārakaṃ vātaṃ upacchindanti, tato ākāse udakaṃ bhassati, tasmiṃ bhassante pathavī bhassati. Puna vāto attano balena antodhamakaraṇe viya udakaṃ ābandhitvā gaṇhāti, tato udakaṃ uggacchati, tasmiṃ uggacchante pathavī uggacchati. Evaṃ udakaṃ kampitaṃ pathaviṃ kampeti. Etañca kampanaṃ yāva ajjakālāpi hotiyeva, bahalabhāvena pana na ogacchanuggacchanaṃ paññāyati.

171. 'When great winds blow' means: at whatever time great winds blow, winds called 'uplifting winds' arise. As they blow, they cut off the wind that supports the water, a mass nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas thick. Then the water, which is in space, falls, and as it falls, the earth falls. Again, the wind by its own power binds and seizes the water, as if within a water-strainer. Then the water rises, and as it rises, the earth rises. In this way, the agitated water causes the earth to shake. And this shaking continues even to the present day, but due to the great thickness, its descending and ascending are not discernible.

Mahiddhiko mahānubhāvoti ijjhanassa mahantatāya mahiddhiko, anubhavitabbassa mahantatāya mahānubhāvo. Parittāti dubbalā. Appamāṇāti balavā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ kampetīti so iddhiṃ nibbattetvā saṃvejento mahāmoggallāno viya, vīmaṃsanto vā mahānāgattherassa bhāgineyyo saṅgharakkhitasāmaṇero viya pathaviṃ kampeti. So kirāyasmā khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ patvā cintesi [V 2.0133] – “atthi nu kho koci bhikkhu, yena pabbajitadivaseyeva arahattaṃ patvā vejayanto pāsādo kampitapubbo”ti? Tato – “natthi kocī”ti ñatvā – “ahaṃ kampessāmī”ti abhiññābalena vejayantamatthake ṭhatvā pādena paharitvā kampetuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ sakkassa nāṭakitthiyo āhaṃsu – “putta saṅgharakkhita, tvaṃ pūtigandheneva sīsena vejayantaṃ kampetuṃ icchasi, suppatiṭṭhito tāta pāsādo, kathaṃ kampetuṃ [P 2.0559] sakkhissasī”ti?

"Of great psychic power and great might": of great psychic power due to the greatness of his accomplishment; of great might due to the greatness of what is to be experienced. "Limited" means weak. "Immeasurable" means strong. "He makes this earth shake": having produced psychic power, causing it to tremble like the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, or investigating like the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew of the Elder Mahānāga, he makes the earth shake. It is said that this venerable one, having attained arahantship at the very touch of the razor, thought: "Is there any monk who, having attained arahantship on the very day of his ordination, has previously shaken the Vejayanta Palace?" Then, knowing "There is none," he thought, "I will shake it." Standing at the pinnacle of the Vejayanta by the power of his supernormal knowledge, he struck it with his foot but was unable to shake it. Then, Sakka’s dancing nymphs said to him: "Son Saṅgharakkhita, do you wish to shake the Vejayanta with your head that has a putrid smell? The palace is well-established, dear one, how will you be able to shake it?"

Sāmaṇero [M 2.0149] – “imā devatā mayā saddhiṃ keḷiṃ karonti, ahaṃ kho pana ācariyaṃ nālatthaṃ, kahaṃ nu kho me ācariyo sāmuddikamahānāgatthero”ti āvajjento mahāsamudde udakaleṇaṃ māpetvā divāvihāraṃ nisinnoti ñatvā tattha gantvā theraṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Tato naṃ thero – “kiṃ, tāta saṅgharakkhita, asikkhitvāva yuddhaṃ paviṭṭhosī”ti vatvā “nāsakkhi, tāta, vejayantaṃ kampetu”nti pucchi. Ācariyaṃ, bhante, nālatthanti. Atha naṃ thero – “tāta tumhādise akampente ko añño kampessati. Diṭṭhapubbaṃ te, tāta, udakapiṭṭhe gomayakhaṇḍaṃ pilavantaṃ, tāta, kapallakapūvaṃ pacantā antantena paricchindanti, iminā opammena jānāhī”ti āha. So – “vaṭṭissati, bhante, ettakenā”ti vatvā pāsādena patiṭṭhitokāsaṃ udakaṃ hotūti adhiṭṭhāya vejayantābhimukho agamāsi.

The novice thought: "These deities are making sport of me, but I have not obtained a teacher. Where can my teacher, the Elder Sāmuddika Mahānāga, be?" Reflecting thus, and discerning that the elder had created a water-cavern in the great ocean and was seated there for his day-sojourn, he went there, paid homage to the elder, and stood to one side. Then the elder said to him: "Why, dear Saṅgharakkhita, have you entered the battle without having trained?" and asked, "Were you unable, dear one, to shake the Vejayanta Palace?" "Venerable sir, I had not obtained a teacher." Then the elder said to him: "Dear one, if one such as you does not shake it, who else will? Have you ever seen, dear one, a lump of cow dung floating on the surface of the water? Dear one, those who bake a potsherd-cake trim it at the very edges. Understand by this simile." He replied: "That much will suffice, venerable sir," and having made the resolution, "Let the place where the palace is established become water," he proceeded towards the Vejayanta.

Devadhītaro taṃ disvā – “ekavāraṃ lajjitvā gato, punapi sāmaṇero eti, punapi etī”ti vadiṃsu. Sakko devarājā – “mā mayhaṃ puttena saddhiṃ kathayittha, idāni tena ācariyo laddho, khaṇena pāsādaṃ kampessatī”ti āha. Sāmaṇeropi pādaṅguṭṭhena pāsādathūpikaṃ pahari. Pāsādo catūhi disāhi oṇamati. Devatā – “patiṭṭhātuṃ dehi, tāta, pāsādassa patiṭṭhātuṃ dehi, tāta, pāsādassā”ti viraviṃsu. Sāmaṇero pāsādaṃ yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā pāsādamatthake ṭhatvā udānaṃ udānesi –

Seeing him, the celestial maidens said: "Having departed once in shame, the novice comes again; he comes again!" Sakka, the king of the gods, said: "Do not jest with my son. Now he has obtained a teacher; in a moment he will shake the palace." The novice, too, struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe. The palace tilted from the four directions. The deities cried out: "Dear one, allow the palace to stand! Dear one, allow the palace to stand!" The novice, having set the palace back in its proper place, stood atop the palace and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Ajjevāhaṃ pabbajito, ajja pattāsavakkhayaṃ;

Ajja kampemi pāsādaṃ, aho buddhassuḷāratā.

"Today I have gone forth; today I have attained the destruction of the taints; today I shake the palace—ah, the magnificence of the Buddha!

Ajjevāhaṃ pabbajito…pe… aho dhammassuḷāratā.

Ajjevāhaṃ pabbajito…pe… aho saṅghassuḷāratāti.

Today I have gone forth... ah, the magnificence of the Dhamma! Today I have gone forth... ah, the magnificence of the Saṅgha!"

Ito [V 2.0134] paresu chasu pathavīkampesu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahāpadāne vuttameva.

Whatever is to be said concerning the six earthquakes subsequent to these has already been stated in the Mahāpadāna Sutta.

Iti imesu aṭṭhasu pathavīkampesu paṭhamo dhātukopena, dutiyo iddhānubhāvena, tatiyacatutthā puññatejena, pañcamo ñāṇatejena, chaṭṭho sādhukāradānavasena, sattamo kāruññabhāvena, aṭṭhamo ārodanena. Mātukucchiṃ okkamante ca tato nikkhamante ca mahāsatte tassa puññatejena pathavī akampittha. Abhisambodhiyaṃ ñāṇatejena abhihatā [M 2.0150] hutvā akampittha. Dhammacakkappavattane [P 2.0560] sādhukārabhāvasaṇṭhitā sādhukāraṃ dadamānā akampittha. Āyusaṅkhārossajjane kāruññasabhāvasaṇṭhitā cittasaṅkhobhaṃ asahamānā akampittha. Parinibbāne ārodanavegatunnā hutvā akampittha. Ayaṃ panattho pathavīdevatāya vasena veditabbo, mahābhūtapathaviyā panetaṃ natthi acetanattāti.

Thus, among these eight earthquakes, the first is due to a disturbance of the elements; the second, due to the power of psychic might; the third and fourth, due to the power of merit; the fifth, due to the power of knowledge; the sixth, by way of giving approval; the seventh, due to a state of compassion; and the eighth, due to lamentation. When the great being descended into his mother’s womb and when he emerged from it, the earth shook due to the power of his merit. At his full enlightenment, it shook, being struck by the power of his knowledge. At the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, it shook as if established in a state of giving approval. At the relinquishing of the life-formation, it shook as if established in a state of compassion, unable to bear the agitation of mind. At the parinibbāna, it shook, being impelled by the force of lamentation. This meaning, however, is to be understood with reference to the earth-deity, for this does not pertain to the great earth-element itself, on account of its being non-sentient.

Ime kho, ānanda, aṭṭha hetūti ettha imeti niddiṭṭhanidassanaṃ. Ettāvatā ca panāyasmā ānando – “addhā ajja bhagavatā āyusaṅkhāro ossaṭṭho”ti sallakkhesi. Bhagavā pana sallakkhitabhāvaṃ jānantopi okāsaṃ adatvāva aññānipi aṭṭhakāni sampiṇḍento – “aṭṭha kho imā”tiādimāha.

In the phrase "These, Ānanda, are the eight causes," the word "these" is a reference to what has just been stated. And by this much, the Venerable Ānanda marked: "Surely, today the Blessed One has relinquished his life-formation." But the Blessed One, though knowing that he had so marked, without giving him an opportunity, and wishing to group together other sets of eight, said, "There are these eight..." and so on.

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Eight Assemblies

172. Tattha anekasataṃ khattiyaparisanti bimbisārasamāgamañātisamāgalicchavīsamāgamādisadisaṃ, sā pana aññesu cakkavāḷesupi labbhateyeva. Sallapitapubbanti ālāpasallāpo katapubbo. Sākacchāti dhammasākacchāpi samāpajjitapubbā. Yādisako tesaṃ vaṇṇoti te odātāpi honti kāḷāpi maṅguracchavīpi, satthā suvaṇṇavaṇṇova. Idaṃ pana saṇṭhānaṃ paṭicca kathitaṃ. Saṇṭhānampi ca kevalaṃ tesaṃ paññāyatiyeva, na pana bhagavā milakkhusadiso hoti, nāpi āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalo, buddhaveseneva nisīdati. Te pana attano samānasaṇṭhānameva passanti. Yādisako tesaṃ saroti te chinnassarāpi honti gaggarassarāpi kākassarāpi, satthā brahmassarova. Idaṃ pana bhāsantaraṃ sandhāya kathitaṃ. Sacepi hi satthā rājāsane nisinno katheti, “ajja rājā madhurena sarena kathetī”ti tesaṃ hoti. Kathetvā pakkante pana bhagavati puna rājānaṃ āgataṃ disvā – “ko nu kho aya”nti vīmaṃsā uppajjati. Tattha ko nu kho ayanti imasmiṃ ṭhāne idāneva māgadhabhāsāya sīhaḷabhāsāya madhurenākārena kathento ko nu kho ayaṃ antarahito, kiṃ devo, udāhu manussoti evaṃ vīmaṃsantāpi [V 2.0135] na jānantīti attho. Kimatthaṃ panevaṃ ajānantānaṃ dhammaṃ desetīti? Vāsanatthāya[M 2.0151]. Evaṃ sutopi hi dhammo anāgate paccayo hoti yevāti anāgataṃ paṭicca deseti. Anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisantiādīnampi soṇadaṇḍakūṭadaṇḍasamāgamādivasena [P 2.0561] ceva aññacakkavāḷavasena ca sambhavo veditabbo.

172. There, hundreds of khattiya assemblies—gatherings like those of Bimbisāra, relatives, and Licchavīs, and similar gatherings—these are found even in other world-systems. 'Having conversed before' means conversation had previously taken place. 'Discussion' refers to Dhamma discussions that had previously taken place. 'Such as their complexion'—some were fair, some dark, some had a brownish hue, but the Teacher was of a golden complexion. This was said with reference to their appearance. Their appearance alone was evident, but the Blessed One was not like a barbarian, nor adorned with jewels and earrings; he sat in the manner of a Buddha. They saw only an appearance similar to their own. 'Such as their voice'—some had cracked voices, some had hoarse voices, some had crow-like voices, but the Teacher had a voice like Brahmā’s. This was said with reference to the language. Even if the Teacher spoke while seated on a royal throne, they thought, 'Today the king is speaking with a sweet voice.' But when the Blessed One had finished speaking and departed, and they saw the king again, they wondered, 'Who is this now?' Here, 'Who is this now?' means that in this place, just now speaking in the Magadhan or Sinhalese language with a sweet tone—who is this who has disappeared? Is it a deva, or a human? Even as they wondered thus, they did not know. Why then did he teach the Dhamma to those who did not understand? For the sake of their latent tendencies. Even Dhamma heard in this way becomes a condition in the future—thus he taught with the future in mind. As for hundreds of brahmin assemblies and the like, the possibility of them occurring should be understood in terms of gatherings like those of Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadaṇḍa, and the like, and in terms of other world-systems.

Imā pana aṭṭha parisā bhagavā kimatthaṃ āhari? Abhītabhāvadassanatthameva. Imā kira āharitvā evamāha – “ānanda, imāpi aṭṭha parisā upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ desentassa tathāgatassa bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā natthi, māraṃ pana ekakaṃ disvā tathāgato bhāyeyyāti ko evaṃ saññaṃ uppādetumarahati. Abhīto, ānanda, tathāgato acchambhī, sato sampajāno āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajī”ti.

Now, for what purpose did the Blessed One bring forth these eight assemblies? It was solely to show his fearlessness. Having brought them forth, he said this: 'Ānanda, even when these eight assemblies approach and the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma, there is no fear or timidity in the Tathāgata. Who could possibly think that the Tathāgata would be afraid on seeing Māra alone? Ānanda, the Tathāgata, fearless, unshaken, mindful, and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-sustaining force.'

Aṭṭhaabhibhāyatanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Eight Spheres of Mastery

173. Abhibhāyatanānīti abhibhavanakāraṇāni. Kiṃ abhibhavanti? Paccanīkadhammepi ārammaṇānipi. Tāni hi paṭipakkhabhāvena paccanīkadhamme abhibhavanti, puggalassa ñāṇuttariyatāya ārammaṇāni.

173. 'The bases of mastery' are the causes of mastery. What do they master? Both opposing qualities and objects. For they master opposing qualities by way of being counteractive, and objects through the superiority of a person's knowledge.

Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññītiādīsu pana ajjhattarūpe parikammavasena ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī nāma hoti. Ajjhattañhi nīlaparikammaṃ karonto kese vā pitte vā akkhitārakāya vā karoti. Pītaparikammaṃ karonto mede vā chaviyā vā hatthapādapiṭṭhesu vā akkhīnaṃ pītakaṭṭhāne vā karoti. Lohitaparikammaṃ karonto maṃse vā lohite vā jivhāya vā akkhīnaṃ rattaṭṭhāne vā karoti. Odātaparikammaṃ karonto aṭṭhimhi vā dante vā nakhe vā akkhīnaṃ setaṭṭhāne vā karoti. Taṃ pana sunīlaṃ supītaṃ sulohitakaṃ suodātakaṃ na hoti, avisuddhameva hoti.

In the case of 'one who perceives form internally,' etc., one is called 'one who perceives form internally' by way of preliminary work on internal form. For one who does preliminary work on blue internally does so on the hair, bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One who does preliminary work on yellow does so on fat, the skin, the backs of the hands and feet, or the yellow part of the eyes. One who does preliminary work on red does so on flesh, blood, the tongue, or the red part of the eyes. One who does preliminary work on white does so on bones, teeth, nails, or the white part of the eyes. But that is not perfectly blue, perfectly yellow, perfectly red, or perfectly white; it is impure.

Eko bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti yassevaṃ parikammaṃ ajjhattaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, nimittaṃ pana bahiddhā, so evaṃ ajjhattaṃ parikammassa bahiddhā ca appanāya vasena – “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti vuccati. Parittānīti avaḍḍhitāni. Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānīti suvaṇṇāni vā honti, dubbaṇṇāni vā. Parittavaseneva idaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tāni abhibhuyyāti yathā nāma sampannagahaṇiko kaṭacchumattaṃ bhattaṃ labhitvā – “kiṃ [M 2.0152] ettha bhuñjitabbaṃ atthī”ti saṅkaḍḍhitvā ekakabaḷameva karoti, evameva ñāṇuttariko puggalo visadañāṇo [V 2.0136] – “kiṃ ettha parittake ārammaṇe samāpajjitabbaṃ atthi, nāyaṃ mama bhāro”ti tāni rūpāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati, saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetīti attho. Jānāmi [P 2.0562] passāmīti iminā panassa ābhogo kathito. So ca kho samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa, na antosamāpattiyaṃ. Evaṃsaññī hotīti ābhogasaññāyapi jhānasaññāyapi evaṃsaññī hoti. Abhibhavanasaññā hissa antosamāpattiyampi atthi, ābhogasaññā pana samāpattito vuṭṭhitasseva.

'One who perceives form internally, seeing forms externally'—when for someone the preliminary work has arisen internally, but the sign is external, he is thus called 'one who perceives form internally, seeing forms externally' by way of the internal preliminary work and the external absorption. 'Limited' means undeveloped. 'Beautiful or ugly' means that they are either beautiful or ugly. It should be understood that this sphere of mastery is spoken of by way of the limited. 'Having mastered them'—just as a person with strong digestion, receiving only a spoonful of food, thinks, 'What is there to eat here?' and gathers it up into a single mouthful, just so a person with superior knowledge, with clear knowledge, thinks, 'What is there to attain in this limited object? This is no burden for me,' masters those forms, and enters into attainment, meaning that absorption is reached simultaneously with the arising of the sign. By 'I know, I see,' his directing of the mind is described. And that is for one who has arisen from the attainment, not while within the attainment. 'He is one with such a perception'—he is one with such a perception through both the perception of directing the mind and the perception of jhāna. For him, the perception of mastery exists even within the attainment, but the perception of directing the mind exists only for one who has arisen from the attainment.

Appamāṇānīti vaḍḍhitappamāṇāni, mahantānīti attho. Abhibhuyyāti ettha pana yathā mahagghaso puriso ekaṃ bhattavaḍḍhitakaṃ labhitvā – “aññampi hotu, kiṃ etaṃ mayhaṃ karissatī”ti taṃ na mahantato passati, evameva ñāṇuttaro puggalo visadañāṇo “kiṃ ettha samāpajjitabbaṃ, nayidaṃ appamāṇaṃ, na mayhaṃ cittekaggatākaraṇe bhāro atthī”ti tāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati, saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetīti attho.

'Immeasurable' means of immeasurable extent, vast is the meaning. 'Having mastered them'—here, just as a gluttonous person, having obtained a single helping of food, thinks, 'Let there be more, what can this do for me?' and does not regard it as large, in the same way, a person with superior knowledge, with clear knowledge, thinks, 'What is there to attain here? This is not immeasurable; there is no burden for me in achieving one-pointedness of mind,' and having mastered them, enters into attainment. The meaning is that here, simultaneously with the arising of the sign, one reaches absorption.

Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti alābhitāya vā anatthikatāya vā ajjhattarūpe parikammasaññāvirahito.

'One who is a non-perceiver of form internally' is devoid of the perception of preliminary work regarding internal form, due to either non-attainment or lack of interest.

Eko bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti yassa parikammampi nimittampi bahiddhāva uppannaṃ, so evaṃ bahiddhā parikammassa ceva appanāya ca vasena – “ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti vuccati. Sesamettha catutthābhibhāyatane vuttanayameva. Imesu pana catūsu parittaṃ vitakkacaritavasena āgataṃ, appamāṇaṃ mohacaritavasena, suvaṇṇaṃ dosacaritavasena, dubbaṇṇaṃ rāgacaritavasena. Etesañhi etāni sappāyāni. Sā ca nesaṃ sappāyatā vitthārato visuddhimagge caritaniddese vuttā.

“One sees forms externally”: for whom both the preliminary work and the sign have arisen externally, he is thus called “one who, not perceiving form internally, sees forms externally” by way of the external preliminary work and absorption. The rest here is in the same manner as stated for the fourth sphere of mastery. Now, among these four, the limited is presented for one of speculative temperament, the immeasurable for one of deluded temperament, the beautiful for one of aversive temperament, and the ugly for one of lustful temperament. Indeed, for these persons, these objects are suitable. And their suitability is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of Temperaments.

Pañcamaabhibhāyatanādīsu nīlānīti sabbasaṅgāhakavasena vuttaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇānīti vaṇṇavasena. Nīlanidassanānīti nidassanavasena, apaññāya mānavivarāni asambhinnavaṇṇāni ekanīlāneva hutvā dissantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Nīlanibhāsānīti idaṃ pana obhāsavasena vuttaṃ, nīlobhāsāni nīlappabhāyuttānīti attho. Etena nesaṃ visuddhataṃ dasseti. Visuddhavaṇṇavaseneva [M 2.0153] hi imāni cattāri abhibhāyatanāni vuttāni. Umāpupphanti etañhi pupphaṃ siniddhaṃ mudu, dissamānampi nīlameva hoti. Girikaṇṇikapupphādīni pana dissamānāni setadhātukāneva honti. Tasmā idameva gahitaṃ, na [P 2.0563] tāni. Bārāṇaseyyakanti bārāṇasisambhavaṃ. Tattha kira kappāsopi [V 2.0137] mudu, suttakantikāyopi tantavāyāpi chekā, udakampi suci siniddhaṃ. Tasmā taṃ vatthaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ hoti; dvīsupi passesu maṭṭhaṃ mudu siniddhaṃ khāyati.

In the fifth sphere of mastery and so on, “blue” is stated in an all-encompassing sense. “Blue in color” is in the sense of color. “Blue in appearance” is in the sense of appearance. “Blue in radiance,” however, is stated in the sense of luminosity, meaning they possess a blue radiance, are endowed with blue light. By this, he indicates their purity. For these four spheres of mastery are stated solely in terms of pure color. As for the umā flower, this flower is smooth and soft, and even when seen, it is entirely blue. But flowers like the girikaṇṇika and so on, when seen, have a white element. Therefore, this one was taken, not those. “Of Bārāṇasī” means originating in Bārāṇasī. There, it is said, the cotton is soft, the female spinners and the weavers are skilled, and the water is pure and smooth. Therefore, that cloth is finished on both sides; on both sides it appears polished, soft, and smooth.

Pītānītiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. “Nīlakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto nīlasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti pupphasmiṃ vā vatthasmiṃ vā vaṇṇadhātuyā vā”tiādikaṃ panettha kasiṇakaraṇañca parikammañca appanāvidhānañca sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vitthārato vuttameva. Imānipi aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni abhītabhāvadassanatthameva ānītāni. Imāni kira vatvā evamāha – “ānanda, evarūpāpi samāpattiyo samāpajjantassa ca vuṭṭhahantassa ca tathāgatassa bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā natthi, māraṃ pana ekakaṃ disvā tathāgato bhāyeyyāti ko evaṃ saññaṃ uppādetumarahati. Abhīto, ānanda, tathāgato acchambhī, sato sampajāno āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajī”ti.

In the case of 'yellow' and so forth, the meaning should be understood in this same way. The method of preparing the kasiṇa, the preliminary work, and the procedure for absorption—all this, beginning with the words, “One who learns the blue kasiṇa grasps the sign in something blue, whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color element,” is indeed explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. These eight spheres of mastery, too, were introduced solely for the purpose of demonstrating fearlessness. It is said that after speaking of these, he said this: “Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who enters and emerges from such attainments, there is no fear or timidity. Who could possibly conceive the thought that the Tathāgata would be afraid upon seeing Māra alone? The Tathāgata, Ānanda, is fearless, untrembling; mindful and fully aware, he relinquished the life-formation.”

Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Eight Liberations.

174. Vimokkhakathā uttānatthāyeva. Imepi aṭṭha vimokkhā abhītabhāvadassanatthameva ānītā. Imepi kira vatvā evamāha – “ānanda, etāpi samāpattiyo samāpajjantassa ca vuṭṭhahantassa ca tathāgatassa bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā natthi…pe… ossajī”ti.

174. The discourse on the liberations is of clear meaning. These eight liberations, too, were introduced solely for the purpose of demonstrating fearlessness. It is said that after speaking of these, he said this: “Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who enters and emerges from these attainments, there is no fear or timidity... he relinquished.”

175. Idānipi bhagavā ānandassa okāsaṃ adatvāva ekamidāhantiādinā nayena aparampi desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha paṭhamābhisambuddhoti abhisambuddho hutvā paṭhamameva aṭṭhame sattāhe.

175. Now, without giving Ānanda an opportunity, the Blessed One began another discourse in the manner of that beginning, “On one occasion I...” Therein, “first fully enlightened” means: having become fully enlightened, in the very first, eighth week.

177. Ossaṭṭhoti vissajjito paricchinno, evaṃ kira vatvā – “tenāyaṃ dasasahassī lokadhātu kampitthā”ti āha.

177. ‘Ossaṭṭho’ means relinquished, determined. It is said that having spoken thus, he said: “At that, this ten-thousandfold world system shook.”

Ānandayācanakathā

The Account of Ānanda's Request.

178. Alanti paṭikkhepavacanametaṃ. Bodhinti catumaggañāṇapaṭiveghaṃ. Saddahasi tvanti evaṃ vuttabhāvaṃ tathāgatassa saddahasīti vadati. Tasmātihānandāti [M 2.0154] yasmā idaṃ vacanaṃ saddahasi, tasmā tuyhevetaṃ dukkaṭanti dasseti.

178. ‘Alaṃ’ is a word of rejection. ‘Bodhi’ means the penetration of the knowledge of the four paths. As for ‘saddahasi tvaṃ,’ he is saying: “Do you have faith that the Tathāgata spoke thus?” As for ‘Tasmātihānanda,’ this shows: “Because you have faith in this statement, therefore this is your own misdeed.”

179. Ekamidāhanti [V 2.0138] idaṃ bhagavā – “na kevalaṃ ahaṃ idheva taṃ āmantesiṃ, aññadāpi āmantetvā oḷārikaṃ nimittaṃ akāsiṃ, tampi [P 2.0564] tayā na paṭividdhaṃ, tavevāyaṃ aparādho”ti evaṃ sokavinodanatthāya nānappakārato therasseva dosāropanatthaṃ ārabhi.

179. The Blessed One began this passage starting with “On one occasion I...” for the purpose of dispelling sorrow and, in various ways, placing the fault on the Elder himself, saying: “It was not only here that I addressed you. On other occasions, too, I addressed you and made a clear hint, but that too was not penetrated by you. This is your own fault.”

183. Piyehi manāpehīti mātāpitābhātābhaginiādikehi jātiyā nānābhāvo, maraṇena vinābhāvo, bhavena aññathābhāvo. Taṃ kutettha labbhāti tanti tasmā, yasmā sabbeheva piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo, tasmā dasa pāramiyo pūretvāpi, sambodhiṃ patvāpi, dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvāpi, yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvāpi, devorohaṇaṃ katvāpi, yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ vata tathāgatassāpi sarīraṃ mā palujjīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, rodantenāpi kandantenāpi na sakkā taṃ kāraṇaṃ laddhunti. Puna paccāvamissatīti yaṃ cattaṃ vantaṃ, taṃ vata puna paṭikhādissatīti attho.

183. “From beloved and dear ones” means from mother, father, brothers, sisters, and so on. ‘Nānābhāvo’ is otherness through birth; ‘vinābhāvo’ is separation through death; ‘aññathābhāvo’ is alteration through existence. “How can that be obtained here?”: ‘taṃ’ means “therefore.” Because there is otherness from all that is beloved and dear, therefore, even after fulfilling the ten perfections, attaining full enlightenment, setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, displaying the Twin Miracle, and performing the descent from the deva world, for the wish, “May the Tathāgata's body—which is born, come to be, conditioned, and subject to dissolution—not dissolve!” there is no basis. Even by weeping and lamenting, that outcome cannot be obtained. “Will return again” means: will one indeed consume again what has been relinquished and vomited?

184. Yathayidaṃ brahmacariyanti yathā idaṃ sikkhāttayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ. Addhaniyanti addhānakkhamaṃ. Ciraṭṭhitikanti cirappavattivasena ciraṭṭhitikaṃ. Cattāro satipaṭṭhānātiādi sabbaṃ lokiyalokuttaravaseneva kathitaṃ. Etesaṃ pana bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ vinicchayo sabbākārena visuddhimagge paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddese vutto. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

184. “So that this holy life” means so that this holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the threefold training. “May be enduring” means able to last a long time. “May be long-standing” means long-standing by way of long continuation. The four establishments of mindfulness and so on are all taught in terms of the mundane and the supramundane. The analysis of these states pertaining to enlightenment, however, is given in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Path. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Tatiyabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Third Recitation Section is concluded.

Nāgāpalokitavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Elephant's Gaze.

186. Nāgāpalokitanti yathā hi mahājanassa aṭṭhīni koṭiyā koṭiṃ āhacca ṭhitāni paccekabuddhānaṃ, aṅkusakalaggāni viya, na evaṃ buddhānaṃ. Buddhānaṃ [M 2.0155] pana saṅkhalikāni viya ekābaddhāni hutvā ṭhitāni, tasmā pacchato apalokanakāle na sakkā hoti gīvaṃ parivattetuṃ. Yathā pana hatthināgo pacchābhāgaṃ apaloketukāmo sakalasarīreneva parivattati, evaṃ parivattitabbaṃ hoti. Bhagavato pana nagaradvāre ṭhatvā – “vesāliṃ apalokessāmī”ti citte uppannamatte – “bhagavā anekāni kappakoṭisahassāni pāramiyo pūrentehi tumhehi na gīvaṃ parivattetvā [V 2.0139] apalokanakammaṃ kata”nti ayaṃ pathavī kulālacakkaṃ viya parivattetvā bhagavantaṃ [P 2.0565] vesālinagarābhimukhaṃ akāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

186. Regarding 'the elephant's gaze': For whereas the bones of the general populace lie with one end touching another, and the bones of Paccekabuddhas are interlocked like hooks, it is not so with the Buddhas. The bones of Buddhas, however, remain bound together like a chain. Thus, at the time of looking back, it is not possible to turn the neck. Just as a great elephant, wishing to look back, must turn its entire body, so too must a turning be done. But when the Blessed One stood at the city gate, and the thought arose in his mind, 'I will gaze upon Vesālī,' this earth turned like a potter's wheel, making the Blessed One face Vesālī, because the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections for countless thousands of aeons, had never performed the act of looking back by turning the neck. This was said in reference to that.

Nanu ca na kevalaṃ vesāliyāva, sāvatthirājagahanāḷandapāṭaligāmakoṭigāmanātikagāmakesupi tato tato nikkhantakāle taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ pacchimadassanameva, tattha tattha kasmā nāgāpalokitaṃ nāpalokesīti? Anacchariyattā. Tattha tattha hi nivattetvā apalokentassetaṃ na acchariyaṃ hoti, tasmā nāpalokesi. Api ca vesālirājāno āsannavināsā, tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ upari vinassissanti. Te taṃ nagaradvāre nāgāpalokitaṃ nāma cetiyaṃ katvā gandhamālādīhi pūjessanti, taṃ nesaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatīti tesaṃ anukampāya apalokesi.

But surely it was not only in Vesālī; when departing from Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, Nālandā, Pāṭaligāma, Koṭigāma, and Nātikagāma, in each case, that was the final glance. Why then was the 'elephant’s gaze' not performed in those places? Because it was not extraordinary. For in those various places, turning back and looking would not have been extraordinary; therefore, he did not gaze back. Moreover, the rulers of Vesālī were near destruction; they would perish after three years. They would build a shrine named the 'Elephant’s Gaze' at that city gate and worship it with perfumes, garlands, and so on, and that would be for their long-term welfare and happiness. Out of compassion for them, he gazed back.

Dukkhassantakaroti vaṭṭadukkhassa antakaro. Cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Parinibbutoti kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto.

‘End-maker of suffering’ means the end-maker of the suffering of the round of existence. ‘Possessed of vision’ means possessing the five eyes. ‘Fully extinguished’ means fully extinguished by the Nibbāna of the defilements.

Catumahāpadesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Four Great References

187. Mahāpadeseti mahāokāse, mahāapadese vā, buddhādayo mahante mahante apadisitvā vuttāni mahākāraṇānīti attho.

187. Regarding 'great references' (mahāpadesa): it means 'in a great context' (mahāokāse), or 'in a great reference' (mahāapadese). The meaning is that they are great reasons (mahākāraṇāni) spoken by referring to great beings such as the Buddha.

188. Neva abhinanditabbanti haṭṭhatuṭṭhehi sādhukāraṃ datvā pubbeva na sotabbaṃ, evaṃ kate hi pacchā “idaṃ na sametī”ti vuccamāno – “kiṃ pubbeva ayaṃ dhammo, idāni na dhammo”ti vatvā laddhiṃ na vissajjeti. Nappaṭikkositabbanti – “kiṃ esa bālo vadatī”ti evaṃ pubbeva na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ vutte hi vattuṃ yuttampi na vakkhati. Tenāha – “anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā”ti. Padabyañjanānīti padasaṅkhātāni byañjanāni. Sādhukaṃ uggahetvāti imasmiṃ [M 2.0156] ṭhāne pāḷi vuttā, imasmiṃ ṭhāne attho vutto, imasmiṃ ṭhāne anusandhi kathito, imasmiṃ ṭhāne pubbāparaṃ kathitanti suṭṭhu gahetvā. Sutte osāretabbānīti sutte otāretabbāni. Vinaye sandassetabbānīti vinaye saṃsandetabbāni.

188. ‘It should not be approved of’ means one should not give a ‘Well said!’ with joy and delight beforehand. For if this is done, when it is later said, ‘This does not conform,’ one does not relinquish one's view, saying, ‘Was this the Dhamma before, and now it is not the Dhamma?’ ‘It should not be rejected’ means one should not say beforehand, ‘What is this fool saying?’ For if this is said, one will not say even what is fitting to be said. Therefore, He said, ‘without approving, without rejecting.’ ‘Words and syllables’ means syllables reckoned as words. ‘Having been well grasped’ means having thoroughly grasped that ‘in this place the Pāli was stated, in this place the meaning was stated, in this place the connection was explained, in this place the sequence was explained.’ ‘They should be checked against the Sutta’ means they should be applied to the Sutta. ‘They should be compared with the Vinaya’ means they should be collated with the Vinaya.

Ettha ca suttanti vinayo. Yathāha – “kattha paṭikkhittaṃ? Sāvatthiyaṃ suttavibhaṅge”ti (cuḷava. 457). Vinayoti khandhako. Yathāha – “vinayātisāre”ti. Evaṃ vinayapiṭakampi na [V 2.0140] pariyādiyati. Ubhatovibhaṅgā pana suttaṃ, khandhakaparivārā vinayoti evaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ pariyādiyati. Athavā suttantapiṭakaṃ suttaṃ, vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayoti evaṃ dveyeva piṭakāni pariyādiyanti. Suttantābhidhammapiṭakāni [P 2.0566] vā suttaṃ, vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayoti evampi tīṇi piṭakāni na tāva pariyādiyanti. Asuttanāmakañhi buddhavacanaṃ nāma atthi. Seyyathidaṃ – jātakaṃ, paṭisambhidā, niddeso, suttanipāto, dhammapadaṃ, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, vimānavatthu, petavatthu, theragāthā, therīgāthā, apadānanti.

And here, 'sutta' means the Vinaya. As it is said: 'Where was it rejected? In Sāvatthī, in the Suttavibhaṅga.' 'Vinaya' means the Khandhaka. As it is said: 'in a transgression of the Vinaya.' In this way, the Vinayapiṭaka is not fully encompassed. But if the two Vibhaṅgas are the 'sutta,' and the Khandhakas and Parivāra are the 'vinaya,' in this way the Vinayapiṭaka is fully encompassed. Alternatively, the Suttantapiṭaka is the 'sutta,' and the Vinayapiṭaka is the 'vinaya.' In this way, only two Piṭakas are encompassed. Or, the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are the 'sutta,' and the Vinayapiṭaka is the 'vinaya.' Even in this way, the three Piṭakas are not yet fully encompassed. For there exists the word of the Buddha that is not named 'sutta.' That is to say: Jātaka, Paṭisambhidā, Niddesa, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and Apadāna.

Sudinnatthero pana – “asuttanāmakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ na atthī”ti taṃ sabbaṃ paṭipakkhipitvā – “tīṇi piṭakāni suttaṃ, vinayo pana kāraṇa”nti āha. Tato taṃ kāraṇaṃ dassento idaṃ suttamāhari –

The elder Sudinna, however, rejected all of that, saying, ‘There is no word of the Buddha that is not named “sutta,”’ and declared: ‘The three Piṭakas are the Sutta, but the Vinaya is the Principle.’ Then, to demonstrate that Principle, he cited this sutta:

“Ye kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi, ime dhammā sarāgāya saṃvattanti no virāgāya, saññogāya saṃvattanti no visaññogāya, ācayāya saṃvattanti no apacayāya, mahicchatāya saṃvattanti no appicchatāya, asantuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti no santuṭṭhiyā, saṅgaṇikāya saṃvattanti no pavivekāya, kosajjāya saṃvattanti no vīriyārambhāya, dubbharatāya saṃvattanti no subharatāya. Ekaṃsena, gotami, dhāreyyāsi – ‘neso dhammo, neso vinayo, netaṃ satthusāsana’nti. Ye ca kho tvaṃ, gotami, dhamme jāneyyāsi, ime dhammā virāgāya saṃvattanti no sarāgāya, visaññogāya saṃvattanti no saññogāya, apacayāya saṃvattanti no ācayāya, appicchatāya saṃvattanti no mahicchatāya, santuṭṭhiyā saṃvattanti no asantuṭṭhiyā, pavivekāya saṃvattanti no saṅgaṇikāya[M 2.0157], vīriyārambhāya saṃvattanti no kosajjāya, subharatāya saṃvattanti no dubbharatāya. Ekaṃsena, gotami, dhāreyyāsi – ‘eso dhammo, eso vinayo, etaṃ satthusāsana’nti” (a. ni. 8.53).

‘Gotamī, those things of which you might know, “These things lead to passion, not to dispassion; they lead to being fettered, not to being unfettered; they lead to accumulation, not to dispersal; they lead to desire, not to modesty; they lead to discontent, not to contentment; they lead to company, not to seclusion; they lead to laziness, not to arousal of energy; they lead to being hard to support, not to being easy to support,” you should definitively bear in mind, Gotamī: “This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction.” And those things of which you might know, Gotamī, “These things lead to dispassion, not to passion; they lead to being unfettered, not to being fettered; they lead to dispersal, not to accumulation; they lead to modesty, not to desire; they lead to contentment, not to discontent; they lead to seclusion, not to company; they lead to arousal of energy, not to laziness; they lead to being easy to support, not to being hard to support,” you should definitively bear in mind, Gotamī: “This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.”’

Tasmā sutteti tepiṭake buddhavacane otāretabbāni. Vinayeti etasmiṃ rāgādivinayakāraṇe saṃsandetabbānīti ayamettha attho. Na ceva sutte osarantīti suttapaṭipāṭiyā katthaci anāgantvā challiṃ uṭṭhapetvā guḷhavessantara-guḷhaummagga-guḷhavinaya-vedallapiṭakānaṃ aññatarato āgatāni paññāyantīti attho. Evaṃ āgatāni hi rāgādivinaye ca na paññāyamānāni chaḍḍetabbāni honti. Tena vuttaṃ – “iti hetaṃ, bhikkhave, chaḍḍeyyāthā”ti. Etenupāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

Therefore, 'in the Sutta' means they should be checked against the Buddha's word in the Tipiṭaka. 'In the Vinaya' means they should be collated with this, the cause for the removal of lust and other defilements—this is the meaning here. 'They do not enter into the Sutta' means that, not appearing anywhere in the sequence of the Suttas, but presenting a counterfeit teaching, they appear to come from one of the hidden collections—such as the Guḷhavessantara, Guḷhaummagga, Guḷhavinaya, or the Vedalla Piṭaka. Indeed, teachings that have come in this way and are not evident in the discipline for the removal of lust and other defilements are to be discarded. Therefore, it is said: 'Thus, monks, you should discard it.' By this method, the meaning should be understood in all cases.

Idaṃ[V 2.0141], bhikkhave, catutthaṃ mahāpadesaṃ dhāreyyāthāti idaṃ [P 2.0567] catutthaṃ dhammassa patiṭṭhānokāsaṃ dhāreyyātha.

The words, 'Monks, you should remember this fourth great authority,' mean that you should remember this as the fourth ground for the establishment of the Dhamma.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne imaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sutte cattāro mahāpadesā, khandhake cattāro mahāpadesā, cattāri pañhabyākaraṇāni, suttaṃ, suttānulomaṃ, ācariyavādo, attanomati, tisso saṅgītiyoti.

Now, in this place, the following miscellaneous points should be understood: in the Suttas, the four great authorities; in the Khandhakas, the four great authorities; the four ways of answering questions; the Sutta, what conforms with the Sutta, the teacher's tradition, one's own opinion, and the three Councils.

Tattha – “ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo”ti dhammavinicchaye patte ime cattāro mahāpadesā pamāṇaṃ. Yaṃ ettha sameti tadeva gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ viravantassapi na gahetabbaṃ.

Therein, when a determination of Dhamma and Vinaya is required, these four great authorities are the standard. Whatever agrees with them should be accepted, and whatever disagrees should not be accepted, even if the speaker is eloquent.

“Idaṃ kappati, idaṃ na kappatī”ti kappiyākappiyavinicchaye patte – “yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā idaṃ na kappatīti appaṭikkhittaṃ, taṃ ce akappiyaṃ anulometi, kappiyaṃ paṭibāhati, taṃ vo na kappatī”tiādinā (mahāva. 305) nayena khandhake vuttā cattāro mahāpadesā pamāṇaṃ. Tesaṃ vinicchayakathā samantapāsādikāyaṃ vuttā. Tattha vuttanayena yaṃ kappiyaṃ anulometi, tadeva kappiyaṃ, itaraṃ akappiyanti evaṃ sanniṭṭhānaṃ kātabbaṃ.

When a determination of what is allowable and unallowable is required, as in 'This is allowable, this is not allowable,' the four great authorities mentioned in the Khandhaka are the standard, according to the method beginning with: 'Whatever, monks, I have not rejected as “this is not allowable,” if it accords with what is unallowable and obstructs what is allowable, that is not allowable for you,' and so on. The discussion on their determination is given in the Samantapāsādikā. There, according to the method described, a conclusion should be reached thus: whatever accords with what is allowable is indeed allowable, and the rest is unallowable.

Ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo pañho, vibhajjabyākaraṇīyo pañho, paṭipucchābyākaraṇīyo pañho, ṭhapanīyo pañhoti imāni cattāri pañhabyākaraṇāni nāma. Tattha “cakkhuṃ anicca”nti puṭṭhena – “āma anicca”nti ekaṃseneva byākātabbaṃ[M 2.0158]. Esa nayo sotādīsu. Ayaṃ ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo pañho. “Aniccaṃ nāma cakkhu”nti puṭṭhena – “na cakkhumeva, sotampi aniccaṃ ghānampi anicca”nti evaṃ vibhajitvā byākātabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vibhajjabyākaraṇīyo pañho. “Yathā cakkhu tathā sotaṃ, yathā sotaṃ tathā cakkhu”nti puṭṭhena “kenaṭṭhena pucchasī”ti paṭipucchitvā “dassanaṭṭhena pucchāmī”ti vutte “na hī”ti byākātabbaṃ, “aniccaṭṭhena pucchāmī”ti vutte āmāti byākātabbaṃ. Ayaṃ paṭipucchābyākaraṇīyo pañho. “Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”ntiādīni puṭṭhena pana “abyākatametaṃ bhagavatā”ti ṭhapetabbo, esa pañho na byākātabbo. Ayaṃ ṭhapanīyo pañho. Iti tenākārena pañhe sampatte imāni cattāri pañhabyākaraṇāni pamāṇaṃ. Imesaṃ vasena so pañho byākātabbo.

A question to be answered definitively, a question to be answered with a distinction, a question to be answered with a counter-question, and a question to be set aside—these are the four ways of answering questions. Therein, when asked, 'Is the eye impermanent?' one should answer definitively, 'Yes, it is impermanent.' This is the method for the ear and so on. This is a question to be answered definitively. When asked, 'Is the impermanent called the eye?' one should answer with a distinction, 'Not only the eye; the ear is also impermanent, the nose is also impermanent.' This is a question to be answered with a distinction. When asked, 'As the eye, so the ear; as the ear, so the eye?' one should first counter-question, 'In what sense do you ask?' If the reply is, 'I ask in the sense of seeing,' then one should answer, 'No.' If the reply is, 'I ask in the sense of impermanence,' then one should answer, 'Yes.' This is a question to be answered with a counter-question. However, when asked questions such as, 'Is that the life principle, that the body?' one should set it aside, saying, 'This has not been declared by the Blessed One.' This question should not be answered. This is a question to be set aside. Thus, when a question is encountered in that manner, these four ways of answering questions are the standard. The question should be answered according to these.

Suttādīsu pana suttaṃ nāma tisso saṅgītiyo ārūḷhāni tīṇi piṭakāni. Suttānulomaṃ nāma anulomakappiyaṃ. Ācariyavādo nāma aṭṭhakathā. Attanomati nāma nayaggāhena [V 2.0142] anubuddhiyā attano paṭibhānaṃ. Tattha suttaṃ appaṭibāhiyaṃ, taṃ paṭibāhantena buddhova paṭibāhito hoti. Anulomakappiyaṃ [P 2.0568] pana suttena samentameva gahetabbaṃ, na itaraṃ. Ācariyavādopi suttena samentoyeva gahetabbo, na itaro. Attanomati pana sabbadubbalā, sāpi suttena samentāyeva gahetabbā, na itarā. Pañcasatikā, sattasatikā, sahassikāti imā pana tisso saṅgītiyo. Suttampi tāsu āgatameva pamāṇaṃ, itaraṃ gārayhasuttaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Tattha otarantānipi hi padabyañjanāni na ceva sutte otaranti, na ca vinaye sandissantīti veditabbāni.

Among these, 'Sutta' means the three Piṭakas that were included in the three Councils. 'Suttānuloma' means what is conformably allowable. 'Ācariyavāda' means the commentaries. 'Attanomati' means one's own ingenuity, gained by grasping the method and by insight. Therein, the Sutta is irrefutable; whoever refutes it, refutes the Buddha himself. What is conformably allowable, however, should be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. The teachers' doctrine, too, should be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. Personal opinion, however, is the weakest of all; that too should be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. The Five Hundred, the Seven Hundred, and the Thousand—these are the three Councils. The Sutta that has come down in them is the standard; other, blameworthy suttas should not be accepted. Indeed, the words and phrases that appear in them should be understood as neither entering into the Sutta nor being found in the Vinaya.

Kammāraputtacundavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Cunda the Smith's Son

189. Kammāraputtassāti suvaṇṇakāraputtassa. So kira aḍḍho mahākuṭumbiko bhagavato paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpanno hutvā attano ambavane vihāraṃ kārāpetvā niyyātesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “ambavane”ti.

189. 'Of the smith's son' means of the goldsmith's son. It is said that he was a wealthy man, the head of a large household. Upon first seeing the Blessed One, he became a stream-enterer, and having had a monastery built in his own mango grove, he presented it. Referring to that, it is said, 'in the mango grove.'

Sūkaramaddavanti nātitaruṇassa nātijiṇṇassa ekajeṭṭhakasūkarassa pavattamaṃsaṃ. Taṃ kira mudu ceva siniddhañca hoti, taṃ paṭiyādāpetvā sādhukaṃ pacāpetvāti [M 2.0159] attho. Eke bhaṇanti – “sūkaramaddavanti pana muduodanassa pañcagorasayūsapācanavidhānassa nāmetaṃ, yathā gavapānaṃ nāma pākanāma”nti. Keci bhaṇanti – “sūkaramaddavaṃ nāma rasāyanavidhi, taṃ pana rasāyanasatthe āgacchati, taṃ cundena – ‘bhagavato parinibbānaṃ na bhaveyyā’ti rasāyanaṃ paṭiyatta”nti. Tattha pana dvisahassadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu devatā ojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu.

Sūkaramaddava means the readily available meat of a prime boar, neither too young nor too old. It is said to be both soft and tender. The meaning is that, having had it prepared, he had it well cooked. Some say: 'Sūkaramaddava is the name for a preparation of soft rice cooked with the juice of the five products of a cow, just as gavapāna is a name for a cooked dish.' Others say: 'Sūkaramaddava is a type of elixir, which is found in the science of elixirs. Cunda prepared this elixir, thinking, “May the Blessed One's final Nibbāna not occur.”' In that food, the deities of the four great continents with their two thousand surrounding islands infused nutritive essence.

Nāhaṃ tanti imaṃ sīhanādaṃ kimatthaṃ nadati? Parūpavādamocanatthaṃ. Attanā paribhuttāvasesaṃ neva bhikkhūnaṃ, na manussānaṃ dātuṃ adāsi, āvāṭe nikhaṇāpetvā vināsesīti hi vattukāmānaṃ idaṃ sutvā vacanokāso na bhavissatīti paresaṃ upavādamocanatthaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadatīti.

Why does he utter this lion's roar, 'I do not see...'? To avert the blame of others. For those who might wish to say, 'He did not give the remainder of what he had consumed to be given to the monks or to humans, but had it buried in a pit and destroyed,' upon hearing this there will be no opportunity for them to speak. Thus, he utters the lion's roar to avert the blame of others.

190. Bhuttassa ca sūkaramaddavenāti bhuttassa udapādi, na pana bhuttapaccayā. Yadi hi abhuttassa uppajjissatha, atikharo bhavissati. Siniddhabhojanaṃ bhuttattā panassa tanuvedanā ahosi. Teneva padasā gantuṃ asakkhi. Virecamānoti abhiṇhaṃ pavattalohitavirecanova samāno[V 2.0143]. Avocāti attanā patthitaṭṭhāne parinibbānatthāya evamāha. Imā pana dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi ṭhapitagāthāyoti veditabbā.

190. "Bhuttassa ca sūkaramaddavenāti"—it arose after he had eaten, but not because he had eaten. For if it had arisen for one who had not eaten, it would have been very severe. However, because he had eaten rich food, his pain was slight. For that very reason, he was able to go on foot. "Virecamānoti" means he was one who was constantly passing bloody stools. "Avocāti" means he spoke thus for the purpose of attaining final Nibbāna in the place he had aspired to reach. These verses, however, should be understood as verses established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma.

Pānīyāharaṇavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Fetching of Water

191. Iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Acchodakāti [P 2.0569] pasannodakā. Sātodakāti madhurodakā. Sītodakāti tanusītalasalilā. Setakāti nikkaddamā. Suppatitthāti sundaratitthā.

191. "Iṅghā" is a particle in the sense of urging. "Acchodakā" means clear water. "Sātodakā" means sweet water. "Sītodakā" means cool, clear water. "Setakā" means free of mud. "Suppatitthā" means having a good ford.

Pukkusamallaputtavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of Pukkusa the Mallian

192. Pukkusoti tassa nāmaṃ. Mallaputtoti mallarājaputto. Mallā kira vārena rajjaṃ kārenti. Yāva nesaṃ vāro na pāpuṇāti, tāva vaṇijjaṃ karonti. Ayampi vaṇijjameva karonto pañca sakaṭasatāni yojāpetvā dhuravāte vāyante purato gacchati, pacchā vāte vāyante satthavāhaṃ purato pesetvā sayaṃ pacchā gacchati. Tadā pana pacchā vāto vāyi, tasmā esa purato satthavāhaṃ pesetvā sabbaratanayāne [M 2.0160] nisīditvā kusinārato nikkhamitvā “pāvaṃ gamissāmī”ti maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tena vuttaṃ – “kusinārāya pāvaṃ addhānamaggappaṭipanno hotī”ti.

192. "Pukkusa" was his name. "Mallaputta" means a son of a Malla king. The Mallas, it is said, rule in turns. For as long as their turn does not arrive, they engage in trade. This man, too, while engaged in trade, having yoked five hundred carts, would go in front when a headwind blew; when a tailwind blew, he would send the caravan ahead and go behind himself. At that time, however, a tailwind was blowing, so he sent the caravan ahead, and seated in a carriage adorned with all manner of jewels, he departed from Kusinārā and set out on the road, thinking, "I will go to Pāvā." Therefore it is said: "He was journeying on the main road from Kusinārā to Pāvā."

Āḷāroti tassa nāmaṃ. Dīghapiṅgalo kireso, tenassa āḷāroti nāmaṃ ahosi. Kālāmoti gottaṃ. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma. Neva dakkhatīti na addasa. Yatrasaddayuttattā panetaṃ anāgatavasena vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi īdisesu ṭhānesu saddalakkhaṇaṃ.

"Āḷāra" was his name. It is said he was tall and had tawny eyes, hence his name was Āḷāra. "Kālāma" was his clan name. "Yatra hi nāma" means "who indeed." "Neva dakkhati" means "he did not see." However, because it is connected with the word "yatra," this is stated in the future tense. For such is the grammatical characteristic in such instances.

193. Niccharantīsūti vicarantīsu. Asaniyā phalantiyāti navavidhāya asaniyā bhijjamānāya viya mahāravaṃ ravantiyā. Navavidhā hi asaniyo – asaññā, vicakkā, saterā, gaggarā, kapisīsā, macchavilolikā, kukkuṭakā, daṇḍamaṇikā, sukkhāsanīti. Tattha asaññā asaññaṃ karoti. Vicakkā ekaṃ cakkaṃ karoti. Saterā saterasadisā hutvā patati. Gaggarā gaggarāyamānā patati. Kapisīsā bhamukaṃ ukkhipento makkaṭo viya hoti. Macchavilolikā vilolitamaccho viya hoti. Kukkuṭakā kukkuṭasadisā hutvā patati. Daṇḍamaṇikā naṅgalasadisā hutvā patati. Sukkhāsanī patitaṭṭhānaṃ samugghāṭeti.

193. "Niccharantīsu" means flashing forth. "Asaniyā phalantiyā" means with the great roar of a ninefold thunderbolt as it splits apart. For there are nine kinds of thunderbolts: the Unconscious-maker, the Wheel-former, the Grass-cutter, the Rumbler, the Monkey-head, the Fish-writher, the Rooster, the Plough-knob, and the Dry-strike. Among them, the Unconscious-maker renders one unconscious. The Wheel-former creates a single wheel. The Grass-cutter falls as if cutting through grass. The Rumbler falls with a rumbling sound. The Monkey-head is like a monkey raising its brow. The Fish-writher is like a writhing fish. The Rooster falls like a rooster. The Plough-knob falls like the knob on a plough handle. The Dry-strike utterly destroys the place where it falls.

Deve [V 2.0144] vassanteti sukkhagajjitaṃ gajjitvā antarantarā vassante. Ātumāyanti ātumaṃ nissāya viharāmi. Bhusāgāreti khalasālāyaṃ. Etthesoti etasmiṃ kāraṇe eso mahājanakāyo sannipatito. Kva ahosīti kuhiṃ ahosi. So taṃ bhanteti so tvaṃ bhante.

"Deve vassante" means when the sky, having thundered with dry thunder, was raining intermittently. "Ātumāyanti" means "I am dwelling near Ātumā." "Bhusāgāre" means in a threshing hall. "Ettheso" means "for this reason, this great crowd has gathered." "Kva ahosīti" means "where were you?" "So taṃ bhanteti" means "that you, venerable sir."

194. Siṅgīvaṇṇanti siṅgīsuvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ. Yugamaṭṭhanti [P 2.0570] maṭṭhayugaṃ, saṇhasāṭakayugaḷanti attho. Dhāraṇīyanti antarantarā mayā dhāretabbaṃ, paridahitabbanti attho. Taṃ kira so tathārūpe chaṇadivaseyeva dhāretvā sesakāle nikkhipati. Evaṃ uttamaṃ maṅgalavatthayugaṃ sandhāyāha. Anukampaṃ upādāyāti mayi anukampaṃ paṭicca. Acchādehīti upacāravacanametaṃ – ekaṃ mayhaṃ dehi, ekaṃ ānandassāti attho. Kiṃ pana thero taṃ gaṇhīti? Āma gaṇhi. Kasmā? Matthakappattakiccattā. Kiñcāpi hesa evarūpaṃ lābhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānaṃ paṭipanno. Taṃ panassa upaṭṭhākakiccaṃ matthakaṃ pattaṃ. Tasmā aggahesi. Ye cāpi evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “anārādhako maññe ānando [M 2.0161] pañcavīsati vassāni upaṭṭhahantena na kiñci bhagavato santikā tena laddhapubba”nti. Tesaṃ vacanokāsacchedanatthampi aggahesi. Api ca jānāti bhagavā – “ānando gahetvāpi attanā na dhāressati, mayhaṃyeva pūjaṃ karissati. Mallaputtena pana ānandaṃ pūjentena saṅghopi pūjito bhavissati, evamassa mahāpuññarāsi bhavissatī”ti therassa ekaṃ dāpesi. Theropi teneva kāraṇena aggahesīti. Dhammiyā kathāyāti vatthānumodanakathāya.

194. "Siṅgīvaṇṇa" means the color of siṅgī-gold. "Yugamaṭṭha" means a polished pair, that is, a pair of fine garments. "Dhāraṇīya" means that it should be worn by me from time to time, that is, it should be put on. It is said that he wore it only on such festive days and put it aside at other times. Thus, he spoke referring to this supreme pair of auspicious cloths. "Anukampaṃ upādāya" means out of compassion for me. "Acchādehi" is a conventional expression, meaning "give one to me and one to Ānanda." But did the Elder accept it? Yes, he accepted it. Why? Because his service had reached its culmination. Although he had undertaken the position of attendant having rejected such gain, that service of his as an attendant had reached its peak. Therefore, he accepted it. And also, to cut off the opportunity for speech for those who might say, "Ānanda, I suppose, is unable to please the Blessed One; though he has been in attendance for twenty-five years, he has never before received anything from the Blessed One," he accepted it. Moreover, the Blessed One knew: "Even having accepted it, Ānanda will not wear it himself but will make an offering of it to me. And when the Malla's son honors Ānanda, the Saṅgha will also be honored, and thus there will be a great accumulation of merit for him." Thus, he had one given to the Elder. The Elder also accepted it for that very reason. "Dhammiyā kathāya" means with a talk of rejoicing over the cloth offering.

195. Bhagavato kāyaṃ upanāmitanti nivāsanapārupanavasena allīyāpitaṃ. Bhagavāpi tato ekaṃ nivāsesi, ekaṃ pārupi. Hataccikaṃ viyāti yathā hatacciko aṅgāro antanteneva jotati, bahi panassa pabhā natthi, evaṃ bahi paṭicchannappabhaṃ hutvā khāyatīti attho.

195. "Bhagavato kāyaṃ upanāmitaṃ" means it was placed upon the Blessed One's body, that is, it was made to adhere by being worn as a lower robe and an upper robe. The Blessed One, too, wore one from that pair as a lower robe and one as an upper robe. "Hataccikaṃ viya" means just as a flameless ember glows only within, but has no radiance outside, so too did he appear, with his radiance concealed externally—this is the meaning.

Imesu kho, ānanda, dvīsupi kālesūti kasmā imesu dvīsu kālesu evaṃ hoti? Āhāravisesena ceva balavasomanassena ca. Etesu hi dvīsu kālesu sakalacakkavāḷe devatā āhāre ojaṃ pakkhipanti, taṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ kucchiṃ pavisitvā pasannarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpassa pasannattā manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni ativiya virocanti. Sambodhidivase cassa – “anekakappakoṭisatasahassasañcito vata me kilesarāsi ajja pahīno”ti āvajjantassa balavasomanassaṃ uppajjati, cittaṃ pasīdati, citte pasanne lohitaṃ pasīdati, lohite pasanne manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni ativiya virocanti. Parinibbānadivasepi – “ajja, dānāhaṃ, anekehi [P 2.0571] buddhasatasahassehi paviṭṭhaṃ amatamahānibbānaṃ nāma nagaraṃ pavisissāmī”ti āvajjantassa [V 2.0145] balavasomanassaṃ uppajjati, cittaṃ pasīdati, citte pasanne lohitaṃ pasīdati, lohite pasanne manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni ativiya virocanti. Iti āhāravisesena ceva balavasomanassena ca imesu dvīsu kālesu evaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Upavattaneti pācīnato nivattanasālavane. Antarena yamakasālānanti yamakasālarukkhānaṃ majjhe.

Why is it, Ānanda, that on these two occasions such a thing happens? It is due to special food and intense joy. For on these two occasions, the deities throughout the entire universe infuse nutritive essence into the food, and when that excellent meal enters the stomach, it produces a radiant physical form. Because the physical form arising from food is radiant, the six sense faculties with the mind as the sixth shine exceedingly bright. And on the day of enlightenment, for him reflecting—‘Indeed, today the mass of my defilements accumulated over countless hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons has been abandoned’—intense joy arises, the mind becomes clear, when the mind is clear the blood becomes clear, and when the blood is clear the six sense faculties with the mind as the sixth shine exceedingly bright. On the day of Parinibbāna as well, for him reflecting—‘Today, I shall enter the city named the Deathless, the great Nibbāna, which has been entered by many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas’—intense joy arises, the mind becomes clear, when the mind is clear the blood becomes clear, and when the blood is clear the six sense faculties with the mind as the sixth shine exceedingly bright. Thus, it should be understood that on these two occasions such a thing happens due to special food and intense joy. ‘Upavattana’ means in the Sāla grove of turning back, from the east. ‘Antarena yamakasālānaṃ’ means in the middle of the twin Sāla trees.

Siṅgīvaṇṇanti gāthā saṅgītikāle ṭhapitā.

The verse beginning with 'Siṅgīvaṇṇa' was established at the time of the Recitation.

196. Nhatvā [M 2.0162] ca pivitvā cāti ettha tadā kira bhagavati nahāyante antonadiyaṃ macchakacchapā ca ubhatotīresu vanasaṇḍo ca sabbaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇameva hoti. Ambavananti tassāyeva nadiyā tīre ambavanaṃ. Āyasmantaṃ cundakanti tasmiṃ kira khaṇe ānandatthero udakasāṭakaṃ pīḷento ohīyi, cundatthero samīpe ahosi. Taṃ bhagavā āmantesi.

196. Regarding ‘Having bathed and drunk’: here, it is said that when the Blessed One was bathing in the river, the fish and turtles within the river and the forest grove on both banks all became the color of gold. ‘Ambavana’ means a mango grove on the bank of that very river. Regarding ‘the Venerable Cundaka’: it is said that at that moment, the Elder Ānanda was left behind while wringing out the bathing cloth, and the Elder Cunda was nearby. The Blessed One addressed him.

Gantvāna buddho nadikaṃ kakudhanti imāpi gāthā saṅgītikāleyeva ṭhapitā. Tattha pavattā bhagavā idha dhammeti bhagavā idha sāsane dhamme pavattā, caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassāni pavattānīti attho. Pamukhe nisīdīti satthu puratova nisīdi. Ettāvatā ca thero anuppatto. Evaṃ anuppattaṃ atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi.

The verses beginning ‘The Buddha, having gone to the river Kakudhā’ were also established at the time of the Recitation. Therein, ‘the Blessed One promulgated the Dhamma here’ means the Blessed One promulgated the Dhamma in this Dispensation; the meaning is that he promulgated the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma. ‘He sat in front’ means he sat right before the Teacher. And by this time, the Elder had arrived. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda who had thus arrived.

197. Alābhāti ye aññesaṃ dānānisaṃsasaṅkhātā lābhā honti, te alābhā. Dulladdhanti puññavisesena laddhampi manussattaṃ dulladdhaṃ. Yassa teti yassa tava. Uttaṇḍulaṃ vā atikilinnaṃ vā ko jānāti, kīdisampi pacchimaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā tathāgato parinibbuto, addhā te yaṃ vā taṃ vā dinnaṃ bhavissatīti. Lābhāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikadānānisaṃsasaṅkhātā lābhā. Suladdhanti tuyhaṃ manussattaṃ suladdhaṃ. Samasamaphalāti sabbākārena samānaphalā.

197. ‘No gain’: those which are reckoned as gains by others, the benefits of giving, are no gain for you. ‘An ill gain’: even the human state, though obtained by special merit, is an ill gain for you. ‘For whom, for you’ means ‘for you whose...’. Someone might say: ‘“Whether undercooked or overcooked,” who knows? Having consumed some kind of last alms-meal, the Tathāgata attained Parinibbāna. Surely what you gave must have been just any old thing.’ ‘Gains’: gains reckoned as the benefits of giving in this life and the next. ‘A good gain’: your human state is a good gain. ‘Of equal fruit’: of equal fruit in every way.

Nanu ca yaṃ sujātāya dinnaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā tathāgato abhisambuddho, so sarāgasadosasamohakāle paribhutto, ayaṃ pana cundena dinno vītarāgavītadosavītamohakāle paribhutto, kasmā ete samaphalāti? Parinibbānasamatāya ca samāpattisamatāya ca anussaraṇasamatāya ca. Bhagavā [P 2.0572] hi sujātāya dinnaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā saupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbuto, cundena dinnaṃ paribhuñjitvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutoti evaṃ parinibbānasamatāyapi samaphalā. Abhisambujjhanadivase ca catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā [V 2.0146] samāpattiyo samāpajji, parinibbānadivasepi sabbā tā samāpajjīti evaṃ samāpattisamatāyapi samaphalā. Sujātā ca aparabhāge assosi – “na kiresā rukkhadevatā, bodhisatto kiresa, taṃ kira piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho[M 2.0163], sattasattāhaṃ kirassa tena yāpanaṃ ahosī”ti. Tassā idaṃ sutvā – “lābhā vata me”ti anussarantiyā balavapītisomanassaṃ udapādi. Cundassāpi aparabhāge – “avasānapiṇḍapāto kira mayā dinno, dhammasīsaṃ kira me gahitaṃ, mayhaṃ kira piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā satthā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbuto”ti sutvā “lābhā vata me”ti anussarato balavasomanassaṃ udapādīti evaṃ anussaraṇasamatāyapi samaphalāti veditabbā.

But is it not so that the alms-meal given by Sujātā, having consumed which the Tathāgata became fully enlightened, was consumed at a time when he had lust, hatred, and delusion, whereas this one given by Cunda was consumed at a time when he was free from lust, hatred, and delusion? Why then are these of equal fruit? Because of the equality of the extinction, the equality of the attainments, and the equality of the recollection. For the Blessed One, having consumed the alms-meal given by Sujātā, was extinguished by means of the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining; having consumed the one given by Cunda, he was extinguished by means of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. Thus, they are of equal fruit because of the equality of the extinction. And on the day of becoming fully enlightened, he entered into meditative attainments numbering twenty-four hundred-thousand crores, and on the day of Parinibbāna, he entered into all of them again. Thus, they are of equal fruit because of the equality of the attainments. And later, Sujātā heard: ‘It seems this is not a tree deity; it seems this is a Bodhisatta. It seems that having consumed that alms-meal, he has become fully enlightened with unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and it seems that it sustained him for seven weeks.’ Hearing this and recollecting, ‘Oh, what a gain for me!’, intense rapture and joy arose in her. For Cunda, too, later, upon hearing, ‘It seems the final alms-meal was given by me; it seems on my account the pinnacle of the Dhamma was attained; it seems that having consumed my alms-meal the Teacher was extinguished by means of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining,’ and recollecting, ‘Oh, what a gain for me!’, intense joy arose in him. Thus, it should be understood that they are of equal fruit because of the equality of the recollection.

Yasasaṃvattanikanti parivārasaṃvattanikaṃ. Ādhipateyyasaṃvattanikanti jeṭṭhakabhāvasaṃvattanikaṃ.

‘Conducive to fame’ means conducive to a following. ‘Conducive to sovereignty’ means conducive to pre-eminence.

Saṃyamatoti sīlasaṃyamena saṃyamantassa, saṃvare ṭhitassāti attho. Veraṃ na cīyatīti pañcavidhaṃ veraṃ na vaḍḍhati. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti kusalo pana ñāṇasampanno ariyamaggena anavasesaṃ pāpakaṃ lāmakaṃ akusalaṃ jahāti. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti so imaṃ pāpakaṃ jahitvā rāgādīnaṃ khayā kilesanibbānena nibbutoti. Iti cundassa ca dakkhiṇaṃ, attano ca dakkhiṇeyyasampattiṃ sampassamāno udānaṃ udānesīti.
