‘For one who restrains’: for one who restrains with the restraint of virtue; the meaning is, for one established in restraint. ‘Hostility is not accumulated’: the five kinds of hostility do not increase. ‘And the skillful one abandons evil’: the skillful one, endowed with knowledge, abandons evil, which is base and unwholesome, without remainder by means of the noble path. ‘He is extinguished through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion’: having abandoned this evil, he is extinguished through the destruction of lust and so forth, by the extinction of the defilements. Thus, seeing clearly both Cunda’s offering and his own accomplishment as one worthy of offerings, he uttered this inspired utterance.

Catutthabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth recitation section is finished.

Yamakasālāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Twin Sāla Trees.

198. Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhinti idha bhikkhūnaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo natthi. Veḷuvagāme vedanāvikkhambhanato paṭṭhāya hi – “na cirena bhagavā parinibbāyissatī”ti sutvā tato tato āgatesu bhikkhūsu ekabhikkhupi pakkanto nāma natthi. Tasmā gaṇanavītivatto saṅgho ahosi. Upavattanaṃ mallānaṃ sālavananti yatheva hi kalambanadītīrato rājamātuvihāradvārena thūpārāmaṃ gantabbaṃ [P 2.0573] hoti, evaṃ hiraññavatiyā pārimatīrato sālavanuyyānaṃ, yathā anurādhapurassa thūpārāmo, evaṃ taṃ kusinārāyaṃ hoti. Yathā thūpārāmato dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisanamaggo pācīnamukho [V 2.0147] gantvā uttarena nivatto, evaṃ uyyānato sālavanaṃ pācīnamukhaṃ gantvā uttarena nivattaṃ. Tasmā taṃ – “upavattana”nti vuccati. Antarena yamakasālānaṃ [M 2.0164] uttarasīsakanti tassa kira mañcakassa ekā sālapanti sīsabhāge hoti, ekā pādabhāge. Tatrāpi eko taruṇasālo sīsabhāgassa āsanno hoti, eko pādabhāgassa. Api ca yamakasālā nāma mūlakhandhaviṭapapattehi aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitvā ṭhitasālāti vuttaṃ. Mañcakaṃ paññapehīti tasmiṃ kira uyyāne rājakulassa sayanamañco atthi, taṃ sandhāya paññapehīti āha. Theropi taṃyeva paññapetvā adāsi.

198. Here, 'with a great assembly of monks' means there was no limit to the number of monks. For, starting from the suppression of feeling at Veḷuvagāma—after hearing, 'Before long, the Blessed One will attain final Nibbāna'—monks came from here and there, and not a single monk departed. Thus, the Saṅgha was beyond counting. 'Upavattana, the Mallas' sal grove'—just as one can go from the Kalamba riverbank through the Rājamātuvihāra gate to reach the Thūpārāma, so too from the far bank of the Hiraññavatī river, one can reach the sal grove park. Just as the Thūpārāma is of Anurādhapura, so that grove is of Kusinārā. As the path from the Thūpārāma entering the city through the southern gate goes east and then turns north, so too from the park, the path to the sal grove goes east and then turns north. Therefore, it is called 'Upavattana.' 'Between the twin sal trees, with the head to the north'—it is said that one row of sal trees was at the head side of that couch, and another at the foot side. There, a young sal tree stood near the head side, and another near the foot side. Moreover, the twin sal trees are described as sal trees whose roots, trunks, branches, and leaves were intertwined with each other. 'Prepare a couch'—it is said that in that park, there was a royal couch. Referring to it, he said, 'Prepare it.' The Elder also had that very one prepared and offered it.

Kilantosmi, ānanda, nipajjissāmīti tathāgatassa hi –

"I am weary, Ānanda. I will lie down." For the Tathāgata indeed—

“Gocari kaḷāpo gaṅgeyyo, piṅgalo pabbateyyako;

Hemavato ca tambo ca, mandākini uposatho;

Chaddantoyeva dasamo, ete nāgānamuttamā”ti. –

"Gocari, Kaḷāpo, Gaṅgeyyo, Piṅgalo, Pabbateyyako; Hemavata, Tambo, Mandākini, Uposatho; Chaddanta indeed is the tenth—these are the foremost among the nāgas."

Ettha yaṃ dasannaṃ gocarisaṅkhātānaṃ pakatihatthīnaṃ balaṃ, taṃ ekassa kaḷāpassāti. Evaṃ dasaguṇavaḍḍhitāya gaṇanāya pakatihatthīnaṃ koṭisahassabalappamāṇaṃ balaṃ, taṃ sabbampi cundassa piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuttakālato paṭṭhāya caṅgavāre pakkhittaudakaṃ viya parikkhayaṃ gataṃ. Pāvānagarato tīṇi gāvutāni kusinārānagaraṃ, etasmiṃ antare pañcavīsatiyā ṭhānesu nisīditvā mahatā ussāhena āgacchantopi sūriyassa atthaṅgamitavelāyaṃ sañjhāsamaye bhagavā sālavanaṃ paviṭṭho. Evaṃ rogo sabbaṃ ārogyaṃ maddanto āgacchati. Etamatthaṃ dassento viya sabbalokassa saṃvegakaraṃ vācaṃ bhāsanto – “kilantosmi, ānanda, nipajjissāmī”ti āha.

Here, the strength of ten ordinary elephants, known as Gocari, equals that of one Kaḷāpa. Thus, by increasing tenfold in this calculation, a strength that amounts to a thousand crores of ordinary elephants was all exhausted like water poured onto a straining cloth from the moment the Blessed One partook of Cunda’s meal. From the city of Pāvā to Kusinārā is a distance of three gāvutas. In this interval, the Blessed One sat down in twenty-five places and, exerting great effort, arrived at the Sāla grove by evening, at the time of sunset. Thus, disease came crushing all health. As if to reveal this fact and to stir urgency in the whole world, he spoke these words: “I am weary, Ānanda, I will lie down.”

Kasmā pana bhagavā evaṃ mahantena ussāhena idhāgato, kiṃ aññattha na sakkā parinibbāyitunti? Parinibbāyituṃ nāma na katthaci na sakkā, tīhi pana kāraṇehi idhāgato, idañhi bhagavā evaṃ passati – “mayi aññattha parinibbāyante mahāsudassanasuttassa atthuppatti na bhavissati, kusinārāyaṃ [P 2.0574] pana parinibbāyante yamahaṃ devaloke anubhavitabbaṃ sampattiṃ manussalokeyeva anubhaviṃ, taṃ dvīhi bhāṇavārehi maṇḍetvā desessāmi, taṃ me sutvā bahū janā kusalaṃ kātabbaṃ maññissantī”ti.

But why did the Blessed One come here with such great effort? Could he not attain final Nibbāna elsewhere? Indeed, final Nibbāna can be attained anywhere. However, he came here for three reasons. The Blessed One saw this: "If I attain final Nibbāna elsewhere, the opportunity for the arising of the Mahāsudassana Sutta will not occur. But if I attain final Nibbāna in Kusinārā, the prosperity that was to be experienced in the heavenly world, I experienced right here in the human world. I will adorn it with two recitations and teach it. Hearing this, many people will consider that good should be done."

Aparampi [M 2.0165] passati – “maṃ aññattha parinibbāyantaṃ subhaddo na passissati, so ca buddhaveneyyo[V 2.0148], na sāvakaveneyyo; na taṃ sāvakā vinetuṃ sakkonti. Kusinārāyaṃ parinibbāyantaṃ pana maṃ so upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchissati, pañhāvissajjanapariyosāne ca saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya mama santike pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā mayi dharamāneyeva arahattaṃ patvā pacchimasāvako bhavissatī”ti.

He also foresaw this: "If I attain final Nibbāna elsewhere, Subhadda will not see me; and he is one fit to be guided by a Buddha, not one fit to be guided by disciples; the disciples are not able to guide him. But if I attain final Nibbāna in Kusinārā, he will approach me and ask a question, and at the conclusion of the answer to his question, he will be established in the refuges, and receiving the going forth and the full ordination in my presence, and taking up a meditation subject, while I am still living, he will attain arahantship, becoming my last disciple."

Aparampi passati – “mayi aññattha parinibbāyante dhātubhājanīye mahākalaho bhavissati, lohitaṃ nadī viya sandissati. Kusinārāyaṃ parinibbute doṇabrāhmaṇo taṃ vivādaṃ vūpasametvā dhātuyo vibhajissatī”ti. Imehi tīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā evaṃ mahantena ussāhena idhāgatoti veditabbo.

He saw yet another reason: "If I attain final Nibbāna elsewhere, at the distribution of the relics there will be a great quarrel; blood will flow like a river. But if I attain final Nibbāna in Kusinārā, the brahmin Doṇa will settle that dispute and distribute the relics." Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One came here with such great effort for these three reasons.

Sīhaseyyanti ettha kāmabhogīseyyā, petaseyyā, sīhaseyyā, tathāgataseyyāti catasso seyyā.

Regarding 'the lion's lying down': Here, there are four kinds of lying down—the lying down of those who enjoy sensual pleasures, the lying down of ghosts, the lion's lying down, and the Tathāgata's lying down.

Tattha – “yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, kāmabhogī sattā vāmena passena sentī”ti ayaṃ kāmabhogīseyyā. Tesu hi yebhuyyena dakkhiṇena passena sayantā nāma natthi.

Among these: "Monks, for the most part, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side." This is the lying posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures. Among them, there are hardly any who lie on their right side.

“Yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, petā uttānā sentī”ti ayaṃ petaseyyā. Appamaṃsalohitattā hi petā aṭṭhisaṅghāṭajaṭitā ekena passena sayituṃ na sakkonti, uttānāva senti.

"Monks, for the most part, ghosts lie face up." This is the lying down of ghosts. Due to their scant flesh and blood, ghosts, matted with a framework of bones, cannot lie on one side; they lie only face up.

“Sīho, bhikkhave, migarājā dakkhiṇena passena seyyaṃ kappeti…pe… attamano hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ sīhaseyyā. Tejussadattā hi sīho migarājā dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne, pacchimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā naṅguṭṭhaṃ antarasatthimhi pakkhipitvā purimapādapacchimapādanaṅguṭṭhānaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā dvinnaṃ purimapādānaṃ matthake sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā sayati. Divasaṃ sayitvāpi pabujjhamāno na utrasanto pabujjhati, sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvā purimapādādīnaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkheti. Sace kiñci ṭhānaṃ vijahitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti – “na yidaṃ tuyhaṃ jātiyā sūrabhāvassa ca anurūpa”nti anattamano hutvā tattheva sayati, na gocarāya pakkamati. Avijahitvā ṭhite pana [P 2.0575] – “tuyhaṃ jātiyā ca sūrabhāvassa ca anurūpamida”nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho uṭṭhāya sīhavijambhitaṃ [M 2.0166] vijambhitvā kesarabhāraṃ vidhunitvā tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā gocarāya pakkamati.

"Bhikkhus, the lion, king of beasts, lies down on his right side… and is content." This is the lion’s posture for lying down. Indeed, due to his great majesty, the lion, king of beasts, places his two front paws in one spot and his hind paws in another spot, tucks his tail between his thighs, marks the position of his front paws, hind paws, and tail, and lies down, resting his head upon his two front paws. Even after sleeping for a whole day, upon awakening, he does not awaken startled. Rather, lifting his head, he observes the position of his front paws and so on. If any part has shifted from its place, thinking, "This is not befitting your birth and courageous nature," he becomes displeased and lies down right there again; he does not go out for prey. But if they have remained in place without shifting, thinking, "This is befitting your birth and courageous nature," joyful and delighted, he rises, gives a lion’s stretch, shakes out his mane, lets out a lion’s roar three times, and goes out for prey.

“Catutthajjhānaseyyā [V 2.0149] pana tathāgatassa seyyāti vuccati” (a. ni. 4.246). Tāsu idha sīhaseyyā āgatā. Ayañhi tejussadairiyāpathattā uttamaseyyā nāma.

"The lying down in the fourth jhāna, however, is said to be the Tathāgata's posture for lying down." Among these, the lion’s posture for lying down is mentioned here. For this is called the supreme posture for lying down, on account of its being a posture of great majesty.

Pāde pādanti dakkhiṇapāde vāmapādaṃ. Accādhāyāti atiādhāya, īsakaṃ atikkamma ṭhapetvā. Gopphakena hi gopphake, jāṇunā vā jāṇumhi saṅghaṭṭiyamāne abhiṇhaṃ vedanā uppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na hoti, seyyā aphāsukā hoti. Yathā pana na saṅghaṭṭeti, evaṃ atikkamma ṭhapite vedanā nuppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, seyyā phāsu hoti. Tasmā evaṃ nipajji. Anuṭṭhānaseyyaṃ upagatattā panettha – “uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā”ti na vuttaṃ. Kāyavasena cettha anuṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ, niddāvasena pana taṃ rattiṃ bhagavato bhavaṅgassa okāsoyeva nāhosi. Paṭhamayāmasmiñhi mallānaṃ dhammadesanā ahosi, majjhimayāme subhaddassa pacchimayāme bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ovadi, balavapaccūse parinibbāyi.

‘Foot upon foot’ means the left foot upon the right foot. ‘Overlapping’ means placing it so as to slightly extend beyond. For when ankle rubs against ankle, or knee against knee, painful feeling arises, the mind does not become concentrated, and the posture for lying down is uncomfortable. But when they are placed so as to extend beyond in such a way that they do not rub, painful feeling does not arise, the mind becomes concentrated, and the posture for lying down is comfortable. Therefore, he lay down in this manner. Because he had entered the state of lying down from which there is no rising, it is not said here, ‘having established in his mind the perception of rising.’ And here, the non-rising should be understood in a physical sense; for in terms of sleep, on that night there was no opportunity at all for the Blessed One’s life-continuum to arise. For in the first watch of the night, there was the teaching of the Dhamma to the Mallas; in the middle watch, to Subhadda; in the last watch, he admonished the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; and at the break of dawn, he attained Parinibbāna.

Sabbaphāliphullāti sabbe samantato pupphitā mūlato paṭṭhāya yāva aggā ekacchannā ahesuṃ, na kevalañca yamakasālāyeva, sabbepi rukkhā sabbapāliphullāva ahesuṃ. Na kevalañhi tasmiṃyeva uyyāne, sakalañhipi dasasahassacakkavāḷe pupphūpagā pupphaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, phalūpagā phalaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, sabbarukkhānaṃ khandhesu khandhapadumāni, sākhāsu sākhāpadumāni, vallīsu vallipadumāni, ākāsesu ākāsapadumāni pathavītalaṃ bhinditvā daṇḍapadumāni pupphiṃsu. Sabbo mahāsamuddo pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchanno ahosi. Tiyojanasahassavitthato himavā ghanabaddhamorapiñchakalāpo viya, nirantaraṃ mālādāmagavacchiko viya, suṭṭhu pīḷetvā ābaddhapupphavaṭaṃsako viya, supūritaṃ pupphacaṅkoṭakaṃ viya ca atiramaṇīyo ahosi.

‘All in full bloom’ means that all the sāla trees were in full bloom all around, covered from root to tip as if by a single canopy. And not only the twin sāla trees, but all the trees were in full bloom. Indeed, not only in that grove, but throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world-system, flowering trees bore flowers, and fruit-bearing trees bore fruit. On the trunks of all trees, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses; on the vines, vine-lotuses; in the sky, sky-lotuses; and breaking through the surface of the earth, stalked lotuses bloomed. The entire great ocean was covered with lotuses of five colors. The Himālaya mountains, three thousand yojanas in breadth, were exceedingly delightful, like a dense cluster of bound peacock feathers, like a window continuously adorned with festoons of flowers, like a floral diadem tightly fastened, and like a well-filled flower basket.

Te tathāgatassa sarīraṃ okirantīti te yamakasālā bhummadevatāhi sañcalitakhandhasākhaviṭapā tathāgatassa sarīraṃ avakiranti, sarīrassa upari pupphāni vikirantīti attho. Ajjhokirantīti ajjhottharantā viya kiranti. Abhippakirantīti abhiṇhaṃ punappunaṃ pakirantiyeva. Dibbānīti [M 2.0167] devaloke nandapokkharaṇīsambhavāni, tāni honti [P 2.0576] suvaṇṇavaṇṇāni paṇṇacchattappamāṇapattāni, mahātumbamattaṃ reṇuṃ gaṇhanti. Na kevalañca mandāravapupphāneva, aññānipi pana dibbāni pāricchattakakoviḷārapupphādīni suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakāni pūretvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyampi tidasapurepi brahmalokepi ṭhitāhi devatāhi paviṭṭhāni, antalikkhā patanti. Tathāgatassa sarīranti antarā avikiṇṇāneva āgantvā pattakiñjakkhareṇucuṇṇehi tathāgatassa sarīrameva okiranti.

‘They shower the Tathāgata’s body’ means that those twin sāla trees, their trunks, branches, and boughs shaken by the earth-deities, scattered flowers upon the Tathāgata’s body; the meaning is that they sprinkled flowers over his body. ‘They shower over’ means they scattered them as if covering him completely. ‘They scatter profusely’ means they scattered them constantly, again and again. ‘Celestial’ refers to those originating from the Nandapokkharanī lake in the deva-world; they are golden in color, with petals the size of a leaf-parasol, and they hold pollen the size of a large gourd. And not only māndārava flowers, but also other celestial flowers such as pāricchattaka and koviḷāra flowers, filling golden caskets, were released by deities stationed at the rim of the world-system, in the city of the Tidasas, and in the Brahmā-world, and they fell from the sky. ‘The Tathāgata’s body’ means that, without being scattered elsewhere along the way, they came and showered only the Tathāgata’s body with the powders of their petals, filaments, and pollen.

Dibbānipi [V 2.0150] candanacuṇṇānīti devatānaṃ upakappanacandanacuṇṇāni. Na kevalañca devatānaṃyeva, nāgasupaṇṇamanussānampi upakappanacandanacuṇṇāni. Na kevalañca candanacuṇṇāneva, kāḷānusārikalohitacandanādisabbadibbagandhajālacuṇṇāni, haritālaañjanasuvaṇṇarajatacuṇṇāni sabbadibbagandhavāsavikatiyo suvaṇṇarajatādisamugge pūretvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiādīsu ṭhitāhi devatāhi paviṭṭhāni antarā avippakiritvā tathāgatasseva sarīraṃ okiranti.

‘Celestial sandalwood powders’ means the sandalwood powders prepared for the devas. And not only the sandalwood powders prepared for the devas, but also for nāgas, supaṇṇas, and humans. And not only sandalwood powders, but all manner of celestial fragrant powders, such as black anusārī, red sandalwood, and so on; powders of orpiment, collyrium, gold, and silver; and all varieties of specially prepared celestial perfumes and incenses—these, having filled caskets of gold, silver, and the like, were released by deities stationed at the rim of the world-system and other such places. Without being scattered along the way, they showered only the Tathāgata’s body.

Dibbānipi tūriyānīti devatānaṃ upakappanatūriyāni. Na kevalañca tāniyeva, sabbānipi tantibaddhacammapariyonaddhaghanasusirabhedāni dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devanāgasupaṇṇamanussānaṃ tūriyāni ekacakkavāḷe sannipatitvā antalikkhe vajjantīti veditabbāni.

‘Celestial musical instruments’ means the musical instruments provided for the deities. And not only those, but it should be understood that all the musical instruments of the devas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and humans throughout the ten-thousandfold world-systems—of all kinds, whether stringed, leather-covered, solid, or hollow—gathered together in one world-system and played in the sky.

Dibbānipi saṅgītānīti varuṇavāraṇadevatā kira nāmetā dīghāyukā devatā – “mahāpuriso manussapathe nibbattitvā buddho bhavissatī”ti sutvā “paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase naṃ gahetvā gamissāmā”ti mālaṃ ganthetumārabhiṃsu. Tā ganthamānāva – “mahāpuriso mātukucchiyaṃ nibbatto”ti sutvā “tumhe kassa ganthathā”ti vuttā “na tāva niṭṭhāti, kucchito nikkhamanadivase gaṇhitvā gamissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Punapi “nikkhanto”ti sutvā “mahābhinikkhamanadivase gamissāmā”ti. Ekūnatiṃsavassāni ghare vasitvā “ajja mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto”tipi sutvā “abhisambodhidivase gamissāmā”ti. Chabbassāni padhānaṃ katvā “ajja abhisambuddho”tipi sutvā “dhammacakkappavattanadivase gamissāmā”ti. “Sattasattāhāni bodhimaṇḍe vītināmetvā [P 2.0577] isipatanaṃ gantvā dhammacakkaṃ pavattita”ntipi sutvā “yamakapāṭihāriyadivase gamissāmā”ti. “Ajja yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karī”tipi [M 2.0168] sutvā “devorohaṇadivase gamissāmā”ti. “Ajja devorohaṇaṃ karī”tipi sutvā “āyusaṅkhārossajjane gamissāmā”ti. “Ajja āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajī”tipi sutvā “na tāva niṭṭhāti, parinibbānadivase gamissāmā”ti. “Ajja bhagavā yamakasālānamantare dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno sīhaseyyaṃ upagato balavapaccūsasamaye parinibbāyissati. Tumhe kassa ganthathā”ti sutvā pana – “kinnāmetaṃ, ‘ajjeva mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, ajjeva mātukucchito nikkhami, ajjeva mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhami, ajjeva buddho ahosi, ajjeva dhammacakkaṃ pavattayi, ajjeva yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi, ajjeva devalokā otiṇṇo, ajjeva āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossaji, ajjeva kira parinibbāyissatī’ti. Nanu nāma dutiyadivase yāgupānakālamattampi ṭhātabbaṃ assa. Dasa pāramiyo pūretvā buddhattaṃ pattassa nāma ananucchavikameta”nti apariniṭṭhitāva mālāyo gahetvā āgamma anto cakkavāḷe [V 2.0151] okāsaṃ alabhamānā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ lambitvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyāva ādhāvantiyo hatthena hatthaṃ gīvāya gīvaṃ gahetvā tīṇi ratanāni ārabbha dvattiṃsa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni chabbaṇṇarasmiyo dasa pāramiyo aḍḍhachaṭṭhāni jātakasatāni cuddasa buddhañāṇāni ārabbha gāyitvā tassa tassa avasāne “mahāyaso, mahāyaso”ti vadanti. Idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ – “dibbānipi saṅgītāni antalikkhe vattanti tathāgatassa pūjāyā”ti.

“Even divine songs”—it is said that the deities named Varuṇa and Vāraṇa, long-lived deities, hearing that “the Great Being will be born in the human realm and become a Buddha,” began to weave garlands, thinking, “On the day of his conception, we will take it and go.” While they were still weaving, they heard, “The Great Being has been conceived in his mother’s womb,” and when asked, “For whom are you weaving?” they replied, “It is not yet finished. On the day he emerges from the womb, we will take it and go.” Again, hearing “He has emerged,” they said, “We will go on the day of his Great Renunciation.” After he had lived at home for twenty-nine years, they heard, “Today he has undertaken the Great Renunciation,” and said, “We will go on the day of his full enlightenment.” After six years of striving, hearing “Today he has attained full enlightenment,” they said, “We will go on the day he sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.” Hearing “After spending seven weeks at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he went to Isipatana and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,” they said, “We will go on the day of the Twin Miracle.” Hearing “Today he performed the Twin Miracle,” they said, “We will go on the day of his descent from the deva realm.” Hearing “Today he descended from the deva realm,” they said, “We will go on the day he relinquishes his life-formation.” Hearing “Today he relinquished his life-formation,” they said, “It is not yet finished. We will go on the day of his Parinibbāna.” Hearing “Today the Blessed One, between the twin sāl trees, has adopted the lion’s posture on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, and will attain Parinibbāna at the time of the powerful dawn. For whom are you weaving?” they then said, “What is this? ‘Today he was conceived in his mother’s womb, today he emerged from the womb, today he undertook the Great Renunciation, today he became a Buddha, today he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, today he performed the Twin Miracle, today he descended from the deva world, today he relinquished his life-formation, and today, it is said, he will attain Parinibbāna.’ Surely, he should have remained at least until the time for drinking rice-gruel on the second day. For one who has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained Buddhahood, this is unfitting.” Taking the still-unfinished garlands, they came, but finding no space within the world-sphere, they hung them on the rim of the world-sphere, and, running along the very rim of the world-sphere, holding hand to hand and neck to neck, they sang in reference to the Three Jewels, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the six-colored rays, the ten perfections, the five hundred and fifty birth stories, and the fourteen Buddha-knowledges. At the end of each, they exclaimed, “Of great fame, of great fame!” It is in reference to this that it was said: “Even divine songs resound in the sky in honor of the Tathāgata.”

199. Bhagavā pana yamakasālānaṃ antarā dakkhiṇena passena nipannoyeva pathavītalato yāva cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyā, cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭito ca yāva brahmalokā sannipatitāya parisāya mahantaṃ ussāhaṃ disvā āyasmato ānandassa ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ…pe… tathāgatassa pūjāyā”ti. Evaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ dassetvā tenāpi attano asakkatabhāvameva dassanto na kho, ānanda, ettāvatātiādimāha.

199. The Blessed One, lying between the twin sāl trees on his right side, saw the great endeavor of the assembly gathered from the surface of the earth up to the rim of the world-sphere, and from the rim of the world-sphere up to the Brahma-world, and he informed the Venerable Ānanda. Therefore it is said: “Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda… for the honor of the Tathāgata.” Having pointed out such great honor, and yet showing that even by this he himself was not truly honored, he said, “Not so, Ānanda, not merely in this way,” and so on.

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ānanda, mayā dīpaṅkarapādamūle nipannena aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā abhinīhāraṃ karontena [P 2.0578] na mālāgandhatūriyasaṅgītānaṃ atthāya abhinīhāro kato, na etadatthāya pāramiyo pūritā. Tasmā na kho ahaṃ etāya pūjāya pūjito nāma homī”ti.

This is the meaning: “Ānanda, when I, lying at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, brought together the eight conditions and made the aspiration, that aspiration was not made for the sake of garlands, perfumes, musical instruments, and songs. The perfections were not fulfilled for this purpose. Therefore, I am not truly honored by this kind of worship.”

Kasmā [M 2.0169] pana bhagavā aññattha ekaṃ umāpupphamattampi gahetvā buddhaguṇe āvajjetvā katāya pūjāya buddhañāṇenāpi aparicchinnaṃ vipākaṃ vaṇṇetvā idha evaṃ mahantaṃ pūjaṃ paṭikkhipatīti? Parisānuggahena ceva sāsanassa ca ciraṭṭhitikāmatāya. Sace hi bhagavā evaṃ na paṭikkhipeyya, anāgate sīlassa āgataṭṭhāne sīlaṃ na paripūressanti, samādhissa āgataṭṭhāne samādhiṃ na paripūressanti, vipassanāya āgataṭṭhāne vipassanāgabbhaṃ na gāhāpessanti. Upaṭṭhāke samādapetvā pūjaṃyeva kārentā viharissanti. Āmisapūjā ca nāmesā sāsanaṃ ekadivasampi ekayāgupānakālamattampi sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Mahāvihārasadisañhi vihārasahassaṃ mahācetiyasadisañca cetiyasahassampi sāsanaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkonti. Yena kammaṃ kataṃ, tasseva hoti. Sammāpaṭipatti pana tathāgatassa anucchavikā pūjā. Sā hi tena patthitā ceva, sakkoti sāsanañca sandhāretuṃ, tasmā taṃ dassento yo kho ānandātiādimāha.

But why does the Blessed One, who elsewhere praises the immeasurable result of offering even a single flax flower while recollecting the virtues of the Buddha—a result that cannot be fathomed even by a Buddha's knowledge—yet here reject such great worship? It is out of compassion for the assembly and the desire for the long-lasting stability of the Dispensation. For if the Blessed One did not reject it, in the future, people would not perfect virtue where virtue should be perfected, nor concentration where concentration should be perfected, nor would they cause the embryo of insight to be conceived where insight should be developed. They would merely have their supporters make offerings, and thus they would dwell. And this material worship cannot sustain the Dispensation even for a single day, or for the time it takes to drink rice-gruel. Indeed, even a thousand monasteries like the Great Monastery or a thousand stupas like the Great Stupa cannot uphold the Dispensation. The kamma that is done belongs only to the one who did it. But the practice of righteousness is the fitting worship for the Tathāgata. For that is what he aspired to, and it is able to sustain the Dispensation. Therefore, to show this, he said, “Whoever, Ānanda,” and so on.

Tattha dhammānudhammappaṭipannoti navavidhassa lokuttaradhammassa anudhammaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno[V 2.0152]. Sāyeva pana paṭipadā anucchavikattā “sāmīcī”ti vuccati. Taṃ sāmīciṃ paṭipannoti sāmīcippaṭipanno. Tameva pubbabhāgapaṭipadāsaṅkhātaṃ anudhammaṃ carati pūretīti anudhammacārī.

Herein, 'one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma and its corollaries' means one who practices the preliminary path, which is the practice that conforms to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. And since that very path is fitting, it is called 'proper.' One who practices that proper path is 'one who practices properly.' One who practices and fulfills that very conforming practice, known as the preliminary path, is 'one who lives in conformity with the Dhamma.'

Pubbabhāgapaṭipadāti ca sīlaṃ ācārapaññatti dhutaṅgasamādānaṃ yāva gotrabhuto sammāpaṭipadā veditabbā. Tasmā yo bhikkhu chasu agāravesu patiṭṭhāya paññattiṃ atikkamati, anesanāya jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ na dhammānudhammappaṭipanno. Yo pana sabbaṃ attano paññattaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ jinavelaṃ jinamariyādaṃ jinakāḷasuttaṃ aṇumattampi na vītikkamati, ayaṃ dhammānudhammappaṭipanno nāma. Bhikkhuniyāpi eseva nayo. Yo upāsako pañca verāni dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattati appeti, ayaṃ na dhammānudhammappaṭipanno. Yo pana tīsu saraṇesu, pañcasupi sīlesu, dasasu sīlesu paripūrakārī hoti, māsassa aṭṭha uposathe karoti, dānaṃ deti, gandhapūjaṃ mālāpūjaṃ karoti, mātaraṃ pitaraṃ [P 2.0579] upaṭṭhāti, dhammike samaṇabrāhmaṇe upaṭṭhāti, ayaṃ dhammānudhammappaṭipanno nāma. Upāsikāyapi eseva nayo.

Morality, the code of conduct, the undertaking of ascetic practices, and the right practice up to the change-of-lineage should be understood as the preliminary practice. Therefore, a monk who, established in the six kinds of disrespect, transgresses a regulation and makes a living by improper means, is not one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. But one who does not transgress in the slightest any training rule laid down—the Victor's boundary, the Victor's limit, the Victor's black measuring line—is called one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. For a nun, this is the same method. A layman who undertakes and engages in the five enmities or the ten unwholesome courses of action is not one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. But a layman who is a fulfiller of the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts; who observes the eight Uposatha days of the month; who gives alms; who makes offerings of scents and garlands; who attends to his mother and father; and who attends to righteous ascetics and brahmins—he is called one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. For a laywoman, this is the same method.

Paramāya [M 2.0170] pūjāyāti uttamāya pūjāya. Ayañhi nirāmisapūjā nāma sakkoti mama sāsanaṃ sandhāretuṃ. Yāva hi imā catasso parisā maṃ imāya pūjessanti, tāva mama sāsanaṃ majjhe nabhassa puṇṇacando viya virocissatīti dasseti.

‘By the highest worship’ means by the supreme worship. For this, indeed, is called the spiritual worship, which is capable of sustaining my Dispensation. He shows that for as long as these four assemblies worship me with this worship, so long will my Dispensation shine in the midst of the sky like the full moon.

Upavāṇattheravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Elder Upavāṇa

200. Apasāresīti apanesi. Apehīti apagaccha. Thero ekavacaneneva tālavaṇṭaṃ nikkhipitvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Upaṭṭhākotiādi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ anibaddhupaṭṭhākabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha. Ayaṃ, bhante, āyasmā upavāṇoti evaṃ therena vutte ānando upavāṇassa sadosabhāvaṃ sallakkheti, ‘handassa niddosabhāvaṃ kathessāmī’ti bhagavā yebhuyyena ānandātiādimāha. Tattha yebhuyyenāti idaṃ asaññasattānañceva arūpadevatānañca ohīnabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Apphuṭoti asamphuṭṭho abharito vā. Bhagavato kira āsannapadese vālaggamatte okāse sukhumattabhāvaṃ māpetvā dasa dasa mahesakkhā devatā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tāsaṃ parato vīsati vīsati. Tāsaṃ parato tiṃsati tiṃsati. Tāsaṃ parato cattālīsaṃ cattālīsaṃ. Tāsaṃ parato paññāsaṃ paññāsaṃ. Tāsaṃ parato saṭṭhi saṭṭhi devatā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tā aññamaññaṃ hatthena vā pādena vā vatthena vā na byābādhenti. “Apehi maṃ, mā ghaṭṭehī”ti vattabbākāraṃ nāma natthi. “Tā [V 2.0153] kho pana devatāyo dasapi hutvā vīsatipi hutvā tiṃsampi hutvā cattālīsampi hutvā paññāsampi hutvā āraggakoṭinitudanamattepi tiṭṭhanti, na ca aññamaññaṃ byābādhentī”ti (a. ni. 1.37) vuttasadisāva ahesuṃ. Ovārentoti āvārento. Thero kira pakatiyāpi mahāsarīro hatthipotakasadiso. So paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupitvā atimahā viya ahosi.

200. ‘Apasāresīti’ means he removed him. ‘Apehīti’ means go away. The elder, with a single word, set down the palm-leaf fan and stood to one side. The phrase ‘attendant’ and so on is said with reference to his being an unassigned attendant during the first period after the enlightenment. When the elder [Ānanda] spoke thus: ‘Venerable sir, this is the venerable Upavāṇa,’ Ānanda perceived Upavāṇa to be at fault. The Blessed One, thinking, ‘Well now, I shall speak of his blamelessness,’ then said, ‘For the most part, Ānanda…’ and so on. Therein, ‘for the most part’ is said with reference to the exclusion of the non-percipient beings and the formless deities. ‘Apphuṭoti’ means untouched or unfilled. It is said that in the immediate vicinity of the Blessed One, even in a space the size of a hair's tip, having created subtle bodies, ten by ten deities of great power stood. Beyond them, twenty by twenty; beyond them, thirty by thirty; beyond them, forty by forty; beyond them, fifty by fifty; and beyond them, sixty by sixty deities stood. They did not obstruct each other with hand, foot, or robe. There was no occasion to say, ‘Move away from me, do not touch me.’ They were just like what is stated (AN 3.137): ‘Those deities, whether ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty, can stand in a space the size of a needle's point and not obstruct one another.’ ‘Ovārentoti’ means obstructing. It is said that the elder was by nature of large physique, like a young elephant. When he donned his robe of discarded rags, he appeared truly immense.

Tathāgataṃ dassanāyāti bhagavato mukhaṃ daṭṭhuṃ alabhamānā evaṃ ujjhāyiṃsu. Kiṃ pana tā theraṃ vinivijjha passituṃ na sakkontīti? Āma, na sakkonti. Devatā hi puthujjane vinivijjha passituṃ sakkonti, na khīṇāsave. Therassa ca mahesakkhatāya [P 2.0580] tejussadatāya upagantumpi na sakkonti. Kasmā [M 2.0171] pana therova tejussado, na aññe arahantoti? Yasmā kassapabuddhassa cetiye ārakkhadevatā ahosi.

‘To see the Tathāgata’ means that, being unable to behold the Blessed One’s face, they complained thus. But can those deities not see by piercing through the elder? Indeed, they cannot. For deities can see by piercing through ordinary people, but not through those whose cankers are destroyed. And due to the elder’s great power and radiance, they cannot even approach him. But why is this elder alone so radiant, and not the other arahants? Because he was a guardian deity at the shrine of Kassapa Buddha.

Vipassimhi kira sammāsambuddhe parinibbute ekagghanasuvaṇṇakkhandhasadisassa dhātusarīrassa ekameva cetiyaṃ akaṃsu, dīghāyukabuddhānañhi ekameva cetiyaṃ hoti. Taṃ manussā ratanāyāmāhi vidatthivitthatāhi dvaṅgulabahalāhi suvaṇṇiṭṭhakāhi haritālena ca manosilāya ca mattikākiccaṃ tilateleneva udakakiccaṃ sādhetvā yojanappamāṇaṃ uṭṭhapesuṃ. Tato bhummā devatā yojanappamāṇaṃ, tato ākāsaṭṭhakadevatā, tato uṇhavalāhakadevatā, tato abbhavalāhakadevatā, tato cātumahārājikā devatā, tato tāvatiṃsā devatā yojanappamāṇaṃ uṭṭhapesunti evaṃ sattayojanikaṃ cetiyaṃ ahosi. Manussesu mālāgandhavatthādīni gahetvā āgatesu ārakkhadevatā gahetvā tesaṃ passantānaṃyeva cetiyaṃ pūjesi.

It is said that when the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Buddha Vipassī, attained final Nibbāna, they made only one shrine for his relic-body, which was like a solid mass of gold. For indeed, there is only one shrine for long-lived Buddhas. Humans built it a yojana high, using golden bricks a `ratana` long, a span wide, and two fingers thick, accomplishing the work of mortar with orpiment and realgar, and the work of water with sesame oil alone. Then the earth-deities raised it a yojana; then the sky-dwelling deities; then the hot-cloud deities; then the storm-cloud deities; then the deities of the Four Great Kings; then the Tāvatiṃsa deities raised it a yojana. Thus the shrine came to be seven yojanas high. When people came bringing garlands, scents, robes, and other offerings, the guardian deities would take them and worship the shrine even as the people looked on.

Tadā ayaṃ thero brāhmaṇamahāsālo hutvā ekaṃ pītakaṃ vatthaṃ ādāya gato. Devatā tassa hatthato vatthaṃ gahetvā cetiyaṃ pūjesi. Brāhmaṇo taṃ disvā pasannacitto “ahampi anāgate evarūpassa buddhassa cetiye ārakkhadevatā homī”ti patthanaṃ katvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatti. Tassa devaloke ca manussaloke ca saṃsarantasseva kassapo bhagavā loke uppajjitvā parinibbāyi. Tassāpi ekameva dhātusarīraṃ ahosi. Taṃ gahetvā yojanikaṃ cetiyaṃ kāresuṃ. So tattha ārakkhadevatā hutvā sāsane antarahite sagge nibbattitvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle tato cuto mahākule paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā nikkhamma pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto. Iti cetiye ārakkhadevatā hutvā āgatattā thero tejussadoti veditabbo.

At that time, this elder was a brahmin of great wealth who took a single yellow cloth and went there. The deities took the cloth from his hand and worshipped the shrine. Seeing this, the brahmin, with a serene mind, made the aspiration: ‘May I too, in the future, become a guardian deity of such a Buddha’s shrine!’ After passing away from there, he was reborn in the deva realm. While he was wandering through the deva and human realms, the Blessed One Kassapa arose in the world and attained final Nibbāna. For him too, there was only one relic-body. Taking it, they had a shrine one yojana high built. He became its guardian deity, and after the Dispensation disappeared, he was reborn in heaven. In our Blessed One’s time, he passed away from there, took rebirth in a great family, went forth from home, became a monk, and attained Arahantship. Thus, it should be understood that the elder is so radiant because he had come from being a guardian deity of a shrine.

Devatā[V 2.0154], ānanda, ujjhāyantīti iti ānanda, devatā ujjhāyanti, na mayhaṃ puttassa añño koci doso atthīti dasseti.

The statement, 'Ānanda, the deities are murmuring,' shows that the deities are murmuring, and that there is no other fault in my son.

201. Kathaṃbhūtā pana, bhanteti kasmā āha? Bhagavā tumhe – “devatā ujjhāyantī”ti vadatha, kathaṃ bhūtā pana tā tumhe manasi karotha[M 2.0172], kiṃ tumhākaṃ parinibbānaṃ adhivāsentīti pucchati. Atha bhagavā – “nāhaṃ adhivāsanakāraṇaṃ vadāmī”ti tāsaṃ anadhivāsanabhāvaṃ dassento santānandātiādimāha.

201. Why did he say, 'Venerable sir, of what sort are they?' He asks: 'Blessed One, you say, "The deities are murmuring." Of what sort are those deities that you have in mind? Do they endure your parinibbāna?' Then the Blessed One, showing their inability to endure, said, 'I do not speak of a reason for enduring,' and began with the words, 'There are, Ānanda...'

Tattha [P 2.0581] ākāse pathavīsaññiniyoti ākāse pathaviṃ māpetvā tattha pathavīsaññiniyo. Kandantīti rodanti. Chinnapātaṃ papatantīti majjhe chinnā viya hutvā yato vā tato vā papatanti. Āvaṭṭantīti āvaṭṭantiyo patitaṭṭhānameva āgacchanti. Vivaṭṭantīti patitaṭṭhānato parabhāgaṃ vaṭṭamānā gacchanti. Apica dve pāde pasāretvā sakiṃ purato sakiṃ pacchato sakiṃ vāmato sakiṃ dakkhiṇato saṃparivattamānāpi – “āvaṭṭanti vivaṭṭantī”ti vuccanti. Santānanda, devatā pathaviyaṃ pathavīsaññiniyoti pakatipathavī kira devatā dhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Tattha hatthako brahmā viya devatā osīdanti. Tenāha bhagavā – “oḷārikaṃ hatthaka, attabhāvaṃ abhinimmināhī”ti (a. ni. 3.128). Tasmā yā devatā pathaviyaṃ pathaviṃ māpesuṃ, tā sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “pathaviyaṃ pathavīsaññiniyo”ti.

Therein, 'those who perceive earth in the sky' means having fashioned earth in the sky, they perceive earth there. 'They weep' means they cry. 'Falling as if cut apart' means they fall as if cut in the middle, falling from here and there. 'Whirling' means they whirl, coming back to the very place where they fell. 'Revolving' means they revolve, turning away from the place where they fell and going to another part. Moreover, even while stretching out their two legs, sometimes forward, sometimes backward, sometimes to the left, sometimes to the right, turning all around, they are called 'whirling and revolving'. Indeed, Ānanda, regarding 'deities who perceive earth on the earth,' ordinary earth, it seems, cannot bear the deities. There, like the Brahmā Hatthaka, the deities sink. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Hatthaka, manifest a gross physical form' (AN 3.128). Thus, this statement—'those who perceive earth on the earth'—was said with reference to those deities who fashioned an earth upon the earth.

Vītarāgāti pahīnadomanassā silāthambhasadisā anāgāmikhīṇāsavadevatā.

'Those free from passion' refers to deities who are non-returners and those whose taints are destroyed, who have abandoned dejection and are like stone pillars.

Catusaṃvejanīyaṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Four Places That Inspire Spiritual Urgency

202. Vassaṃvuṭṭhāti buddhakāle kira dvīsu kālesu bhikkhū sannipatanti upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇatthaṃ, vuṭṭhavassā ca gahitakammaṭṭhānānuyogena nibbattitavisesārocanatthaṃ. Yathā ca buddhakāle, evaṃ tambapaṇṇidīpepi apāragaṅgāya bhikkhū lohapāsāde sannipatiṃsu, pāragaṅgāya bhikkhū tissamahāvihāre. Tesu apāragaṅgāya bhikkhū saṅkārachaḍḍakasammajjaniyo gahetvā āgantvā mahāvihāre sannipatitvā cetiye sudhākammaṃ katvā – “vuṭṭhavassā āgantvā lohapāsāde sannipatathā”ti vattaṃ katvā phāsukaṭṭhānesu vasitvā vuṭṭhavassā āgantvā lohapāsāde pañcanikāyamaṇḍale, yesaṃ pāḷi paguṇā, te pāḷiṃ sajjhāyanti. Yesaṃ aṭṭhakathā paguṇā, te aṭṭhakathaṃ sajjhāyanti. [M 2.0173] Yo pāḷiṃ vā aṭṭhakathaṃ vā virādheti[V 2.0155], taṃ – “kassa santike tayā gahita”nti vicāretvā ujuṃ katvā gāhāpenti. Pāragaṅgāvāsinopi tissamahāvihāre evameva karonti. Evaṃ dvīsu kālesu sannipatitesu bhikkhūsu ye pure vassūpanāyikāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gatā visesārocanatthaṃ āgacchanti, evarūpe sandhāya “pubbe bhante vassaṃvuṭṭhā”tiādimāha.

202. 'Having completed the rains retreat' means that during the Buddha's time, it is said that monks would gather on two occasions: near the commencement of the rains retreat to receive a meditation subject, and after having completed the rains retreat to report the special attainments realized through the practice of the received meditation subject. Just as in the Buddha's time, so too on the island of Tambapaṇṇī, monks from the near side of the Ganges would gather in the Lohapāsāda, and monks from the far side of the Ganges in the Tissamahāvihāra. Among them, the monks from the near side of the Ganges would take rubbish baskets and brooms, come and gather in the Mahāvihāra, perform whitewashing work on the cetiya, and establish the custom: 'After completing the rains retreat, come and gather in the Lohapāsāda.' Then, dwelling in comfortable places, upon completing the rains retreat, they would come and gather in the Lohapāsāda within the assembly circle of the five Nikāyas. Those proficient in the Pāli would recite the Pāli, while those proficient in the commentaries would recite the commentaries. If anyone made a mistake in the Pāli or the commentaries, they would investigate, 'From whom did you receive this?', correct it, and have them learn it properly. The residents of the far side of the Ganges would do the same in the Tissamahāvihāra. Thus, when the monks assembled on these two occasions, those who had previously received a meditation subject before the rains retreat and had gone away would come to report their special attainments. It is with reference to such monks that Ānanda said, 'Formerly, venerable sir, monks who had completed the rains retreat...'

Manobhāvanīyeti manasā bhāvite sambhāvite. Ye vā mano manaṃ bhāventi vaḍḍhenti rāgarajādīni pavāhenti, evarūpeti attho. Thero [P 2.0582] kira vattasampanno mahallakaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā thaddho hutvā na nisīdati, paccuggamanaṃ katvā hatthato chattañca pattacīvarañca gahetvā pīṭhaṃ papphoṭetvā deti, tattha nisinnassa vattaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ paṭijaggitvā deti. Navakaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā tuṇhībhūto na nisīdati, samīpe ṭhatvā vattaṃ karoti. So tāya vattapaṭipattiyā aparihāniṃ patthayamāno evamāha.

'Spiritually inspiring' means cultivated and esteemed in the mind. Or, it means those who cultivate and develop the mind, causing defilements such as lust and passion to be washed away; this is the meaning. It is said that the Elder, being accomplished in his duties, upon seeing a senior monk, would not sit down stiffly. Instead, he would go forward to greet him, take the umbrella, bowl, and robe from his hands, dust off a seat and offer it. Having performed his duties for the one seated there, he would attend to the lodging and offer it. When seeing a junior monk, he would not sit down silently, but would stand nearby and perform his duties. Wishing for no decline in such conduct of his duties, he spoke thus.

Atha bhagavā – “ānando manobhāvanīyānaṃ dassanaṃ na labhissāmī”ti cinteti, handassa, manobhāvanīyānaṃ dassanaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhissāmi, yattha vasanto ito cito ca anāhiṇḍitvāva lacchati manobhāvanīye bhikkhū dassanāyāti cintetvā cattārimānītiādimāha.

Then the Blessed One reflected, 'Ānanda is thinking, "I will no longer get to see the spiritually inspiring monks."' He then thought, 'Well then, let me point out to him a place for seeing spiritually inspiring monks, a place where, by dwelling there, he will be able to see those spiritually inspiring monks without wandering here and there.' Having reflected thus, he spoke the discourse beginning with, 'These four...'

Tattha saddhassāti buddhādīsu pasannacittassa vattasampannassa, yassa pāto paṭṭhāya cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīni sabbavattāni katāneva paññāyanti. Dassanīyānīti dassanārahāni dassanatthāya gantabbāni. Saṃvejanīyānīti saṃvegajanakāni. Ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni, padesaṭhānāneva vā.

Therein, 'of one with faith' means one whose mind is serene with confidence in the Buddha and others, who is accomplished in his duties, for whom from morning onwards all duties, such as the duty of sweeping the cetiya courtyard, are seen to have been performed. 'Worthy of seeing' means worthy of being seen, places to be gone to for the purpose of seeing. 'Inspiring spiritual urgency' means generating spiritual urgency. 'Places' means causes, or simply locations.

Ye hi kecīti idaṃ cetiyacārikāya satthakabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha cetiyacārikaṃ āhiṇḍantāti ye ca tāva tattha tattha cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjantā, āsanāni dhovantā bodhimhi udakaṃ siñcantā āhiṇḍanti, tesu vattabbameva natthi asukavihāre “cetiyaṃ vandissāmā”ti nikkhamitvā pasannacittā antarā kālaṅkarontāpi anantarāyena sagge patiṭṭhahissanti yevāti dasseti.

'Whoever...' – this was said to show the beneficial nature of pilgrimage to shrines. Therein, 'those who wander on pilgrimage to shrines' refers to those who, wandering here and there, sweep the cetiya courtyards, wash the seats, and sprinkle water on the Bodhi tree. Regarding them, there is indeed nothing more to be said. It is shown that even those who, with serene and confident minds, leave their monasteries thinking, 'We will pay homage to the cetiya,' and pass away along the way, will certainly be established in a heavenly world without any impediment.

Ānandapucchākathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse concerning Ānanda's Question

203. Adassanaṃ[V 2.0156][M 2.0174], ānandāti yadetaṃ mātugāmassa adassanaṃ, ayamettha uttamā paṭipattīti dasseti. Dvāraṃ pidahitvā senāsane nisinno hi bhikkhu āgantvā dvāre ṭhitampi mātugāmaṃ yāva na passati, tāvassa ekaṃseneva na lobho uppajjati, na cittaṃ calati. Dassane pana satiyeva tadubhayampi assa. Tenāha – “adassanaṃ ānandā”ti. Dassane bhagavā sati kathanti bhikkhaṃ gahetvā upagataṭṭhānādīsu dassane sati kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti pucchati. Atha bhagavā yasmā khaggaṃ gahetvā – “sace mayā saddhiṃ ālapasi, ettheva te sīsaṃ pātessāmī”ti ṭhitapurisena vā, “sace mayā saddhiṃ ālapasi, ettheva te maṃsaṃ murumurāpetvā khādissāmī”ti [P 2.0583] ṭhitayakkhiniyā vā ālapituṃ varaṃ. Ekasseva hi attabhāvassa tappaccayā vināso hoti, na apāyesu aparicchinnadukkhānubhavanaṃ. Mātugāmena pana ālāpasallāpe sati vissāso hoti, vissāse sati otāro hoti, otiṇṇacitto sīlabyasanaṃ patvā apāyapūrako hoti; tasmā anālāpoti āha. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

203. “Not seeing, Ānanda”—this indicates that not seeing women is the highest practice in this regard. For a bhikkhu sitting in his dwelling with the door closed, as long as he does not see a woman, even one who has come and is standing at the door, greed certainly does not arise in him, nor does his mind waver. But when there is seeing, both of these may occur in him. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Not seeing, Ānanda.” “But if there is seeing, Blessed One, how should one act?”—he asks how one should act if seeing occurs in places one has gone to for alms and so on. Then the Blessed One said that it is better to converse with a man standing holding a sword, saying, “If you speak with me, I will cut off your head right here,” or with a female yakkha standing there, saying, “If you speak with me, I will chew your flesh to a pulp and eat it,” for in that case, only the destruction of this single existence occurs, not the experience of immeasurable suffering in the woeful states. But when there is conversation and discussion with a woman, familiarity arises; when there is familiarity, an opening arises; a person whose mind has entered that opening, having fallen into a transgression of virtue, becomes one who fills the woeful states. Therefore, he said, “No conversation.” And this has been said:

“Sallape asihatthena, pisācenāpi sallape;

Āsīvisampi āsīde, yena daṭṭho na jīvati;

Na tveva eko ekāya, mātugāmena sallape”ti. (a. ni. 5.55);

“One may converse with a man holding a sword, one may converse even with a demon; one may approach a venomous snake, by which if bitten, one does not live; but one should never converse alone with a woman.” (AN 5.55)

Ālapantena panāti sace mātugāmo divasaṃ vā pucchati, sīlaṃ vā yācati, dhammaṃ vā sotukāmo hoti, pañhaṃ vā pucchati, tathārūpaṃ vā panassa pabbajitehi kattabbakammaṃ hoti, evarūpe kāle anālapantaṃ “mūgo ayaṃ, badhiro ayaṃ, bhutvāva baddhamukho nisīdatī”ti vadati, tasmā avassaṃ ālapitabbaṃ hoti. Evaṃ ālapantena pana kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbanti pucchati. Atha bhagavā – “etha tumhe, bhikkhave, mātumattīsu mātucittaṃ upaṭṭhapetha, bhaginimattīsu bhaginicittaṃ upaṭṭhapetha, dhītumattīsu dhītucittaṃ upaṭṭhapethā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.127) imaṃ ovādaṃ sandhāya sati, ānanda, upaṭṭhapetabbāti āha.

“But when one is speaking”—if a woman asks about the day, or requests to undertake the precepts, or wishes to hear the Dhamma, or asks a question, or if there is some duty that should be done for her by the ordained, at such a time, if one does not speak, people will say, “This one is mute, this one is deaf, after eating he just sits there with his mouth shut.” Therefore, one must certainly speak. “But when speaking thus, how should one act?”—he asks. Then the Blessed One, referring to this advice—“Come, bhikkhus, toward those who are of a mother’s age, establish the mind of a mother; toward those who are of a sister’s age, establish the mind of a sister; toward those who are of a daughter’s age, establish the mind of a daughter” (SN 4.111)—said, “Mindfulness, Ānanda, should be established.”

204. Abyāvaṭāti atantibaddhā nirussukkā hotha. Sāratthe ghaṭathāti uttamatthe arahatte ghaṭetha. Anuyuñjathāti tadadhigamāya anuyogaṃ [M 2.0175] karotha. Appamattāti tattha avippamuṭṭhasatī. Vīriyātāpayogena ātāpino. Kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhatāya pahitattā pesitacittā viharatha.

204. “Unoccupied” (abyāvaṭā) means be unentangled, without anxiety. “Strive for the essence” (sāratthe ghaṭatha) means exert yourselves for the highest goal, Arahantship. “Apply yourselves” (anuyuñjatha) means make an effort for its attainment. “Heedful” (appamattā) means with unremitting mindfulness in that regard. “Ardent” (ātāpino) by means of the application of ardent energy. Dwell with a resolute mind, with a mind sent forth (pahitattā pesitacittā), having no concern for body or life.

205. Kathaṃ [V 2.0157] pana, bhanteti tehi khattiyapaṇḍitādīhi kathaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Addhā maṃ te paṭipucchissanti – “kathaṃ, bhante, ānanda tathāgatassa sarīre paṭipajjitabba”nti; “tesāhaṃ kathaṃ paṭivacanaṃ demī”ti pucchati. Ahatena vatthenāti navena kāsikavatthena. Vihatena kappāsenāti supothitena kappāsena. Kāsikavatthañhi sukhumattā telaṃ na gaṇhāti, kappāso pana gaṇhāti. Tasmā “vihatena kappāsenā”ti āha. Āyasāyāti sovaṇṇāya. Sovaṇṇañhi idha “ayasa”nti adhippetaṃ.

205. “But how, venerable sir?”—he asks how those wise nobles and others should proceed. “Surely they will ask me in return: ‘Venerable Ānanda, how should one proceed with regard to the Tathāgata’s body?’ What answer should I give them?”—he asks. “With new cloth” (ahatena vatthena) means with new cloth from Kāsī. “With carded cotton” (vihatena kappāsena) means with well-beaten cotton. For cloth from Kāsī, due to its fineness, does not absorb oil, but cotton does. Therefore, he said, “with carded cotton.” “In an iron one” (āyasāya) means in a golden one. For here, by “iron” (ayasa), gold is intended.

Thūpārahapuggalavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of Persons Worthy of a Stūpa

206. Rājā cakkavattīti ettha kasmā bhagavā agāramajjhe vasitvā kālaṅkatassa rañño thūpārahataṃ anujānāti, na sīlavato puthujjanassa bhikkhussāti? Anacchariyattā. Puthujjanabhikkhūnañhi [P 2.0584] thūpe anuññāyamāne tambapaṇṇidīpe tāva thūpānaṃ okāso na bhaveyya, tathā aññesu ṭhānesu. Tasmā “anacchariyā te bhavissantī”ti nānujānāti. Rājā cakkavattī ekova nibbattati, tenassa thūpo acchariyo hoti. Puthujjanasīlavato pana parinibbutabhikkhuno viya mahantampi sakkāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

206. “A wheel-turning monarch”—in this context, why does the Blessed One permit worthiness for a stūpa for a king who has passed away while living in a household, but not for a virtuous ordinary bhikkhu? Because it is not extraordinary. For if stūpas were permitted for ordinary bhikkhus, to begin with in the island of Tambapaṇṇi there would be no space for stūpas, and likewise in other places. Therefore, thinking, “They would not be extraordinary,” he does not permit it. Only one wheel-turning monarch arises at a time; for that reason his stūpa is extraordinary. But for a virtuous ordinary bhikkhu, it is indeed fitting to show great honor, just as for a bhikkhu who has attained Parinibbāna.

Ānandaacchariyadhammavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Wonderful Qualities of Ānanda

207. Vihāranti idha maṇḍalamālo vihāroti adhippeto, taṃ pavisitvā. Kapisīsanti dvārabāhakoṭiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ aggaḷarukkhaṃ. Rodamāno aṭṭhāsīti so kirāyasmā cintesi – “satthārā mama saṃvegajanakaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ, cetiyacārikāya sātthakabhāvo kathito, mātugāme paṭipajjitabbapañho vissajjito, attano sarīre paṭipatti akkhātā, cattāro thūpārahā kathitā, dhuvaṃ ajja bhagavā parinibbāyissatī”ti, tassevaṃ cintayato balavadomanassaṃ uppajji. Athassa etadahosi – “bhagavato santike rodanaṃ nāma aphāsukaṃ, ekamantaṃ gantvā [M 2.0176] sokaṃ tanukaṃ karissāmī”ti, so tathā akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “rodamāno aṭṭhāsī”ti.

207. “Dwelling” (vihāranti)—here, by “dwelling” (vihāra) is meant the circular hall; having entered it. “Monkey-head” (kapisīsaṃ)—the bolt-post standing at the end of the door-jamb. “Weeping, he stood”—it is said that the venerable one thought: “The Teacher has told me of a dwelling place that inspires a sense of urgency, he has spoken of the benefit of pilgrimage to shrines, he has answered the question of how to act toward women, he has declared how to proceed with regard to his own body, and he has described the four who are worthy of a stūpa. Surely, today the Blessed One will attain Parinibbāna.” As he was thinking thus, strong sorrow arose in him. Then this occurred to him: “It is unseemly to weep in the presence of the Blessed One. I will go to one side and lessen my grief.” He did so. Therefore it was said, “Weeping, he stood.”

Ahañca vatamhīti ahañca vata amhi, ahaṃ vatamhītipi pāṭho. Yo mama anukampakoti yo maṃ anukampati anusāsati, sve dāni paṭṭhāya kassa mukhadhovanaṃ dassāmi, kassa pāde dhovissāmi, kassa senāsanaṃ paṭijaggissāmi, kassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vicarissāmīti bahuṃ vilapi. Āmantesīti bhikkhusaṅghassa antare theraṃ adisvā āmantesi.

“And I, alas, am still a learner”—meaning, “I am indeed a learner with a task yet to be done.” There is also the reading, “I, alas, am…” “He who was my compassionate guide”—meaning, he who has compassion for me and instructs me. “From tomorrow onwards, for whom shall I offer water for washing the face? Whose feet shall I wash? Whose dwelling shall I attend to? Whose bowl and robe shall I take and wander with?”—thus he lamented greatly. “He addressed”—not seeing the Elder amidst the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he addressed them.

Mettena [V 2.0158] kāyakammenāti mettacittavasena pavattitena mukhadhovanadānādikāyakammena. Hitenāti hitavuddhiyā katena. Sukhenāti sukhasomanasseneva katena, na dukkhinā dummanena hutvāti attho. Advayenāti dve koṭṭhāse katvā akatena. Yathā hi eko sammukhāva karoti na parammukhā, eko parammukhāva karoti na sammukhā evaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvā katenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Appamāṇenāti pamāṇavirahitena. Cakkavāḷampi hi atisambādhaṃ, bhavaggampi atinīcaṃ, tayā kataṃ kāyakammameva [P 2.0585] bahunti dasseti.

“With bodily action characterized by loving-kindness”—with bodily action such as offering water for washing the face and so forth, performed with a mind of loving-kindness. “Beneficially”—done for the sake of welfare and increase. “Happily”—done with joy and gladness alone, not with sorrow or displeasure—this is the meaning. “Without division”—done without making two portions. For example, one does it face-to-face, not behind one’s back; another does it behind one’s back, not face-to-face—thus, it is said to be done without making such a division. “Immeasurably”—free from measure. For even the world-sphere is excessively constricted, and the peak of existence is excessively low, yet the bodily action done by you is vast indeed—this is shown.

Mettena vacīkammenāti mettacittavasena pavattitena mukhadhovanakālārocanādinā vacīkammena. Api ca ovādaṃ sutvā – “sādhu, bhante”ti vacanampi mettaṃ vacīkammameva. Mettena manokammenāti kālasseva sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā vivittāsane nisīditvā – “satthā arogo hotu, abyāpajjo sukhī”ti evaṃ pavattitena manokammena. Katapuññosīti kappasatasahassaṃ abhinīhārasampannosīti dasseti. Katapuññosīti ca ettāvatā vissattho mā pamādamāpajji, atha kho padhānamanuyuñja. Evañhi anuyutto khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo, dhammasaṅgītikāle arahattaṃ pāpuṇissasi. Na hi mādisassa katapāricariyā nipphalā nāma hotīti dasseti.

“With verbal action characterized by loving-kindness”—with verbal action, such as announcing the time for washing the face and so forth, performed with a mind of loving-kindness. Furthermore, even saying, “It is good, venerable sir,” upon hearing advice is itself verbal action characterized by loving-kindness. “With mental action characterized by loving-kindness”—having attended to the body early in the morning and sitting in a secluded seat, with mental action thus arisen: “May the Teacher be free from illness, free from affliction, and happy.” “You have made merit”—this shows that you are endowed with an aspiration fulfilled over a hundred thousand eons. And on account of this statement, ‘You have made merit,’ do not become complacent and fall into negligence, but rather, apply yourself to the endeavor. For, being so applied, you will quickly become one without taints; at the time of the Dhamma council, you will attain arahantship. Indeed, service rendered to one such as I is never fruitless—this is shown.

208. Evañca pana vatvā mahāpathaviṃ pattharanto viya ākāsaṃ vitthārento viya cakkavāḷagiriṃ osārento viya sineruṃ ukkhipento viya mahājambuṃ khandhe gahetvā cālento viya āyasmato ānandassa guṇakathaṃ ārabhanto atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi. Tattha “yepi [M 2.0177] te, bhikkhave, etarahī”ti kasmā na vuttaṃ? Aññassa buddhassa natthitāya. Eteneva cetaṃ veditabbaṃ – “yathā cakkavāḷantarepi añño buddho natthī”ti. Paṇḍitoti byatto. Medhāvīti khandhadhātuāyatanādīsu kusalo.

208. And having spoken thus, as if spreading out the great earth, as if expanding the sky, as if making the Cakkavāḷa mountains descend, as if lifting up Mount Sineru, as if seizing the great rose-apple tree by its trunk and shaking it—thus beginning the account of the Venerable Ānanda’s virtues, the Blessed One then addressed the monks. Herein, why was it not said, “O monks, whosoever at present...”? Because of the non-existence of another Buddha. And by this alone it should be understood that just as there is no other Buddha in another world-sphere. “Sagacious” means accomplished. “Intelligent” means skilled in the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth.

209. Bhikkhuparisā ānandaṃ dassanāyāti ye bhagavantaṃ passitukāmā theraṃ upasaṅkamanti, ye ca “āyasmā kirānando samantapāsādiko abhirūpo dassanīyo bahussuto saṅghasobhano”ti therassa guṇe sutvā āgacchanti, te sandhāya “bhikkhuparisā ānandaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamantī”ti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha. Attamanāti savanena no dassanaṃ sametīti sakamanā tuṭṭhacittā. Dhammanti “kacci, āvuso, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci yoniso manasikārena kammaṃ karotha, ācariyupajjhāye vattaṃ pūrethā”ti evarūpaṃ paṭisanthāradhammaṃ. Tattha bhikkhunīsu – “kacci, bhaginiyo, aṭṭha garudhamme samādāya vattathā”ti idampi nānākaraṇaṃ hoti. Upāsakesu āgatesu “upāsaka, na te kacci sīsaṃ vā aṅgaṃ vā [V 2.0159] rujjati, arogā te puttabhātaro”ti na evaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karoti. Evaṃ pana karoti – “kathaṃ upāsakā tīṇi saraṇāni pañca sīlāni rakkhatha, māsassa aṭṭha [P 2.0586] uposathe karotha, mātāpitūnaṃ upaṭṭhānavattaṃ pūretha, dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇe paṭijaggathā”ti. Upāsikāsupi eseva nayo.

209. “The assembly of monks approaches Ānanda to see him”: this refers to those who, wishing to see the Blessed One, approach the Elder, and also those who, having heard of the Elder’s virtues—“The Venerable Ānanda, it is said, is inspiring confidence all around, handsome, pleasing to see, of great learning, and an ornament to the Saṅgha”—come for that reason. With reference to them, it is said, “The assembly of monks approaches Ānanda to see him.” This is the method in all cases. “Delighted”—thinking, ‘Our seeing matches what we have heard,’ they are joyful and with pleased minds. “Dhamma”—this refers to a welcoming talk of this kind: “Friends, I trust you are keeping well? I trust you are comfortable? I trust you are undertaking your practice with wise attention and fulfilling your duties toward your teachers and preceptors?” Among the nuns, there is also this specific point: “Sisters, I trust you are undertaking and observing the eight weighty rules?” When male lay followers arrive, he does not make a greeting like this: “Lay follower, I trust your head or limbs are not aching? Are your sons and brothers in good health?” Rather, he greets them thus: “How is it, lay followers? Do you protect the three refuges and the five precepts? Do you observe the eight Uposatha precepts each month? Do you fulfill your duties of service toward your parents? Do you attend to righteous ascetics and brahmins?” The same method applies to female lay followers as well.

Idāni ānandattherassa cakkavattinā saddhiṃ upamaṃ karonto cattārome bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha khattiyāti abhisittā ca anabhisittā ca khattiyajātikā. Te kira – “rājā cakkavattī nāma abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko ākāsena vicaranto rajjaṃ anusāsati dhammiko dhammarājā”ti tassa guṇakathaṃ sutvā “savanena dassanampi sama”nti attamanā honti. Bhāsatīti kathento – “kathaṃ, tātā, rājadhammaṃ pūretha, paveṇiṃ rakkhathā”ti paṭisanthāraṃ karoti. Brāhmaṇesu pana – “kathaṃ ācariyā mante vācetha, kathaṃ antevāsikā mante gaṇhanti, dakkhiṇaṃ vā vatthāni vā kapilaṃ vā alatthā”ti paṭisanthāraṃ karoti. Gahapatīsu – “kathaṃ tātā, na vo rājakulato daṇḍena vā balinā vā pīḷā atthi, sammā [M 2.0178] devo dhāraṃ anupavecchati, sassāni sampajjantī”ti evaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karoti. Samaṇesu – “kathaṃ, bhante, pabbajitaparikkhārā sulabhā, samaṇadhamme na pamajjathā”ti evaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karoti.

Now, making a comparison of the Venerable Ānanda with a wheel-turning monarch, the Blessed One said the passage beginning, “These four, O monks…” Herein, “nobles” refers to those of the noble caste who have been consecrated. It is said that they, hearing the praise of the wheel-turning monarch—“The king known as the wheel-turner is handsome, pleasing to see, inspiring; traveling through the sky, he governs the kingdom; he is righteous, a king of righteousness”—become delighted, thinking, “Seeing him is the same as hearing of him.” “He speaks”—when speaking, he makes this greeting: “How is it, my good sirs? Do you fulfill the principles of kingship? Do you protect the ancient tradition?” With brahmins, however, he makes this greeting: “How is it, teachers? Do you recite the sacred verses? How do your pupils learn the sacred verses? Have you received a religious donation, or robes, or a tawny cow?” With householders: “How is it, my good sirs? I trust you suffer no oppression from the royal family by way of punishment or taxes? Does the sky-god send down showers properly? Are the crops abundant?” With ascetics, he makes this greeting: “How is it, venerable sirs? Are the requisites of one gone forth easy to obtain? Do you not neglect the duties of an ascetic?”

Mahāsudassanasuttadesanāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse of the Mahāsudassana Sutta

210. Khuddakanagaraketi nagarapatirūpake sambādhe khuddakanagarake. Ujjaṅgalanagaraketi visamanagarake. Sākhānagaraketi yathā rukkhānaṃ sākhā nāma khuddakā honti, evameva aññesaṃ mahānagarānaṃ sākhāsadise khuddakanagarake. Khattiyamahāsālāti khattiyamahāsārappattā mahākhattiyā. Esa nayo sabbattha.

210. “A small town” (khuddakanagaraka) means a small, congested town that is a semblance of a city. “A wilderness town” (ujjaṅgalanagaraka) means a town on uneven ground. “A branch town” (sākhānagaraka) means a small town that is like a branch of other great cities, just as the branches of trees are small. “Nobles of great substance” (khattiyamahāsālā) means great nobles who have attained great wealth. This is the method in all cases.

Tesu khattiyamahāsālā nāma yesaṃ koṭisatampi koṭisahassampi dhanaṃ nikhaṇitvā ṭhapitaṃ, divasaparibbayo ekaṃ kahāpaṇasakaṭaṃ nigacchati, sāyaṃ dve pavisanti. Brāhmaṇamahāsālā nāma yesaṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ nihitaṃ hoti, divasaparibbayo eko kahāpaṇakumbho nigacchati, sāyaṃ ekasakaṭaṃ pavisati. Gahapatimahāsālā nāma yesaṃ cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ nihitaṃ hoti, divasaparibbayo pañca kahāpaṇambaṇāni nigacchanti, sāyaṃ kumbho pavisati.

Among them, wealthy nobles are those who have buried and stored away a billion, or even ten billion, in wealth; their daily expenditure amounts to one cartload of kahāpaṇas, and in the evening, two cartloads come in. Wealthy brahmins are those who have eight hundred million in wealth stored away; their daily expenditure amounts to one pot of kahāpaṇas, and in the evening, one cartload comes in. Wealthy householders are those who have four hundred million in wealth stored away; their daily expenditure amounts to five ambaṇas of kahāpaṇas, and in the evening, a pot comes in.

Mā [V 2.0160] hevaṃ, ānanda, avacāti ānanda, mā evaṃ avaca, na imaṃ “khuddakanagara”nti [P 2.0587] vattabbaṃ. Ahañhi imasseva nagarassa sampattiṃ kathetuṃ – “anekavāraṃ tiṭṭhaṃ nisīdaṃ mahantena ussāhena, mahantena parakkamena idhāgato”ti vatvā bhūtapubbantiādimāha. Subhikkhāti khajjabhojjasampannā. Hatthisaddenāti ekasmiṃ hatthimhi saddaṃ karonte caturāsītihatthisahassāni saddaṃ karonti, iti hatthisaddena avivittā, hoti, tathā assasaddena. Puññavanto panettha sattā catusindhavayuttehi rathehi aññamaññaṃ anubandhamānā antaravīthīsu vicaranti, iti rathasaddena avivittā hoti. Niccaṃ payojitāneva panettha bheriādīni tūriyāni, iti bherisaddādīhipi avivittā hoti. Tattha sammasaddoti kaṃsatāḷasaddo. Pāṇitāḷasaddoti pāṇinā caturassaambaṇatāḷasaddo. Kuṭabherisaddotipi vadanti.

Do not say so, Ānanda. That is, 'Ānanda, do not speak thus.' This should not be called a 'small town.' For having said, 'I have come here with great effort and great exertion, standing and sitting many times, to relate the prosperity of this very town,' he began with 'It happened in the past...'. 'Subhikkhā' means it was endowed with abundant solid and soft food. 'Hatthisaddena' means that when one elephant made a sound, eighty-four thousand elephants would make a sound; thus it was not devoid of the sound of elephants, and likewise with the sound of horses. Here, meritorious beings, with chariots yoked to four Sindh thoroughbreds, followed one another along the streets; thus it was not devoid of the sound of chariots. Moreover, drums and other musical instruments were constantly played here; thus it was not devoid of the sound of drums and the like. Therein, the 'sammasadda' is the sound of brass cymbals. The 'pāṇitāḷasadda' is the sound of a four-ambaṇa drum struck by hand. Some also say it is the sound of a pot-drum.

Asnātha [M 2.0179] pivatha khādathāti asnātha pivatha khādatha. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo, bhuñjatha bhoti iminā dasamena saddena avivittā hoti anupacchinnasaddā. Yathā pana aññesu nagaresu “kacavaraṃ chaḍḍetha, kudālaṃ gaṇhatha, pacchiṃ gaṇhatha, pavāsaṃ gamissāma, taṇḍulapuṭaṃ gaṇhatha, bhattapuṭaṃ gaṇhatha, phalakāvudhādīni sajjāni karothā”ti evarūpā saddā honti, na yidha evaṃ ahosīti dasseti.

'Eat, drink, chew' means 'Eat, drink, chew.' This is the summary here: with this tenth sound, 'Enjoy, sirs!,' it was not devoid of sound; the sound was uninterrupted. For whereas in other towns there are such sounds as, 'Throw away the garbage!,' 'Take the spade!,' 'Take the basket!,' 'We will go on a journey!,' 'Take the bag of rice!,' 'Take the bag of food!,' 'Prepare the shields, weapons, and so forth!,' it is shown that it was not so here.

“Dasamena saddenā”ti ca vatvā “kusāvatī, ānanda, rājadhānī sattahi pākārehi parikkhittā ahosī”ti sabbaṃ mahāsudassanasuttaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā gaccha tvaṃ ānandātiādimāha. Tattha abhikkamathāti abhimukhā kamatha, āgacchathāti attho. Kiṃ pana te bhagavato āgatabhāvaṃ na jānantīti? Jānanti. Buddhānaṃ gatagataṭṭhānaṃ nāma mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ hoti, kenacideva karaṇīyena nisinnattā na āgatā. “Te āgantvā bhikkhusaṅghassa ṭhānanisajjokāsaṃ saṃvidahitvā dassantī”ti tesaṃ santike avelāyampi bhagavā pesesi.

And having said, 'With the tenth sound,' and having concluded the entire Mahāsudassana Sutta with 'Kusāvatī, Ānanda, the royal city was surrounded by seven walls,' he then said, 'Go, Ānanda,' and so on. Therein, 'abhikkamatha' means 'approach forward'; the meaning is 'come.' But did they not know of the Blessed One's arrival? They knew. For wherever Buddhas go, there is a great commotion; they had not come because they were seated due to some duty. Thinking, 'Having come, they will arrange and provide a place for the Saṅgha of monks to stand and sit,' the Blessed One sent a messenger to them even at an inopportune time.

Mallānaṃ vandanāvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Mallas' Veneration

211. Amhākañca noti ettha no kāro nipātamattaṃ. Aghāvinoti uppannadukkhā. Dummanāti anattamanā. Cetodukkhasamappitāti domanassasamappitā. Kulaparivattaso kulaparivattaso ṭhapetvāti ekekaṃ [P 2.0588] kulaparivattaṃ kulasaṅkhepaṃ vīthisabhāgena ceva racchāsabhāgena ca visuṃ visuṃ ṭhapetvā.

211. In 'amhākañca no,' the word 'no' is merely a particle. 'Aghāvino' means having arisen suffering. 'Dummanā' means displeased. 'Cetodukkhasamappitā' means overcome by mental sorrow. 'Kulaparivattaso kulaparivattaso ṭhapetvā' means placing each family circle, each family group, separately by divisions of streets and portions of roads.

Subhaddaparibbājakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Story of Subhadda the Wanderer

212. Subhaddo [V 2.0161] nāma paribbājakoti udiccabrāhmaṇamahāsālakulā pabbajito channaparibbājako. Kaṅkhādhammoti vimatidhammo. Kasmā panassa ajja evaṃ ahosīti? Tathāvidhaupanissayattā. Pubbe kira puññakaraṇakāle dve bhātaro ahesuṃ. Te ekatova sassaṃ akaṃsu. Tattha jeṭṭhakassa – “ekasmiṃ sasse navavāre aggasassadānaṃ mayā dātabba”nti ahosi. So vappakāle bījaggaṃ nāma datvā gabbhakāle kaniṭṭhena saddhiṃ [M 2.0180] mantesi – “gabbhakāle gabbhaṃ phāletvā dassāmā”ti kaniṭṭho – “taruṇasassaṃ nāsetukāmosī”ti āha. Jeṭṭho kaniṭṭhassa ananuvattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā khettaṃ vibhajitvā attano koṭṭhāsato gabbhaṃ phāletvā khīraṃ nīharitvā sappinavanītena saṃyojetvā adāsi, puthukakāle puthukaṃ kāretvā adāsi, lāyanakāle lāyanaggaṃ, veṇikaraṇe veṇaggaṃ, kalāpādīsu kalāpaggaṃ, khalaggaṃ, khalabhaṇḍaggaṃ, koṭṭhagganti evaṃ ekasasse navavāre aggadānaṃ adāsi. Kaniṭṭho pana uddharitvā adāsi.

212. Subhadda was a wanderer with a covered body who had gone forth from a wealthy northern brahmin family. 'Kaṅkhādhammo' means a doctrine of uncertainty. Why did this occur to him today? Because of such a supporting condition. It is said that in the past, at a time of making merit, there were two brothers. They farmed together. The elder thought, 'From a single harvest, I must give the first-fruits of the crop nine times.' At planting time, he gave the first of the seeds. When the grain was in the blade, he consulted with his younger brother, saying, 'At this stage, let us split open the sheath and give the milky grain.' The younger brother said, 'You want to destroy the young crop!' Knowing his younger brother would not follow his wish, the elder divided the field. From his own portion, he split open the sheath, extracted the milky sap, combined it with ghee and fresh butter, and gave it as an offering. At the time for making flattened rice, he had flattened rice made and gave it. At the time of reaping, he gave the first of the reaping; at the time of binding, the first of the sheaves; among the bundles, the first of the bundles; the first of the threshing floor; the first of the threshed grain; and the first of the granary. Thus, from a single harvest, he gave the first-fruits offering nine times. The younger brother, however, gave only after taking the grain from the granary.

Tesu jeṭṭhako aññāsikoṇḍaññatthero jāto. Bhagavā – “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya”nti olokento “aññāsikoṇḍañño ekasmiṃ sasse nava aggadānāni adāsi, imaṃ aggadhammaṃ tassa desessāmī”ti sabbapaṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. So aṭṭhārasahi brahmakoṭīhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Kaniṭṭho pana ohīyitvā pacchā dānassa dinnattā satthu parinibbānakāle evaṃ cintetvā satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmo ahosi.

Of them, the elder brother was reborn as the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña. The Blessed One, considering to whom he should first teach the Dhamma, looked and thought, 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña gave nine first-fruit offerings from one harvest. To him I shall teach this foremost Dhamma.' Thus, he taught the Dhamma to him first of all. He, along with one hundred and eighty million brahmās, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The younger brother, however, having been left behind because he gave his offering later, at the time of the Teacher’s Parinibbāna, thought in this way and became desirous of seeing the Teacher.

Mā tathāgataṃ viheṭhesīti thero kira – “ete aññatitthiyā nāma attano gahaṇameva gaṇhanti, tassa vissajjāpanatthāya bhagavato bahuṃ bhāsamānassa kāyavācāvihesā bhavissati, pakatiyāpi ca kilantoyeva bhagavā”ti maññamāno evamāha. Paribbājako – “na me ayaṃ bhikkhu okāsaṃ karoti, atthikena pana anuvattitvā kāretabbo”ti theraṃ anuvattanto dutiyampi tatiyampi āha.

The elder, it is said, thinking, 'These followers of other sects only take up their own view, and for the purpose of making them abandon it, there will be physical and verbal distress for the Blessed One from speaking much, and the Blessed One is already weary by nature,' spoke thus: 'Do not disturb the Tathāgata.' The wanderer, thinking, 'This monk does not give me an opportunity, but one who has a need should have it done by following persistently,' followed the elder and spoke a second and a third time.

213. Assosi [P 2.0589] khoti sāṇidvāre ṭhitassa bhāsato pakatisoteneva assosi, sutvā ca pana subhaddasseva atthāya mahatā ussāhena āgatattā alaṃ ānandātiādimāha. Tattha alanti paṭikkhepatthe nipāto. Aññāpekkhovāti aññātukāmova hutvā. Abbhaññiṃsūti yathā tesaṃ paṭiññā, tatheva jāniṃsu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace nesaṃ sā paṭiññā niyyānikā, sabbe abbhaññaṃsu, no ce, na abbhaññaṃsu. Tasmā kiṃ tesaṃ paṭiññā niyyānikā, aniyyānikāti [V 2.0162] ayameva [M 2.0181] tassa pañhassa attho. Atha bhagavā tesaṃ aniyyānikabhāvakathanena atthābhāvato ceva okāsābhāvato ca “ala”nti paṭikkhipitvā dhammameva desesi. Paṭhamayāmasmiñhi mallānaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā majjhimayāme subhaddassa, pacchimayāme bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ovaditvā balavapaccūsasamaye parinibbāyissāmicceva bhagavā āgato.

213. The Blessed One indeed heard him speaking while standing at the curtained doorway; he heard with his natural ear. And having heard, because he had come with great effort for the sake of Subhadda himself, he said, 'Enough, Ānanda,' and so on. Therein, 'enough' is a particle in the sense of refusal. 'Desiring to know' means being one who desires to know. 'They understood' means they knew in accordance with their declaration. This is what is meant: if their declaration is liberating, all understood; if not, they did not understand. Therefore, the meaning of that question is simply this: 'Is their declaration liberating or not liberating?' Then the Blessed One, due to the lack of benefit and the lack of opportunity in stating that their views were not liberating, having refused with 'Enough,' taught only the Dhamma. For the Blessed One had come with the very intention of teaching the Dhamma to the Mallas in the first watch, to Subhadda in the middle watch, advising the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in the last watch, and attaining final Nibbāna at the time of strong dawn.

214. Samaṇopi tattha na upalabbhatīti paṭhamo sotāpannasamaṇopi tattha natthi, dutiyo sakadāgāmisamaṇopi, tatiyo anāgāmisamaṇopi, catuttho arahattasamaṇopi tattha natthīti attho. “Imasmiṃ kho”ti purimadesanāya aniyamato vatvā idāni attano sāsanaṃ niyamento āha. Suññā parappavādā samaṇebhīti catunnaṃ maggānaṃ atthāya āraddhavipassakehi catūhi, maggaṭṭhehi catūhi, phalaṭṭhehi catūhīti dvādasahi samaṇehi suññā parappavādā tucchā rittakā. Ime ca subhaddāti ime dvādasa bhikkhū. Sammā vihareyyunti ettha sotāpanno attano adhigataṭṭhānaṃ aññassa kathetvā taṃ sotāpannaṃ karonto sammā viharati nāma. Esa nayo sakadāgāmiādīsu. Sotāpattimaggaṭṭho aññampi sotāpattimaggaṭṭhaṃ karonto sammā viharati nāma. Esa nayo sesamaggaṭṭhesu. Sotāpattimaggatthāya āraddhavipassako attano paguṇaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā aññampi sotāpattimaggatthāya āraddhavipassakaṃ karonto sammā viharati nāma. Esa nayo sesamaggatthāya āraddhavipassakesu. Idaṃ sandhāyāha – “sammā vihareyyu”nti. Asuñño loko arahantehi assāti naḷavanaṃ saravanaṃ viya nirantaro [P 2.0590] assa.

214. 'Not even a recluse is found there' means that the first recluse, the stream-enterer, is not found there, nor the second, the once-returner, nor the third, the non-returner, nor the fourth recluse, the arahant. Regarding 'In this,' having previously spoken without restriction, he now speaks while defining his own dispensation. 'The doctrines of others are empty of recluses'—the doctrines of others are empty, hollow, and void of the twelve kinds of recluses: the four who have undertaken insight practice for the sake of the four paths, the four established in the paths, and the four established in the fruits. 'And these, Subhadda' refers to these twelve bhikkhus. Regarding 'Would live rightly,' herein, a stream-enterer who, having explained his own state of attainment to another, causes that person to become a stream-enterer, is said to live rightly. This is the method for the once-returner and the others. One established in the path of stream-entry who causes another to be established in the path of stream-entry is said to live rightly. This is the method for those established in the remaining paths. One who has undertaken insight practice for the sake of the path of stream-entry who, having explained his own well-practiced meditation subject to another, causes that person to undertake insight practice for the sake of the path of stream-entry, is said to live rightly. This is the method for those who have undertaken insight practice for the sake of the remaining paths. It is with reference to this that he said, 'would live rightly.' 'The world would not be empty of arahants' means it would be continuous, like a forest of reeds or a forest of arrow-reeds.

Ekūnatiṃso vayasāti vayena ekūnatiṃsavasso hutvā. Yaṃ pabbajinti ettha yanti nipātamattaṃ. Kiṃ kusalānuesīti “kiṃ kusala”nti anuesanto pariyesanto.
