Tattha – “kiṃ kusala”nti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, taṃ gavesantoti attho. Yato ahanti yato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ pabbajito, etthantare samadhikāni paññāsa vassāni hontīti dasseti. Ñāyassa dhammassāti ariyamaggadhammassa. Padesavattīti padese vipassanāmagge pavattanto. Ito bahiddhāti mama sāsanato bahiddhā. Samaṇopi [M 2.0182] natthīti padesavattivipassakopi natthi, paṭhamasamaṇo sotāpannopi natthīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'At twenty-nine years of age' means being twenty-nine years of age. Regarding 'When I went forth,' herein 'yaṃ' is merely a particle. 'Seeking what is skillful' means seeking and searching for 'what is skillful.' Therein, by 'what is skillful,' the knowledge of omniscience is intended; the meaning is 'seeking that.' 'Since I' shows that from when I went forth, in this interval more than fifty years have passed. 'Of the true Dhamma' means of the Dhamma of the noble path. 'A partial practitioner' means one proceeding on the path of insight, which is a preliminary part. 'Outside of this' means outside of my dispensation. 'Not even a recluse exists' means that not even a partial practitioner of insight exists, and it is said that not even the first recluse, the stream-enterer, exists.

Ye etthāti ye tumhe ettha sāsane satthārā sammukhā antevāsikābhisekena abhisittā, tesaṃ vo lābhā tesaṃ vo suladdhanti. Bāhirasamaye kira yaṃ antevāsikaṃ ācariyo – “imaṃ pabbājehi[V 2.0163], imaṃ ovada, imaṃ anusāsā”ti vadati, so tena attano ṭhāne ṭhapito hoti, tasmā tassa – “imaṃ pabbajehi, imaṃ ovada, imaṃ anusāsā”ti ime lābhā honti. Therampi subhaddo tameva bāhirasamayaṃ gahetvā evamāha.

'Those here' means: 'You who have been consecrated here in this dispensation by the Teacher in his presence with the consecration of a disciple, it is a gain for you, it is well-gained by you.' It is said that in an external system, when a teacher tells a resident pupil, 'Ordain this one, advise this one, instruct this one,' that pupil is thereby established in the teacher's own place. Therefore, for that pupil, 'Ordain this one, advise this one, instruct this one'—these are his gains. Subhadda, taking that very external system as his reference, spoke thus to the Elder.

Alattha khoti kathaṃ alattha? Thero kira naṃ ekamantaṃ netvā udakatumbato pānīyena sīsaṃ temetvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādāpetvā saraṇāni datvā bhagavato santikaṃ ānesi. Bhagavā upasampādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. So taṃ gahetvā uyyānassa ekamante caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāya ghaṭento vāyamanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā āgamma bhagavantaṃ vanditvā nisīdi. Taṃ sandhāya – “acirūpasampanno kho panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'He did indeed attain,' how did he attain? It is said that the Elder, having led him to a secluded place, moistened his head with water from a water-gourd, taught him the meditation subject of the five parts ending with the skin, had his hair and beard removed, had him clothed in ochre robes, administered the refuges, and brought him into the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave him the higher ordination and explained a meditation subject. Having received it, he determined upon a walking path in a secluded part of the grove, and striving and making an effort, developing insight, he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then he returned, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. It was with reference to him that it was said: 'One who has but recently received the higher ordination...'

So ca bhagavato pacchimo sakkhisāvako ahosīti saṅgītikārakānaṃ vacanaṃ. Tattha yo bhagavati dharamāne pabbajitvā aparabhāge upasampadaṃ labhitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, upasampadampi vā dharamāneyeva labhitvā aparabhāge kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, kammaṭṭhānampi vā dharamāneyeva gahetvā aparabhāge arahattameva pāpuṇāti, sabbopi so pacchimo sakkhisāvako. Ayaṃ pana dharamāneyeva bhagavati [P 2.0591] pabbajito ca upasampanno ca kammaṭṭhānañca gahetvā arahattaṃ pattoti.

“He was the last direct disciple of the Blessed One”—this is the word of the compilers of the Council. Herein, whoever goes forth while the Blessed One is living, and in a later period receives the higher ordination, takes up a meditation subject, and attains arahantship; or, having received the higher ordination while the Blessed One is still living, in a later period takes up a meditation subject and attains arahantship; or, having taken up a meditation subject while the Blessed One is still living, in a later period attains arahantship—every such one is a last direct disciple. This one, however, while the Blessed One was still living, went forth, received the higher ordination, took up a meditation subject, and attained arahantship.

Pañcamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth recitation section is completed.

Tathāgatapacchimavācāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Tathāgata's Last Words

216. Idāni bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādaṃ ārabhi, taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho bhagavātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha desito paññattoti dhammopi desito ceva [M 2.0183] paññatto ca, vinayopi desito ceva paññatto ca. Paññatto ca nāma ṭhapito paṭṭhapitoti attho. So vo mamaccayenāti so dhammavinayo tumhākaṃ mamaccayena satthā. Mayā hi vo ṭhiteneva – “idaṃ lahukaṃ, idaṃ garukaṃ, idaṃ satekicchaṃ, idaṃ atekicchaṃ, idaṃ lokavajjaṃ, idaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ, ayaṃ āpatti puggalassa santike vuṭṭhāti, ayaṃ āpatti gaṇassa santike vuṭṭhāti, ayaṃ saṅghassa santike vuṭṭhātī”ti [V 2.0164] sattāpattikkhandhavasena otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ sakhandhakaparivāro ubhatovibhaṅgo vinayo nāma desito, taṃ sakalampi vinayapiṭakaṃ mayi parinibbute tumhākaṃ satthukiccaṃ sādhessati.

216. Now, he began his exhortation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. To show this, the text beginning ‘Then the Blessed One…’ was spoken. Therein, regarding ‘taught and laid down,’ both the Dhamma was taught and laid down, and the Vinaya was taught and laid down. And ‘laid down’ means established and set forth. Regarding ‘That for you after my passing,’ it means: that Dhamma and Vinaya will be your teacher after my passing. For it was by me, while still present, that the Vinaya—comprising the two Vibhaṅgas with the Khandhakas and the Parivāra—was taught concerning matters that arose, according to the seven classes of offenses, thus: ‘This is a light offense, this is a grave offense; this is curable, this is incurable; this is a worldly fault, this is a fault by enactment; this offense is resolved in the presence of an individual, this offense is resolved in the presence of a group, this offense is resolved in the presence of the Saṅgha.’ That entire Vinaya Piṭaka, when I have attained final Nibbāna, will accomplish the task of a teacher for you.

Ṭhiteneva ca mayā – “ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañca indriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti tena tenākārena ime dhamme vibhajitvā vibhajitvā suttantapiṭakaṃ desitaṃ, taṃ sakalampi suttantapiṭakaṃ mayi parinibbute tumhākaṃ satthukiccaṃ sādhessati. Ṭhiteneva ca mayā – “ime pañcakkhandhā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, cattāri saccāni, bāvīsatindriyāni, nava hetū, cattāro āhārā, satta phassā, satta vedanā, satta saññā, satta sañcetanā, satta cittāni. Tatrāpi ‘ettakā dhammā kāmāvacarā, ettakā rūpāvacarā, ettakā arūpāvacarā, ettakā pariyāpannā, ettakā apariyāpannā, ettakā lokiyā, ettakā lokuttarā’ti” ime dhamme vibhajitvā vibhajitvā catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānaanantanayamahāpaṭṭhānapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ desitaṃ, taṃ sakalampi abhidhammapiṭakaṃ mayi parinibbute tumhākaṃ satthukiccaṃ sādhessati.

And it was by me, while still present, that the Suttanta Piṭaka was taught, having analyzed these teachings again and again in various ways, thus: ‘These are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path.’ That entire Suttanta Piṭaka, when I have attained final Nibbāna, will accomplish the task of a teacher for you. And it was by me, while still present, that the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—adorned with the Mahāpaṭṭhāna of infinite methods and twenty-four conditional relations—was taught, having analyzed these phenomena again and again, thus: ‘These are the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four Noble Truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine causes, the four nutriments, the seven contacts, the seven feelings, the seven perceptions, the seven volitions, the seven consciousnesses.’ And therein also: ‘So many phenomena are of the sense-sphere, so many of the form-sphere, so many of the formless-sphere; so many are included in the round, so many are not included in the round; so many are worldly, so many are supramundane.’ That entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, when I have attained final Nibbāna, will accomplish the task of a teacher for you.

Iti sabbampetaṃ abhisambodhito yāva parinibbānā pañcacattālīsavassāni bhāsitaṃ lapitaṃ – “tīṇi piṭakāni, pañca nikāyā, navaṅgāni, caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti evaṃ mahāpabhedaṃ hoti. Iti [P 2.0592] imāni caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassāni tiṭṭhanti, ahaṃ ekova parinibbāyāmi. Ahañca kho pana dāni ekakova ovadāmi anusāsāmi, mayi parinibbute imāni caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassāni tumhe ovadissanti anusāsissantīti evaṃ bhagavā bahūni kāraṇāni dassento – “so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti ovaditvā puna anāgate cārittaṃ dassento yathā kho panātiādimāha.

Thus, all this that was spoken and uttered for forty-five years, from the full awakening until the final Nibbāna, is of great variety, being: the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine Aṅgas, and the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma. Thus, these eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma remain; I alone attain final Nibbāna. And now, I alone exhort and instruct; when I have attained final Nibbāna, these eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma will exhort and instruct you. In this way, the Blessed One, showing many reasons, gave the exhortation, ‘That will be your teacher after my passing.’ Then, to show the proper conduct for the future, he spoke the words beginning, ‘And how, friends...’

Tattha [M 2.0184] samudācarantīti kathenti voharanti. Nāmena vā gottena vāti navakāti avatvā “tissa, nāgā”ti evaṃ nāmena vā, “kassapa, gotamā”ti evaṃ gottena vā, “āvuso tissa, āvuso kassapā”ti evaṃ āvusovādena vā samudācaritabbo. Bhanteti vā āyasmāti vāti bhante tissa, āyasmā tissāti evaṃ samudācaritabbo. Samūhanatūti ākaṅkhamāno samūhanatu, yadi icchati samūhaneyyāti attho. Kasmā pana samūhanathāti ekaṃseneva avatvā vikappavacaneneva ṭhapesīti? Mahākassapassa balaṃ diṭṭhattā. Passati hi bhagavā [V 2.0165] – “samūhanathāti vuttepi saṅgītikāle kassapo na samūhanissatī”ti. Tasmā vikappeneva ṭhapesi.

Herein, ‘they address’ means they speak, they use terms of address. ‘By name or by clan’ means that, without saying ‘junior bhikkhu,’ one should be addressed by name, such as ‘Tissa’ or ‘Nāga’; or by clan, such as ‘Kassapa’ or ‘Gotama’; or with the term ‘friend,’ such as ‘Friend Tissa’ or ‘Friend Kassapa.’ ‘Or by “Bhante” or by “Āyasmā”’ means one should be addressed as ‘Bhante Tissa’ or ‘Āyasmā Tissa.’ ‘Let him abolish’ means: if wishing, let him abolish; the meaning is, if he wishes, he may abolish it. But why did the Blessed One not state it definitively, saying, ‘You should abolish,’ but instead established it with a word of option? Because he saw the strength of Mahākassapa. For the Blessed One saw: ‘Even if it is said, “You should abolish,” at the time of the council, Kassapa will not abolish it.’ Therefore, he established it with an option.

Tattha – “ekacce therā evamāhaṃsu – cattāri pārājikāni ṭhapetvā avasesāni khuddānukhuddakānī”tiādinā nayena pañcasatikasaṅgītiyaṃ khuddānukhuddakakathā āgatāva vinicchayo pettha samantapāsādikāyaṃ vutto. Keci panāhu – “bhante, nāgasena, katamaṃ khuddakaṃ, katamaṃ anukhuddaka”nti milindena raññā pucchito. “Dukkaṭaṃ, mahārāja, khuddakaṃ, dubbhāsitaṃ anukhuddaka”nti vuttattā nāgasenatthero khuddānukhuddakaṃ jānāti. Mahākassapo pana taṃ ajānanto –

Therein, the discussion on the minor and lesser rules arose in the Council of Five Hundred in this way: some elders said, ‘Setting aside the four Pārājika offenses, the remaining rules are the minor and lesser ones,’ and so on. The decision on this matter is also stated in the Samantapāsādikā. Some, however, say that since it is said that when asked by King Milinda, ‘Venerable Nāgasena, what is a minor rule, and what is a lesser rule?’ he replied, ‘A dukkaṭa offense, great king, is a minor rule; a dubbhāsita offense is a lesser rule,’ the Elder Nāgasena knew what the minor and lesser rules were. But Mahākassapa, not knowing this...

“Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho santamhākaṃ sikkhāpadāni gihigatāni, gihinopi jānanti – “idaṃ vo samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ kappati, idaṃ vo na kappatī”ti. Sace mayaṃ khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni samūhanissāma, bhavissanti vattāro – “dhūmakālikaṃ samaṇena gotamena sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, yāva nesaṃ satthā aṭṭhāsi, tāvime sikkhāpadesu sikkhiṃsu, yato imesaṃ satthā parinibbuto, na dānime sikkhāpadesu sikkhantī”ti. Yadi saṅghassa [P 2.0593] pattakallaṃ, saṅgho apaññattaṃ na paññapeyya, paññattaṃ na samucchindeyya, yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya vatteyya. Esā ñattīti –

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. Our existing training rules are known even to householders—they too know, ‘This is allowable for you, recluses of the Sakyan son; this is not allowable.’ If we uproot the minor and lesser rules of training, there will be those who say, ‘The training rule proclaimed by the recluse Gotama for the disciples was like smoke; as long as their teacher remained, they trained in these training rules; now that their teacher has attained final Nibbāna, they no longer train in these training rules.’ If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should not institute what has not been instituted, nor abolish what has been instituted, but should undertake and practice according to the training rules as they have been established. This is the motion.”

Kammavācaṃ sāvesīti. Na taṃ evaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Nāgasenatthero hi – “paravādino okāso mā ahosī”ti evamāha. Mahākassapatthero “khuddānukhuddakāpattiṃ na samūhanissāmī”ti kammavācaṃ sāvesi.

He announced the formal act. This should not be understood in that way. For the Elder Nāgasena said this so that opponents would have no opportunity to object. The Elder Mahākassapa announced the formal act, saying, “I will not abolish the minor and lesser offenses.”

Brahmadaṇḍakathāpi [M 2.0185] saṅgītiyaṃ āgatattāsamantapāsādikāyaṃ vinicchitā.

The discussion on the brahma-punishment, having come up at the Council, was also decided in the Samantapāsādikā.

Kaṅkhāti dveḷhakaṃ. Vimatīti vinicchituṃ asamatthatā, buddho nu kho, na buddho nu kho, dhammo nu kho, na dhammo nu kho, saṅgho nu kho, na saṅgho nu kho, maggo nu kho, na maggo nu kho, paṭipadā nu kho, na paṭipadā nu khoti yassa saṃsayo uppajjeyya, taṃ vo vadāmi “pucchatha bhikkhave”ti ayamettha saṅkhepattho. Satthugāravenāpi na puccheyyāthāti mayaṃ satthusantike pabbajimha, cattāro paccayāpi no satthu santakāva, te mayaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ kaṅkhaṃ akatvā [V 2.0166] na arahāma ajja pacchimakāle kaṅkhaṃ kātunti sace evaṃ satthari gāravena na pucchatha. Sahāyakopi bhikkhave sahāyakassa ārocetūti tumhākaṃ yo yassa bhikkhuno sandiṭṭho sambhatto, so tassa ārocetu, ahaṃ etassa bhikkhussa kathessāmi, tassa kathaṃ sutvā sabbe nikkaṅkhā bhavissathāti dasseti.

‘Doubt’ is indecisiveness. ‘Uncertainty’ is the inability to decide: ‘Is it the Buddha or not the Buddha? Is it the Dhamma or not the Dhamma? Is it the Saṅgha or not the Saṅgha? Is it the path or not the path? Is it the practice or not the practice?’ If such a doubt should arise in anyone, I say to you, ‘Ask, bhikkhus!’ This is the meaning here in brief. As for ‘You might not ask out of respect for the Teacher’: if, thinking, ‘We went forth in the Teacher’s presence; the four requisites are also the Teacher’s property. Having not had doubts for so long, it is not right for us to have doubts now at this final hour,’ you do not ask out of respect for the Teacher, then ‘Bhikkhus, let a friend tell a friend.’ This shows that whichever of you is an acquaintance or intimate of another bhikkhu, let him tell that bhikkhu; I will speak to that bhikkhu, and having heard his explanation, all of you will be free from doubt.

Evaṃ pasannoti evaṃ saddahāmi ahanti attho. Ñāṇamevāti nikkaṅkhabhāvapaccakkhakaraṇañāṇaṃyeva, ettha tathāgatassa na saddhāmattanti attho. Imesañhi, ānandāti imesaṃ antosāṇiyaṃ nisinnānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ. Yo pacchimakoti yo guṇavasena pacchimako. Ānandattheraṃyeva sandhāyāha.

Thus, ‘confident’ means ‘thus I have faith.’ ‘Only knowledge’ means the knowledge that directly realizes the state of being without doubt; the meaning here is that for the Tathāgata it is not a matter of mere faith. ‘Of these, Ānanda,’ refers to these five hundred bhikkhus sitting behind the curtain. ‘Who was the last’ means who was last in terms of virtue. He is referring only to the Elder Ānanda.

218. Appamādena sampādethāti satiavippavāsena sabbakiccāni sampādeyyātha. Iti bhagavā parinibbānamañce nipanno pañcacattālīsa vassāni dinnaṃ ovādaṃ sabbaṃ ekasmiṃ appamādapadeyeva pakkhipitvā adāsi. Ayaṃ tathāgatassa pacchimā vācāti idaṃ pana saṅgītikārakānaṃ [P 2.0594] vacanaṃ.

218. ‘Strive on with diligence’ means you should accomplish all your duties with non-absence of mindfulness. Thus the Blessed One, lying on his Parinibbāna-couch, having given the teaching for forty-five years, encompassed all of it in this single term, ‘diligence,’ and so gave his final instruction. ‘This was the Tathāgata’s last word’—this, however, is the statement of the compilers of the Council.

Parinibbutakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Attainment of Parinibbāna

219. Ito paraṃ yaṃ parinibbānaparikammaṃ katvā bhagavā parinibbuto, taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho bhagavā paṭhamaṃ jhānantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha parinibbuto bhanteti nirodhaṃ samāpannassa bhagavato assāsapassāsānaṃ abhāvaṃ disvā pucchati. Na āvusoti thero kathaṃ jānāti? Thero kira satthārā saddhiṃyeva taṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjanto yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanā vuṭṭhānaṃ, tāva gantvā idāni bhagavā [M 2.0186] nirodhaṃ samāpanno, antonirodhe ca kālaṅkiriyā nāma natthīti jānāti.

219. Hereafter, to show the preliminary practice for Parinibbāna which the Blessed One performed before attaining Parinibbāna, it was stated: “Then the Blessed One entered the first jhāna,” and so on. Therein, upon seeing the absence of the Blessed One’s in-breaths and out-breaths when he had entered cessation, he asks, “Has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, venerable sir?” “No, friend”—how does the Elder know? It is said that the Elder, having attained each attainment together with the Teacher, having gone up to the emergence from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, knows that the Blessed One has now entered cessation, and that there is no such thing as death within cessation.

Atha kho bhagavā saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhahitvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajji…pe… tatiyajjhānā vuṭṭhahitvā catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjīti ettha bhagavā catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajji, terasasu ṭhānesu dutiyajjhānaṃ, tathā tatiyajjhānaṃ, pannarasasu ṭhānesu catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Kathaṃ? Dasasu asubhesu, dvattiṃsākāre aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu, mettākaruṇāmuditāsu, ānāpāne, paricchedākāseti imesu tāva catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Ṭhapetvā pana dvattiṃsākārañca dasa asubhāni ca sesesu terasasu dutiyajjhānaṃ[V 2.0167], tesuyeva ca tatiyajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Aṭṭhasu pana kasiṇesu, upekkhābrahmavihāre, ānāpāne, paricchedākāse, catūsu arūpesūti imesu pannarasasu ṭhānesu catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Ayampi ca saṅkhepakathāva. Nibbānapuraṃ pavisanto pana bhagavā dhammassāmī sabbāpi catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā samāpattiyo pavisitvā videsaṃ gacchanto ñātijanaṃ āliṅgetvā viya sabbasamāpattisukhaṃ anubhavitvā paviṭṭho.

“Then the Blessed One, emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception… and so on… emerging from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna.” Here, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna in twenty-four instances, the second jhāna in thirteen instances, similarly the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna in fifteen instances. How? In the ten impurities, the thirty-two aspects of the body, the eight kasiṇas, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, mindfulness of breathing, and limited space—in these twenty-four instances, he entered the first jhāna. Excluding the thirty-two aspects of the body and the ten impurities, in the remaining thirteen instances, he entered the second jhāna, and in those same instances, the third jhāna. But in the eight kasiṇas, the brahmavihāra of equanimity, mindfulness of breathing, limited space, and the four immaterial attainments—in these fifteen instances, he entered the fourth jhāna. This too is just a brief account. When entering the city of Nibbāna, the Blessed One, the Master of the Dhamma, having entered all the attainments numbering two hundred and forty million and one hundred thousand, like one embracing relatives when going to a foreign land, having fully experienced the bliss of all attainments, entered.

Catutthajjhānā vuṭṭhahitvā samanantarā bhagavā parinibbāyīti ettha jhānasamanantaraṃ, paccavekkhaṇāsamanantaranti dve samanantarāni. Tattha jhānā vuṭṭhāya bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇassa tattheva parinibbānaṃ jhānasamanantaraṃ nāma. Jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā puna jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇassa tattheva parinibbānaṃ paccavekkhaṇāsamanantaraṃ nāma. Imānipi dve samanantarāneva. Bhagavā pana jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhitvā bhavaṅgacittena abyākatena dukkhasaccena parinibbāyi. Ye [P 2.0595] hi keci buddhā vā paccekabuddhā vā ariyasāvakā vā antamaso kunthakipillikaṃ upādāya sabbe bhavaṅgacitteneva abyākatena dukkhasaccena kālaṅkarontīti. Mahābhūmicālādīni vuttanayānevāti.

In the passage, “Having emerged from the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna immediately thereafter,” there are two kinds of immediacy: immediacy upon emerging from jhāna, and immediacy upon reviewing. Herein, for one who has emerged from jhāna and descended into the life-continuum, final Nibbāna right there is called “immediacy upon emerging from jhāna.” For one who has emerged from jhāna, reviewed the jhāna factors, and then descended into the life-continuum, final Nibbāna right there is called “immediacy upon reviewing.” These two are also immediacies. The Blessed One, however, having entered jhāna, emerged from it, reviewed the jhāna factors, and attained final Nibbāna with the life-continuum consciousness, which is indeterminate and is the truth of suffering. Indeed, all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples—down to the last ant or pupa—pass away with the life-continuum consciousness, which is indeterminate and is the truth of suffering. The great earthquakes and other phenomena occurred in the manner already described.

220. Bhūtāti sattā. Appaṭipuggaloti paṭibhāgapuggalavirahito. Balappattoti dasavidhañāṇabalaṃ patto.

220. Bhūtā means beings. Appaṭipuggala means one without a comparable individual. Balappatta means one who has attained the tenfold power of knowledge.

221. Uppādavayadhamminoti [M 2.0187] uppādavayasabhāvā. Tesaṃ vūpasamoti tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vūpasamo, asaṅkhataṃ nibbānameva sukhanti attho.

221. Uppādavayadhammino means having the nature of arising and passing away. Tesaṃ vūpasamo means the stilling of these formations; the meaning is that the unconditioned Nibbāna itself is happiness.

222. Nāhu assāsapassāsoti na jāto assāsapassāso. Anejoti taṇhāsaṅkhātāya ejāya abhāvena anejo. Santimārabbhāti anupādisesaṃ nibbānaṃ ārabbha paṭicca sandhāya. Yaṃ kālamakarīti yo kālaṃ akari. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “āvuso, yo mama satthā buddhamuni santiṃ gamissāmīti, santiṃ ārabbha kālamakari, tassa ṭhitacittassa tādino idāni assāsapassāso na jāto, natthi, nappavattatī”ti.

222. Nāhu assāsapassāso means in-breath and out-breath did not arise. Anejo means unshaken due to the absence of that agitation which is called craving. Santimārabbha means having taken as object, reached, and intended Nibbāna without remainder of aggregates. Yaṃ kālamakarī means “who passed away.” This is what is said: “Friends, my teacher, the Buddha, the sage, thinking, ‘I shall go to peace,’ passed away having made peace his object. For him, whose mind was steadfast, for such a one, in-breath and out-breath have not arisen, do not exist, do not occur.”

Asallīnenāti alīnena asaṅkuṭitena suvikasiteneva cittena. Vedanaṃ ajjhavāsayīti vedanaṃ adhivāsesi, na vedanānuvattī hutvā ito cito ca samparivatti. Vimokkhoti kenaci dhammena anāvaraṇavimokkho sabbaso apaññattibhāvūpagamo pajjotanibbānasadiso jāto.

Asallīnena means with a mind that is not clinging, not contracted, but fully blossomed. Vedanaṃ ajjhavāsayī means he endured the feeling; he did not, in following the feeling, turn over from here to there. Vimokkha means that a liberation unobstructed by any phenomenon occurred, a complete attainment of the state of non-designation, like the extinguishing of a flame.

223. Tadāsīti [V 2.0168] “saha parinibbānā mahābhūmicālo”ti evaṃ heṭṭhā vuttaṃ bhūmicālameva sandhāyāha. Tañhi lomahaṃsanañca bhiṃsanakañca āsi. Sabbākāravarūpeteti sabbavarakāraṇūpete.

223. Tadāsi refers to the earthquake previously mentioned in the phrase, “With the final Nibbāna, there was a great earthquake.” For it was both hair-raising and terrifying. Sabbākāravarūpete means endowed with all excellent causes.

224. Avītarāgāti puthujjanā ceva sotāpannasakadāgāmino ca. Tesañhi domanassaṃ appahīnaṃ. Tasmā tepi bāhā paggayha kandanti. Ubhopi hatthe sīse ṭhapetvā rodantīti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

224. Avītarāgā means worldlings, as well as stream-enterers and once-returners. For them, grief has not been abandoned. Therefore, they too raise their arms and weep. “Placing both hands on their heads, they cry”—all this should be understood in the same way as before.

225. Ujjhāyantīti “ayyā attanāpi adhivāsetuṃ na sakkonti, sesajanaṃ kathaṃ samassāsessantī”ti vadantiyo ujjhāyanti. Kathaṃbhūtā pana bhante āyasmā anuruddho devatā manasikarotīti devatā, bhante, kathaṃbhūtā āyasmā anuruddho sallakkheti, kiṃ tā satthu parinibbānaṃ adhivāsentīti?

225. Ujjhāyanti means they complain, saying: “The noble ones themselves cannot endure it; how then will they console the remaining people?” The question, “But what kind of deities, venerable sir, does the Venerable Anuruddha attend to?” means they are asking: “Venerable sir, what kind of deities does the Venerable Anuruddha perceive? Do they endure the Teacher’s final Nibbāna?”

Atha tāsaṃ pavattidassanatthaṃ thero santāvusotiādimāha. Taṃ vuttatthameva. Rattāvasesanti [P 2.0596] balavapaccūse parinibbutattā rattiyā avasesaṃ [M 2.0188] cullakaddhānaṃ. Dhammiyā kathāyāti aññā pāṭiyekkā dhammakathā nāma natthi, “āvuso sadevake nāma loke appaṭipuggalassa satthuno ayaṃ maccurājā na lajjati, kimaṅgaṃ pana lokiyamahājanassa lajjissatī”ti evarūpāya pana maraṇapaṭisaṃyuttāya kathāya vītināmesuṃ. Tesañhi taṃ kathaṃ kathentānaṃ muhutteneva aruṇaṃ uggacchi.

Then, to show their state, the Elder spoke the words beginning with “Santā, āvuso.” The meaning of that has already been stated. Rattāvasesaṃ means the remaining small portion of the night, because he attained final Nibbāna at the break of dawn. Dhammiyā kathāya means there was no other specific Dhamma talk; rather, they passed the time with a talk connected with death, of this nature: “Friends, in this world with its devas, this King of Death feels no shame toward the Teacher, who is without peer. What reason, then, would he have to feel shame toward the great mass of worldly people?” For while they were engaged in that talk, in just a moment, the dawn arose.

226. Atha khoti aruṇuggaṃ disvāva thero theraṃ etadavoca. Teneva karaṇīyenāti kīdisena nu kho parinibbānaṭṭhāne mālāgandhādisakkārena bhavitabbaṃ, kīdisena bhikkhusaṅghassa nisajjaṭṭhānena bhavitabbaṃ, kīdisena khādanīyabhojanīyena bhavitabbanti, evaṃ yaṃ bhagavato parinibbutabhāvaṃ sutvā kattabbaṃ teneva karaṇīyena.

226. Atha kho means that as soon as he saw the break of dawn, the Elder said this to the other Elder. Teneva karaṇīyena means by that very duty which must be performed upon hearing of the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, which consists of such things as: ‘What kind of offerings of flowers, scents, and so on, should there be at the place of final Nibbāna? What kind of seating should there be for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus? What kind of food and provisions should there be?’

Buddhasarīrapūjāvaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Veneration of the Buddha’s Bodily Relics

227. Sabbañca tāḷāvacaranti sabbaṃ tūriyabhaṇḍaṃ. Sannipātethāti bheriṃ carāpetvā samāharatha. Te tatheva akaṃsu. Maṇḍalamāḷeti dussamaṇḍalamāḷe. Paṭiyādentāti sajjentā.

227. Sabbañca tāḷāvacaraṃ means all musical instruments. Sannipātethā means, having had the drum beaten, gather them. They did just so. Maṇḍalamāḷe means in circular pavilions of cloth. Paṭiyādenti means arranging.

Dakkhiṇena dakkhiṇanti nagarassa dakkhiṇadisābhāgeneva dakkhiṇadisābhāgaṃ. Bāhirena bāhiranti [V 2.0169] antonagaraṃ appavesetvā bāhireneva nagarassa bāhirapassaṃ haritvā. Dakkhiṇato nagarassāti anurādhapurassa dakkhiṇadvārasadise ṭhāne ṭhapetvā sakkārasammānaṃ katvā jetavanasadise ṭhāne jhāpessāmāti attho.

Dakkhiṇena dakkhiṇaṃ means to the southern quarter by way of the southern quarter of the city. Bāhirena bāhiraṃ means, without having entered the inner city, taking it along the outer side of the city to the outside. Dakkhiṇato nagarassa means the intention is: having placed it in a spot like the southern gate of Anurādhapura and having paid homage and respect, we shall cremate it in a place like Jetavana.

228. Aṭṭha mallapāmokkhāti majjhimavayā thāmasampannā aṭṭhamallarājāno. Sīsaṃ nhātāti sīsaṃ dhovitvā nahātā. Āyasmantaṃ anuruddhanti therova dibbacakkhukoti pākaṭo, tasmā te santesupi aññesu mahātheresu – “ayaṃ no pākaṭaṃ katvā kathessatī”ti theraṃ pucchiṃsu. Kathaṃ pana, bhante, devatānaṃ adhippāyoti bhante, amhākaṃ tāva adhippāyaṃ jānāma. Devatānaṃ kathaṃ adhippāyoti pucchanti. Thero paṭhamaṃ tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ dassento tumhākaṃ khotiādimāha. Makuṭabandhanaṃ nāma mallānaṃ cetiyanti mallarājūnaṃ pasādhanamaṅgalasālāya etaṃ nāmaṃ. Cittīkataṭṭhena panesā “cetiya”nti vuccati.

228. Aṭṭha mallapāmokkhā means eight Malla kings of middle age and endowed with strength. Sīsaṃnhātā means having washed their heads and bathed. Regarding Āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ: the Elder was famous as one who possessed the divine eye; therefore, although other great elders were present, they asked him, thinking, “This one will make it clear and explain it to us.” Kathaṃ pana, bhante, devatānaṃ adhippāyo means they ask: “Venerable sir, we know our own intention. What is the intention of the deities?” The Elder, first indicating their intention, spoke the words beginning with “Tumhākaṃ kho.” Makuṭabandhanaṃ nāma mallānaṃ cetiyaṃ means this was the name of the Malla kings’ auspicious ceremonial hall for adornment. It is called a cetiya because it is an object of reverence.

229. Yāva [P 2.0597][M 2.0189] sandhisamalasaṅkaṭīrāti ettha sandhi nāma gharasandhi. Samalaṃ nāma gūtharāsiniddhamanapanāḷi. Saṅkaṭīraṃ nāma saṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ. Dibbehi ca mānusakehi ca naccehīti upari devatānaṃ naccāni honti, heṭṭhā manussānaṃ. Esa nayo gītādīsu. Apica devatānaṃ antare manussā, manussānaṃ antare devatāti evampi sakkarontā pūjentā agamaṃsu. Majjhena majjhaṃ nagarassa haritvāti evaṃ hariyamāne bhagavato sarīre bandhulamallasenāpatibhariyā mallikā nāma – “bhagavato sarīraṃ āharantī”ti sutvā attano sāmikassa kālaṃ kiriyato paṭṭhāya aparibhuñjitvā ṭhapitaṃ visākhāya pasādhanasadisaṃ mahālatāpasādhanaṃ nīharāpetvā – “iminā satthāraṃ pūjessāmī”ti taṃ majjāpetvā gandhodakena dhovitvā dvāre ṭhitā.

229. As to the phrase 'as far as the joints, filth, and rubbish heaps': herein, 'joints' means the joints of houses. 'Filth' means a drain for removing heaps of excrement. 'Rubbish heap' means a place for rubbish. As to 'with divine and human dances': above were the dances of the deities, and below, those of humans. This same principle applies to songs and so forth. Moreover, among the deities were humans, and among the humans were deities; thus honoring and revering, they proceeded. As to 'carrying it through the middle of the city': while the Blessed One's body was being carried in this way, Mallikā, the wife of the Malla general Bandhula, hearing, 'They are bringing the Blessed One's body,' had the great creeper ornament, which was similar to Visākhā's and had been set aside unused since the time of her husband's death, brought out. Thinking, 'With this I shall honor the Teacher,' she had it polished and washed with scented water, and stood at her gate.

Taṃ kira pasādhanaṃ tāsañca dvinnaṃ itthīnaṃ, devadāniyacorassa geheti tīsuyeva ṭhānesu ahosi. Sā ca satthu sarīre dvāraṃ sampatte – “otāretha, tātā, satthusarīra”nti vatvā taṃ pasādhanaṃ satthusarīre paṭimuñci. Taṃ sīsato paṭṭhāya paṭimukkaṃ yāvapādatalāgataṃ. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ bhagavato sarīraṃ sattaratanamayena mahāpasādhanena pasādhitaṃ ativiya virocittha. Taṃ sā disvā pasannacittā patthanaṃ akāsi – “bhagavā yāva vaṭṭe saṃsarissāmi, tāva me pāṭiyekkaṃ pasādhanakiccaṃ mā hotu, niccaṃ paṭimukkapasādhanasadisameva sarīraṃ hotū”ti.

That ornament, it is said, existed in only three places: in the houses of those two women and of the thief Devadāniya. And when the Teacher's body reached the gate, she said, 'Lower the Teacher's body, my good sirs,' and draped that ornament over the Teacher's body. Placed on from the head, it reached as far as the soles of his feet. The golden-hued body of the Blessed One, adorned with the great seven-jeweled ornament, shone exceedingly. Seeing this, with a serene mind, she made an aspiration: 'Venerable Sir, for as long as I wander in the round of rebirth, may there be no need for me to adorn myself separately; may my body always be as if already adorned.'

Atha bhagavantaṃ sattaratanamayena mahāpasādhanena ukkhipitvā puratthimena dvārena nīharitvā puratthimena nagarassa makuṭabandhanaṃ mallānaṃ cetiyaṃ, ettha bhagavato sarīraṃ nikkhipiṃsu.

Then, having lifted the Blessed One with the great seven-jeweled ornament, they carried him out through the eastern gate to the Mallas' shrine named Makuṭabandhana, to the east of the city. There they laid down the Blessed One's body.

Mahākassapattheravatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Elder Mahākassapa

231. Pāvāya [V 2.0170] kusināranti pāvānagare piṇḍāya caritvā “kusināraṃ gamissāmī”ti addhānamaggappaṭipanno hoti. Rukkhamūle nisīdīti ettha kasmā divāvihāranti na vuttaṃ? Divāvihāratthāya anisinnattā. Therassa hi parivārā bhikkhū sabbe sukhasaṃvaddhitā mahāpuññā. Te majjhanhikasamaye tattapāsāṇasadisāya bhūmiyā padasā gacchantā kilamiṃsu. Thero te disvā – “bhikkhū kilamanti, gantabbaṭṭhānañca na dūraṃ, thokaṃ vissamitvā darathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā sāyanhasamaye kusināraṃ gantvā dasabalaṃ passissāmī”ti maggā [M 2.0190] okkamma aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle [P 2.0598] saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā udakatumbato udakena hatthapāde sītale katvā nisīdi. Parivārabhikkhūpissa rukkhamūle nisīditvā yoniso manasikāre kammaṃ kurumānā tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamānā nisīdiṃsu. Iti darathavinodanatthāya nisinnattā “divāvihāra”nti na vuttaṃ.

231. As to the phrase 'From Pāvā to Kusinārā': having wandered for alms in the city of Pāvā, he set out on the main road, thinking, 'I will go to Kusinārā.' As to 'He sat at the foot of a tree': why is it not said 'for the day's abiding' here? Because he did not sit for the purpose of the day's abiding. For the elder’s retinue of monks were all brought up in comfort and of great merit. At midday, they grew weary walking on foot upon ground that was like a heated stone slab. Seeing them, the elder thought, 'The monks are weary, and the place we must go is not far. Having rested a little and allayed our fatigue, in the evening we shall go to Kusinārā and see the One of Ten Powers.' Stepping off the road, he spread his outer robe at the foot of a certain tree, cooled his hands and feet with water from a water gourd, and sat down. The monks of his retinue also sat down at the foot of the tree, applying themselves to the task of wise attention and speaking of the virtues of the Three Jewels. Thus, because they sat down for the purpose of dispelling fatigue, it is not said 'for the day's abiding.'

Mandāravapupphaṃ gahetvāti mahāpātippamāṇaṃ pupphaṃ āgantukadaṇḍake ṭhapetvā chattaṃ viya gahetvā. Addasa khoti āgacchantaṃ dūrato addasa. Disvā ca pana cintesi –

As to 'having taken a mandārava flower': having placed the flower, which was the size of a large bowl, on an artificial stalk, he held it like an umbrella. As to 'he saw': he saw him coming from afar. And having seen him, he thought:

“Etaṃ ājīvakassa hatthe mandāravapupphaṃ paññāyati, etañca na sabbadā manussapathe paññāyati, yadā pana koci iddhimā iddhiṃ vikubbati, tadā sabbaññubodhisattassa ca mātukucchiokkamanādīsu hoti. Na kho pana ajja kenaci iddhivikubbanaṃ kataṃ, na me satthā mātukucchiṃ okkanto, na kucchito nikkhamanto, nāpissa ajja abhisambodhi, na dhammacakkappavattanaṃ, na yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ, na devorohaṇaṃ, na āyusaṅkhārossajjanaṃ. Mahallako pana me satthā dhuvaṃ parinibbuto bhavissatī”ti.

'This mandārava flower is apparent in the Ājīvaka's hand, and such a flower is not always apparent in the human realm. It appears when someone with psychic power performs a wonder, and also on such occasions as the All-Knowing Bodhisatta's descent into his mother's womb. But today no wonder of psychic power has been performed by anyone. My Teacher has not descended into a mother's womb, nor has he emerged from a womb; nor is today his full awakening, nor the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, nor the Twin Wonder, nor the descent from the world of the gods, nor the relinquishing of the life-force determination. My Teacher, however, is aged. Surely he must have attained final Parinibbāna.'

Tato – “pucchāmi na”nti cittaṃ uppādetvā – “sace kho pana nisinnakova pucchāmi, satthari agāravo kato bhavissatī”ti uṭṭhahitvā ṭhitaṭṭhānato apakkamma chaddanto nāgarājā maṇicammaṃ viya dasabaladattiyaṃ meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupitvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhapetvā satthari katena gāravena ājīvakassa abhimukho hutvā – “āvuso, amhākaṃ satthāraṃ jānāsī”ti āha. Kiṃ pana satthu parinibbānaṃ jānanto pucchi ajānantoti? Āvajjanapaṭibaddhaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ jānanaṃ, anāvajjitattā panesa ajānanto pucchīti [V 2.0171] eke. Thero samāpattibahulo, rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaleṇamaṇḍapādīsu niccaṃ samāpattibaleneva yāpeti, kulasantakampi gāmaṃ pavisitvā dvāre samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhitova bhikkhaṃ gaṇhāti. Thero kira iminā pacchimena attabhāvena mahājanānuggahaṃ karissāmi – “ye mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ vā denti gandhamālādīhi vā sakkāraṃ karonti, tesaṃ taṃ mahapphalaṃ hotū”ti evaṃ [M 2.0191] karoti. Tasmā samāpattibahulatāya na jānāti. Iti ajānantova pucchatīti vadanti, taṃ [P 2.0599] na gahetabbaṃ.

Thereupon, having formed the thought, 'I shall ask him,' he then thought, 'But if I ask while remaining seated, I will have shown disrespect towards the Teacher.' So he rose, and stepping back from where he stood, he draped the dust-heap robe, the color of a raincloud, which had been given by the One of Ten Powers, just as Chaddanta, the elephant king, might drape his jeweled hide. Placing his hands in reverential salutation, resplendent with the joining of his ten fingernails, upon his head, and with the reverence he had for the Teacher, he faced the Ājīvaka and said, 'Friend, do you know our Teacher?' Now, did he ask knowing of the Teacher's final Parinibbāna, or not knowing? The knowledge of those whose cankers are destroyed is dependent on adverting the mind. Some say that because he had not adverted his mind, he asked without knowing. The elder was one who dwelt much in meditative attainment. At his night-time and day-time resting places, in caves, pavilions, and so on, he always sustained himself by the power of meditative attainment. Even when entering a village belonging to his family, he would enter a meditative attainment at the door and would accept almsfood only after emerging from it. It is said that the elder acted thus, thinking, 'In this final existence, I shall bring about the welfare of many people. May the offerings of those who give me almsfood or who honor me with perfumes, garlands, and the like be of great fruit for them.' Therefore, because he dwelt much in meditative attainment, he did not know. Thus they say that he asked without knowing, but that view should not be accepted.

Na hettha ajānanakāraṇaṃ atthi. Abhilakkhitaṃ satthu parinibbānaṃ ahosi, dasasahassilokadhātukampanādīhi nimittehi. Therassa pana parisāya kehici bhikkhūhi bhagavā diṭṭhapubbo, kehici na diṭṭhapubbo, tattha yehipi diṭṭhapubbo, tepi passitukāmāva, yehipi adiṭṭhapubbo, tepi passitukāmāva. Tattha yehi na diṭṭhapubbo, te atidassanakāmatāya gantvā “kuhiṃ bhagavā”ti pucchantā “parinibbuto”ti sutvā sandhāretuṃ nāsakkhissanti. Cīvarañca pattañca chaḍḍetvā ekavatthā vā dunnivatthā vā duppārutā vā urāni paṭipisantā parodissanti. Tattha manussā – “mahākassapattherena saddhiṃ āgatā paṃsukūlikā sayampi itthiyo viya parodanti, te kiṃ amhe samassāsessantī”ti mayhaṃ dosaṃ dassanti. Idaṃ pana suññaṃ mahāaraññaṃ, idha yathā tathā rodantesu doso natthi. Purimataraṃ sutvā nāma sokopi tanuko hotīti bhikkhūnaṃ satuppādanatthāya jānantova pucchi.

Here, there is no cause for not knowing. The Teacher’s final Nibbāna was clearly marked by signs such as the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world-system. In the Elder’s assembly, some monks had seen the Blessed One before, while others had not. Among them, those who had seen him before still wished to see him, and those who had not seen him before also wished to see him. Among those who had not seen him, being overcome by the desire to see him, they would go and ask, “Where is the Blessed One?” Upon hearing, “He has passed into final Nibbāna,” they would be unable to compose themselves. Discarding their robes and bowls, wearing but a single garment, or improperly dressed, or improperly robed, they would beat their breasts and lament. Then people would think, “These rag-robed monks who came with the Elder Mahākassapa are themselves weeping like women; how then will they console us?” Thus they would find fault with me. But this is a vast, secluded forest; here, there is no fault no matter how they weep. Moreover, when one hears of it sooner, the grief itself is lessened. Thus, though he already knew, he asked for the sake of arousing mindfulness in the monks.

Ajja sattāhaparinibbuto samaṇo gotamoti ajja samaṇo gotamo sattāhaparinibbuto. Tato me idanti tato samaṇassa gotamassa parinibbutaṭṭhānato.

The phrase 'The ascetic Gotama has been passed into final Nibbāna for seven days as of today' means: today, it has been seven days since the ascetic Gotama passed into final Nibbāna. The phrase 'From there, this is for me' means: from that place of the ascetic Gotama's final Nibbāna.

232. Subhaddo nāma vuḍḍhapabbajitoti “subhaddo”ti tassa nāmaṃ. Vuḍḍhakāle pana pabbajitattā “vuḍḍhapabbajito”ti vuccati. Kasmā pana so evamāha? Bhagavati āghātena. Ayaṃ kireso khandhake āgate ātumāvatthusmiṃ nahāpitapubbako vuḍḍhapabbajito bhagavati kusinārato nikkhamitvā aḍḍhateḷasehi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ ātumaṃ āgacchante bhagavā āgacchatīti sutvā – “āgatakāle yāgupānaṃ karissāmī”ti sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhite dve putte etadavoca – “bhagavā kira, tātā, ātumaṃ āgacchati mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ aḍḍhateḷasehi bhikkhusatehi; gacchatha tumhe, tātā, khurabhaṇḍaṃ ādāya nāḷiyāvāpakena anugharakaṃ anugharakaṃ āhiṇḍatha loṇampi telampi taṇḍulampi khādanīyampi [P 2.0600] saṃharatha [M 2.0192] bhagavato āgatassa yāgupānaṃ karissāmā”ti (mahāva. 303). Te tathā akaṃsu.

232. Regarding 'Subhaddo, the one who went forth in old age': 'Subhaddo' was his name. He is called 'the one who went forth in old age' because he was ordained in his old age. But why did he speak thus? Out of resentment towards the Blessed One. It is said that this person, mentioned in the Khandhaka in the story of Ātumā, was formerly a barber who had gone forth in old age. He heard that the Blessed One was leaving Kusinārā and coming to Ātumā with twelve hundred and fifty monks, and thought, 'When he arrives, I will prepare rice gruel and drinks.' He then spoke to his two sons, who were novices: 'My dear sons, it is said the Blessed One is coming to Ātumā with a great assembly of monks, twelve hundred and fifty of them. Go, my dears, take your barber's equipment and a measuring bag, and go from house to house. Collect salt, oil, rice, and other edibles. When the Blessed One arrives, we will prepare rice gruel and drinks for him.' (Mahāvagga 303). They did so.

Manussā [V 2.0172] te dārake mañjuke paṭibhāneyyake disvā kāretukāmāpi akāretukāmāpi kārentiyeva. Katakāle – “kiṃ gaṇhissatha tātā”ti pucchanti. Te vadanti – “na amhākaṃ aññena kenaci attho, pitā pana no bhagavato, āgatakāle yāgudānaṃ dātukāmo”ti. Taṃ sutvā manussā aparigaṇetvāva yaṃ te sakkonti āharituṃ, sabbaṃ denti. Yampi na sakkonti, manussehi pesenti. Atha bhagavati ātumaṃ āgantvā bhusāgāraṃ paviṭṭhe subhaddo sāyanhasamayaṃ gāmadvāraṃ gantvā manusse āmantesi – “upāsakā, nāhaṃ tumhākaṃ santikā aññaṃ kiñci paccāsīsāmi, mayhaṃ dārakehi ābhatāni taṇḍulādīniyeva saṅghassa pahonti. Yaṃ hatthakammaṃ, taṃ me dethā”ti. “Idañcidañca gaṇhathā”ti sabbūpakaraṇāni gāhetvā vihāre uddhanāni kāretvā ekaṃ kāḷakaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā tādisameva pārupitvā – “idaṃ karotha, idaṃ karothā”ti sabbarattiṃ vicārento satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā bhojjayāguñca madhugoḷakañca paṭiyādāpesi. Bhojjayāgu nāma bhuñjitvā pātabbayāgu, tattha sappimadhuphāṇitamacchamaṃsapupphaphalarasādi yaṃ kiñci khādanīyaṃ nāma sabbaṃ pakkhipati kīḷitukāmānaṃ sīsamakkhanayoggā hoti sugandhagandhā.

Seeing that the boys were charming and eloquent, people had them perform their services, whether they wished to or not. When the work was done, they would ask, 'What will you take, my dears?' The boys would reply, 'We have no need of anything else, but our father wishes to make an offering of rice gruel to the Blessed One when he arrives.' Hearing this, the people, without counting, gave everything the boys could carry. And what they could not carry, the people had sent by others. Then, when the Blessed One had arrived at Ātumā and entered the chaff-house, Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening and addressed the people: 'Lay devotees, I do not expect anything else from you. The rice and other provisions brought by my sons are sufficient for the Saṅgha. Just provide me with the manual labor.' Saying, 'Take this and that,' he had all the necessary equipment brought. He had ovens set up in the monastery, put on a dark saffron robe, and wore a similar one as an outer robe. All night long, he went about directing, 'Do this, do this,' and spending a hundred thousand, he had a meal-gruel and honey-balls prepared. The meal-gruel is a gruel to be eaten and then drunk. Into it is put every kind of edible thing: ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flower and fruit essences, and so on. It has a fragrant scent and is suitable for anointing the heads of those who wish for amusement.

Atha bhagavā kālasseva sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto piṇḍāya carituṃ ātumanagarābhimukho pāyāsi. Manussā tassa ārocesuṃ – “bhagavā piṇḍāya gāmaṃ pavisati, tayā kassa yāgu paṭiyāditā”ti. So yathānivatthapāruteheva tehi kāḷakakāsāvehi ekena hatthena dabbiñca kaṭacchuñca gahetvā brahmā viya dakkhiṇajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā vanditvā – “paṭiggaṇhātu me, bhante, bhagavā yāgu”nti āha.

Then the Blessed One, having attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, surrounded by the community of monks, set out towards the city of Ātumā for alms. People informed Subhadda: “The Blessed One is entering the village for alms. For whom have you prepared the rice gruel?” So, just as he was, dressed in those dark saffron robes, holding a ladle in one hand and a spoon in the other, like a Brahmā, he placed his right knee on the ground, paid homage, and said: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my rice gruel.”

Tato “jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchantī”ti khandhake āgatanayena bhagavā pucchitvā ca sutvā ca taṃ vuḍḍhapabbajitaṃ vigarahitvā tasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ akappiyasamādānasikkhāpadañca, khurabhaṇḍapariharaṇasikkhāpadañcāti dve sikkhāpadāni [P 2.0601] paññapetvā – “bhikkhave, anekakappakoṭiyo bhojanaṃ pariyesanteheva [M 2.0193] vītināmitā, idaṃ pana tumhākaṃ akappiyaṃ adhammena uppannaṃ bhojanaṃ, imaṃ paribhuttānaṃ anekāni attabhāvasahassāni apāyesveva nibbattissanti, apetha mā gaṇhathā”ti bhikkhācārābhimukho agamāsi. Ekabhikkhunāpi na kiñci gahitaṃ.

Then, in accordance with the principle from the Khandhaka that 'Tathāgatas ask even when they already know,' the Blessed One, after questioning and listening, rebuked that monk who had gone forth in old age. In connection with that incident, he laid down two training rules: the training rule concerning causing the acceptance of what is improper, and the training rule concerning carrying around razor equipment. He said, 'Monks, many crores of aeons have been passed just in the search for food. This food, however, is improper for you, having been acquired unrighteously. For those who consume it, there will be rebirth in the states of woe for many thousands of lifetimes. Go away, do not take it!' So saying, he proceeded on his alms-round. Not even one monk took anything.

Subhaddo anattamano hutvā ayaṃ “sabbaṃ jānāmī”ti āhiṇḍati. Sace na gahitukāmo, pesetvā ārocetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pakkāhāro nāma sabbaciraṃ tiṭṭhanto sattāhamattaṃ tiṭṭheyya. Idañhi mama yāvajīvaṃ pariyattaṃ assa. Sabbaṃ tena nāsitaṃ, ahitakāmo ayaṃ mayhanti [V 2.0173] bhagavati āghātaṃ bandhitvā dasabale dharante kiñci vattuṃ nāsakkhi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ayaṃ uccā kulā pabbajito mahāpuriso, sace kiñci vakkhāmi, maṃyeva santajjessatī”ti. Svāyaṃ ajja “parinibbuto bhagavā”ti sutvā laddhassāso viya haṭṭhatuṭṭho evamāha.

Subhadda, being displeased, thought: 'This one wanders about claiming, “I know everything.” If he did not wish to take it, he should have sent word. This cooked food, even if it were to last a very long time, would only last for seven days. Yet this would have sufficed for my entire life. Everything was ruined by him; this one wishes me ill.' Thus, harboring resentment towards the Blessed One, he could not say anything while the Ten-Powered One was still alive. Indeed, this was his thought: 'This great man has gone forth from a high family; if I say anything, he will rebuke me.' Today, hearing that 'the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna,' he was as if relieved and, overjoyed, spoke thus.

Thero taṃ sutvā hadaye pahāradānaṃ viya matthake patitasukkhāsani viya maññi, dhammasaṃvego cassa uppajji – “sattāhamattaparinibbuto bhagavā, ajjāpissa suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ dharatiyeva, dukkhena bhagavatā ārādhitasāsane nāma evaṃ lahu mahantaṃ pāpakasaṭaṃ kaṇṭako uppanno, alaṃ kho panesa pāpo vaḍḍhamāno aññepi evarūpe sahāye labhitvā sakkā sāsanaṃ osakkāpetu”nti. Tato thero cintesi –

The elder, hearing this, felt as if struck in the heart, as if a dry thunderbolt had fallen on his head, and a sense of spiritual urgency arose in him: “The Blessed One attained final Nibbāna just seven days ago, and even now his golden-hued body still remains. In the Dispensation established with such difficulty by the Blessed One, such a great and wicked scoundrel, a thorn, has so quickly arisen. Indeed, this wicked one, growing, may find other companions like himself and is capable of causing the Dispensation to decline.” Then the elder thought:

“Sace kho panāhaṃ imaṃ mahallakaṃ idheva pilotikaṃ nivāsāpetvā chārikāya okirāpetvā nīharāpessāmi, manussā ‘samaṇassa gotamassa sarīre dharamāneyeva sāvakā vivadantī’ti amhākaṃ dosaṃ dassessanti adhivāsemi tāva.

“If I were to have this old monk dressed in a rag right here, have his head sprinkled with ashes, and have him driven away, people would say, ‘Even while the ascetic Gotama’s body is still present, his disciples are quarreling,’ and they would find fault with us. I will endure this for now.

Bhagavatā hi desito dhammo asaṅgahitapuppharāsisadiso. Tattha yathā vātena pahaṭapupphāni yato vā tato vā gacchanti, evameva evarūpānaṃ pāpapuggalānaṃ vasena gacchante gacchante kāle vinaye ekaṃ dve sikkhāpadāni nassissanti, sutte eko dve pañhāvārā nassissanti, abhidhamme ekaṃ dve bhūmantarāni nassissanti, evaṃ anukkamena mūle naṭṭhe pisācasadisā bhavissāma; tasmā dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ karissāma. Evañhi sati daḷhaṃ [M 2.0194] suttena saṅgahitāni pupphāni viya ayaṃ dhammavinayo niccalo bhavissati.

For the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of flowers not strung together. Just as flowers scattered by the wind go here and there, so too, due to such wicked persons, as time passes, one or two training rules will be lost in the Vinaya, one or two sections of discourse will disappear from the Sutta, and one or two divisions of topics will vanish from the Abhidhamma. Gradually, when the root is lost, we will become like ghosts. Therefore, we shall hold a council of the Dhamma and Vinaya. For when this is done, this Dhamma and Vinaya will become steadfast, like flowers firmly bound by a thread.

Etadatthañhi bhagavā [P 2.0602] mayhaṃ tīṇi gāvutāni paccuggamanaṃ akāsi, tīhi ovādehi upasampadaṃ adāsi, kāyato apanetvā kāye cīvaraparivattanaṃ akāsi, ākāse pāṇiṃ cāletvā candūpamaṃ paṭipadaṃ kathento maṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā kathesi, tikkhattuṃ sakalasāsanadāyajjaṃ paṭicchāpesi. Mādise bhikkhumhi tiṭṭhamāne ayaṃ pāpo sāsane vuḍḍhiṃ mā alattha. Yāva adhammo na dippati, dhammo na paṭibāhiyati. Avinayo na dippati vinayo na paṭibāhiyati. Adhammavādino na balavanto honti, dhammavādino na dubbalā honti; avinayavādino na balavanto honti, vinayavādino na dubbalā honti. Tāva dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyissāmi. Tato bhikkhū attano attano pahonakaṃ gahetvā kappiyākappiyaṃ [V 2.0174] kathessanti. Athāyaṃ pāpo sayameva niggahaṃ pāpuṇissati, puna sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na sakkhissati, sāsanaṃ iddhañceva phītañca bhavissatī”ti.

It was for this very purpose that the Blessed One came three gāvutas to meet me, gave me ordination with three exhortations, took the robe from his body and exchanged it with mine, and, waving his hand in the air while teaching the practice comparable to the moon, he spoke making me a personal witness. Three times he entrusted me with the entire inheritance of the Dispensation. While a monk like me is present, may this wicked one not prosper in the Dispensation. So long as the unrighteous does not flourish and the righteous is not obstructed; so long as indiscipline does not flourish and discipline is not obstructed; so long as speakers of unrighteousness are not powerful and speakers of righteousness are not weak; so long as speakers of indiscipline are not powerful and speakers of discipline are not weak—for that long shall I convene a council of the Dhamma and the Vinaya. Then the monks, each taking up what is appropriate for them, will speak on what is allowable and unallowable. Then this wicked one will by himself meet with censure; he will not be able to raise his head again, and the Dispensation will be successful and prosperous.”

So evaṃ nāma mayhaṃ cittaṃ uppannanti kassaci anārocetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ samassāsesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo…pe… netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti.

Without disclosing to anyone, 'Such a thought has arisen in me,' he reassured the Saṅgha of monks. Therefore, it is said: “Then the Venerable Mahākassapa...pe... this is not possible.”

233. Citakanti vīsaratanasatikaṃ candanacitakaṃ. Āḷimpessāmāti aggiṃ gāhāpessāma. Na sakkonti āḷimpetunti aṭṭhapi soḷasapi dvattiṃsapi janā jālanatthāya yamakayamakaukkāyo gahetvā tālavaṇṭehi bījantā bhastāhi dhamantā tāni tāni kāraṇāni karontāpi na sakkontiyeva aggiṃ gāhāpetuṃ. Devatānaṃ adhippāyoti ettha tā kira devatā therassa upaṭṭhākadevatāva. Asītimahāsāvakesu hi cittāni pasādetvā tesaṃ upaṭṭhākāni asītikulasahassāni sagge nibbattāni. Tattha there cittaṃ pasādetvā sagge nibbattā devatā tasmiṃ samāgame theraṃ adisvā – “kuhiṃ nu kho amhākaṃ kulūpakatthero”ti antarāmagge paṭipannaṃ disvā “amhākaṃ kulūpakattherena avandite citako mā pajjalitthā”ti adhiṭṭhahiṃsu.

233. The funeral pyre—a pyre of sandalwood one hundred and twenty cubits in size. 'We will ignite it,' they said, meaning, 'We will have the fire lit.' But they could not ignite it. Even eight, sixteen, or thirty-two people, taking pairs of torches for kindling, fanning with palm-leaf fans, blowing with bellows, and performing these and other actions, were still unable to have the fire lit. It was due to the intention of the deities. Here, those deities were indeed the attendant deities of the Elder. For, having placed their faith in the eighty great disciples, eighty thousand families who were their supporters were reborn in heaven. Among them, the deities who had placed their faith in the Elder and were reborn in heaven did not see the Elder at the gathering. Thinking, 'Where, indeed, is our family's patron Elder?' and seeing him journeying on the road, they made a resolution: 'May the pyre not ignite until our family's patron Elder has paid homage.'

Manussā [M 2.0195] taṃ sutvā – “mahākassapo kira nāma bho bhikkhu pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ ‘dasabalassa pāde vandissāmī’ti āgacchati. Tasmiṃ kira anāgate citako na pajjalissati. Kīdiso bho so bhikkhu kāḷo odāto dīgho rasso, evarūpe nāma bho bhikkhumhi ṭhite kiṃ dasabalassa parinibbānaṃ nāmā”ti keci [P 2.0603] gandhamālādihatthā paṭipathaṃ gacchiṃsu. Keci vīthiyo vicittā katvā āgamanamaggaṃ olokayamānā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Hearing this, the people said, 'Sirs, it is said that a monk named Mahākassapa is coming with five hundred monks, intending, “I will pay homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One.” It is said that until he arrives, the pyre will not ignite. What kind of monk is he, sirs—dark or fair, tall or short? While such a monk is present, why did the Ten-Powered One have to attain Parinibbāna?' Some, holding perfumes and garlands, went along the road to meet him. Others, having decorated the streets, stood watching the road of his arrival.

234. Atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo yena kusinārā…pe… sirasā vandīti thero kira citakaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā āvajjantova sallakkhesi – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīsaṃ, imasmiṃ ṭhāne pādā”ti. Tato pādānaṃ samīpe ṭhatvā abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya – “arāsahassapaṭimaṇḍitacakkalakkhaṇapatiṭṭhitā dasabalassa pādā saddhiṃ kappāsapaṭalehi pañca dussayugasatāni suvaṇṇadoṇiṃ candanacitakañca dvedhā katvā mayhaṃ uttamaṅge sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhahantū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Saha adhiṭṭhānacittena tāni pañca dussayugasatāni dvedhā katvā valāhakantarā puṇṇacando viya pādā nikkhamiṃsu. Thero vikasitarattapadumasadise hatthe pasāretvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇe satthupāde yāva gopphakā daḷhaṃ gahetvā attano siravare patiṭṭhapesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “bhagavato pāde sirasā vandī”ti.

234. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached Kusinārā… he paid homage with his head. The elder, having circumambulated the pyre, reflected and discerned, “In this place is the head, in this place are the feet.” Then, standing near the feet, he entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for supernormal power. Emerging from it, he resolved, “May the feet of the Ten-Powered One, established with the mark of a wheel adorned with a thousand spokes, splitting in two the five hundred pairs of cloths along with the layers of cotton, the golden trough, and the sandalwood pyre, rest upon my supreme head.” Simultaneously with his mind of resolution, those five hundred pairs of cloths split in two, and the feet emerged from between the clouds like the full moon. The elder, stretching out his hands like blooming red lotuses, firmly grasped the golden-hued Teacher’s feet up to the ankles and placed them upon his own noble head. Therefore, it is said: “He paid homage to the Blessed One’s feet with his head.”

Mahājano [V 2.0175] taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā ekappahāreneva mahānādaṃ nadi, gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā yathāruci vandi. Evaṃ pana therena ca mahājanena ca tehi ca pañcahi bhikkhusatehi vanditamatte puna adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi. Pakatiadhiṭṭhānavaseneva therassa hatthato muccitvā alattakavaṇṇāni bhagavato pādatalāni candanadāruādīsu kiñci acāletvāva yathāṭhāne patiṭṭhahiṃsu, yathāṭhāne ṭhitāneva ahesuṃ. Bhagavato hi pādesu nikkhamantesu vā pavisantesu vā kappāsaaṃsu vā dasikatantaṃ vā telabindu vā dārukkhandhaṃ vā ṭhānā calitaṃ nāma nāhosi. Sabbaṃ yathāṭhāne ṭhitameva ahosi. Uṭṭhahitvā pana atthaṅgate cande viya sūriye viya ca tathāgatassa pādesu antarahitesu mahājano mahākanditaṃ kandi. Parinibbānakālato adhikataraṃ kāruññaṃ ahosi.

Seeing this marvel, the great crowd let out a mighty cry all at once, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and paid homage as they pleased. However, as soon as the elder, the great crowd, and those five hundred monks had paid homage, there was no further need for an act of resolution. By the power of the original resolution alone, the Blessed One’s soles, colored like lac, were released from the elder’s hands and, without moving the sandalwood logs or anything else in the slightest, they settled back into their original place; they were just as they had been before. Indeed, when the Blessed One’s feet emerged or returned, not a fiber of cotton, nor a thread from a fringe, nor a drop of oil, nor a block of wood was moved from its place. Everything remained exactly where it was. But when the Tathāgata’s feet vanished, like the moon or the sun that has risen and then set, the great crowd wept with loud lamentation. The sorrow was even greater than at the time of the final passing away.

Sayameva [M 2.0196] bhagavato citako pajjalīti idaṃ pana kassaci pajjalāpetuṃ vāyamantassa adassanavasena vuttaṃ. Devatānubhāvena panesa samantato ekappahāreneva pajjali.

As for the statement, ‘The Blessed One’s pyre ignited by itself,’ this was said because no one was seen trying to light it. In fact, by the power of the deities, it blazed up from all sides all at once.

235. Sarīrāneva avasissiṃsūti pubbe ekagghanena ṭhitattā sarīraṃ nāma ahosi. Idāni vippakiṇṇattā sarīrānīti vuttaṃ sumanamakuḷasadisā [P 2.0604] ca dhotamuttasadisā ca suvaṇṇasadisā ca dhātuyo avasissiṃsūti attho. Dīghāyukabuddhānañhi sarīraṃ suvaṇṇakkhandhasadisaṃ ekameva hoti. Bhagavā pana – “ahaṃ na ciraṃ ṭhatvā parinibbāyāmi, mayhaṃ sāsanaṃ tāva sabbattha na vitthāritaṃ, tasmā parinibbutassāpi me sāsapamattampi dhātuṃ gahetvā attano attano vasanaṭṭhāne cetiyaṃ katvā paricaranto mahājano saggaparāyaṇo hotū”ti dhātūnaṃ vikiraṇaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi. Kati, panassa dhātuyo vippakiṇṇā, kati na vippakiṇṇāti. Catasso dāṭhā, dve akkhakā, uṇhīsanti imā satta dhātuyo na vippakiriṃsu, sesā vippakiriṃsūti. Tattha sabbakhuddakā dhātu sāsapabījamattā ahosi, mahādhātu majjhe bhinnataṇḍulamattā, atimahatī majjhe bhinnamuggamattāti.

235. Regarding the words, ‘Only the relics remained’: previously, because it existed as a single solid mass, it was called the ‘body’ (sarīra). Now, because they are scattered, they are called ‘relics’ (sarīrāni). The meaning is that relics resembling jasmine buds, washed pearls, and gold remained. Indeed, for Buddhas with long lifespans, their bodily frame is a single mass, like a block of gold. The Blessed One, however, resolved the scattering of the relics, thinking: ‘I will attain final Nibbāna without remaining for long, and my Dispensation has not yet spread everywhere. Therefore, even after I have finally passed away, may the great multitude, by taking even a mustard-seed-sized relic, building a shrine in their own dwelling places, and attending to it, have heaven as their destination.’ How many of his relics were scattered, and how many were not scattered? Four canine teeth, two collarbones, and the frontal bone—these seven relics were not scattered. The remaining ones were scattered. Among them, the smallest relic was the size of a mustard seed, the medium one was the size of a broken rice grain, and the largest was the size of a broken mung bean.

Udakadhārāti aggabāhumattāpi jaṅghamattāpi tālakkhandhamattāpi udakadhārā ākāsato patitvā nibbāpesi. Udakasālatoti parivāretvā ṭhitasālarukkhe sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ, tesampi hi khandhantaraviṭapantarehi udakadhārā nikkhamitvā nibbāpesuṃ. Bhagavato citako mahanto. Samantā pathaviṃ bhinditvāpi naṅgalasīsamattā udakavaṭṭi phalikavaṭaṃsakasadisā uggantvā citakameva gaṇhanti. Gandhodakenāti suvaṇṇaghaṭe rajataghaṭe ca pūretvā ābhatanānāgandhodakena. Nibbāpesunti suvaṇṇamayarajatamayehi aṭṭhadaṇḍakehi vikiritvā candanacitakaṃ nibbāpesuṃ.

Regarding the stream of water: a stream of water forearm-deep, shin-deep, and even as thick as a palm trunk fell from the sky and extinguished the pyre. As for ‘from the water-sāla trees’: this was said in reference to the surrounding sāla trees, for from between their trunks and branches, streams of water also gushed forth and extinguished it. The Blessed One’s pyre was large. From all around, even breaking through the earth, columns of water the size of a ploughshare, resembling crystal ornaments, rose up and fell only upon the pyre. By ‘with fragrant water’ is meant with various fragrant waters brought after being filled into golden and silver pots. They extinguished the sandalwood pyre by scattering water with eight-pronged sprinklers made of gold and silver.

Ettha [V 2.0176] ca citake jhāyamāne parivāretvā ṭhitasālarukkhānaṃ sākhantarehi viṭapantarehi pattantarehi jālā uggacchanti, pattaṃ vā sākhā vā pupphaṃ vā daḍḍhā nāma natthi, kipillikāpi makkaṭakāpi jālānaṃ antareneva vicaranti[M 2.0197]. Ākāsato patitaudakadhārāsupi sālarukkhehi nikkhantaudakadhārāsupi pathaviṃ bhinditvā nikkhantaudakadhārāsupi dhammakathāva pamāṇaṃ. Evaṃ citakaṃ nibbāpetvā pana mallarājāno santhāgāre catujjātiyagandhaparibhaṇḍaṃ kāretvā lājapañcamāni pupphāni vikiritvā upari celavitānaṃ bandhitvā suvaṇṇatārakādīhi khacitvā tattha gandhadāmamālādāmaratanadāmāni olambetvā [P 2.0605] santhāgārato yāva makuṭabandhanasaṅkhātā sīsapasādhanamaṅgalasālā, tāva ubhohi passehi sāṇikilañjaparikkhepaṃ kāretvā upari celavitānaṃ bandhāpetvā suvaṇṇatārakādīhi khacitvā tatthapi gandhadāmamālādāmaratanadāmāni olambetvā maṇidaṇḍavaṇṇehi veṇūhi ca pañcavaṇṇaddhaje ussāpetvā samantā vātapaṭākā parikkhipitvā susammaṭṭhāsu vīthīsu kadaliyo ca puṇṇaghaṭe ca ṭhapetvā daṇḍakadīpikā jāletvā alaṅkatahatthikkhandhe saha dhātūhi suvaṇṇadoṇiṃ ṭhapetvā mālāgandhādīhi pūjentā sādhukīḷitaṃ kīḷantā antonagaraṃ pavesetvā santhāgāre sarabhamayapallaṅke ṭhapetvā upari setacchattaṃ dhāresuṃ. Evaṃ katvā – “atha kho kosinārakā mallā bhagavato sarīrāni sattāhaṃ santhāgāre sattipañjaraṃ karitvā”ti sabbaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Here, while the pyre was burning, flames rose up between the branches, the boughs, and the leaves of the surrounding sāla trees. Not a single leaf, branch, or flower was burned. Even ants and spiders moved about unharmed amidst the flames. Regarding the streams of water falling from the sky, emerging from the sāla trees, and breaking through the earth, the Dhamma discourse itself is the authority. After extinguishing the pyre, the Malla kings had the assembly hall prepared with the four kinds of perfumes. They scattered flowers with parched rice as the fifth, hung a cloth canopy above, and inlaid it with golden stars and so forth. There, they suspended garlands of scents, flowers, and jewels. From the assembly hall up to the auspicious hall for adorning the head, called Makuṭabandhana, they had an enclosure of cloth screens made on both sides, had a cloth canopy hung above, and adorned it with golden stars and so forth. There, too, they hung garlands of scents, flowers, and jewels, and raised five-colored flags on bamboo poles the color of jeweled staffs. All around, they set up wind-banners, and in the well-swept streets, they placed banana trees and full water pots, and lit lamps on stands. Placing the golden urn containing the relics on the back of an adorned elephant, they paid homage with garlands, perfumes, and so forth. Celebrating a joyous festival, they entered the city and placed the urn on a couch with legs in the shape of a Sarabha creature in the assembly hall. Above it, they held a white parasol. Having done so, the entire passage beginning, 'Then, for seven days, the Mallas of Kusinārā, having made a lattice of spears in the assembly hall for the Blessed One's bodily relics...' should be understood.

Tattha sattipañjaraṃ karitvāti sattihatthehi purisehi parikkhipāpetvā. Dhanupākāranti paṭhamaṃ tāva hatthikumbhena kumbhaṃ paharante parikkhipāpesuṃ, tato asse gīvāya gīvaṃ paharante, tato rathe āṇikoṭiyā āṇikoṭiṃ paharante, tato yodhe bāhunā bāhuṃ paharante. Tesaṃ pariyante koṭiyā koṭiṃ paharamānāni dhanūni parikkhipāpesuṃ. Iti samantā yojanappamāṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ sattāhaṃ sannāhagavacchikaṃ viya katvā ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “dhanupākāraṃ parikkhipāpetvā”ti.

Therein, 'having made a lattice of spears' means having caused them to be surrounded by men with spears in hand. As for the 'rampart of bows': first, they had elephants surround them, striking forehead to forehead; then horses, striking neck to neck; then chariots, striking yoke-pin to yoke-pin; then warriors, striking arm to arm. At their perimeter, they had bows placed, striking tip to tip. In this way, for seven days, they arranged protection for the place measuring a yojana all around, making it like a window secured with a lattice. It was in reference to this that it was said: 'having had a rampart of bows set up around them.'

Kasmā panete evamakaṃsūti? Ito purimesu hi dvīsu sattāhesu te bhikkhusaṅghassa ṭhānanisajjokāsaṃ karontā khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ saṃvidahantā sādhukīḷikāya okāsaṃ na labhiṃsu. Tato nesaṃ ahosi – “imaṃ sattāhaṃ sādhukīḷitaṃ kīḷissāma, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati yaṃ amhākaṃ pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā kocideva āgantvā dhātuyo gaṇheyya, tasmā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā kīḷissāmā”ti. Te tathā evamakaṃsu.

But why did they do so? Because in the two preceding weeks, while arranging places for the Sangha of bhikkhus to stand and sit and preparing hard and soft food, they found no opportunity for a joyous festival. Then it occurred to them: 'This week we shall hold a joyous festival. However, the possibility exists that someone, knowing our heedlessness, might come and take away the relics; therefore, having posted a guard, we shall hold our festival.' Thus they did.

Sarīradhātuvibhajanavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Distribution of the Bodily Relics

236. Assosi [V 2.0177][M 2.0198] kho rājāti kathaṃ assosi? Paṭhamameva kirassa amaccā sutvā cintayiṃsu – “satthā nāma parinibbuto, na so sakkā puna āharituṃ. Pothujjanikasaddhāya pana amhākaṃ raññā sadiso natthi, sace esa imināva niyāmena suṇissati, hadayamassa phalissati. Rājā kho pana amhehi anurakkhitabbo”ti te tisso suvaṇṇadoṇiyo āharitvā catumadhurassa pūretvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā etadavocuṃ – “deva[P 2.0606], amhehi supinako diṭṭho, tassa paṭighātatthaṃ tumhehi dukūladupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā yathā nāsāpuṭamattaṃ paññāyati, evaṃ catumadhuradoṇiyā nipajjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Rājā atthacarānaṃ amaccānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “evaṃ hotu tātā”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathā akāsi.

236. Regarding the phrase, 'The king heard': How did he hear? It is said that first his ministers, upon hearing the news, thought: 'The Teacher has attained Parinibbāna; he cannot be brought back. But in terms of the faith of an ordinary person, there is none like our king. If he hears this news in the usual way, his heart will break. The king must certainly be protected by us.' So they brought three golden troughs, filled them with the four sweets, went to the king, and said this: 'Your Majesty, we have seen a bad dream. To counteract it, you should put on a double-layered fine cloth and lie down in this trough of the four sweets in such a way that only your nostrils are visible.' The king, hearing the words of his ministers who sought his welfare, agreed, saying, 'So be it, my dears,' and did as they said.

Atheko amacco alaṅkāraṃ omuñcitvā kese pakiriya yāya disāya satthā parinibbuto, tadabhimukho hutvā añjaliṃ paggayha rājānaṃ āha – “deva, maraṇato muccanakasatto nāma natthi, amhākaṃ āyuvaḍḍhano cetiyaṭṭhānaṃ puññakkhettaṃ abhisekasiñcako so bhagavā satthā kusinārāya parinibbuto”ti. Rājā sutvāva visaññījāto catumadhuradoṇiyaṃ usumaṃ muñci. Atha naṃ ukkhipitvā dutiyāya doṇiyā nipajjāpesuṃ. So puna saññaṃ labhitvā – “tātā, kiṃ vadethā”ti pucchi. “Satthā, mahārāja, parinibbuto”ti. Rājā punapi visaññījāto catumadhuradoṇiyā usumaṃ muñci. Atha naṃ tatopi ukkhipitvā tatiyāya doṇiyā nipajjāpesuṃ. So puna saññaṃ labhitvā “tātā, kiṃ vadethā”ti pucchi. “Satthā, mahārāja, parinibbuto”ti. Rājā punapi visaññījāto, atha naṃ ukkhipitvā nahāpetvā matthake ghaṭehi udakaṃ āsiñciṃsu.

Then a certain minister, taking off his ornaments and letting his hair down, faced the direction where the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, raised his joined palms in reverence, and said to the king: 'Your Majesty, there is no being that is freed from death. Our increaser of life-span, our place of veneration, our field of merit, the one who sprinkles the water of consecration—that Blessed One, the Teacher, has attained Parinibbāna in Kusinārā.' Just on hearing this, the king became unconscious and released a wave of heat into the trough of the four sweets. Then they lifted him up and had him lie down in the second trough. When he regained consciousness, he asked, 'My dears, what did you say?' 'The Teacher, great king, has attained Parinibbāna.' The king again became unconscious and released a wave of heat into the trough of the four sweets. Then they lifted him from there also and had him lie down in the third trough. When he again regained consciousness, he asked, 'My dears, what did you say?' 'The Teacher, great king, has attained Parinibbāna.' The king became unconscious yet again. Then they lifted him up, had him bathed, and poured water from pots over his head.

Rājā saññaṃ labhitvā āsanā vuṭṭhāya gandhaparibhāvite maṇivaṇṇe kese vikiritvā suvaṇṇaphalakavaṇṇāya piṭṭhiyaṃ pakiritvā pāṇinā uraṃ paharitvā pavāḷaṅkuravaṇṇāhi suvaṭṭitaṅgulīhi suvaṇṇabimbisakavaṇṇaṃ uraṃ sibbanto viya gahetvā paridevamāno ummattakavesena antaravīthiṃ otiṇṇo, so alaṅkatanāṭakaparivuto nagarato nikkhamma jīvakambavanaṃ gantvā yasmiṃ ṭhāne nisinnena bhagavatā dhammo desito taṃ oloketvā [M 2.0199] – “bhagavā sabbaññu, nanu imasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīditvā dhammaṃ desayittha, sokasallaṃ me vinodayittha, tumhe mayhaṃ sokasallaṃ nīharittha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ saraṇaṃ gato, idāni pana me paṭivacanampi na detha, bhagavā”ti punappunaṃ paridevitvā “nanu bhagavā ahaṃ aññadā evarūpe kāle ‘tumhe mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivārā [V 2.0178] jambudīpatale cārikaṃ carathā’ti suṇomi, idāni panāhaṃ tumhākaṃ ananurūpaṃ ayuttaṃ pavattiṃ suṇomī”ti evamādīni ca vatvā saṭṭhimattāhi gāthāhi [P 2.0607] bhagavato guṇaṃ anussaritvā cintesi – “mama parideviteneva na sijjhati, dasabalassa dhātuyo āharāpessāmī”ti evaṃ assosi. Sutvā ca imissā visaññibhāvādipavattiyā avasāne dūtaṃ pāhesi. Taṃ sandhāya atha kho rājātiādi vuttaṃ.

Having regained consciousness, the king rose from his seat, scattered his hair—perfumed with fragrance and gem-like in color—over his back, which was the color of a golden slab. He struck his chest with his hand, and with well-rounded fingers like coral sprouts, he clutched his chest, which was the color of a golden plaque, as if stitching it, wailing in the guise of a madman. He went down into the street, surrounded by a troupe of adorned dancers, and left the city for Jīvaka’s mango grove. When he reached the spot where the Blessed One had once sat and taught the Dhamma, he gazed upon it and lamented: 'O Blessed One, the All-Knowing One! Did you not sit in this very place and teach the Dhamma? Did you not dispel the dart of my sorrow? You drew out my dart of sorrow, and I went for refuge to you. Yet now, O Blessed One, you do not even give me a reply!' Again and again, he wailed, saying, 'O Blessed One, did I not hear at other times that you, surrounded by the great Saṅgha of monks, wander on tour in Jambudīpa? But now, I hear news of you that is unbefitting and improper!' Speaking thus, and recalling the virtues of the Blessed One with about sixty verses, he thought, 'My purpose is not accomplished by mere lamenting. I shall have the relics of the Ten-Powered One brought here.' Thus he had heard. And having heard, at the conclusion of this episode of his loss of consciousness and the like, he sent a messenger. It is with reference to this that the passage beginning, 'Then the king...' was spoken.

Tattha dūtaṃ pāhesīti dūtañca paṇṇañca pesesi. Pesetvā ca pana – “sace dassanti, sundaraṃ. No ce dassanti, āharaṇupāyena āharissāmī”ti caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā sayampi nikkhantoyeva. Yathā ca ajātasattu, evaṃ licchavīādayopi dūtaṃ pesetvā sayampi caturaṅginiyā senāya nikkhamiṃsuyeva. Tattha pāveyyakā sabbehi āsannatarā kusinārato tigāvutantare nagare vasanti, bhagavāpi pāvaṃ pavisitvāva kusināraṃ gato. Atha kasmā paṭhamataraṃ na āgatāti ce? Mahāparivārā panete rājāno mahāparivāraṃ karontāva pacchato jātā.

Therein, 'he sent a messenger' means he dispatched both a messenger and a letter. Having sent them, he thought, 'If they give them, it is good. If they do not give them, I will take them by some means of acquisition.' He mustered a fourfold army and set out himself. And just as Ajātasattu did, so too the Licchavis and others sent a messenger and then set out themselves with a fourfold army. Among them, the Pāvans were closer than all the others, residing in a city at a distance of three gāvutas from Kusinārā; for the Blessed One, too, had gone to Kusinārā only after entering Pāvā. If it is asked, 'Then why did they not arrive first?' These kings had large retinues, and it was while preparing their great retinues that they came to be behind.

Te saṅghe gaṇe etadavocunti sabbepi te sattanagaravāsino āgantvā – “amhākaṃ dhātuyo vā dentu, yuddhaṃ vā”ti kusinārānagaraṃ parivāretvā ṭhite – “etaṃ bhagavā amhākaṃ gāmakkhette”ti paṭivacanaṃ avocuṃ. Te kira evamāhaṃsu – “na mayaṃ satthu sāsanaṃ pahiṇimha, nāpi gantvā ānayimha. Satthā pana sayameva āgantvā sāsanaṃ pesetvā amhe pakkosāpesi. Tumhepi kho pana yaṃ tumhākaṃ gāmakkhette ratanaṃ uppajjati, na taṃ amhākaṃ detha. Sadevake ca loke buddharatanasamaṃ ratanaṃ nāma natthi, evarūpaṃ uttamaratanaṃ labhitvā mayaṃ na dassāma. Na kho pana tumhehiyeva mātuthanato khīraṃ pītaṃ, amhehipi mātuthanato khīraṃ pītaṃ. Na tumheyeva purisā, amhepi purisā hotū”ti aññamaññaṃ ahaṃkāraṃ katvā sāsanapaṭisāsanaṃ pesenti, aññamaññaṃ mānagajjitaṃ gajjanti. Yuddhe pana sati kosinārakānaṃyeva jayo abhavissa. Kasmā? Yasmā dhātupāsanatthaṃ [M 2.0200] āgatā devatā nesaṃ pakkhā ahesuṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana – “bhagavā amhākaṃ gāmakkhette parinibbuto, na mayaṃ dassāma bhagavato sarīrānaṃ bhāga”nti ettakameva āgataṃ.

'They addressed the assembly and the group thus' means this: when all those inhabitants of the seven cities had come, surrounded the city of Kusinārā, and stood there saying, 'Either give us the relics, or give us battle!', the Mallas of Kusinārā spoke this reply to them: 'The Blessed One attained final Nibbāna in our village territory.' It is said they spoke thus: 'We did not send a message to the Teacher, nor did we go and bring him. Rather, the Teacher came on his own, sent a message, and had us summoned. Moreover, whatever jewel arises in your village territory, you do not give it to us. And in the world with its gods, there is no jewel equal to the Buddha-jewel.
