Having obtained such a supreme jewel, we will not give it up. It is not only you who have drunk milk from your mothers’ breasts; we too have drunk milk from our mothers’ breasts. You are not the only men; we too are men!' Arousing mutual pride, they sent messages and counter-messages, roaring with arrogance at one another. Had there been a battle, however, the victory would have belonged to the Kosinārakans alone. Why? Because the deities who had come for the purpose of venerating the relics were on their side. In the Pāḷi canon, however, only this much is stated: 'The Blessed One attained final Nibbāna in our village territory; we will not give a share of the Blessed One’s bodily relics.'

237. Evaṃ vutte doṇo brāhmaṇoti doṇabrāhmaṇo imaṃ tesaṃ vivādaṃ sutvā – “ete rājāno bhagavato parinibbutaṭṭhāne vivādaṃ karonti, na kho panetaṃ patirūpaṃ, alaṃ iminā kalahena, vūpasamessāmi na”nti so gantvā te saṅghe gaṇe etadavoca. Kimavoca? Unnatappadese [V 2.0179][P 2.0608] ṭhatvā dvibhāṇavāraparimāṇaṃ doṇagajjitaṃ nāma avoca. Tattha paṭhamabhāṇavāre tāva ekapadampi te na jāniṃsu. Dutiyabhāṇavārapariyosāne – “ācariyassa viya bho saddo, ācariyassa viya bho saddo”ti sabbe niravā ahesuṃ. Jambudīpatale kira kulaghare jātā yebhuyyena tassa na antevāsiko nāma natthi. Atha so te attano vacanaṃ sutvā nirave tuṇhībhūte viditvā puna etadavoca – “suṇantu bhonto”ti etaṃ gāthādvayaṃ avoca.

237. 'When this was said, the brahmin Doṇa' means that Doṇa the brahmin, hearing this dispute of theirs, thought: 'These kings are quarreling at the place where the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna. This is certainly not fitting. Enough of this quarrel; I will quell it.' So he went to that assembly, to that group, and said this. What did he say? Standing in an elevated place, he uttered what is called the 'Roar of Doṇa,' which was the length of two recitation sections. During the first recitation section, they did not recognize even a single word. At the end of the second recitation section, they all became silent, saying, 'Sirs, the sound is like our teacher's! Sirs, the sound is like our teacher's!' It is said that on the continent of Jambudīpa, among those born in noble families, there was almost no one who was not his pupil. Then he, knowing that they had become silent and quiet upon hearing his voice, spoke again, uttering these two verses beginning with, 'Listen, good sirs.'

Tattha amhākaṃ buddhoti amhākaṃ buddho. Ahu khantivādoti buddhabhūmiṃ appatvāpi pāramiyo pūrento khantivāditāpasakāle dhammapālakumārakāle chaddantahatthikāle bhūridattanāgarājakāle campeyyanāgarājakāle saṅkhapālanāgarājakāle mahākapikāle aññesu ca bahūsu jātakesu paresu kopaṃ akatvā khantimeva akāsi. Khantimeva vaṇṇayi. Kimaṅgaṃ pana etarahi iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu tādilakkhaṇaṃ patto, sabbathāpi amhākaṃ buddho khantivādo ahosi, tassa evaṃvidhassa. Na hi sādhu yaṃ uttamapuggalassa, sarīrabhāge siyā sampahāroti na hi sādhuyanti na hi sādhu ayaṃ. Sarīrabhāgeti sarīravibhāganimittaṃ, dhātukoṭṭhāsahetūti attho. Siyā sampahāroti āvudhasampahāro sādhu na siyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, 'our Buddha' means our Buddha. 'He was a teacher of patience' means that even before attaining the state of a Buddha, while fulfilling the perfections—in his existence as the ascetic Khantivādī, as Prince Dhammapāla, as the elephant Chaddanta, as the Nāga King Bhūridatta, as the Nāga King Campeyya, as the Nāga King Saṅkhapāla, as the Great Monkey, and in many other Jātakas—he did not become angry with others but practiced only patience. He praised only patience. How much more so now that he has attained the characteristic of equanimity towards the agreeable and disagreeable? In every way, our Buddha was a teacher of patience. 'For it is not good that there should be a violent clash over the bodily share of the supreme person'—here, 'for it is not good that' means 'this is certainly not good.' 'Over the bodily share' means on account of the division of the body; the meaning is 'for the reason of a share of the relics.' 'There should be a violent clash' means a clash with weapons; it is said that this would not be good.

Sabbeva bhonto sahitāti sabbeva bhonto sahitā hotha, mā bhijjatha. Samaggāti kāyena ca vācāya ca ekasannipātā ekavacanā samaggā hotha. Sammodamānāti cittenāpi aññamaññaṃ sammodamānā hotha. Karomaṭṭhabhāgeti bhagavato sarīrāni aṭṭha bhāge karoma[M 2.0201]. Cakkhumatoti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumato buddhassa. Na kevalaṃ tumheyeva, bahujanopi pasanno, tesu ekopi laddhuṃ ayutto nāma natthīti bahuṃ kāraṇaṃ vatvā saññāpesi.

“All you sirs, be united; do not be divided. Be harmonious in body and speech, with one assembly and one voice. Rejoice together with one another, even in mind. Let us make eight portions of the Blessed One's bodily relics. Of the one with the eyes—the Buddha endowed with the five eyes. Not only are you devoted, but many people are also devoted, and among them there is not one who is unfit to receive a share.” Thus, having stated many reasons, he convinced them.

238. Tesaṃ saṅghānaṃ gaṇānaṃ paṭissutvāti tesaṃ tesaṃ tato tato samāgatasaṅghānaṃ samāgatagaṇānaṃ paṭissuṇitvā. Bhagavato [P 2.0609] sarīrāni aṭṭhadhā samaṃ suvibhattaṃ vibhajitvāti ettha ayamanukkamo – doṇo kira tesaṃ paṭissuṇitvā suvaṇṇadoṇiṃ vivarāpesi. Rājāno āgantvā doṇiyaṃyeva ṭhitā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā dhātuyo disvā – “bhagavā sabbaññu pubbe mayaṃ tumhākaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ chabbaṇṇabuddharasmikhacitaṃ asītianubyañjanasamujjalitasobhaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ addasāma, idāni pana suvaṇṇavaṇṇāva dhātuyo avasiṭṭhā jātā, na yuttamidaṃ bhagavā tumhāka”nti parideviṃsu.

238. “Having listened to those assemblies and groups”: this means having heeded the various assemblies and groups that had gathered from here and there. Regarding the phrase, “having divided the Blessed One's bodily relics into eight equal, well-divided parts,” here is the sequence of events: Doṇa, it is said, having heeded them, had the golden urn opened. The kings came and saw the golden-colored relics that were right in the urn, and lamented: “O Blessed One, previously we saw your golden-colored body, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, embellished with the six-colored Buddha-rays, and resplendent with the eighty minor characteristics. But now, only golden-colored relics have been left remaining. This is not fitting for you, O Blessed One.”

Brāhmaṇopi tasmiṃ samaye tesaṃ pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā dakkhiṇadāṭhaṃ gahetvā veṭhantare ṭhapesi, atha [V 2.0180] pacchā aṭṭhadhā samaṃ suvibhattaṃ vibhaji, sabbāpi dhātuyo pākatikanāḷiyā soḷasa nāḷiyo ahesuṃ, ekekanagaravāsino dve dve nāḷiyo labhiṃsu. Brāhmaṇassa pana dhātuyo vibhajantasseva sakko devānamindo – “kena nu kho sadevakassa lokassa kaṅkhacchedanatthāya catusaccakathāya paccayabhūtā bhagavato dakkhiṇadāṭhā gahitā”ti olokento “brāhmaṇena gahitā”ti disvā – “brāhmaṇopi dāṭhāya anucchavikaṃ sakkāraṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissati, gaṇhāmi na”nti veṭhantarato gahetvā suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭake ṭhapetvā devalokaṃ netvā cūḷāmaṇicetiye patiṭṭhapesi.

The brahmin, at that time, perceiving their negligence, took the right tooth-relic and placed it inside his turban. Then, afterwards, he divided the relics into eight equal, well-divided portions. In total, the relics amounted to sixteen standard measures (nāḷi), and the inhabitants of each city received two measures each. But while the brahmin was dividing the relics, Sakka, the king of the gods, was observing, thinking: “By whom, I wonder, has the Blessed One's right tooth-relic been taken—a relic that is a condition for the teaching of the Four Noble Truths for the purpose of cutting off the doubt of the world with its gods?” Seeing that it had been taken by the brahmin, he thought: “This brahmin will not be able to pay fitting honor to the tooth-relic. I shall take it.” Taking it from inside the turban, he placed it in a golden casket, brought it to the world of the gods, and enshrined it in the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya.

Brāhmaṇopi dhātuyo vibhajitvā dāṭhaṃ apassanto corikāya gahitattā – “kena me dāṭhā gahitā”ti pucchitumpi nāsakkhi. “Nanu tayāva dhātuyo bhājitā, kiṃ tvaṃ paṭhamaṃyeva attano dhātuyā atthibhāvaṃ na aññāsī”ti attani dosāropanaṃ sampassanto – “mayhampi koṭṭhāsaṃ dethā”ti vattumpi nāsakkhi. Tato – “ayampi suvaṇṇatumbo dhātugatikova, yena tathāgatassa dhātuyo mitā, imassāhaṃ thūpaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā imaṃ me bhonto tumbaṃ dadantūti āha.

The brahmin, having divided the relics and not seeing the tooth-relic, was unable even to ask, “By whom was my tooth-relic taken?”, because it had been taken by theft. Foreseeing that blame would be placed upon himself—“Was it not you yourself who divided the relics? Why did you not know from the very beginning of the existence of your own relic?”—he was unable even to say, “Give me a portion as well.” Then, thinking, “This golden vessel is also like a relic, for by it the Tathāgata's relics were measured. I shall make a stūpa for it,” he said, “Honored sirs, give me this vessel.”

Pippalivaniyā [M 2.0202] moriyāpi ajātasattuādayo viya dūtaṃ pesetvā yuddhasajjāva nikkhamiṃsu.

The Moriyas of Pipphalivana, like Ajātasattu and the others, also sent a messenger and marched out prepared for battle.

Dhātuthūpapūjāvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Veneration of the Relic Stūpa.

239. Rājagahe bhagavato sarīrānaṃ thūpañca mahañca akāsīti kathaṃ akāsi? Kusinārato yāva rājagahaṃ pañcavīsati yojanāni, etthantare aṭṭhausabhavitthataṃ samatalaṃ maggaṃ [P 2.0610] kāretvā yādisaṃ mallarājāno makuṭabandhanassa ca santhāgārassa ca antare pūjaṃ kāresuṃ. Tādisaṃ pañcavīsatiyojanepi magge pūjaṃ kāretvā lokassa anukkaṇṭhanatthaṃ sabbattha antarāpaṇe pasāretvā suvaṇṇadoṇiyaṃ pakkhittadhātuyo sattipañjarena parikkhipāpetvā attano vijite pañcayojanasataparimaṇḍale manusse sannipātāpesi. Te dhātuyo gahetvā kusinārato sādhukīḷitaṃ kīḷantā nikkhamitvā yattha yattha suvaṇṇavaṇṇāni pupphāni passanti, tattha tattha dhātuyo sattiantare ṭhapetvā pūjaṃ akaṃsu. Tesaṃ pupphānaṃ khīṇakāle gacchanti, rathassa dhuraṭṭhānaṃ pacchimaṭṭhāne sampatte satta divase sādhukīḷitaṃ kīḷanti. Evaṃ dhātuyo gahetvā āgacchantānaṃ satta vassāni satta māsāni satta divasāni vītivattāni.

239. Regarding the statement, “In Rājagaha, he made a stūpa and a great festival for the Blessed One's bodily relics,” how did he do so? From Kusinārā to Rājagaha is twenty-five yojanas. In between, he had a level, smooth road made, eight usabhas in width. Just as the Malla kings had arranged veneration between the Makuṭabandhana shrine and the assembly hall, he had a similar veneration arranged along the entire twenty-five-yojana road. For the purpose of preventing the people's weariness, he had shops set up everywhere along the way. He had the relics, which were placed in a golden urn, surrounded by a cage of spears, and he had the people from his own territory, within a circumference of five hundred yojanas, assembled. Taking the relics from Kusinārā, they departed, engaging in a noble celebration. Wherever they saw golden-colored flowers, they placed the relics within the enclosure of spears and performed acts of veneration. When those flowers withered, they would proceed. When the front of the chariot reached the final stopping place, they would celebrate for seven days. In this way, as they came bearing the relics, seven years, seven months, and seven days passed.

Micchādiṭṭhikā [V 2.0181] – “samaṇassa gotamassa parinibbutakālato paṭṭhāya balakkārena sādhukīḷitāya upaddutamha sabbe no kammantā naṭṭhā”ti ujjhāyantā manaṃ padosetvā chaḷāsītisahassamattā apāye nibbattā. Khīṇāsavā āvajjitvā “mahājano manaṃ padosetvā apāye nibbattī”ti disvā – “sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ dhātuāharaṇūpāyaṃ kāressāmā”ti tassa santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā – “dhātuāharaṇūpāyaṃ karohi mahārājā”ti āhaṃsu. Sakko āha – “bhante, puthujjano nāma ajātasattunā samo saddho natthi, na so mama vacanaṃ karissati, apica kho māravibhiṃsakasadisaṃ vibhiṃsakaṃ dassessāmi, mahāsaddaṃ sāvessāmi, yakkhagāhakakhipitakaarocake karissāmi, tumhe ‘amanussā mahārāja kupitā dhātuyo āharāpethā’ti vadeyyātha, evaṃ so āharāpessatī”ti. Atha kho sakko taṃ sabbaṃ akāsi.

Those of wrong view, grumbling, “From the time of the ascetic Gotama's final Nibbāna, we have been oppressed by this forced, noble celebration, and all our livelihoods have been ruined,” corrupted their minds, and some eighty-six thousand of them were reborn in a state of loss. The Arahants, reflecting and seeing that a great number of people had corrupted their minds and were reborn in a state of loss, thought, “We shall have Sakka, the king of the gods, arrange a means for bringing the relics.” They went to him, related the matter, and said, “Great king, arrange a means for bringing the relics.” Sakka replied: “Venerable sirs, there is no ordinary person as faithful as Ajātasattu; he will not do as I say. However, I will display a terrifying spectacle like that of Māra; I will cause a great sound to be heard; I will create diseases like possession by yakkhas, digestive ailments, and loss of appetite. You should then say, ‘Great king, the non-human beings are angered. Have the relics brought.’ In this way, he will have them brought.” Then Sakka did all of that.

Therāpi rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “mahārāja, amanussā kupitā, dhātuyo āharāpehī”ti bhaṇiṃsu. Rājā – “na tāva, bhante, mayhaṃ cittaṃ [M 2.0203] tussati, evaṃ santepi āharantū”ti āha. Sattamadivase dhātuyo āhariṃsu. Evaṃ āhatā dhātuyo gahetvā rājagahe thūpañca mahañca akāsi. Itarepi attano attano [P 2.0611] balānurūpena āharitvā sakasakaṭṭhānesu thūpañca mahañca akaṃsu.

The elders approached the king and said, 'Great king, non-human beings are angry. Have the relics brought.' The king replied, 'Not yet, venerable sirs, is my mind satisfied. Even so, let them bring them.' On the seventh day, the relics were brought. Having taken the relics that were brought in this way, he built a stupa and held a great festival in Rājagaha. Others too, according to their own strength, having brought relics, built stupas and held great festivals in their respective places.

240. Evametaṃ bhūtapubbanti evaṃ etaṃ dhātubhājanañceva dasathūpakaraṇañca jambudīpe bhūtapubbanti pacchā saṅgītikārakā āhaṃsu. Evaṃ patiṭṭhitesu pana thūpesu mahākassapatthero dhātūnaṃ antarāyaṃ disvā rājānaṃ ajātasattuṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahārāja, ekaṃ dhātunidhānaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Sādhu, bhante, nidhānakammaṃ tāva mama hotu, sesadhātuyo pana kathaṃ āharāmīti? Na, mahārāja, dhātuāharaṇaṃ tuyhaṃ bhāro, amhākaṃ bhāroti. Sādhu, bhante, tumhe dhātuyo āharatha, ahaṃ dhātunidhānaṃ karissāmīti. Thero tesaṃ tesaṃ rājakulānaṃ paricaraṇamattameva ṭhapetvā sesadhātuyo āhari. Rāmagāme pana dhātuyo nāgā pariggaṇhiṃsu, tāsaṃ antarāyo natthi. “Anāgate laṅkādīpe mahāvihāre mahācetiyamhi nidahissantī”ti tā na āharitvā sesehi sattahi nagarehi āharitvā rājagahassa pācīnadakkhiṇadisābhāge ṭhatvā – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne yo pāsāṇo atthi, so antaradhāyatu, paṃsu suvisuddhā hotu, udakaṃ mā uṭṭhahatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi.

240. 'Thus it was in the past'—this is how the distribution of relics and the construction of ten stupas occurred in Jambudīpa in ancient times. Later, the compilers of the recitations recounted it thus. When the stupas were established, the Venerable Mahākassapa, seeing a danger to the relics, approached King Ajātasattu and said, 'Great king, it is fitting to create a single relic repository.' The king replied, 'Very well, venerable sir, let the work of the repository be my responsibility. But how shall I gather the remaining relics?' The elder said, 'Great king, the task of gathering the relics is not your burden—it is ours.' The king agreed, saying, 'Very well, venerable sir, you gather the relics, and I will construct the relic repository.' The elder then collected the remaining relics, leaving only a small portion for the veneration of the respective royal families. However, the relics at Rāmagāma were guarded by nāgas, so there was no danger to them. Thinking, 'In the future, they will be enshrined in the great cetiya at the Mahāvihāra in Laṅkādīpa,' he did not retrieve those but gathered the rest from the seven cities. He then stood in the southeast part of Rājagaha and made this resolution: 'Let any stones in this place disappear, let the soil become perfectly pure, and let no water rise up here.'

Rājā taṃ ṭhānaṃ khaṇāpetvā tato uddhatapaṃsunā iṭṭhakā kāretvā asītimahāsāvakānaṃ cetiyāni [V 2.0182] kāreti. “Idha rājā kiṃ kāretī”ti pucchantānampi “mahāsāvakānaṃ cetiyānī”ti vadanti, na koci dhātunidhānabhāvaṃ jānāti. Asītihatthagambhīre pana tasmiṃ padese jāte heṭṭhā lohasanthāraṃ santharāpetvā tattha thūpārāme cetiyagharappamāṇaṃ tambalohamayaṃ gehaṃ kārāpetvā aṭṭha aṭṭha haricandanādimaye karaṇḍe ca thūpe ca kārāpesi. Atha bhagavato dhātuyo haricandanakaraṇḍe pakkhipitvā taṃ haricandanakaraṇḍakampi aññasmiṃ haricandanakaraṇḍake, tampi aññasminti evaṃ aṭṭha haricandanakaraṇḍe ekato katvā eteneva upāyena te aṭṭha karaṇḍe aṭṭhasu haricandanathūpesu, aṭṭha haricandanathūpe aṭṭhasu lohitacandanakaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha lohitacandanakaraṇḍe aṭṭhasu lohitacandanathūpesu, aṭṭha lohitacandanathūpe aṭṭhasu dantakaraṇḍesu[P 2.0612], aṭṭha dantakaraṇḍe [M 2.0204] aṭṭhasu dantathūpesu, aṭṭha dantathūpe aṭṭhasu sabbaratanakaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha sabbaratanakaraṇḍe aṭṭhasu sabbaratanathūpesu, aṭṭha sabbaratanathūpe aṭṭhasu suvaṇṇakaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha suvaṇṇakaraṇḍe, aṭṭhasu suvaṇṇathūpesu, aṭṭha suvaṇṇathūpe aṭṭhasu rajatakaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha rajatakaraṇḍe aṭṭhasu rajatathūpesu, aṭṭha rajatathūpe, aṭṭhasu maṇikaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha maṇikaraṇḍe aṭṭhasu maṇithūpesu, aṭṭha maṇithūpe aṭṭhasu lohitaṅkakaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha lohitaṅkakaraṇḍe aṭṭhasu lohitaṅkathūpesu, aṭṭha lohitaṅkathūpe aṭṭhasu masāragallakaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha masāragallakaraṇḍe aṭṭhasu masāragallathūpesu, aṭṭha masāragallathūpe aṭṭhasu phalikakaraṇḍesu, aṭṭha phalikakaraṇḍe aṭṭhasu phalikamayathūpesu pakkhipi.

The king had that site excavated and, using the soil removed from there, had bricks made to construct shrines for the eighty great disciples. When people asked, "What is the king building here?" they would say, "Shrines for the great disciples," but no one knew of it being a relic repository. In that area, which was eighty cubits deep, after having a layer of iron plates spread out at the bottom, he had a copper house built there, the size of the shrine-house at the Thūpārāma, and he had eight caskets and eight stūpas made of sandalwood, etc. Then, the Blessed One's relics were placed in a sandalwood casket, and that sandalwood casket was placed inside another sandalwood casket, and that one inside yet another, and so on, until eight sandalwood caskets were thus nested together. In the same manner, he placed those eight caskets within eight sandalwood stūpas, the eight sandalwood stūpas within eight red sandalwood caskets, the eight red sandalwood caskets within eight red sandalwood stūpas, the eight red sandalwood stūpas within eight ivory caskets, the eight ivory caskets within eight ivory stūpas, the eight ivory stūpas within eight all-jeweled caskets, the eight all-jeweled caskets within eight all-jeweled stūpas, the eight all-jeweled stūpas within eight golden caskets, the eight golden caskets within eight golden stūpas, the eight golden stūpas within eight silver caskets, the eight silver caskets within eight silver stūpas, the eight silver stūpas within eight gem caskets, the eight gem caskets within eight gem stūpas, the eight gem stūpas within eight ruby caskets, the eight ruby caskets within eight ruby stūpas, the eight ruby stūpas within eight beryl caskets, the eight beryl caskets within eight beryl stūpas, the eight beryl stūpas within eight crystal caskets, and the eight crystal caskets within eight crystal stūpas.

Sabbesaṃ uparimaṃ phalikacetiyaṃ thūpārāmacetiyappamāṇaṃ ahosi, tassa upari sabbaratanamayaṃ gehaṃ kāresi, tassa upari suvaṇṇamayaṃ, tassa upari rajatamayaṃ, tassa upari tambalohamayaṃ gehaṃ. Tattha sabbaratanamayaṃ vālikaṃ okiritvā jalajathalajapupphānaṃ sahassāni vippakiritvā aḍḍhachaṭṭhāni jātakasatāni asītimahāthere suddhodanamahārājānaṃ mahāmāyādeviṃ satta sahajāteti sabbānetāni suvaṇṇamayāneva kāresi. Pañcapañcasate suvaṇṇarajatamaye puṇṇaghaṭe ṭhapāpesi, pañca suvaṇṇaddhajasate ussāpesi. Pañcasate suvaṇṇadīpe, pañcasate rajatadīpe kārāpetvā sugandhatelassa pūretvā tesu dukūlavaṭṭiyo ṭhapesi.

The uppermost crystal shrine was the size of the Thūpārāma shrine. Above that, he had a house made of all precious gems constructed; above that, a golden one; above that, a silver one; and above that, a copper one. There, having strewn sand made of all precious gems and scattered thousands of water-born and land-born flowers, he had all these made entirely of gold: the five hundred and fifty Jātaka stories, the eighty great elders, King Suddhodana, Queen Mahāmāyā, and the seven co-nascent ones. He had five hundred golden and five hundred silver full pots placed, and five hundred golden flags raised. He had five hundred golden lamps and five hundred silver lamps made, filled them with fragrant oil, and placed fine cloth wicks in them.

Athāyasmā mahākassapo – “mālā mā milāyantu, gandhā mā vinassantu, dīpā mā vijjhāyantū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe akkharāni chindāpesi –

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having resolved, "May the garlands not wither, may the perfumes not be destroyed, may the lamps not be extinguished," had letters engraved on a golden plate—

“Anāgate piyadāso nāma kumāro chattaṃ ussāpetvā asoko dhammarājā bhavissati. So imā dhātuyo vitthārikā karissatī”ti.

“In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa will raise the royal parasol and become the righteous King Asoka. He will spread these relics far and wide.”

Rājā [V 2.0183] sabbapasādhanehi pūjetvā ādito paṭṭhāya dvāraṃ pidahanto nikkhami, so tambalohadvāraṃ pidahitvā āviñchanarajjuyaṃ kuñcikamuddikaṃ bandhitvā [M 2.0205] tattheva mahantaṃ maṇikkhandhaṃ ṭhapetvā – “anāgate daliddarājā imaṃ maṇiṃ gahetvā [P 2.0613] dhātūnaṃ sakkāraṃ karotū”ti akkharaṃ chindāpesi.

After worshipping with all adornments, the king, beginning from the entrance, went out sealing the doors. He closed the copper door, tied a key and seal to a fastening rope, and placed a large heap of jewels there, having had inscribed: “In the future, let a poor king take this jewel and make offerings to the relics.”

Sakko devarājā vissakammaṃ āmantetvā – “tāta, ajātasattunā dhātunidhānaṃ kataṃ, ettha ārakkhaṃ paṭṭhapehī”ti pahiṇi. So āgantvā vāḷasaṅghāṭayantaṃ yojesi, kaṭṭharūpakāni tasmiṃ dhātugabbhe phalikavaṇṇakhagge gāhetvā vātasadisena vegena anupariyāyantaṃ yantaṃ yojetvā ekāya eva āṇiyā bandhitvā samantato giñjakāvasathākārena silāparikkhepaṃ katvā upari ekāya pidahitvā paṃsuṃ pakkhipitvā bhūmiṃ samaṃ katvā tassa upari pāsāṇathūpaṃ patiṭṭhapesi. Evaṃ niṭṭhite dhātunidhāne yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā theropi parinibbuto, rājāpi yathākammaṃ gato, tepi manussā kālaṅkatā.

Sakka, the king of the gods, summoned Vissakamma and sent him, saying: “Dear one, Ajātasattu has made a relic deposit; establish protection there.” He came and set up a mechanism of interlocking figures of fierce beasts; in that relic chamber, he set up a mechanism with wooden figures holding crystal-colored swords, rotating swiftly like the wind. Having bound it with a single pin, he surrounded it with a stone enclosure in the shape of a brick house, covered it above with a single stone slab, filled it with earth, leveled the ground, and erected a stone stūpa on top of it. When the relic deposit was thus completed, the Elder, having remained for the extent of his lifespan, attained final Nibbāna; the king also passed away according to his kamma, and those people also died.

Aparabhāge piyadāso nāma kumāro chattaṃ ussāpetvā asoko nāma dhammarājā hutvā tā dhātuyo gahetvā jambudīpe vitthārikā akāsi. Kathaṃ? So nigrodhasāmaṇeraṃ nissāya sāsane laddhappasādo caturāsīti vihārasahassāni kāretvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pucchi – “bhante, mayā caturāsīti vihārasahassāni kāritāni, dhātuyo kuto labhissāmī”ti? Mahārāja, – “dhātunidhānaṃ nāma atthī”ti suṇoma, na pana paññāyati – “asukasmiṃ ṭhāne”ti. Rājā rājagahe cetiyaṃ bhindāpetvā dhātuṃ apassanto paṭipākatikaṃ kāretvā bhikkhubhikkhuniyo upāsakaupāsikāyoti catasso parisā gahetvā vesāliṃ gato. Tatrāpi alabhitvā kapilavatthuṃ. Tatrāpi alabhitvā rāmagāmaṃ gato. Rāmagāme nāgā cetiyaṃ bhindituṃ na adaṃsu, cetiye nipatitakudālo khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tatrāpi alabhitvā allakappaṃ veṭhadīpaṃ pāvaṃ kusināranti sabbattha cetiyāni bhinditvā dhātuṃ alabhitvāva paṭipākatikāni katvā puna rājagahaṃ gantvā catasso parisā sannipātāpetvā – “atthi kenaci sutapubbaṃ ‘asukaṭṭhāne nāma dhātunidhāna’nti” pucchi.

In a later time, a prince named Piyadāsa raised the royal parasol and, becoming the righteous King Asoka, took those relics and made them widespread in Jambudīpa. How? Having gained faith in the Dispensation through the novice Nigrodha, he had eighty-four thousand monasteries built and asked the community of monks: “Venerable sirs, I have had eighty-four thousand monasteries built. From where will I obtain relics?” “Great King, we hear that ‘there is a relic repository,’ but it is not known ‘in which place it is.’” The king had the cetiya in Rājagaha broken open, but not seeing the relics, he had it restored to its original state and, taking the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—he went to Vesālī. Not obtaining them there either, he went to Kapilavatthu. Not obtaining them there either, he went to Rāmagāma. In Rāmagāma, the Nāgas did not allow the cetiya to be broken; a pickaxe that fell upon the cetiya shattered into pieces. Thus, not obtaining them there either, he went to Allakappa, Veṭhadīpa, Pāvā, and Kusinārā. Having broken open the cetiyas in all those places and still not obtaining the relics, he had them restored to their original state. Returning again to Rājagaha, he had the fourfold assembly convened and asked: “Has it been heard by anyone that ‘in such-and-such a place there is a relic repository’?”

Tatreko vīsavassasatiko thero – “asukaṭṭhāne dhātunidhāna”nti na jānāmi, mayhaṃ pana pitā mahāthero maṃ sattavassakāle [P 2.0614] mālācaṅkoṭakaṃ gāhāpetvā – “ehi sāmaṇera, asukagacchantare pāsāṇathūpo [M 2.0206] atthi, tattha gacchāmā”ti gantvā pūjetvā – “imaṃ ṭhānaṃ upadhāretuṃ vaṭṭati sāmaṇerā”ti āha. Ahaṃ ettakaṃ jānāmi mahārājāti āha. Rājā “etadeva ṭhāna”nti [V 2.0184] vatvā gacche hāretvā pāsāṇathūpañca paṃsuñca apanetvā heṭṭhā sudhābhūmiṃ addasa. Tato sudhañca iṭṭhakāyo ca hāretvā anupubbena pariveṇaṃ oruyha sattaratanavālukaṃ asihatthāni ca kaṭṭharūpakāni samparivattakāni addasa. So yakkhadāsake pakkosāpetvā balikammaṃ kāretvāpi neva antaṃ na koṭiṃ passanto devatānaṃ namassamāno – “ahaṃ imā dhātuyo gahetvā caturāsītiyā vihārasahassesu nidahitvā sakkāraṃ karomi, mā me devatā antarāyaṃ karontū”ti āha.

There, an elder of one hundred and twenty years said: “I do not know ‘in which place the relic deposit is.’ However, my father, the great elder, when I was seven years old, had me take a flower basket and said, ‘Come, novice, in a certain thicket there is a stone stūpa; let us go there.’ Having gone and paid homage, he said, ‘Novice, it is proper to remember this place.’ I know only this much, Great King.” The king, saying, “This is indeed the place,” had the thicket cleared away. Having removed the stone stūpa and the earth, he saw a plastered surface below. Then, having removed the plaster and the bricks and gradually descending into the enclosure, he saw sand of the seven jewels, and revolving wooden figures with swords in their hands. He summoned the servants of the yakkhas and had offerings made, but seeing neither end nor limit, he paid homage to the deities and said: “I will take these relics, enshrine them in the eighty-four thousand monasteries, and make offerings. May the deities not create an obstacle for me.”

Sakko devarājā cārikaṃ caranto taṃ disvā vissakammaṃ āmantesi – “tāta, asoko dhammarājā ‘dhātuyo nīharissāmī’ti pariveṇaṃ otiṇṇo, gantvā kaṭṭharūpakāni hārehī”ti. So pañcacūḷagāmadārakavesena gantvā rañño purato dhanuhattho ṭhatvā – “harāmi mahārājā”ti āha. “Hara, tātā”ti saraṃ gahetvā sandhimhiyeva vijjhi, sabbaṃ vippakiriyittha. Atha rājā āviñchane bandhaṃ kuñcikamuddikaṃ gaṇhi, maṇikkhandhaṃ passi. “Anāgate daliddarājā imaṃ maṇiṃ gahetvā dhātūnaṃ sakkāraṃ karotū”ti puna akkharāni disvā kujjhitvā – “mādisaṃ nāma rājānaṃ daliddarājāti vattuṃ ayutta”nti punappunaṃ ghaṭetvā dvāraṃ vivarāpetvā antogehaṃ paviṭṭho.

Sakka, the king of the gods, while journeying, saw him and addressed Vissakamma: “Dear one, the righteous King Asoka has descended into the enclosure, thinking, ‘I will remove the relics.’ Go and take away the wooden figures.” So he went in the guise of a village boy with five top-knots and, standing before the king with a bow in hand, said: “Great King, I will remove them.” When the king said, “Remove them, dear one,” he took an arrow and shot it right at the joint, and the entire mechanism was scattered. Then the king took the key-ring tied to the pulling-cord and saw a block of jewels. Seeing the inscription, “In the future, let a poor king take this jewel and pay homage to the relics,” he became angry, thinking, “It is not right to call a king like me a ‘poor king.’” Striving again and again, he had the door opened and entered the inner chamber.

Aṭṭhārasavassādhikānaṃ dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ upari āropitadīpā tatheva pajjalanti. Nīluppalapupphāni taṅkhaṇaṃ āharitvā āropitāni viya, pupphasanthāro taṅkhaṇaṃ santhato viya, gandhā taṃ muhuttaṃ pisitvā ṭhapitā viya rājā suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ gahetvā – “anāgate piyadāso nāma kumāro chattaṃ ussāpetvā asoko nāma dhammarājā bhavissati so imā dhātuyo vitthārikā karissatī”ti vācetvā – “diṭṭho bho, ahaṃ ayyena mahākassapattherenā”ti vatvā vāmahatthaṃ ābhujitvā dakkhiṇena hatthena apphoṭesi. So tasmiṃ ṭhāne paricaraṇadhātumattameva ṭhapetvā sesā dhātuyo gahetvā [P 2.0615] dhātugehaṃ pubbe pihitanayeneva pidahitvā sabbaṃ yathāpakatiyāva katvā upari pāsāṇacetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā caturāsītiyā vihārasahassesu dhātuyo [M 2.0207] patiṭṭhāpetvā mahāthere vanditvā pucchi – “dāyādomhi, bhante, buddhasāsane”ti. Kissa dāyādo tvaṃ, mahārāja, bāhirako tvaṃ sāsanassāti. Bhante, channavutikoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā caturāsīti vihārasahassāni kāretvā ahaṃ na dāyādo, añño ko dāyādoti? Paccayadāyako nāma tvaṃ mahārāja, yo pana attano puttañca dhītarañca pabbājeti, ayaṃ sāsane dāyādo nāmāti. So puttañca dhītarañca pabbājesi. Atha naṃ therā āhaṃsu – “idāni, mahārāja, sāsane dāyādosī”ti.

The lamps that were placed over two hundred and eighteen years ago still burn just as they were. The blue water lily flowers were as if freshly brought and offered at that very moment; the floral arrangement, as if just laid out at that very moment; the fragrances, as if freshly ground and placed at that very instant. The king, taking a golden plaque, read: 'In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa will raise the parasol and become a righteous king named Asoka. He will widely distribute these relics.' Then he said, 'Indeed, I have been seen by the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera!' and bending his left arm, he struck his upper arm with his right hand. At that very spot, he left only a relic sufficient for personal veneration, took the remaining relics, and sealed the relic chamber in the same way it was sealed before, restoring everything to its original state. Then he established a stone stupa above it, enshrined relics in eighty-four thousand monasteries, paid homage to the great elders, and asked, 'Venerable sirs, am I an heir in the Buddha’s dispensation?' 'Great king, in what way are you an heir? You are an outsider to the dispensation.' 'Venerable sirs, having spent ninety-six crores of wealth and built eighty-four thousand monasteries, if I am not an heir, then who is?' 'Great king, you are a donor of requisites. But one who ordains their own son and daughter—such a person is called an heir in the dispensation.' So he ordained his son and daughter. Then the elders said to him, 'Now, great king, you are an heir in the dispensation.'

Evametaṃ [V 2.0185] bhūtapubbanti evaṃ etaṃ atīte dhātunidhānampi jambudīpatale bhūtapubbanti. Tatiyasaṅgītikārāpi imaṃ padaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu.

The phrase 'Evametaṃ bhūtapubbaṃ' means: 'Thus this enshrinement of relics has occurred before in Jambudīpa in the past.' The compilers of the Third Council also established this phrase.

Aṭṭhadoṇaṃ cakkhumato sarīrantiādigāthāyo pana tambapaṇṇidīpe therehi vuttāti.

The verses beginning 'Eight measures of the relics of the One with Vision' are said to have been spoken by the elders on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Mahāparinibbānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta is concluded.

4. Mahāsudassanasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta

Kusāvatīrājadhānīvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Royal City of Kusāvatī

241. Evaṃ [P 2.0616][V 2.0186][M 2.0208] me sutanti mahāsudassanasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – sabbaratanamayoti ettha ekā iṭṭhakā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā, ekā lohitaṅkamayā, ekā masāragallamayā, ekā sabbaratanamayā, ayaṃ pākāro sabbapākārānaṃ anto ubbedhena saṭṭhihattho ahosi. Eke pana therā – “nagaraṃ nāma anto ṭhatvā olokentānaṃ dassanīyaṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā sabbabāhiro saṭṭhihattho, sesā anupubbanīcā”ti vadanti. Eke – “bahi ṭhatvā olokentānaṃ dassanīyaṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā sabbaabbhantarimo saṭṭhihattho, sesā anupubbanīcā”ti. Eke – “anto ca bahi ca ṭhatvā olokentānaṃ dassanīyaṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā majjhe pākāro saṭṭhihattho, anto ca bahi ca tayo tayo anupubbanīcā”ti.

241. 'Thus have I heard'—this is the Mahāsudassana Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of words not previously explained. Regarding 'made of all precious stones': here, one brick was made of gold, one of silver, one of ruby, one of coral, and one of all precious stones. This wall, among all the walls, was sixty cubits high on the inside. Some elders, however, say: 'A city should be beautiful to those standing inside looking out; therefore, the outermost wall was sixty cubits high, and the rest were successively lower.' Others say: 'It should be beautiful to those standing outside looking in; therefore, the innermost wall was sixty cubits high, and the rest were successively lower.' Still others say: 'It should be beautiful to those standing both inside and outside; therefore, the middle wall was sixty cubits high, with three on the inside and three on the outside being successively lower.'

Esikāti esikatthambho. Tiporisaṅgāti ekaṃ porisaṃ majjhimapurisassa attano hatthena pañcahatthaṃ, tena tiporisaparikkhepā pannarasahatthaparimāṇāti attho. Te pana kathaṃ ṭhitāti? Nagarassa bāhirapasse ekekaṃ mahādvārabāhaṃ nissāya ekeko, ekekaṃ khuddakadvārabāhaṃ nissāya ekeko, mahādvārakhuddakadvārānaṃ antarā tayo tayoti. Tālapantīsu sabbaratanamayānaṃ tālānaṃ ekaṃ sovaṇṇamayanti pākāre vuttalakkhaṇameva veditabbaṃ, paṇṇaphalesupi eseva nayo. Tā pana tālapantiyo asītihatthā ubbedhena, vippakiṇṇavāluke samatale bhūmibhāge pākārantare ekekā hutvā ṭhitā.

`Esikā` means a monumental pillar. `Tiporisaṅga` means having a circumference of three `porisas`; one `porisa` is five cubits by the measure of a medium-sized man's hand, so the meaning is a measure of fifteen cubits in circumference. But how were they positioned? On the outer side of the city, one stood by each great gate-post, one by each minor gate-post, and three between each great and minor gate. As for the rows of palm trees, among the palms made of all jewels, one was of gold—this should be understood as having the same characteristics as described for the wall. The same principle applies to the leaves and fruits. Those rows of palm trees were eighty cubits in height, and they stood one by one in the space between the walls on level ground with scattered sand.

Vaggūti cheko sundaro. Rajanīyoti rañjetuṃ samattho. Khamanīyoti divasampi suyyamāno khamateva, na bībhaccheti. Madanīyoti [P 2.0617] mānamadapurisamadajanano. Pañcaṅgikassāti ātataṃ vitataṃ ātatavitataṃ [V 2.0187] susiraṃ ghananti imehi pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatassa. Tattha ātataṃ nāma cammapariyonaddhesu bherīādīsu ekatalaṃ tūriyaṃ. Vitataṃ nāma ubhayatalaṃ. Ātatavitataṃ nāma sabbato pariyonaddhaṃ. Susiraṃ [M 2.0209] nāma vaṃsādi. Ghanaṃ nāma sammādi. Suvinītassāti ākaḍḍhanasithilakaraṇādīhi sumucchitassa. Suppaṭitāḷitassāti pamāṇe ṭhitabhāvajānanatthaṃ suṭṭhu paṭitāḷitassa. Sukusalehi samannāhatassāti ye vādituṃ chekā kusalā, tehi vāditassa. Dhuttāti akkhadhuttā,. Soṇḍāti surāsoṇḍā. Teyeva punappunaṃ pātukāmatāvasena pipāsā. Paricāresunti (dī. ni. 2.132) hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā cāletvā naccantā kīḷiṃsu.

`Vaggū` means skillful and beautiful. `Rajanīya` means capable of delighting. `Khamanīya` means pleasing; even when heard all day, it is pleasing and does not cause aversion. `Madanīya` means intoxicating, arousing the intoxication of pride and the intoxication of manhood. `Pañcaṅgikassa` means endowed with these five parts: ātata, vitata, ātatavitata, susira, and ghana. Among these, `ātata` refers to single-faced instruments like drums covered with hide. `Vitata` refers to double-faced instruments. `Ātatavitata` refers to those entirely covered. `Susira` refers to wind instruments like the flute. `Ghana` refers to solid instruments like cymbals. `Suvinītassa` means skillfully tuned by means of tightening, loosening, and so on. `Suppaṭitāḷitassa` means properly and repeatedly struck to ascertain that it is in the correct measure. `Sukusalehi samannāhatassa` means played by those who are clever and skilled in performance. `Dhuttā` means dice-gamblers. `Soṇḍā` means liquor-addicts. Their thirst (`pipāsā`) is due to their constant desire to drink. `Paricāresuṃ` (Dī. Ni. 2.132) means they played, dancing and moving their hands and feet.

Cakkaratanavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Wheel-Jewel

243. Sīsaṃ nhātassāti sīsena saddhiṃ gandhodakena nahātassa. Uposathikassāti samādinnauposathaṅgassa. Uparipāsādavaragatassāti pāsādavarassa upari gatassa, subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā pāsādavarassa uparimahātale sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sīlāni āvajjantassa. Tadā kira rājā pātova satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ datvā soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi sīsaṃ nahāyitvā katapātarāso suddhaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā uparipāsādassa sirisayane pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno attano dānādimayaṃ puññasamudāyaṃ āvajjanto nisīdi. Ayaṃ sabbacakkavattīnaṃ dhammatā.

243. ‘Having bathed the head’ means one who has bathed with fragrant water, including the head. ‘One observing the Uposatha’ means one who has undertaken the factors of the Uposatha. ‘Having gone to the upper excellent palace’ means one who has gone to the upper part of the excellent palace, and having eaten fine food and entered the glorious inner chamber on the great upper terrace of the palace, is reflecting on his precepts. At that time, it is said, the king, having disbursed a hundred thousand in the early morning and given a great donation, bathed his head with sixteen pots of fragrant water. Having finished his morning meal, he put on a clean upper robe, arranged it over one shoulder, and sat cross-legged on the glorious couch in the upper palace, reflecting on the accumulation of his merit from giving and other meritorious deeds. This is the nature of all universal monarchs.

Tesaṃ taṃ āvajjantānaṃyeva vuttappakārapuññakammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nīlamaṇisaṅghātasadisaṃ pācīnasamuddajalatalaṃ bhindamānaṃ viya, ākāsaṃ alaṅkurumānaṃ viya dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati. Taṃ mahāsudassanassāpi tatheva pāturahosi. Tayidaṃ dibbānubhāvayuttattā dibbanti vuttaṃ. Sahassaṃ assa arānanti sahassāraṃ. Saha nemiyā, saha nābhiyā cāti sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ. Sabbehi ākārehi paripuṇṇanti sabbākāraparipūraṃ.

Even as they were reflecting thus, a divine wheel-jewel appeared, arisen from the season conditioned by their meritorious deeds of the aforementioned kind, resembling a mass of blue gems, as if splitting the surface of the eastern ocean, as if adorning the sky. It had appeared for Mahāsudassana in the same way. This is called ‘divine’ because it is endowed with divine power. ‘It has a thousand spokes’—thus, it is ‘thousand-spoked’. ‘With a rim and with a hub’—thus, it is ‘rimmed and hubbed’. ‘Complete in all aspects’—thus, it is ‘complete in every way’.

Tattha cakkañca taṃ ratijananaṭṭhena ratanañcāti cakkaratanaṃ. Yāya pana taṃ nābhiyā “sanābhika”nti vuttaṃ, sā indanīlamayā hoti, majjhe panassā sārarajatamayā panāḷi, yāya [P 2.0618] suddhasiniddhadantapantiyā hasamānā viya virocati, majjhe chiddena viya candamaṇḍalena, ubhosupi bāhirantesu rajatapaṭṭena kataparikkhepā hoti. Tesu panassa nābhipanāḷiparikkhepapaṭṭesu [M 2.0210] yuttayuttaṭṭhānesu paricchedalekhā suvibhattāva hutvā paññāyanti. Ayaṃ tāva assa nābhiyā sabbākāraparipūratā.

Therein, it is a wheel, and it is a jewel in the sense that it generates delight—thus, a wheel-jewel. Now, that nave by which it is called ‘with a nave’ is made of sapphire. In its middle is a tube made of the finest silver, by which it shines as if smiling with a row of pure, smooth teeth, like the moon-disc with a hole in its center. On both its outer edges, it is enclosed by a silver band. On these silver bands enclosing its nave and tube, the dividing lines are clearly apparent in their respective places, being very well-defined. This, then, is the complete perfection of its nave in every aspect.

Yehi [V 2.0188] pana taṃ – “arehi sahassāra”nti vuttaṃ, te sattaratanamayā sūriyarasmiyo viya pabhāsampannā honti, tesampi ghaṭakamaṇikaparicchedalekhādīni suvibhattāneva hutvā paññāyanti. Ayamassa arānaṃ sabbākāraparipūratā.

And those spokes, by which it is said to be ‘thousand-spoked,’ are made of the seven kinds of gems and are radiant like sunbeams. On them too, the dividing lines of the gem settings and so forth appear very clearly, being well-defined. This is the complete perfection of its spokes in every aspect.

Yāya pana taṃ nemiyā – “sanemika”nti vuttaṃ, sā bālasūriyarasmikalāpasiriṃ avahasamānā viya surattasuddhasiniddhapavāḷamayā hoti. Sandhīsu panassā sañjhārāgasassirikā rattajambunadapaṭṭā vaṭṭaparicchedalekhā suvibhattā hutvā paññāyanti. Ayamassa nemiyā sabbākāraparipūratā.

And that rim, by which it is called ‘rimmed,’ is made of bright red, pure, smooth coral, as if mocking the splendor of a cluster of rays from the morning sun. At its joints, bands of red gold, imbued with the beauty of the evening twilight, appear as clearly marked, circular dividing lines. This is the complete perfection of its rim in every aspect.

Nemimaṇḍalapiṭṭhiyaṃ panassa dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānaṃ antare dhamanavaṃso viya anto susiro chiddamaṇḍalakhacito vātagāhī pavāḷadaṇḍo hoti, yassa vāteritassa sukusalasamannāhatassa pañcaṅgikatūriyassa viya saddo vaggu ca rajanīyo ca kamanīyo ca madanīyo ca hoti. Tassa kho pana pavāḷadaṇḍassa upari setacchattaṃ ubhosu passesu samosaritakusumadāmānaṃ dve pantiyoti evaṃ samosaritakusumadāmapantisatadvayaparivārasetacchattasatadhārinā pavāḷadaṇḍasatena samupasobhitanemiparikkhepassa dvinnampi nābhipanāḷīnaṃ anto dve sīhamukhāni honti, yehi tālakkhandhappamāṇā puṇṇacandakiraṇakalāpasassirīkā taruṇaravisamānarattakambalageṇḍukapariyantā ākāsagaṅgāgatisobhaṃ avahasamānā viya dve muttakalāpā olambanti. Yehi cakkaratanena saddhiṃ ākāse samparivattamānehi tīṇi cakkāni ekato parivattantāni viya khāyanti. Ayamassa sabbaso sabbākāraparipūratā.

On the surface of its rim, between each set of ten spokes, there is a coral rod that catches the wind, hollow inside like a flute and inlaid with perforated discs. When the wind blows through it, its sound is like that of a five-part orchestra skillfully played: melodious, delightful, charming, and intoxicating. Above that coral rod is a white parasol, with two rows of hanging flower garlands on both sides. Thus, the circumference of the rim is adorned with a hundred such coral rods, each bearing a white parasol surrounded by two hundred rows of hanging flower garlands. Inside both of the nave-tubes are two lion-mouths, from which hang two strands of pearls the size of palm trunks, possessing the splendor of a cluster of full moonbeams, bordered by crimson woolen balls like the morning sun, and as if mocking the beauty of the celestial Ganges’s flow. When these revolve in the sky together with the wheel-jewel, it appears as if three wheels are revolving at once. This is its complete perfection in every respect.

Taṃ panetaṃ evaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ pakatiyā sāyamāsabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā attano attano gharadvāre paññattāsanesu nisīditvā pavattakathāsallāpesu manussesu vīthicatukkādīsu [P 2.0619] kīḷamāne dārakajane nātiuccena nātinīcena vanasaṇḍamatthakāsannena ākāsappadesena upasobhayamānaṃ viya, rukkhasākhaggāni dvādasayojanato paṭṭhāya suyyamānena madhurassarena [M 2.0211] sattānaṃ sotāni odhāpayamānaṃ yojanato paṭṭhāya nānappabhāsamudayasamujjalena vaṇṇena nayanāni samākaḍḍhantaṃ viya, rañño cakkavattissa puññānubhāvaṃ ugghosayantaṃ viya, rājadhāniyā abhimukhaṃ āgacchati.

Now, this wheel-jewel, so perfect in every way, approached the royal capital. It did so while people, having customarily eaten their evening meal, were seated on prepared seats at their respective doorsteps engaged in conversation, and while children were playing in the streets and at crossroads. It traveled through a region of the sky neither too high nor too low, near the treetops of a forest grove, as if adorning the tips of the branches. From a distance of twelve leagues, its sweet sound could be heard, captivating the ears of beings. From a league away, it drew their eyes with its appearance, radiant with a glow of various colors, as if proclaiming the power of the wheel-turning king’s merit.

Athassa cakkaratanassa saddasavaneneva – “kuto nu kho, kassa nu kho ayaṃ saddo”ti āvajjitahadayānaṃ puratthimadisaṃ ālokayamānānaṃ tesaṃ manussānaṃ aññataro aññataraṃ evamāha [V 2.0189] – “passatha, bho, acchariyaṃ, ayaṃ puṇṇacando pubbe eko uggacchati, ajjeva pana attadutiyo uggato, etañhi rājahaṃsamithunamiva puṇṇacandamithunaṃ pubbāpariyena gaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghatī”ti. Tamañño āha – “kiṃ kathesi, samma, kuhiṃ nāma tayā dve puṇṇacandā ekato uggacchantā diṭṭhapubbā, nanu esa tapanīyaraṃsidhāro piñcharakiraṇo divākaro uggato”ti, tamañño hasitaṃ katvā evamāha – “kiṃ ummattosi, nanu idāneva divākaro atthaṅgato, so kathaṃ imaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ anubandhamāno uggacchissati? Addhā panetaṃ anekaratanappabhāsamudayujjalaṃ ekassāpi puññavato vimānaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Te sabbepi apasārayantā aññe evamāhaṃsu – “bho, kiṃ bahuṃ vilapatha, nevāyaṃ puṇṇacando, na sūriyo na devavimānaṃ. Na hetesaṃ evarūpā sirisampatti atthi, cakkaratanena pana etena bhavitabba”nti.

Then, just by hearing the sound of that wheel-treasure, those people, their hearts inclined to wonder while looking towards the eastern direction, one among them said to another: ‘Behold, sirs, a marvel! Previously, the full moon would rise alone, but today it has risen as a pair. For this pair of full moons, like a pair of royal swans, traverses the sky one after the other.’ Another said to him: ‘What are you saying, friend? Where indeed have you ever seen two full moons rising together? Is it not this sun, the bearer of golden rays, with tawny beams, that has risen?’ Yet another, laughing, said: ‘Are you mad? Has not the sun just now set? How could it rise again, following this full moon? Surely, this must be the celestial mansion of some meritorious being, resplendent with the accumulated radiance of many jewels.’ But others, dismissing all of them, said: ‘Sirs, why do you prate so much? This is neither the full moon, nor the sun, nor a celestial mansion. For these do not possess such glorious fortune. This must be the wheel-treasure.’

Evaṃ pavattasallāpasseva tassa janassa candamaṇḍalaṃ ohāya taṃ cakkaratanaṃ abhimukhaṃ hoti. Tato tehi – “kassa nu kho idaṃ nibbatta”nti vutte bhavanti vattāro – “na kassaci aññassa, nanu amhākaṃ mahārājā pūritacakkavattivatto, tassetaṃ nibbatta”nti. Atha so ca mahājano, yo ca añño passati, sabbo cakkaratanameva anugacchati. Taṃ cāpi cakkaratanaṃ raññoyeva atthāya attano āgatabhāvaṃ ñāpetukāmaṃ viya sattakkhattuṃ pākāramatthakeneva [P 2.0620] nagaraṃ anusaṃyāyitvā, atha rañño antepuraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, antepurassa ca uttarasīhapañjarasadise ṭhāne yathā gandhapupphādīhi sukhena sakkā hoti pūjetuṃ, evaṃ akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati.

Thus, while such conversation was going on among the people, that wheel-treasure, leaving the orb of the moon, turned towards them. Then, when they asked, ‘For whom, now, has this appeared?’, there were those who replied: ‘For no one else. Is not our great king one who has fulfilled the duties of a wheel-turning monarch? It is for him that this has appeared.’ Then that great crowd, and whoever else saw it, all followed the wheel-treasure. And that wheel-treasure, as if wishing to make known its arrival for the sake of the king, having circled the city seven times just along the top of the ramparts, then, having circumambulated the king’s inner palace to the right, it stood in a place like the northern lion-window of the inner palace, as if fixed to its axle, in such a way that it would be possible to worship it with ease with perfumes, flowers, and so on.

Evaṃ ṭhitassa panassa vātapānachiddādīhi pavisitvā nānāvirāgaratanappabhāsamujjalaṃ antopāsādaṃ alaṅkurumānaṃ pabhāsamūhaṃ disvā dassanatthāya sañjātābhilāso [M 2.0212] rājā hoti. Parijanopissa piyavacanapābhatena āgantvā tamatthaṃ nivedeti. Atha rājā balavapītipāmojjaphuṭasarīro pallaṅkaṃ mocetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā sīhapañjarasamīpaṃ gantvā taṃ cakkaratanaṃ disvā “sutaṃ kho pana meta”ntiādikaṃ cintanaṃ cintayati. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa…pe… assaṃ nu kho ahaṃ rājā cakkavattī”ti. Tattha so hoti rājā cakkavattīti kittāvatā cakkavattī hotīti? Ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi cakkaratane ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavatte idāni tassa pavattāpanatthaṃ yaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ dassento atha kho ānandātiādimāha.

Now, as it stood thus, the king, seeing the mass of rays entering through openings such as windows and adorning the palace interior, making it resplendent with the radiance of various colorful jewels, became filled with the desire to see it. His retinue also, approaching with a gift of pleasing words, informed him of the matter. Then the king, his body suffused with strong joy and delight, releasing his cross-legged posture and rising from his seat, went to the vicinity of the lion-window. Upon seeing the wheel-treasure, he thought the thought beginning with, ‘Indeed, I have heard of this…’. For King Mahāsudassana, all this happened in the very same way. Therefore it was said: ‘Having seen… of King Mahāsudassana… might I be a wheel-turning king?’ Therein, regarding the statement ‘he is a wheel-turning king,’ to what extent is one a wheel-turning king? When the wheel-treasure, having risen into the sky by as much as one or two finger-breadths, rolls forward, one is a wheel-turning king. Now, to show what must be done to make it roll, He said the words beginning with, ‘Then, Ānanda…’

244. Tattha [V 2.0190] uṭṭhāyāsanāti nisinnāsanato uṭṭhahitvā cakkaratanasamīpaṃ āgantvā. Suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvāti hatthisoṇḍasadisapanāḷiṃ suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ ukkhipitvā. Anvadeva rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyāti sabbacakkavattīnañhi udakena abbhukkiritvā – “abhivijinātu bhavaṃ cakkaratana”nti vacanasamanantarameva vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā cakkaratanaṃ pavattati. Yassa pavatti samakālameva so rājā cakkavattī nāma hoti. Pavatte pana cakkaratane taṃ anubandhamānova rājā cakkavattiyānavaraṃ āruyha vehāsaṃ abbhuggacchati. Athassa chattacāmarādihattho parijano ceva antepurajano ca tato nānākārakañcukakavacādisannāhavibhūsitena vividhābharaṇappabhāsamujjalena samussitaddhajapaṭākapaṭimaṇḍitena attano attano balakāyena saddhiṃ uparājasenāpatipabhutayopi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rājānameva parivārenti.

244. Therein, 'rising from his seat' means having risen from the seat where he was sitting and having approached the wheel-treasure. 'Taking the golden vessel' means lifting up the golden vessel with a spout like an elephant's trunk. Regarding 'King Mahāsudassana followed with his fourfold army': for all wheel-turning monarchs, immediately after the wheel-treasure is sprinkled with water and the words, 'May your honor, the wheel-treasure, conquer!' are spoken, it rises into the sky and rolls forward. At the very same time as its rolling, that king becomes known as a wheel-turning monarch. When the wheel-treasure rolls forward, the king, following it, mounts the excellent wheel-turning vehicle and ascends into the sky. Then his retinue, with parasols, fly-whisks, and other regalia in hand, and the people of the inner palace, and also the viceroy, the commander-in-chief, and others, together with their respective armies—adorned with various kinds of armor and mail, resplendent with the radiance of diverse ornaments, and decorated with raised banners and flags—ascend into the sky and surround the king.

Rājayuttā pana janasaṅgahatthaṃ nagaravīthīsu bheriyo carāpenti – “tātā, amhākaṃ rañño cakkaratanaṃ nibbattaṃ, attano vibhavānurūpena maṇḍitapasādhikā sannipatathā”ti. Mahājano [P 2.0621] pana pakatiyā cakkaratanasaddeneva sabbakiccāni pahāya gandhapupphādīni ādāya sannipatitova sopi sabbo vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rājānameva parivāreti. Yassa yassa hi raññā saddhiṃ gantukāmatācittaṃ uppajjati, so so ākāsagatova hoti. Evaṃ dvādasayojanāyāmavitthārā parisā hoti. Tattha ekapurisopi chinnabhinnasarīro vā kiliṭṭhavattho vā [M 2.0213] natthi. Suciparivāro hi rājā cakkavattī. Cakkavattiparisā nāma vijjādharapurisā viya ākāse gacchamānā indanīlamaṇitale vippakiṇṇaratanasadisā hoti. Mahāsudassanassāpi tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “anvadeva rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyā”ti.

Furthermore, royal officials, for the sake of gathering the people, had drums beaten in the city streets, announcing: ‘Sirs, the wheel-treasure of our king has appeared! Assemble, adorned and decorated according to your own means.’ But the great populace, by nature, just by the sound of the wheel-treasure, had already abandoned all their duties, taken up perfumes, flowers, and so on, and assembled. That entire populace also, having risen into the sky, surrounded the king. For whosoever the thought arose of wishing to go with the king, that very person was conveyed to the sky. Thus the assembly was twelve yojanas in length and breadth. Therein, there was not even one person with a cut or broken body, or with soiled clothes. For a wheel-turning king has a pure retinue. The assembly of a wheel-turning monarch, moving through the sky like celestial knowledge-bearers, is like jewels scattered on a surface of sapphire. For King Mahāsudassana also, it was the very same. Therefore it was said: ‘King Mahāsudassana followed with his fourfold army.’

Taṃ pana cakkaratanaṃ rukkhaggānaṃ uparūpari nātiuccena nātinīcena gaganappadesena pavattati. Yathā rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalapallavehi atthikā, tāni sukhena gahetuṃ sakkonti. Yathā ca bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitā “esa rājā, esa uparājā, esa senāpatī”ti sallakkhetuṃ sakkonti. Ṭhānādīsu ca iriyāpathesu yo yena icchati, so teneva gacchati. Cittakammādisippapasutā cettha attano attano kiccaṃ karontāyeva gacchanti. Yatheva hi bhūmiyaṃ, tathā tesaṃ sabbakiccāni ākāseva ijjhanti. Evaṃ cakkavattiparisaṃ gahetvā taṃ cakkaratanaṃ vāmapassena sineruṃ pahāya mahāsamuddassa uparibhāgena sattasahassayojanappamāṇaṃ pubbavidehaṃ gacchati.

That Wheel-Treasure proceeds through a region of the sky above the treetops, neither too high nor too low, so that those who have need of the flowers, fruits, and new shoots of the trees can easily take them, and so that those standing on the ground can recognize, 'This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the commander-in-chief.' And concerning the postures, such as standing, whoever wishes to travel in a particular posture, travels in that very posture. Here, those devoted to crafts such as painting travel while performing their respective duties. For just as on the ground, so too are all their tasks accomplished in the sky itself. Thus, taking with him the retinue of the wheel-turning monarch, that Wheel-Treasure, leaving Mount Sineru on its left, travels over the great ocean to Pubbavideha, the eastern continent, a distance of seven thousand yojanas.

Tattha yo vinibbedhena dvādasayojanāya, parikkhepato chattiṃsayojanāya parisāya sannivesakkhamo [V 2.0191] sulabhāhārūpakaraṇo chāyudakasampanno sucisamatalo ramaṇīyo bhūmibhāgo, tassa uparibhāge taṃ cakkaratanaṃ akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Atha tena saññāṇena so mahājano otaritvā yathāruci nahānabhojanādīni sabbakiccāni karonto vāsaṃ kappeti. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbaṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “yasmiṃ kho panānanda, padese cakkaratanaṃ patiṭṭhāti, tattha so rājā mahāsudassano vāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyā”ti.

There, on a region of land twelve yojanas in length and thirty-six yojanas in circumference—a place suitable for the encampment of the retinue, with easily obtainable food and requisites, endowed with shade and water, clean and level, and delightful—on that very region the Wheel-Treasure comes to a standstill, as if fixed to an axle. Then, by that sign, that great populace descends and, performing all their tasks such as bathing and eating according to their pleasure, they establish their residence. For Mahāsudassana, too, everything occurred in just the same way. Therefore, it was said: 'And wherever, Ānanda, the Wheel-Treasure comes to rest, there King Mahāsudassana took up residence together with his fourfold army.'

Evaṃ vāsaṃ upagate cakkavattimhi ye tattha rājāno, te “paracakkaṃ āgata”nti sutvāpi na balakāyaṃ sannipātetvā yuddhasajjā honti. Cakkaratanassa hi uppattisamanantarameva natthi so satto nāma, yo paccatthikasaññāya taṃ rājānaṃ ārabbha [P 2.0622] āvudhaṃ ukkhipituṃ visaheyya. Ayamānubhāvo cakkaratanassa.

When the Wheel-turning Monarch has thus taken up residence, the kings there, even upon hearing that 'a foreign army has arrived,' do not assemble their forces or prepare for battle. For immediately upon the arising of the Wheel-Treasure, there is no being who would dare to raise a weapon against that king with hostile intent. Such is the power of the Wheel-Treasure.

Cakkānubhāvena [M 2.0214] hi tassa rañño,

Arī asesā damathaṃ upenti;

Arindamaṃ nāma narādhipassa,

Teneva taṃ vuccati tassa cakkanti.

Indeed, by the power of that king's wheel,

All enemies without exception are brought to submission;

For that very reason, the wheel of that lord of men

Is called 'Arindama,' the Tamer of Foes.

Tasmā sabbepi te rājāno attano attano rajjasirivibhavānurūpaṃ pābhataṃ gahetvā taṃ rājānaṃ upagamma onatasirā attano moḷimaṇippabhābhisekena tassa pādapūjaṃ karontā – “ehi kho, mahārājā”tiādīhi vacanehi tassa kiṃkārapaṭisāvitaṃ āpajjanti. Mahāsudassanassāpi tatheva akaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “ye kho, panānanda, puratthimāya disāya…pe… anusāsa, mahārājā”ti.

Therefore, all those kings, taking gifts befitting their own royal splendor and wealth, approached that king and, with heads bowed, honored his feet with the consecration of the radiance from their own crown jewels. With words such as, 'Come, great king,' they placed themselves at his command. They did the same for Mahāsudassana. Hence it was said: 'And then, Ānanda, the kings of the eastern region... “Instruct us, great king.”'

Tattha svāgatanti su āgataṃ. Ekasmiñhi āgate socanti, gate nandanti. Ekasmiṃ āgate nandanti, gate socanti, tādiso tvaṃ āgamananandano, gamanasocano. Tasmā tava āgamanaṃ suāgamananti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ vutte pana rājā cakkavattī nāpi – “ettakaṃ nāma me anuvassaṃ baliṃ upakappethā”ti vadati, nāpi aññassa bhogaṃ acchinditvā aññassa deti. Attano pana dhammarājabhāvassa anurūpāya paññāya pāṇātipātādīni upaparikkhitvā pemanīyena mañjunā sarena – “passatha tātā, pāṇātipāto nāmesa āsevito bhāvito bahulīkato nirayasaṃvattaniko hotī”tiādinā nayena dhammaṃ desetvā “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādikaṃ [V 2.0192] ovādaṃ deti. Mahāsudassanopi tatheva akāsi, tena vuttaṃ – “rājā mahāsudassano evamāha – ‘pāṇo na hantabbo…pe… yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā’ti”. Kiṃ pana sabbepi rañño imaṃ ovādaṃ gaṇhantīti? Buddhassāpi tāva sabbe na gaṇhanti, rañño kiṃ gaṇhissantīti. Tasmā ye paṇḍitā vibhāvino, te gaṇhanti. Sabbe pana anuyantā bhavanti. Tasmā ye kho panānandātiādimāha.

There, 'welcome' means 'well-come.' For with some, their arrival brings grief and their departure brings joy. With others, their arrival brings joy and their departure brings grief. You are one whose arrival brings joy and whose departure brings sorrow. Therefore, your coming is called a 'welcome.' When this is said, the wheel-turning monarch does not say, 'Provide me with such and such tribute annually,' nor does he seize the wealth of one to give to another. Instead, with wisdom befitting his status as a righteous king, he scrutinizes the killing of living beings and so forth, and with an affectionate and sweet voice, he teaches the Dhamma, saying: 'See, dear ones, the killing of living beings, when practiced, developed, and frequently indulged in, is conducive to hell,' and so on. Then he gives the advice: 'Living beings should not be killed,' and so forth. Mahāsudassana did the same, which is why it is said: 'King Mahāsudassana spoke thus: “Living beings should not be killed... and enjoy what has been rightfully obtained.”' But do all kings accept this advice? Even the Buddha’s teachings are not accepted by all—how much less a king’s? Therefore, only the wise and discerning accept it. Yet all become his followers. Hence, it was said: 'And those, Ānanda, who...' and so on.

Atha taṃ cakkaratanaṃ evaṃ pubbavidehavāsīnaṃ ovāde dinne katapātarāse cakkavattibalena vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā puratthimasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhati. Yathā yathā ca taṃ ajjhogāhati, tathā tathā agadagandhaṃ ghāyitvā saṅkhittaphaṇo nāgarājā viya, saṅkhittaūmivipphāraṃ hutvā ogacchamānaṃ mahāsamuddasalilaṃ yojanamattaṃ ogantvā antosamudde veḷuriyabhitti viya tiṭṭhati. Taṅkhaṇaññeva ca tassa rañño puññasiriṃ daṭṭhukāmāni viya mahāsamuddatale vippakiṇṇāni [P 2.0623][M 2.0215] nānāratanāni tato tato āgantvā taṃ padesaṃ pūrayanti. Atha sā rājaparisā taṃ nānāratanaparipūraṃ mahāsamuddatalaṃ disvā yathāruci ucchaṅgādīhi ādiyati, yathāruci ādinnaratanāya pana parisāya taṃ cakkaratanaṃ paṭinivattati. Paṭinivattamāne ca tasmiṃ parisā aggato hoti, majjhe rājā, ante cakkaratanaṃ. Tampi jalanidhijalaṃ palobhiyamānamiva cakkaratanasiriyā, asahamānamiva ca tena viyogaṃ nemimaṇḍalapariyantaṃ abhihanantaṃ nirantarameva upagacchati. Evaṃ rājā cakkavattī puratthimamahāsamuddapariyantaṃ pubbavidehaṃ abhivijinitvā dakkhiṇasamuddapariyantaṃ jambudīpaṃ vijetukāmo cakkaratanadesitena maggena dakkhiṇasamuddābhimukho gacchati. Mahāsudassanopi tatheva agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pavattī”ti.

Then that wheel-treasure, after the advice had been given to the inhabitants of the eastern continent and the morning meal had been taken, rose into the sky with the army of the wheel-turning monarch and plunged into the eastern ocean. As it submerged, the great ocean water, like a serpent king with hood contracted from smelling an antidote, receded a yojana deep with its waves contracted, and stood within the ocean like a wall of beryl. At that very moment, various jewels scattered across the ocean floor, as if eager to witness the splendor of the king’s merit, came from all directions and filled that area. Seeing the ocean floor filled with these various jewels, the royal retinue gathered them as they pleased in their laps and so forth. When the retinue had taken jewels as they pleased, the wheel-treasure turned back. As it retreated, the retinue went ahead, the king was in the middle, and the wheel-treasure was at the rear. That water of the ocean, as if enticed by the splendor of the wheel-treasure, and as if unable to bear separation from it, continuously approached, striking up to the edge of the wheel's rim. Thus, the wheel-turning monarch, having conquered the eastern continent up to the eastern ocean, now desired to conquer Jambudīpa up to the southern ocean. Following the path shown by the wheel-treasure, he proceeded toward the southern ocean. Mahāsudassana also went in the same way. Therefore, it is said: “Then, Ānanda, the wheel-treasure plunged into the eastern ocean and, having emerged, proceeded towards the southern direction.”

Evaṃ pavattamānassa pana tassa pavattanavidhānaṃ, senāsanniveso, paṭirājāgamanaṃ, tesaṃ anusāsanippadānaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddaajjhogāhanaṃ samuddasalilassa ogacchamānaṃ ratanānaṃ ādānanti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

While this was proceeding, the manner of its proceeding, the encampment of the army, the arrival of the opposing kings, the giving of instructions to them, the plunging into the southern ocean, the subsiding of the ocean's waters, and the taking of jewels—all should be understood in the same way as before.

Vijinitvā pana taṃ dasasahassayojanappamāṇaṃ jambudīpaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddatopi paccuttaritvā sattayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ aparagoyānaṃ vijetuṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijinitvā pacchimasamuddatopi uttaritvā aṭṭhayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ uttarakuruṃ vijetuṃ tatheva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijiya uttarasamuddato paccuttarati.

Having conquered that Jambudīpa, ten thousand yojanas in extent, he crossed over from the southern ocean and, as previously described, went to conquer Aparagoyāna, seven thousand yojanas in extent. Having completely conquered that too, up to the ocean's edge, in the same manner, he crossed over from the western ocean and similarly went to conquer Uttarakuru, eight thousand yojanas in extent. Having completely conquered that too, up to the ocean's edge in the same way, he crossed back from the northern ocean.

Ettāvatā [V 2.0193] raññā cakkavattinā cāturantāya pathaviyā ādhipaccaṃ adhigataṃ hoti. So evaṃ vijitavijayo attano rajjasirisampattidassanatthaṃ sapariso uddhaṃ gaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghitvā suvikasitapadumakumudapuṇḍarīkavanavicitte cattāro jātassare viya pañcasatapañcasataparittadīpaparivāre cattāro mahādīpe oloketvā cakkaratanadesiteneva maggena [M 2.0216] yathānukkamaṃ attano rājadhāniṃ paccāgacchati. Atha taṃ cakkaratanaṃ antepuradvāraṃ sobhayamānaṃ viya hutvā tiṭṭhati.

By this much, the wheel-turning monarch attains sovereignty over this earth that is bounded by the four oceans. Having thus achieved victorious conquest, he ascends into the sky with his retinue to behold the splendor and prosperity of his kingdom. He gazes upon the four great continents, each surrounded by five hundred smaller islands, like four Jātassara lakes adorned with forests of fully bloomed lotuses, water lilies, and white lotuses. Then, following the path shown by the wheel-treasure, he returns in due order to his royal capital. There, the wheel-treasure remains, as if adorning the gate of the inner palace.

Evaṃ patiṭṭhite pana tasmiṃ cakkaratane rājantepure ukkāhi vā dīpikāhi vā kiñci [P 2.0624] karaṇīyaṃ na hoti, cakkaratanobhāsoyeva rattiṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamatiyeva. Ye pana andhakāratthikā honti, tesaṃ andhakārameva hoti. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbametaṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “dakkhiṇaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā…pe… evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti.

When the wheel-treasure was thus established, in the royal inner palace there was no need for anything to be done with torches or lamps, for the radiance of the wheel-treasure itself dispelled the darkness of the night. But for those who needed darkness, it was dark for them. For Mahāsudassana too, all this was just the same. Therefore it is said: "Having plunged into the southern ocean... such a wheel-treasure appeared."

Hatthiratanavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Elephant-Treasure

246. Evaṃ pātubhūtacakkaratanasseva cakkavattino amaccā pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ samaṃ sucibhūmibhāgaṃ kāretvā haricandanādīhi surabhigandhehi upalimpāpetvā heṭṭhā vicittavaṇṇasurabhikusumasamokiṇṇaṃ upari suvaṇṇatārakānaṃ antarantarā samosaritamanuññakusumadāmapaṭimaṇḍitavitānaṃ devavimānaṃ viya abhisaṅkharitvā – “evarūpassa nāma deva hatthiratanassa āgamanaṃ cintethā”ti vadanti. So pubbe vuttanayeneva mahādānaṃ datvā sīlāni ca samādāya taṃ puññasampattiṃ āvajjanto nisīdi. Athassa puññānubhāvacodito chaddantakulā vā uposathakulā vā taṃ sakkāravisesaṃ anubhavitukāmo taruṇaravimaṇḍalābhirattacaraṇagīvāmukhapaṭimaṇḍitavisuddhasetasarīro sattapatiṭṭho susaṇṭhitaaṅgapaccaṅgasanniveso vikasitarattapadumacārupokkharo iddhimā yogī viya vehāsagamanasamattho manosilācuṇṇarañjitapariyanto viya rajatapabbato hatthiseṭṭho āgantvā tasmiṃ padese tiṭṭhati. So chaddantakulā āgacchanto sabbakaniṭṭho āgacchati. Uposathakulā āgacchanto sabbajeṭṭho. Pāḷiyaṃ pana uposatho nāgarājā icceva āgataṃ. Nāgarājā nāma kassaci aparibhogo, sabbakaniṭṭho āgacchatīti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Svāyaṃ pūritacakkavattivattānaṃ cakkavattīnaṃ vuttanayeneva cintayantānaṃ āgacchati. Mahāsudassanassa pana sayameva pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā taṃ hatthiṃ apanetvā tattha aṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “puna caparaṃ ānanda…pe… nāgarājā”ti.

246. For a wheel-turning monarch for whom the wheel-treasure has thus appeared, his ministers have a level and clean area prepared at the customary auspicious elephant ground, have it anointed with fragrant substances such as yellow sandalwood, and adorn it like a celestial mansion, scattered below with various colorful and fragrant flowers, and with a canopy above decorated with golden stars and interspersed with hanging, delightful flower garlands. They then say, ‘Your Majesty, please reflect upon the arrival of such an elephant-treasure!’ He, having given great gifts and undertaken the precepts in the manner previously described, sat reflecting on that accomplishment of merit. Then, impelled by the power of his merit, a supreme elephant from the Chaddanta or Uposatha lineage, desiring to experience that special honor, came and stood in that place. Its body was pure white, adorned with feet, neck, and face reddened like the disk of the rising sun; it was firm on seven points; its major and minor limbs were well-proportioned; its beautiful trunk was like a blossomed red lotus; it was possessed of psychic power, capable of traversing the sky like a yogi; and it resembled a silver mountain whose edges are colored with powder of red arsenic. When one comes from the Chaddanta lineage, it is the youngest that comes. When one comes from the Uposatha lineage, it is the eldest. In the Pāli, however, it is stated only that Uposatha, the elephant king, came. In the commentaries it is said that an elephant king is not for anyone’s use, and that it is the youngest that comes. This elephant comes for wheel-turning monarchs who have fulfilled the duties of a wheel-turner when they reflect in the prescribed manner. But for Mahāsudassana, it came by itself to the customary auspicious elephant ground, and having removed the elephant that was there, it stood in its place. Therefore, it was said: ‘Furthermore, Ānanda… the elephant king.’”

Evaṃ [V 2.0194][M 2.0217] pātubhūtaṃ pana taṃ hatthiratanaṃ disvā hatthigopakādayo haṭṭhatuṭṭhā vegena gantvā rañño ārocenti. Rājā turitaturito āgantvā taṃ disvā pasannacitto – “bhaddakaṃ vata bho hatthiyānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā”ti cintayanto hatthaṃ [P 2.0625] pasāreti. Atha so gharadhenuvacchako viya kaṇṇe olambitvā sūratabhāvaṃ dassento rājānaṃ upasaṅkamati. Rājā taṃ ārohitukāmo hoti. Athassa parijanā adhippāyaṃ ñatvā taṃ hatthiratanaṃ suvaṇṇaddhajaṃ suvaṇṇālaṅkāraṃ hemajālapaṭicchannaṃ katvā upanenti. Rājā taṃ anisīdāpetvāva sattaratanamayāya nisseṇiyā āruyha ākāsagamananinnacitto hoti. Tassa saha cittuppādeneva so nāgarājā rājahaṃso viya indanīlamaṇippabhājālaṃ nīlagaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghati. Tato cakkacārikāya vuttanayeneva sakalarājaparisā. Iti sapariso rājā antopātarāseyeva sakalapathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā rājadhāniṃ paccāgacchati. Evaṃ mahiddhikaṃ cakkavattino hatthiratanaṃ hoti. Mahāsudassanassāpi tādisameva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “disvā rañño…pe… pāturahosī”ti.

Then, seeing that elephant-treasure thus manifested, the elephant keepers and others, joyful and delighted, went quickly and informed the king. The king, arriving in great haste and seeing it, with a pleased mind thought, 'Indeed, what a fine elephant vehicle! If only it could attain tameness,' and extended his hand. Then, like the calf of a domestic cow, letting its ears hang down and displaying its gentle nature, it approached the king. The king desired to mount it. Then his attendants, knowing his intention, adorned that elephant-treasure with golden banners and golden ornaments, covered it with a golden net, and brought it to him. The king, without having it kneel, ascended by a staircase made of the seven treasures, his mind inclined to travel in the sky. Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, that king of elephants, like a royal swan, soared towards the blue expanse of the sky, which had a net of radiance like an Indanīla gem. Thereafter, the entire royal retinue followed in the same way as was described for the journey of the wheel-treasure. Thus the king, with his retinue, having journeyed around the entire earth within the time of the morning meal, returned to the royal capital. Such is the elephant-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch, one of great psychic power. For Mahāsudassana, too, it was just so. Therefore it was said: 'Having seen the king... it appeared.'

Assaratanavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Horse-Treasure

247. Evaṃ pātubhūtahatthiratanassa pana cakkavattino amaccā pakatimaṅgalaassaṭṭhānaṃ sucisamatalaṃ kāretvā alaṅkaritvā ca purimanayeneva rañño tassa āgamanacintanatthaṃ ussāhaṃ janenti. So purimanayeneva katadānamānanasakkāro samādinnasīlabbato pāsādatale sukhanisinno puññasampattiṃ samanussarati. Athassa puññānubhāvacodito sindhavakulato vijjulatāvinaddhasaradakālasetavalāhakarāsisassirīko rattapādo rattatuṇḍo candappabhāpuñjasadisasuddhasiniddhaghanasaṃhatasarīro kākagīvā viya indanīlamaṇi viya ca kāḷavaṇṇena sīsena samannāgatattā kāḷasīsoti suṭṭhu kappetvā ṭhapitehi viya muñjasadisehi saṇhavaṭṭaujugatehi kesehi samannāgatattā muñjakeso vehāsaṅgamo valāhako nāma assarājā āgantvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne patiṭṭhāti. Mahāsudassanassa panesa hatthiratanaṃ viya āgato. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ hatthiratane [M 2.0218] vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ sandhāya bhagavā – “puna ca para”ntiādimāha.

247. Now, for the wheel-turning monarch for whom the elephant-treasure had manifested, the ministers, having had the customary auspicious stable ground made clean and level and having adorned it, in the same way as before, generated encouragement for the king for the purpose of contemplating its arrival. He, in the same way as before, having given gifts, shown reverence, and paid respect, and having undertaken the precepts and observances, was seated comfortably on the palace terrace, recollecting the accomplishment of his merit. Then, impelled by the power of his merit, from the Sindhu breed, a horse-king named Valāhaka, a sky-goer, came and stood in that place. He had the splendor of a mass of white clouds in the autumn season entwined with vines of lightning, had red hooves and a red muzzle, and a body pure, smooth, solid, and compact like a heap of moonlight. Because he was endowed with a head of black color, like a crow's neck or an Indanīla gem, he was black-headed. Because he was endowed with a mane like muñja grass, with hairs fine, round, and straight, as if well-cut and placed, he was muñja-maned. For Mahāsudassana, this horse-treasure arrived just like the elephant-treasure. All the rest should be understood in the same way as was stated for the elephant-treasure. It was with reference to such a horse-treasure that the Blessed One said: 'And further...' and so on.

Maṇiratanavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Jewel-Treasure

248. Evaṃ pātubhūtaassaratanassa pana rañño cakkavattino catuhatthāyāmaṃ sakaṭanābhisamapariṇāhaṃ ubhosu antesu kaṇṇikapariyantato viniggatehi suparisuddhamuttākalāpehi dvīhi kañcanapadumehi alaṅkataṃ caturāsītimaṇisahassaparivāraṃ tārāgaṇaparivutassa [V 2.0195] puṇṇacandasassiriṃ pharamānaṃ [P 2.0626] viya vepullapabbatato maṇiratanaṃ āgacchati. Tassevaṃ āgatassa muttājālake ṭhapetvā veḷuparamparāya saṭṭhihatthappamāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ āropitassa rattibhāge samantā yojanappamāṇaṃ okāsaṃ ābhā pharati, yāya sabbo so okāso aruṇuggamanavelā viya sañjātāloko hoti. Tato kassakā kasikammaṃ vāṇijā āpaṇugghāṭanaṃ te te sippino taṃ taṃ kammantaṃ payojenti “divā”ti maññamānā. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “puna ca paraṃ ānanda,…pe… maṇiratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti.

248. Now, for the wheel-turning king for whom the horse-treasure had manifested, a jewel-treasure comes from Mount Vepulla. It is four cubits in length, with a circumference equal to a cart's nave, adorned at both ends with two golden lotuses from the edge of whose pericarps issue clusters of perfectly pure pearls, and it is attended by eighty-four thousand gems, spreading splendor as if of a full moon surrounded by a host of stars. When it has thus arrived and been placed in a net of pearls and raised sixty cubits into the sky on a succession of bamboos, at night its radiance spreads over the space of a yojana all around, by which that entire space becomes illuminated as at the time of sunrise. Then, thinking, 'It is day,' farmers apply themselves to their farm work, merchants to the opening of their shops, and various artisans to their respective tasks. For Mahāsudassana, too, all this was just so. Therefore it was said: 'And further, Ānanda,... the jewel-treasure appeared.'

Itthiratanavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Woman-Treasure

249. Evaṃ pātubhūtamaṇiratanassa pana cakkavattino visayasukhavisesassa visesakāraṇaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati. Maddarājakulato vā hissa aggamahesiṃ ānenti, uttarakuruto vā puññānubhāvena sayaṃ āgacchati. Avasesā panassā sampatti – “puna ca paraṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa itthiratanaṃ pāturahosi, abhirūpā dassanīyā”tiādinā nayena pāḷiyaṃyeva āgatā.

249. Now, for the wheel-turning monarch for whom the jewel-treasure had manifested, the woman-treasure appears, the special cause for a special kind of sensual pleasure. For indeed, they either bring his chief queen from the Madda royal clan, or she comes by herself from Uttarakuru through the power of his merit. Her remaining accomplishments have come in the Pāli text itself, by the method beginning: 'And further, Ānanda, for King Mahāsudassana the woman-treasure appeared, beautiful, lovely...' and so on.

Tattha saṇṭhānapāripūriyā adhikaṃ rūpaṃ assāti abhirūpā. Dissamānāva cakkhūni piṇayati, tasmā aññaṃ kiccavikkhepaṃ hitvāpi daṭṭhabbāti dassanīyā. Dissamānāva somanassavasena cittaṃ pasādetīti pāsādikā. Paramāyāti evaṃ pasādāvahattā uttamāya. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti vaṇṇasundaratāya. Samannāgatāti upetā. Abhirūpā vā yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā. Dassanīyā yasmā nātikisā nātithūlā. Pāsādikā [M 2.0219] yasmā nātikāḷikā nāccodātā. Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā yasmā abhikkantā mānusivaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ. Manussānañhi vaṇṇābhā bahi na niccharati. Devānaṃ pana atidūrampi niccharati.

Therein, she is 'beautiful' (abhirūpā) because she has a superior form due to the complete perfection of her figure. She is 'lovely' (dassanīyā) because, just by being seen, she delights the eyes; therefore, she is to be looked at even having set aside other distracting tasks. She is 'charming' (pāsādikā) because, just by being seen, she pleases the mind by way of gladness. By 'supreme' (paramāya) is meant 'highest' (uttamāya) because she thus brings about serenity. By 'beauty of complexion' (vaṇṇapokkharatāya) is meant 'beauty of color' (vaṇṇasundaratāya). 'Endowed' (samannāgatā) means 'possessed of'. Alternatively, she is 'beautiful' because she is neither too tall nor too short. She is 'charming' because she is neither too dark nor too fair.
