She is 'endowed with supreme beauty of complexion' because she has surpassed human complexion but not attained divine complexion. For the radiance of the complexion of humans does not extend outwards, but that of devas extends even to a great distance.

Tassā pana dvādasahatthappamāṇaṃ padesaṃ sarīrābhā obhāseti. Nātidīghādīsu cassā paṭhamayugaḷena ārohasampatti, dutiyayugaḷena pariṇāhasampatti, tatiyayugaḷena vaṇṇasampatti vuttā. Chahi vāpi etehi kāyavipattiyā abhāvo, atikkantā mānusivaṇṇanti iminā kāyasampatti vuttā. Tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vāti sappimaṇḍe pakkhipitvā ṭhapitassa satavāravihatassa tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vā. Sīteti rañño sītakāle. Uṇheti rañño uṇhakāle. Candanagandhoti niccakālameva supisitassa [P 2.0627] abhinavassa catujjātisamāyojitassa [V 2.0196] haricandanassa gandho kāyato vāyati. Uppalagandho vāyatīti hasitakathitakālesu mukhato taṅkhaṇaṃ vikasitasseva nīluppalassa atisurabhigandho vāyati.

Her body’s radiance illuminates an area of twelve cubits. In the first pair (neither too tall nor too short) her perfection of stature is stated; in the second pair (neither too thin nor too stout) her perfection of proportions; and in the third pair (neither too dark nor too pale) her perfection of complexion. By these six terms is stated the absence of bodily defects, while by ‘surpassing human complexion’ is stated bodily perfection. The phrase ‘of cotton wool or carded cotton’ refers to cotton wool or carded cotton that has been placed in ghee-butter and beaten a hundred times. ‘Cool’ means she is cool to the king in the cold season. ‘Warm’ means she is warm to the king in the hot season. ‘The fragrance of sandalwood’ means that the scent of finely ground, fresh, golden sandalwood blended with the four fragrances always wafts from her body. ‘The fragrance of a lotus wafts forth’ means that when she smiles or speaks, the exceedingly pleasant fragrance of a freshly bloomed blue lotus emanates from her mouth.

Evaṃ rūpasamphassagandhasampattiyuttāya panassā sarīrasampattiyā anurūpaṃ ācāraṃ dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rājānaṃ disvā nisinnāsanato aggidaḍḍhā viya paṭhamameva uṭṭhātīti pubbuṭṭhāyinī. Tasmiṃ nisinne tassa tālavaṇṭena bījanādikiccaṃ katvā pacchā nipatati nisīdatīti pacchānipātinī. Kiṃ karomi, te devāti vācāya kiṃ-kāraṃ paṭisāvetīti kiṃ kārapaṭissāvinī. Rañño manāpameva carati karotīti manāpacārinī. Yaṃ rañño piyaṃ tadeva vadatīti piyavādinī.

Thus, to show the conduct befitting her bodily perfection endowed with perfection of form, touch, and fragrance, the passage beginning ‘Moreover…’ was stated. Herein, ‘one who rises first’ (pubbuṭṭhāyinī) means that upon seeing the king, she rises from her seat first, as if scorched by fire. ‘One who sits down afterward’ (pacchānipātinī) means that when he is seated, after performing for him the service of fanning and so on with a palm-leaf fan, she then sits down. ‘One who is responsive to what is to be done’ (kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī) means that she makes her readiness known by asking, ‘What shall I do for you, lord?’ ‘One of pleasing conduct’ (manāpacārinī) means that she conducts herself and acts only in ways pleasing to the king. ‘One who speaks agreeably’ (piyavādinī) means that she speaks only what is dear to the king.

Idāni – “svāssā ācāro bhāvavisuddhiyāva, na sāṭheyyanā”ti dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tattha no aticarīti na atikkamitvā cari, ṭhapetvā rājānaṃ aññaṃ purisaṃ cittenapi na patthesīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, to show that ‘her conduct is solely due to purity of nature, and not due to deceit,’ the passage beginning ‘Moreover…’ was stated. Herein, ‘she does not transgress’ (no aticarī) means she did not act transgressively; it is said that, setting aside the king, she did not long for another man even with her mind.

Tattha ye tassā ādimhi “abhirūpā”tiādayo, ante “pubbuṭṭhāyinī”tiādayo guṇā vuttā, te pakatiguṇā eva. “Atikkantā mānusivaṇṇa”ntiādayo pana cakkavattino puññaṃ upanissāya cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya purimakammānubhāvena nibbattāti veditabbā.

Herein, the qualities of hers mentioned at the beginning, such as ‘beautiful,’ and at the end, such as ‘one who rises first,’ are indeed her natural qualities. But ‘surpassing human complexion’ and the like should be understood as having arisen through the power of previous kamma, in dependence on the merit of the wheel-turning monarch, beginning from the manifestation of the wheel-treasure.

Abhirūpatādikāpi [M 2.0220] vā cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya sabbākāraparipūrā jātā. Tenāha – “evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti.

Or, her qualities such as beauty also became fully perfected in all respects, beginning from the manifestation of the wheel-treasure. Therefore, he said: ‘Such a woman-treasure manifested.’

Gahapatiratanavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Householder-Treasure

250. Evaṃ pātubhūtaitthiratanassa pana rañño cakkavattino dhanakaraṇīyānaṃ kiccānaṃ yathāsukhaṃ pavattanatthaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pātubhavati. So pakatiyāva mahābhogo, mahābhogakule jāto. Rañño dhanarāsivaḍḍhako seṭṭhigahapati hoti. Cakkaratanānubhāvasahitaṃ panassa kammavipākajaṃ dibbacakkhu pātubhavati, yena antopathaviyampi yojanabbhantare nidhiṃ passati, so taṃ sampattiṃ disvā tuṭṭhamānaso gantvā rājānaṃ dhanena pavāretvā sabbāni dhanakaraṇīyāni sampādeti[V 2.0197]. Mahāsudassanassāpi tatheva sampādesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “puna caparaṃ ānanda…pe… evarūpaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti.

250. For the wheel-turning king for whom the woman-treasure has appeared, the householder-treasure appears for the comfortable execution of duties to be done with wealth. By nature, he is of great wealth, born into a family of great wealth. He is a treasurer-householder who increases the king’s store of wealth. And for him, accompanied by the power of the wheel-treasure, a divine eye born of the result of kamma appears, by which he sees treasure within a yojana even inside the earth. Seeing that accomplishment, with a pleased mind, he approaches the king, makes an offering of wealth, and accomplishes all duties to be done with wealth. He accomplished the same for Mahāsudassana as well. Therefore it was said: ‘Moreover, Ānanda… such a householder-treasure appeared.’”

Pariṇāyakaratanavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Counselor-Treasure

251. Evaṃ [P 2.0628] pātubhūtagahapatiratanassa pana rañño cakkavattissa sabbakiccasaṃvidhānasamatthaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavati. So rañño jeṭṭhaputtova hoti. Pakatiyā eva so paṇḍito byatto medhāvī vibhāvī. Rañño puññānubhāvaṃ nissāya panassa attano kammānubhāvena paracittañāṇaṃ uppajjati. Yena dvādasayojanāya rājaparisāya cittācāraṃ ñatvā rañño hite ca ahite ca vavatthapetuṃ samattho hoti, sopi taṃ attano ānubhāvaṃ disvā tuṭṭhahadayo rājānaṃ sabbakiccānusāsanena pavāreti. Mahāsudassanampi tatheva pavāresi. Tena vuttaṃ – “puna caparaṃ…pe… pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti.

251. For the wheel-turning king for whom the householder-treasure has appeared, the counselor-treasure, capable of managing all affairs, appears. He is indeed the king’s eldest son. By nature, he is wise, competent, intelligent, and discerning. Relying on the power of the king’s merit, knowledge of others’ minds arises in him through the power of his own kamma. By this, having known the mental conduct of the royal assembly within twelve yojanas, he is able to determine what is beneficial and what is harmful to the king. He too, seeing his own power, with a joyful heart, makes an offering of instruction to the king on all duties. He made such an offering to Mahāsudassana in the same way. Therefore it was said: ‘Moreover… the counselor-treasure appeared.’”

Tattha ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetunti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhānantare ṭhapetabbaṃ ṭhapetuṃ.

Herein, ‘to place what should be placed’ means to place in each respective position that which should be placed.

Catuiddhisamannāgatavaṇṇanā

Explanation of Being Endowed with the Four Potencies

252. Samavepākiniyāti samavipācaniyā. Gahaṇiyāti kammajatejodhātuyā. Tattha yassa bhuttamattova āhāro jīrati, yassa vā [M 2.0221] pana puṭabhattaṃ viya tattheva tiṭṭhati, ubhopete na samavepākiniyā samannāgatā. Yassa pana puna bhattakāle bhattachando uppajjateva, ayaṃ samavepākiniyā samannāgatoti.

252. ‘Samavepākiniyā’ means that which digests evenly. ‘Gahaṇiyā’ refers to the element of heat born of kamma. Herein, one whose food digests as soon as it is eaten, or one for whom it remains right there like rice in a bundle, both these are not endowed with even digestion. But one for whom the desire for food arises again only at mealtime, this one is endowed with even digestion.

Dhammapāsādapokkharaṇivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Dhamma Palace and Lotus Pond

253. Māpesi khoti nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā janarāsiṃ kāretvā na māpesi, rañño pana saha cittuppādeneva bhūmiṃ bhinditvā caturāsīti pokkharaṇīsahassāni nibbattiṃsu. Tāni sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Dvīhi vedikāhīti ekāya iṭṭhakānaṃ pariyanteyeva parikkhittā ekāya pariveṇaparicchedapariyante. Etadahosīti kasmā ahosi? Ekadivasaṃ kira nahatvā ca pivitvā ca gacchantaṃ mahājanaṃ mahāpuriso oloketvā ime ummattakaveseneva gacchanti. Sace etesaṃ ettha piḷandhanapupphāni bhaveyyuṃ, bhaddakaṃ siyāti. Athassa etadahosi. Tattha sabbotukanti [V 2.0198] pupphaṃ nāma ekasmiṃyeva utumhi pupphati. Ahaṃ pana tathā karissāmi – “yathā sabbesu utūsu pupphissatī”ti cintesiṃ. Ropāpesīti nānāvaṇṇauppalabījādīni tato tato āharāpetvā na ropāpesi, saha cittuppādeneva panassa sabbaṃ ijjhati. Taṃ loko raññā ropitanti maññi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ropāpesī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya mahājano nānappakāraṃ jalajathalajamālaṃ piḷandhitvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷamāno [P 2.0629] viya gacchati.

253. 'Māpesi kho' means: he did not have them made by having a drum beaten in the city and gathering a crowd of people. Rather, with the mere arising of the king’s thought, the earth split open and eighty-four thousand lotus ponds came into being. It was with reference to these that this was said. 'Dvīhi vedikāhi' means: one railing enclosed them only at the edge of the bricks, and one at the edge of the precinct's boundary. 'Etadahosi' means: why did this thought arise in him? It is said that one day, the Great Being, seeing the great multitude of people going about after bathing and drinking, observed: 'These people go about as if in the guise of madmen. If only they had flowers for adornment here, it would be excellent.' Then this thought arose in him. In this context, 'sabbotuka' means: a flower normally blooms in only one season. But he thought, 'I, however, will act in such a way that they will bloom in all seasons.' 'Ropāpesi' means: he did not have lotus seeds of various colors and so forth brought from here and there and planted. Rather, for him, everything was accomplished with the mere arising of his thought. The world thought, 'It was planted by the king.' Therefore, it was said, 'ropāpesi.' From that time onwards, the great multitude of people, adorned with various kinds of aquatic and terrestrial garlands, went about as if celebrating a festival.

254. Atha rājā tato uttaripi janaṃ sukhasamappitaṃ kātukāmo – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ imāsaṃ pokkharaṇīnaṃ tīre”tiādinā janassa sukhavidhānaṃ cintetvā sabbaṃ akāsi. Tattha nhāpesunti añño sarīraṃ ubbaṭṭesi, añño cuṇṇāni yojesi, añño tīre nahāyantassa udakaṃ āhari, añño vatthāni paṭiggahesi ceva adāsi ca.

254. Then the king, desiring to make the people even more endowed with happiness, considered making arrangements for the people's well-being with the thought beginning, 'What if I were to, on the banks of these lotus ponds…,' and did everything. In that context, 'nhāpesuṃ' means: one person massaged the body, another applied powders, another brought water for one bathing on the bank, and another both received and gave clothes.

Paṭṭhapesi khoti kathaṃ paṭṭhapesi? Itthīnañca purisānañca anucchavike alaṅkāre kāretvā itthimattameva tattha paricāravasena sesaṃ sabbaṃ pariccāgavasena ṭhapetvā rājā mahāsudassano dānaṃ deti, taṃ paribhuñjathāti bheriṃ carāpesi. Mahājano pokkharaṇītīraṃ āgantvā nahatvā vatthāni parivattetvā nānāgandhehi vilitto piḷandhanavicittamālo dānaggaṃ [M 2.0222] gantvā anekappakāresu yāgubhattakhajjakesu aṭṭhavidhapānesu ca yo yaṃ icchati, so taṃ khāditvā ca pivitvā ca nānāvaṇṇāni khomasukhumāni vatthāni nivāsetvā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā yesaṃ tādisāni atthi, te ohāya gacchanti. Yesaṃ pana natthi, te gahetvā gacchanti. Hatthiassayānādīsupi nisīditvā thokaṃ vicaritvā anatthikā ohāya, atthikā gahetvā gacchanti. Varasayanesu nipajjitvā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā anatthikā ohāya, atthikā gahetvā gacchanti. Itthīhipi saddhiṃ sampattiṃ anubhavitvā anatthikā ohāya, atthikā gahetvā gacchanti. Sattavidharatanapasādhanāni ca pasādhetvāpi sampattiṃ anubhavitvā anatthikā ohāya, atthikā gahetvā gacchanti. Tampi dānaṃ uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya dīyateva. Jambudīpavāsikānaṃ aññaṃ kammaṃ natthi, rañño dānaṃ paribhuñjantāva vicaranti.

'Paṭṭhapesi kho' means: how did he establish it? King Mahāsudassana had suitable adornments made for women and men. Keeping only women there by way of service, and setting aside all the rest by way of relinquishment, he had a drum beaten, proclaiming: 'The king gives a gift, come and enjoy it!' The great multitude of people, having come to the bank of the lotus pond, bathed, changed their clothes, and, anointed with various perfumes and adorned with colorful garlands, went to the alms hall. There, from among the many kinds of gruel, cooked rice, solid foods, and eight kinds of beverages, whatever anyone desired, that they ate and drank. Then, having dressed in fine linen garments of various colors and experienced that splendor, those who already possessed such things would depart, leaving them behind. But those who did not, would depart taking them. Also, having sat upon elephants, horses, chariots, and so on, and traveled a short distance, those who had no need would leave them, while those who had need would take them and depart. Having lain on excellent couches and experienced that splendor, those who had no need would leave them, while those who had need would take them and depart. Having experienced splendor together with women, those who had no need would leave them, while those who had need would take them and depart. And having adorned themselves with the seven kinds of jewel ornaments and experienced that splendor, those who had no need would leave them, while those who had need would take them and depart. That gift was given continuously and with great effort. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa had no other work; they went about simply partaking of the king’s gift.

255. Atha brāhmaṇagahapatikā cintesuṃ – “ayaṃ rājā evarūpaṃ dānaṃ dadantopi ‘mayhaṃ taṇḍulādīni vā khīrādīni vā dethā’ti na kiñci āharāpeti, na kho pana amhākaṃ – ‘rājā āharāpetī’ti tuṇhīmāsituṃ patirūpa”nti te bahuṃ sāpateyyaṃ saṃharitvā rañño upanāmesuṃ. Tasmā – “atha kho, ānanda, brāhmaṇagahapatikā”tiādimāha. Evaṃ samacintesunti kasmā evaṃ cintesuṃ? Kassaci gharato appaṃ ābhataṃ, kassaci bahu. Tasmiṃ paṭisaṃhariyamāne [V 2.0199] – “kiṃ taveva gharato sundaraṃ ābhataṃ, na mayhaṃ gharato, kiṃ taveva gharato bahu[P 2.0630], na mayha”nti evaṃ kalahasaddopi uppajjeyya, so mā uppajjitthāti evaṃ samacintesuṃ.

255. Then the brahmins and householders thought: 'This king, even while giving such a gift, does not have anything brought, saying, "Give me rice and so on, or milk and so on." However, it is not proper for us to remain silent just because the king does not have things brought.' So they collected much of their own wealth and presented it to the king. Therefore, the Blessed One said the passage beginning: 'Then, Ānanda, the brahmins and householders…' 'Evaṃ samacintesuṃ' means: why did they think in unison in this way? Because from one person's house a little was brought, from another's much. When it was being collected, the sound of quarrels might arise, such as: 'Was something beautiful brought only from your house, and not from mine? Was much brought only from your house, and not from mine?' They thought in unison in this way so that such quarrels would not arise.

256. Ehi tvaṃ sammāti ehi tvaṃ vayassa. Dhammaṃ nāma pāsādanti pāsādassa nāmaṃ āropetvāva āṇāpesi. Vissakammo pana kīva mahanto deva pāsādo hotūti paṭipucchitvā dīghato yojanaṃ vitthārato aḍḍhayojanaṃ sabbaratanamayova hotūti vuttepi ‘evaṃ hotu, bhaddaṃ tava vacana’nti tassa paṭissuṇitvā dhammarājānaṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā māpesi. Tattha evaṃ bhaddaṃ tavāti kho ānandāti evaṃ bhaddaṃ tava iti kho ānanda. Paṭissutvāti sampaṭicchitvā, vatvāti attho. Tuṇhībhāvenāti samaṇadhammapaṭipattikaraṇokāso [M 2.0223] me bhavissatīti icchanto tuṇhībhāvena adhivāsesi. Sāramayoti candanasāramayo.

256. 'Ehi tvaṃ samma' means: 'Come, you, friend.' 'Dhammaṃ nāma pāsādaṃ' means: he gave the command only after bestowing this name upon the palace. Vissakamma, for his part, asked in return, 'Your Majesty, how large should the palace be?' And even when it was said, 'Let it be a yojana in length, half a yojana in width, and made entirely of all precious gems,' he replied to him, 'So be it, your words are excellent.' Having thus assented and gained the acceptance of the Dhamma King, he created it. In that passage, 'evaṃ bhaddaṃ tavāti kho ānanda' is to be understood as 'evaṃ bhaddaṃ tava iti kho ānanda.' 'Paṭissutvā' means having accepted, that is, having spoken. 'Tuṇhībhāvena' means: desiring, 'There will be an opportunity for me to practice the duties of an ascetic,' he consented through silence. 'Sāramayo' means: made of sandalwood heartwood.

257. Dvīhi vedikāhīti ettha ekā vedikā panassa uṇhīsamatthake ahosi, ekā heṭṭhā paricchedamatthake.

257. Regarding 'Dvīhi vedikāhi,' in this context, one railing was on top of its pinnacle, and one was below, on top of the boundary marker.

258. Duddikkho ahosīti duuddikkho, pabhāsampattiyā duddasoti attho. Musatīti harati phandāpeti niccalabhāvena patiṭṭhātuṃ na deti. Viddheti ubbiddhe, meghavigamena dūrībhūteti attho. Deveti ākāse.

258. 'Duddikkho ahosi' means it was difficult to look up at; the meaning is that it was difficult to see due to its radiant splendor. 'Musati' means it carries away, it causes to tremble, it does not allow one to stand still with stability. 'Viddhe' means scattered; the meaning is 'when it has become distant due to the passing of clouds.' 'Deve' means in the sky.

259. Māpesi khoti ahaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne pokkharaṇiṃ māpemi, tumhākaṃ gharāni bhindathāti na evaṃ kāretvā māpesi. Cittuppādavaseneva panassa bhūmiṃ bhinditvā tathārūpā pokkharaṇī ahosi. Te sabbakāmehīti sabbehi icchiticchitavatthūhi, samaṇe samaṇaparikkhārehi, brāhmaṇe brāhmaṇaparikkhārehi santappesīti.

259. He did not have the lotus pond made by causing it to be done thus: "I will have a lotus pond made in this place; demolish your houses!" Rather, by the power of his thought-arising alone, the earth split open and such a lotus pond came to be. "With all desires" means that he satisfied them with all wished-for things: ascetics with the requisites of ascetics, and brahmins with the requisites of brahmins.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Recitation Section is concluded.

Jhānasampattivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Attainment of Jhāna

260. Mahiddhikoti cittuppādavaseneva caturāsītipokkharaṇīsahassānaṃ nibbattisaṅkhātāya mahatiyā [V 2.0200] iddhiyā samannāgato. Mahānubhāvoti tesaṃyeva anubhavitabbānaṃ mahantatāya mahānubhāvena samannāgato. Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa – “katamesaṃ tiṇṇa”nti attho. Dānassāti sampattipariccāgassa. Damassāti āḷavakasutte paññā damoti āgato. Idha attānaṃ [P 2.0631] damentena kataṃ uposathakammaṃ. Saṃyamassāti sīlassa.

260. "Of great psychic power" means he was endowed with the great psychic power known as the arising of eighty-four thousand lotus ponds merely by the power of his thought. "Of great influence" means he was endowed with great influence due to the vastness of those very things that were to be experienced. "Such as" is a particle, and its meaning is "Which of the three?" "Of generosity" means of the relinquishment of possessions. "Of self-control": in the Āḷavaka Sutta, it is said, "wisdom is self-control." Here, it is the Uposatha observance undertaken by one who controls oneself. "Of restraint" means of morality.

Bodhisattapubbayogavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Bodhisatta's Former Endeavor

Idha ṭhatvā panassa pubbayogo veditabbo – rājā kira pubbe gahapatikule nibbatti. Tena ca samayena dharamānakasseva kassapabuddhassa sāsane eko thero araññe vāsaṃ vasati, bodhisatto attano [M 2.0224] kammena araññaṃ paviṭṭho theraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā therassa nisajjanaṭṭhānacaṅkamanaṭṭhānāni oloketvā pucchi – “idheva, bhante, ayyo vasatī”ti? Āma, upāsakāti sutvā – “idheva ayyassa paṇṇasālaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā attano kammaṃ pahāya dabbasambhāraṃ koṭṭetvā paṇṇasālaṃ katvā chādetvā bhittiyo mattikāya limpitvā dvāraṃ yojetvā kaṭṭhattharaṇaṃ katvā – “karissati nu kho paribhogaṃ, na karissatī”ti ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Thero antogāmato āgantvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kaṭṭhattharaṇe nisīdi. Upāsakopi āgantvā vanditvā samīpe nisinno “phāsukā, bhante, paṇṇasālā”ti pucchi. Phāsukā, bhaddamukha, pabbajitasāruppāti. Vasissatha, bhante, idhāti? Āma, upāsakāti, so adhivāsanākārena vasissatīti ñatvā nibaddhaṃ mayhaṃ gharadvāraṃ āgantabbanti paṭijānāpetvā – “ekaṃ me, bhante, varaṃ dethā”ti āha. Atikkantavarā, upāsaka, pabbajitāti. Bhante, yañca kappati, yañca anavajjanti. Vadehi upāsakāti. Bhante, nibaddhavasanaṭṭhāne nāma manussā maṅgale vā amaṅgale vā āgamanaṃ icchanti, anāgacchantassa kujjhanti. Tasmā aññaṃ nimantitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvāpi mayhaṃ gharaṃ pavisitvāva bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetabbanti. Thero adhivāsesi.

Here, his former endeavor should be understood. It is said that the king was once born into a householder’s family. At that time, during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, while he was still living, a certain elder was dwelling in the forest. The Bodhisatta, having entered the forest for his work, saw the elder, approached him, paid homage, and after observing the elder’s sitting and walking places, asked: “Venerable sir, does the noble one dwell right here?” “Yes, lay follower.” Hearing this, he thought, “It is fitting to build a leaf-hut for the noble one right here.” Abandoning his own work, he cut and gathered the materials, built a leaf-hut, thatched it, plastered the walls with clay, fitted a door, and made a wooden floor. Then, wondering, “Will he use it or not?” he sat to one side. The elder, returning from the village, entered the leaf-hut and sat on the wooden floor. The lay follower also approached, paid homage, and, sitting nearby, asked, “Venerable sir, is the leaf-hut comfortable?” “It is comfortable, good sir, and suitable for a renunciant.” “Venerable sir, will you dwell here?” “Yes, lay follower.” Knowing from this sign of acceptance that he would dwell there, he had him promise, “You must come regularly to my house door,” and then said, “Venerable sir, grant me one boon.” “Lay follower, renunciants have gone beyond boons.” “Venerable sir, grant one that is allowable and blameless.” “Speak, lay follower.” “Venerable sir, when one has a permanent dwelling place, people desire a visit on auspicious or inauspicious occasions, and they become angry with one who does not come. Therefore, even if you have gone to another place where you are invited, the business of your meal should be completed only after entering my house.” The elder consented.

So paṇṇasālāya kaṭasāṭakaṃ pattharitvā mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapesi, apassenaṃ nikkhipi, pādakathalikaṃ ṭhapesi, pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇi, caṅkamaṃ katvā vālikaṃ okiri, mige āgantvā bhittiṃ ghaṃsitvā mattikaṃ pātente disvā kaṇṭakavatiṃ parikkhipi. Pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā udakaṃ āḷulikaṃ karonte disvā anto pāsāṇehi cinitvā bahi kaṇṭakavatiṃ parikkhipitvā antovatipariyante tālapantiyo ropeti, mahācaṅkame sammaṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ āḷulente disvā caṅkamampi vatiyā parikkhipitvā antovatipariyante tālapantiṃ ropesi. Evaṃ [P 2.0632] āvāsaṃ niṭṭhapetvā [V 2.0201] therassa ticīvaraṃ, piṇḍapātaṃ, osadhaṃ, paribhogabhājanaṃ, ārakaṇṭakaṃ, pipphalikaṃ, nakhacchedanaṃ, sūciṃ, kattarayaṭṭhiṃ, upāhanaṃ, udakatumbaṃ, chattaṃ, dīpakapallakaṃ, malaharaṇiṃ. Parissāvanaṃ, dhamakaraṇaṃ, pattaṃ, thālakaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi pabbajitānaṃ paribhogajātaṃ, sabbaṃ adāsi. Therassa bodhisattena adinnaparikkhāro nāma nāhosi. So sīlāni rakkhanto uposathaṃ karonto yāvajīvaṃ [M 2.0225] theraṃ upaṭṭhahi. Thero tattheva vasanto arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyi.

He spread a grass mat in the leaf-hut and prepared a bed and a seat. He placed a leaning-board, set up a foot-scraper, dug a lotus pond, made a walking path, and scattered sand upon it. Seeing that deer would come and rub against the wall, causing the clay to fall off, he enclosed it with a thorny fence. Seeing that they would enter the lotus pond and muddy the water, he lined the inside with stones, enclosed the outside with a thorny fence, and planted rows of palm trees along the boundary of the inner fence. Seeing that the swept ground of the great walking path was being soiled, he also enclosed the walking path with a fence and planted a row of palm trees along the boundary of the inner fence. Having thus completed the dwelling, he gave the elder the three robes, almsfood, medicine, a bowl for use, a bodkin, a small razor, a nail-cutter, a needle, a walking stick, sandals, a water-gourd, an umbrella, a small oil lamp, an ear-pick, a water strainer, a handled water strainer, a bowl, a plate, and whatever other kind of requisite is used by renunciants—he gave everything. There was no requisite that the Bodhisatta did not give to the elder. Guarding his moral virtues and observing the Uposatha, he attended to the elder for as long as he lived. The elder, dwelling right there, attained Arahantship and attained final Nibbāna.

Bodhisattopi yāvatāyukaṃ puññaṃ katvā devaloke nibbattitvā tato cuto manussalokaṃ āgacchanto kusāvatiyā rājadhāniyā nibbattitvā mahāsudassano rājā ahosi.

The Bodhisatta, too, having performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, was reborn in the deva-world. Passing away from there and coming to the human world, he was reborn in the royal city of Kusāvati and became King Mahāsudassana.

“Evaṃ nātimahantampi, puññaṃ āyatane kataṃ;

Mahāvipākaṃ hotīti, kattabbaṃ taṃ vibhāvinā”.

“Thus even a merit not so great, when done in a worthy field, is of great result; therefore it should be done by one who is discerning.”

Mahāviyūhanti rajatamayaṃ mahākūṭāgāraṃ. Tattha vasitukāmo hutvā agamāsi, ettāvatā kāmavitakkāti kāmavitakka tayā ettāvatā nivattitabbaṃ, ito paraṃ tuyhaṃ abhūmi, idaṃ jhānāgāraṃ nāma, nayidaṃ tayā saddhiṃ vasanaṭṭhānanti evaṃ tayo vitakke kūṭāgāradvāreyeva nivattesi.

“Mahāviyūha” is the great, silver, gabled palace. Desiring to dwell there, he went to it. “Thus far, O thought of sensuality! You must turn back at this point. Beyond this is no ground for you. This is called the Jhāna-chamber; it is not a place for dwelling together with you.” In this way, he turned back the three kinds of thought at the very door of the gabled palace.

261. Paṭhamajjhānantiādīsu visuṃ kasiṇaparikammakiccaṃ nāma natthi. Nīlakasiṇena atthe sati nīlamaṇiṃ, pītakasiṇena atthe sati suvaṇṇaṃ, lohitakasiṇena atthe sati rattamaṇiṃ, odātakasiṇena atthe sati rajatanti olokitaolokitaṭṭhāne kasiṇameva paññāyati.

261. In regard to the first jhāna and so on, there is no separate task of preliminary work for the kasiṇas. When there is need for the blue kasiṇa, he looks at a blue gem; when there is need for the yellow kasiṇa, at gold; when there is need for the red kasiṇa, at a red jewel; when there is need for the white kasiṇa, at silver. Thus, in whatever place he looks again and again, only the kasiṇa itself appears.

262. Mettāsahagatenātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbampi visuddhimagge vuttameva. Iti pāḷiyaṃ cattāri jhānāni, cattāri appamaññāneva vuttāni. Mahāpuriso pana sabbāpi aṭṭha samāpattiyo, pañca abhiññāyo ca nibbattetvā anulomapaṭilomādivasena cuddasahākārehi samāpattiyo pavisanto madhupaṭalaṃ paviṭṭhabhamaro madhurasena viya samāpattisukheneva yāpeti.

262. Regarding 'accompanied by loving-kindness,' etc., whatever is to be said has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, in the Pāli text, the four jhānas and the four immeasurables are mentioned. However, the Great Being, having produced all eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, enters the attainments by means of fourteen modes, such as in forward and reverse order. Just as a bee that has entered a honeycomb sustains itself with the taste of honey, so too does he sustain himself solely with the bliss of the attainments.

Caturāsītinagarasahassādivaṇṇanā

The Description of the Eighty-four Thousand Cities, and So Forth

263. Kusāvatīrājadhānippamukhānīti [V 2.0202] kusāvatī rājadhānī tesaṃ nagarānaṃ pamukhā sabbaseṭṭhāti attho. Bhattābhihāroti [P 2.0633] abhiharitabbabhattaṃ.

263. Kusāvatīrājadhānippamukhānīti: The royal capital Kusāvatī is the foremost among those cities, meaning it is the best of all. Bhattābhihāroti: This means 'food that is to be brought.'

264. Vassasatassa [M 2.0226] vassasatassāti kasmā evaṃ cintesi? Tesaṃ saddena ukkaṇṭhitvā, “samāpannassa saddo kaṇṭako”ti (a. ni. 10.72) hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā saddena ukkaṇṭhito mahāpuriso. Atha kasmā mā āgacchantūti na vadati? Idāni rājā na passatīti nibaddhavattaṃ na labhissanti, taṃ tesaṃ mā uppajjitthāti na vadati.

264. Why did he think, 'For a hundred years, for a hundred years'? Because he was distressed by their noise. For it is said, 'Noise is a thorn for one who has attained absorption.' Therefore, the Great Being was distressed by the noise. Then why did he not say, 'Do not come'? He did not say it, thinking: 'Since the king does not see them now, they will not receive their regular allowance; may that not happen to them.'

Subhaddādeviupasaṅkamanavaṇṇanā

The Description of Queen Subhaddā’s Approach

265. Etadahosīti kadā etaṃ ahosi. Rañño kālaṅkiriyadivase. Tadā kira devatā cintesuṃ – “rājā anāthakālaṅkiriyaṃ mā karotu, orodhehi bahūhi dhītūhi puttehi parivāritova karotū”ti. Atha deviṃ āvaṭṭetvā tassā evaṃ cittaṃ uppādesuṃ. Pītāni vatthānīti tāni kira pakatiyā rañño manāpāni, tasmā tāni pārupathāti āha. Ettheva devi tiṭṭhāti devi imaṃ jhānāgāraṃ nāma tumhehi saddhiṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ na hoti, jhānarativindanaṭṭhānaṃ mama, mā idha pāvisīti.

265. Etadahosīti: 'This occurred'—when did this occur? On the day of the king’s death. At that time, it is said, the deities thought: 'Let the king not die unsupported, but let him die surrounded by many concubines, daughters, and sons.' Then, having influenced the queen, they caused such a thought to arise in her. Pītāni vatthānīti: 'Yellow garments'—it is said that these were naturally pleasing to the king, therefore she said, 'Wear them.' Ettheva devi tiṭṭhāti: 'Queen, stand right here.' [The king said:] 'Queen, this is called the jhāna-hall. It is not a place to dwell together with you; it is my place for finding delight in jhāna. Do not enter here.'

266. Etadahosīti loke sattā nāma maraṇāsannakāle ativiya virocanti, tenassa rañño vippasannaindriyabhāvaṃ disvā evaṃ ahosi, tato mā rañño kālaṅkiriyā ahosīti tassa kālaṅkiriyaṃ anicchamānā sampati guṇamassa kathayitvā tiṭṭhamānākāraṃ karissāmīti cintetvā imāni te devātiādimāha. Tattha chandaṃ janehīti pemaṃ uppādehi, ratiṃ karohi. Jīvite apekkhanti jīvite sāpekkhaṃ, ālayaṃ, taṇhaṃ karohīti attho.

266. Etadahosīti: In the world, beings shine exceedingly at the time near death. Because of that, seeing the king's state of exceptionally clear faculties, this thought occurred to her. Then, not wishing his death, thinking, 'May the king not die!', she decided, 'Now, by speaking of his virtues, I will create a reason for him to remain.' Having thought thus, she spoke the words beginning with 'Imāni te, deva...' Therein, chandaṃ janehīti means 'generate affection, create delight.' Jīvite apekkhanti means 'create longing, attachment, and craving for life.'

Evaṃ kho maṃ tvaṃ devīti “mayaṃ kho, deva, itthiyo nāma pabbajitānaṃ upacārakathaṃ na jānāma, kathaṃ vadāma mahārājā”ti rājānaṃ “pabbajito aya”nti maññamānāya deviyā vutte – “evaṃ kho maṃ, tvaṃ devi, samudācarāhī”tiādimāha. Garahitāti buddhehi paccekabuddhehi sāvakehi aññehi ca paṇḍitehi bahussutehi garahitā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Sāpekkhakālakiriyā [V 2.0203] hi attanoyeva gehe yakkhakukkuraajagoṇamahiṃsamūsikakukkuṭaūkāmaṅgulādibhāvena nibbattanakāraṇaṃ hoti.

Evaṃ kho maṃ tvaṃ devīti: When the queen, thinking, 'This king is now a renunciant,' said, 'Your Majesty, we women do not know the proper way to address renunciants; how should we speak, O great king?' he replied with the words beginning, 'Thus, O queen, you should address me.' Garahitāti: 'Censured'—censured by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other wise and learned ones. For what reason? Because dying with attachment is a cause for being reborn in one's own house as a yakkha, dog, goat, ox, buffalo, mouse, chicken, louse, bedbug, or the like.

268. Atha [M 2.0227] kho, ānanda, subhaddā devī assūni puñchitvāti devī ekamantaṃ gantvā roditvā kanditvā assūni puñchitvā etadavoca.

268. Atha kho, ānanda, subhaddā devī assūni puñchitvāti: The queen, having gone to one side, wept and lamented, and having wiped away her tears, said this.

Brahmalokūpagamavaṇṇanā

The Description of Going to the Brahma World

269. Gahapatissa vāti kasmā [P 2.0634] āha? Tesaṃ kira soṇaseṭṭhiputtādīnaṃ viya mahatī sampatti hoti, soṇassa kira seṭṭhiputtassa ekā bhattapāti dve satasahassāni agghati. Iti tesaṃ tādisaṃ bhattaṃ bhuttānaṃ muhuttaṃ bhattasammado bhattamucchā bhattakilamatho hoti.

269. 'Or of a householder'—why was this said? It is said that they have great wealth, like Soṇa the merchant's son and others. A single food bowl of Soṇa the merchant's son, it is said, was worth two hundred thousand. Thus, for those who have eaten such a meal, for a moment there is food-drowsiness, food-stupor, and food-weariness.

271. Yaṃ tena samayena ajjhāvasāmīti yattha vasāmi, taṃ ekaṃyeva nagaraṃ hoti, avasesesu puttadhītādayo ceva dāsamanussā ca vasiṃsu. Pāsādakūṭāgāresupi eseva nayo. Pallaṅkādīsupi ekaṃyeva pallaṅkaṃ paribhuñjati, sesā puttādīnaṃ paribhogā honti. Itthīsupi ekāva paccupaṭṭhāti, sesā parivāramattā honti, paridahāmīti ekameva dussayugaṃ nivāsemi, sesāni parivāretvā vicarantānaṃ asītisahassādhikānaṃ soḷasannaṃ purisasatasahassānaṃ honti. Bhuñjāmīti paramappamāṇena nāḷikodanamattaṃ bhuñjāmi, sesaṃ parivāretvā vicarantānaṃ cattālīsasahassādhikānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ purisasatasahassānaṃ hotīti dasseti. Ekathālipāko hi dasannaṃ janānaṃ pahoti.

271. Yaṃ tena samayena ajjhāvasāmīti: 'Whatever I inhabited at that time'—the city where I lived was only one; in the remaining cities lived my sons, daughters, and so on, as well as slaves and servants. This same principle applies to palaces and gabled chambers. Among couches and so on, I used only one couch; the rest were for the use of my sons and others. Among the women, only one attended to me; the rest were merely my retinue. Paridahāmīti: 'I wear'—I wear only one pair of cloths; the rest were for the one million, six hundred and eighty thousand men who moved about in my retinue. Bhuñjāmīti: 'I eat'—this shows that I eat at most a measure of one nāḷi of cooked rice; the rest was for the eight hundred and forty thousand men who moved about in my retinue. For one pot of cooked food is sufficient for ten people.

Etāni pana caturāsīti nagarasahassāni ceva pāsādasahassāni ca kūṭāgārasahassāni ca ekissāyeva paṇṇasālāya nissandena nibbattāni. Caturāsīti pallaṅkasahassāni nipajjanatthāya dinnamañcakassa nissandena nibbattāni. Caturāsīti hatthisahassāni assasahassāni rathasahassāni nisīdanatthāya dinnapīṭhassa nissandena nibbattāni. Caturāsīti maṇisahassāni ekadīpassa nissandena nibbattāni. Caturāsīti pokkharaṇīsahassāni ekapokkharaṇiyā nissandena nibbattāni. Caturāsīti itthisahassāni puttasahassāni gahapatisahassāni paribhogabhājanapattathālaka dhamakaraṇa parissāvana ārakaṇṭaka pipphalaka nakhacchedana kuñcikakaṇṇamalaharaṇī pādakathalika upāhana chatta kattarayaṭṭhidānassa nissandena nibbattāni. Caturāsīti dhenusahassāni gorasadānassa nissandena nibbattāni. Caturāsīti vatthakoṭisahassāni [V 2.0204] nivāsanapārupanadānassa nissandena nibbattāni[M 2.0228]. Caturāsīti thālipākasahassāni bhojanadānassa nissandena nibbattānīti veditabbāni.

Furthermore, these eighty-four thousand cities, eighty-four thousand palaces, and eighty-four thousand storied mansions arose as a consequence of a single leaf-hut. The eighty-four thousand couches arose as a consequence of a single small bed that was given for lying down. The eighty-four thousand elephants, horses, and chariots arose as a consequence of a single seat that was given for sitting. The eighty-four thousand jewels arose as a consequence of a single lamp. The eighty-four thousand lotus ponds arose as a consequence of a single lotus pond. The eighty-four thousand women, sons, and householders arose as a consequence of the gift of a bowl for use, a plate, a water-strainer, a cloth filter, a bodkin, a small razor, a nail-clipper, a key, an ear-pick, a potsherd for rubbing the feet, sandals, a parasol, and a staff. The eighty-four thousand cows arose as a consequence of the gift of milk-products. The eighty-four thousand sets of garments arose as a consequence of the gift of inner and outer wear. The eighty-four thousand pots of cooked food arose as a consequence of the gift of food—thus it should be understood.

272. Evaṃ bhagavā mahāsudassanassa sampattiṃ ādito paṭṭhāya vitthārena kathetvā sabbaṃ taṃ dārakānaṃ paṃsvāgārakīḷanaṃ [P 2.0635] viya dassento parinibbānamañcake nipannova passānandātiādimāha. Tattha vipariṇatāti pakativijahanena nibbutapadīpo viya apaññattikabhāvaṃ gatā. Evaṃ aniccā kho, ānanda, saṅkhārāti evaṃ hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā.

272. Thus the Blessed One, having spoken in detail from the beginning about the great prosperity of Mahāsudassana, showing it all to be like children's play with a house of dust, then, while lying on the couch of final Nibbāna, spoke the words beginning with, 'See, Ānanda…' Therein, 'have been transformed' means they have gone to a state of non-designation by abandoning their natural condition, like an extinguished lamp. 'Thus, Ānanda, formations are impermanent' means that, having been thus, they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence.

Ettāvatā bhagavā yathā nāma puriso satahatthubbedhe campakarukkhe nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā abhiruhitvā campakapupphaṃ ādāya nisseṇiṃ muñcanto otareyya, evameva nisseṇiṃ bandhanto viya anekavassakoṭisatasahassubbedhaṃ mahāsudassanasampattiṃ āruyha sampattimatthake ṭhitaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ ādāya nisseṇiṃ muñcanto viya otiṇṇo. Teneva pubbe vasabharājā dīghabhāṇakattherānaṃ lohapāsādassa pācīnapasse ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ imaṃ suttaṃ sajjhāyantānaṃ sutvā – “kiṃ, bho, mayhaṃ ayyakena ettha vuttaṃ, attano khāditapītaṭṭhāne sampattimeva kathetī”ti cintento – “evaṃ aniccā kho, ānanda, saṅkhārā”ti vuttakāle “imaṃ, bho, disvā pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumatā evaṃ vutta”nti vāmahatthaṃ samiñjitvā dakkhiṇahatthena apphoṭetvā – “sādhu sādhū”ti tuṭṭhahadayo sādhukāraṃ adāsi.

By this much, the Blessed One, just as a man might fasten a ladder to a campaka tree a hundred cubits high, climb it, take a campaka flower, and then descend while unfastening the ladder, in the very same way, as if fastening a ladder, ascended to the great prosperity of Mahāsudassana, which was as high as many hundred-thousands of crores of years, and standing at the pinnacle of that prosperity, took hold of the characteristic of impermanence and descended as if unfastening the ladder. For this very reason, in the past, King Vasabha, hearing the elder reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya chanting this sutta at Ambalaṭṭhikā on the eastern side of the Lohapāsāda, thought, 'Good sirs, what has my ancestor said here? He speaks only of prosperity in the very place where he ate and drank.' Then, at the moment when it was said, 'Thus, Ānanda, formations are impermanent,' he realized, 'Good sirs, having seen this, the one with the five kinds of vision spoke thus!' and bending his left arm, he struck it with his right hand and, with a delighted heart, gave his approval, saying, 'Excellent, excellent!'

Evaṃ addhuvāti evaṃ udakapupphuḷādayo viya dhuvabhāvavirahitā. Evaṃ anassāsikāti evaṃ supinake pītapānīyaṃ viya anulittacandanaṃ viya ca assāsavirahitā.

'Thus unstable' means that, like water bubbles and so forth, they are devoid of a permanent nature. 'Thus without solace' means that, like water drunk in a dream and like anointed sandalwood, they are devoid of comfort.

Sarīraṃ nikkhipeyyāti sarīraṃ chaḍḍeyya. Idāni aññassa sarīrassa nikkhepo vā paṭijagganaṃ vā natthi kilesapahīnattā, ānanda, tathāgatassāti vadati. Idaṃ pana vatvā puna theraṃ āmantesi, cakkavattino ānubhāvo nāma rañño pabbajitassa sattame divase antaradhāyati. Mahāsudassanassa pana kālaṅkiriyato sattameva divase sattaratanapākārā sattaratanatālā caturāsīti pokkharaṇīsahassāni dhammapāsādo dhammapokkharaṇī cakkaratananti sabbametaṃ antaradhāyīti. Hatthiādīsu pana ayaṃ dhammatā khīṇāyukā saheva kālaṅkaronti. Āyusese [M 2.0229] sati hatthiratanaṃ uposathakulaṃ gacchati, assaratanaṃ valāhakakulaṃ, maṇiratanaṃ vepullapabbatameva [V 2.0205] gacchati. Itthiratanassa [P 2.0636] ānubhāvo antaradhāyati. Gahapatiratanassa cakkhu pākatikameva hoti. Pariṇāyakaratanassa veyyattiyaṃ nassati.

'He should lay down the body' means he should cast off the body. He says, 'Now, Ānanda, for the Tathāgata there is no laying down or tending to another body, because the defilements have been abandoned.' Having said this, he again addressed the elder. The majestic power of a wheel-turning monarch vanishes on the seventh day after the king has gone forth into homelessness. But in the case of Mahāsudassana, on the seventh day after his passing away, the seven-jeweled ramparts, the seven-jeweled palm trees, the eighty-four thousand lotus ponds, the Palace of Dhamma, the Lotus Pond of Dhamma, and the wheel-treasure—all of this vanished. Regarding the elephant-treasure and the others, this is the natural course: those whose lifespans are exhausted pass away together with the monarch. If their lifespan remains, the elephant-treasure returns to the Uposatha clan, the horse-treasure to the Valāhaka clan, and the jewel-treasure goes to Mount Vepulla itself. The majestic power of the woman-treasure vanishes. The eye of the householder-treasure becomes ordinary. The expertise of the counselor-treasure is lost.

Idamavoca bhagavāti idaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āruḷhañca anāruḷhañca sabbaṃ bhagavā avoca. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

Regarding 'Thus spoke the Blessed One': the Blessed One spoke all of this, both what is included in the Pāli text and what is not. The rest is of plain meaning.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Here in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya,

Mahāsudassanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mahāsudassana Sutta is concluded.

5. Janavasabhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Janavasabha Sutta

Nātikiyādibyākaraṇavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Declarations concerning the People of Nātika and Others

273-275. Evaṃ [V 2.0206][M 2.0230][P 2.0637] me sutanti janavasabhasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – parito parito janapadesūti samantā samantā janapadesu. Paricāraketi buddhadhammasaṅghānaṃ paricārake. Upapattīsūti ñāṇagatipuññānaṃ upapattīsu. Kāsikosalesūti kāsīsu ca kosalesu ca, kāsiraṭṭhe ca kosalaraṭṭhe cāti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Aṅgamagadhayonakakambojaassakaavantiraṭṭhesu pana chasu na byākaroti. Imesaṃ pana soḷasannaṃ mahājanapadānaṃ purimesu dasasuyeva byākaroti. Nātikiyāti nātikagāmavāsino.

273-275. 'Thus have I heard' is the Janavasabha Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of words with non-obvious meanings. 'In the surrounding regions' means in the regions all around. 'Attendants' means those who attend upon the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. 'In the rebirths' means in the rebirths resulting from their knowledge, destiny, and merit. 'In Kāsī and Kosala' means in the Kāsī territory and the Kosala territory. This method applies everywhere. However, he does not make a declaration concerning the six regions of Aṅga, Magadha, Yona, Kamboja, Assaka, and Avanti. Of these sixteen great regions, he makes a declaration concerning only the first ten. 'The people of Nātika' means the inhabitants of the village of Nātika.

Tenāti tena anāgāmiādibhāvena. Sutvāti sabbaññutaññāṇena paricchinditvā byākarontassa bhagavato pañhābyākaraṇaṃ sutvā tesaṃ anāgāmiādīsu niṭṭhaṅgatā hutvā. Tena anāgāmiādibhāvena attamanā ahesuṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tenāti te nātikiyāti vuttaṃ. Etasmiṃ atthe na-kāro nipātamattaṃ hoti.

'By that' means by that state of being a non-returner and so on. 'Having heard' means that, having heard the Blessed One's answering of questions, which he delivered after discerning them with his omniscient knowledge, they became established in the states of non-returner and so on. By that state of being a non-returner and so on, they were delighted. In the commentary, however, it is said that `tenā` means `te nātikiyā` (those people of Nātika). In this sense, the letter 'na' is a mere particle.

Ānandaparikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Conversation with Ānanda

277. Bhagavantaṃ kittayamānarūpoti aho buddho, aho dhammo, aho saṅgho; aho dhammo svākkhātoti evaṃ kittayantova kālamakāsi. Bahujano pasīdeyyāti amhākaṃ pitā mātā bhātā bhaginī putto dhītā sahāyako, tena amhehi saddhiṃ ekato bhuttā, ekato sayitā, tassa idañcidañca manāpaṃ akarimha, so kira anāgāmī sakadāgāmī sotāpanno; aho sādhu, aho suṭṭhūti evaṃ bahujano pasādaṃ āpajjeyya.

277. 'Appearing to praise the Blessed One' means: saying, 'Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Saṅgha! Oh, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed!' and so passing away while thus praising. 'That many people might gain faith' means: 'Our father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, or companion, with whom we ate together and slept together, and for whom we did this and that which was pleasing—he, it seems, is a non-returner, a once-returner, or a stream-enterer. Oh, it is good! Oh, it is very good!' Thus, many people would gain faith.

278. Gatinti [V 2.0207] ñāṇagatiṃ. Abhisamparāyanti ñāṇābhisamparāyameva. Addasā khoti kittake jane addasa? Catuvīsatisatasahassāni.

278. 'Gati' means the course of knowledge. 'Abhisamparāya' means the future life attained through knowledge itself. 'Addasā kho' means: how many people did he see? Two million four hundred thousand.

279. Upasantapadissoti [M 2.0231] upasantadassano. Bhātirivāti [P 2.0638] ativiya bhāti, ativiya virocati. Indriyānanti manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ. Addasaṃ kho ahaṃ ānandāti neva dasa, na vīsati, na sataṃ, na sahassaṃ, anūnādhikāni catuvīsatisatasahassāni addasanti āha.

279. 'Upasantapadisso' means of serene appearance. 'Bhātiriva' means 'shines exceedingly,' 'radiates intensely.' 'Indriyāni' means the faculties with the mind as the sixth. 'I saw, Ānanda' means: 'Not ten, not twenty, not a hundred, not a thousand, but I saw no less and no more than two million four hundred thousand,' he said.

Janavasabhayakkhavaṇṇanā

Exposition on Janavasabha the Yakkha

280. Disvā pana me ettako jano maṃ nissāya dukkhā pamuttoti balavasomanassaṃ uppajji, cittaṃ pasīdi, cittassa pasannattā cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ lohitaṃ pasīdi, lohitassa pasannattā manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni pasīdiṃsūti sabbamidaṃ vatvā atha kho ānandātiādimāha. Tattha yasmā so bhagavato dhammakathaṃ sutvā dasasahassādhikassa janasatasahassassa jeṭṭhako hutvā sotāpanno jāto, tasmā janavasabhotissa nāmaṃ ahosi.

280. Having seen that 'so many people have been freed from suffering by relying on me,' strong joy arose in me, my mind became clear; due to the clarity of the mind, the blood originating from the mind became clear; due to the clarity of the blood, the faculties with the mind as the sixth became clear. Having said all this, he then said, 'Then, Ānanda,' and so on. In this context, because he, having heard the Dhamma talk of the Blessed One, became a stream-enterer, being the chief of one hundred and ten thousand people, his name therefore became Janavasabha.

Ito sattāti ito devalokā cavitvā satta. Tato sattāti tato manussalokā cavitvā satta. Saṃsārāni catuddasāti sabbāpi catuddasakhandhapaṭipāṭiyo. Nivāsamabhijānāmīti jātivasena nivāsaṃ jānāmi. Yattha me vusitaṃ pureti yattha devesu ca vessavaṇassa sahabyataṃ upagatena manussesu ca rājabhūtena ito attabhāvato pureyeva mayā vusitaṃ. Pure evaṃ vusitattā eva ca idāni sotāpanno hutvā tīsu vatthūsu bahuṃ puññaṃ katvā tassānubhāvena upari nibbattituṃ samatthopi dīgharattaṃ vusitaṭṭhāne nikantiyā balavatāya ettheva nibbatto.

'From here, seven' means seven who passed away from this deva world. 'From there, seven' means seven who passed away from the human world. 'Fourteen cycles of existence' means all fourteen successions of aggregates. 'I know my abodes' means I know my abodes by way of birth. 'Where I dwelt before' means where, among the devas, having attained companionship with Vessavaṇa, and among humans, having been a king, I dwelt even before this existence. And because I had dwelt thus before, now, having become a stream-enterer and having made much merit in the three objects, although capable of being reborn above by the power of that merit, due to the strength of craving for the place where I had dwelt for a long time, I was reborn right here.

281. Āsā ca pana me santiṭṭhatīti imināhaṃ sotāpannoti na suttappamattova hutvā kālaṃ vītināmesiṃ. Sakadāgāmimaggatthāya pana me vipassanā āraddhā. Ajjeva ajjeva paṭivijjhissāmīti evaṃ saussāho viharāmīti dasseti. Yadaggeti laṭṭhivanuyyāne paṭhamadassane sotāpannadivasaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tadagge ahaṃ, bhante, dīgharattaṃ avinipāto avinipātaṃ sañjānāmīti taṃdivasaṃ ādiṃ katvā, ahaṃ, bhante, purimaṃ catuddasaattabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ dīgharattaṃ avinipāto laṭṭhivanuyyāne sotāpattimaggavasena adhigataṃ avinipātadhammataṃ sañjānāmīti attho. Anacchariyanti [M 2.0232] anuacchariyaṃ. Cintayamānaṃ punappunaṃ acchariyamevidaṃ yaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena gacchanto bhagavantaṃ antarāmagge addasaṃ. Idampi acchariyaṃ [P 2.0639] yañca vessavaṇassa [V 2.0208] mahārājassa sayaṃparisāya bhāsato bhagavato diṭṭhasadisameva sammukhā sutaṃ. Dve paccayāti antarāmagge diṭṭhabhāvo ca vessavaṇassa sammukhā sutaṃ ārocetukāmatā ca.

281. 'And yet, my hope remains established'—by this he shows: 'I did not pass the time heedlessly, thinking, "I am a stream-enterer." Rather, my insight meditation has been undertaken for the sake of the once-returner path. "Today, indeed today, I will penetrate it"—thus I dwell with effort.' 'From that day'—he speaks referring to the day he became a stream-enterer at the first sight in the Laṭṭhivana Grove. The meaning of 'From that day, venerable sir, for a long time I have known that I am not subject to fall' is: 'Taking that day as the beginning, venerable sir, I well know the state of not being subject to fall—attained by means of the stream-entry path in the Laṭṭhivana Grove—throughout the long time of the previous fourteen existences.' 'Repeatedly wonderful' means it is very wonderful. 'When considered again and again, it is indeed wonderful that while going on some business I saw the Blessed One on the way. This too is wonderful: that what was heard face-to-face from the great king Vessavaṇa as he spoke in his own assembly was just like seeing the Blessed One.' 'Two causes' means: the fact of having seen him on the way, and the desire to report what was heard face-to-face from Vessavaṇa.

Devasabhāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Divine Assembly

282. Sannipatitāti kasmā sannipatitā? Te kira catūhi kāraṇehi sannipatanti. Vassūpanāyikasaṅgahatthaṃ, pavāraṇāsaṅgahatthaṃ, dhammasavanatthaṃ, pāricchattakakīḷānubhavanatthanti. Tattha sve vassūpanāyikāti āsāḷhīpuṇṇamāya dvīsu devalokesu devā sudhammāya devasabhāya sannipatitvā mantenti asukavihāre eko bhikkhu vassūpagato, asukavihāre dve tayo cattāro pañca dasa vīsati tiṃsaṃ cattālīsaṃ paññāsaṃ sataṃ sahassaṃ bhikkhū vassūpagatā, etthettha ṭhāne ayyānaṃ ārakkhaṃ susaṃvihitaṃ karothāti evaṃ vassūpanāyikasaṅgaho kato hoti.

282. 'Assembled'—why are they assembled? It is said they assemble for four reasons: for the purpose of supporting those entering the rains-residence, for the purpose of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, and for the purpose of enjoying the sport of the Pāricchattaka tree. In this regard, concerning 'tomorrow is the day for entering the rains-residence'—on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, the devas in the two deva worlds assemble in the Sudhammā assembly hall and deliberate: 'In such-and-such a monastery, one monk has entered the rains-residence; in such-and-such a monastery, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand monks have entered the rains-residence. In these various places, arrange good and proper protection for the venerable ones.' In this way, the support for those entering the rains-residence is accomplished.

Tadāpi eteneva kāraṇena sannipatitā. Idaṃ tesaṃ hoti āsanasminti idaṃ tesaṃ catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ āsanaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tesu nisinnesu atha pacchā amhākaṃ āsanaṃ hoti.

At that time, too, they assembled for this very reason. 'This is their seat' means this is the seat of those four great kings. When they are thus seated, then afterward is our seat.

Yenatthenāti yena vassūpanāyikatthena. Taṃ atthaṃ cintayitvā taṃ atthaṃ mantayitvāti taṃ araññavāsino bhikkhusaṅghassa ārakkhatthaṃ cintayitvā. Etthettha vuṭṭhabhikkhusaṅghassa ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahathāti catūhi mahārājehi saddhiṃ mantetvā. Vuttavacanāpi tanti tettiṃsa devaputtā vadanti, mahārājāno vuttavacanā nāma. Tathā tettiṃsa devaputtā paccānusāsanti, itare paccānusiṭṭhavacanā nāma. Padadvayepi pana tanti nipātamattameva. Avipakkantāti agatā.

'For what purpose' means for the purpose of supporting those entering the rains-residence. 'Having considered that purpose, having deliberated on that purpose' means having considered that purpose of protecting the community of forest-dwelling monks. 'In these various places, arrange protection for the community of monks who have completed the rains-residence'—having deliberated thus with the four great kings. 'And the words were spoken' means the thirty-three devas speak, and the great kings are called 'those to whom words have been spoken.' Likewise, the thirty-three devas instruct them again, and the others, the great kings, are called 'those who have been further instructed.' In both phrases, however, 'taṃ' is merely a particle. 'They had not departed' means they had not gone.

283. Uḷāroti vipulo mahā. Devānubhāvanti yā sā sabbadevatānaṃ vatthālaṅkāravimānasarīrānaṃ pabhā dvādasa yojanāni pharati. Mahāpuññānaṃ pana sarīrappabhā yojanasataṃ pharati. Taṃ devānubhāvaṃ atikkamitvā.

283. 'Sublime' means vast, great. 'The majesty of the devas' refers to the radiance from the garments, ornaments, mansions, and bodies of all the devas, which extends for twelve yojanas. The bodily radiance of those with great merit, however, extends for a hundred yojanas. Surpassing that majesty of the devas.

Brahmuno [M 2.0233] hetaṃ pubbanimittanti yathā sūriyassa udayato etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ yadidaṃ aruṇuggaṃ, evameva brahmunopi etaṃ – “pubbanimitta”nti dīpeti.

"This is the forerunner of Brahmā." Just as the dawn is the forerunner, the preliminary sign of the sun's rising, so too this indicates, "This is the forerunner of Brahmā."

Sanaṅkumārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Sanaṅkumāra Story

284. Anabhisambhavanīyoti [V 2.0209][P 2.0640] apattabbo, na taṃ devā tāvatiṃsā passantīti attho. Cakkhupathasminti cakkhupasāde āpāthe vā. So devānaṃ cakkhussa āpāthe sambhavanīyo pattabbo na hoti, na abhibhavatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Heṭṭhā heṭṭhā hi devatā uparūpari devānaṃ oḷārikaṃ katvā māpitameva attabhāvaṃ passituṃ sakkonti, vedapaṭilābhanti tuṭṭhipaṭilābhaṃ. Adhunābhisitto rajjenāti sampati abhisitto rajjena. Ayaṃ panattho duṭṭhagāmaṇiabhayavatthunā dīpetabbo –

284. ‘Unattainable’ means he cannot be reached; the meaning is that the Tāvatiṃsa gods do not see him. ‘Within the range of vision’ means within the eye’s sensitivity or within the visual field. He is not attainable, not to be reached within the range of the gods’ vision; he cannot be encompassed, is what is said. Indeed, lower deities are able to see only the grosser forms created by the higher deities. ‘Gaining joy’ means gaining satisfaction. ‘Recently anointed with kingship’ means recently anointed with kingship. This meaning, however, should be illustrated by the story of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya.

So kira dvattiṃsa damiḷarājāno vijitvā anurādhapure pattābhiseko tuṭṭhasomanassena māsaṃ niddaṃ na labhi, tato – “niddaṃ na labhāmi, bhante”ti bhikkhusaṅghassa ācikkhi. Tena hi, mahārāja, ajja uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāhīti. So ca uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi. Saṅgho gantvā – “cittayamakaṃ sajjhāyathā”ti aṭṭha ābhidhammikabhikkhū pesesi. Te gantvā – “nipajja tvaṃ, mahārājā,”ti vatvā sajjhāyaṃ ārabhiṃsu. Rājā sajjhāyaṃ suṇantova niddaṃ okkami. Therā – rājānaṃ mā pabodhayitthāti pakkamiṃsu. Rājā dutiyadivase sūriyuggamane pabujjhitvā there apassanto – “kuhiṃ ayyā”ti pucchi. Tumhākaṃ niddokkamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā gatāti. Natthi, bho, mayhaṃ ayyakassa dārakānaṃ ajānanakabhesajjaṃ nāma, yāva niddābhesajjampi jānanti yevāti āha.

It is said that after conquering thirty-two Tamil kings and being anointed in Anurādhapura, he could not sleep for a month due to joyful elation. Then he told the community of bhikkhus, ‘Venerable sirs, I cannot sleep.’ ‘Then, great king, undertake the Uposatha today,’ they said. And so he undertook the Uposatha. The Saṅgha sent eight Abhidhamma-expert bhikkhus, saying, ‘Recite the Cittayamaka.’ They went and, saying, ‘Lie down, great king,’ began the recitation. While listening to the recitation, the king fell asleep. The elders departed, saying, ‘Do not wake the king.’ The next day at sunrise, the king awoke and, not seeing the elders, asked, ‘Where are the venerable ones?’ ‘They left, knowing that you had fallen asleep,’ they replied. ‘Good sirs, there is no medicine, so to speak, unknown to my masters’ disciples; indeed, they even know the medicine for sleep,’ he said.

Pañcasikhoti pañcasikhagandhabbasadiso hutvā. Pañcasikhagandhabbadevaputtassa kira sabbadevatā attabhāvaṃ mamāyanti. Tasmā brahmāpi tādisaṃyeva attabhāvaṃ nimminitvā pāturahosi. Pallaṅkena nisīdīti pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi.

‘Pañcasikha’ means having become similar to the celestial musician Pañcasikha. It is said that all deities cherished the form of the celestial musician Pañcasikha, the son of a deity. Therefore, Brahmā also created a similar form and appeared. ‘He sat cross-legged’ means he sat having folded his legs in a cross-legged posture.

Vissaṭṭhoti sumutto apalibuddho. Viññeyyoti atthaviññāpano. Mañjūti madhuro mudu. Savanīyoti sotabbayuttako kaṇṇasukho. Bindūti [M 2.0234] ekagghano. Avisārīti suvisado avippakiṇṇo. Gambhīroti nābhimūlato paṭṭhāya gambhīrasamuṭṭhito, na jivhādantaoṭṭhatālumattappahārasamuṭṭhito. Evaṃ samuṭṭhito hi amadhuro ca hoti, na ca dūraṃ sāveti. Ninnādīti [P 2.0641] mahāmeghamudiṅgasaddo viya ninnādayutto. Apicettha pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ padaṃ purimassa purimassa atthoyevāti veditabbo. Yathāparisanti yattakā parisā, tattakameva viññāpeti. Anto parisāyaṃ yevassa saddo samparivattati, na bahiddhā vidhāvati. Ye hi kecīti [V 2.0210] ādi bahujanahitāya paṭipannabhāvadassanatthaṃ vadati. Saraṇaṃ gatāti na yathā vā tathā vā saraṇaṃ gate sandhāya vadati. Nibbematikagahitasaraṇe pana sandhāya vadati. Gandhabbakāyaṃ paripūrentīti gandhabbadevagaṇaṃ paripūrenti. Iti amhākaṃ satthu loke uppannakālato paṭṭhāya cha devalokādīsu piṭṭhaṃ koṭṭetvā pūritanāḷi viya saravananaḷavanaṃ viya ca nirantaraṃ jātaparisāti āha.

‘Vissaṭṭha’ means fully freed, unhindered. ‘Viññeyya’ means conveying the meaning. ‘Mañju’ means sweet, soft. ‘Savanīya’ means suitable to be heard, pleasing to the ear. ‘Bindu’ means a single mass. ‘Avisārī’ means very distinct, unscattered. ‘Gambhīra’ means arising deeply from the base of the navel, not arising merely from striking the tongue, teeth, lips, or palate. For a voice arising in such a way is unmelodious and does not carry far. ‘Ninnādī’ means possessing a reverberation like the sound of a great rain cloud or a drum. And here, it should be understood that each later word explains the meaning of each earlier word. ‘According to the assembly’ means he makes it understood only to the extent of that assembly. His sound circulates only within the assembly; it does not go outside. ‘Whatever beings’ and so on is spoken to show his practice for the welfare of many people. ‘Gone for refuge’ does not refer to one who has gone for refuge in just any way; rather, it refers to one who has taken refuge free from doubt. ‘Filling the Gandhabba realm’ means they fill the host of Gandhabba deities. Thus, he said, from the time our Teacher arose in the world, the assemblies of his disciples have been continuous, like a pipe packed with powder, or like a dense reed forest, filling the six heavenly worlds and so forth.

Bhāvitaiddhipādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Developed Bases of Psychic Power

287. Yāvasupaññattā cime tena bhagavatāti tena mayhaṃ satthārā bhagavatā yāva supaññattā yāva sukathitā. Iddhipādāti ettha ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena pādāti veditabbā. Iddhipahutāyāti iddhipahonakatāya. Iddhivisavitāyāti iddhivipajjanabhāvāya, punappunaṃ āsevanavasena ciṇṇavasitāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Iddhivikubbanatāyāti iddhivikubbanabhāvāya, nānappakārato katvā dassanatthāya. Chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgatantiādīsu chandahetuko chandādhiko vā samādhi chandasamādhi, kattukamyatāchandaṃ adhipatiṃ karitvā paṭiladdhasamādhissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā. Catukiccasādhakassa sammappadhānavīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Samannāgatanti chandasamādhinā ca padhānasaṅkhārena ca upetaṃ. Iddhipādanti nipphattipariyāyena ijjhanaṭṭhena vā, ijjhanti etāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iminā vā pariyāyena iddhīti saṅkhyaṃ gatānaṃ abhiññācittasampayuttānaṃ chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena pādabhūto sesacittacetasikarāsīti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “iddhipādoti tathābhūtassa vedanākkhandho, saññākkhandho, saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandho”ti (vibha. 434). Iminā [M 2.0235] nayena sesesupi attho veditabbo. Yatheva [P 2.0642] hi chandaṃ adhipatiṃ karitvā paṭiladdhasamādhi chandasamādhīti vutto, evaṃ vīriyaṃ, cittaṃ, vīmaṃsaṃ adhipatiṃ karitvā paṭiladdhasamādhi vīmaṃsāsamādhīti vuccati. Apica upacārajjhānaṃ pādo, paṭhamajjhānaṃ iddhi. Saupacāraṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ pādo, dutiyajjhānaṃ iddhīti evaṃ pubbabhāge pādo, aparabhāge iddhīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Vitthārena iddhipādakathā visuddhimagge ca vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya ca vuttā.

287. “‘How well proclaimed by the Blessed One’—thus, by that Blessed One, my Teacher, these have been exceedingly well proclaimed, exceedingly well expounded. Regarding ‘bases of psychic power,’ here ‘power’ (iddhi) should be understood in the sense of succeeding, and ‘base’ (pāda) in the sense of foundation. ‘For proficiency in psychic power’ means for the sake of being capable of psychic power. ‘For producing various psychic powers’ means for the state of generating various psychic powers; it is said to be through repeated practice, by way of cultivation. ‘For performing transformations of psychic power’ means for the state of performing transformations of psychic power, for the purpose of demonstrating them after having done so in various ways. In phrases such as ‘endowed with concentration of zeal and striving-formations,’ concentration that has zeal as its cause or has zeal as predominant is ‘concentration of zeal.’ This is a designation for the concentration attained by making the desire-to-act the dominant factor. Formations that are principal are ‘striving-formations.’ This is a designation for the right effort that accomplishes the four tasks. ‘Endowed’ means possessed of both concentration of zeal and striving-formations. Regarding ‘base of psychic power,’ it is so called by way of accomplishment or in the sense of succeeding. Or, because by this beings succeed, prosper, and reach an exalted state, thus, by this method, ‘power’ (iddhi) is the designation for the zeal, concentration, and striving-formations that are associated with the mind of direct knowledge. ‘Base’ (pāda), in the sense of a foundation, is the remaining mass of mind and mental factors. This is the meaning. For this was said: ‘“Base of psychic power” refers to the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, and the consciousness aggregate of one in such a state’ (Vibh. 434). By this method, the meaning should be understood in the remaining cases as well. For just as the concentration attained by making zeal the dominant factor is called ‘concentration of zeal,’ so too the concentration attained by making energy, mind, or investigation the dominant factor is called ‘concentration of investigation.’ Furthermore, access concentration is the base, the first jhāna is the power. The first jhāna with its access is the base, the second jhāna is the power. Thus, the preceding part is the base, and the succeeding part is the power; this is how the meaning should be understood here. The discourse on the bases of psychic power has been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga and in the Vibhaṅga Commentary.

Keci pana “nipphannā iddhi. Anipphanno iddhipādo”ti vadanti, tesaṃ vādamaddanatthāya abhidhamme uttaracūḷikavāro nāma ābhato – “cattāro iddhipādā chandiddhipādo, vīriyiddhipādo, cittiddhipādo, vīmaṃsiddhipādo. Tattha katamo chandiddhipādo? Idha bhikkhu yasmiṃ [V 2.0211] samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti niyyānikaṃ apacayagāmiṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya paṭhamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā vivicceva kāmehi paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati dukkhāpaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ. Yo tasmiṃ samaye chando chandikatā kattukamyatā kusalo dhammacchando, ayaṃ vuccati chandiddhipādo, avasesā dhammā chandiddhipādasampayuttā”ti (vibha. 458). Ime pana lokuttaravaseneva āgatā. Tattha raṭṭhapālatthero chandaṃ dhuraṃ katvā lokuttaraṃ dhammaṃ nibbattesi. Soṇatthero vīriyaṃ dhuraṃ katvā, sambhūtatthero cittaṃ dhuraṃ katvā, āyasmā mogharājā vīmaṃsaṃ dhuraṃ katvāti.

Some, however, say, 'Psychic power is an accomplished reality. The basis of psychic power is an unaccomplished reality.' To refute their view, the following passage from the Uttara Cūḷikavāra is adduced in the Abhidhamma: 'There are four bases of psychic power: the basis of psychic power of desire, the basis of psychic power of energy, the basis of psychic power of mind, and the basis of psychic power of investigation. Therein, what is the basis of psychic power of desire? Here, a bhikkhu develops the supramundane jhāna that is emancipating, that leads to the dismantling of accumulations, for the abandoning of wrong views, for the attainment of the first stage; secluded from sensual pleasures… he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is of difficult practice and slow in direct knowledge. At that time, whatever desire, eagerness, wish-to-do, wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is—this is called the basis of psychic power of desire. The remaining states are associated with the basis of psychic power of desire' (Vibh. 458). These, however, are presented only in the supramundane sense. In this regard, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla produced the supramundane Dhamma by making desire the guiding principle. The Elder Soṇa did so by making energy the guiding principle, the Elder Sambhūta by making mind the guiding principle, and the Venerable Mogharājā by making investigation the guiding principle.

Tattha yathā catūsu amaccaputtesu ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā rājānaṃ upanissāya viharantesu eko upaṭṭhāne chandajāto rañño ajjhāsayañca ruciñca ñatvā divā ca ratto ca upaṭṭhahanto rājānaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇi. Yathā so, evaṃ chandadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabbo.

Therein, it is as with four sons of ministers who were living in dependence on the king, aspiring for a higher position. One of them, becoming zealous in service, came to know the king's disposition and preferences. By attending to him day and night, he pleased the king and attained a higher position. Just as it was with him, so should the one who produces the supramundane Dhamma through the guiding principle of zeal be understood.

Eko pana – “divase divase upaṭṭhātuṃ ko sakkoti, uppanne kicce parakkamena ārādhessāmī”ti kupite paccante raññā pahito parakkamena sattumaddanaṃ katvā ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇi. Yathā so, evaṃ vīriyadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabbo.

Another, thinking, 'Who can attend day by day? When a duty arises, I will please him with my exertion,' was sent by the king to a rebellious border region. Through his exertion, he crushed the enemy and attained a higher position. Just as it was with him, so should the one who produces the supramundane Dhamma through the guiding principle of energy be understood.

Eko [M 2.0236] – “divase divase upaṭṭhānampi urena sattisarapaṭicchannampi [P 2.0643] bhāroyeva, mantabalena ārādhessāmī”ti khattavijjāya kataparicayattā mantasaṃvidhānena rājānaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇāti. Yathā so, evaṃ cittadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabbo.

Another, thinking, 'Both daily attendance and facing spears and arrows with one's chest are just a burden; I will please him with the power of counsel,' and being practiced in the art of statecraft, pleased the king through strategic planning and attained a higher position. Just as it was with him, so should the one who produces the supramundane Dhamma through the guiding principle of mind be understood.

Aparo – “kiṃ imehi upaṭṭhānādīhi, rājāno nāma jātisampannassa ṭhānantaraṃ denti, tādisassa dento mayhaṃ dassatī”ti jātisampattimeva nissāya ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇi, yathā so, evaṃ suparisuddhaṃ vīmaṃsaṃ nissāya vīmaṃsadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabbo.

Yet another, thinking, 'What is the use of these things like attendance? Kings, by nature, grant high positions to one endowed with noble birth. When granting to such a person, he will grant one to me,' attained a higher position by relying solely on his excellence of birth. Just as it was with him, so should the one who produces the supramundane Dhamma through the guiding principle of investigation, relying on thoroughly purified investigation, be understood.

Anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ. Iddhividhanti iddhikoṭṭhāsaṃ.

‘Of various kinds’ means of many sorts. ‘The kinds of psychic power’ means the portion of psychic power.

Tividhaokāsādhigamavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Threefold Attainment of Opportunity

288. Sukhassādhigamāyāti jhānasukhassa maggasukhassa phalasukhassa ca adhigamāya. Saṃsaṭṭhoti [V 2.0212] sampayuttacitto. Ariyadhammanti ariyena bhagavatā buddhena desitaṃ dhammaṃ. Suṇātīti satthu sammukhā bhikkhubhikkhunīādīhi vā desiyamānaṃ suṇāti. Yoniso manasikarotīti upāyato pathato kāraṇato ‘anicca’ntiādivasena manasi karoti. “Yoniso manasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro pathamanasikāro, anicce aniccanti dukkhe dukkhanti anattani anattāti asubhe asubhanti saccānulomikena vā cittassa āvaṭṭanā anvāvaṭṭanā ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro, ayaṃ vuccati yonisomanasikāro”ti. Evaṃ vutte yonisomanasikāre kammaṃ ārabhatīti attho. Asaṃsaṭṭhoti vatthukāmehipi kilesakāmehipi asaṃsaṭṭho viharati. Uppajjati sukhanti uppajjati paṭhamajjhānasukhaṃ. Sukhā bhiyyo somanassanti samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa jhānasukhapaccayā aparāparaṃ somanassaṃ uppajjati. Pamudāti tuṭṭhākārato dubbalapīti. Pāmojjanti balavataraṃ pītisomanassaṃ. Paṭhamo okāsādhigamoti paṭhamajjhānaṃ pañcanīvaraṇāni vikkhambhetvā attano okāsaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “paṭhamo okāsādhigamo”ti vuttaṃ.

288. For the attainment of happiness: that is, for attaining the happiness of jhāna, the happiness of the path, and the happiness of the fruit. Associated: means having a conjoined mind. Noble Dhamma: refers to the Dhamma taught by the Noble One, the Blessed One, the Buddha. Listens: means one hears it in the presence of the Teacher, or when it is being taught by monks, nuns, and others. Applies the mind wisely: means one directs the mind by way of the proper method, the right path, and correct reason, in the manner of contemplating 'impermanent,' and so on. As it is said: "Wise attention is attention by way of the proper method, attention by way of the right path; it is contemplating the impermanent as impermanent, the painful as painful, the non-self as non-self, the foul as foul; or it is the mind's turning, repeated turning, directing, applying, and attending in accordance with the truths. This is called wise attention." Thus, when this wise attention is spoken of, the meaning is that one undertakes the practice. Unassociated: means one dwells unassociated with both sensual objects and sensual defilements. Happiness arises: means the happiness of the first jhāna arises. Joy greater than that happiness: means that for one who has emerged from the attainment, successive joy arises due to the happiness of jhāna as its condition. Gladness: refers to a weaker joy in the form of delight. Rapture: refers to a stronger joy and gladness. The first attainment of opportunity: means the first jhāna, having suppressed the five hindrances, seizes its own opportunity and remains established; therefore, it is called "the first attainment of opportunity."

Oḷārikāti [M 2.0237] ettha kāyavacīsaṅkhārā tāva oḷārikā hontu, cittasaṅkhārā kathaṃ oḷārikāti? Appahīnattā. Kāyasaṅkhārā hi catutthajjhānena pahīyanti, vacīsaṅkhārā dutiyajjhānena, cittasaṅkhārā nirodhasamāpattiyā. Iti kāyavacīsaṅkhāresu pahīnesupi te tiṭṭhantiyevāti pahīne upādāya [P 2.0644] appahīnattā oḷārikā nāma jātā. Sukhanti nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa uppannaṃ catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpattisukhaṃ. Sukhā bhiyyo somanassati phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhitassa aparāparaṃ somanassaṃ. Dutiyo okāsādhigamoti catutthajjhānaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ vikkhambhetvā attano okāsaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “dutiyo okāsādhigamo”ti vuttaṃ. Dutiyatatiyajjhānāni panettha catutthe gahite gahitāneva hontīti visuṃ na vuttānīti.

Gross: Herein, while the bodily and verbal fabrications are gross, how are the mental fabrications gross? Because they are not yet abandoned. For the bodily fabrications are abandoned by the fourth jhāna, the verbal fabrications by the second jhāna, and the mental fabrications by the attainment of cessation. Thus, even when the bodily and verbal fabrications are abandoned, the mental fabrications still remain; therefore, with reference to the abandoned fabrications, they are called 'gross' on account of not being abandoned. Happiness: means the happiness of the fourth-jhāna fruition attainment that has arisen for one emerging from cessation. Joy greater than that happiness: means the successive joy for one who has emerged from the fruition attainment. The second attainment of opportunity: means the fourth jhāna, having suppressed pleasure and pain, seizes its own opportunity and remains established; therefore, it is called "the second attainment of opportunity." Herein, since the second and third jhānas are included when the fourth is attained, they are not mentioned separately.

Idaṃ kusalantiādīsu kusalaṃ nāma dasakusalakammapathā. Akusalanti dasaakusalakammapathā. Sāvajjadukādayopi etesaṃ vaseneva veditabbā. Sabbañceva panetaṃ kaṇhañca sukkañca sappaṭibhāgañcāti kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaṃ. Nibbānameva hetaṃ appaṭibhāgaṃ. Avijjā pahīyatīti vaṭṭapaṭicchādikā avijjā pahīyati. Vijjā uppajjatīti arahattamaggavijjā uppajjati. Sukhanti arahattamaggasukhañceva phalasukhañca. Sukhā bhiyyo somanassanti phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhitassa aparāparaṃ somanassaṃ. Tatiyo okāsādhigamoti arahattamaggo sabbakilese vikkhambhetvā attano okāsaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati, tasmā “tatiyo okāsādhigamo”ti vutto. Sesamaggā pana tasmiṃ gahite antogadhā evāti visuṃ na vuttā.

This is wholesome, and so on: Here, 'wholesome' refers to the ten wholesome courses of action. 'Unwholesome' refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action. The pairs of terms beginning with 'blameworthy' should also be understood in relation to these. Furthermore, all of this is both dark and bright, and has a counterpart; thus it is termed 'dark-bright with a counterpart.' For only Nibbāna is without a counterpart. Ignorance is abandoned: means the ignorance that conceals the round of existence is abandoned. Knowledge arises: means the knowledge of the path to Arahantship arises. Happiness: means both the happiness of the path to Arahantship and the happiness of fruition. Joy greater than that happiness: means the successive joy for one who has emerged from the fruition attainment. The third attainment of opportunity: means the path to Arahantship, having suppressed all defilements, seizes its own opportunity and remains established; therefore, it is called "the third attainment of opportunity." The remaining paths, however, are included within it once it is attained, so they are not mentioned separately.

Ime [V 2.0213] pana tayo okāsādhigamā aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇavasena vitthāretvā kathetabbā. Kathaṃ? Sabbāni ārammaṇāni visuddhimagge vuttanayeneva upacāravasena ca appanāvasena ca vavatthapetvā catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu paṭhamajjhānaṃ “paṭhamo okāsādhigamo”ti kathetabbaṃ. Terasasu ṭhānesu dutiyatatiyajjhānāni, pannarasasu ṭhānesu catutthajjhānañca nirodhasamāpattiṃ pāpetvā “dutiyo okāsādhigamo”ti kathetabbaṃ. Dasa upacārajjhānāni pana maggassa padaṭṭhānabhūtāni tatiyaṃ okāsādhigamaṃ bhajanti. Apica tīsu sikkhāsu adhisīlasikkhā paṭhamaṃ okāsādhigamaṃ bhajati, adhicittasikkhā dutiyaṃ, adhipaññāsikkhā tatiyanti evaṃ sikkhāvasenapi kathetabbaṃ. Sāmaññaphalepi cūḷasīlato yāva paṭhamajjhānā paṭhamo okāsādhigamo[M 2.0238], dutiyajjhānato yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanā dutiyo[P 2.0645], vipassanāto yāva arahattā tatiyo okāsādhigamoti evaṃ sāmaññaphalasuttantavasenapi kathetabbaṃ. Tīsu pana piṭakesu vinayapiṭakaṃ paṭhamaṃ okāsādhigamaṃ bhajati, suttantapiṭakaṃ dutiyaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakaṃ tatiyanti evaṃ piṭakavasenapi kathetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, these three attainments of opportunity should be explained in detail by way of the thirty-eight meditation objects. How? Having distinguished all the meditation objects according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga, by way of both access and absorption, the first jhāna should be explained as "the first attainment of opportunity" in twenty-four instances. In thirteen instances, the second and third jhānas, and in fifteen instances, the fourth jhāna, should be explained as "the second attainment of opportunity," extending up to the attainment of cessation. The ten access jhānas, which serve as the foundation for the path, partake of the third attainment of opportunity. Moreover, among the three trainings, the training in higher virtue partakes of the first attainment of opportunity, the training in higher mind partakes of the second, and the training in higher wisdom partakes of the third—thus it should also be explained by way of the trainings. Also in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, from the minor section on virtue up to the first jhāna is the first attainment of opportunity; from the second jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the second; and from insight up to Arahantship is the third—thus it should also be explained by way of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. And among the three Piṭakas, the Vinaya Piṭaka partakes of the first attainment of opportunity, the Suttanta Piṭaka partakes of the second, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka partakes of the third—thus it should also be explained by way of the Piṭakas.

Pubbe kira mahātherā vassūpanāyikāya imameva suttaṃ paṭṭhapenti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Tīṇi piṭakāni vibhajitvā kathetuṃ labhissāmāti. Tepiṭakena hi samodhānetvā kathentassa dukkathitanti na sakkā vattuṃ. Tepiṭakaṃ bhajāpetvā kathitameva idaṃ suttaṃ sukathitaṃ hotīti.

It is said that in the past, the great elders would establish this very sutta on the day of entering the rains retreat. For what reason?
