Thinking, "We will be able to speak by analyzing it in relation to the three Piṭakas." For when one speaks by connecting it with the Tipiṭaka, it cannot be said that it is poorly spoken. This sutta, when spoken by analyzing it in relation to the Tipiṭaka, is indeed well-spoken.

Catusatipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Four Establishments of Mindfulness

289. Kusalassādhigamāyāti maggakusalassa ceva phalakusalassa ca adhigamatthāya. Ubhayampi hetaṃ anavajjaṭṭhena khemaṭṭhena vā kusalameva. Tattha sammāsamādhiyatīti tasmiṃ ajjhattakāye samāhito ekaggacitto hoti. Bahiddhā parakāye ñāṇadassanaṃ abhinibbattetīti attano kāyato parassa kāyābhimukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ peseti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Sabbattheva ca satimāti padena kāyādipariggāhikā sati, lokoti padena pariggahitakāyādayova loko. Cattāro cete satipaṭṭhānā lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitāti veditabbā.

289. For the attainment of the wholesome—that is, for the attainment of both path-wholesomeness and fruit-wholesomeness. Both of these are indeed wholesome in the sense of being blameless or in the sense of being secure. Therein, 'one is rightly concentrated' (sammāsamādhiyatīti) means one is composed and single-minded in that internal body. 'One generates knowledge and vision externally in another's body' (bahiddhā parakāye ñāṇadassanaṃ abhinibbatteti) means one directs knowledge from one's own body toward another's body. This is the method everywhere. And everywhere, by the term 'mindful' (satimā) is meant the mindfulness that comprehends the body and so forth; and by the term 'world' (loko) is meant the very body and so forth that have been comprehended. And these four foundations of mindfulness should be understood as being described as mixed: mundane and supramundane.

Sattasamādhiparikkhāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Seven Requisites of Concentration

290. Samādhiparikkhārāti ettha tayo parikkhārā. “Ratho sīlaparikkhāro jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.4) hi ettha alaṅkāro parikkhāro nāma. “Sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi [V 2.0214] suparikkhataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 7.67) ettha parivāro parikkhāro nāma. “Gilānapaccayajīvitaparikkhāro”ti (dī. ni. 3.182) ettha sambhāro parikkhāro nāma. Idha pana parivāraparikkhāravasena “satta samādhiparikkhārā”ti vuttaṃ. Parikkhatāti parivāritā. Ayaṃ vuccati so ariyo sammāsamādhīti ayaṃ sattahi ratanehi parivuto cakkavattī viya sattahi aṅgehi parivuto [M 2.0239] “ariyo sammāsamādhī”ti vuccati. Saupaniso itipīti saupanissayo itipi vuccati, saparivāro yevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sammādiṭṭhissāti sammādiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhitassa. Sammāsaṅkappo pahotīti sammāsaṅkappo pavattati. Esa nayo sabbapadesu. Ayaṃ panattho maggavasenāpi phalavasenāpi veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Maggasammādiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhitassa [P 2.0646] maggasammāsaṅkappo pahoti…pe… maggañāṇe ṭhitassa maggavimutti pahoti. Tathā phalasammādiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhitassa phalasammāsaṅkappo pahoti…pe… phalasammāñāṇe ṭhitassa phalavimutti pahotīti.

290. Regarding 'requisites of concentration' (samādhiparikkhārā), there are three kinds of 'requisites'. For in the phrase, 'The chariot has virtue as its requisite, its axle is jhāna, its wheel is energy' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.4), the term 'requisite' (parikkhāro) means 'ornament'. In the phrase, 'It is well-protected by seven city fortifications' (A. Ni. 7.67), the term 'requisite' means 'retinue' or 'surrounding'. In the phrase, 'the requisite of medicine as a support for the sick' (gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro), the term 'requisite' means 'provision'. Here, however, 'the seven requisites of concentration' is said in the sense of a surrounding requisite. 'Equipped' (parikkhatā) means 'surrounded'. 'This is called that noble right concentration' (ayaṃ vuccati so ariyo sammāsamādhi)—just as a wheel-turning monarch is surrounded by seven treasures, so too is this 'noble right concentration' said to be surrounded by seven factors. 'With a supporting condition' (saupaniso itipi) is also expressed as 'with a basis' (saupanissayo itipi), which means 'with its retinue'. 'For one with right view' (sammādiṭṭhissa) means for one established in right view. 'Right intention arises' (sammāsaṅkappo pahoti) means right intention proceeds. This is the method in all instances. This meaning, moreover, should be understood both in terms of the path and in terms of the fruit. How? For one established in path right view, path right intention arises… and so on… for one established in path knowledge, path liberation arises. Similarly, for one established in fruit right view, fruit right intention arises… and so on… for one established in fruit right knowledge, fruit liberation arises.

Svākkhātotiādīni visuddhimagge vaṇṇitāni. Apārutāti vivaṭā. Amatassāti nibbānassa. Dvārāti pavesanamaggā. Aveccappasādenāti acalappasādena. Dhammavinītāti sammāniyyānena niyyātā.

The terms beginning with 'well-expounded' have been explained in the Visuddhimagga. 'Opened' (apārutā) means unveiled. 'Of the Deathless' (amatassa) means of Nibbāna. 'Doors' (dvārā) means the paths of entry. 'With unwavering confidence' (aveccappasādena) means with unshakeable confidence. 'Trained by the Dhamma' (dhammavinītā) means led out by the proper means of guidance.

Atthāyaṃ itarā pajāti anāgāmino sandhāyāha, anāgāmino ca atthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Puññabhāgāti puññakoṭṭhāsena nibbattā. Ottappanti ottappamāno. Tena kadāci nāma musā assāti musāvādabhayena saṅkhātuṃ na sakkomi, na pana mama saṅkhātuṃ balaṃ natthīti dīpeti.

Regarding 'There is this other populace' (atthāyaṃ itarā pajā), this was said in reference to non-returners; it means that non-returners also exist. 'Partakers in merit' (puññabhāgā) means born from a portion of merit. 'They are conscientious' (ottappanti) means being conscientious. Through that, he indicates: 'Lest it might sometimes be false, I am unable to reckon out of fear of false speech; but it is not that I lack the power to reckon.'

291. Taṃ kiṃ maññati bhavanti iminā kevalaṃ vessavaṇaṃ pucchati, na panassa evarūpo satthā nāhosīti vā na bhavissatīti vā laddhi atthi. Sabbabuddhānañhi abhisamaye viseso natthi.

291. By 'What does the worthy one think of this?' (taṃ kiṃ maññati bhavaṃ), he asks Vessavaṇa alone; it is not that he holds the view that 'there was no such Teacher before' or 'there will not be in the future'. For in the direct realization of all Buddhas, there is no difference.

292. Sayaṃparisāyanti attano parisāyaṃ. Tayidaṃ brahmacariyanti taṃ idaṃ sakalaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Imāni pana padāni dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi ṭhapitānīti.

292. 'In his own assembly' (sayaṃparisāyaṃ) means in his own assembly. 'This holy life' (tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ) means this entire holy life of the threefold training. The rest is clear. These passages, however, were inserted by the elders who compiled the Dhamma.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Janavasabhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Janavasabha Sutta is concluded.

6. Mahāgovindasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Mahāgovinda Sutta

293. Evaṃ [V 2.0215][P 2.0647][M 2.0240] me sutanti mahāgovindasuttaṃ. Tatrāyamanuttānapadavaṇṇanā – pañcasikhoti pañcacūḷo pañcakuṇḍaliko. So kira manussapathe puññakammakaraṇakāle daharo pañcacūḷakadārakakāle vacchapālakajeṭṭhako hutvā aññepi dārake gahetvā bahigāme catumaggaṭṭhānesu sālaṃ karonto pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇanto setuṃ bandhanto visamaṃ maggaṃ samaṃ karonto yānānaṃ akkhapaṭighātanarukkhe harantoti evarūpāni puññāni karonto vicaritvā daharova kālamakāsi. Tassa so attabhāvo iṭṭho kanto manāpo ahosi. So kālaṃ katvā cātumahārājikadevaloke navutivassasatasahassappamāṇaṃ āyuṃ gahetvā nibbatti. Tassa tigāvutappamāṇo suvaṇṇakkhandhasadiso attabhāvo ahosi. So sakaṭasahassamattaṃ ābharaṇaṃ pasādhetvā navakumbhamatte gandhe vilimpitvā dibbarattavatthadharo rattasuvaṇṇakaṇṇikaṃ piḷandhitvā pañcahi kuṇḍalakehi piṭṭhiyaṃ vattamānehi pañcacūḷakadārakaparihāreneva vicarati. Tenetaṃ “pañcasikho” tveva sañjānanti.

293. 'Thus have I heard'—the Mahāgovinda Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of the non-obvious terms: 'Pañcasikha' means 'Five-Crested' or 'having five topknots'. It is said that when he was on the human plane, at a time of performing meritorious deeds, he was a young boy with five topknots. As the chief of the cowherd boys, he would take other boys and, outside the village, perform such meritorious deeds as building rest houses at crossroads, digging ponds, constructing bridges, leveling uneven roads, and removing trees that would obstruct the axles of vehicles. Having gone about performing such meritorious deeds, he passed away while still young. That existence of his was wished for, beloved, and pleasing. Having passed away, he was reborn in the devaloka of the Four Great Kings, obtaining a lifespan of nine million years. His body was three gāvutas in size, like a mass of gold. Adorning himself with ornaments amounting to a thousand cartloads, anointing himself with perfumes from nine pots, wearing divine red garments, and wearing a red-gold earring, he goes about with five topknots on his back in the same manner as a boy with five topknots. For that reason, they know him only as 'Pañcasikha'.

Abhikkantāya rattiyāti abhikkantāya khīṇāya rattiyā, ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ atītāyāti attho. Abhikkantavaṇṇoti atiiṭṭhakantamanāpavaṇṇo. Pakatiyāpi hesa kantavaṇṇo, alaṅkaritvā āgatattā pana abhikkantavaṇṇo ahosi. Kevalakappanti anavasesaṃ samantato. Anavasesattho ettha kevalasaddo. Kevalaparipuṇṇanti ettha viya. Samantato attho kappasaddo, kevalakappaṃ jetavanantiādīsu viya. Obhāsetvāti ābhāya pharitvā, candimā viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekapajjotaṃ karitvāti attho.

'When the night was advanced' (abhikkantāya rattiyā) means when the night had advanced, had been spent; the meaning is that one portion had passed. 'Of surpassing beauty' (abhikkantavaṇṇo) means of exceedingly wished for, beloved, and pleasing appearance. By nature he was already of pleasing appearance, but because he came adorned, he became of surpassing beauty. 'The entire' (kevalakappaṃ) means completely, all around. Here, the word 'kevala' has the meaning of 'complete', as in 'completely perfect' (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ). The word 'kappa' has the meaning of 'all around', as in 'the entire Jetavana' (kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ) and so forth. 'Having illuminated' (obhāsetvā) means having pervaded it with his radiance; the meaning is that he made it a single effulgence, a single luster, like the moon or the sun.

Devasabhāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Assembly of the Devas

294. Sudhammāyaṃ sabhāyanti sudhammāya nāma itthiyā ratanamattakaṇṇikarukkhanissandena nibbattasabhāyaṃ[V 2.0216]. Tassā [P 2.0648] kira phalikamayā bhūmi, maṇimayā āṇiyo[M 2.0241], suvaṇṇamayā thambhā, rajatamayā thambhaghaṭikā ca saṅghātā ca, pavāḷamayāni vāḷarūpāni, sattaratanamayā gopānasiyo ca pakkhapāsakā ca mukhavaṭṭi ca, indanīlaiṭṭhakāhi chadanaṃ, sovaṇṇamayaṃ chadanapīṭhaṃ, rajatamayā thūpikā, āyāmato ca vitthārato ca tīṇi yojanasatāni, parikkhepato navayojanasatāni, ubbedhato pañcayojanasatāni, evarūpāyaṃ sudhammāyaṃ sabhāyaṃ.

294. In the Sudhammā Assembly Hall—this refers to the assembly hall that arose as a result of the ratanamaṭṭakaṇṇikā tree of a woman named Sudhammā. Its floor, it is said, was made of crystal, the pegs of gems, the pillars of gold, and the pillar capitals and beams of silver. The figures of beasts were made of coral; the rafters, roof-ribs, and fascia-boards were made of the seven precious substances. The inner roofing was of sapphire bricks, the outer roofing was golden, and the pinnacle was silver. In length and width, it measured three hundred yojanas; in circumference, nine hundred yojanas; and in height, five hundred yojanas. Such was the Sudhammā Assembly Hall.

Dhataraṭṭhotiādīsu dhataraṭṭho gandhabbarājā gandhabbadevatānaṃ koṭisatasahassena parivuto koṭisatasahassasuvaṇṇamayāni phalakāni ca suvaṇṇasattiyo ca gāhāpetvā puratthimāya disāya pacchimābhimukho dvīsu devalokesu devatā purato katvā nisinno.

In the section beginning with 'Dhataraṭṭha,' Dhataraṭṭha, the king of the gandhabbas, surrounded by a hundred thousand crores of gandhabba deities, having caused a hundred thousand crores of golden shields and golden spears to be held, and having placed the deities of two deva-worlds before him, sat in the eastern direction facing west.

Virūḷhako kumbhaṇḍarājā kumbhaṇḍadevatānaṃ koṭisatasahassena parivuto koṭisatasahassarajatamayāni phalakāni ca suvaṇṇasattiyo ca gāhāpetvā dakkhiṇāya disāya uttarābhimukho dvīsu devalokesu devatā purato katvā nisinno.

Virūḷhaka, the king of the kumbhaṇḍas, surrounded by a hundred thousand crores of kumbhaṇḍa deities, having caused a hundred thousand crores of silver shields and golden spears to be held, and having placed the deities of two deva-worlds before him, sat in the southern direction facing north.

Virūpakkho nāgarājā nāgānaṃ koṭisatasahassena parivuto koṭisatasahassamaṇimayāni mahāphalakāni ca suvaṇṇasattiyo ca gāhāpetvā pacchimāya disāya puratthimābhimukho dvīsu devalokesu devatā purato katvā nisinno.

Virūpakkha, the king of the nāgas, surrounded by a hundred thousand crores of nāgas, having caused a hundred thousand crores of great jeweled shields and golden spears to be held, and having placed the deities of two deva-worlds before him, sat in the western direction facing east.

Vessavaṇo yakkharājā yakkhānaṃ koṭisatasahassena parivuto koṭisatasahassapavāḷamayāni mahāphalakāni ca suvaṇṇasattiyo ca gāhāpetvā uttarāya disāya dakkhiṇābhimukho dvīsu devalokesu devatā purato katvā nisinnoti veditabbo.

Vessavaṇa, the king of the yakkhas, surrounded by a hundred thousand crores of yakkhas, having caused a hundred thousand crores of great coral shields and golden spears to be held, and having placed the deities of two deva-worlds before him, sat in the northern direction facing south—thus it should be understood.

Atha pacchā amhākaṃ āsanaṃ hotīti tesaṃ pacchato amhākaṃ nisīdituṃ okāso pāpuṇāti. Tato paraṃ pavisituṃ vā passituṃ vā na labhāma. Sannipātakāraṇaṃ panettha pubbe vuttaṃ catubbidhameva. Tesu vassūpanāyikasaṅgaho vitthārito. Yathā pana vassūpanāyikāya, evaṃ mahāpavāraṇāyapi puṇṇamadivase sannipatitvā “ajja kattha gantvā kassa santike pavāressāmā”ti mantenti. Tattha sakko devānamindo yebhuyyena piyaṅgudīpamahāvihārasmiṃyeva pavāreti. Sesā devatā pāricchattakādīni [M 2.0242] dibbapupphāni ceva dibbacandanacuṇṇāni ca gahetvā attano attano manāpaṭṭhānameva gantvā pavārenti. Evaṃ pavāraṇasaṅgahatthāya sannipatanti[P 2.0649].

Then, afterwards, 'our seat is there' means we get an opportunity to sit behind them. Beyond that, we do not get to enter or to see. The reason for this gathering, however, is just the fourfold one stated previously. Among them, the assembly concerning the rains-retreat has been explained in detail. Just as for the rains-retreat, so too on the full moon day of the great Pavāraṇā, they gather and deliberate, 'Today, where shall we go and in the presence of which elder shall we perform the Pavāraṇā?' There, Sakka, the lord of the devas, usually performs the Pavāraṇā in the great monastery on Piyangu island itself. The remaining deities, taking divine flowers such as the Pāricchattaka and divine sandalwood powder, go to their own pleasing places and perform the Pavāraṇā. Thus, they gather for the purpose of the Pavāraṇā assembly.

Devaloke [V 2.0217] pana āsāvatī nāma latā atthi. Sā pupphissatīti devā vassasahassaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Pāricchattake pupphamāne ekavassaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Te tassa paṇḍupalāsādibhāvato paṭṭhāya attamanā honti. Yathāha –

Now, in the deva world, there is a creeper named Āsāvatī. Thinking, 'It will bloom,' the devas go to attend upon it for a thousand years. When the Pāricchattaka is about to bloom, they go to attend upon it for one year. They become delighted from the time its leaves begin to turn pale yellow. As it is said:

“Yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, samaye devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ pāricchattako koviḷāro paṇḍupalāso hoti, attamanā, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṃsā tasmiṃ samaye honti – ‘paṇḍupalāso kho dāni pāricchattako koviḷāro, na cirasseva pannapalāso bhavissatī’ti. Yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, samaye devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ pāricchattako koviḷāro pannapalāso hoti, khārakajāto hoti, jālakajāto hoti, kuṭumalakajāto hoti, korakajāto hoti. Attamanā, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṃsā tasmiṃ samaye honti – ‘korakajāto dāni pāricchattako koviḷāro na cirasseva sabbapāliphullo bhavissatī’ti (a. ni. 7.69).

‘Bhikkhus, at the time when the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has pale leaves, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are delighted, thinking: “Now the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has pale leaves; before long it will be shedding its leaves.” Bhikkhus, at the time when the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has shed its leaves, has produced shoots, has formed a network of buds, has formed large buds, and has formed opening buds, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are delighted, thinking: “Now the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has formed opening buds; before long it will be in full bloom.”’

Sabbapāliphullassa kho pana, bhikkhave, pāricchattakassa koviḷārassa samantā paññāsa yojanāni ābhāya phuṭaṃ hoti, anuvātaṃ yojanasataṃ gandho gacchati. Ayamānubhāvo pāricchattakassa koviḷārassā”ti.

‘Furthermore, Bhikkhus, of the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree when it is in full bloom, its radiance pervades fifty yojanas all around, and its fragrance travels a hundred yojanas downwind. Such is the spiritual power of the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree.’

Pupphite pāricchattake ārohaṇakiccaṃ vā aṅkusakaṃ gahetvā namanakiccaṃ vā pupphāharaṇatthaṃ caṅkoṭakakiccaṃ vā natthi, kantanakavāto uṭṭhahitvā pupphāni vaṇṭato kantati, sampaṭicchanakavāto sampaṭicchati, pavesanakavāto sudhammaṃ devasabhaṃ paveseti, sammajjanakavāto purāṇapupphāni nīharati, santharaṇakavāto pattakaṇṇikakesarāni naccanto santharati, majjhaṭṭhāne dhammāsanaṃ hoti. Yojanappamāṇo ratanapallaṅko upari tiyojanena setacchattena dhārayamānena, tadanantaraṃ sakkassa devarañño [M 2.0243] āsanaṃ atthariyati. Tato tettiṃsāya devaputtānaṃ, tato aññāsaṃ mahesakkhadevatānaṃ. Aññataradevatānaṃ pana pupphakaṇṇikāva āsanaṃ hoti.

When the Pāricchattaka has blossomed, there is no need for climbing, or for taking a hook to bend the branches, or for a basket to gather the flowers. A cutting wind arises and cuts the flowers from their stems; a receiving wind catches them; an ushering wind brings them into the Sudhammā deva-assembly hall; a sweeping wind removes the old flowers; and a spreading wind, as if dancing, strews the petals, pericarps, and stamens. In the center is the Dhamma seat. There is a jeweled couch, one yojana in size, with a white canopy held three yojanas above it. Next to that, the seat of Sakka, king of the devas, is spread. Then, the seats for the thirty-three devaputtas, and then for other deities of great power. For certain other deities, however, the pericarp of a flower itself serves as their seat.

Devā devasabhaṃ pavisitvā nisīdanti. Tato pupphehi reṇuvaṭṭi uggantvā upari kaṇṇikaṃ āhacca nipatamānā devatānaṃ tigāvutappamāṇaṃ attabhāvaṃ lākhārasaparikammasajjitaṃ viya [P 2.0650] karoti. Tesaṃ sā kīḷā catūhi māsehi pariyosānaṃ gacchati. Evaṃ pāricchattakakīḷānubhavanatthāya sannipatanti.

The devas enter the deva-assembly hall and take their seats. Then, a cloud of pollen rises from the flowers, strikes the pinnacle above, and as it falls, it makes the bodies of the deities, which are three gāvutas in size, appear as if adorned with lac-dye. That sport of theirs comes to an end in four months. Thus, they gather for the purpose of experiencing the sport of the Pāricchattaka.

Māsassa [V 2.0218] pana aṭṭhadivase devaloke mahādhammasavanaṃ ghusati. Tattha sudhammāyaṃ devasabhāyaṃ sanaṅkumāro vā mahābrahmā, sakko vā devānamindo, dhammakathikabhikkhu vā, aññataro vā dhammakathiko devaputto dhammakathaṃ katheti. Aṭṭhamiyaṃ pakkhassa catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ amaccā, cātuddasiyaṃ puttā, pannarase sayaṃ cattāro mahārājāno nikkhamitvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭañca jātihiṅgulakañca gaṇhitvā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo anuvicaranti. Te – “asukā nāma itthī vā puriso vā buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato. Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato. Pañcasīlāni rakkhati. Māsassa aṭṭha uposathe karoti. Mātuupaṭṭhānaṃ pūreti. Pituupaṭṭhānaṃ pūreti. Asukaṭṭhāne uppalahatthakasatena pupphakumbhena pūjā katā. Dīpasahassaṃ āropitaṃ. Akāladhammasavanaṃ kāritaṃ. Chattavedikā puṭavedikā kucchivedikā sīhāsanaṃ sīhasopānaṃ kāritaṃ. Tīṇi sucaritāni pūreti. Dasakusalakammapathe samādāya vattatī”ti suvaṇṇapaṭṭe jātihiṅgulakena likhitvā āharitvā pañcasikhassa hatthe denti. Pañcasikho mātalissa hatthe deti. Mātali saṅgāhako sakkassa devarañño deti.

On the eighth day of the month, a great Dhamma hearing is proclaimed in the deva realm. There, in the Sudhammā divine assembly hall, either Sanankumāra the Mahābrahmā, or Sakka, the lord of devas, or a Dhamma-preaching bhikkhu, or some other Dhamma-preaching devaputta delivers a Dhamma talk. On the eighth day of the fortnight, the ministers of the Four Great Kings, on the fourteenth, their sons, and on the fifteenth, the Four Great Kings themselves go forth, taking golden tablets and genuine vermilion, and wander through villages, towns, and royal cities. They record: 'Such and such a woman or man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; observes the five precepts; observes the eight uposathas of the month; fulfills their duties to their mother and father. In such-and-such a place an offering was made with a hundred handfuls of lotuses and an urn of flowers; a thousand lamps were lit; a Dhamma hearing was arranged at an uncustomary time; a canopied platform, a surrounding platform, a central platform, a lion throne, and a lion staircase were caused to be built. They fulfill the three kinds of good conduct and live having undertaken the ten wholesome courses of action.' Having inscribed this on golden tablets with genuine vermilion, they bring them and place them in the hands of Pañcasikha. Pañcasikha gives them to Mātali, and Mātali, the benefactor, presents them to Sakka, the king of devas.

Yadā puññakammakārakā bahū na honti, potthako khuddako hoti, taṃ disvāva devā – “pamatto, vata bho mahājano viharati, cattāro apāyā paripūrissanti, cha devalokā tucchā bhavissantī”ti anattamanā honti. Sace pana potthako mahā hoti, taṃ disvāva devā – “appamatto, vata bho, mahājano viharati, cattāro apāyā suññā bhavissanti[M 2.0244], cha devalokā paripūrissanti, buddhasāsane puññāni karitvā āgate mahāpuññe purakkhatvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷituṃ labhissāmā”ti attamanā honti. Taṃ potthakaṃ gahetvā sakko devarājā vāceti. Tassa pakatiniyāmena kathentassa saddo dvādasa yojanāni gaṇhāti. Uccena sarena kathentassa ca sakalaṃ dasayojanasahassaṃ devanagaraṃ chādetvā tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ dhammasavanatthāya sannipatanti. Idha pana pavāraṇasaṅgahatthāya sannipatitāti veditabbā.

When the doers of meritorious deeds are few, the record becomes small. Seeing this, the devas are displeased: 'Alas, the multitude lives heedlessly! The four states of woe will be full, and the six heavenly realms will be empty.' But if the record is large, seeing this, the devas are pleased: 'Indeed, the multitude lives heedfully! The four states of woe will be empty, and the six heavenly realms will be full. Having performed meritorious deeds in the Buddha's Dispensation, and having honored the greatly meritorious ones who arrive, we shall have the opportunity to celebrate a festival.' Taking that record, Sakka, the king of devas, recites it. The sound of him speaking in his natural manner extends for twelve yojanas. And when he speaks in a high tone, it stands covering the entire ten-thousand-yojana celestial city. Thus, they assemble to hear the Dhamma. Here, however, it should be understood that they assembled for the purpose of the Pavāraṇā gathering.

Tathāgataṃ namassantāti navahi kāraṇehi tathāgataṃ namassamānā[P 2.0651]. Dhammassa ca sudhammatanti svākkhātatādibhedaṃ dhammassa sudhammataṃ ujuppaṭipannatādibhedaṃ saṅghassa ca suppaṭipattinti attho.

'Paying homage to the Tathāgata' means paying homage to the Tathāgata for nine reasons. 'And the good nature of the Dhamma' means the good nature of the Dhamma, distinguished by being well-proclaimed and so on. And 'the good practice of the Saṅgha' means the good practice of the Saṅgha, distinguished by upright practice and so on. This is the meaning.

Aṭṭhayathābhuccavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Eight Truthful Qualities

296. Yathābhucceti yathābhūte yathāsabhāve. Vaṇṇeti guṇe. Payirudāhāsīti kathesi. Bahujanahitāya [V 2.0219] paṭipannoti kathaṃ paṭipanno? Dīpaṅkarapādamūle aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā buddhatthāya abhinīharamānopi bahujanahitāya paṭipanno nāma hoti.

296. 'Yathābhucca' means as it truly is, according to its true nature. 'Vaṇṇeti' means to describe the qualities. 'Payirudāhāsi' means he spoke. 'Practicing for the welfare of many'—how was he practicing? Even while combining the eight qualities at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara and making an aspiration for Buddhahood, he is said to be practicing for the welfare of many.

Dānapāramī, sīlapāramī, nekkhammapāramī, paññāpāramī, vīriyapāramī, khantipāramī, saccapāramī, adhiṭṭhānapāramī, mettāpāramī, upekkhāpāramīti kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni imā dasa pāramiyo pūrentopi bahujanahitāya paṭipanno.

The perfection of generosity, the perfection of virtue, the perfection of renunciation, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of energy, the perfection of patience, the perfection of truthfulness, the perfection of determination, the perfection of loving-kindness, and the perfection of equanimity—even while fulfilling these ten perfections for four incalculable eons and an additional one hundred thousand kappas, he was practicing for the welfare of many.

Khantivāditāpasakāle, cūḷadhammapālakumārakāle, chaddantanāgarājakāle, bhūridattacampeyyasaṅkhapālanāgarājakāle, mahākapikāle ca tādisāni dukkarāni karontopi bahujanahitāya paṭipanno. Vessantarattabhāve ṭhatvā sattasatakamahādānaṃ datvā sattasu ṭhānesu pathaviṃ kampetvā pāramīkūṭaṃ gaṇhantopi bahujanahitāya paṭipanno. Tato anantare attabhāve tusitapure yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhantopi bahujanahitāya paṭipanno.

During the time he was the ascetic Khantivādī, the prince Cūḷadhammapāla, the elephant king Chaddanta, the nāga kings Bhūridatta, Campeyya, and Saṅkhapāla, and the great monkey—even while performing such difficult deeds, he was practicing for the welfare of many. In his existence as Vessantara, giving the great seven-hundredfold gift, causing the earth to quake in seven places, and reaching the summit of the perfections, he was practicing for the welfare of many. In the existence immediately following that one, dwelling in the Tusita celestial realm for his entire lifespan, he was practicing for the welfare of many.

Tattha pañca pubbanimittāni disvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatāhi yācito pañca mahāvilokanāni viloketvā devānaṃ saṅgahatthāya paṭiññaṃ datvā tusitapurā [M 2.0245] cavitvā mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantopi bahujanahitāya paṭipanno.

There, seeing the five premonitory signs, being requested by the deities of the ten-thousand-world-system, surveying the five great surveys, giving a promise to the devas for their benefit, passing away from the Tusita heaven, and taking conception in his mother's womb—even then, he was practicing for the welfare of many.

Dasa māse mātukucchiyaṃ vasitvā lumbinīvane mātukucchito nikkhamantopi, ekūnatiṃsavassāni agāraṃ ajjhāvasitvā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā anomanadītīre pabbajantopi, chabbassāni padhānena attānaṃ kilametvā bodhipallaṅkaṃ āruyha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhantopi, sattasattāhaṃ bodhimaṇḍe yāpentopi, isipatanaṃ āgamma anuttaraṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavattentopi, yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karontopi, devorohaṇaṃ orohantopi, buddho hutvā pañcacattālīsa vassāni tiṭṭhantopi, āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajantopi, yamakasālānamantare anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyantopi [P 2.0652] bahujanahitāya paṭipanno. Yāvassa sāsapamattāpi dhātuyo dharanti, tāva bahujanahitāya paṭipannoti veditabbo. Sesapadāni etasseva vevacanāni. Tattha pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ purimassa purimassa attho.

Dwelling in his mother’s womb for ten months and emerging in the Lumbinī grove; living in the household for twenty-nine years, going forth in the great renunciation, and becoming ordained on the bank of the river Anomā; wearying himself with striving for six years, ascending the seat of enlightenment, and penetrating the knowledge of omniscience; spending seven weeks at the site of enlightenment; going to Isipatana and setting in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of the Dhamma; performing the twin miracle; descending from the deva realm; living as the Buddha for forty-five years; relinquishing his life-constituent; and attaining final Nibbāna without remainder between the twin sāla trees—in all these instances, he was practicing for the welfare of many. As long as even a mustard seed’s worth of his relics endure, so long should he be understood as one practicing for the welfare of many. The remaining terms are synonyms of this. Therein, each latter term is the meaning of each former term.

Neva atītaṃse samanupassāma, na panetarahīti atītepi buddhato aññaṃ na samanupassāma, anāgatepi na samanupassāma, etarahi pana aññassa satthuno abhāvatoyeva aññatra tena bhagavatā na samanupassāmāti ayamettha attho. Aṭṭhakathāyampi hi – “atītānāgatā buddhā amhākaṃ [V 2.0220] satthārā sadisāyeva, kiṃ sakko kathetī”ti vicāretvā – “etarahi bahujanahitāya paṭipanno satthā amhākaṃ satthāraṃ muñcitvā añño koci natthi, tasmā na passāmāti kathetī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā ca ettha, evaṃ ito paresupi padesu ayamattho veditabbo. Svākkhātādīni ca kusalādīni ca vuttatthāneva.

We do not perceive anyone in the past, nor indeed in the present. This means that in the past we do not perceive anyone other than the Buddha, nor do we perceive anyone in the future, and now, due to the absence of another teacher, we do not perceive anyone other than that Blessed One—this is the meaning here. For in the commentary too, it is said: 'Past and future Buddhas are just like our Teacher. What is Sakka saying?' Having considered this, it is stated: 'Now, there is no other teacher, apart from our Teacher who is practicing for the welfare of many. Therefore, he says, “we do not perceive.”' Just as here, so too in the passages that follow, this meaning should be understood. As for 'well-proclaimed' and 'skillful,' their meanings are as previously stated.

Gaṅgodakaṃ yamunodakenāti gaṅgāyamunānaṃ samāgamaṭṭhāne udakaṃ vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi saṃsandati sameti, majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ekasadisameva hoti, na mahāsamuddaudakena saṃsaṭṭhakāle viya visadisaṃ. Parisuddhassa nibbānassa paṭipadāpi parisuddhāva. Na hi daharakāle vejjakammādīni katvā agocare caritvā mahallakakāle nibbānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ sakkā, nibbānagāminī pana paṭipadā parisuddhāva vaṭṭati ākāsūpamā. Yathā hi ākāsampi alaggaṃ parisuddhaṃ candimasūriyānaṃ ākāse icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantānaṃ viya nibbānaṃ gacchantassa bhikkhuno paṭipadāpi kule vā gaṇe vā alaggā [M 2.0246] abaddhā ākāsūpamā vaṭṭati. Sā panesā tādisāva bhagavatā paññattā kathitā desitā. Tena vuttaṃ – “saṃsandati nibbānañca paṭipadā cā”ti.

The water of the Ganges with the water of the Yamuna—at the confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna, the waters blend and merge in color, fragrance, and taste. In the middle, they become as one, like refined gold, not dissimilar as when mixed with the waters of the great ocean. The path to purified Nibbāna is likewise pure. For it is not possible for one who, in youth, engages in medical practices and wanders in improper places, to see Nibbāna in old age. The path leading to Nibbāna, however, should be pure, like the sky. For just as the sky is unattached and pure for the moon and sun traveling to whatever place they wish, so too the path of a bhikkhu going to Nibbāna should be unattached and unbound to family or group, like the sky. And this very path of such a kind was proclaimed, declared, and taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: 'Nibbāna and the path converge.'

Paṭipannānanti paṭipadāya ṭhitānaṃ. Vusitavatanti vutthavāsānaṃ etesaṃ. Laddhasahāyoti etesaṃ tattha tattha saha ayanato sahāyo. “Adutiyo asahāyo appaṭisamo”ti idaṃ pana asadisaṭṭhena vuttaṃ. Apanujjāti tesaṃ majjhepi phalasamāpattiyā viharanto cittena apanujja, apanujjeva ekārāmataṃ anuyutto viharatīti attho.

'Of those practicing' means of those established in the path. 'Of those who have lived the life' means of those who have completed the dwelling in the holy life. 'He has obtained companions' means he has companions from going together with them here and there. But the phrase 'without a second, without a companion, without an equal' is said in the sense of being incomparable. 'He dispels' means that even while in their midst, dwelling in the attainment of fruition, having dispelled them with his mind—having indeed dispelled them—he dwells devoted to delighting in solitude; this is the meaning.

Abhinipphanno [P 2.0653] kho pana tassa bhagavato lābhoti tassa bhagavato mahālābho uppanno. Kadā paṭṭhāya uppanno? Abhisambodhiṃ patvā sattasattāhaṃ atikkamitvā isipatane dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā anukkamena devamanussānaṃ damanaṃ karontassa tayo jaṭile pabbājetvā rājagahaṃ gatassa bimbisāradamanato paṭṭhāya uppanno. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.70). Satasahassakappādhikesu catūsu asaṅkhyeyyesu ussannapuññanissandasamuppanno lābhasakkāro mahogho viya ajjhottharamāno āgacchati.

Indeed, the gain of that Blessed One was fully accomplished; a great gain arose for that Blessed One. From when did it arise? After attaining full enlightenment, passing seven weeks, setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana, gradually taming gods and humans, ordaining the three matted-hair ascetics, and going to Rājagaha, it arose from the taming of Bimbisāra onwards. In reference to this, it was said: 'At that time the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed; he was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and requisites for the sick.' The gain and honor, produced as the result of abundant merit accumulated over four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand more, came overwhelming like a great flood.

Ekasmiṃ kira samaye rājagahe sāvatthiyaṃ sākete kosambiyaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃ bhagavato paṭipāṭibhattaṃ [V 2.0221] nāma uppannaṃ, tattheko – “ahaṃ sataṃ vissajjetvā dānaṃ dassāmī”ti paṇṇaṃ likhitvā vihāradvāre bandhi. Añño – ahaṃ dve satāni. Añño – ahaṃ pañca satāni. Añño – ahaṃ sahassaṃ. Añño – ahaṃ dve sahassāni. Añño – ahaṃ pañca. Dasa. Vīsati. Paññāsaṃ; añño – ahaṃ satasahassaṃ. Añño – ahaṃ dve satasahassāni vissajjetvā dānaṃ dassāmī”ti paṇṇaṃ likhitvā vihāradvāre bandhi. Janapadacārikaṃ carantampi okāsaṃ labhitvā – “dānaṃ dassāmī”ti sakaṭāni pūretvā mahājano anubandhiyeva. Yathāha – “tena kho pana samayena jānapadā manussā bahuṃ loṇampi telampi taṇḍulampi khādanīyampi sakaṭesu āropetvā bhagavato piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhā honti – ‘yattha paṭipāṭiṃ [M 2.0247] labhissāma, tattha bhattaṃ karissāmā’ti” (mahāva. 282). Evaṃ aññānipi khandhake ca vinaye ca bahūni vatthūni veditabbāni.

It is said that at one time, in Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Bārāṇasī, a turn-by-turn meal offering for the Blessed One arose. There, one person wrote a notice saying, 'I will give a donation, spending one hundred,' and tied it at the monastery gate. Another: 'I, two hundred.' Another: 'I, five hundred.' Another: 'I, one thousand.' Another: 'I, two thousand.' Another: 'I, five.' 'Ten.' 'Twenty.' 'Fifty.' Another: 'I, one hundred thousand.' Another: 'I will give a donation, spending two hundred thousand,' and tied the notice at the monastery gate. Even while the Blessed One was traveling on tour through the countryside, a great crowd, having obtained an opportunity and thinking, 'We will give a donation,' would follow him, having filled their carts. As it is said: 'At that time, people from the countryside loaded much salt, oil, rice, and edible food onto carts and followed right behind the Blessed One, thinking, “Wherever we get our turn, there we will prepare a meal.”' Thus, many other such accounts in the Khandhakas and the Vinaya should be understood.

Asadisadāne panesa lābho matthakaṃ patto. Ekasmiṃ kira samaye bhagavati janapadacārikaṃ caritvā jetavanaṃ sampatte rājā nimantetvā dānaṃ adāsi. Dutiyadivase nāgarā adaṃsu. Puna tesaṃ dānato atirekaṃ rājā, tassa dānato atirekaṃ nāgarāti evaṃ bahūsu divasesu gatesu rājā cintesi – “ime nāgarā divase divase atirekataraṃ karonti, pathavissaro pana rājā nāgarehi dāne parājitoti garahā bhavissatī”ti. Athassa mallikā upāyaṃ ācikkhi. So rājaṅgaṇe sālakalyāṇipadarehi maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā taṃ nīluppalehi [P 2.0654] chādetvā pañca āsanasatāni paññāpetvā pañca hatthisatāni āsanānaṃ pacchābhāge ṭhapetvā ekekena hatthinā ekekassa bhikkhuno setacchattaṃ dhārāpesi. Dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ āsanānaṃ antare sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā ekekā khattiyadhītā catujjātiyagandhaṃ pisati. Niṭṭhitaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ majjhaṭṭhāne gandhambaṇe pakkhipati, taṃ aparā khattiyadhītā nīluppalahatthakena samparivatteti. Evaṃ ekekassa bhikkhuno tisso tisso khattiyadhītaro parivārā, aparā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā itthī tālavaṇṭaṃ gahetvā bījati, aññā dhamakaraṇaṃ gahetvā udakaṃ parissāveti, aññā pattato udakaṃ harati. Bhagavato cattāri anagghāni ahesuṃ. Pādakathalikā ādhārako apassenaphalakaṃ chattapādamaṇīti imāni cattāri anagghāni ahesuṃ. Saṅghanavakassa deyyadhammo satasahassaṃ agghati. Tasmiñca dāne aṅgulimālatthero saṅghanavako ahosi. Tassa āsanasamīpe ānīto hatthī taṃ upagantuṃ nāsakkhi. Tato rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā – “añño hatthī natthī”ti? Duṭṭhahatthī pana atthi, ānetuṃ na sakkāti. Sammāsambuddho – saṅghanavako kataro mahārājāti? Aṅgulimālatthero bhagavāti. Tena hi taṃ duṭṭhahatthiṃ ānetvā ṭhapetu, mahārājāti. Hatthiṃ maṇḍayitvā ānayiṃsu. So therassa tejena nāsāvātasañcaraṇamattampi [V 2.0222] kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Evaṃ nirantaraṃ satta divasāni dānaṃ dīyittha. Sattame divase rājā dasabalaṃ vanditvā – “bhagavā mayhaṃ dhammaṃ desethā”ti āha.

Now, this gain in the Unsurpassed Alms-giving reached its peak. Once, it is said, when the Blessed One, having wandered on tour through the countryside, arrived at Jetavana, the king invited him and gave alms. On the following day, the citizens gave. Again, the king gave more than their gift, and the citizens gave even more than his gift. Thus, after many days had passed, the king thought: 'These citizens give increasingly more each day. But the king, lord of the earth, will be censured for being defeated by the citizens in giving.' Then Mallikā suggested a plan to him. He had a pavilion built in the royal courtyard with planks of the finest sāla wood and arranged five hundred seats. He stationed five hundred elephants behind the seats, causing each elephant to hold a white parasol for each monk. Between every two seats stood a beautifully adorned noble maiden, grinding perfume of four kinds. As it was ground, she placed it in a fragrant container in the middle, and another noble maiden stirred it with a blue lotus. Thus, each monk had three noble maidens as attendants. Another woman, adorned with all ornaments, held a palm-leaf fan and fanned him, while another carried a water strainer and strained water, and another removed the water from the bowl. For the Blessed One there were four priceless items: a foot-stool, a bowl-stand, a leaning-board, and a jewel for the base of the parasol—these four were priceless. The offering for the Sangha's junior-most monk was worth a hundred thousand. At that alms-giving, the Elder Aṅgulimāla was the Sangha's junior-most monk. The elephant that was brought near his seat could not approach him. Then they informed the king. The king asked, 'Is there no other elephant?' They replied, 'There is a rogue elephant, but it is not possible to bring it.' The Perfectly Enlightened One asked, 'Great king, who is the Sangha's junior-most monk?' 'The Elder Aṅgulimāla, Blessed One.' 'Then, great king, have that rogue elephant brought and stationed there.' They adorned the elephant and brought it. But due to the elder’s power, it could not even make the slightest movement of air through its trunk. Thus, for seven days without interruption, the alms were given. On the seventh day, the king paid homage to the Ten-Powered One and said, 'Blessed One, please teach me the Dhamma.'

Tassañca [M 2.0248] parisati kāḷo ca juṇho cāti dve amaccā honti. Kāḷo cintesi – “nassati rājakulassa santakaṃ, kiṃ nāmete ettakā janā karissanti, bhuñjitvā vihāraṃ gantvā niddāyissanteva, idaṃ pana eko rājapuriso labhitvā kiṃ nāma na kareyya, aho nassati rañño santaka”nti. Juṇho cintesi – “mahantaṃ idaṃ rājattanaṃ nāma, ko añño idaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissati? Kiṃ rājā nāma so, yo rājattane ṭhitopi evarūpaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ na sakkotī”ti. Bhagavā parisāya ajjhāsayaṃ olokento tesaṃ dvinnaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā – “sace ajja juṇhassa ajjhāsayena dhammakathaṃ kathemi, kāḷassa sattadhā muddhā phalissati[P 2.0655]. Mayā kho pana sattānuddayatāya pāramiyo pūritā. Juṇho aññasmimpi divase mayi dhammaṃ kathayante maggaphalaṃ paṭivijjhissati, idāni pana kāḷaṃ olokessāmī”ti rañño catuppadikameva gāthaṃ abhāsi –

In that assembly there were two ministers, Kāḷa and Juṇha. Kāḷa thought: 'The royal family's property is being destroyed. What will so many people do? After eating, they will go to the monastery and just sleep. If a single royal official were to obtain this, what would he not do? Alas, the king’s property is being destroyed!' Juṇha thought: 'Great indeed is this kingship! Who else would be capable of doing this? What kind of king is one who, though established in kingship, is unable to give such a gift?' The Blessed One, observing the inclinations of the assembly, understood the intentions of these two. He thought: 'If today I deliver a Dhamma talk in line with Juṇha’s inclination, Kāḷa’s head will split into seven pieces. But I have fulfilled the perfections out of compassion for beings. Juṇha will realize the path and its fruits on another day when I teach the Dhamma. For now, I will be considerate of Kāḷa.' Then he spoke only this four-lined verse to the king:

“Na ve kadariyā devalokaṃ vajanti,

Bālā have nappasaṃsanti dānaṃ;

Dhīro ca dānaṃ anumodamāno,

Teneva so hoti sukhī paratthā”ti. (dha. pa. 177);

The miserly do not go to the world of the gods; fools indeed do not praise giving. But the wise one, rejoicing in giving, thereby is happy hereafter.

Rājā anattamano hutvā – “mayā mahādānaṃ dinnaṃ, satthā ca me mandameva dhammaṃ kathesi, nāsakkhiṃ maññe dasabalassa cittaṃ gahetu”nti. So bhuttapātarāso vihāraṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pucchi – “mayā, bhante, mahantaṃ dānaṃ dinnaṃ, anumodanā ca me na mahatī katā, ko nu kho me, bhante, doso”ti? Natthi, mahārāja, tava doso, parisā pana aparisuddhā, tasmā dhammaṃ na desesinti. Kasmā pana bhagavā parisā na suddhāti? Satthā dvinnaṃ amaccānaṃ parivitakkaṃ ārocesi. Rājā kāḷaṃ pucchi – “evaṃ, tāta, kāḷā”ti? “Evaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Mayi mama santakaṃ dadamāne tava kataraṃ ṭhānaṃ rujjati, na taṃ sakkomi passituṃ, pabbājetha naṃ mama raṭṭhato”ti āha. Tato juṇhaṃ pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “evaṃ kira, tāta, cintesī”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Tava cittānurūpameva hotū”ti tasmiṃyeva maṇḍape evaṃ paññattesuyeva āsanesu pañca bhikkhusatāni nisīdāpetvā tāyeva khattiyadhītaro [V 2.0223] parivārāpetvā rājagehato dhanaṃ gahetvā mayā [M 2.0249] dinnasadisameva satta divasāni dānaṃ dehīti. So tathā adāsi. Datvā sattame divase – “dhammaṃ bhagavā desethā”ti āha.

The king, displeased, thought: 'I have given a great gift, yet the Teacher preached to me only a brief teaching. I suppose I was unable to capture the mind of the Ten-Powered One.' After finishing his morning meal, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and asked: 'Venerable sir, I have given a great gift, yet the discourse of appreciation given for me was not great. What, venerable sir, is my fault?' 'There is no fault in you, great king, but the assembly was impure; therefore I did not teach the Dhamma at length.' 'But why, Blessed One, was the assembly impure?' The Teacher then revealed the thoughts of the two ministers. The king asked Kāḷa: 'Is it so, my dear Kāḷa?' 'It is so, great king.' 'When I am giving away my own property, what concern is it of yours? I cannot bear to see you; banish him from my kingdom!' he said. Then he had Juṇha summoned and asked: 'Is it true, my dear sir, that you thought in this way?' 'Yes, great king.' 'Let it be according to your thought! In that very same pavilion, on those very seats that were prepared, seat five hundred monks, have them attended by those same noble maidens, take wealth from the royal treasury, and for seven days give alms just like those given by me.' So the minister gave accordingly. Having given thus, on the seventh day he said: 'Blessed One, please teach the Dhamma!'

Satthā dvinnampi dānānaṃ anumodanaṃ ekato katvā dve mahānadiyo ekoghapuṇṇā kurumāno viya mahādhammadesanaṃ desesi. Desanāpariyosāne juṇho sotāpanno ahosi. Rājā pasīditvā dasabalassa bāhiravatthuṃ nāma adāsi. Evaṃ abhinipphanno kho pana tassa bhagavato lābhoti veditabbo.

The Teacher, having given the anumodanā for both gifts as one, delivered a great Dhamma discourse, as if making two great rivers full with a single flood. At the end of the discourse, Juṇha became a stream-enterer. The king, pleased, gave an external object to the Ten-Powered One. Thus, it should be understood that the gain of the Blessed One was accomplished.

Abhinipphanno [P 2.0656] silokoti vaṇṇaguṇakittanaṃ. Sopi bhagavato dhammacakkappavattanato paṭṭhāya abhinipphanno. Tato paṭṭhāya hi bhagavato khattiyāpi vaṇṇaṃ kathenti. Brāhmaṇāpi gahapatayopi nāgā supaṇṇā gandhabbā devatā brahmānopi kittiṃ vatvā – “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā. Aññatitthiyāpi vararojassa sahassaṃ datvā samaṇassa gotamassa avaṇṇaṃ kathehīti uyyojesuṃ. So sahassaṃ gahetvā dasabalaṃ pādatalato paṭṭhāya yāva kesantā apalokayamāno likkhāmattampi vajjaṃ adisvā – “vippakiṇṇadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇe asītianubyañjanavibhūsite byāmappabhāparikkhitte suphullitapāricchattakatārāgaṇasamujjalitaantalikkhavicittakusumasassirikanandanavanasadise anavajjaattabhāve avaṇṇaṃ vadantassa mukhampi viparivatteyya, muddhāpi sattadhā phaleyya, avaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ upāyo natthi, vaṇṇameva vadissāmī”ti pādatalato paṭṭhāya yāva kesantā atirekapadasahassena vaṇṇameva kathesi. Yamakapāṭihāriye panesa vaṇṇo nāma matthakaṃ patto. Evaṃ abhinipphanno silokoti.

The accomplished fame is the proclamation of qualities and virtues. This also came to be from the Blessed One's setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma. From that time onward, khattiyas praised the Blessed One; brahmins, householders, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, devas, and even brahmās, proclaiming his glory, saying, 'Indeed, the Blessed One is...' and so on. Even followers of other sects, having given a thousand to Vararoja, urged him, 'Speak ill of the ascetic Gotama.' Taking the thousand, he examined the Ten-Powered One from the soles of his feet up to the end of his hair, and not seeing even a fault the size of a nit's egg, he reflected: 'In one endowed with the thirty-two scattered marks of a great man, adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, like a Nandana Grove splendid with variegated flowers, like the sky illumined by a cluster of stars, like a fully blossomed Pāricchattaka tree—in such a flawless being, the mouth of one speaking ill would surely twist, and his head would split into seven pieces. There is no way to speak ill of him; I will speak only praise.' And so, from the soles of his feet up to the end of his hair, he spoke only praise with more than a thousand verses. This praise, moreover, reached its peak at the Twin Miracle. Thus, his fame was accomplished.

Yāva maññe khattiyāti khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā suddā nāgā supaṇṇā yakkhā asurā devā brahmānoti sabbeva te sampiyāyamānarūpā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā viharanti. Vigatamado kho panāti ettakā maṃ janā sampiyāyamānarūpā viharantīti na madapamatto hutvā davādivasena āhāraṃ āhāreti, aññadatthu vigatamado kho pana so bhagavā āhāraṃ āhāreti.

As far as one might think, nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, nāgas, supaṇṇas, yakkhas, asuras, devas, and brahmās—all of them dwell appearing fond, delighted, and pleased. Indeed, he is without vanity. Thinking, 'So many people dwell appearing fond of me,' he does not become intoxicated with vanity and take food for sport and amusement. Rather, the Blessed One, being truly without vanity, partakes of food.

Yathāvādīti [M 2.0250] yaṃ vācāya vadati, tadanvayamevassa kāyakammaṃ hoti. Yañca kāyena karoti, tadanvayamevassa vacīkammaṃ hoti. Kāyo vā vācaṃ, vācā vā kāyaṃ nātikkamati, vācā kāyena, kāyo ca vācāya sameti. Yathā ca –

As he speaks, so he acts; his bodily action accords with his speech. And what he does with his body, his verbal action accords with that. The body does not transgress speech, nor does speech transgress the body; speech accords with the body, and the body with speech. And just as –

“Vāmena [V 2.0224] sūkaro hoti, dakkhiṇena ajāmigo;

Sarena nelako hoti, visāṇena jaraggavo”ti. –

On the left, he is a boar; on the right, a goat-deer; by his cry, a young bull; by his horns, an old ox.

Ayaṃ sūkarayakkho sūkare disvā sūkarasadisaṃ vāmapassaṃ dassetvā te gahetvā khādati, ajāmige disvā taṃsadisaṃ [P 2.0657] dakkhiṇapassaṃ dassetvā te gahetvā khādati, nelakavacchake disvā vacchakaravaṃ ravanto te gahetvā khādati, goṇe disvā tesaṃ visāṇasadisāni visāṇāni māpetvā te dūratova – “goṇo viya dissatī”ti evaṃ upagate gahetvā khādati. Yathā ca dhammikavāyasajātake sakuṇehi puṭṭho vāyaso – “ahaṃ vātabhakkho, vātabhakkhatāya mukhaṃ vivaritvā pāṇakānañca maraṇabhayena ekeneva pādena ṭhito, tasmā tumhepi –

This boar-demon, seeing boars, shows his boar-like left side, then seizes and devours them; seeing goat-deer, he shows his goat-deer-like right side, then seizes and devours them; seeing young calves, he makes the cry of a calf, then seizes and devours them; seeing bulls, he creates horns similar to theirs, and when they approach from afar thinking, 'It looks like a bull,' he seizes and devours them. And just as in the Dhammika Vāyasajātaka, a crow, when asked by the birds, said: 'I am a wind-eater; because I am a wind-eater, I keep my mouth open, and out of fear for the death of living beings, I stand on one foot. Therefore, you also—

“Dhammaṃ caratha bhaddaṃ vo, dhammaṃ caratha ñātayo;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi cā”ti.

Practice the Dhamma, may good be yours; practice the Dhamma, O kinsmen. One who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily in this world and the next.

Sakuṇesu vissāsaṃ uppādesi, tato –

He inspired trust in the birds, then –

“Bhaddako vatāyaṃ pakkhī, dijo paramadhammiko;

Ekapādena tiṭṭhanto, dhammo dhammoti bhāsatī”ti.

What a good bird this is, a twice-born one of supreme righteousness! Standing on one foot, it proclaims, 'Dhamma, Dhamma!'

Evaṃ vissāsamāgate sakuṇe khādittha. Tena tesaṃ vācā kāyena, kāyo ca vācāya na sameti, na evaṃ bhagavato. Bhagavato pana vācā kāyena, kāyo ca vācāya sametiyevāti dasseti.

Thus, he devoured the birds that had come to trust him. Therefore, for such beings, speech does not accord with the body, nor does the body accord with speech—but it is not so for the Blessed One. Rather, it is shown that the Blessed One's speech indeed accords with his body, and his body with his speech.

Tiṇṇā taritā vicikicchā assāti tiṇṇavicikiccho. “Kathamidaṃ kathamida”nti evarūpā vigatā kathaṃkathā assāti vigatakathaṃkatho. Yathā hi mahājano – “ayaṃ rukkho, kiṃ rukkho nāma, ayaṃ gāmo, ayaṃ janapado, idaṃ raṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ raṭṭhaṃ nāma, kasmā nu kho ayaṃ rukkho ujukkhandho, ayaṃ vaṅkakkhandho, kasmā kaṇṭako koci ujuko hoti, koci vaṅko, pupphaṃ kiñci sugandhaṃ, kiñci duggandhaṃ, phalaṃ kiñci [M 2.0251] madhuraṃ, kiñci amadhura”nti sakaṅkhova hoti, na evaṃ satthā. Satthā hi – “imesaṃ nāma dhātūnaṃ ussannussannattā idaṃ evaṃ hotī”ti vigatakathaṃkathova[P 2.0658]. Yathā ca paṭhamajjhānādilābhīnaṃ dutiyajjhānādīsu kaṅkhā hoti. Paccekabuddhānampi [V 2.0225] hi sabbaññutaññāṇe yāthāvasanniṭṭhānābhāvato vohāravasena kaṅkhā nāma hotiyeva, na evaṃ buddhassa. So hi bhagavā sabbattha vigatakathaṃkathoti dasseti.

His doubt is crossed over, gone beyond; hence, he is 'one who has crossed over doubt.' 'How is this? How is that?'—such wavering is gone in him; hence, he is 'one who is free from wavering.' Just as ordinary people might wonder, 'This is a tree, but what kind of tree is it? This is a village... this is a district... this is a kingdom, but what kind of kingdom is it? Why is this tree straight-trunked, while that one is crooked? Why is one thorn straight and another bent? Why is one flower fragrant and another foul-smelling? Why is one fruit sweet and another not sweet?'—they are indeed doubtful. But it is not so for the Teacher. For the Teacher, knowing, 'This is so because of the predominance of these particular elements,' is indeed free from wavering. And just as those who have attained the first jhāna and so on may have doubts about the second jhāna and so on, and even Paccekabuddhas, due to the absence of a conclusive determination as it truly is regarding omniscience, indeed have doubt in terms of convention—it is not so for the Buddha. For it is shown that the Blessed One is free from wavering in all things.

Pariyositasaṅkappoti yathā keci sīlamattena, keci vipassanāmattena, keci paṭhamajjhānena…pe… keci nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā, keci sotāpannabhāvamattena…pe… keci arahattena, keci sāvakapāramīñāṇena, keci paccekabodhiñāṇena pariyositasaṅkappā paripuṇṇamanorathā honti, na evaṃ mama satthā. Mama pana satthā sabbaññutaññāṇena pariyositasaṅkappoti dasseti.

One whose intention is fulfilled: just as some have their intentions fulfilled and their aspirations completed merely by virtue, some merely by insight, some by the first jhāna... some by the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, some merely by the state of a stream-enterer... some by arahantship, some by the knowledge of a disciple's perfections, or some by the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha—it is not so for my Teacher. Rather, it is shown that my Teacher's intention is fulfilled by the knowledge of omniscience.

Ajjhāsayaṃ ādibrahmacariyanti karaṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ, adhikāsayena uttamanissayabhūtena ādibrahmacariyena porāṇabrahmacariyabhūtena ca ariyamaggena tiṇṇavicikiccho vigatakathaṃkatho pariyositasaṅkappoti attho. “Pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto, balesu ca vasībhāva”nti hi vacanato pariyositasaṅkappatāpi bhagavato ariyamaggeneva nipphannāti.

Ajjhāsayaṃ ādibrahmacariyaṃ is a nominative expression in the instrumental sense. The meaning is: one who has crossed over doubt, is free from wavering, and whose intention is fulfilled by means of the noble path, which is an excellent support, has become the supreme refuge, is the initial holy life, and has become the ancient holy life. For, from the saying, “He himself awakened to the truths in things unheard before, attained omniscience therein, and mastery over the powers,” it is understood that the Blessed One’s state of having a fulfilled intention was also accomplished by means of the noble path alone.

297. Yathariva bhagavāti yathā bhagavā, evaṃ ekasmiṃ jambudīpatale catūsu disāsu cārikaṃ caramānā aho vata cattāro jinā dhammaṃ deseyyunti paccāsisamānā vadanti. Athāpare tīsu maṇḍalesu ekato vicaraṇabhāvaṃ ākaṅkhamānā tayo sammāsambuddhāti āhaṃsu. Apare – “dasa pāramiyo nāma pūretvā catunnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā uppatti dullabhā, sace pana eko nibaddhavāsaṃ vasanto dhammaṃ deseyya, eko cārikaṃ caranto, evampi jambudīpo sobheyya ceva, bahuñca hitasukhamadhigaccheyyā”ti cintetvā aho vata, mārisāti āhaṃsu.

297. Yathariva bhagavā means “just as the Blessed One.” Thus, wandering on pilgrimage in the four directions on the single plane of Jambudīpa, they speak, aspiring, “Oh, that four Conquerors might teach the Dhamma!” Then others, desiring a state of wandering together in three regions, said, “Three Perfectly Enlightened Ones.” Others, thinking, “Having fulfilled the ten perfections, the arising of four or three is rare. But if one were to teach the Dhamma while dwelling in a fixed residence, and another while wandering on pilgrimage, even so Jambudīpa would shine and would attain much welfare and happiness,” said, “Oh, may it be so, sirs!”

298. Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yanti ettha ṭhānaṃ avakāsoti ubhayametaṃ kāraṇādhivacanameva. Kāraṇañhi tiṭṭhati [P 2.0659] ettha tadāyattavuttitāya phalanti ṭhānaṃ. Okāso viya cassa taṃ tena vinā aññattha abhāvatoti avakāso. Yanti karaṇatthe paccattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti [M 2.0252] – “yena kāraṇena ekissā lokadhātuyā dve buddhā ekato uppajjeyyuṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ natthī”ti.

298. In the phrase Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ (“This is impossible, there is no opportunity that...”), both ṭhāna and avakāsa are simply designations for cause. For, because the effect, which has its occurrence dependent on it, stands (tiṭṭhati) in it (the cause), it is called ṭhāna (a standing place). And it is like a space (okāsa) for that effect; because without it (the cause), the effect has no existence elsewhere, it is called avakāsa. The word yaṃ is a nominative in the instrumental sense. This is what is said: “That cause by which two Buddhas might arise simultaneously in one world-system does not exist.”

Ettha ca –

And here:

“Yāvatā [V 2.0226] candimasūriyā, pariharanti disā bhanti virocanā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko, ettha te vattate vaso”ti. (ma. ni. 1.503) –

“As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining, illuminating the directions, so far extends the thousandfold world, over which your power prevails.”

Gāthāya ekacakkavāḷameva ekā lokadhātu. “Sahassī lokadhātu akampitthā”ti (a. ni. 3.126) āgataṭṭhāne cakkavāḷasahassaṃ ekā lokadhātu. “Ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, tathāgato tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātuṃ sarena viññāpeyya, obhāsena ca phareyyā”ti (a. ni. 3.81) āgataṭṭhāne tisahassimahāsahassī ekā lokadhātu. “Ayañca dasasahassī lokadhātū”ti (ma. ni. 3.201) āgataṭṭhāne dasacakkavāḷasahassāni ekā lokadhātu. Taṃ sandhāya ekissā lokadhātuyāti āha. Ettakañhi jātikhettaṃ nāma. Tatrāpi ṭhapetvā imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe jambudīpassa majjhimadesaṃ na aññatra buddhā uppajjanti jātikhettato pana paraṃ buddhānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānameva na paññāyati. Yenatthenāti yena pavāraṇasaṅgahatthena.

In the verse, a single Cakkavāḷa is one world-system. In the passage where it is said, “The thousandfold world-system trembled,” a thousand Cakkavāḷas are one world-system. In the passage where it is said, “If he wished, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could make his voice heard throughout the three-thousand great-thousand world-system, or illuminate it with his radiance,” the three-thousand great-thousand world-system is one world-system. In the passage where it is said, “And this ten-thousandfold world-system,” ten thousand Cakkavāḷas are one world-system. With reference to that, he said, “in one world-system.” For this much is called the field of birth. And even there, Buddhas do not arise anywhere other than the Middle Country of Jambudīpa in this Cakkavāḷa. Furthermore, beyond the field of birth, a place for the arising of Buddhas is simply not known. Yenatthenā means: by the reason of being included for the Pavāraṇā.

Sanaṅkumārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Sanaṅkumāra Story

300. Vaṇṇena ceva yasasā cāti alaṅkāraparivārena ca puññasiriyā cāti attho.

300. Vaṇṇena ceva yasasā ca means: by a retinue of adornments and by the glory of merit.

301. Sādhu mahābrahmeti ettha sampasādane sādhusaddo. Saṅkhāya modāmāti jānitvā modāma.

301. Here, in Sādhu mahābrahme, the word sādhu is for expressing approval. By Saṅkhāya modāma is meant: having known, we rejoice.

Govindabrāhmaṇavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Govinda

304. Yāva dīgharattaṃ mahāpaññova so bhagavāti ettakanti paricchinditvā na sakkā vattuṃ, atha kho yāva dīgharattaṃ aticirarattaṃ mahāpaññova so bhagavā. Noti kathaṃ tumhe maññathāti. Atha sayamevetaṃ pañhaṃ byākātukāmo – “anacchariyametaṃ, mārisā, yaṃ idāni pāramiyo [M 2.0253] pūretvā bodhipallaṅke tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ bhinditvā paṭividdhaasādhāraṇañāṇo so bhagavā mahāpañño bhaveyya, kimettha acchariyaṃ, aparipakkāya pana bodhiyā padesañāṇe [P 2.0660] ṭhitassa sarāgādikālepi mahāpaññabhāvameva vo, mārisā, kathessāmī”ti bhavapaṭicchannakāraṇaṃ āharitvā dassento bhūtapubbaṃ bhotiādimāha.

304. Regarding the phrase, “For a long time, the Blessed One was of great wisdom”: it is not possible to define this and say, “it was for this long.” Rather, for a long time, an exceedingly long time, the Blessed One was of great wisdom. Was he not? What do you think? Then, wishing to answer this question himself, he said: “It is no wonder, sirs, that now, having fulfilled the perfections, having shattered the heads of the three Māras at the seat of enlightenment, and having penetrated the unique and extraordinary knowledge, the Blessed One should be of great wisdom. What is astonishing in this? But, sirs, I will tell you of his state of great wisdom even when his enlightenment was immature, while he stood at the stage of partial knowledge, and even during the time he still had passion and so forth.” Then, showing a reason concealed by a past life, he began with, “Once upon a time, sirs…”

Purohitoti sabbakiccāni anusāsanapurohito. Govindoti govindiyābhisekena abhisitto[V 2.0227], pakatiyā panassa aññadeva nāmaṃ, abhisittakālato paṭṭhāya “govindo”ti saṅkhyaṃ gato. Jotipāloti jotanato ca pālanato ca jotipālo. Tassa kira jātadivase sabbāvudhāni ujjotiṃsu. Rājāpi paccūsasamaye attano maṅgalāvudhaṃ pajjalitaṃ disvā bhīto aṭṭhāsi. Govindo pātova rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sukhaseyyaṃ pucchi rājā – “kuto me ācariya, sukhaseyyā”ti vatvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ārocesi. Mā bhāyi, mahārāja, mayhaṃ putto jāto, tassānubhāvena sakalanagare āvudhāni pajjaliṃsūti. Rājā – “kiṃ nu kho me kumāro paccatthiko bhaveyyā”ti cintetvā suṭṭhutaraṃ bhāyi. “Kiṃ vitakkesi mahārājā”ti ca puṭṭho tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ govindo “mā bhāyi mahārāja, neso kumāro tumhākaṃ dubbhissati, sakalajambudīpe pana tena samo paññāya na bhavissati, mama puttassa vacanena mahājanassa kaṅkhā chijjissati, tumhākañca sabbakiccāni anusāsissatī”ti samassāseti. Rājā tuṭṭho – “kumārassa khīramūlaṃ hotū”ti sahassaṃ datvā “kumāraṃ mahallakakāle mama dassethā”ti āha. Kumāro anupubbena vuḍḍhimanuppatto. Jotitattā panassa pālanasamatthatāya ca jotipālotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “jotanato ca pālanato ca jotipālo”ti.

Purohita means the foremost in instructing in all duties. Govinda is so called because he was anointed with the Govinda consecration; but his original name was different. From the time of his anointing, he came to be known as "Govinda." Jotipāla is so called because of his radiance (jotana) and his protection (pālana). On the day of his birth, it is said, all weapons blazed up. The king, too, at dawn, seeing his own auspicious weapon ablaze, stood terrified. Govinda went early to the king’s presence and inquired about his peaceful rest. The king said, "From where, teacher, comes my peaceful rest?" and told him the reason. "Do not fear, great king, my son has been born, and by his power all the weapons in the city blazed up." The king thought, "Could this boy become my adversary?" and became even more afraid. When asked, "What are you thinking, great king?" he explained the matter. Then Govinda reassured him, saying, "Do not fear, great king, this boy will not harm you. In all of Jambudīpa, none will equal him in wisdom. By my son’s words, the doubts of the people will be dispelled, and he will instruct you in all your duties." The king, pleased, said, "Let the boy have milk-money," and gave a thousand [coins], saying, "When the boy is grown, show him to me." The boy gradually grew up. Because of his radiance and his ability to protect, they named him Jotipāla. Hence it is said, "Because of his radiance and protection, he is called Jotipāla."

Sammā vossajjitvāti sammā vossajjitvā. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Alamatthadasataroti samattho paṭibalo atthadaso alamatthadaso, taṃ alamatthadasaṃ tiretīti alamatthadasataro. Jotipālasseva māṇavassa anusāsaniyāti sopi jotipālaṃyeva pucchitvā anusāsatīti dasseti.

By 'having properly relinquished' (sammā vossajjitvā) is meant 'having properly relinquished.' Or this is the correct reading. By 'alamatthadasatara' is meant: an 'alamatthadasa' is one who is capable, able, and perceives the meaning; one who surpasses that 'alamatthadasa' is an 'alamatthadasatara'. By 'the instruction of the youth Jotipāla' is shown that he too instructed after questioning Jotipāla himself.

305. Bhavamatthu [M 2.0254] bhavantaṃ jotipālanti bhoto jotipālassa bhavo vuddhi visesādhigamo sabbakalyāṇañceva maṅgalañca hotūti attho. Sammodanīyaṃ kathanti? “Alaṃ, mahārāja, mā cintayi, dhuvadhammo esa sabbasattāna”ntiādinā nayena maraṇappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ sokavinodanapaṭisanthārakathaṃ pariyosāpetvā. Mā no bhavaṃ jotipālo anusāsaniyā [P 2.0661] paccabyāhāsīti mā paṭibyākāsi, “anusāsā”ti vutto – “nāhaṃ anusāsāmī”ti no mā anusāsaniyā paccakkhāsīti attho. Abhisambhosīti saṃvidahitvā paṭṭhapesi. Manussā evamāhaṃsūti taṃ pitarā mahāpaññataraṃ sabbakiccāni anusāsantaṃ sabbakamme abhisambhavantaṃ disvā tuṭṭhacittā govindo vata, bho, brāhmaṇo, mahāgovindo vata, bho, brāhmaṇoti evamāhaṃsu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, “govindo vata, bho, brāhmaṇo ahosi etassa pitā; ayaṃ pana mahāgovindo vata, bho, brāhmaṇo”ti.

305. By 'May there be prosperity for you, Jotipāla' (bhavamatthu bhavantaṃ jotipālaṃ) is meant, 'May there be growth, special attainment, and all auspiciousness and blessing for the venerable Jotipāla.' What is the pleasing conversation? Having concluded the comforting conversation that removes sorrow, connected with death, in the manner beginning with 'Enough, great king, do not grieve, this is the constant nature of all beings,' etc. By 'May the venerable Jotipāla not refuse us in instruction' (mā no bhavaṃ jotipālo anusāsaniyā paccabyāhāsi) is meant: 'Do not speak against it; when told, "Instruct!", do not refuse us instruction by saying, "I will not instruct."' By 'abhisambhosī' is meant 'having arranged, he established.' People spoke thus: Seeing him, who was wiser than his father, instructing in all duties and accomplishing all tasks, they, with joyful hearts, said, 'Indeed, sirs, Govinda the brahmin! Indeed, sirs, Mahāgovinda the brahmin!' This is what was meant: 'Indeed, sirs, his father was Govinda the brahmin; but this one, sirs, is indeed Mahāgovinda the brahmin.'

Rajjasaṃvibhajanavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Division of the Kingdom.

306. Yena [V 2.0228] te cha khattiyāti ye te “sahāyā”ti vuttā cha khattiyā, te kira reṇussa ekapitikā kaniṭṭhabhātaro, tasmā mahāgovindo “ayaṃ abhisitto etesaṃ rajjasaṃvibhāgaṃ kareyya vā na vā, yaṃnūnāhaṃ te paṭikacceva reṇussa santikaṃ pesetvā paṭiññaṃ gaṇhāpeyya”nti cintento yena te cha khattiyā tenupasaṅkami. Rājakattāroti rājakārakā amaccā.

306. The phrase 'by whom those six khattiyas' (yena te cha khattiyā) refers to those six khattiyas who were called 'companions'. It seems they were Reṇu's younger brothers by the same father. Therefore, Mahāgovinda, thinking: 'Whether this anointed one will share the kingdom with them or not, it would be better if I first sent them to Reṇu and had them take a pledge,' approached those six khattiyas. Rājakattāro means the royal officials who make kings (rājakārakā amaccā).

307. Madanīyā kāmāti madakarā pamādakarā kāmā. Gacchante gacchante kāle esa anussaritumpi na sakkuṇeyya, tasmā āyantu bhonto āgacchantūti attho.

307. 'Sensual pleasures are maddening' (madanīyā kāmā) means sensual pleasures that cause intoxication and heedlessness. As time passes, he might not even be able to recall them. Therefore, the meaning is, 'Come, good sirs, come!'

308. Sarāmahaṃ bhoti tadā kira manussānaṃ saccavādikālo hoti, tasmā “kadā mayā vuttaṃ, kena diṭṭhaṃ, kena suta”nti abhūtaṃ avatvā “sarāmahaṃ bho”ti āha. Sammodanīyaṃ kathanti kiṃ mahārāja devattaṃ gate raññe mā cintayittha, dhuvadhammo esa sabbasattānaṃ, evaṃbhāvino saṅkhārāti evarūpaṃ paṭisanthārakathaṃ. Sabbāni sakaṭamukhāni paṭṭhapesīti sabbāni cha [M 2.0255] rajjāni sakaṭamukhāni paṭṭhapesi. Ekekassa rañño rajjaṃ tiyojanasataṃ hoti, reṇussa rañño rajjosaraṇapadeso dasagāvutaṃ, majjhe pana reṇussa rajjaṃ vitānasadisaṃ ahosi. Kasmā evaṃ paṭṭhapesīti? Kālena kālaṃ rājānaṃ passituṃ āgacchantā aññassa rajjaṃ apīḷetvā attano attano rajjapadeseneva āgamissanti ceva gamissanti ca. Pararajjaṃ otiṇṇassa hi – “bhattaṃ detha, goṇaṃ dethā”ti vadato manussā ujjhāyanti – “ime rājāno attano attano vijitena na gacchanti, amhākaṃ pīḷaṃ [P 2.0662] karontī”ti. Attano vijitena gacchantassa “amhākaṃ santikā iminā idañcidañca laddhabbamevā”ti manussā pīḷaṃ na maññanti. Imamatthaṃ cintayitvā mahāgovindo “sammodamānā rājāno ciraṃ rajjamanusāsantū”ti evaṃ paṭṭhapesi.

308. 'I remember, sirs' (sarāmahaṃ bho)—at that time, it seems, was the age of truthfulness for people. Therefore, without speaking falsely by saying, 'When did I say this? Who saw it? Who heard it?' he said, 'I remember, sirs.' 'Pleasant conversation' (sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ) means such a consoling talk as: 'O great king, do not grieve over the king who has passed away. This is the constant nature of all beings; such is the nature of conditioned things.' 'He arranged all the chariot entrances' (sabbāni sakaṭamukhāni paṭṭhapesi) means he arranged all six kingdoms to have cart-front shapes. Each king’s realm was three hundred yojanas, while the approach to King Reṇu’s kingdom was ten gāvutas, and in the middle, Reṇu’s kingdom was like a canopy. Why did he arrange it this way? So that when they came to see the king from time to time, they would not encroach on another’s territory but would come and go only through their own respective domains. For if one entered another’s kingdom and said, 'Give us food, give us oxen!'—the people would complain, saying, 'These kings do not travel through their own territories but trouble us.' But if one traveled through their own territory, the people would not feel troubled, thinking, 'From our own vicinity, this and that must be obtained by him.' Reflecting on this, Mahāgovinda arranged it so that 'the kings, living harmoniously, would rule for a long time.'

“Dantapuraṃ kaliṅgānaṃ, assakānañca potanaṃ;

Māhissati avantīnaṃ, sovīrānañca rodukaṃ.

Mithilā ca videhānaṃ, campā aṅgesu māpitā;

Bārāṇasī ca kāsīnaṃ, ete govindamāpitā”ti. –

'Dantapura of the Kaliṅgas, Potana of the Assakas, Māhissati of the Avantis, Roduka of the Sovīras, Mithilā of the Videhas, Campā built in Aṅga, and Bārāṇasī of the Kāsīs—these were planned by Govinda.'

Etāni [V 2.0229] satta nagarāni mahāgovindeneva tesaṃ rājūnaṃ atthāya māpitāni.

These seven cities were built by Mahāgovinda himself for the benefit of those kings.

“Sattabhū brahmadatto ca, vessabhū bharato saha;

Reṇu dve ca dhataraṭṭhā, tadāsuṃ satta bhāradhā”ti. –

Sattabhū and Brahmadatta, Vessabhū together with Bharata, Reṇu and the two Dhataraṭṭhas—these were the seven sovereigns at that time.

Imāni tesaṃ sattannampi nāmāni. Tesu hi eko sattabhū nāma ahosi, eko brahmadatto nāma, eko vessabhū nāma, eko teneva saha bharato nāma, eko reṇu nāma, dve pana dhataraṭṭhāti ime satta jambudīpatale bhāradhā mahārājāno ahesunti.

These were the names of all seven of them. Among them, one was named Sattabhū, one Brahmadatta, one Vessabhū, one Bharata along with him, one Reṇu, and two Dhataraṭṭhas—these seven were great sovereign kings on the continent of Jambudīpa.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Recitation Section is Concluded.

Kittisaddaabbhuggamanavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Rise of the Sound of Fame

311. Upasaṅkamiṃsūti [M 2.0256] “amhākaṃ ayaṃ issariyasampatti na aññassānubhāvena, mahāgovindassānubhāvena nipphannā. Mahāgovindo amhe satta rājāno samagge katvā jambudīpatale patiṭṭhāpesi, pubbūpakārissa pana na sukarā paṭikiriyā kātuṃ. Amhe sattapi jane esoyeva anusāsatu, etaṃyeva senāpatiñca purohitañca karoma, evaṃ no vuddhi bhavissatī”ti cintetvā upasaṅkamiṃsu. Mahāgovindopi – “mayā ete samaggā katā, sace etesaṃ añño senāpati purohito ca bhavissati, tato attano attano senāpatipurohitānaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā aññamaññaṃ bhindissanti, adhivāsemi nesaṃ senāpatiṭṭhānañca purohitaṭṭhānañcā”ti cintetvā “evaṃ bho”ti paccassosi.

311. ‘They approached’ means they approached, thinking: ‘This sovereignty and prosperity of ours has not been achieved through the power of another, but through the power of Mahāgovinda. Mahāgovinda united us seven kings and established us on the continent of Jambudīpa, and it is not easy to make a return for the favor of one who has first been a benefactor. Let this one alone instruct all seven of us; let us appoint him as our commander-in-chief and priest; in this way our prosperity will grow.’ Mahāgovinda also thought: ‘I have united them. If they have another commander-in-chief and priest, then, taking the word of their own respective commanders-in-chief and priests, they will become divided from one another. I shall accept their positions of commander-in-chief and priest.’ Thinking thus, he consented, saying, ‘So be it, sirs.’

Satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāleti “ahaṃ sabbaṭṭhānesu sammukho bhaveyyaṃ vā na vā, yatthāhaṃ sammukho na bhavissāmi, tattheva te kattabbaṃ karissantī”ti satta [P 2.0663] anupurohite ṭhapesi. Te sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ – “satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle”ti. Divasassa dvikkhattuṃ vā sāyaṃ pāto vā nahāyantīti nahātakā. Vatacariyapariyosāne vā nahātā, tato paṭṭhāya brāhmaṇehi saddhiṃ na khādanti na pivantīti nahātakā.

‘And seven great brahmin households’ means he appointed seven deputy priests, thinking: ‘I may or may not be present in all places; wherever I am not present, they will do what needs to be done.’ It is with reference to them that this was said: ‘and seven great brahmin households.’ They are called ‘nahātakas’ (the bathed) because they bathe twice a day, in the evening and morning. Or, they are called ‘nahātakas’ because, having bathed at the conclusion of their religious observances, from then on they do not eat or drink with other brahmins.

312. Abbhuggacchīti [V 2.0230] abhiuggacchi. Tadā kira manussānaṃ “na brahmunā saddhiṃ amantetvā sakkā evaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ anusāsitu”nti nisinnanisinnaṭṭhāne ayameva kathā pavattittha. Na kho panāhanti mahāpuriso kira – “ayaṃ mayhaṃ abhūto vaṇṇo uppanno, vaṇṇuppatti kho pana na bhāriyā, uppannassa vaṇṇassa rakkhanameva bhāriyaṃ, ayañca me acintetvā amantetvā karontasseva vaṇṇo uppannova, cintetvā mantetvā karontassa pana vitthārikataro bhavissatī”ti brahmadassane upāyaṃ pariyesanto taṃ disvā sutaṃ kho pana metantiādiatthaṃ parivitakkesi.

312. ‘It arose’ (abbhuggacchi) means it went up. At that time, it seems, this very talk occurred among people wherever they were seated: ‘It is not possible to govern the entire continent of Jambudīpa without having consulted with Brahmā.’ But the great man, it is said, thought: ‘This unprecedented praise has arisen for me. The arising of praise is not a burden; maintaining the praise that has arisen is the burden. This praise has arisen for me even while acting without thinking or consulting; for one who acts after thinking and consulting, it will become even more widespread.’ Seeking a means to see Brahmā, and having found it, he pondered the matter beginning with, ‘Now, I have heard this...’.

313. Yena [M 2.0257] reṇu rājā tenupasaṅkamīti evaṃ me antarā daṭṭhukāmo vā sallapitukāmo vā na bhavissati, yato chinnapalibodho sukhaṃ viharissāmīti palibodhupacchedanatthaṃ upasaṅkami, esa nayo sabbattha.

313. ‘He approached King Reṇu’ means he did so thinking: ‘Thus, during the interim, there will be no one who wishes to see me or to converse with me. Since my hindrances will be cut off, I will dwell happily.’ He approached for the purpose of cutting off hindrances. This is the method in all instances.

316. Sādisiyoti samavaṇṇā samajātikā.

316. ‘Of a similar kind’ (sādisiyo) means of the same social standing and birth.

317. Navaṃ sandhāgāraṃ kāretvāti rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānacaṅkamanasampannaṃ vassike cattāro māse vasanakkhamaṃ bahi naḷaparikkhittaṃ vicittaṃ āvasathaṃ kāretvā. Karuṇaṃ jhānaṃ jhāyīti karuṇāya tikacatukkajjhānaṃ jhāyi, karuṇāmukhena panettha avasesāpi tayo brahmavihārā gahitāva. Ukkaṇṭhanā paritassanāti jhānabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitassa anabhiratiukkaṇṭhanā vā bhayaparitassanā vā natthi, brahmuno pana āgamanapatthanā āgamanataṇhā ahūti attho.

317. ‘Having had a new assembly hall built’ means having constructed a decorated dwelling, complete with places for the night and day and for walking, suitable for residing in for the four months of the rainy season, and enclosed on the outside with reeds. ‘He meditated on the jhāna of compassion’ means he meditated on the threefold and fourfold jhānas attained through compassion; and here, by way of compassion, the remaining three divine abodes are also taken to be included. ‘Restlessness and agitation’ means that for one established in the jhāna-ground there is no discontent which is restlessness, nor fear which is agitation. But there was a longing for the arrival of Brahmā, a craving for his arrival; this is the meaning.

Brahmunāsākacchāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Conversation with Brahmā

318. Bhayanti cittutrāsabhayameva. Ajānantāti ajānamānā. Kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayanti (dī. ni. 2.179) mayaṃ kinti taṃ jānāma, ayaṃ katthavāsiko, kinnāmo, kiṃ gottotiādīnaṃ ākārānaṃ kena ākārena taṃ dhārayāmāti attho.

318. ‘Fear’ means simply the fear that is mental terror. ‘Not knowing’ means not knowing. ‘How might we know you?’ means: ‘How might we know you? Where does this one dwell? What is his name? What is his clan?’—by which of these characteristics are we to remember you? This is the meaning.

Maṃ ve kumāraṃ jānantīti maṃ “kumāro”ti “daharo”ti jānanti. Brahmaloketi seṭṭhaloke. Sanantananti ciratanaṃ porāṇakaṃ[P 2.0664]. Ahaṃ so porāṇakumāro sanaṅkumāro nāma brahmāti dasseti. Evaṃ govinda jānāhīti govinda paṇḍita, tvaṃ evaṃ jānāhi, evaṃ maṃ dhārehi.

‘They know me as the Youth’ means they know me as ‘the Youth’ or ‘the Young One.’ ‘In the Brahmā world’ means in the highest world. ‘Eternal’ (sanantana) means long-standing, ancient. He reveals: ‘I am that ancient youth, the Brahmā named Sanaṅkumāra.’ ‘Thus, Govinda, know’ means: ‘O wise Govinda, you should know thus; you should remember me thus.’

“Āsanaṃ [V 2.0231] udakaṃ pajjaṃ, madhusākañca brahmuno;

Agghe bhavantaṃ pucchāma, agghaṃ kurutu no bhava”nti. –

“A seat, water, water for the feet, and a honey-offering for Brahmā; we ask your reverence concerning the guest-offering; may your reverence accept the guest-offering from us.”

Ettha agghanti atithino upanāmetabbaṃ vuccati. Teneva idamāsanaṃ paññattaṃ, ettha nisīdatha, idaṃ udakaṃ parisuddhaṃ, ito pānīyaṃ pivatha, pāde dhovatha, idaṃ pajjaṃ pādānaṃ hitatthāya abhisaṅkhataṃ telaṃ, ito pāde makkhetha, idaṃ madhusākanti. Bodhisattassa brahmacariyaṃ na aññesaṃ brahmacariyasadisaṃ hoti, na so “idaṃ sve, idaṃ tatiyadivase bhavissatī”ti sannidhiṃ [M 2.0258] nāma karoti. Madhusākaṃ pana aloṇaṃ adhūpanaṃ atakkaṃ udakena seditasākaṃ, taṃ sandhāyesa – “idaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti vadanto “agghe bhavantaṃ pucchāmā”tiādimāha. Ime sabbepi agghā brahmuno atthi. Te agghe bhavantaṃ pucchāma. Evaṃ pucchantānañca agghaṃ kurutu no bhavaṃ, paṭiggaṇhātu no bhavaṃ idamagghanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ panesa – “ito ekampi brahmā na bhuñjatī”ti idaṃ na jānātīti. No na jānāti, jānantopi attano santike āgato atithi pucchitabboti vattasīsena pucchati.

Herein, that which should be offered to a guest is called a 'hospitable gift' (aggha).
