Therefore: 'This seat has been prepared, sit here; this water is pure, drink from this water; wash your feet; this is foot-oil, a salve prepared for the benefit of the feet, anoint your feet with it; these are sweet greens.' The Bodhisatta’s holy life is not like the holy life of others; he does not make any accumulation, thinking, 'This will be for tomorrow, this for the third day.' Now, the sweet greens were saltless, unspiced, without buttermilk, being greens steamed only with water. With reference to this, while saying, 'Partake of this,' he then said, 'We ask the venerable one for a hospitable gift,' and so on. All these hospitable gifts are for Brahmā. We ask the venerable one for these hospitable gifts. And for those who ask thus, 'May the venerable one grant us a hospitable gift, may the venerable one accept this hospitable gift from us'—this is what is meant. But does he not know this: 'Brahmā does not partake of even one of these things'? No, it is not that he does not know. Even knowing, he asks because a guest who has come into his presence should be asked, making it a point of custom.

Atha kho brahmā – “kiṃ nu kho paṇḍito mama paribhogakaraṇābhāvaṃ ñatvā pucchati, udāhu kohaññe ṭhatvā pucchatī”ti samannāharanto “vattasīse ṭhito pucchatī”ti ñatvā paṭiggaṇhituṃ dāni me vaṭṭatīti paṭiggaṇhāma te agghaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ govinda bhāsasīti āha. Yaṃ tvaṃ govinda bhāsasi – “idamāsanaṃ paññattaṃ, ettha nisīdathā”tiādi, tatra te mayaṃ āsane nisinnā nāma homa, pānīyaṃ pītā nāma homa, pādāpi me dhotā nāma hontu, telenapi makkhitā nāma hontu, udakasākampi paribhuttaṃ nāma hotu, tayā dinnaṃ adhivāsitakālato paṭṭhāya yaṃ yaṃ tvaṃ bhāsasi, taṃ taṃ mayā paṭiggahitameva hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “paṭiggaṇhāma te agghaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ govinda bhāsasī”ti. Evaṃ pana agghaṃ paṭiggaṇhitvā pañhassa okāsaṃ karonto diṭṭhadhammahitatthāyātiādimāha.

Then Brahmā reflected: 'Does this wise one ask knowing that I do not partake, or does he ask out of pretense?' Understanding, 'He asks, standing on the ground of custom,' he thought, 'Now it is proper for me to accept,' and said: 'We accept your hospitable gift, O Govinda, whatever you say.' Whatever you, Govinda, say—such as, 'This seat is prepared, sit here,' and so on—by that, we are considered to be seated on your seat; we are considered to have drunk the water; my feet are considered to be washed; they are considered to be anointed with oil; and the greens steamed in water are considered to have been partaken of. From the moment of consent for what has been offered by you, whatever you say, that very thing is accepted by me. Therefore it was said: 'We accept your hospitable gift, O Govinda, whatever you say.' Having thus accepted the hospitable gift and creating an opportunity for a question, he said, 'For the welfare and benefit in this very life,' and so on.

Kaṅkhī [P 2.0665] akaṅkhiṃ paravediyesūti ahaṃ savicikiccho bhavantaṃ parena sayaṃ abhisaṅkhatattā parassa pākaṭesu paravediyesu pañhesu nibbicikicchaṃ.

'The doubting one asks the undoubting one about matters to be known by others' means: I, who am with doubt, ask the venerable one, who is without doubt concerning questions that are evident to another and are to be known by another, because he has prepared himself.

Hitvā mamattanti idaṃ mama, idaṃ mamāti upakaraṇataṇhaṃ cajitvā. Manujesūti sattesu, manujesu yo koci manujo mamattaṃ hitvāti attho. Ekodibhūtoti ekībhūto, eko tiṭṭhanto eko nisīdantoti. Vacanattho panettha eko udeti pavattatīti ekodi, tādiso bhūtoti ekodibhūto[V 2.0232]. Karuṇedhimuttoti karuṇājhāne adhimutto, taṃ jhānaṃ nibbattetvāti attho. Nirāmagandhoti vissagandhavirahito. Ettha ṭhitoti etesu dhammesu ṭhito. Ettha ca sikkhamānoti [M 2.0259] etesu dhammesu sikkhamāno. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana upari mahāgovindena ca brahmunā ca vuttoyeva.

'Having abandoned what is mine' means having abandoned the craving for requisites, thinking, 'This is mine, this is mine.' 'Among humans' means among beings; the meaning is 'any human among humans who has abandoned what is mine.' 'Become solitary' means become one, standing alone, sitting alone. The etymological meaning here is: 'one arises, one proceeds,' thus 'ekodi'; 'having become such,' thus 'ekodibhūto.' 'Resolved on compassion' means resolved on the jhāna of compassion; the meaning is having produced that jhāna. 'Without the raw stench' means devoid of the fishy smell of defilements. 'Established herein' means established in these states. 'And training herein' means training in these states. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, has already been given above by Mahāgovinda and by Brahmā.

320. Tattha ete avidvāti ete āmagandhe ahaṃ avidvā, na jānāmīti attho. Idha brūhi dhīrāti te me tvaṃ idha dhīra paṇḍita, brūhi, vada. Kenāvaṭā vāti pajā kurutūti katamena kilesāvaraṇena āvaritā pajā pūtikā vāyati. Āpāyikāti apāyūpagā. Nivutabrahmalokāti nivuto pihito brahmaloko assāti nivutabrahmaloko. Katamena kilesena pajāya brahmalokūpago maggo nivuto pihito paṭicchannoti pucchati.

320. Therein, 'not knowing these' means: I am one who does not know these raw stenches; I do not know them—this is the meaning. 'Tell me here, O wise one' means: You, O wise and learned one, tell me, speak to me here. 'By what covered does this generation emit a stench?' means: Covered by what defilement-covering does this generation, being putrid, emit a stench? 'Bound for the plane of misery' means going to the plane of misery. 'With the Brahmā-world obstructed' means one for whom the Brahmā-world is obstructed, closed off; hence 'one with the Brahmā-world obstructed.' He asks: By what defilement is the path for this generation leading to the Brahmā-world obstructed, closed off, and concealed?

Kodho mosavajjaṃ nikati ca dubbhoti kujjhanalakkhaṇo kodho ca, paravisaṃvādanalakkhaṇo musāvādo ca, sadisaṃ dassetvā vañcanalakkhaṇā nikati ca, mittadubbhanalakkhaṇo dubbho ca. Kadariyatā atimāno usūyāti thaddhamacchariyalakkhaṇā kadariyatā ca, atikkamitvā maññanalakkhaṇo atimāno ca, parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā usūyā ca. Icchā vivicchā paraheṭhanā cāti taṇhālakkhaṇā icchā ca, macchariyalakkhaṇā vivicchā ca, vihiṃsālakkhaṇā paraheṭhanā ca. Lobho ca doso ca mado ca mohoti yattha katthaci lubbhanalakkhaṇo lobho ca, dussanalakkhaṇo doso ca, majjanalakkhaṇo mado ca, muyhanalakkhaṇo moho ca. Etesu yuttā anirāmagandhāti etesu cuddasasu kilesesu yuttā pajā nirāmagandhā na hoti, āmagandhā sakuṇapagandhā [P 2.0666] pūtigandhāyevāti vadati. Āpāyikā nivutabrahmalokāti esā pana āpāyikā ceva hoti, paṭicchannabrahmalokamaggā cāti. Idaṃ pana suttaṃ kathentena āmagandhasuttena dīpetvā kathetabbaṃ, āmagandhasuttampi iminā dīpetvā kathetabbaṃ.

'Anger, false speech, deceit, and malice' means: anger, which has the characteristic of rage; false speech, which has the characteristic of deceiving others; deceit, which has the characteristic of cheating by showing something similar; and malice, which has the characteristic of corrupting a friendship. 'Stinginess, conceit, and envy' means: stinginess, which has the characteristic of harsh avarice; conceit, which has the characteristic of thinking in a transgressing manner; and envy, which has the characteristic of finding fault with others' success. 'Desire, selfishness, and harming others' means: desire, which has the characteristic of craving; selfishness, which has the characteristic of avarice; and harming others, which has the characteristic of violence. 'Greed, and hatred, and intoxication, and delusion' means: greed, which has the characteristic of coveting anything whatsoever; hatred, which has the characteristic of corruption of mind; intoxication, which has the characteristic of vanity; and delusion, which has the characteristic of bewilderment. 'Connected with these, one is not without the raw stench' means: a generation connected with these fourteen defilements is not without the raw stench; it has the raw stench, it has the stench of a corpse, it has a putrid stench—thus he speaks. 'Bound for the plane of misery, with the Brahmā-world obstructed' means: this generation is indeed bound for the plane of misery, and the path to the Brahmā-world is concealed. This discourse, when taught, should be taught by illuminating it with the Āmagandha Sutta, and the Āmagandha Sutta should also be taught by illuminating it with this discourse.

Te na sunimmadayāti te āmagandhā sunimmadayā sukhena nimmadetabbā pahātabbā na honti, duppajahā dujjayāti attho. Yassa dāni bhavaṃ govindo kālaṃ maññatīti “yassā pabbajjāya bhavaṃ govindo kālaṃ maññati, ayameva hotu, evaṃ sati mayhampi tava santike āgamanaṃ svāgamanaṃ bhavissati, kathitadhammakathā sukathitā bhavissati, tvaṃ tāta sakalajambudīpe [M 2.0260] aggapuriso daharo paṭhamavaye ṭhito, evaṃ mahantaṃ nāma sampattisirivilāsaṃ pahāya tava pabbajanaṃ nāma gandhahatthino ayabandhanaṃ chinditvā gamanaṃ viya atiuḷāraṃ, buddhatanti nāmesā”ti mahāpurisassa daḷhīkammaṃ katvā brahmā sanaṅkumāro brahmalokameva gato.

'They are not easily subdued' means: these stenches of defilement are not easily subdued, not easily abandoned; they are hard to relinquish, hard to conquer—this is the meaning. 'Now, when does the venerable Govinda think it is time?' means: 'For whose going forth does the venerable Govinda think it is time? Let it be this very one. If it is so, my coming to you will be a welcome coming, and the Dhamma talk spoken will be well spoken. You, dear one, are the foremost person in all Jambudīpa, young, standing in your first youth. Your going forth, abandoning such great prosperity, glory, and splendor, is truly magnificent, like a tusker elephant breaking its iron chains and going forth. This is called the lineage of the Buddhas.' Having strengthened the resolve of the great being, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra returned to the Brahmā world.

Reṇurājaāmantanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Address to King Reṇu

321. Mahāpurisopi [V 2.0233] “mama itova nikkhamitvā pabbajanaṃ nāma na yuttaṃ, ahaṃ rājakulassa atthaṃ anusāsāmi, tasmā rañño ārocessāmi. Sace sopi pabbajissati, sundarameva. No ce pabbajissati, purohitaṭṭhānaṃ niyyātetvā ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkami, tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bho mahāgovindo,…pe… nāhaṃ porohacce rame”ti.

321. The Great Being also thought: "It is not proper for me to go forth, departing from here. I guide the royal family's welfare, so I shall inform the king. If he too goes forth, that would be excellent. If he does not go forth, I will hand over the position of royal chaplain and then I will go forth." Having reflected thus, he approached the king. Therefore it is said: "Then, venerable Mahāgovinda,…pe… I do not delight in the office of chaplain."

Tattha tvaṃ pajānassu rajjenāti tava rajjena tvameva jānāhi. Nāhaṃ porohicce rameti ahaṃ purohitabhāve na ramāmi, ukkaṇṭhitosmi, aññaṃ anusāsakaṃ jānāhi, nāhaṃ porohicce rameti.

Here, 'You yourself must know your kingdom' means 'You yourself must manage your kingdom.' 'I do not delight in the office of chaplain' means 'I do not delight in being a chaplain; I am discontented. Find another advisor; I do not delight in the office of chaplain.'

Atha rājā – “dhuvaṃ cattāro māse paṭisallīnassa brāhmaṇassa gehe bhogā mandā jātā”ti cintetvā dhanena nimantento – “sace te ūnaṃ kāmehi. Ahaṃ paripūrayāmi te”ti vatvā puna – “kinnu kho esa ekako viharanto kenaci vihiṃsito bhaveyyā”ti cintetvā,

Then the king, thinking, "Surely, for the brahmin who has been in seclusion for four months, the wealth in his house has dwindled," inviting him with riches, said, "If you are deficient in sensual pleasures, I will replenish them for you." Then he thought again, "Living alone, could he have been harassed by someone?"

“Yo taṃ hiṃsati vāremi, bhūmisenāpati ahaṃ;

Tuvaṃ pitā ahaṃ putto, mā no govinda pājahī”ti. –

"I shall restrain whoever harms you; I am the commander of the land's army. You are the father, I am the son; Govinda, do not abandon us."

Āha[P 2.0667]. Tassattho – yo taṃ hiṃsati, taṃ vāremi, kevalaṃ tumhe “asuko”ti ācikkhatha, ahamettha kattabbaṃ jānissāmīti. Bhūmisenāpati ahanti atha vā ahaṃ pathaviyā sāmī, svāhaṃ imaṃ rajjaṃ tumheyeva paṭicchāpessāmi. Tuvaṃ pitā ahaṃ puttoti tvaṃ pitiṭṭhāne ṭhassasi, ahaṃ puttaṭṭhāne. So tvaṃ mama manaṃ haritvā attanoyeva manaṃ govinda, pājehi; yathā icchasi tathā pavattassu. Ahaṃ pana tava manaṃyeva anuvattanto tayā dinnapiṇḍaṃ paribhuñjanto taṃ asicammahattho vā upaṭṭhahissāmi, rathaṃ vā te pājessāmi. “Mā no govinda, pajahī”ti vā pāṭho[M 2.0261]. Tassattho – tvaṃ pitiṭṭhāne tiṭṭha, ahaṃ puttaṭṭhāne ṭhassāmi. Mā no tvaṃ bho govinda, pajahi, mā pariccajīti. Atha mahāpuriso yaṃ rājā cintesi, tassa attani abhāvaṃ dassento –

He said. Its meaning is: 'Whoever harms you, him I will restrain; you just tell me "so-and-so," and I will know what needs to be done here.' 'I am the commander of the land's army' means, alternatively, 'I am the lord of the earth, and I will have you alone accept this kingdom.' 'You are the father, I am the son' means 'you will stand in the place of a father, and I in the place of a son.' 'So, Govinda, having won my heart, direct your own mind; act as you wish. But I, following only your mind, enjoying the food given by you, will attend to you with sword and shield in hand, or I will drive your chariot.' 'Govinda, do not abandon us' is also a reading; its meaning is: 'You stand in the place of a father, I will stand in the place of a son. Do not abandon us, venerable Govinda, do not forsake us.' Then the Great Being, showing that what the king had thought was not the case for him, said:

“Na [V 2.0234] matthi ūnaṃ kāmehi, hiṃsitā me na vijjati;

Amanussavaco sutvā, tasmāhaṃ na gahe rame”ti. –

"I have no lack of sensual pleasures, nor have I been harmed; but having heard the word of a non-human, I no longer delight in the household life."

Āha. Tattha na matthīti na me atthi. Gaheti gehe. Atha naṃ rājā pucchi –

He said. Here, 'na matthi' means 'na me atthi' (I do not have). 'Gahe' means 'in the household.' Then the king asked him:

“Amanusso kathaṃ vaṇṇo, kiṃ te atthaṃ abhāsatha;

Yañca sutvā jahāsi no, gehe amhe ca kevalī”ti.

"What was the appearance of the non-human? What matter did he speak of to you? Having heard what do you abandon us, our homes, and all our people?"

Tattha jahāsi no, gehe amhe ca kevalīti brāhmaṇassa sampattibharite gehe saṅgahavasena attano gehe karonto yaṃ sutvā amhākaṃ gehe ca amhe ca kevalī sabbe aparisese jambudīpavāsino jahāsīti vadati.

Here, regarding 'you abandon us, our homes, and all our people': the king speaks, who, by way of patronage, considered the brahmin's houses filled with prosperity as his own. He says: 'Having heard what, do you abandon our houses, and us, indeed all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa without exception?'

Athassa ācikkhanto mahāpuriso upavutthassa me pubbetiādimāha. Tattha upavutthassāti cattāro māse ekībhāvaṃ upagantvā vutthassa. Yiṭṭhakāmassa me satoti yajitukāmassa me [P 2.0668] samānassa. Aggi pajjalito āsi, kusapattaparitthatoti kusapattehi paritthato sappidadhimadhuādīni pakkhipitvā aggi jalayitumāraddho āsi, evaṃ aggiṃ jāletvā “mahājanassa dānaṃ dassāmī”ti evaṃ cintetvā ṭhitassa mamāti ayamettha attho.

Then the Great Being, explaining it to him, said, 'For me, who had been dwelling previously...' and so on. Here, 'upavutthassa' means 'who had dwelt, having attained solitude for four months.' 'Yiṭṭhakāmassa me sato' means 'while I was desirous of sacrificing.' 'The fire was kindled, spread about with kusa grass' means that, having spread kusa leaves and placed ghee, yogurt, honey, and so on, the fire was begun to be lit. The meaning here is: 'while I stood thus, having lit the fire and thinking, "I will give a gift to the multitude."

Sanantanoti sanaṅkumāro brahmā. Tato rājā sayampi pabbajitukāmo hutvā saddahāmītiādimāha. Tattha kathaṃ vattetha aññathāti kathaṃ tumhe aññathā vattissatha. Te taṃ anuvattissāmāti te mayampi tumheyeva anuvattissāma, anupabbajissāmāti attho. “Anuvajissāmā”tipi pāṭho, tassa anugacchissāmāti attho. Akācoti nikkāco akakkaso. Govindassānusāsaneti tava govindassa sāsane. Bhavantaṃ govindameva satthāraṃ karitvā carissāmāti vadati.

'Sanantana' means Sanaṅkumāra, the Brahmā. Then the king, himself desiring to go forth, said, 'I believe,' and so on. Here, 'kathaṃ vattetha aññathā' means 'how could you act otherwise?' 'Te taṃ anuvattissāma' means 'we too will follow you; we will also go forth after you,' this is the meaning. 'Anuvajissāma' is also a reading; its meaning is 'we will go after you.' 'Akāco' means 'flawless, not harsh.' 'Govindassānusāsane' means 'in your instruction, Govinda.' He says: 'Making the venerable Govinda our teacher, we will conduct ourselves.'

Cha khattiyaāmantanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Address to the Six Khattiyas

322. Yena [M 2.0262] te cha khattiyā tenupasaṅkamīti reṇuṃ rājānaṃ “sādhu mahārāja rajjaṃ nāma mātaraṃ pitaraṃ bhātibhaginīādayopi māretvā gaṇhantesu sattesu evaṃ mahantaṃ rajjasiriṃ pahāya pabbajitukāmena uḷāraṃ mahārājena kata”nti upatthambhetvā daḷhataramassa ussāhaṃ katvā upasaṅkami[V 2.0235]. Evaṃ samacintesunti rañño cintitanayeneva kadāci brāhmaṇassa bhogā parihīnā bhaveyyunti maññamānā samacintesuṃ. Dhanena sikkheyyāmāti upalāpeyyāma saṅgaṇheyyāma. Tāvatakaṃ āharīyatanti tāvatakaṃ āharāpiyatu gaṇhiyatu, yattakaṃ icchatha, tattakaṃ gaṇhathāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhavantānaṃyeva vāhasāti bhavante paccayaṃ katvā, tumhehi dinnattāyeva pahūtaṃ sāpateyyaṃ jātaṃ.

322. Regarding Yena te cha khattiyā tenupasaṅkami, he approached King Reṇu, encouraging him and strengthening his resolve by saying, 'Well done, great king. Among beings who seize a kingdom by killing their mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, and others, it is a noble thing that you, a great king, desiring to go forth, have abandoned such vast royal splendor.' As for Evaṃ samacintesuṃ, they reflected in the very same way the king had thought, supposing that the brahmin’s wealth might someday diminish. Regarding Dhanena sikkheyyāma, this means 'we should entice him with wealth, we should win him over.' As for Tāvatakaṃ āharīyataṃ, this means 'let that much be brought and taken,' which is to say, 'take as much as you wish.' Regarding Bhavantānaṃyeva vāhasā, this means 'it is through reliance on you; abundant possessions have arisen precisely because they were given by you.'

323. Sace jahatha kāmānīti sace vatthukāme ca kilesakāme ca pariccajatha. Yattha satto puthujjanoti yesu kāmesu puthujjano satto laggo laggito. Ārambhavho daḷhā hothāti evaṃ sante vīriyaṃ ārabhatha, asithilaparakkamataṃ adhiṭṭhāya daḷhā bhavatha. Khantībalasamāhitāti khantibalena samannāgatā bhavathāti rājūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janeti.

323. Regarding Sace jahatha kāmāni, this means 'if you abandon both material desires and desires which are defilements.' As for Yattha satto puthujjano, this means 'in which desires the ordinary person is attached, stuck, and ensnared.' Regarding Ārambhavho daḷhā hotha, this means 'this being so, arouse your energy; having established unwavering exertion, be firm.' As for Khantībalasamāhitā, this means 'be endowed with the strength of patience.' Thus, he generated enthusiasm in the kings.

Esa maggo ujumaggoti esa karuṇājhānamaggo ujumaggo nāma. Esa maggo anuttaroti eseva [P 2.0669] brahmalokūpapattiyā asadisamaggo uttamamaggo nāma. Saddhammo sabbhi rakkhitoti eso eva ca buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakehi sabbhirakkhitadhammo nāma. Iti karuṇājhānassa vaṇṇabhaṇanenāpi tesaṃ anivattanatthāya daḷhīkammameva karoti.

Regarding Esa maggo ujumaggo, this means 'this path of compassion-jhāna is called the straight path.' As for Esa maggo anuttaro, this means 'this very path, for the purpose of rebirth in the Brahma-world, is called the unequalled path, the supreme path.' Regarding Saddhammo sabbhi rakkhito, this means 'this very Dhamma is called the Dhamma protected by good people, that is, by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples.' Thus, also by speaking in praise of compassion-jhāna, he performed the very act of strengthening them for the sake of their not turning back.

Ko nu kho pana bho jānāti jīvitānanti bho jīvitaṃ nāma udakapupphuḷūpamaṃ tiṇagge ussāvabindūpamaṃ taṅkhaṇaviddhaṃsanadhammaṃ, tassa ko gatiṃ jānāti, kismiṃ khaṇe bhijjissati? Gamanīyo samparāyoti paraloko pana avassaṃ gantabbova, tattha paṇḍitena kulaputtena mantāyaṃ boddhabbaṃ. Mantā vuccati paññā, tāya mantetabbaṃ bujjhitabbaṃ, upaparikkhitabbañca jānitabbañcāti attho. Karaṇatthe vā bhummaṃ. Mantāyaṃ boddhabbanti mantāya bujjhitabbaṃ, ñāṇena jānitabbanti attho. Kiṃ bujjhitabbaṃ? Jīvitassa dujjānatā, samparāyassa [M 2.0263] ca avassaṃ gamanīyatā, bujjhitvā ca pana sabbapalibodhe chinditvā kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ caritabbaṃ brahmacariyaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā natthi jātassa amaraṇaṃ.

Regarding Ko nu kho pana bho jānāti jīvitānaṃ, this means: 'Sirs, life is like a water bubble, like a dewdrop on a blade of grass, having the nature of being destroyed in an instant. Who knows its course? In what moment will it break?' As for Gamanīyo samparāyo, the next world must certainly be gone to; there, a wise clansman should understand through deliberation. Mantā is called wisdom; by it, one should deliberate, understand, investigate, and know. Or, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. Mantāyaṃ boddhabbaṃ means 'it should be understood through deliberation, known through knowledge.' What is to be understood? The difficulty of knowing life and the inevitability of going to the next world. And having understood this, and having cut off all obstacles, one should perform wholesome deeds and live the holy life. Why? Because for one who is born, there is no non-dying.

Brāhmaṇamahāsālādīnaṃ āmantanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Address to the Brahmin Householders of Great Wealth and Others

324. Appesakkhā ca appalābhā cāti bho pabbajjā nāma appayasā ceva, pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya hi rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitaṃ viheṭhetvā viheṭhetvā lāmakaṃ anāthaṃ katvāva kathenti. Appalābhā ca, sakalagāmaṃ caritvāpi ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ dullabhameva. Idaṃ pana brahmaññaṃ [V 2.0236] mahesakkhañca mahāyasattā, mahālābhañca lābhasakkārasampannattā. Bhavañhi etarahi sakalajambudīpe aggapurohito sabbattha aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggabhattaṃ aggagandhaṃ aggamālaṃ labhatīti.

324. Regarding Appesakkhā ca appalābhā ca, this means: 'Sir, the life of renunciation is of little renown and few gains. For from the time of renunciation, people speak of one who has gone forth having abandoned a kingdom only after repeatedly harassing him, making him seem lowly and helpless. And it is of few gains, for even after wandering through an entire village, sustenance is very difficult to obtain. This state of a brahmin, however, is of great influence on account of its great renown, and of great gain on account of being endowed with gains and honor. For you, venerable sir, being now the chief purohita in all of Jambudīpa, receive everywhere the foremost seat, the foremost water, the foremost meal, the foremost perfume, and the foremost garland.'

Rājāva raññanti ahañhi bho etarahi pakatiraññaṃ majjhe cakkavattirājā viya. Brahmāva brahmānanti pakatibrahmānaṃ majjhe mahābrahmasadiso. Devatāva gahapatikānanti avasesagahapatikānaṃ panamhi sakkadevarājasadiso.

Regarding Rājāva raññaṃ, this means: 'Sirs, I am now like a wheel-turning monarch in the midst of ordinary kings.' As for Brahmāva brahmānaṃ, this means: 'In the midst of ordinary brahmās, I am like a Mahābrahmā.' Regarding Devatāva gahapatikānaṃ, this means: 'Among the remaining householders, I am like Sakka, king of the devas.'

Bhariyānaṃ āmantanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Address to the Wives

325. Cattārīsā bhariyā sādisiyoti sādisiyova cattārīsā bhariyā, aññā panassa tīsu vayesu nāṭakitthiyo bahukāyeva.

325. Regarding Cattārīsā bhariyā sādisiyo, this means there were forty wives of equal status. But besides these, he had very many female entertainers in the three stages of life.

Mahāgovindapabbajjāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Mahāgovinda's Going Forth

326. Cārikaṃ caratīti gāmanigamapaṭipāṭiyā cārikaṃ carati, gatagataṭṭhāne [P 2.0670] buddhakolāhalaṃ viya hoti. Manussā “mahāgovindapaṇḍito kira āgacchatī”ti sutvā puretarameva maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā maggaṃ alaṅkaritvā paccuggantvā gaṇhitvā enti, mahālābhasakkāro mahogho viya ajjhottharanto uppajji. Sattapurohitassāti sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ purohitassa. Iti yathā etarahi evarūpesu vā ṭhānesu kismiñcideva dukkhe uppanne “namo buddhassā”ti vadanti, evaṃ tadā “namatthu mahāgovindassa brāhmaṇassa, namatthu sattapurohitassā”ti vadanti.

326. Regarding Cārikaṃ carati, this means he wanders on tour in sequence through villages and towns. In every place he went, there was a commotion like that for a Buddha. Hearing, 'The sage Mahāgovinda is coming, it is said,' people would have a pavilion made beforehand, adorn the path, go out to meet him, and escort him in. Great gain and honor arose, overwhelming him like a great flood. As for sattapurohitassa, this means 'of the purohita of the seven kings.' Thus, just as nowadays when some suffering arises in such situations people say, 'Homage to the Buddha,' so too at that time they would say, 'Homage to the brahmin Mahāgovinda, homage to the purohita of the seven kings.'

327. Mettāsahagatenātiādinā [M 2.0264] nayena pāḷiyaṃ brahmavihārāva āgatā, mahāpuriso pana sabbāpi aṭṭha samāpattiyo ca pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattesi. Sāvakānañca brahmalokasahabyatāya maggaṃ desesīti brahmaloke brahmunā sahabhāvāya maggaṃ kathesi.

327. By the method beginning with Mettāsahagatena, only the divine abodes are mentioned in the Pāli text. The Great Being, however, also produced all eight attainments and the five higher knowledges. And for his disciples, he taught the path to companionship in the Brahma-world; that is, he spoke of the path to a state of being together with Brahmā in the Brahma-world.

328. Sabbenasabbanti ye aṭṭha ca samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattesuṃ. Ye na sabbena sabbaṃ sāsanaṃ ājāniṃsūti ye aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ekasamāpattimpi na jāniṃsu, na sakkhiṃsu nibbattetuṃ. Amoghāti savipākā. Avañjhāti na vañjhā. Sabbanihīnaṃ pasavanti gandhabbakāyaṃ [V 2.0237] pasavi. Saphalāti avasesadevalokūpapattīhi sātthā. Saudrayāti brahmalokūpapattiyā savuḍḍhi.

328. Regarding Sabbenasabbaṃ, this refers to those who produced the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges. As for Ye na sabbena sabbaṃ sāsanaṃ ājāniṃsu, this refers to those who did not know even one of the eight attainments and were not able to produce it. Amoghā means 'with result.' Avañjhā means 'not barren.' Sabbanihīnaṃ pasavi means it produced the host of gandhabbas. Saphalā means it was fruitful with rebirth in the remaining deva worlds. Saudrayā means it was with increase through rebirth in the Brahma-world.

329. Sarāmahanti sarāmi ahaṃ pañcasikha, iminā kira padena ayaṃ suttanto buddhabhāsito nāma jāto. Na nibbidāyāti na vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya. Na virāgāyāti na vaṭṭe virāgatthāya. Na nirodhāyāti na vaṭṭassa nirodhatthāya. Na upasamāyāti na vaṭṭassa upasamanatthāya. Na abhiññāyāti na vaṭṭaṃ abhijānanatthāya. Na sambodhāyāti na kilesaniddāvigamena vaṭṭato pabujjhanatthāya. Na nibbānāyāti na amatanibbānatthāya.

329. “I remember”—I, Pañcasikha, remember. By this phrase, it is said, this discourse became known as spoken by the Buddha. “Not for disenchantment”—not for the purpose of disenchantment with the cycle of existence. “Not for dispassion”—not for the purpose of dispassion toward the cycle of existence. “Not for cessation”—not for the purpose of cessation of the cycle of existence. “Not for peace”—not for the purpose of pacification of the cycle of existence. “Not for higher knowledge”—not for the purpose of knowing the cycle of existence with higher knowledge. “Not for awakening”—not for the purpose of awakening from the cycle of existence through the removal of the sleep of defilements. “Not for Nibbāna”—not for the purpose of deathless Nibbāna.

Ekantanibbidāyāti ekantameva vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya. Ettha pana nibbidāyāti vipassanā. Virāgāyāti maggo. Nirodhāya upasamāyāti nibbānaṃ. Abhiññāya sambodhāyāti maggo. Nibbānāyāti nibbānameva. Evaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vipassanā, tīsu maggo, tīsu nibbānaṃ vuttanti evaṃ vavatthānakathā veditabbā. Pariyāyena pana sabbānipetāni [P 2.0671] maggavevacanānipi nibbānavevacanānipi hontiyeva. Sammādiṭṭhiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ visuddhimagge saccavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva.

“For complete disenchantment” means solely for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the cycle of existence. Herein, “for disenchantment” means insight. “For dispassion” means the path. “For cessation” and “for peace” mean Nibbāna. “For higher knowledge” and “for awakening” mean the path. “For Nibbāna” means Nibbāna itself. Thus, in one place insight is stated, in three the path, and in three Nibbāna—this explanation of classification should be understood in this way. However, by way of alternative meaning, all these terms are indeed synonyms for the path and synonyms for Nibbāna. Whatever should be said regarding right view and so on has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition of the truths.

330. Ye na sabbenasabbanti ye cattāropi ariyamagge paripūretuṃ na jānanti, tīṇi vā dve vā ekaṃ vā nibbattenti. Sabbesaṃyeva imesaṃ kulaputtānanti brahmacariyaciṇṇakulaputtānaṃ. Amoghā…pe… saphalā saudrayāti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

330. “Those who not in every way”—those who do not know how to fulfill all four noble paths, but bring into being one, two, or three. “Of all these sons of good families” means of the sons of good families who have practiced the holy life. “Not barren… fruitful, with increase”—he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Bhagavantaṃ [M 2.0265] abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvāti (dī. ni. 2.188) bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ cittena sampaṭicchanto abhinanditvā vācāya pasaṃsamāno anumoditvā mahantaṃ añjaliṃ sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhapetvā pasannalākhārase nimujjamāno viya dasabalassa chabbaṇṇarasmijālantaraṃ pavisitvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā bhagavantaṃ abhitthavanto abhitthavanto satthu purato antaradhāyitvā attano devalokameva agamāsīti.

“Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him”—accepting the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma in his mind and rejoicing, praising it with his voice and approving, he placed his great clasped hands upon his head. As if plunging into clear lac-dye, he entered into the net of the six-colored rays of the One with Ten Powers. Having paid homage in four places and circumambulated him three times, repeatedly praising the Blessed One, he disappeared from the Teacher's presence and went to his own deva-world.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Mahāgovindasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta is concluded.

7. Mahāsamayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta

Nidānavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Introduction

331. Evaṃ [V 2.0238][P 2.0672][M 2.0266] me sutanti mahāsamayasuttaṃ. Tatrāyamapubbapadavaṇṇanā – sakkesūti ambaṭṭhasutte vuttena uppattinayena “sakyā vata, bho kumārā”ti udānaṃ paṭicca sakkāti laddhanāmānaṃ rājakumārānaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīsaddena “sakkā”ti vuccati, tasmiṃ sakkesu janapade. Mahāvaneti sayaṃjāte aropite himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhe mahati vane. Sabbeheva arahantehīti imaṃ suttaṃ kathitadivaseyeva pattaarahattehi.

331. “Thus have I heard” is the Mahāsamaya Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of the initial words: “Among the Sakyans”—by the method of origin stated in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, on account of the inspired utterance, “Capable indeed, sirs, are the princes!” the royal princes received the name “Sakyā.” Their dwelling place, even a single district, is called “Sakyā” by conventional usage; in that Sakyan district. “In the Great Forest” means in a great forest that was self-grown, not planted, and continuously connected with the Himalayas. “With all the Arahants” means with those who had attained Arahantship on the very day this sutta was spoken.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – sākiyakoliyā kira kapilavatthunagarassa ca koliyanagarassa ca antare rohiṇiṃ nāma nadiṃ ekeneva āvaraṇena bandhāpetvā sassāni karonti, atha jeṭṭhamūlamāse sassesu milāyantesu ubhayanagaravāsikānampi kammakarā sannipatiṃsu. Tattha koliyanagaravāsino āhaṃsu – “idaṃ udakaṃ ubhato hariyamānaṃ na tumhākaṃ na amhākaṃ pahossati, amhākaṃ pana sassaṃ ekena udakeneva nipphajjissati, idaṃ udakaṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti. Kapilavatthunagaravāsino āhaṃsu – “tumhesu koṭṭhe pūretvā ṭhitesu mayaṃ rattasuvaṇṇanīlamaṇikāḷakahāpaṇe ca gahetvā pacchipasibbakādihatthā na sakkhissāma tumhākaṃ gharadvāre vicarituṃ, amhākampi sassaṃ ekeneva udakena nipphajjissati, idaṃ udakaṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti. “Na [P 2.0673] mayaṃ dassāmā”ti. “Mayampi na dassāmā”ti. Evaṃ kalahaṃ vaḍḍhetvā eko uṭṭhāya ekassa pahāraṃ adāsi, sopi aññassāti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ paharitvā rājakulānaṃ jātiṃ ghaṭṭetvā kalahaṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsu.

Herein is the sequential account: It is said that the Sākyas and Koliyas had a single dam built across the Rohiṇī River, between the city of Kapilavatthu and the city of Koliya, and cultivated their crops. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops were withering, the laborers of the residents of both cities gathered. There, the residents of the city of Koliya said, “This water, being drawn from both sides, will not suffice for either you or us. Our crops, however, can be brought to fruition with just one more watering. Give this water to us.” The residents of the city of Kapilavatthu said, “When your granaries are full, we will not be able to wander at your house-doors with red gold, blue gems, and black coins in hand, with baskets, bags, and the like. Our crops too can be brought to fruition with just one more watering. Give this water to us.” “We will not give it.” “We too will not give it.” Thus, having escalated the quarrel, one rose and struck another, and that one struck someone else. In this way, striking one another and insulting the lineage of the royal families, they intensified the quarrel.

Koliyakammakarā vadanti – “tumhe kapilavatthuvāsike gahetvā gajjatha, ye soṇasiṅgālādayo viya attano bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvasiṃsu. Etesaṃ hatthino ca assā ca phalakāvudhāni [V 2.0239] ca amhākaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? Sākiyakammakarāpi vadanti – “tumhe dāni kuṭṭhino dārake gahetvā gajjatha, ye anāthā niggatikā tiracchānā viya kolarukkhe vasiṃsu, etesaṃ hatthino ca assā ca phalakāvudhāni ca amhākaṃ [M 2.0267] kiṃ karissantī”ti? Te gantvā tasmiṃ kamme niyuttaamaccānaṃ kathesuṃ, amaccā rājakulānaṃ kathesuṃ, tato sākiyā – “bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsikānaṃ thāmañca balañca dassessāmā”ti yuddhasajjā nikkhamiṃsu. Koliyāpi – “kolarukkhavāsīnaṃ thāmañca balañca dassessāmā”ti yuddhasajjā nikkhamiṃsu.

The Koliyan laborers said, “You boast, relying on the residents of Kapilavatthu, who, like dogs, jackals, and so on, cohabited with their own sisters. What can their elephants, horses, and shields-and-weapons do to us?” The Sākyan laborers also said, “Now you boast, relying on those leprous children who, helpless and without refuge, lived in a Kola tree like animals. What can their elephants, horses, and shields-and-weapons do to us?” They went and told the ministers appointed to that work, and the ministers told the royal families. Then the Sākyas, declaring, “We will show the strength and power of those who cohabit with their sisters!” marched out prepared for battle. The Koliyas also, declaring, “We will show the strength and power of those who live in the Kola tree!” marched out prepared for battle.

Bhagavāpi rattiyā paccūsasamayeva mahākaruṇāsamāpattito vuṭṭhāya lokaṃ volokento ime evaṃ yuddhasajje nikkhamante addasa. Disvā – “mayi gate ayaṃ kalaho vūpasamissati nu kho udāhu no”ti upadhārento – “ahamettha gantvā kalahavūpasamanatthaṃ tīṇi jātakāni kathessāmi, tato kalaho vūpasamissati. Atha sāmaggidīpanatthāya dve jātakāni kathetvā attadaṇḍasuttaṃ desessāmi. Desanaṃ sutvā ubhayanagaravāsinopi aḍḍhatiyāni aḍḍhatiyāni kumārasatāni dassanti, ahaṃ te pabbajissāmi, tadā mahāsamāgamo bhavissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānamakāsi. Tasmā imesu yuddhasajjesu nikkhamantesu kassaci anārocetvā sayameva pattacīvaramādāya gantvā dvinnaṃ senānaṃ antare ākāse pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajjetvā nisīdi.

The Blessed One, having risen at dawn from his meditation on great compassion and surveying the world, saw these people marching out thus prepared for battle. Reflecting, “If I go, will this conflict subside, or not?” he resolved, “I will go there and tell three Jātakas to pacify the quarrel; then the quarrel will subside. Then, to illuminate harmony, I will tell two Jātakas and teach the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. After hearing the teaching, the residents of both cities will each offer two hundred and fifty princes; I will ordain them, and then there will be a great gathering.” Thus, he made his decision. Therefore, without informing anyone, he himself took his bowl and robe and went. Seating himself cross-legged in the sky between the two armies, he emitted the six-colored rays and sat there.

Kapilavatthuvāsino bhagavantaṃ disvāva – “amhākaṃ ñātiseṭṭho satthā āgato, diṭṭho nu kho tena amhākaṃ kalahakāraṇabhāvo”ti cintetvā – “na kho pana sakkā bhagavati āgate amhehi parassa sarīre satthaṃ pātetuṃ, koliyanagaravāsino amhe [P 2.0674] hanantu vā pacantu vā”ti āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Koliyanagaravāsinopi tatheva cintetvā āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu.

The residents of Kapilavatthu, upon seeing the Blessed One, thought, “Our Teacher, the most excellent of our kinsmen, has come. Has he seen the cause of our quarrel?” Thinking thus, they reflected, “Now, with the Blessed One having arrived, it is not possible for us to strike another’s body with a weapon. Let the residents of Koliya kill us or cook us!” So they discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. The residents of Koliya also, thinking in the same manner, discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down.

Bhagavā jānantova – “kasmā āgatattha mahārājā”ti pucchi. Bhagavā, na titthakīḷāya na pabbatakīḷāya na nadīkīḷāya na giridassanatthaṃ, imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne saṅgāmaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā āgatamhāti. Kiṃ nissāya vo kalaho mahārājāti? Udakaṃ, bhanteti. Udakaṃ kiṃ agghati mahārājāti? Appagghaṃ, bhanteti. Pathavī nāma kiṃ agghati mahārājāti? Anagghā, bhanteti. Khattiyā kiṃ agghanti mahārājāti? Khattiyā nāma anagghā bhanteti. Appamūlakaṃ udakaṃ nissāya kimatthaṃ anagghe khattiye nāsetha, mahārājāti? “Kalahe assādo nāma natthi, kalahavasena mahārājā aṭṭhāne veraṃ katvā ekāya rukkhadevatāya kāḷasīhena saddhiṃ baddhāghāto [V 2.0240] sakalampi [M 2.0268] imaṃ kappaṃ anuppattoyevā”ti vatvā phandanajātakaṃ kathesi. Tato “parapattiyena nāma mahārājā na bhavitabbaṃ. Parapattiyā hutvā hi ekassa sasakassa kathāya tiyojanasahassavitthate himavante catuppadagaṇā mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhandino ahesuṃ. Tasmā parapattiyena na bhavitabba”nti vatvā pathavīundriyajātakaṃ kathesi. Tato – “kadāci, mahārājā, dubbalopi mahabbalassa randhaṃ vivaraṃ passati, kadāci mahabbalo dubbalassa. Laṭukikāpi hi sakuṇikā hatthināgaṃ ghātesī”ti vatvā laṭukikajātakaṃ kathesi. Evaṃ kalahavūpasamatthāya tīṇi jātakāni kathetvā sāmaggiparidīpanatthāya dve jātakāni kathesi. Kathaṃ? Samaggānañhi mahārājā koci otāraṃ nāma passituṃ na sakkotīti vatvā rukkhadhammajātakaṃ kathesi. Tato “samaggānaṃ mahārājā koci vivaraṃ passituṃ nāsakkhi. Yadā pana aññamaññaṃ vivādamakaṃsu, atha te nesādaputto jīvitā voropetvā ādāya gato. Vivāde assādo nāma natthī”ti vatvā vaṭṭakajātakaṃ kathesi. Evaṃ imāni pañca jātakāni kathetvā avasāne attadaṇḍasuttaṃ kathesi.

The Blessed One, though knowing, asked, “For what purpose have you come here, great kings?” “Venerable sir, we have not come for amusement at a ford, amusement on a mountain, amusement at a river, or to see the mountains, but having prepared for a battle in this place, we have come.” “On what account is your quarrel, great kings?” “Over water, venerable sir.” “What is water worth, great kings?” “It is of little worth, venerable sir.” “What is the earth worth, great kings?” “It is priceless, venerable sir.” “What are warrior-nobles worth, great kings?” “Warrior-nobles, venerable sir, are priceless.” “For the sake of water, which is of little worth, why do you destroy priceless warrior-nobles, great kings? There is no satisfaction in quarreling. Through quarreling, great kings, enmity is wrongly made; a certain tree-deity, having bound hatred with a black bear, has continued in it for this entire eon,” and having said this, he narrated the Phandana Jātaka. Then he said, “One should not be credulous, great kings. For, being credulous, on the word of a single hare, the four-footed creatures plunged into the great ocean from the Himalayas, which are three thousand leagues wide. Therefore, one should not be credulous,” and having said this, he narrated the Pathavīundriya Jātaka. Then he said, “Sometimes, great kings, even the weak see an opening or a gap in the strong; sometimes the strong see it in the weak. For even a little quail bird once killed a great elephant,” and having said this, he narrated the Laṭukika Jātaka. Thus, to pacify the quarrel, he narrated three Jātakas. To illustrate harmony, he narrated two Jātakas. How so? “For those who are united, great kings, no one can find an opportunity against them,” and having said this, he narrated the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka. Then he said, “When united, great kings, no one could find a gap. But when they quarreled among themselves, a fowler’s son took their lives and carried them away. There is no satisfaction in strife,” and having said this, he narrated the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. Thus, having narrated these five Jātakas, at the end he taught the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

Rājāno [P 2.0675] pasannā – “sace satthā nāgamissa, mayaṃ sahatthā aññamaññaṃyeva vadhitvā lohitanadiṃ pavattayissāma, amhākaṃ puttabhātaro gehadvāre na passeyyāma, sāsanapaṭisāsanampi no āharaṇako na bhavissati. Satthāraṃ nissāya no jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ. Sace pana satthā agāraṃ ajjhāvasissa, dvisahassadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu rajjamassa hatthagataṃ abhavissa, atirekasahassaṃ kho panassa puttā abhavissaṃsu, tato khattiyaparivārova avicarissa. Taṃ kho panesa sampattiṃ pahāya nikkhamitvā sambodhiṃ patto, idānipi khattiyaparivāroyeva vicaratū”ti ubhayanagaravāsino aḍḍhatiyāni aḍḍhatiyāni kumārasatāni adaṃsu. Bhagavā te pabbājetvā mahāvanaṃ agamāsi. Tesaṃ garugāravavasena na attano ruciyā pabbajitānaṃ anabhirati uppajji. Purāṇadutiyikāyopi nesaṃ “ayyaputtā ukkaṇṭhantu, gharāvāso na saṇṭhātī”tiādīni vatvā sāsanaṃ pesenti. Te atirekataraṃ ukkaṇṭhiṃsu.

The kings were pleased. They thought: “If the Teacher had not come, we would have struck each other with our own hands and caused a river of blood to flow, and we would not have seen our sons and brothers at our doorsteps, and there would have been no one to bring us messages and replies. Our lives have been obtained by relying on the Teacher. But if the Teacher had lived in a house, his rule would have been in his hands over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands, and he would have had more than a thousand sons; then he would have wandered attended only by a retinue of khattiyas. Yet, having abandoned such prosperity, he went forth and attained perfect enlightenment. Even now, let him wander attended by a retinue of khattiyas.” Thus, the residents of both cities gave two hundred and fifty princes each. The Blessed One ordained them and went to the Great Forest. Discontent arose in those who had gone forth not of their own liking, but out of great reverence. Even their former wives sent messages to them, saying, “Noble sirs, be discontent! Household life is not stable,” and so on. They became even more disheartened.

Bhagavā āvajjanto tesaṃ anabhiratabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ime bhikkhū mādisena buddhena saddhiṃ ekato vasantā ukkaṇṭhanti, handa nesaṃ kuṇāladahassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā tattha netvā anabhiratiṃ vinodessāmī”ti [M 2.0269] kuṇāladahassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Te taṃ daṭṭhukāmā ahesuṃ. Daṭṭhukāmattha, bhikkhave, kuṇāladahanti? Āma bhagavāti. Yadi evaṃ, etha, gacchāmāti. Iddhimantānaṃ bhagavā gamanaṭṭhānaṃ mayaṃ kathaṃ gamissāmāti? Tumhe gantukāmā hotha, ahaṃ mamānubhāvena gahetvā gamissāmīti. Sādhu, bhanteti. Atha bhagavā pañca bhikkhusatāni gahetvā ākāse uppatitvā [V 2.0241] kuṇāladahe patiṭṭhāya te bhikkhū āha – “bhikkhave, imasmiṃ kuṇāladahe yesaṃ macchānaṃ nāmaṃ na jānātha, tesaṃ nāmaṃ pucchathā”ti.

The Blessed One, reflecting and knowing their state of discontent, thought: 'These monks, living together with a Buddha like me, are disheartened. Come, I will describe the beauty of Lake Kuṇāla to them and, taking them there, dispel their discontent.' So he spoke of the beauty of Lake Kuṇāla. They became desirous of seeing it. The Blessed One asked, 'Monks, do you wish to see Lake Kuṇāla?' The monks replied, 'Blessed One, how shall we go to a place that is a destination for those with psychic power?' The Blessed One said, 'If you are desirous of going, I will take you there by my power.' 'Very well, Lord,' they said. Then the Blessed One, taking the five hundred monks, rose into the sky, landed at Lake Kuṇāla, and said to those monks: 'Monks, in this Lake Kuṇāla, ask the names of those fish whose names you do not know.'

Te pucchiṃsu, bhagavā pucchitapucchitaṃ kathesi. Na kevalaṃ macchānaṃyeva, tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe rukkhānampi pabbatapāde dvipadacatuppadasakuṇānampi nāmāni pucchāpetvā kathesi. Atha dvīhi sakuṇehi mukhatuṇḍakena ḍaṃsitvā gahitadaṇḍake nisinno kuṇālasakuṇarājā purato pacchato ubhosu passesu sakuṇasaṅghaparivuto āgacchati. Bhikkhū taṃ disvā – “esa, bhante, imesaṃ sakuṇānaṃ rājā bhavissati, parivārā ete etassā”ti [P 2.0676] maññāmāti. Evameva, bhikkhave, ayampi mama vaṃso mama paveṇīti. Idāni tāva mayaṃ, bhante, ete sakuṇe passāma. Yaṃ pana bhagavā “ayampi mama vaṃso mama paveṇī”ti āha, taṃ sotukāmamhāti. Sotukāmattha bhikkhaveti? Āma, bhagavāti. Tena hi suṇāthāti tīhi gāthāsatehi maṇḍetvā kuṇālajātakaṃ kathento anabhiratiṃ vinodesi. Desanāpariyosāne sabbepi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu, maggeneva ca nesaṃ iddhipi āgatā. Bhagavā – “hotu tāva ettakaṃ etesaṃ bhikkhūna”nti ākāse uppatitvā mahāvanameva agamāsi. Tepi bhikkhū gamanakāle dasabalassa ānubhāvena gantvā āgamanakāle attano ānubhāvena bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā mahāvane otariṃsu.

They asked, and the Blessed One answered each question that was asked. Not only of the fish, but having them ask the names of the trees in that forest grove and of the two-legged and four-legged creatures at the foot of the mountain, he also told them. Then, the kuṇāla bird-king arrived, seated on a perch held in the beaks of two birds, surrounded by a flock of birds before, behind, and on both sides. Seeing him, the monks said, 'Venerable Sir, we suppose this is the king of these birds, and these are his retinue.' 'Just so, monks. This one is also of my lineage, my ancestry.' 'Venerable Sir, we see these birds now. But we wish to hear of that which the Blessed One spoke, saying, "This one is also of my lineage, my ancestry."' 'Do you wish to hear, monks?' 'Yes, Blessed One.' 'In that case, listen.' Then, adorning it with three hundred verses, he told the Kuṇāla Jātaka and dispelled their discontent. At the conclusion of the discourse, all were established in the fruit of stream-entry, and psychic power also came to them along with the path. The Blessed One, thinking, 'Let this much suffice for these monks for now,' rose into the sky and went to the Great Forest. Those monks, too, having gone by the power of the Ten-Powered One on the way there, returned by their own power, surrounding the Blessed One, and descended in the Great Forest.

Bhagavā paññattāsane nisīditvā te bhikkhū āmantetvā – “etha, bhikkhave, nisīdatha, uparimaggattayavajjhānaṃ vo kilesānaṃ pahānāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathessāmī”ti kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Bhikkhū cintesuṃ – “bhagavā amhākaṃ anabhiratabhāvaṃ ñatvā kuṇāladahaṃ netvā anabhiratiṃ vinodesi, tattha sotāpattiphalappattānaṃ no idāni idha tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi, na kho panamhehi ‘sotāpannā maya’nti vītināmetuṃ vaṭṭati, uttamapurisasadisehi no bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti te dasabalassa pāde vanditvā uṭṭhāya nisīdanaṃ papphoṭetvā visuṃ visuṃ pabbhārarukkhamūlesu nisīdiṃsu.

The Blessed One sat down on the designated seat and addressed the monks: "Come, monks, sit down. I will teach you a meditation subject for the abandonment of your defilements that are to be destroyed by the three higher paths." Then he taught the meditation subject. The monks thought: "The Blessed One, knowing our discontent, led us to Lake Kuṇāla and dispelled our discontent. There, for us who had attained the fruit of stream-entry, he has now given a meditation subject for the three higher paths here. But it is not fitting for us to pass the time thinking, 'We are stream-enterers.' It is fitting for us to become like supreme men." They paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, rose, shook out their sitting cloths, and each sat down separately at the foot of a cliff-side tree.

Bhagavā [M 2.0270] cintesi – “ime bhikkhū pakatiyāpi avissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhānā, laddhupāyassa pana bhikkhuno kilamanakāraṇaṃ nāma natthi. Gacchantā gacchantā ca vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ patvā – “attanā attanā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ ārocessāmā’ti mama santikaṃ āgamissanti. Etesu āgatesu dasasahassacakkavāḷe devatā ekacakkavāḷe sannipatissanti, mahāsamayo bhavissati, vivitte okāse mayā nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tato vivitte okāse buddhāsanaṃ paññapetvā nisīdi.

The Blessed One thought: 'These monks, by their very nature, do not neglect their meditation subject; and for a monk who has found the means, there is no cause for weariness. As they continue on their way, they will develop insight, attain arahantship, and then come to me, thinking, "We will each announce the special quality we have attained." When they have arrived, deities from ten thousand world-systems will gather in one world-system, and there will be a great assembly. It is fitting for me to sit in a secluded place.' Therefore, having prepared the Buddha's seat in a secluded spot, he sat down.

Sabbapaṭhamaṃ [V 2.0242] kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gatathero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tato aparo tato aparoti pañcasatāpi paduminiyaṃ padumāni viya vikasiṃsu. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ [P 2.0677] arahattappattabhikkhu – “bhagavato ārocessāmī”ti pallaṅkaṃ vinibbhujitvā nisīdanaṃ papphoṭetvā uṭṭhāya dasabalābhimukho ahosi. Evaṃ aparopi aparopīti pañcasatāpi bhattasālaṃ pavisantā viya paṭipāṭiyāva āgamaṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ āgato vanditvā nisīdanaṃ paññapetvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ ārocetukāmo – “atthi nu kho añño koci, natthī”ti nivattitvā āgamanamaggaṃ olokento aparampi addasa aparampi addasa. Iti sabbepi te āgantvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā ayaṃ imassa harāyamāno na kathesi, ayaṃ imassa harāyamāno na kathesīti. Khīṇāsavānaṃ kira dve ākārā honti – “aho vata mayā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ sadevako loko khippameva paṭivijjheyyā”ti cittaṃ uppajjati. Paṭiladdhabhāvaṃ pana nidhiladdhapuriso viya na aññassa ārocetukāmo hoti.

The very first elder to take up the meditation subject and depart attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then another, and another after that—all five hundred blossomed like lotuses in a lotus pond. The first monk to attain arahantship thought, 'I will announce it to the Blessed One.' Breaking his cross-legged posture, he shook out his sitting mat, stood up, and faced the Ten-Powered One. In this way, another and another—all five hundred arrived in succession, just as one enters a refectory. The first to arrive paid homage, prepared a seat, and sat to one side. Intending to announce the special quality he had attained, he wondered, 'Is there anyone else coming, or not?' Turning back to look at the path of their approach, he saw another, and then another. Thus, all of them arrived and sat to one side. This one, feeling shy before that one, did not speak; and that one, feeling shy before this one, did not speak. It is said that there are two modes for those whose taints are destroyed: the thought arises, 'Oh, that the world with its devas might quickly penetrate the quality I have attained!' Or, like a person who has found a hidden treasure, one has no desire to announce the attainment to another.

Evaṃ osīdamatte pana tasmiṃ ariyamaṇḍale pācīnayugandharaparikkhepato abbhā, mahikā, dhūmo, rajo, rāhūti imehi upakkilesehi vippamuttaṃ buddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitassa lokassa rāmaṇeyyakadassanatthaṃ pācīnadisāya ukkhittarajatamayamahāādāsamaṇḍalaṃ viya, nemivaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā parivattiyamānarajatacakkasassirikaṃ puṇṇacandamaṇḍalaṃ ullaṅghitvā anilapathaṃ paṭipajjittha. Iti evarūpe khaṇe laye muhutte bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ mahāvane mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi sabbeheva arahantehi.

Now, at that very moment, when that noble circle had thus settled down, the full moon's orb—free from such defilements as clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu from the circumference of the eastern Yugandhara, like a great silver mirror-disc raised in the eastern direction for the sake of showing the delightfulness of the world adorned by the arising of a Buddha, and possessing the splendor of a silver wheel held by its rim and made to revolve—having risen up, entered the path of the wind. Thus, at such a moment, instant, and juncture, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Great Wood, together with a great Saṅgha of monks, with about five hundred monks, all of them arahants.

Tattha bhagavāpi mahāsammatassa vaṃse uppanno, tepi pañcasatā bhikkhū mahāsammatassa kule uppannā. Bhagavāpi khattiyagabbhe jāto, tepi khattiyagabbhe [M 2.0271] jātā. Bhagavāpi rājapabbajito, tepi rājapabbajitā. Bhagavāpi setacchattaṃ pahāya hatthagataṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ nissajjetvā pabbajito, tepi setacchattaṃ pahāya hatthagatāni rajjāni nissajjetvā pabbajitā. Iti bhagavā parisuddhe okāse parisuddhe rattibhāge sayaṃ parisuddho parisuddhaparivāro vītarāgo vītarāgaparivāro vītadoso vītadosaparivāro vītamoho vītamohaparivāro nittaṇho nittaṇhaparivāro nikkileso nikkilesaparivāro santo santaparivāro danto dantaparivāro mutto muttaparivāro ativiya virocatīti. Vaṇṇabhūmi [P 2.0678] nāmesā, yattakaṃ sakkoti, tattakaṃ vattabbaṃ. Iti ime bhikkhū sandhāya vuttaṃ – “pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi sabbeheva arahantehī”ti.

Therein, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of Mahāsammata, and those five hundred monks were born in the family of Mahāsammata. The Blessed One was born of the khattiya caste, and they too were born of the khattiya caste. The Blessed One went forth from the royal state, and they too went forth from the royal state. The Blessed One, having abandoned the white parasol and relinquished the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch that was in his grasp, went forth; they too, having abandoned the white parasol and relinquished the kingdoms that were in their grasp, went forth. Thus, the Blessed One—in a pure place, in a pure part of the night, himself pure, with a pure retinue; free from lust, with a retinue free from lust; free from hatred, with a retinue free from hatred; free from delusion, with a retinue free from delusion; free from craving, with a retinue free from craving; free from defilements, with a retinue free from defilements; peaceful, with a peaceful retinue; tamed, with a tamed retinue; liberated, with a liberated retinue—shone forth exceedingly. This is called the ground for praise; as much as one is able, so much should be said. Thus, with reference to these monks, it was said: “with about five hundred monks, all of them arahants.”

Yebhuyyenāti [V 2.0243] bahutarā sannipatitā, mandā na sannipatitā asaññā arūpāvacaradevatā samāpannadevatā ca. Tatrāyaṃ sannipātakkamo mahāvanassa kira sāmantā devatā caliṃsu – “āyāma, bho buddhadassanaṃ nāma bahūpakāraṃ, dhammassavanaṃ bahūpakāraṃ, bhikkhusaṅghadassanaṃ bahūpakāraṃ, āyāma āyāmā”ti mahāsaddaṃ kurumānā āgantvā bhagavantañca taṃmuhuttaṃ arahattappattakhīṇāsave ca vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Eteneva upāyena tāsaṃ tāsaṃ saddaṃ sutvā saddantaraaḍḍhagāvutagāvutaaḍḍhayojanayojanādivasena tiyojanasahassavitthate himavante, tikkhattuṃ tesaṭṭhiyā nagarasahassesu, navanavutiyā doṇamukhasatasahassesu, channavutiyā paṭṭanakoṭisatasahassesu, chapaṇṇāsāya ratanākaresūti sakalajambudīpe, pubbavidehe, aparagoyāne, uttarakurumhi, dvīsu parittadīpasahassesūti sakalacakkavāḷe, tato dutiyatatiyacakkavāḷeti evaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatā sannipatitāti veditabbā. Dasasahassacakkavāḷañhi idha dasalokadhātuyoti adhippetā. Tena vuttaṃ – “dasahi ca lokadhātūhi devatā yebhuyyena sannipatitā hontī”ti.

By 'for the most part' (yebhuyyena) is meant that the majority had gathered, while a few had not—namely, the non-percipient deities, the formless-realm deities, and the deities absorbed in meditative attainment. Here is the sequence of the gathering: It is said that the deities in the vicinity of the Great Forest stirred, saying, “Come, friends! Seeing the Buddha is of great benefit, hearing the Dhamma is of great benefit, seeing the Saṅgha of monks is of great benefit. Come, come!” Making a great sound, they approached, paid homage to the Blessed One and to the taint-destroyed ones who had attained arahantship at that very moment, and then stood to one side. In this same way, hearing the calls of those various deities, deities gathered from within earshot—from distances of half a gāvuta, a gāvuta, half a yojana, a yojana, and so forth—throughout the Himalayas, which extend for three thousand yojanas; in the sixty-three thousand cities; in the ninety-nine hundred thousand market towns; in the ninety-six million port cities; in the fifty-six sources of gems—that is, throughout the entire Jambudīpa, as well as in Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and the two thousand minor islands; that is, throughout the entire world-system, and then from the second and third world-systems. Thus it should be understood that deities from ten thousand world-systems gathered. For here, 'ten thousand world-systems' is intended by the term 'ten world-spheres'. Therefore it was said: “And deities from ten world-spheres have, for the most part, gathered.”

Evaṃ sannipatitāhi devatāhi sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ yāva brahmalokā sūcighare nirantaraṃ pakkhittasūcīhi viya paripuṇṇaṃ hoti. Tatra brahmalokassa evaṃ uccattanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Lohapāsāde kira sattakūṭāgārasamo pāsāṇo brahmaloke ṭhatvā adho khitto catūhi [M 2.0272] māsehi pathaviṃ pāpuṇāti. Evaṃ mahante okāse yathā heṭṭhā ṭhatvā khittāni pupphāni vā dhūmo vā upari gantuṃ, upari vā ṭhatvā khittasāsapā heṭṭhā otarituṃ antaraṃ na labhanti, evaṃ nirantaraṃ devatā ahesuṃ. Yathā kho pana cakkavattirañño nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ asambādhaṃ hoti, āgatāgatā mahesakkhā khattiyā okāsaṃ labhantiyeva, parato parato pana atisambādhaṃ hoti, evameva bhagavato nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ asambādhaṃ, āgatāgatā mahesakkhā devatā ca mahābrahmāno ca okāsaṃ labhantiyeva. Apisudaṃ [P 2.0679] bhagavato āsannāsannaṭṭhāne mahāparinibbāne vuttanayeneva vālaggakoṭinitudanamatte padese dasapi vīsampi sabbaparato tiṃsampi devatā sukhume sukhume attabhāve māpetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Saṭṭhi saṭṭhi devatā aṭṭhaṃsu.

With the deities thus assembled, the entire interior of the world-system, up to the Brahma-world, became as full as a needle case packed tightly with needles, leaving no space between. Therein, the height of the Brahma-world should be understood thus: it is said that a stone the size of the Lohapāsāda with its seven pinnacled chambers, if dropped from the Brahma-world, would take four months to reach the earth. In such a vast space, just as flowers or smoke thrown from below cannot find an interval to rise upwards, or mustard seeds thrown from above cannot find an interval to descend, so densely packed were the deities. Yet, just as the sitting place of a wheel-turning monarch is uncrowded, and eminent khattiyas who arrive always find space, though further away it becomes extremely crowded, so too was the Blessed One’s sitting place uncrowded, and the eminent deities and great Brahmās who arrived always found space. Moreover, in the area nearest to the Blessed One, as is said in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, even in a space the size of that pricked by a hair-tip, ten, twenty, and at the very back even thirty deities stood, having created exceedingly subtle forms. Sixty by sixty, deities stood.

Suddhāvāsakāyikānanti suddhāvāsavāsīnaṃ. Suddhāvāsā nāma suddhānaṃ anāgāmikhīṇāsavānaṃ āvāsā pañca brahmalokā. Etadahosīti kasmā ahosi? Te kira brahmāno samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā yathāparicchedena vuṭṭhitā brahmabhavanaṃ olokentā pacchābhatte bhattagehaṃ viya suññataṃ addasaṃsu. Tato “kuhiṃ brahmāno gatā”ti āvajjantā mahāsamāgamaṃ ñatvā – “ayaṃ samāgamo mahā, mayaṃ ohīnā, ohīnakānaṃ okāso dullabho hoti, tasmā [V 2.0244] gacchantā atucchahatthā hutvā ekekaṃ gāthaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā gacchāma. Tāya mahāsamāgame ca attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpessāma, dasabalassa ca vaṇṇaṃ bhāsissāmā”ti. Iti tesaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhāya āvajjitattā etadahosi.

‘Of the Suddhāvāsa group’ (suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ) means ‘of the dwellers in the Pure Abodes.’ The Pure Abodes are the five Brahma-worlds that are the dwelling places of the pure ones: the non-returners and the taint-destroyed ones. Why did ‘this thought occur to them’ (etadahosi)? It is said that those Brahmās, having entered meditative attainment and emerged after their determined period, surveyed their Brahma-abode and saw it was empty, like a dining hall after the meal. Then, reflecting, “Where have the Brahmās gone?” they learned of the great assembly and thought: “This assembly is great, and we have been left behind. For those who are left behind, a place is difficult to obtain. Therefore, let us not go empty-handed, but let each of us compose a verse and then go. By means of these verses, we will make known our arrival at the great assembly and also speak in praise of the Ten-Powered One.” Thus, because they had emerged from their attainment and reflected in this way, this thought occurred to them.

332. Bhagavato purato pāturahesunti pāḷiyaṃ bhagavato santike abhimukhaṭṭhāneyeva otiṇṇā viya katvā vuttā, na kho panettha evaṃ attho veditabbo. Te pana brahmaloke ṭhitāyeva gāthā abhisaṅkharitvā eko puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otari, eko dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ, eko pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ, eko uttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otari. Tato puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otiṇṇabrahmā nīlakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā nīlarasmiyo vissajjitvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ maṇicammaṃ paṭimuñcanto viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā buddhavīthi [M 2.0273] nāma kenaci ottharituṃ na sakkā, tasmā pahaṭabuddhavīthiyāva āgantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito attanā abhisaṅkhataṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

332. Regarding the phrase 'they appeared before the Blessed One' (bhagavato purato pāturahesuṃ), in the Pāli text it is stated as if they had descended right in front of the Blessed One; however, this is not the meaning to be understood here. Rather, those Brahmās, while still in the Brahma world, each composed a verse. One descended at the rim of the eastern world-system, one at the rim of the southern world-system, one at the rim of the western world-system, and one at the rim of the northern world-system. Then, the Brahmā who descended at the rim of the eastern world-system entered the blue kasiṇa, emitted blue rays, and, as if clothing the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system in jeweled armor, made his arrival known. The Buddha's path cannot be obstructed by anyone; therefore, having come along the clear Buddha-path, he paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side, and, while standing there, recited the verse he had composed.

Dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otiṇṇabrahmāpi pītakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā pītarasmiyo suvaṇṇapabhaṃ muñcitvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭaṃ pārupento viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā tatheva aṭṭhāsi. Pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ [P 2.0680] otiṇṇabrahmāpi lohitakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā lohitarasmiyo muñcitvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ rattavarakambalena parikkhipanto viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā tatheva aṭṭhāsi. Uttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otiṇṇabrahmāpi odātakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā odātarasmiyo muñcitvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ sumanapaṭaṃ pārupanto viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā tatheva aṭṭhāsi.

The Brahmā who descended at the rim of the southern world-system also entered the yellow kasiṇa, emitted yellow rays of golden radiance, and, as if draping a golden cloth upon the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system, made his arrival known and stood there in the same manner. The Brahmā who descended at the rim of the western world-system also entered the red kasiṇa, emitted red rays, and, as if enveloping the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system with a fine red blanket, made his arrival known and stood there in the same manner. The Brahmā who descended at the rim of the northern world-system also entered the white kasiṇa, emitted white rays, and, as if draping a cloth of jasmine flowers upon the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system, made his arrival known and stood there in the same manner.

Pāḷiyaṃ pana “bhagavato purato pāturahesuṃ. Atha kho tā devatā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsū”ti evaṃ ekakkhaṇaṃ viya purato pātubhāvo ca abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitabhāvo ca vutto, so iminā anukkamena ahosi, ekato katvā pana dassito. Gāthābhāsanaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ visuṃ visuṃyeva vuttaṃ.

In the Pāli text, however, it is stated: "They appeared before the Blessed One. Then those deities, having paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side." Thus, their appearance before him, their paying homage, and their standing to one side are spoken of as if occurring in a single moment. But this occurred in the sequence described, though it is presented as a single event. The speaking of the verses, however, is stated separately in the Pāli text.

Tattha mahāsamayoti mahāsamūho. Pavanaṃ vuccati vanasaṇḍo. Ubhayenapi bhagavā imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe ajja mahāsamūho mahāsannipātoti āha. Tato yesaṃ so sannipāto, te dassetuṃ devakāyā [V 2.0245] samāgatāti āha. Tattha devakāyāti devaghaṭā. Āgatamha imaṃ dhammasamayanti evaṃ samāgate devakāye disvā mayampi imaṃ dhammasamūhaṃ āgatā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅghaṃ, kenaci aparājitaṃ ajjeva tayo māre madditvā vijitasaṅgāmaṃ imaṃ aparājitasaṅghaṃ dassanatthāya āgatamhāti attho. So pana brahmā imaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Therein, 'a great occasion' (mahāsamayo) means a great assembly. A forest grove is called a 'wood' (pavanaṃ). By both terms, the Blessed One indicated, "Today in this forest grove there is a great assembly, a great gathering." Then, to show whose assembly it was, he said, "Hosts of devas have assembled." Therein, 'hosts of devas' (devakāyā) means groups of deities. Regarding the line, 'We have come to this Dhamma assembly' (āgatamha imaṃ dhammasamayanti), the meaning is: "Having seen the hosts of devas thus assembled, we too have come to this Dhamma assembly. For what reason? To see the unconquered Saṅgha." That is, "We have come to see this unconquered Saṅgha, undefeated by anyone, which has this very day crushed the three Māras and won the battle." That Brahmā, having spoken this verse, paid homage to the Blessed One and stood right at the rim of the eastern world-system.

Atha dutiyo vuttanayeneva āgantvā abhāsi. Tattha tatra bhikkhavoti tasmiṃ sannipātaṭṭhāne bhikkhū. Samādahaṃsūti samādhinā yojesuṃ. Cittamattano ujukaṃ akaṃsūti attano cittaṃ sabbe vaṅkakuṭilajimhabhāve haritvā ujukaṃ akariṃsu. Sārathīva nettāni gahetvāti [M 2.0274] yathā samappavattesu sindhavesu odhastapatodo sārathi sabbayottāni gahetvā acodento avārento tiṭṭhati, evaṃ chaḷaṅgupekkhāsamannāgatā guttadvārā sabbepete pañcasatā bhikkhū indriyāni rakkhanti paṇḍitā, ete daṭṭhuṃ idhāgatamha bhagavāti. Sopi gantvā yathāṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Then the second Brahmā came in the manner described and spoke. Therein, 'the bhikkhus there' (tatra bhikkhavo) refers to the bhikkhus in that place of assembly. 'Composed themselves' (samādahaṃsu) means they yoked their minds with concentration. 'They made their own minds straight' (cittamattano ujukaṃ akaṃsu) means they all removed any state of crookedness, perversity, or deviousness from their minds and made them straight. 'Like a charioteer holding the reins' (sārathīva nettāni gahetvā): just as a charioteer, with goad laid down, holds all the reins while his thoroughbreds proceed evenly, neither urging them on nor holding them back, so too do these five hundred bhikkhus—wise, with guarded sense-doors, and endowed with six-factored equanimity—guard their faculties. The meaning is: 'O Blessed One, we have come here to see them.' He too went and stood in his proper place.

Atha [P 2.0681] tatiyo vuttanayeneva āgantvā abhāsi. Tattha chetvā khīlanti rāgadosamohakhīlaṃ chinditvā. Palighanti rāgadosamohapalighameva. Indakhīlantipi rāgadosamohaindakhīlameva. Ūhacca manejāti ete taṇhāejāya abhāvena anejā bhikkhū indakhīlaṃ ūhacca samūhanitvā. Te carantīti catūsu disāsu appaṭihatacārikaṃ caranti. Suddhāti nirupakkilesā. Vimalāti nimmalā. Idaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Cakkhumatāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumantena. Sudantāti cakkhutopi dantā, sotatopi ghānatopi jivhātopi kāyatopi manatopi dantā. Susunāgāti taruṇanāgā. Te evarūpena anuttarena yogācariyena damite taruṇanāge dassanāya āgatamha bhagavāti. Sopi gantvā yathāṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Then the third Brahmā came in the manner described and spoke. Therein, 'having cut the stake' (chetvā khīlaṃ) means having cut the stake of greed, hatred, and delusion. 'The cross-bar' (palighaṃ) refers to the cross-bar of greed, hatred, and delusion. 'The threshold-post' (indakhīlaṃ) is also the threshold-post of greed, hatred, and delusion. 'Having uprooted that which wavers' (ūhacca maneja): these bhikkhus, being unwavering due to the absence of the agitation of craving, have uprooted and removed the threshold-post. 'They wander' (te caranti): they wander with unobstructed travel in the four directions. 'Pure' (suddhā): free from defilements. 'Stainless' (vimalā): immaculate; this is a synonym for the former. 'By the one with vision' (cakkhumatā): by the one endowed with the five eyes. 'Well-tamed' (sudantā): tamed as to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. 'Excellent young nāgas' (susunāgā): young noble ones. The meaning is: 'O Blessed One, we have come to see those young noble ones, tamed by such an unsurpassed master of the practice.' He too went and stood in his proper place.

Atha catuttho vuttanayeneva āgantvā abhāsi. Tattha gatāseti nibbematikasaraṇagamanena gatā. Sopi gantvā yathāṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Then the fourth Brahmā came in the manner described and spoke. Therein, 'they have gone' (gatāse) means they have gone for refuge without any doubt. He too went and stood in his proper place.

Devatāsannipātavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Assembly of Deities

333. Atha bhagavā olokento pathavītalato yāva cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiparicchedā yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā devatāsannipātaṃ disvā cintesi – “mahā ayaṃ devatāsamāgamo, bhikkhū pana evaṃ mahā devatāya samāgamoti na jānanti, handa, nesaṃ ācikkhāmī”ti, evaṃ cintetvā [V 2.0246] “atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesī”ti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Tattha etaparamāti etaṃ paramaṃ pamāṇaṃ etesanti etaparamā. Idāni buddhānaṃ pana abhāvā “yepi te, bhikkhave, etarahī”ti tatiyo vāro na vutto. Ācikkhissāmi, bhikkhaveti kasmā āha? Devatānaṃ cittakallatājananatthaṃ. Devatā kira cintesuṃ – “bhagavā evaṃ mahante samāgame mahesakkhānaṃyeva devatānaṃ nāmagottāni kathessati, appesakkhānaṃ kiṃ kathessatī”ti? Atha [M 2.0275] bhagavā “imā devatā kiṃ cintentī”ti āvajjanto mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetvā hadayamaṃsaṃ maddanto viya sabhaṇḍaṃ coraṃ gaṇhanto viya ca taṃ tāsaṃ cittācāraṃ ñatvā – “dasasahassacakkavāḷato āgatāgatānaṃ appesakkhamahesakkhānaṃ sabbāsampi devatānaṃ nāmagottaṃ kathessāmī”ti cintesi.

333. Then the Blessed One, surveying from the surface of the earth up to the boundary of the world-system's circumference and up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world, saw the gathering of devas and thought: "This is a great assembly of devas, but the bhikkhus do not know that such a great assembly of devas has come. Come now, I shall inform them." Having thought thus, the passage beginning, "Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus," should all be elaborated. Therein, 'etaparamā' means 'this is the highest measure for them.' But now, due to the absence of other Buddhas, the third instance beginning with 'those who, bhikkhus, are now' was not spoken. Why did he say, 'I shall explain, bhikkhus'? To generate mental readiness in the devas. It is said that the devas thought: "In such a great assembly, the Blessed One will only state the names and clans of the devas of great power. What will he say of those with little power?" Then the Blessed One, adverting to their thoughts—as if putting his hand into his mouth and squeezing the flesh of his heart, and as if seizing a thief with his stolen goods—knew their mental disposition and thought: "I shall state the names and clans of all the devas, both of little and great power, who have come from the ten-thousand world-systems."

Buddhā nāma mahantā ete sattavisesā, yaṃ sadevakassa [P 2.0682] lokassa diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, na kiñci katthaci nīlādivasena vibhattarūpārammaṇesu rūpārammaṇaṃ vā bherīsaddādivasena vibhattasaddārammaṇādīsu visuṃ visuṃ saddādiārammaṇaṃ vā atthi, yaṃ etesaṃ ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ nāgacchati. Yathāha –

These beings called Buddhas are great and special. Of that which is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and mentally traversed by the world with its devas, there is no form-object among form-objects distinguished by blue and other colors, nor any sound-object or other sense-object among sound-objects and so forth distinguished by the sound of a drum and other sounds, that does not come into the range of their knowledge. As it is said:

“Yaṃ bhikkhave sadevakassa lokassa…pe… sadevamanussāya diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, tamahaṃ jānāmi, tamahaṃ passāmi, tamahaṃ abbhaññāsi”nti (a. ni. 4.24).

"Whatever, bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... with its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or traversed by the mind—that I know, that I see, that I have directly known." (A. Ni. 4.24)

Evaṃ sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇo bhagavā sabbāpi tā devatā bhabbābhabbavasena dve koṭṭhāse akāsi. “Kammāvaraṇena vā samannāgatā”tiādinā nayena vuttā sattā abhabbā nāma. Te ekavihāre vasantepi buddhā na olokenti. Viparītā pana bhabbā nāma, te dūre vasantepi gantvā saṅgaṇhanti. Tasmā tasmimpi devatāsannipāte ye abhabbā, te pahāya bhabbe pariggahesi. Pariggahetvā – “ettakā ettha rāgacaritā, ettakā dosacaritā, ettakā mohacaritā”ti caritavasena cha koṭṭhāse akāsi. Atha nesaṃ sappāyaṃ dhammadesanaṃ upadhārayanto – “rāgacaritānaṃ devatānaṃ sammāparibbājaniyasuttaṃ kathessāmi, dosacaritānaṃ kalahavivādasuttaṃ, mohacaritānaṃ mahābyūhasuttaṃ, vitakkacaritānaṃ cūḷabyūhasuttaṃ, saddhācaritānaṃ tuvaṭṭakapaṭipadaṃ, buddhicaritānaṃ purābhedasuttaṃ kathessāmī”ti desanaṃ vavatthapetvā puna taṃ parisaṃ manasākāsi – “attajjhāsayena nu kho jāneyya, parajjhāsayena atthuppattikena pucchāvasenā”ti. Tato “pucchāvasena jāneyyā”ti ñatvā “atthi nu kho koci devatānaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ gahetvā caritavasena pañhaṃ pucchituṃ samattho”ti “tesu pañcasatesu bhikkhūsu ekopi [V 2.0247] na sakkotī”ti addasa. Tato asītimahāsāvake dve aggasāvake ca samannāharitvā “tepi [M 2.0276] na sakkontī”ti disvā cintesi “sace paccekabuddho bhaveyya, sakkuṇeyya nu kho”ti “sopi na sakkuṇeyyā”ti ñatvā “sakkasuyāmādīsu koci sakkuṇeyyā”ti samannāhari. Sace hi tesu koci sakkuṇeyya, taṃ pucchāpetvā attanā vissajjeyya, na pana tesupi koci sakkoti.

Thus, the Blessed One, with unobstructed knowledge in all things, divided all those devas into two categories: the capable and the incapable. Beings spoken of in the manner beginning, 'Or endowed with the obstruction of kamma,' are called incapable. Even if they dwell in the same monastery, the Buddhas do not see them. Conversely, the capable, even if they dwell far away, the Buddhas go and gather them. Therefore, in that assembly of devas, having set aside the incapable, he embraced the capable. Having embraced them, he divided them into six categories according to their temperament: 'So many here are of lustful temperament, so many of hateful temperament, so many of deluded temperament.' Then, considering a suitable Dhamma teaching for them, he determined: 'For the devas of lustful temperament, I will teach the Sammāparibbājaniya Sutta; for those of hateful temperament, the Kalahavivāda Sutta; for those of deluded temperament, the Mahābyūha Sutta; for those of speculative temperament, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta; for those of faithful temperament, the Tuvaṭṭaka Practice; and for those of intellectual temperament, the Purābheda Sutta.' Having thus established the teaching, he once again focused his mind on that assembly, considering: 'Should I know how to proceed by my own inclination, by another's inclination, by the arising of a cause, or by way of a question?' Then, realizing, 'I should know by way of a question,' he considered, 'Is there anyone capable of grasping the devas' inclination and asking a question according to their temperament?' He saw that not even one among the five hundred bhikkhus was able. Then, bringing to mind the eighty great disciples and the two chief disciples, he saw that even they were incapable. He thought, 'If there were a Paccekabuddha, would he be able?' Knowing that even he would not be able, he considered, 'Could anyone among Sakka, Suyāma, and others do it?' For if anyone among them could, he would have them ask the question and then answer it himself. But none of them were capable either.

Athassa [P 2.0683] etadahosi – “mādiso buddhoyeva sakkuṇeyya, atthi pana katthaci añño buddho”ti anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantañāṇaṃ pattharitvā olokento aññaṃ buddhaṃ na addasa. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ idāni attanā samaṃ na passeyya, so jātadivasepi brahmajālavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena attanā samaṃ apassanto – “aggohamasmi lokassā”ti appaṭivattiyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi. Evaṃ aññaṃ attanā samaṃ apassitvā cintesi – “sace ahaṃ pucchitvā ahameva vissajjeyyaṃ, evampetā devatā na sakkhissanti paṭivijjhituṃ. Aññasmiṃ pana buddheyeva pucchante mayi ca vissajjante accherakaṃ bhavissati, sakkhissanti ca devatā paṭivijjhituṃ, tasmā nimmitabuddhaṃ māpessāmī”ti abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya – “pattacīvaragahaṇaṃ ālokitavilokitaṃ samiñjitapasāritañca mama sadisaṃyeva hotū”ti kāmāvacaracittehi parikammaṃ katvā pācīnayugandharaparikkhepato ullaṅghamānaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā nikkhamantaṃ viya rūpāvacaracittena adhiṭṭhāsi.

Then this thought occurred to him: "Only a Buddha like me would be able. But is there another Buddha somewhere?" Spreading his infinite knowledge across the infinite world-systems, he searched but saw no other Buddha. And this was no wonder, that he would not now see anyone equal to himself. On the day of his birth too, as described in the commentary to the Brahmajāla Sutta, not seeing anyone equal to himself, he roared the irrefutable lion's roar: "I am the highest in the world." Thus, not seeing anyone equal to himself, he thought: "If I were to ask a question and answer it myself, these devas would not be able to comprehend it. But if another Buddha were to ask and I were to answer, it would be astonishing, and the devas would be able to comprehend. Therefore, I shall create an emanated Buddha." Having entered the jhāna that is the basis for the higher knowledges and emerged, he resolved: "Let the taking of the bowl and robe, the looking forward and around, the bending and stretching, be just like mine."
