"'Upanaccantiyā'ti: While dancing. It is said that at one time she went with the devas of the Four Great Kings to display a dance for Sakka, the king of the devas. And at that very moment, Sakka was proclaiming the eight true qualities of the Tathāgata. Thus, on that day, having gone there, she heard this while dancing.

Sakkūpasaṅkamavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on Sakka's Approach

350. Paṭisammodatīti “saṃsandati kho te”tiādīni vadanto bhagavā sammodati, pañcasikho paṭisammodati. Gāthā ca bhāsanto pañcasikho sammodati, bhagavā paṭisammodati. Āmantesīti jānāpesi. Tassa kirevaṃ ahosi “ayaṃ pañcasikho mayā mama kammena pesito attano kammaṃ karoti. Evarūpassa satthu santike ṭhatvā kāmaguṇūpasañhitaṃ ananucchavikaṃ kathesi, naṭā nāma nillajjā honti, kathento vippakārampi dasseyya, handa naṃ mama kammaṃ jānāpemī”ti cintetvā āmantesi.

350. "Paṭisammodati" means the Blessed One rejoiced, saying things like, "You are in harmony," and Pañcasikha rejoiced in return. While reciting the verse, Pañcasikha rejoiced, and the Blessed One reciprocated. "Āmantesi" means he addressed. It occurred to him: "This Pañcasikha, sent by me for my task, is doing his own work. Standing in the presence of such a Teacher, he speaks what is unfitting, associated with sensual qualities. Actors are indeed shameless; while speaking, he might even display impropriety. Come, let me make him aware of my task." Having reflected thus, he addressed him.

351. Evañca [P 3.0705][V 2.0267] pana tathāgatāti dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi ṭhapitavacanaṃ. Abhivadantīti abhivādanasampaṭicchanena vaḍḍhitavacanena vadanti. Abhivaditoti vaḍḍhitavacanena vutto.

351. "'Evañca pana tathāgatā'ti: This is a statement inserted by the elders who compiled the Dhamma. 'Abhivadanti'ti: They speak with words of blessing in acceptance of homage. 'Abhivadito'ti: Spoken to with words of blessing.

Urundā samapādīti mahantā vivaṭā ahosi, andhakāro guhāyaṃ antaradhāyi. Āloko udapādīti yo pakatiyā guhāyaṃ andhakāro, so antarahito, āloko jāto. Sabbametaṃ dhammasaṅgāhakānaṃ vacanaṃ.

"'Urundā samapādī'ti: It became great and open; the darkness in the cave disappeared. 'Āloko udapādī'ti: The darkness that was naturally in the cave vanished, and a light arose. All this is the word of the compilers of the Dhamma.

352. Cirapaṭikāhaṃ, bhanteti cirato ahaṃ, cirato paṭṭhāyāhaṃ dassanakāmoti attho. Kehici kehici kiccakaraṇīyehīti devānaṃ dhītā ca puttā ca aṅke nibbattanti, pādaparicārikā itthiyo sayane nibbattanti, tāsaṃ maṇḍanapasādhanakārikā devatā sayanaṃ parivāretvā nibbattanti, veyyāvaccakarā antovimāne nibbattanti, etesaṃ atthāya aḍḍakaraṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ye pana sīmantare nibbattanti, te “tava santakā, mama santakā”ti nicchetuṃ asakkontā aḍḍaṃ karonti, sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ pucchanti. So “yassa vimānaṃ āsannataraṃ, tassa santakā”ti vadati. Sace [M 2.0298] dvepi samaṭṭhāne honti, “yassa vimānaṃ olokentī ṭhitā, tassa santakā”ti vadati. Sace ekampi na oloketi, taṃ ubhinnaṃ kalahupacchedanatthaṃ attano santakaṃ karoti. Kīḷādīnipi kiccāni karaṇīyāneva. Evarūpāni tāni karaṇīyāni sandhāya “kehici kehici kiccakaraṇīyehī”ti āha.

352. "For a long time, venerable sir," means "for a long time, from long ago, I have desired to see you." "By some, by some duties to be done": the daughters and sons of the devas are born in their laps; female attendants who attend to their feet are born on their couches; devatās who adorn and beautify them are born surrounding the bed; servants are born inside the celestial mansions. For these, there is no such thing as arbitration. But those who are born on the borders, unable to decide, create a dispute, saying, "They are yours, they are mine." They ask Sakka, the king of the devas. He says, "They belong to whoever's mansion is nearer." If both are in an equal place, he says, "They belong to whomever's mansion she stands looking at." If she does not look at either one, he makes it his own to settle the dispute between the two. Even playful activities and other duties must be performed. Referring to such duties, he said, "By some, by some duties to be done."

Salaḷāgāraketi salaḷamayagandhakuṭiyaṃ. Aññatarena samādhināti tadā kira bhagavā sakkasseva aparipākagataṃ ñāṇaṃ viditvā okāsaṃ akāretukāmo phalasamāpattivihārena nisīdi. Taṃ esa ajānanto “aññatarena samādhinā”ti āha. Bhūjati ca nāmāti bhūjatīti tassā nāmaṃ. Paricārikāti pādaparicārikā devadhītā. Sā kira dve phalāni pattā, tenassā devaloke abhiratiyeva natthi. Niccaṃ bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā añjaliṃ sirasi ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ namassamānā tiṭṭhati. Nemisaddena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhitoti “samāpanno saddaṃ suṇātī”ti no vata re vattabbe, nanu bhagavā sakkassa devānamindassa [P 3.0706] “apicāhaṃ āyasmato cakkanemisaddena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhito”ti bhaṇatīti. Tiṭṭhatu nemisaddo, samāpanno nāma antosamāpattiyaṃ kaṇṇamūle dhamamānassa saṅkhayugaḷassāpi asanisannipātassāpi saddaṃ na suṇāti. Bhagavā pana “ettakaṃ kālaṃ sakkassa okāsaṃ na karissāmī”ti paricchinditvā kālavasena phalasamāpattiṃ samāpanno. Sakko “na dāni me satthā okāsaṃ karotī”ti gandhakuṭiṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rathaṃ nivattetvā devalokābhimukhaṃ pesesi. Gandhakuṭipariveṇaṃ [V 2.0268] rathasaddena samohitaṃ pañcaṅgikatūriyaṃ viya ahosi. Bhagavato yathāparicchinnakālavasena samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa rathasaddeneva paṭhamāvajjanaṃ uppajji, tasmā evamāha.

"In the salaḷa hall" means in the fragrant hut made of salaḷa wood. "By a certain concentration": at that time, it is said, the Blessed One, knowing that Sakka’s knowledge was not yet mature and not wishing to grant him an opportunity, sat in the abiding of fruition attainment. He, not knowing this, said, "by a certain concentration." "And her name is Bhūjati": Bhūjati is her name. "An attendant": a celestial maiden who was a foot-attendant. It is said she had attained two fruits; therefore, she had no delight at all in the deva world. Constantly coming to attend upon the Blessed One, she would stand paying homage to him with her hands reverently placed on her head. Regarding "arisen from that concentration by the sound of the wheel-rim": it should not be said that one who has attained absorption hears a sound. But did not the Blessed One say to Sakka, the lord of the devas, "Moreover, venerable one, I arose from that concentration by the sound of your wheel-rim"? Let the sound of the wheel-rim be. One who has attained absorption, while in absorption, does not hear the sound even of a pair of conches being blown near the ear, nor of a thunderclap. But the Blessed One, having determined, "For this much time I will not grant Sakka an opportunity," entered the fruition attainment according to that period of time. Sakka, thinking, "Now the Teacher does not grant me an opportunity," and after circumambulating the fragrant hut, turned his chariot around and sent it toward the deva world. The precinct of the fragrant hut, filled with the sound of the chariot, was like a five-limbed orchestra. For the Blessed One, who arose from the attainment according to the predetermined period of time, the first moment of advertence arose precisely with the sound of the chariot. Therefore, he spoke thus.

Gopakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Gopaka Story

353. Sīlesu paripūrakārinīti pañcasu sīlesu paripūrakārinī. Itthittaṃ virājetvāti itthittaṃ nāma alaṃ, na hi itthitte ṭhatvā cakkavattisiriṃ, na sakkamārabrahmasiriyo paccanubhavituṃ, na paccekabodhiṃ, na sammāsambodhiṃ gantuṃ sakkāti evaṃ itthittaṃ virājeti nāma. Mahantamidaṃ purisattaṃ nāma seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ, ettha ṭhatvā sakkā etā sampattiyo pāpuṇitunti evaṃ [M 2.0299] pana purisattaṃ bhāveti nāma. Sāpi evamakāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “itthittaṃ virājetvā purisattaṃ bhāvetvā”ti. Hīnaṃ gandhabbakāyanti hīnaṃ lāmakaṃ gandhabbanikāyaṃ. Kasmā pana te parisuddhasīlā tattha uppannāti? Pubbanikantiyā. Pubbepi kira nesaṃ etadeva vasitaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā nikantivasena tattha uppannā. Upaṭṭhānanti upaṭṭhānasālaṃ. Pāricariyanti paricaraṇabhāvaṃ. Gītavāditehi amhe paricarissāmāti āgacchanti.

353. "One who fulfills the virtues" means one who fulfills the five precepts. "Having become dispassionate towards femininity": the state of being a woman is called "inadequate," for while established in femininity, one cannot experience the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, nor the majesty of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, nor is it possible to attain Paccekabodhi or perfect enlightenment. In this way, one is said to "become dispassionate towards femininity." And one is said to "cultivate manhood" by thinking thus: "This state of manhood is great, excellent, supreme. Established in this, it is possible to attain these accomplishments." She also acted in this way. Therefore, it is said: "Having become dispassionate towards femininity, having cultivated manhood." "To the inferior host of gandhabbas" means to the inferior, base company of gandhabbas. But why were they, of pure virtue, reborn there? Because of a former delight. It is said that in the past, this very place was their dwelling place; therefore, because of that delight, they were reborn there. "For attendance" means to the attendance hall. "For service" means for the state of being an attendant. They come thinking, "We will serve them with song and music."

Paṭicodesīti sāresi. So kira te disvā “ime devaputtā ativiya virocenti ativaṇṇavanto, kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ katvā āgatā”ti āvajjanto “bhikkhū ahesu”nti addasa. Tato “bhikkhū hontu, sīlesu paripūrakārino”ti upadhārento “paripūrakārino”ti addasa. “Paripūrakārino hontu, añño guṇo atthi [P 3.0707] natthī”ti upadhārento “jhānalābhino”ti addasa. “Jhānalābhino hontu, kuhiṃ vāsikā”ti upadhārento “mayhaṃva kulūpakā”ti addasa. Parisuddhasīlā nāma chasu devalokesu yatthicchanti, tattha nibbattanti. Ime pana uparidevaloke ca na nibbattā. Jhānalābhino nāma brahmaloke nibbattanti, ime ca brahmaloke na nibbattā. Ahaṃ pana etesaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā devalokasāmikassa sakkassa devānamindassa pallaṅke putto hutvā nibbatto, ime hīne gandhabbakāye nibbattā. Aṭṭhivedhapuggalā nāmete vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā gāḷhaṃ vijjhitabbāti cintetvā kutomukhā nāmātiādīhi vacanehi paṭicodesi.

"He admonished them" means he reminded them. It is said that upon seeing them, he reflected, "These devaputtas shine exceedingly, they are extremely beautiful. What kamma, I wonder, have they done to have come here?" Reflecting thus, he perceived that they had been monks. Then, investigating, "Let them be monks, but are they fulfillers of the precepts?" he perceived that they were fulfillers. Investigating, "Let them be fulfillers of the precepts, but is there any other quality or not?" he perceived that they were attainers of jhāna. Investigating, "Let them be attainers of jhāna, but where were their residences?" he perceived, "They were my own family preceptors!" Those of pure virtue are reborn wherever they wish in the six deva worlds. But these were not reborn in the higher deva worlds. Those who are attainers of jhāna are reborn in the Brahma world, but these were not reborn in the Brahma world. As for me, having stood firm in their instruction, I was reborn as the son of Sakka, lord of the devas, master of the deva world, on his couch. But these were reborn in the inferior host of gandhabbas. Thinking, "These are persons to be pierced to the bone! They should be pierced strongly, turning them over and over," he admonished them with words such as, "From where have you come?"

Tattha kutomukhāti bhagavati abhimukhe dhammaṃ desente tumhe kutomukhā kiṃ aññā vihitā ito cito ca olokayamānā udāhu niddāyamānā? Duddiṭṭharūpanti duddiṭṭhasabhāvaṃ daṭṭhuṃ ayuttaṃ[V 2.0269]. Sahadhammiketi ekassa satthu sāsane samāciṇṇadhamme katapuññe. Tesaṃ bhanteti tesaṃ gopakena devaputtena evaṃ vatvā puna “aho tumhe nillajjā ahirikā”tiādīhi vacanehi paṭicoditānaṃ dve devā diṭṭheva dhamme satiṃ paṭilabhiṃsu.

Herein, regarding 'kutomukhā': While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma facing you, from what direction were your minds turned? Were you with minds directed elsewhere, looking here and there, or were you dozing off? Regarding 'duddiṭṭharūpaṃ': a nature wrongly seen, something unsuitable to be seen. Regarding 'sahadhammike': those who have practiced the Dhamma in the dispensation of the one Teacher, who have made merit. Regarding 'tesaṃ bhante': Of them, who were thus reproached by the devaputta Gopaka with words such as, 'Ah, you are shameless, without modesty!', two of the devas regained mindfulness in that very life.

Kāyaṃ brahmapurohitanti te kira cintayiṃsu – “naṭehi nāma naccantehi gāyantehi vādentehi āgantvā dāyo nāma labhitabbo assa, ayaṃ pana [M 2.0300] amhākaṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya pakkhittaloṇaṃ uddhanaṃ viya taṭataṭāyateva, kiṃ nu kho ida”nti āvajjantā attano samaṇabhāvaṃ parisuddhasīlataṃ jhānalābhitaṃ tasseva kulūpakabhāvañca disvā “parisuddhasīlā nāma chasu devalokesu yathārucite ṭhāne nibbattanti, jhānalābhino brahmaloke. Mayaṃ uparidevalokepi brahmalokepi nibbattituṃ nāsakkhimha. Amhākaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā ayaṃ itthikā upari nibbattā, mayaṃ bhikkhū samānā bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ caritvā hīne gandhabbakāye nibbattā. Tena no ayaṃ evaṃ niggaṇhātī”ti ñatvā tassa kathaṃ suṇantāyeva tesu dve janā paṭhamajjhānasatiṃ paṭilabhitvā jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasantā anāgāmiphaleyeva patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ so paritto [P 3.0708] kāmāvacarattabhāvo dhāretuṃ nāsakkhi. Tasmā tāvadeva cavitvā brahmapurohitesu nibbattā. So ca nesaṃ kāyo tattha ṭhitānaṃyeva nibbatto. Tena vuttaṃ – “tesaṃ, bhante, gopakena devaputtena paṭicoditānaṃ dve devā diṭṭheva dhamme satiṃ paṭilabhiṃsu kāyaṃ brahmapurohita”nti.

Regarding 'kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ': It is said that they thought: 'Actors, by dancing, singing, and playing instruments, should receive a gift. But this one, from the moment we saw him, just crackles like a stove with salt thrown on it. What can this be?' Reflecting thus, they saw their own state as recluses, their purity of virtue, their attainment of jhāna, and their own role as frequenters of his family. 'Those of pure virtue are reborn in the six deva worlds according to their wish, and those who attain jhāna are reborn in the Brahma world. We were unable to be reborn in a higher deva world or in the Brahma world. This woman, by following our advice, was reborn in a higher realm, while we, though monks who lived the holy life under the Blessed One, were reborn in an inferior gandhabba body. That is why he rebukes us so.' Understanding this, even as they listened to his words, two among them regained the mindfulness of the first jhāna. Making that jhāna their foundation and contemplating conditioned phenomena, they were established in the fruit of non-returning. Then their limited existence in the sense-sphere realm could no longer sustain them. Therefore, they passed away at that very moment and were reborn among the Brahma ministers. And that body of theirs was formed even while they were standing there. Therefore it is said: 'Venerable sir, of them who were reproached by the devaputta Gopaka, two devas regained mindfulness in that very life, and their body became that of the Brahma ministers.'

Tattha diṭṭheva dhammeti tasmiññeva attabhāve jhānasatiṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Tattheva ṭhatvā cutā pana kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ brahmapurohitasarīraṃ paṭilabhiṃsūti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Eko pana devoti eko devaputto nikantiṃ chindituṃ asakkonto kāme ajjhavasi, tattheva āvāsiko ahosi.

Herein, 'diṭṭheva dhamme' means that they regained mindfulness of jhāna in that very existence. Having passed away while dwelling right there, they then obtained a body of a Brahma minister, the form of a Brahma minister—thus the meaning should be understood. As for 'eko pana devo': one devaputta, being unable to cut off delight, continued to dwell in sensual pleasures; he became a resident right there.

354. Saṅghañcupaṭṭhāsinti saṅghañca upaṭṭhāsiṃ.

354. 'Saṅghañcupaṭṭhāsiṃ' means: and I attended upon the Sangha.

Sudhammatāyāti dhammassa sundarabhāvena. Tidivūpapannoti tidive tidasapure upapanno. Gandhabbakāyūpagate vasīneti gandhabbakāyaṃ āvāsiko hutvā upagate. Ye ca mayaṃ pubbe manussabhūtāti ye pubbe manussabhūtā mayaṃ annena pānena upaṭṭhahimhāti iminā saddhiṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo.

'Sudhammatāya' means: by the beautiful nature of the Dhamma. 'Tidivūpapanno' means: reborn in Tidiva, the city of the Tidasas. 'Gandhabbakāyūpagate vasīne' means: having gone to the gandhabba host, having become a resident there. 'Ye ca mayaṃ pubbe manussabhūtā': the meaning should be understood by connecting this with the word 'upaṭṭhahimha' thus: 'we, who were formerly human beings, attended upon them with food and drink'.

Pādūpasaṅgayhāti [V 2.0270] pāde upasaṅgayha pādadhovanapādamakkhanānuppadānena pūjetvā ceva vanditvā ca. Sake nivesaneti attano ghare. Imassāpi padassa upaṭṭhahimhāti imināva sambandho.

'Pādūpasaṅgayha' means: having approached the feet, and having both honored and paid homage by means of offering foot-washing and foot-anointing. 'Sake nivesane' means: in one's own house. This phrase is also connected with 'upaṭṭhahimha' ('we attended').

Paccattaṃ veditabboti attanāva veditabbo. Ariyāna subhāsitānīti tumhehi vuccamānāni buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ subhāsitāni.

'Paccattaṃ veditabbo' means: to be known by oneself. 'Ariyāna subhāsitāni' means: the well-spoken words of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, which are spoken by you.

Tumhe [M 2.0301] pana seṭṭhamupāsamānāti uttamaṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ upāsamānā anuttare buddhasāsane vā. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Bhavatūpapattīti bhavantānaṃ upapatti.

'Tumhe pana seṭṭhamupāsamānā' means: approaching the supreme Buddha, the Blessed One, or in the unsurpassed Dispensation of the Buddha. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' means: the noble conduct. 'Bhavatūpapatti' means: the rebirth of the venerable ones.

Agāre vasato mayhanti gharamajjhe vasantassa mayhaṃ.

'Agāre vasato mayhaṃ' means: of me, dwelling in the midst of a house.

Svajjāti so ajja. Gotamasāvakenāti idha gopako gotamasāvakoti vutto. Sameccāti samāgantvā.

'Svajja' means: he, today. 'Gotamasāvakena' means: here Gopaka is called a disciple of Gotama. 'Samecca' means: having come together.

Handa [P 3.0709] viyāyāma byāyāmāti handa uyyamāma byāyamāma. Mā no mayaṃ parapessā ahumhāti noti nipātamattaṃ, mā mayaṃ parassa pesanakārakāva ahumhāti attho. Gotamasāsanānīti idha pakatiyā paṭividdhaṃ paṭhamajjhānameva gotamasāsanānīti vuttaṃ, taṃ anussaraṃ anussaritvāti attho.

'Handa viyāyāma byāyāma' means: come, let us strive, let us exert ourselves. 'Mā no mayaṃ parapessā ahumhā': here 'no' is a mere particle; the meaning is, 'Let us not be those who do another's bidding.' 'Gotamasāsanāni': here, the first jhāna itself, which had been naturally penetrated, is called 'the teachings of Gotama'; the meaning is recollecting, having recollected that.

Cittāni virājayitvāti pañcakāmaguṇikacittāni virājayitvā. Kāmesu ādīnavanti vikkhambhanavasena paṭhamajjhānena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ addasaṃsu, samucchedavasena tatiyamaggena. Kāmasaṃyojanabandhanānīti kāmasaññojanāni ca kāmabandhanāni ca. Pāpimayogānīti pāpimato mārassa yogabhūtāni, bandhanabhūtānīti attho. Duraccayānīti duratikkamāni. Saindā devā sapajāpatikāti indaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā upaviṭṭhā saindā pajāpatiṃ devarājānaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā upaviṭṭhā sapajāpatikā. Sabhāyupaviṭṭhāti sabhāyaṃ upaviṭṭhā, nisinnāti attho.

'Cittāni virājayitvā' means: having become dispassionate towards the thoughts associated with the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Kāmesu ādīnavaṃ': they saw the danger in sensual pleasures by way of suppression with the first jhāna, and by way of eradication with the third path. 'Kāmasaṃyojanabandhanāni' means: the fetters of sensual pleasure and the bonds of sensual pleasure. 'Pāpimayogāni' means: things that are the yokes of Māra, the Evil One; the meaning is, they are bonds. 'Duraccayāni' means: hard to overcome. 'Saindā devā sapajāpatikā': those seated with Indra as their chief are 'saindā'; those seated with Pajāpati, the king of devas, as their chief are 'sapajāpatikā'. 'Sabhāyupaviṭṭhā' means: seated in the assembly hall; the meaning is, seated.

Vīrāti sūrā. Virāgāti vītarāgā. Virajaṃ karontāti virajaṃ anāgāmimaggaṃ karontā uppādentā. Nāgova sannāni guṇānīti kāmasaññojanabandhanāni chetvā deve tāvatiṃse atikkamiṃsu. Saṃvegajātassāti jātasaṃvegassa sakkassa.

'Vīrā' means: heroes. 'Virāgā' means: free from lust. 'Virajaṃ karontā' means: making the stainless path of non-returning, generating it. Regarding 'Nāgova sannāni guṇāni': having cut the fetters and bonds of sensual pleasure, they surpassed the Tāvatiṃsa devas. 'Saṃvegajātassa' means: of Sakka, in whom spiritual urgency had arisen.

Kāmābhibhūti [V 2.0271] duvidhānampi kāmānaṃ abhibhū. Satiyā vihīnāti jhānasativirahitā.

'Kāmābhibhū' means: one who has overcome sensual pleasures, one who has overcome both kinds of sensual pleasures. 'Satiyā vihīnā' means: devoid of mindfulness, that is, devoid of the mindfulness of jhāna.

Tiṇṇaṃ tesanti tesu tīsu janesu. Āvasinettha ekoti tattha hīne kāye ekoyeva āvāsiko jāto. Sambodhipathānusārinoti anāgāmimaggānusārino. Devepi hīḷentīti dve devaloke [M 2.0302] hīḷentā adhokarontā upacārappanāsamādhīhi samāhitattā attano pādapaṃsuṃ devatānaṃ matthake okirantā ākāse uppatitvā gatāti.

Tiṇṇaṃ tesaṃ means 'of those three,' that is, among those three persons. Āvasinettha eko means 'one dweller here,' that is, in that inferior Gandhabba-body, only one was born as a resident. Sambodhipathānusārino means 'following the path to full enlightenment,' that is, following the path of non-returning. Devepi hīḷenti means 'they even despise the devas,' that is, the two devas, despising and humbling the deva worlds, being well-concentrated through access and attainment concentration, scattering the dust from their own feet upon the heads of the deities, rose into the sky and departed.

Etādisī dhammappakāsanetthāti ettha sāsane evarūpā dhammappakāsanā, yāya sāvakā etehi guṇehi samannāgatā honti. Na [P 3.0710] tattha kiṃ kaṅkhati koci sāvakoti kiṃ tattha tesu sāvakesu koci ekasāvakopi buddhādīsu vā cātuddisabhāve vā na kaṅkhati “sabbadisāsu asajjamāno agayhamāno viharatī”ti. Idāni bhagavato vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇanto “nitiṇṇaoghaṃ vicikicchachinnaṃ, buddhaṃ namassāma jinaṃ janinda”nti āha. Tattha vicikicchachinnanti chinnavicikicchaṃ. Janindanti sabbalokuttamaṃ.

Etādisī dhammappakāsanā ettha means 'such a proclamation of the Dhamma is here,' that is, in this Dispensation there is such a proclamation of the Dhamma by which the disciples become endowed with these qualities. Na tattha kiṃ kaṅkhati koci sāvako means 'no disciple there has any doubt,' that is, among those disciples, not even a single disciple doubts the Buddha and so forth, or their existence in the four directions. Such a one dwells unattached and ungrasped in all directions. Now, wishing to speak in praise of the Blessed One, he said: 'We pay homage to the Buddha, the Victor, the Lord of Men, who has crossed the flood, whose doubt is cut off.' Here, vicikicchachinnaṃ means 'one whose doubt is severed.' Janindanti sabbalokuttamaṃ.

Yaṃ te dhammanti yaṃ tava dhammaṃ. Ajjhagaṃsu teti te devaputtā adhigatā. Kāyaṃ brahmapurohitanti amhākaṃ passantānaṃyeva brahmapurohitasarīraṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ tava dhammaṃ jānitvā tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ te dve visesagū amhākaṃ passantānaṃyeva kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ adhigantvā maggaphalavisesaṃ ajjhagaṃsu, mayampi tassa dhammassa pattiyā āgatamhāsi mārisāti. Āgatamhaseti sampattamha. Katāvakāsā bhagavatā, pañhaṃ pucchemu mārisāti sace no bhagavā okāsaṃ karoti, atha bhagavatā katāvakāsā hutvā pañhaṃ, mārisa, puccheyyāmāti attho.

Yaṃ te dhammaṃ means 'that Dhamma of yours,' that is, your Dhamma. Ajjhagaṃsu te means 'they attained,' that is, those devaputtas attained. Kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ means 'the body of a Brahma-purohita,' that is, the body of a Brahma-purohita even while we were looking on. This is what is said: 'Knowing your Dhamma, those two distinguished ones among those three persons, having attained the body of a Brahma-purohita even while we were looking on, attained the distinction of path and fruit. We too, sir, have come for the attainment of that Dhamma.' Āgatamhāsi means 'we have come,' that is, we have arrived. Katāvakāsā bhagavatā, pañhaṃ pucchemu, mārisa means 'having been given an opportunity by the Blessed One, we would ask a question, sir,' that is, if the Blessed One grants us an opportunity, then, having been given an opportunity by the Blessed One, we would ask a question, sir—such is the meaning.

Maghamāṇavavatthu

The Story of Magha the Young Man

355. Dīgharattaṃ visuddho kho ayaṃ yakkhoti cirakālato pabhuti visuddho. Kīva cirakālato? Anuppanne buddhe magadharaṭṭhe macalagāmake maghamāṇavakālato paṭṭhāya. Tadā kiresa ekadivasaṃ kālasseva vuṭṭhāya gāmamajjhe manussānaṃ gāmakammakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā attano ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ pādanteneva paṃsukacavaraṃ apanetvā ramaṇīyamakāsi, añño āgantvā tattha aṭṭhāsi. So tāvatakeneva satiṃ paṭilabhitvā majjhe gāmassa khalamaṇḍalamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ sodhetvā vālukaṃ okiritvā [V 2.0272] dārūni āharitvā sītakāle aggiṃ karoti, daharā ca mahallakā ca āgantvā tattha nisīdanti.

355. Dīgharattaṃ visuddho kho ayaṃ yakkho means 'this yakkha has been purified for a long time,' that is, purified from a long time ago. How long ago? From the time of Magha the young man in the village of Macala in the Magadha country, before the Buddha arose. It is said that at that time, he rose early one day and went to the middle of the village, to the place where people did communal work. With the tip of his foot, he swept away the dust and rubbish from where he stood, making it pleasant. Another person came and stood there. Just by that, he regained mindfulness. He then cleaned a space the size of a threshing floor in the middle of the village, sprinkled sand, brought firewood, and made a fire in the cold season. Both young and old would come and sit there.

Athassa [M 2.0303] ekadivasaṃ etadahosi – “mayaṃ nagaraṃ gantvā rājarājamahāmattādayo passāma, imesupi candimasūriyesu ‘cando nāma devaputto, sūriyo nāma devaputto’ti [P 3.0711] vadanti. Kiṃ nu kho katvā ete etā sampattiyo adhigatā”ti? Tato “nāññaṃ kiñci, puññakammameva katvā”ti cintetvā “mayāpi evaṃvidhasampattidāyakaṃ puññakammameva kattabba”nti cintesi.

Then one day this thought occurred to him: 'When we go to the city, we see kings, royal ministers, and others. Even regarding this moon and sun, they say, "The moon is a devaputta named Canda, the sun is a devaputta named Suriya." Having done what, indeed, have they attained these accomplishments?' Then, thinking, 'It is nothing else; it is only by having done meritorious deeds,' he resolved, 'I too must do meritorious deeds that bestow such accomplishments.'

So kālasseva vuṭṭhāya yāguṃ pivitvā vāsipharasukudālamusalahattho catumahāpathaṃ gantvā musalena pāsāṇe uccāletvā pavaṭṭeti, yānānaṃ akkhapaṭighātarukkhe harati, visamaṃ samaṃ karoti, catumahāpathe sālaṃ karoti, pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇati, setuṃ bandhati, evaṃ divasaṃ kammaṃ katvā atthaṅgate sūriye gharaṃ eti. Taṃ añño pucchi – “bho, magha, tvaṃ pātova nikkhamitvā sāyaṃ araññato esi, kiṃ kammaṃ karosī”ti? Puññakammaṃ karomi. Saggagāmimaggaṃ sodhemīti. Kimidaṃ, bho, puññaṃ nāmāti? Tvaṃ na jānāsīti? Āma, na jānāmīti. Nagaraṃ gatakāle diṭṭhapubbā te rājarājamahāmattādayoti? Āma, diṭṭhapubbāti. Puññakammaṃ katvā tehi taṃ ṭhānaṃ laddhaṃ, ahampi evaṃvidhasampattidāyakaṃ kammaṃ karomi. “Cando nāma devaputto, sūriyo nāma devaputto”ti sutapubbaṃ tayāti? Āma sutapubbanti. Etassa saggassa gamanamaggaṃ ahaṃ sodhemīti. Idaṃ pana puññakammaṃ kiṃ taveva vaṭṭati, aññassa na vaṭṭatīti? Na kassacetaṃ vāritanti. Yadi evaṃ sve araññaṃ gamanakāle mayhampi saddaṃ dehīti. Punadivase taṃ gahetvā gato, evaṃ tasmiṃ gāme tettiṃsa manussā taruṇavayā sabbe tasseva anuvattakā ahesuṃ. Te ekacchandā hutvā puññakammāni karontā vicaranti. Yaṃ disaṃ gacchanti, maggaṃ samaṃ karontā ekadivaseneva karonti, pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇantā, sālaṃ karontā, setuṃ bandhantā ekadivaseneva niṭṭhāpenti.

He would rise early in the morning, drink rice gruel, and then go to the crossroads carrying an adze, axe, spade, and mallet. With the mallet, he would dislodge stones and roll them away. He would remove trees that obstructed the axles of carts, level uneven ground, build a rest house at the crossroads, dig a pond, and construct a bridge. After working all day like this, he would return home at sunset. Another person asked him, 'Friend Magha, you leave early in the morning and return from the forest in the evening—what work do you do?' He replied, 'I do meritorious deeds. I clear the path leading to heaven.' The other asked, 'Friend, what is this thing called merit?' 'Do you not know?' 'Indeed, I do not know.' 'When you go to the city, have you not seen kings, royal ministers, and others?' 'Indeed, I have.' 'It is by doing meritorious deeds that they have obtained that position. I too am doing deeds that bestow such accomplishments. Have you not heard it said, "The moon is a devaputta, the sun is a devaputta"?' 'Indeed, I have.' 'I am clearing the path to that heaven.' 'But is this meritorious deed only for you? Is it not for others?' 'It is not forbidden to anyone.' 'If so, then when you go to the forest tomorrow, call for me too.' The next day, he took that man and went. In this way, thirty-three young men in that village all became his followers. Being of one accord, they went about performing meritorious deeds. Whichever direction they went, when leveling a road, they would do it in a single day; when digging a pond, building a rest house, or constructing a bridge, they would complete it in a single day.

Atha nesaṃ gāmabhojako cintesi – “ahaṃ pubbe etesu suraṃ pivantesu pāṇaghātādīni karontesu ca kahāpaṇādivasena ceva daṇḍabalivasena ca dhanaṃ labhāmi. Idāni etesaṃ puññakaraṇakālato paṭṭhāya ettako āyo natthi, handa ne rājakule paribhindāmī”ti rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā [P 3.0712] core, mahārāja, passāmīti. Kuhiṃ, tātāti? Mayhaṃ gāmeti. Kiṃ corā nāma, tātāti? Rājāparādhikā devāti. Kiṃ jātikāti? Gahapatijātikā devāti. Gahapatikā kiṃ karissanti, tayā [M 2.0304] jānamānena kasmā mayhaṃ na kathitanti? Bhayena, mahārāja, na [V 2.0273] kathemi, idāni mā mayhaṃ dosaṃ kareyyāthāti. Atha rājā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ mahāravaṃ ravatī”ti saddahitvā “tena hi gaccha, tvameva ne ānehī”ti balaṃ datvā pesesi. So gantvā divasaṃ araññe kammaṃ katvā sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā gāmamajjhe nisīditvā “sve kiṃ kammaṃ karissāma, kiṃ maggaṃ samaṃ karoma, pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāma, setuṃ bandhāmā”ti mantayamāneyeva te parivāretvā “mā phandittha, rañño āṇā”ti bandhitvā pāyāsi. Atha kho nesaṃ itthiyo “sāmikā kira vo ‘rājāparādhikā corā’ti bandhitvā niyyantī”ti sutvā “aticirena kūṭā ete ‘puññakammaṃ karomā’ti divase divase araññeva acchanti, sabbakammantā parihīnā, gehe na kiñci vaḍḍhati, suṭṭhu baddhā suṭṭhu gahitā”ti vadiṃsu.

Then their village headman thought: 'Previously, when these men were drinking liquor and committing acts such as killing living beings, I gained wealth through kahāpaṇas and the like, and by means of fines and taxes. Now, from the time they began performing meritorious deeds, there has been no such income. Come now, I shall slander them in the royal court.' He approached the king and said, 'Great King, I see thieves.' 'Where, my dear man?' the king asked. 'In my village.' 'What sort of thieves, my dear man?' 'They are offenders against the king, Your Majesty.' 'Of what caste are they?' 'They are of the householder caste, Your Majesty.' 'What can householders do? Knowing this, why did you not tell me?' 'Out of fear, Great King, I did not speak. Now, please do not hold this fault against me.' Then the king, thinking, 'This man is raising a great alarm on my behalf,' believed him and said, 'Very well, go and bring them here yourself.' And giving him a contingent of men, he sent him off. The headman went, and while they—having worked in the forest for the day, eaten their evening meal, and sat down in the middle of the village—were discussing, 'What work shall we do tomorrow? Which road shall we level? Shall we dig a pond, or shall we build a causeway?', he surrounded them, saying, 'Do not move! It is the king’s command!' and, having bound them, led them away. Then their wives, hearing, 'It seems your husbands are being led away, bound as “thieves who are offenders against the king,”' said: 'For a very long time these men have been deceitful. Saying, “Let us do meritorious deeds,” they spend day after day in the forest. All their work is neglected, and nothing in the household prospers. It is good they are bound! It is good they are caught!'

Gāmabhojakopi te netvā rañño dassesi. Rājā anupaparikkhitvāyeva “hatthinā maddāpethā”ti āha. Tesu nīyamānesu magho itare āha – “bho, sakkhissatha mama vacanaṃ kātu”nti? Tava vacanaṃ karontāyevamha imaṃ bhayaṃ pattā, evaṃ santepi tava vacanaṃ karoma, bhaṇa bho, kiṃ karomāti? Ettha bho vaṭṭe carantānaṃ nāma nibaddhaṃ etaṃ, kiṃ pana tumhe corāti? Na coramhāti. Imassa lokassa saccakiriyā nāma avassayo, tasmā sabbepi “yadi amhe corā, hatthī maddatu, atha na corā, mā maddatū”ti saccakiriyaṃ karothāti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Hatthī upagantumpi na sakkoti, viravanto palāyati, hatthiṃ tuttatomaraṅkusehi koṭṭentāpi upanetuṃ na sakkonti. “Hatthiṃ upanetuṃ na sakkomā”ti rañño ārocesuṃ. Tena hi upari kaṭena paṭicchādetvā maddāpethāti. Upari kaṭe dinne diguṇaravaṃ viravanto palāyati.

The village headman also took them and presented them to the king. The king, without any investigation, commanded, 'Have them trampled by an elephant.' As they were being led away, Magha said to the others, 'Friends, will you be able to do as I say?' 'It is by doing as you say that we have come into this peril,' they replied. 'Even so, we shall do as you say. Speak, friend, what shall we do?' 'Friends, for those wandering in the round of existence, such a fate is inevitable. But tell me, are you thieves?' 'We are not thieves.' 'In this world, an act of truth is a refuge. Therefore, let all of us make an act of truth, saying: “If we are thieves, may the elephant trample us; but if we are not thieves, may it not trample us.”' They did so. The elephant could not even approach them; trumpeting, it fled. Even when its handlers struck it with goads, pikes, and hooks, they could not bring it near. They reported to the king, 'We cannot make the elephant approach.' 'In that case,' he said, 'cover them with a mat from above and have them trampled.' When a mat was placed over them, the elephant fled, trumpeting with twice the volume.

Rājā sutvā pesuññakārakaṃ pakkosāpetvā āha – “tāta, hatthī maddituṃ na icchatī”ti? Āma, deva, jeṭṭhakamāṇavo mantaṃ jānāti, mantasseva ayamānubhāvoti. Rājā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “manto kira te atthī”ti pucchi? Natthi, deva, mayhaṃ [P 3.0713] manto, saccakiriyaṃ pana mayaṃ karimha – “yadi amhe rañño corā, maddatu, atha na corā, mā maddatū”ti, saccakiriyāya no esa ānubhāvoti. Kiṃ pana, tāta, tumhe kammaṃ karothāti? Amhe, deva, maggaṃ samaṃ karoma, catumahāpathe sālaṃ karoma[M 2.0305], pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāma, setuṃ bandhāma, evarūpāni puññakammāni karontā vicarimhāti.

Hearing this, the king had the slanderer summoned and said, 'My dear man, the elephant does not wish to trample them.' 'Yes, Your Majesty. The eldest youth knows a mantra; this is the power of that mantra.' The king had the youth summoned and asked, 'I hear that you have a mantra. Is that so?' 'I have no mantra, Your Majesty. We simply performed an act of truth, saying: “If we are the king’s thieves, let it trample us; but if we are not thieves, may it not trample us.” This is the power of our act of truth.' 'But what sort of work do you do, my dear men?' 'Your Majesty, we level roads, we build rest-houses at the crossroads, we dig ponds, and we construct causeways. We go about performing such meritorious deeds as these.'

Ayaṃ tumhe kimatthaṃ pisuṇesīti? Amhākaṃ pamattakāle idañcidañca labhati, appamattakāle taṃ natthi, etena kāraṇenāti. Tāta, ayaṃ hatthī nāma tiracchāno, sopi tumhākaṃ [V 2.0274] guṇe jānāti. Ahaṃ manusso hutvāpi na jānāmi, tumhākaṃ vasanagāmaṃ tumhākaṃyeva puna aharaṇīyaṃ katvā demi, ayampi hatthī tumhākaṃyeva hotu, pesuññakārakopi tumhākaṃyeva dāso hotu. Ito paṭṭhāya mayhampi puññakammaṃ karothāti dhanaṃ datvā vissajjesi. Te dhanaṃ gahetvā vārena vārena hatthiṃ āruyha gacchantā mantayanti “bho puññakammaṃ nāma anāgatabhavatthāya kariyati, amhākaṃ pana antoudake pupphitaṃ nīluppalaṃ viya imasmiññeva attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Idāni atirekaṃ puññaṃ karissāmā”ti, kiṃ karomāti? Catumahāpathe thāvaraṃ katvā mahājanassa vissamanasālaṃ karoma, itthīhi pana saddhiṃ apattikaṃ katvā karissāma, amhesu hi “corā”ti gahetvā nīyamānesu itthīnaṃ ekāpi cintāmattakampi akatvā “subaddhā sugahitā”ti uṭṭhahiṃsu, tasmā tāsaṃ pattiṃ na dassāmāti. Te attano gehāni gantvā hatthino tettiṃsapiṇḍaṃ denti, tettiṃsa tiṇamuṭṭhiyo āharanti, taṃ sabbaṃ hatthissa kucchipūraṃ jātaṃ. Te araññaṃ pavisitvā rukkhe chindanti, chinnaṃ chinnaṃ hatthī kaḍḍhitvā sakaṭapathe ṭhapesi. Te rukkhe tacchetvā sālāya kammaṃ ārabhiṃsu.

The king asked, 'Why did this man slander you?' 'When we were heedless,' they replied, 'he would receive this and that gain. Since we have been heedful, there is nothing for him. It is for this reason.' 'My dear men,' said the king, 'this elephant is but an animal, yet even it knows your virtues. I, though a human being, did not know them. I give you your home village, to be yours irrevocably. This elephant shall also be yours, and this slanderer shall be your slave. From this day forward, perform meritorious deeds for me as well.' Having given them wealth, he dismissed them. Taking the wealth, they went on their way, taking turns riding the elephant, and they conferred among themselves: 'Friends, meritorious deeds are usually performed for the sake of a future existence, but for us, the result has appeared in this very life, like a blue water lily blossoming in the water. Now let us perform even more merit.' 'What shall we do?' 'At the great crossroads, let us build a permanent rest-hall for the people. However, we shall do it without giving the women a share. For when we were seized as “thieves” and led away, not a single one of our wives showed even a moment's concern; instead, they exclaimed, “It is good they are bound! It is good they are caught!” Therefore, we shall not give them a share of the merit.' They went to their homes and brought thirty-three handfuls of grass for the elephant, and all of it was enough to fill its belly. They entered the forest and cut down trees. As each tree was felled, the elephant dragged it and placed it on the cart track. They then prepared the timber and began the work on the hall.

Maghassa gehe sujātā, sudhammā, cittā, nandāti catasso bhariyāyo ahesuṃ. Sudhammā vaḍḍhakiṃ pucchati – “tāta, ime sahāyā kālasseva gantvā sāyaṃ enti, kiṃ kammaṃ karontī”ti? “Sālaṃ karonti, ammā”ti. “Tāta, mayhampi sālāya pattiṃ katvā dehī”ti. “Itthīhi apattikaṃ [P 3.0714] karomā”ti ete vadantīti. Sā vaḍḍhakissa aṭṭha kahāpaṇe datvā “tāta, yena kenaci upāyena mayhaṃ pattikaṃ karohī”ti āha. So “sādhu ammā”ti vatvā puretaraṃ vāsipharasuṃ gahetvā gāmamajjhe ṭhatvā “kiṃ bho ajja imasmimpi kāle na nikkhamathā”ti uccāsaddaṃ katvā “sabbe maggaṃ āruḷhā”ti ñatvā “gacchatha tāva tumhe, mayhaṃ papañco atthī”ti te [M 2.0306] purato katvā aññaṃ maggaṃ āruyha kaṇṇikūpagaṃ rukkhaṃ chinditvā tacchetvā maṭṭhaṃ katvā āharitvā sudhammāya gehe ṭhapesi – “mayā dehīti vuttadivase nīharitvā dadeyyāsī”ti.

In Magha's house, there were four wives: Sujātā, Sudhammā, Cittā, and Nandā. Sudhammā asked the carpenter, 'Dear sir, these companions go out early and return in the evening—what work do they do?' 'They are making a hall, mother,' he said. 'And these men say, "We are making it without a share for women."' She gave the carpenter eight kahāpaṇas and said, 'Dear sir, by some means or other, make me a shareholder.' He agreed, 'Very well, mother,' and taking his adze and axe beforehand, he stood in the middle of the village. He shouted loudly, 'Sirs, why have you not set out even at this time today?' Knowing they had all set out on the road, he sent them on ahead, saying, 'You all go on, I have some business.' Taking another path, he cut down a tree suitable for a finial, planed it, made it smooth, and brought it to Sudhammā’s house, placing it there. 'On the day I say, "Give it," you should bring it out and give it,' he instructed.

Atha niṭṭhite dabbasambhārakamme bhūmikammato paṭṭhāya cayabandhanathambhussāpana saṅghāṭayojana kaṇṇikamañcabandhanesu katesu so vaḍḍhakī kaṇṇikamañce nisīditvā catūhi disāhi gopānasiyo ukkhipitvā “bho ekaṃ pamuṭṭhaṃ atthī”ti āha. Kiṃ bho pamuṭṭhaṃ, sabbameva tvaṃ pamussasīti. Imā bho gopānasiyo kattha patiṭṭhahissantīti? Kaṇṇikā nāma laddhuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Kuhiṃ bho idāni sakkā laddhunti? Kulānaṃ gehe sakkā laddhunti. Āhiṇḍantā pucchathāti. Te antogāmaṃ pavisitvā pucchitvā sudhammāya gharadvāre “imasmiṃ ghare kaṇṇikā atthī”ti [V 2.0275] āhaṃsu. Sā “atthī”ti āha. Handa mūlaṃ gaṇhāhīti. Mūlaṃ na gaṇhāmi, sace mama pattiṃ karotha, dassāmīti. Etha bho mātugāmassa pattiṃ na karoma, araññaṃ gantvā rukkhaṃ chindissāmāti nikkhamiṃsu.

Then, when the work of gathering the timber was finished, and when the tasks from leveling the ground to building up the foundation, raising the pillars, joining the beams, and constructing the scaffolding for the finial were completed, the carpenter sat on the finial scaffolding. Lifting the rafters from the four directions, he said, 'Sirs, one thing has been forgotten.' 'What has been forgotten, sir? You forget everything!' they replied. 'Sirs, where will these rafters be established?' he asked. 'A finial must be obtained.' 'Where, sir, can one be obtained now?' 'It can be obtained in the house of a family.' 'Go and ask around.' They entered the village and inquired, and at Sudhammā’s door, they said, 'Is there a finial in this house?' She said, 'There is.' 'Come now, take a price for it.' 'I will not take a price. If you make me a shareholder, I will give it.' 'Come, sirs, we do not make a share for a woman. Let us go to the forest and cut a tree,' they said, and departed.

Tato vaḍḍhakī “kiṃ na laddhā, tāta, kaṇṇikā”ti pucchi. Te tamatthaṃ ārocayiṃsu. Vaḍḍhakī kaṇṇikamañce nisinnova ākāsaṃ ulloketvā “bho ajja nakkhattaṃ sundaraṃ, idaṃ aññaṃ saṃvaccharaṃ atikkamitvā sakkā laddhuṃ, tumhehi ca dukkhena ābhatā dabbasambhārā, te sakalasaṃvaccharena imasmiññeva ṭhāne pūtikā bhavissanti. Devaloke nibbattakāle tassāpi ekasmiṃ koṇe sālā hotu, āharatha na”nti āha. Sāpi yāva te na puna āgacchanti, tāva kaṇṇikāya heṭṭhimatale “ayaṃ sālā sudhammā nāmā”ti akkharāni chindāpetvā ahatena vatthena veṭhetvā ṭhapesi. Kammikā āgantvā – “āhara, re kaṇṇikaṃ[P 3.0715], yaṃ hotu taṃ hotu. Tuyhampi pattiṃ karissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Sā nīharitvā “tātā, yāva aṭṭha vā soḷasa vā gopānasiyo na ārohanti, tāva imaṃ vatthaṃ mā nibbeṭhayitthā”ti vatvā adāsi. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā gahetvā gopānasiyo āropetvāva vatthaṃ nibbeṭhesuṃ.

Then the carpenter asked, 'Dear sirs, why was the finial not obtained?' They told him the matter. The carpenter, still seated on the finial scaffolding, looked up at the sky and said, 'Sirs, today the constellation is auspicious. Such a one can only be obtained after another year has passed. The timber you have brought with such difficulty will rot in this very place over a whole year. When we are reborn in the world of the devas, let her also have a hall in one corner. Bring it!' While they had not yet returned, she had the letters 'This hall is named Sudhammā' carved on the underside of the finial, wrapped it in new cloth, and set it aside. The workers came and said, 'Bring the finial! Let what will be, be. We will make a share for you also.' She brought it out and, giving it to them, said, 'Dear sirs, until eight or sixteen rafters are mounted, do not unwrap this cloth.' They agreed, saying 'Very well,' took it, and only after mounting the rafters did they unwrap the cloth.

Eko mahāgāmikamanusso uddhaṃ ullokento akkharāni disvā “kiṃ, bho, ida”nti akkharaññuṃ manussaṃ pakkosāpetvā dassesi. So “sudhammā [M 2.0307] nāma ayaṃ sālā”ti āha. “Haratha, bho, mayaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya sālaṃ katvā nāmamattampi na labhāma, esā ratanamattena kaṇṇikarukkhena sālaṃ attano nāmena kāretī”ti viravanti. Vaḍḍhakī tesaṃ viravantānaṃyeva gopānasiyo pavesetvā āṇiṃ datvā sālākammaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

A prominent man of the village, looking up, saw the letters and asked, 'Sirs, what is this?' He had a literate man summoned and showed it to him. That man said, 'This hall is named Sudhammā.' 'Take it down, sirs!' they cried out. 'We, having built this hall from the very beginning, do not receive even the mention of our names, yet this woman, for a mere finial, is having the hall named after herself!' But while they were still crying out, the carpenter inserted the rafters, drove in the pins, and completed the work on the hall.

Sālaṃ tidhā vibhajiṃsu, ekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse issarānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ akaṃsu, ekasmiṃ duggatānaṃ, ekasmiṃ gilānānaṃ. Tettiṃsa janā tettiṃsa phalakāni paññapetvā hatthissa saññaṃ adaṃsu – “āgantuko āgantvā yassa atthate phalake nisīdati, taṃ gahetvā phalakasāmikasseva gehe patiṭṭhapehi. Tassa pādaparikammapiṭṭhiparikammakhādanīyabhojanīyasayanāni sabbāni phalakasāmikasseva bhāro bhavissatī”ti. Hatthī āgatāgataṃ gahetvā phalakasāmikassa gehaṃ neti, so tassa taṃ divasaṃ kattabbaṃ karoti.

They divided the hall into three parts. In one section, they made a place for the influential to stay; in one, for the poor; and in one, for the sick. The thirty-three men prepared thirty-three planks and gave this instruction to a man named Hatthi: 'When a traveler arrives and sits on a spread-out plank, take him and establish him in the house of that plank's owner. All services for his feet and back, hard and soft food, and lodging shall be the responsibility of the plank's owner.' Hatthi would take each arriving traveler to the house of the respective plank's owner, and that owner would perform the duties required for that day.

Maghamāṇavo sālato avidūre ṭhāne koviḷārarukkhaṃ ropāpesi, mūle cassa pāsāṇaphalakaṃ atthari. Nandā nāmassa bhariyā avidūre pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāpesi, cittā mālāvacche [V 2.0276] ropāpesi, sabbajeṭṭhikā pana ādāsaṃ gahetvā attabhāvaṃ maṇḍayamānāva vicarati. Magho taṃ āha – “bhadde, sudhammā, sālāya pattikā jātā, nandā pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāpesi, cittā mālāvacche ropāpesi. Tava pana puññakammaṃ nāma natthi, ekaṃ puññaṃ karohi, bhadde”ti sā “tvaṃ kassa kāraṇā karosi, nanu tayā kataṃ mayhamevā”ti vatvā attabhāvamaṇḍanameva anuyuñjati.

The young man Magha had a koviḷāra tree planted in a place not far from the hall, and at its base, he had a stone slab laid. His wife named Nandā had a lotus pond dug nearby. Cittā had a pleasure grove planted. The eldest wife, Sujātā, however, just took up her mirror and went about adorning her own person. Magha said to her, 'Good lady, Sudhammā has become a shareholder in the hall, Nandā has had a lotus pond dug, and Cittā has had a pleasure grove planted. But as for you, you have no meritorious deed to your name. Do at least one meritorious deed, good lady.' But she replied, 'For whose sake do you act? Is not what is done by you mine as well?' and applied herself only to her self-adornment.

Magho yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cavitvā tāvatiṃsabhavane sakko hutvā nibbatti, tepi tettiṃsa gāmikamanussā [P 3.0716] kālaṅkatvā tettiṃsa devaputtā hutvā tasseva santike nibbattā. Sakkassa vejayanto nāma pāsādo satta yojanasatāni uggacchi, dhajo tīṇi yojanasatāni uggacchi, koviḷārarukkhassa nissandena samantā tiyojanasataparimaṇḍalo pañcadasayojanapariṇāhakkhandho pāricchattako nibbatti, pāsāṇaphalakassa [M 2.0308] nissandena pāricchattakamūle saṭṭhiyojanikā paṇḍukambalasilā nibbatti. Sudhammāya kaṇṇikarukkhassa nissandena tiyojanasatikā sudhammā devasabhā nibbatti. Nandāya pokkharaṇiyā nissandena paññāsayojanā nandā nāma pokkharaṇī nibbatti. Cittāya mālāvacchavatthunissandena saṭṭhiyojanikaṃ cittalatāvanaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ nibbatti.

Magha, having lived for the extent of his lifespan, passed away from there and was reborn as Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Those thirty-three villagers also passed away and were reborn as thirty-three divine sons in his very presence. Sakka's palace, named Vejayanta, rose seven hundred yojanas, and its banner rose three hundred yojanas. As a result of the koviḷāra tree, the Pāricchattaka tree arose, with a perimeter of three hundred yojanas all around and a trunk fifteen yojanas in girth. As a result of the stone slab, the Paṇḍukambala stone slab, sixty yojanas in extent, arose at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. As a result of Sudhammā's kaṇṇikāra tree, the Sudhammā divine assembly hall, three hundred yojanas in extent, arose. As a result of Nandā's pond, the pond named Nandā, fifty yojanas in extent, arose. As a result of Cittā's plot for flowering shrubs, the pleasure grove named Cittalatāvana, sixty yojanas in extent, arose.

Sakko devarājā sudhammāya devasabhāya yojanike suvaṇṇapallaṅke nisinno tiyojanike setacchatte dhāriyamāne tehi devaputtehi tāhi devakaññāhi aḍḍhatiyāhi nāṭakakoṭīhi dvīsu devalokesu devatāhi ca parivārito mahāsampattiṃ olokento tā tisso itthiyo disvā “imā tāva paññāyanti, sujātā kuhi”nti olokento “ayaṃ mama vacanaṃ akatvā girikandarāya bakasakuṇikā hutvā nibbattā”ti disvā devalokato otaritvā tassā santikaṃ gato. Sā disvāva sañjānitvā adhomukhā jātā. “Bāle, idāni kiṃ sīsaṃ na ukkhipasi? Tvaṃ mama vacanaṃ akatvā attabhāvameva maṇḍayamānā vītināmesi. Sudhammāya ca nandāya ca cittāya ca mahāsampatti nibbattā, ehi amhākaṃ sampattiṃ passā”ti devalokaṃ netvā nandāya pokkharaṇiyā pakkhipitvā pallaṅke nisīdi.

Sakka, the king of the devas, seated on a golden throne one yojana in size in the Sudhammā divine assembly hall, with a white parasol spanning three yojanas held over him, and surrounded by those divine sons, two and a half crores of dancing women, and deities in two deva worlds, was surveying his great fortune. He saw those three women and, looking about, thought, “These are visible, but where is Sujātā?” He then saw, “This one, not heeding my words, was reborn as a female crane in a mountain gorge.” Having seen this, he descended from the deva world and went to her. She, upon seeing him, recognized him and lowered her face. “O foolish one, why do you not raise your head now? Not heeding my words, you spent your time only adorning your own person. For Sudhammā, Nandā, and Cittā, great fortune has arisen. Come, see our fortune.” Having led her to the deva world, he placed her in the Nandā pond and sat on the throne.

Nāṭakitthiyo “kuhiṃ gatattha, mahārājā”ti pucchiṃsu. So anārocetukāmopi tāhi nippīḷiyamāno “sujātāya santika”nti āha. Kuhiṃ nibbattā, mahārājāti? Kandarapādeti. Idāni kuhinti? Nandāpokkharaṇiyaṃ me vissaṭṭhāti. Etha, bho, amhākaṃ ayyaṃ passāmāti sabbā tattha agamaṃsu. Sā pubbe sabbajeṭṭhikā hutvā tā avamaññittha. Idāni [V 2.0277] tāpi taṃ disvā – “passatha, bho amhākaṃ ayyāya mukhaṃ kakkaṭakavijjhanasūlasadisa”ntiādīni vadantiyo keḷiṃ akaṃsu. Sā ativiya aṭṭiyamānā sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ āha – “mahārāja, imāni [P 3.0717] suvaṇṇarajatamaṇivimānāni vā nandāpokkharaṇī vā mayhaṃ kiṃ karissati, jātibhūmiyeva mahārāja sattānaṃ sukhā, maṃ tattheva kandarapāde vissajjehī”ti. Sakko taṃ tattha vissajjetvā “mama vacanaṃ karissasī”ti āha. Karissāmi, mahārājāti. Pañca sīlāni gahetvā akhaṇḍāni katvā rakkha, katipāhena taṃ etāsaṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ karissāmīti. Sā tathā akāsi.

The dancing women asked, “Where have you been, great king?” Though he did not wish to tell, being pressed by them, he said, “To Sujātā.” They asked, “Where was she reborn, great king?” “At the foot of the gorge,” he replied. “And where is she now?” “She was released by me in the Nandā pond.” Saying, “Come, friends, let us see our lady,” they all went there. Previously, having been the eldest of them all, she had looked down upon them. Now they too, seeing her, made sport of her, saying such things as, “Look, friends, our lady’s beak is like a stake for piercing crabs!” Being extremely distressed, she said to Sakka, the king of the devas: “Great king, what will these mansions of gold, silver, and jewels, or the Nandā pond, do for me? For beings, great king, the place of birth itself is happiness. Release me right there at the foot of the gorge.” Sakka, having released her there, asked, “Will you heed my words?” “I will, great king,” she replied. “Undertake the five precepts, keep them unbroken, and guard them. In a few days, I will make you the chief among these.” She did so.

Sakko [M 2.0309] katipāhassa accayena “sakkā nu kho sīlaṃ rakkhitu”nti gantvā maccharūpena uttānako hutvā tassā purato udakapiṭṭhe osarati, sā “matamacchako bhavissatī”ti gantvā sīse aggahesi. Maccho naṅguṭṭhaṃ cālesi. Sā “jīvati maññe”ti udake vissajjesi. Sakko ākāse ṭhatvā “sādhu, sādhu, rakkhasi sikkhāpadaṃ, evaṃ taṃ rakkhamānaṃ katipāheneva nāṭakānaṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Tassāpi pañca vassasatāni āyu ahosi. Ekadivasampi udarapūraṃ nālatthaṃ, sukkhitvā parisukkhitvā milāyamānāpi sīlaṃ akhaṇḍetvā kālaṅkatvā bārāṇasiyaṃ kumbhakāragehe nibbatti.

Sakka, after a few days had passed, went to test her, thinking, “Is she truly able to guard her virtue?” Taking the form of a fish lying on its back, he appeared on the surface of the water before her. She, thinking, “It must be a dead fish,” went and took it by the head. The fish moved its tail. She, thinking, “I suppose it is alive,” released it into the water. Sakka, standing in the air, said: “Excellent, excellent! You guard the training rule. As you continue to guard it thus, in just a few days I will make you chief of the dancers.” Her lifespan as a crane was five hundred years. Not even for a single day did she get enough to fill her stomach; though she was dried up, utterly parched, and withering, she did not break her virtue. After passing away, she was reborn in a potter’s house in Bārāṇasī.

Sakko “kuhiṃ nibbattā”ti olokento disvā “tato idha ānetuṃ na sakkā, jīvitavuttimassā dassāmī”ti suvaṇṇaeḷālukānaṃ yānakaṃ pūretvā majjhe gāmassa mahallakavesena nisīditvā “eḷālukāni gaṇhathā”ti ukkuṭṭhimakāsi. Samantā gāmavāsikā āgantvā “dehi, tātā”ti āhaṃsu. Ahaṃ sīlarakkhakānaṃ demi, tumhe sīlaṃ rakkhathāti. Tāta mayaṃ sīlaṃ nāma kīdisantipi na jānāma, mūlena dehīti. “Sīlarakkhakānaṃyeva dammī”ti āha. “Etha, re kosi ayaṃ eḷālukamahallako”ti sabbe nivattiṃsu.

Sakka, looking to see where she had been reborn, saw her and thought, “It is not possible to bring her here from there; I will give her a means of livelihood.” Having filled a small cart with golden cucumbers, he sat in the middle of the village in the guise of an old man and cried out, “Get your cucumbers!” The villagers from all around came and said, “Give us some, father.” He replied, “I give to those who guard virtue. Do you guard virtue?” They said, “Father, we do not even know what this thing called virtue is like. Give them to us for a price.” He said, “I give only to those who guard virtue.” Saying, “Come on, friends, what sort of old cucumber man is this?” they all turned back.

Sā dārikā pucchi – “amma, tumhe eḷālukatthāya gatā tucchahatthāva āgatā”ti. Kosi, amma, eḷālukamahallako “ahaṃ sīlarakkhakānaṃ dammī”ti vadati, nūnimassa dārikā sīlaṃ khāditvā vattanti, mayaṃ sīlameva na jānāmāti. Sā “mayhaṃ ānītaṃ bhavissatī”ti gantvā “eḷālukaṃ, tāta, dehī”ti āha. “Tvaṃ sīlāni rakkhasi ammā”ti? “Āma, tāta rakkhāmī”ti. Idaṃ mayā tuyhameva ābhatanti gehadvāre yānena saddhiṃ ṭhapetvā pakkāmi. Sāpi yāvajīvaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhitvā cavitvā vepacittiasurassa dhītā hutvā nibbatti. Sīlanissandena [V 2.0278] pāsādikā ahosi. So [P 3.0718] “dhītuvivāhamaṅgalaṃ karissāmī”ti asure sannipātesi.

The girl asked, “Mother, you went for cucumbers but have come back empty-handed?” Her mother replied, “My dear, who knows what sort of old cucumber man he is. He says, ‘I give to those who guard virtue.’ Surely his daughters must live by eating virtue! We do not even know what virtue is.” The girl, thinking, “It must have been brought for me,” went and said, “Father, give me a cucumber.” He asked, “Do you guard the precepts, my dear?” “Yes, father, I guard them.” “This was brought by me for you alone,” he said, and placing it, together with the cart, at the house door, he departed. She too guarded her virtue for her whole life and, after passing away, was reborn as the daughter of Vepacitti, the asura. As a result of her virtue, she was lovely. He, thinking, “I will perform my daughter’s wedding ceremony,” assembled the asuras.

Sakko “kuhiṃ nibbattā”ti olokento “asurabhavane nibbattā, ajjassā vivāhamaṅgalaṃ karissantī”ti disvā “idāni yaṃkiñci katvā ānetabbā mayā”ti asuravaṇṇaṃ nimminitvā gantvā asurānaṃ antare aṭṭhāsi. “Tava [M 2.0310] sāmikaṃ vadehī”ti tassā hatthe pitā pupphadāmaṃ adāsi “yaṃ icchasi, tassūpari khipāhī”ti. Sā olokentī sakkaṃ disvā pubbasannivāsena sañjātasinehā “ayaṃ me sāmiko”ti tassūpari dāmaṃ khipi. So taṃ bāhāya gahetvā ākāse uppati, tasmiṃ khaṇe asurā sañjāniṃsu. Te “gaṇhatha, gaṇhatha, jarasakkaṃ, veriko amhākaṃ, na mayaṃ etassa dārikaṃ dassāmā”ti anubandhiṃsu. Vepacitti pucchi “kenāhaṭā”ti? “Jarasakkena mahārājā”ti. “Avasesesu ayameva seṭṭho, apethā”ti āha. Sakko naṃ netvā aḍḍhatiyakoṭināṭakānaṃ jeṭṭhikaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā sakkaṃ varaṃ yāci – “mahārāja, mayhaṃ imasmiṃ devaloke mātā vā pitā vā bhātā vā bhaginī vā natthi, yattha yattha gacchasi, tattha tattha maṃ gahetvāva gaccha mahārājā”ti. Sakko “sādhū”ti paṭiññaṃ adāsi.

Sakka, looking about and thinking, “Where has she been reborn?” saw, “She has been reborn in the realm of the asuras; today they will hold her wedding ceremony.” Having seen this, he thought, “Now I must bring her here by some means or other.” Creating the appearance of an asura, he went and stood among the asuras. Her father, saying, “Declare your husband,” placed a flower garland in her hand with the words, “Throw it upon whomever you desire.” As she was looking about, she saw Sakka, and with affection arisen due to past association, she said, “This is my husband,” and threw the garland upon him. He took her by the arm and flew up into the sky. At that moment, the asuras recognized him. They pursued him, shouting, “Seize him, seize him, the old Sakka! He is our enemy! We will not give our daughter to him!” Vepacitti asked, “By whom has she been carried away?” “By the old Sakka, great king!” they replied. “Among the rest, he is the best. Stand aside!” he said. Sakka took her and established her in the position of chief among the twenty-five million celestial dancers. She asked a boon of Sakka: “Great king, in this deva-world I have no mother, father, brother, or sister. Wherever you go, great king, please take me with you.” Sakka gave his promise, saying, “Very well.”

Evaṃ macalagāmake maghamāṇavakālato paṭṭhāya visuddhabhāvamassa sampassanto bhagavā “dīgharattaṃ visuddho kho ayaṃ yakkho”ti āha. Atthasañhitanti atthanissitaṃ kāraṇanissitaṃ.

Thus, clearly perceiving his state of purity from the time he was the youth Magha in the village of Macala, the Blessed One said, “For a long time this yakkha has indeed been pure.” ‘Connected with welfare’ means based on welfare, based on cause.

Pañhaveyyākaraṇavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Question

357. Kiṃ saṃyojanāti kiṃ bandhanā, kena bandhanena baddhā hutvā. Puthukāyāti bahujanā. Averāti appaṭighā. Adaṇḍāti āvudhadaṇḍadhanadaṇḍavinimuttā. Asapattāti apaccatthikā. Abyāpajjāti vigatadomanassā. Viharemu averinoti aho vata kenaci saddhiṃ averino vihareyyāma, katthaci kopaṃ na uppādetvā accharāya gahitakaṃ jaṅghasahassena saddhiṃ paribhuñjeyyāmāti dānaṃ datvā pūjaṃ katvā ca patthayanti. Iti ca nesaṃ hotīti evañca nesaṃ ayaṃ patthanā hoti. Atha ca panāti evaṃ patthanāya satipi.

357. ‘What are the fetters?’ means what are the bonds, by what bond are they bound? ‘The multitude’ means many people. ‘Without enmity’ means without aversion. ‘Without punishment’ means freed from punishment by weapons and punishment by fines. ‘Without adversaries’ means without opponents. ‘Without ill will’ means with dejection departed. ‘May we dwell without enmity’ means: “Oh, would that we could dwell without enmity towards anyone! Would that, without generating anger towards anyone, we could share a morsel taken with a snap of the fingers with a thousand others!” Thus they make an aspiration after giving gifts and making offerings. ‘And so it is for them’ means: and thus this is their aspiration. ‘And yet’ means: even when there is such an aspiration.

Issāmacchariyasaṃyojanāti parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā issā, attasampattiyā parehi sādhāraṇabhāvassa [V 2.0279] asahanalakkhaṇaṃ [P 3.0719] macchariyaṃ, issā ca macchariyañca saṃyojanaṃ etesanti issāmacchariyasaṃyojanā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana issāmacchariyāni abhidhamme vuttāneva.

‘Fettered by envy and stinginess’ means: envy has the characteristic of resenting others' prosperity; stinginess has the characteristic of being unable to bear one's own prosperity being shared with others. They for whom envy and stinginess are a fetter are said to be 'fettered by envy and stinginess.' This is the summary here. In detail, however, envy and stinginess are explained in the Abhidhamma.

Āvāsamacchariyena [M 2.0311] panettha yakkho vā peto vā hutvā tasseva āvāsassa saṅkāraṃ sīsena ukkhipitvā vicarati. Kulamacchariyena tasmiṃ kule aññesaṃ dānādīni karonte disvā “bhinnaṃ vatidaṃ kulaṃ mamā”ti cintayato lohitampi mukhato uggacchati, kucchivirecanampi hoti, antānipi khaṇḍākhaṇḍāni hutvā nikkhamanti. Lābhamacchariyena saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā santake lābhe maccharāyitvā puggalikaparibhogena paribhuñjitvā yakkho vā peto vā mahāajagaro vā hutvā nibbattati. Sarīravaṇṇaguṇavaṇṇamacchariyena pana pariyattidhammamacchariyena ca attanova vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇeti, na paresaṃ vaṇṇaṃ, “kiṃ vaṇṇo eso”ti taṃ taṃ dosaṃ vadanto pariyattiñca kassaci kiñci adento dubbaṇṇo ceva eḷamūgo ca hoti.

Here, due to stinginess regarding dwellings, one becomes a yakkha or a peta and wanders about carrying the rubbish of that very dwelling on one's head. Due to stinginess regarding families, upon seeing others performing acts of giving in that family, one thinks, “Alas, this family of mine is ruined!” and blood may even come from one's mouth, and one's intestines may come out in pieces. Due to stinginess regarding gains, having been miserly with gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group and having consumed them for personal use, one is reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great python. Furthermore, due to stinginess regarding the beauty of one's body and virtues, and regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures, one praises only one's own qualities and not those of others. Saying of this or that fault, “What kind of quality is that?” and not imparting any of the scriptures to anyone, one becomes ugly and a drooling mute.

Apica āvāsamacchariyena lohagehe paccati. Kulamacchariyena appalābho hoti. Lābhamacchariyena gūthaniraye nibbattati. Vaṇṇamacchariyena bhave nibbattassa vaṇṇo nāma na hoti. Dhammamacchariyena kukkuḷaniraye nibbattati. Idaṃ pana issāmacchariyasaṃyojanaṃ sotāpattimaggena pahīyati. Yāva taṃ nappahīyati, tāva devamanussā averatādīni patthayantāpi verādīhi na parimuccantiyeva.

Moreover, due to stinginess regarding dwellings, one is tormented in an iron house hell. Due to stinginess regarding family, one has little gain. Due to stinginess regarding gains, one is reborn in the excrement hell. Due to stinginess regarding appearance, for one reborn in existence, there is no such thing as beauty. Due to stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one is reborn in the hot embers hell. This fetter of envy and stinginess is abandoned by the path of stream-entry. As long as it is not abandoned, gods and humans, even while aspiring for freedom from enmity and so forth, are by no means freed from enmity and the like.

Tiṇṇā mettha kaṅkhāti etasmiṃ pañhe mayā tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā kaṅkhā tiṇṇāti vadati, na maggavasena tiṇṇakaṅkhataṃ dīpeti. Vigatā kathaṃkathāti idaṃ kathaṃ, idaṃ kathanti ayampi kathaṃkathā vigatā.

‘My doubt is crossed here’ means he is saying: “Regarding this question, having heard your words, my doubt is crossed.” It does not indicate that doubt has been crossed by means of the path. ‘Perplexity is gone’ means that the state of asking, “How is this? How is that?”—this very perplexity—is gone.

358. Nidānādīni vuttatthāneva. Piyāppiyanidānanti piyasattasaṅkhāranidānaṃ macchariyaṃ, appiyasattasaṅkhāranidānā issā. Ubhayaṃ vā ubhayanidānaṃ. Pabbajitassa hi saddhivihārikādayo, gahaṭṭhassa puttādayo hatthiassādayo vā sattā piyā honti keḷāyitā mamāyitā, muhuttampi te apassanto adhivāsetuṃ na sakkoti. So aññaṃ tādisaṃ piyasattaṃ labhantaṃ disvā issaṃ karoti. “Iminā amhākaṃ kiñci kammaṃ atthi, muhuttaṃ tāva [P 3.0720] naṃ dethā”ti tameva aññehi yācito “na sakkā dātuṃ, kilamissati vā ukkaṇṭhissati vā”tiādīni [V 2.0280] vatvā macchariyaṃ karoti. Evaṃ tāva ubhayampi piyasattanidānaṃ hoti. Bhikkhussa pana pattacīvaraparikkhārajātaṃ, gahaṭṭhassa vā alaṅkārādiupakaraṇaṃ piyaṃ hoti manāpaṃ, so aññassa [M 2.0312] tādisaṃ uppajjamānaṃ disvā “aho vatassa evarūpaṃ na bhaveyyā”ti issaṃ karoti, yācito vāpi “mayampetaṃ mamāyantā na paribhuñjāma, na sakkā dātu”nti macchariyaṃ karoti. Evaṃ ubhayampi piyasaṅkhāranidānaṃ hoti. Appiye pana te vuttappakāre satte ca saṅkhāre ca labhitvā sacepissa te amanāpā honti, tathāpi kilesānaṃ viparītavuttitāya “ṭhapetvā maṃ ko añño evarūpassa lābhī”ti issaṃ vā karoti, yācito tāvakālikampi adadamāno macchariyaṃ vā karoti. Evaṃ ubhayampi appiyasattasaṅkhāranidānaṃ hoti.

358. The terms beginning with 'cause' have already been explained. As for the cause of the dear and the not-dear: stinginess has dear beings and formations as its cause, and envy has not-dear beings and formations as its cause. Or, both have both as their cause. For a renunciant, co-resident disciples and others are dear, cherished, and regarded as one’s own. For a householder, children and others, or elephants, horses, and other beings are dear, cherished, and regarded as one’s own. Not seeing them even for a moment, one cannot endure. Seeing another obtain such a dear being, one generates envy. When asked by others for that very person, “We have some work with this person; please give him to us for a moment,” one generates stinginess, saying such things as, “It is not possible to give him; he will become weary or discontented.” Thus, both have dear beings as their cause. Furthermore, for a bhikkhu, the collection of requisites such as the bowl and robes, or for a householder, ornaments and other accessories, are dear and pleasing. Seeing such a thing arise for another, one generates envy, thinking, “Oh, if only he did not have such a thing!” Or, when asked, one generates stinginess, saying, “We ourselves, cherishing this as our own, do not use it; it cannot be given.” Thus, both have dear formations as their cause. Furthermore, regarding not-dear beings and formations of the aforementioned kind, having obtained them, even if they are displeasing to him, nevertheless, due to the perverse nature of the defilements, one generates envy, thinking, “Besides me, who else is a gainer of such a thing?” Or, when asked, not giving it even for a short while, one generates stinginess. Thus, both have not-dear beings and formations as their cause.

Chandanidānanti ettha pariyesanachando, paṭilābhachando, paribhogachando, sannidhichando, vissajjanachandoti pañcavidho chando.

Herein, regarding 'having desire as its cause,' desire is of five kinds: the desire for seeking, the desire for acquisition, the desire for enjoyment, the desire for storing, and the desire for giving away.

Katamo pariyesanachando? Idhekacco atitto chandajāto rūpaṃ pariyesati, saddaṃ. Gandhaṃ. Rasaṃ. Phoṭṭhabbaṃ pariyesati, dhanaṃ pariyesati. Ayaṃ pariyesanachando.

What is the desire for seeking? Here, a certain person, unsatisfied, with desire arisen, seeks form, sound, smell, taste, and tangible objects; he seeks wealth. This is the desire for seeking.

Katamo paṭilābhachando? Idhekacco atitto chandajāto rūpaṃ paṭilabhati, saddaṃ. Gandhaṃ. Rasaṃ. Phoṭṭhabbaṃ paṭilabhati, dhanaṃ paṭilabhati. Ayaṃ paṭilābhachando.

What is the desire for acquisition? Here, a certain person, unsatisfied, with desire arisen, acquires form, sound, smell, taste, and tangible objects; he acquires wealth. This is the desire for acquisition.

Katamo paribhogachando? Idhekacco atitto chandajāto rūpaṃ paribhuñjati, saddaṃ. Gandhaṃ. Rasaṃ. Phoṭṭhabbaṃ paribhuñjati, dhanaṃ paribhuñjati. Ayaṃ paribhogachando.

What is the desire for enjoyment? Here, a certain person, unsatisfied, with desire arisen, enjoys form, sound, smell, taste, and tangible objects; he enjoys wealth. This is the desire for enjoyment.

Katamo sannidhichando? Idhekacco atitto chandajāto dhanasannicayaṃ karoti “āpadāsu bhavissatī”ti. Ayaṃ sannidhichando.

What is the desire for accumulation? Here, a certain person, unsatisfied and with desire arisen, makes an accumulation of wealth, thinking, “It will be for times of adversity.” This is the desire for accumulation.

Katamo vissajjanachando? Idhekacco atitto chandajāto dhanaṃ vissajjeti, hatthārohānaṃ, assārohānaṃ, rathikānaṃ, dhanuggahānaṃ – “ime maṃ rakkhissanti gopissanti mamāyissanti samparivārayissantī”ti. Ayaṃ vissajjanachando. Ime pañca chandā. Idha taṇhāmattameva, taṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ.

What is the desire for giving away? Here, a certain person, unsatisfied, with desire arisen, gives away wealth to elephant-riders, horse-riders, charioteers, and archers, thinking, “These will protect me, guard me, cherish me as their own, and surround me.” This is the desire for giving away. These are the five desires. Herein, they are merely craving, and it is with reference to that that this was said.

Vitakkanidānoti ettha “lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo”ti (dī. ni. 2.110) evaṃ vutto [V 2.0281] vinicchayavitakko vitakko nāma. Vinicchayoti dve vinicchayā taṇhāvinicchayo [M 2.0313] ca, diṭṭhivinicchayo ca. Aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritaṃ taṇhāvinicchayo nāma. Dvāsaṭṭhi [P 3.0721] diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhivinicchayo nāmāti evaṃ vuttataṇhāvinicchayavasena hi iṭṭhāniṭṭhapiyāppiyavavatthānaṃ na hoti. Tadeva hi ekaccassa iṭṭhaṃ hoti, ekaccassa aniṭṭhaṃ paccantarājamajjhimadesarājūnaṃ gaṇḍuppādamigamaṃsādīsu viya. Tasmiṃ pana taṇhāvinicchayavinicchite paṭiladdhavatthusmiṃ “ettakaṃ rūpassa bhavissati, ettakaṃ saddassa, ettakaṃ gandhassa, ettakaṃ rasassa, ettakaṃ phoṭṭhabbassa bhavissati, ettakaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissati, ettakaṃ parassa bhavissati, ettakaṃ nidahissāmi, ettakaṃ parassa dassāmī”ti vavatthānaṃ vitakkavinicchayena hoti. Tenāha “chando kho, devānaminda, vitakkanidāno”ti.

Herein, regarding 'having thought as its cause': as stated, 'judgment is conditioned by acquisition,' the thought associated with judgment is what is called 'thought' (vitakka). 'Judgment' (vinicchaya) is twofold: judgment by craving and judgment by views. The one hundred and eight movements of craving are called 'judgment by craving.' The sixty-two views are called 'judgment by views.' For, based on judgment by craving, there is no fixed determination of what is desirable and undesirable, dear and not-dear. Indeed, the very same thing is desirable to one person and undesirable to another, as in the case of the grub and deer meat for kings of border regions and the middle country. However, with regard to an object that has been obtained and decided upon through judgment by craving, the determination—'This much will be for form, this much for sound, this much for smell, this much for taste, this much for tangible objects; this much will be for me, this much for another; this much I will store away, this much I will give to another'—occurs through the judgment of thought. Therefore, He said: 'Desire, O lord of the devas, has thought as its cause.'

Papañcasaññāsaṅkhānidānoti tayo papañcā taṇhāpapañco, mānapapañco, diṭṭhipapañcoti. Tattha aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritaṃ taṇhāpapañco nāma. Navavidho māno mānapapañco nāma. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhipapañco nāma. Tesu idha taṇhāpapañco adhippeto. Kenaṭṭhena papañco? Mattapamattākārapāpanaṭṭhena papañco. Taṃsampayuttā saññā papañcasaññā. Saṅkhā vuccati koṭṭhāso “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā”tiādīsu viya. Iti papañcasaññāsaṅkhānidānoti papañcasaññākoṭṭhāsanidāno vitakkoti attho.

Regarding 'having the collections of perceptions of proliferation as its cause': there are three proliferations (papañca): proliferation of craving, proliferation of conceit, and proliferation of views. Therein, the one hundred and eight movements of craving are called 'proliferation of craving.' The nine kinds of conceit are called 'proliferation of conceit.' The sixty-two views are called 'proliferation of views.' Among these, the proliferation of craving is intended here. In what sense is it 'proliferation'? It is 'proliferation' in the sense of causing a state of intoxication and heedlessness. Perception associated with that is 'perception of proliferation.' Saṅkhā is said to be a collection, as in such passages as, 'For the collections of proliferations have perception as their cause.' Thus, the meaning of 'having the collections of perceptions of proliferation as its cause' is that thought has the collection of perceptions of proliferation as its cause.

Papañcasaññāsaṅkhānirodhasāruppagāmininti etissā papañcasaññāsaṅkhāya khayā nirodho vūpasamo, tassa sāruppañceva tattha gāminiṃ cāti saha vipassanāya maggaṃ pucchati.

Regarding 'leading to what is suitable for the cessation of the collections of perceptions of proliferation': the cessation (nirodha) and appeasement (vūpasama) of this collection of perceptions of proliferation is its destruction. He asks about the path together with insight, which is both suitable for that cessation and leads thereto.

Vedanākammaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Meditation Subject of Feelings

359. Athassa bhagavā somanassaṃpāhanti tisso vedanā ārabhi. Kiṃ pana bhagavatā pucchitaṃ kathitaṃ, apucchitaṃ, sānusandhikaṃ, ananusandhikanti? Pucchitameva kathitaṃ, no apucchitaṃ, sānusandhikameva, no ananusandhikaṃ. Devatānañhi rūpato arūpaṃ pākaṭataraṃ, arūpepi vedanā pākaṭatarā. Kasmā? Devatānañhi karajakāyaṃ sukhumaṃ, kammajaṃ balavaṃ, karajakāyassa sukhumattā, kammajassa balavattā ekāhārampi atikkamitvā na tiṭṭhanti, uṇhapāsāṇe [M 2.0314] ṭhapitasappipiṇḍi viya vilīyantīti sabbaṃ brahmajāle vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tasmā bhagavā sakkassa tisso vedanā ārabhi. Duvidhañhi kammaṭṭhānaṃ – rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ, arūpakammaṭṭhānañca. Rūpapariggaho, arūpapariggahotipi etadeva [P 3.0722] vuccati. Tattha bhagavā yassa rūpaṃ [V 2.0282] pākaṭaṃ, tassa saṅkhepamanasikāravasena vā vitthāramanasikāravasena vā catudhātuvavatthānaṃ vitthārento rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ katheti. Yassa arūpaṃ pākaṭaṃ, tassa arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ katheti. Kathento ca tassa vatthubhūtaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvāva katheti, devānaṃ pana arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭanti arūpakammaṭṭhānavasena vedanā ārabhi.

359. Then the Blessed One, arousing joy in him, began to speak about the three kinds of feeling. Now, did the Blessed One speak of what was asked or unasked, of what was connected or unconnected? What was spoken was only what was asked, not what was unasked; only what was connected, not what was unconnected. For deities, the formless is more evident than form, and even among the formless, feeling is more evident. Why? Because the physical bodies of deities are subtle and their kamma-born heat is powerful; due to the subtlety of their physical bodies and the power of their kamma-born heat, they cannot last having gone beyond a single day's food, but dissolve like a lump of ghee placed on a hot stone. All this should be understood in the same way as it was explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta. Therefore, the Blessed One began to speak to Sakka about the three kinds of feeling. For the meditation subject is twofold: the form meditation subject and the formless meditation subject. The grasping of form and the grasping of the formless are also terms for this. Therein, for one for whom form is evident, the Blessed One teaches the form meditation subject by elaborating on the analysis of the four elements, either by way of brief attention or detailed attention. For one for whom the formless is evident, he teaches the formless meditation subject. And when teaching it, he teaches only after having shown the form meditation subject, which serves as its basis. But for deities, the formless meditation subject is evident; therefore, he began to speak about feeling by way of the formless meditation subject.

Tividho hi arūpakammaṭṭhāne abhiniveso – phassavasena, vedanāvasena, cittavasenāti. Kathaṃ? Ekaccassa hi saṅkhittena vā vitthārena vā pariggahite rūpakammaṭṭhāne tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ paṭhamābhinipāto taṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusanto uppajjamāno phasso pākaṭo hoti. Ekaccassa taṃ ārammaṇaṃ anubhavantī uppajjamānā vedanā pākaṭā hoti. Ekaccassa taṃ ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā taṃ vijānantaṃ uppajjamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti.

Indeed, the application of mind to the formless meditation subject is threefold: by way of contact, by way of feeling, and by way of mind. How so? For a certain person, when the form meditation subject has been grasped, whether briefly or in detail, contact becomes prominent—arising as the initial impact of mind and mental factors upon that object, touching that object. For another person, feeling becomes prominent—arising and experiencing that object. For yet another person, consciousness becomes prominent—arising, having grasped that object and cognizing it.

Tattha yassa phasso pākaṭo hoti, sopi na kevalaṃ phassova uppajjati, tena saddhiṃ tadeva ārammaṇaṃ anubhavamānā vedanāpi uppajjati, sañjānamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatīti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. Yassa vedanā pākaṭā hoti, sopi na kevalaṃ vedanāva uppajjati, tāya saddhiṃ tadeva ārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi uppajjati, sañjānamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatīti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. Yassa viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, sopi na kevalaṃ viññāṇameva uppajjati, tena saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi uppajjati, anubhavamānā vedanāpi, sañjānamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi uppajjatīti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti.

Therein, for one for whom contact is prominent, it is not the case that only contact arises. Together with it, feeling also arises experiencing that same object, perception also arises perceiving it, volition also arises intending, and consciousness also arises cognizing it. Thus, one grasps just the pentad with contact as the fifth. For one for whom feeling is prominent, it is not the case that only feeling arises. Together with it, contact also arises touching that same object, perception also arises perceiving it, volition also arises intending, and consciousness also arises cognizing it. Thus, one grasps just the pentad with contact as the fifth. For one for whom consciousness is prominent, it is not the case that only consciousness arises. Together with it, contact also arises touching that same object, feeling also arises experiencing it, perception also arises perceiving it, and volition also arises intending. Thus, one grasps just the pentad with contact as the fifth.

So “ime phassapañcamakā dhammā kiṃ nissitā”ti upadhārento “vatthunissitā”ti pajānāti. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ [M 2.0315] – “idañca pana me viññāṇaṃ ettha sitaṃ ettha paṭibaddha”nti. So atthato bhūtāni ceva upādārūpāni ca. Evamettha vatthu rūpaṃ, phassapañcamakā nāmanti nāmarūpamattameva passati. Rūpañcettha rūpakkhandho, nāmaṃ cattāro arūpino khandhāti pañcakkhandhamattaṃ hoti. Nāmarūpavinimuttā hi pañcakkhandhā, pañcakkhandhavinimuttaṃ vā nāmarūpaṃ natthi. So “ime pañcakkhandhā kiṃ [P 3.0723] hetukā”ti upaparikkhanto “avijjādihetukā”ti passati.
