Tato “paccayo ceva paccayuppannañca idaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthi, suddhasaṅkhārapuñjamattamevā”ti sappaccayanāmarūpavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti sammasanto vicarati[V 2.0283], so ajja ajjāti paṭivedhaṃ ākaṅkhamāno tathārūpe divase utusappāyaṃ, puggalasappāyaṃ, bhojanasappāyaṃ, dhammasavanasappāyaṃ vā labhitvā ekapallaṅkena nisinnova vipassanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Evamimesampi tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ hoti.

That person, considering, 'Upon what do these dhammas of the contact-pentad depend?' understands, 'They depend on a physical basis.' The physical basis is the physical body, in reference to which it was said: 'And this consciousness of mine is dependent on this and bound to this.' In essence, that is the primary elements and derived materiality. Thus, herein, the physical basis is form and the contact-pentad is name; in this way, one sees only name-and-form. And herein, form is the form-aggregate, and name is the four formless aggregates; thus, it is merely the five aggregates. For the five aggregates are not separate from name-and-form, nor is name-and-form separate from the five aggregates. Then, investigating, 'What is the cause of these five aggregates?' one sees, 'They have ignorance and so on as their cause.' Thereafter, applying the three characteristics to name-and-form together with its causes, one proceeds by way of the sequence of insight, contemplating, 'Impermanent, suffering, not-self,' and reflecting: 'This is only a condition and what is conditionally arisen; there is no other being or person, but only a mere heap of pure formations.' Aspiring for penetration, thinking, 'Today! Today!' on a suitable day—having found a favorable climate, suitable people, suitable food, or a suitable Dhamma talk—one sits in a single posture, brings insight to its culmination, and becomes established in arahantship. In this way, the meditation subject has been taught for these three kinds of persons, all the way up to arahantship.

Idha pana bhagavā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento vedanāsīsena kathesi. Phassavasena hi viññāṇavasena vā kathiyamānaṃ etassa na pākaṭaṃ hoti, andhakāraṃ viya khāyati. Vedanāvasena pana pākaṭaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Vedanānaṃ uppattiyā pākaṭatāya. Sukhadukkhavedanānañhi uppatti pākaṭā. Yadā sukhaṃ uppajjati, tadā sakalaṃ sarīraṃ khobhentaṃ maddantaṃ pharamānaṃ abhisandayamānaṃ satadhotasappiṃ khādāpayantaṃ viya, satapākatelaṃ makkhayamānaṃ viya, ghaṭasahassena pariḷāhaṃ nibbāpayamānaṃ viya, “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti vācaṃ nicchārayamānameva uppajjati. Yadā dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tadā sakalasarīraṃ khobhentaṃ maddantaṃ pharamānaṃ abhisandayamānaṃ tattaphālaṃ pavesentaṃ viya, vilīnatambalohena āsiñcantaṃ viya, sukkhatiṇavanappatimhi araññe dāruukkākalāpaṃ khipamānaṃ viya “aho dukkhaṃ, aho dukkha”nti vippalāpayamānameva uppajjati. Iti sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ uppatti pākaṭā hoti.

Here, however, the Blessed One, while explaining the formless meditation subject, explained it with feeling as the focal point. For when explained in terms of contact or consciousness, it does not become clear to him—it appears like darkness. But when explained in terms of feeling, it becomes clear. Why? Because the arising of feelings is evident. Indeed, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is evident. When pleasure arises, it arises shaking the entire body, crushing, pervading, and suffusing it—like causing one to consume ghee washed a hundred times, like being anointed with oil cooked a hundred times, like extinguishing a burning fever with a thousand pots of water—while causing one to utter the words, 'Ah, pleasure! Ah, pleasure!' When pain arises, it arises shaking the entire body, crushing, pervading, and suffusing it—like inserting a hot ploughshare, like being drenched with molten copper, like throwing a bundle of firebrands into a forest of dry grass and trees—while causing one to lament, 'Ah, pain! Ah, pain!' Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is evident.

Adukkhamasukhā pana duddīpanā andhakārena viya abhibhūtā. Sā sukhadukkhānaṃ apagame sātāsātapaṭikkhepavasena majjhattākārabhūtā adukkhamasukhā vedanāti nayato gaṇhantassa pākaṭā hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā antarā piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ āruhitvā palātassa migassa anupadaṃ gacchanto [M 2.0316] migaluddako piṭṭhipāsāṇassa orabhāgepi parabhāgepi padaṃ disvā majjhe apassantopi “ito āruḷho, ito oruḷho, majjhe piṭṭhipāsāṇe iminā padesena gato bhavissatī”ti nayato jānāti[P 3.0724]. Evaṃ āruḷhaṭṭhāne padaṃ viya hi sukhavedanāya uppatti pākaṭā hoti, oruḷhaṭṭhāne padaṃ viya dukkhavedanāya uppatti pākaṭā hoti, ito āruyha, ito oruyha, majjhe evaṃ gatoti nayato gahaṇaṃ viya sukhadukkhānaṃ apagame sātāsātapaṭikkhepavasena majjhattākārabhūtā adukkhamasukhā vedanāti nayato gaṇhantassa pākaṭā hoti. Evaṃ bhagavā paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nivattetvā dassesi.

The neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, however, is difficult to illuminate, being as if overwhelmed by darkness. It becomes evident to one who grasps it by inference as the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which is of a neutral character by way of rejecting the agreeable and disagreeable upon the cessation of pleasant and painful feelings. How so? Just as a deer hunter, following the tracks of a deer that has fled after climbing onto a flat rock, sees footprints on both the near and far sides of the rock but not in the middle, and yet knows by inference: 'It climbed up from here and descended from there; in the middle, on the flat rock, it must have passed through this spot.' In the same way, the arising of pleasant feeling is evident like a footprint at the place of ascent, and the arising of painful feeling is evident like a footprint at the place of descent. Just as one grasps by inference, 'Having climbed from here and descended from there, it passed through the middle in this way,' so too, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which is of a neutral character by way of rejecting the agreeable and disagreeable upon the cessation of pleasant and painful feelings, becomes evident to one who grasps it by inference. Thus, the Blessed One first taught the material meditation subject and afterwards distinguished and showed the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling.

Na kevalañca idheva evaṃ dassesi, mahāsatipaṭṭhāne, majjhimanikāyamhi satipaṭṭhāne, cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaye, mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaye, cūḷavedallasutte, mahāvedallasutte, raṭṭhapālasutte, māgaṇḍiyasutte, dhātuvibhaṅge, āneñjasappāye, sakale vedanāsaṃyutteti evaṃ anekesu suttantesu paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā [V 2.0284] pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nivattetvā dassesi. Yathā ca tesu tesu, evaṃ imasmimpi sakkapañhe paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nivattetvā dassesi. Rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ panettha vedanāya ārammaṇamattakaṃyeva saṅkhittaṃ, tasmā pāḷiyaṃ nāruḷhaṃ bhavissati.

And not only here did he teach in this way. In the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya, the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the Mahāvedalla Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the Āneñjasappāya Sutta, and in the entire Vedanāsaṃyutta—in these many discourses, he first taught the material meditation subject and afterwards distinguished and showed the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling. And just as in those various discourses, so too in this Sakkapañha Sutta, he first taught the material meditation subject and afterwards distinguished and showed the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling. Here, the material meditation subject is summarized as merely an object for feeling; therefore, it will not have been included in the Pāḷi text.

360. Arūpakammaṭṭhāne yaṃ tassa pākaṭaṃ vedanāvasena abhinivesamukhaṃ, tameva dassetuṃ somanassaṃpāhaṃ, devānamindātiādimāha. Tattha duvidhenāti dvividhena, dvīhi koṭṭhāsehīti attho. Evarūpaṃ somanassaṃ na sevitabbanti evarūpaṃ gehasitasomanassaṃ na sevitabbaṃ. Gehasitasomanassaṃ nāma “tattha katamāni cha gehasitāni somanassāni? Cakkhuviññeyyānaṃ rūpānaṃ iṭṭhānaṃ kantānaṃ manāpānaṃ manoramānaṃ lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ paṭilābhaṃ vā paṭilābhato samanupassato, pubbe vā paṭiladdhapubbaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ vipariṇataṃ samanussarato uppajjati somanassaṃ, yaṃ evarūpaṃ somanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati gehasitaṃ somanassa”nti evaṃ chasu dvāresu vuttakāmaguṇanissitaṃ somanassaṃ (ma. ni. 3.306).

360. Regarding the immaterial meditation subject, in order to show that very entry-point for mental application which is evident to him by way of feeling, the Buddha said, 'Joy, O king of the devas...' and so on. Therein, 'of two kinds' means twofold, by two divisions. 'Such joy should not be cultivated' means such joy based on the household life should not be cultivated. What is called joy based on the household life? 'Therein, what are the six kinds of joy based on the household life? When one sees or considers the acquisition of forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, and connected with worldly allurements; or when one recollects those formerly obtained which are past, ceased, and altered, joy arises. Whatever joy is of such a kind, this is called joy based on the household life.' Thus, it is the joy dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure spoken of in relation to the six sense doors.

Evarūpaṃ [M 2.0317] somanassaṃ sevitabbanti evarūpaṃ nekkhammasitaṃ somanassaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Nekkhammasitaṃ somanassaṃ nāma – “tattha katamāni cha nekkhammasitāni somanassāni? Rūpānaṃ [P 3.0725] tveva aniccataṃ viditvā vipariṇāmavirāganirodhaṃ pubbe ceva rūpā etarahi ca sabbe te rūpā aniccā, dukkhā, vipariṇāmadhammāti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato uppajjati somanassaṃ, yaṃ evarūpaṃ somanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati nekkhammasitaṃ somanassa”nti (ma. ni. 3.308) evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ussukkāpetuṃ sakkontassa “ussukkitā me vipassanā”ti somanassajātassa uppannaṃ somanassaṃ. Sevitabbanti idaṃ nekkhammavasena, vipassanāvasena, anussativasena, paṭhamajjhānādivasena ca uppajjanakasomanassaṃ sevitabbaṃ nāma.

'Such joy should be cultivated' means such joy based on renunciation should be cultivated. What is called joy based on renunciation? 'Therein, what are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation? Having known the impermanence of forms themselves, their alteration, fading away, and cessation, and that forms both formerly and now—all those forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to alteration—for one who sees this as it really is with right wisdom, joy arises. Whatever joy is of such a kind, this is called joy based on renunciation.' Thus, it is the joy that arises for one who is able to arouse effort by establishing insight based on impermanence and so forth when a desirable object comes into the range of the six sense doors, and in whom joy is born from the thought, 'My insight has been initiated.' 'It should be cultivated' means that the joy which is fit to arise by way of renunciation, by way of insight, by way of recollection, and by way of the first jhāna and so forth, is what is to be cultivated.

Tattha yaṃ ce savitakkaṃ savicāranti tasmimpi nekkhammasite somanasse yaṃ nekkhammavasena, vipassanāvasena, anussativasena, paṭhamajjhānavasena ca uppannaṃ savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ somanassanti jāneyya. Yaṃ ce avitakkaṃ avicāranti yaṃ pana dutiyatatiyajjhānavasena uppannaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ somanassanti jāneyya. Ye avitakke avicāre, te paṇītatareti etesupi dvīsu yaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ, taṃ paṇītataranti attho.

Herein, regarding that which is 'with thought and with examination': even in joy based on renunciation, one should understand as joy with thought and with examination that which arises by means of renunciation, by means of insight, by means of recollection, and by means of the first jhāna. And regarding that which is 'without thought and without examination': one should understand as joy without thought and without examination that which arises by means of the second and third jhāna. 'Those without thought, without examination, are more sublime' means that of these two, that which is without thought and without examination is more sublime.

Iminā [V 2.0285] kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Dvinnaṃ arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Kathaṃ? Eko kira bhikkhu savitakkasavicāre somanasse vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā “idaṃ somanassaṃ kiṃ nissita”nti upadhārento “vatthunissita”nti pajānātīti phassapañcamake vuttanayeneva anukkamena arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Eko avitakkaavicāre somanasse vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā vuttanayeneva arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Tattha abhiniviṭṭhasomanassesupi savitakkasavicārato avitakkaavicāraṃ paṇītataraṃ. Savitakkasavicārasomanassavipassanātopi avitakkaavicāravipassanā paṇītatarā. Savitakkasavicārasomanassaphalasamāpattitopi avitakkaavicārasomanassaphalasamāpattiyeva paṇītatarā. Tenāha bhagavā “ye avitakke avicāre, te paṇītatare”ti.

What is taught by this? The Arahantship of two individuals is taught. How so? It is said that one monk, having established insight in joy that is with thought and with examination, and investigating, 'Upon what is this joy dependent?', understands, 'It is dependent on a basis.' Thus, in due course, in the very manner stated in the section on the pentad of contact, he becomes established in Arahantship. Another monk, having established insight in joy that is without thought and without examination, becomes established in Arahantship in the very manner stated. Therein, even among joys in which one is absorbed, that which is without thought and without examination is more sublime than that with thought and with examination. Insight without thought and without examination is also more sublime than insight into joy with thought and with examination. The attainment of fruition associated with joy without thought and without examination is indeed more sublime than the attainment of fruition associated with joy with thought and with examination. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Those without thought, without examination, are more sublime.'

361. Evarūpaṃ [M 2.0318] domanassaṃ na sevitabbanti evarūpaṃ gehasitadomanassaṃ na sevitabbaṃ. Gehasitadomanassaṃ nāma – “tattha katamāni cha gehasitāni domanassāni? Cakkhuviññeyyānaṃ rūpānaṃ iṭṭhānaṃ kantānaṃ manāpānaṃ manoramānaṃ lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ appaṭilābhaṃ vā appaṭilābhato [P 3.0726] samanupassato pubbe vā apaṭiladdhapubbaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ vipariṇataṃ samanussarato uppajjati domanassaṃ, yaṃ evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati gehasitadomanassa”nti (ma. ni. 3.307). Evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ nānubhaviṃ, nānubhavissāmi, nānubhavāmīti vitakkayato uppannaṃ kāmaguṇanissitaṃ domanassaṃ.

361. 'Such displeasure should not be cultivated' means that such displeasure based on the household life should not be cultivated. What is displeasure based on the household life? 'Herein, what are the six kinds of displeasure based on the household life? Displeasure arises for one who perceives the non-attainment of forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, and connected with the baits of the world, or who, from their non-attainment, or who, recollecting what was not obtained in the past—which is past, ceased, and altered—, such displeasure that arises is called displeasure based on the household life.' Thus, it is the displeasure dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure that arises for one who thinks regarding a desirable object at the six doors: 'I have not experienced it, I will not experience it, I am not experiencing it.'

Evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ sevitabbanti evarūpaṃ nekkhammasitadomanassaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Nekkhammasitadomanassaṃ nāma – “tattha katamāni cha nekkhammasitāni domanassāni? Rūpānaṃ tveva aniccataṃ viditvā vipariṇāmavirāganirodhaṃ pubbe ceva rūpā etarahi ca sabbe te rūpā aniccā, dukkhā, vipariṇāmadhammāti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sampappaññāya disvā anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpeti ‘kudāssu nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ, upasampajja viharissāmi, yadariyā etarahi āyatanaṃ upasampajja viharantī’ti. Iti anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato uppajjati pihapaccayā domanassaṃ, yaṃ evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati nekkhammasitadomanassa”nti (ma. ni. 3.307) evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate anuttaravimokkhasaṅkhātaariyaphaladhammesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā tadadhigamāya aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ussukkāpetumasakkontassa imampi pakkhaṃ, imampi māsaṃ, imampi saṃvaccharaṃ vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyabhūmiṃ pāpuṇituṃ nāsakkhinti anusocato uppannaṃ domanassaṃ. Sevitabbanti idaṃ nekkhammavasena, vipassanāvasena, anussativasena, paṭhamajjhānādivasena ca uppajjanakadomanassaṃ sevitabbaṃ nāma.

'Such displeasure should be cultivated' means that such displeasure based on renunciation should be cultivated. What is displeasure based on renunciation? 'Herein, what are the six kinds of displeasure based on renunciation? Having known the impermanence of forms, their alteration, fading away, and cessation, and having seen with right understanding, as it truly is, that "Both forms in the past and forms at present—all those forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change," one establishes a longing for the unsurpassed liberations: "Oh, when shall I enter and dwell in that sphere which the noble ones now enter and dwell in?" Thus, for one who establishes a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, displeasure arises conditioned by that longing. Such displeasure as this is called displeasure based on renunciation.' Thus, when a desirable object comes into the range of the six doors, it is the displeasure that arises for one who, having established a longing for the noble fruition-states known as the unsurpassed liberations and having established insight by way of impermanence and so on for their attainment, is unable to exert himself and laments, 'Having striven in insight this fortnight, this month, this year, I was not able to reach the noble plane.' 'Should be cultivated' means that this displeasure which arises by means of renunciation, by means of insight, by means of recollection, and by means of the first jhāna and so on, is what is to be cultivated.

Tattha [V 2.0286] yaṃ ce savitakkasavicāranti tasmimpi duvidhe domanasse gehasitadomanassameva savitakkasavicāradomanassaṃ nāma. Nekkhammavasena, vipassanāvasena, anussativasena, paṭhamadutiyajjhānavasena ca uppannadomanassaṃ pana avitakkaavicāradomanassanti veditabbaṃ. Nippariyāyena pana avitakkaavicāradomanassaṃ nāma natthi. Domanassindriyañhi ekaṃsena akusalañceva savitakkasavicārañca, etassa pana bhikkhuno maññanavasena [P 3.0727] savitakkasavicāranti ca avitakkaavicāranti ca vuttaṃ.

Herein, regarding that which is 'with thought and with examination': even in that twofold displeasure, it is displeasure based on the household life that is called displeasure with thought and with examination. However, the displeasure that arises by means of renunciation, by means of insight, by means of recollection, and by means of the first and second jhānas should be understood as displeasure without thought and without examination. But in an absolute sense, there is no such thing as displeasure without thought and without examination. For the faculty of displeasure is exclusively unwholesome and with thought and with examination. It is, however, spoken of as 'with thought and with examination' and 'without thought and without examination' by way of this monk's own conceiving.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 2.0319] nayo – idha bhikkhu domanassapaccayabhūte savitakkasavicāradhamme avitakkaavicāradhamme ca domanassapaccayā eva uppanne maggaphaladhamme ca aññesaṃ paṭipattidassanavasena domanassanti gahetvā “kadā nu kho me savitakkasavicāradomanasse vipassanā paṭṭhapitā bhavissati, kadā avitakkaavicāradomanasse”ti ca “kadā nu kho me savitakkasavicāradomanassaphalasamāpatti nibbattitā bhavissati, kadā avitakkaavicāradomanassaphalasamāpattī”ti cintetvā temāsikaṃ, chamāsikaṃ, navamāsikaṃ vā paṭipadaṃ gaṇhāti. Temāsikaṃ gahetvā paṭhamamāse ekaṃ yāmaṃ jaggati, dve yāme niddāya okāsaṃ karoti, majjhime māse dve yāme jaggati, ekaṃ yāmaṃ niddāya okāsaṃ karoti, pacchimamāse caṅkamanisajjāyeva yāpeti. Evaṃ ce arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce pāpuṇāti, visesetvā chamāsikaṃ gaṇhāti. Tatrāpi dve dve māse vuttanayena paṭipajjitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ asakkonto visesetvā navamāsikaṃ gaṇhāti. Tatrāpi tayo tayo māse tatheva paṭipajjitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ asakkontassa “na ladvaṃ vata me sabrahmacārīhi saddhiṃ visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāretu”nti āvajjato domanassaṃ uppajjati, assudhārā pavattanti gāmantapabbhāravāsīmahāsīvattherassa viya.

Here is the method: In this tradition, a monk, taking as 'displeasure' the states accompanied by applied and sustained thought and those without applied and sustained thought that are conditioned by displeasure, as well as the path and fruition states that have arisen conditioned by displeasure itself—all by way of seeing the practice of others—reflects: 'When, I wonder, will insight based on displeasure with applied and sustained thought be established for me? When will it be based on displeasure without applied and sustained thought?' And also: 'When, I wonder, will the fruition attainment based on displeasure with applied and sustained thought be produced for me? When will the fruition attainment based on displeasure without applied and sustained thought be produced?' Having reflected thus, he undertakes a three-month, six-month, or nine-month period of practice. Having undertaken the three-month practice, in the first month he stays awake for one watch of the night and makes opportunity for sleep for two watches. In the middle month, he stays awake for two watches and makes opportunity for sleep for one watch. In the final month, he passes the time solely in walking and sitting. If he attains Arahantship in this way, that is excellent. If he does not attain it, he makes a special effort and undertakes a six-month practice. There too, practicing in the manner described for two months at a time, if he is unable to attain Arahantship, he makes a special effort and undertakes a nine-month practice. There too, practicing in the same way for three months at a time, if he is unable to attain Arahantship, displeasure arises in him as he reflects: 'Alas, I have not had the opportunity to perform the Pavāraṇā of purity together with my companions in the holy life.' Upon reflecting thus, displeasure arises in him, and streams of tears flow—just as they did for the great elder Mahāsīva, who dwelt in the mountain cave near the village.

Mahāsīvattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Mahāsīva

Thero kira aṭṭhārasa mahāgaṇe vācesi. Tassovāde ṭhatvā tiṃsasahassā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Atheko bhikkhu “mayhaṃ tāva abbhantare guṇā appamāṇā, kīdisā nu kho me ācariyassa guṇā”ti āvajjanto puthujjanabhāvaṃ passitvā “amhākaṃ ācariyo aññesaṃ avassayo hoti, attano bhavituṃ na sakkoti, ovādamassa dassāmī”ti ākāsena gantvā vihārasamīpe otaritvā divāṭṭhāne nisinnaṃ ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vattaṃ dassetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

It is said that the elder taught eighteen great assemblies. Abiding by his instruction, thirty thousand monks attained Arahantship. Then a certain monk, reflecting, 'The virtues within me are indeed immeasurable; what sort of virtues, I wonder, does my teacher possess?' and perceiving his teacher's state to be that of a worldling, thought: 'Our teacher is a support for others, but is unable to be one for himself. I will give him instruction.' Then, having gone through the sky and descended near the monastery, he approached the teacher, who was seated in his daytime dwelling, showed his respects, and sat down to one side.

Thero [V 2.0287] – “kiṃ kāraṇā āgatosi piṇḍapātikā”ti āha. Ekaṃ anumodanaṃ gaṇhissāmīti āgatosmi, bhanteti. Okāso na bhavissati, āvusoti? Vitakkamāḷake ṭhitakāle pucchissāmi, bhanteti. Tasmiṃ ṭhāne aññe [P 3.0728] pucchantīti. Bhikkhācāramagge, bhanteti. Tatrāpi aññe pucchantīti. Dupaṭṭanivāsanaṭṭhāne, saṅghāṭipārupanaṭṭhāne, pattanīharaṇaṭṭhāne, gāme [M 2.0320] caritvā āsanasālāyaṃ yāgupītakāle, bhanteti. Tattha aṭṭhakathātherā attano kaṅkhaṃ vinodenti, āvusoti. Antogāmato nikkhantakāle pucchissāmi, bhanteti. Tatrāpi aññe pucchanti, āvusoti. Antarāmagge, bhante, bhojanasālāyaṃ bhattakiccapariyosāne, bhante, divāṭṭhāne, pādadhovanakāle, mukhadhovanakāle, bhanteti? Tadā aññe pucchantīti. Tato paṭṭhāya yāva aruṇā apare pucchanti, āvusoti. Dantakaṭṭhaṃ gahetvā mukhadhovanatthaṃ gamanakāle, bhanteti? Tadā aññe pucchantīti. Mukhaṃ dhovitvā āgamanakāle, bhanteti? Tatrāpi aññe pucchantīti. Senāsanaṃ pavisitvā nisinnakāle, bhanteti? Tatrāpi aññe pucchantīti. Bhante, nanu mukhaṃ dhovitvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā tayo cattāro pallaṅke usumaṃ gāhāpetvā yonisomanasikāre kammaṃ karontānaṃ okāsakālena bhavitabbaṃ siyā, maraṇakhaṇampi na labhissatha, bhante, phalakasadisattha bhante parassa avassayo hotha, attano bhavituṃ na sakkotha, na me tumhākaṃ anumodanāya atthoti ākāse uppatitvā agamāsi.

The elder asked, "For what reason have you come, alms-goer?" "I have come to learn a discourse of appreciation, venerable sir." "There will be no opportunity, friend." "I will ask when you are standing in the Hall of Reflection, venerable sir." "Others are asking at that place." "On the alms-round path, venerable sir." "There too, others are asking." "At the place for putting on the double-layered lower robe, at the place for putting on the outer robe, at the place for taking out the bowl, after going through the village, at the time of drinking gruel in the assembly hall, venerable sir." "There, friend, the elders of the commentaries are dispelling their own doubts." "I will ask at the time of leaving the village, venerable sir." "There too, friend, others are asking." "On the path between villages, venerable sir; in the dining hall at the end of the meal, venerable sir; in the daytime quarters; at the time of washing the feet; at the time of washing the face, venerable sir?" "At that time, others are asking." "From then until dawn, friend, others are asking." "When taking a tooth-stick and going to wash the face, venerable sir?" "At that time, others are asking." "When returning after having washed the face, venerable sir?" "There too, others are asking." "After entering the lodging and sitting down, venerable sir?" "There too, others are asking." "Venerable sir, surely after washing the face and entering the lodging, having generated warmth through three or four meditation sessions while engaged in the practice of wise attention, there ought to be a time of opportunity? You will not obtain even a moment for yourself, even at the time of death! Venerable sir, you are like a plank: you are a support for others, but you cannot be a support for yourself. I have no need for your discourse of appreciation," and he leapt into the sky and departed.

Thero – “imassa bhikkhuno pariyattiyā kammaṃ natthi, mayhaṃ pana aṅkusako bhavissāmīti āgato”ti ñatvā “idāni okāso na bhavissati, paccūsakāle gamissāmī”ti pattacīvaraṃ samīpe katvā sabbaṃ divasabhāgaṃ paṭhamayāmamajjhimayāmañca dhammaṃ vācetvā pacchimayāme ekasmiṃ there uddesaṃ gahetvā nikkhante pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā teneva saddhiṃ nikkhanto. Nisinnaantevāsikā ācariyo kenaci papañcena nikkhantoti maññiṃsu. Nikkhanto thero koci deva samānācariyabhikkhūti saññaṃ akāsi.

The elder, knowing, "This monk has no more work to do with the scriptures, but has come thinking, 'I will be his goad,'" thought, "Now there will be no opportunity; I will go at dawn." Having placed his bowl and robe nearby, and having had the Dhamma recited throughout the day and during the first and middle watches of the night, in the last watch, when a certain elder had taken his recitation passage and departed, he took his bowl and robe and left with that very elder. The resident pupils who were seated thought, "The teacher has left on some minor business." The departing elder gave the impression of being just some monk from the same lineage.

Thero kira “mādisassa arahattaṃ nāma kiṃ, dvīhatīheneva pāpuṇitvā paccāgamissāmī”ti antevāsikānaṃ anārocetvāva āsāḷhīmāsassa juṇhapakkhaterasiyā nikkhanto gāmantapabbhāraṃ gantvā caṅkamaṃ āruyha kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto taṃ divasaṃ arahattaṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhi. Uposathadivase sampatte “dvīhatīhena arahattaṃ gaṇhissāmīti āgato[P 3.0729], gahetuṃ pana nāsakkhiṃ. Tayo māse pana tīṇi divasāni viya yāva mahāpavāraṇā tāva jānissāmī”ti vassaṃ upagantvāpi gahetuṃ nāsakkhi. Pavāraṇādivase cintesi – “ahaṃ dvīhatīhena [V 2.0288] arahattaṃ gaṇhissāmīti āgato[M 2.0321], temāsenāpi nāsakkhiṃ, sabrahmacārino pana visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavārentī”ti. Tassevaṃ cintayato assudhārā pavattanti. Tato “na mañce mayhaṃ catūhi iriyāpathehi maggaphalaṃ uppajjissati, arahattaṃ appatvā neva mañce piṭṭhiṃ pasāressāmi, na pāde dhovissāmī”ti mañcaṃ ussāpetvā ṭhapesi. Puna antovassaṃ pattaṃ, arahattaṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhiyeva. Ekūnatiṃsapavāraṇāsu assudhārā pavattanti. Gāmadārakā therassa pādesu phālitaṭṭhānāni kaṇṭakehi sibbanti, davaṃ karontāpi “ayyassa mahāsīvattherassa viya pādā hontū”ti davaṃ karonti.

The elder, it is said, thought, "What is Arahantship to one such as I? I shall attain it within two or three days and return." Without informing his resident pupils, he departed on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon in the month of Āsāḷhī. Having gone to a mountain slope near a village and ascended a walking path, he was attending to his meditation subject, but on that day, he was unable to grasp Arahantship. When the Uposatha day arrived, he thought, "I came thinking I would grasp Arahantship in two or three days, but I have been unable to grasp it. Now, for the three months until the great Pavāraṇā, I will know it, treating this period like three days." Yet, even after entering the rains-residence, he was unable to grasp it. On the day of the Pavāraṇā, he reflected, "I came thinking I would grasp Arahantship in two or three days, but even after three months, I have been unable. My fellow practitioners, however, are performing the Pavāraṇā of purity." As he thought thus, streams of tears flowed. Then he resolved, "The path and fruit will not arise for me on a couch in any of the four postures. Until I attain Arahantship, I shall neither stretch my back on a couch nor wash my feet." He then set his couch upright. Again, the rains-residence was completed, but he was still unable to grasp Arahantship. For twenty-nine Pavāraṇās, streams of tears flowed. Village boys would stitch the cracked places on the elder's feet with thorns, and even while making sport, they would say in jest, "May your feet be like those of the venerable Mahāsīva."

Thero tiṃsasaṃvacchare mahāpavāraṇādivase ālambaṇaphalakaṃ nissāya ṭhito “idāni me tiṃsa vassāni samaṇadhammaṃ karontassa, nāsakkhiṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ, addhā me imasmiṃ attabhāve maggo vā phalaṃ vā natthi, na me laddhaṃ sabrahmacārīhi saddhiṃ visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāretu”nti cintesi. Tassevaṃ cintayatova domanassaṃ uppajji, assudhārā pavattanti. Atha avidūraṭṭhāne ekā devadhītā rodamānā aṭṭhāsi. “Ko ettha rodasī”ti? “Ahaṃ, bhante, devadhītā”ti. “Kasmā rodasī”ti? “Rodamānena maggaphalaṃ nibbattitaṃ, tena ahampi ekaṃ dve maggaphalāni nibbattessāmīti rodāmi, bhante”ti.

In the thirtieth year, on the day of the great Pavāraṇā, the elder stood leaning against a support board and thought, "It has now been thirty years that I have been practicing the duty of a recluse, yet I have been unable to attain Arahantship. Surely, for me in this existence, there is neither path nor fruit. I have not had the opportunity to perform the Pavāraṇā of purity with my fellow practitioners." As he was thinking thus, sorrow arose, and streams of tears flowed. Then, in a place not far off, a certain devadhītā stood weeping. He asked, "Who is weeping here?" "Venerable sir, I am a devadhītā." "Why do you weep?" "Venerable sir, since the path and fruit are produced by one who weeps, I too am weeping, thinking, 'I shall produce one or two paths and fruits.'"

Tato thero – “bho mahāsīvatthera, devatāpi tayā saddhiṃ keḷiṃ karonti, anucchavikaṃ nu kho te eta”nti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ aggahesi. So “idāni nipajjissāmī”ti senāsanaṃ paṭijaggitvā mañcakaṃ paññapetvā udakaṭṭhāne udakaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā “pāde dhovissāmī”ti sopānaphalake nisīdi.

Thereupon the elder, reflecting, "Venerable Mahāsīva, even deities make sport of you. Is this truly fitting for you?" developed his insight and grasped Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thinking, "Now I shall lie down," he tended to his lodging, prepared a small couch, made water ready at the water-place, and thinking, "I shall wash my feet," he sat down on the plank at the head of the stairs.

Antevāsikāpissa “amhākaṃ ācariyassa samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ gacchantassa tiṃsa vassāni, sakkhi nu kho visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ, nāsakkhī”ti āvajjayamānā “arahattaṃ patvā pādadhovanatthaṃ nisinno”ti disvā “amhākaṃ ācariyo amhādisesu antevāsikesu tiṭṭhantesu ‘attanāva pāde dhovissatī’ti aṭṭhānametaṃ, ahaṃ dhovissāmi ahaṃ dhovissāmī”ti tiṃsasahassānipi ākāsena gantvā vanditvā “pāde [P 3.0730] dhovissāma, bhante”ti [M 2.0322] āhaṃsu. Āvuso, idāni tiṃsa vassāni honti mama pādānaṃ adhotānaṃ, tiṭṭhatha, tumhe, ahameva dhovissāmīti.

His resident pupils, reflecting, "It has been thirty years since our teacher went to practice the duty of a recluse. Has he been able to produce a special attainment, or has he not?" and seeing that he had attained Arahantship and was seated for the purpose of washing his feet, thought, "While we, his resident pupils, are present, it is inappropriate that our teacher should wash his own feet. I will wash them! I will wash them!" Then, thirty thousand of them, having gone through the air and paid homage, said, "Venerable sir, we shall wash your feet." "Friends, it has now been thirty years that my feet have been unwashed. You stay put; I myself shall wash them."

Sakkopi āvajjanto – “mayhaṃ ayyo mahāsīvatthero arahattaṃ patto tiṃsasahassānaṃ antevāsikānaṃ ‘pāde dhovissāmā’ti āgatānaṃ pāde dhovituṃ na deti. Mādise pana upaṭṭhāke tiṭṭhante [V 2.0289] ‘mayhaṃ ayyo sayaṃ pāde dhovissatī’ti aṭṭhānametaṃ, ahaṃ dhovissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā sujātāya deviyā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa santike pāturahosi. So sujaṃ asurakaññaṃ purato katvā “apetha, bhante, mātugāmo”ti okāsaṃ kāretvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā purato ukkuṭiko nisīditvā “pāde dhovissāmi, bhante”ti āha. Kosiya, idāni me tiṃsa vassāni pādānaṃ adhotānaṃ, devatānañca pakatiyāpi manussasarīragandho nāma jeguccho, yojanasate ṭhitānampi kaṇṭhe āsattakuṇapaṃ viya hoti, ahameva dhovissāmīti. Bhante, ayaṃ gandho nāma na paññāyati, tumhākaṃ pana sīlagandho cha devaloke atikkamitvā upari bhavaggaṃ patvā ṭhito. Sīlagandhato añño uttaritaro gandho nāma natthi, bhante, tumhākaṃ sīlagandhenamhi āgatoti vāmahatthena gopphakasandhiyaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇahatthena pādatalaṃ parimajji. Daharakumārasseva pādā ahesuṃ. Sakko pāde dhovitvā vanditvā devalokameva gato.

Sakka also, reflecting, "My venerable Mahāsīva has attained Arahantship. He does not permit the thirty thousand resident pupils who have come saying, 'We shall wash your feet,' to do so. But while an attendant such as I is present, it is inappropriate that my venerable one should wash his own feet. I shall wash them," made a resolution. Together with the devī Sujātā, he appeared in the presence of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Placing the Asura maiden Sujā before him and saying, "Step aside, venerable sirs, it is a woman," he had a space made. Approaching the elder and paying homage, he sat down before him in a squatting posture and said, "Venerable sir, I shall wash your feet." "Kosiya, it has now been thirty years that my feet have been unwashed. And for devas, the scent of a human body is by nature repulsive; even to those standing a hundred yojanas away, it is like a corpse stuck in the throat. I myself shall wash them." "Venerable sir, this scent is not perceived. Your fragrance of virtue, however, having surpassed the six deva worlds, has reached the peak of existence above. There is no other fragrance more excellent than the fragrance of virtue, venerable sir. It is because of your fragrance of virtue that I have come." Taking hold of the ankle joint with his left hand, he stroked the sole of the foot with his right hand. The elder's feet became like those of a young boy. Sakka, having washed the feet and paid homage, went back to the deva world.

Evaṃ “na labhāmi sabrahmacārīhi saddhiṃ visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāretu”nti āvajjantassa uppannaṃ domanassaṃ nissāya bhikkhuno maññanavasena vipassanāya ārammaṇampi vipassanāpi maggopi phalampi savitakkasavicāradomanassanti ca avitakkāvicāradomanassanti ca vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be understood that for a bhikkhu reflecting, 'I am not able to perform the Pavāraṇā of purity with my fellow practitioners,' the object of insight, insight itself, the path, and the fruit—relying on the sorrow that arose by way of his conceiving—are spoken of as 'sorrow with initial and sustained thought' and 'sorrow without initial and sustained thought'.

Tattha eko bhikkhu savitakkasavicāradomanasse vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā idaṃ domanassaṃ kiṃ nissitanti upadhārento vatthunissitanti pajānātīti phassapañcamake vuttanayeneva anukkamena arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Eko avitakkāvicāre domanasse vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā vuttanayeneva arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Tattha abhiniviṭṭhadomanassesupi savitakkasavicārato avitakkaavicāraṃ paṇītataraṃ. Savitakkasavicāradomanassavipassanātopi avitakkāvicāradomanassavipassanā [P 3.0731] paṇītatarā. Savitakkasavicāradomanassaphalasamāpattitopi avitakkāvicāradomanassaphalasamāpattiyeva paṇītatarā[M 2.0323]. Tenāha bhagavā – “ye avitakkaavicāre te paṇītatare”ti.

Therein, one bhikkhu establishes insight into displeasure with initial and sustained application. Reflecting, 'Upon what is this displeasure dependent?', he understands that it is dependent on a physical basis. Thus, in the manner stated regarding the fivefold group with contact, he is gradually established in Arahantship. Another bhikkhu establishes insight into displeasure without initial and sustained application and is established in Arahantship in the same way. Therein, even among firmly held displeasures, that without initial and sustained application is more sublime than that with initial and sustained application. Insight into displeasure without initial and sustained application is more sublime than insight into displeasure with initial and sustained application. The fruition attainment related to displeasure without initial and sustained application is indeed more sublime than the fruition attainment related to displeasure with initial and sustained application. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Those without initial and sustained application are more sublime.'

362. Evarūpā upekkhā na sevitabbāti evarūpā gehasitaupekkhā na sevitabbā. Gehasitaupekkhā nāma “tattha katamā cha gehasitaupekkhā. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjati upekkhā bālassa mūḷhassa puthujjanassa anodhijinassa avipākajinassa anādīnavadassāvino assutavato puthujjanassa, yā evarūpā upekkhā, rūpaṃ sā nātivattati, tasmā sā upekkhā gehasitāti vuccatī”ti evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate guḷapiṇḍike nilīnamakkhikā [V 2.0290] viya rūpādīni anativattamānā tattheva laggā laggitā hutvā uppannā kāmaguṇanissitā upekkhā na sevitabbā.

362. When it is said, 'Such equanimity should not be cultivated,' it means such household-based equanimity should not be cultivated. What is household-based equanimity? 'Herein, what are the six kinds of household-based equanimity? When a foolish, deluded ordinary person—one who has not conquered the boundaries, who has not conquered the results, who does not see the danger, an unlearned ordinary person—sees a form with the eye, equanimity arises. Such equanimity does not transcend the form; therefore, that equanimity is called 'household-based'.' In this way, when agreeable objects come into range at the six sense doors, like a fly settled on a lump of molasses, the equanimity that arises dependent on sensual pleasures—not transcending forms and so on, but stuck right there, clinging and attached—should not be cultivated.

Evarūpā upekkhā sevitabbāti evarūpā nekkhammasitā upekkhā sevitabbā. Nekkhammasitā upekkhā nāma – “tattha katamā cha nekkhammasitā upekkhā? Rūpānaṃ tveva aniccataṃ viditvā vipariṇāmavirāganirodhaṃ ‘pubbe ceva rūpā etarahi ca, sabbe te rūpā aniccā, dukkhā, vipariṇāmadhammā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato uppajjati upekkhā, yā evarūpā upekkhā, rūpaṃ sā ativattati, tasmā sā upekkhā nekkhammasitāti vuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.308). Evaṃ chasu dvāresu iṭṭhāniṭṭhaārammaṇe āpāthagate iṭṭhe arajjantassa, aniṭṭhe adussantassa, asamapekkhanena asammuyhantassa uppannā vipassanā ñāṇasampayuttā upekkhā. Apica vedanāsabhāgā tatra majjhattupekkhāpi ettha upekkhāva. Tasmā sevitabbāti ayaṃ nekkhammavasena vipassanāvasena anussatiṭṭhānavasena paṭhamadutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānavasena ca uppajjanakaupekkhā sevitabbā nāma.

'Such equanimity should be cultivated' means that such renunciation-based equanimity should be cultivated. Renunciation-based equanimity is defined as: 'Herein, what are the six kinds of renunciation-based equanimity? Having known the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation, equanimity arises in one who sees this with right wisdom as it really is: "Forms both previously and now—all those forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change." Such equanimity transcends form; therefore, that equanimity is called 'renunciation-based'.' Thus, when agreeable and disagreeable objects come into range at the six sense doors, it is the equanimity associated with insight-knowledge that arises in one who is not attached to the agreeable, not repulsed by the disagreeable, and not deluded through improper seeing. Moreover, the equanimity of specific neutrality, which is of the same nature as feeling, is also included as equanimity here. Therefore, 'should be cultivated' refers to this equanimity that arises by way of renunciation, by way of insight, by way of the foundations of recollection, and by way of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas; this is called 'equanimity to be cultivated'.

Ettha yaṃ ce savitakkaṃ savicāranti tāyapi nekkhammasitaupekkhāya yaṃ nekkhammavasena vipassanāvasena anussatiṭṭhānavasena paṭhamajjhānavasena ca uppannaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ upekkhanti jāneyya. Yaṃ ce avitakkaṃ avicāranti yaṃ pana dutiyajjhānādivasena uppannaṃ avitakkāvicāraṃ upekkhanti jāneyya. Ye [P 3.0732] avitakke avicāre te paṇītatareti etāsu dvīsu yā avitakkaavicārā, sā paṇītatarāti attho. Iminā kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti[M 2.0324]? Dvinnaṃ arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Eko hi bhikkhu savitakkasavicāraupekkhāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ayaṃ upekkhā kiṃ nissitāti upadhārento vatthunissitāti pajānātīti phassapañcamake vuttanayeneva anukkamena arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Eko avitakkāvicārāya upekkhāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā vuttanayeneva arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Tattha abhiniviṭṭhaupekkhāsupi savitakkasavicārato avitakkāvicārā paṇītatarā. Savitakkasavicāraupekkhāvipassanātopi avitakkāvicāraupekkhāvipassanāpaṇītatarā. Savitakkasavicāraupekkhāphalasamāpattitopi avitakkāvicārupekkhāphalasamāpattiyeva paṇītatarā. Tenāha bhagavā “ye avitakke avicāre te paṇītatare”ti.

Herein, regarding 'that which is with initial and sustained application': of that renunciation-based equanimity, one should know that which has arisen by way of renunciation, by way of insight, by way of the foundations of recollection, and by way of the first jhāna, as 'equanimity with initial and sustained application'. And regarding 'that which is without initial and sustained application': one should know that which has arisen by way of the second jhāna and so on as 'equanimity without initial and sustained application'. 'Those without initial and sustained application are more sublime' means that between these two, that which is without initial and sustained application is more sublime. What is taught by this? The Arahantship of two bhikkhus is taught. For one bhikkhu, having established insight upon equanimity with initial and sustained application and reflecting, 'Upon what does this equanimity depend?', understands that it is dependent on a physical basis. Thus, in the manner stated regarding the fivefold group with contact, he is gradually established in Arahantship. Another bhikkhu, having established insight upon equanimity without initial and sustained application, is established in Arahantship in the same way. Therein, even among the equanimities one is devoted to, that without initial and sustained application is more sublime than that with initial and sustained application. Insight upon equanimity without initial and sustained application is more sublime than insight upon equanimity with initial and sustained application. The fruition attainment of equanimity without initial and sustained application is indeed more sublime than the fruition attainment of equanimity with initial and sustained application. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Those that are without initial and sustained application are more sublime.'

363. Evaṃ paṭipanno kho, devānaminda, bhikkhu papañcasaññāsaṅkhānirodhasāruppagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hotīti bhagavā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Sakko pana sotāpattiphalaṃ [V 2.0291] patto. Buddhānañhi ajjhāsayo hīno na hoti, ukkaṭṭhova hoti. Ekassapi bahūnampi dhammaṃ desentā arahatteneva kūṭaṃ gaṇhanti. Sattā pana attano anurūpe upanissaye ṭhitā keci sotāpannā honti, keci sakadāgāmī, keci anāgāmī, keci arahanto. Rājā viya hi bhagavā, rājakumārā viya veneyyā. Yathā hi rājā bhojanakāle attano pamāṇena piṇḍaṃ uddharitvā rājakumārānaṃ upaneti, te tato attano mukhappamāṇeneva kabaḷaṃ karonti, evaṃ bhagavā attajjhāsayānurūpāya desanāya arahatteneva kūṭaṃ gaṇhāti. Veneyyā attano upanissayappamāṇena tato sotāpattiphalamattaṃ vā sakadāgāmianāgāmiarahattaphalameva vā gaṇhanti. Sakko pana sotāpanno jāto. Sotāpanno ca hutvā bhagavato puratoyeva cavitvā taruṇasakko hutvā nibbatti, devatānañhi cavamānānaṃ attabhāvassa gatāgataṭṭhānaṃ nāma na paññāyati, dīpasikhāgamanaṃ viya hoti. Tasmā sesadevatā na jāniṃsu. Sakko pana sayaṃ cutattā bhagavā ca appaṭihatañāṇattā dveva janā jāniṃsu. Atha sakko cintesi [P 3.0733] “mayhañhi bhagavatā tīsu ṭhānesu nibbattitaphalameva kathitaṃ, ayañca pana maggo vā phalaṃ vā sakuṇikāya viya uppatitvā gahetuṃ na sakkā, āgamanīyapubbabhāgapaṭipadāya assa bhavitabbaṃ. Handāhaṃ upari khīṇāsavassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ pucchāmī”ti.

363. Thus, O Sakka, lord of devas, a bhikkhu who practices in this way is practicing the path suitable for the cessation of the classifications of perception and proliferation.' The Blessed One concluded the discourse with Arahantship as its pinnacle. Sakka, however, attained the fruit of stream-entry. For the disposition of the Buddhas is never inferior, but always supreme. Whether teaching the Dhamma to one or to many, they take Arahantship as the pinnacle. Beings, however, established in their own corresponding supporting conditions, some become stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some Arahants. For the Blessed One is like a king, and those to be trained are like princes. Just as a king at mealtime, having taken a portion according to his own measure, presents it to the princes, and they then take a mouthful from it according to the size of their own mouths, so too the Blessed One, with a teaching corresponding to his own disposition, takes Arahantship as the pinnacle. Those to be trained, according to the measure of their own supporting conditions, take from that teaching just the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, or even the fruit of Arahantship itself. Now, Sakka became a stream-enterer. And having become a stream-enterer, he passed away right there in the presence of the Blessed One and was reborn as the young Sakka. For when devas pass away, the place of their existence's coming and going is not discernible; it is like the going of a lamp's flame. Therefore, the other devas did not know. But Sakka himself, because he had passed away, and the Blessed One, because of his unobstructed knowledge—only these two persons knew. Then Sakka thought: 'The Blessed One has spoken to me only of the fruit that is brought about in three instances; but this path or fruit cannot be grasped by flying up like a bird. There must be a preliminary practice for its attainment. Come now, I will ask further about the preliminary practice of one whose taints are destroyed.'

Pātimokkhasaṃvaravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Pātimokkha Restraint

364. Tato [M 2.0325] taṃ pucchanto kathaṃ paṭipanno pana, mārisātiādimāha. Tattha pātimokkhasaṃvarāyāti uttamajeṭṭhakasīlasaṃvarāya. Kāyasamācārampītiādi sevitabbakāyasamācārādivasena pātimokkhasaṃvaradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlakathā ca nāmesā kammapathavasena vā paṇṇattivasena vā kathetabbā hoti.

364. Then, wishing to ask that, he said, 'But how, venerable sir, does one practice?' and so on. Therein, 'for the Pātimokkha restraint' means for the supreme and foremost restraint of virtue. 'Bodily conduct' and so on are stated to show the Pātimokkha restraint by way of such things as bodily conduct that should be cultivated. And this discourse on virtue should be given either in terms of the paths of action or in terms of the designations.

Tattha kammapathavasena kathentena asevitabbakāyasamācāro tāva pāṇātipātaadinnādānamicchācārehi kathetabbo. Paṇṇattivasena kathentena kāyadvāre paññattasikkhāpadavītikkamavasena kathetabbo. Sevitabbakāyasamācāro pāṇātipātādiveramaṇīhi ceva kāyadvāre paññattasikkhāpadaavītikkamena ca kathetabbo. Asevitabbavacīsamācāro musāvādādivacīduccaritena ceva vacīdvāre paññattasikkhāpadavītikkamena ca kathetabbo. Sevitabbavacīsamācāro musāvādādiveramaṇīhi ceva vacīdvāre paññattasikkhāpadaavītikkamena ca kathetabbo.

Therein, when speaking in terms of the paths of action, bodily conduct that should not be cultivated should first be discussed in terms of killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. When speaking in terms of designation, it should be discussed in terms of the transgression of the training precepts designated at the body-door. Bodily conduct that should be cultivated should be discussed both in terms of abstaining from killing and so on, and through non-transgression of the training precepts designated at the body-door. Verbal conduct that should not be cultivated should be discussed both in terms of verbal misconduct such as false speech and so on, and through transgression of the training precepts designated at the speech-door. Verbal conduct that should be cultivated should be discussed both in terms of abstaining from false speech and so on, and through non-transgression of the training precepts designated at the speech-door.

Pariyesanā [V 2.0292] pana kāyavācāhi pariyesanāyeva. Sā kāyavacīsamācāragahaṇena gahitāpi samānā yasmā ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlaṃ nāma etasmiññeva dvāradvaye uppajjati, na ākāse, tasmā ājīvaṭṭhamakasīladassanatthaṃ visuṃ vuttā. Tattha nasevitabbapariyesanā anariyapariyesanāya kathetabbā. Sevitabbapariyesanā ariyapariyesanāya. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Now, the search is a search by means of body and speech. Although it is included by the undertaking of bodily and verbal conduct, because the virtue that has livelihood as its eighth component arises only in this pair of doors, and not in the sky, it is therefore stated separately to show this virtue with livelihood as its eighth component. Therein, the search that should not be cultivated should be explained as the ignoble search. The search that should be cultivated should be explained as the noble search. For this was stated:

“Dvemā, bhikkhave, pariyesanā anariyā ca pariyesanā, ariyā ca pariyesanā. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, anariyā pariyesanā? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhammaṃyeva pariyesati, attanā jarādhammo, byādhidhammo, maraṇadhammo, sokadhammo, saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

'Monks, there are these two searches: the ignoble search and the noble search. And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, a certain person, being himself subject to birth, seeks what is also subject to birth; being himself subject to aging, to illness, to death, to sorrow, to defilement, he seeks what is also subject to defilement.

Kiñca, bhikkhave, jātidhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave[P 3.0734], jātidhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ jātidhammaṃ ajeḷakaṃ jātidhammaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ jātidhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ jātidhammaṃ, jātarūparajataṃ jātidhammaṃ. Jātidhammā [M 2.0326] hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo, etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you call subject to birth? Children and wives, monks, are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; chickens and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to birth. Being greedy, infatuated, and engrossed in these, one who is himself subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth.

Kiñca, bhikkhave, jarādhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, jarādhammaṃ…pe… jarādhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you call subject to aging? Children and wives, monks, are subject to aging...pe... one seeks only what is subject to aging.

Kiñca, bhikkhave, byādhidhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, byādhidhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ byādhidhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ byādhidhammaṃ. Byādhidhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo, etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā byādhidhammo samāno byādhidhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you call subject to illness? Children and wives, monks, are subject to illness; male and female slaves are subject to illness; goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to illness. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to illness. Being greedy, infatuated, and engrossed in these, one who is himself subject to illness seeks only what is subject to illness.

Kiñca, bhikkhave, maraṇadhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, maraṇadhammaṃ…pe… maraṇadhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you call subject to death? Children and wives, monks, are subject to death...pe... one seeks only what is subject to death.

Kiñca, bhikkhave, sokadhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ…pe… sokadhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you call subject to sorrow? Children and wives...pe... one seeks only what is subject to sorrow.

Kiñca, bhikkhave, saṃkilesadhammaṃ vadetha…pe… jātarūparajataṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃ. Saṃkilesadhammā[V 2.0293], hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo, etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva pariyesati. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, anariyā pariyesanāti (ma. ni. 1.274).

And what, monks, do you say is a thing subject to defilement? … Gold and silver are things subject to defilement. These acquisitions, monks, are things subject to defilement. Being tied to, infatuated with, and attached to them, one who is himself subject to defilement seeks that which is subject to defilement. This, monks, is the ignoble search.

Apica kuhanādivasena pañcavidhā, agocaravasena chabbidhā vejjakammādivasena ekavīsatividhā, evaṃ pavattā sabbāpi anesanā anariyapariyesanāyevāti veditabbā.

Moreover, all such wrong seeking—whether fivefold by way of deceit and the like, sixfold by way of improper haunts, or twenty-onefold by way of medical practices and the like—should be understood as the ignoble search.

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, ariyā pariyesanā? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajātaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati, attanā jarādhammo, byādhi, maraṇa, soka, saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ [M 2.0327] yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati. Ayaṃ ariyā pariyesanāti (ma. ni. 1.275).

And what, monks, is the noble search? Here, monks, someone, being himself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna. Being himself subject to aging… sickness… death… sorrow… being himself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, he seeks the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna. This is the noble search.

Apica pañca kuhanādīni cha agocare ekavīsatividhañca anesanaṃ vajjetvā bhikkhācariyāya dhammena samena pariyesanāpi ariyapariyesanāyevāti veditabbā.

Moreover, having avoided the five kinds of deceit and so forth, the six improper resorts, and the twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood, seeking by means of the alms-round, in accordance with the Dhamma and equitably, should also be understood as the noble search.

Ettha ca yo yo [P 3.0735] “na sevitabbo”ti vutto, so so pubbabhāge pāṇātipātādīnaṃ sambhārapariyesanāpayogakaraṇagamanakālato paṭṭhāya na sevitabbova. Itaro ādito paṭṭhāya sevitabbo, asakkontena cittampi uppādetabbaṃ. Apica saṅghabhedādīnaṃ atthāya parakkamantānaṃ devadattādīnaṃ viya kāyasamācāro na sevitabbo, divasassa dvattikkhattuṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ upaṭṭhānagamanādivasena pavatto dhammasenāpatimahāmoggallānattherādīnaṃ viya kāyasamācāro sevitabbo. Dhanuggahapesanādivasena vācaṃ bhindantānaṃ devadattādīnaṃ viya vacīsamācāro na sevitabbo, tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇakittanādivasena pavatto dhammasenāpatimahāmoggallānattherādīnaṃ viya vacīsamācāro sevitabbo. Anariyapariyesanaṃ pariyesantānaṃ devadattādīnaṃ viya pariyesanā na sevitabbā, ariyapariyesanameva pariyesantānaṃ dhammasenāpatimahāmoggallānattherādīnaṃ viya pariyesanā sevitabbā.

Herein, whatever is said to be 'not to be cultivated' should not be cultivated from the preliminary stage, starting from the time of going, making the effort, and searching for the means for killing living beings and so forth. The other kind should be cultivated from the outset; and if one is unable, even the thought should be aroused. Furthermore, bodily conduct like that of Devadatta and others, who strive for the purpose of creating a schism in the Sangha and so forth, should not be cultivated. Bodily conduct like that of the General of the Dhamma Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and others, which consists of going to attend upon the Three Jewels two or three times a day, should be cultivated. Verbal conduct like that of Devadatta and others, who uttered speech by way of dispatching archers and so forth, should not be cultivated. Verbal conduct like that of the General of the Dhamma Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and others, which consists of extolling the virtues of the Three Jewels, should be cultivated. Seeking like that of Devadatta and others, who engaged in the ignoble search, should not be cultivated. Seeking like that of the General of the Dhamma Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and others, who engaged only in the noble search, should be cultivated.

Evaṃ paṭipanno khoti evaṃ asevitabbaṃ kāyavacīsamācāraṃ pariyesanañca pahāya sevitabbānaṃ pāripūriyā paṭipanno, devānaminda, bhikkhu pātimokkhasaṃvarāya uttamajeṭṭhakasīlasaṃvaratthāya [V 2.0294] paṭipanno nāma hotīti bhagavā khīṇāsavassa āgamanīyapubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ kathesi.

Indeed, Devānaminda, a monk who practices thus—abandoning such bodily and verbal conduct and seeking as should not be pursued, and practicing for the fulfillment of such as should be pursued—is said to be practicing for the restraint of the Pātimokkha, for the purpose of the highest and foremost restraint of virtue. Thus, the Blessed One taught the preliminary practice that leads to one whose taints are destroyed.

Indriyasaṃvaravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Restraint of the Faculties

365. Dutiyapucchāyaṃ indriyasaṃvarāyāti indriyānaṃ pidhānāya, guttadvāratāya saṃvutadvāratāyāti attho. Vissajjane panassa cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpampītiādi sevitabbarūpādivasena indriyasaṃvaradassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha evaṃ vutteti heṭṭhā somanassādipañhāvissajjanānaṃ sutattā imināpi evarūpena bhavitabbanti sañjātapaṭibhāno bhagavatā evaṃ vutte sakko devānamindo [M 2.0328] bhagavantaṃ etadavoca, etaṃ imassa kho ahaṃ, bhanteti ādikaṃ vacanaṃ avoca. Bhagavāpissa okāsaṃ datvā tuṇhī ahosi. Kathetukāmopi hi yo atthaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkoti, atthaṃ sampādetuṃ sakkonto vā na kathetukāmo hoti, na tassa bhagavā okāsaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ pana yasmā kathetukāmo ceva, sakkoti ca atthaṃ sampādetuṃ tenassa bhagavā okāsamakāsi.

365. In the second question, 'for the restraint of the faculties' means for the closing of the faculties, for having guarded doors, for being with restrained doors—this is the meaning. In the reply, the passage beginning 'forms cognizable by the eye' was stated for the purpose of showing the restraint of the faculties by way of forms and so forth that should be cultivated. Here, when this was said—because the answers to the previous questions about joy and so forth had been heard, his ready wit arose that this too should be of such a nature. When the Blessed One spoke thus, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One, the words beginning, 'Venerable sir, of this…' And the Blessed One, having given him an opportunity, remained silent. For if one wishes to speak but cannot accomplish the meaning, or can accomplish the meaning but does not wish to speak, the Blessed One does not grant an opportunity to such a one. But since this one both wished to speak and was able to accomplish the meaning, the Blessed One granted him an opportunity.

Tattha evarūpaṃ na sevitabbanti ādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepo – yaṃ [P 3.0736] rūpaṃ passato rāgādayo uppajjanti, taṃ na sevitabbaṃ na daṭṭhabbaṃ na oloketabbanti attho. Yaṃ pana passato asubhasaññā vā saṇṭhāti, pasādo vā uppajjati, aniccasaññāpaṭilābho vā hoti, taṃ sevitabbaṃ.

Therein, in the passages beginning 'such a form should not be cultivated,' this is the summary: whatever form, when seen, gives rise to lust and so forth, that should not be cultivated, not looked at, not gazed upon—this is the meaning. But whatever form, when seen, establishes the perception of unattractiveness, or gives rise to serenity, or results in the gaining of the perception of impermanence, that should be cultivated.

Yaṃ cittakkharaṃ cittabyañjanampi saddaṃ suṇato rāgādayo uppajjanti, evarūpo saddo na sevitabbo. Yaṃ pana atthanissitaṃ dhammanissitaṃ kumbhadāsigītampi suṇantassa pasādo vā uppajjati, nibbidā vā saṇṭhāti, evarūpo saddo sevitabbo.

Whatever sound, elaborate in its syllables and expressions, when heard, gives rise to lust and so forth, such a sound should not be cultivated. But whatever sound is based on the meaning and based on the Dhamma—even the song of a potter’s maid—when heard, gives rise to serenity or establishes disenchantment, such a sound should be cultivated.

Yaṃ gandhaṃ ghāyato rāgādayo uppajjanti, evarūpo gandho na sevitabbo. Yaṃ pana gandhaṃ ghāyato asubhasaññādipaṭilābho hoti, evarūpo gandho sevitabbo.

Whatever scent, when smelled, gives rise to lust and so forth, such a scent should not be cultivated. But whatever scent, when smelled, leads to the attainment of the perception of foulness and the like, such a scent should be cultivated.

Yaṃ rasaṃ sāyato rāgādayo uppajjanti, evarūpo raso na sevitabbo. Yaṃ pana rasaṃ sāyato āhāre paṭikūlasaññā ceva uppajjati, sāyitapaccayā ca kāyabalaṃ nissāya ariyabhūmiṃ [V 2.0295] okkamituṃ sakkoti, mahāsīvattherabhāgineyyasīvasāmaṇerassa viya paribhuñjantasseva kilesakkhayo vā hoti, evarūpo raso sevitabbo.

Whatever taste, when savored, gives rise to lust and so forth, such a taste should not be cultivated. But whatever taste, when savored, gives rise to the perception of repulsiveness in food, and by relying on the bodily strength gained from having eaten, one is able to enter the noble plane; or, like the novice Sīva, the nephew of the Elder Mahāsīva, the destruction of the taints occurs even while one is consuming—such a taste should be cultivated.

Yaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusato rāgādayo uppajjanti, evarūpaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ na sevitabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana phusato sāriputtattherādīnaṃ viya āsavakkhayo ceva, vīriyañca supaggahitaṃ, pacchimā ca janatā diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpādanena anuggahitā hoti, evarūpaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Sāriputtatthero kira tiṃsa vassāni mañce piṭṭhiṃ na pasāresi. Tathā mahāmoggallānatthero. Mahākassapatthero vīsavassasataṃ mañce piṭṭhiṃ na pasāresi. Anuruddhatthero paññāsa vassāni. Bhaddiyatthero tiṃsa vassāni. Soṇatthero aṭṭhārasa [M 2.0329] vassāni. Raṭṭhapālatthero dvādasa. Ānandatthero pannarasa. Rāhulatthero dvādasa. Bākulatthero asīti vassāni. Nāḷakatthero yāvaparinibbānā mañce piṭṭhiṃ na pasāresīti.

Whatever tangible object, when touched, gives rise to lust and other defilements—such a tangible object should not be cultivated. But whatever tangible object, when touched, leads to the destruction of the taints—as in the case of the Elder Sāriputta and others—and strengthens effort, and later generations are helped by following their example—such a tangible object should be cultivated. It is said that the Elder Sāriputta did not stretch out his back on a bed for thirty years. Likewise, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. The Elder Mahākassapa did not stretch out his back on a bed for one hundred and twenty years. The Elder Anuruddha for fifty years. The Elder Bhaddiya for thirty years. The Elder Soṇa for eighteen years. The Elder Raṭṭhapāla for twelve. The Elder Ānanda for fifteen. The Elder Rāhula for twelve. The Elder Bākula for eighty years. The Elder Nāḷaka did not stretch out his back on a bed until his final attainment of Nibbāna.

Ye manoviññeyye dhamme samannāharantassa rāgādayo uppajjanti, “aho, vata yaṃ paresaṃ paravittūpakaraṇaṃ taṃ mamassā”tiādinā nayena vā abhijjhādīni āpāthamāgacchanti evarūpā dhammā na sevitabbā. “Sabbe sattā averā hontū”ti evaṃ mettādivasena, ye vā pana tiṇṇaṃ therānaṃ dhammā, evarūpā sevitabbā. Tayo kira therā vassūpanāyikadivase kāmavitakkādayo [P 3.0737] akusalavitakkā na vitakketabbāti katikaṃ akaṃsu. Atha pavāraṇadivase saṅghatthero saṅghanavakaṃ pucchi – “āvuso, imasmiṃ temāse kittake ṭhāne cittassa dhāvituṃ dinna”nti? Na, bhante, pariveṇaparicchedato bahi dhāvituṃ adāsinti. Dutiyaṃ pucchi – “tava āvuso”ti? Nivāsagehato, bhante, bahi dhāvituṃ na adāsinti. Atha dvepi theraṃ pucchiṃsu “tumhākaṃ pana, bhante”ti? Niyakajjhattakhandhapañcakato, āvuso, bahi dhāvituṃ na adāsinti. Tumhehi, bhante, dukkaraṃ katanti. Evarūpo manoviññeyyo dhammo sevitabbo.

Whatever mind-cognizable phenomena, when attended to, give rise to lust and other defilements—such as, "Oh, if only what belongs to others, the wealth and implements of others, were mine!"—or when covetousness and the like arise—such phenomena should not be cultivated. But thoughts like, "May all beings be free from enmity!"—cultivated through loving-kindness and the like—or the qualities of the three elders—such phenomena should be cultivated. It is said that three elders made a resolution on the day of entering the rains retreat not to entertain unwholesome thoughts such as sensual thoughts. Then, on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the senior elder of the Sangha asked the junior elder, "Friend, during these three months, how far was the mind allowed to wander?" "Venerable sir, it was not allowed to wander beyond the boundaries of the monastery." He asked the second elder, "And you, friend?" "Venerable sir, it was not allowed to wander beyond my dwelling." Then both of them asked the senior elder, "And you, venerable sir?" "Friends, it was not allowed to wander beyond the five aggregates of my own person." "Venerable sir, you have done what is difficult." Such a mind-cognizable phenomenon should be cultivated.

366. Ekantavādāti ekoyeva anto vādassa etesaṃ, na dvedhā gatavādāti ekantavādā, ekaññeva vadantīti pucchati. Ekantasīlāti ekācārā. Ekantachandāti ekaladdhikā. Ekantaajjhosānāti ekantapariyosānā.

366. Regarding 'ekantavādā': For these, there is only one side to their doctrine; their doctrine does not go in two ways, hence they are 'ekantavādā'. He asks, 'Do they speak only one thing?' Regarding 'ekantasīlā': this means those of singular conduct. Regarding 'ekantachandā': this means those of a singular view. Regarding 'ekantaajjhosānā': this means those of a singular finality.

Anekadhātu nānādhātu kho, devānaminda, lokoti devānaminda, ayaṃ loko anekajjhāsayo nānajjhāsayo. Ekasmiṃ gantukāme eko ṭhātukāmo hoti. Ekasmiṃ ṭhātukāme eko sayitukāmo hoti. Dve sattā ekajjhāsayā nāma dullabhā. Tasmiṃ anekadhātunānādhātusmiṃ [V 2.0296] loke yaṃ yadeva dhātuṃ yaṃ yadeva ajjhāsayaṃ sattā abhinivisanti gaṇhanti, taṃ tadeva. Thāmasā parāmāsāti thāmena ca parāmāsena ca. Abhinivissa voharantīti suṭṭhu gaṇhitvā voharanti, kathenti dīpenti kittenti. Idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti idaṃ amhākameva vacanaṃ saccaṃ, aññesaṃ vacanaṃ moghaṃ tucchaṃ niratthakanti.

Regarding the phrase, 'Indeed, O lord of the devas, the world is of many elements, of diverse elements': this means, O lord of the devas, that this world is of many inclinations, of diverse inclinations. When one desires to go, another desires to stand. When one desires to stand, another desires to lie down. Two beings with the same inclination are indeed rare. In this world of many and diverse elements, whatever element, whatever inclination beings adhere to and grasp, that very thing they hold to. The phrase 'by force and by misapprehension' means by strength and by wrongful grasping. 'They declare, having firmly adhered' means having grasped firmly, they declare, speak, explain, and proclaim. 'This alone is true, all else is false' means: 'This word of ours alone is true; the word of others is vain, empty, and worthless.'

Accantaniṭṭhāti [M 2.0330] anto vuccati vināso, antaṃ atītā niṭṭhā etesanti accantaniṭṭhā. Yā etesaṃ niṭṭhā, yo paramassāso nibbānaṃ, taṃ sabbesaṃ vināsātikkantaṃ niccanti vuccati. Yogakkhemoti nibbānasseva nāmaṃ, accanto yogakkhemo etesanti accantayogakkhemī. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmaṃ ariyamaggaṃ carantīti brahmacārī. Accantatthāya brahmacārī accantabrahmacārī. Pariyosānantipi nibbānassa nāmaṃ. Accantaṃ pariyosānaṃ etesanti accantapariyosānā.

Regarding 'accantaniṭṭhā': 'Anta' (end) is here called destruction. Those whose consummation has gone beyond that end are 'accantaniṭṭhā'. That consummation of theirs, which is the supreme solace, Nibbāna, is said to be eternal, having transcended all destruction. 'Yogakkhema' is a name for Nibbāna itself; 'accantayogakkhemī' are those for whom there is the ultimate security from bondage. Because they practice the supreme life, the Noble Path, in the sense of what is highest, they are 'brahmacārī'. An 'accantabrahmacārī' is one who lives the holy life for the sake of the ultimate. 'Pariyosāna' is also a name for Nibbāna. 'Accantapariyosānā' are those for whom there is an ultimate conclusion.

Taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttāti [P 3.0738] taṇhāsaṅkhayoti maggopi nibbānampi. Maggo taṇhaṃ saṅkhiṇāti vināsetīti taṇhāsaṅkhayo. Nibbānaṃ yasmā taṃ āgamma taṇhā saṅkhiyati vinassati, tasmā taṇhāsaṅkhayo. Taṇhāsaṅkhayena maggena vimuttā, taṇhāsaṅkhaye nibbāne vimuttā adhimuttāti taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā.

Regarding 'taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā': 'Taṇhāsaṅkhayo' (the destruction of craving) refers to both the path and Nibbāna. The path wears down and destroys craving, hence it is called 'taṇhāsaṅkhayo'. Nibbāna is called 'taṇhāsaṅkhayo' because, on reaching it, craving is worn down and destroyed. Those liberated by the path that is the destruction of craving, or those liberated and resolved upon Nibbāna which is the destruction of craving, are called 'taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā'.

Ettāvatā ca bhagavatā cuddasapi mahāpañhā byākatā honti. Cuddasa mahāpañhā nāma issāmacchariyaṃ eko pañho, piyāppiyaṃ eko, chando eko, vitakko eko, papañco eko, somanassaṃ eko, domanassaṃ eko, upekkhā eko, kāyasamācāro eko, vacīsamācāro eko, pariyesanā eko, indriyasaṃvaro eko, anekadhātu eko, accantaniṭṭhā ekoti.

And with this much, the Blessed One has explained the fourteen great questions. The fourteen great questions are: envy and stinginess as one question, what is liked and disliked as one, desire as one, thought as one, proliferation as one, mental pleasure as one, mental pain as one, equanimity as one, bodily conduct as one, verbal conduct as one, seeking as one, sense restraint as one, the manifold elements as one, and ultimate consummation as one.

367. Ejāti calanaṭṭhena taṇhā vuccati. Sā pīḷanaṭṭhena rogo, anto padussanaṭṭhena gaṇḍo, anuppaviṭṭhaṭṭhena sallaṃ. Tasmā ayaṃ purisoti yasmā ejā attanā katakammānurūpena purisaṃ tattha tattha abhinibbattatthāya kaḍḍhati, tasmā ayaṃ puriso tesaṃ tesaṃ bhavānaṃ vasena uccāvacaṃ āpajjati. Brahmaloke ucco hoti, devaloke avaco. Devaloke ucco, manussaloke avaco. Manussaloke ucco, apāye avaco. Yesāhaṃ, bhanteti yesaṃ ahaṃ bhante. Sandhivasena panettha “yesāha”nti hoti. Yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattanti yathā mayā suto ceva uggahito ca, evaṃ. Dhammaṃ desemīti sattavatapadaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Na cāhaṃ tesanti ahaṃ pana tesaṃ sāvako na [M 2.0331] sampajjāmi. Ahaṃ kho pana, bhantetiādinā attano sotāpannabhāvaṃ jānāpeti.

367. Craving is called 'ejā' in the sense of agitation. It is a 'disease' (rogo) in the sense of oppressing, a 'boil' (gaṇḍo) in the sense of corrupting within, and an 'arrow' (sallaṃ) in the sense of having penetrated. Therefore, 'this person' (ayaṃ puriso) is so called because craving (ejā), in accordance with deeds done by oneself, pulls a person here and there for the purpose of being reborn there. Thus, this person attains various high and low states according to those various existences. In the Brahma realm, one is high; in the deva realm, low. In the deva realm, one is high; in the human realm, low. In the human realm, one is high; in the plane of misery, low. 'Yesāhaṃ, bhante' is 'yesaṃ ahaṃ bhante'. Here, by euphonic combination, it becomes 'yesāhaṃ'. 'As heard, as learned' means 'just as it was heard and learned by me, so...'. 'I teach the Dhamma' means 'I teach the Dhamma of seven items of practice'. 'But I am not theirs' means 'But I do not become their disciple'. By the phrase beginning with 'But I, venerable sir...', he makes known his own attainment of stream-entry.

Somanassapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Acquisition of Gladness

368. Vedapaṭilābhanti [V 2.0297] tuṭṭhipaṭilābhaṃ. Devāsurasaṅgāmoti devānañca asurānañca saṅgāmo. Samupabyūḷhoti samāpanno nalāṭena nalāṭaṃ paharaṇākārappatto viya. Etesaṃ kira kadāci mahāsamuddapiṭṭhe saṅgāmo hoti tattha pana chedanavijjhanādīhi aññamaññaṃ ghāto nāma natthi, dārumeṇḍakayuddhaṃ viya jayaparājayamattameva hoti. Kadāci devā jinanti, kadāci asurā. Tattha yasmiṃ saṅgāme devā puna apaccāgamanāya asure [P 3.0739] jiniṃsu, taṃ sandhāya tasmiṃ kho pana bhantetiādimāha. Ubhayametanti ubhayaṃ etaṃ. Duvidhampi ojaṃ ettha devaloke devāyeva paribhuñjissantīti evamassa āvajjantassa balavapītisomanassaṃ uppajji. Sadaṇḍāvacaroti sadaṇḍāvacarako, daṇḍaggahaṇena satthaggahaṇena saddhiṃ ahosi, na nikkhittadaṇḍasatthoti dasseti. Ekantanibbidāyāti ekanteneva vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāyāti sabbaṃ mahāgovindasutte vuttameva.

368. Vedapaṭilābhaṃ means the attainment of joy. The battle of devas and asuras refers to the conflict between the devas and the asuras. Samupabyūḷho means they were drawn up for battle, as if having reached the point of striking forehead against forehead. It is said that their battle sometimes takes place on the surface of the great ocean. There, however, there is no killing of one another by cutting, piercing, and so on; there is only victory and defeat, like a battle of wooden rams. Sometimes the devas win, sometimes the asuras. Referring to the battle in which the devas defeated the asuras so that they could not return again, he said, 'But then, venerable sir...' and so on. Ubhayametaṃ means 'both of these.' Thus, as he was reflecting, 'In this deva world, the devas alone will enjoy both kinds of nutriment,' strong joyous gladness arose in him. Sadaṇḍāvacaro means one who moves about with a rod; he was with the taking up of the rod and the sword, showing that he had not laid down the rod and the sword. Ekantanibbidāya means solely for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the round of existence. All this has been explained in the Mahāgovinda Sutta.

369. Pavedesīti kathesi dīpesi. Idhevāti imasmiññeva okāse. Devabhūtassa me satoti devassa me sato. Punarāyu ca me laddhoti puna aññena kammavipākena me jīvitaṃ laddhanti, iminā attano cutabhāvaṃ ceva upapannabhāvañca āvikaroti.

369. Pavedesi means he spoke, he explained. Idheva means in this very place. Devabhūtassa me sato means 'of me, being a deva.' Punarāyu ca me laddho means 'and again a lifespan has been obtained by me'; that is, 'by another result of kamma, life has been obtained by me.' By this, he reveals both his passing away and his taking rebirth.

Diviyā kāyāti dibbā attabhāvā. Āyuṃ hitvā amānusanti dibbaṃ āyuṃ jahitvā. Amūḷho gabbhamessāmīti niyatagatikattā amūḷho hutvā. Yattha me ramatī manoti yattha me mano ramissati, tattheva khattiyakulādīsu gabbhaṃ upagacchissāmīti sattakkhattuṃ deve ca mānuse cāti imamatthaṃ dīpeti.

Diviyā kāyā means divine existences. Āyuṃ hitvā amānusaṃ means having abandoned the divine lifespan. Amūḷho gabbhamessāmi means being undeluded because of having a fixed destiny. Yattha me ramatī mano means 'wherever my mind will delight, right there in a khattiya family or the like, I will enter a womb.' This explains the meaning: 'seven times among devas and humans.'

Ñāyena viharissāmīti manussesu upapannopi mātaraṃ jīvitā voropanādīnaṃ abhabbattā ñāyena kāraṇena samena viharissāmīti attho.

Ñāyena viharissāmi means: even when reborn among humans, because of being incapable of such acts as depriving one's mother of life, I will dwell according to the right method, for the right reason, and equitably. This is the meaning.

Sambodhi [M 2.0332] ce bhavissatīti idaṃ sakadāgāmimaggaṃ sandhāya vadati, sace sakadāgāmī bhavissāmīti dīpeti. Aññātā viharissāmīti aññātā ājānitukāmo hutvā viharissāmi. Sveva anto bhavissatīti so eva me manussaloke anto bhavissatīti.

Sambodhi ce bhavissati: this is said with reference to the path of the once-returner; it explains, 'if I become a once-returner.' Aññātā viharissāmi means I will dwell as one desiring to know. Sveva anto bhavissati means that very life in the human world will be my last.

Puna [V 2.0298] devo bhavissāmi, devalokasmiṃ uttamoti puna devalokasmiṃ uttamo sakko devānamindo bhavissāmīti vadati.

Puna devo bhavissāmi, devalokasmiṃ uttamo means he says: 'Again in the deva world, I shall become the supreme one, Sakka, lord of the devas.'

Antime vattamānamhīti antime bhave vattamāne. So nivāso bhavissatīti ye te āyunā ca paññāya ca akaniṭṭhā jeṭṭhakā sabbadevehi paṇītatarā devā, avasāne me so nivāso bhavissati[P 3.0740]. Ayaṃ kira tato sakkattabhāvato cuto tasmiṃ attabhāve anāgāmimaggassa paṭiladdhattā uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī hutvā avihādīsu nibbattanto avasāne akaniṭṭhe nibbattissati. Taṃ sandhāya evamāha. Esa kira avihesu kappasahassaṃ vasissati, atappesu dve kappasahassāni, sudassesu cattāri kappasahassāni, sudassīsu aṭṭha, akaniṭṭhesu soḷasāti ekatiṃsa kappasahassāni brahmaāyuṃ anubhavissati. Sakko devarājā anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati visākhā mahāupāsikāti tayopi hi ime ekappamāṇaāyukā eva, vaṭṭābhiratasattā nāma etehi sadisā sukhabhāgino nāma natthi.

Antime vattamānamhi means when existing in the final life. So nivāso bhavissati means: 'Those devas who are the Akaniṭṭhas, the eldest, superior to all devas in lifespan and wisdom—that will be my dwelling at the end.' It is said that this one, having passed away from that state as Sakka and having attained the path of the non-returner in that existence, becomes one who goes upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
