Being reborn in the Aviha realm and so on, he will at the end be reborn in the Akaniṭṭha realm. It was with reference to this that he spoke thus. It is said that he will dwell in the Aviha realm for a thousand aeons, in the Atappa realm for two thousand aeons, in the Sudassa realm for four thousand aeons, in the Sudassī realm for eight thousand, and in the Akaniṭṭha realm for sixteen thousand. Thus, for thirty-one thousand aeons he will experience the lifespan of a Brahmā. Sakka, king of the devas; Anāthapiṇḍika, the householder; and Visākhā, the great female lay disciple—these three all have lifespans of equal measure. There are no beings who delight in the round of existence who are partakers of happiness comparable to these.

370. Apariyositasaṅkappoti aniṭṭhitamanoratho. Yassu maññāmi samaṇeti ye ca samaṇe pavivittavihārinoti maññāmi.

370. Apariyositasaṅkappo means with unfulfilled aspiration. Yassu maññāmi samaṇe means 'and those ascetics whom I consider to be dwellers in seclusion.'

Ārādhanāti sampādanā. Virādhanāti asampādanā. Na sampāyantīti sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkonti.

Ārādhanā means accomplishment. Virādhanā means non-accomplishment. Na sampāyanti means they are not able to accomplish it and then speak.

Ādiccabandhunanti ādiccopi gotamagotto, bhagavāpi gotamagotto, tasmā evamāha. Yaṃ karomasīti yaṃ pubbe brahmuno namakkāraṃ karoma. Samaṃ devehīti devehi saddhiṃ, ito paṭṭhāya idāni amhākaṃ brahmuno namakkārakaraṇaṃ natthīti dasseti. Sāmaṃ karomāti namakkāraṃ karoma.

Ādiccabandhunaṃ: The sun is of the Gotama clan, and the Blessed One is also of the Gotama clan; therefore, he spoke thus. Yaṃ karomasi means the homage we formerly paid to Brahmā. Samaṃ devehi means 'together with the devas'; this shows that from now on, there is no paying of homage to Brahmā for us. Sāmaṃ karoma means we pay homage.

371. Parāmasitvāti [M 2.0333] tuṭṭhacitto sahāyaṃ hatthena hatthamhi paharanto viya pathaviṃ paharitvā, sakkhibhāvatthāya vā paharitvā “yathā tvaṃ niccalo, evamahaṃ bhagavatī”ti. Ajjhiṭṭhapañhāti ajjhesitapañhā patthitapañhā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

371. Parāmasitvā means, with a pleased mind, having struck the earth as if striking a companion's hand with his own; or, having struck it for the purpose of bearing witness, saying, 'Just as you are unmoving, so am I unmoving in my faith in the Blessed One.' Ajjhiṭṭhapañhā means requested questions, desired questions. The rest is clear everywhere.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

Sakkapañhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Sakkapañha Sutta is concluded.

9. Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta

Uddesavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Summary Section

373. Evaṃ [P 3.0741][V 2.0299][M 2.0334] me sutanti mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ. Tatrāyamapubbapadavaṇṇanā – ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggoti kasmā bhagavā idaṃ suttamabhāsi? Kururaṭṭhavāsīnaṃ gambhīradesanāpaṭiggahaṇasamatthatāya. Kururaṭṭhavāsino kira bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo utupaccayādisampannattā tassa raṭṭhassa sappāyautupaccayasevanena niccaṃ kallasarīrā kallacittā ca honti. Te cittasarīrakallatāya anuggahitapaññābalā gambhīrakathaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ samatthā honti. Tena nesaṃ bhagavā imaṃ gambhīradesanāpaṭiggahaṇasamatthataṃ sampassanto ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu kammaṭṭhānaṃ arahatte pakkhipitvā idaṃ gambhīratthaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ abhāsi. Yathā hi puriso suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakaṃ labhitvā tattha nānāpupphāni pakkhipeyya, suvaṇṇamañjūsaṃ vā pana labhitvā sattaratanāni pakkhipeyya, evaṃ bhagavā kururaṭṭhavāsiparisaṃ labhitvā gambhīradesanaṃ desesi. Tenevettha aññānipi gambhīratthāni imasmiṃ dīghanikāye mahānidānaṃ majjhimanikāye [P 3.0742] satipaṭṭhānaṃ, sāropamaṃ, rukkhopamaṃ, raṭṭhapālaṃ, māgaṇḍiyaṃ, āneñjasappāyanti aññānipi suttāni desesi.

373. "Thus have I heard" refers to the Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta. Here follows the explanation of the initial words: "Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path"—why did the Blessed One speak this sutta? It was because the inhabitants of the Kuru country were capable of receiving a profound teaching. It is said that the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen of the Kuru country, because that country is endowed with a suitable climate, requisites, and so on, and by partaking of the suitable climate and requisites, are always of sound body and sound mind. Through the soundness of their minds and bodies, their faculty of wisdom being supported, they are capable of receiving profound discourse. Observing their ability to receive a profound teaching, the Blessed One, having placed the meditation subject in twenty-one instances culminating in Arahantship, taught this Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta of profound meaning. Just as a person who obtains a golden casket might fill it with various flowers, or who obtains a golden chest might fill it with the seven treasures, so the Blessed One, having found the assembly of inhabitants from the Kuru country, taught them a profound teaching. For that very reason, he also taught other suttas of profound meaning here: in this Dīghanikāya, the Mahānidāna; and in the Majjhimanikāya, the Satipaṭṭhāna, Sāropama, Rukkhopama, Raṭṭhapāla, Māgaṇḍiya, and Āneñjasappāya suttas.

Apica tasmiṃ janapade catasso parisā pakatiyāva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā viharanti, antamaso dāsakammakaraparijānāpi satipaṭṭhānapaṭisaṃyuttameva kathaṃ kathenti. Udakatitthasuttakantanaṭṭhānādīsupi niratthakakathā nāma nappavattati. Sace kāci itthī “amma, tvaṃ kataraṃ satipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ manasikarosī”ti pucchitā “na kiñcī”ti vadati, taṃ garahanti “dhiratthu tava jīvitaṃ, jīvamānāpi tvaṃ matasadisā”ti. Atha naṃ “mā dāni puna evamakāsī”ti ovaditvā aññataraṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhāpenti. Yā pana “ahaṃ asukasatipaṭṭhānaṃ nāma manasikaromī”ti vadati, tassā “sādhu sādhū”ti sādhukāraṃ katvā “tava [V 2.0300] jīvitaṃ sujīvitaṃ, tvaṃ nāma manussattaṃ pattā, tavatthāya sammāsambuddho uppanno”tiādīhi pasaṃsanti. Na kevalañcettha manussajātikāva satipaṭṭhānamanasikārayuttā, te nissāya viharantā tiracchānagatāpi.

Moreover, in that country, the four assemblies by their very nature dwell devoted to the practice of the development of the foundations of mindfulness. Even down to the slaves, workers, and servants, they engage only in conversations connected with the foundations of mindfulness. At watering places, spinning places, and the like, what is called pointless talk does not occur. If any woman is asked, "Mother, which development of the foundations of mindfulness do you attend to?" and she says, "None," they rebuke her, saying, "Fie on your life! Though living, you are like one dead." Then, advising her, "Do not do so again," they have her learn one of the foundations of mindfulness. But as for the one who says, "I attend to such-and-such a foundation of mindfulness," they give cries of approval, saying, "Good, good!" and praise her with such words as: "Your life is a life well-lived! You have indeed attained the human state, and for your sake the Perfectly Enlightened One has arisen!" Not only are human beings here devoted to attending to the foundations of mindfulness, but also the animals who live in dependence on them.

Tatridaṃ [M 2.0335] vatthu – eko kira naṭako suvapotakaṃ gahetvā sikkhāpento vicarati. So bhikkhunupassayaṃ upanissāya vasitvā gamanakāle suvapotakaṃ pamussitvā gato. Taṃ sāmaṇeriyo gahetvā paṭijaggiṃsu. Buddharakkhito tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ purato nisinnaṃ disvā mahātherī āha – “buddharakkhitā”ti. Kiṃ, ayyeti? Atthi te koci bhāvanāmanasikāroti? Natthi, ayyeti. Āvuso, pabbajitānaṃ santike vasantena nāma vissaṭṭhaattabhāvena bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, kocideva manasikāro icchitabbo, tvaṃ pana aññaṃ na sakkhissasi, “aṭṭhi aṭṭhī”ti sajjhāyaṃ karohīti. So theriyā ovāde ṭhatvā “aṭṭhi aṭṭhī”ti sajjhāyanto carati.

Here is the account: A certain actor, it is said, was traveling around while training a young parrot. Having stayed near a nunnery, he left one day, forgetting the young parrot. The novice nuns took it and cared for it. They named it Buddharakkhita. One day, seeing it sitting in front of her, the great elder nun said, "Buddharakkhita!" "What is it, venerable lady?" it replied. "Do you have any development of the mind or attention?" "No, venerable lady." "Friend, for one living near those who have gone forth, it is not fitting to be of a neglected self. Some form of attention should be desired. But you are incapable of anything else—recite ‘bone, bone.’" Following the elder nun’s advice, it went about reciting, "bone, bone."

Taṃ ekadivasaṃ pātova toraṇagge nisīditvā bālātapaṃ tapamānaṃ eko sakuṇo nakhapañjarena aggahesi. So “kiri kirī”ti saddamakāsi. Sāmaṇeriyo sutvā “ayye buddharakkhito sakuṇena gahito, mocema na”nti leḍḍuādīni gahetvā anubandhitvā mocesuṃ[P 3.0743]. Taṃ ānetvā purato ṭhapitaṃ therī āha – “buddharakkhita, sakuṇena gahitakāle kiṃ cintesī”ti? Na, ayye, aññaṃ kiñci cintesiṃ, aṭṭhipuñjova aṭṭhipuñjaṃ gahetvā gacchati, katarasmiṃ ṭhāne vippakirissatīti, evaṃ ayye aṭṭhipuñjameva cintesinti. Sādhu, sādhu, buddharakkhita, anāgate bhavakkhayassa te paccayo bhavissatīti. Evaṃ tattha tiracchānagatāpi satipaṭṭhānamanasikārayuttā. Tasmā nesaṃ bhagavā satipaṭṭhānabuddhimeva janento idaṃ suttamabhāsi.

One day, early in the morning, while it was sitting at the top of the gateway warming itself in the early morning sun, a bird of prey caught it in its talons. It cried, "Kiri, kirī!" Hearing this, the novice nuns said, "Venerable lady, Buddharakkhita has been caught by a bird—let’s free him!" They picked up clods of earth and other things, chased after it, and freed him. They brought him back and placed him before the elder nun. She asked, "Buddharakkhita, what did you think when you were caught by the bird?" "Venerable lady, I thought nothing else. A heap of bones is carrying off a heap of bones; I wondered, 'In which place will it scatter them?' Thus, venerable lady, I only reflected on the heap of bones." "Good, good, Buddharakkhita! In the future, this will be a condition for the destruction of your existence." Thus, even those born as animals there were engaged in attending to the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, the Blessed One, arousing in them the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness, spoke this discourse.

Tattha ekāyanoti ekamaggo. Maggassa hi –

Herein, 'ekāyana' means the one path. For of the path—

“Maggo pantho patho pajjo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ;

Nāvā uttarasetū ca, kullo ca bhisisaṅkamo”ti.

"Path, road, way, course, straight path, track; boat, ferry, bridge, raft, and lotus-stalk crossing."

Bahūni nāmāni. Svāyamidha ayananāmena vutto, tasmā ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggoti ettha ekamaggo ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo na dvidhā pathabhūtoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā [V 2.0301] ekena ayitabboti ekāyano. Ekenāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya vūpakaṭṭhena pavivittacittena. Ayitabbo paṭipajjitabbo, ayanti vā etenāti ayano, saṃsārato [M 2.0336] nibbānaṃ gacchantīti attho. Ekassa ayano ekāyano. Ekassāti seṭṭhassa. Sabbasattaseṭṭho ca bhagavā, tasmā bhagavatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi hi tena aññepi ayanti, evaṃ santepi bhagavatova so ayano tena uppāditattā. Yathāha “so hi, brāhmaṇa, bhagavā anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.79). Ayatīti vā ayano, gacchati pavattatīti attho. Ekasmiṃ ayanoti ekāyano, imasmiññeva dhammavinaye pavattati, na aññatthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “imasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214). Desanābhedoyeva heso, atthato pana ekova. Apica ekaṃ ayatīti ekāyano. Pubbabhāge nānāmukhabhāvanānayappavattopi aparabhāge ekaṃ nibbānameva [P 3.0744] gacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha brahmā sahampati –

Many are the names. Herein, it is called by the name 'path' (ayana); therefore, 'This is the one path, bhikkhus.' Here this path is a single path, bhikkhus, not a divided path—this meaning should be seen. Or, it is to be traveled by one—thus, 'the one path.' 'By one' means abandoning company and crowds, with a withdrawn, secluded mind. 'To be traveled' means to be practiced; 'ayana' means the path by which one goes, the meaning is going from saṃsāra to Nibbāna. The path of the One is 'the one path.' 'Of the One' means of the best. The Blessed One is the best of all beings, hence it is said to be 'of the Blessed One.' Although others also travel by it, even so, it is the Blessed One's path because it was originated by him. As it is said: 'For, brahmin, the Blessed One is the originator of the unarisen path,' etc. (MN 3.79). Or, 'ayana' means it goes, it proceeds. 'In one' means 'the one path'; it proceeds in this very Dhamma-Vinaya, not elsewhere—this is said. As it is said: 'In this Dhamma-Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found' (DN 2.214). This is merely a difference in teaching, but in meaning, it is one. Furthermore, 'it goes to one'—thus, 'the one path.' Though in the preliminary stage it proceeds by various methods of development, in the final stage it goes solely to the one Nibbāna—this is said. As Brahmā Sahampati said:

Ekāyanaṃ jātikhayantadassī,

Maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe,

Tarissanti ye ca taranti oghanti. (saṃ. ni. 5.409);

The Seer of the destruction of birth, compassionate for their welfare, knows the one path; by this path they crossed over in the past, and by it they will cross, and are crossing, the flood.

Keci pana “na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yantī”ti gāthānayena yasmā ekavāraṃ nibbānaṃ gacchati, tasmā “ekāyano”ti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati. Imassa hi atthassa sakiṃ ayanoti iminā byañjanena bhavitabbaṃ. Yadi pana ekaṃ ayanamassa ekā gati pavattīti evaṃ atthaṃ yojetvā vucceyya, byañjanaṃ yujjeyya, attho pana ubhayathāpi na yujjati. Kasmā? Idha pubbabhāgamaggassa adhippetattā. Kāyādicatuārammaṇappavatto hi pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggo idhādhippeto, na lokuttaro, so ca anekavārampi ayati, anekañcassa ayanaṃ hoti.

But some say, 'Because, according to the verse, “they do not go to the far shore a second time,” it goes to Nibbāna once, it is therefore called “the one path.”' This is not correct. For this meaning, the expression should be 'sakiṃ-ayano' (once-going). If, however, it were stated, connecting the meaning as 'having one destination, one course,' the wording would fit, but the meaning would not fit in either case. Why? Because here the preliminary path is intended. For here, the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness, which proceeds with the four objects beginning with the body, is intended, not the supramundane path. And that path goes many times, and its course is manifold.

Pubbepi ca imasmiṃ pade mahātherānaṃ sākacchā ahosiyeva. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggoti āha. Ācariyo panassa tipiṭakacūḷasumatthero missakamaggoti āha. Pubbabhāgo bhanteti? Missako, āvusoti. Ācariye pana punappunaṃ bhaṇante appaṭibāhitvā [M 2.0337] tuṇhī ahosi. Pañhaṃ avinicchinitvāva uṭṭhahiṃsu. Athācariyatthero nahānakoṭṭhakaṃ gacchanto “mayā missakamaggo kathito, cūḷanāgo pubbabhāgamaggoti ādāya voharati, ko nu kho ettha nicchayo”ti suttantaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya parivattento “yo hi koci[V 2.0302], bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya satta vassānī”ti imasmiṃ ṭhāne sallakkhesi. Lokuttaramaggo uppajjitvā satta vassāni tiṭṭhamāno nāma natthi, mayā vutto missakamaggo na labbhati. Cūḷanāgena diṭṭho pubbabhāgamaggova labbhatīti ñatvā aṭṭhamiyaṃ dhammasavane saṅghuṭṭhe agamāsi.

Even in the past, there was indeed a discussion among the great elders regarding this term. The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said it was the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness. But his teacher, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷasumana, said it was a mixed path. 'Is it the preliminary part, venerable sir?' 'It is mixed, friend.' But when the teacher repeatedly stated this, without objecting, he remained silent. Without deciding the question, they rose. Then the teacher-elder, while going to the bathing chamber, was reviewing the sutta from the beginning, thinking: 'I have said it is a mixed path, but Cūḷanāga holds that it is the preliminary path. What is the correct decision here?' He then reflected on this passage: 'Bhikkhus, whoever should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years...' He considered: 'There is no such thing as a supramundane path that, having arisen, remains for seven years. The mixed path I spoke of is not tenable. The preliminary path that Cūḷanāga saw is what is tenable.' Realizing this, he went when the Dhamma recitation was announced on the eighth day.

Porāṇakattherā kira piyadhammasavanā honti, saddaṃ sutvāva “ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ, ahaṃ paṭhama”nti ekappahāreneva osaranti. Tasmiñca divase cūḷanāgattherassa vāro, tena [P 3.0745] dhammāsane nisīditvā bījaniṃ gahetvā pubbagāthāsu vuttāsu therassa āsanapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhitassa etadahosi – “raho nisīditvā na vakkhāmī”ti. Porāṇakattherā hi anusūyakā honti. Na attano rucimeva ucchubhāraṃ viya evaṃ ukkhipitvā vicaranti, kāraṇameva gaṇhanti, akāraṇaṃ vissajjenti. Tasmā thero “āvuso, cūḷanāgā”ti āha. So ācariyassa viya saddoti dhammaṃ ṭhapetvā “kiṃ bhante”ti āha. Āvuso, cūḷanāga, mayā vutto missakamaggo na labbhati, tayā vutto pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggova labbhatīti. Thero cintesi – “amhākaṃ ācariyo sabbapariyattiko tepiṭako sutabuddho, evarūpassāpi nāma bhikkhuno ayaṃ pañho āluḷeti, anāgate mama bhātikā imaṃ pañhaṃ āluḷessantīti suttaṃ gahetvā imaṃ pañhaṃ niccalaṃ karissāmī”ti paṭisambhidāmaggato “ekāyanamaggo vuccati pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggo”.

The ancient elders, it is said, were fond of hearing the Dhamma. Upon hearing the call, they would rush forward at once, saying, 'I first, I first!' On that day, it was the turn of the Elder Cūḷanāga. He had seated himself on the Dhamma seat and taken up the fan. While the introductory verses were being recited, it occurred to his teacher-elder, who was standing at the back of the seat, 'I will not wait to speak in private.' For the ancient elders were without envy. They did not go about carrying their own preferences like a load of sugar cane, but accepted what was reasonable and dismissed what was unreasonable. Therefore, the elder said, 'Friend, Cūḷanāga.' Recognizing the voice as his teacher's, he set aside the Dhamma recitation and said, 'What is it, venerable sir?' 'Friend, Cūḷanāga, the mixed path I spoke of is not tenable; the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness you spoke of is what is tenable.' The Elder Cūḷanāga then reflected, 'Our teacher is a master of all the scriptures, a Tipiṭaka-master, one awakened by what he has heard. Yet even a bhikkhu such as he is confused by this question. In the future, my spiritual brothers will be confused by this question. I will take a sutta as authority and settle this question immovably.' From the Paṭisambhidāmagga he cited: 'The one-way path is called the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness.'

Maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko seṭṭho, saccānaṃ caturo padā;

Virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṃ, dvipadānañca cakkhumā.

Of paths, the Eightfold is the best; of truths, the Four Noble Truths; of states, dispassion is the best; and of two-footed beings, the One with Vision.

Eseva maggo natthañño, dassanassa visuddhiyā;

Etañhi tumhe paṭipajjatha, mārasenappamaddanaṃ;

Etañhi tumhe paṭipannā, dukkhassantaṃ karissathāti. –

This is the only path, there is no other, for the purification of vision. Enter upon this path, and you will confound the army of Māra. Having entered upon this path, you will make an end of suffering.

Suttaṃ āharitvā ṭhapesi.

Having cited the discourse, he established the point.

Maggoti [M 2.0338] kenaṭṭhena maggo? Nibbānagamanaṭṭhena nibbānatthikehi magganīyaṭṭhena ca. Sattānaṃ visuddhiyāti rāgādīhi malehi abhijjhāvisamalobhādīhi ca upakkilesehi kiliṭṭhacittānaṃ sattānaṃ visuddhatthāya. Tathā hi imināva maggena ito satasahassakappādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ [P 3.0746] asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ [V 2.0303] upari ekasmiṃyeva kappe nibbatte taṇhaṅkaramedhaṅkarasaraṇaṅkaradīpaṅkaranāmake buddhe ādiṃ katvā sakyamunipariyosānā aneke sammāsambuddhā anekasatā paccekabuddhā gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā ariyasāvakā cāti ime sattā sabbe cittamalaṃ pavāhetvā paramavisuddhiṃ pattā. Rūpamalavasena pana saṃkilesavodānapaññattiyeva natthi. Tathā hi –

In what sense is it a 'path' (magga)? In the sense that it leads to Nibbāna and is to be sought by those who seek Nibbāna. 'For the purification of beings' means for the purification of the minds of beings that are defiled by impurities such as greed, and by defilements such as covetousness and unrighteous greed. Indeed, by this very path, starting with the Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara, who arose in a single aeon more than four incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons ago, up to Sakyamuni, numerous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, hundreds of Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples beyond calculation have all washed away the defilements of the mind and reached supreme purity. However, with respect to the stain of form, there is no designation of defilement and purification. For it is said:

“Rūpena saṃkiliṭṭhena, saṃkilissanti māṇavā;

Rūpe suddhe visujjhanti, anakkhātaṃ mahesinā.

"By defiled form, beings are defiled; by pure form, they are cleansed—this was not declared by the Great Seer.

Cittena saṃkiliṭṭhena, saṃkilissanti māṇavā;

Citte suddhe visujjhanti, iti vuttaṃ mahesinā”.

With a defiled mind beings are defiled; with a pure mind they are purified—thus was it said by the Great Sage."

Yathāha – “cittasaṃkilesā, bhikkhave, sattā saṃkilissanti, cittavodānā visujjhantī”ti. Tañca cittavodānaṃ iminā satipaṭṭhānamaggena hoti. Tenāha “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti.

As it is said: "Monks, beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind; beings are purified by the purification of the mind." And this purification of the mind comes about through this path of the establishments of mindfulness. Therefore, it is said, "for the purification of beings."

Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyāti sokassa ca paridevassa ca samatikkamāya pahānāyāti attho, ayañhi maggo bhāvito santatimahāmattādīnaṃ viya sokasamatikkamāya, paṭācārādīnaṃ viya paridevasamatikkamāya saṃvattati. Tenāha “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”ti. Kiñcāpi hi santatimahāmatto –

'For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation' means for the transcending and abandoning of sorrow and lamentation. This path, when developed, leads to the overcoming of sorrow, as in the case of the great minister Santati and others, and to the overcoming of lamentation, as in the case of Paṭācārā and others. Therefore, it is said, "for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation." Although the great minister Santati—

“Yaṃ pubbe taṃ visodhehi, pacchā te mātu kiñcanaṃ;

Majjhe ce no gahessasi, upasanto carissasī”ti. (su. ni. 945);

"Purify what was done before, let there be nothing for you after. If you do not grasp at what is in between, you will go about at peace."

Imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvāva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patto. Paṭācārā –

Having heard this verse, he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. As for Paṭācārā—

“Na santi puttā tāṇāya, na pitā nāpi bandhavā;

Antakenādhipannassa, natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā”ti. (dha. pa. 288);

"Sons are no protection, nor father, nor relatives. For one overcome by the Ender, there is no protection among kinsmen."

Imaṃ [P 3.0747][M 2.0339] gāthaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā. Yasmā pana kāyavedanācittadhammesu kañci dhammaṃ [V 2.0304] anāmasitvā bhāvanā nāma natthi, tasmā tepi imināva maggena sokaparideve samatikkantāti veditabbā.

Having heard this verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry. But since there is no cultivation without attending to some phenomenon among body, feeling, mind, or dhammas, it should be understood that they too overcame sorrow and lamentation by this very path.

Dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāyāti kāyikadukkhassa cetasikadomanassassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ atthaṅgamāya, nirodhāyāti attho. Ayañhi maggo bhāvito tissattherādīnaṃ viya dukkhassa, sakkādīnaṃ viya ca domanassassa atthaṅgamāya saṃvattati.

'For the disappearance of pain and displeasure' means for the disappearance, that is, the cessation, of these two: bodily pain and mental displeasure. For this path, when developed, conduces to the disappearance of pain, as in the case of the Elder Tissa and others, and to the disappearance of displeasure, as in the case of Sakka and others.

Tatrāyaṃ atthadīpanā – sāvatthiyaṃ kira tisso nāma kuṭumbikaputto cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo pahāya pabbajitvā agāmake araññe viharati. Tassa kaniṭṭhabhātu bhariyā “gacchatha, naṃ jīvitā voropethā”ti pañcasate core pesesi. Te gantvā theraṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Thero āha – “kasmā āgatattha upāsakā”ti? Taṃ jīvitā voropessāmāti. Pāṭibhogaṃ me upāsakā, gahetvā ajjekarattiṃ jīvitaṃ dethāti. Ko te, samaṇa, imasmiṃ ṭhāne pāṭibhogo bhavissatīti? Thero mahantaṃ pāsāṇaṃ gahetvā dve ūruṭṭhīni bhinditvā “vaṭṭati upāsakā pāṭibhogo”ti āha. Te apakkamitvā caṅkamanasīse aggiṃ katvā nipajjiṃsu. Therassa vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā sīlaṃ paccavekkhato parisuddhaṃ sīlaṃ nissāya pītipāmojjaṃ uppajji. Tato anukkamena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento tiyāmarattiṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā aruṇuggamane arahattaṃ patto imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Here is an illustration of the meaning: In Sāvatthī, it is said, a householder's son named Tissa, having abandoned forty crores of gold, went forth and lived in a remote wilderness. His younger brother's wife sent five hundred thieves, saying, "Go, deprive him of his life." They went, surrounded the elder, and sat down. The elder asked, "Why have you come, lay followers?" They replied, "To deprive you of your life." He said, "Lay followers, accept a pledge from me and grant me life for just this one night." They asked, "Who can be your pledge in this place, ascetic?" The elder took a large rock, broke both his thigh bones, and said, "Is this pledge sufficient, lay followers?" They departed, made a fire at the head of his walking path, and lay down. For the elder, having suppressed the pain and reflecting on his virtue, joy and gladness arose in reliance on his pure virtue. Then, gradually developing insight, he performed the duties of an ascetic for the three watches of the night. At the break of dawn, he attained arahantship and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Ubho pādāni bhinditvā, saññapessāmi vo ahaṃ;

Aṭṭiyāmi harāyāmi, sarāgamaraṇaṃ ahaṃ.

"Having broken both my legs, I will make you understand. I am distressed and ashamed of dying with lust.

Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, yathābhūtaṃ vipassisaṃ;

Sampatte aruṇuggamhi, arahattamapāpuṇi”nti.

Having reflected thus, I saw things as they truly are; at the arrival of dawn, I attained arahantship."

Aparepi tiṃsa bhikkhū bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññavihāre vassaṃ upagantvā “āvuso, tiyāmarattiṃ [P 3.0748] samaṇadhammova kātabbo, na aññamaññassa santikaṃ āgantabba”nti vatvā vihariṃsu. Tesaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā paccūsasamaye pacalāyantānaṃ eko byaggho āgantvā ekekaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā gacchati. Na koci “maṃ byaggho gaṇhī”ti vācampi nicchāresi. Evaṃ pañcasu dasasu bhikkhūsu khāditesu uposathadivase “itare, āvuso[M 2.0340], kuhi”nti pucchitvā ñatvā ca “idāni gahitena gahitomhīti vattabba”nti vatvā vihariṃsu[V 2.0305]. Atha aññataraṃ daharabhikkhuṃ purimanayeneva byaggho gaṇhi. So “byaggho bhante”ti āha. Bhikkhū kattaradaṇḍe ca ukkāyo ca gahetvā mocessāmāti anubandhiṃsu. Byaggho bhikkhūnaṃ agatiṃ chinnataṭaṭṭhānamāruyha taṃ bhikkhuṃ pādaṅguṭṭhakato paṭṭhāya khādituṃ ārabhi. Itarepi “idāni sappurisa, amhehi kattabbaṃ natthi, bhikkhūnaṃ viseso nāma evarūpe ṭhāne paññāyatī”ti āhaṃsu. So byagghamukhe nipannova taṃ vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento yāva gopphakā khāditasamaye sotāpanno hutvā, yāva jaṇṇukā khāditasamaye sakadāgāmī, yāva nābhiyā khāditasamaye anāgāmī hutvā, hadayarūpe akhāditeyeva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Furthermore, thirty monks received a meditation subject from the Blessed One and, having entered a forest monastery for the rainy season, dwelt there after agreeing, “Friends, for the three watches of the night, only the practice of a recluse is to be done; one should not approach another.” As they were practicing the recluse’s practice, at dawn, while they were nodding off, a tiger came and carried away one monk at a time. Not one of them even uttered the words, “A tiger has seized me!” In this way, after five or ten monks had been devoured, on the Uposatha day, they asked, “Friends, where are the others?” Upon realizing what had happened, they said, “From now on, whoever is seized must say, ‘I have been seized!’” and they continued to dwell there. Then a young monk was seized by the tiger in the same manner as before. He cried out, “Venerable sirs, a tiger!” The monks, taking knives, staves, and torches, pursued it, intending to free him. The tiger, seeing no escape from the monks, climbed a steep, sheer bank and began to devour the monk, starting from his big toe. The others said, “Now, good sir, there is nothing we can do. The distinction of a monk becomes known in such a situation.” Lying in the tiger’s mouth, he suppressed the pain and developed insight. By the time he was eaten up to the ankles, he became a stream-enterer; by the time he was eaten up to the knees, he became a once-returner; by the time he was eaten up to the navel, he became a non-returner; and before his heart-base was eaten, he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Sīlavā vatasampanno, paññavā susamāhito;

Muhuttaṃ pamādamanvāya, byagghenoruddhamānaso.

“Though virtuous, accomplished in vows, wise, and well-composed, having for a moment given way to heedlessness, my mind was overwhelmed by the tiger.

Pañjarasmiṃ gahetvāna, silāya uparī kato;

Kāmaṃ khādatu maṃ byaggho, aṭṭhiyā ca nhārussa ca;

Kilese khepayissāmi, phusissāmi vimuttiya”nti.

Caught in its jaws, placed upon a rock, let the tiger devour me at will, my bones and sinews; I shall destroy the defilements, I shall attain liberation.”

Aparopi pītamallatthero nāma gihikāle tīsu rajjesu paṭākaṃ gahetvā tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ āgamma rājānaṃ passitvā raññā [P 3.0749] katānuggaho ekadivasaṃ kilañjakāpaṇasāladvārena gacchanto “rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha, taṃ vo pahīnaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti na tumhākavākyaṃ sutvā cintesi “neva kira rūpaṃ attano, na vedanā”ti. So taṃyeva aṅkusaṃ katvā nikkhamitvā mahāvihāraṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajito upasampanno dvemātikā paguṇā katvā tiṃsa bhikkhū gahetvā gabalavāliyaaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi. Pādesu avahantesu jaṇṇukehi caṅkamati. Tamenaṃ rattiṃ eko migaluddako migoti maññamāno pahari. Satti vinivijjhitvā gatā, so taṃ sattiṃ harāpetvā paharaṇamukhāni tiṇavaṭṭiyā pūrāpetvā pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ attānaṃ nisīdāpetvā okāsaṃ kāretvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saha [M 2.0341] paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā ukkāsitasaddena āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ byākaritvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Another, the Elder Pītamalla, in his time as a householder, had been a champion in three kingdoms. Coming to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, he met the king and received his favor. One day, while passing by the door of a mat-shop hall, he heard the words, “Form, monks, is not yours; abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.” Hearing this “not yours” statement, he thought, “Indeed, form is not one’s own, nor is feeling.” Taking this very thing as a goad, he went forth from home, went to the Great Monastery, and requested the going forth. Having gone forth and received the higher ordination, he mastered the two Mātikās, took thirty monks, and went to the Gabalavāliya courtyard to practice the recluse’s duty. When his feet were worn away, he did walking meditation on his knees. One night, a deer hunter, mistaking him for a deer, struck him. The spear pierced right through him. He had the spear removed, had the openings of the wound filled with wads of grass, and had himself seated on a flat stone. Having created the opportunity, he developed insight and, together with the analytical knowledges, attained arahantship. When the monks arrived at the sound of his clearing his throat, he declared his attainment and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Bhāsitaṃ buddhaseṭṭhassa, sabbalokaggavādino;

Na tumhākamidaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ jaheyyātha bhikkhavo.

“Spoken by the supreme Buddha, the foremost speaker in all the world: ‘This form is not yours, O monks, you should abandon it.

Aniccā [V 2.0306] vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino;

Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”ti.

Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned formations, subject to arising and passing away. Having arisen, they cease; their stilling is bliss.’”

Evaṃ tāva ayaṃ maggo tissattherādīnaṃ viya dukkhassa atthaṅgamāya saṃvattati.

Thus, this path leads to the cessation of suffering, just as it did for the Elder Tissa and others.

Sakko pana devānamindo attano pañcavidhapubbanimittaṃ disvā maraṇabhayasantajjito domanassajāto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchi. So upekkhāpañhavissajjanāvasāne [P 3.0750] asītisahassāhi devatāhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Sā cassa upapatti puna pākatikāva ahosi.

Sakka, the lord of the gods, seeing his own fivefold premonitions of death, was terrified by the fear of death and became sorrowful. He approached the Blessed One and asked a question. At the conclusion of the answer to the question on equanimity, he, along with eighty thousand deities, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. And his state of existence was restored as before.

Subrahmāpi devaputto accharāsahassaparivuto saggasampattiṃ anubhoti. Tattha pañcasatā accharāyo rukkhato pupphāni ocinantiyo cavitvā niraye uppannā. So “kiṃ imā cirāyantī”ti upadhārento tāsaṃ niraye nibbattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “kittakaṃ nu kho mama āyū”ti upaparikkhanto attano āyuparikkhayaṃ viditvā cavitvā tattheva niraye nibbattanabhāvaṃ disvā bhīto ativiya domanassajāto hutvā “imaṃ me domanassaṃ satthā vinayissati, na añño”ti avasesā pañcasatā accharāyo gahetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchi –

The young god Subrahma, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, was experiencing heavenly bliss. There, five hundred nymphs, while picking flowers from a tree, passed away and arose in hell. He, considering, “Why are they taking so long?” came to know of their rebirth in hell. Examining his own lifespan, “How long, I wonder, is my life?” he saw the exhaustion of his own lifespan and saw that after passing away he would be reborn right there in hell. Frightened and exceedingly sorrowful, thinking, “The Teacher will dispel this sorrow of mine, no one else,” he took the remaining five hundred nymphs, approached the Blessed One, and asked a question:

“Niccaṃ utrastamidaṃ cittaṃ, niccaṃ ubbiggidaṃ mano;

Anuppannesu kicchesu, atho uppatitesu ca;

Sace atthi anutrastaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchitoti. (saṃ. ni. 1.98);

“Ever terrified is this mind, ever agitated is this heart, concerning troubles not yet arisen and also those that have arisen. If there is a state without terror, explain that to me upon being asked.”

Tato naṃ bhagavā āha –

Then the Blessed One said to him:

“Nāññatra bojjhā tapasā, nāññatrindriyasaṃvarā;

Nāññatra sabbanissaggā, sotthiṃ passāmi pāṇina”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.98);

“Apart from awakening, austerity, restraint of the senses, and the relinquishing of all, I see no safety for living beings.”

So [M 2.0342] desanāpariyosāne pañcahi accharāsatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya taṃ sampattiṃ [V 2.0307] thāvaraṃ katvā devalokameva agamāsīti. Evaṃ ayaṃ maggo bhāvito sakkādīnaṃ viya domanassassa atthaṅgamāya saṃvattatīti veditabbo.

At the conclusion of the discourse, he, together with the five hundred celestial nymphs, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Having made that attainment stable, he went to the deva world. Thus, it should be understood that this path, when developed, leads to the cessation of sorrow, just as it did for Sakka and others.

Ñāyassa adhigamāyāti ñāyo vuccati ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, tassa adhigamāya, pattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi pubbabhāge lokiyo satipaṭṭhānamaggo bhāvito lokuttaramaggassa [P 3.0751] adhigamāya saṃvattati. Tenāha “ñāyassa adhigamāyā”ti. Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyāti taṇhāvānavirahitattā nibbānanti laddhanāmassa amatassa sacchikiriyāya, attapaccakkhatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi maggo bhāvito anupubbena nibbānasacchikiriyaṃ sādheti. Tenāha “nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti.

For the attainment of the right way—the right way is called the Noble Eightfold Path; for its attainment, for its reaching, this is said. Indeed, in the preliminary stage, the mundane path of the establishments of mindfulness, when developed, conduces to the attainment of the supramundane path. Therefore, it is said, "for the attainment of the right way." For the realization of Nibbāna—for the realization of the deathless, which has obtained the name Nibbāna because it is devoid of the thicket of craving, for direct personal experience, this is said. Indeed, when this path is developed, it gradually accomplishes the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, "for the realization of Nibbāna."

Tattha kiñcāpi “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti vutte sokasamatikkamādīni atthato siddhāneva honti, ṭhapetvā pana sāsanayuttikovide aññesaṃ na pākaṭāni, na ca bhagavā paṭhamaṃ sāsanayuttikovidaṃ janaṃ katvā pacchā dhammaṃ deseti. Tena teneva pana suttena taṃ taṃ atthaṃ ñāpeti. Tasmā idha yaṃ yaṃ atthaṃ ekāyanamaggo sādheti, taṃ taṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassento “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”tiādimāha. Yasmā vā yā sattānaṃ visuddhi ekāyanamaggena saṃvattati, sā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamena hoti. Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamo dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamena, dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamo ñāyassādhigamena, ñāyassādhigamo nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya. Tasmā imampi kamaṃ dassento “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti vatvā “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”tiādimāha.

Here, although when it is said "for the purification of beings," the overcoming of sorrow and the like are already accomplished in meaning, they are not evident to others, except for those skilled in the connections of the Teaching. Nor does the Blessed One first make people skilled in the connections of the Teaching and then later preach the Dhamma. Instead, he makes those meanings known through this or that sutta. Therefore, here, showing whatever meaning the direct path accomplishes by making it evident, he stated, "for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation," and so on. Or, because the purification of beings that is brought about by the direct path occurs through the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation; and the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation occurs through the disappearance of pain and displeasure; and the disappearance of pain and displeasure occurs through the attainment of the right way; and the attainment of the right way occurs through the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, showing this sequence as well, after stating "for the purification of beings," he says, "for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation," and so on.

Apica vaṇṇabhaṇanametaṃ ekāyanamaggassa. Yatheva hi bhagavā – “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsessāmi yadidaṃ chachakkānī”ti (ma. ni. 3.420) chachakkadesanāya aṭṭhahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi. Yathā ca ariyavaṃsadesanāya “cattārome, bhikkhave, ariyavaṃsā aggaññā rattaññā vaṃsaññā porāṇā asaṃkiṇṇā asaṃkiṇṇapubbā na [M 2.0343] saṅkīyanti na saṅkīyissanti, appaṭikuṭṭhā samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhī”ti (a. ni. 4.28) navahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi; evaṃ imassāpi ekāyanamaggassa sattānaṃ visuddhiyātiādīhi sattahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi. Kasmāti ce, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ. Vaṇṇabhāsanañhi sutvā te bhikkhū “ayaṃ kira maggo hadayasantāpabhūtaṃ sokaṃ, vācāvippalāpabhūtaṃ [P 3.0752] paridevaṃ, kāyikaasātabhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ, cetasikaasātabhūtaṃ domanassanti [V 2.0308] cattāro upaddave hanati, visuddhiṃ ñāyaṃ nibbānanti tayo visese āvahatī”ti ussāhajātā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ dhāretabbaṃ, vācetabbaṃ, imañca maggaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ maññissanti. Iti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi. Kambalavāṇijādayo kambalādīnaṃ vaṇṇaṃ viya.

Moreover, this is a commendation of the direct path. Just as the Blessed One—"Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with meaning and phrasing; I will make known the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure, that is, the six sixes"—thus, in the discourse on the six sixes, he praised it with eight expressions. And as in the discourse on the noble lineages—"Monks, these four noble lineages are original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never previously adulterated, not being adulterated now, nor will they be in the future, unrebuked by wise ascetics and brahmins"—he praised it with nine expressions. Similarly, he praised this direct path with seven expressions, beginning with "for the purification of beings." Why? To generate enthusiasm in those monks. For upon hearing this commendation, those monks would think, "This path, it seems, eliminates the four afflictions—sorrow which is heartache, lamentation which is wailing, pain which is bodily unpleasantness, and displeasure which is mental unpleasantness—and brings the three special qualities: purification, the right way, and Nibbāna." Inspired, they would resolve: 'This teaching of the Dhamma should be learned, mastered, remembered, recited, and this path should be developed.' Thus, he praised it to generate enthusiasm in those monks, just as merchants praise their blankets and other goods.

Yathā hi satasahassagghanikapaṇḍukambalavāṇijena ‘kambalaṃ gaṇhathā’ti ugghositepi asukakambaloti na tāva manussā jānanti. Kesakambalavāḷakambalādayopi hi duggandhā kharasamphassā kambalātveva vuccanti. Yadā pana tena gandhārako rattakambalo sukhumo ujjalo sukhasamphassoti ugghositaṃ hoti, tadā ye pahonti, te gaṇhanti. Ye nappahonti, tepi dassanakāmā honti; evameva ‘ekāyano, bhikkhave, ayaṃ maggo’ti vuttepi asukamaggoti na tāva pākaṭo hoti. Nānappakārakā hi aniyyānikamaggāpi maggātveva vuccanti. “Sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”tiādimhi pana vutte “ayaṃ kira maggo cattāro upaddave hanati, tayo visese āvahatī”ti ussāhajātā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ dhāretabbaṃ vācetabbaṃ, imañca maggaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ maññissantīti vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanto “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”tiādimāha. Yathā ca satasahassagghanikapaṇḍukambalavāṇijūpamā; evaṃ rattajambunadasuvaṇṇaudakappasādakamaṇiratanasuvisuddhamuttaratanapavāḷādivāṇijūpamādayopettha āharitabbā.

Just as when a merchant selling a pale blanket worth a hundred thousand calls out, 'Buy a blanket!' people do not yet know which blanket it is. For blankets of human hair, horse-tail hair, and so forth are foul-smelling and rough to the touch, yet they are still called blankets. But when he announces, 'A fragrant, red blanket, soft, bright, and pleasant to the touch!' then those who can afford it buy it, and even those who cannot still wish to see it. In the same way, when it is said, 'Monks, this is the direct path,' the specific path is not yet apparent. For there are many kinds of paths that do not lead to deliverance, yet they are still called paths. But when 'For the purification of beings...' and so on, is said, then people become inspired, thinking, 'This path, it seems, destroys four afflictions and brings three special qualities!' They will consider that this teaching should be learned, mastered, remembered, and recited, and this path should be developed. Thus, speaking in praise of it, he says, 'For the purification of beings...' and so on. Just as the simile of the merchant selling the pale blanket worth a hundred thousand, so too should the similes of merchants selling red Jambu-river gold, water-purifying gems, exceedingly pure pearl-gems, coral, and so forth, be brought in here.

Yadidanti nipāto, ye imeti ayamassa attho. Cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Tena na tato heṭṭhā, na uddhanti satipaṭṭhānaparicchedaṃ dīpeti. Satipaṭṭhānāti tayo satipaṭṭhānā satigocaropi tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatāpi, satipi. “Catunnaṃ[M 2.0344], bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi, taṃ suṇātha…pe… ko ca, bhikkhave, kāyassa samudayo. Āhārasamudayā kāyassa samudayo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.408) hi [P 3.0753] satigocaro satipaṭṭhānanti vuccati. Tathā “kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ no sati, sati pana upaṭṭhānañceva sati cā”tiādīsupi (paṭi. ma. 3.35). Tassattho – patiṭṭhāti asminti paṭṭhānaṃ. Kā patiṭṭhāti? Sati. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, padhānaṃ ṭhānanti vā paṭṭhānaṃ. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ hatthiṭṭhānaassaṭṭhānādīni viya.

The word 'yadidaṃ' is a particle; 'ye ime' is its meaning. 'Cattāro' is a numerical determination. By this, it indicates the determination of the foundations of mindfulness as neither fewer nor more. The term 'satipaṭṭhāna' refers to the three foundations of mindfulness, the sphere of mindfulness, the Teacher's transcendence of aversion and attachment regarding disciples who have embarked on the threefold practice, and also mindfulness itself. For in passages such as, “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the arising and cessation of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that… and so on… And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of the body? From the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of the body,” the sphere of mindfulness is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Similarly, in passages like, “The body is an establishment, not mindfulness; mindfulness, however, is both an establishment and mindfulness.” Its meaning is as follows: that in which something is established is a 'paṭṭhāna'. What is established? Mindfulness. The establishment of mindfulness is 'satipaṭṭhāna'; or, 'paṭṭhāna' means a principal standing place. The establishment of mindfulness is 'satipaṭṭhāna', like an elephant's standing place, a horse's standing place, and so forth.

“Tayo satipaṭṭhānā yadariyo sevati, yadariyo sevamāno satthā gaṇamanusāsituṃ arahatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.311) ettha tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatā “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttā. Tassattho – paṭṭhapetabbato paṭṭhānaṃ, pavattayitabbatoti [V 2.0309] attho. Kena paṭṭhapetabbatoti? Satiyā. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta sambojjhaṅge paripūrentī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.147) pana satiyeva “satipaṭṭhānaṃ”ti vuccati. Tassattho – paṭṭhātīti paṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhāti okkanditvā pakkhanditvā pattharitvā pavattatīti attho. Satiyeva satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Atha vā saraṇaṭṭhena sati, upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ. Iti sati ca sā paṭṭhānaṃ cātipi satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Idamidhādhippetaṃ.

In the passage, “There are three foundations of mindfulness that the noble one cultivates, and by cultivating them, the Teacher is worthy to instruct the group,” the Teacher's transcendence of aversion and attachment regarding disciples who have embarked on the threefold practice is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Its meaning is: 'paṭṭhāna' because it is to be established, meaning it is to be set in motion. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness. The establishment by mindfulness is 'satipaṭṭhāna'. In passages such as, “When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment,” mindfulness itself is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Its meaning is: it is 'paṭṭhāna' because it is present, meaning it is present, having descended, having rushed forth, having spread out, having occurred. Mindfulness itself is 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Alternatively, 'sati' is in the sense of remembering, and 'paṭṭhāna' is in the sense of presence. Thus, it is 'satipaṭṭhāna' because it is both mindfulness (sati) and an establishment (paṭṭhāna). This is what is intended here.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā “satipaṭṭhānā”ti bahuvacanaṃ? Satibahuttā. Ārammaṇabhedena hi bahukā etā satiyo. Atha maggoti kasmā ekavacanaṃ? Maggaṭṭhena ekattā. Catassopi hi etā satiyo maggaṭṭhena ekattaṃ gacchanti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “maggoti kenaṭṭhena maggo? Nibbānagamanaṭṭhena. Nibbānatthikehi magganīyaṭṭhena cā”ti. Catassopi cetā aparabhāge kāyādīsu ārammaṇesu kiccaṃ sādhayamānā nibbānaṃ gacchanti, ādito paṭṭhāya ca nibbānatthikehi maggiyanti, tasmā catassopi eko maggoti vuccanti. Evañca sati vacanānusandhinā sānusandhikāva desanā hoti, “mārasenappamaddanaṃ, vo bhikkhave, maggaṃ desessāmi, taṃ suṇātha…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, mārasenappamaddano maggo? Yadidaṃ satta bojjhaṅgā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.224) viya. Yathā mārasenappamaddanoti ca, satta bojjhaṅgāti ca atthato ekaṃ, byañjanamevettha nānaṃ[M 2.0345]. Evaṃ “ekāyanamaggo”ti [P 3.0754] ca “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti ca atthato ekaṃ, byañjanamevettha nānaṃ, tasmā maggaṭṭhena ekattā ekavacanaṃ. Ārammaṇabhedena satibahuttā bahuvacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

If that is so, why is 'satipaṭṭhānā' in the plural? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulnesses. For these mindfulnesses are many due to the distinction of their objects. Then why is 'maggo' in the singular? Because of their unity in the sense of path. For these four mindfulnesses attain unity in the sense of path. For it has been said: “In what sense is it a path? In the sense of leading to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna.” For these four, subsequently accomplishing their task in regard to objects such as the body, go to Nibbāna, and from the beginning they are sought by those who desire Nibbāna; therefore, all four are called one path. And thus, by the connection of the words, the teaching becomes coherent, as in: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the path that crushes the army of Māra; listen to that… and so on… And what, bhikkhus, is the path that crushes the army of Māra? Namely, the seven factors of enlightenment.” Just as 'crushing the army of Māra' and 'the seven factors of enlightenment' are one in meaning, differing only in expression, so too 'the direct path' and 'the four foundations of mindfulness' are one in meaning, differing only in expression. Therefore, the singular is used because of their unity in the sense of path. The plural should be understood as due to the multiplicity of mindfulnesses because of the distinction of their objects.

Kasmā pana bhagavatā cattārova satipaṭṭhānā vuttā anūnā anadhikāti? Veneyyahitattā. Taṇhācaritadiṭṭhicaritasamathayānikavipassanāyānikesu hi mandatikkhavasena dvedhā dvedhā pavattesu veneyyesu mandassa taṇhācaritassa oḷārikaṃ kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa sukhumaṃ vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Diṭṭhicaritassapi mandassa nātippabhedagataṃ cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa atippabhedagataṃ dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo. Samathayānikassa ca mandassa akicchena adhigantabbanimittaṃ paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa oḷārikārammaṇe asaṇṭhahanato dutiyaṃ. Vipassanāyānikassapi mandassa nātippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ tatiyaṃ, tikkhassa atippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ catutthaṃ. Iti cattārova vuttā anūnā anadhikāti.

But why did the Blessed One teach only four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more? For the welfare of those to be trained. For among those to be trained—those of craving-temperament, those of view-temperament, those whose vehicle is serenity, and those whose vehicle is insight—who proceed in two ways each, as dull and sharp: for the dull one of craving-temperament, the coarse contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness is the path of purification; for the sharp one, the subtle contemplation of feelings. For the dull one of view-temperament, the contemplation of mind, not gone to excessive differentiation, is the path of purification; for the sharp one, the contemplation of phenomena, gone to extreme differentiation. And for the dull one whose vehicle is serenity, the first foundation of mindfulness, whose sign is to be attained without difficulty, is the path of purification; for the sharp one, the second is the path, because of not settling on coarse objects. And for the dull one whose vehicle is insight, the third, whose object is not gone to excessive differentiation, is the path of purification; for the sharp one, the fourth, whose object is gone to extreme differentiation. Thus, only four are taught, neither fewer nor more.

Subhasukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsappahānatthaṃ [V 2.0310] vā. Kāyo hi asubho, tattha ca subhavipallāsavipallatthā sattā. Tesaṃ tattha asubhabhāvadassanena tassa vipallāsassa pahānatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Sukhaṃ niccaṃ attāti gahitesupi ca vedanādīsu vedanā dukkhā, cittaṃ aniccaṃ, dhammā anattā, tesu ca sukhaniccaattavipallāsavipallatthā sattā. Tesaṃ tattha dukkhādibhāvadassanena tesaṃ vipallāsānaṃ pahānatthaṃ sesāni tīṇi vuttānīti evaṃ subhasukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsappahānatthaṃ vā cattārova vuttā anūnā anadhikāti veditabbā. Na kevalañca vipallāsappahānatthameva, atha kho caturoghayogāsavaganthaupādānaagatipahānatthampi catubbidhāhārapariññatthañca cattārova vuttāti veditabbā. Ayaṃ tāva pakaraṇanayo.

Or, it is for the abandonment of the perversions regarding the beautiful, pleasure, permanence, and self. For the body is unbeautiful, and beings are perverted by the perversion regarding the beautiful in it. To abandon that perversion by seeing its unbeautiful nature, the first foundation of mindfulness is taught. And also, regarding feelings and so on that are taken as pleasure, permanence, and self: feelings are suffering, consciousness is impermanent, and phenomena are non-self; yet beings are perverted by the perversions regarding pleasure, permanence, and self in them. To abandon those perversions by seeing their nature as suffering and so on, the remaining three are taught. Thus, it should be understood that the four are taught for the abandonment of the perversions regarding the beautiful, pleasure, permanence, and self—neither fewer nor more. And it should be understood that the four are taught not only for the abandonment of perversions, but also for the abandonment of the four floods, yokes, taints, bonds, clingings, and wrong courses, and for the full understanding of the four kinds of nutriment. This, for now, is the method of the treatise.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana saraṇavasena ceva ekattasamosaraṇavasena ca ekameva satipaṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇavasena cattāroti etadeva vuttaṃ. Yathā [P 3.0755] hi catudvāre nagare pācīnato āgacchantā pācīnadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, dakkhiṇato. Pacchimato. Uttarato āgacchantā uttaradisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā uttaradvārena nagarameva pavisanti; evaṃ – sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nagaraṃ viya [M 2.0346] hi nibbānamahānagaraṃ, dvāraṃ viya aṭṭhaṅgiko lokuttaramaggo, pācīnadisādayo viya kāyādayo.

In the commentary, however, it is stated that by way of its function of recollection and by way of its convergence on a single goal, there is only one establishment of mindfulness, but by way of its objects, there are four. For just as in a city with four gates, those coming from the east take goods originating in the eastern region and enter the city through the eastern gate, and similarly those coming from the south, west, and north take goods originating in their respective regions and enter through their respective gates—so too should this matter be understood. The great city of Nibbāna is like the city, the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path is like the gate, and the body and so on are like the eastern and other directions.

Yathā pācīnato āgacchantā pācīnadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ kāyānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā kāyānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti. Yathā dakkhiṇato āgacchantā dakkhiṇāya disāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ vedanānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā vedanānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti. Yathā pacchimato āgacchantā pacchimadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pacchimadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ cittānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā cittānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti. Yathā uttarato āgacchantā uttaradisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā uttaradvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ dhammānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā dhammānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti. Evaṃ saraṇavasena ceva ekattasamosaraṇavasena ca ekameva satipaṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇavasena cattārova vuttāti veditabbā.

Just as those coming from the east, taking goods originating in the eastern direction, enter the city through the eastern gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of the body, having developed the contemplation of the body in its fourteen aspects, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the Noble Path produced by the power of developing the contemplation of the body. Just as those coming from the south, taking goods originating in the southern direction, enter the city through the southern gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of feeling, having developed the contemplation of feeling in its nine aspects, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the Noble Path produced by the power of developing the contemplation of feeling. Just as those coming from the west, taking goods originating in the western direction, enter the city through the western gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of consciousness, having developed the contemplation of consciousness in its sixteen aspects, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the Noble Path produced by the power of developing the contemplation of consciousness. Just as those coming from the north, taking goods originating in the northern direction, enter the city through the northern gate, so too, those approaching by way of the contemplation of phenomena, having developed the contemplation of phenomena in its five aspects, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the Noble Path produced by the power of developing the contemplation of phenomena. Thus, it should be understood that by way of its function of recollection and by way of its convergence on a single goal, there is only one establishment of mindfulness, but by way of its objects, there are four.

Katame [V 2.0311] cattāroti kathetukamyatā pucchā. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Bhikkhaveti dhammapaṭiggāhakapuggalālapanametaṃ. Bhikkhūti paṭipattisampādakapuggalanidassanametaṃ. Aññepi ca devamanussā paṭipattiṃ sampādentiyeva, seṭṭhattā pana paṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanato ca “bhikkhū”ti āha. Bhagavato hi anusāsaniṃ sampaṭicchantesu bhikkhu seṭṭho, sabbappakārāya anusāsaniyā bhājanabhāvato. Tasmā seṭṭhattā “bhikkhū”ti [P 3.0756] āha. Tasmiṃ gahite pana sesā gahitāva honti, rājagamanādīsu rājaggahaṇena sesaparisā viya. Yo ca imaṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjati, so bhikkhu nāma hotīti paṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanatopi “bhikkhū”ti āha. Paṭipannako hi devo vā hotu manusso vā, bhikkhūti saṅkhyaṃ gacchatiyeva yathāha –

What are the four? This is a question posed out of a desire to explain. Here—in this Dispensation. “Bhikkhus”—this is an address to the individuals who receive the Dhamma. “A bhikkhu”—this is an indication of an individual who accomplishes the practice. Other devas and humans also accomplish the practice, but the term “bhikkhu” is used because of the excellence of the practice and because it reveals the state of a bhikkhu. For among those who accept the Blessed One’s instruction, the bhikkhu is the most excellent, being a vessel for all kinds of instruction. Therefore, due to this excellence, the term “bhikkhu” is used. When such a one is taken, the others are also taken, just as in royal processions and so on, by taking the king, the rest of the retinue is implied. And whoever undertakes this practice is called a bhikkhu—thus, also because the practice reveals the state of a bhikkhu, the term “bhikkhu” is used. For whether a deva or a human, one who has entered upon the practice is reckoned as a bhikkhu, as it is said—

“Alaṅkato [M 2.0347] cepi samaṃ careyya,

Santo danto niyato brahmacārī;

Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ,

So brāhmaṇo so samaṇo sa bhikkhū”ti. (dha. pa. 142);

“Though adorned, if one lives equanimously, calm, tamed, resolute, a celibate; having laid down the rod towards all beings—he is a brahmin, he is a recluse, he is a bhikkhu.”

Kāyeti rūpakāye. Rūpakāyo hi idha aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kesādīnañca dhammānaṃ samūhaṭṭhena hatthikāyarathakāyādayo viya kāyoti adhippeto. Yathā ca samūhaṭṭhena, evaṃ kucchitānaṃ āyaṭṭhena. Kucchitānañhi paramajegucchānaṃ so āyotipi kāyo. Āyoti uppattideso. Tatthāyaṃ vacanattho. Āyanti tatoti āyo. Ke āyanti? Kucchitā kesādayo. Iti kucchitānaṃ āyoti kāyo.

“Body” means the form-body. For here, the form-body is intended as “body” in the sense of an aggregation—like an elephant-body or a chariot-body—due to being an aggregate of limbs and parts, and of constituents such as hair. And just as it is a 'body' in the sense of an aggregation, so it is also in the sense of being a resort for the repulsive. For since it is a resort for what is repulsive and utterly disgusting, it is called a 'body' (kāya). “Resort” (āya) means the place of origination. Here is the etymological meaning: They come (āyanti) to it, therefore it is a resort (āyo). What comes? Repulsive things like hair and so on. Thus, because it is a resort for repulsive things, it is a 'body'.

Kāyānupassīti kāye anupassanasīlo kāyaṃ vā anupassamāno. Kāyeti ca vatvāpi puna kāyānupassīti dutiyakāyaggahaṇaṃ asammissato vavatthānaghanavinibbhogādidassanatthaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Tena na kāye vedanānupassī vā, cittadhammānupassī vā, atha kho kāyānupassīyevāti kāyasaṅkhāte vatthusmiṃ kāyānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā na kāye aṅgapaccaṅgavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, nāpi kesalomādivinimuttaitthipurisānupassī, yopi cettha kesalomādiko bhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhāto kāyo, tatthapi na bhūtupādāyavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, atha kho rathasambhārānupassako viya aṅgapaccaṅgasamūhānupassī, nagarāvayavānupassako viya kesalomādisamūhānupassī, kadalikkhandhapattavaṭṭivinibbhujako viya rittamuṭṭhiviniveṭhako viya ca bhūtupādāyasamūhānupassīyevāti nānappakārato samūhavaseneva kāyasaṅkhātassa vatthuno dassanena ghanavinibbhogo [V 2.0312] dassito hoti. Na hettha [P 3.0757] yathāvuttasamūhavinimutto kāyo vā itthī vā puriso vā añño vā koci dhammo dissati, yathāvuttadhammasamūhamatteyeva pana tathā tathā sattā micchābhinivesaṃ karonti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

“Observing the body” means one whose nature is to observe the body, or one who is observing the body. Even after saying “in the body,” the repetition of “body” in the term “observing the body” should be understood as being for the purpose of showing the unmixed determination, the analysis of the compact, and so on. Thus, it is not observing feelings in the body, nor observing consciousness or phenomena, but solely observing the body. By this, in showing the very mode of contemplating the body in the object designated as 'body', the unmixed determination is shown. Similarly, it is not observing a single phenomenon detached from limbs and parts in the body, nor observing a man or woman separate from hair, body-hair, etc. Even in the case of the body here, which is designated as a collection of the primary elements and derived matter, it is not observing a single phenomenon apart from the primary elements and derived matter. Instead, just as one observes the assembled parts of a chariot, or the components of a city, or as one peels away the layers of a banana trunk, or as one unfolds an empty fist, so too is one observing the body as an aggregate of primary elements and derived matter. In this way, the analysis of the compact is shown by viewing the object designated as 'body' only in terms of its composite nature in various ways. For here, no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon is seen apart from the aforementioned aggregate. Yet beings wrongly cling to this very aggregate of phenomena in various ways. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yaṃ passati na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passati;

Apassaṃ bajjhate mūḷho, bajjhamāno na muccatī”ti.

“What one sees is not seen; what is seen, that one does not see. Not seeing, the deluded one is bound; being bound, one is not freed.”

Ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthanti [M 2.0348] vuttaṃ, ādisaddena cettha ayampi attho veditabbo. Ayañhi etasmiṃ kāye kāyānupassīyeva, na añña dhammānupassīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā anudakabhūtāyapi marīciyā udakānupassino honti, na evaṃ aniccadukkhānattaasubhabhūteyeva imasmiṃ kāye niccasukhaattasubhabhāvānupassī, atha kho kāyānupassī aniccadukkhānattaasubhākārasamūhānupassīyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yvāyaṃ parato “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā…pe… so satova assasatī”tiādinā nayena assāsapassāsādicuṇṇikajātaaṭṭhikapariyosāno kāyo vutto, yo ca “idhekacco pathavīkāyaṃ aniccato anupassati, āpokāyaṃ tejokāyaṃ vāyokāyaṃ kesakāyaṃ lomakāyaṃ chavikāyaṃ cammakāyaṃ maṃsakāyaṃ rudhirakāyaṃ nhārukāyaṃ aṭṭhikāyaṃ aṭṭhimiñjakāya”nti (paṭi. ma. 3.35) paṭisambhidāyaṃ kāyo vutto, tassa sabbassa imasmiññeva kāye anupassanato kāye kāyānupassīti evampi attho veditabbo.

It is said for the purpose of seeing the dissolution of solidity, etc., and by the word 'etc.,' this meaning should also be understood here. For here, one is a contemplator of the body in the body, not a contemplator of other phenomena—this is what is meant. Just as people perceive water in a mirage, though it is waterless, so too, in this body—which is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure—one does not perceive it as permanent, pleasant, self, or pure. Rather, one contemplates the body as a collection of characteristics that are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure—this is what is meant. Alternatively, there is the body described later in the passage, 'Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest... mindfully breathes in,' and so on, up to the description of bones reduced to powder, as well as the body described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'Here, someone contemplates the earth element as impermanent, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the hair element, the body hair element, the skin element, the hide element, the flesh element, the blood element, the sinew element, the bone element, the bone marrow element' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.35)—because one contemplates all of that within this very body, the meaning 'contemplating the body in the body' should also be understood in this way.

Atha vā kāye ahanti vā mamanti vā evaṃ gahetabbassa yassa kassaci ananupassanato, tassa tasseva pana kesalomādikassa nānādhammasamūhassa anupassanato kāye kesādidhammasamūhasaṅkhātakāyānupassīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood thus: because one does not contemplate anyone in the body who is to be grasped as 'I' or 'mine,' but rather contemplates that very aggregation of diverse phenomena such as hair and so forth, one is a contemplator of the body in the body, that is, one who contemplates the body as an aggregation of phenomena such as hair.

Apica “imasmiṃ kāye aniccato anupassati, no niccato”tiādinā anukkamena paṭisambhidāyaṃ āgatanayassa sabbasseva aniccalakkhaṇādino ākārasamūhasaṅkhātassa kāyassa anupassanatopi kāye kāyānupassīti evampi attho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā [P 3.0758] hi ayaṃ kāye kāyānupassanāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhu imaṃ kāyaṃ aniccānupassanādīnaṃ sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena aniccato anupassati, no niccato. Dukkhato anupassati, no sukhato. Anattato anupassati, no attato. Nibbindati, no nandati, virajjati, no rajjati, nirodheti. No samudeti, paṭinissajjati, no ādiyati. So taṃ aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati[V 2.0313], dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ pajahati, anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ pajahati, nibbindanto nandiṃ pajahati[M 2.0349], virajjanto rāgaṃ pajahati, nirodhento samudayaṃ pajahati, paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahatīti veditabbo.

Furthermore, according to the method presented in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, beginning with the statement 'in this body, one contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent,' and so on, the meaning should also be understood thus: because one contemplates the entire body, which is designated as a collection of characteristics beginning with the mark of impermanence, this is also 'contemplating the body in the body.' For indeed, a monk who has embarked on this practice of contemplating the body in the body contemplates this body by way of the seven contemplations: he contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent; as suffering, not as pleasant; as non-self, not as self; he becomes disenchanted, he does not delight; he becomes dispassionate, he is not passionate; he brings it to cessation, he does not cause it to arise; he relinquishes, he does not grasp. Thus, it should be understood that by contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence; by contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure; by contemplating it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self; by becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight; by becoming dispassionate, he abandons passion; by bringing it to cessation, he abandons arising; by relinquishing, he abandons grasping.

Viharatīti iriyati. Ātāpīti tīsu bhavesu kilese ātāpetīti ātāpo, vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ātāpo assa atthīti ātāpī. Sampajānoti sampajaññasaṅkhātena ñāṇena samannāgato. Satimāti kāyapariggāhikāya satiyā samannāgato. Ayaṃ pana yasmā satiyā ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā paññāya anupassati, na hi sativirahitassa anupassanā nāma atthi, tenevāha – “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Tasmā ettha “kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”ti ettāvatā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yasmā anātāpino antosaṅkhepo antarāyakaro hoti, asampajāno upāyapariggahe anupāyaparivajjane ca sammuyhati, muṭṭhassati upāyāpariccāge anupāyāpariggahe ca asamattho hoti, tenassa taṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sampajjati. Tasmā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ānubhāvena taṃ sampajjati, tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ “ātāpī sampajāno satimā”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“He dwells” means he comports himself. “Ardent” refers to ardor, which is a term for energy, because it burns up the defilements in the three realms of existence. One who possesses this ardor is called “ardent.” “Clearly comprehending” means endowed with the knowledge known as clear comprehension. “Mindful” means endowed with the mindfulness that apprehends the body. Moreover, since one apprehends the object with mindfulness and contemplates it with wisdom—for there is no such thing as contemplation for one devoid of mindfulness—it is said: “Indeed, monks, I say that mindfulness is beneficial everywhere” (SN 5.234). Thus, here, by the phrase 'he dwells contemplating the body in the body,' the establishment of mindfulness with regard to the contemplation of the body is stated. Alternatively, for one who is not ardent, inner sloth becomes an obstacle; one who is not clearly comprehending is confused about adopting the right means and avoiding the wrong means; and one who is not mindful is incapable of relinquishing the wrong means and adopting the right means. For such a one, that meditation subject does not succeed. Therefore, to show the qualities by whose power it does succeed, it should be understood that this was said: “ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful.”

Iti kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ sampayogaṅgañcassa dassetvā idāni pahānaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti vuttaṃ. Tattha vineyyāti tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā vinayitvā. Loketi tasmiññeva kāye. Kāyo hi idha lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti adhippeto. Yasmā panassa na kāyamatteyeva abhijjhādomanassaṃ pahīyati, vedanādīsupi pahīyatiyeva. Tasmā pañcapi upādānakkhandhā lokoti vibhaṅge vuttaṃ. Lokasaṅkhātattā [P 3.0759] vā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ atthuddhāranayenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panāha – “tattha katamo loko? Sveva kāyo loko”ti, ayamevettha attho. Tasmiṃ loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ vineyyāti evaṃ sambandho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā panettha abhijjhāggahaṇena kāmacchando, domanassaggahaṇena byāpādo saṅgahaṃ gacchati, tasmā nīvaraṇapariyāpannabalavadhammadvayadassanena nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, having shown the establishment of mindfulness regarding the body and its associated factor, now, to show the factor of abandoning, it is said: 'having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world.' Herein, 'having subdued' means having subdued either by substitution or by suppression. 'In the world' refers to that very body. For here, the body is intended as 'the world' in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating. However, since covetousness and displeasure are not abandoned with regard to the body alone, but are also abandoned with regard to feelings and so forth, it is therefore said in the Vibhaṅga that the five aggregates subject to clinging are 'the world.' Or, this is said by way of extracting the meaning, because these phenomena are designated as 'the world.' But when it is said: 'Herein, what is the world? Just this body is the world,' this is the meaning here. The connection should be seen thus: 'having subdued covetousness and displeasure in that world.' Moreover, since here the term 'covetousness' includes sensual desire, and the term 'displeasure' includes ill will, it should be understood that the abandoning of the hindrances is spoken of by showing these two powerful states included among the hindrances.

Visesena [M 2.0350] cettha abhijjhāvinayena kāyasampattimūlakassa anurodhassa, domanassavinayena kāyavipattimūlakassa virodhassa, abhijjhāvinayena ca kāye abhiratiyā, domanassavinayena kāyabhāvanāya anabhiratiyā, abhijjhāvinayena kāye abhūtānaṃ subhasukhabhāvādīnaṃ pakkhepassa, domanassavinayena [V 2.0314] kāye bhūtānaṃ asubhāsukhabhāvādīnaṃ apanayanassa ca pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena yogāvacarassa yogānubhāvo yogasamatthatā ca dīpitā hoti. Yogānubhāvo hi esa, yadidaṃ anurodhavirodhavippamutto aratiratisaho abhūtapakkhepabhūtāpanayanavirahito ca hoti. Anurodhavirodhavippamutto cesa aratiratisaho abhūtaṃ apakkhipanto bhūtañca anapanayanto yogasamattho hotīti.

Here, in particular, the abandoning of attraction rooted in bodily attainment through the removal of covetousness is stated; the abandoning of aversion rooted in bodily adversity through the removal of displeasure; through the removal of covetousness, delight in the body; through the removal of displeasure, discontent regarding the cultivation of the body; through the removal of covetousness, the imputation of unreal states such as beauty, pleasure, etc., to the body; and through the removal of displeasure, the removal of real states such as ugliness, suffering, etc., from the body. Thus, the meditator's meditative power and competence in meditation are revealed. For this is meditative power: that one is free from attraction and aversion, is able to endure discontent and delight, and is devoid of projecting the unreal and removing the real. And being free from attraction and aversion, enduring discontent and delight, not projecting the unreal, and not removing the real—one is competent in meditation.

Aparo nayo “kāye kāyānupassī”ti ettha anupassanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. “Viharatī”ti ettha vuttavihārena kammaṭṭhānikassa kāyapariharaṇaṃ, “ātāpī”tiādīsu pana ātāpena sammappadhānaṃ, satisampajaññena sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ, kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇūpāyo vā. Satiyā vā kāyānupassanāvasena paṭiladdhasamatho, sampajaññena vipassanā abhijjhādomanassavinayena bhāvanābalaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Another method: Here, by 'contemplating the body in the body,' the meditation subject for contemplation is stated. By 'he dwells,' the meditator's proper conduct in maintaining the body is stated. And in 'ardent,' etc., ardour signifies right effort; mindfulness and clear comprehension signify the meditation subject in all aspects, or the means of maintaining the meditation subject. Or, through mindfulness, tranquility is attained by way of contemplating the body; through clear comprehension, insight; and through the removal of covetousness and displeasure, the strength of development—this should be understood.

Vibhaṅge pana anupassīti tattha “katamā anupassanā? Yā paññā pajānanā vicayo pavicayo dhammavicayo sallakkhaṇā upalakkhaṇā paccupalakkhaṇā paṇḍiccaṃ kosallaṃ nepuññaṃ vebhabyā cintā upaparikkhā bhūrīmedhā pariṇāyikā vipassanā sampajaññaṃ patodo paññā paññindriyaṃ paññābalaṃ paññāsatthaṃ paññāpāsādo paññāāloko paññāobhāso paññāpajjoto paññāratanaṃ amoho dhammavicayo sammādiṭṭhi, ayaṃ vuccati anupassanā. Imāya anupassanāya upeto hoti samupeto upagato samupagato upapanno samannāgato, tena vuccati anupassīti. Viharatīti iriyati pavattati pāleti yapeti yāpeti carati viharati, tena vuccati viharatīti. Ātāpīti tattha katamaṃ ātāpaṃ? Yo cetasiko vīriyārambho nikammo parakkamo uyyāmo vāyāmo ussāho ussoḷhī thāmo dhiti asithilaparakkamatā anikkhittaddandatā anikkhittadhuratā dhurasampaggāhī vīriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ vīriyabalaṃ sammāvāyāmo, idaṃ vuccati ātāpaṃ. Iminā ātāpena upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato[P 3.0760], tena vuccati ātāpīti. Sampajānoti tattha katamaṃ sampajaññaṃ? Yā paññā pajānanā vicayo pavicayo dhammavicayo sallakkhaṇā upalakkhaṇā paccupalakkhaṇā paṇḍiccaṃ kosallaṃ nepuññaṃ vebhabyā cintā upaparikkhā bhūrīmedhā pariṇāyikā vipassanā sampajaññaṃ patodo paññā paññindriyaṃ paññābalaṃ paññāsatthaṃ paññāpāsādo paññāāloko paññāobhāso paññāpajjoto paññāratanaṃ amoho dhammavicayo sammādiṭṭhi, idaṃ vuccati sampajaññaṃ. Iminā sampajaññena upeto hoti [V 2.0315] …pe… samannāgato, tena vuccati sampajānoti. Satimāti tattha katamā sati? Yā sati anussati paṭissati sati saraṇatā dhāraṇatā apilāpanatā asammusanatā sati satindriyaṃ satibalaṃ sammāsati[M 2.0351], ayaṃ vuccati sati. Imāya satiyā upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato, tena vuccati satimāti.

In the Vibhaṅga, regarding “one who contemplates”: What is contemplation? It is wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, marking, examining, counter-examining, expertise, skill, intelligence, analysis, reflection, scrutiny, abundant wisdom, guidance, insight, clear comprehension, the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the pinnacle of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called contemplation. One who is endowed with this contemplation, fully endowed, has approached it, fully approached, attained it, and is possessed of it, is called “one who contemplates.” “Dwells”: moves, proceeds, maintains, conducts, keeps going, behaves, dwells—thus it is called “dwells.” “Ardent”: What is ardour? It is the mental stirring of energy, commencement, exertion, endeavour, effort, striving, zeal, enthusiasm, strength, resolve, unrelaxed exertion, not laying aside the burden, not shirking responsibility, bearing responsibility, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, right effort—this is called ardour. One who is endowed with this ardour… possessed of it, is called “ardent.” “Clearly comprehending”: What is clear comprehension? It is wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, marking, examining, counter-examining, expertise, skill, intelligence, analysis, reflection, scrutiny, abundant wisdom, guidance, insight, clear comprehension, the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the pinnacle of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called clear comprehension. One who is endowed with this clear comprehension… possessed of it, is called “clearly comprehending.” “Mindful”: What is mindfulness?
