It is mindfulness, recollection, remembrance, mindfulness, remembering, retention, non-forgetfulness, non-confusion, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness—this is called mindfulness. One who is endowed with this mindfulness… possessed of it, is called “mindful.”

Vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti tattha katamo loko? Sveva kāyo loko. Pañcapi upādānakkhandhā loko, ayaṃ vuccati loko. Tattha katamā abhijjhā? Yo rāgo sārāgo anunayo anurodho nandī nandirāgo cittassa sārāgo, ayaṃ vuccati abhijjhā. Tattha katamaṃ domanassaṃ? Yaṃ cetasikaṃ asātaṃ cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ cetosamphassajā asātā dukkhā vedanā, idaṃ vuccati domanassaṃ. Iti ayañca abhijjhā, idañca domanassaṃ imamhi loke vinītā honti paṭivinītā santā samitā vūpasamitā atthaṅgatā abbhatthaṅgatā appitā byappitā sositā visositā byantīkatā, tena vuccati vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa”nti (vibha. 357-362).

“Having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world”—here, what is the world? Indeed, this body is the world. The five aggregates subject to clinging are the world; this is called the world. Here, what is covetousness? That which is lust, intense lust, affection, attraction, delight, lustful delight, intense lust of the mind—this is called covetousness. Here, what is displeasure? Whatever is mental unpleasantness, mental suffering, the unpleasant, painful feeling born of mind-contact—this is called displeasure. Thus, this covetousness and this displeasure, having been removed, utterly removed, calmed, quieted, pacified, extinguished, passed away, disappeared, dismissed, dispelled, dried up, completely dried up, brought to an end in this world—therefore it is said, ‘having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.’

Evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho vutto. Tena saha ayaṃ aṭṭhakathānayo yathā saṃsandati, evaṃ veditabbo. Ayaṃ tāva kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānuddesassa atthavaṇṇanā.

Thus the meaning of these terms has been stated. And in connection with this, the method of the commentary should be understood as it corresponds. This, then, is the exposition of the meaning of the summary section on the contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness.

Idāni vedanāsu. Citte. Dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati…pe… vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti ettha vedanāsu vedanānupassīti evamādīsu vedanādīnaṃ puna vacane payojanaṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī. Citte cittānupassī. Dhammesu dhammānupassīti ettha pana vedanāti tisso vedanā, tā ca lokiyā eva. Cittampi lokiyaṃ, tathā dhammā. Tesaṃ vibhāgo niddesavāre pākaṭo bhavissati. Kevalaṃ panidha yathā vedanā anupassitabbā, tathā tā anupassanto “vedanāsu vedanānupassī”ti veditabbo. Esa nayo cittadhammesupi. Kathañca vedanā anupassitabbāti? Sukhā tāva vedanā dukkhato, dukkhā sallato, adukkhamasukhā aniccato. Yathāha –

Now, regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena: ‘one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena… having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.’ Here, the purpose of the repetition of terms like ‘contemplating feelings in feelings’ and so on, regarding feelings and the rest, should be understood in the same way as was stated in the contemplation of the body. As for ‘contemplating feelings in feelings,’ ‘mind in mind,’ and ‘phenomena in phenomena,’ here ‘feelings’ refers to the three kinds of feelings, and these are only mundane. The mind is also mundane, and so are phenomena. Their classification will become clear in the exposition section. However, here it should simply be understood that just as feelings are to be contemplated, so one who contemplates them thus is to be known as ‘one who contemplates feelings in feelings.’ The same method applies to mind and phenomena. And how are feelings to be contemplated? Pleasant feeling, first, as suffering; painful feeling as a dart; and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it is said:

“Yo [M 2.0352][P 3.0761] sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, addakkhi naṃ aniccato;

Sa ve sammaddaso bhikkhu, upasanto carissatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 4.253);

“He who saw pleasure as suffering, saw suffering as a dart; saw the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant as impermanent—truly, that monk, rightly seeing, will fare on, calmed.”

Sabbā [V 2.0316] eva cetā “dukkhā”tipi anupassitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ, taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259). Sukhadukkhatopi ca anupassitabbā. Yathāha “sukhā vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.465) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Apica aniccādisattaanupassanāvasenapi anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ niddesavāreyeva pākaṭaṃ bhavissati.

All these, too, are to be contemplated as “suffering.” For it has been said: “Whatever is felt, that I declare to be in suffering.” And they are also to be contemplated in terms of pleasure and pain. As it is said: “Pleasant feeling is pleasant while it lasts, and painful when it changes.” All this should be elaborated. Moreover, they are also to be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence. The rest will become clear in the exposition section itself.

Cittadhammesupi cittaṃ tāva ārammaṇādhipatisahajātabhūmikammavipākakiriyādinānattabhedānaṃ aniccādianupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasarāgādibhedānañca vasena anupassitabbaṃ. Dhammā salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇānaṃ suññatadhammassa aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasantādibhedānañca vasena anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Kāmañcettha yassa kāyasaṅkhāte loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ pahīnaṃ, tassa vedanādīsupi taṃ pahīnameva. Nānāpuggalavasena pana nānācittakkhaṇikasatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāvasena ca sabbattha vuttaṃ. Yato vā ekattha pahīnaṃ sesesupi pahīnaṃ hoti, tenevassa tattha pahānadassanatthampi etaṃ vuttanti veditabbanti.

As for mind and phenomena, the mind, first, is to be contemplated by way of the various distinctions such as object, dominance, co-arising, bases, kamma, result, and functional activity; by way of the contemplations beginning with impermanence; and by way of the distinctions beginning with passion that appear in the exposition section. Phenomena are to be contemplated by way of their specific characteristics and general characteristics, by way of the phenomenon of emptiness, by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence, and by way of the distinctions beginning with the serene that appear in the exposition section. The rest is to be understood in the same way as stated. Although for one in whom covetousness and displeasure have been abandoned in the world designated as the body, they are abandoned in feelings and the rest as well. However, it has been stated everywhere by way of different individuals and by way of the cultivation of the establishments of mindfulness at different moments of consciousness. Or, because what is abandoned in one place is also abandoned in the remaining places, this has been stated to show its abandonment there as well.

Uddesavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on the summary section is concluded.

Kāyānupassanā ānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Contemplation of the Body: The Section on In-and-Out Breathing

374. Idāni seyyathāpi nāma cheko vilīvakārako thūlakilañjasaṇhakilañjacaṅkoṭakapeḷāpuṭādīni upakaraṇāni kattukāmo ekaṃ mahāveṇuṃ labhitvā catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ veṇukhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā phāletvā taṃ taṃ upakaraṇaṃ kareyya, evameva bhagavā satipaṭṭhānadesanāya sattānaṃ anekappakāraṃ [P 3.0762] visesādhigamaṃ kattukāmo ekameva sammāsatiṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame [M 2.0353] cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”tiādinā nayena ārammaṇavasena catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā kāyaṃ vibhajanto “kathañca bhikkhave”tiādinā nayena niddesavāraṃ vattumāraddho.

374. Now, just as a skilled basket-maker, wishing to make various implements such as coarse mats, fine mats, baskets, and boxes, would obtain a large bamboo, split it into four parts, and then take each piece of bamboo, split it further, and fashion the desired implement—in the same way, the Blessed One, wishing to enable beings to attain various kinds of special attainments through the teaching of the establishments of mindfulness, took the single right mindfulness and divided it into four parts by way of objects, saying, “There are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body,” and so on. Then, taking each establishment of mindfulness, he began to set forth the exposition section by analyzing the body, saying, “And how, monks…”

Tattha kathañcātiādi vitthāretukamyatāpucchā. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave, kena ca [V 2.0317] pakārena bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatīti? Esa nayo sabbapucchāvāresu. Idha bhikkhave bhikkhūti bhikkhave imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Ayañhettha idhasaddo sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano ca. Vuttañhetaṃ “idheva bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139). Tena vuttaṃ “imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū”ti.

Here, the phrase “And how…” is a question indicating the desire to elaborate. This is the concise meaning here: “Monks, in what way does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body?” This is the method in all question sections. “Here, monks” means “a monk in this dispensation.” For here, the word “here” elucidates the dispensation as the support for a person who brings forth all kinds of contemplation of the body, and also denies such a state in other dispensations. As it is said: “Here alone, monks, is there a recluse… empty are the doctrines of others.” Therefore, it is said, “a monk in this dispensation.”

Araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vāti idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ. Imassa hi bhikkhuno dīgharattaṃ rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu anuvisaṭaṃ cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ otarituṃ na icchati, kūṭagoṇayuttaratho viya uppathameva dhāvati. Tasmā seyyathāpi nāma gopo kūṭadhenuyā sabbaṃ khīraṃ pivitvā vaḍḍhitaṃ kūṭavacchaṃ dametukāmo dhenuto apanetvā ekamante mahantaṃ thambhaṃ nikhaṇitvā tattha yottena bandheyya. Athassa so vaccho ito cito ca vipphanditvā palāyituṃ asakkonto tameva thambhaṃ upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā, evameva imināpi bhikkhunā dīgharattaṃ rūpārammaṇādirasapānavaḍḍhitaṃ duṭṭhacittaṃ dametukāmena rūpādiārammaṇato apanetvā araññaṃ vā rukkhamūlaṃ vā suññāgāraṃ vā pavisitvā tattha satipaṭṭhānārammaṇatthambhe satiyottena [P 3.0763] bandhitabbaṃ. Evamassa taṃ cittaṃ ito cito ca vipphanditvāpi pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇaṃ alabhamānaṃ satiyottaṃ chinditvā palāyituṃ asakkontaṃ tamevārammaṇaṃ upacārappanāvasena upanisīdati ceva upanipajjati ca. Tenāhu porāṇā –

“Whether he has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling”—this elucidates the selection of a suitable dwelling conducive to the development of the establishments of mindfulness. For this monk’s mind, long engrossed in objects such as forms, does not wish to enter the path of the meditation subject; like a cart yoked to a rogue ox, it runs only on the wrong path. Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a rogue calf grown strong by drinking all the milk of a rogue cow, would take it away from its mother, drive a large post firmly into the ground, and tie the calf there with a rope—then that calf, struggling and thrashing here and there, unable to escape, would eventually settle down by sitting or lying near that very post—in the same way, this monk, wishing to tame his vicious mind long nourished by the taste of objects such as forms, should withdraw from such objects, enter the forest, the root of a tree, or an empty dwelling, and there bind it to the post of the object of mindfulness with the rope of mindfulness. Thus, though his mind struggles and thrashes here and there, unable to find its previously familiar objects, and unable to break the rope of mindfulness and escape, it settles down by approaching and resting upon that very object in terms of access and absorption. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Yathā thambhe nibandheyya, vacchaṃ damaṃ naro idha;

Bandheyyevaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ, satiyārammaṇe daḷha”nti.

“Just as a man here would tie a calf to be tamed to a post, so should he bind his own mind firmly to the object with mindfulness.”

Evamassetaṃ [M 2.0354] senāsanaṃ bhāvanānurūpaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpana”nti.

Thus, this dwelling is suitable for his development. Therefore, it is said: “This is an elucidation of the selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of the establishments of mindfulness.”

Apica yasmā idaṃ kāyānupassanāya muddhabhūtaṃ sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ itthipurisahatthiassādisaddasamākulaṃ gāmantaṃ apariccajitvā na sukaraṃ sampādetuṃ, saddakaṇḍakattā jhānassa. Agāmake pana araññe sukaraṃ yogāvacarena idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva [V 2.0318] jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasitvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ, tasmāssa anurūpasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā, “araññagato vā”tiādimāha.

Moreover, since this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing—the pinnacle of the contemplation of the body and the basis for special attainments and a pleasant dwelling in this very life for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples—is difficult to accomplish without abandoning a village vicinity filled with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and the like, because sound is a thorn to jhāna. However, in a forest without villages, it is easy for a practitioner to grasp this meditation subject, bring forth the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, and then, using that very jhāna as a basis, to comprehend formations and attain the supreme fruit, arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing a suitable dwelling place for him, said, “Gone to the forest or…” and so on.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya hi bhagavā. So yathā vatthuvijjācariyo nagarabhūmiṃ passitvā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā “ettha nagaraṃ māpethā”ti upadisati, sotthinā ca nagare niṭṭhite rājakulato mahāsakkāraṃ labhati, evameva yogāvacarassa anurūpasenāsanaṃ upaparikkhitvā “ettha kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjitabba”nti upadisati, tato tattha kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjantena yoginā anukkamena arahatte patte “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā”ti mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhati.

Indeed, the Blessed One is like a master of site-science. Just as such a master, having seen and thoroughly examined a city site, instructs, “Build the city here,” and upon the successful completion of the city, receives great honor from the royal family, in the same way, the Blessed One, having examined a suitable dwelling place for a practitioner, instructs, “The meditation subject should be practiced here.” Then, as the practitioner practices the meditation subject there and gradually attains arahantship, the Blessed One receives great honor with the words, “Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”

Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu dīpisadisoti vuccati. Yathā hi mahādīpirājā araññe tiṇagahanaṃ vā vanagahanaṃ vā pabbatagahanaṃ vā nissāya nilīyitvā vanamahiṃsagokaṇṇasūkarādayo mige gaṇhāti, evameva ayaṃ araññādīsu kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto [P 3.0764] bhikkhu yathākkamena cattāro magge ceva cattāri ariyaphalāni ca gaṇhāti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

This monk, however, is said to be like a leopard. Just as a great leopard king, relying on a thicket of grass, a dense part of the forest, or a mountain thicket in the wilderness, lies in wait and seizes wild buffalo, gokaṇṇa, boar, and other animals, so too this monk, practicing the meditation subject in the forest and other such places, gradually grasps the four paths and the four noble fruits. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yathāpi dīpiko nāma, nilīyitvā gaṇhatī mige;

Tathevāyaṃ buddhaputto, yuttayogo vipassako;

Araññaṃ pavisitvāna, gaṇhāti phalamuttama”nti.

“Just as a leopard, indeed, lying in wait, seizes its prey; so too this son of the Buddha, devoted to the practice, an insight practitioner, entering the forest, grasps the supreme fruit.”

Tenassa parakkamajavayoggabhūmiṃ araññasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā “araññagato vā”tiādimāha. Ito paraṃ imasmiṃ ānāpānapabbe yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho bhamakāro vāti idañhi upamāmattameva iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāyeti idaṃ appanāmattameva ca tattha anāgataṃ, sesaṃ āgatameva.

Therefore, showing the forest dwelling as the ground suitable for his exertion and vigor, the Blessed One said, “Gone to the forest or…” and so on. From here onwards, whatever should be said in this section on mindfulness of breathing has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. However, “Just as, monks, a skilled turner…”—this, which is merely a simile—and “Internally the body…”—this, which is merely the application—are not mentioned there; the rest is mentioned.

Yaṃ [M 2.0355] pana anāgataṃ, tattha dakkhoti cheko. Dīghaṃ vā añchantoti mahantānaṃ bherīpokkharādīnaṃ likhanakāle hatthe ca pāde ca pasāretvā dīghaṃ kaḍḍhanto. Rassaṃ vā añchantoti khuddakānaṃ dantasūcivedhakādīnaṃ likhanakāle mandamandaṃ rassaṃ kaḍḍhanto. Evameva khoti evaṃ ayampi bhikkhu addhānavasena ittaravasena ca pavattānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ vasena dīghaṃ vā assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatīti. Tassevaṃ sikkhato assāsapassāsanimitte cattāri jhānāni uppajjanti, so jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā assāsapassāse vā pariggaṇhāti jhānaṅgāni vā.

As for what is not mentioned, there 'skilled' means 'expert'. 'Drawing a long line' refers to when marking large items like kettle-drums and drumheads, stretching out his hands and feet and pulling the line long. 'Drawing a short line' refers to when marking small items like ivory carvings, needles, and awls, gently pulling the line short. Just so, this monk, regarding the in-breaths and out-breaths that occur for a long or short duration, knows, “When breathing in long, I breathe in long”… and so on, and he trains in the same way. As he trains thus, the four jhānas arise based on the sign of the in-breaths and out-breaths. Having emerged from jhāna, he comprehends either the in-breaths and out-breaths or the jhāna factors.

Tattha [V 2.0319] assāsapassāsakammiko “ime assāsapassāsā kiṃ nissitā? Vatthunissitā. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo, karajakāyo nāma cattāri mahābhūtāni upādārūpañce”ti evaṃ rūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti. Tato tadārammaṇe phassapañcamake nāmanti. Evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggahetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaṭiccasamuppādaṃ disvā “paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī”ti [P 3.0765] vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Idaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhaṃ.

Herein, the practitioner of in-and-out breathing considers: “On what are these in-breaths and out-breaths dependent? They are dependent on a base. The base is the body born of kamma; the body born of kamma is the four great elements and derived form.” Thus, he comprehends form. Then, with that as the object, he discerns name in the group with contact as the fifth. Having comprehended name-and-form in this way, seeking its cause and seeing dependent origination beginning with ignorance, he becomes free from doubt, thinking: “This is merely phenomena arisen from conditions and their causes; there is no other being or person.” Imposing the three characteristics upon name-and-form together with its conditions, he develops insight and gradually attains arahantship. This is a door to deliverance up to arahantship for one monk.

Jhānakammikopi “imāni jhānaṅgāni kiṃ nissitāni, vatthunissitāni, vatthu nāma karajakāyo jhānaṅgāni nāmaṃ, karajakāyo rūpa”nti nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaccayākāraṃ disvā “paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī”ti vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Idamekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhaṃ.

A practitioner of jhāna also distinguishes name-and-form thus: “On what do these jhāna factors depend? They depend on a base. The base is the body born of kamma; the jhāna factors are name, and the body born of kamma is form.” Having distinguished name-and-form, he seeks its condition. Seeing the mode of conditions beginning with ignorance, he becomes free from doubt, thinking: “This is merely phenomena arisen from conditions and their causes; there is no other being or person.” Imposing the three characteristics upon name-and-form together with its conditions, he develops insight and gradually attains arahantship. This is a door to deliverance up to arahantship for one monk.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā assāsapassāsakāye kāyānupassī viharati. Bahiddhā vāti parassa vā assāsapassāsakāye. Ajjhattabahiddhā vāti kālena attano, kālena parassa assāsapassāsakāye. Etenassa paguṇakammaṭṭhānaṃ aṭṭhapetvā aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakālo kathito. Ekasmiṃ kāle panidaṃ ubhayaṃ na labbhati.

Thus, 'internally' means one dwells contemplating the body in the body with regard to one's own body of in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Externally' means with regard to another's body of in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Internally and externally' means at one time with regard to one's own, and at another time with regard to another's, body of in-breaths and out-breaths. By this is explained the time for alternating practice, after one has established a proficient meditation subject. However, at one and the same time, this pair cannot be obtained.

Samudayadhammānupassī [M 2.0356] vāti yathā nāma kammārassa bhastañca gaggaranāḷiñca tajjañca vāyāmaṃ paṭicca vāto aparāparaṃ sañcarati, evaṃ bhikkhuno karajakāyañca nāsapuṭañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsakāyo aparāparaṃ sañcarati. Kāyādayo dhammā samudayadhammā, te passanto “samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī”ti vuccati. Vayadhammānupassī vāti yathā bhastāya apanītāya gaggaranāḷiyā bhinnāya tajje ca vāyāme asati so vāto nappavattati, evameva kāye bhinne nāsapuṭe viddhaste citte ca niruddhe assāsapassāsakāyo nāma nappavattatīti kāyādinirodhā assāsapassāsanirodhoti evaṃ passanto “vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī”ti vuccati. Samudayavayadhammānupassī vāti kālena samudayaṃ kālena vayaṃ anupassanto. Atthi kāyoti vā panassāti kāyova atthi, na satto, na puggalo, na itthī, na puriso, na attā, na attaniyaṃ, nāhaṃ, na mama, na koci, na kassacīti evamassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti.

Or, he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body: just as, dependent on a blacksmith's bellows, the nozzle-pipe, and the appropriate effort, the wind moves back and forth, so too, dependent on the monk's body born of kamma, the nostrils, and the mind, the body of in-and-out breaths moves back and forth. The body and other phenomena are of an arising nature; seeing them, he is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of arising in the body.' Or, he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body: just as, when the bellows are taken away, the nozzle-pipe is broken, and the appropriate effort is absent, that wind does not proceed, so too, when the body is broken, the nostrils are destroyed, and the mind has ceased, the so-called body of in-and-out breaths does not proceed. Thus, seeing that with the cessation of the body and so on there is the cessation of in-and-out breathing, he is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of passing away in the body.' Or, he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body by contemplating arising at one time and passing away at another. Or, his mindfulness is established with the thought: 'There is a body'—to the extent that there is just a body, not a being, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not what belongs to a self, not 'I,' not 'mine,' not anyone, not anyone's.

Yāvadevāti [V 2.0320][P 3.0766] payojanaparicchedavavatthāpanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā sā sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti, sā na aññadatthāya. Atha kho yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya aparāparaṃ uttaruttari ñāṇapamāṇatthāya ceva satipamāṇatthāya ca, satisampajaññānaṃ vuḍḍhatthāyāti attho. Anissito ca viharatīti taṇhānissayadiṭṭhinissayānaṃ vasena anissitova viharati. Na ca kiñci loke upādiyatīti lokasmiṃ kiñci rūpaṃ vā…pe… viññāṇaṃ vā “ayaṃ me attā vā attaniyaṃ vā”ti na gaṇhāti. Evampīti upari atthaṃ upādāya sampiṇḍanattho pi-kāro. Iminā pana padena bhagavā ānāpānapabbadesanaṃ niyyātetvā dasseti.

‘To the extent that’ (yāvadeva) serves to establish the delimitation of the purpose. This is what is said: that mindfulness which is established is not for any other purpose. Rather, it is just for the sake of knowledge, for the progressive, step-by-step increase in the measure of knowledge and the measure of mindfulness; the meaning is that it is for the growth of mindfulness and clear comprehension. ‘And he dwells independent’ means he dwells independent by way of the two dependencies: dependence on craving and dependence on views. ‘And he does not cling to anything in the world’ means that in the world he does not grasp any form… or consciousness as ‘this is my self’ or ‘what belongs to my self.’ ‘In this way too’ (evampi): the particle ‘pi’ (too) has the sense of summarizing, with reference to the meaning that has gone before. With this phrase, the Blessed One concludes and presents the discourse on the section about mindfulness of breathing.

Tattha assāsapassāsapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa assāsapassāsavasena abhiniviṭṭhassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Therein, the mindfulness that comprehends the in-and-out breaths is the truth of suffering. The pre-existing craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The Noble Path—which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object—is the truth of the path. Thus, having striven by way of the Four Truths, one attains Nibbāna. For a monk who is devoted to the in-and-out breaths, this is the gateway to liberation, leading all the way to Arahantship.

Ānāpānapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Mindfulness of Breathing is finished.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Postures

375. Evaṃ [M 2.0357] assāsapassāsavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni iriyāpathavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha kāmaṃ soṇasiṅgālādayopi gacchantā “gacchāmā”ti jānanti, na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ na pajahati, attasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ pajahati, attasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti kammaṭṭhānañceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. Idañhi “ko gacchati, kassa gamanaṃ, kiṃ kāraṇā gacchatī”ti evaṃ sampajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo.

375. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of in-and-out breathing, now, in order to analyze it by way of the postures, he says, ‘Again, further,’ and so on. In this regard, although even dogs, jackals, and so on know, ‘We are walking,’ when they are walking, this was not said with reference to that kind of knowing. For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not uproot the notion of a self, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness. But this monk's knowing does abandon the perception of a being, does uproot the notion of a self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of the foundations of mindfulness. For this was said with reference to such clear comprehension as: ‘Who walks? Whose is the walking? For what reason does one walk?’ The same method applies to standing and the other postures.

Tattha ko gacchatīti? Na koci satto vā puggalo vā gacchati. Kassa gamananti? Na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā gamanaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā gacchatīti[P 3.0767]? Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena gacchati. Tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti – “gacchāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati[V 2.0321], taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalakāyassa purato abhinīhāro gamananti vuccati. Ṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo.

Therein, who walks? No being or person walks. Whose is the walking? It is the walking of no being or person. For what reason does one walk? One walks by the impulse of the wind element that is an activity of the mind. Therefore, one understands thus: The thought ‘I am walking’ arises. That generates effort. The effort generates intimation. The forward movement of the entire body by the impulse of the wind element that is an activity of the mind is called ‘walking.’ The same method applies to standing and the other postures.

Tatrāpi hi “tiṭṭhāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalakāyassa koṭito paṭṭhāya ussitabhāvo ṭhānanti vuccati. “Nisīdāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena heṭṭhimakāyassa samiñjanaṃ uparimakāyassa ussitabhāvo nisajjāti vuccati. “Sayāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalasarīrassa tiriyato pasāraṇaṃ sayananti vuccatīti.

In that case too, the thought ‘I am standing’ arises. That generates effort. The effort generates intimation. The upright state of the entire body, beginning from the tips, by the impulse of the wind element that is an activity of the mind, is called ‘standing.’ The thought ‘I am sitting’ arises. That generates effort. The effort generates intimation. The bending of the lower body and the upright state of the upper body, by the impulse of the wind element that is an activity of the mind, is called ‘sitting.’ The thought ‘I am lying down’ arises. That generates effort. The effort generates intimation. The horizontal extension of the entire body, by the impulse of the wind element that is an activity of the mind, is called ‘lying down.’

Tassa evaṃ pajānato evaṃ hoti “satto gacchati, satto tiṭṭhatī”ti vuccati, atthato pana koci satto gacchanto vā ṭhito vā natthi. Yathā pana “sakaṭaṃ gacchati, sakaṭaṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti vuccati, na ca kiñci sakaṭaṃ nāma gacchantaṃ vā ṭhitaṃ vā atthi, cattāro pana goṇe yojetvā chekamhi sārathimhi pājente “sakaṭaṃ gacchati, sakaṭaṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti vohāramattameva [M 2.0358] hoti, evameva ajānanaṭṭhena sakaṭaṃ viya kāyo, goṇā viya cittajavātā, sārathi viya cittaṃ. “Gacchāmi tiṭṭhāmī”ti citte uppanne vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena gamanādīni pavattanti, tato “satto gacchati, satto tiṭṭhati, ahaṃ gacchāmi, ahaṃ tiṭṭhāmī”ti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Tenāha –

When one understands thus, it occurs to one: “It is said, ‘a being goes, a being stands,’ but in reality, there is no being who goes or stands.” Just as it is said, “the cart goes, the cart stands,” yet there is no cart that goes or stands; but when four oxen are yoked and a skilled driver urges them on, it is merely a verbal convention to say, “the cart goes, the cart stands.” Similarly, the body is like the cart, the mind-generated air-elements are like the oxen, and the mind is like the driver. When the thought “I go, I stand” arises, the air element arises generating bodily intimation; and due to the impulse of the air element produced by mental activity, going and so forth occur; then it is merely a verbal convention to say, “a being goes, a being stands; I go, I stand.” Therefore, it is said:

“Nāvā mālutavegena, jiyāvegena tejanaṃ;

Yathā yāti tathā kāyo, yāti vātāhato ayaṃ.

“As a boat by the force of the wind, as an arrow by the force of a bowstring, goes, so this body, impelled by the air element, goes.

Yantaṃ [P 3.0768] suttavaseneva, cittasuttavasenidaṃ;

Payuttaṃ kāyayantampi, yāti ṭhāti nisīdati.

Just as a machine moves by means of strings, so too this bodily machine, set in motion by the mind's strings, goes, stands, and sits.

Ko nāma ettha so satto, yo vinā hetupaccaye;

Attano ānubhāvena, tiṭṭhe vā yadi vā vaje”ti.

Who indeed is that being here, who, without cause and condition, by his own power, could stand or move?”

Tasmā evaṃ hetupaccayavaseneva pavattāni gamanādīni sallakkhento esa “gacchanto vā gacchāmīti [V 2.0322] pajānāti, ṭhito vā, nisinno vā, sayāno vā sayānomhīti pajānātī”ti veditabbo.

Therefore, one who observes that activities such as walking occur solely by the power of cause and condition is to be understood as the one who, “when walking, knows, ‘I am walking’; or when standing, knows, ‘I am standing’; or when sitting, knows, ‘I am sitting’; or when lying down, knows, ‘I am lying down.’”

Yathā yathā vā panassa kāyo paṇihito hoti, tathā tathā naṃ pajānātīti sabbasaṅgāhikavacanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yena yena vā ākārenassa kāyo ṭhito hoti, tena tena naṃ pajānāti. Gamanākārena ṭhitaṃ gacchatīti pajānāti. Ṭhānanisajjasayanākārena ṭhitaṃ sayānoti pajānātīti.

“And in whatever way his body is disposed, he knows it accordingly”—this is a comprehensive statement. What is meant is this: in whatever manner his body is positioned, he knows it in that manner. He knows a body positioned in the manner of walking as walking. He knows a body positioned in the manner of standing, sitting, or lying down as standing, sitting, or lying down.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Bahiddhā vāti parassa vā catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena. Ajjhattabahiddhā vāti kālena attano, kālena parassa catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vātiādīsu pana avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayotiādinā nayena pañcahākārehi rūpakkhandhassa samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Tañhi sandhāya idha “samudayadhammānupassī vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atthi kāyoti vā panassātiādi vuttasadisameva.

Thus, “internally”—in this way, by comprehending the four modes of deportment in one's own case, one dwells contemplating the body in the body. “Externally”—by comprehending the four modes of deportment in another's case. “Both internally and externally”—at times comprehending the four modes of deportment in one's own case, at times in another's case, one dwells contemplating the body in the body. Regarding “contemplating the nature of arising,” and so forth, the arising and passing away of the form aggregate should be deduced in five ways according to the method beginning with “with the arising of ignorance, form arises.” It is with reference to that, that “contemplating the nature of arising,” and so forth, is stated here. “There exists a body”—this and the rest are just as said before.

Idhāpi [M 2.0359] catuiriyāpathapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa catuiriyāpathapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Here too, mindfulness that comprehends the four modes of deportment is the truth of suffering. The prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The noble path—which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object—is the truth of the path. Thus, having striven by way of the four truths, one attains extinguishment. This is the gateway to liberation, up to arahantship, for a monk who comprehends the four modes of deportment.

Iriyāpathapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Deportment is concluded.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Fourfold Clear Comprehension

376. Evaṃ iriyāpathavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni catusampajaññavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha[P 3.0769]. Tattha abhikkantetiādīni sāmaññaphale vaṇṇitāni. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ catusampajaññapariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Idhāpi samudayavayadhammānupassītiādīsu [V 2.0323] rūpakkhandhasseva samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Sesaṃ vuttasadisameva.

376. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body in terms of postures, now, in order to analyze it in terms of the four kinds of clear comprehension, he begins again with the passage “Furthermore,” and so forth. Here, “going forward,” and so forth, are as explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. “Thus, internally”—in this way, by comprehending the four kinds of clear comprehension, one dwells contemplating the body in the body, either in one's own body or in another's body, at times in one's own body, at times in another's body. Here too, regarding “contemplating the nature of arising and passing away,” and so forth, the arising and passing away of the form aggregate itself should be deduced. The rest is similar to what has been stated.

Idha catusampajaññapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, vuttappakāro ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa catusampajaññapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno vasena yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Here, mindfulness that comprehends the four kinds of clear comprehension is the truth of suffering. The prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The noble path of the kind described is the truth of the path. Thus, having striven by way of the four truths, one attains extinguishment. This is the gateway to liberation, up to arahantship, for a monk who comprehends the four kinds of clear comprehension.

Catusampajaññapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Fourfold Clear Comprehension is concluded.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of Repulsiveness

377. Evaṃ catusampajaññavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni paṭikūlamanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha imameva kāyantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ sabbākārena vitthārato visuddhimagge kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne vuttaṃ. Ubhatomukhāti heṭṭhā ca upari cāti dvīhi mukhehi yuttā. Nānāvihitassāti nānāvidhassa.

377. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body in terms of the four kinds of clear comprehension, now, in order to analyze it in terms of contemplation of repulsiveness, he begins again with the passage “Furthermore,” and so forth. Here, regarding “this same body,” and so forth, whatever should be said has all been explained in every way and in detail in the Visuddhimagga under the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body. “Open at both ends” means “furnished with two openings, that is, below and above.” “Of various kinds” means “of various types.”

Idaṃ [M 2.0360] panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ – ubhatomukhā putoḷi viya hi cātumahābhūtiko kāyo, tattha missetvā pakkhittanānāvidhadhaññaṃ viya kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, cakkhumā puriso viya yogāvacaro, tassa taṃ putoḷiṃ muñcitvā paccavekkhato nānāvidhadhaññassa pākaṭakālo viya yogino dvattiṃsākārassa vibhūtakālo veditabbo. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ kesādipariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha dvattiṃsākārapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti [P 3.0770] evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

Here is the comparison: the body composed of the four great elements is like a sack with openings on both sides; the thirty-two aspects beginning with hair are like the various kinds of grains poured into it after being mixed; the yogi is like a man with eyes; and the time when the thirty-two aspects become manifest to the yogi should be understood as being like the time when the various kinds of grains become apparent to him as he unties the sack and inspects them. Thus, 'internally'—in this way, by comprehending the aspects beginning with hair, one dwells contemplating the body in one’s own body or in another’s body, at times in one’s own body, at times in another’s body. From this point onwards, the method is as stated. Only here, mindfulness that apprehends the thirty-two aspects is the truth of suffering—thus, having made this connection, the gateway to deliverance should be understood. The rest is similar to what has been stated.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Contemplation of Repulsiveness is concluded.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of the Elements

378. Evaṃ [V 2.0324] paṭikūlamanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni dhātumanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tatthāyaṃ opammasaṃsandanena saddhiṃ atthavaṇṇanā – yathā koci goghātako vā tasseva vā bhattavetanabhato antevāsiko gāviṃ vadhitvā vinivijjhitvā catasso disā gatānaṃ mahāpathānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte catumahāpathe koṭṭhāsaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā nisinno assa, evameva bhikkhu catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhitattā yathāṭhitaṃ, yathāṭhitattā ca yathāpaṇihitaṃ kāyaṃ “atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu…pe… vāyodhātū”ti evaṃ paccavekkhati.

378. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the contemplation of repulsiveness, now, in order to analyze it by way of the contemplation of the elements, he begins again with the passage 'Furthermore,' etc. Here is the explanation of the meaning together with the comparison: Just as a cattle butcher or his apprentice who is fed and paid, having slaughtered a cow and dismembered it, might sit at the four great crossroads—the place considered the center for the great paths going in the four directions—having cut it into portions; even so, a monk examines this body, which is positioned in any of the four postures, and which is arranged as it is positioned, thus: 'In this body, there is the earth element... the air element.'

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā goghātakassa gāviṃ posentassāpi āghātanaṃ āharantassāpi āharitvā tattha bandhitvā ṭhapentassapi vadhentassāpi vadhitaṃ mataṃ passantassāpi tāvadeva gāvīti saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva naṃ padāletvā bilaso na vibhajati. Vibhajitvā nisinnassa panassa gāvīti saññā antaradhāyati, maṃsasaññā pavattati. Nāssa evaṃ [M 2.0361] hoti – “ahaṃ gāviṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime gāviṃ harantī”ti. Atha khvassa “ahaṃ maṃsaṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime maṃsaṃ haranti” cceva hoti; evameva imassāpi bhikkhuno pubbe bālaputhujjanakāle gihibhūtassāpi pabbajitassāpi tāvadeva sattoti vā puggaloti vā saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā dhātuso na paccavekkhati. Dhātuso paccavekkhato panassa sattasaññā antaradhāyati, dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati. Tenāha bhagavā – “‘imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū’ti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho goghātako vā…pe… vāyodhātū”ti. Goghātako viya hi yogī, gāvīti saññā viya sattasaññā, catumahāpatho viya catuiriyāpatho, bilaso vibhajitvā [P 3.0771] nisinnabhāvo viya dhātuso paccavekkhaṇanti ayamettha pāḷivaṇṇanā. Kammaṭṭhānakathā pana visuddhimagge vitthāritā.

What is meant? Just as for the cattle butcher—whether he is feeding the cow, leading it to the slaughter-place, having brought it there and tied it up, killing it, or seeing it killed and dead—the perception 'cow' does not disappear until he has cut it up and divided it into portions. But once he has divided it and sits down, the perception 'cow' disappears, and the perception 'meat' arises. He no longer thinks, 'I am selling a cow; these people are taking a cow.' Instead, he thinks, 'I am selling meat; these people are taking meat.' Similarly, for this monk—whether in the past as a foolish ordinary person, as a householder, or even after going forth—the perception 'being' or 'person' does not disappear until he has, having broken up the compactness of this very body, however it is positioned and arranged, examined it by way of the elements. But when he examines it by way of the elements, the perception 'being' disappears, and his mind settles on the elements alone. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'He examines this very body, however positioned or arranged, by way of the elements: "In this body, there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element." Just as, monks, a skilled butcher... the air element.' Here, the yogi is like the butcher, the perception 'being' is like the perception 'cow,' the four postures are like the four great paths, and the state of sitting after dividing into portions is like examining by way of the elements—this is the explanation of the Pāli text. But the discussion on the meditation subject has been expanded upon in the Visuddhimagga.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ catudhātupariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha catudhātupariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ, sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally'—in this way, by comprehending the four elements, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body or in another's body, at times in one's own body, at times in another's body. From this point onwards, the method is as stated. Only here, mindfulness that apprehends the four elements is the truth of suffering—thus, having made this connection, the gateway to deliverance should be understood. The rest is similar to what has been stated.

Dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Contemplation of the Elements is concluded.

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Nine Charnel Ground Sections

379. Evaṃ [V 2.0325] dhātumanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni navahi sivathikapabbehi vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha seyyathāpi passeyyāti yathā passeyya. Sarīranti matasarīraṃ. Sivathikāya chaḍḍitanti susāne apaviddhaṃ. Ekāhaṃ matassa assāti ekāhamataṃ. Dvīhaṃ matassa assāti dvīhamataṃ. Tīhaṃ matassa assāti tīhamataṃ. Kammārabhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena uddhumātattā uddhumātaṃ, uddhumātameva uddhumātakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ uddhumātanti uddhumātakaṃ. Vinīlaṃ vuccati [M 2.0362] viparibhinnavaṇṇaṃ, vinīlameva vinīlakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ. Maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa nīlaṭṭhānesu nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paribhinnaṭṭhānehi navahi vā vaṇamukhehi vissandamānapubbaṃ vipubbaṃ, vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ. Vipubbakaṃ jātaṃ tathābhāvaṃ gatanti vipubbakajātaṃ.

379. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of contemplation of the elements, now, to analyze it by way of the nine charnel ground sections, it begins with the words 'again, further' and so on. Herein, 'just as if one were to see' (seyyathāpi passeyya) means 'as one would see' (yathā passeyya). 'A body' (sarīraṃ) means a dead body (matasarīraṃ). 'Discarded in a charnel ground' (sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ) means 'thrown away in a charnel ground' (susāne apaviddhaṃ). 'One day dead' (ekāhaṃ matassa assa) means 'dead for one day' (ekāhamataṃ). 'Two days dead' (dvīhaṃ matassa assa) means 'dead for two days' (dvīhamataṃ). 'Three days dead' (tīhaṃ matassa assa) means 'dead for three days' (tīhamataṃ). 'Bloated' (uddhumātaṃ) means swollen due to a state of distension (sūnabhāvena) that has arisen successively from the wind rising upwards after the cessation of life, like a blacksmith's bellows (kammārabhastā viya). 'Bloated' (uddhumātaṃ) itself is called `uddhumātakaṃ`. Or, because it is repulsive (paṭikūlattā), a contemptible bloated thing (kucchitaṃ uddhumātaṃ) is called `uddhumātakaṃ`. 'Discolored' (vinīlaṃ) is said of what has a changed color (viparibhinnavaṇṇaṃ); 'discolored' (vinīlaṃ) itself is called `vinīlakaṃ`. Or, because it is repulsive (paṭikūlattā), a contemptible discolored thing (kucchitaṃ vinīlaṃ) is called `vinīlakaṃ`. This is a designation for a corpse (chavasarīrassa) that is red in places where flesh is abundant, white in places where pus has collected, and mostly blue in the blue areas, like one wrapped in a blue cloth. 'Festering' (vipubbaṃ) means with pus oozing (vissandamānapubbaṃ) from the broken places (paribhinnaṭṭhānehi) or from the nine wound-openings (navahi vā vaṇamukhehi). 'Festering' (vipubbaṃ) itself is called `vipubbakaṃ`. Or, because it is repulsive (paṭikūlattā), a contemptible festering thing (kucchitaṃ vipubbaṃ) is called `vipubbakaṃ`. 'Having become festering' (vipubbakajātaṃ) means having reached that state (tathābhāvaṃ gataṃ).

So imameva kāyanti so bhikkhu imaṃ attano kāyaṃ tena kāyena saddhiṃ ñāṇena upasaṃharati upaneti. Kathaṃ? Ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatītoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – āyu, usmā, viññāṇanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ atthitāya ayaṃ [P 3.0772] kāyo ṭhānagamanādikhamo hoti, imesaṃ pana vigamā ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃ pūtikasabhāvoyeva, evaṃbhāvī evaṃ uddhumātādibhedo bhavissati, evaṃanatīto evaṃ uddhumātādibhāvaṃ anatikkantoti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ uddhumātādipariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

'He compares this very body' (so imameva kāyaṃ) means that the monk compares this very body of his (imaṃ attano kāyaṃ) with that [dead] body (tena kāyena saddhiṃ) by means of knowledge (ñāṇena), considering it thus: 'This body, too, (ayampi kho kāyo) is of such a nature (evaṃdhammo), is of such a state (evaṃbhāvī), and has not gone beyond this (evaṃanatīto).' This is said to mean: due to the existence of these three things—life-faculty (āyu), heat (usmā), and consciousness (viññāṇaṃ)—this body is capable of standing, moving, etc. (ṭhānagamanādikhamo hoti); but with their disappearance, this body, too, is of such a nature (evaṃdhammo), that is, of a putrid nature (evaṃ pūtikasabhāvova), it will be of such a state (evaṃbhāvī), that is, it will become bloated and so on (evaṃ uddhumātādibhedo bhavissati), and it has not gone beyond this (evaṃanatīto), meaning it has not gone beyond the state of being bloated and so on (evaṃ uddhumātādibhāvaṃ anatikkanto). Thus, 'internally' (iti ajjhattaṃ vā) means that by thus comprehending the bloated state and so on (evaṃ uddhumātādipariggaṇhanena), he dwells contemplating the body in the body (kāyānupassī viharati), either in his own body (attano vā kāye) or in another's body (parassa vā kāye), or at times in his own body (kālena vā attano) and at times in another's body (kālena vā parassa kāye).

Khajjamānanti udarādīsu nisīditvā udaramaṃsaoṭṭhamaṃsaakkhikūṭādīni luñcitvā luñcitvā khādiyamānaṃ. Samaṃsalohitanti sāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ. Nimaṃsalohitamakkhitanti maṃse khīṇepi lohitaṃ na sussati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “nimaṃsalohitamakkhita”nti. Aññenāti aññena disābhāgena. Hatthaṭṭhikanti catusaṭṭhibhedampi hatthaṭṭhikaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vippakiṇṇaṃ. Pādaṭṭhikādīsupi eseva nayo.

'Being devoured' (khajjamānaṃ) means being eaten (khādiyamānaṃ) by tearing apart again and again (luñcitvā luñcitvā) the flesh of the belly, the flesh of the lips, the eye sockets, etc. (udaramaṃsa-oṭṭhamaṃsa-akkhikūṭādīni) after perching on the belly and so on (udarādīsu nisīditvā). 'With flesh and blood' (samaṃsalohitaṃ) means endowed with remaining flesh and blood (sāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ). 'Fleshless, but smeared with blood' (nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ) means that even when the flesh is gone (maṃse khīṇepi), the blood does not dry up (lohitaṃ na sussati); it is said with reference to that (taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ). 'In another direction' (aññenāti) means in another directional part (aññena disābhāgena). 'A hand bone' (hatthaṭṭhikanti) means any of the sixty-four kinds of hand bones (catusaṭṭhibhedampi hatthaṭṭhikaṃ) scattered about individually (pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vippakiṇṇaṃ). The same method applies to a foot bone and so on (pādaṭṭhikādīsupi eseva nayo).

Terovassikānīti atikkantasaṃvaccharāni. Pūtīnīti abbhokāse ṭhitāni vātātapavuṭṭhisamphassena [V 2.0326] terovassikāneva pūtīni honti, antobhūmigatāni pana cirataraṃ tiṭṭhanti. Cuṇṇakajātānīti cuṇṇaṃ cuṇṇaṃ hutvā vippakiṇṇāni. Sabbattha so imamevāti vuttanayena khajjamānādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ khajjamānādipariggaṇhanena yāva cuṇṇakabhāvā attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

'More than a year old' (terovassikāni) means having passed years (atikkantasaṃvaccharāni). 'Rotten' (pūtīni) means that those left in the open air (abbhokāse ṭhitāni), affected by contact with wind, sun, and rain (vātātapavuṭṭhisamphassena), become rotten after more than a year (terovassikāneva pūtīni honti); but those buried underground (antobhūmigatāni pana) last much longer (cirataraṃ tiṭṭhanti). 'Reduced to powder' (cuṇṇakajātāni) means having become powder (cuṇṇaṃ cuṇṇaṃ hutvā) and scattered (vippakiṇṇāni). In every case, the phrase 'he compares this very body' (so imamevāti) means that the connection (yojanā) should be made in the manner stated (vuttanayena) with regard to the state of being devoured and so on (khajjamānādīnaṃ vasena). Thus, 'internally' (iti ajjhattaṃ vā) means that by thus comprehending the state of being devoured and so on (evaṃ khajjamānādipariggaṇhanena) up to the state of being powder (yāva cuṇṇakabhāvā), he dwells contemplating the body in the body (kāyānupassī viharati), either in his own body (attano vā kāye) or in another's body (parassa vā kāye), or at times in his own body (kālena vā attano) and at times in another's body (kālena vā parassa kāye).

Idha [M 2.0363] pana ṭhatvā navasivathikā samodhānetabbā. Ekāhamataṃ vāti hi ādinā nayena vuttā sabbāpi ekā, kākehi vā khajjamānantiādikā ekā, aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhanti ekā, nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandhanti ekā, apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhanti ekā, aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhānītiādikā ekā aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgānīti ekā, puñjakitāni terovassikānīti ekā, pūtīni cuṇṇakajātānīti ekāti.

At this point (idha pana ṭhatvā), the nine charnel ground contemplations (navasivathikā) should be brought together (samodhānetabbā). All those stated by the method beginning with 'one day dead' (ekāhamataṃ vā) are one; that beginning with 'being devoured by crows' (kākehi vā khajjamānaṃ) is one; the 'skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews' (aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ) is one; the 'fleshless, smeared with blood, held together by sinews' (nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ) is one; the 'fleshless and bloodless, held together by sinews' (apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ) is one; that beginning with 'bones disjoined' (aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhānīti) is one; the 'bones white, like the color of a conch shell' (aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgāni) is one; the 'piled up, more than a year old' (puñjakitāni terovassikāni) is one; the 'rotten, reduced to powder' (pūtīni cuṇṇakajātāni) is one.

Evaṃ kho, bhikkhaveti idaṃ navasivathikā dassetvā kāyānupassanaṃ niṭṭhapento āha. Tattha navasivathikapariggāhikā [P 3.0773] sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idaṃ navasivathikapariggāhakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

'Thus, O monks' (evaṃ kho, bhikkhave) was said by him to conclude the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanaṃ niṭṭhapento āha), having shown these nine charnel ground contemplations (idaṃ navasivathikā dassetvā). Herein, mindfulness that comprehends the nine charnel ground contemplations (navasivathikapariggāhikā sati) is the truth of suffering (dukkhasaccaṃ); the previous craving (purimataṇhā) that gives rise to it (tassā samuṭṭhāpikā) is the truth of the origin (samudayasaccaṃ); the non-occurrence of both (ubhinnaṃ appavatti) is the truth of cessation (nirodhasaccaṃ); the Noble Path (ariyamaggo) that fully understands suffering (dukkhaparijānano), abandons the origin (samudayapajahano), and takes cessation as its object (nirodhārammaṇo) is the truth of the path (maggasaccaṃ). Thus, by advancing (ussakkitvā) by way of the four truths (evaṃ catusaccavasena), one attains Nibbāna (nibbutiṃ pāpuṇāti)—this is the means of deliverance (niyyānamukhaṃ) up to Arahantship (yāva arahattā) for monks who comprehend the nine charnel ground contemplations (navasivathikapariggāhakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ).

Navasivathikapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Nine Charnel Ground Contemplations is concluded.

Ettāvatā ca ānāpānapabbaṃ, iriyāpathapabbaṃ, catusampajaññapabbaṃ, paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ, dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ, navasivathikapabbānīti cuddasapabbā kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā hoti. Tattha ānāpānapabbaṃ, paṭikūlamanasikārapabbanti imāneva dve appanākammaṭṭhānāni, sivathikānaṃ pana ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā sesāni dvādasāpi upacārakammaṭṭhānānevāti.

Thus far (ettāvatā), the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) consisting of fourteen sections (cuddasapabbā) is concluded: the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānapabbaṃ), the section on postures (iriyāpathapabbaṃ), the section on clear comprehension (catusampajaññapabbaṃ), the section on reflection on repulsiveness (paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ), the section on reflection on the elements (dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ), and the nine sections on the charnel ground contemplations (navasivathikapabbāni). Of these (tattha), only the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānapabbaṃ) and the section on reflection on repulsiveness (paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ)—these two alone (imāneva dve)—are meditation subjects for absorption (appanākammaṭṭhānāni); but the remaining twelve (sesāni dvādasāpi) are only meditation subjects for access concentration (upacārakammaṭṭhānāneva), because the charnel ground contemplations (sivathikānaṃ pana) are stated by way of contemplating their danger (ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā).

Kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of the Body is concluded.

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Contemplation of Feeling

380. Evaṃ [V 2.0327] bhagavā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sukhaṃ vedananti kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno “ahaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti pajānātīti attho. Tattha [M 2.0364] kāmaṃ uttānaseyyakāpi dārakā thaññapivanādikāle sukhaṃ vedayamānā “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmā”ti pajānanti, na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ na jahati, attasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ jahati, attasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānañceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. Idañhi “ko vedayati, kassa vedanā, kiṃ kāraṇā vedanā”ti evaṃ sampajānavediyanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

380. Having thus explained the establishment of mindfulness in the contemplation of the body in fourteen ways, the Blessed One now, in order to explain the contemplation of feelings in nine ways, said the passage beginning, 'And how, bhikkhus?' Herein, 'experiencing a pleasant feeling' means that when experiencing either a bodily or a mental pleasant feeling, he understands, 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.' In this regard, even infants lying on their backs (uttānaseyyakāpi dārakā), while suckling milk and so on (thaññapivanādikāle), know they are experiencing pleasant feeling, but this is not the kind of knowing being referred to. For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being (sattūpaladdhiṃ), does not uproot the notion of self (attasaññaṃ), and is neither a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhānaṃ) nor the development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā). But this bhikkhu’s knowing abandons the perception of a being, uproots the notion of self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. For this is said with reference to experiencing with clear comprehension (sampajānavediyanaṃ), as in the questions: 'Who feels? Whose is the feeling? What is the cause of feeling?'

Tattha ko vedayatīti na koci satto vā puggalo vā vedayati. Kassa vedanāti na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā vedanā. Kiṃ kāraṇā vedanāti vatthuārammaṇāva panassa vedanā, tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti “taṃ taṃ sukhādīnaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayati taṃ pana vedanāya pavattiṃ [P 3.0774] upādāya’ahaṃ vedayāmī’ti vohāramattaṃ hotī”ti. Evaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatīti sallakkhento esa “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānātī”ti veditabbo cittalapabbate aññataratthero viya.

Herein, 'Who feels?' (ko vedayatīti). No being or person feels. 'Whose is the feeling?' (kassa vedanāti). It is the feeling of no being or person. 'What is the cause of feeling?' (kiṃ kāraṇā vedanāti). Feeling has a basis and an object (vatthuārammaṇāva panassa vedanā). Therefore, one understands thus: 'Having made this or that basis and object of pleasure, etc., its support, it is merely feeling that feels. But on account of the occurrence of that feeling, there is the mere convention, “I feel.”' Thus, by observing that it is merely feeling that feels, having made a basis and an object its support, it should be understood that one knows, 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling,' like a certain elder on Cittalapabbata.

Thero kira aphāsukakāle balavavedanāya nitthunanto aparāparaṃ parivattati, tameko daharo āha – “kataraṃ vo, bhante, ṭhānaṃ rujjatī”ti. Āvuso, pāṭiyekkaṃ rujjanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatīti. Evaṃ jānanakālato paṭṭhāya adhivāsetuṃ vaṭṭati no, bhante,ti. Adhivāsemi, āvusoti. Adhivāsanā, bhante, seyyoti. Thero adhivāsesi. Vāto yāva hadayā phālesi, mañcake antāni rāsikatāni ahesuṃ. Thero daharassa dassesi “vaṭṭatāvuso, ettakā adhivāsanā”ti. Daharo tuṇhī ahosi. Thero vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi.

It is said that during a time of illness, the elder, groaning from severe pain, kept tossing and turning. A certain young bhikkhu then asked him, “Venerable sir, which part of your body is in pain?” “Friend, there is no specific spot that hurts; it is feeling itself that feels, taking a basis and an object,” the elder replied. “Since you understand it this way, should you not endure it, venerable sir?” “I am enduring it, friend.” “Endurance is excellent, venerable sir.” The elder endured. The internal wind tore him apart up to his heart, and his intestines were piled up on the bed. The elder showed the young bhikkhu, saying, “Friend, is this much endurance sufficient?” The young bhikkhu remained silent. The elder, applying balanced effort, attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then, with his head level, he attained final Nibbāna.

Yathā ca sukhaṃ, evaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno “nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti pajānāti. Iti bhagavā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento yasmā phassavasena cittavasena vā kathiyamānaṃ pākaṭaṃ na hoti[V 2.0328], andhakāraṃ viya khāyati, vedanānaṃ pana uppattipākaṭatāya vedanāvasena pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā sakkapañhe viya idhāpi vedanāvasena arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Tattha “duvidhañhi [M 2.0365] kammaṭṭhānaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ arūpakammaṭṭhānañcā”tiādi kathāmaggo sakkapañhe vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Just as with pleasant feeling, so too with painful feeling... and experiencing unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: "I am experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling." Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the meditation subject of form, proceeded to explain the meditation subject of the formless. Because when explained by way of contact or by way of consciousness, it is not clear—it appears as if in darkness—but due to the evident nature of the arising of feelings, it becomes clear by way of feelings. Therefore, just as in the 'Questions of Sakka,' here too the meditation subject of the formless was explained by way of feeling. In this context, the line of explanation beginning with, "There are two kinds of meditation subjects: the meditation subject of form and the meditation subject of the formless," should be understood in the same way as stated in the 'Questions of Sakka.'

Tattha sukhaṃ vedanantiādīsu ayaṃ aparopi pajānanapariyāyo, sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānātīti sukhavedanākkhaṇe dukkhavedanāya abhāvato sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno “sukhaṃ vedanaṃyeva vedayāmī”ti pajānāti. Tena yā [P 3.0775] pubbe bhūtapubbā dukkhavedanā, tassa idāni abhāvato imissā ca sukhāya vedanāya ito paṭhamaṃ abhāvato vedanā nāma aniccā adhuvā vipariṇāmadhammā, itiha tattha sampajāno hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

Herein, in the phrases beginning with 'feels a pleasant feeling,' this is another method of full understanding: one understands, 'I feel a pleasant feeling.' Thus, at the moment of a pleasant feeling, due to the absence of painful feeling, one who feels a pleasant feeling understands, 'I feel only a pleasant feeling.' By this, because the painful feeling that was formerly present is now absent, and because this pleasant feeling was absent before this, one is clearly aware that feelings are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. And this was stated by the Blessed One:

“Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, sukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye dukkhaṃ…pe… adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, adukkhamasukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Sukhāpi, kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Dukkhāpi, kho…pe… adukkhamasukhāpi kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā…pe… nirodhadhammā. Evaṃ passaṃ, aggivessana, sutavā ariyasāvako sukhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, dukkhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, adukkhamasukhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati, vimuttasmiṃ ‘vimuttamī’ti ñāṇaṃ hoti, ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti (ma. ni. 2.205).

“Aggivessana, at a time when one feels a pleasant feeling, one does not at that time feel a painful feeling, nor a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; one feels only a pleasant feeling at that time. Aggivessana, at a time when one feels a painful feeling... or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not at that time feel a pleasant feeling, nor a painful feeling; one feels only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling at that time. Moreover, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of a nature to be destroyed, of a nature to vanish, of a nature to fade away, of a nature to cease. A painful feeling also... a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling also, Aggivessana, is impermanent... of a nature to cease. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, disenchanted with painful feeling, and disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

Sāmisaṃ vā sukhantiādīsu sāmisā sukhā nāma pañcakāmaguṇāmisasannissitā cha gehasitasomanassavedanā. Nirāmisā sukhā nāma cha nekkhammasitasomanassavedanā. Sāmisā dukkhā nāma cha gehasitadomanassavedanā. Nirāmisā dukkhā nāma cha nekkhammasitadomanassavedanā. Sāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma cha gehasitaupekkhāvedanā. Nirāmisā adukkhamasukhā [M 2.0366] nāma cha nekkhammasitaupekkhāvedanā. Tāsaṃ vibhāgo sakkapañhe vuttoyeva.

In the phrases beginning with 'worldly pleasant feeling,' worldly pleasant feelings are the six feelings of mental pleasure associated with the household life, which are dependent on the bait of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Unworldly pleasant feelings are the six feelings of mental pleasure associated with renunciation. Worldly painful feelings are the six feelings of mental pain associated with the household life. Unworldly painful feelings are the six feelings of mental pain associated with renunciation. Worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are the six feelings of equanimity associated with the household life. Unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are the six feelings of equanimity associated with renunciation. Their classification is as stated in the 'Questions of Sakka.'

Iti [V 2.0329] ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ sukhavedanādipariggaṇhanena attano vā vedanāsu, parassa vā vedanāsu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati. Samudayavayadhammānupassī vāti ettha pana avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayotiādīhi pañcahi pañcahi ākārehi vedanānaṃ samudayañca [P 3.0776] vayañca passanto “samudayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, kālena samudayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu, kālena vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharatī”ti veditabbo. Ito paraṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha vedanāpariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā vedanāpariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ, sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on. In this way, by comprehending pleasant feeling and so on, one dwells contemplating feelings in one's own feelings, or in the feelings of another, or at times in one's own feelings and at times in the feelings of another. 'Contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away,' and so on. Here, by seeing the arising and passing away of feelings in five ways each, such as 'with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling,' it should be understood that 'one dwells contemplating the phenomena of arising in feelings, or one dwells contemplating the phenomena of passing away in feelings, or one dwells contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away in feelings.' From this point on, the method is the same as that stated in the contemplation of the body. Only here, having made the connection that 'the mindfulness that comprehends feeling is the truth of suffering,' the outlet for the bhikkhu who comprehends feeling should be understood. The rest is the same.

Vedanānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of Feeling is concluded.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Contemplation of Consciousness

381. Evaṃ navavidhena vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sarāganti aṭṭhavidhalobhasahagataṃ. Vītarāganti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Idaṃ pana yasmā sammasanaṃ na dhammasamodhānaṃ tasmā idha ekapadepi lokuttaraṃ na labbhati. Sesāni cattāri akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Sadosanti duvidhadomanassasahagataṃ. Vītadosanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Sesāni dasa akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Samohanti vicikicchāsahagatañceva, uddhaccasahagatañcāti duvidhaṃ. Yasmā pana moho sabbākusalesu uppajjati, tasmā sesānipi idha vaṭṭantiyeva. Imasmiññeva hi duke dvādasākusalacittāni pariyādinnānīti. Vītamohanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Saṅkhittanti thinamiddhānupatitaṃ. Etañhi saṅkuṭitacittaṃ nāma. Vikkhittanti uddhaccasahagataṃ, etañhi pasaṭacittaṃ nāma.

381. Having thus explained the establishment of mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings in nine ways, now, to explain the contemplation of mind in sixteen ways, he began with, 'And how, bhikkhus?' Here, 'with lust' refers to that which is accompanied by the eight kinds of greed. 'Without lust' refers to the mundane wholesome and indeterminate. However, because this is examination, not a combination of phenomena, here not even a single supramundane state is found. The remaining four unwholesome minds belong neither to the former term nor to the latter. 'With hate' refers to that which is accompanied by the two kinds of aversion. 'Without hate' refers to the mundane wholesome and indeterminate. The remaining ten unwholesome minds belong neither to the former term nor to the latter. 'With delusion' refers to the two kinds: that accompanied by doubt and that accompanied by restlessness. But since delusion arises in all unwholesome states, the remaining ones are also applicable here. Indeed, in this very pair, the twelve unwholesome minds are fully included. 'Without delusion' refers to the mundane wholesome and indeterminate. 'Contracted' refers to that which has fallen into sloth and torpor, for this is called a contracted mind. 'Scattered' refers to that which is accompanied by restlessness, for this is called a scattered mind.

Mahaggatanti rūpārūpāvacaraṃ. Amahaggatanti kāmāvacaraṃ. Sauttaranti kāmāvacaraṃ. Anuttaranti rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacarañca. Tatrāpi sauttaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ, anuttaraṃ [M 2.0367] arūpāvacarameva. Samāhitanti yassa appanāsamādhi upacārasamādhi vā atthi. Asamāhitanti ubhayasamādhivirahitaṃ[V 2.0330]. Vimuttanti tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttīhi vimuttaṃ. Avimuttanti ubhayavimuttivirahitaṃ. Samucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttīnaṃ pana idha okāsova natthi.

'Developed' refers to that of the form and formless spheres. 'Undeveloped' refers to that of the sensual sphere. 'Surpassable' refers to that of the sensual sphere. 'Unsurpassable' refers to that of the form and formless spheres. And even there, that of the form sphere is surpassable, while that of the formless sphere alone is unsurpassable. 'Concentrated' refers to that which has either absorption concentration or access concentration. 'Unconcentrated' refers to that which is devoid of both concentrations. 'Liberated' refers to that liberated by liberation-by-substitution and liberation-by-suppression. 'Unliberated' refers to that which is devoid of both liberations. But here there is no opportunity at all for the liberations of cutting off, tranquilization, and escape.

Iti [P 3.0777] ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ sarāgādipariggaṇhanena yasmiṃ yasmiṃ khaṇe yaṃ yaṃ cittaṃ pavattati, taṃ taṃ sallakkhento attano vā citte, parassa vā citte, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa citte cittānupassī viharati. Samudayavayadhammānupassīti ettha pana avijjāsamudayā viññāṇasamudayoti evaṃ pañcahi pañcahi ākārehi viññāṇassa samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha cittapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ padayojanaṃ katvā cittapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on. In this way, by comprehending with categories such as 'with lust,' at whatever moment whatever mind occurs, by observing that very mind, one dwells contemplating the mind in one's own mind, or in another's mind, or at times in one's own mind and at times in another's mind. As for 'contemplating the nature of arising and passing away,' here the arising and passing away of consciousness should be deduced in five ways each, thus: 'from the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of consciousness.' From this point on, the method is as has been stated. Only here, having made the connection of terms thus: 'the mindfulness that comprehends the mind is the truth of suffering,' the gateway to liberation for the bhikkhu who comprehends the mind should be known. The rest is just the same.

Cittānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of Mind is concluded.

Dhammānupassanā nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā

The Contemplation of Phenomena: The Exposition of the Section on the Hindrances

382. Evaṃ soḷasavidhena cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Apica bhagavatā kāyānupassanāya suddharūpapariggaho kathito, vedanācittānupassanāhi suddhaarūpapariggaho. Idāni rūpārūpamissakapariggahaṃ kathetuṃ “kathañca, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Kāyānupassanāya vā rūpakkhandhapariggahova kathito, vedanānupassanāya vedanākkhandhapariggahova, cittānupassanāya viññāṇakkhandhapariggahova idāni saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhapariggahampi kathetuṃ “kathañca, bhikkhave”tiādimāha.

382. Having thus explained the establishment of mindfulness through the contemplation of mind in sixteen ways, now, to explain the contemplation of phenomena in five ways, he began with, 'And how, bhikkhus?' Furthermore, the Blessed One has taught the comprehension of pure matter in the contemplation of the body, and the comprehension of pure non-matter in the contemplations of feelings and mind. Now, to explain the comprehension of the mixture of matter and non-matter, he begins with, 'And how, bhikkhus?' Or, in the contemplation of the body, only the comprehension of the aggregate of matter was taught; in the contemplation of feelings, only the comprehension of the aggregate of feeling; in the contemplation of mind, only the comprehension of the aggregate of consciousness. Now, to also explain the comprehension of the aggregates of perception and formations, he begins with, 'And how, bhikkhus?'

Tattha santanti abhiṇhasamudācāravasena saṃvijjamānaṃ. Asantanti asamudācāravasena vā pahīnattā vā asaṃvijjamānaṃ. Yathā cāti yena kāraṇena kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Tañca pajānātīti tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Iti iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

Here, 'present' refers to what is existing by way of frequent occurrence. 'Not present' refers to what is not existing either by way of non-occurrence or because it has been abandoned. 'And how' means the reason by which the arising of sensual desire occurs. 'And he understands that' means he understands that reason. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Tattha subhanimitte ayonisomanasikārena kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Subhanimittaṃ nāma [V 2.0331] subhampi subhanimittaṃ, subhārammaṇampi subhanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro [M 2.0368] nāma anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāro anicce niccanti vā, dukkhe sukhanti vā, anattani attāti vā, asubhe subhanti vā manasikāro. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, subhanimittaṃ, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāya uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti [P 3.0778] (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Herein, sensual desire arises through unwise attention to an attractive sign. An 'attractive sign' means both the attractive itself is an attractive sign, and an attractive object is an attractive sign. 'Unwise attention' means attention that is not the proper means, attention that is a wrong path; it is attention to the impermanent as permanent, or to suffering as happiness, or to non-self as self, or to the foul as attractive. For one who frequently applies that, sensual desire arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is an attractive sign. Therein, the frequent practice of unwise attention—this is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the increase and expansion of arisen sensual desire' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Asubhanimitte pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Asubhanimittaṃ nāma asubhampi asubhārammaṇampi. Yonisomanasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro pathamanasikāro anicce aniccanti vā, dukkhe dukkhanti vā, anattani anattāti vā, asubhe asubhanti vā manasikāro. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, asubhanimittaṃ, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

But through wise attention to the unattractive sign, its abandonment occurs. An 'unattractive sign' means both the unattractive itself and an unattractive object.
