'Wise attention' means attention that is the proper means, attention that is the path; it is attention to the impermanent as impermanent, or to suffering as suffering, or to non-self as non-self, or to the foul as foul. For one who frequently applies that, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is the unattractive sign. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention—this is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattanti asubhanimittassa uggaho, asubhabhāvanānuyogo, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Dasavidhañhi asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati, bhāventassāpi indriyesu pihitadvārassāpi catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ ālopānaṃ okāse sati udakaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlatāya bhojanamattaññunopi. Teneva vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of sensual desire: the apprehension of the sign of unattractiveness, frequent practice of the meditation on unattractiveness, guarding the doors of the senses, moderation in food, good friendship, and suitable talk. For sensual desire is abandoned for one who apprehends the ten kinds of signs of unattractiveness, for one who develops it, for one who has guarded the doors of the senses, and for one who is moderate in food, accustomed to sustain himself by drinking water when there is still room for four or five morsels. Therefore it was said:

“Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

'Four or five morsels, / Without eating [more], one should drink water; / Enough for easeful living, / For a bhikkhu who has dedicated himself.' (Theragāthā 983)

Asubhakammikatissattherasadise asubhabhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassapi kāmacchando pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu dasaasubhanissitasappāyakathāya pahīyati, tena vuttaṃ – “cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnakāmacchandassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Sensual desire is abandoned for one who cultivates good friends, like the venerable Asubhakammika Tissa, who delights in the practice of contemplating unattractiveness. Sensual desire is abandoned through suitable talk based on the ten aspects of unattractiveness in regard to postures, seating, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: 'Six things conduce to the abandoning of sensual desire.' Moreover, for one whose sensual desire has been abandoned by these six things, it is understood that there is no further arising of it in the future by way of the path of arahantship.

Paṭighanimitte [M 2.0369] ayonisomanasikārena pana byāpādassa uppādo hoti. Tattha paṭighampi paṭighanimittaṃ[V 2.0332], paṭighārammaṇampi paṭighanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro sabbattha ekalakkhaṇova. Taṃ tasmiṃ nimitte bahulaṃ pavattayato byāpādo uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, paṭighanimittaṃ[P 3.0779], tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa uppādāya uppannassa vā byāpādassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

The arising of ill-will occurs through unwise attention to the sign of aversion. Herein, aversion itself is the sign of aversion, and the object of aversion is also the sign of aversion. Unwise attention has the same characteristic in all cases. When one frequently engages with that sign, ill-will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'There is, monks, a sign of aversion. When one frequently engages in unwise attention to it, this is the nourishment for the arising of unarisen ill-will and for the increase and expansion of arisen ill-will' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Mettāya pana cetovimuttiyā yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tattha mettāti vutte appanāpi upacāropi vaṭṭati. Cetovimuttīti appanāva. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇova. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato byāpādo pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, mettā cetovimutti, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā byāpādassa pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

But by the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, through wise attention, the abandoning of ill-will occurs. Herein, when 'loving-kindness' is spoken of, both absorption and access are included. 'Liberation of mind' means only absorption. 'Wise attention' has the characteristic already stated. For one who frequently cultivates this, ill-will is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Monks, there is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness. Herein, the frequent cultivation of wise attention is the nourishment for the non-arising of unarisen ill-will and for the abandoning of arisen ill-will' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattanti mettānimittassa uggaho mettābhāvanānuyogo kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇā paṭisaṅkhānabahulatā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇānañhi aññataravasena mettaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati, odhisoanodhisopharaṇavasena mettaṃ bhāventassāpi. “Tvaṃ etassa kuddho kiṃ karissasi, kimassa sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissasi, nanu tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissasi, parassa kujjhanaṃ nāma vītaccitaṅgāra tattaaya salākagūthādīni gahetvā paraṃ paharitukāmatāsadisaṃ hoti. Esopi tava kuddho kiṃ karissati, kiṃ te sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissati, esa attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissati, appaṭicchitapaheṇakaṃ viya paṭivātaṃ khittarajomuṭṭhi viya ca etassevesa kodho matthake patissatī”ti evaṃ attano ca parassa ca kammassakataṃ paccavekkhatopi, ubhayakammassakataṃ paccavekkhitvā paṭisaṅkhāne ṭhitassāpi, assaguttattherasadise mettābhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu mettānissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cha [M 2.0370] dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi [P 3.0780] pahīnassa byāpādassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of ill-will: grasping the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of kamma, frequent wise consideration, good friendship, and suitable talk. For one who grasps loving-kindness in any way—whether by radiating it in specific or non-specific directions—ill-will is abandoned; similarly, for one who develops loving-kindness by radiating it in specific or non-specific directions. Reflecting thus: 'Being angry at this person, what will you accomplish? Will you be able to destroy his virtue and so on? Surely, you have come by your own kamma and will depart by your own kamma. Being angry at another is like wanting to strike that person after picking up live coals, a heated iron spike, or excrement. And this person, being angry at you, what will he accomplish? Will he be able to destroy your virtue and so on? He has come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma. Like an unaccepted gift or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger of his will fall right upon his own head.' By reflecting in this way on the ownership of kamma—both one's own and others'—ill-will is abandoned. Even for one who stands in wise consideration after reflecting on the ownership of kamma of both, ill-will is abandoned. By associating with good friends who delight in the development of loving-kindness, like the Elder Assagutta, ill-will is abandoned. By engaging in suitable talk grounded in loving-kindness in standing, sitting, and so on, ill-will is abandoned. Therefore it is said: 'Six things conduce to the abandoning of ill-will.' Moreover, one understands that ill-will, abandoned by these six things, does not arise again in the future by means of the non-returner's path.

Aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikārena thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti. Tandī nāma kāyālasiyatā. Vijambhitā nāma kāyavinamanā. Bhattasammado nāma bhattamucchā bhattapariḷāho. Cetaso līnattaṃ nāma cittassa līnākāro. Imesu aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato [V 2.0333] thinamiddhaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, arati tandī vijambhitā bhattasammado cetaso līnattaṃ, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Through unwise attention to discontent and so forth, the arising of sloth and torpor occurs. Lethargy is bodily sluggishness. Yawning is bodily bending. Drowsiness after meals is the stupor or burning caused by food. Mental sinking is the sunken state of mind. When one frequently applies unwise attention to these—discontent and so forth—sloth and torpor arise. Therefore he said: 'Monks, there is discontent, lethargy, yawning, drowsiness after meals, and mental sinking. Herein, the frequent cultivation of unwise attention is the nourishment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the increase and expansion of arisen sloth and torpor' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Ārambhadhātuādīsu pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Ārambhadhātu nāma paṭhamārambhavīriyaṃ. Nikkamadhātu nāma kosajjato nikkhantatāya tato balavataraṃ. Parakkamadhātu nāma paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavataraṃ. Imasmiṃ tippabhede vīriye yonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa anuppādāya, uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

But through wise attention to the element of initiative and so forth, its abandoning occurs. The element of initiative means initial energy. The element of exertion means stronger energy due to emerging from laziness. The element of vigorous exertion means even stronger energy due to advancing from stage to stage. When one frequently applies wise attention to these three kinds of energy, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore he said: 'Monks, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of vigorous exertion. Herein, the frequent cultivation of wise attention is the nourishment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – atibhojane nimittaggāho, iriyāpathasamparivattanatā, ālokasaññāmanasikāro, abbhokāsavāso, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Āharahatthaka tatravaṭṭaka alaṃsāṭaka kākamāsaka bhuttavamitakabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhāne nisinnassa hi samaṇadhammaṃ karoto thinamiddhaṃ mahāhatthī viya ottharantaṃ āgacchati, catupañcaālopaokāsaṃ pana ṭhapetvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlassa bhikkhuno taṃ na hotīti evaṃ atibhojane nimittaṃ gaṇhantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Yasmiṃ iriyāpathe thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, tato aññaṃ parivattentassāpi, rattiṃ candālokadīpālokaukkāloke [P 3.0781] divā sūriyālokaṃ manasikarontassāpi, abbhokāse [M 2.0371] vasantassāpi, mahākassapattherasadise pahīnathinamiddhe kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa thinamiddhassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: grasping the sign of moderation in eating, changing postures, attention to the perception of light, dwelling in the open air, good friendship, and suitable talk. For one who, having eaten food to repletion—licking the hand, licking the bowl, eating until one says 'enough,' until a crow could take a morsel, and until one vomits—sits down in a place for seclusion by day or night and engages in the duties of a recluse, sloth and torpor come upon them, overwhelming them like a great elephant. But for a bhikkhu whose practice is to sustain himself by drinking water after leaving a space for four or five mouthfuls, that does not happen. Thus, by grasping the sign of moderation in eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. By changing to another posture from the one in which sloth and torpor have overtaken one, by attending to the perception of moonlight, lamplight, or torchlight at night, or sunlight by day, by dwelling in the open air, by associating with good friends who have abandoned sloth and torpor, like the Elder Mahākassapa, and by engaging in suitable talk connected with the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) in standing, sitting, and so forth—sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore it is said: 'Six things conduce to the abandoning of sloth and torpor.' One understands that for sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things, there is no future arising through the path of arahantship.

Cetaso avūpasame ayonisomanasikārena uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti. Avūpasamo nāma avūpasantākāro, uddhaccakukkuccamevetaṃ atthato. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato uddhaccakukkuccaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso avūpasamo, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa [V 2.0334] uppādāya, uppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti.

Through unwise attention to the mind's lack of tranquility, the arising of restlessness and remorse occurs. Lack of tranquility means the state of not being tranquil; in essence, this is restlessness and remorse. When one frequently applies unwise attention to this, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore he said: 'Monks, there is the mind's lack of tranquility. Herein, the frequent cultivation of unwise attention is the nourishment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the increase and expansion of arisen restlessness and remorse.'

Samādhisaṅkhāte pana cetaso vūpasame yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso vūpasamo, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa anuppādāya, uppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāyā”ti.

But through wise attention to the mind's tranquility, which is called concentration, its abandoning occurs. Therefore he said: 'Monks, there is the mind's tranquility. Herein, the frequent cultivation of wise attention is the nourishment for the non-arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the abandoning of arisen restlessness and remorse.'

Apica cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattanti bahussutatā paripucchakatā vinaye pakataññutā vuddhasevitā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Bāhussaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā dve vā tayo vā cattāro vā pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati. Kappiyākappiyaparipucchābahulassāpi, vinayapaññattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasibhāvatāya pakataññunopi, vuḍḍhe mahallakatthere upasaṅkamantassāpi, upālittherasadise vinayadhare kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu kappiyākappiyanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīne uddhaccakukkucce uddhaccassa arahattamaggena[P 3.0782], kukkuccassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse: extensive learning, frequent questioning, familiarity with the Discipline, associating with elders, good friendship, and suitable talk. For even for one who, through extensive learning, learns one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas by way of the text and by way of the meaning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. Also for one who frequently questions about what is allowable and what is not, who is familiar with the Vinaya regulations through having practiced them and mastered them, who approaches the senior and elder monks, who associates with good friends who are masters of the Discipline, like the Elder Upāli, and who engages in suitable talk grounded in what is allowable and what is not, in standing, sitting, and so forth—restlessness and remorse are abandoned. Therefore it is said: 'Six things conduce to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.' One understands that for restlessness and remorse abandoned by these six things, the future non-arising of restlessness occurs through the path of arahantship, and that of remorse through the path of the non-returner.

Vicikicchāṭhānīyesu dhammesu ayonisomanasikārena vicikicchāya uppādo hoti. Vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā nāma punappunaṃ vicikicchāya kāraṇattā [M 2.0372] vicikicchāva. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato vicikicchā uppajjati. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya uppādāya, uppannāya vā vicikicchāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Unwise attention to things that are grounds for doubt gives rise to doubt. Things that are grounds for doubt are themselves doubt, being repeatedly a cause for doubt. Therein, doubt arises in one who frequently applies unwise attention. Therefore it is said: “Monks, there are things that are grounds for doubt. The frequent cultivation of unwise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt and for the increase and abundance of arisen doubt.”

Kusalādidhammesu yonisomanasikārena panassā pahānaṃ hoti, tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā sāvajjānavajjā dhammā sevitabbāsevitabbā dhammā hīnapaṇītā dhammā kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro, anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya anuppādāya; uppannāya vā vicikicchāya pahānāyā”ti.

However, through wise attention to states beginning with the wholesome, it is abandoned. Therefore it is said: “Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, states to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, inferior and superior states, dark and bright states with their counterparts. The frequent cultivation of wise attention to them is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen doubt and for the abandoning of arisen doubt.”

Apica [V 2.0335] cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattanti bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, adhimokkhabahulatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Bāhussaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā…pe… pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena ca atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati, tīṇi ratanāni ārabbha paripucchābahulassāpi, vinaye ciṇṇavasībhāvassāpi, tīsu ratanesu okappaniyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāpi, saddhādhimutte vakkalittherasadise kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnāya vicikicchāya sotāpattimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Moreover, six things conduce to the abandoning of doubt: much learning, questioning, proficiency in the Vinaya, abundance of conviction, good friendship, and suitable talk. For indeed, through much learning, even if one learns one or… up to five Nikāyas by text and meaning, doubt is abandoned. For one who frequently questions concerning the Three Jewels, doubt is abandoned. For one who is skilled and practiced in the Vinaya, doubt is abandoned. For one who has abundant conviction, reckoned as unwavering faith in the Three Jewels, doubt is abandoned. For one who associates with good friends like the venerable Vakkali, who is released by faith, doubt is abandoned. For one who engages in suitable talk grounded in the virtues of the Three Jewels while standing, sitting, and so on, doubt is abandoned. Therefore, it is said: “Six things conduce to the abandoning of doubt.” Furthermore, one understands that when doubt is abandoned by these six things, its non-arising in the future is achieved through the path of stream-entry.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ pañcanīvaraṇapariggaṇhanena attano vā dhammesu, parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha subhanimittaasubhanimittādīsu ayonisomanasikārayonisomanasikāravasena [P 3.0783] pañcasu nīvaraṇesu vuttāyeva nīharitabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha nīvaraṇapariggāhikā [M 2.0373] sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā nīvaraṇapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on. In this way, by comprehending the five hindrances, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—whether in one’s own phenomena, in another’s phenomena, or at times in one’s own and at times in another’s phenomena. Here, arising and passing away should be derived from what has already been stated regarding the five hindrances by way of unwise and wise attention to attractive and unattractive signs, and so on. From this point on, the method is just as has been stated. Here, however, the monk who comprehends the hindrances should know the doorway to deliverance by making the connection that 'the mindfulness that comprehends the hindrances is the truth of suffering.' The rest is just the same.

Nīvaraṇapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Hindrances is concluded.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Aggregates

383. Evaṃ pañcanīvaraṇavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni pañcakkhandhavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha pañcasu upādānakkhandhesūti upādānassa khandhā upādānakkhandhā, upādānassa paccayabhūtā dhammapuñjā dhammarāsayoti attho. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana khandhakathā visuddhimagge vuttā.

383. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five hindrances, now, in order to analyze it by way of the five aggregates, he begins with 'Furthermore,' and so on. Herein, 'in the five aggregates of clinging' means aggregates that are objects of clinging; that is, heaps or masses of phenomena that are conditions for clinging—this is the meaning. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, is given in the exposition on the aggregates in the Visuddhimagga.

Iti rūpanti idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ atthīti sabhāvato rūpaṃ pajānāti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārena pana rūpādīni visuddhimagge [V 2.0336] khandhakathāyameva vuttāni. Iti rūpassa samudayoti evaṃ avijjāsamudayādivasena pañcahākārehi rūpassa samudayo. Iti rūpassa atthaṅgamoti evaṃ avijjānirodhādivasena pañcahākārehi rūpassa atthaṅgamo. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge udayabbayañāṇakathāya vutto.

'Thus, form' means: 'this is form,' 'this much is form,' 'there is no form beyond this'—thus one understands form by its intrinsic nature. The same method applies to feeling and so on. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation of form and so on is given in the Visuddhimagga’s exposition on the aggregates. 'Thus, the arising of form' means that in this way, through five aspects beginning with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form. 'Thus, the cessation of form' means that in this way, through five aspects beginning with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form. The same method applies to feeling and so on. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is given in the Visuddhimagga’s exposition on the knowledge of arising and passing away.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ pañcakkhandhapariggaṇhanena attano vā dhammesu, parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādīnaṃ pañcasu khandhesu vuttānaṃ paññāsāya lakkhaṇānaṃ vasena nīharitabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha khandhapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā khandhapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on. In this way, by comprehending the five aggregates, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—whether in one’s own phenomena, in another’s phenomena, or at times in one’s own and at times in another’s phenomena. Here, arising and passing away should be derived by way of the fifty characteristics stated in relation to the five aggregates, such as 'with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form.' From this point on, the method is just as has been stated. Here, however, the monk who comprehends the aggregates should know the doorway to deliverance by making the connection that 'the mindfulness that comprehends the aggregates is the truth of suffering.' The rest is just the same.

Khandhapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Aggregates is concluded.

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Sense Bases

384. Evaṃ [P 3.0784][M 2.0374] pañcakkhandhavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni āyatanavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesūti cakkhu sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhā kāyo manoti imesu chasu ajjhattikesu, rūpaṃ saddo gandho raso phoṭṭhabbo dhammoti imesu chasu bāhiresu. Cakkhuñca pajānātīti cakkhupasādaṃ yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti. Rūpe ca pajānātīti bahiddhā catusamuṭṭhānikarūpañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti. Yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojananti yañca taṃ cakkhuṃ ceva rūpe cāti ubhayaṃ paṭicca. Kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭigha, māna, diṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāsa, bhavarāga, issā, macchariya, avijjāsaṃyojananti dasavidhaṃ saṃyojanaṃ uppajjati, tañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti.

384. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the five aggregates, now, to analyze it by way of the sense bases, he begins with 'Furthermore,' and so on. Herein, 'in the six internal and external sense bases' refers to these six internal ones: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and these six external ones: form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena. 'He understands the eye' means he understands the eye-sensitivity according to its own essential characteristic. 'He understands forms' means he understands external form, which arises from the four causes, according to its own essential characteristic. 'And whatever fetter arises dependent on both' means whatever fetter arises dependent on both, that is, the eye and forms. The ten kinds of fetters arise: the fetter of sensual desire, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, adherence to rites and vows, craving for existence, envy, stinginess, and ignorance—and he understands these according to their own essential characteristic.

Kathaṃ panetaṃ uppajjatīti? Cakkhudvāre tāva āpāthagataṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ kāmassādavasena assādayato abhinandato kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Aniṭṭhārammaṇe kujjhato paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ [V 2.0337] uppajjati. “Ṭhapetvā maṃ ko añño etaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ samattho atthī”ti maññato mānasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvanti gaṇhato diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ satto nu kho, sattassa nu kho”ti vicikicchato vicikicchāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Sampattibhave vata no idaṃ sulabhaṃ jāta”nti bhavaṃ patthentassa bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Āyatimpi evarūpaṃ sīlabbataṃ samādiyitvā sakkā laddhu”nti sīlabbataṃ samādiyantassa sīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Aho vata taṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ aññe na labheyyu”nti usūyato issāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Attanā laddhaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ aññassa maccharāyato macchariyasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Sabbeheva sahajātaaññāṇavasena avijjāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati.

But how does this arise? First, at the eye-door, when a desirable object comes into range, for one who savors it by way of sensual taste and rejoices in it, the fetter of sensual desire arises. When an undesirable object is encountered, for one who becomes angry, the fetter of aversion arises. For one who thinks, 'Except for me, who else is capable of discerning this object?' the fetter of conceit arises. For one who grasps this form-object as permanent and lasting, the fetter of views arises. For one who doubts, 'Is this form-object a being, or does it belong to a being?' the fetter of doubt arises. For one who longs for existence, thinking, 'In a fortunate existence, this would indeed be easily obtained for us,' the fetter of craving for existence arises. For one who undertakes precepts and vows, thinking, 'By undertaking such precepts and vows in the future, it may be possible to obtain this,' the fetter of adherence to rites and vows arises. For one who is envious, thinking, 'Oh, may others not obtain that form-object!' the fetter of envy arises. For one who is stingy towards another regarding a form-object one has obtained, the fetter of stinginess arises. By way of the ignorance co-arisen with all of these, the fetter of ignorance arises.

Yathā ca anuppannassāti yena kāraṇena asamudācāravasena anuppannassa tassa dasavidhassāpi saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti, tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Yathā ca uppannassāti [P 3.0785] appahīnaṭṭhena pana samudācāravasena vā uppannassa tassa dasavidhassāpi saṃyojanassa yena kāraṇena pahānaṃ hoti, tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Yathā ca pahīnassāti tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānavasena pahīnassāpi tassa dasavidhassa saṃyojanassa [M 2.0375] yena kāraṇena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti, tañca pajānāti. Kena kāraṇena panassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti? Diṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsaissāmacchariyabhedassa tāva pañcavidhassa saṃyojanassa sotāpattimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti. Kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojanadvayassa oḷārikassa sakadāgāmimaggena, aṇusahagatassa anāgāmimaggena, mānabhavarāgāvijjāsaṃyojanattayassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti. Sotañca pajānāti sadde cātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Apicettha āyatanakathā vitthārato visuddhimagge āyatananiddese vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

And how the unarisen fetter arises: he understands the cause by which that tenfold fetter, unarisen due to its non-manifestation, comes to arise. And how the arisen fetter is abandoned: he understands the cause by which that tenfold fetter, having arisen in the sense of not being abandoned or through its manifestation, is abandoned. And how the abandoned fetter does not arise again in the future: he understands the cause by which that tenfold fetter, even when abandoned through abandonment by substitution and by suppression, does not arise again in the future. And by what cause does it not arise again in the future? For the fivefold fetter—consisting of identity view, doubt, clinging to rites and rituals, envy, and stinginess—its non-arising again in the future occurs through the path of stream-entry. For the coarse pair of fetters, sensual desire and ill will, their non-arising occurs through the path of once-returning; for their subtle forms, through the path of non-returning. For the threefold fetter—conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance—its non-arising again in the future occurs through the path of arahantship. The same method applies also to 'he understands the ear and sounds,' and so on. Moreover, the detailed discussion of the sense bases should be understood in the way described in the Visuddhimagga’s exposition on the sense bases.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ ajjhattikāyatanapariggaṇhanena attano vā dhammesu bāhirāyatanapariggaṇhanena parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha “avijjāsamudayā cakkhusamudayo”ti rūpāyatanassa rūpakkhandhe, arūpāyatanesu manāyatanassa viññāṇakkhandhe, dhammāyatanassa sesakkhandhesu vuttanayena nīharitabbā. Lokuttaradhammā na gahetabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha āyatanapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā āyatanapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally,' etc., means that one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena in oneself by comprehending the internal sense bases, or in others by comprehending the external sense bases, or at times in oneself and at times in others. As for arising and passing away here, it should be deduced according to the stated method: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the eye'—thus, for the form base in the form aggregate; among the formless bases, for the mind base in the consciousness aggregate; and for the dhamma base in the remaining aggregates. The supramundane dhammas are not to be included. From this point on, the method is as stated. For here, having made the connection that 'mindfulness that comprehends the sense bases is the truth of suffering,' the doorway to liberation for the bhikkhu who comprehends the sense bases should be understood. The rest is just the same.

Āyatanapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the sense bases is finished.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on the Factors of Awakening

385. Evaṃ [V 2.0338] cha ajjhattikabāhirāyatanavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni bojjhaṅgavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha bojjhaṅgesūti bujjhanakasattassa aṅgesu. Santanti paṭilābhavasena saṃvijjamānaṃ. Satisambojjhaṅganti satisaṅkhātaṃ sambojjhaṅgaṃ. Ettha hi sambujjhati āraddhavipassakato paṭṭhāya yogāvacaroti sambodhi. Yāya vā so satiādikāya sattadhammasāmaggiyā sambujjhati [P 3.0786] kilesaniddāto uṭṭhāti, saccāni vā paṭivijjhati, sā dhammasāmaggī sambodhi. Tassa sambodhissa, tassā vā sambodhiyā aṅganti sambojjhaṅgaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “satisaṅkhātaṃ sambojjhaṅga”nti. Sesasambojjhaṅgesupi imināva nayena vacanattho veditabbo.

385. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena in terms of the six internal and external sense bases, now, to analyze it in terms of the factors of awakening, the text begins with 'Again, furthermore,' and so on. Herein, 'in the factors of awakening' means in the factors of a being who awakens. 'Present' means existing by way of attainment. 'The factor of awakening of mindfulness' means the factor of awakening designated as mindfulness. For here, the practitioner, starting from one who has undertaken insight meditation, awakens; hence he is 'one who awakens' (sambodhi). Or, that harmony of seven states beginning with mindfulness, by which one awakens—rises from the sleep of the defilements or penetrates the truths—is 'awakening' (sambodhi). A factor of that one who awakens, or of that awakening, is a 'factor of awakening.' Therefore it is said: 'the factor of awakening designated as mindfulness.' The meaning of the words for the remaining factors of awakening should also be understood in this same way.

Asantanti [M 2.0376] appaṭilābhavasena avijjamānaṃ. Yathā ca anupannassātiādīsu pana satisambojjhaṅgassa tāva “atthi, bhikkhave, satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha satiyeva satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇoyeva. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

‘Non-existent’ means not existing by way of non-attainment. Now, regarding 'how the unarisen arises,' and so on, for the mindfulness factor of awakening, its arising occurs thus: 'There are, monks, states that are a basis for the mindfulness factor of awakening; frequent wise attention to them—this is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen mindfulness factor of awakening, or for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen mindfulness factor of awakening' (SN 5.66). Herein, mindfulness itself constitutes the states that are a basis for the mindfulness factor of awakening. Wise attention is as previously described. For one who frequently applies that there, the mindfulness factor of awakening arises.

Apica cattāro dhammā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti satisampajaññaṃ muṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanatā upaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Abhikkantādīsu hi sattasu ṭhānesu satisampajaññena, bhattanikkhittakākasadise muṭṭhassatipuggale parivajjanena, tissadattattheraabhayattherasadise upaṭṭhitassatipuggale sevanena, ṭhānanisajjādīsu satisamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatāya ca satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, four states conduce to the arising of the mindfulness factor of awakening: mindfulness and clear comprehension; avoiding persons of lapsed mindfulness; associating with persons of established mindfulness; and being intent on that. For the mindfulness factor of awakening arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven activities beginning with going forward; by avoiding persons of lapsed mindfulness, like a crow that has dropped its food; by associating with persons of established mindfulness, like the venerable Tissadatta and the venerable Abhaya; and by having a mind that is sloped, inclined, and directed towards arousing mindfulness in postures such as standing and sitting. Thus, he understands that for this factor, having arisen from these four causes, the fulfillment of its development occurs through the path of arahantship.

Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa pana “atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā…pe… kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Now, for the investigation-of-states factor of awakening, its arising occurs thus: 'There are, monks, skillful and unskillful states... states that are dark and bright, with their counterparts. Herein, frequent wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-states factor of awakening, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen investigation-of-states factor of awakening.' Thus is its arising.

Apica [V 2.0339] satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paripucchakatā vatthuvisadakiriyā [P 3.0787] indriyasamattapaṭipādanā duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā paññavantapuggalasevanā gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha paripucchakatāti khandhadhātuāyatanaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgasamathavipassanānaṃ atthasannissitaparipucchābahulatā. Vatthuvisadakiriyāti ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yadā hissa kesanakhalomāni dīghāni honti, sarīraṃ vā ussannadosañceva sedamalamakkhitañca, tadā ajjhattikaṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Yadā pana cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ [M 2.0377] duggandhaṃ hoti, senāsanaṃ vā uklāpaṃ, tadā bāhiravatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Tasmā kesādichedāpanena uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi sarīrasallahukabhāvakaraṇena ucchādananahāpanena ca ajjhattikavatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sūcikammadhovanarajanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇādīhi bāhiravatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Etasmiñhi ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi avisade uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ aparisuddhāni dīpakapallavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Visade pana ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi visadaṃ hoti parisuddhāni dīpakapallavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Tena vuttaṃ “vatthuvisadakiriyā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattatī”ti.

Furthermore, seven states conduce to the arising of the investigation-of-states factor of awakening: questioning, clarifying the basis, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on the domain of profound knowledge, and being intent on that. Herein, questioning means frequently inquiring about the meaning related to the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, path factors, jhāna factors, serenity, and insight. Clarifying the basis means making the internal and external bases clear. For when one’s head hair, body hair, and nails are long, or when the body is afflicted with excessive humors, sweat, and dirt, then the internal basis is unclear and impure. And when the robe is worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, or the dwelling is untidy, then the external basis is unclear and impure. Therefore, the internal basis should be made clear by cutting the head hair, nails, etc., by making the body light by means of emetics and purgatives, and by anointing and bathing. The external basis should be made clear by needlework, washing, dyeing, mending, etc. For when the internal and external bases are unclear, the knowledge that arises in the mind and mental factors is also unclear and impure—like the light of a lamp flame that arises dependent on an unclean lamp, wick, and oil. But when the internal and external bases are clear, the knowledge that arises in the mind and mental factors is also clear—like the light of a lamp flame that arises dependent on a clean lamp, wick, and oil. Therefore, it is said: “Clarifying the basis conduces to the arising of the investigation-of-states factor of awakening.”

Indriyasamattapaṭipādanā nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Sace hissa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, itarāni mandāni, tato vīriyindriyaṃ paggahakiccaṃ, satindriyaṃ upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ avikkhepakiccaṃ, paññindriyaṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā, yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena hāpetabbaṃ. Vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassanaṃ. Sace pana vīriyindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, atha saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, na itarāni itarakiccabhedaṃ. Tasmā taṃ [P 3.0788] passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabbaṃ. Tatrāpi soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi ekassa balavabhāve sati itaresaṃ attano kiccesu asamatthatā veditabbā.

Balancing the faculties means making the faculties of faith and so on equal. If one's faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of striving, the faculty of mindfulness cannot perform its function of attending, the faculty of concentration cannot perform its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom cannot perform its function of seeing. Therefore, it should be reduced by reflecting on the nature of phenomena, or by not attending in the way that made it strong. The story of the Venerable Vakkali is an illustration here. But if the faculty of energy is strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform its function of conviction, nor can the others perform their respective functions. Therefore, it should be reduced by cultivating tranquility and so forth. Here too, the story of the Venerable Soṇa should be shown. Similarly, in the remaining cases, when one is strong, it should be understood that the others are incapable of performing their own functions.

Visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samataṃ pasaṃsanti. Balavasaddho hi mandapañño mudhappasanno hoti, avatthusmiṃ pasīdati. Balavapañño mandasaddho kerāṭikapakkhaṃ bhajati, bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hoti. Cittuppādamatteneva kusalaṃ hotīti atidhāvitvā dānādīni akaronto niraye uppajjati. Ubhinnaṃ samatāya vatthusmiṃyeva pasīdati. Balavasamādhiṃ pana mandavīriyaṃ samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā kosajjaṃ abhibhavati. Balavavīriyaṃ [V 2.0340] mandasamādhiṃ vīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā uddhaccaṃ abhibhavati. Samādhi pana vīriyena saṃyojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati, vīriyaṃ samādhinā saṃyojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ [M 2.0378] na labhati. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti.

In particular, they praise the balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy. For one with strong faith but weak wisdom is blindly confident and has confidence in what is unworthy. One with strong wisdom but weak faith inclines to the side of a trickster and is as incurable as a disease caused by medicine. Thinking that merit comes merely from the arising of a thought, such a person overreaches and, by not practicing generosity and so on, is reborn in hell. With a balance of both, one has confidence only in what is worthy. When concentration is strong but energy is weak, one is overcome by sloth, since concentration sides with sloth. When energy is strong but concentration is weak, one is overcome by restlessness, since energy sides with restlessness. But concentration yoked with energy cannot fall into sloth, and energy yoked with concentration cannot fall into restlessness. Therefore, both should be made equal, for with the balance of both, absorption occurs.

Apica samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇissati. Samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanākammikassa paññā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhinnaṃ pana samatāyapi appanā hotiyeva. Sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭati. Sati hi cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ saddhāvīriyapaññānaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato, kosajjapakkhikena ca samādhinā kosajjapātato rakkhati. Tasmā sā loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu, sabbakammikaamacco viya ca, sabbarājakiccesu sabbattha icchitabbā. Tenāha – “sati ca pana sabbatthikā vuttā bhagavatā, kiṃ kāraṇā? Cittañhi satipaṭisaraṇaṃ, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā ca sati, na vinā satiyā cittassa paggahaniggaho hotī” ti. Duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā nāma khandhādibhede anogāḷhapaññānaṃ dummedhapuggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Paññavantapuggalasevanā nāma samapaññāsalakkhaṇapariggāhikāya [P 3.0789] udayabbayapaññāya samannāgatapuggalasevanā. Gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā nāma gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evaṃ uppannassa pannassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Moreover, for one practicing concentration, strong faith is required. Thus believing and resolving, one will attain absorption. But among concentration and wisdom, for one practicing concentration, strong one-pointedness is required. For in this way, he attains absorption. For one practicing insight, strong wisdom is required. For in this way, he attains penetration of characteristics. But absorption occurs even with equality of the two. Mindfulness, however, is required everywhere as a strong factor. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation due to faith, energy, and wisdom, which belong to the side of agitation, and from falling into sloth due to concentration, which belongs to the side of sloth. Therefore, like salt for seasoning in all dishes, or like a minister for all royal duties, it should be desired everywhere. Hence it was said: “And mindfulness is declared by the Blessed One as applicable everywhere. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its recourse, and mindfulness has protection as its mode of presentation. Without mindfulness, there is no uplifting and restraining of the mind.” Avoiding unwise individuals means keeping far away from dull-witted individuals whose wisdom has not penetrated the divisions of the aggregates and so on. Associating with wise individuals means keeping company with individuals endowed with wisdom that grasps the characteristics of equal wisdom—wisdom of arising and passing away. Reflecting on profound knowledge means reflecting on the distinctions with the profound wisdom that operates in the profound aggregates and so on. Being inclined towards that means having a mind inclining, tending, and sloping toward the arising of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor in standing, sitting, and so forth. Thus one understands that the development of the arisen wisdom reaches perfection through the path of arahantship.

Vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa “atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ uppādo hoti.

For the energy enlightenment factor, its arising comes about thus: “Monks, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of striving. Frequently applying wise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen energy enlightenment factor, and for the increase, growth, development, and perfection of the arisen energy enlightenment factor.”

Apica ekādasa dhammā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇatā ānisaṃsadassāvitā gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā piṇḍapātāpacāyanatā dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇatā jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti.

Moreover, eleven things conduce to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: reflecting on the fear of the lower realms, seeing the advantages, reflecting on the path to be trodden, reverencing alms-food, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of one’s birth, reflecting on the greatness of one’s spiritual companions, avoiding lazy persons, associating with energetic persons, and inclination towards that.

Tattha [V 2.0341][M 2.0379] nirayesu pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāya mahādukkhānubhavanakālepi, tiracchānayoniyaṃ jālakhipanakumīnādīhi gahitakālepi, pājanakaṇṭakādippahāratunnassa sakaṭavahanādikālepi, pettivisaye anekānipi vassasahassāni ekaṃ buddhantarampi khuppipāsāhi āturībhūtakālepi, kālakañcikaasuresu saṭṭhihatthaasītihatthappamāṇena aṭṭhicammamatteneva attabhāvena vātātapādidukkhānubhavanakālepi na sakkā vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ uppādetuṃ, ayameva te bhikkhu kālo vīriyakaraṇāyāti evaṃ apāyabhayaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi vīriyasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

Herein, in the hells, starting from the fivefold binding and torture, even while experiencing great suffering; in the animal realm, even when seized by those who cast nets, hooks, and so on, or while being pierced by goads, thorns, and so on, or while pulling carts and so on; in the realm of ghosts, even while afflicted by hunger and thirst for many thousands of years, for an entire Buddha-interval; or among the Kālakañjaka asuras, where, with bodies of only bone and skin sixty or eighty cubits in measure, one experiences the suffering of wind, sun, and so on—it is impossible to arouse the energy enlightenment factor. “Now, monk, is the time for you to exert energy”—thus, for one reflecting on the fear of the lower realms, the energy enlightenment factor arises.

Na sakkā kusītena navalokuttaradhammaṃ laddhuṃ, āraddhavīriyeneva sakkā ayamānisaṃso vīriyassāti [P 3.0790] evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinopi uppajjati. Sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhamahāsāvakehi te gatamaggo gantabbo, so ca na sakkā kusītena gantunti evaṃ gamanavīthiṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati. Ye taṃ piṇḍapātādīhi upaṭṭhahanti, ime te manussā neva ñātakā, na dāsakammakarā, nāpi taṃ nissāya jīvissāmāti te paṇītāni cīvarādīni denti. Atha kho attano kārānaṃ mahapphalataṃ paccāsīsamānā denti. Satthārāpi “ayaṃ ime paccaye paribhuñjitvā kāyadaḷhībahulo sukhaṃ viharissatī”ti na evaṃ sampassatā tuyhaṃ paccayā anuññātā. Atha kho “ayaṃ ime paribhuñjamāno samaṇadhammaṃ katvā vaṭṭadukkhato muccissatī”ti te paccayā anuññātā, so dāni tvaṃ kusīto viharanto na taṃ piṇḍaṃ apacāyissati. Āraddhavīriyasseva hi piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ nāma hotīti evaṃ piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati ayyamittattherassa viya.

It is impossible for a lazy person to attain the ninefold supramundane Dhamma; it is possible only for one with aroused energy. “This is the benefit of energy”—thus it arises for one who sees the benefits. The path trodden by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples is to be trodden by you, and it cannot be trodden by the lazy—thus it arises for one reflecting on the path to be trodden. Those who support you with alms-food and so on are neither your relatives, nor your slaves or servants, nor do they sustain themselves by depending on you. Rather, they give choice robes and other requisites, hoping for great fruit from their actions. The Teacher did not permit requisites for you with the thought: “Having used these, he will live happily with a strong body.” Rather, he permitted those requisites with the thought: “Using these, he will practice the ascetic’s duties and be freed from the suffering of the cycle.” So now, if you dwell lazily, you will not be reverencing that alms-food. For reverencing alms-food is only for one with aroused energy—thus it arises for one reflecting on reverencing alms-food, as in the case of the Elder Ayyamitta.

Thero kira kassakaleṇe nāma paṭivasati. Tassa ca gocaragāme ekā mahāupāsikā theraṃ puttaṃ katvā paṭijaggati. Sā ekadivasaṃ araññaṃ gacchantī dhītaraṃ āha – “amma, asukasmiṃ ṭhāne purāṇataṇḍulā, asukasmiṃ sappi, asukasmiṃ khīraṃ, asukasmiṃ phāṇitaṃ, tava bhātikassa ayyamittassa āgatakāle bhattaṃ pacitvā khīrasappiphāṇitehi saddhiṃ dehi, tvañca bhuñjeyyāsi. Ahaṃ pana hiyyo pakkapārivāsikabhattaṃ kañjiyena bhuttāmhī”ti. Divā kiṃ bhuñjissasi ammā,ti? Sākapaṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā kaṇataṇḍulehi ambilayāguṃ pacitvā ṭhapehi ammā,ti.

The Elder, it is said, lived in a cave called Kassakaleṇa. In his alms-village, a great laywoman cared for him, treating him like a son. One day, while going to the forest, she told her daughter: “Dear, in such-and-such a place there is old rice, in such-and-such a place ghee, in such-and-such a place milk, in such-and-such a place molasses. When your brother, the Elder Ayyamitta, arrives, cook a meal and give it to him together with milk, ghee, and molasses, and you may eat too. As for me, yesterday I ate a probationer’s meal with rice gruel.” “Mother, what will you eat during the day?” “Dear, add a vegetable leaf, cook some sour gruel with broken rice, and keep it aside.”

Thero [M 2.0380] cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ nīharantova taṃ saddaṃ sutvā attānaṃ ovadi “mahāupāsikā kira kañjiyena pārivāsikabhattaṃ bhuñji, divāpi kaṇapaṇṇambilayāguṃ bhuñjissati[V 2.0342], tuyhaṃ atthāya pana purāṇataṇḍulādīni ācikkhati, taṃ nissāya kho panesā neva khettaṃ na vatthuṃ na bhattaṃ na vatthaṃ paccāsīsati, tisso pana sampattiyo patthayamānā deti, tvaṃ etissā tā sampattiyo dātuṃ sakkhissasi, na sakkhissasīti, ayaṃ kho pana piṇḍapāto tayā sarāgena sadosena [P 3.0791] samohena na sakkā gaṇhitu”nti pattaṃ thavikāya pakkhipitvā gaṇṭhikaṃ muñcitvā nivattitvā kassakaleṇameva gantvā pattaṃ heṭṭhāmañce cīvaraṃ cīvaravaṃse ṭhapetvā “arahattaṃ apāpuṇitvā na nikkhamissāmī”ti vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā nisīdi. Dīgharattaṃ appamatto hutvā nivutthabhikkhu vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā purebhattameva arahattaṃ patvā vikasamānamiva padumaṃ mahākhīṇāsavo sitaṃ karontova nisīdi. Leṇadvāre rukkhamhi adhivatthā devatā –

The Elder, having put on his robe and while taking out his bowl, heard that sound and admonished himself: “The great lay follower, it seems, has eaten a meal for one who has completed probation with rice gruel, and during the day she will eat sour gruel of broken rice and leaves. Yet for your sake, she points out old rice and the like. In return for this, she does not expect fields, property, food, or cloth. Instead, desiring three kinds of success, she gives. Will you be able to give her those successes or not? Moreover, this almsfood cannot be taken by you with lust, hatred, or delusion.” He placed the bowl back into the bag, untied the knot, turned back, and went to Kassaka’s cave. There, he set the bowl down on the lower bed and hung his robe on the robe rack, having resolved, “I will not leave until I attain arahantship.” He sat down, exerting himself with diligence. Having been heedful for a long time, the monk who had completed the holy life developed insight and attained arahantship before the meal. Like a blooming lotus, the great one with destroyed taints sat smiling. The deity dwelling in the tree at the cave’s entrance—

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te āsavā khīṇā, dakkhiṇeyyosi mārisā”ti. –

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred among men, homage to you, O supreme among men; whose taints are destroyed, you are worthy of offerings, O venerable one.”

Udānaṃ udānetvā “bhante, piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ tumhādisānaṃ arahantānaṃ bhikkhaṃ datvā mahallakitthiyo dukkhā muccissantī”ti āha. Thero uṭṭhahitvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā kālaṃ olokento “pātoyevā”ti ñatvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ pāvisi.

Having uttered an exclamation of joy, she said, “Venerable sir, by giving alms to arahants like you who have entered for alms, old women will be freed from suffering.” The Elder rose, opened the door, and observing the time, knowing it was still early, took his bowl and robe and entered the village.

Dārikāpi bhattaṃ sampādetvā “idāni me bhātā āgamissati, idāni āgamissatī”ti dvāraṃ olokayamānā nisīdi. Sā there gharadvāraṃ sampatte pattaṃ gahetvā sappiphāṇitayojitassa khīrapiṇḍapātassa pūretvā hatthe ṭhapesi. Thero “sukhaṃ hotū”ti anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sāpi taṃ olokayamānā aṭṭhāsi. Therassa hi tadā ativiya parisuddho chavivaṇṇo ahosi, vippasannāni indriyāni, mukhaṃ bandhanā pavuttatālapakkaṃ viya ativiya virocittha.

The girl, having prepared the meal, sat watching the door, thinking, “Now my brother will come, now he will come.” When the Elder reached the house door, she took his bowl, filled it with milk-rice almsfood mixed with ghee and molasses, and placed it in his hands. The Elder said, “May you be happy,” gave his blessing, and departed. She stood watching him. At that time, the Elder’s complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were exceedingly clear, and his face shone brilliantly like a ripe palm fruit released from its stalk.

Mahāupāsikā araññā āgantvā “kiṃ, amma, bhātiko te āgato”ti pucchi. Sā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Upāsikā “ajja [M 2.0381] mama puttassa pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ patta”nti ñatvā “abhiramati te, amma, bhātā buddhasāsane, na ukkaṇṭhatī”ti āha.

The great lay follower, having come from the forest, asked, “Dear, has your brother come?” She related all that had happened. The lay follower, knowing, “Today the purpose of my son's going forth has reached its culmination,” said, “Dear, your brother delights in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not discontent.”

Mahantaṃ kho panetaṃ satthudāyajjaṃ yadidaṃ satta ariyadhanāni nāma, taṃ na sakkā kusītena gahetuṃ. Yathā hi vippaṭipannaṃ puttaṃ mātāpitaro “ayaṃ amhākaṃ aputto”ti [P 3.0792] paribāhiraṃ [V 2.0343] karonti, so tesaṃ accayena dāyajjaṃ na labhati, evaṃ kusītopi idaṃ ariyadhanadāyajjaṃ na labhati, āraddhavīriyova labhatīti dāyajjamahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

Moreover, this great inheritance of the Teacher, namely the seven noble treasures, cannot be obtained by a lazy person. Just as parents disown a wayward child, saying, “This is not our child,” and exclude him, so he does not receive their inheritance after their passing away; in the same way, a lazy person does not obtain this noble treasure inheritance—only an energetic person does. Thus, by reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, energy arises.

Mahā kho pana te satthā, satthuno hi te mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhigaṇhanakālepi abhinikkhamanepi abhisambodhiyampi dhammacakkappavattanayamakapāṭihāriyadevorohanaāyusaṅkhāravossajjanesupi parinibbānakālepi dasasahassilokadhātu akampittha, yuttaṃ nu te evarūpassa satthu sāsane pabbajitvā kusītena bhavitunti evaṃ satthumahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

Indeed, great was your Teacher, for at the time of your Teacher’s conception in his mother’s womb, his Great Renunciation, his supreme enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the twin miracle, the descent from the world of the devas, the relinquishing of the life-formation, and at his final passing away—the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. Is it fitting for you, having gone forth in such a Teacher’s Dispensation, to be lazy? Thus, by reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, energy arises.

Jātiyāpi tvaṃ idāni na lāmakajātiko, asambhinnāya mahāsammatapaveṇiyā āgataukkākarājavaṃse jātosi, suddhodanamahārājassa ca mahāmāyādeviyā ca nattā, rāhulabhaddassa kaniṭṭho, tayā nāma evarūpena jinaputtena hutvā na yuttaṃ kusītena viharitunti evaṃ jātimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

By birth too, you are now not of low lineage. You were born into the unbroken noble line of the Okkāka kings, descended from the lineage of Mahāsammata; you are the grandson of the great King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of the venerable Rāhula. For one like you, a son of the Conqueror, it is not fitting to live lazily. Thus, by reflecting on the greatness of one's birth, energy arises.

Sāriputtamahāmoggallānā ceva asīti ca mahāsāvakā vīriyeneva lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsu, tvaṃ etesaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjasi, na paṭipajjasīti evaṃ sabrahmacārimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna, along with the eighty great disciples, penetrated the supramundane Dhamma through energy alone. Are you treading the path of these fellow practitioners, or are you not? Thus, by reflecting on the greatness of one's fellow practitioners, energy arises.

Kucchiṃ pūretvā ṭhitaajagarasadise vissaṭṭhakāyikacetasikavīriye kusītapuggale parivajjantassāpi āraddhavīriye pahitatte puggale sevantassāpi ṭhānanisajjādīsu vīriyuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Energy also arises for one who avoids lazy people—who are like well-fed pythons, with slackened bodily and mental energy—and associates with energetic and resolute people; and for one with a mind inclined, prone, and tending to generate energy in postures such as standing and sitting. One understands that for whom energy has thus arisen, the perfection of development comes about through the path of arahantship.

Pītisambojjhaṅgassa “atthi, bhikkhave, pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ uppādo hoti[M 2.0382]. Tattha pītiyeva pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma. Tassā uppādakamanasikāro yonisomanasikāro nāma.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of joy: “There are, bhikkhus, states that are a foundation for the enlightenment factor of joy. Frequent wise attention to them is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of joy and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of joy.” Thus its arising occurs. Herein, joy itself is the state that is the foundation for the enlightenment factor of joy. The attention that produces it is called wise attention.

Apica ekādasa dhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti buddhānussati, dhamma, saṅgha[V 2.0344], sīla, cāga, devatānussati [P 3.0793] upasamānussati lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā siniddhapuggalasevanatā pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Buddhaguṇe anussarantassāpi hi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati, dhammasaṅghaguṇe anussarantassāpi, dīgharattaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā rakkhitaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihinopi dasasīlaṃ pañcasīlaṃ pañcavekkhantassāpi, dubbhikkhabhayādīsu paṇītabhojanaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ datvā “evaṃ nāma adamhā”ti cāgaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihinopi evarūpe kāle sīlavantānaṃ dinnadānaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, yehi guṇehi samannāgatā devatā devattaṃ pattā, tathārūpānaṃ guṇānaṃ attani atthitaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, samāpattiyā vikkhambhitā kilesā saṭṭhipi sattatipi vassāni na samudācarantīti paccavekkhantassāpi, cetiyadassanabodhidassanatheradassanesu asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve buddhādīsu pasādasinehābhāvena gadrabhapiṭṭhe rajasadise lūkhapuggale parivajjantassāpi, buddhādīsu pasādabahule muducitte siniddhapuggale sevantassāpi, ratanattayaguṇaparidīpake pasādanīyasuttante paccavekkhantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu pītiuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Moreover, eleven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy: recollection of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, virtue, generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace, avoiding rough persons, associating with gentle persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and inclination toward them. For one who recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, suffusing the entire body up to the level of access concentration. The same occurs when recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma and the Sangha. When reflecting on virtue long maintained unbroken and guarded in purity through the fourfold purification, or when a lay follower reflects on the five or ten precepts, joy arises. When reflecting on generosity after giving fine food to fellow practitioners during times of famine, thinking, "This is what we have done," or when a lay follower reflects on gifts given to virtuous ones on such occasions, joy arises. When reflecting on the qualities present in oneself that deities possess, which led them to attain divine status, joy arises. When reflecting on how defilements suppressed by meditative attainment do not recur even for sixty or seventy years, joy arises. When avoiding rough persons—who, due to negligence in showing respect at shrines, Bodhi trees, or to elders, display a lack of faith and affection for the Buddha and others, resembling dust on a donkey's back—joy arises. When associating with gentle persons who are abundant in faith in the Buddha and others, and who are tender-hearted, joy arises. When reflecting on inspiring discourses that illuminate the qualities of the Triple Gem, joy arises. When one's mind is inclined, prone, and tending toward generating joy in postures like standing or sitting, joy arises. One understands that when joy arises in this way, its development is fulfilled by the path to arahantship.

Passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa “atthi, bhikkhave, kāyapassaddhi cittapassaddhi, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of tranquility: "There is, bhikkhus, bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Frequent wise attention to that is nutriment for the arising of the unarisen tranquility enlightenment factor, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen tranquility enlightenment factor." Thus its arising occurs.

Apica satta dhammā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paṇītabhojanasevanatā utusukhasevanatā iriyāpathasukhasevanatā majjhattapayogatā sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā passaddhakāyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Paṇītañhi siniddhaṃ sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassāpi, sītuṇhesu [P 3.0794] ca utūsu ṭhānādīsu ca iriyāpathesu sappāyautuñca iriyāpathañca sevantassāpi [M 2.0383] passaddhi uppajjati. Yo pana mahāpurisajātiko sabbautuiriyāpathakkhamo hoti, na taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa sabhāgavisabhāgatā atthi, tasseva visabhāge utuiriyāpathe vajjetvā sabhāge sevantassa uppajjati. Majjhattapayogo vuccati attano ca parassa ca kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇā. Iminā majjhattapayogena uppajjati. Yo leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paraṃ viheṭhayamāno vicarati, evarūpaṃ sāraddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ parivajjantassāpi, saṃyatapādapāṇiṃ passaddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu passaddhiuppādanatthāya ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi [V 2.0345] uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, seven things conduce to the arising of the tranquility enlightenment factor: consuming agreeable food, dwelling in a pleasant climate, maintaining comfortable postures, practicing moderation, avoiding restless individuals, associating with calm individuals, and being inclined towards it. For one who eats fine, smooth, and suitable food, or who dwells in a suitable climate and maintains suitable postures, tranquility arises. However, this is not stated with regard to a great being who can endure all climates and postures. But for one who has both agreeable and disagreeable states, it arises by avoiding disagreeable climates and postures and cultivating agreeable ones. Moderation is called reflecting on one's own and others' ownership of actions. Through this moderation, tranquility arises. For one who avoids a restless individual who goes around harming others with clods and sticks, who associates with a restrained and calm individual, and whose mind is inclined, prone, and tending to arouse tranquility in standing, sitting, and other postures—tranquility arises. When it has thus arisen, one understands that its full development is achieved through the path of arahantship.

Samādhisambojjhaṅgassa “atthi, bhikkhave, samathanimittaṃ abyagganimittaṃ, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro, anuppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha samathova samathanimittaṃ avikkhepaṭṭhena ca abyagganimittanti.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration: "There is, bhikkhus, the serenity-sign, the non-agitation-sign. Frequent wise attention to that is nutriment for the arising of the unarisen concentration enlightenment factor, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen concentration enlightenment factor." Thus its arising occurs. Herein, serenity itself is the serenity-sign; and in the sense of non-distraction, it is the non-agitation-sign.

Apica ekādasa dhammā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti vatthuvisadakiriyatā indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā nimittakusalatā samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatā samaye cittassa niggaṇhanatā samaye sampahaṃsanatā samaye ajjhupekkhanatā asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā samāhitapuggalasevanatā jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha vatthuvisadakiriyatā ca indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā ca vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Moreover, eleven things conduce to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor: clarifying the object, balancing the faculties, skill in the sign, uplifting the mind at the right time, restraining the mind at the right time, gladdening the mind at the right time, viewing with equanimity at the right time, avoiding persons who are not concentrated, associating with persons who are concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and being resolved on that. Herein, clarifying the object and balancing the faculties should be understood in the way already stated.

Nimittakusalatā nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahaṇakusalatā. Samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatāti yasmiṃ samaye atisithilavīriyatādīhi līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa paggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatāti yasmiṃ samaye āraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhataṃ [P 3.0795] cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa niggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye sampahaṃsanatāti yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānadhigamena vā nirassādaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti[M 2.0384]. Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma jāti jarā byādhi maraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena ca pasādaṃ janeti, ayaṃ vuccati “samaye sampahaṃsanatā”ti.

Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasiṇa sign. Uplifting the mind at the proper time: when the mind is sluggish due to excessive slackness of energy and the like, at that time, one uplifts it by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of states, energy, and rapture. Restraining the mind at the proper time: when the mind is restless due to excessive energy and the like, at that time, one restrains it by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Gladdening the mind at the proper time: when the mind is joyless due to dullness in the application of wisdom or failure to attain the bliss of peace, at that time, one inspires it by reflecting on the eight grounds for spiritual urgency. The eight grounds for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; the suffering of the lower worlds, the fifth; suffering rooted in the past round of existence; suffering rooted in the future round of existence; and suffering rooted in the present search for food. One also generates confidence by recollecting the qualities of the Three Jewels. This is called 'gladdening the mind at the proper time.'

Samaye ajjhupekkhanatā nāma yasmiṃ samaye sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadāssa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu na byāpāraṃ āpajjati, sārathi viya samappavattesu assesu. Ayaṃ vuccati – “samaye ajjhupekkhanatā”ti. Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā nāma upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ [V 2.0346] vā appattānaṃ vikkhittacittānaṃ puggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Samāhitapuggalasevanā nāma upacārena vā appanāya vā samāhitacittānaṃ sevanā bhajanā payirupāsanā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu samādhiuppādanatthaṃyeva ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evañhi paṭipajjato esa uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Looking on with equanimity at the proper time: when, through proper practice, the mind is neither sluggish nor agitated, not joyless, and proceeds evenly in its object, having entered the path of serenity, then one does not engage in uplifting, restraining, or gladdening it, like a charioteer with horses that are proceeding evenly. This is called 'looking on with equanimity at the proper time.' Avoiding individuals who are not concentrated means avoiding from afar individuals whose minds are distracted and who have not attained access concentration or absorption. Associating with concentrated individuals means serving, associating with, and attending upon those whose minds are concentrated through access concentration or absorption. Inclination towards that means having a mind inclined, bent, and leaning towards arousing concentration in standing, sitting, and other postures. For one who practices thus, this arises. And when this has arisen, one understands that the perfection of its development comes about through the path of arahantship.

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa “atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha upekkhāva upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma.

For the equanimity enlightenment factor, its arising is thus: "There are, bhikkhus, states that are grounds for the equanimity enlightenment factor. Frequent cultivation of wise attention to them is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor." Here, equanimity itself is what is meant by states that are grounds for the equanimity enlightenment factor.

Apica pañca dhammā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti sattamajjhattatā saṅkhāramajjhattatā sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā [P 3.0796] sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha dvīhākārehi sattamajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti “tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissasi, esopi attanova kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissati, tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī”ti evaṃ kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇena, “paramatthato sattoyeva natthi, so tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī”ti evaṃ nissattapaccavekkhaṇena cāti. Dvīhevākārehi saṅkhāramajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – “idaṃ cīvaraṃ anupubbena vaṇṇavikāratañceva jiṇṇabhāvañca upagantvā pādapuñchanacoḷakaṃ hutvā yaṭṭhikoṭiyā chaḍḍanīyaṃ bhavissati, sace panassa sāmiko [M 2.0385] bhaveyya, nāssa evaṃ vinassituṃ dadeyyā”ti evaṃ assāmikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena ca, “anaddhaniyaṃ idaṃ tāvakālika”nti evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena cāti. Yathā ca cīvare, evaṃ pattādīsupi yojanā kātabbā.

Furthermore, five states conduce to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor: neutrality towards beings, neutrality towards formations, avoiding individuals attached to beings and formations, associating with individuals who are neutral towards beings and formations, and inclination towards that. Herein, one arouses neutrality towards beings in two ways: by reflecting on ownership of kamma thus: 'You have come by your own kamma and will go by your own kamma; this one too has come by their own kamma and will go by their own kamma. To whom are you attached?'; and by reflecting on the absence of a being thus: 'Ultimately, there is no being. To whom are you attached?' One arouses neutrality towards formations in two ways: by reflecting on the absence of an owner thus: 'This robe, gradually undergoing a change of color and aging, will become a foot-wiping cloth and then will be discarded on the end of a stick. If it had an owner, they would not allow it to be destroyed like this'; and by reflecting on its temporariness thus: 'This is not lasting, only temporary.' Just as with the robe, so too should this be applied to the bowl and other requisites.

Sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatāti ettha yo puggalo gihi vā attano puttadhītādike, pabbajito vā attano antevāsikasamānupajjhāyakādike mamāyati, sahattheneva nesaṃ kesacchedanasūcikammacīvaradhovanarajanapattapacanādīni karoti, muhuttampi apassanto “asuko sāmaṇero kuhiṃ asuko daharo kuhi”nti bhantamigo viya ito cito ca oloketi, aññena kesacchedanādīnaṃ atthāya “muhuttaṃ asukaṃ pesethā”ti yāciyamānopi “amhepi taṃ attano kammaṃ na kārema, tumhe naṃ gahetvā kilamessathā”ti na deti, ayaṃ sattakelāyano nāma.

Regarding 'avoiding individuals attached to beings and formations': Here, a person, whether a householder who regards their own sons, daughters, and so on as 'mine,' or one gone forth who regards their own pupils, co-residents, preceptors, and so on as 'mine,' personally performs for them tasks such as cutting hair, needlework, washing and dyeing robes, cooking for the bowl, and so on. If they do not see them even for a moment, they look around here and there like a bewildered deer, thinking: 'Where is that novice? Where is that young one?' Even when asked by another for the sake of hair-cutting and so on, 'Send so-and-so for a moment,' they do not let them go, saying: 'We ourselves do not make them do our own work; you will tire them by taking them.' This one is called 'one attached to beings.'

Yo [V 2.0347] pana cīvarapattathālakakattarayaṭṭhiādīni mamāyati, aññassa hatthena parāmasitumpi na deti, tāvakālikaṃ yācito “mayampi idaṃ mamāyantā na paribhuñjāma, tumhākaṃ kiṃ dassāmā”ti vadati, ayaṃ saṅkhārakelāyano nāma. Yo pana tesu dvīsupi vatthūsu majjhatto udāsino, ayaṃ sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto nāma. Iti ayaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo evarūpaṃ sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaṃ ārakā parivajjantassāpi, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu taduppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi [P 3.0797] uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

One who regards robes, bowls, plates, staffs, and so on as 'mine,' and does not allow others to even touch them with their hands, and when asked for them temporarily says: 'Even we, cherishing this as our own, do not use it; what could we give to you?'—this one is called 'one attached to formations.' But one who is neutral and indifferent in both these matters is called 'one who is neutral towards beings and formations.' Thus, this equanimity enlightenment factor arises in one who avoids from afar such a person who is attached to beings and formations, who associates with a person who is neutral towards beings and formations, and whose mind is inclined, bent, and leaning towards arousing it in standing, sitting, and other postures.
