When it has thus arisen, one understands that the perfection of its development comes about through the path of arahantship.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā satta sambojjhaṅge pariggaṇhitvā, parassa vā, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa sambojjhaṅge pariggaṇhitvā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha sambojjhaṅgānaṃ nibbattinirodhavasena veditabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha bojjhaṅgapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā bojjhaṅgapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Thus, having comprehended the seven enlightenment factors in oneself, or in another, or at times in oneself and at times in another, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. Here, the arising and passing away of the enlightenment factors should be understood in terms of their production and cessation. Beyond this, the method is just as stated previously. Only here, mindfulness that comprehends the enlightenment factors is the truth of suffering; having made this connection, the gateway to liberation for the bhikkhu who comprehends the enlightenment factors should be understood. The rest is just the same.

Bojjhaṅgapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Enlightenment Factors is concluded.

Catusaccapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Four Truths

386. Evaṃ [M 2.0386] sattabojjhaṅgavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni catusaccavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ tebhūmakadhamme “idaṃ dukkha”nti yathāsabhāvato pajānāti, tasseva kho pana dukkhassa janikaṃ samuṭṭhāpikaṃ purimataṇhaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti, ubhinnaṃ appavattinibbānaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti, dukkhaparijānanaṃ samudayapajahanaṃ nirodhasacchikaraṇaṃ ariyamaggaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadā”ti yathāsabhāvato pajānātīti attho. Avasesā ariyasaccakathā ṭhapetvā jātiādīnaṃ padabhājanakathaṃ visuddhimagge vitthāritāyeva.

386. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment, now, in order to analyze it in terms of the four truths, the text states, 'Furthermore...' and so on. Herein, 'he understands as it really is, "This is suffering"' means that he understands the phenomena of the three realms—setting aside craving—as 'This is suffering,' in accordance with their true nature. He understands the aforesaid craving, which generates and originates that very suffering, as 'This is the origin of suffering.' He understands Nibbāna, the non-occurrence of both, as 'This is the cessation of suffering.' And he understands the Noble Path—which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and realizes cessation—as 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,' in accordance with its true nature. The remaining discussion on the Noble Truths, except for the word-analysis of terms such as birth, is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Dukkhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering

388. Padabhājane [V 2.0348] pana katamā ca, bhikkhave, jātīti bhikkhave, yā jātipi dukkhāti evaṃ vuttā jāti, sā katamāti evaṃ sabbapucchāsu attho veditabbo. Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānanti idaṃ “imesaṃ nāmā”ti niyamābhāvato sabbasattānaṃ pariyādānavacanaṃ. Tamhi tamhi sattanikāyeti idampi sabbasattanikāyapariyādānavacanaṃ jananaṃ jāti savikārānaṃ paṭhamābhinibbattakkhandhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sañjātīti idaṃ tassā eva upasaggamaṇḍitavevacanaṃ. Sā eva anupaviṭṭhākārena okkamanaṭṭhena okkanti. Nibbattisaṅkhātena abhinibbattanaṭṭhena abhinibbatti. Iti ayaṃ catubbidhāpi sammutikathā nāma[P 3.0798]. Khandhānaṃ pātubhāvoti ayaṃ pana paramatthakathā. Ekavokārabhavādīsu ekacatupañcabhedānaṃ khandhānaṃyeva pātubhāvo, na puggalassa, tasmiṃ pana sati puggalo pātubhūtoti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Āyatanānaṃ paṭilābhoti āyatanāni pātubhavantāneva paṭiladdhāni nāma honti, so tesaṃ pātubhāvasaṅkhāto paṭilābhoti attho.

388. Now, in the word-analysis, in all questions such as, 'And what, bhikkhus, is birth?', the meaning should be understood as: 'That birth which was spoken of as suffering, what is it?' The phrase 'of those various beings' is a term encompassing all beings, as there is no restriction such as 'of these by name.' The phrase 'in whatever order of beings' is also a term encompassing all orders of beings. 'Generation' (janana) is birth (jāti); this is a designation for the first arising of the aggregates with their alterations. 'Conception' (sañjāti) is a synonym for that, adorned with a prefix. 'Descent' (okkanti) is that same thing, in the sense of descending, in the manner of entering. 'Production' (abhinibbatti) is in the sense of arising, termed 'coming to be.' Thus, these four are what is called conventional speech. 'The manifestation of the aggregates,' however, is the ultimate teaching. In the one-constituent existence and so on, it is only the manifestation of the aggregates—divided as one, four, or five—not of a person. But when that is present, that a 'person' has manifested is a mere convention. 'The acquisition of the sense bases' means that the sense bases, as they manifest, are said to be acquired; thus, their manifestation is termed 'acquisition.'

389. Jarāti sabhāvaniddeso. Jīraṇatāti ākārabhāvaniddeso. Khaṇḍiccantiādi vikāraniddeso. Daharakālasmiñhi dantā samasetā honti. Teyeva paripaccante anukkamena vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjitvā tattha tattha pattanti. Atha patitañca ṭhitañca upādāya khaṇḍitadantā khaṇḍitā [M 2.0387] nāma. Khaṇḍitānaṃ bhāvo khaṇḍiccanti vuccati. Anukkamena paṇḍarabhūtāni kesalomāni palitāni nāma. Palitāni sañjātāni assāti palito, palitassa bhāvo pāliccaṃ. Jarāvātappahārena sositamaṃsalohitatāya valiyo tacasmiṃ assāti valittaco, tassa bhāvo valittacatā. Ettāvatā dantakesalomatacesu vikāradassanavasena pākaṭībhūtā pākaṭajarā dassitā.

389. 'Aging' is the exposition of its inherent nature. 'Decaying' is the exposition of its characteristic. 'Broken-toothedness,' and so on, is the exposition of its alteration. For in youth, the teeth are even and white. As they mature, they gradually undergo a change in color and fall out here and there. Then, with reference to what has fallen and what remains, the teeth are called 'broken.' The state of being broken is called 'broken-toothedness' (khaṇḍicca). Gradually, the head-hair and body-hair, having become white, are called 'gray' (palitāni). One for whom gray hairs have arisen is 'gray-haired' (palito); the state of being gray-haired is 'grayness' (pālicca). Because of the striking of the wind of aging, due to the drying up of flesh and blood, one has wrinkles on the skin and is 'wrinkle-skinned' (valittaco); the state of being so is 'wrinkledness' (valittacatā). Thus far, manifest aging has been shown by way of the visible alterations in the teeth, head-hair, body-hair, and skin.

Yatheva hi udakassa vā vātassa vā aggino vā tiṇarukkhādīnaṃ saṃbhaggapalibhaggatāya vā jhāmatāya vā gatamaggo pākaṭo hoti, na ca so gatamaggo tāneva udakādīni, evameva jarāya dantādīnaṃ khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, cakkhuṃ ummiletvāpi gayhati, na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarā. Na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā hoti. Yasmā pana jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati, tasmā jarā “āyuno saṃhānī”ti phalūpacārena vuttā. Yasmā daharakāle suppasannāni sukhumampi attano visayaṃ sukheneva ca gaṇhanasamatthāni cakkhādīni indriyāni jaraṃ pattassa paripakkāni ālulitāni avisadāni oḷārikampi attano visayaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthāni honti, tasmā “indriyānaṃ paripāko”tipi phalūpacāreneva vuttā.

For just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire is made manifest by the breaking and shattering or by the burning of grass, trees, and so on—and yet that path taken is not the water and so on themselves—even so the path taken by aging is made manifest by the brokenness of teeth and so on, and can be grasped even by opening the eye; and yet the brokenness of teeth and so on is not aging itself. For aging is not cognizable by the eye. But because the life-faculty of one who has reached old age declines, aging is called 'the decline of the life-faculty' by a figurative expression based on its effect. And because the faculties, such as the eye, which in youth are very clear and able to easily grasp even a subtle object in their own sphere, become, for one who has reached old age, overripe, confused, unclear, and unable to grasp even a coarse object in their own sphere, it is also called 'the ripening of the faculties'—again, by a figurative expression based on its effect.

390. Maraṇaniddese [V 2.0349] yanti maraṇaṃ sandhāya napuṃsakaniddeso, yaṃ maraṇaṃ cutīti vuccati, cavanatāti vuccatīti ayamettha yojanā. Tattha cutīti sabhāvaniddeso. Cavanatāti ākārabhāvaniddeso. Maraṇaṃ pattassa khandhā bhijjanti ceva antaradhāyanti ca adassanaṃ gacchanti, tasmā taṃ bhedo antaradhānanti vuccati. Maccumaraṇanti maccumaraṇaṃ, na khaṇikamaraṇaṃ. Kālakiriyāti maraṇakālakiriyā. Ayaṃ sabbāpi sammutikathāva. Khandhānaṃ bhedoti ayaṃ pana paramatthakathā. Ekavokārabhavādīsu ekacatupañcabhedānaṃ khandhānaṃyeva bhedo, na [P 3.0799] puggalassa, tasmiṃ pana sati puggalo matoti vohāramattaṃ hoti.

390. In the exposition of death, the word 'that' (yaṃ) is a neuter designation referring to death. The application here is: 'that death which is called 'passing away' (cuti) and is called 'the state of passing away' (cavanatā).' Herein, 'passing away' is the exposition of its inherent nature. 'The state of passing away' is the exposition of its characteristic. For one who has reached death, the aggregates break up and disappear, they go out of sight; therefore, it is called 'dissolution' and 'disappearance.' 'Death as dying' (maccumaraṇa) means death, not momentary death. 'The doing of time' (kālakiriyā) means the doing of the time of death. All this is conventional speech. 'The dissolution of the aggregates,' however, is the ultimate teaching. In the one-constituent existence and so on, it is only the dissolution of the aggregates—divided as one, four, or five—not of a person. But when that occurs, that a 'person' has died is a mere convention.

Kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti attabhāvassa nikkhepo. Maraṇaṃ pattassa hi niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ attabhāvo patati, tasmā taṃ kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti vuttaṃ. Jīvitindriyassa upacchedo pana sabbākārato paramatthato maraṇaṃ. Etadeva [M 2.0388] sammutimaraṇanti pi vuccati. Jīvitindriyupacchedameva hi gahetvā lokiyā “tisso mato, phusso mato”ti vadanti.

The casting off of the corpse is the casting off of individual existence. For one who has reached death, the individual existence falls away like a useless log; therefore, it is called 'the casting off of the corpse.' The cessation of the life faculty, however, is death in every aspect and in the ultimate sense. This is also called conventional death. For worldly people, taking it as just the cessation of the life faculty, say, 'Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead.'

391. Byasanenāti ñātibyasanādīsu yena kenaci byasanena. Dukkhadhammenāti vadhabandhādinā dukkhakāraṇena. Phuṭṭhassāti ajjhotthaṭassa abhibhūtassa. Sokoti yo ñātibyasanādīsu vā vadhabandhanādīsu vā aññatarasmiṃ sati tena abhibhūtassa uppajjati socanalakkhaṇo soko. Socitattanti socitabhāvo. Yasmā panesa abbhantare sosento parisosento uppajjati, tasmā antosoko antoparisokoti vuccati.

391. 'By calamity' means through any calamity, such as the calamity of relatives. 'By a painful state' means through a cause of suffering, such as execution or imprisonment. 'Afflicted' means touched, overwhelmed, overcome. 'Sorrow' is the sorrow characterized by grieving that arises in one who is overcome by any of the calamities, such as the calamity of relatives, or by execution, imprisonment, and so on. 'State of sorrowing' means the state of being in sorrow. And because this arises while wasting away internally, while completely wasting away, it is therefore called internal sorrow, internal complete wasting away.

392. “Mayhaṃ dhītā, mayhaṃ putto”ti evaṃ ādissa ādissa devanti paridevanti etenāti ādevo. Taṃ taṃ vaṇṇaṃ parikittetvā devanti etenāti paridevo. Tato parā dve tasseva bhāvaniddesā.

392. 'My daughter, my son'—lamenting thus, mentioning this again and again, is lamentation (ādeva). Extolling this and that quality while lamenting is lamentation (parideva). After that, there are two expositions of its nature.

393. Kāyikanti kāyapasādavatthukaṃ. Dukkhamanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ. Asātanti amadhuraṃ. Kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhanti kāyasamphassato jātaṃ dukkhaṃ. Asātaṃ vedayitanti amadhuraṃ vedayitaṃ.

393. 'Bodily' means having the body-sensitivity as its basis. 'Pain' is pain in the sense of being difficult to bear. 'Unpleasant' means not delightful. 'Pain born of bodily contact' means pain born from bodily contact. 'Unpleasant feeling' means a feeling that is not delightful.

394. Cetasikanti cittasampayuttaṃ. Sesaṃ dukkhe vuttanayameva.

394. 'Mental' means associated with the mind. The rest is in the same way as was stated for pain.

395. Āyāsoti saṃsīdanavisīdanākārappatto cittakilamatho. Balavataraṃ āyāso upāyāso. Tato parā dve attattaniyābhāvadīpakā bhāvaniddesā.

395. 'Distress' is the mental fatigue that has the characteristic of sinking and collapsing. A stronger distress is great distress. After that, the two are expositions of its nature, which illuminate the state of 'self' and 'what belongs to self'.

398. Jātidhammānanti [V 2.0350] jātisabhāvānaṃ. Icchā uppajjatīti taṇhā uppajjati. Aho vatāti patthanā. Na kho panetaṃ icchāyāti evaṃ jātiyā anāgamanaṃ vinā maggabhāvanaṃ na icchāya pattabbaṃ. Idampīti etampi upari sesāni upādāya pikāro. Yampicchanti yenapi dhammena alabbhaneyyavatthuṃ icchanto na labhati, taṃ alabbhaneyya vatthumhi icchanaṃ dukkhaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

398. 'Subject to birth' means those whose nature is to be born. 'Desire arises' means craving arises. 'If only' is a wish. 'But this is not to be had by wishing' means that the non-arising of birth is not to be attained by wishing, without the development of the path. Regarding 'this too' (idampi), the particle 'pi' is used with reference to the remaining items that follow. When one desires an unobtainable object and does not get it, that desire for an unobtainable object is suffering. This is the method in all cases.

399. Khandhaniddese [M 2.0389] rūpañca taṃ upādānakkhandho cāti rūpupādānakkhandho evaṃ sabbattha.

399. In the exposition of the aggregates, 'the form clinging-aggregate' means 'it is form and it is a clinging-aggregate.' This applies in all cases.

Samudayasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Origin

400. Yāyaṃ taṇhāti yā ayaṃ taṇhā. Ponobbhavikāti punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punobbhavo, punobbhavo sīlaṃ assāti ponobbhavikā. Nandīrāgena saha gatāti nandīrāgasahagatā. Nandīrāgena saddhiṃ atthato ekattameva gatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatratatrābhinandinīti [P 3.0800] yatra yatra attabhāvo, tatra tatra abhinandinī. Rūpādīsu vā ārammaṇesu tatra tatra abhinandinī, rūpābhinandinī sadda, gandha, rasa, phoṭṭhabba, dhammābhinandinīti attho. Seyyathidanti nipāto. Tassa sā katamā ceti attho. Kāme taṇhā kāmataṇhā, pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Bhave taṇhā bhavataṇhā, bhavapatthanāvasena uppannassa sassatadiṭṭhisahagatassa rūpārūpabhavarāgassa ca jhānanikantiyā cetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vibhave taṇhā vibhavataṇhā, ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

400. 'This craving' means 'this which is craving.' 'Leading to renewed existence' means that which causes renewed existence; renewed existence is its nature, thus it leads to renewed existence. 'Accompanied by delight and lust' means it goes together with delight and lust. This means it is said to have gone to oneness in meaning with delight and lust. 'Finding delight here and there' means finding delight wherever there is individual existence. Or, it means finding delight in this and that object, such as form, and so on; that is, delighting in form, sound, smell, taste, tactile objects, and mental objects. 'That is to say' is a particle, and its meaning is, 'And which is it?' Craving for sensual pleasures is sensual craving; this is a name for the passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Craving for existence is existence-craving; this is a designation for the lust for existence in the form and formless realms that arises by way of the aspiration for existence, accompanied by the eternalist view, and for the delight in jhāna. Craving for non-existence is non-existence-craving; this is a designation for the lust accompanied by the annihilationist view.

Idāni tassā taṇhāya vatthuṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ sā kho panesātiādimāha. Tattha uppajjatīti jāyati. Nivisatīti punappunaṃ pavattivasena patiṭṭhahati. Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpanti yaṃ lokasmiṃ piyasabhāvañceva madhurasabhāvañca. Cakkhu loketiādīsu lokasmiñhi cakkhādīsu mamattena abhiniviṭṭhā sattā sampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhitā attano cakkhuṃ ādāsatalādīsu nimittaggahaṇānusārena vippasannaṃ pañcapasādaṃ suvaṇṇavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇisīhapañjaraṃ viya maññanti, sotaṃ rajatapanāḷikaṃ viya, pāmaṅgasuttaṃ viya ca maññanti, “tuṅganāsā”ti laddhavohāraṃ ghānaṃ vaṭṭitvā ṭhapitaharitālavaṭṭaṃ viya maññanti, jivhaṃ rattakambalapaṭalaṃ viya mudusiniddhamadhurasadaṃ maññanti, kāyaṃ sālalaṭṭhiṃ viya, suvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya ca maññanti, manaṃ aññesaṃ manena asadisaṃ uḷāraṃ maññanti. Rūpaṃ suvaṇṇakaṇikārapupphādivaṇṇaṃ viya, saddaṃ mattakaravīka kokilamandadhamitamaṇivaṃsanigghosaṃ viya, attanā paṭiladdhāni catusamuṭṭhānikagandhārammaṇādīni [V 2.0351] “kassaññassa evarūpāni atthī”ti maññanti. Tesaṃ evaṃ maññamānānaṃ tāni cakkhādīni piyarūpāni ceva sātarūpāni ca honti. Atha nesaṃ tattha anuppannā ceva taṇhā uppajjati[M 2.0390], uppannā ca taṇhā punappunaṃ pavattivasena nivisati. Tasmā bhagavā “cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī”tiādimāha. Tattha uppajjamānāti yadā uppajjamānā hoti, tadā ettha uppajjatīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Now, to show in detail the basis of that craving, he said, 'Now, this craving,' and so on. Therein, 'arises' means is born. 'Settles' means it becomes established by way of repeated occurrence. 'Whatever in the world is endearing and agreeable' means whatever in the world has an endearing nature and a pleasing nature. Regarding 'the eye in the world,' and so on: in the world, beings who are attached with a sense of 'mine' to the eye and so on, established in their acquisitions, regard their own eye—the clear fivefold sensitivity—according to the grasping of signs in a mirror surface and so on, as like an opened jeweled lion-window in a golden palace. They regard the ear as like a silver pipe or a plumb line. They regard the nose, which has received the designation 'prominent nose,' as like a rolled and placed stick of yellow orpiment. They regard the tongue as like a layer of red wool, soft, smooth, and sweet-sounding. They regard the body as like a sāla sapling or a golden archway. They regard their mind as unlike the minds of others, as sublime. They regard form as like the color of a golden kaṇikāra flower, and so on; sound as like the sound of a jeweled flute gently blown by intoxicated karavīka birds and cuckoos. And regarding the olfactory objects and so on, which arise from the four sources, that they have obtained, they think, 'Who else has such things?' For those who think in this way, those things, the eye and so on, become endearing and agreeable. Then, for them, craving that has not yet arisen arises, and craving that has arisen settles by way of repeated occurrence. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'The eye in the world is endearing and agreeable; it is here that this craving, when arising, arises,' and so on. Therein, 'when arising' means that when it is in the process of arising, it arises here. This is the method in all cases.

Nirodhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation

401. Asesavirāganirodhotiādīni sabbāni nibbānavevacanāneva. Nibbānañhi āgamma taṇhā asesā virajjati nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ “tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho”ti vuccati. Nibbānañca āgamma taṇhā cajiyati paṭinissajjiyati vimuccati na [P 3.0801] allīyati, tasmā nibbānaṃ “cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo”ti vuccati. Ekameva hi nibbānaṃ, nāmāni panassa sabbasaṅkhatānaṃ nāmapaṭipakkhavasena anekāni honti. Seyyathidaṃ, asesavirāgo asesanirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo taṇhakkhayo anuppādo appavattaṃ animittaṃ appaṇihitaṃ anāyūhanaṃ appaṭisandhi anupapatti agati ajātaṃ ajaraṃ abyādhi amataṃ asokaṃ aparidevaṃ anupāyāsaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhanti.

401. "Complete fading away, cessation," and so forth—all these are synonyms for Nibbāna. For it is by relying on Nibbāna that craving utterly fades away and ceases; therefore, it is called "the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving." And by relying on Nibbāna, craving is abandoned, relinquished, released, and does not cling; thus, Nibbāna is called "abandonment, relinquishment, liberation, non-attachment." Indeed, Nibbāna is one, but its names are many by way of being the opposite of the names of all conditioned things. These include: complete fading away, complete cessation, abandonment, relinquishment, liberation, non-attachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, non-recurrence, signlessness, desirelessness, non-accumulation, non-rebirth, non-reappearance, no destination, the unborn, the unaging, the unailing, the deathless, the sorrowless, the lamentless, the distressless, the undefiled.

Idāni maggena chinnāya nibbānaṃ āgamma appavattipattāyapi ca taṇhāya yesu vatthūsu tassā uppatti dassitā, tattheva abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ sā kho panesātiādimāha. Tattha yathā puriso khette jātaṃ tittaalābuvalliṃ disvā aggato paṭṭhāya mūlaṃ pariyesitvā chindeyya, sā anupubbena milāyitvā apaññattiṃ gaccheyya. Tato tasmiṃ khette tittaalābu niruddhā pahīnāti vucceyya, evameva khette tittaalābu viya cakkhādīsu taṇhā. Sā ariyamaggena mūlacchinnā nibbānaṃ āgamma appavattiṃ gacchati. Evaṃ gatā pana tesu vatthūsu khette tittaalābu viya na paññāyati.

Now, to show the non-existence of craving in those very objects where its arising was shown, even though it has been cut off by the path and has reached non-recurrence by relying on Nibbāna, he said, "But this..." and so forth. Here, just as a man, seeing a bitter gourd vine grown in a field, might seek its root from the top downwards and cut it, and it would gradually wither away and cease to be discernible. Then it could be said that the bitter gourd in that field has ceased and been abandoned. In the same way, craving is like the bitter gourd in the field of the eye and so on. It is cut off at the root by the noble path and reaches non-recurrence by relying on Nibbāna. When it has gone thus, it is no longer discernible in those objects, just as the bitter gourd is no longer discernible in the field.

Yathā ca aṭavito core ānetvā nagarassa dakkhiṇadvāre ghāteyyuṃ, tato aṭaviyaṃ corā matāti vā māritāti vā vucceyyuṃ, evaṃ aṭaviyaṃ corā viya cakkhādīsu taṇhā. Sā dakkhiṇadvāre corā viya nibbānaṃ āgamma niruddhattā nibbāne niruddhā. Evaṃ niruddhā panetesu [V 2.0352] vatthūsu aṭaviyaṃ corā viya na paññāyati, tenassā tattheva nirodhaṃ dassento [M 2.0391] “cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhatī”tiādimāha.

Just as if bandits were brought from the forest and executed at the southern gate of the city, then it would be said that the bandits had died in the forest or had been killed; so too with craving in regard to the eye and so on—craving is like bandits in the forest. That craving, like the bandits at the southern gate, is ceased in Nibbāna, having been brought to cessation by relying on Nibbāna. Thus ceased in these bases, it is no longer discernible, just as the bandits are no longer discernible in the forest. Therefore, to show its cessation right there, he said: "The eye is a beloved and agreeable thing in the world. It is here that this craving is abandoned when being abandoned, and ceases when ceasing," and so forth.

Maggasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path

402. Ayamevāti aññamaggapaṭikkhepanatthaṃ niyamanaṃ. Ariyoti taṃ taṃ maggavajjhehi kilesehi ārakattā ariyabhāvakarattā ca ariyo. Dukkhe ñāṇantiādinā catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ. Tattha purimāni dve saccāni vaṭṭaṃ, pacchimāni vivaṭṭaṃ. Tesu bhikkhuno vaṭṭe kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso hoti, vivaṭṭe natthi abhiniveso. Purimāni hi dve saccāni “pañcakkhandhā dukkhaṃ, taṇhā samudayo”ti evaṃ saṅkhepena ca “katame pañcakkhandhā, rūpakkhandho”tiādinā nayena vitthārena ca ācariyassa santike uggaṇhitvā vācāya punappunaṃ parivattento yogāvacaro kammaṃ karoti. Itaresu pana dvīsu saccesu nirodhasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ, maggasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpanti evaṃ savanena kammaṃ [P 3.0802] karoti. So evaṃ karonto cattāri saccāni ekapaṭivedheneva paṭivijjhati ekābhisamayena abhisameti. Dukkhaṃ pariññāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, samudayaṃ pahānapaṭivedhena, nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāpaṭivedhena, maggaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati. Dukkhaṃ pariññābhisamayena…pe… maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti. Evamassa pubbabhāge dvīsu saccesu uggahaparipucchāsavanadhāraṇasammasanapaṭivedho hoti, dvīsu pana savanapaṭivedhoyeva. Aparabhāge tīsu kiccato paṭivedho hoti, nirodhe ārammaṇapaṭivedho. Paccavekkhaṇā pana pattasaccassa hoti. Ayañca ādikammiko, tasmā sā idha na vuttā.

402. 'This very' is a determination for the purpose of rejecting other paths. 'Noble' (ariya) is so called because it is far from those defilements to be avoided by the path, and because it brings about the state of nobility. 'Knowledge of suffering,' and so forth—by this the meditation subject of the four truths is indicated. Among them, the first two truths pertain to the cycle of existence, while the latter two pertain to liberation from the cycle. For a bhikkhu, there is an absorption in the meditation subject with regard to the cycle of existence, but no absorption with regard to liberation from the cycle. For the first two truths—'The five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin'—the yogi, having learned them briefly and in detail from the teacher, such as 'What are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form,' and so forth, engages in the practice by repeatedly reciting them verbally. Regarding the other two truths, the truth of cessation is desirable, pleasing, and agreeable, and the truth of the path is likewise desirable, pleasing, and agreeable—thus, one engages in the practice through hearing. So doing, one penetrates all four truths with a single penetration and comprehends them with a single comprehension. Suffering is penetrated through the penetration of full understanding, the origin through the penetration of abandonment, cessation through the penetration of realization, and the path through the penetration of development. Suffering is comprehended through the comprehension of full understanding, and so on up to the path through the comprehension of development. Thus, in the preliminary stage, there is the penetration of learning, questioning, hearing, retention, and examination regarding the first two truths, while for the latter two, there is only the penetration of hearing. In the later stage, penetration occurs in terms of function for three truths, while for cessation, it is penetration of the object. Reviewing, however, pertains to the truth that has been attained. This is for the one just beginning, therefore it is not discussed here.

Imassa ca bhikkhuno pubbe pariggahato “dukkhaṃ parijānāmi, samudayaṃ pajahāmi, nirodhaṃ sacchikaromi, maggaṃ bhāvemī”ti ābhogasamannāhāramanasikārapaccavekkhaṇā natthi, pariggahato paṭṭhāya hoti. Aparabhāge pana dukkhaṃ pariññātameva…pe… maggo bhāvitova hoti. Tattha dve saccāni duddasattā gambhīrāni, dve gambhīrattā duddasāni. Dukkhasaccañhi uppattito pākaṭaṃ, khāṇukaṇṭakapahārādīsu “aho dukkha”nti vattabbatampi āpajjati. Samudayampi khāditukāmatābhuñjitukāmatādivasena uppattito pākaṭaṃ. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhato pana ubhayampi gambhīraṃ. Iti tāni duddasattā gambhīrāni. Itaresaṃ pana dvinnaṃ dassanatthāya payogo bhavaggagahaṇatthaṃ hatthappasāraṇaṃ [M 2.0392] viya avīciphusanatthaṃ pādappasāraṇaṃ viya satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā [V 2.0353] koṭipādanaṃ viya ca hoti. Iti tāni gambhīrattā duddasāni. Evaṃ duddasattā gambhīresu gambhīrattā ca duddasesu catūsu saccesu uggahādivasena pubbabhāgañāṇuppattiṃ sandhāya idaṃ dukkhe ñāṇantiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭivedhakkhaṇe pana ekameva taṃ ñāṇaṃ hoti.

Moreover, for this bhikkhu, before comprehension, there is no reflection, attention, consideration, or reviewing such as, 'I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, I develop the path.' But from comprehension onwards, it is present. Later on, suffering is fully understood...the path is fully developed. Here, two truths are profound because they are hard to see, and two are hard to see because they are profound. For the truth of suffering is evident in its arising, as seen when one exclaims, 'Ah, suffering!' upon being struck by a thorn or splinter, and so forth. The origin is also evident in its arising, such as the desire to eat or the desire to enjoy, and so forth. But both are profound when it comes to penetration of their characteristics. Thus, they are profound because they are hard to see. As for the other two, the effort to see them is like stretching out the hand to grasp the highest point of existence, like stretching out the foot to touch the Avīci hell, or like placing the tip of a hair split a hundred times onto another hair tip. Thus, they are hard to see because of their profundity. In this way, regarding the four truths—which are profound because they are hard to see, and hard to see because they are profound—this statement 'knowledge of suffering,' and so forth, refers to the arising of knowledge in the preliminary stage through learning, and so on. But at the moment of penetration, there is only one knowledge.

Nekkhammasaṅkappādayo kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāviramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu tīsu ṭhānesu uppannassa akusalasaṅkappassa padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamāno ekova kusalasaṅkappo uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāsaṅkappo nāma.

Thoughts of renunciation and so forth are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from sensual desire, ill-will, and harmfulness. However, at the moment of the path, a single wholesome thought arises, fulfilling the path factor by cutting off the root of the unwholesome thought that has arisen in these three instances and thereby establishing its non-arising. This is called right thought.

Musāvādāveramaṇiādayopi musāvādādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu catūsu ṭhānesu uppannāya akusaladussīlyacetanāya padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāvācā nāma[P 3.0803].

Abstaining from false speech and so forth—these too are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from false speech and so forth. However, at the moment of the path, a single wholesome abstention arises, fulfilling the path factor by cutting off the root of the unwholesome immoral volition that has arisen in these four instances and thereby establishing its non-arising. This is called right speech.

Pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādayopi pāṇātipātādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu tīsu ṭhānesu uppannāya akusaladussīlyacetanāya akiriyato padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati, ayaṃ sammākammanto nāma.

Abstaining from killing living beings and so forth—these too are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from killing and so forth. However, at the moment of the path, a single wholesome abstention arises, fulfilling the path factor by cutting off the root of the unwholesome immoral volition that has arisen in these three instances and thereby establishing its non-arising through non-performance. This is called right action.

Micchāājīvanti khādanīyabhojanīyādīnaṃ atthāya pavattitaṃ kāyavacīduccaritaṃ. Pahāyāti vajjetvā. Sammāājīvenāti buddhapasatthena ājīvena. Jīvitaṃ kappetīti jīvitappavattiṃ pavatteti. Sammāājīvopi kuhanādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesuyeva sattasu ṭhānesu uppannāya micchājīvadussīlyacetanāya padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati, ayaṃ sammāājīvo nāma.

Wrong livelihood is bodily and verbal misconduct undertaken for the sake of food, drink, and so on. 'Abandoning' means avoiding. 'By right livelihood' means by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. 'He makes a living' means he maintains the continuity of life. Right livelihood, too, due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from deceit and so on, is diverse in the preliminary stage. However, at the moment of the path, a single wholesome abstention arises, fulfilling the path factor by cutting off the root of the volition of wrong livelihood and immorality that has arisen in these very seven instances, and thereby establishing its non-arising. This is called right livelihood.

Anuppannānanti ekasmiṃ vā bhave tathārūpe vā ārammaṇe attano na uppannānaṃ. Parassa pana uppajjamāne disvā “aho vata me evarūpā pāpakā akusaladhammā na uppajjeyyu”nti evaṃ anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ [M 2.0393] dhammānaṃ anuppādāya. Chandaṃ janetīti tesaṃ anuppādakapaṭipattisādhakaṃ vīriyachandaṃ janeti. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti [V 2.0354] vīriyaṃ pavatteti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti vīriyena cittaṃ paggahitaṃ karoti. Padahatīti kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca aṭṭhi ca avasissatūti padahanaṃ pavatteti.

'Unarisen' means those that have not arisen in oneself in a particular existence or in such an object. But seeing them arising in another, one thinks: 'Oh, that such evil, unwholesome states would not arise in me!' Thus, for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, he generates desire. 'He generates desire' means he generates the energetic desire that accomplishes the practice for their non-arising. 'He exerts' means he makes an effort. 'He arouses energy' means he sets energy in motion. 'He uplifts the mind' means with energy he makes the mind uplifted. 'He strives' means he sets striving in motion, thinking, 'Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain!'

Uppannānanti samudācāravasena attano uppannapubbānaṃ. Idāni tādise na uppādessāmīti tesaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānanti appaṭiladdhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ. Uppannānanti tesaṃyeva paṭiladdhānaṃ. Ṭhitiyāti punappunaṃ uppattipabandhavasena ṭhitatthaṃ. Asammosāyāti avināsanatthaṃ. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti uparibhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Bhāvanāya pāripūriyāti bhāvanāya paripūraṇatthaṃ. Ayampi sammāvāyāmo anuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ anuppādanādicittānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesuyeva catūsu ṭhānesu kiccasādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānaṃ ekameva kusalavīriyaṃ uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāvāyāmo nāma.

'Arisen' refers, by way of habitual conduct, to those that have previously arisen in oneself. Thinking, 'I will not let such states arise now,' one generates desire for their abandonment. 'Unarisen wholesome states' refers to those not yet attained, such as the first jhāna and so on. 'Arisen' refers to those very same states already attained. 'For their maintenance' means for the sake of stability, by way of a continuous sequence of repeated arising. 'For non-confusion' means for the sake of non-destruction. 'For increase' means for a superior state. 'For abundance' means for an expanded state. 'For development and fulfillment' means for the sake of completing the cultivation. This right effort, too, in the preliminary stage is diverse due to the diversity of thoughts, such as those for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. But at the moment of the path, only a single wholesome energy arises, fulfilling the path factor by accomplishing its function in these very four instances. This is called right effort.

Sammāsatipi kāyādipariggāhakacittānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana catūsu ṭhānesu kiccasādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva sati uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāsati nāma.

Right mindfulness, too, because of the diversity of the consciousness that encompasses the body, etc., is diverse in the preliminary stage. But at the moment of the path, a single mindfulness arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of accomplishing its function in the four foundations. This is called right mindfulness.

Jhānāni pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi [P 3.0804] nānā, pubbabhāge samāpattivasena nānā, maggakkhaṇe nānāmaggavasena. Ekassa hi paṭhamamaggo paṭhamajjhāniko hoti, dutiyamaggādayopi paṭhamajjhānikā vā dutiyajjhānādīsu aññatarajhānikā vā. Ekassapi paṭhamamaggo dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajhāniko hoti, dutiyādayopi dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajjhānikā vā paṭhamajjhānikā vā. Evaṃ cattāropi maggā jhānavasena sadisā vā asadisā vā ekaccasadisā vā honti. Ayaṃ panassa viseso pādakajjhānaniyamena hoti.

The jhānas differ both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. In the preliminary stage, they differ in terms of attainment, while at the moment of the path, they differ according to the different paths. For one person, the first path may be associated with the first jhāna, and the second path and so on may be associated with the first jhāna or any of the other jhānas. For another person, the first path may be associated with any of the other jhānas, and the second path and so on may be associated with any of the other jhānas or the first jhāna. Thus, the four paths may be similar, dissimilar, or partially similar in terms of jhāna. But this distinction is determined by the foundational jhāna.

Pādakajjhānaniyamena tāva paṭhamajjhānalābhino paṭhamajjhānā vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno maggo paṭhamajjhāniko hoti. Maggaṅgabojjhaṅgāni panettha paripuṇṇāneva honti. Dutiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno dutiyajjhāniko hoti. Maggaṅgāni panettha satta honti. Tatiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno tatiyajjhāniko. Maggaṅgāni panettha satta[M 2.0394], bojjhaṅgāni cha honti. Esa nayo catutthajjhānato vuṭṭhāya yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ.

First, by the determination of the foundational jhāna: for one who has attained the first jhāna, emerges from the first jhāna, and then develops insight, the path that arises is connected to the first jhāna. Here, the path factors and enlightenment factors are fully complete. For one who emerges from the second jhāna and develops insight, the path that arises is connected to the second jhāna. Here, there are seven path factors. For one who emerges from the third jhāna and develops insight, the path that arises is connected to the third jhāna. Here, there are seven path factors and six enlightenment factors. This is the method up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having emerged from the fourth jhāna.

Āruppe [V 2.0355] catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ uppajjati, tañca lokuttaraṃ, no lokiyanti vuttaṃ, ettha kathanti? Etthāpi paṭhamajjhānādīsu yato vuṭṭhāya sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭilabhitvā arūpasamāpattiṃ bhāvetvā so āruppe uppanno, taṃ jhānikāvassa tattha tayo maggā uppajjanti. Evaṃ pādakajjhānameva niyameti.

It is said: 'In the formless realm, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise, and these are supramundane, not mundane.' How is this here? Here too, if one emerges from the first jhāna or others, attains the path of stream-entry, and then cultivates the formless attainments, and that person is reborn in the formless realm, then for him, the three subsequent paths associated with that jhāna arise there. Thus, it is the foundational jhāna alone that determines this.

Keci pana therā “vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentī”ti vadanti. Keci “puggalajjhāsayo niyametī”ti vadanti. Keci “vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā niyametī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ vādavinicchayo visuddhimagge vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanādhikāre vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

However, some elders say, "The aggregates, being the object of insight, determine it." Some say, "The disposition of the individual determines it." Some say, "Insight leading to emergence determines it." The adjudication of these views should be understood according to the method explained in the Visuddhimagga in the section on insight leading to emergence.

Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhīti ayaṃ pubbabhāge lokiyo aparabhāge lokuttaro sammāsamādhīti vuccati.

This, bhikkhus, is called right concentration: this is called mundane right concentration in the preliminary stage and supramundane right concentration in the later stage.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā cattāri saccāni pariggaṇhitvā, parassa vā, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa cattāri saccāni pariggaṇhitvā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha catunnaṃ saccānaṃ yathāsambhāvato uppattinivattivasena veditabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha catusaccapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ [P 3.0805] yojanaṃ katvā saccapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ, sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally' means having grasped the four truths in oneself, or in another, or at times in oneself and at times in another, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. Here, the arising and passing away of these four truths should be understood in terms of origination and cessation, according to their respective possibilities. Beyond this, the method is as previously stated. Only here, the mindfulness that grasps the four truths, by making the application 'the truth of suffering,' should be understood as the gateway to deliverance for the bhikkhu who grasps the truths. The rest is similar.

Catusaccapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the Four Truths is concluded.

404. Ettāvatā ānāpānapabbaṃ catuiriyāpathapabbaṃ catusampajaññapabbaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ catudhātuvavatthānaṃ navasivathikā vedanānupassanā cittānupassanā nīvaraṇapariggaho khandhapariggaho āyatanapariggaho bojjhaṅgapariggaho saccapariggahoti ekavīsati kammaṭṭhānāni. Tesu ānāpānaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ navasivathikāti ekādasa appanākammaṭṭhānāni honti. Dīghabhāṇakamahāsīvatthero pana “navasivathikā ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttā”ti āha. Tasmā tassa matena dveyeva appanākammaṭṭhānāni, sesāni upacārakammaṭṭhānāni. Kiṃ panetesu sabbesu abhiniveso [M 2.0395] jāyatīti? Na jāyati. Iriyāpathasampajaññanīvaraṇabojjhaṅgesu hi abhiniveso na jāyati, sesesu jāyatīti. Mahāsīvatthero panāha “etesupi abhiniveso jāyati. Ayañhi ‘atthi nu kho me cattāro iriyāpathā udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me catusampajaññaṃ udāhu [V 2.0356] natthi, atthi nu kho me pañcanīvaraṇā udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me sattabojjhaṅgā udāhu natthī’ti evaṃ pariggaṇhāti. Tasmā sabbattha abhiniveso jāyatī”ti.

404. Up to this point, there are twenty-one meditation subjects: the section on mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, the four kinds of clear comprehension, the thirty-two parts, the analysis of the four elements, the nine charnel ground contemplations, contemplation of feelings, contemplation of mind, the grasping of the hindrances, the grasping of the aggregates, the grasping of the sense bases, the grasping of the enlightenment factors, and the grasping of the truths. Among these, mindfulness of breathing, the thirty-two parts, and the nine charnel ground contemplations—eleven in total—are subjects for absorption. However, the elder Dīghabhāṇaka Mahāsīva says, "The nine charnel ground contemplations are stated by way of contemplation of the repulsive." Therefore, according to his view, there are only two absorption subjects; the rest are access concentration subjects. But does adherence arise regarding all these? It does not. Adherence does not arise regarding postures, clear comprehension, hindrances, or enlightenment factors, but it does arise regarding the rest. However, the elder Mahāsīva says, "Adherence arises even in these. For one grasps thus: 'Do I have the four postures or not? Do I have the four kinds of clear comprehension or not? Do I have the five hindrances or not? Do I have the seven enlightenment factors or not?' Therefore, adherence arises in all cases."

Yo hi koci, bhikkhaveti yo hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā upāsako vā upāsikā vā. Evaṃ bhāveyyātiādito paṭṭhāya vuttena bhāvanānukkamena bhāveyya. Pāṭikaṅkhanti paṭikaṅkhitabbaṃ icchitabbaṃ avassaṃbhāvīti attho. Aññāti arahattaṃ. Sati vā upādiseseti upādānasese vā sati aparikkhīṇe. Anāgāmitāti anāgāmibhāvo.

"For whoever, bhikkhus"—for whatever bhikkhu, bhikkhuni, male lay follower, or female lay follower. "Should develop in this way"—beginning from the start, one should develop according to the sequence of development described. "One may expect"—it should be expected, wished for; the meaning is that it is certain to happen. "Final knowledge"—arahantship. "Or, if there is a residue of clinging"—or, if there is a residue of clinging remaining, unexhausted. "Non-returning"—the state of a non-returner.

Evaṃ sattannaṃ vassānaṃ vasena sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassetvā puna tato appatarepi kāle dassento tiṭṭhantu, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Sabbampi cetaṃ majjhimassa veneyyapuggalassa vasena vuttaṃ, tikkhapaññaṃ pana sandhāya “pātova anusiṭṭho sāyaṃ visesaṃ adhigamissati, sāyaṃ [P 3.0806] anusiṭṭho pāto visesaṃ adhigamissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Iti bhagavā “evaṃ niyyānikaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāsana”nti dassetvā ekavīsatiyāpi ṭhānesu arahattanikūṭena desitaṃ desanaṃ niyyātento “ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo…pe… iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti āha. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti. Desanāpariyosāne pana tiṃsa bhikkhusahassāni arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

Having thus shown the liberating nature of the Teaching with respect to seven years, and then showing it again for an even shorter time, he said, 'Let alone, bhikkhus,' and so on. All this was spoken with reference to a person of middling capacity for being trained. But with reference to one of sharp wisdom, it was said, "If instructed in the morning, one will attain distinction by evening; if instructed in the evening, one will attain distinction by morning." Thus, the Blessed One, having shown, "Bhikkhus, my Teaching is thus liberating," and delivering a discourse that culminates in arahantship in twenty-one instances, said, "Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path... etc. ... Thus, that which was spoken was spoken in reference to this." The rest is clear in meaning. At the conclusion of the discourse, thirty thousand monks were established in arahantship.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya.

Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta is concluded.

10. Pāyāsirājaññasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Pāyāsi Rājañña Sutta

406. Evaṃ [V 2.0357][P 3.0807][M 2.0396] me sutanti pāyāsirājaññasuttaṃ. Tatrāyamapubbapadavaṇṇanā – āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ. Kumārakassapoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kumārakāle pabbajitattā pana bhagavatā “kassapaṃ pakkosatha, idaṃ phalaṃ vā khādanīyaṃ vā kassapassa dethā”ti vutte “katarakassapassā”ti. “Kumārakassapassā”ti evaṃ gahitanāmattā tato paṭṭhāya vuḍḍhakālepi “kumārakassapo” tveva vuccati. Apica rañño posāvanikaputtattāpi taṃ kumārakassapoti sañjāniṃsu.

406. "Thus I have heard"—this is the Pāyāsi Rājañña Sutta. Herein is the explanation of words not previously explained: "Venerable" (āyasmā) is an affectionate term. "Kumārakassapa" is his name. Because he went forth in his youth, when the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa, give this fruit or food to Kassapa," and someone asked, "Which Kassapa?", he replied, "Kumārakassapa." Thus, having acquired this name, from then on, even in his old age he was called "Kumārakassapa." Moreover, because he was a son raised by the king, they recognized him as Kumārakassapa.

Ayaṃ panassa pubbayogato paṭṭhāya āvibhāvakathā – thero kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle seṭṭhiputto ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ citrakathiṃ ekaṃ attano sāvakaṃ etadagge ṭhapentaṃ disvā bhagavato sattāhaṃ dānaṃ datvā “ahampi bhagavā anāgate ekassa buddhassa ayaṃ thero viya citrakathī sāvako bhavāmī”ti patthanaṃ katvā puññāni karonto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tadā kira parinibbutassa bhagavato sāsane osakkante pañca bhikkhū nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā pabbataṃ āruyha samaṇadhammaṃ akaṃsu. Saṅghatthero tatiyadivase arahattaṃ patto, anuthero catutthadivase anāgāmī ahosi, itare tayo visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkontā devaloke nibbattā.

This is the account of his manifestation, beginning with his former endeavors: It is said that the Elder was the son of a wealthy man during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Then one day, seeing the Blessed One establishing a certain disciple of his as foremost in varied discourse, he gave alms to the Blessed One for a week and made the aspiration, "O Blessed One, in the future, may I also become a disciple skilled in varied discourse, like this Elder, under a Buddha." Making merit, he went forth in the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, but was unable to bring about any special attainment. At that time, it is said that when the dispensation of the Blessed One who had attained final Nibbāna was decaying, five monks made a ladder, climbed a mountain, and practiced the ascetic life. The Saṅgha-elder attained arahantship on the third day; the next elder became a non-returner on the fourth day; and the other three, being unable to bring about any special attainment, were reborn in the deva-world.

Tesaṃ ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sampattiṃ anubhavantānaṃ eko takkasilāyaṃ rājakule nibbattitvā pakkusāti nāma rājā hutvā bhagavantaṃ uddissa pabbajitvā rājagahaṃ uddissa āgacchanto kumbhakārasālāyaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā anāgāmiphalaṃ patto. Eko [P 3.0808] ekasmiṃ samuddapaṭṭane kulaghare nibbattitvā nāvaṃ āruyha bhinnanāvo dārucīrāni nivāsetvā lābhasampattiṃ patto “ahaṃ arahā”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā “na tvaṃ arahā, gaccha, satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchā”ti atthakāmāya devatāya codito tathā katvā arahattaphalaṃ patto.

Of them, after experiencing prosperity among devas and humans for one buddha-interval, one was reborn in a royal family at Takkasilā, became King Pukkusāti, went forth on account of the Buddha, and while traveling to Rājagaha, heard the Buddha’s teaching in a potter’s workshop and attained the fruit of non-returning. Another was reborn in a respectable family in a coastal town, boarded a ship, and when the ship broke, wearing clothes made of bark, attained gain, and thought, 'I am an arahant.' A deva, wishing for his welfare, admonished him, 'You are not an arahant; go and ask the Teacher a question.' He did so and attained the fruit of arahantship.

Eko [V 2.0358] rājagahe ekissā kuladārikāya kucchimhi uppanno. Sā ca paṭhamaṃ mātāpitaro yācitvā pabbajjaṃ alabhamānā kulagharaṃ gantvā gabbhaṃ gaṇhi[M 2.0397]. Gabbhasaṇṭhitampi ajānanti sāmikaṃ ārādhetvā tena anuññātā bhikkhunīsu pabbajitā, tassā gabbhanimittaṃ disvā bhikkhuniyo devadattaṃ pucchiṃsu. So “assamaṇī”ti āha. Dasabalaṃ pucchiṃsu. Satthā upālittheraṃ sampaṭicchāpesi. Thero sāvatthinagaravāsīni kulāni visākhañca upāsikaṃ pakkosāpetvā sodhento “pure laddho gabbho, pabbajjā arogā”ti āha. Satthā “suvinicchitaṃ adhikaraṇa”nti therassa sādhukāramadāsi. Sā bhikkhunī suvaṇṇabimbasadisaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ gahetvā rājā pasenadi kosalo posāpesi. “Kassapo”ti cassa nāmaṃ katvā aparabhāge alaṅkaritvā satthu santikaṃ netvā pabbājesi. Iti naṃ rañño posāvanikaputtattāpi “kumārakassapo”ti sañjāniṃsūti. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ andhavane samaṇadhammaṃ karontaṃ atthakāmā devatā pañhe uggahāpetvā “ime pañhe bhagavantaṃ pucchā”ti āha. Thero pañhe pucchitvā pañhavissajjanāvasāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Bhagavāpi taṃ citrakathikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

One was conceived in the womb of a young woman of good family in Rājagaha. At first, having asked her parents for permission to go forth and not receiving it, she entered the household life and conceived. Not knowing she was pregnant, she pleased her husband, and with his permission, went forth among the bhikkhunīs. When the bhikkhunīs saw the signs of her pregnancy, they asked Devadatta. He declared, 'She is not an ascetic.' They then asked the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher had the Elder Upāli accept the case. The elder summoned families residing in the city of Sāvatthi and the lay devotee Visākhā, and while investigating the matter, he declared, 'The conception occurred beforehand; the going forth is valid.' The Teacher gave his approval to the elder, saying, 'The legal question has been well-decided.' That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son like a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala took him and had him raised. He was named 'Kassapa,' and later, having been adorned, he was brought to the Teacher and given the going forth. Thus, because he was the king's foster son, he was known as 'Kumāra Kassapa.' One day, while he was practicing the ascetic's duties in the Andhavana forest, a deity desiring his welfare had him learn some questions and said, 'Ask these questions to the Blessed One.' The elder asked the questions, and at the conclusion of the explanation, he attained arahantship. The Blessed One also placed him in the foremost position among the bhikkhus skilled in varied discourse.

Setabyāti tassa nagarassa nāmaṃ. Uttarena setabyanti setabyato uttaradisāya. Rājaññoti anabhisittakarājā. Diṭṭhigatanti diṭṭhiyeva. Yathā gūthagataṃ muttagatanti vutte na gūthādito aññaṃ atthi, evaṃ diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ. Itipi natthīti taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ apadisitvā evampi natthīti vadati. Purā…pe… saññāpetīti yāva na saññāpeti.

Setabyā is the name of that city. 'North of Setabyā' means in the northern direction from Setabyā. `Rājañña` means an unconsecrated king. `Diṭṭhigata` means just the view itself. Just as when it is said 'dung heap, urine heap,' there is nothing else apart from dung and urine, so `diṭṭhigata` is just the view itself. 'Thus it does not exist' means, having pointed out this or that reason, one says, 'Even this does not exist.' The phrase 'Before... until he convinces' means 'as long as he has not yet convinced'.

Candimasūriyaupamāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Simile of the Moon and Sun

411. Ime bho, kassapa, candimasūriyāti so kira therena pucchito cintesi “ayaṃ samaṇo paṭhamaṃ candimasūriye upamaṃ āhari, candimasūriyasadiso bhavissati paññāya, anabhibhavanīyo [P 3.0809] aññena, sace panāhaṃ ‘candimasūriyā imasmiṃ loke’ti bhaṇissāmi, ‘kiṃ nissitā ete, kittakapamāṇā, kittakaṃ uccā’tiādīhi paliveṭhessati. Ahaṃ kho panetaṃ nibbeṭhetuṃ na sakkhissāmi, ‘parasmiṃ loke’ iccevassa kathessāmī”ti. Tasmā evamāha.

411. 'These, venerable Kassapa, are the moon and sun.' When asked thus by the elder, he thought: 'This ascetic first used the simile of the moon and sun; he will be like the moon and sun in wisdom, unconquerable by another. But if I say, "The moon and sun are in this world," he will entangle me with questions like, "On what do they depend? How large are they? How high are they?" and so on. I, however, will not be able to unravel this; therefore I will say to him, "They are in another world."' That is why he spoke thus.

Bhagavā [M 2.0398] pana tato pubbe na cirasseva sudhābhojanīyajātakaṃ kathesi. Tattha “cande cando devaputto, sūriye sūriyo devaputto”ti āgataṃ. Bhagavatā ca kathitaṃ jātakaṃ vā suttantaṃ vā sakalajambudīpe [V 2.0359] patthaṭaṃ hoti, tena so “ettha nivāsino devaputtā natthī”ti na sakkā vattunti cintetvā devā te na manussāti āha.

But the Blessed One, not long before that, had narrated the Sudhābhojanīya Jātaka. In it, this occurs: 'In the moon is the devaputta Canda; in the sun is the devaputta Sūriya.' And a Jātaka or Suttanta spoken by the Blessed One spreads throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Therefore, thinking, 'It is not possible to say that devaputtas dwelling therein do not exist,' he said, 'Those are devas, not humans.'

412. Atthi pana, rājañña, pariyāyoti atthi pana kāraṇanti pucchati. Ābādhikāti visabhāgavedanāsaṅkhātena ābādhena samannāgatā. Dukkhitāti dukkhappattā. Bāḷhagilānāti adhimattagilānā. Saddhāyikāti ahaṃ tumhe saddahāmi, tumhe mayhaṃ saddhāyikā saddhāyitabbavacanāti attho. Paccayikāti ahaṃ tumhe pattiyāmi, tumhe mayhaṃ paccayikā pattiyāyitabbāti attho.

412. 'Is there, O king, a way?' means he asks if there is a reason. 'Afflicted' means possessed of illness, characterized as disagreeable sensation. 'In pain' means having encountered suffering. 'Grievously ill' means extremely ill. 'Trustworthy' means, 'I trust you; you are trustworthy to me, one whose words are to be trusted'—that is the meaning. 'Reliable' means, 'I have confidence in you; you are reliable to me, one to be relied upon'—that is the meaning.

Corādiupamāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Simile of Thieves, and so on

413. Uddisitvāti tesaṃ attānañca paṭisāmitabhaṇḍakañca dassetvā, sampaṭicchāpetvāti attho. Vippalapantassāti “putto me, dhītā me, dhanaṃ me”ti vividhaṃ palapantassa. Nirayapālesūti niraye kammakāraṇikasattesu. Ye pana “kammameva kammakāraṇaṃ karoti, natthi nirayapālā”ti vadanti. Te “tamenaṃ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā”ti devadūtasuttaṃ paṭibāhanti. Manussaloke rājakulesu kāraṇikamanussā viya hi niraye nirayapālā honti.

413. 'Having pointed out' means having shown both themselves and the goods to be returned; the meaning is 'having made them accept.' 'Of one who babbles' refers to one who chatters variously, saying, 'My son, my daughter, my wealth.' 'Hell wardens' means the beings in hell who inflict the punishment. But those who say, 'Karma alone carries out the punishment; there are no hell wardens,' they reject the Devadūta Sutta, which says, 'Then, monks, the hell wardens...' For just as in the human world there are executioners in royal families, so in hell there are hell wardens.

415. Veḷupesikāhīti veḷuvilīvehi. Sunimmajjathāti yathā suṭṭhu nimmajjitaṃ hoti, evaṃ nimmajjatha, apanethāti attho.

415. `Veḷupesikāhi` means with strips of bamboo. `Sunimmajjatha` means, 'Just as something is thoroughly cleansed, so you should cleanse'; the meaning is 'remove'.

Asucīti amanāpo. Asucisaṅkhātoti asucikoṭṭhāsabhūto asucīti ñāto vā. Duggandhoti [P 3.0810] kuṇapagandho. Jegucchoti jigucchitabbayutto. Paṭikūloti dassaneneva paṭighāvaho. Ubbādhatīti divasassa dvikkhattuṃ nhatvā tikkhattuṃ vatthāni parivattetvā alaṅkatapaṭimaṇḍitānaṃ cakkavattiādīnampi manussānaṃ gandho yojanasate ṭhitānaṃ devatānaṃ kaṇṭhe āsattakuṇapaṃ viya bādhati.

'Unclean' means unpleasant. 'Counted as impure' means being a portion of impurity, or known as impure. 'Foul-smelling' means the smell of a corpse. 'Disgusting' means connected with what is to be loathed. 'Repulsive' means causing aversion by the mere sight of it. 'It oppresses' means that the odor of human beings—even of universal monarchs and others who bathe twice a day, change their clothes three times, and are adorned and decorated—afflicts deities standing a hundred yojanas away like a corpse tied to their necks.

416. Puna [M 2.0399] pāṇātipātādipañcasīlāni samādāyavattentānaṃ vasena vadati. Tāvatiṃsānanti idañca dūre nibbattā tāva mā āgacchantu, ime kasmā na entīti vadati.

416. Again, he speaks in reference to those who undertake and maintain the five precepts, beginning with abstaining from killing living beings. ‘Tāvatiṃsā’ means: ‘Let those born far away not come just yet; why do these not come?’

418. Jaccandhūpamo [V 2.0360] maññe paṭibhāsīti jaccandho viya upaṭṭhāsi. Araññavanapatthānīti araññakaṅgayuttatāya araññāni, mahāvanasaṇḍatāya vanapatthāni. Pantānīti dūrāni.

418. ‘He seems to me like one born blind’ means he appeared as one born blind. ‘Forests and woodland thickets’ refers to forests because of their association with wilderness, and woodland thickets because of their great expanse of woods. ‘Remote’ means distant.

419. Kalyāṇadhammeti teneva sīlena sundaradhamme. Dukkhapaṭikūleti dukkhaṃ apatthente. Seyyo bhavissatīti paraloke sugatisukhaṃ bhavissatīti adhippāyo.

419. ‘One of lovely virtue’ means one of beautiful qualities due to that very morality. ‘Averse to suffering’ means one who rejects suffering. ‘It will be better’ means the intention is that in the next world there will be the happiness of a good destination.

420. Upavijaññāti upagatavijāyanakālā, paripakkagabbhā na cirasseva vijāyissatīti attho. Opabhoggā bhavissatīti pādaparicārikā bhavissati. Anayabyasananti mahādukkhaṃ. Ayoti sukhaṃ, na ayo anayo, dukkhaṃ. Tadetaṃ sabbaso sukhaṃ byasati vikkhipatīti byasanaṃ. Iti anayova byasanaṃ anayabyasanaṃ, mahādukkhanti attho. Ayonisoti anupāyena. Apakkaṃ na paripācentīti apariṇataṃ akhīṇaṃ āyuṃ antarāva na upacchindanti. Paripākaṃ āgamentīti āyuparipākakālaṃ āgamenti. Dhammasenāpatināpetaṃ vuttaṃ –

420. ‘Upavijaññā’ means the time for giving birth has arrived, the womb is fully matured; the meaning is, she will give birth very soon. ‘Opabhoggā bhavissati’ means she will become a foot attendant. ‘Anayabyasana’ means great suffering. ‘Aya’ is happiness; ‘na ayo’ is anaya, suffering. That which completely destroys (byasati) and scatters (vikkhipati) this happiness is ruin (byasana). Thus, anaya which is also byasana is anayabyasana, meaning great suffering. ‘Ayoniso’ means improperly. ‘They do not ripen what is unripe’ means they do not prematurely cut off a life that is immature and unexhausted. ‘They await the ripening’ means they await the time of life’s full maturity. This was also said by the General of the Dhamma.

“Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathāti. (theragā. 1001)

“I do not delight in death, nor do I delight in life; I await my time, like a hired worker his wages.”

421. Ubbhinditvāti mattikālepaṃ bhinditvā.

421. ‘Ubbhinditvā’ means having broken through the clay plaster.

422. Rāmaṇeyyakanti [P 3.0811] ramaṇīyabhāvaṃ. Velāsikāti khiḍḍāparādhikā. Komārikāti taruṇadārikā. Tuyhaṃ jīvanti supinadassanakāle nikkhamantaṃ vā pavisantaṃ vā jīvaṃ api nu passanti. Idha cittācāraṃ “jīva”nti gahetvā āha. So hi tattha jīvasaññīti.

422. ‘Rāmaṇeyyaka’ means the state of being delightful. ‘Velāsikā’ means one who is prone to playful misconduct. ‘Komārikā’ means a young girl. Do they see your life-force (jīva) when it is going out or entering in a dream? Here, taking the mental activity as ‘life-force,’ it is said. For he perceives it there as a living being.

423. Jiyāyāti dhanujiyāya, gīvaṃ veṭhetvāti attho. Patthinnataroti thaddhataro. Iminā kiṃ dasseti? Tumhe jīvakāle sattassa pañcakkhandhāti [M 2.0400] vadanti, cavanakāle pana rūpakkhandhamattameva avasissati, tayo khandhā appavattā honti, viññāṇakkhandho gacchati. Avasiṭṭhena rūpakkhandhena lahutarena bhavitabbaṃ, garukataro ca hoti. Tasmā natthi koci kuhiṃ gantāti imamatthaṃ dasseti.

423. ‘Jiyāya’ means by a bowstring; the meaning is ‘having wrapped it around the neck.’ ‘Patthinnataro’ means stiffer. What does this indicate? You say that during life a being has five aggregates, but at the moment of death only the form aggregate remains; three aggregates become inoperative, and the consciousness aggregate departs. The remaining form aggregate should be lighter, but it becomes heavier. Therefore, it indicates this meaning: no one goes anywhere.

424. Nibbutanti vūpasantatejaṃ.

424. ‘Nibbuta’ means with its heat extinguished.

425. Anupahaccāti [V 2.0361] avināsetvā. Āmato hotīti addhamato marituṃ āraddho hoti. Odhunāthāti orato karotha. Sandhunāthāti parato karotha. Niddhunāthāti aparāparaṃ karotha. Tañcāyatanaṃ na paṭisaṃvedetīti tena cakkhunā taṃ rūpāyatanaṃ na vibhāveti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

425. ‘Anupahacca’ means without destroying. ‘Āmato hoti’ means he is half-dead; he has begun to die. ‘Odhunātha’ means shake it off from this side. ‘Sandhunātha’ means shake it off from the other side. ‘Niddhunātha’ means shake it off again and again. ‘He does not experience that sense-base’ means he does not discern that form-base with that eye. This same method applies everywhere.

426. Saṅkhadhamoti saṅkhadhamako. Upalāpetvāti dhamitvā.

426. ‘Saṅkhadhamo’ means a conch-blower. ‘Upalāpetvā’ means having blown.

428. Aggikoti aggiparicārako. Āpādeyyanti nipphādeyyaṃ, āyuṃ vā pāpuṇāpeyyaṃ. Poseyyanti bhojanādīhi bhareyyaṃ. Vaḍḍheyyanti vaḍḍhiṃ gameyyaṃ. Araṇīsahitanti araṇīyugaḷaṃ.

428. ‘Aggiko’ means a fire-attendant. ‘Āpādeyyaṃ’ means I would produce, or I would cause life to be attained. ‘Poseyyaṃ’ means I would nourish with food and so on. ‘Vaḍḍheyyaṃ’ means I would cause to grow. ‘Araṇīsahita’ means a pair of fire-sticks.

429. Tirorājānopīti tiroraṭṭhe aññasmimpi janapade rājāno jānanti. Abyattoti avisado acheko. Kopenapīti ye maṃ evaṃ vakkhanti, tesu uppajjanakena kopenapi etaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ harissāmi pariharissāmīti gahetvā vicarissāmi. Makkhenāti tayā vuttayuttakāraṇamakkhalakkhaṇena makkhenāpi. Palāsenāti tayā saddhiṃ yugaggāhalakkhaṇena palāsenāpi.

429. ‘Tirorājānopi’ means kings in an outside kingdom, in another country, also know. ‘Abyatto’ means not clear, unskillful. ‘Kopenapi’ means: I will live holding this view, thinking, ‘I will carry and maintain this view even with the anger that arises towards those who will speak to me thus.’ ‘Makkhena’ means even with the disparagement characterized by denigrating the reason you have stated. ‘Palāsena’ means even with the contentiousness characterized by rivalry with you.

430. Haritakapaṇṇanti [P 3.0812] yaṃ kiñci haritakaṃ, antamaso allatiṇapaṇṇampi na hotīti attho. Sannaddhakalāpanti sannaddhadhanukalāpaṃ. Āsittodakāni vaṭumānīti paripuṇṇasalilā maggā ca kandarā ca. Yoggānīti balibadde.

430. ‘Haritakapaṇṇa’ means any green thing; the meaning is that not even a fresh blade of grass is present. ‘Sannaddhakalāpa’ means a bound quiver. ‘Āsittodakāni vaṭumāni’ means paths and ravines are full of water. ‘Yoggāni’ means draught oxen.

Bahunikkhantaroti bahunikkhanto ciranikkhantoti attho. Yathābhatena bhaṇḍenāti yaṃ vo tiṇakaṭṭhodakabhaṇḍakaṃ āropitaṃ, tena yathābhatena yathāropitena, yathāgahitenāti attho.

‘Bahunikkhanta’ means having gone out much; the meaning is long departed. ‘Yathābhatena bhaṇḍena’ means with whatever goods—grass, wood, or water—have been loaded by you, with them as brought, as loaded, as taken; this is the meaning.

Appasārānīti appagghāni. Paṇiyānīti bhaṇḍāni.

‘Appasārāni’ means of little worth. ‘Paṇiyāni’ means goods.

Gūthabhārikādiupamāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Simile of the Dung-Carrier and Others

432. Mama [M 2.0401] ca sūkarabhattanti mama ca sūkarānaṃ idaṃ bhattaṃ. Uggharantanti upari gharantaṃ. Paggharantanti [V 2.0362] heṭṭhā parissavantaṃ. Tumhe khvettha bhaṇeti tumhe kho ettha bhaṇe. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Tathā hi pana me sūkarabhattanti tathā hi pana me ayaṃ gūtho sūkarānaṃ bhattaṃ.

432. ‘Mama ca sūkarabhattaṃ’ means ‘and this is food for my pigs.’ ‘Uggharantaṃ’ means oozing upwards. ‘Paggharantaṃ’ means trickling downwards. ‘Tumhe khvettha bhaṇe’ means ‘you, indeed, speak here.’ Or this is the reading: ‘Tathā hi pana me sūkarabhattaṃ’ means ‘for this dung is indeed food for my pigs.’

434. Āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilatīti āgatāgataṃ parājayaguḷaṃ gilati. Pajjohissāmīti pajjohanaṃ karissāmi, balikammaṃ karissāmīti attho. Akkhehi dibbissāmāti guḷehi kīḷissāma. Littaṃ paramena tejasāti paramatejena visena littaṃ.

434. ‘Āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilati’ means he swallows the ball of defeat as it comes. ‘Pajjohissāmi’ means I will make an offering; the meaning is, I will perform a ritual offering. ‘Akkhehi dibbissāma’ means we will play with dice. ‘Littaṃ paramena tejasā’ means smeared with poison of the highest potency.

436. Gāmapaṭṭanti vuṭṭhitagāmapadeso vuccati. “Gāmapada”ntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Sāṇabhāranti sāṇavākabhāraṃ. Susannaddhoti subaddho. Tvaṃ pajānāhīti tvaṃ jāna. Sace gaṇhitukāmosi, gaṇhāhīti vuttaṃ hoti.

436. ‘Gāmapaṭṭa’ is said to be a deserted village area. ‘Gāmapada’ is also a reading, and the meaning is the same. ‘Sāṇabhāra’ means a load of hemp fiber. ‘Susannaddho’ means well-bound. ‘Tvaṃ pajānāhi’ means ‘you know.’ This means: ‘If you wish to take it, take it.’

Khomanti khomavākaṃ. Ayanti kāḷalohaṃ. Lohanti tambalohaṃ. Sajjhanti rajataṃ. Suvaṇṇanti [P 3.0813] suvaṇṇamāsakaṃ. Abhinandiṃsūti tussiṃsu.

‘Khoma’ means linen fiber. ‘Aya’ means black iron. ‘Loha’ means copper. ‘Sajjha’ means silver. ‘Suvaṇṇa’ means a gold māsaka coin. ‘Abhinandiṃsu’ means they rejoiced.

437. Attamanoti sakamano tuṭṭhacitto. Abhiraddhoti abhippasanno. Pañhāpaṭibhānānīti pañhupaṭṭhānāni. Paccanīkaṃ kattabbanti paccanīkaṃ paṭiviruddhaṃ viya kattabbaṃ amaññissaṃ, paṭilomagāhaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsinti attho.

437. ‘Attamano’ means one whose mind is his own, with a delighted mind. ‘Abhiraddho’ means greatly pleased. ‘Pañhāpaṭibhānāni’ means the presentation of questions. ‘Paccanīkaṃ kattabbaṃ’ means: I would not have thought that something contrary, something opposed, should be done; I would have stood holding a perverse view. This is the meaning.

438. Saṅghātaṃ āpajjantīti saṅghātaṃ vināsaṃ maraṇaṃ āpajjanti. Na mahapphaloti vipākaphalena na mahapphalo hoti. Na mahānisaṃsoti guṇānisaṃsena mahānisaṃso na hoti. Na mahājutikoti ānubhāvajutiyā mahājutiko na hoti. Na mahāvipphāroti vipākavipphāratāya mahāvipphāro na hoti. Bījanaṅgalanti bījañca naṅgalañca. Dukkhetteti duṭṭhukhette nissārakhette. Dubbhūmeti visamabhūmibhāge. Patiṭṭhāpeyyāti ṭhapeyya. Khaṇḍānīti chinnabhinnāni. Pūtīnīti nissārāni. Vātātapahatānīti [M 2.0402] vātena ca ātapena ca hatāni pariyādinnatejāni. Asārādānīti taṇḍulasārādānarahitāni palālāni. Asukhasayitānīti yāni sukkhāpetvā koṭṭhe ākiritvā ṭhapitāni, tāni sukhasayitāni nāma. Etāni pana na tādisāni. Anuppaveccheyyāti anupaveseyya, na sammā vasseyya, anvaddhamāsaṃ anudasāhaṃ anupañcāhaṃ na vasseyyāti attho. Api nu tānīti api nu evaṃ khettabījavuṭṭhidose sati tāni bījāni aṅkuramūlapattādīhi uddhaṃ vuddhiṃ heṭṭhā virūḷhiṃ samantato ca vepullaṃ āpajjeyyunti[V 2.0363]. Evarūpo kho rājañña yaññoti evarūpaṃ rājañña dānaṃ parūpaghātena uppāditapaccayatopi dāyakatopi pariggāhakatopi avisuddhattā na mahapphalaṃ hoti.

438. “Saṅghātaṃ āpajjanti” means they come to ruin, destruction, death. “Na mahapphalo” means it is not of great fruit in terms of resultant fruit. “Na mahānisaṃso” means it is not of great benefit in terms of the advantages of qualities. “Na mahājutiko” means it is not of great radiance in terms of the radiance of power. “Na mahāvipphāro” means it is not of great expansion in terms of the expansion of its result. “Bījanaṅgala” means both seeds and a plow. “Dukkhette” means in a bad field, an unproductive field. “Dubbhūme” means in an uneven area of land. “Patiṭṭhāpeyya” means would place. “Khaṇḍāni” means broken and shattered. “Pūtīni” means without essence. “Vātātapahatāni” means damaged by wind and sun, with their potency diminished. “Asārādāni” means stalks without the essence of rice grains. “Asukhasayitāni” means those that, having been dried and piled up in a granary, are called well-stored; but these are not like that. “Anuppaveccheyya” means would not cause to enter, would not rain properly; that is, would not rain every half-month, every ten days, or every five days—this is the meaning. “Api nu tāni” means, given such faults in the field, seed, and rain, would those seeds attain upward growth with sprout, root, and leaf, downward rooting, and widespread increase all around? “Evarūpo kho rājañña yañño” means such a gift, O nobleman, is not of great fruit, due to being impure in respect of its arising from causes produced through harming others, and in respect of both the giver and the receiver.

Evarūpo kho rājañña yaññoti evarūpaṃ rājaññadānaṃ aparūpaghātena uppannapaccayatopi aparūpaghātitāya sīlavantadāyakatopi [P 3.0814] sammādiṭṭhiādiguṇasampannapaṭiggāhakatopi mahapphalaṃ hoti. Sace pana guṇātirekaṃ nirodhā vuṭṭhitaṃ paṭiggāhakaṃ labhati, cetanā ca vipulā hoti, diṭṭheva dhamme vipākaṃ detīti.

“Evarūpo kho rājañña yañño” means such a gift, O nobleman, is of great fruit, because its requisites arise without harming others, because the giver is virtuous and does not harm others, and because the recipient is endowed with qualities such as right view. But if one obtains a recipient of surpassing qualities who has arisen from cessation, and the volition is vast, it yields its result in this very life.

439. Imaṃ pana therassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pāyāsirājañño theraṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ therassa mahādānaṃ datvā tato paṭṭhāya mahājanassa dānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Taṃ sandhāya atha kho pāyāsi rājaññotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kaṇājakanti sakuṇḍakaṃ uttaṇḍulabhattaṃ. Bilaṅgadutiyanti kañjikadutiyaṃ. Dhorakāni ca vatthānīti thūlāni ca vatthāni. Guḷavālakānīti guḷadasāni, puñjapuñjavasena ṭhitamahantadasānīti attho. Evaṃ anuddisatīti evaṃ upadisati. Pādāpīti pādenapi.

439. Having heard this Dhamma talk of the Elder, the nobleman Pāyāsi invited the Elder and gave great alms to him for seven days. From then on, he established almsgiving for the great multitude. Regarding that, it is said, “Then the nobleman Pāyāsi,” and so on. Here, “kaṇājaka” means broken rice with husks. “Bilaṅgadutiya” means accompanied by sour gruel. “Dhorakāni ca vatthāni” means coarse cloths. “Guḷavālakāni” means pieces of molasses, meaning large pieces placed heap upon heap. “Evaṃ anuddisati” means thus he instructs. “Pādāpi” means even with the foot.

440. Asakkaccanti saddhāvirahitaṃ assaddhadānaṃ. Asahatthāti na sahatthena. Acittīkatanti cittīkāravirahitaṃ, na cittīkārampi paccupaṭṭhāpetvā na paṇītacittaṃ katvā adāsi. Apaviddhanti chaḍḍitaṃ vippatitaṃ. Suññaṃ serīsakanti serīsakaṃ nāma ekaṃ tucchaṃ rajatavimānaṃ upagato. Tassa kira dvāre mahāsirīsarukkho, tena taṃ “serīsaka”nti vuccati.

440. “Asakkaccaṃ” means without reverence, a gift without faith. “Asahatthā” means not with one’s own hand. “Acittīkataṃ” means lacking respect; he gave without establishing respect and without making his mind sublime. “Apaviddha” means discarded, rejected. “Suññaṃ serīsakaṃ” means he went to an empty silver mansion called Serīsaka. It is said that at its entrance was a great Sirīsa tree, therefore it was called “Serīsaka.”

441. Āyasmā [M 2.0403] gavaṃpatīti thero kira pubbe manussakāle gopāladārakānaṃ jeṭṭhako hutvā mahato sirīsassa mūlaṃ sodhetvā vālikaṃ okiritvā ekaṃ piṇḍapātikattheraṃ rukkhamūle nisīdāpetvā attanā laddhaṃ āhāraṃ datvā tato cuto tassānubhāvena tasmiṃ rajatavimāne nibbatti. Sirīsarukkho vimānadvāre aṭṭhāsi. So paññāsāya vassehi phalati, tato paññāsa vassāni gatānīti devaputto saṃvegaṃ āpajjati. So aparena samayena amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle manussesu nibbattitvā satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā arahattaṃ patto. Pubbāciṇṇavasena pana divāvihāratthāya tadeva vimānaṃ abhiṇhaṃ gacchati, taṃ kirassa utusukhaṃ hoti. Taṃ sandhāya “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā gavaṃpatī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

441. “Āyasmā Gavaṃpati” means it is said that the Elder, in a previous human existence, was the eldest of some cowherd boys. Having cleaned the base of a large sirīsa tree, scattered sand, and seated an alms-pilgrim elder at the foot of the tree, he gave him the food he had obtained. After passing away from there, due to the power of that deed, he was reborn in that silver mansion. The sirīsa tree stood at the gate of the mansion. It bears fruit every fifty years; when fifty years have passed, the young deva experiences a sense of urgency. Later, in the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn among humans. After hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma talk, he attained arahantship. Due to his habit from the past, he frequently visited that very mansion for his daytime abiding, as it was said to be climatically pleasant for him. With reference to that, it is said: “At that time, the Venerable Gavampati…” and so on.

So [P 3.0815][V 2.0364] sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvāti so parassa santakampi dānaṃ sakkaccaṃ datvā. Evamārocesīti “sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ dethā”tiādinā nayena ārocesi. Tañca pana therassa ārocanaṃ sutvā mahājano sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā devaloke nibbatto. Pāyāsissa pana rājaññassa paricārakā sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvāpi nikantivasena gantvā tasseva santike nibbattā. Taṃ kira disācārikavimānaṃ vaṭṭaniaṭaviyaṃ ahosi. Pāyāsidevaputto ca ekadivasaṃ vāṇijakānaṃ dassetvā attano katakammaṃ kathesīti.

“So sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā” means he gave carefully even the gift that belonged to another. “Evaṃ ārocesi” means he announced in this way: “Give gifts carefully,” and so on. And having heard the Elder’s announcement, the great multitude gave gifts carefully and were reborn in the heavenly world. But the attendants of the nobleman Pāyāsi, though they gave gifts carefully, did so reluctantly and were reborn in his very presence. That celestial mansion of a direction-farer, it is said, was in the Vaṭṭaniya forest. And the deva Pāyāsi, having shown himself to some merchants one day, recounted the deeds he had done.

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Thus in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīghanikāya,

Pāyāsirājaññasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Pāyāsi Sutta is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca mahāvaggassatthavaṇṇanā.

And the Explanation of the Mahāvagga is completed.

Mahāvaggaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāvagga is concluded.
